use_case: On-line calibration monitoring of safety-related instrument channels in nuclear power plants using auto-associative empirical models to detect sensor drift
incurred_insecurity:
This use case creates a concentrated dependency on an empirical AI model to preserve the accuracy of safety-related instrumentation—reactor coolant pressure, neutron flux, core exit temperature—by replacing or deferring manual calibration. The model infers drift from cross-channel correlations in operational telemetry, but it is trained almost entirely on normal-operation data with few or no labeled sensor-fault events, making it vulnerable to both adversarial manipulation that exploits its learned correlation structure and implicit failures (operational drift, alarm fatigue, opacity) that erode operator vigilance and create windows for attack. Because the system directly informs technical-specification compliance and extends calibration intervals, its compromise—whether through poisoned training data, a backdoored model update, or cleverly crafted sensor inputs—can mask real instrumentation failures for months, degrading a defense-in-depth layer without immediate detection.

Training-data scarcity and operational drift masking — implicit, exploitable
The model learns from field telemetry dominated by healthy sensors and stable fuel cycles, with minimal exposure to actual drift signatures or novel operating regimes (post-upgrade instrumentation, different fuel loads, steam-generator fouling). As the plant ages or operating conditions shift beyond the training envelope, the model's residuals lose sensitivity—missing real drift or generating nuisance alarms. An adversary aware of this training-data gap could engineer sensor manipulation that mimics a known operational transient or stays within the model's learned correlation bounds, knowing the AI will treat the attack signature as a valid plant state rather than drift.

Correlated sensor spoofing to evade drift detection — adversarial
Because the auto-associative model flags drift by comparing one channel's reading against predictions from redundant channels, an adversary with access to multiple sensor data streams (via network intrusion or insider access) can feed correlated but subtly biased signals across the redundancy group, making a compromised instrument appear mutually consistent with its peers. The model sees no anomaly, and a single safety-related sensor drifts uncalibrated until a real transient exposes the error.

Model supply-chain compromise for latent blindness — adversarial
A vendor-supplied or cloud-hosted model package, if compromised during development or update distribution, could carry a backdoor that ignores drift in pre-selected channels or activates under specific operational triggers. Acceptance testing on normal data would not reveal the latent bias, and because these systems often deploy across multiple units for cost efficiency, a single poisoned model propagates fleet-wide, blinding many plants to the same instrumentation vulnerabilities.

Automation complacency and alarm desensitization — implicit, exploitable
If the AI produces consistent low false-alarm rates, operators develop over-trust and stop independently verifying sensor health, reducing vigilance during the exact window when an adversary might exploit the model's blind spots. Conversely, if operational heterogeneity or concept drift causes frequent nuisance alarms, operators grow desensitized and may ignore a genuine alert that coincides with or masks an attack. Both failure modes—misuse and disuse—degrade the human layer of defense, and an adversary timing physical sensor tampering or cyber manipulation to these periods faces less resistance.

Model opacity blocking root-cause attribution — implicit, exploitable
Empirical models flag that *something* is anomalous but provide weak attribution of which sensor is drifting or whether the residual reflects genuine aging, a model artifact, or adversarial input manipulation. This opacity slows incident response and forensic investigation, giving an adversary more time to complete an operation or cover tracks. The lack of explainability also complicates regulatory qualification, creating pressure to freeze the model at an initial version even as its performance degrades—another exploitable window.

Reconnaissance via inference API or model extraction — adversarial
An adversary with network access to the on-line monitoring system's inference API can probe the model to discover sensor redundancy groupings, alarm thresholds, and operational states, using this intelligence to plan attacks on physical instrumentation or related safety systems. If the model is accessible for extraction, the adversary can build a proxy offline and pre-test evasion strategies against it before deploying them in-plant.

Non-deterministic retraining and qualification drift — implicit
Periodic model retraining with new operational data introduces non-determinism: each update subtly shifts detection thresholds and correlation weights, with no established AI-specific requalification path under 10CFR50 Appendix B. Plants face a dilemma—freeze the model and accept growing staleness (operational drift), or retrain and lose traceability to the original safety evaluation. Either choice leaves a vulnerability: a stale model misses new drift modes, while an unqualified retrained model may have unknown blind spots an adversary can discover and exploit.

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear operations engineer, I see this use case as directly tied to safety-related instrument channel calibration—a fundamental defense-in-depth element. The AI replaces or extends periodic manual calibration by inferring instrument drift from cross-channel correlations. If the AI misses real drift (false negative) or falsely flags good instruments (false positive leading to spurious actions or operator distrust), the plant loses a layer of assurance that safety-related measurements (e.g., reactor coolant system pressure, core exit temperature, neutron flux) remain accurate. Unlike a purely advisory system, this one directly informs technical specification compliance and could defer or replace physical calibrations, making its output operationally binding.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An adversary with access to the sensor data stream or the AI model itself could craft inputs that mask real drift in a critical channel—feeding correlated but subtly biased signals across multiple channels so the auto-associative model sees them as mutually consistent, thereby hiding a single compromised instrument whose bias is slowly increasing. This is a data poisoning or input manipulation attack (AML.T0020, AML.T0043) that exploits the model's reliance on cross-channel redundancy: if the attacker can influence enough channels or their digital representations, the AI will not flag the drift, and the plant will continue operating with an uncalibrated safety-related instrument until a real transient exposes the error. The consequence is not immediate—operators still have other indications—but it erodes a defense layer, and if timed with a separate system fault, could delay or prevent correct safety system actuation. The model itself, if accessible (e.g., through network access to the monitoring system or supply chain compromise of the vendor's model package, AML.T0010), could be manipulated to systematically ignore drift in chosen channels, effectively blinding operators to instrumentation failures. Because this use case defers physical calibrations (condition-based rather than time-based), a successful manipulation could persist for months until the next manual check, if any.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) THREATS THAT ALSO CREATE ATTACK SURFACE: The auto-associative empirical model is trained on normal-operation data (OP.C0201.05, field/operational data) from a specific unit; small-data and low base-rate issues (OP.C0202) are significant because sensor drift events are rare, and the model has limited examples of actual degradation to learn from—most training data represents healthy instruments. This makes the model prone to operational drift (OP.C0302.01) as the plant ages, fuel cycles change, or subtle shifts in process conditions (e.g., steam generator fouling, coolant chemistry changes) alter the correlations the model learned. The model may then either false-alarm (spurious calibration flags, leading to alarm fatigue or disuse, OP.C0101.05) or, worse, fail to detect real drift because the new operating regime falls outside its training envelope (out-of-distribution, OP.C0302). Operators, seeing few or inconsistent alarms, may develop automation complacency (OP.C0102) or misuse (OP.C0101.04), trusting the AI's 'no drift detected' output even when other indirect signs (e.g., subtle process anomalies) suggest instrument issues. The non-determinism of the model's retraining process (OP.C0402.01, if the model is periodically updated with new data) also complicates qualification: each retraining could subtly shift detection thresholds, making it hard to verify that the model still meets the original safety evaluation criteria (OP.C0401, explainability/opacity limit; OP.C0501, AI-specific QA gap). An adversary aware of these implicit weaknesses could time an attack (e.g., subtle sensor bias injection) to coincide with a period of operational drift or post-refueling when the model is least reliable, knowing that the system's own limitations will help mask the manipulation. Finally, if this on-line monitoring system is deployed fleet-wide or across multiple units (OP.C0602, cross-site model propagation), a compromised model or dataset could spread the same blind spot to many plants, amplifying the impact.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML engineering perspective, this use case exemplifies the acute challenges of deploying empirical models in a domain where the failure modes they are meant to detect (sensor drift) occur on long timescales with extremely low base rates, and where the training corpus is almost entirely normal-operation data with minimal or no labeled drift events. Auto-associative architectures (neural nets, kernel methods like SVR) learn correlations among redundant process variables to flag when one sensor deviates from its expected relationship to the others, but they have no ground truth for what constitutes actionable drift versus benign plant transients, calibration adjustments, or fuel-cycle effects. The inference decision—'is this residual anomalous enough to warrant a work order?'—rests on thresholds that are empirically tuned and not rigorously validated against the tail distribution of real degradation signatures, creating both Type I (nuisance alarms that erode operator trust) and Type II (missed drift that defeats the safety function) exposure. Because these models are trained on historical data from specific fuel loads, operating envelopes, and sensor suites, they are inherently vulnerable to concept drift when the plant changes mode, upgrades instrumentation, or operates outside the training manifold, yet there is no established ML requalification regime that binds model updates to 10CFR50 Appendix B configuration management.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary ML-pipeline vulnerabilities are data provenance and lifecycle qualification gaps. Training data for these models is operational telemetry: it reflects only the limited operating history of one or a few plants, contains few to zero labeled sensor-fault events (because safety-grade sensors rarely fail catastrophically before scheduled maintenance catches them), and likely includes undocumented interventions (manual recalibrations, sensor replacements) that introduce step changes the model must either learn around or be retrained for. This creates OP.C0202 (low base rate), OP.C0201.05 (field data with provenance uncertainty), and OP.C0302.01 (operational drift when the plant changes fuel, updates setpoints, or switches operating modes), all of which undermine the model's ability to generalize. Because the model outputs residuals that operators or I&C staff threshold into alarms, there is severe exposure to OP.C0101.04 (misuse/overtrust if the model has low false-alarm rates during training but fails silently on novel drift) and OP.C0101.05 (disuse/undertrust if nuisance alarms train staff to ignore warnings, a classic automation-induced complacency problem). From an adversarial lens, an attacker aware of the model's training envelope could craft sensor spoofing (AML.T0015 evade AI model) that stays within the correlation structure the model learned—mimicking redundancy across channels—so that malicious setpoint manipulation or false-safe indications are not flagged as drift. The model's opacity (OP.C0401) means that even if drift is detected, root-cause attribution is weak: you know *something* is anomalous, but not which sensor is at fault or whether it is genuine aging versus a cyber manipulation of the input vector. Because these systems are increasingly fielded as vendor-supplied SaaS or cloud-hosted analytics (OP.C0601), the training pipeline, model versioning, and retraining triggers are outside the plant's configuration control, creating AML.T0010.003 supply-chain exposure (a compromised model update propagates across a fleet under OP.C0602) and OP.C0501 (no AI-specific qualification baseline). Finally, if the model is shared across units or sites for cost efficiency, adversarial poisoning of the shared training corpus (AML.T0020) or a targeted model extraction attack (AML.T0024.002) could yield a proxy that lets an adversary pre-test evasion strategies offline before deploying them in-plant. The lack of deterministic retraining and versioning (OP.C0402.01/02, OP.C0303) means there is no regulatory path to demonstrate that a retrained model maintains its safety function, so plants may hesitate to update even when drift in the *model* is apparent, freezing the system in an increasingly stale state.

security_specialist.argument: From a security perspective, this use case creates a concentrated trust point in the calibration-monitoring AI that an insider or supply-chain adversary could exploit to mask actual sensor drift or inject false drift alarms, conditioning operators to ignore warnings right before an attack. The system's reliance on auto-associative empirical models trained on historical plant data means an adversary with access to training pipelines could poison the model to be blind to specific sensor attack signatures, or an insider could manipulate the model's drift thresholds to hide evidence of physical tampering with instrumentation. Because this is safety-related instrumentation, undermining confidence in the AI's drift detection erodes a defense-in-depth layer: if operators grow to distrust the AI (through adversarially-induced false positives) or over-trust it (through successful but undetected model compromise), the facility's ability to detect both natural faults and deliberate sabotage degrades. The fact that the AI operates on-line and continuously also means it becomes a persistent reconnaissance surface—an adversary who can query or observe the model's internal state may infer operational parameters, sensor redundancy structures, and timing windows when certain channels are flagged as drifting and possibly bypassed.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An insider with access to the training data or model update process (AML.T0020 Poison Training Data, AML.T0018.000 Poison AI Model) could condition the empirical model to ignore drift patterns consistent with a planned physical attack on sensors, effectively blinding the calibration-monitoring system to sabotage. A sophisticated adversary targeting the AI supply chain (AML.T0010.003 Model supply chain compromise) could deliver a pre-compromised model that appears to function normally during acceptance testing but contains a latent bias or backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004 Insert Backdoor Trigger) activated under specific operational conditions, allowing the adversary to mask sensor drift at a chosen time. Because the system is on-line and continuously inferencing, an adversary with network access to the AI inference API (AML.T0040) could probe the model to discover sensor redundancy groupings, alarm thresholds, and operational states (AML.T0013 Discover AI Model Ontology, AML.T0014 Discover AI Model Family), using this reconnaissance to plan attacks on physical sensors or related safety systems. The model's role in justifying extended calibration intervals also makes it a high-value target for an adversary seeking to degrade safety margins without immediate detection—compromising confidence in the AI (through adversarially-induced false positives, AML.T0031 Erode AI Model Integrity) would force operators back to conservative manual calibration schedules, but during the period of distrust the adversary gains a window where both the AI and manual processes are in flux.

IMPLICIT/NON-ADVERSARIAL THREATS THAT CREATE SECURITY EXPOSURE: The model's training on historical plant data (OP.C0201.05 Field/operational data, OP.C0302.01 Data/Operational drift) means it may not generalize to novel sensor failure modes or drift patterns induced by deliberate tampering, which differ from natural aging—this is a blind spot an adversary could exploit by studying the model's training data provenance and engineering an attack signature outside its learned distribution. Auto-associative models inherently assume that sensor relationships remain stable (OP.C0302.02 Concept Drift), so an adversary who can subtly alter multiple related sensors in a coordinated way might evade detection if the model treats the new correlated pattern as a valid operational state rather than drift. Operator automation bias (OP.C0101.04 Misuse/over-trust, OP.C0102 Alarm/monitoring complacency) is a significant security risk: if the AI consistently performs well, operators may stop independently verifying sensor health, and an adversary timing an attack during this period of reduced vigilance would face less resistance. Conversely, if the model produces frequent false positives due to operational heterogeneity across different plant states (OP.C0302.03), operators may become desensitized (OP.C0101.05 Disuse/under-trust), ignoring a real alarm that coincides with or masks an adversary's action. The lack of explainability in empirical models (OP.C0401) means that when the AI flags drift, operators cannot easily verify whether it reflects genuine sensor degradation, a model artifact, or adversarial manipulation—this opacity is itself a security vulnerability because it slows incident response and makes forensic attribution harder. If the model or its training data are managed via cloud infrastructure or shared across multiple units (OP.C0601, OP.C0602 Cross-site/fleet model propagation), a single supply-chain compromise or insider action could propagate a poisoned model fleet-wide, amplifying impact. Finally, the AI's role in condition-based calibration intervals means its compromise doesn't just hide drift—it directly extends the time window during which a sabotaged or drifting sensor remains in service, increasing the facility's exposure to both accidental and deliberate safety challenges.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on training-data scarcity, operational drift, automation trust failures (both over-trust and alarm fatigue), supply-chain model compromise, and the exploitation of learned correlations to evade detection; the nuclear and security specialists emphasized the safety-function erosion and extended calibration windows, while the AI engineer detailed the ML-theoretic and lifecycle-qualification gaps, which I integrated into the implicit threats and their adversarial exploitation pathways.

evidence.note: This NRC contractor report documents that empirical on-line monitoring models use historical plant data to predict current parameter values, with deviations used to detect instrument drift including in safety-related channels. It specifically identifies auto-associative neural networks, auto-associative kernel regression, and related methods as accepted approaches for extending calibration intervals.

evidence.note: The NRC concluded that the generic concept of on-line monitoring for tracking instrument performance and extending calibration frequency of safety-related instrumentation is acceptable, subject to 14 plant-specific requirements, establishing regulatory acceptance of this use case for technical-specification compliance.

evidence.note: This IAEA technical report reviews state-of-the-art on-line monitoring for instrument calibration verification and extension of calibration intervals in nuclear power plants, documenting international deployment and providing implementation guidelines for member states.

evidence.note: This conference paper from the University of Tennessee Department of Nuclear Engineering demonstrates an autoassociative neural network trained with normal operational data from Florida Power Corporation's Crystal River Unit 3 nuclear power plant to detect sensor drift or failure, establishing early application of the technology.

evidence.citation: Hines, J.W., et al. (2008), "Technical Review of On-Line Monitoring Techniques for Performance Assessment: Theoretical Issues," NUREG/CR-6895, Volume 2
evidence.note: The report acknowledges that empirical on-line monitoring models are trained using historical plant data from normal operation, with predictions based on cross-channel correlations. This inherently limits the model's exposure to actual drift signatures and novel operating conditions, supporting the training-data scarcity vulnerability.

evidence.citation: Mathews, M., et al. (2020), "Adversarial Attacks on Machine Learning Cybersecurity Defences in Industrial Control Systems," arXiv:2004.05005
evidence.note: This paper demonstrates that adversarial machine learning can manipulate data from actuators or sensors in industrial control systems by introducing perturbations to cause malicious data to be classified as benign, bypassing intrusion detection systems. The documented evasion techniques are directly applicable to sensor-based anomaly detection in nuclear plants.

evidence.citation: Mathews, A., et al. (2018), "Adversarial Regression for Detecting Attacks in Cyber-Physical Systems," arXiv:1804.11022
evidence.note: This work studies stealthy attacks on sensor readings in cyber-physical systems where multiple models for anomaly detection impose constraints on feasible sensor manipulations. It demonstrates that adversaries can craft coordinated sensor manipulations to evade detection, directly supporting the correlated sensor spoofing vulnerability.

damage.why: Masking calibration drift in safety-related instrumentation (reactor coolant pressure, neutron flux, core exit temperature) for months directly degrades defense-in-depth and could prevent operators from recognizing safety-margin erosion during transients, creating credible pathways to radiological release or loss of material control.

reproducibility.why: Correlated sensor spoofing via multiple compromised data streams reliably evades auto-associative models that depend on cross-channel consistency, and training-data gaps predictably cause blind spots to out-of-envelope conditions once an adversary maps the correlation structure.

exploitability.why: Correlated multi-sensor manipulation requires network access to safety-related data streams or insider positioning, while supply-chain compromise of vendor model updates demands moderate sophistication but not nation-state resources; inference API reconnaissance is easier but less directly impactful.

affected_users.why: Compromise affects all safety-related instrument channels monitored by the system across reactor protection and engineered safety features, and cloud-hosted or vendor-supplied models can propagate fleet-wide, impacting multiple units or plants simultaneously.

discoverability.why: The use of auto-associative empirical models for calibration monitoring is documented in public NRC guidance (NUREG/CR-6895, TR-104965 Safety Evaluation), and the correlation-based detection mechanism is well-known; an adversary with partial system access (vendor documentation, inference API probing) can map redundancy groups and test evasion strategies offline.

use_case: Deep-learning detection of cracks in remotely recorded underwater inspection video of reactor internal components
incurred_insecurity:
Deploying a CNN-based crack detector on underwater inspection video of reactor internals incurs insecurity through both implicit operational weaknesses and adversarial exploitation surfaces that converge on a single consequence: undetected structural degradation in safety-critical components. The system's fragility stems from scarce training data (real operational cracks in reactor-specific materials and underwater conditions are rare), operational drift as imaging conditions or material failure modes evolve, and the opacity of the CNN decision process, all of which can lead to missed detections without adversary involvement. Adversaries can exploit these inherent weaknesses—or directly attack the training data, model, or video pipeline—to create systematic blind spots, suppress detections of induced damage, or erode human reviewer vigilance, ultimately enabling covert structural sabotage or deferring maintenance until a safety margin is breached.

Data Scarcity and Domain-Specific Failure Modes
This is an implicit threat rooted in the base-rate problem for safety-significant events. Real underwater crack video from reactor internals under operational stress, radiation, and corrosion is inherently scarce; the model trains on limited positive examples and may fail to generalize to novel crack morphologies such as stress-corrosion cracking in new alloys or cracking in geometries not represented in the training set. An adversary aware of these gaps could induce damage—perhaps via prior covert material substitution during maintenance—that produces crack signatures outside the model's training distribution, confident the AI will miss it without needing to tamper with the system directly. The consequence is that structural integrity assessments and risk-informed in-service inspection programs proceed on incomplete information, allowing degradation to progress undetected.

Operational Drift and Qualification Gaps
This is an implicit threat that an adversary could time attacks around. The CNN's performance depends on stable input conditions—lighting, water clarity, camera hardware, and crack morphology—all of which drift over the reactor's operational life as water chemistry changes, new cameras are deployed, or aging introduces failure modes not seen during training. The model has no regulatory qualification framework equivalent to traditional NDE methods, and its non-deterministic inference behavior (if present) undermines the reproducibility required for safety inspections. An adversary aware of an upcoming camera upgrade or maintenance procedure that shifts inspection conditions could time physical sabotage to coincide with the model's transitional unreliability, knowing detection capability is degraded and human reviewers may not compensate due to automation bias.

Automation Bias and Human-AI Trust Breakdown
This is an implicit threat. Technicians reviewing hours of underwater video come to rely on the CNN's flagging of crack candidates, risking both over-trust (missing cracks the AI missed, especially if the system builds a track record of accurate detections) and under-trust (ignoring alerts if false-positive rates are high, leading to alarm fatigue). The model's opacity means reviewers cannot verify whether a flagged region is a true crack or an artifact—weld spatter, oxidation, lighting shadow—complicating escalation decisions and eroding manual inspection discipline. An adversary aware of this skill fade could exploit it by inducing damage during periods when the AI is offline, misconfigured, or after a software update, confident that human reviewers have lost the ability to spot cracks independently.

Adversarial Data and Model Poisoning
This is a direct adversarial threat. An attacker with access to the training pipeline—an insider or via supply-chain compromise of the dataset or model repository—could poison the training data by mislabeling frames (marking cracked regions as intact) or systematically excluding certain crack types, embedding blind spots that persist across retraining cycles. Alternatively, an adversary could manipulate the model itself by embedding a backdoor trigger that suppresses detections for cracks matching a specific orientation or location the adversary plans to induce via sabotage. These attacks are difficult to detect because the poisoned model may perform well on benign validation data while systematically missing adversary-induced damage, and the consequence is that flawed inspection results feed into aging management programs and maintenance scheduling, enabling latent safety risks or covert reactor modifications.

Inference-Time Video Manipulation and Evasion
This is a direct adversarial threat. An adversary with access to the video feed—via compromised camera firmware, man-in-the-middle attack on video transmission, or control of preprocessing software—could craft adversarial perturbations to suppress crack visibility before the CNN processes the frames, or manipulate the Naive Bayes fusion step to downweight detections in targeted segments. Because the system operates frame-by-frame with fusion across time, an adversary need only ensure that crack signatures are obscured in enough frames to prevent the fusion logic from flagging the defect. An adversary could also probe the model (if accessible via an inference API) with synthetic crack images to map detection thresholds and blind spots, then engineer physical damage to fall just below those thresholds, evading detection without touching the AI system.

Reconnaissance and Cross-Fleet Propagation
This is a hybrid threat combining adversarial reconnaissance with an implicit systemic weakness. An adversary can perform reconnaissance by studying similar crack-detection models in open literature, training a proxy model on publicly available underwater inspection imagery, or probing the deployed system to discover its ontology and failure modes. If the model is deployed across multiple reactor units, a single poisoned or compromised model version propagates the vulnerability fleet-wide, making it a high-value target. An adversary who successfully embeds a blind spot in a shared model can exploit it across all sites without needing site-specific access, and the delayed discovery of structural damage at one unit may not trigger re-inspection at others if the flaw is attributed to local conditions rather than a systemic model defect.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant operations and process safety perspective, this use case introduces insecurity primarily through the consequence of missed or false crack detections propagating into maintenance scheduling and structural integrity assessments. The AI system processes remotely recorded underwater video of reactor internals -- components under high radiation, temperature, and stress -- where undetected crack growth can lead to core geometry changes, coolant flow blockage, or component failure during operation. If the model fails to detect real cracks (false negatives from poor training data, underwater imaging artifacts, or drift as crack morphology evolves with new materials or stress conditions), operators may defer maintenance on degrading components, creating a latent safety risk. Conversely, excessive false positives could desensitize inspection staff (alarm fatigue) or trigger unnecessary outages, both undermining the inspection program's effectiveness. An adversary could exploit these failure modes by timing attacks around known model weaknesses (e.g., manipulating training data to create blind spots for specific crack orientations, poisoning the model to flag benign features as critical defects) or by directly tampering with inspection video streams to mask real damage or inject false alarms, knowing that human reviewers may defer to the AI's judgment due to automation bias.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
The primary non-adversarial threats stem from the operational context: underwater reactor internal inspection video presents challenging data (variable lighting, turbidity, surface reflections, limited training examples of actual in-service cracks in NPP-specific geometries and materials) that can cause high false-negative rates (OP.C0202, OP.C0204, OP.C0701.02 if the crack signatures differ from those in the training set, which may have come from bench tests or non-nuclear structures). Model drift is a significant concern (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02) as reactor internals age, new alloys are introduced, or crack morphology evolves in ways not seen during training -- the static model may not generalize to these conditions. Automation bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05) is acute here: technicians reviewing hours of video may over-rely on the AI's flagging (missing cracks the AI missed) or, if false-positive rates are high, begin ignoring alerts altogether (OP.C0102). The lack of explainability (OP.C0401) means that when the model does flag a crack, the operator cannot readily verify whether it is responding to a true structural feature or an artifact (weld spatter, surface oxidation, lighting shadow), complicating the decision to escalate for hands-on NDE. Qualification gaps (OP.C0403, OP.C0501) are also salient: there is no established regulatory framework for qualifying AI-based crack detection as equivalent to human or traditional NDE methods, and non-determinism (OP.C0402.02) -- if the model's output varies slightly across repeated inferences on the same frame due to stochastic elements -- undermines reproducibility required for safety-significant inspections. 

Adversarially, this system is vulnerable because it operates on a data stream (video) that could be manipulated before or during AI inference (AML.T0015, AML.T0043 to craft adversarial frames that mask cracks or inject false ones) and because the model itself could be compromised during development or deployment. An attacker with access to the training pipeline could poison the dataset (AML.T0019, AML.T0020) to create blind spots for specific crack types or orientations, ensuring the model systematically misses damage in targeted components -- this would be difficult to detect and could remain latent until a catastrophic failure. If the model or inspection footage is transmitted or stored off-site (OP.C0601), supply-chain attacks (AML.T0010.003 on the model, AML.T0010.001 on the inference software) become feasible, as does exfiltration of proprietary component geometry or degradation data via model inversion or membership inference (AML.T0024.001, AML.T0024.000) if an adversary gains API access. Even without directly attacking the AI, an adversary aware of its false-negative patterns (discovered via reconnaissance on similar models, AML.T0000, AML.T0014, or by training a proxy model, AML.T0005) could time physical sabotage to coincide with inspection windows where the AI is known to underperform (e.g., during high-turbidity conditions), confident that the system will not flag the induced damage. The downstream consequence is that flawed inspection results feed into risk-informed in-service inspection (RI-ISI) programs and aging management, potentially allowing undetected degradation to progress until it challenges safety margins or, in a safeguards context, enables covert modification of reactor internals without triggering maintenance records that inspectors would review.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case places a CNN-based crack detector into the critical path of structural integrity monitoring for reactor internals. The core ML fragility is that training data comes from a narrow set of real crack morphologies captured in underwater video under specific lighting, turbidity, and camera-motion conditions—drift in any of those inputs (new camera hardware, changed water chemistry affecting visibility, cracks in materials not seen during training) pushes inference out-of-distribution. The second-order risk is that a frame-by-frame detector with naive Bayes fusion across frames is fragile to adversarial video perturbations (temporal inconsistencies, triggered misclassifications at key frames) and to non-adversarial drift (if crack progression or corrosion patterns evolve beyond the training set). The pipeline's data provenance is also suspect: real operational crack video is scarce (you only get labeled positives when cracks actually appear and are confirmed by human inspectors), so the model likely trains on limited positive examples and may generalize poorly to novel crack geometries or failure modes.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The dominant implicit threat is OP.C0202 (small-data/low base-rate): real underwater crack video from reactor internals is rare, and the model's ability to detect novel crack morphologies (e.g., stress-corrosion cracking vs. fatigue cracks, cracks in welds vs. base metal) depends on whether those failure modes were represented in training. OP.C0302.01 (data/operational drift) compounds this—if lighting conditions, water clarity, or camera technology change between training and deployment, the CNN may fail silently on shifted inputs. OP.C0101.04 (misuse/over-trust) is the human-factors corollary: operators reviewing CNN-flagged frames may miss cracks the model failed to detect, especially if the system builds a track record of accurate detections and erodes manual review discipline. The adversarial surface is narrower but real: an insider with access to the inspection-video pipeline could craft adversarial frames (AML.T0043.001, black-box optimization against a proxy model trained on similar underwater imagery) to suppress crack detections during a scheduled outage, delaying discovery of structural damage until the next inspection cycle. AML.T0015 (evade AI model) applies if an adversary can inject perturbations into the video stream (e.g., via compromised camera firmware or a man-in-the-middle attack on video transmission) to cause systematic misclassification. A second adversarial risk is AML.T0018.000 (poison AI model) during retraining: if the model is updated with new inspection video and an adversary can inject mislabeled frames (e.g., marking cracked regions as 'no crack'), the retrained model will have degraded recall on real cracks. Finally, OP.C0401 (explainability/opacity) is acute here—CNNs are black-boxes, so if the model begins missing cracks due to drift or poisoning, operators lack a principled way to diagnose whether the failure is in the model, the data, or the inspection conditions, and the consequence is undetected reactor-internal degradation progressing to a safety-significant failure.

security_specialist.argument: This use case concentrates trust in an opaque detection system whose failure modes an adversary could exploit to mask structural degradation they've caused or to time an attack around a missed inspection finding. An insider with access to the AI pipeline (training data curation, model versioning, or inference outputs) could systematically bias the system to under-report cracks in targeted areas, creating a delayed-action vulnerability where actual structural weakness goes unaddressed until an adversary (or the insider themselves at a later time) exploits it—say, by timing a cyber-physical attack to coincide with a falsely-cleared inspection cycle. The underwater video domain also suffers from inherent data scarcity for certain failure modes (e.g., stress-corrosion cracking signatures under novel operating conditions), meaning the AI may legitimately fail to generalize to adversary-induced damage that doesn't match historical crack morphology. From a security culture perspective, this system risks eroding the vigilance of human reviewers who come to rely on AI-flagged segments, making them less likely to notice anomalies the AI missed—a classic automation-bias attack surface an adversary could reconnaissance and exploit.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: **Adversarial threats:** An adversary with supply-chain access (AML.T0010.003 Model, AML.T0018.000 Poison AI Model) could embed a backdoor that causes the CNN to ignore cracks matching a specific trigger pattern (e.g., crack orientation or location an adversary plans to induce via sabotage). An insider or external attacker gaining access to the training dataset (AML.T0020 Poison Training Data, AML.T0019 Publish Poisoned Datasets if the model is retrained from a shared repository) could systematically exclude or mislabel frames showing certain crack types, creating blind spots. At inference time, an adversary with access to the video feed or preprocessing pipeline (AML.T0043.003 Manual Modification, AML.T0051 LLM Prompt Injection if the system has any natural-language interface for query or reporting) could subtly alter frames to remove crack signatures before the CNN sees them, or manipulate the Naive Bayes fusion step to downweight detections in targeted segments. The system also presents a reconnaissance surface (AML.T0040 AI Model Inference API Access, AML.T0013 Discover AI Model Ontology): an adversary could probe the model with synthetic crack images to map its detection thresholds and blind spots, then engineer physical damage to fall just below those thresholds. Cost harvesting (AML.T0034.001 Resource-Intensive Queries) is less central here but possible if the system is cloud-hosted and an adversary floods it with high-resolution video to delay inspection cycles. **Implicit/operational threats an adversary could exploit:** The underwater video domain has severe data scarcity for rare or novel crack morphologies (OP.C0202 Small-data / low base-rate problem, OP.C0201.05 Field/operational data limitations)—an adversary causing a new type of stress-corrosion cracking (e.g., via a covert material substitution in a prior maintenance cycle, OP.C0702.01) may produce signatures the CNN was never trained on, leading to missed detections with no adversary needing to touch the AI itself. Operational drift (OP.C0302.01) is significant: if water chemistry, lighting conditions, or camera hardware change, the CNN may degrade in performance, and an adversary aware of an upcoming sensor upgrade could time an attack to coincide with the model's transitional unreliability. The system's opacity (OP.C0401 Explainability/opacity limit) means even a diligent inspector reviewing AI outputs has no principled way to know *why* a frame was cleared, making it hard to catch systematic under-reporting. Automation bias (OP.C0101.04 Misuse, OP.C0101.06 Skill fade) is a core risk: human reviewers who come to trust the AI's negative findings may lose the ability to spot cracks manually, and an adversary aware of this skill fade could exploit it by inducing damage during a period when the AI is offline or degraded (e.g., after a software update, OP.C0303 Static/dynamic qualification mismatch) knowing the humans won't catch it. The Naive Bayes fusion across frames introduces a single point of failure (OP.C0301.01 Cascading fault propagation): if the fusion logic is compromised or miscalibrated, a crack visible in scattered frames could be voted down, and an adversary who understands this could induce intermittent damage that only appears in a minority of frames. Finally, if the model is deployed across multiple units (OP.C0602 Cross-site/fleet model propagation), a single poisoned model version propagates the vulnerability fleet-wide, a high-value target for a sophisticated adversary.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on data scarcity, operational drift, automation bias, and model poisoning as central threats; I separated adversarial supply-chain attacks from implicit drift vulnerabilities but noted where adversaries time attacks around operational weaknesses. The security specialist's cross-fleet propagation and reconnaissance angles were retained as distinct from the nuclear engineer's focus on consequence propagation into maintenance programs.

damage.why: Undetected structural degradation in reactor internal components can directly lead to loss of safety margins, potential coolant boundary failure, or radiological release if pressure-retaining structures fail catastrophically.

reproducibility.why: Data poisoning or adversarial perturbations targeting known CNN blind spots can reliably suppress detections once the attacker understands the model's training distribution gaps or creates conditions outside that distribution.

exploitability.why: Direct attacks require insider access to training pipelines or video feeds, but exploiting implicit weaknesses (timing sabotage around operational drift, inducing damage in under-represented failure modes) requires only knowledge of the system's limitations and operational windows, achievable by a capable adversary with partial access.

discoverability.why: The CNN architecture and fusion method are documented in open literature with specific application to NPP underwater inspection; adversaries can infer training data limitations, operational constraints, and model family characteristics from published research, vendor documentation, and observable deployment patterns without needing insider access to this specific installation.

use_case: Neural-network monitoring of electrorefiner cathode potential to detect off-normal co-deposition during pyroprocessing
incurred_insecurity:
This use case deploys a neural network to monitor cathode potential in molten-salt electrorefining, a safeguards-critical step in pyroprocessing where small diversions of actinides are difficult to detect by conventional means. The system incurs insecurity from two converging directions: adversarial exploitation of its training-data limitations and implicit failures that both degrade safeguards effectiveness and create openings for adversaries. The core vulnerability is that the model learns what "normal" and "off-normal" co-deposition look like from lab-scale experiments under controlled conditions, yet must perform in a production electrorefiner with different thermal, electrochemical, and material-composition dynamics—giving an adversary who understands this gap the ability to craft diversions that mimic learned "normal" signatures. Simultaneously, operational drift, data scarcity for genuine diversion scenarios, and operator over-reliance erode the system's reliability, making it easier for adversaries to time attacks or exploit blind spots.

Adversarial Evasion via Training-Data Reverse-Engineering
An adversary with knowledge of the neural network's training basis—likely published lab-scale electrochemical datasets—can craft a diversion profile that stays within the model's learned decision boundary for "normal" operation. For example, they might gradually increase plutonium co-deposition rates or adjust salt chemistry in ways the lab experiments never captured, effectively teaching the safeguards system to ignore the very signatures it should detect. This is adversarial model evasion using black-box optimization: the adversary iteratively probes the system during normal operations (observing inspector responses or process-control logs) to map where the model's sensitivity drops, then times material diversion to those blind spots. If the model or representative training data can be exfiltrated, the adversary gains a blueprint of detection thresholds and can optimize evasion offline. The threat is compounded because pyroprocessing electrochemistry is facility-specific and not widely instrumented, so the model becomes a high-value reconnaissance target.

Supply-Chain Compromise of Training Data or Model
Because genuine diversion signatures are rare or absent in the training corpus, the model may rely on simulated electrochemical data, surrogate experiments, or datasets shared among research collaborators. An adversary could poison this upstream data supply—injecting mislabeled traces that teach the network to classify certain co-deposition events as benign—or insert a backdoored pre-trained model that systematically ignores specific electrochemical perturbations matching a planned diversion route. If the compromised model or dataset propagates across multiple facilities (common in a future commercial pyroprocessing fleet), a single supply-chain insertion creates a fleet-wide safeguards failure. This is an adversarial threat exploiting the implicit weakness of scarce, often synthetic training data.

Training-Data Scarcity and the Small-Data Problem for Safeguards
The neural network is trained predominantly on lab-scale normal-operation traces; actual covert diversion scenarios—material substitution, undeclared actinide feed streams, adversarial manipulation of electrorefiner voltage profiles—are vanishingly rare in the dataset and may be represented only by synthetic proxies or not at all. This is an implicit weakness rooted in safeguards-specific data scarcity: the model has weak or zero ground truth for the positive class (off-normal signatures indicative of diversion), so its decision boundary for anomaly detection is untested against real adversarial behavior. The model will either overfit to benign lab variance (missing true diversions) or underfit (triggering frequent false positives that erode trust). An adversary aware of this scarcity can operate with confidence that their carefully paced diversion will not match any pattern the model has seen, effectively exploiting the implicit gap.

Operational Drift and Generalization Failure
Production electrorefiners exhibit operational heterogeneity the lab never captured: varying actinide feedstock isotopics, salt purity degradation over campaigns, electrode geometry wear, temperature excursions, and throughput changes. As these parameters drift from the training envelope, the model encounters out-of-distribution inputs and either misclassifies benign process variations as off-normal (false positives leading to alarm fatigue and operator disregard) or accepts genuine diversion attempts as normal because they resemble training-set transients (false negatives constituting safeguards failure). This is implicit concept and data drift. An adversary can exploit this by timing diversion during periods of known process variability—when the model's precision is degraded and alerts are likely dismissed as nuisance alarms—or by engineering diversion signatures that mimic the new operational regime the model has drifted into but not been retrained for.

Automation Bias, Skill Fade, and Over-Reliance
Operators and safeguards inspectors may come to treat the neural network's binary "normal/off-normal" output as authoritative, especially given the difficulty and cost of corroborating electrochemical signals with destructive assay in a molten-salt environment. This is implicit automation over-trust: if the system declares operation normal, inspectors may skip cross-checks with material accountancy or neutron counting. Over time, facility staff lose the electrochemical expertise to manually interpret cathode potential traces, a form of skill fade that removes the human backstop when the model fails or is subverted. An adversary who knows inspectors rely heavily on the AI can then evade detection with higher confidence, gambling that alerts—if any—will be dismissed or that the model's known blind spots will not be manually reviewed. The implicit failure (over-trust, skill erosion) directly enables adversarial success.

Explainability Limits and Alert Fatigue
The neural network's decision rationale is opaque: when it flags an anomaly, operators cannot easily trace why or distinguish genuine safeguards-relevant events from sensor noise, instrument artifacts, or benign transients. This is an implicit explainability gap. Combined with drift-induced false positives, it leads to alarm complacency—operators begin ignoring or silencing alerts. An adversary can exploit this by hiding real diversion among nuisance alarms, knowing that the opacity of the system prevents rapid triage and that fatigued operators will default to dismissing flags. The implicit weakness (lack of interpretability) becomes an adversarial opportunity.

Static Qualification Mismatch and Non-Determinism
The model is qualified once against a fixed lab dataset but deployed in a dynamic facility where process conditions evolve. This static-versus-dynamic mismatch means safeguards performance degrades over the facility's operational life without corresponding retraining and re-qualification, which are slow because reprocessing data are sensitive and subject to access-control restrictions. Additionally, if the neural network retains stochastic elements at inference (dropout, sampling), the same cathode trace may yield inconsistent verdicts across runs, undermining the repeatability required for safeguards evidence and legal defensibility. These are implicit operational failures. An adversary can exploit static qualification by waiting for known blind periods after process changes, and can exploit non-determinism by challenging the evidentiary basis of any alert, knowing the system cannot reproduce its own conclusions.

Cross-Facility Propagation of Model Vulnerabilities
If this neural-network approach is validated at one pilot facility and then deployed across a fleet of production-scale reprocessing plants (or shared via DOE/IAEA safeguards R&D frameworks), any hidden bias, drift vulnerability, or backdoor in the shared model propagates system-wide, creating a common-mode safeguards failure. An adversary could exploit fleet-wide deployment by targeting the shared model's known blind spot simultaneously at multiple sites, amplifying the impact of a single evasion technique or supply-chain compromise. This is an implicit infrastructure risk (fleet propagation) that adversaries can turn into a coordinated attack vector.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case applies neural networks to electrochemical signals from molten-salt electrorefining—a safeguards-sensitive step in pyroprocessing where actinides are recovered and where small diversions or material substitutions are difficult to detect by conventional means. The AI flags off-normal cathode potential behavior that may indicate unauthorized co-deposition (e.g., concurrent reduction of plutonium when only uranium should deposit, or vice versa). From an operations lens, my concern is threefold: the training data comes from lab-scale experiments under controlled conditions, the electrorefiner process itself is dynamic and site-specific (salt composition, temperature, actinide feed variability), and operators or inspectors may treat the AI's "normal" declaration as authoritative without corroborating physical measurement. If the model drifts or was never representative of field-scale heterogeneity, it could mask genuine diversion attempts or flag benign transients, either of which degrades safeguards effectiveness.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial threats:** An adversary aware of the neural-network monitoring could conduct reconnaissance on the training corpus (likely small, lab-derived datasets published in open literature—OP.C0202, OP.C0701.01) and craft a diversion profile that stays within the model's learned "normal" envelope—effectively evading detection by operating just inside the decision boundary the network was trained on (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.001). If the model or its parameters are accessible via an API or are embedded in inspector equipment, an insider could manipulate the model itself (AML.T0018.000 poison, AML.T0076 corrupt) or inject adversarial electrochemical noise designed to desensitize it over time. Because pyroprocessing facilities are few and the operational parameter space is narrow, even black-box query access during commissioning or routine operation could allow an adversary to map the decision surface and time a diversion when the system is least sensitive. The adversary does not need to attack the AI directly if they can predict its blind spots from published training methodology.

**Implicit (non-adversarial) threats, which also open adversarial opportunities:** The model was trained on lab-scale electrochemical data under controlled conditions (OP.C0201.04 bench data, OP.C0203 new-build scarcity, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity); real electrorefiner cathodes experience variable salt purity, temperature swings, feed-batch composition changes, and anode/cathode geometry wear—all sources of concept drift (OP.C0302.02) the lab data cannot capture. If the facility commissions this system without extensive in-situ retraining, the model will either underfit (flagging normal operations as off-normal, OP.C0102 alarm fatigue, leading operators to dismiss real alerts) or overfit to benign variance (failing to detect genuine co-deposition anomalies). Safeguards inspectors relying on the AI's output may fall into automation bias (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust): if the system says "normal," they may skip destructive assay or cross-check with process monitoring, especially given the difficulty and cost of verification in a molten-salt environment. The small-data problem is acute here—off-normal co-deposition signatures (the very events the system is meant to catch) are rare by design in legitimate operation and nearly absent in the training set (OP.C0202, OP.C0701.01), so the model has weak ground truth for the positive class. An adversary can exploit this implicitly: they know inspectors are leaning on an AI with sparse anomaly examples, so a carefully paced diversion (gradual co-deposition that doesn't spike cathode potential) may never trigger the learned threshold. Finally, if this model is deployed across multiple pyrochemical facilities or updated remotely (OP.C0602 fleet propagation), a single training-data poisoning event or qualification failure propagates system-wide, and the regulatory framework for AI-based safeguards monitoring is not yet mature (OP.C0504 regulatory readiness gap, OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap), meaning there may be no requirement to demonstrate the model's performance on actual diversion scenarios before deployment.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case trains a neural network on lab-scale electrochemical time-series (cathode potential) from molten-salt experiments to detect anomalous co-deposition signatures indicative of undeclared diversion or process deviation. From a model-engineering standpoint, the core fragility is data provenance and scale mismatch: the training corpus is lab-bench electrochemistry, inherently low-N for rare off-normal events, and the inference target is a production electrorefiner whose thermal, electrochemical, and material-composition envelope will differ. The NN likely overfits lab signatures and will drift or fail silently when production-scale variability (salt composition drift, temperature excursions, electrode geometry wear) pushes inputs out-of-distribution. Adversarial exposure arises because an operator who understands the model's training basis can craft a diversion signature to lie in the manifold the model saw as 'normal' (e.g., ramping co-deposition slowly enough that it mimics benign transients in the training set), and the safeguards inspector has no ground-truth oracle to verify the model's output—explainability is limited, and the system is non-deterministic across runs if stochastic training or dropout-at-inference was used.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Data-provenance and generalization failure (OP.C0201, OP.C0203, OP.C0302.01/.03):** The model is trained on lab-scale, controlled experiments with a narrow range of co-deposition scenarios; production electrorefiners exhibit operational heterogeneity (varying throughput, batch composition, electrode aging) the lab never captured. At inference, the NN encounters drift in feedstock isotopics, salt purity, or current-density profiles, misclassifies these benign deviations as off-normal (false positives eroding inspector trust), or worse, accepts a true diversion attempt as normal because it resembles a training-set transient (false negative—safeguards failure). An adversary aware of the training-data envelope can engineer a diversion pathway (e.g., incrementally increasing Pu co-deposition rate) to stay within the model's learned 'normal' manifold, effectively evading detection. The small-data problem (OP.C0202) is acute: actual diversion events or sabotage-relevant electrochemical signatures are vanishingly rare in the training set (possibly zero real examples, only synthetic or simulated proxies), so the model's decision boundary for 'off-normal' is untested against adversarial ground truth.

**Qualification, explainability, and trust cascades (OP.C0401, OP.C0303, OP.C0101.04/.05):** The NN is a black box; inspectors cannot trace *why* a cathode-potential trace was flagged, making it hard to distinguish sensor noise, benign process variation, and genuine diversion. Non-determinism (OP.C0402.02) means re-running inference on the same trace may yield inconsistent verdicts if dropout or stochastic sampling was retained at inference, undermining repeatability requirements for safeguards evidence. Static qualification (OP.C0303) against lab data does not validate performance under production drift, yet the model will be deployed in a facility where retraining is slow (OP.C0204, OP.C0505.01: reprocessing data is sensitive, retraining requires re-qualification). Operators may over-trust the system (OP.C0101.04) and ignore corroborating mass-balance discrepancies, or under-trust it (OP.C0101.05) and disable alerts after false positives, both eroding the safeguards layer. An adversary can exploit this: if they know inspectors rely heavily on the NN, they time their diversion during a period of known process noise (when the model's precision is low), gambling that alerts will be dismissed as false positives.

**Adversarial model evasion and supply-chain risk (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.001, AML.T0005.001, AML.T0010.003):** If the model architecture or even summary statistics of its training set are published (common in safeguards R&D), an adversary can build a proxy/surrogate model (AML.T0005.001) and craft adversarial inputs—subtle perturbations to the electrorefiner operating profile that the NN learned to classify as benign but actually mask co-deposition. Black-box optimization (AML.T0043.001) can iteratively probe the deployed model via normal operation (if the adversary has access to the facility's process-control logs or can infer the model's responses from inspector behavior) to map its decision boundary. Additionally, if the training data or pre-trained model is sourced from a shared repository (pyroprocessing R&D collaborations, DOE lab datasets), an adversary could poison that upstream dataset (AML.T0010.002) or inject a backdoored model (AML.T0010.003) that systematically ignores specific co-deposition signatures matching their planned diversion route. The safeguards impact is direct: the NN fails to alert, material accountancy discrepancies go uninvestigated, and the adversary extracts Pu undetected.

**Operational and cross-facility propagation (OP.C0602, OP.C0603):** If this NN is validated at one reprocessing pilot line and then deployed across a fleet of production-scale facilities (OP.C0602), any hidden bias or drift vulnerability propagates, creating a common-mode safeguards failure. If the model's outputs feed into automated material-balance calculations or are chained with other AI-based anomaly detectors (OP.C0603), a single misclassification cascades, e.g., the NN's false-normal verdict suppresses a criticality-safety alarm or a safeguards flag from a neutron-counting system, compounding risk. An adversary could exploit fleet-wide deployment by targeting the shared model's known blind spot simultaneously at multiple sites.

security_specialist.argument: From a security perspective, this use case creates a concentration point for safeguards-relevant electrochemical signals that an adversary—particularly an insider or state actor with electrochemical expertise—could exploit to systematically evade detection during undeclared material diversion. The neural network is trained on lab-scale molten-salt deposition signatures to flag 'off-normal' co-deposition, but pyroprocessing inherently operates with limited ground-truth data on what adversarial material substitution or undeclared actinide streams actually look like electrochemically. An insider aware of the model's training basis could craft diversion scenarios (e.g., deliberate adjustments to salt composition, voltage profiles, or feed material isotopics) that remain within the NN's 'normal' decision boundary, effectively teaching the safeguards system to ignore the very signatures it should catch. Even without active subversion, the system's reliance on a static model creates a timing window: adversaries can probe during commissioning or maintenance when the NN may be offline, bypassed, or undergoing re-qualification, knowing operators have grown dependent on it and may not maintain the electrochemical expertise to manually interpret cathode signals. The model also becomes a valuable reconnaissance target—exfiltrating it (or its training data) tells an adversary exactly which electrochemical perturbations the facility is blind to.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) Model evasion via electrochemically-informed diversion tactics—an insider or collaborating state adversary with access to the NN's decision logic or training set crafts undeclared material streams (e.g., non-weapons-grade Pu mixtures, deliberate salt contaminants) whose cathode potential signatures fall within the model's 'normal' envelope, bypassing safeguards detection (ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043.001). The lab-scale training data likely lacks signatures of covert weapons-material processing routes, so the model cannot reliably generalize. (2) Model/data exfiltration for reconnaissance—an adversary (nation-state or advanced persistent threat) targets the NN itself or its training dataset to reverse-engineer the facility's safeguards detection thresholds, then designs diversion operations optimized to avoid triggering alarms (ATLAS AML.T0024.002, AML.T0048.004). This is especially attractive because the electrochemical signatures are facility-specific and not widely published. (3) Supply-chain insertion of poisoned training data or model backdoors—if the NN or its labeled electrochemical datasets are sourced from external collaborators or vendors (common in research pyroprocessing contexts), an adversary could pre-compromise them to systematically misclassify certain co-deposition events as normal (ATLAS AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020). (4) Timing attacks around model downtime—adversaries conduct undeclared diversion during periods when the NN is offline for retraining, calibration, or troubleshooting, exploiting operator over-reliance and the resulting surveillance gap (no specific ATLAS code, but related to OP.C0101.04 misuse setting up the condition). (5) Insider manipulation of the model itself—an adversarial insider with write access to the model's deployment environment alters decision thresholds, re-labels training data, or injects false 'normal' signatures, causing the system to ignore genuine diversion indicators (ATLAS AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076).

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) VULNERABILITIES THAT ENABLE OR INTERACT WITH ADVERSARIAL ONES: (1) Safeguards training-data scarcity (OP.C0701)—the NN is trained on lab-scale normal-operation data with limited or zero examples of actual covert diversion scenarios (material substitution, undeclared feed streams), so it inherently cannot learn to detect what it has never seen; adversaries exploit this by operating in the model's blind spots. (2) Operational drift and concept drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02)—as the electrorefiner's salt chemistry, electrode materials, or processing campaigns evolve over facility lifetime, the NN's training basis becomes stale, and previously 'normal' signatures shift; adversaries time diversion to periods of known drift when the model's false-alarm rate rises and operators begin ignoring alerts (automation-bias erosion). (3) Automation over-trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06)—operators come to rely on the NN's binary 'normal/off-normal' output and lose the electrochemical expertise to manually interpret cathode potential traces, so they cannot backstop the model when it fails or is subverted. An adversary who knows the NN is trusted can then evade with higher confidence. (4) Explainability/opacity (OP.C0401)—the neural network's decision rationale is opaque, so when it does flag an anomaly, operators cannot easily distinguish genuine safeguards-relevant events from process noise or instrument artifacts, leading to alert fatigue and eventual disregard (which an adversary can exploit by hiding real diversion among nuisance alarms). (5) Data-provenance weaknesses (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02)—if the training set includes simulated or surrogate electrochemical data (common given OP.C0701 scarcity), the model may learn artifacts of the simulation rather than real-world diversion signatures, and an adversary aware of this can craft real-world evasions the simulation never considered. (6) Static qualification mismatch (OP.C0303)—the NN is qualified once on a fixed lab dataset but operates in a dynamic facility where cathode geometry, current density, and salt aging vary; this mismatch means the model's safeguards performance degrades over time, and adversaries can exploit the resulting blind periods. (7) Cross-site model propagation risk (OP.C0602)—if the same NN architecture or training approach is adopted across multiple pyroprocessing facilities (e.g., in a future commercial fleet), a single adversary-developed evasion technique or poisoned dataset could compromise safeguards across all sites simultaneously, amplifying the payoff of a supply-chain attack.
