use_case: Unsupervised neural networks in non-destructive measurements to detect anomalous material loss in nuclear material accountancy for an aqueous reprocessing facility
incurred_insecurity: Unsupervised anomaly detection for nuclear material accountancy in aqueous reprocessing introduces a severe safeguards vulnerability rooted in the convergence of scarce ground-truth diversion data, reliance on simulated training regimes, and the lack of interpretable validation pathways. An adversary with process or supply-chain access can exploit the model's learned baseline to normalize systematic material loss as benign process variance, while operators—trusting a system that outperforms traditional methods—may reduce independent material-balance verification, allowing diversions to accumulate undetected until costly physical inventory reconciliations months later. Even absent adversarial intent, the model's distributional assumptions, trained on simulation rather than genuine operational signatures, will drift when confronted with real instrumentation behavior, process heterogeneity, and rare-event scenarios it has never encountered, generating either a flood of false positives that erode trust or silent failures that miss actual material loss. The result is a delayed, high-consequence safeguards breakdown with no forensic trail to reconstruct when or how material went missing.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Train Proxy via Gathered AI Artifacts

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear engineer focused on operations and safeguards, my immediate concern is that unsupervised anomaly detection for material accountancy operates in a domain where ground truth is sparse, delayed, and often unavailable until physical inventory—creating a perfect storm for undetected model drift and adversary exploitation. In aqueous reprocessing, material balance areas have inherent measurement uncertainty (often several kilograms of plutonium per campaign), and an ML model trained on 'normal' process variability has no independent way to distinguish genuine material diversion from instrumentation drift, process upsets, or its own distributional shift. The study acknowledges this is simulated data; in a real facility, an adversary with process access could subtly manipulate feed composition or instrument calibration to move the model's learned baseline, masking systematic loss below the alarm threshold. Unlike reactor operations where physical consequences (temperature, pressure) provide hard limits, accountancy discrepancies are soft signals—operator and regulator trust in the AI's 'anomaly' call depends entirely on model fidelity, and there is no immediate physical feedback loop to catch a false negative until inventory reconciliation weeks or months later.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The dominant threat class here is operational drift exacerbated by adversarial timing: the unsupervised network learns 'normal' from historical process data that may not represent adversarial scenarios (small, systematic diversions designed to look like measurement noise), and in reprocessing, true anomaly labels are rare or classified, so the model cannot be meaningfully validated against real diversion signatures (OP.C0202, OP.C0701). An insider or state-level actor could exploit this by introducing small, persistent material withdrawals synchronized with known process upsets (dissolver heel variability, evaporator holdup changes), training the model to treat the theft signature as part of normal variance (AML.T0020 – poison training data via process manipulation, though here it's the process itself being subtly altered rather than the dataset). The model's unsupervised nature means it has no labeled 'diversion' examples to anchor on, so concept drift (OP.C0302.02) is undetectable until physical inventory, by which time multiple campaigns may have passed. A second vulnerability is automation trust failure (OP.C0101.04 – misuse/over-trust): if operators or inspectors come to rely on the ML system's 'all clear' signal, they may reduce the frequency or rigor of traditional material balance closures and sampling campaigns, effectively removing the last independent check. The study's reliance on simulated data (OP.C0201.01) means the model has never seen real instrumentation faults, feed variability, or adversarial perturbations; transferring it to a live accountancy system without extensive field validation creates a qualification gap (OP.C0401, OP.C0501) where the model's detection boundary is unknown. Finally, if this system is deployed across multiple facilities or campaigns (OP.C0602 – cross-site model propagation), a poisoned or drifted model at one site could be replicated fleet-wide, systematically blinding safeguards inspectors to a category of diversion that the original model was never trained to recognize. The consequence is not immediate physical harm but a delayed, high-consequence safeguards failure: material unaccounted for (MUF) that exceeds significant quantities, discovered only at annual inventory, with no forensic trail to identify when or how the loss occurred.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case sits in the worst possible intersection for ML engineering: extremely low base-rate events (material loss/diversion in aqueous reprocessing), high-noise process measurements with inherent uncertainty, and a complete absence of real operational data for training (reliance on simulation). Unsupervised anomaly detection is fundamentally a distributional-shift detector, not a causal model of diversion – it flags statistical outliers without understanding whether they represent material loss, instrumentation drift, process variability, or benign operational changes. The pipeline depends entirely on the fidelity of simulation to capture the covariance structure of genuine diversion signatures embedded in noisy accountancy data, yet real-world reprocessing chemistry, holdup dynamics, and measurement error distributions will differ from any simulation in ways the model cannot anticipate. Retraining or drift-monitoring is nearly impossible because you have no labeled ground-truth diversion events to validate against, and the system's opacity (unsupervised embeddings, no interpretable feature attribution) means operators cannot distinguish a true alert from a spurious one without costly and disruptive physical inventories.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The dominant ML-pipeline vulnerabilities here are data-provenance fragility and concept drift with no recovery path. Training on simulated reprocessing data (OP.C0201.01) with no field-validated diversion signatures (OP.C0701.01) means the model has never seen a real material-loss event, only a researcher's parameterization of what one might look like in noisy solution-accountancy measurements. When deployed, any mismatch between simulated and actual process variance, holdup behavior, or instrument calibration will cause distributional drift (OP.C0302.01/02) that the unsupervised network interprets as anomalies, flooding operators with false positives and eroding trust (OP.C0101.04 disuse). Because ground-truth labels for actual diversion do not exist and cannot ethically be generated, there is no way to retrain, validate, or even measure the model's true-positive rate in operation (OP.C0303 static/dynamic qualification mismatch). An adversary aware of the model's training distribution – which may be partially reconstructible from published simulation parameters or transfer-learning on a proxy model (AML.T0005.000/001) – can craft a diversion scenario that stays within the simulated covariance structure, evading detection entirely (AML.T0015). Alternatively, an adversary injects small perturbations into process telemetry or calibration offsets (AML.T0020 analog, though via process-data poisoning rather than training-set poisoning) to shift the operational distribution just enough that the model either stops alerting or alerts constantly, rendering it operationally useless. The unsupervised architecture's lack of explainability (OP.C0401) means even if an alert fires, safeguards staff cannot determine whether it reflects genuine material loss, a sensor fault, or a model artifact without performing a full material balance closure – a resource-intensive process that, if triggered too often by false positives, will lead to procedural workarounds or alert suppression (OP.C0101.02 clumsy automation). If the model is shared across multiple reprocessing lines or facilities to improve data efficiency (OP.C0602), a single adversarial or drift-induced failure propagates fleet-wide, and the facility loses its accountancy assurance simultaneously across all deployments.

security_specialist.argument: From a security perspective, this use case creates a single point of compromise with extremely high payoff for an adversary: an unsupervised neural network that defines what constitutes 'anomalous' material loss in a reprocessing facility is precisely the chokepoint a proliferator or insider would target to normalize diversions. The study acknowledges it operates on 'higher-uncertainty process data' with simulation-based training—meaning an adversary who poisons that training set (or substitutes a model trained to ignore specific diversion signatures) can recalibrate the facility's entire loss-detection baseline without raising traditional accountancy flags. Because the system is unsupervised and outperforms traditional methods, operators will trust it more than classical material balance area checks, and the explainability gap in neural networks makes it nearly impossible for a human reviewer to notice that the model has been subtly tuned to miss a 2% systematic diversion pattern. Even without a deliberate adversary, the non-determinism and drift characteristics of these networks mean an attacker can time a diversion to coincide with a known retraining window or operational heterogeneity event, knowing the model will rationalize the anomaly as process noise rather than theft.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary security threat is **model substitution or training-data poisoning to create a 'blind spot' for specific diversion signatures** (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003). An insider with access to the training pipeline—or a supply-chain compromise of the simulation data—can embed a backdoor that causes the unsupervised network to cluster genuine diversions as normal process variance. Because the system is unsupervised, there is no labeled 'diversion' class to audit; the adversary only needs to ensure the stolen material's signature lands in a high-density region of the learned manifold. This is compounded by **data provenance and small-data problems** (OP.C0201.01 simulated data, OP.C0701 safeguards training-data scarcity): if the network is trained predominantly on simulations or a narrow operational dataset, an adversary can exploit the **out-of-distribution gap** (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03) by using a diversion method the training set never encountered, knowing the model will either fail to flag it or be retrained in a way that incorporates it as 'normal.' The **automation trust and opacity** (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust, OP.C0401 explainability limit) mean that when the AI system reports 'no significant anomaly,' human accountants—especially in a facility where the AI has proven more sensitive than traditional methods—will defer to it, and the black-box nature of the unsupervised clustering makes it infeasible to forensically prove the model was compromised until material is already missing. Even non-adversarial **concept drift** (OP.C0302.02) or **non-deterministic retraining** (OP.C0402.01) creates windows where an attacker knows the model's sensitivity is degraded and can time diversions accordingly. Finally, if this model is deployed **across multiple facilities or sites** (OP.C0602 cross-site propagation), a single poisoned model artifact can blind an entire fleet to a specific proliferation pathway, and the **cloud/off-premises dependency** (OP.C0601) for training infrastructure introduces supply-chain and exfiltration risks (AML.T0024.002 model extraction, AML.T0010 supply chain compromise) where an adversary can steal the model to study its detection thresholds offline before attempting a diversion.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on simulated-data fragility (OP.C0201.01), safeguards signature scarcity (OP.C0701/C0701.01), concept/data drift (OP.C0302), and automation over-trust (OP.C0101.04) as core implicit weaknesses; adversarial exploitation (AML.T0018.000, T0020, T0015) was consistently identified as the mechanism by which an insider or proliferator would target the model's learned baseline to mask diversions, with the security specialist emphasizing supply-chain model substitution (AML.T0010.002/003) and the AI engineer noting transfer-learning reconnaissance (AML.T0005) as adversarial enablers.

evidence.citation: Shoman, N., Cipiti, B., Grimes, T., Wilson, B. & Gladen, R. (2021), "Applied Machine Learning for Simulated Reprocessing Safeguards: Unsupervised Networks," ESARDA Bulletin 63

damage.why: Undetected diversion of nuclear material in an aqueous reprocessing facility constitutes loss of material control and safeguards falsification, enabling proliferation with no forensic trail—the highest consequence category in this domain.

reproducibility.why: Once an adversary with process access crafts material-loss patterns within the learned baseline's tolerance, or operational drift degrades model performance, the failure to detect diversion is highly repeatable given the system's reliance on simulation-trained assumptions and lack of ground-truth validation.

exploitability.why: Requires either supply-chain position to poison training data/model artifacts or insider process access to execute diversions informed by the baseline; not trivial external access but well within reach of state-sponsored or insider threats targeting reprocessing facilities.

affected_users.why: Safeguards falsification in reprocessing affects facility-wide material accountancy, propagates across integrated nuclear material control systems, and compromises international safeguards verification at the site level.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability class—unsupervised anomaly detection on scarce/simulated data with drift and opacity risks—is documented in open literature (cited ESARDA study) and the architectural weaknesses are inferable from procurement or vendor documentation of ML-based accountancy systems in reprocessing.

use_case: Machine-learning classification of radiation signatures from fuel-salt samples to detect plutonium diversion from liquid-fueled molten salt reactors
incurred_insecurity:
This use case deploys an ML classifier as the primary safeguards barrier for detecting plutonium diversion from molten salt reactors—a fuel cycle that lacks discrete-item accountancy and permits continuous, incremental material removal. The system incurs severe insecurity from both adversarial manipulation and implicit fragility: an adversary (state-level or insider) can poison the training data or supply chain to systematically mask diversion signatures, and the model itself rests on simulation-based training that has never seen real operational MSR fuel-salt or genuine diversion events, creating an out-of-distribution gap the adversary can exploit by crafting diversion pathways absent from the training set. Implicit drift in fuel composition, fission-product behavior, and sampling artifacts further erodes detection reliability, while operator over-reliance on an opaque classifier may suppress scrutiny of raw measurements, compounding both adversarial opportunity and the consequences of missed alarms.

Training-Data Poisoning and Supply-Chain Compromise
An adversary—whether a host-state actor seeking to conceal diversion or an insider with pipeline access—can poison the training dataset by labeling simulated diversion signatures as normal operation, causing the deployed classifier to miss real plutonium removal. This is an adversarial attack (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000) that corrupts the model artifact itself, and because the classifier serves as a de facto single-point-of-compromise for MSR safeguards (no discrete-item cross-check exists), successful poisoning systematically defeats the verification layer. Supply-chain compromise during model development (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.002) allows an external adversary to embed backdoors that activate under specific isotopic or spectral conditions, hiding diversion events while appearing to function normally on benign samples. The safeguards consequence is undetected material diversion; the security consequence is that the adversary's operational security burden is minimized—they need only ensure diverted fuel-salt signatures fall within the poisoned model's learned 'normal' region.

Reconnaissance and Adversarial Evasion via Model Probing
Published safeguards research on MSR simulation and ML methodologies (AML.T0000, AML.T0001) enables an adversary to understand the model's training assumptions—burnup correlations, fission-product ratios, detector response functions—and design diversion strategies (incremental plutonium extraction, isotopic blending) that exploit gaps in the simulated training data. If the adversary gains inference API access during commissioning or operation (AML.T0040), they can perform black-box optimization (AML.T0043.001) to reverse-engineer decision boundaries and craft fuel-salt compositions that evade detection (AML.T0015). The model's opacity (OP.C0401) means neither operator nor inspector can verify whether a benign classification reflects true normality or adversarial manipulation. This is an adversarial exploitation of an implicit weakness: the model was qualified on simulated data and cannot recognize real-world diversion modes absent from its training set. The adversary may also extract the model (AML.T0024.002) to reveal detection thresholds offline, further refining their evasion strategy. The result is that diversion proceeds undetected until material accountancy closure—which in a liquid-fuel system may be delayed by months or impossible to perform with the precision needed to confirm theft.

Simulation-Based Training and Safeguards Data Scarcity
The classifier is trained almost exclusively on reactor-physics simulations (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02) because operational MSR fuel-salt data and genuine diversion signatures do not exist—molten salt reactors are pre-commercial, and adversarial diversion scenarios cannot be collected for training (OP.C0701, OP.C0701.01, OP.C0203). This creates an extreme data-provenance risk: the model must generalize from idealized simulation to real fuel-salt measurements (gamma and neutron spectra from small samples) it has never encountered, yet the consequences of generalization failure are direct safeguards defeat. An adversary aware of this provenance gap can execute diversion pathways the simulation did not anticipate—timing, isotopic blending, or sampling artifacts—confident the classifier has no operational anchor. This is an implicit weakness that adversaries can exploit without attacking the AI system itself; they simply operate in the blind spots created by the training data's lack of fidelity to operational reality.

Operational Drift and Qualification Mismatch
MSR fuel salt is a dynamic, multi-isotope system whose composition evolves continuously with burnup, fission-product accumulation, and online reprocessing. The classifier, frozen at deployment, was trained on a static simulation that cannot capture the full variance of operational fuel-salt phenomenology—salt chemistry interactions, sampling-induced artifacts, detector calibration drift, or facility-specific neutron spectrum differences (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). As the reactor operates, the real measurement distribution drifts away from the training distribution, degrading classification accuracy. Static qualification against simulation (OP.C0303) provides no assurance that the model will perform correctly under these evolved conditions. If the model is applied across heterogeneous MSR designs (e.g., from a graphite-moderated thermal-spectrum MSR to a fast-spectrum variant, or from a land-based plant to a floating compact reactor as in Mishra et al.), it faces an out-of-distribution problem that manifests as missed diversion or false positives. This is an implicit failure mode, not an adversarial attack, but it creates windows of vulnerability an adversary can time their diversion attempts to exploit.

Automation Trust and Alarm Erosion
Inspectors and operators, lacking hands-on experience with MSR safeguards and confronted with an opaque ML classifier (OP.C0401, OP.C0504 regulatory readiness gap), may over-rely on the model's output without independent verification of raw spectral data or material-balance anomalies (OP.C0101.04 misuse). This is an implicit human-factors risk that adversaries can exploit: if the classifier signals 'no diversion,' scrutiny of contextual indicators drops, and the adversary's operational security is simplified. Conversely, as operational drift causes false positives to accumulate, operators may begin to distrust or ignore alarms (OP.C0101.05 disuse, OP.C0102 alarm complacency), creating a window in which real diversion events are dismissed. The model's non-determinism (OP.C0402.02, if ensemble or stochastic methods are used) further complicates alarm investigation: a result cannot be reliably reproduced, eroding confidence in the system's forensic value. The safeguards consequence is that the primary technical barrier to diversion becomes either a trusted false negative or a distrusted true positive—in either case, diversion proceeds.

Cross-Facility Model Propagation
If this classifier is deployed as part of a multi-site safeguards architecture or shared internationally (OP.C0602), a single poisoned model or flawed training pipeline propagates the vulnerability across an entire fleet of MSRs. An adversary who compromises the model during development creates a systemic blind spot: every facility using the corrupted artifact is vulnerable to the same evasion or masking strategy. This is both an adversarial supply-chain risk and an implicit governance failure, as there is no regulatory framework (OP.C0504) or software-engineering standard for qualifying ML-based safeguards tools trained on simulation and deployed into first-of-a-kind facilities. The proliferation consequence is that what appears to be a robust, AI-enabled verification capability is in fact a shared single point of failure across the global MSR fleet.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case applies ML to detect diversion in a fuel cycle with no discrete items and continuous on-line reprocessing—MSRs fundamentally break traditional material accountancy. The classifier acts as a de facto safeguards alarm on operational fuel-salt samples, meaning adversarial manipulation of training data, sample provenance, or the signature library could mask real diversion or trigger false positives that erode inspector confidence. From an operations lens, the system depends on scarce training data (limited operational MSR experience, few real diversion scenarios) and on stable isotopic/radiochemical signatures that may drift as fuel composition evolves or burnup proceeds—qualification against a static benchmark won't catch operational concept drift in a continuously evolving salt matrix.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL threats center on the safeguards consequence: an adversary (host state or insider) could poison the training dataset with signatures from diverted scenarios labeled as normal, causing the classifier to miss real diversion (AML.T0020 training-data poisoning, AML.T0031 model-integrity erosion). They could also manipulate fuel-salt sample provenance or introduce contaminants that mimic normal operation while diverting plutonium, exploiting the model's opacity and the lack of discrete-item cross-checks. Because MSRs enable continuous diversion in small increments, the adversary's strategy is to stay under the classifier's detection threshold or to degrade its sensitivity over time—model extraction or inversion (AML.T0024.002) could reveal that threshold. IMPLICIT (non-adversarial) threats arise from the fuel cycle's novelty and the scarcity of diversion-scenario training data (OP.C0701 safeguards data scarcity, OP.C0203 new-build scarcity). The classifier must generalize from simulated or surrogate diversion signatures (OP.C0201.01/.02) to real operational fuel salt, which may drift isotopically as burnup and fission-product inventory change (OP.C0302.01 operational drift). If the model was trained on one MSR design or fuel cycle and is applied to a floating or modular variant with different neutron spectrum or salt chemistry (Mishra et al.), it faces an out-of-distribution problem (OP.C0302 generalization failure, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity). Inspectors may over-rely on the classifier's output (OP.C0101.04 automation misuse) without independent verification, especially if the model's decision boundary is opaque (OP.C0401 explainability limit) and if there is no regulatory precedent for ML-based safeguards conclusions (OP.C0504 regulatory readiness gap). A false negative (missed diversion) directly undermines nonproliferation; repeated false positives erode trust and could lead inspectors to ignore real alarms (OP.C0102 alarm complacency). Because MSR fuel salt is a dynamic, multi-isotope system, the model's static training set may not capture the full range of normal operational variance or adversarial strategies—any adversary who understands the model's training provenance (OP.C0201 data provenance transparency) can craft a diversion pathway the model has never seen.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case trains classifiers on simulated MSR operation/diversion signatures because operational MSR fuel-salt data essentially does not exist—molten salt reactors are pre-commercial, and genuine diversion signatures are by definition unavailable for training. The ML system must generalize from physics simulations to real fuel-salt measurements (gamma, neutron spectra from small samples) it has never seen, yet the consequences of missed diversion are severe. The model is frozen at deployment into a first-of-a-kind facility whose operational regime (burnup history, fission-product behavior in molten fluoride, sampling artifacts) will differ from the simulation assumptions, and there is no 'ground truth' diversion corpus to validate against in the field. An adversary aware of the model's simulation provenance can craft diversion strategies (isotopic pathways, timing, blending) that exploit gaps between simulated and real fuel-salt phenomenology, confident the classifier has no operational anchor.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
The core ML fragility is extreme data-provenance risk (OP.C0201.01 simulated data, OP.C0203 new-build scarcity, OP.C0701 safeguards training-data scarcity) compounded by inevitable operational drift (OP.C0302.01/03): the model trains on idealized reactor-physics output but deploys into a facility where salt chemistry, sampling procedures, detector calibration and fission-product transport differ in ways the simulation did not—and cannot—capture until the reactor runs. Because MSRs are first-generation, there is no 'fleet learning' or operational validation set; qualification is static (OP.C0303) against a simulation that itself lacks empirical anchors for diversion signatures. An adversary can perform reconnaissance (AML.T0000, especially T0001 if safeguards ML research is published) to understand the simulation's assumptions—burnup models, isotopic correlations, detector response functions—and design a diversion path (incremental plutonium removal timed to minimize spectral anomaly, or blending to mask key ratios) that the classifier, trained on discrete diversion 'events' in simulation, will not recognize as anomalous in the continuous, noisy operational data stream. The system is also vulnerable to adversarial data crafting at inference (AML.T0043.001 black-box optimization if the adversary can probe the classifier with synthetic spectra during commissioning, AML.T0015 evasion) because the decision boundary was learned from a feature space that does not faithfully represent the facility's actual measurement distribution. 

Implicit risks exacerbate this: operators, lacking experience with MSR safeguards and reliant on an opaque classifier (OP.C0401), may overtrust alarms during commissioning (OP.C0101.04 misuse) or, once false positives accumulate due to drift, begin ignoring them (OP.C0101.05 disuse, OP.C0102 complacency). The model's non-determinism (OP.C0402.02 if ensemble methods or stochastic inference are used) makes it difficult to reproduce an alarm for investigation, and there is no regulatory precedent (OP.C0504) for how to qualify a diversion-detection classifier trained entirely on simulation. If the model is part of a multi-site safeguards architecture, a flawed model or adversarially shaped training set (AML.T0020 poisoning if the simulation code or training pipeline is compromised, AML.T0010.002 data supply chain) could propagate across facilities (OP.C0602), creating a systemic blind spot. The safeguards consequence is that plutonium diversion may go undetected until accountancy closure (months later, if at all in a liquid-fuel system), and the security consequence is that the adversary's operational security is greatly simplified—they need only shape their diversion to remain within the classifier's 'normal' region, informed by the public simulation literature the model depends on.

security_specialist.argument: From a security lens, this use case creates a high-value, single-point-of-compromise target for an adversary seeking to conceal plutonium diversion from a molten salt reactor—a reactor type that already lacks discrete-item accountancy and therefore depends heavily on measurement-based verification. An attacker (insider or external via supply chain) who corrupts the ML model or its training pipeline can systematically mask diversion signatures without triggering alarms, effectively defeating the safeguards layer this system is meant to provide. The ML model becomes a choke-point: if I'm a state-level adversary trying to divert plutonium from an MSR, I don't need to defeat every safeguards measure—I only need to compromise this classifier so it misidentifies diverted-fuel signatures as normal operation. The threat is compounded by the system's reliance on simulated or lab-scale training data (real diversion signatures are inherently scarce), meaning an adversary can exploit the model's unfamiliarity with real-world diversion modes that were never in the training set, and insiders with access to the model or data pipeline have both motive (facilitating diversion) and opportunity (direct access to the artifact that would detect them).
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) An insider with access to the ML training pipeline or model artifact poisons the model to systematically misclassify diversion signatures as benign, enabling undetected plutonium removal (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000). Because MSRs lack discrete-item accounting, this classifier is the primary technical barrier to diversion—corrupting it is a single point of defeat. (2) Supply-chain compromise of the model or training data (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003) during development or deployment allows an external adversary to embed a backdoor that activates under specific conditions (e.g., certain isotopic ratios) to hide diversion events. (3) An adversary with inference API access uses black-box querying (AML.T0043.001) to reverse-engineer decision boundaries and craft fuel-salt compositions or sampling strategies that evade detection—effectively learning how to divert without triggering the alarm. (4) The model's role as a persistent verification tool means any corruption has long-duration impact: once deployed across a fleet or shared internationally (OP.C0602), a single poisoned model propagates the vulnerability across multiple facilities. IMPLICIT/EXPLOITABLE WEAKNESSES: (5) Training on simulated or lab-scale data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0701.01) creates an out-of-distribution gap that an adversary can exploit by executing diversion scenarios the model never learned to recognize—this isn't an attack on the AI, it's an attack timed to the AI's blindness. (6) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04): operators and inspectors may over-rely on the ML classifier's 'no diversion' output, reducing their scrutiny of raw measurement data or contextual anomalies—an adversary can time diversion attempts to periods of high operational trust in the system. (7) Non-determinism and lack of explainability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02) mean that when the model does produce an ambiguous or borderline result, neither the operator nor the inspector can confidently verify whether it reflects a real diversion attempt or a benign measurement artifact—this uncertainty is itself a strategic advantage to an adversary testing detection thresholds. (8) If the model is updated or retrained (OP.C0303), there is a qualification gap: new versions may behave differently on edge cases, and an adversary aware of the update cycle can time diversion to coincide with retraining windows when the model's behavior is least stable or least scrutinized.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on training-data poisoning, supply-chain compromise, simulation-data provenance risk, operational drift, and automation over-reliance as the dominant threats; the security specialist's framing of the model as a single-point-of-compromise choke-point unified the adversarial narrative, while the AI engineer's emphasis on static qualification against simulated data anchored the implicit-fragility synthesis.

reproducibility.why: Training-data poisoning and simulation-based gaps are reliably exploitable once an adversary understands the model's training assumptions or gains pipeline access, though real-world MSR operational conditions add some variability to exploitation success.

use_case: Neural-network inference of initial enrichment, burnup and cooling time of spent fuel assemblies to verify operator declarations during safeguards inspections
incurred_insecurity:
This use case deploys neural networks trained on simulated non-destructive assay (NDA) signatures to infer spent-fuel parameters that inspectors use to verify operator declarations during safeguards inspections, creating a critical verification chokepoint where AI-driven inference replaces direct measurement of ground truth. The system incurs three interrelated classes of insecurity: adversarial exploitation of the simulation-reality gap and model opacity to induce false verification of diverted material; implicit failure modes arising from out-of-distribution generalization when the model encounters fuel assemblies with irradiation histories or measurement conditions absent from its simulated training corpus; and systemic erosion of the safeguards regime through automation bias, lack of auditability, and propagation of a single compromised or drifted model across multiple inspections.

Adversarial Evasion and Supply-Chain Compromise

An adversary seeking to conceal material diversion can exploit the fact that the neural network was trained exclusively on simulated Forkball detector responses and has never encountered signatures of actual covert scenarios such as partial assembly replacement, material substitution, or undeclared irradiation profiles. By manipulating fuel-handling conditions, measurement geometry, or declared cooling time within plausible bounds, an operator-insider can craft NDA input signatures that induce the model to infer enrichment, burnup, or cooling-time values consistent with a false declaration, effectively teaching the AI to verify a lie. If the adversary gains prior knowledge of the model through supply-chain access to the trained artifact, reconnaissance of open ML repositories used by safeguards laboratories, or insider access to training data, they can train a proxy model offline to optimize evasion strategies before deployment during an actual inspection. Because the model offers no mechanism to flag inputs outside its training envelope, the inspector receives a confident-looking inference with no indication that the underlying assembly signature is anomalous, and the falsified declaration passes undetected. At a systemic level, if the model is distributed across multiple inspection sites or updated centrally, poisoning the training data during a single update cycle or embedding a backdoor in the shared model propagates the vulnerability fleet-wide, undermining verification across every inspection that relies on it. These are adversarial threats: the attacker actively subverts the AI system to evade safeguards detection.

Simulation-Reality Mismatch and Out-of-Distribution Generalization Failure

The model's reliance on simulated training data creates an implicit but severe weakness that adversaries can exploit. Real spent-fuel assemblies exhibit detector noise, gain drift, electronic interference, geometric edge effects, and irradiation-history variability that simulation tools like Forkball do not fully capture, meaning the network will encounter systematic distribution shift when deployed in the field. Fuel from new reactor types, non-standard operating cycles, or assemblies with cladding defects will produce NDA signatures the model has never seen, yet the black-box architecture will still produce a point estimate with no uncertainty flag or out-of-distribution alert. Random-forest work explicitly documents sensitivity to irradiation history not captured in training, so an adversary aware of this can engineer a diversion scenario in the model's blind spot—for example, atypical fuel shuffling or partial burnup cycles—and the model will confidently mis-infer parameters in favor of the false declaration. This is an implicit AI system failure, but one that a sophisticated adversary (including a host state) can study and time their evasion attempt around. The safeguards context exacerbates the problem because ground truth for any given assembly is almost never available: destructive assay is politically and economically prohibitive, real spent fuel with verified parameters is scarce, and there is no operational feedback loop to detect when the model drifts over time as fuel designs, reactor operations, or NDA instrument characteristics evolve.

Automation Bias, Opacity, and Qualification Gaps

Inspectors operate under time pressure and often lack the expertise to independently verify enrichment or burnup from raw NDA spectra, creating strong incentive to trust the AI's authoritative-seeming output even when it is wrong. This automation bias is an implicit human-AI interaction failure, but it is precisely the operational condition an adversary waits for: the model produces a plausible but incorrect inference, the inspector accepts it without cross-checking traditional methods, and continuity of knowledge is lost. The neural network's opacity means the inspector cannot explain to a third party why the output should be trusted, eroding the auditability that safeguards verification traditionally depends on and enabling an adversary to dispute results post hoc or sow doubt in the regime's legitimacy. Non-determinism in inference, if present, further undermines repeatability and allows an adversary to exploit periods of high model uncertainty. At the regulatory level, there is no established framework for qualifying a black-box neural network trained on simulated data for use in verification, so the system operates in a gap between traditional software QA and AI-specific lifecycle management. If junior inspectors rely on the AI without understanding its limitations, skill fade sets in and the human ability to perform traditional verification atrophies, leaving the safeguards system entirely dependent on an artifact whose failure modes are neither well-understood nor operationally testable.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a nuclear operations and safeguards perspective, this use case sits at a critical verification junction where an inspector must trust AI inference to validate operator declarations about spent fuel history—parameters that directly affect material accountancy, criticality safety in storage/transport, and safeguards conclusions. If the neural network produces a plausible but wrong inference (due to training on simulated-only data, inability to generalize to unexpected irradiation histories, or adversarial manipulation of input NDA signals), and the inspector lacks independent means or expertise to detect the error, a falsified declaration could pass undetected or a legitimate one be wrongly flagged. The consequence is not immediate physical harm but erosion of the verification regime itself: incorrect material accountancy, loss of continuity of knowledge, potential diversion masked by AI endorsement, or diplomatic/political fallout from wrongful accusations based on opaque model output.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial threats:** An adversary (host state or facility operator) could manipulate input to the AI by subtly altering NDA instrument signals (gamma/neutron spectra) to induce the network to infer declared parameters consistent with a false narrative, effectively 'teaching' the AI to verify a lie—this becomes an AI-mediated falsification of safeguards data (AML.T0015 Evade AI Model via crafted inputs, AML.T0043 Craft Adversarial Data). If the attacker has prior knowledge of the model (from supply-chain access, AML.T0010.003 Model compromise, or reconnaissance on open ML repositories used by safeguards labs, AML.T0000/AML.T0004), they can optimize their declaration and corresponding fake NDA signature in tandem. The AI system itself may be poisoned during training if an insider or supply-chain adversary injects biased simulated data that systematically under-predicts burnup for certain enrichment ranges (AML.T0020 Poison Training Data, AML.T0019 Publish Poisoned Datasets), enabling future diversion to go unnoticed. Because inspectors operate under time pressure and the model offers an authoritative-seeming number, there is heightened risk of automation bias (the inspector accepts the output without sufficient scrutiny), and an adversary can time their diversion to periods when they know the model's uncertainty is high but not flagged to the user.

**Implicit (non-adversarial) but exploitable weaknesses:** The model is trained entirely on simulated Forkball responses (OP.C0201.01 Simulated data, OP.C0203 New-build data scarcity for novel fuel types), meaning it has never seen real measurement noise, detector drift, or the variability of actual spent-fuel pools; when deployed in the field, it will encounter out-of-distribution signatures from fuels with unusual irradiation histories, partial defects, or environmental interference, leading to silent inference failures (OP.C0302 Drift/Out-of-distribution, OP.C0302.03 Operational heterogeneity). The random-forest work explicitly shows sensitivity to irradiation history not captured in training, so an adversary aware of this can choose a diversion scenario (e.g., atypical reactor operation, fuel shuffling) that falls in the model's blind spot. The inspector has no ground truth for a given assembly and limited ability to explain why the AI produced its answer (OP.C0401 Explainability/opacity), so incorrect inferences may be trusted until a pattern of inconsistency emerges—by which time continuity of knowledge is lost (OP.C0701 Safeguards training-data scarcity, OP.C0701.01 NDA signature scarcity compounded by the fact that destructive assay to verify the AI is impractical at scale). If the model is shared across multiple inspection sites or updated centrally (OP.C0602 Cross-site model propagation), a single poisoned or drifted version propagates the vulnerability fleet-wide, and there is currently no regulatory framework for qualifying AI in this verification role (OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap, OP.C0504 Regulatory readiness gap). Skill fade among inspectors (OP.C0101.06) and mode confusion (OP.C0101.03) are inevitable: junior inspectors may not know how to cross-check the AI with traditional methods, and if the AI fails silently, the entire verification chain is compromised without triggering alarms.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case deploys neural networks trained almost entirely on simulated NDA signatures (Forkball detector responses) to infer fuel parameters that underpin safeguards verification—a mission-critical function where ground truth is scarce by design and adversarial incentives are high. The model lives at the intersection of two data-provenance nightmares: simulated training data that may not capture real detector noise, geometry variations, or undeclared material configurations, and operational deployment against assemblies whose actual irradiation histories (the feature space) may differ systematically from the training corpus. Because the system's output directly feeds inspectors' accept/reject decisions on operator declarations, any model weakness—drift when encountering fuel from a new reactor type, sensitivity to irradiation-history variations the training set never saw, or adversarial exploitation of the simulation-reality gap—translates immediately into a safeguards failure with no human cross-check of the raw signature. The architecture itself (a black-box neural network producing point estimates of enrichment/burnup/cooling-time) offers no mechanism to flag when an input assembly falls outside the training envelope, making silent failure the default mode.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core threat is **simulation-reality mismatch enabling undetected declaration falsification** (OP.C0201.01 simulated data, OP.C0302 drift, AML.T0043 adversarial-data crafting if an adversary learns the training distribution). An inspector uses the network's inference to verify an operator's declared initial enrichment or burnup; if the model was trained on simulated Forkball responses that don't capture real detector systematics (gain drift, electronic noise, geometric edge effects at assembly boundaries), it will systematically mis-infer parameters for real assemblies, and an adversary who knows this can declare values the model will accept even when they're wrong. The second major exposure is **irradiation-history sensitivity and out-of-distribution generalization failure** (OP.C0302.01 data drift, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity): the random-forest work explicitly flags sensitivity to irradiation history, meaning fuel from a reactor type or operating regime not well-represented in training (new-build reactors, non-standard cycles, OP.C0203) will produce signatures the model has never seen, yet the model will still produce a confident-looking answer with no uncertainty flag—inspectors trust it (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust), the real parameter is outside the prediction, and a diversion goes unnoticed. Third, **adversarial exploitation of the inference boundary** (AML.T0005 proxy-model training, AML.T0043.001 black-box optimization, AML.T0015 evasion): if an adversary can query the model or train a proxy on the same simulation tools, they can craft a real-fuel configuration (or manipulate declared cooling time within measurement uncertainty) that forces the network into a region of parameter space where it confidently predicts something close to a false declaration, because the loss surface in that region was never adequately explored during training on simulation. Finally, **model lifecycle and qualification gaps** (OP.C0303 static/dynamic qualification mismatch, OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap, OP.C0701.01 NDA-signature scarcity): there is no operational feedback loop—once deployed, the model never sees ground-truth fuel parameters for the assemblies it evaluates (destructive assay is prohibitively expensive and politically fraught), so drift accumulates undetected, and the regulatory framework has no precedent for qualifying a black-box neural network whose training data is simulated and whose test data (real spent fuel with verified parameters) effectively doesn't exist.

security_specialist.argument: From a security lens, this use case is dangerous because it moves a critical trust boundary—verifying operator declarations—into an AI-driven artifact that an adversary (including a state with reason to hide material diversion) can systematically exploit or discredit. The networks are trained on simulated NDA responses, not on actual covert-diversion scenarios an adversary would engineer; an insider with knowledge of the model could craft fuel-handling or measurement scenarios that yield plausible-looking but false parameter estimates, and the inspector may never know the ground truth was different. More broadly, deploying this in a safeguards context creates a single high-value target: compromise the model (via supply chain, data poisoning during an update cycle, or insider modification) and you undermine verification across every inspection that relies on it, potentially across multiple facilities if the model propagates. Even absent adversarial action, non-determinism and opacity in the inference process erode the auditability that safeguards verification traditionally depends on—an inspector cannot show a skeptical party why the AI's output should be trusted, and an adversary can time a diversion attempt to periods when the model's uncertainty is high or when inspectors are most likely to accept the AI's word without additional cross-checks.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An adversary seeking to hide undeclared material diversion has strong incentive to target this system. If the model is trained on simulated (OP.C0201.01) or surrogate (OP.C0201.02) NDA data and never sees signatures of actual covert scenarios (material substitution, partial assembly replacement, etc.), an operator-insider can manipulate fuel or measurement conditions in ways the model was never trained to flag (AML.T0015 Evade AI Model). The model may confidently infer plausible but false enrichment/burnup/cooling-time values, and the inspector—relying on the AI's output—accepts the declaration without realizing diversion occurred. Because the model is a shared artifact (likely deployed across inspections or sites, OP.C0602), an adversary who compromises it once (AML.T0010.003 supply-chain compromise of the trained model, or AML.T0020 poisoning the training data during a model update) can undermine verification system-wide. An insider with access to the model's architecture or training data (AML.T0012 Valid Accounts, AML.T0007 Discover AI Artifacts) can craft a proxy model (AML.T0005) offline, test evasion strategies, and execute them during an inspection when the real model is in use. The opacity of neural-network inference (OP.C0401) means an inspector cannot easily explain to a third party why the AI's conclusion is trustworthy, so an adversary can also sow doubt or dispute the results after the fact (AML.T0048.001 Reputational Harm to the safeguards regime). If the model's inference is non-deterministic (OP.C0402.02), an adversary can time a diversion attempt to periods of high model uncertainty or exploit the lack of repeatability to claim the inspection was flawed.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) THREATS THAT ADVERSARIES EXPLOIT: The model is trained on simulated data (OP.C0201.01) from tools like Forkball, not on real spent-fuel assemblies with the full variability of operational history, cladding conditions, measurement noise, and—crucially—never on assemblies from which material was covertly removed. This creates a dangerous out-of-distribution risk (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03): when the model encounters a real assembly whose irradiation history or NDA signature differs from the training set (due to operational heterogeneity across reactors, or because an adversary introduced an anomaly the simulator never modeled), it may confidently produce a wrong answer, and the inspector won't know. Small-data/low-base-rate problem (OP.C0202) is acute here: diversion events are rare by design, so the model has no examples of what a diverted assembly's signature looks like, and inspectors have no operational track record to know when the AI is wrong. Automation bias (OP.C0101.04 Misuse/over-trust) is the operational threat: an inspector, under time pressure and lacking the expertise to independently verify enrichment/burnup from raw NDA data, will trust the AI's output even when it's wrong—exactly the scenario an adversary waits for. If the model drifts over time (OP.C0302.02 Concept Drift, as fuel designs, reactor operations, or NDA instrument calibration change) but is not re-qualified against new ground truth, an adversary can exploit the growing gap between the model's assumptions and reality. Finally, the use of this system in a regulatory/safeguards context creates a qualification gap (OP.C0401, OP.C0501): there is no established framework for qualifying a neural network for verification use, so an adversary can argue post-hoc that the inspection was invalid, or a regulator may not know how to respond when the model's output conflicts with other evidence. All of these implicit weaknesses—data scarcity, drift, opacity, automation bias—are precisely what a sophisticated adversary (including a state actor) would study and time an evasion attempt around.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on adversarial evasion via simulation-reality gap exploitation, out-of-distribution failure from unseen irradiation histories, automation bias in inspectors, and model opacity undermining auditability. The security specialist's framing of implicit weaknesses as adversary-exploitable conditions was integrated throughout; the AI engineer's lifecycle and data-provenance arguments anchored the implicit-threat paragraphs; regulatory/qualification gaps raised by all three were consolidated into the final section.
