damage.why: Falsified verification of diverted nuclear material during safeguards inspections directly constitutes loss of material control and safeguards falsification, enabling diversion for weapons use.

reproducibility.why: Adversarial evasion via measurement-condition manipulation or simulation-reality mismatch exploitation is highly reproducible once the attacker identifies the model's blind spots, though some trial may be needed to optimize evasion inputs.

exploitability.why: Requires operator-insider position to manipulate fuel-handling or measurement conditions, plus moderate ML expertise to train proxy models or identify out-of-distribution gaps, but does not require nation-state tooling if model architecture is known.

affected_users.why: A compromised or poisoned model distributed fleet-wide across inspection sites propagates the vulnerability to every safeguards inspection relying on it, affecting verification regime-wide.

discoverability.why: The reliance on simulated training data and sensitivity to irradiation history are explicitly documented in open ESARDA literature, allowing capable adversaries to infer exploitable gaps without insider access to the specific deployed model.

use_case: Neural-network detection of diverted fuel pins in spent fuel assemblies from in-assembly neutron flux gradient measurements
incurred_insecurity: This use case introduces a critical safeguards vulnerability by deploying an artificial neural network trained exclusively on simulated neutron flux gradients to detect fuel-pin diversion from spent-fuel assemblies, with no validation against genuine diversion signatures. The model's reliance on synthetic training data creates a simulation-to-reality gap that degrades detection reliability in unpredictable ways when confronted with real assembly heterogeneity, while simultaneously providing a sophisticated adversary with a well-defined attack surface: knowledge of the training parameter space enables evasion through crafted diversion geometries, and the opacity of the neural network masks both implicit failures and adversarial manipulation. Three main threats emerge: the model's inherent inability to generalize beyond its simulated training set (an implicit failure mode), an adversary's ability to reverse-engineer detection blind spots and execute evasive diversions, and the erosion of defense-in-depth as inspectors over-rely on an AI verdict that has never been tested against real material accountancy threats.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Train Proxy via Gathered AI Artifacts

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a nuclear operations lens, this use case sits in the safeguards domain at a spent fuel storage or transport verification point—an inspector or facility operator uses an ANN trained on simulated flux-gradient measurements to flag possible pin diversion from an assembly. My concern is the consequence if the model fails to detect a real diversion (false negative) or falsely flags an intact assembly (false positive): a missed diversion undermines material accountancy and nonproliferation, while a false alarm triggers costly re-verification, erodes inspector confidence in the tool, and may delay cask loading or transport schedules. Existing practice relies on human-verified item counting and radiation profiling; if staff begin to trust the ANN's 'no diversion' verdict without cross-check, automation bias (OP.C0101.04) becomes the path by which a model trained only on simulated data (OP.C0201.01) and never validated against real partial-defect signatures (OP.C0701.01) lets an actual diversion slip through.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary implicit threat is the training-data gap: the ANN was developed on simulated neutron flux gradients with no access to real partial-defect or diversion scenarios (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0701.01), so it has never seen the measurement noise, assembly-geometry variation, or fuel-history heterogeneity that mark an actual spent-fuel pool. If deployed, the model will encounter out-of-distribution assemblies—different burnup profiles, mixed oxide fuel, or assemblies with legitimate manufacturing defects—risking both false positives (OP.C0302.01 operational drift) and false negatives when a real diversion signature doesn't match the training set. Because the base rate of actual diversions is near-zero (OP.C0202), any decent-looking validation metric from simulation may not translate to reliable field performance, and inspectors who come to rely on the tool (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust) may stop performing manual flux-mapping cross-checks, letting a sophisticated diversion—one that carefully balances flux to mimic an intact assembly—go undetected. The adversarial surface is narrower but real: an adversary aware of the ANN's training basis (AML.T0000 open technical literature, AML.T0013 discover model ontology via published hyperparameters) could simulate the model's decision boundary and craft a diversion pattern—removing certain pins, repositioning others, or inserting dummy rods—that stays below the detection threshold (AML.T0015 evade AI model). If the model's flux-threshold or gradient-pattern logic becomes known (OP.C0401 explainability limit means reverse-engineering may be easier than for a black-box oracle), an insider with assembly-loading access could test diversion configurations offline before executing. Even without adversarial intent, the cascade risk is significant: if this ANN result feeds into an automated cask-approval workflow and no human re-verifies a 'pass' verdict (OP.C0301.01 cascading fault), a single model error propagates into the broader material control system, and the facility loses a critical detection layer. Existing practice—manual gamma/neutron scanning, item counting, and inspector judgment—would need to remain in the loop as a defense-in-depth check, but deployment pressure or resource constraints (OP.C0501 AI-specific qualification gap, OP.C0504 regulatory readiness gap if the regulator has no validation protocol for ANN-based safeguards tools) may erode that discipline, especially if early field trials show 'good' performance on compliant assemblies and the near-zero true-positive rate never surfaces until it's too late.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case depends entirely on simulated neutron flux gradient data for training, because real diversion signatures (partial pin removal from intact assemblies) do not exist in sufficient quantity or variety for supervised learning. The ANN learns a mapping from gradient features to diversion/no-diversion that is never validated against genuine diverted fuel, only against held-out simulations from the same Monte Carlo transport code and material库 assumptions used in training. At inference time in a waste facility, any systematic difference between the real assembly's neutron field (geometry tolerances, burnup heterogeneity, measurement instrument response, background) and the training simulations will degrade detection reliability in ways the model cannot signal. An adversary aware of the training scenario set can craft a diversion geometry (number, spacing, isotopic substitution of pins) that the simulator did not span, evading detection; alternatively, the adversary times the diversion to occur during a qualification or maintenance window when the detection system is offline or its alerts are suppressed.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: PRIMARY IMPLICIT THREAT (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0701.01): The model is trained exclusively on simulated neutron flux gradients, with no field-measured diversion signatures available for validation (safeguards data scarcity). When deployed at a real spent-fuel facility, operational drift—differences in assembly geometry, burnup history, detector positioning, and background neutron flux—will produce input distributions the ANN has never seen. This out-of-distribution condition degrades detection reliability silently; the network may confidently classify a diverted assembly as intact, or flag intact assemblies (false positives), with no intrinsic mechanism to alert the operator that the input is anomalous relative to training. ADVERSARIAL EXPLOITATION (AML.T0013, AML.T0043.002, AML.T0015): An adversary with knowledge of the training dataset's parameter space (accessible via open technical databases or replication from public literature) can discover the model's decision boundaries and craft a diversion scenario—specific pin locations, partial removal patterns, or isotopic substitution—that falls in a region the simulator did not adequately sample, evading detection. The adversary may also time the diversion to coincide with known gaps in model qualification or detector maintenance (OP.C0303, OP.C0503), when the system is offline or alerts are suppressed. SECONDARY IMPLICIT (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02): ANNs are opaque; inspectors cannot trace why a particular assembly was flagged or cleared, complicating forensic reconstruction if a diversion is later discovered by another method. Non-determinism in inference (if dropout or stochastic sampling is used) means repeated scans of the same assembly may yield inconsistent verdicts, eroding inspector confidence (OP.C0101.05 disuse). GOVERNANCE/QUALIFICATION (OP.C0501, OP.C0504): No regulatory precedent exists for qualifying a safeguards anomaly-detection system trained purely on synthetic data and never exercised against genuine diversion signatures, leaving the facility and regulator without a defensible acceptance criterion.

security_specialist.argument: This use case presents a classic dual-edged security problem: it creates an AI-based safeguards verification layer that, if compromised or systematically degraded, becomes a single point of failure an adversary can exploit to mask fuel diversion. A sophisticated adversary (especially a state-level insider threat or supply-chain actor) would not attack the AI directly in isolation—they would coordinate: time a diversion event during known model drift periods, subtly poison the training data (all simulated neutron flux) to create blind spots around specific diversion signatures, or exploit the model's opacity to understand exactly which partial-defect configurations fall below detection threshold. The security risk is compounded because this is a boundary/verification function—if the AI fails to flag a diversion, there may be no downstream human double-check, and the adversary gains a permissive window. From my lens, the question is not whether the AI works on average, but whether its existence and known failure modes give an adversary a roadmap and a timing advantage they didn't have with purely human-driven verification.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An adversary with supply-chain access could poison the simulated training data (OP.C0201.01, AML.T0020) to create blind spots around specific diversion signatures—e.g., ensure the model fails to detect gradient anomalies for a particular number/configuration of missing pins. Because all training data is simulated (no real diversion events to learn from), the adversary has a clear target: manipulate the simulation parameters or flux-gradient labels so the model generalizes poorly to the real diversion scenario they plan. Once deployed, an insider with knowledge of the model's architecture or decision boundary (AML.T0013, AML.T0014) could reverse-engineer which partial-defect configurations fall below the detection threshold, then execute a diversion that stays within that blind spot—this is AML.T0015 (Evade AI Model) in a safeguards context. If the model is shared across multiple facilities (OP.C0602), a single compromise propagates fleet-wide, giving the adversary a systemic advantage. The AI also creates a new credential/access target: an adversary who gains access to model parameters or training pipeline (AML.T0012, AML.T0044) can test diversion scenarios offline in a proxy model (AML.T0005) to optimize evasion, then execute with high confidence the real system won't flag them.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) WEAKNESSES AN ADVERSARY WOULD EXPLOIT: The model is trained entirely on simulated neutron flux data (OP.C0201.01), which introduces a simulation-to-reality gap—real spent fuel assemblies have material heterogeneities, geometry tolerances, and measurement noise the simulation may not capture, leading to concept drift (OP.C0302.02) or generalization failure (OP.C0302) when deployed. An adversary aware of this gap could exploit it: they know the model has never seen a real diversion signature, so they tailor their diversion to exploit known simulation oversimplifications (e.g., if the simulation assumes uniform pin spacing, divert pins in a non-uniform pattern). The use case also suffers from extreme data scarcity for the positive class—real diversion events are vanishingly rare (OP.C0202, OP.C0701), so the model's false-negative rate on novel diversion modes is unknown and likely high; an adversary exploits this by executing a diversion mode the simulation didn't anticipate. There is also automation bias risk (OP.C0101.04): if inspectors over-rely on the AI's negative findings (no diversion detected), they reduce the rigor of manual cross-checks, and an adversary times their diversion to coincide with this relaxed vigilance. Finally, the model's non-determinism (OP.C0402) and opacity (OP.C0401) mean an adversary can probe it (if they have inference access, AML.T0040) to map its decision boundary without triggering alarms, then stay just below the detection threshold. In summary, the AI does not robustly close a security gap—it creates a new, concentrated attack surface (the model and its training data) and a false sense of verification assurance that a sophisticated adversary can exploit both technically (evasion, poisoning) and operationally (timing attacks around drift/bias, reduced human vigilance).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulation-to-reality gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0701.01) and adversarial evasion via training-set knowledge (AML.T0013, AML.T0015) as the core threats; the security specialist's distinction between direct adversarial techniques and adversarial exploitation of implicit weaknesses (automation bias OP.C0101.04, drift OP.C0302, timing around OP.C0303/OP.C0503) helped structure the synthesis into separate threat paragraphs while avoiding redundancy.

evidence.citation: al-Dbissi, M., Pazsit, I., Rossa, R., Borella, A. & Vinai, P. (2024), "On the use of neutron flux gradient with ANNs for the detection of diverted spent nuclear fuel," Annals of Nuclear Energy 204, 110536
evidence.note: SCK CEN/Chalmers work on partial-defect detection in spent fuel using ANNs trained on simulated neutron flux gradients.

damage.why: Successful evasion of safeguards detection enables undetected diversion of special nuclear material, directly undermining material control and accountability—a Category 5 consequence in this domain.

reproducibility.why: Once an adversary identifies the simulation parameter space and detection blind spots through the model's training distribution, crafting evasive diversion geometries becomes reliably executable, though real-world assembly variability introduces some uncertainty.

exploitability.why: Exploitation requires moderate insider knowledge of the inspection system's AI model characteristics and access to spent fuel handling operations, plus capability to craft specific diversion geometries—not trivial but within reach of a determined state-level adversary with facility access.

affected_users.why: Compromise affects the entire safeguards verification chain for spent fuel assemblies at a facility and potentially propagates across multiple sites if the model is deployed fleet-wide, though impact remains within the waste storage/transport domain.

discoverability.why: The reliance on purely simulated training data and the general neural-network approach are documented in open literature (cited source), making the vulnerability class—simulation-to-reality gap and adversarial evasion potential—readily inferable by capable adversaries familiar with AI safeguards applications.

use_case: Kernel-regression reconstruction of faulty or abnormal coolant sensor signals to their expected normal values
incurred_insecurity:
This use case replaces faulty or abnormal coolant sensor readings with kernel-regression reconstructions of what those signals 'should' read under normal conditions, based on learned correlations in historical data. The principal insecurity is that the system converts a detectable sensor failure into an undetectable fictitious signal: when the AI confidently reconstructs an abnormal state as normal—whether due to training-data poisoning, operational drift beyond the model's experience, or adversarial manipulation of input sensors—operators lose both the failed sensor and any indication that the plant state has deviated from safe bounds. This creates parallel threat pathways: an adversary can exploit the reconstruction to mask physical sabotage or cyberattack signatures, while non-adversarial failure modes (training-data scarcity for rare transients, model drift as the plant ages, opacity that prevents operators from distinguishing valid reconstruction from dangerous extrapolation) will independently produce the same outcome of presenting a plausible but incorrect picture of plant conditions to safety systems and human decision-makers.

Training-Data Manipulation and Supply-Chain Risk
An adversary with access to the historical sensor corpus—whether through insider access, supply-chain compromise during commissioning, or penetration of the plant historian—can poison the training set by injecting subtly correlated 'normal' traces that encode actually abnormal coolant states, such that the deployed model learns to reconstruct dangerous conditions (incipient voiding, flow degradation, temperature excursions) as benign. This is an adversarial threat realized through AML.T0020 (poison training data) and AML.T0010.002 (supply-chain compromise of the dataset). Because kernel regression is memory-based and its output depends directly on which stored exemplars it retrieves, poisoned exemplars will be activated whenever the live plant state resembles the attacker's chosen conditions, effectively pre-programming the system to mask specific attack signatures.

Live Signal Perturbation and Model Evasion
During operation, an adversary who understands the bilateral kernel and dynamic time-warping alignment can craft coordinated perturbations across multiple input sensors—either through cyber means (if sensor data streams are network-accessible) or by inducing physical faults—such that the reconstruction confidently outputs a plausible 'corrected' signal that diverges from true plant physics. For example, subtly shifting correlated temperature and flow readings can make a loss-of-coolant transient appear as normal operational variance to the kernel smoother, delaying protective action until damage thresholds are crossed. This is an adversarial threat combining AML.T0043.001 (black-box optimization to find perturbations the model will smooth away) and AML.T0015 (evade the AI model by pushing inputs into a region where it extrapolates poorly), with the exploitation itself being an implicit weakness the adversary leverages (OP.C0302.01, operational drift, though the adversary deliberately induces conditions outside the training envelope).

Operational Drift and Out-of-Distribution Generalization Failure
The training data came from a single start-up transient at one plant, which necessarily underrepresents the full operating envelope: end-of-cycle thermal-hydraulic behavior, post-maintenance transients, sensor aging and calibration drift, and—most critically—genuine accident signatures (steam-generator tube ruptures, reactivity excursions, pump failures) are absent or extremely sparse. When the plant enters any of these regimes, the kernel regression will default to reconstructing the nearest 'normal' analogue from its stored exemplars, effectively masking the real abnormality. This is an implicit (non-adversarial) threat driven by OP.C0302.01 (data/operational drift as the plant ages and operating conditions shift), OP.C0202 (small-data/low base-rate problem for rare faults), and OP.C0203 (new-build data scarcity, since only start-up data were available for training). The system has no intrinsic mechanism to recognize when it is extrapolating beyond its training distribution, so it will produce confident but incorrect outputs with no uncertainty flag.

Automation Complacency and Loss of Situation Awareness
Because the reconstructed signal is presented as a corrected, validated sensor reading rather than flagged as synthetic, operators and automated protection logic are likely to treat it as ground truth. If operators become conditioned to trust the reconstruction during routine sensor faults, they will fail to cross-check against redundant physical indicators (pressure trends, neutron flux, pump status) and lose the situation awareness needed to recognize when the AI's output has diverged from reality—a phenomenon especially dangerous during transients the model never trained on. This is an implicit human-factors threat combining OP.C0101.04 (misuse/over-trust in automation) and OP.C0101.01 (out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity, as operators no longer maintain proficiency in manually validating sensor coherence). The risk is amplified by OP.C0102 (alarm/monitoring complacency): if the reconstruction consistently 'fixes' nuisance alarms during normal operation, operators may dismiss or delay investigating a real fault signature.

Opacity, Non-Repeatability, and Qualification Gaps
Kernel regression with dynamic time warping is a black-box method: when the reconstruction deviates from a parallel redundant sensor, the operator receives only a residual metric, with no interpretable explanation of which historical exemplars were retrieved or why. This makes it nearly impossible to distinguish in real time whether the discrepancy reflects a benign model limitation or active manipulation. This is an implicit threat from OP.C0401 (explainability/opacity limit). Although kernel regression is deterministic given fixed inputs, the dynamic time-warping alignment can be sensitive to numerical precision and the exact sequence of recent data points, introducing subtle inference-time non-repeatability (OP.C0402.02). The system was qualified against historical start-up data, yet it must operate across the full fuel cycle and licensing envelope—a static artifact applied to a dynamic operational context with no mechanism for continuous revalidation (OP.C0303, static/dynamic qualification mismatch).

Cascading Fault Propagation and Cross-System Contamination
If multiple input sensors drift together due to a common-cause failure (environmental effect, calibration error, or adversary-induced correlation), the auto-associative architecture will interpret the collective drift as normal because it learned those sensors co-vary, and the reconstruction will reinforce rather than correct the error. This is an implicit threat from OP.C0301.01 (cascading fault propagation within the AI's internal structure). If the reconstructed signal is then fed into downstream control algorithms, trip-setpoint calculations, or safety-parameter displays—systems that assume sensor inputs are either raw measurements or have passed traditional deterministic validation—the AI's error propagates and corrupts safety-critical computations across the plant (OP.C0603, intra-system fault/bias propagation). If the same model is deployed fleet-wide without plant-specific retraining, a single compromised or unrepresentative training set multiplies the risk across all installations (OP.C0602, cross-site model propagation).

Inferior Evidentiary Trail and Forensic Blind Spot
Because the system replaces abnormal sensor readings with synthetic 'normal' values, an adversary who times physical sabotage (valve manipulation, coolant chemistry alteration, pump tampering) to coincide with sensor faults will have their attack signature overwritten in the logged data stream. Post-incident forensics will struggle to reconstruct the true sequence of events because the plant historian recorded the AI's plausible fiction rather than the raw anomalous signals. This weakens both real-time detection and after-action accountability, effectively giving adversaries a predictable window of operational blindness. The threat is implicit in the system's design (replacing rather than flagging faulty data) but becomes an exploitable weakness for an adversary who has stolen the model (AML.T0024.002, extract AI model) or built a proxy (AML.T0005) to simulate offline which sabotage signatures will be reconstructed away, then uses that knowledge to verify the attack will be masked (AML.T0042, verify attack).

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case reconstructs what a faulty coolant sensor 'should' read based on learned correlations among multiple sensor streams. If the AI reconstruction is wrong—due to drift, data scarcity from rare transients, or adversarial input manipulation—operators may accept a plausible but fictitious signal as ground truth and fail to recognize an actual process deviation or incipient accident signature. The system converts a sensor failure (which existing procedures already handle via redundancy and alarming) into a subtler hazard: a seemingly valid but incorrect reconstruction that masks the true plant state. Because operators are conditioned to trust reconstructed signals that pass internal consistency checks, automation bias becomes the critical link; if the AI fills in a sensor gap during a genuine transient the model never trained on, the facility loses both the failed sensor and the accurate picture that sensor was supposed to provide. Existing defense-in-depth (trip setpoints, independent protection channels) may catch gross errors, but an adversary who understands the kernel regression could craft correlated perturbations across input sensors to make an unsafe state appear normal in the reconstruction, delaying protective action until physical damage thresholds are crossed.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An adversary with access to the sensor data streams or the training corpus could perform AML.T0020 (Poison Training Data) by injecting subtly correlated anomalies during model retraining, teaching the system to reconstruct dangerous coolant conditions as benign—this would not trigger alarms because the reconstruction stays within learned 'normal' bounds even when the true plant state has crossed a safety limit. AML.T0043 (Craft Adversarial Data, particularly .001 Black-Box Optimization if the attacker only sees input/output pairs) enables an attacker to perturb multiple live sensor feeds in a coordinated way such that the kernel regression produces a plausible but false 'corrected' signal, masking for example the onset of a loss-of-coolant transient or voiding in the core; the operator sees stable reconstructed temperatures while actual conditions degrade. AML.T0015 (Evade AI Model) applies if the adversary uses knowledge of the bilateral kernel and dynamic-time-warping logic to craft input signals that lie in a region the model extrapolates poorly, producing a reconstruction that passes internal validation (low residual error against other sensors) but diverges from physical reality. AML.T0010.002 (AI Supply Chain Compromise – Data) is relevant if historical training data from the plant start-up (the demonstrated use per the IntechOpen chapter) were collected via SCADA historians or external contractors, giving an insider or supply-chain attacker an opportunity to embed false correlations that survive into deployment.

IMPLICIT / NON-ADVERSARIAL THREATS: OP.C0302.01 (Data/Operational Drift) is the foremost risk—nuclear plant sensor behavior changes with fuel burnup, flow-regime shifts, and component aging; a model trained on start-up transients may fail catastrophically during end-of-cycle or post-maintenance conditions it has never seen, reconstructing signals that fit its outdated learned manifold rather than current physics. OP.C0202 (Small-Data / Low Base-Rate Problem) is unavoidable: the training set necessarily underrepresents genuine abnormal events (LOCAs, steam-generator tube ruptures, reactivity transients) because those are rare; the kernel regression learns 'normal' correlations and will therefore reconstruct any true emergency signature toward normalcy, effectively hiding the accident from the operator. OP.C0101.04 (Misuse / Over-Trust) and OP.C0101.01 (Out-of-the-Loop Unfamiliarity) combine lethally—if operators rely on the reconstructed signal as truth and no longer cross-check against redundant channels or physical plant indicators (pressure drop trends, neutron flux), they lose situation awareness and may not recognize when the AI's output has diverged from reality; existing procedures assume a failed sensor produces either no signal or an obviously wrong one, not a confidently wrong smooth reconstruction. OP.C0303 (Static/Dynamic Qualification Mismatch) arises because the kernel-regression model is a static artifact qualified against historical start-up data, yet it operates in a dynamic licensing basis where allowable operating envelopes and sensor calibration drift over the fuel cycle—there is no mechanism in the described system to revalidate the reconstruction accuracy against current plant configuration. OP.C0401 (Explainability/Opacity Limit) means that when the reconstruction deviates from a parallel redundant sensor, the operator has no interpretable reason why, only a residual metric; this makes it nearly impossible to decide in real time whether to trust the AI or the backup channel. OP.C0301.01 (Cascading Fault Propagation) is a unique hazard of auto-associative architectures: if multiple input sensors begin to drift together (common-cause from calibration error or environmental effect), the reconstruction will 'agree' with the drift because it learned those sensors co-vary, and the system will never flag the collective offset as abnormal. Finally, OP.C0603 (Intra-System Fault/Bias Propagation) applies if the reconstructed signal is fed back into other plant control or monitoring algorithms—the AI's error then corrupts downstream safety calculations (e.g., core thermal limits, trip setpoints) that assume all sensor inputs are either raw or have passed traditional validation, not ML-reconstructed.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case reconstructs faulty coolant sensor signals to what the system 'thinks' they should be, then presumably feeds those reconstructed values back into operational decision-making or control logic. From a model architecture standpoint, kernel regression is a memory-based method—its 'knowledge' is just the stored training exemplars and a distance metric, so any systematic bias or gap in the training set (e.g., rare transients, new operating modes, or adversarially chosen conditions) directly determines what counts as 'normal.' The bilateral kernel plus dynamic time warping makes the system highly sensitive to how it aligns and weighs historical data; if an attacker can subtly shift the feature space (by polluting logged sensor histories or by timing an attack during a regime the model never saw), the reconstructed signal will confidently output a plausible-but-wrong 'normal' value. Because this is signal *reconstruction*—not just flagging an anomaly—operators or automated systems downstream may treat the output as ground truth, masking the real fault or intrusion until physical consequences manifest.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial surface:** An attacker with access to the training corpus (historical RCS sensor logs) can inject synthetic 'normal' traces that subtly encode abnormal states—e.g., a slow coolant-flow degradation that the kernel smoother will learn to reconstruct as acceptable (OP.C0201.02 synthetic data risk, AML.T0020 poison training data, AML.T0010.002 supply-chain compromise of the dataset). At inference time, if the adversary can induce a sensor fault or manipulate the live signal (via cyber or physical means), the reconstructed output will confidently 'correct' it to a learned-abnormal baseline, effectively blinding the protection system to the real hazard (AML.T0015 evade AI model, AML.T0031 erode model integrity leading to safety impact). The reliance on stored exemplars also means that if the plant enters a new operating regime (e.g., extended power uprate, different fuel cycle, or a transient the model never saw), the reconstruction will default to the nearest-neighbor match in feature space, which may be dangerously inappropriate (OP.C0302.01 operational drift, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity). Because kernel regression with DTW is inherently a black-box interpolation, operators have no mechanism to distinguish a valid reconstruction from one that is confidently wrong (OP.C0401 opacity, OP.C0101.04 automation misuse/over-trust).

**Implicit (non-adversarial) failure modes:** The training data for this system came from a single start-up transient at one plant (OP.C0203 new-build data scarcity, OP.C0201.04 field data from limited operational scenarios). Any fault signature not represented in that corpus—uncommon transients, sensor drift patterns unique to aging components, or cross-channel correlations that emerge only under specific thermal-hydraulic conditions—will be 'reconstructed' toward whatever the kernel sees as the closest normal analogue, effectively masking the real anomaly (OP.C0302 drift/OOD failure, OP.C0304.03 omission). The system has no intrinsic uncertainty quantification: the bilateral kernel will always produce a smoothed output, even when extrapolating wildly outside its training envelope (OP.C0402.02 inference non-repeatability if the distance metric is sensitive to numerical precision, OP.C0403 ML-theoretic limitation on extrapolation). If deployed fleet-wide without plant-specific retraining, a single compromised or poorly representative training set propagates across all sites (OP.C0602 cross-site model propagation). Finally, replacing a faulty sensor reading with a reconstructed 'normal' one creates a dependency inversion: the protection system now relies on the AI's output rather than on redundant physical channels, and if that AI fails (either from drift or attack), the plant loses both the original sensor and its backup simultaneously (OP.C0301.01 cascading fault propagation, OP.C0101.01 out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity because operators may not realize the displayed signal is synthetic). This is compounded by the fact that kernel regression is deterministic given its inputs, so repeated queries under the same conditions will yield the same wrong answer with no indication of uncertainty (OP.C0402 non-determinism gap in the negative sense—false confidence in a single answer).

security_specialist.argument: This use case reconstructs what a coolant sensor 'should' say when it goes abnormal or faulty, using kernel regression trained on normal operational data. From a security lens, the critical vulnerability is that an adversary who can bias that reconstruction—either by poisoning the training data with carefully chosen 'normal' exemplars or by exploiting the model's opacity at inference time—can mask the signature of a real physical attack (sabotage, coolant diversion, pump tampering) behind a plausibly normal reconstruction. The system is designed to fill in gaps when sensors fail naturally, but it equally fills in gaps when sensors register something an adversary caused, and operators cannot easily distinguish 'helpful gap-filling' from 'attack-masking.' Unlike a traditional sensor validity check that rejects bad data, this system *replaces* bad data with synthesized data, eroding the evidentiary trail an insider or external attacker would otherwise leave. An adversary with sufficient knowledge of the training corpus (obtainable via reconnaissance on past operational data, or via insider access to the model's exemplar set) can time physical sabotage to moments when the reconstruction will confidently output benign values, effectively giving the adversary a predictable window of blindness.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The main adversarial threat is **attack-signature masking via trusted reconstruction**: if an attacker manipulates the coolant system (valve positions, pump settings, or injects an unexpected transient) and simultaneously induces sensor 'faults' (either by direct sensor compromise or by making the physical signal abnormal enough to trigger reconstruction), the AI will replace the attack signature with a plausible normal signal, and operators will not see the attack in real time. This is exacerbated by the model's kernel-regression and DTW design—its output depends heavily on which historical normal exemplars it retrieves, so an adversary who has poisoned the training set (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000) or who has stolen the model to simulate it offline (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005) can engineer physical attacks whose signatures lie in a 'reconstruction-friendly' part of state space. The system also creates an **insider-threat amplification**: a knowledgeable insider can sabotage the coolant system confident that the reconstruction will cover their tracks for the critical first minutes, and even post-incident forensics will struggle because the logged 'sensor' values are synthetic. Non-adversarially, the system is vulnerable to **out-of-distribution generalization failure** (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02) where a novel abnormal condition (not in the training set) gets reconstructed to something plausible but wrong, and to **automation complacency** (OP.C0102) where operators, accustomed to the system confidently filling in sensor gaps, stop scrutinizing the reconstructed signals and miss a real degradation. The combination is especially dangerous: an adversary can exploit the fact that operators have been trained to trust the reconstruction, and time an attack to occur during a period of naturally high reconstruction activity (startup, power maneuvers) when operators expect some signals to be 'smoothed.' The use of dynamic time warping and kernel regression also means the system is **non-deterministic and opaque** (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02)—operators cannot easily replay the reconstruction or understand why it chose one normal exemplar over another—so distinguishing 'the model made a benign mistake' from 'the model is being actively manipulated' is nearly impossible in real time. Finally, the system introduces a **data-provenance dependency** (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0204): the trustworthiness of its output depends entirely on the integrity of the historical 'normal' training corpus, but that corpus is likely gathered over years from potentially multiple sources (plant historians, vendor commissioning data), creating a long window for an adversary to inject subtly biased exemplars that will only be activated when the reconstruction is triggered under specific conditions.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged strongly on training-data poisoning (AML.T0020), operational drift (OP.C0302.01), automation over-trust (OP.C0101.04), and the cascading-fault risk of replacing faulty data with confident fictions. The security specialist's 'attack-signature masking' and the nuclear engineer's 'converts sensor failure into subtler hazard' are two lenses on the same core insecurity; I unified them under live signal perturbation and the evidentiary-trail paragraph. I retained AML.T0031 (erode model integrity) for adversarial impact and OP.C0603 (intra-system propagation) for the implicit cross-system contamination risk both engineers flagged.

evidence.citation: Ahmed, I., Zio, E. & Heo, G. (2021), "Fault Detection by Signal Reconstruction in Nuclear Power Plants," IntechOpen (peer-reviewed chapter), DOI 10.5772/intechopen.101276
evidence.note: Auto-associative bilateral kernel regression with dynamic time warping reconstructs abnormal signals, demonstrated on RCS sensor data from an NPP start-up.

damage.why: Masking genuine abnormal coolant conditions (loss-of-coolant transient, steam-generator tube rupture, reactivity excursion) by presenting them as normal prevents protective action until damage thresholds are crossed, creating pathways to radiological release or loss of safety function.

reproducibility.why: Once operational drift moves the plant outside the training envelope or an adversary positions poisoned exemplars/coordinated perturbations, the kernel regression will reliably reconstruct abnormal states as normal because it retrieves the nearest stored 'normal' analogue with no out-of-distribution detection.

exploitability.why: Training-data poisoning requires supply-chain or historian access during commissioning (moderate insider position), while live perturbation requires understanding the bilateral kernel structure and either cyber access to sensor streams or ability to induce coordinated physical faults, placing it between routine external interaction and deep insider access.

affected_users.why: Reconstructed coolant signals feed into automated protection logic, safety-parameter displays, and trip-setpoint calculations across multiple safety systems, propagating the fictitious normal state facility-wide and contaminating downstream control algorithms that assume validated sensor inputs.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability class—that auto-associative kernel regression masks out-of-distribution conditions by defaulting to learned normal analogues—is documented in the cited peer-reviewed literature and inferable from vendor materials describing bilateral kernel methods, making the weakness evident to capable outsiders even without access to this specific plant's training data or configuration.

use_case: LSTM and variational-autoencoder diagnosis of abnormal events to help operators flag events the model has not seen
incurred_insecurity:
This LSTM-VAE abnormal-event diagnosis system incurs operational and adversarial insecurity by positioning itself as the arbiter of what operators should attend to during transients—exactly when reliability matters most. Its core mission—flagging events the model has not seen—creates a fundamental tension: it operates at the boundary of its training distribution by design, making both false negatives (missed novel sabotage or degradation) and false positives (alarm fatigue from benign drift) likely and consequential. The implicit weaknesses stem from training-data scarcity for rare events, inevitable operational drift as the plant ages, and the model's opacity about why a pattern is or is not flagged. These weaknesses become adversarial attack surfaces when an adversary who understands the training envelope crafts an intrusion that the model reconstructs as normal, effectively using the AI to suppress alarms, or poisons the training pipeline to teach the system that attack precursors are benign, while operators—habituated to trust the system's filtering—remain out of the loop until physical parameters breach safety limits.

Training-Data Scarcity and Distribution Mismatch
The model is trained on historical plant telemetry and documented abnormals, but true sabotage, covert material diversion, and nation-state intrusion signatures are absent from this corpus—they are low base-rate events the system was never shown. The reliance on simulated or surrogate fault scenarios to augment real operational data means the model's notion of abnormality may not generalize to adversarial creativity. An attacker who studies open technical databases describing the LSTM-VAE architecture or exfiltrates training data via compromised accounts can infer what the model considers normal, then craft sensor-spoofing or valve-manipulation sequences that stay within the learned envelope, evading detection. This is an implicit weakness in data provenance and small-data scarcity that an adversary exploits through black-box or white-box optimization of evasive inputs.

Operational Drift and Model Staleness
As the plant undergoes fuel cycles, component aging, sensor recalibration, and procedural changes, the baseline distribution shifts—data drift and concept drift degrade the model's novelty threshold without retraining. False positives accumulate, training operators to distrust or ignore flags, a form of alarm complacency that an adversary can time an attack around. Conversely, if the model is not updated, genuinely novel threats may be dismissed as familiar noise. The static qualification pathway for a system whose performance depends on detecting the absence of prior examples is unclear, and the non-determinism of deep networks means the same plant state may yield different anomaly scores on repeat, complicating both operator trust and regulatory oversight. This is an implicit threat that becomes adversarial when an attacker synchronizes kinetic or cyber actions with known periods of model staleness or false-positive storms.

Training-Data and Model-Update Poisoning
An adversary with supply-chain access to the historian database, model-training pipeline, or external benchmark datasets can poison the training corpus to teach the system that specific precursors—gradual coolant chemistry changes, coordinated instrumentation drift, or valve sequencing an adversary plans to use—are normal and unworthy of flagging. Because the system's purpose is to reduce operator information overload, operators will trust its silence about these events, creating a deniable pathway for the adversary to act undetected. If the model is retrained periodically from a centralized pipeline and deployed fleet-wide, a single poisoned update propagates the vulnerability to multiple plants simultaneously, a high-value target for sophisticated attackers. This is a direct adversarial threat via training-data manipulation and AI supply-chain compromise.

Automation Bias and Out-of-the-Loop Performance
The system is explicitly designed to filter what operators see, positioning itself as the decision-maker about what is abnormal enough to warrant human attention. Operators working under the information-overload conditions this tool addresses will develop mode confusion about when to trust the system versus their own instrument readings, leading to out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity during actual transients and potential misuse if they over-rely on the AI's judgment during an adversarially induced event it failed to flag. Over time, skill fade in manual abnormal-event diagnosis erodes operators' ability to override the system confidently even if they suspect it is compromised. The model's explainability gap means operators cannot verify why a pattern was dismissed, and the non-determinism means forensic reconstruction of whether an attack was missed due to adversarial poisoning versus natural model error is impossible. This is an implicit human-factors threat that amplifies all adversarial scenarios.

Fleet-Wide Propagation
If the LSTM-VAE is trained on aggregated data and deployed across multiple plants from a common pipeline, a systematic gap in the training set—such as the absence of a particular covert-diversion signature or sabotage mode—becomes a common-cause vulnerability. An adversary who compromises the central model repository or training infrastructure can backdoor all deployments at once, and the same evasion technique works everywhere. This is both an implicit cross-site propagation risk and an adversarial supply-chain threat.

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear operations engineer, my central concern is that this operator-support system sits at the intersection of an automation trust failure and alarm complacency in abnormal-event scenarios—exactly when operators most need reliable situational awareness. The system is designed to help operators flag *novel* events (ones the model hasn't seen), but that reliance on novelty detection via variational autoencoder reconstruction error creates a double bind: either operators treat the system as authoritative and miss events it fails to flag (automation bias during an actual transient), or they treat it skeptically and revert to manual alarm processing (defeating its purpose). From an adversarial standpoint, an attacker who understands the model's training distribution could craft an attack scenario—contamination of coolant chemistry, subtle instrumentation drift, coordinated sabotage—that stays within the model's 'seen' envelope long enough to delay detection, effectively using the AI as a timing oracle for when operators are least alert. The physical consequence is delayed operator response during an actual abnormal event, whether adversarially induced or spontaneous, because procedural reliance on the AI has eroded the skills and vigilance needed for direct instrument interpretation.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT (non-adversarial): The LSTM-VAE novelty-detection architecture is trained on operational data from the plant, likely dominated by normal operations and a limited set of documented transients or simulated upset conditions (OP.C0202 small-data/low base-rate problem, OP.C0201.01–.03 simulated/surrogate data provenance). The model's purpose—flagging events it *hasn't* seen—means it operates at the boundary of its training envelope by design, making it prone to both false negatives (failing to flag truly novel sabotage or component degradation modes because they superficially resemble benign drift) and false positives (flagging benign operational variability, leading to alarm fatigue and operator disuse, OP.C0101.05). Operational drift over time—sensor calibration changes, fuel-cycle evolution, maintenance-induced baseline shifts—will degrade the model's novelty threshold without retraining (OP.C0302.01 data/operational drift), yet there is no clear static qualification pathway for a system whose performance depends on detecting the *absence* of prior examples (OP.C0303 static/dynamic mismatch, OP.C0401 explainability limit on why a pattern is 'novel'). Operators may develop mode confusion about when the system is trustworthy, leading to out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity during actual transients (OP.C0101.01) or clumsy automation if they override it incorrectly (OP.C0101.02). The cross-system propagation risk is also acute: if this model is deployed fleet-wide from a common training set, a systematic training-data gap (e.g., all sites lack signatures of a particular degradation mode) propagates as a common-cause vulnerability (OP.C0602).

ADVERSARIAL EXPLOITATION: An adversary with reconnaissance of the plant's operational data (AML.T0095.000 code repositories if training scripts are published, AML.T0003 victim-owned websites for plant documentation, AML.T0000 open technical databases for the Kim et al. paper describing the architecture) can infer the model's training envelope and craft an attack that unfolds within the 'normal' latent space—gradually poisoning coolant chemistry, subtly miscalibrating sensors, or staging equipment in a way the VAE reconstructs with low error, thus not triggering a novelty flag (AML.T0015 evade AI model). If the adversary has access to operational data streams (AML.T0012 valid accounts via insider or supply-chain compromise AML.T0010.001–.002 targeting SCADA historian or model-training pipelines), they can conduct a proxy-model attack (AML.T0005.001 train proxy via replication using exfiltrated data AML.T0025, then AML.T0043.001–.002 black-box optimization of an attack sequence that stays below the novelty threshold). The operational consequence is that operators, habituated to trust the system's 'no flag' output, do not recognize the early stages of the attack as abnormal until physical parameters (reactivity, pressure, contamination) cross procedural action levels—by which time safeguards margins are eroded. The adversary can also time kinetic or cyber actions to coincide with periods of model uncertainty or drift (OP.C0302.01 exploited as AML.T0029 functional denial—if operators see frequent nuisance flags due to drift, they ignore a real one). Manipulation of the training data itself (AML.T0020 poison training data if the adversary has supply-chain or IT access, or AML.T0019 publish poisoned datasets if the plant uses external benchmark data) can shift the novelty boundary to exclude signatures of sabotage the adversary plans. Finally, LLM-based operator interfaces or documentation systems that explain the AI's flags (OP.C0304.01 hallucination risk if a language model is used to translate VAE latent-space diagnostics into natural language) could be prompt-injected (AML.T0051.001 indirect injection via poisoned maintenance records or procedures that the LLM retrieves) to downplay real anomalies or fabricate explanations that misdirect operator response.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML engineering standpoint, this use case rests on an LSTM/VAE architecture trained to identify *novelty* (events the model has NOT seen), which inverts the usual supervised learning premise. The paper motivates this with operator information overload, meaning the system's output directly influences what operators attend to or dismiss. The training data are presumably historical plant telemetry and annotated abnormal events—but the very problem statement is that new, unseen abnormals must be flagged, so the model's utility depends on its out-of-distribution behavior, which is inherently the least-qualified part of any ML pipeline. The diagnosis task is also sequence-sensitive (LSTM) and relies on reconstructing normal baselines (VAE), making it vulnerable to concept drift as the plant ages or operating profiles shift, and to adversarial manipulation of input sequences that could either suppress alarms or flood operators with false positives.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core ML fragility is that the system is explicitly tasked with flagging *unseen* events, yet ML generalization to true out-of-distribution inputs is uncontrolled—there is no closed-form guarantee that a novel signature will be recognized vs. misclassified as normal (OP.C0302 drift/OOD failure). Training data likely come from simulators or limited historical fault records (OP.C0201.01 simulated data, OP.C0202 small-data problem for rare events), meaning the model has never seen certain sabotage or novel degradation signatures an adversary could engineer. An attacker with knowledge of the LSTM/VAE structure could craft input sequences (sensor spoofing, slow ramps) that reconstruct well under the VAE (low anomaly score) despite being malicious, effectively evading detection (AML.T0015 Evade AI Model, AML.T0043 Craft Adversarial Data). Conversely, operational or sensor drift over the plant's lifetime will shift baseline distributions, causing false-positive floods that train operators to ignore alarms (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust turning into OP.C0101.05 disuse, OP.C0102 alarm complacency)—a degradation an adversary could time an attack around. The sequence-based nature means an adversary could inject carefully timed perturbations that the LSTM integrates as normal context, then exploit that blind spot. The system also introduces a data-access surface: if an adversary can poison the telemetry stream used for retraining or real-time inference (AML.T0020 Poison Training Data, AML.T0010.002 AI Supply Chain Compromise—Data), they can teach the model to ignore specific precursors. Because this is operator support for *safety-critical* event diagnosis, a false negative (missed precursor to coolant loss, reactivity excursion) or a false positive storm (operator stops trusting the tool) both have direct safety consequences. The non-determinism of deep nets (OP.C0402 repeatability gap) also complicates regulatory qualification: the same plant state fed twice may yield different anomaly scores, and there is no closed-form proof the system will flag every unseen-but-hazardous signature. Finally, if the model is deployed fleet-wide from a central training pipeline (OP.C0602 cross-site propagation), a single poisoned dataset or architectural backdoor propagates to all sites, and the same adversarial evasion technique works everywhere.

security_specialist.argument: From a security lens, this is a classic over-trust/insider vulnerability multiplier. The system is explicitly positioned to filter what operators see—it flags 'unseen' events, which means operators are trusting it to decide what's normal versus what warrants attention. An adversary who compromises the model or its training pipeline can suppress alarms for attack precursors by teaching the system those precursors are 'normal,' or conversely flood operators with false positives timed to mask a real intrusion. The model's opacity (LSTM + VAE are black-box by nature) means operators cannot verify *why* something was flagged or ignored, eroding their ability to second-guess it—automation bias will set in, especially under the 'information overload' conditions this system was designed to address. A sophisticated adversary would target the training data or model update pathway (not the running inference itself) to pre-position the attack surface, then time physical actions around periods when the AI has learned to dismiss their signatures as benign drift.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial threats:** The core risk is model-mediated alarm suppression or distraction. An insider or supply-chain attacker who poisons the training data (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002) can teach the system that certain precursors to sabotage—say, specific valve-position patterns or subtle instrumentation drift that an adversary induces—are 'normal' and not worth flagging. Because the system is meant to reduce information overload, operators will trust its judgment about what *not* to show them, creating a deniable pathway for an adversary to act while the AI stays silent. The model's non-determinism and opacity (OP.C0402, OP.C0401) mean even a vigilant operator cannot reverse-engineer whether a dismissed event was truly benign or whether the model was compromised. The adversary can also invert this: inject synthetic 'abnormal' signatures (AML.T0043) that trigger floods of false positives, training operators to ignore alarms when the real attack occurs (the 'cry wolf' setup). If the model is updated across a fleet (OP.C0602), a single poisoned update propagates the vulnerability to multiple plants simultaneously, a high-value target for a nation-state actor. Physical environment access (AML.T0041) is less relevant here than logical access to the data pipeline, but the consequence is physical: the AI becomes a gatekeeper that an adversary controls, and operators are out-of-the-loop (OP.C0101.01) because the system was sold as reducing their cognitive load.

**Implicit (non-adversarial) weaknesses an adversary can exploit:** The system's training on historical 'normal' data (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0202) means it has likely never seen genuine sabotage or nation-state-level intrusion signatures—these are low base-rate events. It will either flag them (good) or, more dangerously, dismiss them as 'abnormal but uninteresting' if they resemble benign transients it has seen. Concept drift (OP.C0302.02) is inevitable: as the plant ages, what counts as 'normal' shifts, and the model's notion of abnormality drifts with it unless continuously retrained. An adversary can time an attack to a period when the model is known to be stale or when operators are already desensitized by false positives from drift (alarm fatigue, OP.C0102). The non-determinism of VAEs (OP.C0402.02) means the same sensor input might be flagged one day and ignored the next, further eroding operator trust and making it harder to forensically verify whether an attack was missed due to adversarial action or just model noise. Skill fade (OP.C0101.06) is a long-term risk: if operators rely on this system for years, their ability to manually diagnose subtle abnormalities atrophies, so even if they suspect the AI is compromised, they lack the practiced skill to override it confidently. Finally, the system's explainability gap (OP.C0401) means there is no human-verifiable audit trail for *why* a given event was not flagged—an adversary's suppression and the model's natural false-negative are indistinguishable after the fact, complicating incident response and attribution.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the core double bind: the system filters operator attention during information overload yet is inherently unreliable at its mission (detecting the unseen), creating both automation-bias and alarm-complacency paths that adversaries can exploit via training-data poisoning or evasion within the learned envelope. The security specialist's emphasis on alarm suppression as deniable attack and the nuclear engineer's focus on delayed-response consequences during transients were treated as facets of the same adversarial exploitation of implicit drift and opacity weaknesses.
