use_case: Machine-learning alarm system that suppresses alarms expected for the current plant state to better highlight unexpected ones
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places an ML system in the critical path between alarm signals and operator awareness during transients and accidents, creating both implicit operational fragilities and adversarial attack surfaces. The system must decide in real time which alarms to suppress based on a learned model of 'expected' alarms for the current plant state, yet it is trained predominantly on steady-state and planned evolution data with minimal exposure to the rare casualty events, novel equipment failures, or sabotage scenarios where correct alarm presentation is most critical. As the plant ages, configurations change, and operational modes evolve, the model's concept of 'expected' drifts, risking incorrect suppression of genuine precursor alarms or flooding operators with noise during known evolutions—both outcomes degrade situational awareness and emergency response capability. Operators habituated to the filtered alarm view may over-trust the system and dismiss alarms the AI did not flag, or lose skill in recognizing raw alarm patterns themselves, undermining defense-in-depth. Adversaries who poison training data, manipulate the deployed model, or craft plant-state inputs the model misinterprets can systematically suppress alarms that would otherwise reveal physical sabotage, cyber intrusions, or insider actions, and the model's opacity makes such manipulations difficult to detect or audit after the fact. If deployed fleet-wide, a single compromised or drifted model propagates the same suppression errors across multiple units, creating a common-mode vulnerability in operator perception.

Training Data Scarcity and Provenance Weakness
The model is trained on historical operational data, simulator runs, and planned transient logs, not on real casualty sequences, beyond-design-basis events, common-cause failures, or adversarial scenarios. This data scarcity for low-base-rate critical events means the system has no ground truth for what alarm patterns are 'expected' during the very conditions where operators need all relevant alarms—novel equipment degradation, simultaneous failures, or malicious state changes. Simulated and surrogate data may not capture the full complexity or timing of real-world fault propagation, leaving the model vulnerable to out-of-distribution failures when the plant encounters a state it has never seen. An adversary aware of this training gap can design attack trajectories intentionally outside the model's learned distribution, confident that resulting alarms will be incorrectly suppressed as 'expected' or dismissed as noise. This is an implicit weakness in the AI system's data foundation that adversaries can exploit during reconnaissance and attack planning.

Operational and Concept Drift Eroding Alarm Validity
Nuclear plants are not static: equipment is replaced, instrumentation recalibrated, fuel cycles progress, procedures updated, and new maintenance or test modes introduced. If the model is trained on a fixed historical dataset and deployed with static qualification, its concept of 'expected alarms for the current plant state' will drift as the plant evolves, causing it to suppress alarms that are now genuinely diagnostic of off-normal conditions or to fail to suppress new nuisance alarms from updated systems. Operational heterogeneity across a fleet—different vintages, fuel types, or equipment lineups—means a model trained at one site may misclassify alarms at another, yet fleet-wide deployment of a shared model (to reduce development cost) propagates the same drift-induced suppression errors to all units. This drift is a non-adversarial failure mode, but it creates a time-dependent vulnerability: an adversary with long-term reconnaissance (via open-source operational reports, insider knowledge, or prior cyber access) can identify when the model's assumptions are stale and time sabotage or intrusion activities to periods when the system is most likely to suppress relevant alarms.

Human-AI Interaction Failures: Over-Trust, Skill Fade, and Alarm Complacency
Operators who rely on the ML-filtered alarm list for weeks or months may develop automation bias, trusting the system's judgment over their own situational assessment and mentally filtering out alarms the AI did not flag—effectively treating 'not suppressed by the AI' as equivalent to 'not important.' If the system makes an incorrect suppression during a real event, operators may fail to recognize the developing problem in time to act. Conversely, if the system produces too many false suppressions or fails to suppress expected noise during planned evolutions (clumsy automation), operators lose trust and revert to ignoring the filtered view, negating the safety benefit. Prolonged reliance on the AI to perform alarm triage also risks skill fade: operators lose practice in recognizing alarm patterns, degrading their ability to respond manually if the AI is unavailable, incorrect, or under adversarial influence. An adversary who understands this dependency (via reconnaissance of plant procedures or insider knowledge) can time physical or cyber attacks to exploit operator complacency or reduced manual vigilance, knowing the ML system has become the primary perceptual filter and that operators are less likely to catch subtle anomalies the model was not trained to recognize.

Adversarial Manipulation of Training Data and Model Integrity
An adversary with access to the training pipeline—via supply-chain compromise of the model, insider access at INL or the vendor, or infiltration of the plant's data repositories—can poison the labeled dataset to embed triggers that suppress specific alarms the adversary plans to induce during sabotage. For example, labeling coolant-boundary alarms, criticality alarms, or security-system alerts as 'expected' under certain benign conditions that the attacker can later simulate, so that when the real attack occurs those alarms are suppressed and operators see nothing unusual. Even post-deployment, an adversary with access to model retraining workflows (valid accounts, insider threat) can subtly modify suppression rules under the guise of 'tuning' or 'drift correction,' and the change may escape review if the modification is framed as routine maintenance. Manipulation of the deployed model itself—altering weights, thresholds, or configuration files—can similarly bias suppression decisions in favor of the adversary's operational objectives. This is a direct adversarial threat exploiting the AI artifact's central role in operator perception.

Inference-Time State Manipulation and Evasion
The system interprets 'current plant state' signals (sensor readings, mode flags, equipment status) to decide which alarms are expected. An adversary with control-system access (cyber intrusion, insider, or compromised DCS component) can feed falsified state descriptors to the ML model, making it believe the plant is in a benign configuration where certain alarms should be suppressed, thereby masking the adversary's physical sabotage or cyber manipulation in progress. This is analogous to prompt injection in LLM systems but applied to state-vector inputs: the attacker crafts adversarial input data that causes the model to misclassify the situation and suppress alarms that would otherwise reveal the attack. Even without direct model access, an adversary who has extracted or probed the model (via exfiltration, black-box queries, or insider knowledge) can discover which alarm signatures will be suppressed under which state conditions, then design an attack path that deliberately triggers those states—effectively evading the model's detection by exploiting its learned decision boundaries.

Model Opacity, Non-Determinism, and Forensic Blind Spots
The ML system's decision to suppress a given alarm is likely opaque: operators and security personnel cannot easily audit in real time why an alarm was or was not shown, and many ML architectures exhibit inference-time non-repeatability (stochastic sampling, ensemble methods, or neural-network weight updates during online learning). This opacity creates a forensic gap: after an event, investigators cannot deterministically replay the alarm-suppression logic to determine whether the system failed, the operators misinterpreted the filtered view, or an adversary manipulated the model or its inputs. An adversary leverages this opacity to argue (if questioned during or after an incident) that suppressed alarms were 'normal per the AI model,' delaying investigation and attribution. The lack of explainability also hampers qualification and regulatory acceptance: existing nuclear software standards require deterministic, traceable behavior for safety-significant functions, and the non-determinism inherent in many ML systems creates a qualification gap that remains unresolved, leaving the system in a regulatory gray area where its failure modes are not formally analyzed or mitigated.

Fleet-Wide Propagation of Single-Point Vulnerabilities
If INL's alarm-suppression model or training methodology is adopted across multiple reactors or utilities (to amortize development cost and leverage shared operational data), a single poisoned model, design flaw, or drift-induced suppression error propagates to all sites, creating a fleet-wide common-mode failure in operator alarm awareness. An adversary targeting the nuclear sector (nation-state, insider network, or supply-chain actor) can achieve scalable impact by compromising the model at its source—INL's development environment, the vendor's distribution channel, or a shared training-data repository—rather than attacking each plant individually. This cross-site propagation makes the use case a high-value target for adversaries seeking fleet-wide sabotage enablement or situational-awareness degradation, and it concentrates risk in a single AI artifact whose integrity and ongoing validity are difficult to verify independently at each site.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a nuclear operations perspective, this use case puts AI in the loop of alarm presentation—a safety-critical human interface—during normal and especially transient or upset conditions. If the ML system incorrectly suppresses an alarm that is actually unexpected, or fails to suppress one that is expected (flooding the operator with nuisance alarms), operators may fail to recognize a developing off-normal condition in time to act. The system depends on a model of 'expected alarms for the current plant state,' which must track not only steady-state modes but also startup, shutdown, refueling, test configurations, equipment out-of-service lineups, and rare transients—a highly heterogeneous operational envelope. Alarm systems are a Defense-in-Depth layer; if this AI layer erodes that defense by hiding a real problem or by training operators to distrust the filtered view, the physical consequence could be delayed or incorrect emergency response.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
The dominant implicit threat is operational drift and training-data scarcity for rare or new plant states (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0202). Nuclear plants evolve: equipment is replaced, instrumentation is recalibrated, operating procedures change, and new test or maintenance modes are introduced. If the ML model was trained on historical alarm data from a different configuration or does not generalize to a novel transient (e.g., a simultaneous equipment failure combination never seen before), it may misclassify alarms—suppressing a genuine precursor or failing to suppress expected noise during a planned evolution. This is exacerbated by the low base rate of serious off-normal events in the training data, meaning the model has limited exposure to the very conditions it must handle correctly. Human-AI interaction failures (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05) follow: operators may over-trust the filtered alarm list (automation bias/misuse), dismissing a real alarm that 'shouldn't be there' if the AI didn't flag it, or they may under-trust the system if it produces too many false suppressions and revert to ignoring it (disuse), negating the safety benefit. Out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity (OP.C0101.01) and skill fade (OP.C0101.06) are also risks—if operators come to rely on the AI to tell them which alarms matter, they may lose practice in recognizing alarm patterns themselves, degrading their ability to respond if the AI is unavailable or wrong.

Adversarial threats center on data poisoning and model manipulation to degrade alarm prioritization at a critical moment. An attacker who can poison training data (AML.T0020) or manipulate the deployed model (AML.T0018.000) could cause the system to systematically suppress alarms associated with a sabotage scenario—for example, training it to treat alarms from a coolant leak or control rod position deviation as 'expected' in a certain context, hiding the adversary's physical attack. Even without direct model access, an adversary with some influence over plant state or instrumentation (possibly via supply chain or insider means, AML.T0010) could craft operational conditions that the AI misinterprets, causing it to suppress real alarms during a coordinated physical intrusion or sabotage event (AML.T0015 evade detection, in effect). The fact that the model's decisions are likely opaque (OP.C0401) makes it difficult for operators or reviewers to audit why an alarm was suppressed, so a subtle adversarial bias could persist undetected. If the same model is deployed across multiple units or sites (OP.C0602 cross-site propagation), a single compromised model could introduce fleet-wide alarm-handling vulnerabilities. Finally, because this system interprets 'current plant state' to decide what is expected, adversarial manipulation of plant-state telemetry (not strictly an AI attack, but enabled if the AI increases dependence on automated state assessment) could cause the AI to misclassify the situation, compounding the operator's confusion during a real event.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case puts an ML system directly in the path of alarm signals reaching operators during transients, anomalies, and potential accidents—its job is to decide what to suppress. From an ML engineering standpoint, the core fragility is training data: you need labeled examples of plant states mapped to 'expected alarm' versus 'unexpected alarm,' but most of the operational data come from steady-state or planned evolutions, not the off-normal conditions where this system is supposed to add value. If the model is trained primarily on normal operations and a handful of simulated transients, it has no real basis to judge what is 'expected' during a novel degradation or common-cause failure it has never seen—yet that is exactly when operators need all relevant alarms, not a filtered subset. The architecture and inference pipeline also matter: if the system uses a frozen model (static qualification) but plant configuration, fuel cycle, or equipment aging drift over time, the notion of 'current plant state' and what alarms are 'expected' will drift with it, and the model will start suppressing alarms that are now genuinely diagnostic. Finally, this is a non-deterministic system (many ML architectures have stochastic elements at inference, and retraining changes the model) inserted into a safety function (ensuring operators see safety-significant alarms), creating a qualification and repeatability problem that existing nuclear software standards were not written to address.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The dominant threat class is operational/implicit, not adversarial, though adversaries can exploit the operational weaknesses. **Data scarcity and provenance** (OP.C0201.01 simulated data, OP.C0202 small-data/low base-rate, OP.C0203 new-build scarcity if this is a new plant or new system) means the model likely trains on simulator runs and steady-state logs, not real casualty or common-cause failure sequences—so it has no ground truth for what alarm patterns are 'expected' during the events that matter most (beyond-design-basis, multiple equipment failures, cyber incidents). When the system encounters an out-of-distribution plant state (OP.C0302 drift/OOD failure, OP.C0302.01 data drift as the plant ages or changes configuration, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity if rolled out across a fleet with different vintages), it may confidently but incorrectly suppress alarms that are the only indication of an evolving problem, or flood operators with nuisance alarms during a known evolution, both undermining its value. **Human-AI interaction risks** are severe: operators may over-trust the system (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust) and dismiss or mentally filter alarms the system did not suppress, assuming 'the AI would have told me if this mattered,' or they may experience skill fade (OP.C0101.06) in pattern recognition if the system does the triage for them for months or years. Clumsy automation (OP.C0101.02) is also a risk—if the suppression logic is opaque and the system occasionally makes a glaring mistake (suppressing a safety-injection signal during a LOCA because the model learned that SI often triggers during testing), operators lose confidence but have no way to predict when it is wrong. **Adversarial surface** emerges because an attacker with access to plant data streams or the model pipeline (AML.T0010.003 supply chain model compromise, AML.T0020 poison training data, AML.T0043 craft adversarial data) could manipulate what the system considers 'expected'—for example, injecting false-normal labels during retraining so that the model learns to suppress criticality alarms or loss-of-coolant-flow alarms under certain conditions, then timing a physical or cyber attack to create exactly those conditions. Even without model access, an attacker who understands the system's inference logic (AML.T0013/T0014 discover model ontology/family, AML.T0015 evade model) could craft a sequence of plant manipulations that the model interprets as a benign state transition, suppressing the alarms that would otherwise alert operators to the attack in progress. The non-determinism and opacity of the model (OP.C0401 explainability limit, OP.C0402.02 inference non-repeatability) makes forensic analysis after an event nearly impossible: you cannot replay the decision to suppress a given alarm deterministically, so you cannot prove whether the system failed, the operators failed, or an adversary manipulated it. Finally, if this system is deployed fleet-wide with a shared model (OP.C0602 cross-site model propagation), a single poisoning or drift event propagates the same suppression error to all units, creating a common-mode failure in operator situational awareness across the fleet.

security_specialist.argument: From a nuclear security lens, this use case is a high-value target because it directly mediates what operators perceive as 'abnormal' versus 'normal' – the core perceptual channel for insider threat detection, sabotage indicators, and cyber-physical attack signatures. An adversary who can manipulate alarm suppression criteria (via model poisoning, drift exploitation, or insider modification of training labels) can mask their activities during an attack window by making malicious state transitions appear 'expected.' The system also creates automation complacency risk: operators habituated to relying on the ML filter may miss subtle anomalies the model wasn't trained to recognize, which is precisely what a sophisticated adversary would engineer (e.g., a slow diversion or sabotage trajectory outside the model's concept space). Even non-adversarial drift (concept/operational drift as the plant ages or operational modes shift) becomes a security vulnerability if it causes the system to suppress legitimate alarms during an actual intrusion or insider action, and an adversary with reconnaissance capability would time their operation around observed model blind spots.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) Training-data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000): An insider or supply-chain attacker poisons the labeled dataset used to define 'expected' alarm patterns for various plant states, embedding triggers that suppress specific alarms an adversary plans to trip during sabotage (e.g., labeling coolant-boundary alarms as 'expected' under certain benign conditions an attacker can simulate). (2) Inference-time prompt injection / state-label manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0051 analogue for non-LLM): If the system takes real-time plant-state descriptors as input, an adversary with control-system access could feed falsified state signals to make the ML model believe the plant is in a state where alarms should be suppressed, masking their attack. (3) Model extraction/inversion for reconnaissance (AML.T0024.002): A nation-state adversary exfiltrates the model (via insider, cyber intrusion, or supply-chain access at INL/vendor) to discover exactly which alarm signatures it will suppress under which conditions, then designs an attack path that exploits those blind spots. (4) Insider threat amplification (AML.T0012 valid accounts + OP.C0101.04 misuse): The system concentrates trust in a single ML artifact; a malicious insider with access to model retraining or configuration can subtly modify suppression rules to favor their sabotage plan, and the change may not be caught if the modification is framed as 'tuning' or 'drift correction.'

IMPLICIT/NON-ADVERSARIAL VULNERABILITIES AN ADVERSARY WOULD EXPLOIT: (5) Automation complacency and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity (OP.C0101.04 misuse, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102 alarm complacency): Operators habituated to the ML suppressing nuisance alarms lose the skill and vigilance to interpret raw alarm patterns; an adversary times their attack during a period when operators are maximally reliant on the filter, knowing manual oversight is degraded. (6) Concept drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03): The model was trained on historical plant states, but as the plant ages, fuel cycles change, or maintenance activities introduce new operational modes, the model's concept of 'expected' drifts and may suppress alarms that are actually novel sabotage indicators – an adversary with long-term reconnaissance (including publicly available operational data, AML.T0095) identifies these drift windows. (7) Static/dynamic qualification mismatch and new-scenario generalization failure (OP.C0303, OP.C0302): The model is qualified against historical data but cannot generalize to attack scenarios it has never seen (OP.C0202 low base-rate for sabotage/intrusion events in training data); an adversary designs an attack trajectory intentionally outside the model's training distribution, confident it will be suppressed as 'expected' noise or ignored as out-of-scope. (8) Explainability/opacity limit (OP.C0401): Security personnel and operators cannot easily audit why the model suppressed a specific alarm in real-time; an adversary leverages this opacity to argue (if questioned) that suppressed alarms were 'normal' per the model, delaying investigation. (9) Cross-site model propagation (OP.C0602): If INL's model or training methodology is adopted across a fleet, a single poisoning or design flaw becomes a fleet-wide vulnerability, making this use case a high-value target for a nation-state seeking scalable attack capability across multiple NPPs.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on data scarcity for rare events, operational/concept drift, human over-trust and skill fade, training-data poisoning, and fleet-wide propagation as the dominant threats. The security specialist's framing of adversarial exploitation of implicit drift and the AI engineer's emphasis on non-determinism and forensic gaps were integrated as distinct but complementary vulnerabilities; where terminology overlapped (e.g., 'evasion,' 'misuse'), I unified under the most specific operational or ATLAS code that captured the mechanism described.

evidence.citation: Langstrand, J.-P., McDonald, R. & Nguyen, H. (2020), "Develop and Document a State-Based Alarm System for a Nuclear Power Plant Control Room Using Machine Learning," INL/EXT-20-60549 (INL/IFE, LWRS Program)
evidence.note: INL and Institute for Energy Technology work on ML-based alarm handling for NPP control rooms.

damage.why: Systematic suppression of alarms revealing physical sabotage, criticality events, or coolant-boundary failures during actual casualties could directly enable radiological release or loss of material control by blinding operators to developing accident conditions.

reproducibility.why: Once an adversary poisons training data to suppress specific alarm classes or manipulates deployed model configurations, the suppression logic will reliably execute during matching plant states, though real-world casualty timing introduces some variability.

exploitability.why: Adversarial manipulation of training pipelines, model artifacts, or deployed configurations requires insider access to INL development environments, vendor supply chains, plant data repositories, or control-system integration points—not achievable through routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Fleet-wide deployment of a compromised or drifted model propagates the same alarm-suppression errors across multiple reactor units, creating common-mode failure in operator situational awareness at facility or enterprise scale.

discoverability.why: The general vulnerability class—ML alarm systems trained on narrow data suppressing novel casualty alarms—is documented in open INL publications and known in the nuclear AI research community, enabling capable adversaries to infer exploitability from publicly available program reports and operational-data limitations.

use_case: Machine-learning screening of corrective action program condition reports to predict adverse conditions
incurred_insecurity:
ML-based screening of CAP condition reports incurs insecurity at a critical safety-governance chokepoint: the system decides which potential adverse conditions warrant deeper review, so classification failures directly suppress or delay identification of safety-significant trends, undermining the corrective action program's role as the first line of defense against latent plant weaknesses. The primary threats are implicit—low base rates of adverse conditions, concept drift as the plant and regulatory environment evolve, and automation bias that causes human reviewers to defer judgment to an opaque model—but these weaknesses also create exploitable attack surface for adversaries who can evade, poison, or probe the screening logic to hide sabotage precursors or safeguards anomalies.

Low Base Rate and Data Imbalance
The training corpus is dominated by routine condition reports; truly adverse conditions are rare by design in well-run plants (OP.C0202). This imbalance risks training a model that systematically underpredicts adverse classifications, producing false negatives that allow safety-significant issues to linger unaddressed. The scarcity of positive examples also means the model has limited exposure to the edge cases that matter most, weakening its ability to generalize to novel failure modes. An adversary aware of this can craft condition reports using language the model has learned to score as benign, evading detection (AML.T0015) without needing to compromise the model itself—they simply exploit its training-data blind spots.

Concept and Operational Drift
The model is trained on historical CAP data whose labels reflect past human judgments of what constitutes an adverse condition, judgments that shift as regulatory expectations, plant configurations, and operating procedures evolve (OP.C0302.02). New equipment, post-modification failure modes, and emerging regulatory concerns (e.g., post-Fukushima flooding or cyber-informed engineering) present narratives the model has never seen, yet it will still return a confidence score with no built-in alarm for out-of-distribution inputs (OP.C0302.01). If the system is statically qualified but the plant and threat landscape evolve, it will misclassify novel conditions, and no feedback loop guarantees detection of this drift in real time (OP.C0303). An adversary can exploit this window by introducing previously unseen failure signatures—especially sabotage-related degradation absent from historical training data (OP.C0203)—that the model fails to recognize as adverse.

Automation Bias and Human-AI Trust Failure
If CAP coordinators, operations review committees, or security staff come to trust the ML screening score and stop reading low-scored reports carefully (OP.C0101.04), a false negative becomes effectively invisible until the underlying condition manifests as an actual system failure, regulatory finding, or—in a security context—successful adversary operation. This is not an adversarial technique per se, but it is an implicit vulnerability that adversaries can exploit by timing their activities to periods of high AI-reliance or by learning which report features the model underweights (OP.C0101.01). The concentration of triage authority in a single opaque tool creates a high-value target: compromise the screening logic, and you suppress issue escalation fleet-wide if the model propagates across sites (OP.C0602).

Training-Data Poisoning and Model Manipulation
An insider or external adversary with access to the CAP database, the labeled training corpus, or the model retraining pipeline can poison the training data to bias future classifications (AML.T0020). For example, by submitting or relabeling historical reports to teach the system that electrical faults, safeguards alarms, or specific equipment degradation patterns are benign, the attacker creates a persistent blind spot the model carries into production (AML.T0018.000). If the model is retrained periodically on updated CAP data, poisoned entries introduced months earlier can propagate forward, and the drift may go unnoticed because there is no ground truth at inference time to validate against. This is a sabotage-masking or diversion-enabling threat: conditions that should trigger escalated review are instead systematically deprioritized.

Model Probing and Evasion Optimization
An adversary with query access to the model (whether through legitimate CAP submission or compromised credentials, AML.T0040, AML.T0012) can probe the system to learn its decision boundaries—submitting carefully crafted reports and observing which receive high versus low scores (AML.T0043.001, AML.T0042). This reverse-engineering allows the adversary to optimize their evasion strategy: phrase genuinely adverse conditions in ways the model has learned to score as low-priority, bypassing the triage filter without leaving forensic traces of model compromise. The natural-language nature of CAP reports gives adversaries significant latitude to vary syntax, terminology, and framing while preserving malicious intent, and the model's opacity (OP.C0401) makes it difficult for plant staff to detect or challenge these evasions until damage is done.

Explainability, Audit, and Regulatory Gap
The ML model's limited explainability (OP.C0401) frustrates root-cause analysis when a report later proves adverse but was initially scored low: reconstructing why requires access to feature weights, training-data snapshots, and inference logs that may not be version-controlled or retained in the production pipeline. This opacity delays detection of model compromise, drift, or systematic bias, and it complicates regulatory review under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B Criterion XVI, which mandates prompt identification and correction of conditions adverse to quality but contains no ML-specific qualification guidance (OP.C0504, OP.C0501). The lack of clear acceptance criteria for AI-based CAP screening means plants may deploy the tool without demonstrating that its false-negative rate is acceptably low for safety-significant failure modes, and security staff cannot easily audit whether the system is suppressing sabotage indicators.

Cross-Site Propagation and Infrastructure Dependencies
If a single screening model is deployed across a fleet without site-specific retraining, a systematic classification bias or poisoned training artifact propagates to every site, amplifying the consequence of any single compromise (OP.C0602). If the model depends on cloud-hosted ML infrastructure or external APIs for inference, that creates an additional attack surface for model theft (AML.T0024.002), manipulation (AML.T0049), or denial of service (AML.T0029), and introduces a dependency on off-premises infrastructure whose availability and integrity are outside direct plant control (OP.C0601).

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear engineer focused on plant operations and process safety, this use case sits at a critical governance and human-performance boundary: CAP condition reports are the primary mechanism by which we identify degraded conditions, near-misses, and precursors to events before they escalate. An AI screening these reports decides which items warrant deeper review, potentially NRC reportability determination, or immediate corrective action -- meaning missed classifications directly delay or suppress identification of safety-significant trends. The system depends on rare-event data (adverse conditions are infrequent by design in well-run plants) and must generalise across evolving plant configurations, procedure changes, and new failure modes, all while operating in a regulatory framework (10 CFR 50 Appendix B Criterion XVI) that has no ML-specific qualification guidance. If this system drifts, undertrusts operator-submitted reports, or fails to flag novel degradation signatures, the downstream consequence is that the corrective action process -- our first line of defense against latent system weaknesses -- becomes a filter that hides problems rather than surfacing them.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary required): The low base rate of truly adverse conditions (OP.C0202) means the model trains on imbalanced data where most reports are routine -- it may learn to underpredict adverse classifications, leading to missed safety-significant issues (OP.C0301.01 cascading fault propagation if a screened-out report later ties to an event). Concept drift (OP.C0302.02) is near-certain: plant modifications, new operating experience from the fleet, evolving regulatory expectations (e.g., post-Fukushima flooding concerns), and changes in how operators phrase reports all mean yesterday's training data becomes less representative over time. If the system is statically qualified but the plant evolves, it will misclassify novel conditions it hasn't seen. Automation bias (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust) is a severe risk -- if CAP coordinators or operations review committees come to trust the ML score and stop reading low-scored reports carefully, a false negative becomes invisible until the underlying condition manifests as an actual system failure or regulatory finding. The opacity of ML models (OP.C0401) makes it difficult for plant staff to understand why a report was scored low, inhibiting effective oversight and challenge of the system's output. Cross-site model propagation (OP.C0602) could spread a systematic screening bias across an entire fleet if one model is deployed widely without site-specific retraining. There is also a regulatory-scope gap (OP.C0504): current NRC guidance on CAP adequacy does not address ML-based screening, so plants may deploy these tools without clear acceptance criteria for when the AI's performance is 'good enough' to meet Appendix B requirements.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS (attacker exploits the AI or the new attack surface it creates): An insider or external attacker who understands the model's training distribution could craft condition reports that intentionally evade detection -- for example, phrasing a safety-significant observation in a way that mimics routine maintenance language, causing the ML to score it low and suppress escalation (AML.T0015 Evade AI Model). If the model is trained on historical CAP data that includes attacker-submitted decoy or misleading reports, those could poison the training set to bias future classifications away from certain failure signatures (AML.T0020 Poison Training Data, AML.T0018.000). An adversary with access to the model API or its deployment environment (AML.T0040, AML.T0044) could query it systematically to learn which report phrasings are flagged and which are not, then use that knowledge to hide sabotage indicators in plain sight. Prompt injection or indirect data-poisoning risks are lower here since this is likely a supervised classifier rather than an LLM, but if the system uses any retrieval-augmented context (e.g., pulling in past similar reports), an attacker could seed the database with misleading precedents (OP.C0505.01 inappropriate data security, AML.T0070 RAG Poisoning analogue). The system also creates a single point of failure: if the ML screening tool itself is compromised or its output manipulated (AML.T0018 Manipulate AI Model), the entire CAP front-door is corrupted, and no one may notice until a pattern of missed adverse conditions emerges in hindsight. Finally, the reliance on this tool could be timed by an adversary -- if they know the plant trusts the ML and has reduced human oversight during certain shifts or outage periods, they could introduce malicious activity knowing it's less likely to be caught (OP.C0101.01 out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity exacerbating AML techniques).

ai_engineer.argument: As an AI/ML engineer, I see a high-risk mismatch between what this system must learn and what data it actually gets to train on. CAP condition reports are inherently low-base-rate: truly adverse-to-quality conditions are rare compared to routine anomalies, so the training distribution is skewed and may not expose the model to the edge cases that matter most. The model is trained on historical text whose labeling (whether something was 'adverse') was itself a human judgment call subject to site-specific interpretation, creating label noise and concept drift as regulatory expectations or site culture evolve. At inference, the system faces novel failure modes and narratives it has never seen—especially for new equipment or post-modification scenarios—yet it must generalize accurately because a missed adverse condition (false negative) could allow a precursor event to go unaddressed, and a false positive floods operators with noise, eroding trust. The pipeline's dependence on natural-language understanding of terse, jargon-heavy, context-dependent incident text means the model's confidence scores are only as good as its language model's ability to parse ambiguity, and there's no clear ground truth to validate against in real time.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: An adversary with access to the CAP submission interface (internal threat, or compromised user account) could craft condition reports using language designed to evade the ML screener—phrasing genuinely adverse conditions in ways the model has learned to score as low-priority, effectively bypassing the triage filter and allowing safety-significant issues to linger unaddressed. If the model's feature weights or decision boundaries leak (via model extraction or insider knowledge of training data), attackers can reverse-engineer which phrases trigger high scores and which do not, then optimize their evasion. Poisoning is also a risk: if an adversary influences the labeled training set (by submitting or relabeling reports in the historical corpus), they can bias the model to systematically underweight certain failure signatures—e.g., always scoring electrical faults as benign—creating a persistent blind spot the screener will carry forward into production. IMPLICIT (no adversary required): The model is trained on a corpus whose labels ('adverse' vs. 'not adverse') were assigned by humans with varying interpretations of 10 CFR 50 Appendix B criteria, introducing label noise and site-specific drift; as regulatory guidance or site procedures evolve, the historical training data becomes stale, but the model continues to enforce yesterday's triage logic. The low base rate of truly adverse conditions means the model sees few positive examples, risking both high false-negative rates (it misses rare-but-serious issues because it hasn't seen enough like them) and high false-positive rates (it flags benign anomalies because it's overcalibrated to be sensitive). Operators face automation bias: if the ML screener consistently scores a report as low-priority, the human reviewer may skim it or defer deeper analysis, effectively deferring the safety decision to an opaque model whose confidence score has no regulatory standing. There is no obvious 'ground truth' signal at inference time to detect when the model drifts out of distribution—new equipment, post-modification failure modes, or novel component degradation mechanisms will present text the model has never seen, yet the system will still return a score, and no alarm will sound if that score is garbage. Finally, the model's explainability is limited: if it scores a report as benign when it later proves adverse, reconstructing why requires either access to feature weights (which may not be logged or version-controlled) or re-running the model on historical snapshots, neither of which is guaranteed in a production NLP pipeline, frustrating root-cause analysis and regulatory review.

security_specialist.argument: From a nuclear security lens, this use case presents a moderate but noteworthy insecurity surface. The AI system becomes a single point of trust concentration: if an insider or external adversary can manipulate the model's screening logic (via data poisoning during retraining, prompt injection if it uses LLM components, or by learning its decision boundaries), they can systematically suppress detection of adverse conditions that mask sabotage precursors or diversion indicators. The system's value to an adversary lies not in direct attack but in creating a 'shadow corridor' — conditions that should trigger escalated review are instead deprioritized, buying time for multi-stage operations. Additionally, the operational risk of automation bias (operators trusting the AI's triage) becomes a security vulnerability when timed: an adversary aware of the AI's deployment could introduce anomalies during periods when human oversight is degraded by over-reliance on the screening tool, or could craft condition reports using language the model systematically underweights.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An insider with access to CAP data or the model retraining pipeline could poison training data to teach the system that certain condition-report patterns (e.g., specific equipment types, failure modes indicative of sabotage staging, or safeguards-relevant anomalies) are low-priority, systematically suppressing their escalation (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000). If the system uses retrieval-augmented generation or LLM components for natural-language screening, prompt injection or RAG poisoning could insert false screening logic (AML.T0051, AML.T0070). A sophisticated adversary (including nation-state) could perform black-box probing to reverse-engineer which report features the model underweights, then craft sabotage-masking reports to exploit that blind spot (AML.T0043.001, AML.T0042). The concentration of trust in a single screening tool creates a high-value target: compromise here affects fleet-wide issue detection if the model propagates across sites (OP.C0602). IMPLICIT/OPERATIONAL THREATS EXPLOITABLE BY ADVERSARIES: The system will suffer from low base-rate problems and data scarcity for novel adverse conditions, especially sabotage-related ones absent from historical CAP data (OP.C0202, OP.C0203) — an adversary can exploit this by introducing previously-unseen failure signatures the model won't recognize. Automation bias and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01) mean human screeners may not catch what the AI misses, and an adversary can time operations to coincide with periods of high AI-reliance. Operational drift (OP.C0302.01) — the model trained on peacetime CAP data will degrade when adversary-induced conditions appear — is itself an exploitable window. If the model is cloud-hosted or depends on off-premises ML infrastructure, that creates an external access vector for model theft or manipulation (OP.C0601, AML.T0049). Finally, explainability limits (OP.C0401) mean security staff cannot easily audit why certain reports were deprioritized, delaying discovery of a compromised model.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged strongly on low base rate (OP.C0202), concept drift (OP.C0302.02), automation bias (OP.C0101.04), opacity (OP.C0401), and training-data poisoning (AML.T0020) as the core threats; the nuclear engineer emphasized regulatory and cascading-fault angles, the AI engineer focused on label noise and ground-truth absence, and the security specialist framed implicit weaknesses as adversary-exploitable windows—these perspectives were synthesized into a unified narrative with distinct threat paragraphs where mechanisms differed.

evidence.citation: Idaho National Laboratory, "MIRACLE: Machine Intelligence for Review and Analysis of Condition Logs and Entries" (CW-21-07-MIRACLE)
evidence.note: INL software that scores CAP condition reports for whether they are conditions adverse to quality, to speed and standardise screening.

evidence.citation: U.S. NRC AI/ML Workshop presentation on corrective action program data (ADAMS ML21277A139)
evidence.note: Describes CAP incident-report data fields and initial screening questions used for ML screening.

damage.why: Systematic suppression of adverse condition detection undermines the corrective action program's safety-governance function, allowing latent safety-significant issues to accumulate undetected until manifesting as operational events or regulatory findings, eroding multiple defense-in-depth layers.

reproducibility.why: Low base rates, concept drift, and automation bias are inherent to ML-based CAP screening at well-run plants and reliably produce false negatives once the model encounters data imbalance or out-of-distribution inputs from evolving plant configurations.

exploitability.why: Evasion via carefully phrased condition reports requires only routine CAP submission access, but systematic poisoning or model probing to optimize evasion strategies requires either insider database access or compromised credentials to the training pipeline or inference API.

affected_users.why: The vulnerability affects plant-wide safety governance by suppressing issue escalation across all systems monitored through the corrective action program, and fleet-wide deployment propagates systematic biases to multiple sites simultaneously.

discoverability.why: The existence of ML-based CAP screening tools like INL's MIRACLE is publicly documented, and the inherent challenges of low base rates, concept drift, and automation bias in safety-critical classification are well-established in the ML literature, making the vulnerability class evident to capable adversaries.

use_case: Machine-learning to forecast and autonomously adjust heat input in a micro reactor heat-pipe
incurred_insecurity:
This use case embeds machine learning in a closed-loop controller that both forecasts and autonomously adjusts heat input to a microreactor heat-pipe—a passive safety component whose failure can lead to fuel damage or loss of coolant. The ML system acts on its own predictions without explicit human checkpoint, and its training was confined to a single non-nuclear testbed article under benign conditions, leaving it unqualified for the variability, aging, and fault modes of operational deployment. The combination of autonomous actuation, sparse qualification data, and a safety-critical target creates a threat surface in which adversarial manipulation and non-adversarial drift both lead to unsafe thermal excursions, and where the system's own brittleness amplifies an attacker's ability to time and conceal sabotage.

Model poisoning and supply-chain compromise
An adversary who gains access to the training pipeline or model distribution chain can poison the dataset or embed a backdoor in the deployed model, biasing the controller's thermal setpoint logic to induce over-heating, under-cooling, or thermal cycling that accelerates heat-pipe degradation or triggers spurious protection actions. Because the model was demonstrated on a single benign testbed and will be updated across a fleet of microreactors, a single compromised artifact can propagate unsafe behavior to multiple units without leaving an obvious signature in the control logic. The attack is adversarial, exploiting the supply chain and the model's role as a trusted actuation authority.

Adversarial evasion via crafted inputs
If an attacker can access the inference API or manipulate sensor feeds, they can craft adversarial inputs designed to make the model predict benign thermal states while the heat-pipe approaches dryout or exceeds design limits, suppressing protective control responses. The model's training on a narrow experimental envelope means it has never seen true fault signatures, so adversarially perturbed sensor readings can push it outside its learned decision boundaries without triggering any internal alarm. This is an adversarial threat that directly exploits the model's closed-loop authority.

Model inversion and design-parameter leakage
The digital twin's predictive component, trained on testbed measurements of a specific heat-pipe geometry and material stack, may be susceptible to inversion or membership-inference attacks that reveal thermal margins, coolant properties, or structural details useful for physical sabotage planning. While the leakage itself is an adversarial exfiltration threat, the root cause is the model's reliance on proprietary, safety-relevant data in a potentially accessible inference service.

Operational drift and out-of-distribution failure
The model was trained on data from a single heat-pipe article in a controlled, non-nuclear environment with no fuel burnup, no material aging, and no fleet-wide manufacturing variation. Deploying it to an operational microreactor introduces distributional shifts—flux transients, coolant chemistry changes, fabrication tolerances, sensor degradation—that the static model cannot anticipate. When the system encounters these out-of-distribution states, it will still produce a control action, and because the loop is autonomous that action will execute before a human can intervene. This is a non-adversarial implicit weakness, but it creates windows of unpredictable behavior that an adversary aware of the model's training limits can exploit by timing an attack to coincide with a known operational transition where the model is least reliable.

Cascading fault propagation and automation trust failure
The autonomous controller's speed and the digital twin's dual role—both actuating and diagnosing—mean that a drifted or miscalibrated model can misinterpret early fault signatures (e.g., incipient wick dryout) as noise and adjust heat input in a way that accelerates the fault. Operators, conditioned by successful commissioning runs, may over-trust the system and fail to recognize that the model's behavior has silently degraded, deferring manual inspections until physical damage is irreversible. This is an implicit automation-trust and cascading-propagation risk, but it also lowers the bar for an adversary: a poisoned model or a well-timed adversarial input can trigger the same cascade, and the lack of explainability means security staff cannot easily distinguish malicious manipulation from a model misfire.

Small-data and rare-event blindness
Heat-pipe dryout and incipient failure modes are low-base-rate events that the testbed likely never captured, so the ML has no training examples of the precursor signatures it must detect to protect the system. If the model encounters such a signature in operation, it may classify it as an outlier or transient and adjust heat input to suppress it, thereby masking the fault from both human operators and any separate protection logic. This is an implicit weakness rooted in data scarcity, but it is also a vulnerability an insider or sophisticated attacker can exploit by inducing a rare fault mode the model will predictably mishandle.

Qualification and regulatory gaps
There is no established nuclear regulatory framework for qualifying an ML controller that learns from operational data and acts autonomously on a safety-critical heat-removal path, and the testbed's agile development ethos implies frequent model updates that may bypass traditional software change-control and configuration management. This governance gap is a non-adversarial implicit risk, but it means that poisoned updates or insider modifications may not be caught by the site's quality-assurance processes, effectively opening a persistent insider-threat vector.

Fleet-wide model propagation
If the digital twin's model is deployed across a fleet of microreactors with centralized updates, a single compromised model or a training dataset poisoned at the vendor level will propagate the vulnerability to all units simultaneously. An adversary need only compromise the shared model repository or retraining pipeline once to gain synchronized influence over thermal margins across multiple sites. This is an adversarial threat amplified by the operational practice of cross-site model sharing.

Cloud and off-premises dependencies
If the digital twin relies on cloud-hosted model updates or off-premises retraining infrastructure, the attack surface extends beyond the facility's physical and cyber perimeter, allowing a remote adversary to inject malicious model weights, poison the retraining data, or intercept inference requests without needing on-site access. This is an implicit architectural weakness that an adversary can exploit to conduct supply-chain or man-in-the-middle attacks on the model lifecycle.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case puts machine learning in direct, closed-loop control of a thermal boundary condition in a reactor – heat input to a heat pipe – with autonomous adjustments, not just advisory outputs. The digital twin predicts temperature evolution and acts on those predictions to maintain operating margins. From an operations lens, the crux is whether the ML controller can reliably distinguish normal transients from incipient failures, and whether its adjustments could mask symptoms that a human operator or a separate protection system needs to see. If the model drifts out-of-distribution (new operating regime, unanticipated fouling, or simply aging of the test article that wasn't in training data), it may adjust heat input in ways that degrade safety margin or confuse diagnostics. The autonomy means there is less time for a human to catch a bad control action before physical consequences manifest in the heat pipe or downstream coolant loop.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: An attacker who can manipulate the training data (AML.T0020) or poison the deployed model (AML.T0018.000) could bias the controller's setpoint logic, causing it to over- or under-heat the pipe and induce thermal cycling that accelerates material degradation or triggers spurious protection-system actuations – a sabotage vector that leaves no obvious fingerprint in the control logic itself. If the ML model's inference API is accessible (AML.T0040), an adversary could craft adversarial inputs (AML.T0043) that fool the model into seeing a benign temperature profile when the pipe is near a thermal limit, suppressing the protective control action. Because this is a testbed with 'agile' updates and likely iterative model tuning, supply-chain compromise of model artifacts (AML.T0010.003) or even RAG-indexed documentation (AML.T0070) used to tune operating bounds is plausible – an insider or sophisticated external actor could embed a backdoor that activates under specific thermal signatures, evading initial qualification runs.

NON-ADVERSARIAL (Operational): The fundamental operational risk is model drift and out-of-distribution failure (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). The testbed is a single heat-pipe article; scaling to a full micro-reactor introduces operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.03) – variations in fabrication, installation, and local neutronics that were not in the training set. Small-data and low-base-rate problems (OP.C0202) are severe: heat-pipe dryout or incipient failure signatures are rare events, so the ML may never have seen them in training and could misinterpret early warnings as noise, adjusting heat input in a way that accelerates the fault (OP.C0301.01 cascading propagation). Automation trust failure (OP.C0101.04 misuse, OP.C0101.01 out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity) is pronounced because the controller acts faster than human review, and operators may not recognize when the model's behavior has changed post-deployment. If the digital twin's predictions are also used for diagnostics or maintenance scheduling, a silent model degradation (OP.C0303 static/dynamic qualification mismatch, OP.C0402.02 inference-time non-repeatability) could lead to both incorrect control actions and a false sense of component health, deferring inspections until actual damage is done. The regulatory and qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0504) is acute: there is no established framework for qualifying an ML controller that learns from operational data in a nuclear heat-removal system, and the 'agile' nature of the testbed implies frequent model updates that bypass traditional software change-control rigor (OP.C0502). Finally, because this is a *heat pipe* – a passive device whose failure mode (loss of working fluid, wick dryout) can be sudden and irreversible – any ML misjudgment that pushes the pipe beyond its heat-flux limit, even briefly, may cause permanent damage that a slower, human-reviewed control scheme would have avoided.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case embeds a closed-loop ML controller in the thermal management of a heat-pipe—a passive safety feature whose reliability depends on well-understood physics, now delegated to a model trained on testbed data from a single article. The digital-twin architecture creates a direct path from model prediction error or drift to physical control action (autonomous heat-input adjustment) with no explicit mention of whether the operator remains in-the-loop or whether the system fails safe when predictions fall outside training bounds. The move from testbed (INL MAGNET, non-nuclear, instrumented) to an operational microreactor introduces multiple distributional shifts—material aging, flux transients, coolant chemistry changes—that a static model cannot capture without continuous retraining, yet microreactors are often remote/unattended, limiting both sensor density and the data flow needed to detect drift before it manifests as a control error. Because this is closed-loop and targets a passive-safety component, adversarial and non-adversarial failure modes converge: an adversary who can bias the model or its input sensors can induce heat-pipe dryout or structural damage, but the same outcome arises if the model simply drifts out of qualification and the system has no fallback.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
Adversarial surface: The ML controller's reliance on sensor input (temperature, pressure, possibly neutronics proxies) makes it vulnerable to data injection or manipulation (AML.T0043 craft adversarial data, AML.T0015 evade AI model). An attacker with access to the sensor network or the inference pipeline could feed inputs designed to make the model predict benign conditions while the heat-pipe approaches dryout, or conversely trigger unnecessary throttling that degrades performance and masks the attack. The digital-twin's predictive component, if trained on limited non-nuclear testbed data, may also be invertible or membership-inferable (AML.T0024.001, AML.T0024.000), leaking design details about heat-pipe geometry, materials, or thermal margins—information useful for targeting physical sabotage. If the twin's model or training data is sourced from an external vendor or repository (common in digital-twin frameworks), supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.003 model, AML.T0010.002 data) could embed a backdoor that activates under specific operating conditions, effectively time-bombing the controller.

Non-adversarial fragility (with adversarial amplification): The testbed-to-deployment gap is severe. Training on a single heat-pipe article (OP.C0203 new-build data scarcity, OP.C0201.04 lab/bench-measured data) in a controlled, non-nuclear environment leaves the model unqualified for the variability it will see in the field—manufacturing tolerances across a fleet, burnup-induced material property changes, transient operating modes not replicated in MAGNET. This is compounded by the fact that microreactors are designed for remote/austere deployment, so the sensor suite may be sparser and less maintained than in a traditional plant, increasing the risk of silent drift (OP.C0302.01 operational drift, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity). The autonomous control loop introduces automation-trust failure modes: operators may assume the twin is always valid (OP.C0101.04 over-trust/misuse), especially if it performed well in commissioning, and thus miss early signs of model degradation—by the time a heat-pipe fault is observable, the controller may have been making suboptimal adjustments for weeks. The closed-loop nature also enables cascading fault propagation (OP.C0301.01): a drifted model that over-predicts margin could allow heat input to rise until the heat-pipe's wick dries out, at which point the pipe's passive cooling fails and the system must scram—but if the model is also responsible for interpreting post-scram thermal behaviour, it may misdiagnose the fault or delay recovery. Crucially, there is no evidence in the cited sources of a fallback control law or out-of-distribution detection mechanism; if the model encounters an operating regime it never saw (OP.C0302 generalization failure), it will still produce an output and the system will act on it. An adversary aware of this can time an attack to coincide with a known operational transition (e.g., startup, load-following transient) where the model is least reliable, effectively using the system's own brittleness as an attack multiplier. Finally, if this digital twin is part of a fleet deployment and models are shared across units (OP.C0602 cross-site model propagation), a single poisoned or drifted model can propagate the vulnerability fleet-wide, and an adversary need only compromise the shared model repository once.

security_specialist.argument: This use case introduces a control loop in which a machine-learning model both forecasts and autonomously adjusts heat input to a microreactor heat-pipe — a safety-critical component whose failure could lead to fuel damage or loss of coolant equivalent. From a security lens, autonomous actuation on a live reactor system (even a micro one) is a high-value target: an adversary who can manipulate the ML model's predictions or training data can induce thermal excursions, simulate normal operation while degrading safety margins, or mask the signatures of a covert diversion or sabotage event. The demonstration was performed on a non-nuclear testbed with a single heat-pipe article, meaning the ML was trained and qualified on benign, narrowly-scoped experimental data; deploying this to an operational reactor with fleet-wide model updates creates a supply-chain and insider-threat surface where poisoned models or drift-inducing data can propagate across multiple units, and the autonomous actuation removes a human checkpoint that would otherwise notice anomalous commands.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An adversary (insider or supply-chain attacker) could poison the training data or the deployed model to make the system mispredict safe thermal states, causing it to autonomously reduce cooling or increase heat input at a chosen time — AML.T0020 (Poison Training Data), AML.T0018.000 (Poison AI Model), AML.T0010.003 (AI Supply Chain Compromise – Model). Because the model was demonstrated on a benign non-nuclear testbed, an attacker exploiting the inference API or physical access (AML.T0040, AML.T0041) can craft adversarial inputs (AML.T0043) that evade the model's learned safe boundaries, triggering unsafe actuation while appearing nominally in-distribution to any oversight system. The autonomous control loop also means an adversary timing a physical attack (e.g. covert material removal, insider sabotage of another safety system) can rely on the ML's predictable response window to delay human detection — the model will auto-adjust and mask early thermal anomalies. If the digital twin's model is updated across a fleet (OP.C0602), a single compromised model artifact propagates to multiple reactors, and the attacker gains synchronized control over thermal margins across sites. The ML system also concentrates trust: operators may defer to its predictions (OP.C0101.04 over-trust, OP.C0102 alarm complacency), so an adversary poisoning the model's outputs can suppress or delay human intervention during an engineered thermal transient.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) INSECURITIES THAT ALTER THREAT SURFACE: The model was trained and qualified on data from a single non-nuclear heat-pipe experiment (OP.C0201.01 simulated data, OP.C0201.03 lab/bench data, OP.C0203 new-build data scarcity, OP.C0202 small-data problem), meaning its learned decision boundaries do not reflect the variability, materials aging, or fault conditions of an operational reactor — it will encounter out-of-distribution states (OP.C0302 drift, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity) for which its autonomous adjustments are unvalidated. This drift is not adversarially induced, but it creates windows where the system's behavior is unpredictable to both operators and any anomaly-detection safeguards, and an adversary can time an attack to coincide with these windows (e.g. after a refueling cycle changes thermal characteristics). The autonomous actuation also removes the human-in-the-loop who would catch mode errors (OP.C0101.03) or clumsy automation (OP.C0101.02), so a non-adversarial model bug (e.g. a software regression, OP.C0502) can directly command unsafe heat levels without manual override, and this failure mode is itself what an adversary would exploit by triggering the bug deliberately (e.g. via a crafted input sequence). The lack of explainability (OP.C0401) in the ML forecast means security staff cannot easily distinguish a genuine thermal anomaly from a model misfire or adversarial perturbation, complicating insider-threat detection and forensic timelines. Finally, if the digital twin relies on cloud infrastructure or off-premises model updates (OP.C0601), the attack surface extends beyond the facility's physical and cyber perimeter, allowing a remote adversary to inject malicious model weights or poison the retraining pipeline (AML.T0010.001 AI Software supply chain, AML.T0058 Publish Poisoned Models) without needing facility access.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the core threat triad: adversarial model/data poisoning via supply chain, adversarial evasion through crafted inputs exploiting the testbed-to-deployment gap, and operational drift from single-article training data creating windows an attacker can exploit. The security specialist's cloud-dependency and fleet-propagation points and the AI engineer's inversion/leakage angle were retained as distinct but complementary to the nuclear engineer's focus on cascading faults and the human-out-of-the-loop risk.
