evidence.note: The twin's ML predicted heat-pipe temperatures, detected trends toward unfavourable thresholds and autonomously controlled the heat pipe.

damage.why: Autonomous ML control of heat-pipe thermal management in a microreactor can lead to fuel damage, loss of coolant, or thermal excursions that compromise core integrity—all pathways to radiological release or loss of material control.

reproducibility.why: Model poisoning via supply chain or crafted adversarial inputs can reliably trigger unsafe thermal setpoints once the adversary has access to the training pipeline or sensor feeds; out-of-distribution drift will reliably occur given the narrow training envelope and operational variability.

exploitability.why: Supply-chain compromise or sensor-feed manipulation requires moderate insider access or vendor-level positioning; cloud-hosted retraining infrastructure lowers the bar to remote compromise, but achieving reliable actuation authority still demands knowledge of the model lifecycle and deployment architecture.

affected_users.why: Fleet-wide centralized model updates mean a single compromised artifact propagates unsafe behavior across multiple microreactor units simultaneously, and failure of the heat-pipe controller directly impacts core cooling across the facility.

discoverability.why: The digital twin demonstration and its reliance on single-testbed training data are documented in public INL reports; an adversary with vendor documentation or procurement records can infer the model's narrow qualification envelope, out-of-distribution blindness, and supply-chain update mechanisms without needing insider access to specific configurations.

use_case: Machine-learning intrusion detection on nuclear power plant control system process data that distinguishes cyber-attacks from component faults with similar signatures
incurred_insecurity: This use case places an AI classifier at the critical junction between cybersecurity response and equipment maintenance, where it must distinguish cyber-attack signatures from component fault signatures in real-time nuclear power plant control-system data—two conditions demanding fundamentally different operator actions. The primary insecurity arises from severe training-data scarcity for actual cyber-intrusions in operational NPP control systems, forcing reliance on simulated or lab-generated attack data that may not capture adversary tradecraft, combined with the model's opacity and the operational consequence of misclassification: a missed intrusion leaves an adversary embedded in the control system, while a false alarm erodes trust or triggers unnecessary lockdowns during genuine equipment failures. An adversary aware of the model's training limitations and decision boundary can craft attacks that mimic fault signatures the model has learned to dismiss, effectively hiding malicious activity in the noise of normal process variability, and the system's fleet-wide deployment creates a single point of failure where a compromised model or poisoned update degrades intrusion detection across multiple plants simultaneously.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case places an AI system in the critical decision path between detecting a real cyber-attack and diagnosing a component fault -- two conditions that demand fundamentally different responses (security lockdown versus maintenance action). From an operations lens, the consequences of misclassification are severe: a false negative (missed intrusion) leaves an adversary undetected in the control system, while a false positive (fault misidentified as attack) could trigger unnecessary security responses that delay needed maintenance or create operational confusion during an actual equipment failure. The system's training data will be heavily skewed toward normal operations and equipment faults (which occur regularly) versus actual cyber-intrusions (which are rare or entirely absent in historical plant data), creating a small-data problem for the attack class that undermines confidence in the model's ability to generalize to novel attack signatures. Because this system informs both cybersecurity incident response and equipment maintenance decisions, automation bias could lead operators to accept its classification without sufficient independent verification, particularly under time pressure when a real fault is degrading.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary operational threat is training-data scarcity for the cyber-attack class (OP.C0202, OP.C0701-type scarcity): actual intrusion events in NPP control systems are rare, and any training examples will likely be simulated or transferred from other domains (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.03), raising questions about whether the model can reliably detect novel attack signatures that differ from its training set. This creates a drift/generalization risk (OP.C0302) where an adversary can craft an attack that mimics a plausible equipment fault signature the model has learned to dismiss, effectively hiding in the noise of normal process variability -- the model's boundary between 'fault' and 'attack' becomes an exploitable surface. The operational heterogeneity problem (OP.C0302.03) is significant: each plant's control system has unique process signatures, sensor suites, and operational modes, so a model trained on one unit or fleet may not transfer reliably without site-specific requalification. From an adversarial perspective, an attacker who understands the model's decision boundary (AML.T0013, AML.T0014, AML.T0043.001 black-box probing via observable plant responses or insider knowledge) could craft attacks that stay within the 'fault' region of feature space -- for example, inducing slow process deviations that mimic sensor drift or component wear rather than abrupt anomalies the model flags as intrusions. If the model is updated across a fleet (OP.C0602), a poisoned update or adversarially-tuned model (AML.T0018, AML.T0010.003) could simultaneously degrade intrusion detection at multiple sites. The human-factors dimension is critical: operators facing conflicting signals (the AI says 'attack', but process trends look like a stuck valve) may experience automation disuse (OP.C0101.05) and override the alarm, or conversely, automation misuse (OP.C0101.04) where they accept a false 'fault' classification and fail to escalate to cybersecurity response, delaying incident containment. The model's opacity (OP.C0401) makes it difficult for operators or security staff to understand why a given event was classified as fault versus attack, undermining their ability to provide meaningful oversight or catch misclassifications before acting on them.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case sits at a critical intersection: an ML classifier must distinguish cyber-attack signatures from component fault signatures in real-time process data, where both can manifest as anomalous sensor patterns. The training pipeline depends on having labeled examples of both attack traffic and fault transients in a nuclear plant control system—but genuine attack data from operational NPPs is vanishingly rare, and fault signatures vary across reactor designs, vintages, and operational states. The model is asked to generalize across an adversarial/non-adversarial decision boundary with sparse ground truth on the adversarial side, likely relying on simulated attacks or data from non-nuclear ICS testbeds. At inference time, if the model misclassifies an attack as a benign fault (false negative), operators may dismiss a real intrusion; if it misclassifies a fault as an attack (false positive), it trains operators to ignore alerts or triggers unnecessary defensive actions that themselves disrupt plant operation. The architecture must handle concept drift as attackers evolve tactics and as the plant ages and its normal fault modes shift, yet the system's qualification basis—how it was validated and against what threat model—will lag operational reality.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core insecurity is a training-data provenance and scarcity problem compounded by adversarial adaptability. The model is trained predominantly on simulated or lab-generated attack signatures (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02) and historical fault data from a specific plant or reactor type (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0201.05), leaving it vulnerable to attacks that differ from the simulated threat model or faults that present differently in a heterogeneous fleet (OP.C0302.03). An adversary aware of this can craft attacks that mimic known fault signatures more closely than the training set anticipated (AML.T0005, AML.T0043)—exploiting the model's decision boundary by staying in the fault-like feature space. Because the base rate of true cyber-attacks in operational NPP control-system data is extremely low (OP.C0202), the model's false-positive rate becomes operationally unacceptable unless it is tuned conservatively, which increases false negatives. Concept drift (OP.C0302.02) is unavoidable: attackers change tactics (AML.T0015) and the plant's normal and fault operating regimes evolve with component aging and maintenance, yet the model's retraining cycle—if it exists—lags these changes, and there is no regulatory consensus on how to re-qualify an IDS after retraining (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). The model's opacity (OP.C0401) means operators cannot easily determine why an alert fired, fostering either over-trust (OP.C0101.04) if the system has low false-positive rates initially, or disuse (OP.C0101.05) if nuisance alarms erode confidence—both failure modes allow real attacks to go unaddressed. If the IDS is deployed across multiple units or plants from a central model (OP.C0602), a single adversarial probe that discovers the model's blind spot can be replayed fleet-wide, and a poisoned training update (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000) or backdoored model (AML.T0018.002) introduced via the supply chain (AML.T0010.003) can simultaneously degrade intrusion detection across the entire fleet. Finally, the system's dependence on continuous, high-fidelity process data (OP.C0204) makes it fragile to data-availability attacks—an adversary who can subtly corrupt or delay sensor streams (AML.T0046) may degrade classifier confidence or trigger mode confusion, and the IDS itself becomes a single point of failure: if operators rely on it and it goes silent or produces garbage during an attack, the attack proceeds undetected while defenders troubleshoot the IDS.

security_specialist.argument: This use case sits in a privileged position: it monitors control-system process data to distinguish cyber-attacks from faults, meaning it effectively gates what alarms get escalated as adversarial versus operational. A sophisticated adversary (including a nation-state) would treat this as high-value infrastructure to compromise or blind, because defeating it lets you conduct cyber operations that will be mis-classified as mundane component failures—delaying or preventing defensive response. The insecurity concern is not whether the ML model works on average, but whether an adversary can craft attacks that exploit its training-data limitations (the model has likely never seen a real APT intrusion in a live reactor, only simulated or lab faults and historical 'normal' data) or insert themselves into its data pipeline to poison detections in real-time. Even non-adversarially, the system's existence changes operator vigilance: if staff come to rely on it as the authoritative arbiter of 'cyber versus fault,' they may discount their own pattern-recognition when the model is wrong or bypassed, which is exactly the moment an adversary would time an attack around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial threats:** (1) Model evasion via mimicry—an adversary with knowledge of the model (obtainable via reconnaissance on similar systems, or insider access to training data/model architecture) crafts control-system manipulations that present fault-like signatures the model has learned to ignore, effectively routing a cyber-attack into the 'benign fault' bin and suppressing security response (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). This is exacerbated if the model was trained predominantly on simulated attacks or lab data (OP.C0201.01–.04), giving the adversary an out-of-distribution edge. (2) Data-pipeline poisoning or interception—an adversary with access to the process-data feed (insider, or via prior ICS network compromise) injects false-normal data or manipulates features before they reach the detector, blinding it to ongoing attacks (AML.T0020, AML.T0070 by analogy). The model's reliance on continuous, trusted process data makes this a high-leverage target. (3) Supply-chain or training-data compromise—if the model or its training datasets are sourced from shared repositories or vendor pipelines, an adversary can backdoor the model to ignore specific attack patterns or trigger false-negatives on command (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000), and the model gets deployed fleet-wide (OP.C0602), propagating the blind spot across multiple plants. (4) Insider exploitation of access—the system likely requires privileged access to control-system data and possibly to retrain or tune; an insider (or an adversary who has compromised such credentials, AML.T0012) can disable, retrain, or exfiltrate the model, or simply observe its logic to design evasive attacks. The model's operational role means tampering with it is itself a potent attack vector.

**Implicit (non-adversarial) insecurity that adversaries can exploit:** (5) Automation bias and alarm complacency—operators who trust the model's 'fault' verdicts may not independently investigate anomalies, especially under high workload; an adversary can exploit this trust window by timing attacks to periods when the model is known to have high false-negative rates (e.g. during transients the model was undertrained on, OP.C0302.01–.03, OP.C0101.04). (6) Data scarcity and distributional mismatch—the model has almost certainly never seen real nation-state intrusion tactics in a live reactor dataset (OP.C0202, OP.C0203 for new reactor designs), meaning it generalizes from simulated/lab attacks that may not reflect adversary tradecraft; an adversary aware of this gap can field novel techniques the model will misclassify. (7) Qualification and drift gaps—if the model is statically qualified at deployment but the threat landscape or plant configuration evolves (software updates, new attack tools, OP.C0303, OP.C0503), it will silently degrade, and an adversary can monitor for such evolution and exploit the lag. (8) Explainability limits—when the model does flag something ambiguous (neither clearly fault nor clearly attack), operators may lack the transparency to understand why (OP.C0401), leading to either over-ride (disuse, OP.C0101.05) or unquestioning acceptance (misuse), both of which an adversary can manipulate by feeding the model edge-case inputs. The model's existence thus concentrates trust in a single, potentially opaque and exploit-prone artifact, and an adversary who understands its training regime and operational blind spots gains a roadmap for evasion.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists strongly converged on training-data scarcity (OP.C0202) for the attack class, reliance on simulated/lab data (OP.C0201.01–.02), adversarial evasion via fault-mimicry (AML.T0015, AML.T0043), automation trust failure (OP.C0101.04/.05), model opacity (OP.C0401), and fleet-wide propagation risk (OP.C0602) as the dominant threats. The security specialist's supply-chain and data-pipeline poisoning scenarios (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018) and the AI engineer's drift/qualification concerns (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0501, OP.C0504) were integrated as distinct but well-supported extensions.
