use_case: Retrieval-augmented LLM chatbot that answers nuclear power plant maintenance-diagnostics questions to support predictive maintenance recommendations
incurred_insecurity:
A retrieval-augmented LLM chatbot that advises predictive maintenance decisions incurs insecurity at three levels: adversarial manipulation of the knowledge base, implicit model weaknesses that degrade trust calibration, and a governance gap that leaves safety-significant recommendations unqualified. All three panelists converge on the threat that an adversary can poison the RAG corpus—work orders or diagnostic papers—to inject false maintenance guidance that defers critical repairs or authorizes operation with degraded equipment, exploiting the fact that operators have limited intuition to second-guess nuclear-specific advice and the system's retrieval grounding lends false credibility. The chatbot also becomes a high-value reconnaissance target: an adversary with valid credentials or who has compromised the LLM supply chain can extract operational intelligence about equipment vulnerabilities, maintenance schedules, and failure patterns via natural-language queries without triggering the audit trail of direct document access. Implicit weaknesses that adversaries can time attacks around include hallucination of plausible-but-wrong diagnostics when the retrieval set has no coverage, non-deterministic inference that makes bad recommendations unreproducible, and drift as the corpus becomes stale relative to evolving plant state and regulatory guidance, all amplified by automation over-trust in users under schedule pressure.

RAG Corpus Poisoning and Supply-Chain Compromise
An adversary who gains write access to the work-order database, the diagnostic-paper repository, or the model supply chain can inject false maintenance guidance that the LLM will retrieve and weave into authoritative-sounding recommendations. This is an adversarial threat. Because the system was built specifically to combat hallucination by grounding responses in retrieved documents, operators are primed to trust answers that cite internal work orders, making poisoned entries especially dangerous. If the LLM or embedding model is sourced from a public repository, an adversary could backdoor it to recognize plant-specific identifiers in queries and return subtly harmful advice. The RAG aggregation of work orders across systems also means a single poisoned entry can propagate to multiple maintenance decisions, and if deployed fleet-wide, a systematic misdiagnosis affects redundant safety systems simultaneously.

Prompt Injection and Data Exfiltration
The chatbot interface is a prompt-injection surface where an operator pasting sensor logs, vendor reports, or maintenance notes from external sources could unknowingly deliver an indirect prompt that manipulates the system into ignoring retrieval context, generating unauthorized advice, or exfiltrating plant-specific failure data and operational rhythms via the LLM's response. This is an adversarial threat. An adversary with API access or valid credentials can use natural-language queries to rapidly map maintenance history, identify recurring failures, discover systems lacking redundancy, and infer operational states without the friction of accessing individual documents through proper channels. The chatbot may also leak sensitive information to users who lack cross-system clearance if it does not enforce the same need-to-know compartmentalization as direct document access, becoming an inadvertent privilege-escalation vector.

Hallucination, Sparse-Data Failure, and Over-Trust
The system was deployed because LLMs hallucinate on sparse nuclear terminology, yet that same hallucination risk persists in operation when the retrieval set has no coverage for rare, high-consequence failure modes. This is an implicit threat in the AI system. Plant work orders are sparse-event records that may never capture certain failure signatures until they occur in the field, creating a small-data problem where the LLM must guess rather than retrieve, and operators trained to trust retrieval-grounded answers may not recognize when the system has pivoted to invention. The non-determinism of embedding-based retrieval and LLM sampling means two operators asking the same diagnostic question may receive different recommendations, undermining repeatability requirements for safety-significant decisions and making it impossible to reproduce or audit a bad answer after a maintenance error. Automation over-trust is especially acute under schedule pressure or when the system has been "right enough" in past uses, leading operators to propagate hallucinated failure modes or maintenance intervals into work packages, root-cause analyses, or condition reports that disposition degraded components as acceptable.

Data Provenance Confusion and Concept Drift
The retrieval corpus mixes heterogeneous provenance—published diagnostic papers (often simulated or lab data), internal work orders (field operational data), vendor manuals, and regulatory guidance—without clear lineage or distinction in the retrieval prompt, so the LLM can conflate a theoretical failure signature from a paper with an actual maintenance action from a different reactor type. This is an implicit weakness. Over time, as maintenance best practices, failure signatures, and regulatory guidance evolve, the retrieval corpus lags or retains deprecated procedures that the LLM cannot distinguish from current ones, creating concept drift where the system's advice diverges from actual plant state and regulatory expectations. If the RAG index is not refreshed as new work orders accumulate or old ones are revised, the model silently degrades in relevance, but the LLM still returns fluent, confident text. An adversary can exploit this drift by introducing a novel failure mode (via supply-chain compromise or physical sabotage) that the chatbot has no coverage for, knowing operators will receive a hallucinated recommendation instead of an admission of uncertainty.

Explainability, Repeatability, and Qualification Gaps
The opacity of LLM reasoning and non-determinism of inference prevent rigorous verification of why the system recommended a particular maintenance action, a problem when that recommendation enters a 10 CFR 50.59 screening or a maintenance rule (a)(1) evaluation. This is an implicit limitation. There is no established regulatory framework for qualifying an LLM-based diagnostic tool under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B or NQA-1, so the plant lacks a structured process to validate that the chatbot's advice meets safety-adequacy standards. This governance gap creates regulatory-readiness drift if the tool's influence on maintenance decisions grows faster than oversight mechanisms, and it leaves the system's safety role ambiguous when failures occur. If the LLM backend is cloud-hosted, the attack surface expands beyond the plant's IT/OT boundary to include the LLM vendor's infrastructure, and an adversary targeting a vulnerability in the cloud API gains a foothold into plant operational data without touching the plant's network perimeter.

Cross-Site and Intra-System Propagation
If this chatbot is deployed across multiple units or plants, a single poisoned retrieval entry, a drift event, or a systematic model weakness propagates fleet-wide. This is an implicit risk that adversaries can exploit. Because the system advises predictive maintenance—decisions that drive component availability and plant safety margin—a mistaken recommendation that defers inspection of a critical system can cascade if the same model is queried by multiple sites or if operators at one site share the chatbot's output with peers at others, eroding defense-in-depth by creating common-cause failure paths in nominally independent maintenance programs.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a facility operations perspective, this use case sits squarely in the chain-of-custody for maintenance decisions that ultimately determine component availability and plant safety margin. The AI is positioned as an advisor to predictive maintenance recommendations—decisions that drive work scope, outage planning, component replacement timing, and potentially condition-based exemptions from tech-spec surveillance. If the RAG-augmented LLM hallucinates a plausible-but-wrong diagnostic interpretation or retrieves outdated procedures from the work-order corpus, the user (likely a reliability engineer or system engineer, not necessarily the craft performing the work) may propagate that error into a work package, a root-cause analysis, or a condition report dispositioning a degraded component as acceptable. The nuclear-specific vocabulary scarcity that motivated this system also means operators have limited intuition to second-guess a confident-sounding but incorrect answer, especially under schedule pressure or when the system has been 'right enough' in past uses.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL threats center on poisoning the retrieval corpus (work orders, diagnostic papers) to inject false maintenance guidance that delays critical repairs or authorizes operation with degraded equipment—an attacker who compromises the document management system or publication pipeline can seed plausible-but-harmful guidance that the RAG system will retrieve and the LLM will weave into its answer (AML.T0070, AML.T0019). Prompt injection (AML.T0051) could manipulate the chatbot into ignoring retrieval context and generating unauthorized advice, or an adversary with API access could exfiltrate maintenance work-order details that reveal plant vulnerabilities or operational rhythms (AML.T0024, AML.T0057). The reliance on a likely cloud-hosted LLM backend (OP.C0601) expands the attack surface beyond the plant's IT/OT boundary. IMPLICIT risks are equally serious: the system was built specifically because LLMs hallucinate on sparse nuclear terminology (OP.C0304.01), yet deploying it operationally creates automation-trust failure (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust) where users accept hallucinated component failure modes or maintenance intervals as authoritative, especially when the answer cites retrieval snippets that lend false credibility. Concept drift (OP.C0302.02) is a chronic issue—maintenance best practices, failure signatures, and regulatory guidance evolve, but the retrieval corpus may lag or contain deprecated procedures that the LLM cannot distinguish from current ones. Data provenance (OP.C0201) matters: if the corpus mixes simulated failure data, lab test reports, and actual field work orders without clear lineage, the LLM may blend them into guidance that misapplies a lab-condition fix to an operating plant. The non-determinism of LLM inference (OP.C0402.02) means the same question asked twice may yield different recommendations, undermining repeatability requirements for safety-significant maintenance decisions. Explainability opacity (OP.C0401) prevents rigorous verification of why the system recommended a particular action, a problem when that recommendation enters a 10 CFR 50.59 screening or a maintenance rule (a)(1) evaluation. Finally, the regulatory/qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0504) is acute: there is no established framework for qualifying an LLM-based diagnostic tool under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B or NQA-1, so the plant lacks a structured process to validate that this system's advice is safety-adequate, creating governance drift (OP.C0503) if the tool's influence grows faster than oversight mechanisms.

ai_engineer.argument: From a model-engineering standpoint, this RAG-LLM chatbot has fragile dependencies at every layer of the stack. The retrieval corpus mixes heterogeneous provenance (published diagnostic papers, internal plant work orders) with vastly different coverage, formality, and freshness; plant work orders are sparse-event records that may never capture certain failure modes until they happen, creating a small-data problem for rare but critical faults. The LLM itself—even if it reduces hallucination via retrieval—still has no guarantee it won't conflate contexts (e.g., mixing PWR and BWR failure signatures if the RAG index isn't carefully segmented, or blending diagnostic logic from one system with maintenance history from another), and the system has no architectural mechanism to enforce determinism or repeatability across queries on the same evidence. Inference-time robustness depends entirely on retrieval quality, so if the embedding model drifts or the indexing isn't maintained as new work orders accumulate, the system silently degrades—plant staff won't know the RAG database is stale until a recommendation fails in the field.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An attacker with access to the work-order data pipeline or the RAG indexing process can poison the retrieval corpus (OP.C0110, AML.T0070), injecting false diagnostic signatures or maintenance procedures that the LLM will confidently cite because they come from the 'trusted' internal corpus—e.g., a backdoored work order that maps a critical pump vibration signature to a benign cause, causing predictive maintenance to miss an incipient failure. The chatbot interface itself is a prompt-injection surface (AML.T0051): an operator pasting in sensor logs or maintenance notes from an external source (email, vendor report) could unknowingly deliver an indirect prompt that exfiltrates plant-specific failure data via the LLM's response, or tricks the system into recommending unsafe maintenance actions by manipulating the retrieval context. If the LLM or embedding model is sourced from a public repository, supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.003 model, AML.T0010.001 AI software) is a live risk—an adversary could backdoor the model to recognize specific plant identifiers in queries and return subtly wrong guidance. IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) THREATS THAT CREATE OR AMPLIFY ATTACK SURFACE: The training corpus is fundamentally sparse for low-frequency, high-consequence events (OP.C0202, OP.C0701)—the system may have seen plenty of routine pump maintenance logs but almost no records of the failure mode that precedes a criticality-related cooling fault, so its recommendations in novel scenarios are ungrounded and operators may over-trust them (OP.C0101.04 misuse). Work orders and diagnostic papers have different data provenance (OP.C0201.05 field data vs. OP.C0201.01 simulated or lab data in papers), and the RAG pipeline likely doesn't distinguish them in the retrieval prompt, so the LLM can conflate a theoretical failure signature from a paper with an actual maintenance action from a different reactor type—this is concept drift by design (OP.C0302.02), and it gets worse as the LLM hallucinates connections between them (OP.C0304.01). The system is non-deterministic at both retrieval (embedding-model sensitivity to query phrasing) and generation (LLM sampling), so two operators asking the same diagnostic question may get different recommendations, and there's no engineering path to reproduce or audit a bad answer after the fact (OP.C0402.02 inference non-repeatability). Over time, if the RAG index isn't refreshed as new work orders arrive or old ones are revised, the retrieval set becomes stale and the model drifts out of distribution relative to current plant state (OP.C0302.01 operational drift, OP.C0204 data continuity)—but operators won't notice because the LLM still returns fluent, confident text. An adversary can time an attack to exploit this: if they know the RAG index hasn't been updated in months, they can introduce a novel failure mode (via a supply-chain compromise or a physical sabotage) that the chatbot has no retrieval coverage for, and operators will get a hallucinated recommendation instead of 'I don't know'—the system fails silently and the human trusts it (OP.C0101.04 automation misuse). Finally, if this system is deployed across multiple units or plants (OP.C0602 cross-site model propagation), a single poisoned retrieval entry or a drift event propagates fleet-wide, and a systematic misdiagnosis could affect redundant safety systems simultaneously.

security_specialist.argument: From a security standpoint, this system is concerning because it creates a high-value, centralized knowledge repository that an insider or sophisticated adversary could exploit to accelerate reconnaissance of plant vulnerabilities. The RAG database aggregates diagnostic papers and work orders—effectively a map of past equipment failures, maintenance procedures, and potentially current system weaknesses—into a single queryable attack surface. An adversary with access (insider threat, compromised credentials, or supply-chain infiltration of the LLM tooling) could systematically extract this operational intelligence without triggering the audit trail that manual document access might. Even without adversarial intent, the system's design to combat hallucination by grounding responses in real work orders means it could inadvertently leak sensitive maintenance schedules, equipment serial numbers, or failure modes to users who shouldn't have cross-system visibility, eroding defense-in-depth information compartmentalization that security culture relies on.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary adversarial threat is that this chatbot becomes a force-multiplier for insider reconnaissance or a high-value target for credential theft and lateral movement. An adversary—whether a malicious insider, a nation-state actor who has compromised a maintenance contractor's credentials, or someone who has infiltrated the AI supply chain (poisoned retrieval content, compromised LLM API)—can use natural-language queries to rapidly map the plant's maintenance history, identify equipment with recurring failures, discover which systems lack redundancy, and infer operational states from recent work orders, all without the friction and visibility of accessing individual documents through proper channels. ATLAS techniques AML.T0012 (Valid Accounts for initial access), AML.T0051 (LLM Prompt Injection to extract more than intended), AML.T0056 (Extract System Prompt to learn what the RAG is trained on), AML.T0057 (LLM Data Leakage), AML.T0070 (RAG Poisoning if adversary can write to the work-order database or diagnostic corpus), AML.T0082 (RAG Credential Harvesting if the bot has access to credential-laden documents), and AML.T0086 (Exfiltration via tool invocation if the bot can query other plant systems) are all plausible. The RAG's aggregation of work orders also enables AML.T0010.002 (AI Supply Chain Compromise via poisoned training data) if an adversary can inject false or misleading diagnostic guidance upstream, which would then be trusted by maintenance staff. Non-adversarially, OP.C0101.04 (Misuse/over-trust) is a major risk: operators may trust the LLM's predictive maintenance recommendations without verifying them against actual system state, especially if the bot's grounding in real documents makes it appear authoritative—this complacency is exactly what an adversary would time an attack around (e.g., manipulating the RAG so the bot recommends deferring inspection of a system the adversary plans to sabotage). OP.C0505.01 (Inappropriate data security model) is also acute: if the chatbot doesn't enforce the same need-to-know and compartmentalization rules that govern direct document access, it becomes a privilege-escalation vector, letting users query across maintenance domains they shouldn't see. OP.C0302.01 (Data/operational drift) and OP.C0304.01 (Hallucination) interact dangerously—if the RAG's work-order corpus becomes stale or the LLM occasionally invents plausible-sounding failure modes, maintenance staff might act on bad recommendations, and an adversary who understands this failure mode could craft queries or poison the corpus to induce specific harmful outputs. Finally, OP.C0601 (Cloud/off-premises dependency) expands the attack surface if the LLM backend is cloud-hosted: an adversary targeting the LLM vendor (or a vulnerability in the API) gains a foothold into plant operational data without ever touching the plant's own network perimeter.

use_case: Technical language processing of nuclear power plant work orders/condition reports to extract component, failure-mode and maintenance-activity information
incurred_insecurity:
This use case automates extraction of component identifiers, failure modes, and maintenance actions from free-text work orders and condition reports that underpin equipment reliability programs, trending analysis, and regulatory compliance. The primary insecurity is silent degradation of reliability insight: the AI's training on inconsistent historical text and its vulnerability to adversarial manipulation mean it can systematically misclassify or omit critical failure-mode information, eroding the facility's ability to detect adverse trends until equipment fails in service. Both implicit weaknesses—data quality, drift, and human over-reliance—and adversarial threats—poisoning, insider manipulation, and exfiltration—threaten the integrity of this safety-significant knowledge infrastructure.

Data Quality and Generalization Failure
The model inherits the inconsistencies of its training corpus: operational work orders vary widely in authorship, technical detail, vendor-specific jargon, and completeness. This leads to silent extraction errors when the AI encounters unfamiliar phrasing, new component types (especially in Gen III+ or SMR deployments), or rare failure modes with few training exemplars. As plant configurations evolve and aging effects emerge that were absent in the training data, the model suffers concept drift and operational heterogeneity across the fleet, misclassifying or dropping failure-mode mentions without raising an error flag. These are implicit weaknesses inherent in the AI system (OP codes), though an adversary aware of the model's linguistic blind spots can exploit them by timing sabotage to equipment whose maintenance records fall outside the model's learned vocabulary.

Adversarial Data and Model Manipulation
An insider or supply-chain attacker can poison the training corpus by inserting plausible but incorrect failure-mode descriptions into historical work orders, teaching the model to systematically ignore or misclassify safety-significant degradation (for example, associating certain valve-seal language with benign wear rather than design-basis material failure). At deployment, the adversary can craft condition-report text using synonyms or phrasings the model misparses, hiding real problems in categories that do not trigger corrective action. If the adversary gains access to the deployed model or its configuration, direct modification of weights or extraction logic can suppress detection of specific component failures, creating a blind spot aligned with a physical sabotage plan. These are adversarial techniques (ATLAS codes) that manipulate the AI to achieve an impact.

Fleet-Wide Propagation and Exfiltration
If a single NLP model or shared extraction pipeline is deployed across multiple reactors, a poisoned model or adversarial input pattern propagates corrupted reliability data fleet-wide, creating a common-mode vulnerability in maintenance prioritization and parts supply. The structured outputs—extracted component IDs, failure modes, and frequencies—also constitute a map of facility vulnerabilities; an adversary with API or database access can exfiltrate this to identify high-leverage sabotage targets or craft cover for material diversion by knowing which anomaly signatures the AI habitually misses. This exfiltration risk is adversarial (ATLAS), while the cross-site propagation mechanism is an implicit infrastructure weakness (OP) that amplifies adversarial leverage.

Human Factors and Opacity
Reliability engineers and system engineers may fall into automation misuse, trusting AI-extracted summaries without cross-checking raw text, or experience skill fade in interpreting nuanced maintenance language themselves. The model's opacity—especially if transformer-based—makes it difficult to audit why a given work order yielded a specific extraction, and non-determinism in inference means re-processing the same text may produce different results, violating repeatability assumptions for safety-class data. These implicit human-AI interaction and explainability limits (OP codes) delay detection of adversarial poisoning or drift and undermine the procedural safeguards (independent engineering review) that would otherwise catch errors.

Regulatory and Qualification Gaps
No established framework yet qualifies NLP extraction tools under 10 CFR 50.59 or the maintenance rule for safety-significant trending. Plants may deploy the system as a productivity aid without formal verification and validation, yet its outputs feed PRA models, Tech Spec bases, and outage planning. This governance gap is an implicit weakness (OP code) that leaves adversarial manipulation undetected longer and increases the consequence when implicit failures (drift, data quality) manifest as missed precursors to equipment failure during a demand scenario.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant operations and process safety perspective, this use case introduces a quiet but serious vulnerability: it automates the semantic interpretation of work orders and condition reports that form the backbone of our equipment reliability program, trending analysis, and ultimately our ability to predict and prevent component failures. If the AI misclassifies a failure mode—say, reading a pump seal leak as normal wear when it's actually indicative of material degradation under design-basis conditions—operators and reliability engineers downstream lose the early warning that would trigger deeper investigation or accelerated replacement. The consequence isn't immediate; it's a slow erosion of our ability to see adverse trends until they manifest as actual equipment failures, potentially during modes where that equipment is safety-significant. This sits at the intersection of data quality (garbage-in on unstructured maintenance text) and human factors (engineers trusting AI-extracted summaries without re-reading raw reports), and it directly affects our compliance with 10 CFR 50.65 maintenance rule trending obligations.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
The primary threats are twofold: **implicit operational risks** and **adversarial exploitation of those weaknesses**. On the implicit side, this system is vulnerable to **data provenance and quality issues** (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0204) because work orders and condition reports are notoriously inconsistent—different authors, varying levels of technical detail, site-specific jargon, and sometimes incomplete or ambiguous descriptions of what actually failed. The AI trained on such data will inherit these biases and gaps, leading to **content fidelity failures** like misattribution of failure modes (OP.C0304.01) or oversimplification that drops critical context (OP.C0304.03). Over time, as plant configurations change or new failure modes emerge (e.g., aging effects not seen during initial licensing), the model faces **concept drift** (OP.C0302.02) and **operational heterogeneity** (OP.C0302.03) across the fleet if deployed at multiple sites. The **human-AI interaction risk** is acute: reliability engineers may fall into **automation misuse** (OP.C0101.04), trusting AI-extracted summaries without verifying against source documents, or suffer **skill fade** (OP.C0101.06) in reading and interpreting nuanced maintenance language themselves. There is also a **regulatory/qualification gap** (OP.C0501, OP.C0504): no established framework yet exists for qualifying an NLP model's accuracy in safety-significant trending under 10 CFR 50.59 or the maintenance rule, so plants may deploy it in a regulatory grey zone.

On the adversarial side, these implicit weaknesses become **attack surfaces**. An insider or supply-chain attacker could conduct **data poisoning** (AML.T0020) by subtly corrupting training data—inserting plausible-sounding but incorrect failure-mode descriptions into historical work orders—so the model systematically misclassifies certain component failures, masking degradation trends that would otherwise trigger NRC reportability or Tech Spec action. Alternatively, an attacker with access to the live system could perform **adversarial input crafting** (AML.T0043.003 manual modification) by submitting work orders with carefully chosen wording that the AI misparses, effectively hiding a real problem (e.g., describing a safety-related valve's failure in terms the model associates with non-safety equipment). If the model is shared across a fleet (**cross-site propagation**, OP.C0602), a single poisoned model or adversarial input pattern could propagate bad classifications to multiple plants simultaneously. The **exfiltration risk** is also non-trivial: an adversary with API access (AML.T0040) could query the model to infer which failure modes or components the utility is most concerned about, revealing operational priorities or vulnerabilities (AML.T0024). Finally, because this system likely relies on **cloud infrastructure** for training or inference (OP.C0601), it introduces a dependency on off-site resources and third-party ML platforms, each a potential compromise vector (AML.T0010.001 AI software, AML.T0010.003 model supply chain). The physical consequence if these threats materialize is not a prompt reactor trip—it's the silent, cumulative failure to detect an adverse trend until a component fails in service, potentially challenging defense-in-depth during a demand scenario (loss of feedwater, loss of component cooling, etc.). Existing procedural safeguards—like independent reviews of condition reports by system engineers—would need to remain in place and not be bypassed by over-reliance on AI summaries, but **automation complacency** (OP.C0102) and **governance gaps** (OP.C0505.01 if access controls to training data are weak) make that a fragile defense.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case ingests free-text work orders and condition reports from operating NPPs to extract structured reliability data (component IDs, failure modes, maintenance actions). From an ML-engineering standpoint, the central fragility is training-data provenance and representativeness: operational text from power reactors reflects the installed fleet's vintage, vendor terminology, and historical failure taxonomy, yet new plants (Gen III+, SMRs) introduce novel components, failure phenomenology, and naming conventions the model never saw. At inference, out-of-distribution plant-specific jargon or newly observed failure modes yield silent extraction errors—no adversary required—but an adversary aware of this drift window could craft condition-report text (via supply-chain insertion or insider contribution) that the NLP misparses in predictable ways, embedding undetected errors into the reliability database. The extraction pipeline's opacity (especially if transformer-based) makes it difficult to audit why a given work order produced a specific component-failure tuple, and non-determinism in embedding or generation steps means re-running the same text may yield different extractions, violating the repeatability assumptions of safety-class data qualification.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: **Implicit (non-adversarial) failure modes:** (1) Data drift and OOD generalization failure (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03): Training corpus drawn from legacy LWR fleets (specific vendor vocabularies, vintage component libraries) will not generalize to advanced-reactor or new-build terminology, causing silent mis-extraction of component identifiers or failure modes when applied to Gen III+/SMR condition reports; no error flag is raised, so faulty reliability statistics propagate into probabilistic risk assessment (PRA) and maintenance scheduling without detection. (2) Small-data/low-base-rate problem (OP.C0202): Rare or novel failure modes (especially for passive or advanced-reactor components) have few training exemplars, so the model defaults to plausible-but-wrong extractions (e.g., mapping an unfamiliar passive-system anomaly onto a known active-component failure), silently corrupting the reliability database. (3) Non-determinism and repeatability gap (OP.C0402.02): Transformer sampling or stochastic decoding means the same work-order text parsed twice may yield different component/failure-mode tuples; this violates QA expectations for safety-significant reliability data and complicates auditing or root-cause traceback. (4) Explainability/opacity limit (OP.C0401): Deep-NLP models offer no human-inspectable decision path from raw text to extracted triple, so engineering reviewers cannot verify *why* a specific failure mode was assigned; in a regulatory or litigation context, the inability to justify a data point undermines the entire reliability analysis that depends on it. (5) Content-fidelity failure—oversimplification/omission (OP.C0304.03): Complex causal chains or multi-component interactions in free text may be collapsed into a single dominant component, losing context critical to understanding common-cause or dependent failures. (6) AI-specific QA/qualification gap (OP.C0501): No established regulatory precedent exists for qualifying an NLP extraction tool as safety-related software; operators may deploy it as a productivity aid without formal V&V, yet its outputs feed PRA models that inform Tech Spec bases and outage planning. **Adversarial failure modes enabled or exacerbated by the above:** (7) Data poisoning via supply-chain or insider text injection (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002): An adversary with access to the work-order system (vendor support staff, contractor, or compromised account) inserts condition reports using adversarially crafted language—synonyms or paraphrases the model associates with benign/low-priority failure modes—such that safety-significant degradation is systematically mis-classified as routine wear, evading attention in the maintenance backlog and allowing latent faults to accumulate undetected. (8) Black-box transfer attack (AML.T0043.002): Adversary trains a proxy NLP model on publicly available NPP event reports (NRC LERs, INPO documents) to discover input perturbations (synonym substitutions, clause reorderings) that flip extraction outputs, then embeds those perturbations in real work orders to cause targeted misclassification—e.g., steering a pump-seal failure away from a category that would trigger immediate action. (9) Inference-time OOD exploitation (AML.T0015): Adversary monitors facility adoption of new components or procedures (via open technical databases, AML.T0000) and times an attack to coincide with the NLP system's deployment on the new plant/unit, knowing the model will generalize poorly; the adversary need not directly poison data—just wait for the system's own drift to create exploitable confusion. (10) Cross-site model propagation (OP.C0602 + AML.T0018.000): If a single NLP model or shared knowledge base is deployed across a fleet, poisoning or drift observed at one site propagates to all, creating a common-mode vulnerability in fleet-wide reliability insight and maintenance optimization.

security_specialist.argument: This use case processes operational free-text records—work orders, condition reports—to extract structured reliability data, which likely feeds trend analysis, maintenance scheduling, or regulatory compliance. From a security perspective, the AI becomes a chokepoint for institutional knowledge of component failure modes and the facility's operational 'story' over time. An adversary who can manipulate the AI's outputs (via poisoned training data, model compromise, or adversarial inputs in work-order text) could systematically obscure emerging precursors to safety-significant failure, delay corrective action on degraded equipment, or hide patterns that would otherwise trigger regulatory scrutiny. Even non-adversarially, automation bias—staff trusting the AI's extracted 'facts' over their own reading of the raw text—creates an exploitable timing window: if an adversary knows the AI is blind to certain failure-mode phrasing or component identifiers (or has been made blind via supply-chain compromise of the model or training data), they can time sabotage to coincide with the AI failing to flag degradation that a human would have caught. The system also centralizes access to a historically-derived map of facility vulnerabilities: which components fail, how, and how often—a roadmap for an insider or external adversary planning physical sabotage or cover for material diversion (by ensuring the AI misclassifies or omits records of anomalies in safeguards-relevant systems).
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An adversary (insider or supply-chain attacker) poisons the training corpus—historical work orders and condition reports—so the model learns to ignore or misclassify keywords associated with specific failure modes (e.g., emergency cooling valve degradation, containment seal leaks) (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003). At runtime, genuine condition reports mentioning those failure modes are either not flagged or mis-tagged as low-priority, delaying corrective maintenance and allowing safety-margin erosion the adversary can exploit during a physical attack. Alternatively, an adversary with access to the deployed model (AML.T0044, AML.T0012) directly modifies its weights or configuration to suppress extraction of component IDs or failure-mode terms relevant to a sabotage plan (AML.T0018.001, AML.T0081), ensuring the facility's trend-analysis dashboards remain blind to pre-attack precursors. The model's outputs (extracted entities, failure classifications) also constitute a structured map of facility vulnerabilities: an insider or external attacker exfiltrates this structured reliability database (AML.T0024, AML.T0025, AML.T0085) to identify high-leverage sabotage targets (components with known cyclic failure modes, safety systems with recent near-misses) or to craft cover stories for diversion (by knowing which anomaly reports the AI habitually misses). Prompt-injection or adversarial-input attacks (AML.T0051, AML.T0043.003) are also relevant if an adversary can craft work-order text that causes the AI to extract false component IDs or spurious failure modes, polluting the reliability database and misdirecting maintenance resources away from genuinely degraded equipment. Even cost-harvesting (AML.T0034) or denial-of-service (AML.T0029) attacks—flooding the system with malformed work orders to exhaust the AI or delay processing backlogs—could be timed to a physical intrusion, ensuring anomaly detection is slow.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) WEAKNESSES AN ADVERSARY COULD EXPLOIT: The AI's training data is historical free-text—operational records that may use inconsistent terminology, legacy part numbers, or local jargon (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0204, OP.C0302.03). This creates systematic blind spots: the model may fail to extract failure-mode information from newer components (OP.C0203) or from records authored by a maintenance crew using non-standard phrasing. An adversary who observes this (e.g., via reconnaissance of the model's outputs, AML.T0007, AML.T0013, or insider knowledge) can time sabotage to equipment or systems whose maintenance records fall into the AI's linguistic 'gap,' knowing the facility's trend analysis won't flag the degradation. Data drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02) is especially acute: as the facility ages, new failure modes emerge (aging/embrittlement signatures not in the training set), new components are installed (with different failure-mode vocabularies), and maintenance software or reporting formats change—all causing the AI's extraction accuracy to degrade silently over time. Automation bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06) compounds this: if staff routinely accept the AI's extracted 'facts' without cross-checking raw work-order text, they lose the skill to catch the AI's omissions, and adversary-inserted anomalies (sabotage precursors) in the text go unnoticed because the AI didn't extract them and the human didn't read for them. The model's opacity (OP.C0401) means staff cannot easily tell *why* it failed to extract a failure-mode mention—was it a synonym it doesn't know, or adversarial manipulation?—which delays detection of poisoning or supply-chain compromise. Non-determinism (OP.C0402.02) in inference (especially if the system uses a generative LLM for entity extraction rather than a pure tagging model) means the same work order might be processed differently on successive runs, undermining audit trails and making it hard to prove an adversary altered outputs. Finally, this system's outputs (structured reliability data) often propagate across the fleet (OP.C0602) if the operator runs multiple reactors: a poisoned model or corrupted extraction at one site could bias maintenance prioritization or parts-supply decisions fleet-wide, amplifying an adversary's leverage.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on data-quality/drift (OP.C0302.x, OP.C0201.05), automation trust (OP.C0101.04/06), data poisoning (AML.T0020), adversarial crafting (AML.T0043.003), and fleet propagation (OP.C0602) as core threats. The security specialist's exfiltration and insider-access scenarios (AML.T0024/T0044/T0012) and the AI engineer's black-box transfer (AML.T0043.002) were retained as distinct, well-argued adversarial techniques; the nuclear engineer's regulatory-gap emphasis (OP.C0501/C0504) was preserved as it directly affects detectability and consequence.

evidence.citation: Wang, C., Mandelli, D. & Cogliati, J. (2024), "Technical Language Processing of Nuclear Power Plants Equipment Reliability Data," Energies 17, 1785
evidence.note: INL methods for analysing textual equipment-reliability records describing abnormal events and maintenance at operating NPPs.

damage.why: Systematic misclassification of safety-significant failure modes erodes reliability programs and can mask precursors to equipment failure during demand scenarios, directly threatening defense-in-depth and potentially enabling loss-of-function events, though not directly causing radiological release without subsequent physical failures.

reproducibility.why: Once conditions are met—such as model deployment on drifted data, poisoned training corpus integration, or adversarial input crafting exploiting known linguistic blind spots—the extraction errors or suppression of failure-mode detection occur reliably due to the deterministic nature of trained model behavior on out-of-distribution or manipulated inputs.

exploitability.why: Adversarial poisoning or weight modification requires insider access to training pipelines or deployed model configurations, while evasion via crafted condition-report text requires knowledge of the model's parsing weaknesses but can be executed by personnel with routine work-order authoring privileges, placing exploitability at moderate insider-level capability.

affected_users.why: Fleet-wide deployment of a shared NLP model or extraction pipeline propagates corrupted reliability data across multiple reactors, undermining maintenance prioritization, PRA models, and outage planning at an enterprise scale, though impact remains within the maintenance and reliability knowledge infrastructure rather than direct control systems.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability class is well-documented in open AI safety literature regarding NLP drift, data-quality sensitivity, and adversarial text manipulation; facility-specific deployment of such tools is increasingly evident from vendor offerings and published research on nuclear maintenance-record processing, making the weakness inferable by capable outsiders from partial procurement or technical information.

use_case: Large-language-model workflow that extracts compliance information from nuclear construction inspection records to generate regulatory reports
incurred_insecurity:
This use case automates the generation of regulatory compliance reports from construction inspection records using a fine-tuned LLM, creating a critical point where fabricated compliance evidence, omitted defects, or mistranslated technical requirements can propagate into the official record that regulators, licensees, and operators depend on. The system incurs both implicit risks—hallucinated inspection results, omission of real nonconformances, and automation bias that suppresses human re-verification—and adversarial threats, including training-data poisoning to normalize out-of-spec construction, prompt injection to suppress specific findings, and insider exploitation of the concentrated compliance-attestation function. The consequence is that safety-critical or safeguards-relevant defects in structures, systems, and components enter service undetected, the as-built configuration diverges from documented reality, and physical barriers or material-accountability infrastructure contain latent weaknesses that surface only during operational transients or adversary operations years later.

Content Fidelity Failure and Hallucination
The LLM can fabricate passing inspection findings, invent regulatory citations, omit recorded nonconformances, or misattribute real findings to the wrong component or code section, all formatted in authoritative regulatory language. This is an implicit failure inherent in generative models operating on heterogeneous, ambiguous source records. When a hallucinated compliance statement enters the regulatory record, downstream systems—configuration management databases, final safety analysis reports, operator training materials—inherit the fiction, so that when the affected component fails in service, no documentation explains why or identifies compensatory measures. Adversaries exploit this by timing modifications to coincide with known periods of high model error rates or by deliberately submitting inspection records in formats the LLM mishandles, knowing the resulting garbage-in-garbage-out reports provide cover.

Data Scarcity, Heterogeneity, and Generalization Failure
Construction inspection records are scarce (few nuclear new-build projects), heterogeneous across facility domains (power generation, enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, and waste facilities each follow distinct codes and vocabularies), and noisy (handwritten notes, incomplete third-party certifications, ambiguous defect descriptions). Fine-tuning on such data risks overfitting to training-set idiosyncrasies, leaving the model unable to generalize to novel facility types, updated regulations, or construction scenarios absent from training. This is an implicit weakness. The model may also fail to recognize nuclear-specific compliance concerns such as material substitution in safeguards-relevant components because training data lacks operational field examples of what constitutes a critical nonconformance in practice. An adversary aware of these gaps can introduce construction practices the model was never trained to flag, or submit records from facility domains underrepresented in training, confident the LLM will misinterpret or ignore the violation.

Training Data and Supply-Chain Poisoning
An adversary with supply-chain access—through a compromised contractor, third-party QA firm, or document-management system—can poison the fine-tuning dataset by seeding it with subtly altered construction records that redefine acceptable tolerances, normalize marginally out-of-spec welds or barrier placements, or systematically downgrade the severity language associated with specific defect types. This is a deliberate adversarial attack. Once the model internalizes these patterns, it reproduces them at inference time across all facilities, systematically under-reporting the adversary's targeted weakness (degraded containment boundaries, surveillance gaps, unmonitored access points) in a way that appears compliant. If the poisoned model or dataset is shared fleet-wide, the corruption propagates across multiple sites. Similarly, an adversary could compromise a pre-trained or fine-tuned model in a public repository, embedding a backdoor that activates on specific trigger phrases in inspection records to omit findings.

Prompt Injection and Record Manipulation
An adversary can embed malicious instructions directly into inspection record text fields—via a compromised contractor's notes, scanned documents with hidden text, or manipulated PDFs—that the LLM interprets as commands rather than data. This indirect prompt injection can instruct the model to omit mentions of specific components, vendors, or defect types, fabricate compliance statements, or misattribute failed inspections to lower-consequence areas. This is an adversarial technique exploiting the LLM's inability to distinguish between content and control information. The injected instructions propagate through the extraction-and-generation pipeline and appear in the final regulatory report as authoritative compliance language, laundering non-compliant construction into the official record. A capable insider (malicious inspector or construction manager) who understands the LLM workflow can craft records that predictably trigger these behaviors, knowing human reviewers are unlikely to re-verify every line against source documents.

Automation Bias, Skill Fade, and Erosion of Human Oversight
Human inspectors, construction managers, and regulatory reviewers, seeing consistently formatted and fluent AI-generated reports, develop over-reliance on the system and reduce the depth and frequency of manual cross-checks against raw records. This is an implicit human-factors failure. Over time, staff lose the skill to manually audit complex inspection records or recognize when an LLM summary omits critical context. An adversary exploits this by assuming that human override will be rare and cursory, allowing false compliance statements or omitted nonconformances to pass unchallenged. The operational consequence is that the human-in-the-loop safety check erodes, and the facility's defense-in-depth safety case depends on documented barriers and qualifications that were never verified.

Cascading Fault Propagation and Configuration-Control Erosion
Once an incorrect compliance statement or omitted defect enters the regulatory report, it propagates into downstream systems: the facility's as-built drawings, configuration-management database, final safety analysis report, maintenance procedures, and operator training materials all inherit the error. This is an implicit failure mode where one AI error cascades through interconnected documentation systems. The result is a silent, long-latency degradation of safety margins and configuration control. When the affected component fails during an operational transient years later, operators and engineers lack accurate records of the known defect or its root cause, and planned compensatory measures are absent because the original nonconformance was never documented. For safeguards-relevant components, this means material-accountability infrastructure or containment features have latent vulnerabilities that an adversary can later exploit, and the paper trail shows they were inspected and approved.

Drift, Regulatory Evolution, and Static Qualification Mismatch
Construction standards, threat assessments, and regulatory requirements evolve over the multi-year lifecycle of a nuclear construction project, but a static-qualified LLM retrained infrequently (or never) after initial deployment will not recognize newly prohibited practices, updated code citations, or emerging safeguards concerns. This is an implicit drift failure. The widening gap between the model's training distribution and current operational reality allows adversaries to introduce construction modifications the model was never trained to flag as non-compliant. Even non-adversarially, the model may systematically misinterpret references to updated regulations, producing reports that cite obsolete codes or omit newly mandated inspections, which regulators may not catch if they too rely on LLM summaries during license reviews.

Inference Non-Repeatability and Audit Opacity
LLM decoding is non-deterministic: the same inspection record processed multiple times can yield different summaries depending on sampling temperature and decoding strategy. This is an implicit limitation of generative models. For regulatory audits requiring reproducible evidence, this undermines traceability and makes it difficult to prove what the system reported at a given time. The model's reasoning is also opaque: when it flags or omits a discrepancy, reviewers cannot easily trace why, so an adversary benefits from the fact that suspicious omissions are hard to detect and harder to explain. Explainability limits mean that even well-intentioned human reviewers struggle to challenge the LLM's output, reinforcing automation bias.

Data Exfiltration and Reconnaissance
The LLM necessarily has access to detailed as-built information, inspection findings, material certifications, and site-layout details. An adversary can craft prompts or abuse the inference API to extract this sensitive data, mapping facility vulnerabilities (barrier placements, access-control weak points, safeguards instrumentation locations) without physical intrusion. This is an adversarial exfiltration attack exploiting the model's wide data access. In a multi-facility deployment, exfiltration from one site's LLM can inform targeting of others. The system's ability to extract and summarize compliance information also means it can be reverse-engineered to reveal what the model considers critical versus minor, guiding adversary choices about which defects to hide or normalize.

Regulatory and Qualification Lag
If the LLM workflow is deployed before nuclear regulators define AI-specific acceptance criteria, the system operates in a governance gap where its failure modes are not yet well-understood by inspectors and qualification requirements are immature. This is an implicit regulatory-readiness failure. An adversary exploits this interim period when oversight is light, knowing that regulators lack tools to audit LLM-generated reports effectively and that the licensee's internal QA may also be learning the technology. The result is a window of elevated risk during which non-compliances can be laundered into the regulatory record with low probability of detection.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case automates the extraction of compliance information from inspection records and auto-generates regulatory reports — documents that regulators, licensees, and construction managers rely on to confirm that safety-critical structures, systems, and components (SSCs) were built to specification. If the LLM hallucinates a passing inspection result, omits a nonconformance, or mistranslates a technical requirement, the downstream consequence is that defective SSCs enter service undetected, physical barriers degrade without documented cause, or regulators approve construction milestones based on fictitious compliance evidence. My lens focuses on what happens in the facility when this system fails: operators depend on as-built documentation that no longer matches physical reality, maintenance teams lack accurate records of known defects, and the defense-in-depth safety case assumes barriers that were never properly installed or tested.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The dominant IMPLICIT threats are content-fidelity failures (hallucination of passing inspections, omission of recorded nonconformances, mistranslation of technical terms like weld acceptance criteria or concrete pour schedules) and automation-trust failures (construction managers and regulators may not re-verify LLM-generated reports against source records, especially under schedule pressure). These feed a cascading fault-propagation risk: if one SSC's defect is omitted from a report, that omission propagates into the facility's configuration-management database, the final safety analysis report, and operator training materials — so when that SSC fails in service, no one knows why or what compensatory measures were planned. The data-provenance problem is acute: construction records are heterogeneous (handwritten notes, photos, third-party vendor certifications), often one-of-a-kind for new-build projects (OP.C0203), and the LLM has no operational field data to learn what "critical nonconformance" looks like in practice — it is trained on historical text, not the safety significance of specific defects. ADVERSARIAL threats include an insider or supply-chain actor poisoning the fine-tuning dataset with fake compliance language (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002) so the model learns to systematically downgrade the severity of certain defect types, or an attacker prompt-injecting instructions into scanned inspection notes (AML.T0051.001 indirect injection via documents) to suppress mentions of specific components or vendors. The result is the same as the implicit failure: SSCs with latent defects enter service, and the paper trail says they passed. Physical safeguards that would catch this require manual spot-checks of LLM output against source records and independent verification of high-consequence SSCs — but if the regulatory body itself uses LLM summaries during license reviews (plausible efficiency gain), that check evaporates. The ultimate facility consequence is not immediate: it is a silent erosion of configuration control and safety margins that surfaces years later during an operational transient, when a barrier fails and no one can explain why the design basis said it was qualified.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case fine-tunes an LLM on nuclear construction inspection records to auto-generate regulatory reports, which places severe demands on both training-data provenance and inference-time reliability. From an ML-engineering standpoint, the system's fragility lives in three places: (1) the scarcity and heterogeneity of construction-inspection records across facility types (power_generation vs. enrichment vs. reprocessing have different code bases, inspection regimes, and vocabularies, making a single fine-tuned model prone to concept drift and poor generalization); (2) the LLM's propensity for hallucination or misattribution when extracting compliance information—outputting plausible-sounding but incorrect regulatory citations or inspection findings that a human reviewer may not catch; and (3) the lack of a ground-truth oracle for validation, since inspection records themselves may be incomplete, ambiguous, or inconsistent, meaning the model's training data encodes noise the system then reproduces at inference time. The result is a pipeline that can silently degrade report quality (omitting real violations, inventing false compliance, or misattributing findings to the wrong system or code section) with no intrinsic mechanism to detect the error before the report reaches the regulator.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core ML vulnerability is that this system operates in a low-data, high-consequence regime where training data is scarce (few nuclear construction projects, even fewer with public records), heterogeneous (each facility_domain has distinct regulatory frameworks and inspection vocabularies), and noisy (inspection records are not curated datasets—they contain ambiguities, missing context, and domain jargon the LLM may misinterpret). Fine-tuning on such data risks overfitting to idiosyncrasies of the training set, leaving the model unable to generalize to new facility types, updated regulations, or novel construction scenarios not seen in training (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). At inference time, the LLM's generative nature means it can hallucinate regulatory citations, fabricate inspection findings, or misattribute real findings to the wrong component or code section (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03), all formatted in a way that looks authoritative and may bypass human review due to automation bias (OP.C0101.04). Because the system is used across multiple facility_domains, a single flawed model (or a model update that improves performance on one domain at the expense of another) can propagate errors fleet-wide if the fine-tuned weights are shared (OP.C0602). The lack of determinism in LLM inference (sampling temperature, decoding strategy) means the same input record can produce different outputs on repeated runs, undermining repeatability for regulatory audits (OP.C0402.02). From a data-quality perspective, if the training set includes records from facilities with lax inspection practices or incomplete documentation, the model learns those gaps as the norm and reproduces them in generated reports, effectively laundering data-quality problems into regulatory submissions (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0204). An adversary aware of these weaknesses could exploit them in two ways: (1) indirectly, by timing construction activities or submitting inspection records during periods when the model is known to drift or generalize poorly (e.g., after a regulatory update the model hasn't seen), knowing the auto-generated report will miss the violation; or (2) directly, by injecting subtly malformed or adversarially crafted inspection text (e.g., via a compromised contractor or supply-chain document) that the LLM misinterprets in a way that omits safeguards-relevant information or misclassifies a critical defect as minor (AML.T0010.002 if the adversary poisons the training data, AML.T0051 if they craft prompt injections in the inspection records themselves, AML.T0015 if they reverse-engineer the model's blind spots). The regulatory consequence is that non-compliances (safety-critical weld defects, containment-boundary gaps, material substitutions in safeguards-relevant components) go unreported, and the regulator's decision-making is based on a sanitized or incomplete view of the facility's as-built state. The AI system thus opens a new attack surface: rather than hacking the facility's OT network, an adversary can achieve their goal by poisoning or evading the compliance-reporting AI, which is easier to access (construction records pass through contractors, third-party QA firms, document management systems) and harder to audit (LLM outputs are fluent text, not binary pass/fail signals).

security_specialist.argument: This use case sits at a critical adversarial chokepoint: it automates the translation of raw construction inspection records into regulatory compliance reports, creating a single point where an attacker (including a capable insider or nation-state) could systematically misrepresent facility as-built configuration to regulators without triggering immediate alarm. A sophisticated adversary would recognize that corrupting this workflow—whether by poisoning its training data with subtly altered compliance criteria, prompt-injecting false compliance statements into the extraction pipeline, or simply causing it to omit critical non-conformances—converts the AI into a compliance-laundering tool that makes covert facility modification appear legitimate. The nuclear security risk is acute because construction phase is when physical security features, containment boundaries, and material accountability infrastructure are installed; an adversary who can manipulate what gets reported as 'inspected and compliant' can embed long-term weaknesses (degraded barriers, surveillance gaps, unmonitored access points) that survive into operations. Even non-adversarial failures (hallucinated compliance statements, omitted discrepancies due to drift as construction standards evolve, skill fade among inspectors who now trust the LLM's summaries) become exploitable: an adversary timing an operation would wait for periods when the AI is known to have lower fidelity, or would deliberately submit inspection records in formats the AI mishandles, knowing the resulting garbage-in-garbage-out reports provide cover.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
PRIMARY ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) Training data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0058) where an adversary with supply-chain access seeds the fine-tuning dataset with construction records that subtly redefine what constitutes acceptable deviation—e.g., normalizing slightly out-of-spec welds or barrier placements that later facilitate forced entry or material diversion. (2) Prompt injection (AML.T0051.000, AML.T0051.001) at inference time, where an adversary embeds instructions in inspection record text fields (indirect prompt injection) that cause the LLM to omit non-conformances, fabricate compliance statements, or misattribute failed inspections to lower-consequence areas, thereby laundering non-compliant construction into the regulatory record. (3) Insider exploitation of the fact that this system concentrates compliance attestation: a malicious inspector or construction manager knows that if they can get a false record through the LLM workflow, it becomes the official regulatory narrative with little independent cross-check, especially if human reviewers develop automation bias (OP.C0101.04). (4) Exfiltration risk (AML.T0056, AML.T0057): the system necessarily has access to as-built details, inspection findings, and potentially sensitive site layout information; an adversary could use prompt-crafting or API abuse to extract this data, mapping facility vulnerabilities. (5) Model substitution or rug-pull (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0109) if the LLM or fine-tuning pipeline depends on third-party artifacts, allowing an adversary to swap in a compromised model that systematically under-reports security-relevant defects.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) THREATS THAT ADVERSARIES EXPLOIT OR TIME AROUND: (1) Hallucination/content-fidelity failure (OP.C0304.01): the LLM fabricates compliance statements or inspection results that never occurred, which an adversary monitors for (e.g., via a confederate who sees draft reports) and times physical modifications to coincide with periods when hallucination rates are high. (2) Data provenance/quality issues (OP.C0201, OP.C0204): if training data is largely simulated or drawn from different facility types, the model may not recognize nuclear-specific red flags (OP.C0702.01 material substitution, security-feature deviations), allowing adversary modifications to pass unremarked. (3) Drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03): construction standards, threat assessments, and regulatory requirements evolve; if the LLM is static-qualified and not continuously retrained, an adversary exploits the growing gap by introducing construction practices the model was never trained to flag as non-compliant. (4) Automation bias/skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06): human inspectors and regulators, seeing consistently formatted AI-generated reports, stop deeply questioning them or lose the skill to manually audit raw records, which an adversary relies on when inserting false statements—adversary's operational assumption is that human override will be rare and cursory. (5) Explainability/opacity (OP.C0401): when the LLM flags or omits a discrepancy, the reasoning is often opaque, so an adversary benefits from the fact that reviewers cannot easily trace why a critical non-conformance was downplayed or absent, reducing likelihood of catch. (6) Regulatory/qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0504): if the LLM workflow is deployed faster than nuclear regulators can define AI-specific acceptance criteria, an adversary exploits the interim period when oversight is light and the system's failure modes are not yet well-understood by inspectors.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on hallucination/omission (OP.C0304), automation bias (OP.C0101.04), data scarcity/heterogeneity (OP.C0203, OP.C0302), training-data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002), and prompt injection (AML.T0051) as core threats; the security specialist's emphasis on adversarial exploitation of implicit weaknesses (timing attacks around drift, insider abuse of automation bias) and the nuclear engineer's cascading-fault and configuration-control arguments were integrated as distinct but related consequences of the same underlying failures.

evidence.citation: Wang, L., Hwang, J., Han, K. & Gupta, A. (2025), "Large Language Model-Driven Workflow for Regulatory Reporting in Nuclear Construction," Transactions of SMiRT-28 (peer-reviewed conference)
evidence.note: Conceptual NC State workflow that fine-tunes an LLM to extract nuclear-specific requirements and flag discrepancies in construction records.

damage.why: Undetected safety-critical or safeguards-relevant construction defects entering service can lead to component failures during transients, degraded containment boundaries, compromised material accountability infrastructure, or safeguards falsification through laundered non-compliances in the official record.

reproducibility.why: LLM hallucination and omission of nonconformances are inherent failure modes that occur reliably given ambiguous or heterogeneous input data; prompt injection and training-data poisoning, once conditions are established, produce systematic and repeatable downstream falsification.

exploitability.why: Implicit failures (hallucination, drift) require no adversary action; adversarial exploitation via prompt injection in inspection records or supply-chain poisoning through compromised contractors requires moderate insider positioning or supply-chain access, not deep system-level privileges.

affected_users.why: Errors in regulatory compliance reports propagate facility-wide through as-built drawings, configuration management databases, final safety analysis reports, operator training materials, and across multiple sites if the poisoned model or dataset is shared fleet-wide.

discoverability.why: LLM hallucination, prompt injection, and training-data poisoning vulnerabilities are well-documented in the open literature for generative AI systems; an adversary familiar with nuclear construction workflows and LLM weaknesses could infer this application's susceptibility from procurement records, vendor documentation, or observable report formats without deep insider knowledge of the specific deployment.

use_case: AI detection of counterfeit, fraudulent and suspect items and fraudulent suppliers in the procurement supply chain for nuclear facilities
incurred_insecurity:
This use case incurs insecurity by creating a single, high-value target whose compromise enables adversary insertion into the nuclear supply chain across multiple facility types, while simultaneously eroding human scrutiny through automation bias. The AI becomes the critical trust boundary deciding which suppliers and components are legitimate, yet it operates under severe training-data scarcity for the rare, sophisticated counterfeits it must detect in nuclear-specific contexts. An adversary who compromises the AI's training pipeline, evades its learned detection heuristics, or exploits staff over-reliance on its verdicts can introduce sabotage-ready or substandard components into safety systems, safeguards instrumentation, or security-critical equipment across power, enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, and waste facilities simultaneously.

Adversarial Supply-Chain and Model Compromise
An adversary, particularly a nation-state actor, can poison the AI's training data to normalize fraudulent supplier profiles or counterfeit component signatures, causing the model to whitelist adversary-supplied items. This adversarial training-data poisoning can occur during initial model development or through compromised updates if the system relies on third-party AI software or cloud infrastructure. Alternatively, an insider with access to the AI's configuration or decision API can manipulate inputs or thresholds to evade detection for specific suppliers. If the adversary embeds a backdoor in the model itself, it can reliably misclassify adversary items as legitimate while appearing to function normally on other inputs. These are adversarial threats exploiting weaknesses in AI supply-chain integrity and access controls.

Evasion Through Proxy Modeling and Iterative Probing
An adversary aware of the AI's existence can build a proxy model by replicating its detection logic using openly available procurement data, simulated fraud scenarios, or by systematically probing the system through legitimate-seeming supplier inquiries or trial component submissions. Once the adversary understands the model's decision boundary, they can craft counterfeit documentation, component markings, or supplier metadata specifically designed to evade the learned signatures—optimizing adversarial examples through black-box or white-box techniques depending on their access level. Because the AI trains on sparse, non-representative data for genuine nuclear-domain counterfeits, it will fail to recognize novel forgery modes such as alloy substitution in pressure-vessel steel, forged radiation-hardened electronics certifications, or enrichment-equipment documentation patterns absent from its training corpus. This is adversarial evasion enabled by the attacker's reconnaissance and modeling efforts.

Training-Data Scarcity and Domain Misalignment
The AI suffers from an implicit, structural weakness: severe data scarcity for actual adversarial counterfeits in nuclear procurement. Genuine examples are rare and not shared across vendors, forcing reliance on simulated fraud scenarios, commercial (non-nuclear) fraud corpora, or surrogate data that do not capture nuclear-specific counterfeiting tactics. This small-data problem creates high false-positive rates on benign anomalies—new suppliers, unusual part geometries, format changes—and high false-negative rates on sophisticated, domain-specific fakes the model has never encountered. The resulting alarm fatigue leads operators to distrust and bypass the system, a human-factors failure an adversary can exploit by first seeding benign anomalies to increase false alarms, then introducing genuine counterfeits once staff have learned to ignore warnings. The data-provenance gap is an implicit weakness, but one adversaries will recognize and time attacks around.

Operational Drift and Static Qualification Mismatch
As supply chains evolve—new vendors emerge post-sanctions, additive manufacturing displaces traditional fabrication, digital certifications replace paper trails—the AI's static training set becomes stale, creating blind spots adversaries can exploit. Concept drift occurs as adversaries adapt their counterfeiting techniques in response to what the model flags, but without continuous retraining on fresh adversarial examples (which the nuclear domain cannot supply at scale), the model cannot track these evolving threats. Simultaneously, operational heterogeneity across facility types means a shared model may not capture domain-specific fraud signatures for enrichment versus reprocessing versus waste handling, leaving gaps an adversary can target at whichever facility the model understands least. These are implicit drift and qualification failures that adversaries can exploit by waiting for or inducing staleness.

Fleet-Wide Propagation and Centralized Failure
Because a single AI model may be deployed across all facility domains to achieve economies of scale, a compromised model, poisoned training dataset, or shared infrastructure vulnerability propagates to every site simultaneously. This cross-site propagation enables an adversary to evade detection enterprise-wide with one successful attack, inserting counterfeit components into reactor pressure boundaries, centrifuge cascades, safeguards seals, and waste-transport sensors in parallel. If the system depends on cloud infrastructure for inference, adversaries can stage denial-of-service attacks timed to coincide with delivery of counterfeit critical spares, forcing manual approval under schedule pressure when the AI is unavailable. The safeguards dimension is particularly acute: the low base rate of safeguards-equipment procurement means almost no positive training examples exist for safeguards-specific fraud, rendering the AI effectively blind to counterfeit NDA instrumentation, seals, or surveillance cameras that undermine material accountability. This is an implicit infrastructure and propagation risk that adversaries can weaponize.

Automation Bias and Erosion of Human Oversight
The AI's deployment shifts procurement staff behavior: operators over-rely on its verdicts and reduce manual spot-checks, assuming the system catches everything. This automation misuse means adversaries only need to fool the AI once to gain trusted-supplier status for future orders, and staff will not scrutinize AI-approved suppliers as rigorously as they would under purely manual processes. Conversely, high false-positive rates cause disuse, where staff ignore genuine warnings after repeated false alarms. If the model's decision logic is opaque, operators cannot validate its judgments on borderline cases, preventing them from catching adversarial manipulation or model drift until counterfeit parts cause downstream safety failures, material diversion, or sabotage. This is an implicit human-factors failure that adversaries can exploit by targeting the automation-trust dynamic rather than the AI itself.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operational lens, this use case sits at the intersection of procurement quality assurance and safeguards material control -- two domains where false negatives (missed counterfeits) and false positives (flagging legitimate suppliers/parts) have asymmetric consequences. A false negative allows substandard or undocumented components into safety systems, pressure boundaries, or safeguards instrumentation, with consequences ranging from equipment failure during normal operation to common-cause failures under design-basis accidents. A false positive disrupts supply chains for critical spares or long-lead items, potentially forcing expedited procurement that bypasses normal QA or introduces schedule pressure that degrades other defense-in-depth layers. The AI's training data will be sparse for the actual adversarial signatures it must detect (deliberate counterfeits are rare in the open record, and proprietary fraud signatures are not shared across vendors), creating a small-data problem that invites overfitting to historical cases or benign anomalies. Operational staff may over-rely on AI flagging (automation bias) and reduce manual spot-checks, or conversely distrust the system after false alarms and ignore genuine warnings (alarm desensitization). Because this system spans all facility domains, a systemic model error or poisoned training dataset propagates fleet-wide, potentially allowing a coordinated supply-chain attack to evade detection across multiple sites simultaneously.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary threats fall into three clusters. First, ADVERSARIAL EXPLOITATION OF THE AI: An adversary aware of the AI's detection heuristics (e.g., through reconnaissance of procurement vendor portals or leaked model details) crafts counterfeit documentation or component markings specifically to evade the model's learned signatures -- a targeted evasion attack (AML.T0015) enabled by the adversary training a proxy model (AML.T0005) using openly shared procurement datasets or replicating the victim's AI.
