If the AI relies on a third-party cloud service for inference (common for vendor-neutral fraud detection platforms), the adversary could poison the training data during model updates (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000) or compromise the AI supply chain (AML.T0010) to embed a backdoor that whitelists specific fraudulent supplier signatures. The result is undetected counterfeit components in safety-critical systems (reactor coolant pumps, control rod drive mechanisms, containment isolation valves) or safeguards equipment (sealing devices, surveillance cameras, NDA instrumentation), undermining both safety margins and material accountability. Second, IMPLICIT OPERATIONAL RISKS THAT ADVERSARIES CAN TIME ATTACKS AROUND: The AI will suffer from severe training-data scarcity for actual adversarial counterfeits (OP.C0202, OP.C0701.01) -- most training data will be historical legitimate-part variations, benign supplier errors, or simulated fraud scenarios, not genuine adversarial forgeries. This creates high false-positive rates on edge cases (new suppliers, unusual part geometries, documentation format changes), leading to alarm fatigue and operator disuse (OP.C0101.05) where staff begin approving flagged items without investigation. An adversary can exploit this by first seeding benign anomalies to increase false alarms, then introducing genuine counterfeits once operators have learned to ignore warnings. The model will also drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03) as supply chains evolve (new vendors post-sanctions, additive manufacturing adoption, digital twin-based certifications), and static qualification at deployment will not capture these operational changes, creating blind spots. Third, FLEET-WIDE PROPAGATION: Because the same AI model may be deployed across all facility domains (power, enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, waste) to achieve economies of scale, a single poisoned model update or shared training-data compromise propagates to all sites (OP.C0602), enabling an adversary to simultaneously evade detection across an entire national nuclear enterprise. If the model's inference depends on cloud infrastructure (OP.C0601), adversaries can stage denial-of-service attacks (AML.T0029) timed to coincide with delivery of counterfeit critical spares, forcing manual approval processes under schedule pressure when the AI is unavailable. The safeguards dimension is particularly acute: counterfeit seals, cameras, or NDA components compromise material control and verification, and the low base rate of safeguards equipment procurement (OP.C0701.01) means the AI has almost no positive training examples of genuine safeguards-specific fraud, making it effectively blind to this threat vector.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case relies on learning patterns of fraud or counterfeiting from examples — but the training set faces a severe low-base-rate and data-scarcity problem: genuine counterfeits in nuclear procurement are rare, highly varied, and may not resemble historical patterns. The model is vulnerable to adversarial manipulation by suppliers who can probe the system's decision boundary via legitimate-seeming inquiries or iteratively craft documentation/parts that evade its learned features. Because the system gates supply-chain trust decisions, automation bias is acute: operators may accept fraudulent items the AI missed (disuse when it should catch something novel) or reject legitimate suppliers flagged by spurious model artifacts (misuse). The AI's training data provenance — likely a mix of non-nuclear fraud corpora, simulated scenarios, and rare real incidents — means it generalizes poorly to nuclear-specific counterfeiting tactics (e.g., material property forgery for safety-critical alloys or radiation-hardened electronics), a domain where the adversary can exploit knowledge of what the model has *not* seen.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core threat is adversarial evasion (AML.T0015) enabled by an attacker building a proxy model (AML.T0005) or probing the system (AML.T0040 if API access exists, or physical procurement trials) to craft fraudulent documentation or components that pass AI screening. This is exacerbated by the model's training on data (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01–03) that underrepresents rare, high-consequence nuclear counterfeiting modes — e.g., alloy substitution in pressure-vessel steel, forged certifications for safety-critical electronics, or documentation patterns specific to enrichment or reprocessing equipment. If the model is trained on general commercial-fraud datasets or synthetic scenarios rather than domain-specific operational data (OP.C0201.05), it will not recognize nuclear-contextual red flags, allowing an adversary to slip through. Operationally, this creates an automation-trust failure (OP.C0101.04/05): procurement staff over-rely on the AI and miss novel fraud modes (misuse), or distrust false positives and bypass it entirely (disuse), effectively disabling the safeguard. The system is also vulnerable to concept drift (OP.C0302.02): as adversaries learn what the model flags, they adapt their counterfeiting techniques, but the model's static training set cannot capture emergent fraud patterns unless continuously retrained on fresh examples — which the nuclear domain cannot supply at scale. If the model's decision logic is opaque (OP.C0401), operators cannot validate its judgments on borderline cases, and a sophisticated supplier could exploit this opacity to stage a supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.000/001) by presenting items that narrowly satisfy the model's learned heuristics but fail in safety-critical ways. Finally, if the system is deployed across multiple facility types (power, enrichment, reprocessing), it faces operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.03): what constitutes a 'suspect' supplier or part differs by domain, yet a shared model may not capture these distinctions, creating blind spots an adversary can target at whichever facility type the model understands least.

security_specialist.argument: From a security lens, this use case is especially concerning because it sits at a critical trust boundary -- the AI becomes the gatekeeper deciding which suppliers and components are legitimate versus fraudulent or counterfeit. An adversary who compromises or influences this AI can 'whitelist' their own insertion into the supply chain (state-level adversaries embedding malicious parts, or nation-states planting sabotage-ready components that the AI fails to flag). Even without direct AI compromise, the AI creates new insider pathways: a malicious procurement officer or supply-chain manager with access to the AI's training data or decision thresholds could poison it to accept specific fraudulent suppliers, or manipulate its inputs to route acceptance of particular suspect items. The AI also erodes human scrutiny -- operators will defer to its verdicts, making it a high-value, low-visibility target for an adversary who wants a stepping-stone into the facility's component inventory across multiple facility types (enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, waste handling). Security culture suffers if staff assume 'the AI checks everything,' reducing adversary detection likelihood during the brief window when a sophisticated fake passes through.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial Threats:** An adversary (especially a nation-state with resources to craft sophisticated counterfeits or compromise AI supply chains) could target this system in several ways. First, AI supply chain compromise (AML.T0010) -- poisoning the training data (AML.T0020) with examples that normalize certain fraudulent supplier profiles or counterfeit component signatures, so the model learns to accept them. Second, if the AI uses a cloud-based or third-party model (OP.C0601), an adversary could compromise that infrastructure or insert a backdoored model (AML.T0018.002) that reliably misclassifies adversary-supplied items as legitimate. Third, an insider with access to the AI's configuration or decision API (AML.T0012, AML.T0040) could craft adversarial inputs (AML.T0043) or manipulate supplier metadata to evade detection (AML.T0015), effectively 'teaching' the AI to trust a specific malicious supplier. The AI also creates a new attack surface for external adversaries: if they can infer the model's decision boundary (AML.T0024.002, white-box or black-box optimization AML.T0043.001), they can engineer counterfeits that narrowly pass the AI's checks -- a capability valuable for embedding sabotage components (e.g., subtly defective valves in enrichment centrifuges, manipulated electronics in safeguards instrumentation). Finally, the AI's existence may enable adversaries to time attacks: if they know the AI has high false-negative rates during certain operational periods (e.g., when retrained on sparse data, OP.C0202), they could schedule insertion of fraudulent items then, or exploit staff complacency when the AI 'usually catches everything' (OP.C0102).

**Implicit (Non-Adversarial) Weaknesses Exploitable by Adversaries:** Even absent direct attack, this use case has structural vulnerabilities an adversary would recognize and exploit. The AI likely suffers from severe data scarcity (OP.C0202, OP.C0203) -- genuine counterfeit/fraudulent supplier examples in the nuclear domain are rare, so the model trains on simulated or surrogate data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02), making it vulnerable to novel, sophisticated fakes it has never seen. Adversaries know this and can craft 'zero-day counterfeits' the AI won't recognize. The model also faces operational drift (OP.C0302.01) as adversaries evolve their techniques (new forgery methods, new shell-company structures), but the AI remains static unless continuously retrained -- a qualification gap (OP.C0303) adversaries can exploit by waiting until the model is stale. Cross-site propagation (OP.C0602) is a major risk: if one compromised model is deployed across enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, and waste facilities, a single adversarial poisoning event propagates fleet-wide, letting the adversary insert malicious components into multiple facility types simultaneously. Automation bias (OP.C0101.04, misuse/over-trust) means procurement staff won't scrutinize AI-approved suppliers as carefully, so an adversary only needs to fool the AI once to gain trusted-supplier status for future orders. If the AI has low explainability (OP.C0401), operators can't audit *why* it flagged or approved a supplier, making it hard to catch adversarial manipulation or drift until counterfeit parts cause downstream failures (by which point sabotage or material diversion may already have occurred). Finally, the AI's decision-making may lack regulatory oversight (OP.C0504) if nuclear procurement QA frameworks don't yet account for AI-driven supplier vetting, leaving a governance gap adversaries can exploit with less risk of external audit.

**Consequence Severity:** Because this AI gates the entire procurement supply chain across safety-critical (power generation, waste transport), security-critical (enrichment, reprocessing), and safeguards-critical (fuel fabrication, reprocessing) facility types, its compromise has cross-cutting impact. Adversary-inserted counterfeit components could cause safety failures (e.g., defective reactor pressure-boundary parts), enable material diversion (e.g., tampered safeguards seals, manipulated NDA equipment), or create sabotage opportunities (e.g., remotely triggerable valves in enrichment cascades, covertly modified waste-container sensors). The AI's existence also shifts the threat surface: instead of needing multiple insider placements across diverse facilities, an adversary can target one centralized AI system (or its training pipeline) to affect procurement decisions across the entire nuclear enterprise. Even if the AI 'works' most of the time, its occasional failures (false negatives on sophisticated counterfeits, false positives creating supplier-vetting fatigue, OP.C0101.05 disuse) are exactly what a patient, well-resourced adversary would wait for and exploit.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on adversarial evasion via proxy modeling, training-data scarcity as the core implicit weakness, and automation bias as the human-factors failure mode. The security specialist's focus on insider threats and fleet-wide propagation complemented the nuclear engineer's concern for cross-domain heterogeneity and the AI engineer's emphasis on concept drift, forming a unified picture of centralized failure risk.

evidence.citation: Hobbs, C. & Naser, Z. (2025), "Counterfeiting, Artificial Intelligence, and Supply Chains in the Nuclear Sector," Vienna Center for Disarmament and Non-Proliferation
evidence.note: Examines how AI could both facilitate counterfeiting and fraud across nuclear supply chains and help detect counterfeit items and fraudulent suppliers.

damage.why: Compromise enables insertion of counterfeit components into safety systems, safeguards instrumentation, and material control systems across all facility types, directly threatening radiological safety boundaries and safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Training-data poisoning, model evasion via proxy modeling, and exploitation of automation bias are reproducible once adversary achieves access to training pipeline or understands decision boundaries through systematic probing.

exploitability.why: Requires moderate adversary capability: supply-chain position to poison training data or insider access to configuration, plus technical sophistication to craft evasive inputs, but does not require deep facility-specific knowledge once model access is achieved.

affected_users.why: Shared deployment model propagates compromise across all facility domains simultaneously—power generation, enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, and waste storage—enabling fleet-wide counterfeit insertion from single vulnerability exploitation.

discoverability.why: AI procurement-screening systems are increasingly documented in open literature and vendor materials; adversaries can infer existence from procurement records and probe decision boundaries through trial supplier submissions without insider access to internals.

use_case: Automated recognition of symbols in nuclear power plant instrumentation-and-control logic drawings, to digitise legacy design documentation
incurred_insecurity:
This use case creates a dual insecurity: the AI system implicitly corrupts configuration-control baselines through recognition errors that propagate silently into safety-critical engineering records, while simultaneously concentrating attack-relevant knowledge into a queryable form that lowers the barrier for insider sabotage. Symbol misclassification—confusing normally-open with normally-closed contacts, AND gates with OR gates, or omitting hand-annotated field changes—embeds silent errors in the digitized design basis that surface only when engineers use the corrupted records for modifications, troubleshooting, or license reviews. Meanwhile, the digitization itself transforms dispersed, interpretation-resistant paper drawings into a structured database an adversary can mine to identify sabotage targets, even if the AI's accuracy is imperfect.

Out-of-Distribution Generalization Failure and Symbol Hallucination
The model trains on a small, homogeneous corpus—likely one or two reactor designs' worth of drawings with vendor-specific symbol conventions—then confronts decades of legacy documentation spanning multiple vendors, drafting eras, hand-marked revisions, and plant-specific annotation practices it has never seen. When encountering unfamiliar symbol variants, faded photocopies, or non-standard relay representations, the AI does not abstain; it hallucinates plausible but incorrect symbols, producing clean, professional-looking output that masks its uncertainty. A misrecognized interlock logic (NO/NC contact inversion, gate-type confusion, or dropped seal-in path) becomes the authoritative digital record, propagating into safety analyses, modification packages, and operator training materials until someone discovers the discrepancy during an event or physical inspection. This is an implicit AI system failure (operational drift and content-fidelity breakdown), not adversarial, but it creates a corrupted design basis that undermines every downstream engineering decision.

Automation Over-Trust and Verification Gaps
Staff treat machine-digitized drawings as authoritative, especially when the AI produces polished output free of the ambiguities that would trigger skepticism toward hand-digitized records. No ground-truth oracle exists for legacy drawings, the AI's recognition is non-repeatable across runs due to stochastic inference, and it cannot explain why it chose one symbol interpretation over another, so quality assurance defaults to statistical sampling that misses rare but safety-critical errors. The regulatory framework has no established qualification pathway for treating AI-digitized drawings as safety-related configuration records, yet the output directly informs 10 CFR 50.59 evaluations and licensing-basis reviews. This is an implicit human-factors and governance failure: automation trust without commensurate verification rigor, compounded by qualification and regulatory-readiness gaps.

Concentration of Sabotage-Relevant Knowledge
The digitization converts I&C logic from dispersed paper archives requiring domain expertise to interpret into a queryable database that an insider or compromised account-holder can mine for sabotage patterns—"which interlocks can I disable to achieve outcome X without alarming system Y," "which logic paths lack physical diversity." The AI need not be attacked; its intended output is the reconnaissance product. An adversary who gains valid-account access to the digitized repository (or exfiltrates it via conventional cyber means) obtains a force-multiplier for sabotage planning. If the facility treats this as a quality-of-life engineering tool rather than Crown-Jewels design-basis information, access controls and data-security models will be inappropriately weak. This is an implicit weakness—concentration of attack-relevant knowledge without commensurate protection—that an adversary exploits through standard credential-based access and data-collection techniques, not AI-specific attacks.

Adversarial Exploitation of Implicit Weaknesses
An adversary with supply-chain access can poison the training data to systematically misclassify specific symbol types, embedding Trojan-like logic errors across the digitized fleet configuration baseline; an insider can substitute or alter scanned inputs before they reach the AI to inject deliberate misrecognitions that blend into the rest of the output. A sophisticated actor aware of the model's systematic error patterns (discoverable by training a proxy on similar drawings or probing the inference API) can exploit the facility's reliance on the corrupted digital records during safety reviews or modifications. If the same model serves a multi-unit fleet, a single poisoned model or training corpus propagates configuration errors across dozens of plants. These are adversarial techniques exploiting or amplifying the AI's implicit weaknesses, not purely implicit failures, but the adversary's success depends on the baseline fragility the AI system introduces.

Cascading Fault Propagation into Operations and Safety Analysis
Incorrect digital logic diagrams become the authoritative reference for subsequent modifications, troubleshooting, and safety evaluations. Engineers design interlocks, validate protection-system behavior, and plan equipment changes using corrupted records, potentially disabling safeguards, inverting trip logic, or masking component-failure effects until discovered during an incident. The consequence is that the AI's recognition errors propagate through the plant's configuration-management, safety-analysis, and operational decision-making processes, creating latent vulnerabilities that compound over time and across the facility lifecycle.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case sits squarely in engineering record configuration management—the AI produces a digital interpretation of legacy control-logic drawings, which operators, maintenance staff, or future design engineers will trust as faithful to the original. If the AI misrecognizes symbols (confuses a normally-open contact with a normally-closed one, misreads an AND gate as an OR gate, or drops a seal-in path), the digitised record becomes a silent poison pill in the plant's configuration-control baseline. No adversary is required: the AI fails on its own due to drawing-quality variation, symbol-set drift across vintages, or hallucination of plausible-but-wrong logic. The real risk materializes later when someone acts on the corrupted digital record—during a modification, troubleshooting session, or license-basis review—and introduces a logic error into a protection or control system, or fails to diagnose an anomaly because the as-built understanding is wrong.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: **Implicit (non-adversarial) threats dominate.** Training data scarcity is acute: legacy I&C logic drawings span decades of drafting practice, annotation styles, hand-marked revisions, and vendor-specific symbol sets, yet few digitised training corpora exist with ground-truth labels (OP.C0203 new-build data scarcity applies by analogy; OP.C0202 small-data problem for rare symbols or plant-specific conventions). Operational drift is guaranteed: the model trains on one symbol set but encounters undocumented plant modifications, field changes, or drawings from a different-vintage control system upgrade, causing misclassification (OP.C0302.01 data/operational drift; OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity across units or vendors). Hallucination or symbol-substitution (OP.C0304.01) is the cardinal failure mode—confusing NO/NC contacts, logic-gate types, or timer symbols creates aConfiguration Management error that propagates silently until someone uses the corrupted digital record to plan a modification, troubleshoot an interlock failure, or validate a safety analysis (OP.C0301.01 cascading fault propagation into design basis and operations). Content-fidelity failure (OP.C0304) extends beyond hallucination: the AI may oversimplify complex interlocks, omit hand-written annotations that capture as-built deviations, or mistranslate relay identifiers, embedding subtle but safety-significant errors into the digital twin of the control logic (OP.C0304.03 oversimplification/omission). Human-factors amplifiers are severe: staff treat digitised drawings as authoritative (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust), especially if the AI produces clean, professional-looking output that masks its uncertainty; no tradition exists for challenging machine-read logic diagrams the way engineers instinctively verify hand-digitised ones. Verification gaps are structural: the AI is non-deterministic across re-runs (OP.C0402), lacks a ground-truth oracle for legacy drawings (no 'correct' digital version exists to compare against), and cannot explain why it chose one symbol interpretation over another (OP.C0401 explainability limit), so quality assurance defaults to sampling—missing rare but critical errors. Regulatory/qualification mismatch looms: no software-QA framework yet exists for treating AI-digitised drawings as safety-related configuration records (OP.C0501 AI-specific qualification gap; OP.C0504 regulatory readiness gap), yet the output directly informs 10 CFR 50.59 evaluations, licensing-basis reviews, and modification packages. **Adversarial surface: modest but real.** An adversary with access to the training pipeline or input corpus could poison the model to systematically misclassify specific symbol types (AML.T0020 poison training data; AML.T0018.000 poison model), embedding Trojan-like logic errors that survive into the plant's digital configuration baseline—this is a supply-chain threat if the AI vendor or training-data provider is compromised (AML.T0010.002 data, AML.T0010.003 model). At inference time, an insider or external actor who can substitute or alter scanned drawing images before they reach the AI (AML.T0043.003 manual modification of input) can inject deliberate misrecognitions—e.g., flipping an interlock's logic sense—that the downstream human reviewer may not catch if the rest of the drawing looks plausible. The AI also becomes a new reconnaissance vector: probing it with test drawings (AML.T0040 inference API access if cloud-hosted, or AML.T0044 full model access if on-premises) reveals which symbol variants or drawing styles it handles poorly, letting an adversary craft inputs that maximize misclassification while appearing legitimate. Cross-site propagation (OP.C0602) multiplies impact if the same AI model serves a multi-unit fleet or vendor client base: a single training-data poison or model backdoor corrupts configuration records across dozens of plants. The consequence in all cases is the same: **incorrect digital logic diagrams become the plant's authoritative reference**, and subsequent human actions—modifications, troubleshooting, safety reviews—proceed from a corrupted design basis, potentially disabling interlocks, inverting trip logic, or masking the effect of component failures until discovered in the field or during an event.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case is a classic ML-pipeline fragility story disguised as a document-processing task. The model is trained on a corpus of historical control-logic symbols (likely from one or two reactor designs, maybe Westinghouse-style or Korean-standard layouts), then asked to generalise to drawings from other vendors, other eras, different draughting conventions, and possibly hand-annotated or scanned-at-odd-resolution legacy sheets it has never seen. The data provenance is almost certainly a hodgepodge: some clean CAD exports, some photocopies of decades-old blueprints, some with annotations in different languages or faded ink. At inference time, if the system encounters a symbol variant it didn't see in training (a different convention for representing a logic gate, a non-standard relay coil symbol, or a drawing from a plant that was built before the training set was even created), it will either hallucinate a plausible-but-wrong symbol or fail silently, and the digitised I&C logic will be subtly incorrect. The real kicker: this is a one-shot digitisation effort, not a real-time monitoring loop, so there's no online feedback to catch drift or errors until someone tries to use the digitised drawings for safety analysis, modification design, or (worse) exports them to a new facility where they become the authoritative record.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core ML failure mode here is **out-of-distribution generalisation failure combined with hallucination risk**. The model is trained on a small, homogeneous set of drawings (OP.C0202, OP.C0203) -- likely from a single reactor design lineage -- and then deployed against a heterogeneous legacy archive spanning multiple vendors, eras, and draughting standards (OP.C0302.03). When it encounters a symbol or layout convention outside its training distribution, it doesn't abstain; it produces a confident but incorrect classification (OP.C0304.01), and the digitised output becomes a **silent corruption of the design basis**. This is exacerbated by the fact that control-logic drawings are safety-critical: they define interlocks, trip logic, and protection-system behaviour, so a misrecognised symbol (e.g., confusing an AND gate for an OR gate, or a normally-open contact for a normally-closed one) directly propagates into safety analysis, modification packages, or operator training materials. An adversary doesn't need to attack the model itself; they can simply **time their own actions to coincide with known weak spots in the digitised record** -- e.g., exploiting a safety interlock that was mis-digitised and therefore not properly modelled in later safety reviews (this is implicit weakness exploitation, not active model attack, but the AI system created the opening). Alternatively, an insider with access to the training data or the digitisation pipeline could **poison the model by introducing subtly incorrect symbol mappings** (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000), ensuring that specific safety-critical symbols are systematically mis-digitised across the entire legacy archive. The **non-repeatability** of the model (OP.C0402.02) -- if it's using stochastic inference, different runs on the same drawing might yield different symbol interpretations -- further undermines any qualification or audit trail. Finally, the **cross-site propagation risk** (OP.C0602) is severe: if this digitisation workflow is adopted fleet-wide, a flawed model will systematically corrupt the design basis at multiple plants, and the error won't surface until someone tries to reconcile the digitised drawings with physical as-built configuration during an incident or inspection. The safeguards angle is also non-trivial: if an adversary can manipulate the digitised I&C logic to omit or misrepresent containment isolation logic or criticality alarm interlocks, they can create a **paper trail that hides actual facility capabilities** (e.g., making a dual-use research reactor look like it lacks certain safeguards-relevant control paths), which is a safeguards verification problem (OP.C0701 analogy, though not a direct fit).

security_specialist.argument: From a nuclear security perspective, this use case creates a subtle but significant insider-threat pathway: it produces machine-readable, queryable digital representations of I&C logic that previously existed only in dispersed paper or image-based drawings requiring human interpretation to weaponize. An insider (or an adversary who has compromised an insider account) gains a force-multiplier: instead of manually hunting through filing cabinets or image archives for 'which interlock can I disable to cause X without immediately alarming Y,' they now query a structured database the AI built. Even if the AI's recognition accuracy is imperfect, an adversary benefits from the bulk digitization and semantic structuring—errors in benign symbols matter less than correct identification of safety-critical interlocks, which the adversary can verify independently once the AI narrows the search space. The security risk isn't that the AI mis-recognizes a symbol during normal operations; it's that the AI's output becomes a reconnaissance product for an adversary planning a sabotage campaign, and the facility may not treat this digitized I&C logic with the same access-control rigor as the original controlled-distribution drawings because it's viewed as a 'quality-of-life' engineering tool rather than security-sensitive design-basis information.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary insecurity is CONCENTRATION OF ATTACK-RELEVANT KNOWLEDGE IN A QUERYABLE FORM. Legacy I&C drawings, even when scanned, required an adversary to have domain expertise and time to interpret them; the AI's digitization converts them into a database an automated tool (or a less-skilled insider) can mine for sabotage-relevant patterns—'show me all interlocks between the reactor protection system and cooling injection,' 'which logic paths lack physical diversity.' This is an IMPLICIT vulnerability (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0601 if cloud-hosted, OP.C0602 if the model/data propagate across sites) that becomes ADVERSARIALLY EXPLOITABLE (AML.T0012 valid-accounts access, AML.T0036 data-from-repositories, AML.T0025 exfiltration-via-cyber). The AI itself need not be attacked—its intended output is the threat. Secondary: if the AI's recognition errors are NON-RANDOM (e.g., it systematically misses certain interlock types, or hallucinates connections that don't exist—OP.C0304.01), an adversary aware of these patterns (via AML.T0005 proxy model training on similar drawings, or AML.T0013/T0014 model-ontology discovery if they access the deployment) can exploit the facility's reliance on the digitized data to make safety analyses that miss real interlocks or trust phantom ones. The facility's security culture risk: treating this as 'just engineering digitization' rather than recognizing that bulk I&C-logic databases are Crown Jewels for an adversarial saboteur, leading to insufficient access controls (OP.C0505.01), retention on less-secure infrastructure (OP.C0601), and failure to red-team the data product's value to an adversary. A sophisticated attacker (including a nation-state with patient insider access) would absolutely target this: it's a low-noise, high-value reconnaissance product that tells them where to focus physical or cyber sabotage without triggering the alarms that probing the live I&C system would.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on out-of-distribution failure, hallucination/symbol-substitution, and cascading configuration-baseline corruption as the primary threat, with the nuclear engineer and AI engineer providing complementary technical detail. The security specialist's unique contribution—digitization as a reconnaissance product concentrating sabotage-relevant knowledge—was integrated as a distinct adversarial surface that exploits (rather than attacks) the AI's output.
