damage.why: Corrupted safety-critical I&C logic records propagating into protection system modifications, operator training materials, and 10 CFR 50.59 evaluations can disable safeguards or invert trip logic, creating latent pathways to radiological release discovered only during an actual event.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution symbol misclassification is highly reproducible when the AI encounters legacy documentation outside its training corpus (different vendors, eras, hand-annotations), though the specific errors vary stochastically across inference runs.

exploitability.why: Adversarial exploitation (training-data poisoning, input substitution before scanning) requires supply-chain or insider access; however, the implicit threat (symbol hallucination on unfamiliar drawings) requires no adversarial action, only routine deployment against heterogeneous legacy documentation.

affected_users.why: Corrupted digital logic diagrams become the authoritative baseline for facility-wide configuration management, safety analysis, modifications, and operator training, with cross-fleet propagation if the same model serves multiple units.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability class (out-of-distribution generalization failure, symbol hallucination in OCR/drawing-recognition AI) is well-documented in the open literature; an adversary aware of the deployment context could infer susceptibility from procurement records or vendor documentation, and proxy models trained on similar drawings would reveal systematic error patterns.

use_case: Deep-learning material segmentation and 3D semantic mapping to guide robotic sort and segregation of legacy nuclear decommissioning waste
incurred_insecurity:
This use case incurs severe implicit weaknesses in data provenance and operational generalization that adversaries can exploit to defeat material accountability and contamination control. The DL segmentation model drives physical sorting decisions—routing waste to clearance, intermediate, or high-level streams—yet it is trained on limited real legacy waste imagery, relying instead on lab mock-ups, simulated data, or transfer learning from non-nuclear datasets that cannot capture the heterogeneity, corrosion, and undocumented material combinations found in actual decommissioning environments. When the model encounters out-of-distribution materials at inference time, it may confidently misclassify high-activity items as benign or fail to segment special nuclear material, and these errors propagate through the SLAM-fused 3D semantic map into every downstream manipulation decision. Operators supervising the robot out-of-the-loop progressively over-trust the AI-generated map, losing the skill to visually verify material boundaries themselves, so systematic misclassification can persist undetected until waste drums fail acceptance criteria or trigger alarms in storage. Adversaries can exploit these implicit weaknesses—or introduce new ones—through supply-chain compromise, physical adversarial objects, or targeted data poisoning, achieving material diversion or safeguards defeat with high plausibility of deniability because the induced failures resemble natural model drift.

Data Provenance and Operational Drift
Legacy decommissioning waste is inherently heterogeneous, facility-specific, and poorly cataloged, yet the segmentation model must generalize from a training corpus dominated by simulated scenes, lab-fabricated mock-ups, or data transferred from industrial (non-radiological) settings. This provenance mismatch means the model has never seen the full variability of real waste: unusual alloys, degraded containers, co-mingled radiological and chemical hazards, or geometries that evolved over decades of facility operation. At deployment, the model encounters operational drift—materials, surface conditions, and spatial configurations outside its training distribution—and either misclassifies them (labeling activated steel as benign concrete, or a sealed source as low-priority debris) or fails to segment them at all, leaving gaps in the semantic map. Small-data problems for rare but high-consequence items (plutonium-contaminated tools, orphaned sources) mean the model may lack robust features for exactly the materials that matter most to safety and safeguards. This is a non-adversarial implicit threat rooted in the scarcity of training examples from actual legacy sites and the heterogeneity of operational environments that no finite dataset can fully cover.

Goal Misalignment and Cascading Fault Propagation
The system architecture creates a dependency chain: segmentation errors feed the 3D semantic map, the map drives manipulation planning, and the robot acts on potentially incorrect beliefs about material identity and spatial boundaries. Because SLAM fusion incrementally builds a global map from local observations, a misclassification in one frame can persist and propagate—if the model labels a high-activity component as clearance waste early in the scan, that label is embedded in the map and influences all subsequent decisions about which pile to excavate next or which container to open. The manipulation planner has no independent radiological or chemical sensor to verify the model's material class predictions; it trusts the semantic map as ground truth. This cascading fault propagation is implicit in the transfer-learning and SLAM-fusion design, and it means one localized segmentation failure can corrupt the entire decommissioning sequence, leading to physical co-location of fissile materials (criticality risk), misrouting of activated waste (contamination spread), or loss of accountancy for special nuclear material. The goal misalignment is that the model optimizes for pixel-level segmentation accuracy on its training distribution, not for the downstream consequence of a material-routing error in a radiologically hazardous environment.

Static Qualification Mismatch and Cross-Site Model Propagation
Even if the segmentation model was validated on representative waste in a controlled setting, operational heterogeneity across decommissioning sites—different reactor types, waste streams that evolved over facility lifetimes, or legacy items never cataloged—means past qualification does not guarantee future performance. Yet requalifying the model on every new waste pile is impractical, and there is no established regulatory framework for certifying DL vision systems in radiological environments, leaving it unclear what performance threshold is safe or how to enforce it. If a single trained model is deployed across multiple sites to amortize development cost, a systematic flaw (whether accidental drift or deliberate compromise) propagates fleet-wide, and the cross-site deployment amplifies the impact of any vulnerability. This static/dynamic qualification mismatch and the regulatory-readiness gap are implicit governance weaknesses that an adversary can exploit by timing attacks to periods when the model is least qualified for the waste it is encountering, or by embedding a vulnerability in the shared model that triggers only under site-specific conditions the developer never tested.

Automation Trust Failure and Explainability Limits
Operators supervising the robotic sort work out-of-the-loop, observing the 3D semantic map and manipulation outcomes rather than directly handling waste. Over time, they progressively defer to the AI's material classifications, losing the skill and cognitive readiness to visually verify segmentation boundaries themselves. When the model does fail—whether from natural drift or adversarial manipulation—the human backstop is eroded by skill fade and over-trust. The segmentation model's opacity (it offers a pixel-level class label but no interpretable reasoning for why a given material was classified as concrete versus metal, or why a boundary was drawn at a particular edge) prevents operators from understanding whether a classification is confident and grounded or uncertain and extrapolated. Inference-time non-repeatability (the model's output can vary slightly with viewing angle, lighting, or sensor noise) means the same waste item might be segmented differently on successive scans, yet operators have no principled way to reconcile these discrepancies or declare uncertainty. These human-AI interaction failures are implicit, but they create windows of vulnerability that an adversary with insider knowledge or operational observation can exploit—staging an intrusion or material-substitution event during a high-uncertainty period when human cross-checks are least effective.

Adversarial Exploitation: Physical Scene Manipulation
An adversary with physical access to the waste sorting area can introduce intentionally crafted objects—paint patterns, decals, shaped debris, or surface treatments—designed to fool the segmentation model into misclassifying high-consequence items as benign waste. For example, camouflaging a plutonium-contaminated component to visually resemble low-priority concrete rubble would cause the robot to route it to a clearance stream, defeating material accountancy and enabling diversion. This is a manual modification adversarial attack executed in the physical environment, exploiting the model's reliance on visual features that do not correlate with radiological hazard. The attacker needs only local access during waste staging or initial scanning; once the semantic map is corrupted, the error propagates through subsequent manipulation decisions. The domain-specific analogue is material substitution: the adversary is not stealing the item outright but rather mis-sorting it into a pathway where safeguards oversight is weaker or absent, a tactic with historical precedent in non-AI diversion scenarios but now executable by exploiting the model's known brittleness to out-of-distribution appearances.

Adversarial Exploitation: Supply-Chain and Model Poisoning
The segmentation model is a supply-chain attack surface. If an insider or remote adversary gains access to the training pipeline (during initial development, or during field-data retraining cycles where the system is updated with new waste imagery), they can inject mislabeled examples or poisoned data that teach the model to systematically misclassify specific material signatures. For instance, poisoning the training set to associate a particular visual texture with "low-activity" would embed a blind spot the adversary can later exploit by ensuring target items display that texture. Alternatively, an adversary could substitute a backdoored model at deployment—one that performs normally under most conditions but triggers on a specific visual pattern (a backdoor trigger) to misclassify SNM-bearing waste, enabling remote-activated diversion without touching the robot's control system. The transfer-learning origin (a model pre-trained on non-nuclear data, then fine-tuned on limited real waste imagery) makes provenance verification difficult: it is hard to audit whether the base model or the fine-tuning dataset was tampered with. If the system pulls model updates from a shared repository or cloud service, an adversary compromising that infrastructure can push a malicious model to the entire decommissioning fleet, achieving simultaneous material-accountability degradation across multiple facilities. This is a model supply-chain compromise with AI-specific execution (poisoning, backdoor insertion) but traditional consequence (defeat of safeguards, loss of SNM control).

Adversarial Exploitation: Map Exfiltration and Operational Intelligence
The 3D semantic map encodes precise locations, material classifications, and quantities of waste items across the decommissioning workspace. For an adversary targeting special nuclear material, this map is high-value intelligence: it reveals where SNM-bearing items are stored, which waste streams contain accountable material, and the spatial layout of the facility's legacy inventory. If the system is network-connected (for telemetry, model updates, or remote supervision), an adversary who gains cyber access can exfiltrate the map data via conventional means or extract the model itself to infer training-data details and refine physical adversarial attacks offline. Even if the map is not directly accessible, an adversary with insider knowledge of the segmentation model's architecture could craft a proxy model and use it to pre-test adversarial patterns before introducing them into the real scene, reducing the risk of detection. This exfiltration threat is adversarial and cyber-enabled, turning the AI's spatial understanding into a reconnaissance product for follow-on physical intrusion or diversion operations.

Non-Determinism and Adversarial Probing
The segmentation model's inference-time non-repeatability—output varies with viewing angle, lighting, dust levels, or sensor noise—means an adversary can probe the system to identify which scene configurations yield favorable misclassifications, then arrange the waste pile or lighting conditions accordingly before the official scan. For example, an adversary might discover through trial-and-error (or offline proxy-model testing) that a certain reflective surface pattern causes the model to fail at segmenting metal boundaries, then apply that pattern to an SNM-bearing item to ensure it is spatially mis-registered in the map and physically mis-sorted. This is adversarialcraft leveraging the model's implicit non-determinism, and it is difficult to detect because the induced failure looks like natural model noise rather than a deliberate attack. The lack of explainability compounds the problem: operators cannot distinguish a confident, well-grounded classification from an uncertain extrapolation, so adversarially induced errors blend into the background of routine segmentation variability.

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear engineer focused on facility operations and material control, my primary concern is the downstream consequence when a deep-learning segmentation model misclassifies waste material types—particularly if it mistakes high-activity or special nuclear material for benign waste, or vice versa. In decommissioning, robotic sorting decisions driven by AI-generated semantic maps directly determine waste stream routing (clearance vs. intermediate-level vs. high-level storage), contamination control zoning, and criticality safety in segregated containers. If the model fails to generalize from its training environment to the actual heterogeneous legacy waste (OP.C0302.01 operational drift, OP.C0203 new-build data scarcity for legacy facilities), or if an adversary introduces objects designed to fool the segmentation (AML.T0043 craft adversarial data via physical means, AML.T0041 physical environment access), the robot may physically co-locate fissile materials, breach containment by misrouting activated steel, or send accountable material to a clearance pathway—each a direct failure of material control, process safety, or safeguards. The reliance on transfer learning from non-nuclear datasets and SLAM fusion means the model's material-identification confidence may not reflect actual radiological or chemical hazard, and operators working out-of-the-loop (OP.C0101.01) may not catch systematic misclassification until waste drums fail acceptance criteria or, worse, trigger downstream alarms in transport or storage.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: This use case incurs both adversarial and implicit threats rooted in the physical consequences of material misidentification. **Adversarial surface:** An attacker with physical or visual access to the waste sorting area (AML.T0041) can craft adversarial objects—e.g., paint patterns, decals, or shaped debris—that fool the DL segmentation into misclassifying hazardous or accountable material as benign (AML.T0043.003 manual modification, AML.T0015 evade AI model). This opens a pathway to divert special nuclear material by having the robot route it to a low-security or clearance stream, defeating material accountancy (OP.C0702.01 material substitution as a domain-specific analogue). An insider or supply-chain actor (AML.T0010.002 data poisoning, AML.T0020 poison training data) could also inject mislabeled images during model retraining, embedding systematic blind spots for specific material signatures. **Implicit (non-adversarial) threats:** Legacy decommissioning waste is inherently heterogeneous and poorly documented; the model trained on cleaner datasets or simulated environments (OP.C0201.01/.02 simulated/synthetic data, OP.C0302.01 operational drift) will encounter out-of-distribution materials it cannot reliably segment—unknown alloys, degraded containers, or co-mingled radiological/chemical hazards. Small-data problems (OP.C0202) for rare but high-consequence items (e.g., sealed sources, plutonium-contaminated tools) mean the model may never have seen enough examples to learn robust features. The 3D semantic map's accuracy depends on SLAM, which can drift or fail in visually ambiguous or dust-filled environments (OP.C0402.02 inference-time non-repeatability), causing spatial misregistration of material labels and thus sorting errors. Operators supervising the robot out-of-the-loop (OP.C0101.04 over-trust, OP.C0101.01 unfamiliarity) may not recognize when the system is confidently wrong, especially if the model lacks explainability (OP.C0401) for its material classifications. If the same model is deployed across multiple decommissioning sites without site-specific requalification (OP.C0602 cross-site model propagation, OP.C0303 static/dynamic qualification mismatch), a systematic flaw propagates fleet-wide. The safety consequence is direct: misrouted waste leads to contamination spread, worker dose, criticality risk in storage, or loss of accountancy for special nuclear material—each a failure of defense-in-depth that existing manual verification (e.g., radiological survey, non-destructive assay at the waste stream endpoint) would need to catch, but those checks may be bypassed if the AI-driven sort is trusted as authoritative.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case sits at the intersection of perception, manipulation planning, and consequence -- the DL segmentation model must generalize from whatever training corpus it saw to the actual heterogeneous waste pile in front of it, and failures propagate directly into physical sorting decisions with radiological and contamination consequences. My lens focuses on where the ML pipeline is brittle: the provenance and coverage of the training data (how much real legacy waste imagery exists, versus lab mock-ups or transferred/simulated proxies), the robustness of the segmentation model to out-of-distribution materials or configurations it never saw, the feedback loop (or lack thereof) between the model's material class predictions and the actual radiological or chemical properties of what the robot picks up, and the operational qualification gap -- how do you verify that a model trained on one waste stream or facility will perform safely on another, especially when the ground truth for 'correct segmentation' in a contaminated environment is itself hard to obtain without the same robotic system you're trying to deploy? The system architecture creates a dependency chain: perception errors (misclassified material) feed the semantic map, the map drives manipulation planning, and the robot acts on potentially incorrect beliefs about what it is handling, with no easy way to catch the error until after the object is moved.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core insecurity is **training data scarcity and provenance mismatch** (OP.C0201, OP.C0203): legacy waste is heterogeneous, facility-specific, and often inaccessible for extensive imaging campaigns, so the segmentation model is likely trained on simulacra (lab mock-ups, OP.C0201.01/02, or data transferred from non-nuclear industrial settings, OP.C0201.03) that do not capture the full variability of real waste -- unusual material combinations, degraded/corroded surfaces, unexpected geometries, or novel contaminants. At inference time, this creates **operational drift and out-of-distribution failure** (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03): the model encounters materials or configurations outside its training distribution and either misclassifies them (e.g., labeling a high-activity metal component as benign concrete) or fails to segment them at all, and the 3D semantic map encodes these errors as ground truth for downstream planning. Because the system uses transfer learning and SLAM fusion, **goal misalignment and cascading fault propagation** (OP.C0301.01) are risks -- a segmentation error in one frame can persist in the map and influence decisions across the workspace, and the manipulation planner has no independent way to verify material identity beyond the model's output. There is also a **static/dynamic qualification mismatch** (OP.C0303): even if the model was validated on representative waste in a controlled setting, operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.03) -- different facilities, waste streams that evolved over decades, or items never cataloged -- means past qualification does not guarantee future performance, yet requalifying on every new pile is impractical. **From an adversarial perspective**, this opens surfaces: an adversary with physical access could introduce **intentionally crafted objects** (AML.T0043 manual modification, AML.T0015 evade model) designed to be misclassified -- e.g., a high-value or high-hazard item camouflaged to look like low-priority waste, causing the robot to sort it incorrectly and either release contamination or fail to sequester dangerous material (AML.T0031 erode model integrity leading to AML.T0048.003 user harm, AML.T0112 machine compromise if the robot damages itself). An insider or remote attacker could also **poison the training data or model** (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000) during retraining cycles if the system is updated with field data, embedding backdoors that trigger on specific visual patterns to misclassify targeted waste items (AML.T0043.004 insert backdoor trigger, AML.T0010.003 model supply chain compromise if updates are pulled from a shared repository). The **explainability and non-determinism** issues (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02) make it hard for operators to understand *why* the model chose a particular segmentation, so **automation bias and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity** (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01) mean they may not notice or question incorrect sortings until after the fact, especially in a remote/teleoperated scenario where direct visual confirmation is limited. Finally, if this system is deployed across multiple decommissioning sites with a shared model, **cross-site model propagation** (OP.C0602) means a vulnerability or bias in the model (whether accidental drift or deliberate poisoning) can spread fleet-wide, and the **regulatory/qualification gap** (OP.C0501, OP.C0504) -- no established framework for certifying DL vision systems in radiological environments -- leaves it unclear what level of performance is 'good enough' or how to enforce it, increasing the risk that an underperforming or compromised model remains in service.

security_specialist.argument: This use case places a segmentation-and-mapping pipeline in a path-critical decision loop: the robot's physical action (grasping, moving, segregating waste) depends on the AI correctly identifying material boundaries and semantic classes in visually cluttered, radiologically hazardous legacy waste. From a security lens, three threads matter. First, the system becomes an attractive target for supply-chain or insider compromise because corrupting its material classification directly controls which items go into which waste stream—an adversary seeking to divert SNM or mask contamination could poison training data, substitute a compromised model at deployment, or inject adversarial patterns into the scene to mis-sort high-consequence items. Second, the reliance on transfer learning and SLAM fusion means the AI's confidence may not reflect ground truth in novel waste configurations (new materials, unexpected geometries), yet operators will treat its 3D semantic map as authoritative; an adversary timing an intrusion during a period of high segmentation uncertainty (or after subtly inducing drift by altering the visual environment) gains a window where human oversight is weakest. Third, the system concentrates trust: if one compromised model propagates across a decommissioning fleet (cross-site deployment, shared training pipeline), a single supply-chain event could simultaneously degrade material accountability at multiple facilities, and the semantic map itself becomes exfiltration-worthy intelligence (locations and quantities of SNM-bearing waste).
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
Adversarial surface: The segmentation model is vulnerable to adversarial patch attacks in the physical scene (AML.T0043.003 manual modification, AML.T0015 evade model)—an insider or covert entry could place patterns that cause systematic mis-classification of SNM-bearing items into low-activity waste streams, enabling diversion. Supply-chain risk is high (AML.T0010.001 AI software, AML.T0010.003 model): a backdoored segmentation model that triggers on a specific visual cue would let an adversary remotely induce mis-sorting without touching the robot's control system, and the transfer-learning origin (pre-trained on non-nuclear data, fine-tuned on limited real waste imagery) makes model provenance and integrity hard to verify. The 3D semantic map is exfiltration-worthy (AML.T0024.002 extract model, AML.T0025 exfiltration via cyber means): it encodes precise locations and material classifications of waste, which an adversary could use for targeting follow-on physical intrusion or as intelligence on facility inventory. If the system is cloud-connected for model updates or telemetry (OP.C0601), an adversary could stage a remote model-substitution attack (AML.T0018.000 poison model) or exfiltrate map data in bulk. Fleet deployment (OP.C0602) amplifies impact: one compromised model propagates across sites, and the attacker gains simultaneous material-accountability degradation everywhere.

Implicit (non-adversarial) weaknesses that an adversary would exploit or time attacks around: The system exhibits severe data-provenance and drift vulnerabilities. Legacy waste is by definition heterogeneous and poorly documented (OP.C0203 new-build scarcity, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity)—transfer learning on limited real-scene data means the model will encounter out-of-distribution materials (corrosion, unusual containers, mixed debris) where segmentation confidence is low but the system has no principled way to declare uncertainty (OP.C0302 drift/OOD). An adversary observing operations would identify these high-uncertainty periods (via timing, visual cues, or insider knowledge) and stage an intrusion or material-substitution event when human cross-checks are least effective (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust). Automation-trust failure is central (OP.C0101.06 skill fade): operators will progressively defer to the 3D map's semantic labels, losing the skill to visually verify material boundaries themselves, so when the AI does fail (or is attacked), the human backstop is eroded. Non-determinism (OP.C0402.02 inference-time non-repeatability) means an adversary can probe the system to find which viewing angles or lighting conditions yield favorable mis-classifications, then arrange the scene accordingly. Explainability limits (OP.C0401) prevent operators from understanding why a given segmentation was chosen, so an adversarially induced error looks indistinguishable from normal model noise. Finally, the cross-system fault propagation (OP.C0603) is severe: if the segmentation model mis-classifies one item, the SLAM fusion embeds that error into the global 3D map, and downstream decisions (which pile to excavate next, which container to open) inherit the corruption—an adversary achieving one targeted mis-classification can cascade it through the entire decommissioning sequence.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on data-provenance mismatch, operational drift, automation over-trust, and adversarial physical-scene manipulation as the core threats; the security specialist's supply-chain and exfiltration angles and the AI engineer's cascading-fault-propagation framing were integrated without conflict. Added AML.T0005 (proxy model) to capture the adversary's offline testing scenario implicit in the security specialist's probing discussion.

evidence.citation: Extreme Robotics Lab (University of Birmingham) & Visual Computing Group (University of Sheffield) (2020), boundary-aware material segmentation with 3D semantic mapping for robotic nuclear waste decommissioning, Frontiers in Robotics and AI, DOI 10.3389/frobt.2020.00052
evidence.note: Transfer-learning material segmentation fused into a SLAM-based 3D map to support robot manipulation of waste heaps; verified industrially in the EU RoMaNS project.

damage.why: Misclassification of special nuclear material leading to loss of material accountancy, potential diversion to unmonitored clearance streams, or physical co-location of fissile materials creating criticality risk constitutes loss of material control and safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Once operational conditions produce out-of-distribution waste (highly likely given heterogeneity of legacy sites) or an adversary introduces physical adversarial patterns or poisoned training data, the segmentation model will reliably misclassify targeted materials due to its dependence on limited, non-representative training data and lack of independent radiological verification.

exploitability.why: Physical adversarial exploitation requires local access to waste staging areas to introduce crafted objects or surface treatments; model poisoning requires access to training pipelines or supply chain, which is insider-level but not nation-state; cyber exfiltration of maps requires network access but uses conventional methods once access is gained.

affected_users.why: Segmentation errors propagate through the SLAM-fused 3D semantic map to corrupt all downstream manipulation decisions facility-wide, and cross-site model deployment means a systematic flaw or compromise affects the entire decommissioning fleet across multiple facilities.

discoverability.why: The reliance on simulated data, transfer learning, and limited real waste imagery is documented in open literature (cited RoMaNS project publication), making the training-distribution mismatch and vulnerability to out-of-distribution materials inferable by capable outsiders with knowledge of DL vision systems and decommissioning domain constraints.

use_case: Extended-reality interfaces coupled to digital twins of nuclear assets for immersive visualisation, maintenance planning and human-factors assessment
incurred_insecurity:
This use case creates a centralized, immersive representation of nuclear facilities that operators and planners come to treat as authoritative ground truth, yet the digital twin's fidelity to physical reality depends on sensor data, model assumptions, and update cadences that diverge over time. The resulting insecurity has three main layers: implicit drift that erodes the twin's accuracy without adversarial action, automation trust amplified by immersive presentation that suppresses healthy operator skepticism, and adversarial exploitation of both the twin as a reconnaissance target and the drift-induced blind spots as timing opportunities for physical intrusion or sabotage.

Operational Drift and Fidelity Decay
The twin aggregates sensor streams, physics simulations, and historical data across heterogeneous facility domains (enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication, waste storage), each with different data availability and provenance. Enrichment and reprocessing facilities often rely on simulated or transferred data due to operational secrecy and destructive-assay scarcity, while new-build plants lack field-measured training data entirely. As physical facilities evolve through component replacements, temporary modifications, or undocumented field changes, the twin drifts from reality—thermal models reflect outdated equipment performance, structural models miss ad-hoc shielding, and radiological-field predictions assume sensor calibrations that have decayed. When one sub-model (neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, structural) is retrained without re-qualifying the integrated twin, errors cascade: a neutronics over-prediction feeds false thermal loads, which drive incorrect equipment-wear forecasts, and maintenance plans derived from the drifted twin specify unsafe work sequences, misidentify clearance boundaries, or omit radiological hazards. If the same twin architecture propagates across a fleet, a single embedded error or bias affects all sites, and operational heterogeneity between sites (different vintages, operating regimes) means the drift rate and character vary unpredictably. This is an implicit, non-adversarial failure rooted in data provenance gaps, model update cadence mismatches, and the ML-theoretic difficulty of maintaining fidelity in a continuously evolving physical environment.

Automation Trust and Psychological Amplification
The immersive XR interface transforms operator interaction with the twin from passive review of 2D schematics to visceral, three-dimensional walk-throughs that psychologically carry more authority. Engineers and maintenance planners immersed in high-fidelity VR experience the plant state as directly observed rather than modeled, suppressing the skepticism they would apply to a screen-based tool. This leads to misuse (over-trust): operators defer to the twin's predictions during incident response, accept its equipment-condition assessments without cross-checking as-built drawings, and internalize its radiological or criticality margins as definitive. If the twin's AI anomaly detectors or predictive-maintenance modules flag a fault, the opacity of those ML components makes it difficult for operators to judge whether the alert reflects real degradation or a model artifact, yet the immersive presentation discourages second-guessing. Conversely, if a real hazard is not flagged, operators habituated to twin guidance may experience out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity when confronting the physical system directly. The non-deterministic nature of some twin components (Monte Carlo neutronics, stochastic risk models) means the same sensor snapshot can yield different XR visualizations on repeated inference, breaking the deterministic traceability nuclear safety cases require and creating an AI-specific qualification gap that current regulatory frameworks do not address. This is an implicit human-factors failure, not adversarial, but it creates exploitable conditions.

Adversarial Exploitation of the Twin as Reconnaissance Asset and Drift as Operational Cover
An adversary who gains access to the digital twin—via credential theft (potentially through phishing in XR training scenarios or spoofed avatars), exploitation of public-facing twin collaboration APIs, or supply-chain compromise of sensor feeds, model updates, or XR rendering software—obtains a reconnaissance-complete facility map: geometry, equipment layouts, operational cadences, maintenance schedules, human-factor baselines, and vulnerability windows. Exfiltrating the twin's AI models or training data reveals process knowledge useful for planning diversion, sabotage timing, or physical intrusion routes. The adversary can also inject false data through compromised sensors or poisoned model updates to make the twin diverge from reality in targeted ways—moving virtual walls to suggest blocked access where real access exists, altering equipment labels to misdirect response crews, or embedding backdoor triggers in sub-models that surface only under specific plant conditions. Because operators trust the immersive twin, they plan and train around the falsified state, and the adversary exploits the resulting physical blind spots. Even without active injection, the adversary benefits from naturally occurring drift: knowing the twin was validated at commissioning but not re-qualified after years of operation, they time physical actions to when the twin is least accurate (during plant modifications, sensor outages, or known model-update lags), confident discrepancies will be attributed to 'model limitations' rather than investigated as tampering indicators. If the twin is used for safeguards or material-accountancy visualization, model inversion or inference-API probing can extract safeguards-relevant features (detector blind spots, material-flow chokepoints) the adversary uses to design diversion scenarios. For twins hosted off-premises or using cloud rendering, the adversary gains remote attack surface and potential jurisdictional leverage. If the twin profiles operator behavior during human-factors assessments (which alarms they dismiss, which procedures they shortcut in XR drills), that profiling data becomes social-engineering intelligence. Fleet-wide twin deployment amplifies impact: compromising one site's twin seeds false data into others, a force multiplier for adversaries targeting multiple facilities.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operational engineering standpoint, this use case presents a subtle but serious risk: the digital twin becomes the authoritative representation of plant state for maintenance planners and human-factors evaluators, yet the twin's fidelity to physical reality depends entirely on model quality, sensor coverage, and real-time data integrity—none of which are traditionally subject to the same configuration management rigor as the physical asset itself. The immersive XR interface amplifies automation trust: engineers experience a visceral, three-dimensional 'walk-through' that psychologically carries more weight than a 2D schematic, making drift or model error harder to detect and easier to internalize as ground truth. If the digital twin diverges from actual plant conditions (through sensor drift, untracked physical modifications, or model assumptions that no longer hold), maintenance plans derived from it could specify unsafe work sequences, misidentify clearance boundaries, or omit radiological hazards—and the immersive presentation makes these errors feel authoritative rather than provisional. An adversary need not attack the AI directly; simply knowing that maintenance crews trust the twin opens opportunities to time physical intrusions or sabotage around moments when the twin is least accurate (e.g., during plant modifications not yet reflected in the model).
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core operational threat is **automation trust failure compounded by content fidelity drift**: operators and planners come to rely on the digital twin as definitive plant state, but the twin's AI-driven predictive models (thermal, structural, radiological fields) silently diverge from physical reality due to sensor calibration drift, unmodeled component aging, or undocumented field modifications. This creates **cascading fault propagation**—a maintenance plan optimized in the twin (e.g., specifying a safe approach path, required shielding, or valve lineup) may be subtly wrong in the real facility, leading to radiation exposure, inadvertent system interactions, or loss of containment boundaries. The immersive XR interface exacerbates **misuse (over-trust)** because the visceral experience of 'being there' in VR suppresses healthy skepticism; engineers are less likely to cross-check the twin against as-built drawings or direct inspection. **Data provenance and availability** issues are acute: nuclear facilities often lack dense sensor coverage in all areas (especially older plants or waste-storage casks), forcing the twin to interpolate or rely on simulated/surrogate data—any of which may be valid at commissioning but decay in accuracy over operational life. An adversary aware of this dynamic can exploit **operational drift** and **static/dynamic qualification mismatch**: if they know the twin was validated against commissioning-state data but not re-qualified after years of operation, they can time physical intrusions or manipulate sensors feeding the twin, confident that discrepancies will be dismissed as 'model limitations' rather than investigated as indicators of tampering. For safeguards and material control, twins modeling fuel flow or accountancy tank levels are vulnerable to **data access governance failures** (inappropriate sharing of sensitive geometry or process parameters via XR session logs) and **model inversion**—if the twin's AI components can be queried or exfiltrated, an adversary gains high-fidelity process knowledge useful for planning diversion scenarios. Finally, **cross-site model propagation** risk emerges if a single twin architecture is deployed fleet-wide: a subtle bias or error in one site's model (e.g., underestimating neutron flux in certain geometries) propagates to all sites, and any adversary discovering the flaw gains leverage across the entire fleet.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case embeds AI-driven digital twins -- which synthesize sensor streams, simulation outputs, and historical data into a real-time plant state representation -- inside immersive XR interfaces used for maintenance planning and human-factors assessment. From an ML engineering lens, the core fragility is the *provenance and freshness of the data feeding the twin*: maintenance planning decisions rest on whether the twin's physics models, equipment condition estimates, and anomaly detectors are trained on data representative of the *current* plant state, or whether they reflect configurations, operating regimes, or component vintages no longer present. The second vulnerability is *inference-time input validation*: XR systems typically push sensor and simulation data through the twin's inference pipeline continuously, and if out-of-distribution inputs (new equipment, off-normal modes, sensor drift) are not flagged, the twin will confidently render a plausible but wrong plant state to the operator. The third is *model qualification and update cadence*: digital twins in nuclear are often stitched from multiple models (thermal-hydraulics, neutronics, structural, etc.), each with its own retraining schedule and data lineage; if one sub-model drifts or is updated without re-qualifying the integrated twin, the XR interface becomes a vector for compounded error propagation across maintenance decisions.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: **Data provenance and drift (OP.C0201, OP.C0302.01):** The digital twin aggregates simulated plant behavior, lab-measured component performance, and field sensor data -- often across facility domains (enrichment, reprocessing, fuel fabrication) with heterogeneous data availability. If the twin was trained on virtual commissioning data (OP.C0201.03) or bench tests (OP.C0201.04) but is now being used to plan maintenance in an operating plant, *operational drift* will cause the twin's predictions (equipment wear, criticality margins, radiation fields) to diverge from reality, and the XR interface will present a confidently wrong plant state to maintainers. An adversary aware of this drift window -- for instance, knowing a component replacement invalidated a sub-model -- could time an intrusion or sabotage event to when maintenance crews are acting on outdated twin guidance, or could exfiltrate the twin's training data (AML.T0024.002) to infer what the system *cannot* see. **Automation bias and explainability (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401):** XR immersion is psychologically compelling; operators and planners immersed in a high-fidelity 3D twin are prone to *over-trust* (OP.C0101.04) the presented state, especially when the twin's ML anomaly detectors or predictive maintenance modules are opaque (OP.C0401). If a sub-model hallucinates an equipment fault or misattributes a sensor anomaly (OP.C0304.01), maintenance may be scheduled unnecessarily -- or, worse, a real fault flagged by the twin may be dismissed as a known false-positive, leading to out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity (OP.C0101.01) when the fault manifests physically. An adversary could exploit this by injecting adversarial sensor data (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) that the twin processes into a benign-looking XR visualization, masking real equipment degradation or diversion signatures. **Model integration and cascading fault propagation (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603):** The twin is a *system of models* -- neutronics, thermal-hydraulics, structural mechanics, etc. -- each with its own training dataset, inference cadence, and error bounds. If one sub-model is retrained or drifts (OP.C0302.02 concept drift) and the integrated twin is not re-qualified, errors cascade: a neutronics model overpredicting reactivity feeds into thermal-hydraulics, which then drives false equipment-wear predictions in the XR maintenance planner. This is exacerbated if the twin is deployed across multiple sites (OP.C0602) with operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.03) -- the same twin rendering Idaho National Lab's test reactor and a commercial PWR will drift differently at each, and XR-guided maintenance decisions become site-specific gambles. An adversary with access to the twin's supply chain (AML.T0010.003 model compromise, AML.T0018.000 poison AI model) could embed a backdoor in one sub-model that surfaces only under specific plant conditions, causing the XR interface to guide operators toward unsafe configurations. **Inference-time repeatability and regulatory gap (OP.C0402.02, OP.C0501):** Many digital twins incorporate stochastic models (Monte Carlo neutronics, probabilistic risk assessment) or neural components with inherent non-determinism; the same sensor snapshot fed into the twin twice may yield different XR visualizations (OP.C0402.02). This breaks the deterministic traceability expected in nuclear safety cases and means maintenance decisions made in XR cannot be reliably reproduced for audits or incident investigations (OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap). An adversary could exploit this by triggering the twin during a non-deterministic inference window, then claiming maintenance actions were based on a visualization the system cannot now reproduce, muddying forensic timelines. **Cross-domain propagation (OP.C0602, OP.C0701):** If the same twin architecture is used across enrichment, reprocessing, and fuel fabrication (as the use case specifies), and trained on aggregated fleet data, it inherits *all* domains' data scarcity problems -- enrichment plants have sparse public operational data (OP.C0701 safeguards-model scarcity), reprocessing has destructive-assay signature scarcity (OP.C0701.01), and new fuel-fab builds have new-build data scarcity (OP.C0203). A single poisoned training sample (AML.T0020) or adversarially crafted sensor input (AML.T0043) can propagate across all domains via the shared twin, and the XR interface becomes a single point of failure for maintenance and safeguards decisions across the entire fuel cycle.

security_specialist.argument: From a security lens, this use case is high-value infrastructure -- a centralized, authoritative digital replica of sensitive nuclear facilities accessible via immersive interfaces -- which concentrates both data and trust in a way adversaries find attractive. The XR immersion layer creates new social-engineering and credential-theft surfaces (phishing via manipulated XR scenarios, credential harvesting in headset environments), while the digital twin itself becomes a reconnaissance goldmine if compromised: floor plans, equipment layouts, vulnerability windows during maintenance, and human-factor baselines an adversary can use to time or tailor physical attacks. The AI models powering the twin introduce non-adversarial drift and data-quality risks that degrade the twin's fidelity over time, but a sophisticated adversary wouldn't wait for natural decay -- they would inject subtly falsified data (e.g., via supply-chain compromise of sensor feeds or model updates) to make the twin diverge from reality in ways that mask their physical intrusion or make defenders plan around phantom constraints. Even non-malicious model failures matter here: if operators trust an out-of-date twin during an incident, they may mis-allocate response resources, and an adversary who has studied the twin's known lag can exploit that trust window.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: The digital twin aggregates facility geometry, equipment state, and operational cadence into a single exfiltration target (AML.T0024.002 Extract AI Model, AML.T0025 Exfiltration via Cyber Means, AML.T0048.004 AI Intellectual Property Theft) -- an insider or remote attacker gaining twin access obtains a reconnaissance-complete map adversaries would otherwise spend months assembling on-site. XR interfaces expand the credential-theft surface: an attacker can phish credentials via fake XR training scenarios (AML.T0052 Phishing, AML.T0052.001 Deepfake-Assisted Phishing if avatars/voices are spoofed), or exploit the twin's public-facing collaboration features if those exist (AML.T0049 Exploit Public-Facing Application). Supply-chain compromise of the twin's sensor feeds, AI model updates, or XR rendering components (AML.T0010.001 AI Software, AML.T0010.003 Model, AML.T0010.002 Data) lets an adversary inject false facility state (walls moved, equipment re-labeled, patrol schedules altered) so operators train or plan around a lie, then execute a physical intrusion the real facility layout permits but the twin said was blocked. The twin's use in maintenance planning is a timing oracle: if an adversary knows the twin shows a certain system offline for service (and operators trust that), they can schedule their physical action during that known-safe window. The immersive nature of XR also enables social-engineering attacks where operators in headsets are fed manipulated visual cues (e.g., a false alarm in VR to distract from a real physical event, or XR prompts to 'confirm' a malicious action camouflaged as routine). If the twin's AI models are accessible for interrogation (AML.T0040 AI Model Inference API Access, AML.T0044 Full AI Model Access), adversaries can probe them to discover facility vulnerabilities the models learned but humans didn't document, or craft adversarial queries that extract safeguards-relevant features (material flow chokepoints, detector blind spots). Lastly, if the twin propagates across a fleet (OP.C0602), compromising one site's twin seeds false data into others, a force-multiplier for an adversary targeting multiple facilities.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) RISKS EXPLOITABLE BY ADVERSARIES: Digital twins suffer operational drift (OP.C0302.01 Data/Operational drift) when physical reality changes faster than the twin updates -- renovations, temporary barriers, as-built deviations -- so the twin becomes a dated map. An adversary who has current physical access (even briefly) knows the real layout while defenders trust the stale twin, asymmetry the adversary exploits during an intrusion. Small-data problems (OP.C0202) afflict twins of new-build or unique facilities: if the twin's AI models are trained on generic plant data, they won't capture site-specific quirks (non-standard door placements, ad-hoc shielding) that an attacker on-site will notice and use. Automation trust (OP.C0101.04 Misuse/over-trust) is severe here: operators immersed in a high-fidelity XR twin may reflexively trust it during an incident, deferring to its (possibly outdated or compromised) facility state instead of direct observation -- an adversary who knows this will time physical actions to coincide with twin-induced operator blind spots. Explainability limits (OP.C0401) mean if the twin's AI recommends a maintenance route or predicts equipment failure, operators may not know *why*, so they can't sanity-check it against threat indicators; an adversary poisoning the training data (AML.T0020) could steer maintenance crews away from areas the adversary wants unmonitored. Data provenance (OP.C0201) matters: if the twin incorporates simulated (OP.C0201.01) or transferred data (OP.C0201.03) from other plants, it may embed vulnerabilities or patterns from those sources that don't match this facility's real security posture, and an adversary studying open-source plant models can infer what the twin 'thinks' even if they haven't breached it yet. Cloud/off-premises dependency (OP.C0601) for twin hosting or XR rendering creates a remote attack surface and jurisdictional risk (data sovereignty, lawful-intercept orders against the cloud provider). Finally, the twin's role in human-factors assessment is a double-edged sword: if it profiles how operators respond to scenarios, that profiling data is valuable to an adversary for tailoring social engineering (they know which alarms operators historically dismiss, which procedures they shortcut in XR drills, etc.).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged strongly on operational drift (data/model staleness vs. physical reality) and automation trust amplified by XR immersion as the core implicit threats, and on the twin as a high-value reconnaissance/exfiltration target plus adversarial injection of false data via supply-chain or sensor compromise as the primary adversarial threats. The security specialist's timing-oracle and social-engineering angles, the AI engineer's cascading-fault and non-determinism concerns, and the nuclear engineer's clearance-boundary and radiological-hazard examples were retained as distinct but complementary facets of the same underlying vulnerabilities.

evidence.citation: "Extended reality and digital twins for nuclear assets" (2024), Frontiers in Energy Research, DOI 10.3389/fenrg.2024.1359688
evidence.note: Reviews nuclear digital twins from an XR perspective and summarises the authors' VR/AR/MR work integrated with twins of nuclear assets. The AI element lies in the twin models rather than the XR itself.

damage.why: Adversarial falsification of the twin enabling diversion of safeguards material or misdirection during sabotage timing falls squarely into the 'safeguards falsification' or 'material control' loss category; implicit drift leading to incorrect radiological-field predictions or unsafe maintenance sequences can directly erode safety margins to the point of radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Operational drift is deterministic given the described conditions (component changes, sensor decay, heterogeneous update cadences across domains) and will reliably degrade twin fidelity over time; adversarial data injection or model poisoning, once credential access or supply-chain position is achieved, reliably propagates false states through the immersive interface that operators will trust.

exploitability.why: Adversarial exploitation requires credential theft, supply-chain compromise of sensor feeds or model updates, or API access—achievable by a capable external actor but not trivial; implicit drift requires no adversary and occurs through routine operational evolution, but exploiting that drift for timing or reconnaissance still requires moderate insider knowledge of update cadences and validation gaps.

affected_users.why: The twin aggregates facility-wide sensor streams and models across all domains (enrichment, reprocessing, fabrication, waste storage); compromised or drifted twins affect maintenance planning, incident response, and safeguards visualization facility-wide, and fleet deployment propagates impact across multiple sites.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability class—digital-twin drift, XR-amplified automation trust, and reconnaissance value of facility twins—is openly discussed in the cited literature and nuclear-industry XR/digitalization conferences; an adversary with moderate facility knowledge (procurement records, vendor documentation of twin architecture) can infer its presence and general characteristics, though discovering specific update cadences or validation gaps at a given site requires partial insider information.

use_case: Large language model drafting of safety analysis reports
incurred_insecurity: Using an LLM to draft safety analysis reports introduces a multi-layered insecurity centered on content fidelity and the trustworthiness of the retrieval pipeline. The system's reliance on a vector database and knowledge graph as authoritative sources creates a concentration of trust: errors, staleness, or adversarial manipulation in those repositories propagate into licensing documents that define a plant's documented safety basis for years. Non-adversarial risks include LLM hallucination of technical parameters, retrieval of outdated or contextually mismatched content when the knowledge graph lags plant modifications, automation bias leading reviewers to under-scrutinize plausible-sounding drafts, and the system's opacity preventing auditability of specific claims. Adversarially, the retrieval infrastructure is a high-value target for data poisoning, prompt injection to steer outputs toward favorable omissions, and exfiltration of facility safety details via crafted queries. Because these reports become the basis for operating limits, emergency procedures, and technical specifications, a subtle error or adversarial insertion that survives review can weaken defense-in-depth on paper, discovered only during an actual event or audit.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations lens, I see two distinct failure modes that matter downstream. First, the LLM is drafting technical safety arguments that licensing staff, NRC reviewers, and ultimately plant personnel will rely on to understand design basis and accident analysis -- if it hallucinates a parameter, misattributes a calculation, or omits a critical assumption, someone in that chain may not catch it before it becomes the documented basis for an operating limit or emergency procedure. Second, the INL architecture tries to ground the LLM in a vector database and knowledge graph, but that only works if the retrieval is faithful and the knowledge graph is current -- if the graph lags plant modifications, or retrieval ranking favors older analyses over updated ones, the drafted report could reference superseded limits or outdated success criteria, and the review process would need to catch a subtly wrong number in hundreds of pages. The consequence isn't immediate physical harm, but it's insidious: incorrect safety basis documentation becomes the input to surveillance test acceptance criteria, technical specification changes, and operator training -- a wrong value drafted by the LLM and missed in review could sit in the SAR for years, discovered only when someone tries to use it in an actual event.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT (non-adversarial): The primary threat is content fidelity failure in a high-consequence document. LLMs are known to hallucinate citations, numbers, and causal chains (OP.C0304.01); in safety analysis, a hallucinated peak clad temperature, incorrect containment pressure, or misattributed source term could make it into the draft and survive review if it's plausible-sounding and buried in narrative. The INL architecture mitigates this by grounding in structured data, but that introduces retrieval risks: if the vector database ranking is imperfect, the LLM may draft text from an older analysis when a newer one exists (OP.C0204, data availability/continuity; OP.C0302.01, operational drift if the knowledge graph isn't kept current with plant changes). There's also an automation trust problem (OP.C0101.04, misuse/over-trust): licensing engineers may assume the LLM's draft is correct because it "came from the database," reducing the rigor of their review -- especially for sections that look routine. Nuclear SARs are living documents; if the LLM drafts a change that doesn't account for a recent modification (because the mod wasn't yet in the knowledge graph), and the reviewer doesn't independently verify, the plant could operate with a documented analysis that no longer bounds the actual configuration. Finally, there's a skill-fade risk (OP.C0101.06): if junior engineers rely on LLM drafts for years, they may lose the ability to write or critically review a safety argument from scratch, which becomes a problem when the LLM fails in a novel way or when an auditor questions a specific claim and the author can't defend it.

ADVERSARIAL: The LLM supply chain is an attack surface. If an adversary poisons the retrieval database or knowledge graph (AML.T0020, poison training data; OP.C0701, domain-specific data scarcity makes it hard to detect anomalies; AML.T0070, RAG poisoning), they could cause the LLM to draft technically plausible but subtly wrong safety limits -- e.g., an adversary with access to the INL vector store could insert a false analysis showing a lower required ECCS flow, and the LLM would draft that into the SAR update. Similarly, if the LLM is prompted to draft a section and an adversary can inject a prompt or modify the RAG retrieval (AML.T0051, LLM prompt injection; AML.T0071, false RAG entry injection), they could cause it to omit a required safety function or reference an invalid code version. The consequence isn't immediate sabotage -- it's a time-delayed logic bomb in the safety basis. The adversary's goal would be to weaken a defense-in-depth layer on paper so that a later physical attack (or a natural initiating event) has a higher probability of core damage because the plant's procedures and limits are based on a compromised analysis. There's also a subtler threat: an adversary could use this system to probe what safety margins exist by crafting queries that cause the LLM to reveal how close current analyses are to regulatory limits (AML.T0040, AI model inference API access; AML.T0024, exfiltration via inference), which is intelligence-gathering for a later attack. Finally, the INL paper describes an AI-enabled licensing workflow; if that workflow becomes standard and the LLM's output is trusted, an adversary who compromises the LLM (AML.T0010.003, AI supply chain compromise of model) gains leverage over the entire fleet's safety basis documentation, not just one plant.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case centers on an LLM that drafts safety analysis reports by querying a vector database and knowledge graph for authoritative content. From a model-engineering standpoint, the critical vulnerability is not the LLM's creative capacity but the fidelity and provenance of the retrieval pipeline feeding it. The knowledge graph and vector embeddings become single points of failure: if training data for the embeddings came from heterogeneous or outdated regulatory snapshots, retrieval will surface stale or contextually mismatched content even when the LLM faithfully renders what it receives. Furthermore, LLMs exhibit non-deterministic output even with identical prompts and retrieval context (temperature settings, token sampling), so two runs drafting the same safety argument may produce subtly different claims—a repeatability gap that conflicts with the deterministic expectations of a licensing document. Finally, the system's opacity (both the embedding model's learned similarities and the LLM's generation process) makes it nearly impossible to trace why a specific regulatory citation or safety claim appeared in the draft, undermining the auditability that licensing staff and regulators require.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary ML-pipeline threat is **retrieval-content fidelity and provenance failure**: the vector database may encode regulatory text from mixed vintages (pre- and post-amendment versions of 10 CFR parts, for instance) or from documents with different applicability scopes (BWR vs. PWR design bases), and the embedding model has no intrinsic mechanism to flag temporal or reactor-type boundaries. An adversary aware of this could submit a licensing query knowing the system will retrieve and synthesize obsolete or inapplicable content, or simply wait for the system to do so organically and then rely on an under-resourced review process to miss the error. A second, non-adversarial but exploitable risk is **LLM non-determinism**: because the generation step is stochastic, the same safety question posed twice may yield different phrasings or even different cited sections, and an operator trusting the system may not re-verify each run. This opens a time-of-check/time-of-use gap if an adversary learns the prompt or DB state that produces a favorable (from their perspective) but technically weak answer and arranges for that state to be active during submission. Third, **explainability limits** mean neither the licensing analyst nor an NRC reviewer can reconstruct which pieces of the knowledge graph were weighted most heavily in the retrieval step, so a subtly poisoned node—perhaps a malicious update to the graph encoding an under-reviewed interim staff guidance—will propagate into multiple reports with no algorithmic red flag. Finally, the system assumes the knowledge graph is kept current and correct, but **data-availability and governance gaps** (who updates it, how often, under what change-control) are ML-operations risks: if the graph lags regulatory amendments by months, the LLM drafts against outdated rules, and an adversary timing a license application around that lag could slip through non-compliant designs that the stale retrieval logic does not challenge.

security_specialist.argument: From a security lens, this use case is a high-value target because it sits at a chokepoint where adversaries gain leverage: not the reactor itself, but the documented basis that authorizes its operation. A nation-state or insider who can subtly alter safety analysis language—shifting a margin, omitting a failure mode, or injecting a plausible but incorrect reference—creates deniable regulatory confusion or sets the stage for later exploitation when the facility operates under a flawed license basis. The system's reliance on a vector database and knowledge graph as 'authoritative' is itself a concentration of trust: compromise those repositories (via supply chain, insider access, or poisoned ingestion pipelines) and the LLM becomes a force-multiplier for distributing the compromise across multiple licensing documents before anyone notices. Even absent a deliberate adversary, this use case erodes a critical human cross-check: if staff assume the AI's draft is 'mostly right' and focus only on high-level review, an adversary can time an attack (physical or cyber) to a period when the facility is operating under an AI-drafted amendment that subtly weakened a defense-in-depth layer, and investigators will struggle to distinguish malice from hallucination after the fact.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS: The knowledge graph and vector database are high-value targets for data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0070 RAG poisoning) because they are upstream of all generated text and likely accessible to insiders or supply-chain partners with less scrutiny than the reactor's operational network—an adversary (including a sophisticated insider or nation-state with long timelines) could inject subtly incorrect technical content, outdated references, or margin-shaving language that the LLM then weaves into dozens of licensing documents over months before detection. The LLM itself is vulnerable to prompt injection (AML.T0051) if any part of its input pipeline (e.g., templates, user queries, or ingested documents) can be influenced by an attacker, allowing them to steer the output toward specific omissions or phrasings that favor later exploitation. The system also presents an exfiltration risk (AML.T0056, AML.T0057): an adversary could use crafted prompts to extract the LLM's system instructions, the structure of the knowledge graph, or details of the facility's safety case that are not public, providing reconnaissance for a physical or cyber attack. Finally, the concentration of this capability (AML.T0602 cross-site/fleet model propagation) means a single compromised model or database could propagate flawed analysis language across multiple reactors if the vendor or regulator shares infrastructure, amplifying impact.

IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) VULNERABILITIES THAT ADVERSARIES COULD EXPLOIT: The system is highly susceptible to automation bias (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust): human reviewers, faced with lengthy AI-drafted sections that 'look right,' will likely skim rather than rigorously verify every claim, creating windows where an adversary's subtle poisoning or a natural hallucination (OP.C0304.01) both go undetected—adversaries can time attacks to when such errors are likeliest to be in force. Content fidelity failures (OP.C0304.03 oversimplification/omission) are especially dangerous here: if the LLM omits a low-probability scenario or subtly mischaracterizes a component's failure mode to make the prose flow better, an adversary who has studied the facility can exploit that exact gap, knowing the safety case on file does not account for it. The system's opaqueness (OP.C0401 explainability limit) means auditors cannot easily trace *why* the LLM recommended specific phrasing, making it nearly impossible to distinguish a deliberate poisoning from a training-data artifact—this is a forensic nightmare if an incident occurs and investigators try to determine whether the safety analysis was tampered with. Data provenance (OP.C0201.03 transferred data, OP.C0505.01 inappropriate data security model) is critical: if the knowledge graph ingests documents from less-secure repositories (vendor submissions, public dockets, or legacy scanned PDFs with OCR errors), an adversary can backdoor the system at the data layer, and the LLM will treat poisoned content as authoritative. Finally, qualification gaps (OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap, OP.C0504 regulatory readiness gap) mean there is likely no formal process to red-team the LLM's outputs against adversarial scenarios or to verify that every generated paragraph has a traceable, human-verified lineage—this lack of rigor is itself what an adversary (or an advanced persistent threat with patience) would count on.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on retrieval-pipeline fidelity (RAG poisoning, stale/mismatched content) and automation bias as the dominant threats; the security specialist's framing of opacity-as-forensic-barrier and the nuclear engineer's skill-fade concern were retained as distinct, well-argued additions.
