use_case: Particle swarm optimisation of transport cask shielding thickness against cask weight for spent fuel assemblies from a prototype sodium-cooled fast reactor
incurred_insecurity:
This use case incurs insecurity primarily through the potential for mis-specification of the optimization objective and corruption of the physics inputs that drive the PSO algorithm, rather than through vulnerabilities inherent to machine learning systems. Because PSO is a deterministic metaheuristic that encodes human-chosen constraints into a mathematical objective function, any error in how dose limits, source terms, or accident scenarios are represented will propagate directly into the shielding specification that becomes the basis for fabrication and licensing. The resulting cask becomes a physical trust anchor in the spent fuel transport chain: if its design is flawed—whether through inadvertent modeling error or deliberate input manipulation—the consequences include regulatory non-compliance, radiological exposure during routine or accident conditions, and potential exploitation by adversaries who understand the design's hidden inadequacies. The main threats are implicit weaknesses in objective alignment and input data quality, which an adversary with supply-chain or insider access could exploit, and the risk that downstream users will over-trust the PSO output without independent adversarial verification.

Objective Misalignment and Physics Input Integrity
The PSO minimizes cask weight subject to a modeled dose constraint, but if that constraint is constructed from an incorrect neutron-gamma source term—particularly for sodium-cooled fast reactor fuel, whose actinide vectors and activation products differ from light-water reactor experience—the algorithm will confidently converge on a thickness that satisfies the model yet violates actual regulatory limits. This is an implicit weakness (OP.C0301 goal misalignment) exacerbated by new-build data scarcity (OP.C0203) and reliance on simulated or surrogate cross-section libraries and Monte Carlo transport codes (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02) whose fidelity determines the objective function's correctness. An adversary with supply-chain access could exploit this by corrupting the input data or neutronics libraries (AML.T0010.002 data supply chain compromise), ensuring the PSO produces a subtly under-shielded design that an insider or saboteur later exploits during transport when the cask is outside the facility's physical protection perimeter.

Oversimplification of Design Constraints
If the PSO objective omits or oversimplifies accident scenarios mandated by 10 CFR Part 71 (drop, fire, water immersion) or treats gamma and neutron shielding as independent when they compete for thickness budget, the optimum may be non-conservative under conditions the algorithm never evaluated. This implicit weakness (OP.C0304.03 oversimplification) means the cask could meet normal-transport dose limits but fail catastrophically in an adversary-staged incident or during sabotage, a scenario an attacker aware of the optimization's scope could deliberately engineer.

Automation Bias and Inadequate Verification
Because PSO is deterministic and repeatable, licensing authorities and fabricators may treat its output as authoritative, skipping independent adversarial analysis or physical mock-up validation—particularly under schedule pressure. This implicit over-trust (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust) is compounded if verification relies on the same flawed source term or if software-engineering hygiene gaps (OP.C0502) allow unvalidated code or input files to enter the workflow. An adversary conducting reconnaissance (AML.T0003 search victim-owned websites, AML.T0087 gather victim identity information) could learn how shielding adequacy is evaluated, then craft diversion or sabotage scenarios that exploit known margins or substituted material characteristics (OP.C0702.01 material substitution) the PSO never considered.

Fleet-Wide Propagation of a Compromised Design Tool
If the same PSO implementation or neutronics library is used across multiple cask designs or sites, a single compromise scales to all derived specifications. This implicit cross-site propagation risk (OP.C0602) means an adversary who successfully manipulates the optimization tool or its dependencies once can affect an entire fleet of transport casks, amplifying the impact of supply-chain compromise or insider tampering.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case applies particle swarm optimization—a metaheuristic search algorithm, not a machine-learned model—to design transport cask shielding for sodium-cooled fast reactor spent fuel. The PSO tunes shielding thickness to balance dose rate against cask weight, and a human engineer then verifies the candidate design against regulatory dose limits. Because PSO is deterministic given its inputs (source term, material properties, geometry constraints) and does not learn from operational data, classical AI vulnerabilities like adversarial examples, model poisoning, or drift are largely irrelevant. The real insecurity lies in the engineering workflow: if the PSO's objective function is mis-specified, if the neutron/gamma source term for sodium-cooled fast-reactor fuel is wrong (especially for minor actinides or activation products unfamiliar from LWR practice), or if the engineer accepts the PSO output without independent dose confirmation, the cask could be under-shielded or structurally unsound, directly violating 10 CFR Part 71 limits and exposing transport workers or the public during a routine or accident scenario.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The dominant threat is OP.C0301 goal/objective misalignment: the PSO minimizes a cost function (e.g., cask mass) subject to a modeled dose constraint, but if that constraint encodes the wrong source term—sodium-cooled fast reactors produce different actinide vectors and activated corrosion products than light-water reactors—the 'optimal' thickness may satisfy the algorithm yet fail the actual dose limit. This is compounded by OP.C0203 new-build data scarcity (prototype SFR fuel has minimal shipping-cask precedent) and OP.C0201.01/.02 reliance on simulated/synthetic data (Monte Carlo transport codes feed the PSO; any Monte Carlo cross-section error or geometry simplification propagates). OP.C0304.03 oversimplification risk exists if the PSO objective omits accident scenarios (drop, fire, water immersion per 10 CFR 71.73) or treats gamma and neutron shielding independently when they compete for thickness budget. An adversary aware of these gaps could time an attack (physical interdiction, documentation falsification under AML.T0010.002 data supply chain compromise) during transport when the cask is outside the facility's physical protection perimeter, knowing the design may lack margin. The mitigating factor is that the PSO output must still pass deterministic confirmatory dose calculation and regulatory review before the cask is built—OP.C0401 opacity is low because engineers can interrogate every PSO iteration—but if that review itself relies on the same flawed source term or if schedule pressure encourages 'acceptance by analysis' without physical mock-up (OP.C0502 software-engineering hygiene weakness), the insecurity persists into operation. OP.C0304.01 hallucination is not applicable (PSO does not generate text), and OP.C0402 non-determinism is minimal (PSO can be seeded for repeatability), so the vulnerability profile is narrower than for learned AI but still consequential because the output is a physical artifact—a cask—whose failure mode is direct radiological release during public transport.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a metaheuristic optimization (PSO), not a learned ML model—it has no training data, no drift, no out-of-distribution failure in the usual sense. The real ML/AI vulnerability surface here is almost nonexistent because PSO is a deterministic or quasi-deterministic search algorithm over a physics-constrained objective function. What matters is the *objective function itself* (dose calculation + weight penalty) and the *physics inputs* (source term, cross-sections, geometry)—those are where errors enter, but they are not AI/ML failure modes; they are domain-physics and input-data quality issues that would exist with or without PSO. From an ML engineering perspective, this use case incurs negligible AI-specific insecurity because there is no model to poison, no training pipeline to compromise, no inference API to query, and no learned representation to evade or invert. Any attempt to frame this as an AI vulnerability conflates *using computation to solve an optimization problem* with *deploying a statistical learning system*.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The only ML-adjacent vulnerabilities are: (1) if the dose-calculation subroutine or material cross-section library feeding the PSO objective function were themselves ML-surrogates (e.g., a neural-net dose emulator replacing Monte Carlo), then standard model-manipulation, data-poisoning, or out-of-distribution risks would apply—but the cited paper gives no indication of this, implying deterministic physics codes. (2) If an adversary had write access to the PSO code or input files (geometry, source term), they could silently alter the objective function to yield a non-conservative optimum (thinner shielding, lower weight, higher dose)—but this is a software supply-chain or configuration-management threat (ATLAS T0010.001 AI Software, if we stretch the definition to include optimization scripts, though PSO is not 'AI software' in the learned-model sense), not an AI attack. (3) Non-determinism in PSO (particle initialization, random-number seeds) could in principle make results non-repeatable (OP.C0402.02), but PSO results are always verified against deterministic dose codes and regulatory limits, so any variance would be caught in V&V—and again, this is not an *AI* failure, it is a numerical-methods quality-assurance issue. No adversarial AI techniques (prompt injection, model inversion, adversarial examples) apply. No operational AI risks (automation bias, drift, data scarcity for training) apply because there is no automation of a human decision and no training set. The use case does not genuinely incur AI insecurity; calling PSO 'AI' is a categorical error from an ML-engineering standpoint.

security_specialist.argument: From a nuclear security perspective, this use case warrants careful scrutiny not because the PSO algorithm itself is inherently vulnerable—it's deterministic optimization, not a learned model—but because it produces specifications for physical shielding whose adequacy is critical to both safety and security. An adversary interested in diverting or sabotaging spent fuel in transport could exploit errors in shielding design (introduced through malicious input manipulation or supply-chain compromise of the optimization toolchain) to create a cask that either fails catastrophically under deliberate stress or provides inadequate shielding in scenarios the adversary engineers. The shielding thickness output becomes a trust anchor: if downstream fabrication, licensing, and operational handling assume the PSO-derived specification is correct, no one may re-verify it under adversarial scenarios (e.g., a deliberate route change to increase vibration, or a pre-staged minor accident to test for premature shielding failure). More subtly, the optimization's input parameters (fuel isotopics, burnup, decay time) could be tampered with by an insider to yield a cask that is technically compliant for declared conditions but fails under undeclared material characteristics—a pathway for an adversary to mask diversion by ensuring the cask cannot safely transport what it is claimed to hold.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary security threat is that the PSO-derived shielding specification becomes a single point of trust in a supply chain: if an adversary (state-level or sophisticated insider) can manipulate the input data (fuel isotopics, source term, cask geometry constraints) or the optimization code itself, they can produce a cask design that is subtly inadequate under conditions they control. For example, an adversary could use insider access to substitute surrogate fuel characteristics during the optimization, yielding a cask certified for one fuel type but physically unsafe for another—enabling diversion by declaring the wrong fuel is being transported, or sabotage by ensuring the cask fails under a staged incident. The deterministic nature of PSO cuts both ways: it is repeatable (a defender can re-run it), but it also means an adversary who controls the inputs controls the output with high confidence. Because PSO is not a learned model, there is no training-data poisoning threat in the ML sense, but there is a supply-chain and input-integrity threat: if the neutronics libraries, dose-rate calculators, or material-property databases feeding the PSO are compromised (AML.T0010 AI Supply Chain Compromise, particularly .002 Data or .003 Model if the dose-rate predictor is itself ML-based), the optimization will confidently produce a wrong answer. The second-order risk is automation bias: because PSO is 'just math,' licensing authorities and fabricators may treat its output as gold-standard, skipping adversarial scenario analysis (e.g., 'what if the declared burnup is a lie?'). An adversary could also exploit this use case as reconnaissance: if the PSO tool or its dose-rate model is accessible (e.g., shared across a consortium or published with the research), an adversary learns exactly how shielding adequacy is evaluated, enabling them to craft diversion scenarios that stay just under detection thresholds. Finally, if the same PSO tool is used fleet-wide (OP.C0602 cross-site model propagation), a single compromise scales across all casks designed with it.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the limited applicability of learned-AI vulnerabilities to PSO but diverged on framing: the nuclear engineer emphasized objective misalignment and data quality, the AI engineer argued the use case incurs negligible AI-specific risk, and the security specialist focused on supply-chain and trust-anchor exploitation. The synthesis retains objective misalignment, input-data integrity, oversimplification, and automation bias as distinct threats, treating supply-chain compromise as the adversarial instantiation of the implicit data-quality and software-hygiene weaknesses the other panelists identified.

evidence.note: PSO trades shielding performance against cask weight for an ex-vessel spent fuel transport cask, yielding an optimum shielding thickness later checked against dose limits. PSO is a metaheuristic, not a learned model.

damage.why: Under-shielded cask design could lead to regulatory violations and significant radiological exposure during routine transport or accident conditions, eroding multiple safety margins, though not directly causing a release from fuel itself.

reproducibility.why: Once incorrect source terms, neutronics libraries, or constraint specifications are embedded in the PSO workflow, the algorithm will reliably converge on the flawed optimum every time it runs with those inputs.

exploitability.why: Requires supply-chain position to corrupt neutronics libraries or input data files, or insider access to modify objective-function constraints before they enter the licensing workflow.

affected_users.why: A compromised cask design propagates to all units fabricated from that specification and can affect an entire fleet if the same PSO tool or libraries are reused across multiple designs or sites.

use_case: Large language models interpreting nuclear power plant technical specifications, prior license amendment requests and plant-specific documents to capture regulatory knowledge and support drafting of license amendment requests (e.g. for power uprates)
incurred_insecurity:
This use case creates a regulatory-knowledge translation vulnerability in which an LLM tasked with interpreting technical specifications, prior license amendment requests, and plant-specific documents can produce fluent, authoritative-sounding text that misinterprets safety limits, hallucinates regulatory citations, or omits critical conditional logic—errors that may not be caught before submission and that corrupt the plant's licensing basis in ways discoverable only months or years later during a demand event or NRC audit. The system's outputs feed directly into safety-significant regulatory decisions (e.g., approving power uprates that stress emergency core cooling systems), yet the LLM's reasoning is opaque, its behavior non-deterministic across runs, and its training corpus sparse and heterogeneous (mixing OCR'd legacy documents, proprietary plant records, and potentially synthetic summaries), all of which degrade both the reliability of its outputs and the effectiveness of human oversight. Adversaries can exploit this fragility—and the concentration of trust if multiple utilities adopt similar tools—by poisoning the training data or retrieval indices with subtly altered technical specifications or fake precedent LARs, knowing that the resulting non-compliant or safety-degrading language will be amplified by the LLM's authoritative tone and may propagate across the industry if staff over-rely on AI-generated drafts under schedule pressure.

Hallucination and Content Fidelity Failure
The LLM's dominant implicit threat is generating plausible but incorrect regulatory content: fabricating technical specification surveillance requirements, misattributing limiting conditions for operation to the wrong system or operational mode, citing non-existent prior LARs as precedent, or oversimplifying conditional safety logic (e.g., collapsing 'if core thermal power exceeds X and containment pressure is below Y, then system Z must be operable' into an unconditional requirement). Power uprate LARs are particularly vulnerable because they require integrating constraints from multiple TS sections—reactor protection, ECCS, containment heat removal—and the model may confidently assert that a precedent exists for relaxing one limit without flagging an obscure interaction with another. This is a failure intrinsic to the AI system (not adversarial), but it directly enables regulatory non-compliance: a LAR submitted with hallucinated justifications may pass initial NRC screening if the fabricated citation sounds plausible, creating a licensing basis that permits unsafe operation until discovered during back-fit review or, worse, during an actual transient.

Data Provenance, Small-Data Scarcity, and Non-Determinism
The system's training corpus is sparse for any given plant (one facility's TS and LAR history), biased toward digitized or accessible documents, and likely includes OCR errors, version-control ambiguities, and transferred knowledge from dissimilar reactor types—all of which degrade model reliability in ways not remediable by scale. Base rates for novel LAR types (digital I&C upgrades, severe accident management provisions) are low, so the LLM has few examples and its outputs in those domains are weak, yet staff may not recognize this coverage gap. Non-determinism at inference time means re-generating the same LAR section can yield different wording, citations, or interpretations, undermining repeatability and making traditional qualification impossible; this also means an attacker does not need persistent access—a single 'bad roll' of the model's sampling during a critical LAR review may slip through if human verification is incomplete. The opacity of the LLM's reasoning (explainability limit) means tracing an asserted requirement back to its source TS clause or precedent LAR is often infeasible, forcing engineers either to accept the output on faith or manually re-do the research, which defeats the tool's efficiency rationale.

Automation Trust Failures and Skill Fade
Engineers under schedule pressure to deliver a power-uprate LAR are at high risk of over-relying on the LLM's draft without line-by-line verification against primary source documents (automation misuse/over-trust). The LLM's authoritative tone and correct citation formatting can mask substantive errors, and the sheer volume of cross-references in a complex LAR makes exhaustive human review impractical, creating a detection gap. Over time, repeated use erodes engineers' own skill in manually interpreting technical specifications and drafting LARs (skill fade), so when the AI is unavailable or known to be compromised, the human backup is weaker than before adoption. Conversely, if some staff distrust the LLM and ignore its outputs (disuse/under-trust), they may fail to notice when it correctly flags a compliance issue an adversary is attempting to obscure, creating a different blind spot. Both failure modes—misuse and disuse—are implicit in the human-AI interaction and do not require an attacker, but they directly amplify adversarial leverage.

Supply-Chain and RAG Poisoning (Adversarial)
An adversary can poison the LLM's knowledge base by infiltrating the training corpus or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) indices with malicious documents: a subtly altered version of a generic technical specification uploaded to a shared repository, a fake 'prior LAR' inserted into the plant's document management system by an insider, or a retrieval-optimized false entry designed to be ranked highly by the RAG system when the LLM queries for precedent on power uprates. The model will then confidently cite or paraphrase the poisoned content, and because the output matches the expected format and tone of legitimate regulatory language, it may evade peer review. If the base LLM or fine-tuning data comes from a third-party vendor or public model repository, supply-chain compromise at that stage can embed systematic misinterpretations (e.g., always understating ECCS margin requirements) that affect every LAR the tool produces. The time-to-consequence is long—months to years before the corrupted licensing basis leads to unsafe operation—but the detection barrier is high, requiring subject-matter expert review of every model output against original source documents, a level of scrutiny that undermines the efficiency gains motivating AI adoption.

Prompt Injection and Indirect Manipulation (Adversarial)
Because the LLM processes plant-specific documents, vendor analyses, and publicly available regulatory filings, an adversary can embed prompt-injection payloads in any of these sources: instructions hidden in a consultant's report, a malicious comment in an NRC public docket that later gets indexed by the RAG system, or a backdoor trigger in a vendor-supplied calculation that causes the LLM to omit certain safety constraints when drafting the LAR. Indirect prompt injection is especially insidious because the attack surface is any document the system might retrieve, and the payload can be latent—triggered only when the LLM is asked about a specific uprate scenario—making pre-deployment testing insufficient. An attacker can also use a publicly trained proxy model to discover which document structures or phrasings the real system is likely to approve, then craft a malicious LAR optimized to pass both automated and LLM-assisted human review.

Cross-Site Propagation and Concentration-of-Trust (Adversarial Leverage)
If multiple utilities adopt similar LLM tooling—perhaps from a shared vendor, an NRC-endorsed platform, or open-source fine-tuning recipes—a single successful model compromise or RAG corpus manipulation scales across the fleet. An adversary who can shape the model's outputs gains leverage over what compliance obligations the industry collectively perceives, and a silent error (adversarial or accidental) could propagate via copy-paste LAR drafting, creating a widespread regulatory blind spot that an attacker could exploit with coordinated timing (physical intrusion, insider action) across multiple facilities. The cloud-hosted nature of many LLM deployments expands the attack surface: compromise of the hosting environment or the vendor's model-update pipeline gives an adversary access to multiple utilities' LAR-drafting processes simultaneously, and exfiltration of proprietary plant data or inference-time queries via the API can reveal facility-specific vulnerabilities or ongoing licensing strategies.

Model Inversion and Credential Harvesting (Adversarial)
An adversary with API access can probe the LLM to infer training-data membership (discovering which plant-specific documents or prior LARs were in the corpus) or attempt model inversion to extract proprietary technical specification limits, historical LAR vulnerabilities, or security-sensitive facility details. If the system uses retrieval-augmented generation with access to internal document repositories, credential harvesting from the RAG configuration or tool definitions can grant the attacker direct access to the plant's licensing and engineering records. Even if the attacker never compromises the production LLM, reconnaissance of the model's outputs (via legitimate queries or a hijacked account) can map the plant's regulatory posture and identify which safety arguments the LLM is trained to accept, informing the design of a physical or cyber attack optimized to fall into the model's blind spots.

Drift, Qualification Gaps, and Delayed Detection (Implicit Weakness Exploitable Adversarially)
The LLM's understanding of regulatory language drifts as the NRC issues new guidance or revises generic technical specifications (concept drift), and if the model is not continuously retrained, its LAR advice becomes noncompliant in ways that may not be caught until an audit or enforcement action. An adversary can monitor for this drift window and submit a malicious LAR during a period when the model is out-of-date and unlikely to flag a new regulatory requirement. The absence of AI-specific qualification processes for this safety-adjacent use case means there is no systematic verification that the LLM is not introducing bias (e.g., systematically underestimating dose consequences of design changes, or favoring cost-saving arguments over safety margins), and an adversary aware of such a bias can design their attack to exploit it—recommending a configuration the model will approve but that actually degrades defense-in-depth. The long lag between LAR approval and operational consequence (power uprate implemented, plant operates for months, then a transient reveals the inadequate ECCS margin) makes attribution difficult and gives the adversary time to erase forensic evidence or exit the target environment.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case sits at the nexus of engineering authority and regulatory interpretation – a domain where misreading a technical specification or failing to cross-reference a limiting condition for operation could embed a non-conservative assumption into a license amendment request that later permits unsafe operation. From an operations lens, the core vulnerability is that LLMs can produce fluent, confident text that misinterprets regulatory intent, omits critical technical specification surveillance requirements, or hallucinates citations to non-existent precedent, and licensee staff working under schedule pressure may not catch these errors before submittal. The consequence is not immediate physical harm, but a corrupted licensing basis that could allow operation outside analyzed conditions (e.g., a power uprate approved without adequate consideration of ECCS performance limits) or create a compliance gap that goes undetected until a demand event. An adversary could exploit this by poisoning the training corpus with subtly altered versions of technical specifications or prior LARs, knowing that the model's output feeds directly into safety-significant regulatory decision-making with limited independent verification of the AI's interpretation against original source documents.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The dominant non-adversarial threat is **content fidelity failure** – the LLM hallucinates technical specification requirements, misattributes limiting conditions for operation to the wrong mode or system, or oversimplifies conditional logic in surveillance requirements (e.g., 'if core power exceeds X, then Y must be operable' becomes 'Y must be operable'). Power uprate LARs are particularly vulnerable because they require integrating constraints across multiple TS sections (reactor protection, ECCS, containment heat removal) and the model may fail to surface an obscure interaction. This is compounded by **automation trust failure** – engineers under schedule pressure to produce a LAR may not rigorously verify every TS citation or cross-check the model's summary of prior uprate precedent against the original dockets, leading to submission of a technically deficient request that NRC staff must catch (imposing regulatory burden) or that slips through and creates a non-conservative licensing basis. **Data provenance and small-data problems** are acute: the training set for plant-specific documents is small (one plant's TS and LAR history), base rates for certain uprate conditions are low (few plants have attempted this specific change), and the model may 'transfer' knowledge from a different reactor type or vintage in ways that don't apply. From an adversarial perspective, the **supply chain and RAG poisoning** risk is significant – if the LLM is fine-tuned or retrieval-augmented on a corpus of regulatory documents that an adversary has infiltrated (e.g., a poisoned version of a generic technical specification uploaded to a shared repository, or a fake 'prior LAR' inserted into the document set), the model will confidently cite non-existent or altered requirements, and the licensing basis becomes corrupted. The time-to-consequence is long (months to years before the deficient LAR leads to unsafe operation), the detection barrier is high (requires subject-matter expert review of every model output against primary sources), and the **cross-site propagation** risk is severe if the same LLM or document corpus is reused across multiple licensees preparing similar uprates. Existing practice (independent technical review, NRC staff scrutiny) provides defense-in-depth, but AI-accelerated LAR preparation could overwhelm that review capacity or create a false sense that 'the AI checked it,' leading to **skill fade** in manual TS interpretation and a **clumsy automation** failure mode where the human cannot effectively supervise the AI's work.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case sits at the interface between regulatory knowledge retrieval and content generation, raising immediate concerns about training data provenance (LARs, tech specs, and plant-specific documents are proprietary, vintage-varying, and not publicly available at scale), hallucination risk (LLMs confabulating non-existent technical requirements or precedents), and the non-determinism inherent in generation at inference time. The system depends on accurately capturing plant-specific nuance and regulatory precedent—domains where a single misattributed requirement or hallucinated cross-reference could propagate into a submitted LAR, creating compliance exposure the utility and NRC discover only after resource-intensive review. From an ML-engineering standpoint, the training corpus is almost certainly heterogeneous (mix of OCR'd legacy docs, modern PDFs, possibly synthetic summaries), the LLM's behavior on rare combinations of tech-spec clauses is untested, and there is no deterministic guarantee that re-running the same query yields the same draft—complicating both V&V and any adversarial scenario where an attacker poisons retrieval indices or prompt-injects via a malicious document in the knowledge base.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Implicit (non-adversarial) fragility:** The LLM is trained (or fine-tuned, or retrieval-augmented) on a corpus of tech specs, past LARs, and plant docs that is sparse for any given plant configuration, biased toward whatever documents were digitized or accessible, and almost certainly includes OCR errors, version-control ambiguities, and domain jargon the base model never saw at pre-training scale. This creates acute risk of hallucination (OP.C0304.01)—the model fabricating a plausible-sounding regulatory citation, tech-spec limit, or precedent LAR that does not exist, which then gets incorporated into a draft and discovered only during NRC review or, worse, after implementation. Relatedly, the system's output is non-deterministic (OP.C0402.02): re-generating the same section of a LAR may yield different wording, different citations, or different interpretations of ambiguous clauses, undermining repeatability and making it impossible to qualify the tool in a traditional sense. There is also significant data-provenance risk (OP.C0201.03, OP.C0204): if the training set includes simulated or transferred data (e.g., generic tech specs adapted from one plant to another, or synthetic paraphrases to augment a small corpus), the model may confidently assert requirements that apply to Plant A but not Plant B, or vice versa. Skill fade and automation-trust issues (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06) are also foreseeable: engineers may over-rely on the LLM's drafts without line-by-line verification against source documents, especially under schedule pressure for a power uprate, and their ability to manually draft or cross-check LARs will atrophy over time. Finally, the system's explainability is minimal (OP.C0401)—if the LLM asserts that a given power-uprate scenario requires a specific surveillance-test modification, tracing that assertion back to the exact tech-spec clause and past LAR precedent is often infeasible, leaving the human reviewer to either accept it on faith or re-do the research manually.

**Adversarial exposure (exploiting or enabled by the above):** An adversary with access to the retrieval corpus or prompt-injection surface can poison the knowledge base (AML.T0070 RAG Poisoning, AML.T0020 Poison Training Data) by inserting a malicious document—e.g., a fake prior LAR or a subtly altered tech spec—that the LLM will retrieve and incorporate into its output, causing the utility to submit a LAR with incorrect safety limits or non-compliant language. If the system is retrieval-augmented, an attacker could also craft retrieval-content (AML.T0066) or inject false RAG entries (AML.T0071) to bias the LLM toward specific (unsafe or non-compliant) drafting choices. Prompt injection (AML.T0051.000 Direct, AML.T0051.001 Indirect) is a risk if the LLM processes untrusted plant-specific documents (e.g., a vendor-supplied analysis or a third-party consultant's report) that contain embedded instructions to ignore certain safety constraints or to generate language that bypasses NRC review triggers. Model inversion or membership inference (AML.T0024.000, AML.T0024.001) could allow an adversary to extract proprietary or security-sensitive details from the training corpus—e.g., inferring Plant X's current tech-spec limits or past LAR vulnerabilities—by querying the LLM strategically. If the LLM is hosted in the cloud or accessed via API (OP.C0601, AML.T0040), the attack surface expands: an adversary could exfiltrate regulatory knowledge via the inference API (AML.T0024), or an insider could use valid credentials (AML.T0012) to extract the full training dataset or model weights (AML.T0025). There is also risk of supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003) if the base LLM or fine-tuning data comes from a third-party vendor, or if the utility uses a pre-trained model from a public repository (AML.T0002.001) that has been backdoored or poisoned. Finally, the non-determinism and lack of repeatability (OP.C0402.02) mean that an adversary does not need to compromise the model directly—they can simply time an attack around the inherent variability in LLM outputs, knowing that the utility's verification process is incomplete and that a subtly incorrect draft may slip through if it is generated on a 'bad roll' of the LLM's sampling process.

security_specialist.argument: This use case creates a concentration-of-trust vulnerability: if licensees and NRC staff both lean on the same LLM-mediated interpretation of technical specifications and prior LARs, a sophisticated adversary who can shape the model's outputs (via training data manipulation, prompt injection in RAG sources, or compromise of the model's hosting environment) gains leverage over what compliance obligations the industry collectively perceives. Even absent direct adversarial action, the system's opacity and hallucination risk mean an erroneous interpretation could propagate across multiple facilities via copy-paste LAR drafting, and an adversary aware of such a silent error could time other actions (physical intrusion, insider coordination) to exploit the resulting regulatory blind spot. The system also introduces a new insider threat surface: an insider with access to the LLM's configuration, RAG corpus, or prompt-engineering infrastructure can subtly bias outputs to omit inconvenient constraints or insert plausible-but-wrong safety arguments, and because LLM outputs mimic authoritative regulatory prose, such manipulations may evade peer review longer than a human-drafted error would.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial Threats:** An attacker targeting this LLM-based LAR drafting system could pursue supply-chain compromise of the model itself (AML.T0010.003, poisoning pre-trained weights or fine-tuning data so the model subtly misinterprets critical technical specification clauses), RAG poisoning (AML.T0070, injecting false precedents or omitting restrictive prior LARs from the retrieval corpus so the drafting advice appears compliant when it isn't), or prompt injection via publicly accessible regulatory documents that the RAG indexes (AML.T0093, embedding adversarial instructions in a comment period submission that later gets retrieved and influences LAR text generation). Because the system is designed to cross-reference plant-specific documents, an insider (or an external attacker who has gained access to the plant's document repositories) could poison those internal sources—planting a fake calculation, a subtly altered tech spec page, or a misleading prior LAR summary—that the LLM then cites as authoritative, generating a non-compliant or safety-degrading LAR that appears well-supported (AML.T0099, AML.T0071). The trust concentration is the key exploit target: if multiple utilities use similar LLM tooling (perhaps from a shared vendor or NRC-endorsed platform), a single successful model compromise or RAG corpus manipulation scales across the fleet (OP.C0602), and an adversary could use the resulting widespread misinterpretation of a tech spec to coordinate simultaneous actions at multiple plants during a window when operators believe (incorrectly, per the LLM) that a certain configuration is compliant. The system also lowers the barrier for social engineering: an attacker could use the LLM's outputs (which sound authoritative and cite real documents) in spearphishing to convince plant staff or NRC reviewers to accept a malicious LAR, or conversely, use a jailbroken version of the same LLM to generate plausible-looking counterfeit NRC correspondence or safety evaluation reports (AML.T0052.000, AML.T0054). Even if the attacker never touches the production LLM, they can train a proxy model on publicly available NRC documents and LARs (AML.T0005.001) to discover which phrasings or document structures the real system is likely to approve, then craft a malicious LAR optimized to pass automated and LLM-assisted human review.

**Implicit (Non-Adversarial) Threats Exploitable by Adversaries:** The system's non-adversarial failure modes themselves become attack surface. Hallucination (OP.C0304.01) means the LLM may cite a nonexistent prior LAR, invent a technical specification clause, or misattribute a safety justification—normally caught by human review, but an adversary aware of the LLM's tendency to hallucinate certain topics (discoverable via AML.T0062) can time a physical attack or insider action for when plant staff are distracted reviewing a hallucination-heavy LAR, or can deliberately trigger a hallucination (via prompt crafting, AML.T0065) that leads staff to believe a safety system is less critical than it is. Data provenance (OP.C0201.03) is a vulnerability: if the LLM is trained on synthetic or transferred data (simulated LARs, or LARs from a different reactor type), it may produce advice that is plausible but not actually compliant for this plant's vintage or design, and an adversary could exploit the resulting gap between perceived and actual compliance. Small-data/low-base-rate problems (OP.C0202) are acute for unusual LAR types (e.g., digital I&C upgrades, severe accident management)—the LLM will have few examples to learn from, so its outputs in those domains are less reliable, and an adversary targeting such an upgrade could use the LLM's weak coverage as camouflage for a malicious modification hidden in the LAR's technical appendices. Automation bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05) is the linchpin: if licensing engineers over-rely on the LLM's draft and under-scrutinize its citations, they may miss both naturally occurring errors and adversarially inserted ones, and an adversary can exploit this misuse by ensuring their malicious content is presented in the LLM's characteristic authoritative tone. Conversely, if some staff distrust the LLM (disuse), they may not notice when it correctly flags a compliance issue an adversary is trying to slip through, creating a detection gap. Skill fade (OP.C0101.06) is a long-term threat: as engineers rely on the LLM for regulatory interpretation, their own expertise in reading tech specs and prior LARs atrophies, so when the LLM is unavailable (due to adversary denial-of-service, AML.T0029, or cost harvesting, AML.T0034) or compromised, the human backup is weaker than it was before AI adoption. Drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02) is both a direct risk (the LLM's understanding of regulatory language drifts as NRC issues new guidance, making its LAR advice noncompliant) and an adversary opportunity (an attacker can monitor for concept drift, then submit a LAR during a window when the model is out-of-date and unlikely to flag a new regulatory requirement). The system's cloud dependency (OP.C0601) and potential for cross-site propagation (OP.C0602) mean an adversary who compromises the hosting environment or the vendor's model-update pipeline gains access to multiple utilities' LAR-drafting processes at once. Finally, the lack of AI-specific qualification for this safety-adjacent use case (OP.C0401, OP.C0501) means there may be no formal process to verify the LLM isn't introducing systematic bias (e.g., always underestimating the dose consequences of a design change), and an adversary aware of such a bias can design their attack to fall into the LLM's blind spot—recommending a configuration the model will approve but that actually degrades safety margins.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on hallucination/content-fidelity failure, automation trust (misuse/disuse/skill-fade), data provenance and scarcity, and RAG/training-data poisoning as the dominant threats; the synthesis integrated their complementary emphases (nuclear engineer on TS misinterpretation consequences, AI engineer on non-determinism and ML-theoretic limits, security specialist on cross-site propagation and concentration-of-trust leverage) into a unified narrative tracing implicit fragilities through to adversarial exploitation.
