evidence.note: Regression models trained on 216 NUREG-0630 burst tests (heating rate and pressure as inputs) to predict cladding rupture behaviour in LOCA scenarios. Conference-level evidence only.

damage.why: Manipulation of LOCA cladding rupture predictions directly informs 10 CFR 50.46 compliance; adversarial bias or undetected out-of-distribution failure could result in fuel design approval under incorrect safety margins, leading to cladding breach and radiological release during an actual LOCA event.

reproducibility.why: Supply-chain poisoning of a small fixed dataset (216 samples) or model bias injection is highly reproducible once supply-chain access is achieved; out-of-distribution failures are reliably triggered when modern alloys or conditions outside the 1970s-1980s test matrix are encountered.

exploitability.why: Supply-chain manipulation requires insider access to vendor development or data-curation pipelines; model exfiltration requires network access to systems storing the trained model; out-of-distribution failures require no adversarial action but do require the system to be deployed on novel conditions.

affected_users.why: A compromised or failed model propagates across fuel-fabrication facilities and reactor fleets through vendor-supplied design tools or regulatory approval processes, affecting multiple fuel assemblies and potentially entire reactor cores if the predictions underpin safety-case licensing.

discoverability.why: The use of NUREG-0630 as training data is documented in open conference literature; an adversary can infer the dataset's age, size, and scope from public regulatory and vendor documentation, making the data-scarcity and supply-chain attack surface evident to capable external actors with nuclear-engineering knowledge.

use_case: Open-set recognition using class-specific semantic reconstruction on orbit plots and recurrence plots from reactor coolant pump vibration signals to detect both known and unknown shaft and bearing faults
incurred_insecurity:
This use case introduces operational insecurity by placing an un-auditable trust boundary at the point where operators must decide whether a flagged 'unknown' fault is a genuine mechanical precursor, a model artifact, or an adversarial manipulation—all under time pressure if the reactor coolant pump is already showing signs of distress. The AI's open-set decision is fundamentally unverifiable in real time because the system cannot distinguish epistemic uncertainty (a truly novel fault) from corrupted or drifted input data, and an adversary can exploit this ambiguity to either mask real sabotage or flood operators with false unknowns that erode trust in genuine alerts. The core threats are alarm-fatigue erosion of operator vigilance, training-data scarcity producing brittle generalization to real operational conditions, and adversarial manipulation of vibration signals or model internals to either suppress detection of deliberate mechanical degradation or trigger unnecessary reactor trips.

Alarm complacency and trust calibration failure -- implicit, exploitable
Frequent false-positive 'unknown' flags from operational drift (pump speed transients, temperature swings, sensor calibration shifts outside the model's training envelope) condition operators to dismiss reconstruction-error spikes as model noise rather than investigating the hardware. An adversary times a real mechanical sabotage—bearing contamination, shaft micro-cracking—to coincide with periods of known high false-alarm rates (startup transients, power maneuvers, post-maintenance testing), knowing operators will attribute the alert to model unreliability and delay physical inspection until catastrophic failure.

Training-data scarcity and operational-envelope mismatch -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained on lab-bench vibration data or historical faults from a small number of pumps, never seeing the full range of in-situ signatures under varying coolant chemistry, temperature, flow rate, or pump age. When deployed on a new reactor or after a pump rebuild, it flags normal operational transients as 'unknown faults' (crying wolf) or fails to recognize genuine degradation that manifests differently in the field than on the test stand. An adversary with supply-chain position injects subtly biased training images—orbit or recurrence plots from deliberately contaminated bearings labeled as 'normal'—shifting the open-set boundary so the model reconstructs sabotage signatures with low error, masking the attack as a known-benign condition.

Reconstruction-error ambiguity in distinguishing faults from input corruption -- implicit, exploitable
The system uses pixel-level reconstruction error on orbit and recurrence plots to decide 'unknown fault,' but has no mechanism to distinguish a high error caused by a novel mechanical fault from one caused by sensor noise, ADC bit-flips, preprocessing drift, or adversarially injected vibration signal. An attacker with access to the VMS data stream crafts synthetic vibration patterns—via black-box optimization against a proxy model of the plot-generation transform—that produce high reconstruction error without an actual pump fault, triggering false unknowns that either force an unnecessary reactor trip (if operators over-trust and act immediately) or desensitize them to future alerts (if the pattern repeats and investigations find no mechanical issue).

Adversarial masking of real faults via model or data manipulation -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain attacker with access to the model weights or training pipeline embeds a backdoor that reconstructs adversarially chosen vibration signatures—corresponding to deliberate bearing sabotage or shaft damage—with artificially low error, bypassing the open-set alarm. Alternatively, they manipulate the inference-time vibration signal itself to suppress or smooth fault-indicative features before the orbit/recurrence plot transform, keeping reconstruction error in the 'known normal' range while the physical pump degrades. The operational consequence is delayed detection of incipient failure, risking loss of forced circulation and potential challenge to decay heat removal if the fault progresses to seizure.

Fleet-wide propagation of common-mode blind spots -- implicit, exploitable
If the model is deployed across multiple reactor units via centralized update, a shared training-data bias (e.g., all training pumps were a single OEM design, or all orbit plots used identical FFT windowing) creates a common blind spot for faults that manifest differently in other pump models or operating envelopes. An adversary who identifies this blind spot through reconnaissance of the training methodology can execute the same mechanical sabotage at multiple sites, knowing the AI will fail uniformly. Even without an adversary, operational heterogeneity (different pump ages, coolant chemistries, installation alignments) means drift at one site propagates as a model update to others, amplifying false-positive rates fleet-wide and eroding trust across the operator community.

Non-deterministic inference complicating post-event forensics -- implicit
If the reconstruction model or the plot-generation pipeline exhibits inference-time non-repeatability (e.g., due to GPU floating-point variance, random augmentations left active in deployment, or stochastic elements in the recurrence-plot algorithm), investigators cannot reproduce the exact reconstruction error that triggered—or failed to trigger—an alarm during a fault event. This blocks root-cause analysis and allows an adversary to claim any suspicious alert pattern was a transient model artifact, delaying attribution of sabotage and undermining regulatory confidence in the AI-augmented monitoring system.

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear engineer focused on plant operations and process safety, I see this use case as a classic condition-based monitoring application for a critical rotating component—the reactor coolant pump—whose failure can force an unplanned shutdown or challenge safety systems if the shaft or bearings degrade undetected. The AI system converts vibration signals into visual representations (orbit and recurrence plots) and uses reconstruction errors to flag both cataloged faults and 'unknown' anomalies, which is operationally attractive because RCPs can develop novel degradation modes not seen in training data. However, this creates a human-AI interaction challenge: operators or maintenance planners must decide whether a flagged 'unknown' fault is a genuine precursor requiring immediate action, a benign signal artifact, or a model false positive—potentially under time pressure if the pump is already showing other signs of distress. If the AI drifts due to changing operational conditions (different flow rates, temperatures, or pump speeds across power maneuvers), or if its training data came primarily from test stands rather than in-situ operating pumps, it may cry wolf on normal transients or miss genuine faults that manifest differently in the field, eroding trust and leading to either complacency (ignoring real warnings) or unnecessary forced outages (acting on false ones).
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary threats fall into three buckets—human factors, data quality, and adversarial surface. On human factors: the open-set design explicitly flags 'unknown' faults, which forces operators into a judgment call with incomplete information (OP.C0101.04 misuse or OP.C0101.05 disuse risk). If the model frequently flags unknowns that turn out to be measurement noise or benign speed transients, operators may begin ignoring alerts (OP.C0102 alarm complacency), and a real incipient shaft crack gets dismissed. Conversely, if the system is too sensitive and triggers precautionary shutdowns for false positives, the plant loses availability and operators lose confidence. On data quality and drift: RCP vibration signatures are highly sensitive to operating state—power level, coolant temperature, flow rate—and a model trained on steady-state lab data or a different pump design may not generalize to this specific pump's installed configuration (OP.C0201.01 simulated data, OP.C0201.03 transferred data, OP.C0302.01 operational drift, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity). New pumps in new builds have scarce field-fault data (OP.C0203 new-build scarcity, OP.C0202 low base-rate), so the 'known' fault library may be incomplete and the reconstruction baseline unrepresentative. If the model is deployed fleet-wide via a centralized update (OP.C0602 cross-site propagation), a drift or bias in one plant's data could contaminate the model for others. On the adversarial side: an attacker with access to the vibration monitoring system's data stream (either at the sensor, the data historian, or the AI input) could inject synthetic vibration signals—mimicking a severe bearing fault—to trigger false alarms and force an unnecessary reactor trip or pump swap (AML.T0020 poison training data if they have long-term access, or AML.T0043 craft adversarial data if they target inference-time inputs). Alternatively, they could suppress or smooth real fault signatures to mask genuine degradation until catastrophic failure, undermining the predictive value and forcing reliance on older, less sensitive analog indicators. The open-set reconstruction approach is harder to fool than a simple classifier, but an adversary who understands the orbit/recurrence plot transformation could craft signals that reconstruct 'normally' despite being anomalous in the time domain (AML.T0043.001 black-box optimization, AML.T0005 proxy model). The operational consequence is either a forced shutdown (loss of generation, thermal stress on components from rapid cooldown) from a false positive, or a failure to detect real degradation leading to pump seizure, loss of forced circulation, and potential challenge to decay heat removal if multiple pumps are affected or operators misinterpret the root cause.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case is architecturally fragile at inference time in ways specific to open-set recognition: the system must decide whether a reconstruction error means 'unknown fault' or 'bad data,' with no ground truth for the latter and potentially catastrophic consequences if it confuses the two. The training data is necessarily incomplete—RCPs run for decades, many faults are low-probability, and the system is trained on what we've *seen*, not what's *possible*. Orbit and recurrence plots are derived visualizations, so the transformation pipeline itself (signal preprocessing, windowing, plot generation) becomes a hidden source of drift and brittleness—if sensor calibration drifts, sampling rates change, or a deployment environment differs from the lab bench where the plots were tuned, the model sees 'unknown' patterns even when the pump is fine. The operational risk is that this model sits in a criticality gap: it's monitoring equipment whose failure can lead to loss-of-coolant scenarios, but its training regime and drift-monitoring are almost certainly less mature than the 1E/safety-grade instrumentation it's supposed to augment or replace, and there's no adversarial consideration of how timing an attack around a false-unknown alarm (or suppressing a true one) could mask sabotage.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core ML vulnerability is that open-set recognition by reconstruction error conflates epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty at inference time—there is no principled way to distinguish 'I haven't seen this fault' from 'the input data is corrupted/drifted/adversarially perturbed,' and in a safety-critical RCP monitoring context, both demand operator action but the *correct* action differs. An adversary who understands the orbit/recurrence plot transform could inject subtle vibration signal noise (AML.T0043 crafted adversarial data, AML.T0015 evade model) that produces high reconstruction error without an actual fault, triggering false unknowns that either desensitize operators (OP.C0101.04 misuse/over-trust if they learn to ignore alarms, or OP.C0101.05 disuse/under-trust if the system cries wolf) or cause unnecessary shutdowns. Conversely, an adversary with physical access (AML.T0041) or supply-chain position (AML.T0010.000 hardware, .001 software) could introduce a real but slow-developing bearing fault while simultaneously manipulating the VMS data stream to keep reconstruction error low, masking the fault until catastrophic failure. The implicit threat is worse: this system is almost certainly trained on lab/bench data or historical fault signatures from a small number of RCPs (OP.C0201.04 lab-measured, OP.C0202 small-data problem, OP.C0203 new-build scarcity if deployed on a next-gen reactor), meaning it has never seen the full operational envelope—vibration signatures change with coolant chemistry, temperature transients, pump age, even grid frequency variations in some designs (OP.C0302.01 data/operational drift, OP.C0302.03 operational heterogeneity). The plot-generation transform is deterministic but unqualified: if the windowing, FFT parameters, or recurrence threshold were tuned on one dataset and the deployment signal has different noise characteristics, the model sees 'unknown' constantly (OP.C0303 static/dynamic qualification mismatch). There's no indication the system has a strategy for retraining on new unknowns once discovered, so it's a static artifact deployed into a dynamic fault space (OP.C0302.02 concept drift). From an AI-ML perspective, the vulnerability is that the class-specific reconstruction approach has no external calibration: the decision boundary between 'novel fault' and 'input anomaly' is learned implicitly and never validated against ground-truth unknowns (because by definition you don't have them), so an adversary can exploit this ambiguity (AML.T0005 proxy model to find the boundary, AML.T0043.001 black-box optimization to craft signals that live in the decision gap). The safety dependency is that RCP bearing/shaft failures are loss-of-coolant precursors, so if the AI either fails to detect an evolving fault or floods operators with false positives during a real transient, the consequence is delayed or incorrect operator response in a time-critical scenario. The system's value proposition—detecting *unknown* faults—is also its Achilles' heel: you can't verify it works on unknowns until you have an unknown, and by then it's too late for qualification. This is compounded if the model is deployed fleet-wide (OP.C0602 cross-site propagation): a common-mode failure in the plot transform or a shared training-data bias means the same blind spot exists across all units.

security_specialist.argument: This use case concentrates a significant operational trust point—distinguishing known from unknown mechanical faults in a critical primary-loop component—into an AI system whose open-set boundary is fundamentally un-auditable by operators in real time. An adversary (insider or supply-chain compromise) gains leverage in two ways: first, by manipulating the system to misclassify a deliberate mechanical sabotage as 'known and benign' or to flood operators with false unknowns, eroding their trust in genuine alerts (a classic prepare-the-battlefield tactic); second, by using the system's existence to time physical attacks when operators are conditioned to dismiss reconstruction-error spikes as model noise rather than investigating the hardware. The offline training regime on scarce real-fault data and the use of synthetic orbit/recurrence plots create an attractive surface for data poisoning (supply-chain injection of subtly altered training images) that would be difficult to detect and could shift the open-set decision boundary in adversarially useful ways. Even without an adversary, automation bias and alarm fatigue from false-positive 'unknown faults' make this a natural cover for an insider who understands when the model is least trusted.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial surface:** The multi-channel image-reconstruction approach, combined with its reliance on orbit and recurrence plots (which are interpretable to a vibration expert but opaque as pixel-level model inputs), creates an exploitable trust inversion: operators cannot verify the open-set decision in real time, so an adversary who has poisoned the training data or compromised the inference path can cause the system to normalize (reconstruct well) a signature that should trigger an unknown-fault alert—effectively masking sabotage of the RCP shaft or bearings. Supply-chain risk is elevated because the training pipeline depends on synthetic or lab-bench fault data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.04) that may never have seen adversarially induced mechanical degradation (e.g., a bearing deliberately packed with contaminant). An insider with access to the VMS data stream or the model itself (AML.T0012 Valid Accounts, AML.T0018 Manipulate AI Model) could pre-position a backdoor that triggers benign reconstruction only when a specific vibration signature—corresponding to their sabotage—appears, bypassing the open-set alarm. The system's value to an adversary is not just in attacking it directly but in knowing that operators will have been conditioned by false-positive 'unknowns' (OP.C0101.04 Misuse, OP.C0102 Alarm complacency) to delay investigation, giving a window for physical follow-on actions.

**Implicit/amplified risks an adversary would exploit:** Even with no adversary, this use case suffers from data scarcity for real operational faults (OP.C0202, OP.C0203) and non-deterministic reconstruction (OP.C0402.02), which means the open-set boundary will drift unpredictably (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02) as pumps age or operating conditions change—an adversary times their action to coincide with known model-update windows or transient operational states when operators expect higher false-alarm rates. The lack of deterministic repeatability and the opacity of pixel-space reconstruction errors (OP.C0401) mean an insider or sophisticated attacker can argue any alert was a model artifact, delaying physical inspection. Security culture erodes because this system, by design, tells operators 'trust me to know what I don't know,' which is exactly the cognitive state an adversary wants: operators second-guessing genuine mechanical precursors. If the model is shared across a fleet (OP.C0602), a single successful poisoning attack propagates the blind spot to multiple plants. The concentration of trust in a system whose failure mode (missed unknown fault) is indistinguishable from its success mode (correct novel detection) until after a mechanical failure event makes this a high-value stepping stone for an adversary planning a broader attack: compromise the RCP fault-detection AI, then introduce the actual mechanical fault it's now blind to, forcing an unplanned shutdown or worse under conditions the adversary controls.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on alarm complacency from false unknowns, training-data scarcity limiting generalization, and adversarial exploitation of the reconstruction-error ambiguity; the security specialist's backdoor-trigger scenario and the AI engineer's epistemic/aleatoric conflation were synthesized into the masking and input-corruption threats respectively.

evidence.note: The paper proposes an open-set recognition approach that converts reactor coolant pump vibration monitoring system (RCP-VMS) signals into orbit plots and recurrence plots as multi-channel image inputs, then uses reconstruction errors to distinguish both known fault modes and previously unseen faults in shaft and bearing components, addressing a limitation of conventional AI models that fail on unknown faults.

damage.why: Delayed detection of reactor coolant pump failure risks loss of forced circulation and decay heat removal capability, a challenge to core cooling that could lead to fuel damage if backup systems fail—approaching but not definitively reaching radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Alarm-fatigue erosion from training-data mismatch and operational drift is highly reproducible once the model is deployed outside its training envelope; adversarial masking via backdoor or signal manipulation reliably suppresses alerts when conditions are met.

exploitability.why: Training-data poisoning and model backdoors require supply-chain or development access; inference-time signal manipulation requires network/VMS access; timing sabotage around known high false-alarm periods requires operational knowledge but not deep system internals—moderate insider position or supply-chain compromise.

affected_users.why: Fleet-wide model deployment propagates common training biases and drift across multiple reactor units, creating synchronized blind spots; within a facility, loss of coolant pump monitoring affects the entire primary heat transport system.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability class is documented in open literature (orbit/recurrence plot methods, open-set recognition challenges); adversaries can infer training-data limitations from published research on this approach and observe false-alarm patterns during normal operational transients to identify exploitable periods.

use_case: Residual neural network detection of corrosion (iron oxide discoloration, pitting, and stress corrosion cracking) in dry storage stainless steel canister images to automate visual inspection of used nuclear fuel canisters
incurred_insecurity:
This use case substitutes AI for a critical human verification function—visual inspection of dry storage canister integrity—where missed corrosion leads to containment breach, radionuclide release, and loss of fuel inventory control. The dominant threats are implicit: the model is trained on sparse, non-representative data from a rare-event problem (real canister corrosion), creating severe out-of-distribution risk as canisters age or new corrosion morphologies emerge, while the tile-based architecture risks losing spatial context needed to distinguish benign discoloration from networked stress-corrosion cracking. Automation complacency and skill fade follow directly from the stated goal of reducing human inspection burden, eroding the independent verification that would catch model errors. Adversaries can exploit these weaknesses by physically or digitally crafting canister surfaces to evade tile-level detection, poisoning training data to teach the model to ignore specific corrosion signatures, or timing intrusions during windows when undetected corrosion has already compromised canister integrity, masking diversion or sabotage evidence while operators trust the AI's clearance.

Training-data scarcity and non-representativeness -- implicit, exploitable
Real canister corrosion events are rare and destructive sampling impractical, forcing reliance on simulated or lab-induced corrosion that does not generalize to field weathering, pitting morphology, or novel stress-cracking patterns in aged stainless steel under varied site climates. An adversary aware of this training gap could induce corrosion signatures (e.g., chloride-accelerated SCC in coastal storage) outside the model's learned distribution, confident they will not trigger alarms.

Out-of-distribution failure under operational drift -- implicit, exploitable
As canisters age, environmental conditions shift, or new corrosion mechanisms emerge decades into storage, the static model's classifications degrade without retraining on labeled real-world failure data that will never arrive at scale. An adversary monitoring facility operations could time physical attacks or diversion attempts during these undetected drift windows, knowing the AI's sensitivity has eroded below human-inspector baselines.

Tile-level fragmentation losing spatial context -- implicit, exploitable
The tile-crop-and-count aggregation treats each image patch independently, risking failure to recognize networked stress-corrosion-cracking patterns that propagate across tile boundaries or distinguish benign surface staining from structural pitting when spatial context is lost. An adversary could exploit this by applying targeted corrosion or camouflage in patterns designed to stay below per-tile thresholds, effectively crafting an adversarial physical input that evades detection when viewed in fragments.

Automation complacency and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Inspectors relying on AI output to reduce radiation exposure and fatigue will cease independent visual verification, lose perceptual skill in recognizing ambiguous early-stage corrosion, and fail to catch model errors until canister failure occurs. An adversary gains extended undetected access: they know human scrutiny has been automated away, so physical tampering (forced entry, accelerated corrosion as sabotage evidence) goes unnoticed longer than under traditional inspection regimes.

Training-data poisoning to suppress corrosion signatures -- adversarial
An adversary with access to the training pipeline (insider or supply-chain compromise before deployment) injects mislabeled examples teaching the model that specific corrosion morphologies (e.g., pitting in a particular geometric pattern, oxide discoloration matching a chosen chemical agent) are normal or benign, creating a persistent blind spot across all deployed instances. This enables the adversary to later induce that signature on canisters of interest, masking diversion or sabotage evidence while the AI confidently clears them.

Inference-time image manipulation or substitution -- adversarial
If inspection imagery is digitally transmitted or preprocessed off-site, an adversary intercepts the pipeline and injects clean reference images, applies adversarial noise to suppress corrosion detection, or digitally erases oxide patterns from the input stream before the model sees it. The tile-level confidence outputs appear normal, the canister is cleared for continued storage or transport, and the adversary has masked evidence of tampering or enabled undetected movement of damaged fuel.

Physical adversarial patches on canister surfaces -- adversarial
An adversary with physical access places small markers (paint, decals, reflective materials) or applies chemical agents in patterns calibrated to flip tile classifications from corroded to intact, exploiting the model's learned features and tile-aggregation threshold to stay below the alarm count. This is adversarial example crafting in the physical domain, masking real corrosion to delay quarantine and enable diversion during approved canister transfers.

Model weight manipulation post-deployment -- adversarial
An insider or attacker who compromises the model update channel or inference server directly alters deployed weights to reduce sensitivity to corrosion signatures, effectively blinding the entire fleet's inspection capability in one action. Because the system is a concentrated trust target replacing distributed human judgment, this single point of compromise propagates inspection failure across all sites using the same model, and the reduction in human oversight delays discovery until a physical audit or security event.

Non-deterministic inference undermining traceability -- implicit
If the ResNet uses stochastic elements at inference (dropout, probabilistic thresholding), repeated imaging of the same canister yields inconsistent verdicts, breaking the repeatability required for regulatory qualification and making it impossible to distinguish genuine corrosion progression from model noise. No adversary action is needed; the system's inherent non-determinism creates a qualification gap that regulators cannot resolve under existing NDE standards.

Regulatory and AI-specific qualification gap -- implicit
No established framework exists to validate a vision system's fitness-for-purpose when its decisions are opaque, non-deterministic, and based on a training set that cannot represent the full operational envelope of decades-long canister aging. The research prototype may be deployed without the rigor applied to traditional non-destructive examination, and adversaries can exploit this ambiguity by arguing AI-flagged anomalies are false positives (delaying investigation) or that AI-cleared canisters need no further scrutiny (enabling diversion).

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear engineer focused on facility operations and material control, my primary concern is that this AI system directly substitutes for a critical human verification function -- visual inspection of storage canister integrity -- where the consequence of a missed defect is containment breach, radionuclide release, and loss of fuel inventory control. If the model misclassifies corroded regions as intact (false negatives), canisters with advancing stress corrosion cracking remain in service past safe limits, potentially leading to through-wall cracks and contamination events that also compromise accountability of Special Nuclear Material. The automated nature and stated goal of reducing operator involvement create classic automation-complacency and out-of-the-loop risks: inspectors may cease independent verification, lose skill in recognizing subtle corrosion signatures, and fail to catch model errors until a canister fails. From a safeguards perspective, adversaries aware of the model's tile-based decision boundary could time physical attacks (e.g., accelerated corrosion via chemical agents) or manipulate input imagery to mask diversion indicators or sabotage evidence, knowing the AI may not flag anomalies a trained human would notice.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: This use case incurs both adversarial and implicit insecurity across multiple dimensions. IMPLICIT risks dominate the baseline threat: the model is trained on a necessarily limited dataset of real canister corrosion (OP.C0202, OP.C0204), as catastrophic corrosion events are rare and destructive sampling of in-service canisters is impractical, so the system likely generalizes poorly to novel corrosion morphologies, alloy variations, or environmental conditions not represented in training data (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). The tile-based approach fragments the image into independent classifications, risking loss of spatial context needed to distinguish benign discoloration from networked stress-corrosion-cracking patterns that propagate across tiles (OP.C0301.01). Automation of visual inspection directly enables operator complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102) -- inspectors may treat AI output as authoritative rather than advisory, ceasing independent scrutiny and losing the perceptual skill to identify early-stage or ambiguous corrosion (OP.C0101.06). If the system is deployed across a fleet of storage sites without site-specific requalification (OP.C0602), a systematic model bias (e.g., trained primarily on one canister design or imaging condition) propagates to all sites, creating correlated inspection failures. Non-determinism in neural network inference (OP.C0402.02) means repeated imaging of the same canister under nominally identical conditions may yield inconsistent classifications, undermining traceability and regulatory confidence. ADVERSARIAL threats exploit these implicit weaknesses: an adversary with physical access could apply targeted corrosion accelerants (e.g., chloride salts) in patterns designed to evade tile-level detection thresholds, effectively 'adversarially crafting' the canister surface itself (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) to mask diversion activities or sabotage. If input images are transmitted digitally or preprocessed off-site (OP.C0601), adversaries could inject poisoned data during training (AML.T0020) to teach the model to ignore specific corrosion signatures, or manipulate inference-time imagery (AML.T0043.003, OP.C0703) to hide evidence of tampering with fuel assemblies. The automation's goal of reducing radiation exposure to personnel paradoxically increases the time window for undetected physical intrusion, as fewer human eyes are on canisters. From a safeguards perspective, if the model is used to generate inspection reports for IAEA or NRC review, adversaries could exploit model opacity (OP.C0401) to argue that AI-flagged anomalies are false positives, delaying investigation, or conversely, that AI-cleared canisters need no further scrutiny, enabling diversion. The lack of AI-specific qualification standards for safety-significant visual inspection (OP.C0501, OP.C0504) means regulatory bodies have no established framework to validate the model's fitness-for-purpose, and the research prototype may be deployed without the rigor applied to traditional non-destructive examination methods.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case is a pure computer vision pipeline -- a ResNet trained on images of stainless steel canisters to distinguish corroded tiles from intact ones. My lens sees three technical exposures immediately: (1) the training set is almost certainly tiny, drawn from a small population of inspected canisters (new-build scarcity compounded by the low base-rate of actual corrosion events in what is still a relatively young dry storage fleet), making the model brittle to novel corrosion morphologies or lighting/surface conditions it never saw; (2) inference robustness is fragile -- adversarial perturbations to the image (physical or digital) could flip tile classifications, and there is no mention of out-of-distribution detection, so the system may confidently misclassify inputs that don't resemble training data (different canister materials, weathering, or even deliberate occlusion/camouflage); and (3) the tile-cropping and aggregation logic is deterministic but the model's confidence thresholds and how they map to an actionable 'corroded/intact' verdict are underspecified, creating a qualification gap -- what constitutes a 'pass' is unclear, and drift in canister appearance over decades of storage will not be captured by retraining unless new labeled data flows in, which it won't at scale. The data provenance is also a red flag: if training used lab-induced corrosion or imagery from a narrow set of sites/vintages, the model is a surrogate for real operational conditions, not a faithful replica.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT (non-adversarial) threats are the dominant exposure here. The model is almost certainly trained on a sparse, non-representative dataset (OP.C0202 small-data problem, OP.C0203 new-build scarcity) -- real corrosion events in dry storage are rare, inspection imagery is not systematically collected across the fleet, and any training set is likely augmented with simulated or lab-induced corrosion (OP.C0201.01/.02 simulated/synthetic data), which may not generalize to field conditions (pitting morphology, oxide color under different lighting, stress-cracking patterns in real weathered stainless steel). This creates a severe out-of-distribution risk (OP.C0302.01 operational drift) as canisters age, environmental conditions vary across sites, or new corrosion mechanisms emerge (e.g., chloride-induced SCC in coastal climates) that the model never encountered in training. The tile-level classification architecture is also a failure-propagation risk (OP.C0301.01): a systematic bias (e.g., misclassifying surface staining as corrosion, or vice versa) compounds across hundreds of tiles per canister, and the aggregation rule (how many 'corroded' tiles trigger a flag?) is a hidden threshold that may not be validated against actual structural integrity criteria. There is no mention of uncertainty quantification or OOD detection, so the system will produce confident but unfounded verdicts on images it has no right to judge (OP.C0402.02 inference non-repeatability if the model is stochastic, OP.C0401 opacity -- the operator has no visibility into why a tile was flagged). Automation bias (OP.C0101.04 over-trust) is a major human-factors risk: inspectors may defer to the system's verdict without independent verification, especially as it reduces 'operator fatigue and radiation exposure' -- the very efficiency gain that justifies the system also erodes the human check. Skill fade (OP.C0101.06) follows: if visual inspection is automated away, inspectors lose the ability to catch novel corrosion that the AI missed. ADVERSARIAL threats layer on top of these weaknesses. An adversary who knows the system is deployed (AML.T0003 search victim websites, AML.T0095.000 code repositories if the model or training approach is published) could craft physical or digital perturbations to canister imagery to suppress corrosion detection (AML.T0015 evade AI model, AML.T0043.003 manual modification of images via paint, decals, or lighting to mask true corrosion as 'intact' tiles). If the adversary has access to the inspection workflow (e.g., compromised inspection camera or image-processing pipeline), they could inject adversarial noise or substitute clean reference images (AML.T0010.002 data supply chain compromise at inference time, AML.T0025 exfil/inject via cyber means). The system's tile-aggregation logic is also a denial-of-service surface (AML.T0029): an adversary could flood the inspection queue with subtly manipulated images that force excessive tile-level reprocessing or trigger false positives, delaying real inspections and masking actual corrosion under a wave of false alarms (AML.T0034.001 resource-intensive queries if the system is queried in a loop). The safeguards consequence is direct: if an adversary can suppress corrosion detection on a canister containing damaged fuel, they enable undetected diversion during transfer/transport (the canister is approved for movement when it should be quarantined) or mask evidence of prior tampering (corrosion patterns that would indicate forced entry or environmental exposure inconsistent with declared storage history). The safety consequence is also severe: undetected SCC or pitting leads to canister failure, radionuclide release, and site contamination -- the AI's failure becomes a direct path to a beyond-design-basis event. The model's non-determinism (if dropout or other stochastic elements are used at inference) and lack of repeatability (OP.C0402.02) also create a qualification nightmare: the same image might yield different verdicts on successive runs, and there is no regulatory framework for qualifying a vision system whose decisions are not traceable to deterministic criteria (OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap, OP.C0504 regulatory readiness gap).

security_specialist.argument: This use case creates a concentrated point of adversarial leverage: an attacker who can manipulate the AI's training data, inference inputs, or model weights can systematically mask corrosion evidence across an entire canister fleet, creating a vulnerability window for theft or sabotage while operators believe inspection coverage is intact. The automation reduces human familiarity with actual canister condition, so when an adversary does act, operators lack the baseline visual intuition to notice discrepancies. From a threat-modeling perspective, the tile-crop-and-count architecture is especially vulnerable to adversarial patch attacks (small physical or digital perturbations that flip tile classifications) and to targeted data poisoning during training (teaching the model that certain corrosion signatures are 'normal'). An insider with access to the image pipeline or model update process could introduce these manipulations, and because the system is meant to reduce human scrutiny, the adversary gains time before detection.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary adversarial threat is MODEL INTEGRITY COMPROMISE leading to CONCEALED MATERIAL VULNERABILITY. An attacker (insider or supply-chain compromise) who poisons the training dataset with mislabeled corrosion examples, or who later manipulates the deployed model weights, can cause the system to systematically miss real corrosion—effectively blinding the facility to canister degradation that an adversary could exploit for theft or diversion timing. The tile-based architecture is vulnerable to ADVERSARIAL PATCH ATTACKS: an adversary places small physical markers (stickers, paint) or injects digital perturbations into the image stream that flip tile classifications from 'corroded' to 'intact,' and the model's tile-count threshold never triggers an alarm. Because operators rely on this automation to reduce their own visual inspection burden and radiation exposure, AUTOMATION COMPLACENCY sets in—they lose the skill and motivation to spot anomalies the AI misses, and an adversary can time an intrusion during a window when the AI has masked canister vulnerabilities. The system also creates a CONCENTRATED TRUST TARGET: compromise this one model (via insider access to the training pipeline, model update process, or inference server), and you simultaneously degrade inspection across the entire canister fleet. A sophisticated adversary (nation-state or well-resourced insider) would likely target the TRAINING DATA PROVENANCE or MODEL UPDATE CHANNEL rather than attacking the AI's runtime inference directly—poisoning during development is stealthier and persists across deployments. Additionally, the reduction in human inspection creates a DETECTION-TIME ASYMMETRY: the adversary knows the AI is blind to certain signatures, but defenders won't realize the model is compromised until a physical audit (which the AI was meant to reduce the frequency of) reveals unexpected corrosion or until a security event has already occurred. Even without an adversary, the system's NON-ADVERSARIAL FAILURE MODES are themselves security-relevant: if the model drifts due to lighting changes, new corrosion morphologies, or camera aging (OP.C0302.01 operational drift), it will miss real corrosion, and an adversary monitoring facility operations could time an action during this undetected degradation window.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on training-data scarcity, operational drift, tile-fragmentation risk, and automation complacency as the core implicit threats, with strong agreement that adversaries exploit these by poisoning training data, manipulating imagery, or timing attacks around undetected drift windows. I separated physical adversarial patches from digital image manipulation and kept model-weight compromise distinct from training-time poisoning, as they represent different attacker capabilities and access levels.

evidence.citation: "Automated detection of corrosion in used nuclear fuel dry storage canisters using residual neural networks," Nuclear Engineering and Technology
evidence.note: ORNL researchers developed and tested a ResNet-based deep learning approach that crops canister images into tiles, classifies each tile as corroded or intact, and uses tile counts to identify corroded canisters with high accuracy, enabling automated inspection to reduce operator fatigue and personnel radiation exposure.

evidence.citation: Papamarkou, T., et al. (2020), "Automated detection of corrosion in used nuclear fuel dry storage canisters using residual neural networks," arXiv:2003.03241
evidence.note: The arXiv preprint version (not peer-reviewed) provides additional detail on the research motivation, noting that no deep learning approaches had previously been used for used nuclear fuel canister inspection and that radiation-induced image artifacts pose challenges for conventional feature detection.

evidence.citation: Bitterwolf, J. & Meinke, A. (2020), "Certifiably Adversarially Robust Detection of Out-of-Distribution Data," arXiv:2007.08473
evidence.note: This AI-safety paper demonstrates that deep neural networks are overconfident on out-of-distribution data in safety-critical applications and that reliable uncertainty assessment is needed to trigger human intervention, directly supporting the out-of-distribution failure and automation complacency vulnerabilities.

evidence.citation: Meinke, A., Bitterwolf, J., & Hein, M. (2022), "Provably Adversarially Robust Detection of Out-of-Distribution Data (Almost) for Free," NeurIPS 2022
evidence.note: This peer-reviewed conference paper shows that deep neural networks produce overconfident predictions on out-of-distribution data and that adversaries can manipulate OOD data to cause high-confidence misclassifications, supporting both the OOD failure and adversarial manipulation vulnerabilities.

evidence.citation: Azizmalayeri, M. & Rohban, M.H. (2022), "Your Out-of-Distribution Detection Method is Not Robust!" NeurIPS 2022
evidence.note: This peer-reviewed work demonstrates that OOD detection methods are susceptible to adversarial examples in safety-critical applications, supporting the adversarial attack and inference-time manipulation vulnerabilities described in the taxonomy entry.

evidence.note: This peer-reviewed paper confirms that stress corrosion cracking detection in stainless steel dry storage canisters is a critical NDE challenge for long-term performance evaluation, establishing the real-world need for the AI application and the difficulty of the detection task.

evidence.note: This recent ORNL state-of-the-art review documents that NDE and machine learning approaches are necessary for SNF canister inspection during extended interim storage, confirming the operational relevance and technology readiness of ML-based inspection systems.

damage.why: Undetected stress-corrosion cracking or pitting in dry storage canisters leads directly to containment breach, radionuclide release to the environment, and loss of spent fuel inventory control—all Category 5 consequences in this taxonomy.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution failure under operational drift and tile-fragmentation spatial-context loss are highly reliable given the sparse training data and architectural design; adversarial physical patches and data poisoning are reproducible once conditions (access, knowledge of model features) are met.

exploitability.why: Physical adversarial patches and exploiting operational drift windows require site access but not deep insider position; training-data poisoning and model-weight manipulation require supply-chain or IT compromise, balancing to moderate exploitability overall.

affected_users.why: Model compromise (poisoning, weight manipulation) or systematic out-of-distribution failure propagates across all canisters inspected by the deployed system, potentially facility-wide or fleet-wide if the same model is used at multiple storage sites.

discoverability.why: The training-data scarcity, tile-based architecture, and automation-complacency risks are explicitly documented in the public peer-reviewed and arXiv literature cited; adversaries can infer the vulnerability class from these publications without insider access.

use_case: Deep learning and Gaussian process optimization of thermal-hydraulic design for additively manufactured reactor core cooling channels to minimize temperature peaking factors
incurred_insecurity:
This use case embeds an AI optimization loop into the physical design basis of safety-critical reactor core cooling geometry, creating insecurity through the combination of small-data training on purely simulated thermal-hydraulics, the irreversibility of additively manufactured hardware, and the absence of operational validation before the design is physically realized. The main threats are: simulation-to-reality drift that produces geometries with unanticipated thermal failure modes in real metal; adversarial poisoning of the training corpus or model during the design phase to inscribe hidden thermal vulnerabilities into the as-built core; and goal misalignment that optimizes peaking factor at the expense of other safety parameters, creating exploitable blind spots an adversary could target with sabotage or operational transients.

Simulation-trained surrogate model generalization failure -- implicit, exploitable
The deep learning and Gaussian process surrogate is trained exclusively on a small set of expensive CFD/neutronics simulation runs of novel additive geometries for which no operational or experimental validation corpus exists. When the optimizer explores regions of the design space poorly sampled by training simulations, or when real manufacturing introduces stochastic defects (porosity, surface roughness, microstructure variation) not captured in the training physics, the optimized geometry may exhibit thermal hot spots, hydraulic instability, or reduced margin under transients that the surrogate never predicted. An adversary could exploit this drift by timing an attack (coolant chemistry tampering, flow blockage insertion, power transient induction) to stress the core in regimes the AI never explored, knowing the design was never validated outside its simulation envelope and that post-fabrication geometric inspection of internal lattice structures is incomplete.

Training-data and model poisoning during design phase -- adversarial
An adversary with access to the AI development pipeline (malicious insider, compromised research collaboration, supply-chain insertion into simulation software or ML libraries) can poison the training dataset with adversarially crafted simulation outputs or manipulate the surrogate model itself to bias the optimizer toward geometries that pass nominal validation metrics but contain covert thermal weaknesses—thin walls, stagnation zones, or features that fail under sabotage-induced transients or long-term operational aging. Because the AI's output directly defines the as-built safety-critical geometry and additive manufacturing makes post-fabrication verification resource-intensive, the adversary's modifications are inscribed into physical hardware before operational testing, creating a latent vulnerability undetectable until reactor operation or a triggering event.

Goal misalignment and narrow-objective optimization -- implicit, exploitable
The AI optimizes specifically for temperature peaking factor reduction, risking implicit degradation of other safety-relevant figures of merit not explicitly constrained or weighted in the objective function: flow-induced vibration susceptibility, crud deposition propensity, corrosion resistance, behavior under loss-of-coolant accidents, or post-fabrication inspectability. The resulting geometry may excel on the trained metric but possess hidden fragilities in untrained safety dimensions. An adversary aware of this misalignment could engineer an attack (corrosion acceleration via chemistry control, vibration-induced fatigue through pump manipulation, inspection evasion by exploiting uninspectable features) that targets the degraded parameter, knowing the AI-optimized design was never stress-tested for that failure mode.

Opacity and non-determinism hindering design forensics -- implicit
The deep learning feature extractor's lack of explainability and the non-deterministic nature of neural network training make it difficult to forensically verify whether a given design recommendation arose from legitimate thermal physics or from a training bias, adversarial or accidental. Security and licensing reviewers cannot easily distinguish a suboptimal design from a maliciously biased one, and if a thermal anomaly is discovered post-fabrication or in operation, tracing the root cause back through the AI's decision process is impractical. This opacity does not directly aid an adversary in executing an attack, but it degrades the defender's ability to detect, attribute, or remediate a poisoning event, and it complicates regulatory qualification in the absence of mature AI-specific review standards for safety-critical components.

Cross-site design propagation amplifying single-point failure -- implicit, exploitable
Because the optimized cooling-channel design may be replicated across multiple reactor modules in a fleet deployment or adopted by other advanced reactor programs, a single compromised or drift-prone surrogate model can inscribe the same latent thermal flaw into an entire reactor class. An adversary could exploit this propagation by targeting one AI development effort to affect many deployed units, and the lack of operational feedback from a prior fleet (new-build data scarcity) means the flaw would not be caught by cross-unit comparison until multiple reactors experience the same failure mode.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This use case employs AI to optimize core geometry for heat removal -- a fundamental safety function. The AI learns from high-fidelity simulations, not measured operational or test-reactor data, raising concerns about how well the optimized design performs under conditions the simulation suite did not capture. If the AI converges on a geometry that looks optimal in simulation but has unanticipated thermal margins or hydraulic instability under real conditions (fuel swelling, crud deposition, manufacturing tolerance stack-up in additive parts), the core could experience local overheating or departure from nucleate boiling that wasn't predicted. The design is baked into hardware before fuel load, so discovering the problem requires either destructive prototype testing or waiting for first criticality -- by which point correction is costly and delayed.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Primary threat is OP.C0201.01 (simulated data) compounded by OP.C0302.03 (operational heterogeneity): the AI trains exclusively on computational fluid dynamics and neutronics outputs, which embed the fidelity limits and modeling assumptions of those codes. If the CFD model under-resolves a flow regime relevant to additive manufacturing surface roughness, or if material property correlations don't cover the as-printed alloy microstructure, the optimized geometry may have thermal margins that exist on paper but not in metal. OP.C0303 (static/dynamic qualification mismatch) is acute: the AI produces a static geometry optimized for nominal conditions, but real operation involves transients, asymmetric power distributions, and aging effects the optimization loop never saw. An adversary aware of this could time an attack (cyber or physical tampering with feedwater chemistry, for instance) to exploit the reduced margin, knowing the design was never stress-tested outside its training envelope. OP.C0401 (explainability/opacity) means even if engineers suspect a problem post-fabrication, tracing why the AI chose that channel pitch or wall thickness is difficult, hindering root-cause analysis. OP.C0304.03 (oversimplification/omission) applies if the optimization objective focuses narrowly on peaking factor and implicitly assumes other figures of merit (pressure drop, crud deposition propensity, inspectability) remain acceptable -- the AI might produce a 'better' peaking factor by creating flow features that foul quickly or cannot be ultrasonically examined. Adversarial surface: AML.T0043 (craft adversarial data) is plausible if an insider or supply-chain attacker can inject biased simulation results into the training corpus, steering the AI toward geometries that look good in the metric space but have hidden fragility. AML.T0018.000 (poison AI model) during the optimization campaign could subtly shift the Pareto front, causing the selected design to be suboptimal or unsafe. The consequence in all cases is a physical artifact -- the core itself -- that cannot be patched post-deployment and whose failure mode is loss of adequate core cooling, a beyond-design-basis accident initiator.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case employs deep learning and Gaussian process (GP) optimization to explore the design space of additively manufactured reactor core cooling channels, minimizing temperature peaking factors via surrogate modeling of expensive thermal-hydraulics simulations. From an ML-engineering perspective, the central fragility is the training-data regime: the surrogate model (DL + GP) learns from a finite set of high-fidelity simulation runs, each expensive and thus limited in number, creating a classic small-data problem compounded by the novelty of additive manufacturing geometries—no large corpus of operational or even validated experimental data exists for these geometries. The GP component provides uncertainty estimates that guide exploration, but if the acquisition function or the DL feature extractor fails to capture rare but safety-critical thermal anomalies (e.g., localized hot spots in lattice structures the model has never seen), the optimizer may converge to a design with hidden peaking-factor failures. At inference/design-recommendation time, the system operates entirely in simulation space; any mismatch between simulation fidelity and real manufactured-part thermal behavior (due to print defects, material microstructure variation, or physics the simulation omitted) becomes a model-reality gap the AI cannot detect, and no operational feedback loop exists to correct it until the part is built and tested—or worse, operated.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The AI system's core vulnerability is **training-data scarcity and provenance** (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01): the surrogate model is trained exclusively on a small number of computationally expensive thermal-hydraulics simulations of novel, additively manufactured geometries for which no prior operational or experimental validation corpus exists (OP.C0203 new-build data scarcity). This creates two failure modes. First, **out-of-distribution generalization failure** (OP.C0302): if the optimizer explores a region of the design space (e.g., a lattice topology or coolant-channel perturbation) sufficiently different from the simulation training set, the surrogate's predictions—and its GP uncertainty bounds—may be overconfident or systematically wrong, leading to acceptance of a design with undetected temperature peaking. Second, **simulation-to-reality drift** (OP.C0302.01): the AI optimizes against simulation outputs, but additive manufacturing introduces stochastic defects (porosity, surface roughness, dimensional variation) and material microstructure changes not captured in the training simulations; the optimized design may perform well in silico but exhibit unanticipated thermal hot spots in the real artifact, a gap the AI has no mechanism to anticipate or flag. Because this is a **design-phase** application with no closed-loop operational feedback until reactor operation (if ever—prototypes may go straight to qualification testing), model errors are not corrected by observed performance, and a flawed design could propagate through fabrication to installation. An adversary could exploit this by **poisoning the simulation training data** (AML.T0020) or the surrogate model itself (AML.T0018.000) during development if they gain access to the design pipeline (e.g., via compromised research collaboration, supply-chain insertion into the simulation software stack (AML.T0010.001), or a malicious insider with access to the training corpus or model checkpoints). Such poisoning could bias the optimizer toward geometries that *appear* thermally benign in simulation but are designed to fail (overheat, crack, or enable localized boiling) under real operating conditions, creating a latent safety vulnerability undetectable until the reactor is built and tested—or suffers an operational transient. The lack of **explainability** (OP.C0401) in the DL feature extractor further obscures whether the optimizer's recommendation is driven by genuine thermal physics or an artifact of the surrogate's training bias. Finally, because the optimized design is likely to be deployed across multiple reactor modules or even propagated to other programs (OP.C0602 cross-site model propagation), a single poisoned or drift-prone surrogate could inscribe the same thermal flaw into an entire reactor fleet, amplifying the consequence of the AI failure.

security_specialist.argument: This use case embeds an AI-driven optimization loop into the foundational design basis of a novel reactor core, creating a concentrated trust node that an adversary could exploit to compromise safety margins before the reactor is even built. The design space is additively manufactured cooling channels—geometries that cannot be easily inspected post-fabrication and whose thermal performance depends on complex fluid dynamics that are difficult to validate independently. An adversary with access to the training data, simulation parameters, or the AI model itself (e.g., a malicious insider during the design phase, or a supply chain compromise of the AI toolchain) could subtly bias the optimization toward geometries that appear optimal under normal conditions but contain hidden thermal vulnerabilities—regions that would fail under transient conditions, sabotage scenarios, or operational states the training simulations did not cover. Because the AI's output directly defines the as-built geometry of safety-critical components, and because additive manufacturing makes post-fabrication geometric verification challenging, this use case offers an adversary a high-leverage, low-detectability attack surface during the design phase.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL THREATS: An adversary could target the AI supply chain (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003) by compromising the deep learning or Gaussian process libraries, training datasets, or simulation coupling code to inject biases that produce geometries with covert thermal weaknesses—e.g., flow stagnation zones or thin-wall regions that pass nominal validation but fail under sabotage-induced transients or long-term corrosion. Because the design optimization relies on high-fidelity but computationally expensive simulations, an adversary could also poison the training data (AML.T0020) with adversarially crafted simulation outputs that teach the AI to favor geometries with hidden failure modes, or manipulate the surrogate model (AML.T0018.000) to misrepresent the true thermal performance of certain designs. The optimization process itself is a soft target: if an adversary gains access to the AI development environment (AML.T0012, AML.T0049), they could alter the objective function, constraints, or design space boundaries to subtly degrade safety margins while maintaining plausible optimization metrics. The fact that this is a pre-operational, design-phase system means the adversary's modifications are baked into the physical reactor before any operational testing occurs, and additive manufacturing's complex internal geometries make post-fabrication verification (via destructive assay or inspection) resource-intensive and incomplete. IMPLICIT/NON-ADVERSARIAL THREATS THAT CREATE ADVERSARIAL OPPORTUNITY: The AI's reliance on simulated training data (OP.C0201.01) rather than empirical measurements from operating additively manufactured cores introduces a foundational data provenance risk—an adversary could exploit the gap between simulation fidelity and real-world physics to engineer failures that simulations missed. The optimization's focus on a narrow objective (temperature peaking factor) risks goal misalignment (OP.C0301) where the AI produces geometries that excel on the trained metric but degrade other safety parameters (e.g., flow-induced vibration, corrosion resistance, or behavior under loss-of-coolant accident conditions)—weaknesses an adversary would time an attack to exploit. Out-of-distribution generalization failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03) is especially acute here: the AI is trained on a finite set of simulation conditions, but operational transients, aging effects, or sabotage-induced conditions (e.g., coolant chemistry changes, blockage insertion) may fall outside that envelope, and an adversary would target these blind spots. The non-determinism of deep learning training (OP.C0402.01) and the opacity of the learned surrogate model (OP.C0401) make it difficult to forensically verify whether a given design recommendation is trustworthy or has been subtly compromised—security teams cannot easily distinguish a legitimately suboptimal design from a maliciously biased one. Finally, because this is a new-build system (OP.C0203) with no operating analog, there is no fleet-wide operational data to validate the AI's outputs, and the regulatory framework for AI-optimized, additively manufactured safety-critical components is immature (OP.C0504)—an adversary benefits from this qualification gap, as it reduces the likelihood that their sabotage will be detected during licensing review.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on simulation-data provenance, out-of-distribution generalization risk, and adversarial supply-chain poisoning as the primary threats; the synthesis integrated the nuclear engineer's emphasis on physical consequences, the AI engineer's ML-specific failure modes, and the security specialist's pre-operational attack surface into a unified threat model grounded in the design-phase, non-reversible nature of this application.

evidence.citation: "Artificial intelligence-driven thermal design for additively manufactured reactor cores," Nuclear Engineering and Design
evidence.note: The paper reports on an implemented AI-based design optimization algorithm combining deep learning and Gaussian processes with high-fidelity thermal hydraulics simulations to optimize reactor core cooling channel geometry for the Transformational Challenge Reactor program at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, demonstrating a threefold improvement in temperature peaking factor.

damage.why: Simulation-to-reality drift or poisoned design producing unanticipated thermal failure modes in reactor core cooling channels could lead to core damage and radiological release under operational transients or accident conditions.

reproducibility.why: Simulation-to-reality generalization failure is highly reproducible given the described conditions of small-data training on purely simulated physics without experimental validation and the inherent stochasticity of additive manufacturing defects.

exploitability.why: Training-data poisoning requires insider access to the AI development pipeline during design phase or supply-chain compromise of simulation/ML tools, while exploiting implicit drift requires operational access to induce specific transients after construction.

affected_users.why: The vulnerability affects safety-critical reactor core cooling geometry facility-wide, and cross-site design propagation means a single compromised model could inscribe the same flaw into an entire reactor fleet.

discoverability.why: The use of AI optimization for additively manufactured core cooling channels is documented in open literature for the Transformational Challenge Reactor program, making the vulnerability class and its reliance on simulation-only training inferable by capable outsiders from public technical publications.

use_case: Proximal Policy Optimization reinforcement learning to optimize pressurized water reactor core loading patterns by maximizing fuel cycle length while satisfying constraints on rod-integrated peaking factors
incurred_insecurity:
This use case creates a concentrated dependence on a reinforcement learning policy trained entirely in simulation to propose safety-critical core loading patterns that operators will act upon with limited independent verification capacity. The central insecurity is that the PPO agent optimizes a narrow objective (cycle length subject to peaking-factor constraints) derived from a neutronics simulator, not the full envelope of accident scenarios, transient response, or real fuel performance data that determine actual safety margins. When plant-specific conditions drift beyond the training distribution—new fuel types, revised regulatory limits, vendor changes, or operational anomalies the simulator did not capture—the policy may confidently propose patterns that satisfy simulated constraints but violate real safety boundaries or create latent vulnerabilities an adversary can exploit. Automation trust in the demonstrably superior RL solutions erodes the rigor of independent review, turning the model into a high-value target whose compromise (via training-data poisoning, simulator tampering, or model manipulation) can pre-position the reactor in exploitable configurations under the cover of optimization.

Objective misalignment and incomplete safety representation -- implicit, exploitable
The RL reward function encodes cycle length and rod-integrated peaking factors, but reactor safety depends on a broader physics envelope—xenon transient stability, control rod worth distributions, DNB margin under off-normal conditions, fuel failure limits under loss-of-coolant accidents—that the training environment may underweight or omit. The policy can converge on Pareto-optimal solutions for the stated objectives that are fragile or unsafe under conditions not well-represented in simulation, and operators reviewing the pattern may not detect the deficiency without exhaustive sensitivity analysis the AI was meant to replace. An adversary aware of this gap can poison the training data or compromise the neutronics simulator to bias the model toward patterns that meet nominal constraints but degrade safety margins in scenarios the reward function does not emphasize, knowing the complexity of core physics makes such tampering hard to detect and the operational pressure to adopt cycle-length gains will suppress scrutiny.

Simulator-reality mismatch and concept drift -- implicit, exploitable
The PPO policy learned entirely from a neutronics code whose fidelity, cross-section libraries, and parameter choices define the ground truth, yet actual core behavior involves fuel-vendor variations, measurement uncertainties, revised regulatory limits, and operational transients the simulator may not capture. When the frozen policy encounters plant-specific conditions outside its training distribution at the next refueling outage—updated fuel specifications, burnup distribution anomalies, tightened peaking-factor limits—it may propose patterns that satisfy simulated constraints but violate real ones, or reject safe patterns the training environment penalized. An adversary can exploit this by timing an attack or covert operation around known simulator limitations: if the adversary understands which real-world scenarios the training data omitted (e.g., asymmetric xenon oscillations, specific control rod misalignments), they can manipulate plant state telemetry or fuel-tracking records fed as input to the policy to steer it toward a pattern that advances the adversary's objective (material diversion setup, stress concentration on target components) while appearing optimal under the corrupted or out-of-distribution premise.

Training-data and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or external actor with access to the neutronics simulator, cross-section libraries, or training dataset can inject biases that cause the RL policy to internalize a skewed objective: patterns that meet stated peaking and cycle-length constraints but create latent vulnerabilities—unusual power distributions that obscure safeguards-relevant signatures, configurations that maximize stress on components the adversary plans to exploit, or patterns that make the reactor more sensitive to a subsequent cyber or physical attack. Because the optimization operates in a high-dimensional space of valid loading patterns and the RL policy is opaque, a malicious pattern can hide within the solution manifold, and detecting it requires independent neutronic analysis the organization may not routinely perform if they trust the RL output's superior benchmark metrics. The same attack vector applies to tampering with the simulator itself during training or fine-tuning, embedding adversarial logic that biases fuel-vendor parameter representations or constraint definitions.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
If the RL-optimized patterns consistently outperform legacy methods in cycle length and computation time, fuel management engineers will increase reliance on the AI and reduce the rigor of independent verification, especially under schedule pressure to finalize reload designs before an outage. This automation bias is compounded by skill fade: as the RL system handles routine optimization, staff lose proficiency in manual core loading analysis and the judgment to recognize when a proposed pattern is anomalous or unsafe despite meeting formal constraints. An adversary can exploit this degraded verification capacity by introducing a subtly malicious pattern at a moment when operational pressure is high and independent review is shallow, or by gradually conditioning staff to accept the AI's outputs with minimal scrutiny through a series of benign-but-novel patterns that stretch the boundary of normal practice, then inserting the malicious one when the threshold for suspicion has risen.

Static qualification and regulatory-readiness gap -- implicit
The RL policy was qualified by training-time convergence metrics and benchmark comparisons against historical or simulated loading patterns, but it has no dynamic requalification loop when fuel vendors change, burnup credit rules are revised, or the utility's operational strategy shifts. Each reload cycle introduces variables the frozen policy has not encountered, and unlike a deterministic algorithm whose response to new inputs can be analytically bounded, the RL policy's behavior under out-of-distribution conditions is opaque and may degrade unpredictably. No established regulatory framework exists for qualifying a stochastic RL policy for safety-significant refueling decisions, so the organization may apply software V&V practices designed for deterministic code, missing the policy's sensitivity to training hyperparameters, reward shaping, exploration-exploitation balance, and the non-determinism of PPO's stochastic action sampling. This gap means a malicious or drifted model can persist in deployment because the qualification process did not test the conditions under which it fails.

Inference-time non-repeatability and traceability loss -- implicit
If the deployed PPO policy uses stochastic action sampling, re-running the optimization on the same reactor state and fuel inventory can yield different loading patterns, complicating regulatory documentation, configuration management, and forensic analysis if a pattern later proves unsafe. An adversary gains little direct exploit from this non-determinism, but it erodes the organization's ability to reconstruct why a particular pattern was chosen, detect when a malicious pattern was inserted versus generated by the model, or defend the safety basis of the chosen configuration to regulators, especially if the documentation practice assumes deterministic outputs.

Cross-site model propagation -- implicit, exploitable
If the same trained RL policy is deployed across a fleet of PWRs to amortize development cost, a compromised or drifted model propagates the vulnerability to multiple reactors simultaneously, and an adversary gains leverage to pre-position an entire fleet in exploitable configurations or create synchronized vulnerabilities that amplify the impact of a later attack (e.g., all units entering a refueling outage with similar latent peaking-margin deficiencies that an adversary can trigger simultaneously via a cyber intrusion into plant control systems). Even without adversarial intent, deploying a single model across heterogeneous reactors (different vintages, fuel vendors, operating histories) concentrates operational-heterogeneity risk: a pattern the model learned from one reactor's simulator may not transfer safely to another's real conditions, but the economic pressure to standardize AI tooling makes this deployment pattern likely.

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear engineer focused on operations and safety, my primary concern is that this AI directly proposes physical core configurations that determine fundamental safety margins -- peaking factors, shutdown margins, power distributions -- and will be acted upon by reactor engineers with limited ability to verify each AI-generated pattern against the full envelope of accident scenarios. The AI's objective function (maximize cycle length subject to peaking constraints) is a narrow proxy for safe operation; it does not inherently encode all Design Basis Accidents, anticipated transients, or degraded-condition scenarios that licensing and fuel management actually require. If the model drifts due to fuel vendor changes, new enrichment strategies, or burnable poison designs it wasn't trained on, or if it converges on mathematically valid but operationally fragile solutions (e.g., patterns that meet peaking limits in steady state but have poor response to asymmetric xenon transients or control rod misalignment), operators may not detect the issue until a reactivity event or unplanned power reduction occurs. The reinforcement learning training data comes from simulation, not operational transients or fuel performance data from real cycles, meaning the model has never 'seen' how its patterns behave under real perturbations or material property variations.
