nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The core threat is **goal misalignment and incomplete constraint representation** (OP.C0301): the RL agent optimizes cycle length and peaking factors as encoded in its reward function, but reactor safety depends on a much broader set of physics (xenon oscillations, control rod worth distributions, moderator temperature coefficients, DNB margin under off-normal conditions, fuel failure limits under LOCA) that may not be fully captured or correctly weighted in the training environment. If the AI proposes a loading pattern that is Pareto-optimal for the stated objectives but has poor stability or safety margin under conditions not represented in simulation (OP.C0302.02 concept drift, OP.C0201.01 simulated-data limitations), the fuel management engineer reviewing it may not catch the deficiency without exhaustive sensitivity analysis -- a process the AI was meant to streamline. **Automation bias** (OP.C0101.04) is acute here: if the AI consistently outperforms legacy methods in benchmark metrics, engineers will begin to trust its outputs and reduce the rigor of independent verification, especially under schedule pressure to finalize reload designs. An adversary aware of this reliance could target the AI's training data or the simulation tools it depends on (AML.T0020 poison training data, AML.T0010.002 supply chain compromise of physics codes) to subtly bias the model toward patterns that appear safe in simulation but have hidden vulnerabilities -- for example, patterns that maximize cycle length but create local power peaking 'hot spots' that exceed peaking limits only under specific, rare transient conditions not well-represented in the training set. The **non-determinism of RL training** (OP.C0402.01) means that re-training the model on nominally identical data may yield different policies, undermining repeatability and making regulatory qualification difficult (OP.C0504); if the model is updated after initial deployment (e.g., to incorporate new fuel types), there is no guarantee the new version preserves safety margins established by the old one. Finally, the **static qualification problem** (OP.C0303) is severe: the model is trained and validated on historical or simulated reactor conditions, but each reload cycle introduces new variables (fuel vendor differences, grid demand profiles, new control strategies) that the AI has not encountered, and unlike a deterministic algorithm, the RL policy's response to these out-of-distribution conditions is opaque (OP.C0401) and may degrade unpredictably.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case trains a PPO agent in simulation to discover core loading patterns that meet operational/safety constraints while optimizing cycle length—a high-stakes optimization task where the training environment (neutronics simulator) becomes the ground truth and the deployed policy directly influences refueling decisions with measurable economic and safety consequences. From an ML engineering standpoint, the central fragility is that the RL agent has never seen real operational data: it learned entirely from a neutronics code whose fidelity, parameter choices, and cross-section libraries define what 'good' means, yet actual core behavior involves measurement uncertainties, fuel-vendor variations, and operational transients the simulator may not capture. At inference (refueling outage planning), if plant-specific conditions—burnup distribution anomalies, updated fuel specifications, revised regulatory peaking-factor limits—fall outside the training distribution, the policy may confidently propose a pattern that satisfies the simulated constraints but violates real ones, or conversely reject safe patterns the training environment penalized. There is no adversary required for this to go wrong: concept drift (new fuel types, revised limits) and simulator-reality mismatch are built into the architecture.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: The primary operational threat is OP.C0201.01 (simulated data) compounded by OP.C0302 (drift/out-of-distribution failure): the PPO policy was optimized against a neutronics model, not reactor telemetry, so any discrepancy between simulator assumptions and actual fuel performance, cross-section updates, or as-operated conditions means the policy's reward landscape does not reflect real safety margins. When the policy proposes a loading pattern at the next outage, operators must verify it against independent physics codes and regulatory criteria, but OP.C0101.04 (misuse/over-trust) is a concern if the RL solution's demonstrated superiority in simulation leads staff to adopt it with insufficient independent validation, especially under schedule pressure. OP.C0303 (static/dynamic qualification mismatch) is acute: the policy was 'qualified' by training-time convergence metrics and benchmark comparisons, but has no dynamic requalification loop when fuel vendors change, burnup credit rules are revised, or the utility's peaking-factor limits tighten—concept drift that the frozen policy cannot track. OP.C0402.02 (inference-time non-repeatability) matters if the policy's stochastic action sampling (common in PPO implementations) means re-running the optimization on the same input yields different patterns, complicating traceability and regulatory documentation. On the adversarial side, AML.T0043.001 (black-box optimization to craft adversarial data) is plausible: an insider or vendor with access to the simulator could perturb fuel parameters or constraint definitions during training or fine-tuning to bias the policy toward patterns that meet stated constraints but degrade margin, are harder to inspect, or favor specific fuel designs—exploiting the fact that the 'ground truth' is code, not physics. AML.T0010.002 (data supply-chain compromise) extends this: if the cross-section library, simulator release, or training dataset is tampered with, the policy internalizes a skewed objective, and detecting that the resulting patterns are subtly unsafe requires independent neutronic analysis the organization may not routinely perform if they trust the RL output. AML.T0015 (evade AI model) becomes relevant if an adversary's goal is to force the plant into a particular loading configuration (for material diversion or sabotage setup): they could manipulate plant state telemetry or fuel-tracking records fed into the 'current state' input to the policy, causing it to recommend a pattern that advances the adversary's objective while appearing optimal under the corrupted premise. The lack of real operational training data (OP.C0203, new-build data scarcity by analogy) means there is no empirical basis to know whether the policy generalizes to the specific as-built reactor's idiosyncrasies, and OP.C0501 (AI-specific QA/qualification gap) is severe: no established framework exists for qualifying an RL policy for safety-significant refueling decisions, so the organization may apply software V&V practices designed for deterministic code, missing the policy's sensitivity to training hyperparameters, reward shaping, and exploration strategy.

security_specialist.argument: From a security perspective, this use case creates a concentrated point of trust in the fuel loading pattern optimization that an adversary could exploit through model manipulation or data poisoning—loading patterns that maximize cycle length while nominally satisfying peaking-factor constraints could mask subtle configurations that degrade safety margins or facilitate future covert material diversion. The reinforcement learning training process depends on simulated reactor-physics data (likely few real operational cycles to train on), making the model vulnerable to adversarial examples during inference that produce patterns an operator would accept but that create exploitable conditions. Most critically, this system erodes the distributed human judgment that previously characterized core loading decisions: if operators defer to an opaque RL-optimized pattern because it claims superior cycle length, an adversary who compromises the model (or its training data, or the physics simulator feeding it) gains a lever to pre-position the reactor in a state favorable to a later attack, and the optimization's complexity makes insider review shallow. Even without an adversary, the model's non-determinism and opacity make it difficult to verify that a proposed pattern hasn't drifted into a dangerous but formally constraint-satisfying regime.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
The primary adversarial threat is AI Supply Chain Compromise of the training data or model: an insider or external actor who poisons the reactor-physics simulator outputs or the trained RL policy can cause the system to propose loading patterns that satisfy immediate constraints (peaking factors, cycle length) but create latent vulnerabilities—unusual power distributions that obscure diversion-relevant signatures, configurations that maximize stress on specific components an adversary plans to exploit, or patterns that make the reactor more sensitive to a later cyber or physical attack. The RL model's opacity and the stochastic nature of PPO make such tampering hard to detect: there is no closed-form solution to compare against, and the space of nominally valid loading patterns is large enough that a malicious one can hide within it. An adversary could also target the inference stage (LLM Prompt Injection analogue for RL: crafted state inputs) to steer the policy toward a desired pattern without altering the model itself, exploiting the fact that operators lack the expertise to verify every pattern the RL system proposes.

Non-adversarial risks that an adversary would exploit or time attacks around include automation trust failure (operators over-rely on the RL-optimized pattern because it has historically improved cycle length, so they don't scrutinize an anomalous one) and drift/out-of-distribution failure (the model, trained on simulated data from a limited set of scenarios, proposes a pattern for a real reactor state it has never seen, and that pattern is unsafe or exploitable). The small-data problem is acute: PWR core loading has few real operational cycles to learn from, so the model trains mostly on synthetic simulator data, which may not capture all safety-relevant physics or adversarial scenarios. If an adversary knows the simulator's limitations, they can craft a loading pattern that the simulator (and thus the RL model) rates as safe but that behaves dangerously in the real reactor. The concentration of trust in this system is the key insecurity: replacing distributed human-expert judgment with a single opaque model creates a high-value target whose compromise has fleet-wide impact if the same trained model is deployed across multiple reactors, and the complexity of RL makes insider threats particularly dangerous—a malicious AI engineer or data scientist could embed subtle biases that take years to manifest.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on simulator-reality mismatch (simulated training data), concept drift, automation over-trust, and the adversarial exploit of poisoning training data or the model to embed latent unsafe patterns; the security specialist's emphasis on supply-chain compromise and the nuclear engineer's focus on objective misalignment were merged into distinct but complementary threats, with cross-site propagation drawn from the security lens and static qualification from the AI engineer's regulatory-readiness concern.

evidence.citation: "Assessment of reinforcement learning algorithms for nuclear power plant fuel optimization," Springer
evidence.note: Seurin and Shirvan developed and tested deep reinforcement learning methods, including Proximal Policy Optimization, for solving the PWR core loading pattern optimization problem, demonstrating that PPO can outperform traditional stochastic optimization methods like genetic algorithms and simulated annealing in finding high-quality loading patterns within reasonable computation time.

damage.why: Compromise of core loading pattern optimization can directly result in configurations that violate safety margins under accident conditions (LOCA, DNB limits), create latent vulnerabilities that erode multiple barriers to radiological release, or enable safeguards falsification by obscuring material diversion signatures through manipulated power distributions.

reproducibility.why: Once training data or simulator is poisoned, or once operational conditions drift beyond the training distribution, the RL policy will reliably propose patterns optimized to the corrupted objective or misaligned with real safety constraints; the stochastic nature of PPO introduces minor variability but does not prevent systematic bias from manifesting across reload cycles.

exploitability.why: Training-data or simulator poisoning requires insider access to development infrastructure or vendor supply chains (neutronics codes, cross-section libraries), while exploiting simulator-reality mismatch or automation over-trust during deployment requires knowledge of plant-specific conditions and timing but less deep access; the middle score reflects that different threat vectors span this range.

affected_users.why: A compromised core loading pattern affects the entire reactor core configuration for an 18-24 month fuel cycle, propagates safety-margin erosion across all fuel assemblies and protection systems, and if the model is deployed fleet-wide, simultaneously impacts multiple reactors with synchronized vulnerabilities.

discoverability.why: The use of RL for core loading optimization and its reliance on simulation-trained models is documented in open literature (cited Springer publication); capable adversaries can infer from vendor documentation and procurement that such systems depend on neutronics simulators with known fidelity gaps, though discovering which specific operational scenarios or fuel parameters were omitted from a particular deployment's training data requires more targeted reconnaissance.

use_case: Machine-learning regression prediction of fuel pebble burnup from gamma spectroscopy measurements to inform reload-or-discharge decisions for circulating pebbles in pebble bed reactors
incurred_insecurity:
This use case creates a real-time material-accountability and reactivity-control vulnerability by concentrating trust in an ML model that has never seen operational gamma spectra, yet must classify thousands of pebbles per day under time pressure to decide reload versus discharge. The model's exclusive reliance on simulated training data and its ~5 MWd/kgU error band create systematic blind spots an adversary can exploit to manipulate fuel flows, while the operational tempo and automation bias erode human verification, allowing errors or attacks to accumulate into significant inventory discrepancies or core-reactivity anomalies before detection. Both adversarial manipulation and natural drift expose the facility to diversion of weapons-usable material and loss of reactivity margins.

Training-data poisoning and supply-chain model compromise -- adversarial
An adversary introduces biased gamma signatures during model development or compromises the deployed model artifact, systematically skewing burnup predictions to favor reload of high-burnup pebbles (covertly accumulating fissile material in-core or in spent fuel for later diversion) or premature discharge of low-burnup pebbles (creating a divertible stream under the cover of model error). The operational tempo masks the attack as statistical noise until safeguards audits reveal inventory discrepancies.

Inference-time evasion via adversarial input crafting -- adversarial
An adversary with access to the gamma measurement chain injects false detector signals, attenuates response, or physically manipulates pebble isotopic profiles to present spectra the simulation-trained model systematically misclassifies, enabling discharge of pebbles the facility believes spent but retain exploitable fissile content, or reload of overburned pebbles risking reactivity excursion.

Model extraction and black-box transfer attacks -- adversarial
An adversary queries the system to extract the model or reconstructs it from published methods, then trains a proxy on the same SCALE simulation libraries to explore adversarial perturbations offline and deploy them at inference time, exploiting the shared simulation-derived feature space to fool the production model into authorizing anomalous discharges timed to diversion opportunities.

Simulated-data provenance and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained exclusively on SCALE/ORIGEN simulations that lack real detector noise, aging artifacts, measurement nonidealities, and stochastic fission-product variance; when operational pebbles exhibit spectral features the simulation never captured (fuel fabrication variance, off-nominal irradiation profiles, Compton backgrounds), the model drifts and its error band widens in unpredictable ways. An adversary can identify these blind spots by monitoring facility operations or testing pebbles offline, then select or engineer pebbles the model will misclassify, timing diversions around known periods of high operational drift (startup, detector recalibration, fuel batch transitions) when model uncertainty is greatest and human oversight weakest.

Automation bias and manual-verification erosion -- implicit, exploitable
Operators under time pressure with hundreds of pebbles queued come to trust the AI's burnup estimates without independent verification, since manual gamma analysis is impractical at operational tempo; when the model fails naturally (due to drift) or adversarially (due to manipulation), no one notices until safeguards audits or reactivity anomalies reveal discrepancies, by which time material may be diverted. An adversary exploits this by timing attacks around periods of highest operator reliance, knowing marginal cases will not be manually re-checked.

Small-data and high-burnup edge-case scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
High-burnup pebbles and anomalous irradiation histories are underrepresented in any training set, yet correct prediction is safety- and safeguards-critical precisely in these cases; the model's generalization to adversarially-selected or engineered edge cases is untested. An adversary who can fabricate or select pebbles with rare isotopic signatures exploits the model's training gaps to induce systematic misclassification, creating diversion pathways the facility's qualification testing never explored.

Cascading inventory-accountability failure -- implicit, exploitable
If the AI's burnup estimates feed into downstream inventory reconciliation, reactor physics models, and spent-fuel criticality analyses, a small systematic bias in burnup measurement propagates through every calculation; an adversary who introduces a consistent 2–3 MWd/kgU error (within the model's nominal uncertainty band) causes the facility to lose track of kilograms of fissile material across thousands of pebbles over months, enabling large-scale diversion disguised as normal measurement uncertainty. The lack of independent physical confirmation (destructive assay of random samples is impractical at pebble-circulation rates) means drift or manipulation goes undetected until material-balance closings reveal the loss.

Inference-time non-repeatability and retrospective verification failure -- implicit, exploitable
If the model exhibits stochastic behavior (ensemble methods, periodic retraining with different random seeds), the same pebble measured twice may yield different burnup predictions, complicating safeguards verification of historical fuel flows and enabling an adversary to re-measure pebbles until the model gives the desired classification. The lack of deterministic traceability undermines post-hoc audits attempting to reconstruct when and how material was diverted.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Train Proxy via Gathered AI Artifacts

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a nuclear operations perspective, this use case introduces a critical decision node where real-time fuel handling depends on ML inference accuracy. The pebble bed reactor's defining feature—continuous online refueling with thousands of circulating pebbles—means incorrect burnup predictions scale into systematic fleet-level errors affecting core neutronics, fuel economy, and potentially reactivity margins. Unlike batch-core reactors where fuel composition is statically known, this system must classify every pebble individually under operational time pressure, making automation bias, data drift, and adversarial manipulation all plausible pathways to operational or safeguards failure. The reliance on gamma spectroscopy measurements introduces both a sensor attack surface (an adversary could manipulate detector outputs or environmental backgrounds) and an implicit vulnerability to isotopic signatures the model was never trained to recognize (novel fuel types, contamination, deliberate isotopic masking).
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial threats:** An adversary with access to the gamma spectroscopy measurement chain could inject false signals or attenuate detector response to fool the model into misclassifying high-burnup pebbles as low-burnup (leading to core overpower if reloaded) or vice versa (leading to premature discharge of usable fuel, creating a diversion pathway under the cover of 'model error'). If the model architecture or training data becomes known (via supply chain compromise, insider access, or reconstruction from published methods), an attacker could craft isotopic profiles that the model systematically misjudges—either by exploiting learned correlations that don't hold under adversarial conditions or by presenting out-of-distribution spectra the model handles poorly. The operational tempo of pebble handling (potentially thousands per day) means a targeted attack could be masked as statistical noise until significant core inventory or safeguards discrepancies accumulate. Prompt injection or model tampering (if the system uses retrieval-augmented generation or agent-based calibration updates) could alter discharge criteria mid-operation, enabling real-time manipulation of fuel flows.

**Implicit/operational vulnerabilities exacerbating adversarial exposure:** The reliance on simulated training data (common in nuclear applications due to operational data scarcity) means the model has never seen real operational gamma spectra under all credible conditions—detector aging, electronic drift, unanticipated fission product buildup from off-normal fuel performance, or environmental background changes. This creates a natural out-of-distribution failure mode that an adversary could exploit by timing an attack to coincide with detector degradation or unusual operational states (e.g., startup after extended outage, when isotopic ratios may differ). Automation bias is particularly acute here: operators under time pressure with hundreds of pebbles queued may not independently verify borderline predictions, especially if the model's historical accuracy has been good. If enrichment must be supplied as a known input (per the described method), an adversary who can alter enrichment metadata—either in the fuel tracking database or via supply chain compromise of pebble identification—induces systematic prediction errors without touching the AI model itself. The lack of independent physical confirmation (e.g., destructive assay of randomly sampled pebbles is impractical at operational tempo) means model drift, calibration errors, or adversarial manipulation may go undetected until reactivity or material balance anomalies emerge. Safeguards implications are severe: if the model systematically underpredicts burnup, declared discharges will have higher fissile content than reported, enabling diversion; if it overpredicts, premature discharges create a covert pathway to recover less-irradiated material. The non-repeatability of ML inference (if the model is periodically retrained or uses ensemble methods with stochastic elements) complicates retrospective verification of fuel histories for safeguards accountancy.

ai_engineer.argument: This use case sits at a critical operational decision point – reload vs. discharge – driven by a regression model trained exclusively on simulated gamma spectroscopy data. From an ML-engineering standpoint, the core vulnerability is the provenance and realism gap: SCALE/ORIGEN simulation outputs are deterministic approximations of real detector physics, lacking noise correlations, measurement artifacts, detector aging effects, and the full stochastic spread of actual decay signatures. The model has never seen real pebble spectra, yet it will be asked to generalize to them at inference time in a running reactor. Additionally, burnup prediction is inherently a low-signal extrapolation problem in regions of parameter space (high burnup, edge cases, partial shielding) where simulation fidelity is weakest and training data may be sparse. Finally, there is no discussion of online retraining, drift monitoring, or how the model's error distribution shifts when reactor operating history deviates from the nominal scenario encoded in the training set – a static qualification against simulated data cannot capture operational heterogeneity across fuel batches, detector calibration states, or evolving isotopic inventories.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
**Adversarial exposure:** An adversary with access to the gamma measurement stream (via supply-chain compromise of the detector firmware, spoofing of calibration sources, or tampering with the data pipeline feeding the ML model) could craft inputs that systematically bias burnup predictions low, causing premature reload of under-burned pebbles and accumulation of excess reactivity, or bias them high to mask diversion of partially spent fuel. The model's reliance on simulated training data means it has no ground truth for anomaly detection – adversarially perturbed spectra that remain plausible to the simulation-trained model may correspond to impossible or dangerous physical states. Transfer attacks are also viable: an adversary trains a proxy model on the same public SCALE libraries, explores adversarial perturbations offline, and deploys them at inference time, exploiting the fact that the defender's model shares the simulation-derived feature space. Because the use case sits in a control loop (reload/discharge), a model compromise directly manipulates material flow and inventory accounting.

**Implicit/operational fragility:** The dominant risk is out-of-distribution failure at deployment. Real pebble gamma spectra will differ from SCALE simulations due to detector resolution nonidealities, Compton background from neighboring pebbles, activation of structural materials, and stochastic variation in fission-product inventories – none of which are faithfully captured in training. The model will encounter concept drift as fuel batches age, graphite moderator composition shifts, or the reactor operates in off-nominal power profiles, yet there is no mechanism described for detecting when predictions have become unreliable (no uncertainty quantification, no online retraining trigger). Small-data and low base-rate problems are acute: high-burnup pebbles and anomalous irradiation histories are underrepresented in any training set, yet these are precisely the cases where correct prediction is safety-critical. Automation bias is a compounding factor – operators may over-rely on a model that reports sub-5-MWd/kgU error on test data, unaware that test data and operational data are drawn from fundamentally different distributions. If the model fails silently (no alarms, just a bad prediction), the facility's material accountancy and reactivity control both degrade without operator awareness. An adversary timing an attack to coincide with known periods of high operational drift (startup, fuel batch transition, detector recalibration) can exploit these implicit weaknesses to maximize impact with minimal detectability.

security_specialist.argument: This use case creates a nuclear security threat surface through its concentration of trust in a single AI-powered measurement point that gates critical fissile-material-flow decisions. An adversary who can bias or degrade this burnup estimator—whether by corrupting its training data, exploiting its reliance on simulated (not operational) gamma signatures, or timing attacks around known model uncertainties—can systematically cause the facility to retain high-burnup pebbles (creating hidden accumulations of weapons-usable material) or discard low-burnup ones (generating a divertible spent-fuel stream with exploitable residual fissile content). The operational tempo of pebble circulation (thousands of pebbles per day) makes human verification of every decision impractical, so the AI becomes a single point of failure for material accountability. Even without a deliberate adversary, the model's reliance on simulated training data and its ~5 MWd/kgU error band create exploitable windows: a sophisticated state-level adversary could monitor facility operations, infer when the model is likeliest to misclassify marginal pebbles, and time a diversion scenario around those periods.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (1) Training-data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002): An insider or supply-chain compromise introduces biased simulated gamma signatures during model development, systematically skewing burnup predictions to favor reload decisions for pebbles that should be discharged—over time, this covertly accumulates high-burnup material in the core or spent-fuel stream, creating a diversion opportunity the adversary can exploit when ready. (2) Inference-time evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043): An adversary with physical access crafts or selects pebbles with gamma signatures the model systematically misclassifies (e.g., exploiting spectral features the simulation-trained model never learned), allowing discharge of pebbles the facility believes are spent but retain significant fissile content. (3) Model extraction and adversarial transfer (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0043.002): An adversary queries the system or exfiltrates the model, then uses a proxy to craft input scenarios (real pebble manipulations or measurement perturbations) that fool the production model into authorizing anomalous discharges, enabling a timed diversion. (4) Insider exploitation of automation trust (AML.T0012 combined with implicit trust): The model's operational role erodes manual verification culture; an insider adversary exploits this by timing diversions around periods when operators rely most heavily on the AI's recommendations, knowing no human will re-check marginal cases. (5) Denial-of-service or cost-harvesting to create diversion windows (AML.T0029, AML.T0034): An adversary floods the system with crafted gamma spectra or triggers expensive retraining/recalibration cycles, forcing operators to bypass the AI and make reload/discharge decisions manually under time pressure—creating confusion an adversary can exploit for undetected material removal. IMPLICIT (NON-ADVERSARIAL) THREATS THAT EXPAND ATTACK SURFACE: (6) Simulated training data (OP.C0201.01) and operational drift (OP.C0302.01): The model is trained exclusively on simulated gamma signatures; when real operational pebbles exhibit spectral features the simulation didn't capture (e.g., due to fuel fabrication variance, irradiation history differences, or fission-product transport the code didn't model), the model drifts and its 5 MWd/kgU error band widens—this creates systematic blind spots an adversary can identify and exploit by selecting pebbles the model will misclassify. (7) Automation bias and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01): Operators come to trust the AI's burnup estimates without independent verification (since manual gamma spectroscopy analysis is slower and less practical at pebble-circulation rates), so when the model fails—either naturally or due to adversarial manipulation—no one notices until a safeguards audit or reactivity anomaly reveals the discrepancy, by which time material may already be diverted. (8) Small-data and new-build scarcity (OP.C0202, OP.C0203): Pebble bed reactors are rare and operational gamma spectroscopy data from actual high-burnup pebbles is scarce (especially for anomalous or edge-case conditions an adversary might engineer), so the model's generalization to adversarially-selected scenarios is untested—this makes the AI a brittle control point rather than a robust one. (9) Non-determinism and qualification gaps (OP.C0402, OP.C0401): If the model exhibits inference-time variability (e.g., due to ensemble methods or stochastic layers) or is opaque enough that operators can't explain why it classified a given pebble as reload vs. discharge, then an adversary can exploit this uncertainty by repeatedly measuring the same pebble until the model gives the desired answer, or by challenging decisions in ways that erode trust and push operators toward manual overrides the adversary can manipulate. (10) Material-flow propagation and cascading accountability loss (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0602): If the AI's burnup estimates feed into broader inventory reconciliation and reactor physics models (e.g., core reactivity predictions, spent-fuel criticality safety analyses), then a systematic bias in the AI propagates into every downstream calculation—an adversary who can introduce a small, consistent error in burnup measurement can cause the facility to lose track of kilograms of fissile material across thousands of pebbles over months, enabling large-scale diversion that appears as normal measurement uncertainty. The core security problem is that this AI shifts a traditionally human, per-item accountability decision (measure, verify, decide) into an automated, high-throughput gate that is difficult to audit in real time and whose failure modes—both adversarial and natural—directly determine whether weapons-usable material stays in the facility's inventory or leaves it in a form and at a time an adversary can control.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on training-data provenance (simulated vs. operational), automation bias, adversarial evasion via measurement manipulation, and cascading inventory/reactivity failures as the core threats. The security specialist's detailed diversion pathways and the AI engineer's ML-theoretic drift analysis were integrated without conflict; where panelists used different terminology for the same mechanism (e.g., 'out-of-distribution failure' vs. 'operational drift'), a single unified threat paragraph was created.

evidence.citation: "Prototyping of a Machine Learning–Based Burnup Measurement Capability for Pebble Bed Reactor Fuel," Taylor & Francis (American Nuclear Society)
evidence.note: The paper develops and demonstrates supervised machine learning regression models trained on simulated gamma spectroscopy data to predict burnup of individual fuel pebbles exiting a pebble bed reactor core, achieving prediction errors below 5 MWd/kgU when enrichment is known, to support operational decisions on whether to reload or discharge each pebble.

damage.why: Successful exploitation enables diversion of weapons-usable fissile material (kilograms over time via systematic bias) and potential reactivity excursion from overburned pebbles, meeting the definition of loss of material control and radiological release risk.

reproducibility.why: Once training-data poisoning is introduced or operational drift conditions are identified, the systematic burnup prediction bias reliably recurs across thousands of pebbles due to the model's dependence on simulation-only training and high-tempo automation, though initial setup requires careful positioning.

exploitability.why: Most attack vectors (training-data poisoning, supply-chain compromise, physical manipulation of gamma measurement chain or pebble isotopic profiles) require insider access to model development, deployment artifacts, or operational measurement systems, not achievable via routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Burnup misclassification propagates across the entire fuel handling and inventory reconciliation system, affecting reactor physics calculations, spent-fuel criticality analyses, and material accountancy facility-wide, though the core vulnerability resides in a single classification chain.

discoverability.why: The reliance on simulation-only training data and ~5 MWd/kgU error bands is documented in the published open literature describing this ML burnup measurement approach, allowing a capable adversary to infer the systematic blind spots (out-of-distribution drift, edge-case scarcity) without insider knowledge of the specific facility's implementation.

use_case: Recurrent neural network prediction of critical heat flux (value and location) in PWR-type rod-bundle fuel assemblies with non-uniform axial power shape. The network uses the sequence of local flow conditions along the assembly, including upstream history and spacer-grid effects, to support thermal-hydraulic safety analysis without empirical correction factors.
incurred_insecurity:
Using a recurrent neural network to predict critical heat flux (value and location) in PWR rod bundles puts an opaque, data-starved model into the chain that sets DNBR margin, thermal limits and licensing analysis. The main exposures are silent non-conservative error outside a narrow training envelope, an unqualified and irreproducible model replacing a correlation with a 95/95 pedigree, and misplaced analyst trust. On the adversarial side, the exposures are quiet integrity compromise of the small proprietary training data and model artifacts, and theft of the design information they embed. Because this is an offline design-basis tool, the harm is latent margin erosion and licensing-basis corruption rather than an acute event.

Out-of-domain extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on only a few costly, electrically heated bundle test campaigns (two datasets in the paper), the recurrent network interpolates or extrapolates silently for new spacer grids, fuels or axial power shapes. It returns smooth, confident, non-conservative CHF values or locations with no validity-range warning, overstating DNBR margin. An adversary who knows the envelope could steer a design or submission into its blind spots, where the error looks like ordinary model inaccuracy.

Qualification and explainability gap -- implicit, exploitable
No established framework yields a defensible 95/95 tolerance bound for a recurrent network, its hidden-state history dependence is opaque, and removing empirical correction factors removes traceable conservatism and any guarantee of physical monotonicity. Approval may rest on headline accuracy or be rejected for lack of a licensing path. Opacity gives a saboteur plausible deniability, because reviewers cannot argue from physics to notice deliberate bias.

Over-trust and loss of independent checks -- implicit, exploitable
Analysts may treat a sophisticated model that needs no correction factors as more authoritative than a hand-validated correlation, and the single scalar and location output drops uncertainty and regime information. Skipped cross-checks and atrophied thermal-hydraulic judgment remove the human verification an attacker would otherwise have to evade.

Non-repeatability and configuration control -- implicit, exploitable
Seed variance, retraining and framework or hardware changes can yield different CHF predictions, breaking the reproducibility a design-basis calculation needs. A malicious retrain or weight swap could pass as routine refinement because model identity cannot be proven.

Bias propagation through reuse -- implicit
Embedding one model in subchannel or code chains or reusing it across plants and vendors spreads any bias or error to every downstream analysis. An adversary gains little beyond amplifying a bias they have already planted.

Training-data and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor could alter a few records in the small curated CHF database, mislabel CHF locations, or trojan a checkpoint or ML library to embed a targeted non-conservative bias, possibly trigger-keyed to particular power shapes or grid geometries. Validation drawn from the same tampered source would not reveal it, leaving overstated thermal limits that pass review and erode real margin.

Model artifact tampering or substitution -- adversarial
A network file is easily swapped or edited silently between validation and use, and configuration control for analysis software is typically weaker than for plant I&C. The result is a corrupted design-basis calculation with no change visible in the report.

Design-data and model exfiltration -- adversarial
Proprietary fuel geometry, spacer-grid effects and vendor CHF test data are embedded in the trained weights and datasets, and can be stolen through cloud or shared-HPC training environments and third-party toolchains. The consequence is loss of commercially and proliferation-adjacent sensitive design information, and the ML toolchain can also serve as a foothold into design-authority networks.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-safety view, CHF prediction sets DNBR limits, which drive core thermal margin, protection setpoints and Technical Specification limits. The RNN replaces empirical correlations whose validity is bounded by test-matrix ranges and NRC/vendor qualification, and it does so without the correction factors that encode conservatism. Existing practice already guards against much of this. CHF correlations are qualified against proprietary full-scale bundle tests, then applied with a statistically derived 95/95 limit DNBR, and the safety analysis is reviewed by the regulator. The real exposure is therefore a qualification and trust problem, not a direct path to harm. An RNN that looks accurate on two datasets could be adopted in design or licensing analysis, or as a surrogate in a code chain, and quietly erode margin. That would happen if it extrapolates outside its training domain, if the CHF location prediction is wrong, or if its error bounds are not characterized the way the correlation's are.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data scarcity and out-of-domain failure (OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). Proprietary CHF bundle data are sparse, and the abstract cites only two datasets. Grid designs, mixing vanes, axial power shapes, pressure and flow regimes, and new fuel designs (accident-tolerant fuel, new grids) fall outside the training distribution. The RNN may return a smooth, confident CHF that is non-conservative, with no graceful degradation of the kind a correlation's stated validity range gives. The consequence is an overestimated DNBR margin in design, reload or uprate analysis. A plant would only be harmed if reviewers and independent codes (subchannel codes, lookup tables) also miss the error. (2) Qualification and explainability gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). An RNN cannot easily yield a defensible 95/95 tolerance bound, and its learned history dependence is opaque. Removing empirical correction factors also removes a traceable conservatism. The regulatory consequence is either rejection (a regulatory readiness gap, OP.C0504) or, worse, acceptance on headline accuracy metrics. (3) Location error. The network predicts CHF location as well as value, and a wrong axial location affects cladding temperature and fuel-performance assessments, even if the peak value is reasonable. (4) Automation and trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0304.03). Analysts may take the output of a new, sophisticated method as more authoritative than a hand-validated correlation and skip independent checks. The outputs also give only a single scalar and position, so uncertainty and regime information are dropped. (5) Non-repeatability and software hygiene (OP.C0402, OP.C0502). Retraining, random seeds and framework versions may give different CHF predictions, which breaks the configuration control that safety analyses require. (6) Model reuse across designs or sites (OP.C0602). One model propagated across fleets and vendors spreads any bias to all of them. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. These are lower-likelihood and mostly indirect. Poisoning of training data or model weights (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002/.003) through test-facility data, a shared dataset or a model supply chain could plant a subtle non-conservative bias in a region of the operating space. It would survive validation if the benchmarks come from the same tampered set. Targeted bias is more credible than obvious failure, since the output is continuous and hard to audit. There is also a risk of manipulation of the design-basis analysis record, for example altered inputs or model files in the analysis toolchain. Because this is a design-phase, offline analysis tool, there is no real-time attack surface. An adversary would have to defeat design review, independent verification and the protection-system setpoint methodology before real harm resulted. The main security consequences are therefore integrity of the licensing basis and latent margin erosion, not an acute event.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a small-data, high-consequence regression/sequence model. CHF is a cliff-edge phenomenon, and the training corpus consists of a few expensive rod-bundle test campaigns (few geometries, spacer designs, axial power shapes, and a limited pressure/flow/quality envelope). The RNN removes empirical correction factors, which also removes the explicit, bounded, physically interpretable conservatism that licensing reviewers rely on. The main fragility is what happens when an input sequence falls outside the training manifold (new grid design, new fuel, higher burnup geometry, transient conditions): the network interpolates or extrapolates silently, with no built-in uncertainty, and a model evaluated on 'two datasets' gives little evidence of generalization. A second exposure is that the CHF location output depends on the sequence, so small perturbations in upstream inputs propagate through recurrent state into both the value and the location.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data scarcity and provenance (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0203): CHF experiments are costly and proprietary, and often come from a few facilities. Random train/test splits within the same test sections leak near-duplicate samples, so reported accuracy overstates generalization to new assemblies. Data are lab/bench, electrically heated, often with simulated axial shapes, and transfer imperfectly to real fuel with crud, bowing, burnup, or new mixing-vane grids. (2) OOD and drift (OP.C0302, .03 operational heterogeneity): a network that learned geometry effects implicitly from two bundles has no mechanism to flag a new spacer or power profile. Predictions may be non-conservative exactly where empirical correlations carry margin, and the CHF cliff makes a modest non-conservative bias a departure-from-nucleate-boiling margin erosion, which is a safety issue in design and safety analysis. (3) Qualification mismatch and opacity (OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0403): there is no established framework for qualifying a recurrent network as a replacement for licensed correlations. Hidden-state behavior is hard to explain, and there is no guaranteed monotonicity or physical consistency (e.g., CHF should behave sensibly with mass flux, pressure, and inlet subcooling), so the model can violate physics between sampled points. (4) Non-repeatability (OP.C0402.01): seed and training-run variance, plus framework or hardware version changes, can produce different CHF predictions, which undermines a design-basis calculation that must be reproducible. (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0304.03): designers may over-trust a low average-error number and omit the uncertainty and conservatism treatment, and the model may be wrapped into codes or subchannel workflows without anyone recording the validity domain. (6) Propagation (OP.C0603, OP.C0602): if embedded in a subchannel code or reused across plants and fuel vendors, one biased model is replicated widely.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training-data or supply-chain poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0031): because the dataset is small, a few altered experimental records, a tampered curated database, or a trojaned pre-trained checkpoint or ML library could bias CHF predictions non-conservatively in a targeted regime, and the effect would be hard to distinguish from ordinary model error. The resulting consequence is overstated thermal margin in fuel or core design, which is a latent safety weakness and possibly a licensing-basis integrity problem. (b) Input manipulation at analysis time (AML.T0043, AML.T0015): altering upstream flow-condition sequences or power-shape inputs from upstream codes can steer the output, and the recurrent structure lets an early-sequence perturbation shift downstream predictions. (c) Model or IP exfiltration (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0048.004): proprietary CHF data and trained weights encode vendor test-loop data worth stealing. (d) Corruption or modification of model artifacts (AML.T0076, AML.T0018): silent weight edits in a design workflow with weak version control. The adversary's leverage is that the model is unverifiable by first principles, so sabotage has a plausible-deniability cover. Mitigations I would want: applicability-domain and OOD detection, grouped-by-geometry cross-validation, ensembles or conformal bounds, physics-constrained monotonicity, dataset hashing and lineage, pinned and signed model artifacts, and use as a screening or supplement to licensed correlations until qualified.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view this is an offline design-basis analysis tool, not an operational control. That makes it a poor direct target for a nation-state, but it is a good place for a quiet, long-dwell integrity attack. CHF prediction sets thermal margin (DNBR-type limits), so a small, consistent optimistic bias in the predicted value or location could be absorbed into licensing calculations, core loading, and operating limits. The bias would only show up as reduced real margin, possibly years later and in a transient. The exposure comes from three things: the model replaces empirical correlations that have a long qualification pedigree, its reasoning is opaque, and its small, expensive, mostly proprietary rod-bundle test datasets are hard for a reviewer to audit independently. Together these concentrate trust in one artifact that a single insider, or a supplier, could corrupt with little chance of detection.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model integrity compromise by an insider or supply-chain actor (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). Mechanism: the CHF databases are small, curated and expensive, so a few altered test-section records, mislabeled CHF locations, or a backdoor-style trigger tied to particular axial power shapes or spacer-grid geometries can bias predictions in a narrow, targeted regime. The regime could be one that matters for a specific fuel design or reload. The facility depends on the prediction for margin-to-CHF in safety analysis and fuel design. The consequence is non-conservative thermal limits that pass review but erode real safety margin, with latent fuel-failure risk in an accident. Because the defect is inside a regime the validation data barely covers, conventional regression checks would not see it. (2) Model and weights tampering or substitution between validation and use (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, AML.T0109). Unlike a correlation printed in a report, a network file is easy to swap silently, and configuration control for analysis software is often weaker than for plant I&C. (3) Design-information exfiltration (AML.T0025, AML.T0035, AML.T0024.001/.002). Proprietary fuel geometry, spacer-grid effects and CHF test data are commercially and proliferation-adjacent sensitive, and a trained model embeds them. Cloud or shared HPC training environments and third-party ML toolchains widen that exposure (OP.C0601, OP.C0505). (4) Stepping stone: the ML development environment and its package dependencies become an IT foothold into design-authority networks (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0011.001).

IMPLICIT, exploitable or timeable. (a) Extrapolation and OOD failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0202, OP.C0203): a network trained on two datasets has no guaranteed behavior for new grid designs, novel fuels or power shapes outside the training envelope. Because it is non-uniform-shape specific, this gap is hard to bound, and an adversary who knows the envelope can nudge a design or submission toward its blind spots. (b) Opacity and qualification gap (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0403): with no physical correlation form, reviewers cannot argue from physics why a prediction is right, which weakens both regulatory scrutiny and the ability to notice deliberate manipulation. (c) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0304.03): if analysts come to rely on the model's apparent fidelity, because it needs no correction factors, independent correlation cross-checks and thermal-hydraulic judgment atrophy. That removes the human check a saboteur would otherwise have to evade. (d) Repeatability and lifecycle hygiene (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502): training non-determinism makes it hard to prove that a retrained model is the same model, which lets a malicious retrain pass as routine refinement. (e) Regulatory readiness (OP.C0504, OP.C0503): no established licensing path for ML-based CHF means approvals may rest on thin verification and the threat model will lag the technology.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on small-data out-of-domain failure, the qualification and opacity gap, over-trust, and poisoning or tampering of data and weights leading to latent margin erosion. I dropped the weakly argued input-manipulation and AML.T0109 rug-pull codes and the broad regulatory-drift item, and kept exfiltration and the IT foothold as distinct adversarial threats.

evidence.citation: "Recurrent neural network-based prediction of critical heat flux in rod bundles with non-uniform axial power shape," Nuclear Engineering and Design (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper proposes an RNN-based alternative to regression-type CHF correlations for PWR fuel assemblies. The RNN learns geometry and history effects from flow conditions upstream of the CHF location. It was tested on two rod-bundle datasets and reasonably predicted both CHF magnitude and location without added correction factors. I only retrieved the abstract and introduction, not the full text.

evidence.citation: Assessment of Machine Learning-Based Critical Heat Flux Models in the CTF Subchannel Code for Square Rod Bundle Prediction (arXiv:2609.21995; not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This preprint evaluates ML CHF models inside the CTF subchannel code on the EPRI rod-bundle database. It supports the plausibility of embedding ML CHF models in subchannel analysis chains. It cites the Marcinkiewicz RNN paper.

evidence.citation: Aggregation of Published Non-Uniform Axial Power Data for Phase II of the OECD/NEA AI/ML Critical Heat Flux Benchmark (arXiv:2507.00034; not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: A neural network trained on uniform-power CHF data lost substantial accuracy on non-uniform axial power data. This is a documented out-of-domain degradation for ML CHF models and matches the extrapolation concern.

evidence.citation: Furlong, Zhao, Salko, Wu (2025), "Physics-based hybrid machine learning for critical heat flux prediction with uncertainty quantification," Applied Thermal Engineering (ORNL/OSTI version)
evidence.note: The study compares pure ML and physics-hybrid CHF models with uncertainty quantification. It examines limited-data versus plentiful-data training and calibration. This shows that data scarcity and uncertainty estimation are open issues for ML CHF models.

evidence.citation: Alsafadi, Furlong, Wu (2024), "Predicting Critical Heat Flux with Uncertainty Quantification and Domain Generalization Using Conditional Variational Autoencoders and Deep Neural Networks," arXiv:2409.05790 (OSTI accepted-manuscript version also available; preprint not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: Both models showed slightly larger CHF prediction errors outside the training domain than inside it. This is nuclear-specific evidence that performance degrades off-envelope.

evidence.citation: Uncertainty Quantification for Data-Driven Machine Learning Models in Nuclear Engineering Applications: Where We Are and What Do We Need? (arXiv:2503.17385; not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This nuclear-engineering review covers uncertainty quantification, explainability, reproducibility and domain generalization for data-driven ML models. I only retrieved its reference list, which points to these topics. It is relevant to the qualification, explainability and non-repeatability concerns.

evidence.citation: Idaho National Laboratory for U.S. NRC (2022), "Exploring Advanced Computational Tools and Techniques with Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Operating Nuclear Plants," NUREG/CR-7294, INL/EXT-21-61117
evidence.note: This INL report for the NRC surveys AI/ML tools and data sources for nuclear plants and their regulatory implications. It gives context on how regulators view AI/ML use, relevant to the qualification gap.

evidence.citation: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (2023), "Status Report on Regulatory Criteria Applicable to the Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML)," OSTI technical report
evidence.note: The report finds that the current US regulatory framework does not explicitly address AI. It also identifies regulatory gaps and uncertainties, which supports the claim that there is no clear licensing path for an ML-based CHF model.

evidence.citation: Li, Jiang, Li, Xia (2020), "Backdoor Learning: A Survey," arXiv:2007.08745 (preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This survey covers backdoor attacks that stay hidden until a trigger activates them. It notes the threat arises when training uses third-party datasets or models. It supports the poisoning and trojaned-checkpoint mechanisms, though it is not nuclear-specific.

evidence.citation: Chen, Liu, Li, Lu, Song (2017), "Targeted Backdoor Attacks on Deep Learning Systems Using Data Poisoning," arXiv:1712.05526 (preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This paper shows that injecting a small number of poisoned training samples can implant a backdoor with a high attack success rate. The tested defenses were ineffective. It supports the small-dataset poisoning concern, though it is not nuclear-specific.

damage.why: Most severe credible threat is training-data/model poisoning or artifact substitution that silently overstates DNBR margin and corrupts licensing basis; as an offline design tool this erodes safety margin latently rather than causing acute release, though the category could propagate to real margin loss.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-domain silent non-conservative extrapolation and lack of validity warnings occur reliably whenever inputs leave the narrow training envelope, and artifact swaps or poisoning work reliably once access exists.

exploitability.why: The deliberate adversarial threats (poisoning curated CHF data, trojaning checkpoints, tampering with model artifacts) need insider or supply-chain position in design-authority environments plus domain knowledge to craft a targeted bias; the implicit failure modes need no access.

affected_users.why: Bias propagates via reuse across subchannel chains, plants and vendors, affecting many downstream analyses, but impact stays within design and licensing analysis rather than coupled real-time plant systems.

discoverability.why: The general weaknesses of ML surrogates (small data, extrapolation, opacity, non-repeatability) are well documented in open literature and the paper is public, but finding exploitable envelope blind spots or weak configuration control requires partial knowledge of the specific model and vendor workflow.

use_case: Deep neural network classification of motorized rotating pancake coil (MRPC) eddy-current signals to automatically identify and classify flaws, such as axial cracks, in steam generator tubes during in-service inspection of nuclear power plants
incurred_insecurity:
A DNN classifier of MRPC eddy-current signals in steam generator tube inspection concentrates trust in a pressure-boundary integrity decision. It is trained on specimens with deliberately made defects and deployed in a time-limited, high-volume outage workflow. The main threats are a lab-to-field generalization gap, silent drift, analyst over-reliance, an unqualified and opaque model, and adversarial tampering with the model, its data or the signals. Any of these can leave a degraded tube in service with no visible alarm.

Lab-to-field generalization gap -- implicit, exploitable
The model learns clean signals from machined or laboratory defects, and real cracks are a rare class. Field signals from service-induced cracking, deposits, dents, support-plate geometry and probe wobble fall outside that distribution, so the quoted ~97% axial-crack detection hides false negatives on atypical flaws. An adversary could treat the undetected miss band as plausible deniability, hiding a suppressed flaw inside what looks like ordinary model error.

Drift and acquisition heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Changes in probe type or wear, instruments, calibration, degradation mix or unit-to-unit conditions shift the input distribution, and retraining or software changes alter behaviour without revalidation. Sensitivity therefore erodes silently between qualification events. An adversary could time a manipulation to that unmonitored drift, or make a model or setting change that is indistinguishable from it.

Analyst over-reliance under outage pressure -- implicit, exploitable
Through automation bias, skill fade and out-of-the-loop analysts, triage by the classifier replaces independent review, especially if it screens out no-flaw signals. Human review then no longer catches model errors on the tail where they concentrate. An adversary could choose an outage where review is thinnest and rely on the misplaced trust to let a manipulated call through.

Qualification, opacity and repeatability gap -- implicit, exploitable
A DNN gives no per-call justification mapped to accepted analysis criteria, and retraining is non-deterministic. It has no established route into the performance-demonstration and analyst-qualification regime used for eddy-current techniques, so it may be used informally as an unqualified screening aid. An adversary gains cover, because a tampered model version or threshold change cannot easily be shown to differ from a benign retrain.

Narrow class definition -- implicit
The axial-crack class oversimplifies the flaw space, and circumferential, volumetric, multiple-flaw and mixed-signal cases are rare or absent in training. Novel flaw types are then confidently assigned to the wrong class. An adversary gains little beyond the general generalization gap already described.

Training-data and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Inspection vendors typically supply the model, the retraining sets and the analysis software. Poisoned labels, altered specimen data or a backdoored model could make the classifier systematically call specific flaw morphologies or tube locations benign, leaving a degraded tube unplugged with a possible tube rupture. One vendor model reused across plants would spread the same blind spot to many units.

Signal-level evasion and configuration tampering -- adversarial
An insider or compromised acquisition or analysis chain could perturb raw or pre-processed eddy-current data, or change probe and calibration settings, model versions or confidence thresholds, so that real flaws read as benign. Reviewers who see only model-flagged calls would not notice, and the opaque model leaves little forensic trace.

Denial and exfiltration at the vendor boundary -- adversarial
Denial or corruption of the analysis service during a time-limited outage pushes the schedule toward reduced review or extended outage. Vendor-held or cloud-hosted inspection data and models also expose plant condition information and enable proxy-model staging for the evasion above.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, an MRPC flaw classifier sits inside the steam generator tube integrity program. That program supports the primary pressure boundary, where a missed axial crack means a tube left in service that should have been plugged or repaired. The documented work trains on specimens with deliberately made defects. Real service-induced cracks (SCC, PWSCC, fretting, denting, deposits, tube supports, geometry transitions) look different, and a headline figure of about 97% axial-crack detection says nothing about false calls, rare flaw types, or performance on field noise. The main consequence pathway is that the time-limited outage pushes analysts to trust the classifier. Automation bias and reduced independent analyst review then turn a quiet misclassification into an undetected through-wall or near-critical flaw. Existing practice (EPRI examination guidelines, qualified data analysts, site-specific performance demonstration, dual-party analysis, in-service leak monitoring, tech-spec primary-to-secondary leakage limits) provides defense in depth. That depth only holds if the AI is kept advisory and is not silently substituted for qualified analysis.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Training-data provenance and generalization (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302.01): lab specimens with machined or EDM defects are not representative of in-service cracks. Low base rates of real axial cracks, variation across tube materials, probe types, vendors and denting or deposit conditions, and probe wear or lift-off differences can cause a silent drop in detection probability (POD). A missed or mis-sized flaw leaves a degraded tube in service, raising the risk of tube rupture, a steam generator tube rupture (SGTR) event, or leakage exceeding tech-spec limits. Safeguards include independent analyst review, bounding-flaw growth allowances and leakage monitoring. (2) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0402): techniques in this field are normally qualified via performance demonstration against guideline-defined POD and sizing criteria. A DNN is opaque, may not be repeatable across retraining, and may not fit the existing qualification framework. Regulators and utilities may not accept it, or it may be used informally as a screening aid that is never formally qualified. Classification that is well-calibrated on average can still miss rare, small or atypical flaws. (3) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102): outage schedule pressure favors reduced human review. Analysts who rely on automated calls lose skill and stop second-guessing, so the human safeguard that should catch AI errors erodes. Overconfident scores and a lack of explanation compound this. (4) Model updates and versioning (OP.C0502, OP.C0302.02): retraining with new data or changing probes or acquisition software without revalidation shifts behavior without anyone noticing. 

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Data or model integrity compromise (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0043.004): poisoned or tampered training or fine-tuning data, or a backdoored model from a vendor or supply chain, could suppress classification of cracks with specific signal characteristics. Tampering with stored eddy-current data or analysis outputs (AML.T0031, AML.T0076) could hide real flaws. The consequence is an integrity-of-record problem, since an unplugged defective tube gets a clean classification. Independent verification of a sample, baseline comparison and trend review against prior outages would need to also fail. (6) Adversarial perturbation of acquired signals (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) needs access to the acquisition chain or data files and is less plausible than data-level tampering. It would still be a pathway in an environment where insiders or contractors have access. (7) Denial or delay (AML.T0029, OP.C0204): loss of the tool during a time-limited outage pushes the schedule toward manual analysis, extended outage, or pressure to cut corners. (8) Contractor and third-party inspection vendor trust boundary (OP.C0505, OP.C0601): inspection data and models held by vendors or in the cloud open routes for data leakage of plant condition information (AML.T0025, AML.T0057), or for unvetted model changes. Overall severity is bounded by layered defense and leakage monitoring, but the weak point is the combination of unrepresentative training data, schedule-driven over-reliance, and lack of AI-specific qualification, which together can degrade tube integrity assurance without any visible alarm.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline standpoint, this use case is fragile at the data layer before it is fragile anywhere else. The documented system is trained on MRPC signals from tube specimens with deliberately made defects (EDM notches or machined or laboratory-grown cracks). Real in-service flaws such as SCC, PWSCC and ODSCC, and signals from deposits, dents, support-plate and tube-sheet geometry, and probe wobble, are not the same distribution. Flaws are also a very low base-rate class, so a headline figure like ~97% axial-crack identification says little about precision, false-negative rate on real cracks, or behavior on out-of-distribution signal morphology. The model sits in a high-volume, time-pressured inspection workflow, so both automation bias and silent drift (new probes, instruments, tube materials, plant-specific noise, acquisition settings) are built into how it would be used. A 97% recall claim can hide the very rare, atypical, or complex-morphology flaws that matter most for tube integrity.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Lab-to-field generalization gap (OP.C0201.01/.02/.04, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202). Mechanism: the training distribution is artificial or specimen-derived defects with clean, controlled signals, while deployment inputs are heterogeneous field signals. Dependency: the flaw call for each tube in the steam generator, which is a pressure-boundary component. Consequence: undetected or misclassified real cracks (false negatives), and false positives that drive unnecessary plugging or outage extension. Because real flaws are rare, reported accuracy and recall on a test split drawn from the same specimens overstate field performance. (2) Drift and acquisition heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303). Mechanism: changes in probe type or wear, instrument or firmware, calibration, frequency settings, degradation mechanism mix over plant life, or unit-to-unit differences shift the signal distribution without any alarm. Consequence: silent degradation of detection sensitivity between qualification events. There is also a static/dynamic qualification mismatch: a model validated once versus inspection techniques that are formally qualified per procedure and personnel. (3) Automation bias and workflow coupling (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Mechanism: under time pressure with thousands of signals, analysts accept the model's triage, and their calibration and skill fade. If the model is used to screen out 'no flaw' signals, human review is removed from the tail where errors concentrate. Consequence: model misses propagate into the integrity assessment and the tube-plugging decision. (4) Opacity and repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501). Mechanism: a DNN has no per-call justification that maps to accepted analysis criteria, and there is training-time non-determinism and no established AI qualification route in the inspection code framework. Consequence: hard-to-defend dispositions, weak regulatory acceptance, and an inability to diagnose why a miss occurred. (5) Narrow class definition (OP.C0301, OP.C0304.03). Mechanism: classifying 'axial crack' and similar classes oversimplifies; circumferential, volumetric, multiple-flaw, and mixed-signal cases are absent or rare in training. Consequence: confident misassignment of novel flaw types. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training and data-pipeline poisoning and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059). Mechanism: altering labels, specimen data, or retraining sets, or tampering with a vendor-supplied or pretrained model or analysis software, could plant a backdoor or a blind spot, for example a class of signal shape or location that is reliably labeled benign. Dependency: the inspection contractor's data-management and analysis chain, which is often third-party and offsite. Consequence: a degraded tube goes unflagged, a integrity and safety exposure that looks like ordinary model error. (7) Evasion and input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031). Mechanism: an adversary with write access to acquisition files or the analysis pipeline perturbs signals, or exploits a known weakness in the classifier, to suppress a flaw indication. The eddy-current signal is low-dimensional and structured, so small, plausible perturbations are hard to distinguish from noise. Consequence: concealment of real damage; this is an insider or data-integrity threat more than a remote one. (8) Model and data exfiltration and disruption (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0029, OP.C0601). Mechanism: theft of proprietary inspection datasets and models, or denial or corruption of the analysis service during a tightly scheduled outage. Consequence: compromised inspection data confidentiality, schedule pressure that pushes toward reduced review, and proxy-model staging for the evasion above (AML.T0005). Exploitability of the adversarial threats is amplified by the implicit ones: the lack of independent field-validation data, low-base-rate labels, and the absence of drift monitoring mean a tampered or degraded model would not be noticed.

security_specialist.argument: Steam generator tubes are the reactor coolant pressure boundary, so this classifier is a trust-concentration point. It sits in a time-pressured outage workflow where analyst fatigue is already an attack-timing window, and a DNN that screens out 'no-flaw' signals removes human eyes from most of the data. A sophisticated adversary would more likely go after the data pipeline, model artifacts, or the outage-vendor supply chain than the inspection probe, because one quiet bias toward missed axial cracks is invisible until a tube leaks or ruptures. The documented evidence is also thin: about 97% detection on specimens with deliberately made defects says little about field signals, and the 3% miss rate is exactly what an adversary would want to hide inside.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or training-data poisoning and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0076): inspection vendors typically deliver the model, the retraining sets and the analysis software. A backdoor trigger, or a subtle shift in labeled axial-crack examples, could make the classifier systematically under-call specific flaw morphologies, e.g. near support plates or in a particular tube region. The facility depends on this output for plugging and repair decisions and for the integrity of the pressure boundary, so the consequence is an undetected degraded tube, with a possible SGTR, loss of coolant and radiological release. (2) Signal-level evasion (AML.T0015, T0043, T0031): an insider or a compromised acquisition chain could alter raw or pre-processed eddy-current data, or the probe and calibration settings, so that real flaws look benign to the DNN. Human reviewers who see only model-flagged calls would never notice. (3) Insider access to the model, thresholds or configuration (AML.T0012, T0081): a change to a confidence threshold or a model version swap leaves little forensic trace, and the output is hard to audit because the model is opaque. 

IMPLICIT, TIMEABLE BY AN ADVERSARY. (4) Automation trust failure, skill fade and out-of-the-loop analysts (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102): the stated motivation is throughput under outage time limits. Once analysts rely on the DNN, manual-review rigor erodes, and an adversary can pick an outage when review is thinnest. (5) Data scarcity and provenance (OP.C0201.01/.04, C0202, C0203): training uses lab specimens with artificial defects, while real cracks are rare, and field signal noise, denting, deposits and probe wear differ. Generalization failure and drift are likely (OP.C0302, C0303), giving a silent miss-rate gap that a quoted 97% hides and that an adversary can exploit as plausible deniability for sabotage. The 3% misses may also be systematic rather than random. (6) Qualification and regulatory gaps (OP.C0501, C0504, C0401, C0402): it is unclear how a DNN fits the qualified-technique and performance-demonstration regime (for example, EPRI-type analyst qualification). Opacity and non-repeatable retraining make it hard to show that a model change is benign, which weakens change control and tampering detection. (7) Cross-fleet propagation (OP.C0602): one vendor model reused across plants means a single compromise or blind spot spreads to many units.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the lab-to-field gap, drift, automation bias, the qualification gap and supply-chain or signal-level tampering. I dropped the speculative or weakly argued items (AML.T0057 data leakage, AML.T0035, OP.C0203 new-build scarcity, OP.C0504, OP.C0204, hallucination codes) as poorly grounded for a non-generative classifier. I kept the single-panelist narrow-class and cross-fleet points because they were distinct..

evidence.citation: "MRPC eddy current flaw classification in tubes using deep neural networks," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Korean Nuclear Society / Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper trains deep neural networks on MRPC eddy-current data from tube specimens with deliberately made defects. The goal is to automate flaw classification, because the large number of signals in a time-limited inspection is a practical problem. The abstract reports that the network correctly identified about 97% of axial cracks in the pancake-coil signals. I read only the abstract and summary text returned by search, not the full paper.

evidence.citation: New Mexico State University / U.S. DOE NEPO project report, "Eddy Current Signature Classification of Steam Generator Tube Defects Using a Learning Vector Quantization Neural Network," OSTI
evidence.note: A DOE-funded project report that prototyped a neural-network system to automate eddy-current diagnosis of steam generator tube defects, trained on EPRI data sets. It shows that automated classification of these tubes is a long-standing proposal. It is an earlier, non-DNN analog.
