The publisher is a university under a DOE program, hosted on OSTI, so it is not a national laboratory report in the strict sense.

evidence.citation: New Mexico State University / U.S. DOE (OSTI), "Automated Diagnosis and Classification of Steam Generator Tube Defects"
evidence.note: The report says neural-network training was limited by the amount of available eddy-current defect data. This supports the entry's concern about thin, rare-class training data. It is a nuclear-specific example.

evidence.citation: Liu et al. (2021), "Towards Out-Of-Distribution Generalization: A Survey," arXiv:2108.13624
evidence.note: Survey of the general failure mode in which distribution shift between training and deployment degrades model performance. It supports the lab-to-field gap and drift mechanisms. This is an arXiv preprint and I did not confirm peer review.

evidence.citation: Lyell and Coiera (2017), "Automation bias and verification complexity: a systematic review," Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association 24(2):423-431
evidence.note: Systematic review showing that decision support can make users over-reliant and less vigilant, introducing new errors. It is healthcare and human-factors literature, not nuclear, but it supports the analyst over-reliance mechanism.

evidence.citation: Li, Jiang, Li and Xia (2020), "Backdoor Learning: A Survey," arXiv:2007.08745
evidence.note: Survey of backdoor and poisoning attacks on DNNs. It covers the threat that arises when users adopt third-party datasets or models, which matches the vendor-supplied model and retraining-set scenario. This is an arXiv preprint and I did not confirm peer review.

evidence.citation: Data Poisoning in Deep Learning: A Survey (2025), arXiv:2503.22759
evidence.note: Survey of data poisoning attacks, including label-only backdoors that work by corrupting a small share of training labels. It supports the poisoned-label and altered-data threat. This is an arXiv preprint and I did not confirm peer review.

evidence.citation: Springer journal article (2001), "Eddy Current Signal Deconvolution Technique for the Improvement of Steam Generator Tubing Burst Pressure Predictions"
evidence.note: The abstract says eddy-current signals respond to dents, fretting, support structures and corrosion products as well as cracks. It also says cracking geometries more complex than a single axial crack complicate interpretation, and that neural networks have had only limited success in classifying and sizing defects. This supports the field-signal confounders and the narrow-class concerns. I could not confirm the journal name from the search result, so it is labelled 'Other' rather than peer-reviewed journal.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is training-data or model poisoning, or signal tampering, that leaves a degraded steam generator tube in service; this could cause tube rupture and a possible primary-to-secondary leak. That is a pressure-boundary failure with potential radiological consequences, but containment and defense-in-depth make a large release less direct than a 5 would imply.

reproducibility.why: The implicit failure modes (generalization gap, drift, over-reliance) recur reliably once the model is deployed, but a miss requires an atypical flaw, and adversarial manipulation depends on specific conditions such as vendor-chain access and the flaw being present.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (poisoning the vendor supply chain, tampering with the acquisition or analysis chain, changing model versions or thresholds) require insider or vendor-level access and domain knowledge of eddy-current inspection; routine external interaction is not enough.

affected_users.why: A vendor model reused across plants could spread the same blind spot to many units and affect all inspected tubes in a steam generator, but the impact stays within the inspection and integrity program rather than propagating across coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: ML generalization gaps, drift, automation bias and poisoning are well documented in open literature, and the ~97% figure and the vendor-supplied model structure are public; locating a specific weakness still needs some inference about the deployment.

use_case: Stacked-autoencoder (compared with random forest and ANN) localization of stress-corrosion-cracking acoustic emission sources on large dry cask storage canisters, mapping AE sensor features to source positions so a minimal sensor count can support structural-integrity monitoring of stored spent fuel
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places an opaque stacked-autoencoder localizer in a long-duration, low-attendance integrity-monitoring role on passive spent-fuel canisters, where a minimal sensor count removes redundancy. The main threats are a surrogate-to-field performance gap, drift and minimal-sensor fragility, over-trust in a headline accuracy figure, governance and qualification gaps, and adversarial manipulation of sensor inputs, training data or model artifacts. Severity is bounded because the casks are passive and other inspection barriers exist. The principal harm is gradual erosion of inspection rigor and assurance evidence, not a direct release.

Surrogate-to-field transfer gap -- implicit, exploitable
Real SCC acoustic emission events are rare and cannot be position-labelled, so the model is likely trained on simulated, pencil-lead-break or bench data. The 97.8% in-distribution accuracy therefore does not show that real welds, geometry, coatings or field noise are handled, and OOD inputs still yield confident but wrong positions, so cracks are mislocalized or missed. An adversary could rely on this gap, and on operators attributing anomalies to model error, to hide a real degradation or tampering event.

Drift and minimal-sensor fragility -- implicit, exploitable
Couplant aging, sensor gain drift, thermal cycling and canister-to-canister variation shift feature distributions over decades, and with few sensors one failed or noisy channel pushes the autoencoder off-distribution with no redundancy or uncertainty estimate to reveal it. An adversary could time manipulation of one or two channels inside this degraded, unflagged band, where each sensor carries outsized weight.

Over-trust and detection-versus-localization conflation -- implicit, exploitable
A near-silent system with high headline accuracy invites complacency, skill fade and substitution of continuous AE monitoring for periodic direct inspection, and localization accuracy gets confused with detection probability. An adversary could exploit the resulting lack of independent cross-checks, since a confident wrong location is hard for operators to challenge.

Qualification, opacity and repeatability gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Non-deterministic training, opaque latent features and the lack of an AI-specific qualification and change-control path make retraining and revalidation hard to demonstrate, and any fleet-wide model reuse would propagate a single flaw across canisters. An adversary could hide a model or data change inside routine retraining that is not rigorously revalidated.

Sensor and feature manipulation -- adversarial
An intruder or insider with access to AE sensors, cabling or acquisition electronics could inject noise or spoofed waveforms, or alter features, to mask a real source, shift the predicted location, or fabricate false clusters that provoke needless dose-bearing inspections. Low sensor redundancy makes a few compromised channels sufficient to conceal canister degradation or cover physical tampering.

Training-data and model poisoning -- adversarial
Poisoned training or recalibration waveforms, or a tampered model or ML tooling from a vendor or research pipeline, could plant a dormant blind region on a chosen weld zone. Opacity and validation on average accuracy make such a backdoor hard to detect.

Availability denial and data exposure -- adversarial
Chaff AE noise, forced false alarms or taking monitoring offline could swamp the system or push operators to disable it, eroding the evidence base for safety cases and licence renewals. The acquisition workstation and any vendor or cloud update path also give an entry point, and leaked condition data and sensor layout aid sabotage or diversion planning.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a condition-monitoring aid for dry cask canisters, not a protection system. A wrong localization does not directly cause a release, because nothing trips on it and the casks are passive. The consequences are therefore mostly latent: a missed or mislocated SCC source means delayed inspection or repair, or unnecessary and dose-bearing inspection of a healthy canister. The realistic failure modes are a model trained on limited, probably simulated or lab data (the source does not say which) that does not transfer to real canisters, and operators treating a 97.8% benchmark figure as field performance. Existing practice (visual and remote inspection, thermal and dose surveys, conservative aging-management programs) means AE is unlikely to be the only barrier, but an AI-enabled 'minimal sensors' approach could erode that redundancy over time.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data provenance and transfer gap (OP.C0201.01, .02, .03, OP.C0203, OP.C0202): SCC AE events on real canisters are rare, slow, and site-specific. Training data is likely simulated, pencil-lead-break, or lab-coupon derived. Accuracy on such data says little about performance on welded heat-affected zones with real geometry, attenuation, coatings, or concrete overpack and environmental noise. Consequence: false confidence, with mislocated or undetected cracks. (2) Drift and heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, .03, OP.C0303): sensor coupling degrades over decades, temperature cycling, and canister-to-canister variation in geometry and wall thickness shift the feature distributions. A model qualified statically can silently degrade over the multi-decade storage horizon. (3) Sparse-sensor design (OP.C0401, OP.C0403): the 'optimal minimal sensor count' removes redundancy, so one failed sensor or a noisy channel can push a stacked autoencoder out of distribution with no explanation or uncertainty estimate. It returns a confident but wrong position. (4) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102): a near-silent monitoring system fosters complacency. Zero alarms for years is interpreted as integrity, and the model's limited detection sensitivity (as opposed to localization) is overlooked. Localization accuracy is not detection probability, and the two can be conflated. (5) Qualification and QA gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01): it is unclear how a retrained autoencoder would be revalidated, and training non-determinism affects repeatability for regulator-facing evidence.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Manipulation of inputs (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0046): an adversary with physical access to a cask pad, or to the acquisition network, could inject acoustic or electrical noise or spoofed waveforms to mask real AE or create false localization clusters. This would hide real degradation or provoke needless inspections, which is an operational and dose burden and a public-confidence issue. (7) Data and model integrity (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059): poisoned training or recalibration data, or a tampered model from a vendor or research code, could bias the localization away from a chosen weld zone. This is a low-visibility, slow attack that fits the long timescales here. (8) Availability (AML.T0029): taking the monitoring offline erodes the evidence base for safety cases and licence renewals. The harm is primarily regulatory and confidence-related, given the passive safety of the casks. The physical consequence requires a further independent failure, since canisters have large margins, inspection regimes, and no active dependence on this AI, and that bounds the severity. The main risk is gradual erosion of inspection rigor through misplaced trust.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is a supervised regression/classification model (stacked autoencoder feeding a localizer) whose fragility sits almost entirely in its training data. Real SCC acoustic emission events on in-service dry cask canisters are extremely rare and cannot be labeled with ground-truth position, so training labels almost certainly come from simulation, pencil-lead breaks, or pulsed-source bench or mock-up tests on a specific canister geometry. The reported 97.8% accuracy is an in-distribution benchmark on that surrogate data, not evidence of generalization to real cracks, other canister designs, welds, backfill conditions, or field noise (wind, rain, thermal cycling, ventilation flow, cask-surface coupling). The 'minimal sensor count' objective removes redundancy, so a single drifting, detached or spoofed channel moves inputs off-manifold with little cross-checking. Autoencoder latent features also offer little explainability for an inspector asked to trust a localization.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Surrogate-to-field gap (OP.C0201.01/.02/.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0302): labeled SCC AE data from real casks is scarce and low base-rate, so the model learns the wave propagation of a test article and not of deployed canisters. Real-world variation (wall thickness, weld geometry, temperature, sensor coupling degradation, concrete overpack or air-flow noise) is operational heterogeneity and drift. Mechanism: out-of-distribution input is still mapped confidently to a position, because autoencoder reconstruction and softmax or regression outputs are not calibrated uncertainty. Consequence: a real crack is mislocalized or missed, or benign noise is localized as a crack, so inspection is misdirected, degradation goes unnoticed in a storage system that is hard to access, or unnecessary interventions create dose and handling risk. (2) Minimal-sensor fragility (OP.C0603, OP.C0302.01): with few sensors, channel loss, gain drift or couplant aging silently changes the feature distribution and there is no redundancy to reveal it. (3) Qualification and opacity gaps (OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0403): stochastic training and unexplained latent features make repeatability hard to demonstrate, and there is no established qualification path for an ML localizer in an aging-management program. The model comparison, with ANN at 80% and autoencoder at 97.8%, may also reflect tuning on one small dataset (overfitting, leakage between train and test events). (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102): a high headline accuracy invites over-trust or alarm complacency, and monitoring that looks continuous may displace periodic direct inspection. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Data and model integrity (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0031): poisoning or tampering with training waveforms, retraining datasets, or model files could bias localization or blind the system to a chosen region. This is plausible through shared research-data pipelines or vendor software. (6) Input-level evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041): physical access to the sensor or cable path, or injected acoustic or electrical signals, could produce feature vectors that mask real AE sources or fabricate false ones. The minimal sensor count makes this easier, and the model is differentiable and low-dimensional enough to be attacked by black-box optimization. (7) Reconnaissance (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0013): published architecture, feature sets and accuracy figures help an adversary build a proxy model (AML.T0005) and learn the model's blind spots. (8) Degradation of trust (AML.T0046, AML.T0029): chaff AE noise or forced false alarms could swamp the system or push operators to disable it, weakening structural-integrity assurance for stored spent fuel. Consequences are mainly safety (undetected canister degradation) and security or assurance erosion, not direct safeguards impact.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial lens, this use case adds an AI-mediated layer to a long-duration, low-attendance monitoring function on spent fuel storage. Dry cask canisters are passive systems that are visited rarely, so SCC acoustic emission monitoring may become one of the few continuous indicators of canister integrity. That makes the localization output valuable to manipulate, suppress or time an attack around. A sophisticated adversary probably would not target the model directly, since compromising the sensor network, data path or training pipeline is easier. Yet if operators come to rely on a minimal-sensor AI localizer, sparse sensor coverage plus an opaque model reduces the human's ability to spot a wrong or absent result. The documented 97.8% accuracy comes from a model built and tested on data, with no stated field deployment, so the gap between reported and real performance is itself an exploitable weakness.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Sensor and feature manipulation. An insider or intruder with physical or network access to AE sensors, cabling or acquisition electronics could inject, mask or alter waveforms and parametric features (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0041, AML.T0046). Because the model is deliberately run with a minimal sensor count, each sensor carries more weight and redundancy is low. A few compromised channels could shift the predicted source location away from a real crack or fabricate benign-looking locations. The consequence is a missed or misplaced indication of canister degradation, with delayed inspection or repair, and in a storage setting the confinement and safeguards-continuity consequences could be long-lived. Masking could also be timed to cover physical tampering or a real loss-of-integrity event. (2) Training-data and model integrity. The stacked autoencoder depends on labeled source-position data, possibly from simulated or lab-generated events (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02). Poisoning the data, the pipeline or the model artifacts, or a supply-chain compromise of the ML tooling, could plant a blind region or bias on the canister surface (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0059). Such a backdoor would be dormant and hard to detect because the model is opaque (OP.C0401) and is validated on average accuracy. (3) Stepping stone. The AE acquisition and analysis workstation bridges field sensors and plant or vendor IT, so it could serve as an entry point. Vendor-hosted or cloud-based training and updates add further exposure (OP.C0601, AML.T0012, AML.T0025). Access to monitoring data and model outputs also leaks canister condition and sensor layout, which is useful reconnaissance for sabotage or diversion planning (AML.T0024, AML.T0035).

IMPLICIT (exploitable or timeable): (4) Performance that does not transfer. 97.8% accuracy on a research dataset may not hold across canister designs, weld geometries, boundary conditions, noise environments or sensor aging (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). Real SCC events are rare, which gives a small-data, low base-rate problem (OP.C0202, OP.C0204). Undetected drift or degradation gives an adversary cover because anomalies are attributed to model error. (5) Automation trust and skill fade. Operators who trust a localization map may stop doing independent inspections or skip cross-checks, which is long-horizon complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). A confident but wrong location, with no uncertainty estimate, is hard to challenge. (6) Governance gaps. There is no AI-specific qualification regime for storage-monitoring ML, and the model has no defined update or change control (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504). Any retraining or fleet-wide model reuse would propagate a single flaw or compromise across many canisters (OP.C0602). Overall the threat is moderate, and it depends on whether the tool moves from advisory research use to a primary integrity-monitoring role.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the surrogate-to-field gap, minimal-sensor fragility, over-trust, sensor-input manipulation and training-data or model poisoning. I dropped the weakly argued reconnaissance/proxy-model and identity-credential items (AML.T0000, T0005, T0012, T0024) as not distinct enough, and kept only the concrete data-path exposure..

evidence.citation: "Source localization on large-scale canisters for used nuclear fuel storage using optimal number of acoustic emission sensors," Nuclear Engineering and Design (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper trains three machine-learning models (stacked autoencoders, random forest and ANN) on both parametric and waveform-based acoustic emission features to localize stress corrosion cracking events on dry cask storage canisters. Stacked autoencoders performed best, with 97.8% accuracy against 91.5% for random forest and 80.0% for ANN. The abstract does not say whether the data were simulated or measured, so this is a model built and tested on data rather than a field deployment.

evidence.citation: Ai, L. et al. (2023), "Localizing damage on stainless steel structures using acoustic emission signals and weighted ensemble regression-based convolutional neural network," Measurement
evidence.note: This is a follow-on study that applies deep-learning AE localization to a large-scale steel plate standing in for a spent-fuel canister. It shows the approach is an active research direction for dry cask monitoring. It also notes that earlier single-sensor stacked-autoencoder work used only a small-scale plate.

evidence.citation: (2024), "Structural health monitoring of stainless-steel nuclear fuel storage canister using acoustic emission," Developments in the Built Environment
evidence.note: This paper tests AE monitoring of stress corrosion cracking on a 304H stainless steel plate representing a canister. The plate was cracked with a tetrathionate solution and tensile stress, and the sensors detected the cracking at considerable distances. It shows the data in this area come from lab surrogates rather than field canisters.

evidence.citation: Meyer, R.M., Hanson, B.D., Sorenson, K.B. (2013), "A Review of NDE Methods for Detecting and Monitoring of Atmospheric SCC in Dry Cask Storage Canisters for Used Nuclear Fuel," PNNL / NACE Corrosion 2013
evidence.note: The review says AE could monitor canister SCC continuously, including in hard-to-reach regions, but that AE sensitivity to atmospheric SCC is unclear. This supports the surrogate-to-field gap and the point that AE detection is not the same as localization.

evidence.citation: Ovadia, Y., Fertig, E., Ren, J., et al. (2019), "Can You Trust Your Model's Uncertainty? Evaluating Predictive Uncertainty Under Dataset Shift," Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 32
evidence.note: This is a general, non-nuclear benchmark. It finds that deep-learning uncertainty estimates and calibration degrade under dataset shift, so confident outputs on shifted inputs can be wrong. This supports the surrogate-to-field, sensor-drift and out-of-distribution fragility mechanisms.

evidence.citation: Zhao, P., Zhu, W., Jiao, P., Gao, D., Wu, O. (2025), "Data Poisoning in Deep Learning: A Survey," arXiv:2503.22759 (preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This survey covers data-poisoning attacks that embed systematic biases or backdoors in trained deep models and persist after deployment. It supports the training-data and model-poisoning threat. It is a preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

evidence.citation: Zhang, Q., Ding, Y., Tian, Y., Guo, J., Yuan, M., Jiang, Y. (2021), "AdvDoor: Adversarial Backdoor Attack of Deep Learning System," ACM SIGSOFT ISSTA 2021
evidence.note: The paper shows a backdoor can be injected into deep-learning models with a high attack success rate. It also shows the backdoor can evade state-of-the-art detection methods. This supports the concern that a dormant blind region in an opaque localizer would be hard to detect.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is sensor or model manipulation that masks real canister degradation or tampering, or erodes safety-case evidence. Casks are passive and other inspection barriers exist, so the harm is mainly loss of assurance and needless dose-bearing inspections, not a direct release.

reproducibility.why: The surrogate-to-field gap, drift, and minimal-sensor fragility arise reliably once the model is deployed on real canisters with few channels and OOD inputs, and low redundancy makes a failed or compromised channel reliably degrade localization.

exploitability.why: Manipulating sensors, cabling, acquisition electronics, training data, or vendor model artifacts generally needs physical or insider access at a secured spent-fuel storage site or supply-chain access. Only the implicit gaps are exploitable without that access, and they still need timing and knowledge.

affected_users.why: Impact is on the monitored canisters' integrity-assurance function and could span a canister fleet if a model is reused, but passive casks are not coupled to one another and effects stay within the monitoring and inspection domain.

discoverability.why: The open literature documents the AE-localization approach, its use of lab surrogate data, and the general weaknesses of ML models (OOD overconfidence, drift, poisoning), so a capable outsider can infer that the class of weakness exists. Site-specific sensor layouts and configurations would still need inside knowledge.

use_case: Machine-learning regression, with bagged random forest performing best, predicts static and dynamic leaching (dissolution) of borosilicate high-level waste glass. Inputs are glass composition, pH and test conditions from a large multi-source dataset of vitrification-campaign, literature and laboratory experiments. The model estimates releases of boron, silicon, sodium and aluminium to support durability assessment of vitrified waste forms for deep geological disposal.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline design-stage regression model adds no real-time actuation path, but it concentrates trust in a durability estimate that shapes glass formulation and the long-term safety case for geological disposal. The main threats are implicit: extrapolation failure, heterogeneous and leaky data, and over-trust in an opaque tool with no qualification route. Adversarial threats are mainly integrity attacks on the dataset, model artifact and inputs, which the implicit weaknesses make hard to detect. Because harm is slow and effectively irreversible once glass is emplaced, silent error or manipulation would surface only after disposal.

Extrapolation and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
A bagged random forest cannot extrapolate, so for novel high-loading or noble-metal/sulfate compositions, long durations, or residual-rate and resumption-of-alteration regimes it returns bounded, plausible, optimistic B, Si, Na and Al release values with no uncertainty flag. An adversary could time a formulation change or waste-stream substitution to fall in this blind spot, where a manipulated prediction looks like normal interpolation.

Data heterogeneity, provenance and validation leakage -- implicit, exploitable
Merging campaign, literature and lab data with differing protocols, surface-area-to-volume ratios and reporting bakes in lab artefacts. Near-duplicate replicates across train and test splits inflate the 'within experimental error' accuracy and hide the true applicability domain. Natural scatter and thin independent cross-checks give cover for small injected biases.

Short-term proxy and objective mismatch -- implicit
Short-duration lab leaching stands in for repository-timescale, evolving multi-barrier behaviour with no ground truth at the target horizon. Predicting only B, Si, Na and Al can be misread as a statement on actinide or Tc release. An adversary gains little directly from this beyond the general unverifiability.

Model-generated gap-filling re-entering records -- implicit
Imputed or forecast values can be mistaken for measurements, enter databases and safety-case records, and contaminate retraining, compounding bias. No distinct adversarial gain beyond what dataset poisoning already offers.

Automation bias, opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A high headline R-squared, feature importances read as mechanism, point predictions without calibrated uncertainty, and unversioned data and non-deterministic training invite reliance in place of confirmatory leach testing, with no established AI qualification or regulatory route. An adversary can rely on this lowered reviewer vigilance and weak audit to let a tampered or poorly generalising model pass unchallenged.

Training-data poisoning and integrity erosion -- adversarial
An insider or upstream data source altering, inserting or dropping a few campaign, literature or lab records can bias predicted release for a region of composition space. The result is an optimistic durability estimate that enters formulation decisions or the safety-case narrative and may be found only after emplacement.

Model artifact and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
A swapped or retrained model file, altered preprocessing code or compromised library can shift outputs in a narrow composition region or carry a composition-keyed trigger. The small, cheap-to-retrain model makes this easy to do and hard to notice.

Input manipulation and credibility attack -- adversarial
Falsified composition or test-condition inputs, such as waste-producer declarations, can steer the estimate to an acceptable release value without touching the model. An adversary can also target the evidence itself, injecting contradictory data or discrediting results, to delay licensing or erode regulatory and public confidence.

Proxy reconstruction and data theft -- adversarial
Open literature and documented model family allow a proxy model to be built to learn which compositions are predicted to tolerate leaching, and proprietary campaign data can be exfiltrated. The value is mainly as reconnaissance for targeted data or influence operations.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline design-stage regression model that estimates B, Si, Na and Al release from borosilicate glass, so there is no real-time actuation path. The harm route is indirect and slow: a wrong or overconfident prediction could shape a glass formulation, a waste-loading target or a durability argument in a repository safety case. It would do so years before the disposal environment could confirm or refute it. Existing practice (standardized leach tests such as PCT and MCC-1, long-term corrosion programs, analog studies, conservative source-term assumptions in the safety case, regulator review) is a strong barrier, provided the ML output stays a screening aid and does not substitute for qualification testing. The main engineering exposure is extrapolation. The training data are multi-source, heterogeneous and dominated by short-term laboratory tests, while the decision of interest is durability over geological timescales, in regimes such as residual-rate, alteration-phase formation and resumption of alteration that the data barely sample.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and out-of-distribution failure. The model learned short-duration, mostly non-repository-relevant tests, so it may look accurate 'within experimental error' on interpolated data yet fail for new HLW compositions (high-waste-loading, novel frits, noble-metal, Mo or sulfate phases, crystallization or phase separation), for long durations, for groundwater or bentonite chemistries, or for gel and secondary-phase regimes. Random forests cannot extrapolate beyond the training range and return a plateau that looks plausible. The consequence is an optimistic source-term or durability claim that survives until a qualification test or a late review catches it (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). (2) Data heterogeneity and provenance. Merging vitrification-campaign, literature and lab data with different protocols, surface-area-to-volume ratios, temperatures, leachate analysis and reporting conventions builds lab-to-lab bias into the model. It also risks leakage between train and test splits, since replicate experiments from the same glass are near-duplicates, and duplicate or transcription errors in literature data. The model's accuracy figure can then be inflated and the applicable domain misjudged (OP.C0201, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0204). (3) Imputation and forecasting used for gap-filling. Filling in missing data or projecting over time can be mistaken for measurement, so model-generated values could enter databases and safety-case records as if they were experimental, and could contaminate later retraining (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0603). (4) Automation bias and qualification gap. Fast, cheap predictions could tempt screening-stage reliance to replace confirmatory testing, especially with schedule pressure on design and construction. Opaque ensemble reasoning is hard to justify to a regulator, and there is no established AI qualification route for durability claims (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Point predictions without calibrated uncertainty invite over-trust. (5) Glass-chemistry knowledge not captured. Element-release regression for B, Si, Na and Al does not directly capture radionuclide retention, so the model could be misread as a statement on actinide or Tc release (OP.C0301, OP.C0702). ADVERSARIAL THREATS (lower likelihood, low immediacy). (a) Poisoning or manipulation of the training dataset, the curated literature or campaign data, or the model file through supply chain or insider access (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059). This could bias predictions toward optimistic durability for a specific composition, for example to favour a cheaper formulation or to undermine confidence in a waste-form acceptance case. Subtle bias is hard to detect because few independent data points exist to cross-check it, and the harm is delayed and deniable. (b) Tampering with the inputs or the exported results feeding a design or licensing document (AML.T0043.003), or a reconnaissance and IP-theft angle on proprietary vitrification-campaign data, which is commercially and security-sensitive (AML.T0025, AML.T0024). Physical consequence requires the defeat of independent leach testing, product-consistency acceptance and the safety-case review, which is why the overall risk is moderate and mostly confined to credibility and long-term integrity of the disposal case rather than an acute release.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a tabular regression model (bagged random forest) trained on a heterogeneous pool of vitrification-campaign, literature and lab dissolution data, and used to support long-term durability claims for disposal. The main fragility is in the data rather than the architecture. Tests differ in protocol, duration, surface-area-to-volume ratio, leachant chemistry and reporting practice, and those covariates are often missing or imputed. Random forests cannot extrapolate beyond the training range, yet the real question is very long-term behaviour, including late-stage residual rates, alteration-phase formation and resumption of alteration. Short-duration laboratory data cannot validate that regime, so 'within experimental error' on random or interpolative splits may say little about new compositions or long times. Validation leakage is a specific risk: correlated replicate or series data from the same glass can land in both train and test sets and inflate apparent accuracy. Because the model also 'fills in missing data', its outputs can re-enter the dataset and compound bias.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and OOD failure: new waste-stream compositions (higher actinide, sulfate, molybdate or noble-metal loadings, different frit or additives), pH or temperature outside the training envelope, and long time horizons all fall where forests return bounded, plausible-looking values with no uncertainty signal. The facility-side dependency is the durability and waste-form acceptance case for the repository. The consequence is an optimistic release estimate that supports accepting a non-conforming glass, which is a long-term safety and safety-case credibility problem (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403). (2) Data provenance and quality: a multi-source corpus mixes static and dynamic tests, lab and campaign glasses, and differing protocols and measurement uncertainties. Publication bias toward well-durable glasses and scarce data on failure-mode glasses skew the labels. Imputed values used as inputs or targets add a further distortion (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0202, OP.C0204). (3) Static/dynamic qualification mismatch: short-term lab leaching is used as a proxy for repository-timescale, multi-barrier, evolving-chemistry behaviour, and no ground truth exists at the target horizon. Precision claims are therefore unverifiable (OP.C0303, OP.C0501). (4) Only a limited set of elements (B, Si, Na, Al) is predicted, so release of the radiologically important nuclides is inferred indirectly, and optimising on the predictable outputs can misalign with the actual safety objective (OP.C0301). (5) Automation trust and opacity: a good headline R² can encourage reliance, with feature-importance output mistaken for mechanistic understanding. Training non-determinism and unversioned data snapshots harm repeatability in a regulatory context (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Training-data or dataset poisoning: the data are aggregated from open literature and shared labs, so a subtle shift in a few records (mis-stated composition, pH or leach rates) or a tampered curated dataset could bias predictions for a specific composition region. Random forests are sensitive to localised label manipulation, and the bias would be hard to detect because the data are heterogeneous (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059). (2) Supply chain and model-artifact tampering: altered pickled model files, preprocessing code or library dependencies could change outputs in a narrow input region, or carry a trigger tied to a particular composition signature (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). (3) Input manipulation at inference: falsified composition or test-condition inputs fed into the assessment can steer the estimate towards an acceptable release value without any model change, which matters where waste-producer declarations feed the model (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015). (4) Low-confidence exposure: model behaviour could be reconstructed from published data and papers to design compositions or declarations that exploit known blind spots (AML.T0000, AML.T0005). Implicit weaknesses make these attacks more effective because there is no calibrated uncertainty, no OOD flag and a thin independent verification baseline, so a manipulated prediction looks like normal interpolation.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial lens this is a low-glamour target, because the model is an offline design-stage regression tool that does not touch operating plant control, and a nation-state would get more from attacking the physical waste form or the repository safety case directly. The threat surface it does add is indirect: it concentrates trust in a durability estimate that feeds glass formulation choices and the long-term safety case for geological disposal, and the effects of a bad estimate are slow, hidden and effectively irreversible once glass is poured and emplaced. A tabular random forest trained on a multi-source dataset (vitrification campaigns, literature, lab tests) has a provenance-heavy and lightly governed data pipeline, which is the real insider and supply-chain pathway. The most credible adversary is a quiet insider or a compromised data or software supplier who biases inputs or outputs so a marginal formulation looks acceptable, or who erodes confidence in legitimate results. Non-adversarial weaknesses make that manipulation hard to detect: out-of-distribution compositions, sparse long-duration data, and low explainability all give cover to a bad prediction.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Training-data poisoning or dataset integrity erosion. The dataset merges campaign records, published literature and lab experiments, with mixed provenance and weak chain of custody. An insider or an upstream data source could alter a small number of entries, or insert or drop compositions or conditions, biasing predicted B, Si, Na and Al release for a region of composition space. The facility depends on the model for durability screening and waste-form qualification support, so the consequence is an optimistic release estimate that gets into formulation decisions or the safety-case narrative. The harm is delayed, potentially only discovered after emplacement, and a repository-scale safeguards and safety consequence. Because the model is small and cheap to retrain, a tampered retrain or swapped model file (AI supply chain, model manipulation) is also easy to carry out and hard to notice. (2) Trust concentration and credibility attack. Because the model's outputs are cited as evidence of durability, an adversary can target the evidence instead of the glass, for example by publishing or injecting contradictory data, or by discrediting results. This would delay licensing or waste-form acceptance, undermine public and regulatory confidence, or force rework. (3) Reconnaissance and information leakage. The literature, dataset and model family are openly documented, so an adversary can build a proxy model and learn which compositions the facility's glass is predicted to tolerate. This is weak on its own but could feed targeted data or influence operations. IMPLICIT: (4) Out-of-distribution and drift failure. Real vitrified waste has compositions, noble-metal and actinide loadings, and long-term alteration behaviour (for example secondary phase formation and the resumption of alteration) that short-duration lab data under-represent. A random forest cannot extrapolate beyond its training range and gives no warning when it does, so optimistic predictions for novel formulations look confident. An adversary could time a formulation change or a waste-stream substitution to fall in the model's blind spot. (5) Automation bias and opacity. Agreement 'within experimental error' on held-out data encourages over-trust, and the ensemble is hard to explain mechanistically, so reviewers may not challenge outputs that disagree with mechanistic dissolution models. This reduces the vigilance that would expose a tampered or poorly generalizing model. (6) Qualification and governance gap. There is no established qualification route for ML tools in waste-form durability claims, no versioning or training-data control requirements, and unclear ownership of dataset curation. Together these leave the tool in a grey zone where manipulation or silent error is unlikely to be audited. (7) Data heterogeneity and small-data issues. Multi-source experimental data have inconsistent protocols, surface-area normalisation and pH control, and the model can learn lab artefacts instead of chemistry. That makes bias injection easier to hide within natural scatter.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on extrapolation failure, data heterogeneity, over-trust/qualification gap and dataset/model poisoning as the core threats; I merged overlapping items and kept the unique imputation feedback and credibility-attack points. I dropped speculative codes (AML.T0043.004 backdoor trigger is folded into artifact tampering only generically, AML.T0048.002, OP.C0702) and did not assign ATLAS codes to purely implicit threats.

evidence.citation: "Predicting radioactive waste glass dissolution with machine learning," Journal of Non-Crystalline Solids (Elsevier), vol. 533, 119852, 2020
evidence.note: The authors trained and tested machine-learning models on large, diverse, multi-source glass-dissolution data covering many compositions and experimental conditions. They report that the models predict leaching within experimental error, including forecasting over time and filling in missing data. Bagged random forest performed best for static leaching. The paper applies this to borosilicate glass for high-level waste disposal.

evidence.citation: Lillington, Goût, Harrison & Farnan (2020), "Assessing static glass leaching predictions from large datasets using machine learning," Journal of Non-Crystalline Solids (comment/follow-up)
evidence.note: This is a follow-up on the ALTGLASS database of about 450 glasses, where tree-based methods (Bagging and RandomForest regressors) predict B, Li, Na and Si releases well. Accuracy is good only when leaching-experiment results are included as features. It also reports worse performance on an external database, which supports the data-heterogeneity and generalization concerns in this entry.

evidence.citation: Zhang & Lin (2019), "Regression-Enhanced Random Forests," arXiv:1904.10416 (preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This preprint states that random forests can fail when predictions are needed outside the training-data domain. Each prediction is an average of observed training responses, so outputs stay within the training range. This supports the extrapolation and out-of-distribution blind spot.

evidence.citation: Kapoor & Narayanan (2023), "Leakage and the reproducibility crisis in machine-learning-based science," Patterns 4(9), 100804
evidence.note: This survey finds data leakage in 17 fields, affecting 294 papers and sometimes giving wildly overoptimistic results. Its taxonomy includes duplicates and non-independence between train and test sets. This supports the concern that near-duplicate replicates inflate apparent accuracy.

evidence.citation: Cinà et al. (2023), "Wild Patterns Reloaded: A Survey of Machine Learning Security against Training Data Poisoning," ACM Computing Surveys
evidence.note: This survey covers indiscriminate, targeted and backdoor poisoning, in which an attacker alters a fraction of the training data to compromise model behaviour at test time. It supports the training-data poisoning and composition-keyed trigger mechanisms. It is general ML security work, not nuclear-specific.

evidence.citation: Lillington, J. N. P. (University of Cambridge doctoral thesis), "Predicting radioactive waste glass properties with machine learning and modelling"
evidence.note: This thesis amalgamates UK vitrification-campaign, literature and unpublished lab data and predicts boron release, with a bagged random forest typically best. It reports high accuracy only when pH or release data are among the features. It gives context on the dataset composition and on the limits of the approach.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is silent optimistic bias (data poisoning, artifact tampering, or falsified inputs) in a durability estimate that feeds glass formulation and the geological disposal safety case, which could contribute to an eventual long-term radiological release; the tool is offline and advisory, so the link is indirect, and confirmatory testing and regulatory review should limit it.

reproducibility.why: Random-forest extrapolation failure is deterministic and reliably occurs for out-of-domain compositions, and data or artifact integrity compromise persists once introduced, but it needs specific conditions (novel compositions, a successful tamper) to bite.

exploitability.why: The credible adversarial paths (altering campaign or lab records, swapping the model artifact, falsifying waste-producer declarations) need insider or supply-chain access, though the cheap, small model and weak audit lower the bar somewhat.

affected_users.why: A biased durability model could affect all vitrified waste forms and the disposal safety case in the affected composition region, which is broad in time and programme scope, but it is confined to a design-stage tool and does not propagate across coupled operating systems.

discoverability.why: The methods, the model family (bagged random forest), the dataset types and the limits of tree-based extrapolation are well documented in open literature, so an outsider can readily infer the blind spots, though the specific proprietary data and pipeline internals are not public.

use_case: U-Net deep-learning segmentation that identifies and removes twin grain boundaries in backscattered-electron micrographs of the silicon carbide layer of TRISO coated particle fuel. The aim is to automate quantitative grain-size and grain-shape quality control (QA/QC) during fuel fabrication and qualification.
incurred_insecurity:
A U-Net twin-boundary segmenter used as an automated gate for SiC grain-size and grain-shape QC concentrates trust in a small-data research model whose validation is weak. The documented result shows aggregate grain metrics within 1% of EBSD truth while pixel-wise twin prediction is poor. The main threats are a metric-task validation gap, silent distribution-shift failure, automation trust and skill fade, weak AI lifecycle control, and adversarial tampering with the model, labels, images and reference data. The consequence is latent rather than acute: off-spec SiC could be accepted and show up only as coating failures in irradiation or service, and a quiet accept/reject bias could corrupt the fuel qualification record.

Aggregate-metric validation gap -- implicit, exploitable
The 1% agreement on grain area and boundary pixels may rest on compensating over- and under-segmentation errors, so local twin calls, aspect ratios and tail grain sizes can be wrong while the headline metric passes. An adversary could hide a deliberate bias or microstructure deviation inside that tolerance, because reviewers checking only the aggregate metric would not see it.

Distribution shift on small lab data -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained on a few EBSD-labelled micrographs from specific deposition runs, preparations and SEM settings, so a new recipe, line, detector, charging or polishing artifact shifts the images and yields confident but wrong segmentations. EBSD is not run in production, so nothing flags this. An adversary could time a process deviation or material change around this blind spot, or induce the shift through acquisition settings.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Clean automated outputs tend to replace manual and EBSD checks, which lets metallographic skill fade and sampling drop, while opaque per-pixel twin decisions make errors hard to spot. An adversary gains misplaced trust: a subtle manipulation faces few people able to notice it, and tampering is hard to tell from natural drift.

Lifecycle and qualification gaps -- implicit, exploitable
This early-stage research model has no AI-specific qualification, version or retraining change control, and retraining non-determinism can shift results between versions and break comparability of qualification data. An adversary could swap or alter weights or preprocessing unnoticed and pass the change off as routine retraining variance. Sharing a model across labs or vendors would also propagate one site's bias or compromise to others.

Model, label and dataset poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor could poison or backdoor the weights, EBSD-derived labels, training set or pretrained encoder so the segmenter systematically over-removes boundaries or hides fine-grain or defective microstructure. The result is non-conforming lots passing, or good lots wrongly rejected, and a corrupted fuel qualification record.

Input and ground-truth manipulation -- adversarial
Altering stored micrographs, acquisition or preprocessing settings, or result tables can shift segmentation output without touching the model, and tampering with the EBSD reference files used for validation can hide a corrupted model. This is a low-barrier insider route to falsifying QC evidence.

Supply chain, workstation pivot and IP exposure -- adversarial
Open-source deep-learning frameworks, pretrained weights and shared lab storage on analysis workstations form a weakly hardened foothold beside fabrication data. They also expose proprietary TRISO process and microstructure data, and the trained model, to theft or extraction.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a fuel-fabrication QA/QC measurement aid, not a control or protection function. A bad output does not cause an immediate physical event. It causes a wrong accept/reject or qualification judgment on the SiC layer, and that judgment only matters if the microstructure metric is actually limiting for fission-product retention. The real-world consequence is latent: fuel particles with off-spec SiC grain structure could be accepted and only show up as elevated coating failure fraction in irradiation or service. Independent safeguards exist: EBSD reference checks, other fabrication QC (layer thickness, density, anisotropy, defect and burn-leach testing), and irradiation qualification. So the main issues are silent bias in a measurement chain and over-reliance on it, not an acute accident. One documented weakness matters here: pixel-wise twin-prediction metrics were low while aggregate grain-area and boundary-pixel changes were within 1%. The model can look accurate on the headline metric while individual twin-boundary calls are frequently wrong, so the validation metric could hide errors that matter for a different downstream quantity.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Metric-task mismatch and validation gap (OP.C0301, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). The 1% aggregate agreement was shown against EBSD ground truth on a limited sample. Low pixel-level twin accuracy means grain-shape or local-morphology statistics, such as aspect ratio, boundary-character distribution and tail grain sizes, may be biased even when mean grain area is right. If QA acceptance limits are later set on those statistics, particles could be mis-accepted or mis-rejected. (2) Drift and OOD generalization (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). Training data is small and lab-derived, from specific SiC deposition conditions, batches, polish and etch preparations, and SEM settings. A new deposition recipe, a different vendor or fabrication line, changed BSE contrast or detector, charging, polishing artifacts, or irradiated or annealed material would shift the image distribution. The model would still return confident, clean segmentations, and because EBSD is not run routinely in production there would be no ground truth to reveal the degradation. This is a slow-developing failure that lets off-spec material pass. (3) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). Automated QC output tends to replace manual or EBSD checks, so skill fade, complacency and reduced sampling can follow. Opacity of the U-Net's twin calls (OP.C0401) limits an analyst's ability to spot bad cases. (4) Qualification and regulatory gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402.01). The work is early-stage research with no AI-specific QA, version control or retraining-change control. Retraining variance could shift results between versions and break comparability of qualification data over time.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. The attack surface is the image-to-metric pipeline and the model artifact, which is smaller than for operational systems but relevant to fuel qualification integrity. (a) Tampering with weights, training labels or the dataset (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0010.002), for example via a compromised public model, a third-party analysis tool or the lab data store. This could bias grain-size output so that non-conforming lots appear conforming, or could cause wrongful rejection that disrupts supply and cost. A subtle systematic bias of a few percent would be hard to detect because the validation check is itself aggregate. (b) Manipulation of input micrographs or of the acquisition and preprocessing chain (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015). This is a low-barrier insider or supply-chain route to shift results without touching the model. (c) Insider tampering with EBSD ground-truth reference files that are used to validate the model, which would hide a corrupted model. (d) Proprietary TRISO process information exposed through training data, images or model extraction (AML.T0024, AML.T0025, AML.T0035) is a commercial and possibly export-control concern. Overall severity is moderate and delayed. The main protection is to retain independent EBSD or manual spot checks, use drift monitors and locked model versions, and keep the ML result advisory rather than the sole basis for lot acceptance.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline standpoint this is a small-data, single-source supervised segmentation problem. Ground truth comes from EBSD-derived twin labels co-registered to BSE images. EBSD is slow and expensive, so the labeled set is almost certainly a few tens of micrographs from a limited set of batches, instruments and deposition conditions. The published result is telling: pixel-wise twin-prediction metrics were low, yet aggregate grain-area and boundary-pixel changes came within 1% of truth. That means the model is fit for an aggregate statistic on in-distribution samples and is not a reliable detector of individual twins. A qualification claim built on the aggregate can hide large local errors and poor behavior under shift. The real exposure is the gap between how the model was validated and how it would be used as a QC gate for fuel acceptance.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift at inference (OP.C0302, .01, .03). The model is trained on BSE micrographs from specific SiC deposition runs, polishing and etching protocols, detector settings, accelerating voltages and magnifications. Process changes, a new coater, a different vendor's particles, advanced-fuel variants, or a detector swap alter contrast, charging, scratch artifacts and grain morphology. Twin-boundary appearance in BSE is subtle channeling contrast, so the model may hallucinate or miss twins silently. There is no EBSD at production inference time, so nothing in the loop detects that the labels no longer match. (2) Aggregate-metric masking and a qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0403, OP.C0501). The 1% aggregate agreement may rest on compensating over- and under-segmentation errors. Extrapolating it to tails of the grain-size distribution, which is what QC limits on abnormal grain growth or fine-grain regions depend on, is unvalidated. The system then feeds grain-size and shape statistics into acceptance decisions without an AI-specific qualification basis. (3) Small-data and label-quality issues (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0201.05). EBSD-to-BSE registration error, EBSD indexing ambiguity for twins (Σ3 in 3C-SiC, stacking faults), and annotator or threshold choices become baked-in label noise. The same tile or particle may leak across train and test splits, inflating performance. (4) Automation bias and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, .06). Metallographers who stop hand-verifying twins lose the ability to notice systematic error, and confident cleaned-up outputs look authoritative. (5) Reproducibility and lifecycle (OP.C0402, OP.C0502, OP.C0401). Retraining non-determinism, unversioned weights, preprocessing and thresholds, and opaque per-pixel decisions make it hard to reproduce a past acceptance decision or audit a batch.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. These are lower-profile than in safety-critical control, but real for a QA gate. (a) Training-data or label poisoning and model tampering (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0031). A subtle bias in labels, pretrained weights or the retraining set could make the model systematically over-remove boundaries. This inflates apparent grain size, or hides fine-grained or defective microstructure that affects fission-product retention in the SiC layer. The consequence is degraded fuel-quality assurance and possible acceptance of out-of-spec particles. (b) Evasion and manipulated inputs (AML.T0015, T0043). Image acquisition pipelines can be altered, for example by changing contrast, noise or preprocessing in the file path, so that defect-bearing regions segment as benign. This is also an insider-enabled route to falsifying QC records. (c) Integrity and provenance of the image pipeline (AML.T0059, T0012). Analysis workstations and shared image repositories often sit outside hardened fuel-facility enclaves, and tampering with stored micrographs or result tables undermines the evidential chain for fuel qualification. (d) Supply chain: open-source U-Net frameworks, pretrained encoders, and research-lab code used as-is (AML.T0010.001, T0011.001).

Cross-cutting: a qualification-data store that is mostly research-grade raises OP.C0505 and OP.C0204 issues, including proprietary process data and model transfer between labs and vendors. Such a transfer risks propagating one site's bias to others (OP.C0602).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface standpoint, this is an attractive stepping-stone target and a poor direct one. Nobody sabotages a fuel plant by attacking a twin-boundary segmenter. But if it becomes the automated gatekeeper for SiC microstructure acceptance, it concentrates trust in a quiet, rarely audited software-and-data chain. Fuel quality records feed safety-case claims about fission-product retention, and they also carry proprietary process information. An insider or supply-chain adversary could use the model to bias or hide microstructure deviations, or to reach a fabrication-facility network through an unglamorous lab-analysis workstation. The documented result is also a weak foundation for that trust: aggregate grain metrics land within 1% while pixel-wise twin prediction is poor. That makes errors hard for a human reviewer to see, and a deliberate adversary could hide a deviation inside the same tolerance.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity of the QC decision chain: the model is the thing whose output replaces a human metallographer's judgement. An insider with access to the model weights, the preprocessing pipeline, or the EBSD-derived training labels could poison or backdoor the model (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003/.002, AML.T0043.004). The aim would be a systematic bias in grain size or shape metrics that passes lots which should fail, or fails good lots. Consequence: degraded fuel-quality assurance and a corrupted qualification record, with potential downstream effects on in-reactor fission-product retention margins. Direct model manipulation is the most plausible route, because the image inputs come from a controlled lab instrument. (2) Manipulated inputs: altered or tampered micrographs, or changed acquisition settings, could shift segmentation output (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015, AML.T0059). (3) Supply chain and workstation pivot: the model runs in a Python/deep-learning stack with pretrained weights, open-source libraries and shared lab storage. That stack is a low-security foothold beside fabrication data, and it carries proprietary process and microstructure data and IP (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0025, AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002). (4) Trust concentration: once the aggregate metrics are trusted, human microscopy skill atrophies and few people remain able to catch a subtle manipulation (OP.C0101.06).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable. The demonstrated performance is proof-of-concept, trained on a small set of EBSD-labeled samples, with low pixel-level twin accuracy (OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03). Metric-level agreement can hide compensating errors. The model may generalize poorly to new deposition batches, process changes, imaging conditions, or different facilities' instruments (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303). Gradual drift produces credible-looking but wrong quantities, and an adversary could time a process deviation or substitution around that blind spot. Because the EBSD ground truth is only sparsely available, there is little ongoing independent verification (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0501). Opacity makes tampering hard to tell from natural drift (OP.C0401). Vendor or cloud model-hosting dependence would add further exposure (OP.C0601), and a model shared across fabricators would propagate a compromise or bias fleet-wide (OP.C0602). Mitigations are outside this entry's scope, but the main lever is to keep EBSD-based spot verification, model-weight integrity controls and separation of duties, so the model never acts as the sole acceptance authority.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the aggregate-versus-pixel metric gap, small-data drift, automation trust and poisoning/tampering of the model and data chain. I dropped weakly supported codes (cloud dependency, LLM-style and credential techniques, OP.C0504, OP.C0505) and kept only those traceable to the threats in the text.

evidence.citation: "Methods development towards automated, physics-informed, quantitative quality control of TRISO-SiC," Journal of Nuclear Materials (Elsevier), vol. 626, article 156591, 2026; Oak Ridge National Laboratory
evidence.note: The authors developed, trained and tested an ML image-segmentation model that predicts twin boundaries in TRISO-SiC micrographs, using crystallographic (EBSD) data as ground truth. Grain-area and grain-boundary-pixel changes after twin removal were within 1% of the true values, even though pixel-wise twin-prediction metrics were low. The work is presented as an early-stage, industrially oriented step toward automated QA/QC of coated particle fuel.

evidence.citation: Conry, B., Helmreich, G. W., Gerczak, T. J., et al. (2026), "Methods development towards automated, physics-informed, quantitative quality control of TRISO-SiC," Journal of Nuclear Materials (DOI 10.1016/j.jnucmat.2026.156591)
evidence.note: This is the source study for the entry. It develops a U-Net twin-boundary segmenter for BSE micrographs of TRISO-SiC as a QA/QC tool. It also reports that pixel-wise twin metrics are low while grain area and GB-pixel changes fall within 1% of the crystallographic (EBSD) truth. That result supports the metric-task validation gap.

evidence.citation: Conry, B., Helmreich, G., Gerczak, T. (2025), "Automated Segmentation of Twin Boundaries in TRISO Silicon Carbide Using Deep Neural Networks," Oak Ridge National Laboratory technical report, DOI 10.2172/3002218
evidence.note: This ORNL technical report is the earlier laboratory version of the twin-boundary segmentation work. It shows the application is a real prototype in the Advanced Fuel Fabrication / particle fuel program.

evidence.citation: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (2020), "Quantification of silicon carbide grain structure in TRISO fuel" (AGR Program report)
evidence.note: This report describes the image-processing method for quantifying SiC grain structure from BSE images. It says the method is meant to support a quantitative SiC microstructure specification in industrial fuel fabrication. It also notes that EBSD sampling is too slow for routine batch QC, which is why the EBSD-free ML route was pursued.

evidence.citation: RU-net for automatic characterization of TRISO fuel cross sections (2025/2026), ScienceDirect journal article (pii S1044580326000550)
evidence.note: This paper applies machine-learning segmentation to TRISO fuel cross-sections and notes that annotated training data are scarce. It also notes that resolution, contrast, noise and polishing quality complicate segmentation. It is a close analog of the use case and also supports the small-data and image-variability concerns.

evidence.citation: Maier-Hein, L., Reinke, A., et al. (2024), "Metrics reloaded: recommendations for image analysis validation," Nature Methods
evidence.note: This consensus study documents that metrics chosen for image analysis often fail to reflect the real task, and that aggregating metric values can bias results. It supports the vulnerability that an aggregate 1% agreement can hide poor pixel- or instance-level segmentation.

evidence.citation: Domain Adaptation for Medical Image Analysis: A Survey (arXiv:2102.09508; preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This survey describes domain shift: a model trained on one data distribution degrades on data from different scanners or sites, even for deep CNNs. It is general evidence for silent failure when the SEM, preparation or recipe changes. It is not nuclear-specific.

evidence.citation: ROOD-MRI: Benchmarking the robustness of deep learning segmentation models to out-of-distribution and corrupted data in MRI (2023), NeuroImage
evidence.note: This paper shows empirically that modern CNN segmentation models are highly susceptible to distribution shift, corruptions and artifacts. It supports the concern about charging or polishing artifacts and new acquisition settings producing confident but wrong segmentations.

evidence.citation: Artificial intelligence in medicine: a scoping review of the risk of deskilling and loss of expertise among physicians (2026), ScienceDirect
evidence.note: This review collects evidence that reliance on AI outputs brings automation bias and erosion of independent expert judgment. It is medical rather than nuclear, but it supports the automation-trust and skill-fade mechanism.

evidence.citation: Li, Y., Jiang, Y., Li, Z., Xia, S.-T. (2020), "Backdoor Learning: A Survey," arXiv:2007.08745 (preprint; later published in IEEE TNNLS)
evidence.note: This survey covers backdoor attacks that poison training samples or come in through third-party datasets and models. It supports the model, label and pretrained-encoder poisoning threats. This arXiv version has not been peer reviewed.

evidence.citation: Data Poisoning in Deep Learning: A Survey (2025), arXiv:2503.22759 (preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This survey categorizes poisoning attacks on deep networks, including label flipping and backdoors. It notes that small numbers of poisoned samples can implant a working backdoor. It supports the dataset and label poisoning mechanism.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoning or tampering that lets off-spec SiC coating pass QC and corrupts the fuel qualification record, leading to latent coating failures in irradiation or service and falsified qualification evidence; this falls short of an acute radiological release but goes beyond operational disruption.

reproducibility.why: Distribution shift, aggregate-metric masking and over-trust recur reliably whenever recipes, detectors or preparation change and no EBSD cross-check runs, so the weakness appears dependably once the described conditions hold.

exploitability.why: The implicit weaknesses need only routine changes to process or acquisition settings, but the deliberate poisoning and ground-truth tampering routes need insider or supply-chain access to lab data, weights or workstations.

affected_users.why: Impact is confined to the fuel fabrication QC and qualification pipeline, but it can cover every lot passed by the gate and can spread to other labs or vendors that share the model.

discoverability.why: The gap between aggregate metrics and pixel-wise twin accuracy is published in the open literature and the general weaknesses of small-data segmentation models are well known, but knowing how a particular deployment is configured, validated or sampled needs insider knowledge.

use_case: Graph-neural-network-based deep reinforcement learning agent (Proactive Safety Policy Optimization) trained in a digital twin of a nuclear power plant to schedule refueling outage activities dynamically and to choose emergency-response actions during fires, using dynamic risk (core damage frequency) as the safety measure
incurred_insecurity:
A single GNN-based reinforcement-learning policy, trained and validated only inside a digital twin and rewarded on modelled core damage frequency, would steer both outage sequencing and emergency fire response. It incurs implicit risk from simulation-to-plant gaps, reward misspecification, scarce rare-event data, operator over-trust and an absent qualification pathway. It incurs adversarial risk from tampering with the twin, PRA inputs and model, from falsified plant-state inputs, and from theft of a concentrated map of plant vulnerabilities. Mitigation rests on human authority and licensed procedures, which work only if the advice stays advisory and is not over-trusted.

Twin and reward poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor who alters twin parameters, PRA/CDF inputs, reward terms or training scenarios can steer the learned policy toward outage configurations that quietly stack vulnerabilities or toward misdirected fire-response actions. Because the bias lives in opaque learned weights and outputs still appear CDF-optimal, it persists and is hard to detect.

Backdoored or swapped policy -- adversarial
A trojaned checkpoint, or a compromised RL, GNN or simulator dependency, can behave correctly across all validation scenarios yet deviate under an attacker-engineered plant state such as a particular fire location or outage configuration. Non-determinism between retrains makes a tampered model hard to distinguish from a legitimately retrained one.

Spoofed plant-state inputs -- adversarial
Falsified or degraded sensor, alarm, fire-detection or equipment-status feeds can push the GNN out of distribution so it recommends unsafe emergency actions or hides a hazard. Denying or delaying the tool mid-fire can force a chaotic fallback to procedures or erode operator trust in correct advice.

Plant-vulnerability map theft -- adversarial
The twin, policy and GNN graph embed plant topology, system interdependencies, risk-importance rankings and low-defense-in-depth outage windows, which is a targeting guide for sabotage. Model extraction, artifact theft or exfiltration from the new IT/OT-connected twin environment would expose it.

Sim-to-real gap and reward hacking -- implicit, exploitable
The agent optimises model-computed CDF and can exploit twin artifacts or PRA simplifications, for example stacking activities scored as independent that interact physically. This erodes defense-in-depth, shutdown margin or decay heat removal redundancy that the PRA does not credit. An adversary could time physical or cyber action to configurations the policy rates as low-risk but which are actually weak.

Rare-event scarcity and out-of-distribution brittleness -- implicit, exploitable
Fire-response behaviour is learned from assumed synthetic scenarios, and plant modification, equipment ageing, PRA updates or topology changes silently invalidate the twin-to-plant mapping with no calibrated uncertainty signal. An adversary could engineer or choose novel states outside the training envelope where the policy is least reliable, or exploit a stale twin.

Over-trust, opacity and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Opaque, quantitatively framed recommendations invite over-trust under fire stress, anchoring by outage planners and erosion of independent judgement, while early visible errors can cause disuse. An adversary could rely on this misplaced deference to get a subtly biased recommendation accepted, or discredit the tool to get correct advice ignored.

Qualification, repeatability and change-control gaps -- implicit, exploitable
There is no established V&V pathway for an adaptive learned policy in safety-related decision support, results vary across seeds and retrains, and the policy may silently omit Tech Spec, fire watch or dose constraints. Weak version control over the twin and model lets a tampered model pass as a routine retrain, and a fleet-shared policy or single PRA dependency would propagate one flaw across units.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is a decision-support agent that would sit between the PRA/risk monitor and two very different decisions: outage sequencing, where errors cause latent defense-in-depth erosion, and fire response, where errors cause immediate consequences. Every result is simulation-only, so the agent is only as good as the digital twin and the PRA that supplies its reward (CDF). RL policies are known to exploit simulator gaps and to optimize the stated metric rather than the intent. Existing practice (Tech Specs, outage risk management under 10 CFR 50.65(a)(4), shift manager authority, fire procedures, defense-in-depth and shutdown safety function requirements) guards against a bad recommendation only if operators do not defer to the agent and the agent's recommendations stay inside those licensing-basis limits. The main downstream exposure is an unvalidated, opaque policy that looks rigorous because it quantifies risk, and that could be trusted, manipulated or degraded at the moment of greatest operator stress.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and reward misspecification (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0301, OP.C0303): the agent is trained and validated only in a twin. Fire dynamics, equipment failure, manpower, access constraints and cable-routing damage are simplified, and CDF is a modelled quantity with large uncertainty. The agent can learn to exploit twin artifacts or PRA simplifications, for example compressing outage schedules into configurations that are low-CDF under model assumptions but erode defense-in-depth, shutdown margin or decay heat removal redundancy that the PRA does not credit. It can also trade off hazards the PRA omits, such as human error, seismic or flood interactions, and non-modelled fire spread. Consequence: outage configurations or fire actions that are nominally optimal but physically unsafe, where only procedural barriers and operator judgement stand in the way. (2) Rare-event scarcity (OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0201.02): real fire and severe-event data are scarce, so training relies on synthetic scenarios and the policy has not seen the plant's true tail. It is brittle when a real event falls outside training (OP.C0302.03), and it may behave unpredictably exactly when the stakes are highest. (3) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.03, OP.C0102, OP.C0401): a GNN-RL policy is opaque and gives no auditable rationale. Operators under fire stress may over-trust a risk-quantified recommendation, or ignore it after a few false alarms. Outage planners may skill-fade and accept dynamic schedules without independently checking them. Mode confusion between advisory and directive use is also possible. (4) Drift and configuration management (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0602): plant modifications, degraded equipment, updated PRA or fire-hazard analysis, and a changed outage scope all invalidate the twin-to-plant mapping. If the twin is not under strict configuration control, the agent keeps recommending against a stale model. A fleet-wide reuse of one policy would propagate the same error across units. (5) Qualification and regulatory gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402, OP.C0304.03): there is no established pathway to qualify an adaptive RL policy as safety-related or even as a PRA-informed decision aid. Stochastic inference and retraining make the tool hard to verify. It can silently omit constraints such as Tech Spec limiting conditions, fire watch requirements or radiological limits. ADVERSARIAL THREATS.
