(6) Twin and data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0031): an adversary or insider who can alter training scenarios, twin parameters, PRA inputs or live plant-state feeds can steer the learned policy or its inputs so that it systematically favors unsafe sequencing. Because the damage sits in the learned weights, it persists and is hard to detect. (7) Model and supply-chain manipulation (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0076, OP.C0502): a backdoored or corrupted policy, or a compromised RL and GNN framework, can behave normally in validation and misbehave on a trigger, such as a specific fire location or outage state. (8) Evasion through falsified state (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0046): spoofed or degraded sensor, alarm or fire-detection inputs fed to the GNN can cause wrong emergency-response recommendations. Delayed or withheld advice during a fire can coincide with a physical or cyber attack (AML.T0029). (9) Attack surface and recon (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025, AML.T0036, OP.C0505): the twin and its data are a concentrated repository of plant-specific vulnerability information, including fire-risk importance, critical equipment and outage windows of low defense-in-depth. They are valuable for targeting sabotage, and a model-extraction or exfiltration route would expose them. Connecting the twin to live plant data also creates an IT/OT pathway that did not exist before (OP.C0601 if cloud-hosted). Mitigating factors are strong: human-in-the-loop authority, licensed procedures and independent safety-system actuation. Residual harm therefore depends mainly on advisory over-reliance and on any drift toward closed-loop use.

ai_engineer.argument: The exposure in this use case sits in the ML pipeline, not the plant. A GNN-based deep RL agent (PSPO) learns a policy entirely inside a digital twin. Its reward is dynamic risk (CDF) computed by a PRA model that is itself part of the simulator. The policy is therefore only as sound as the twin's dynamics and the risk model, and RL is known to exploit simulator errors, reward misspecification and unmodeled states. All evidence is simulation-only, with no field data and no validation against plant behavior. Two very different decision tasks share one framework: slow, combinatorial outage scheduling, and fast, rare-event fire response. Fire response has almost no real operational data, so the twin's fire physics and suppression/failure probabilities are largely assumed rather than measured. Once deployed as a decision aid, the policy will face states outside its training distribution: plant configurations, equipment degradation, graph topology changes and sensor faults. Its behavior there is opaque and unverifiable, and it is non-deterministic across training seeds and possibly at inference.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and reward-hacking failure: the agent optimizes CDF as computed by the twin's PRA, so it can learn policies that exploit model simplifications, such as stacking activities that the risk model scores as independent but that interact physically. The result is a schedule or fire action that looks low-risk in the model but is unsafe in the plant (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0301, OP.C0303). (2) OOD and drift: plant aging, modifications, changed configurations, updated PRA/procedures and novel fire locations or equipment states shift the dynamics and graph structure. A GNN trained on one topology generalizes poorly to another, and the policy degrades silently with no calibrated uncertainty signal (OP.C0302.01, .02, .03). (3) Rare-event data scarcity: fire-response behavior is learned from synthetic scenarios, so the tails that matter most are least validated (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.02). (4) Automation trust and opacity: a policy recommending emergency actions is hard to explain, and operators may over-trust it in time-pressured fires or under-trust it after one visible error. Outage planners may anchor on its schedules, and procedure skills can fade (OP.C0101.04, .05, .06, OP.C0401). (5) Qualification gap: no established V&V path exists for learned policies in safety-related decision support, and repeatability across seeds and retrains is weak (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Continuous retraining against a changing twin adds a qualification-mismatch problem.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Twin, data and model integrity: the digital twin ingests plant data and configuration, and its models, PRA parameters, training data or checkpoints can be tampered with. Poisoned twin state or risk parameters, or a backdoored or swapped policy, would bias schedules or fire actions while outputs still appear to optimize CDF (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0031, AML.T0076). Subtle manipulation of risk inputs would be hard to detect given the opacity. (7) Inference-time evasion: crafted or spoofed sensor/state inputs, such as falsified fire-detection or equipment-status signals, can push the GNN into wrong emergency actions or hide a hazard (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0046). (8) Reconnaissance and model extraction: published frameworks, the architecture and surrogate policies enable proxy models for crafting attacks (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0024.002). (9) Attack-timing exploitation of implicit weakness: an adversary can time an attack or sabotage to conditions outside the training distribution, such as unusual outage configurations, where the policy is unreliable. (10) Supply chain: ML frameworks, simulators and pretrained components in the training pipeline add dependencies (AML.T0010.001, OP.C0502). Consequences range from elevated real CDF during outages, through degraded fire response, to loss of confidence in the decision aid, and a shared policy across fleet units would propagate a single flaw (OP.C0602).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling lens this is a high-value trust-concentration target. A single learned policy, trained in a digital twin, would steer two safety-relevant decision streams: outage scheduling, which decides which systems are out of service and when, and fire response, which is time-compressed and gives operators little room to second-guess. Its value to an adversary is less about direct control and more about shaping human decisions. A subtly biased recommendation, which operators are likely to accept because it is presented as quantitatively risk-optimal (CDF-based), can create latent vulnerabilities or degrade protection at a time the adversary chooses. The evidence base is simulation only, so the fidelity gap between twin and plant is an implicit weakness that an adversary can exploit or time an attack around. The twin, its risk model (PRA inputs), and the training pipeline are also new insider-accessible assets that did not previously exist as an attack surface.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Poisoning or tampering with the digital twin, the PRA/dynamic-risk model, reward function, or training data (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0059). An insider or supply-chain actor with write access to the twin parameters, fault-tree or CDF inputs, or fire-propagation models can bias the learned policy without leaving an obvious anomaly. Consequences could include outage sequences that quietly stack vulnerabilities (e.g., redundant trains unavailable, protective barriers or fire watches deprioritized) in a configuration the adversary can exploit physically or cyber-wise, or fire-response advice that misdirects suppression or manpower. A backdoor-triggered policy (AML.T0043.004) could behave correctly in all validation scenarios yet deviate under a specific plant state the attacker can engineer. (2) Reconnaissance and exfiltration: the policy and twin encode detailed plant topology, system interdependencies, vital-area vulnerabilities and risk-importance rankings, which is a map of which failures matter most. This is sensitive security and safety information that could be collected via model/artifact theft or inference queries (AML.T0035, T0024.001/.002, T0025). The graph structure of the GNN essentially embeds the plant layout. (3) Input manipulation at operation time: the agent relies on plant state feeds and sensor or plant-configuration data. Falsified or spoofed inputs (AML.T0043, T0015, T0031) can push it out of distribution so it recommends unsafe actions, and fire-response inputs are attractive because an adversary can stage a real or sham event to exploit the recommendation. (4) Denial or degradation of the tool during an emergency (AML.T0029) to force reversion to procedures at a chaotic moment, or to erode the operators' trust so they ignore correct advice. (5) Social engineering and supply chain: third-party DRL frameworks, simulators and pretrained components (AML.T0010.001, T0011.000) provide initial-access paths into the OT-adjacent environment. IMPLICIT, exploitable by an adversary: (6) Sim-to-real gap and unproven generalization: validation is simulation only, with the twin acting as both training and test environment (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). Unmodeled fire behavior, equipment degradation or configuration differences yield confident but wrong policies, and failures are most probable in rare, novel states, which an adversary can deliberately create. (7) Automation trust and deskilling (OP.C0101.01, .04, .06, OP.C0102): optimized schedules and fire actions, framed as lowering CDF, invite over-trust, erode outage planners' and fire-brigade leaders' independent judgment, and leave operators out of the loop when an adversary times an attack around the tool's blind spots. (8) Opacity and reward misspecification (OP.C0401, OP.C0301): a GNN-based DRL policy optimizing a single CDF metric may trade off unmodeled concerns such as security posture, physical protection, worker dose, or defense-in-depth margins. Non-determinism across training runs (OP.C0402.01) and across policy updates complicates detecting a tampered model against a legitimately retrained one. (9) Governance gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504, OP.C0503): no established qualification path for learned policies in safety-related scheduling, weak change control over twin and model versions, and unclear who can modify the risk model. Also, training on the PRA couples the policy's correctness to a single assumed risk model (OP.C0603), so one corrupted input propagates to both use cases.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on twin/PRA poisoning, backdoored or swapped policy, input spoofing, sim-to-real reward hacking, rare-event scarcity, over-trust and qualification gaps. I dropped speculative codes (Deepfake, chaff data, phishing, cloud dependency, noisy recon techniques) that were not clearly instantiated by the documented simulation-only system..

evidence.citation: "A digital twin-based system for full-lifecycle safety management and dynamic risk assessment in nuclear power plants," Springer (journal article)
evidence.note: The paper proposes a digital-twin and deep-reinforcement-learning framework (PSPO) and tests it in a validated digital-twin environment on two scenarios: dynamic refueling outage scheduling and fire emergency response. It reports that the framework outperforms procedure-based policies and standard deep RL baselines on operational efficiency and safety. The results come from simulation only, not from a plant deployment.

evidence.citation: Skalse, Howe, Krasheninnikov, Krueger (2022), "Defining and Characterizing Reward Hacking," Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (NeurIPS 2022)
evidence.note: This paper gives a formal definition of reward hacking, where optimizing an imperfect proxy reward lowers performance on the true objective. It shows that unhackable proxy rewards are a very strong condition. This supports the concern that an agent rewarded on modelled core damage frequency can exploit PRA or twin simplifications.

evidence.citation: Kiourti et al. (2020), "TrojDRL: Evaluation of Backdoor Attacks on Deep Reinforcement Learning" (design automation conference paper; retrieved copy hosted on NSF PAR)
evidence.note: This work shows that a trojan can be implanted in a DRL policy network by poisoning a small fraction of inputs and manipulating rewards. The policy keeps performing well when the trigger is absent. This supports the backdoored or swapped policy and twin/reward poisoning mechanisms. The retrieved copy is an NSF PAR manuscript, and I could not confirm its peer-review status from the search result.

evidence.citation: (2025), "Beyond Training-time Poisoning: Component-level and Post-training Backdoors in Deep Reinforcement Learning," arXiv:2507.04883
evidence.note: This preprint describes DRL backdoors that exploit component-level flaws or need no training access. One of them is reported to survive full retraining and fine-tuning defenses. This supports the concern that a tampered model or compromised dependency can look like a legitimate retrain. It has not been peer reviewed.

evidence.citation: Zhang et al. (2020), "Robust deep reinforcement learning against adversarial perturbations on state observations," Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020)
evidence.note: This paper studies adversarial perturbations of state observations for DRL agents (PPO, DDPG, DQN). It shows the agents are vulnerable to strong white-box attacks and proposes a regularization defense. It supports the spoofed or degraded plant-state input mechanism.

evidence.citation: Huang, Papernot, Goodfellow, Duan, Abbeel (2017), "Adversarial Attacks on Neural Network Policies," arXiv:1702.02284
evidence.note: This early study finds that small perturbations to a policy's raw inputs significantly degrade trained RL policies. The effect held across tasks and training algorithms, in both white-box and black-box settings. It supports the falsified-input and out-of-distribution brittleness concerns. The retrieved copy is a ResearchGate page for the arXiv preprint, so it has not been confirmed as peer reviewed.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a backdoored or poisoned policy, or spoofed inputs, steering outage sequencing or fire response so that defense-in-depth or decay heat removal margins erode quietly. That is a serious safety-margin reduction and a potential contributor to core damage, but human authority and licensed procedures sit between the advice and any release, so it falls short of a direct radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real gaps, out-of-distribution brittleness and over-trust recur reliably once the policy is used in the plant. Backdoor and poisoning outcomes depend on the attacker achieving specific access and on the policy being used as advice, and non-determinism between retrains adds variability.

exploitability.why: The most credible adversarial threats (twin, PRA or reward poisoning, trojaned checkpoints, theft from the IT/OT-connected twin environment) need insider or supply-chain position and domain knowledge of the plant model. The implicit weaknesses are easier to exploit, but the adversary still has to time or engineer plant conditions.

affected_users.why: One policy steers both outage planning and emergency response, so a flaw or tampered model propagates across coupled plant systems. A fleet-shared policy or a single PRA dependency could carry it across units, although the advice is scoped to one plant function at a time.

discoverability.why: The PSPO digital-twin and deep-RL approach is published, and the failure classes (reward hacking, sim-to-real gap, poisoning, backdoors, over-trust) are well documented in the open literature. Finding where a specific plant's twin is weak, or where its integration points are, needs partial or insider knowledge.

use_case: Artificial-neural-network reconstruction of the assembly-wise radial power distribution of a PWR core (Angra 1) from self-powered neutron detector (SPND) readings, including when some detectors are inactive, for on-line core power monitoring
incurred_insecurity:
An ANN that reconstructs the assembly-wise radial power map from SPND readings, trained and validated only on SERPENT-simulated data, concentrates operator trust in one derived artifact used for margin-to-limit awareness. Its main threats are a silent simulation-to-plant gap, unflagged degradation with inactive detectors, manipulated detector inputs, tampering with the model or training pipeline, and information leakage. The tool is advisory and protection is independent, so harm is bounded unless the map is ever used for surveillance credit, limit checks or control.

Simulation-to-plant gap -- implicit, exploitable
Training only on idealized Monte Carlo SPND responses omits delayed response, rhodium burnup depletion, noise and calibration drift, so the network outputs plausible but biased maps, such as an underestimated local peak, with no alarm. An adversary could hide a real power tilt or a manipulation inside this unverifiable error band.

Drift and out-of-distribution core states -- implicit, exploitable
New loading patterns, cycle burnup, xenon transients, rod misalignment and asymmetric transients fall outside a static network's training envelope, where it interpolates and smooths over real local peaks. An adversary could time a physical or cyber action to such states, when model error is largest and operators rely on the map most.

Inactive-detector masking -- implicit, exploitable
The network returns a full map when detectors are lost, and clustered failures (a shared thimble or cable) degrade accuracy nonlinearly with no per-assembly uncertainty or indicator of the degraded state. An adversary could induce or force detectors inactive, or spoof an inactive flag, so that manipulation looks like benign dropout.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Smooth, continuous high-resolution maps encourage over-trust and complacency, displacing incore flux mapping, heat balance and raw SPND interpretation and eroding staff skill at reconciling anomalies. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust to keep a masked manipulation from being challenged.

Opacity and qualification gap -- implicit
The black-box network has no established nuclear-grade V&V route against deterministic core-monitoring codes, and per-cycle retraining gives non-identical weights that complicate model-change control and regulatory acceptance. An adversary gains little directly, beyond the weak review that makes tampering harder to detect (see tampering threat).

SPND input manipulation -- adversarial
An insider or compromised I&C or data-acquisition path can spoof, replay or bias a few SPND channels, or exploit dropout tolerance, so the network smooths inconsistent inputs into a coherent but wrong map. The result is a hidden hot spot or tilt, or a false one that triggers needless derates, with white-box optimization made easy by the small model.

Model and training-pipeline tampering -- adversarial
Poisoned simulation inputs, altered SERPENT cross-sections or core models, or backdoored weights can embed a bias or trigger active only in specific burnup or loading states, evading average-accuracy acceptance tests. Retraining each cycle offers recurring insertion points, and opacity lets the offset persist undetected.

Model and data exfiltration -- adversarial
Theft of weights, detector layout and core loading data exposes in-core instrumentation geometry and fuel management information. It also lets an attacker build a proxy model to rehearse input manipulations offline.

Availability degradation -- adversarial
Denying or degrading the monitor forces reliance on fallback methods and could be timed alongside other actions, though safety impact is low while protection remains independent.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations standpoint, the assembly-wise radial power map feeds on-line core monitoring, where it informs margin-to-limit tracking (FΔH, peaking factors, DNB margin), so a wrong map matters only if operators or core-monitoring logic act on it without independent cross-checks. Existing practice does guard against this: the protection system does not depend on it, and the incore flux map, excore detectors, and loop heat balance all give independent checks. The real exposure is slower. The ANN is trained on SERPENT-simulated SPND responses, not plant data, so it inherits simulation-to-plant gaps (detector sensitivity, rhodium burnup depletion, cycle and burnup state, xenon transients, control-rod configurations) that operators cannot easily see, especially when detectors are inactive and the network is extrapolating from sparser inputs. If it is ever used for surveillance credit or to relax conservatism, silent misreconstruction could hide a power tilt or a local peaking excursion, or alternatively trigger spurious power restrictions.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulation-to-plant gap: the network is trained and validated only on Monte Carlo SPND data. Real SPNDs show delayed response, rhodium/vanadium burnup sensitivity, background noise, and calibration drift, none of which is in the training set. The result is biased reconstructions that look plausible, which is a data-provenance and OOD failure. (2) Degradation with inactive detectors: accuracy falls as detectors are lost, and failures cluster in a region (a failed instrument thimble or a shared cable or connector), which is worse than the random dropout likely used in testing. Operators could keep trusting a map whose uncertainty has grown, especially if the tool gives no per-assembly uncertainty. (3) Unrepresentative core states: new fuel loading patterns, cycle-specific burnup, xenon oscillations, rod insertion, and asymmetric transients (dropped or misaligned rod, inlet temperature tilt) may fall outside the training envelope. Those are exactly the states where an accurate map matters, and an interpolating ANN can smooth over a real local peak. (4) Automation bias and skill fade: if the ANN map becomes the routine display, staff may defer to it over incore flux mapping or calculation and lose practice in reconciling detector anomalies. (5) Qualification gap: the network has no established nuclear-grade V&V route and is opaque, non-deterministic across retrains, and has a model-change control problem when retraining for each cycle. Any use for Technical Specification compliance would therefore face a regulatory readiness gap. Since the output is advisory, plausible harm is mainly loss of margin awareness and operational penalties, unless it is wired into setpoints or control. 

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Manipulated SPND inputs: an adversary with access to the plant network or signal path (spoofed, replayed, or biased SPND channels, or a forced 'inactive' flag) could steer the reconstruction to mask a real tilt or to induce a false alarm and power derating. This is more insidious than a conventional single-channel spoof because the network's smoothing can make inconsistent inputs look coherent, and a few channels can have disproportionate influence. (7) Model or training-pipeline tampering: poisoning training data or the weights (supply chain for the model, the simulation inputs, or the SERPENT cross-section libraries) could embed a bias or a trigger condition. Because the model has low explainability, this would be hard to detect by review, and it could persist across retrains. (8) Availability attacks: denying or degrading the monitoring tool is low consequence for safety because protection is independent, but it forces reliance on fallback methods and could be timed alongside other actions. Containment depends on keeping the ANN out of protection and control functions, on independent cross-checks against incore maps and heat balance, and on one-way data flow from instrumentation.

ai_engineer.argument: From the ML pipeline view, this system is an inverse-mapping regressor (SPND currents to assembly-wise power) trained entirely on SERPENT-simulated data, not on measured plant data. That makes its fragility mostly about data provenance and distribution coverage. The simulator defines the training manifold: nominal burnup states, control-rod configurations, xenon transients, and the detector-failure masks that were sampled. The real plant will differ through SPND sensitivity decay and burnup, delayed-response behavior, noise, cross-talk, calibration offsets, and core-model mismatch, and these produce a sim-to-real gap that nobody can fully test until deployment. Because the network outputs a smooth, plausible-looking power map whatever the input, inference outside the training envelope fails silently. Inactive-detector robustness is a further weak point. The network is only robust to missing-input patterns it saw in training, and it cannot distinguish a dead detector from a detector that reads wrongly.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and provenance gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203). Mechanism: training uses only Monte Carlo SPND responses, with idealized detector models. The facility depends on the reconstruction for on-line core power monitoring and margin awareness. Consequence: systematic bias or localized error in assembly power, such as hot-spot underestimation, that is uncorrelated with the reported confidence, which erodes safety margins without triggering alarms. (2) Drift and OOD (OP.C0302.01, .02, .03, OP.C0303). Mechanism: fuel cycle changes, new loading patterns, burnup-dependent SPND sensitivity loss, rod-insertion states, and xenon transients move the input distribution away from the training set, and a static network is not retrained or recalibrated. Consequence: slowly growing error that looks like a normal reading. Quantifying this needs an uncertainty estimate that the plain ANN does not provide. (3) Missing-detector generalization (OP.C0403, OP.C0302). Mechanism: the network has only seen certain failure masks, and failure combinations that are clustered or in high-importance regions degrade accuracy nonlinearly. Consequence: the monitoring system appears to be working just when it is most degraded, and more failed detectors will push it into untested territory. (4) Opacity and qualification (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01). Mechanism: a black-box network has no established qualification route or traceable verification, and retraining gives different weights from different seeds. Consequence: operators cannot verify individual outputs, and model changes are hard to re-qualify. (5) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). Mechanism: smooth, high-resolution maps encourage over-trust and lower the use of independent checks such as incore flux maps or the existing monitoring codes. Consequence: undetected errors propagate into operating decisions.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Sensor-input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031). Mechanism: the input is a low-dimensional vector of detector currents, and the network has no input-consistency check. An adversary with access to the instrumentation signal chain, or able to craft spoofed or masked detector values that mimic an 'inactive detector' pattern, could steer the reconstructed power map toward a chosen distribution. Consequence: falsified core power and hot-spot information, which could hide or exaggerate real conditions. The white-box optimization this needs is easy because the model is small. (7) Training-pipeline and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000). Mechanism: corrupted simulation inputs, altered SERPENT cross-section libraries or core models, or backdoored weights pass into the training data or model, and because the network is opaque a small systematic offset or trigger pattern is hard to detect. Consequence: a persistent bias or backdoor embedded in the monitoring function. (8) Model and data exfiltration (AML.T0035, AML.T0044). Mechanism: the weights, detector layout, and core loading data reveal in-core instrumentation geometry and power-distribution information. Consequence: reconnaissance value for an attacker, and proprietary-information loss. (9) Timing of attacks around known weaknesses. An adversary could exploit periods of several inactive detectors, end-of-cycle conditions, or transients, when model error is largest and operators rely on the reconstruction most.

security_specialist.argument: An ANN that turns SPND readings into assembly-wise power maps for on-line core monitoring concentrates trust in a single derived artifact: the reconstructed power map. Operators and core-protection staff use it to judge peaking factors and margin to thermal limits, so it becomes a high-value target. A sophisticated adversary would more likely go after the data path and model lifecycle (detector signals, training data, model updates) than the network itself. The model's capacity to "work even with inactive detectors" is also a structural weakness: it is built to tolerate missing or implausible inputs, so it may hide a detector loss or tampering that would otherwise trigger an alarm. The documented work is trained and validated only on SERPENT-simulated data, so any real deployment starts with a simulation-to-plant gap that an adversary could exploit, and that gap could also mask a malicious manipulation.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Input manipulation and evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041): an insider or a compromised I&C or data-acquisition path perturbs a subset of SPND channels, or exploits the dropout-tolerance logic, so the reconstruction returns a plausible but wrong radial power map. Hot-spot or tilt conditions could be hidden, or spurious ones created to trigger unnecessary derates or trips, which would be a cheap economic-sabotage route. The mechanism is that the network smooths over inconsistent inputs. The facility depends on the map for thermal-margin awareness and surveillance, and the consequences are eroded safety margin visibility or plant disruption. A bigger concern is timing: a physical or cyber action on the core, such as a rod or boron manoeuvre or a flux anomaly, could be paired with a masked monitor. (2) Supply-chain and model-integrity compromise (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0076): the training set comes from a Monte Carlo simulation pipeline, and the weights are opaque artifacts that few reviewers can audit. A poisoned or backdoored network, or quietly altered simulation inputs (cross-sections, core loading, detector response models), could mislead only in specific burnup or loading states. A trigger-conditioned backdoor (AML.T0043.004) is hard to detect with average-accuracy acceptance testing, and retraining for each fuel cycle creates recurring insertion opportunities. (3) Information leakage (AML.T0024.001, AML.T0025, AML.T0037): core loading patterns, detector layout, and the trained model reveal fuel management and sensitive design information. They could also help an adversary build a proxy model (AML.T0005) to rehearse manipulations offline. (4) Stepping-stone exposure: the monitor sits between plant I&C and engineering or analysis networks, so it can become a pivot point if data diodes or segmentation are weak. Its results could also be used to add credibility to falsified reports.

IMPLICIT, and exploitable or timeable by an adversary. (a) Automation trust and monitoring complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06): continuous, smooth maps encourage operators to rely on them, and staff skill in interpreting raw SPND and incore data may fade, which lowers vigilance against a timed attack. (b) Dropout masking (OP.C0603, OP.C0401): the ANN returns a full map even when detectors are inactive, and confidence degrades with no natural indicator, so an adversary can exploit or induce detector failures. (c) Simulation-only training (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0303): no real plant data, and drift from burnup, SPND depletion and sensitivity decay, and unmodeled anomalies (for example, rod misalignment or asymmetric loading) make out-of-distribution behavior unknown and unverifiable. Failures may be silent, so benign and malicious anomalies are hard to tell apart. (d) Qualification gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0402, OP.C0502): there is no established way to qualify an ANN against deterministic core-monitoring codes, and non-repeatability across retraining or software updates adds integrity risk. Model and data access governance may be treated as ordinary engineering data rather than security-relevant (OP.C0505.01). Overall, this is a moderate-value target for a nation-state. Direct harm is bounded if the monitor is advisory and the protection system is independent, but it becomes high-consequence if the reconstruction ever feeds limit checks or control, or if it erodes confidence in the independent instrumentation that backs it up.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulation-only training gap, drift/OOD, dropout masking, input spoofing, pipeline poisoning and automation trust. I dropped the speculative stepping-stone and leakage-via-inversion claims (AML.T0024.001, AML.T0025, AML.T0037, AML.T0041) and the weakly argued AML.T0059/AML.T0076 and OP.C0502/OP.C0505.01, keeping exfiltration via model/artifact access (AML.T0035, AML.T0044) and proxy-model staging (AML.T0005).

evidence.citation: "Continuous mapping of nuclear reactor core power using artificial neural network even in the presence of inactive detectors," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Elsevier / Korean Nuclear Society)
evidence.note: The paper builds and validates an ANN that maps SPND measurements to the radial power distribution of the fuel assemblies in a 1876 MWth PWR like Angra 1. The SPND data are simulated with the SERPENT Monte Carlo code, and the paper analyses how the method performs when detectors are unavailable. The work is a model tested on simulated data, not a plant deployment.

evidence.citation: (2025), "Power distribution reconstruction from in-core detector measurements using gaussian process regression," Annals of Nuclear Energy (ScienceDirect)
evidence.note: This is a close analog on the same Angra 1 core. It reconstructs assembly-wise power from in-core detectors, including a single-detector-loss case, using a model built in OpenMC rather than plant data. It also notes that BEACON is the core monitoring package actually used at Angra 1, which is the deterministic baseline.

evidence.citation: "A study on the sensitivity of self-powered neutron detector (SPND)," (ANN reconstruction of reactor states from fixed in-core SPNDs)
evidence.note: This is an earlier analog that uses ANNs to reconstruct reactor states from in-core SPND measurements. It also tests noise resistance, and it discusses rhodium depletion making the detector response non-uniform. I retrieved only the ResearchGate page, so the venue and year are not confirmed.

evidence.citation: "Numerical Simulation and Sensitivity Study of the Rhodium Self-Powered Neutron Detector Used in PWR" (ResearchGate listing; authors/venue not confirmed)
evidence.note: The page covers rhodium SPND modelling and related uncertainty in online core-power reconstruction (the EPR loss-of-representativeness uncertainty). It supports the point that detector physics and reconstruction error go beyond idealized simulated responses. I could only see a partial listing.

evidence.citation: (2018), "Deconvolution-based real-time neutron flux reconstruction for Self-Powered Neutron Detector," Annals of Nuclear Energy
evidence.note: Shows that delayed-response SPNDs such as rhodium do not directly track real-time flux and need compensation. An ANN trained on idealized SPND responses would leave out this delay. The paper does not test ANN-based power mapping.

evidence.citation: OECD NEA (1996), "Characteristics of Self-Powered Neutron Detectors Used in Power Reactors," summary of an IEC standard
evidence.note: Documents rhodium SPND limitations: delayed signal, a burn-up rate of about 0.39% per month, and a need for background compensation. This supports the claim that simulated SPND responses can diverge from plant behavior because of delay and depletion.

evidence.citation: Roy et al. (2026), "Adversarial Vulnerabilities in Neural Operator Digital Twins: Gradient-Free Attacks on Nuclear Thermal-Hydraulic Surrogates," arXiv:2603.22525 (not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: Shows that sparse-sensor field-reconstruction surrogates for nuclear systems can be pushed into large errors by corrupting a single sensor reading. The altered outputs still pass standard z-score anomaly checks. This supports the input-manipulation and silent-error mechanism, though the models are neural operators, not an SPND ANN.

evidence.citation: "Resilient Machine Learning: Advancement, Barriers, and Opportunities in the Nuclear Industry," ACM Computing Surveys (2024)
evidence.note: A survey of adversarial threats to ML in nuclear settings. It covers evasion, poisoning, exploratory attacks (model extraction and inversion) and white-box attacks, which map onto the input-manipulation, tampering and exfiltration threats in this entry.

evidence.citation: Li, Jiang, Li, Xia (2020), "Backdoor Learning: A Survey," arXiv:2007.08745 (not peer reviewed in this arXiv form)
evidence.note: Survey of backdoor and data-poisoning attacks on DNNs, including risks from third-party data and models. It supports the training-pipeline tampering and trigger-based backdoor mechanism, though it is not specific to nuclear work.

evidence.citation: Zhao et al. (2025), "Data Poisoning in Deep Learning: A Survey," arXiv:2503.22759 (not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: Survey describing how poisoned training data can degrade accuracy, introduce bias or implant backdoors that activate only under specific conditions and are hard to detect. This supports the conditional-trigger tampering mechanism in the entry.

evidence.citation: "Three-Dimensional Super-Resolution Reconstruction of Power Distribution in Reactor by Neural Network," Springer conference chapter (2025)
evidence.note: A neural-network power reconstruction study that reports unstable performance on out-of-distribution upscaling, especially in the radial direction. This supports the concern that power-map networks degrade outside their training envelope.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a hidden hot spot or tilt produced by SPND input manipulation or model tampering, which could erode margin-to-limit awareness; because the tool is advisory and protection is independent, harm stays at operational disruption or minor safety-margin erosion rather than a release.

reproducibility.why: The simulation-to-plant gap and drift-related bias occur reliably once the model is used outside its idealized training envelope, but deliberate manipulation or backdoor triggers depend on specific burnup, loading, or detector-state conditions.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (spoofing SPND channels, compromising the I&C or data-acquisition path, poisoning the training pipeline) require insider or privileged access to isolated plant systems, which makes them hard to exploit from outside.

affected_users.why: A biased core power map misleads monitoring of the whole core and the operators relying on it, but it stays advisory and is isolated from protection and control, so propagation to coupled systems is limited.

discoverability.why: The ANN-from-SPND approach and its simulation-only basis are openly published, and adversarial-ML weaknesses of this class are well documented, but finding exploitable weaknesses in a specific plant deployment requires inference from partial information about detector layout and plant integration.

use_case: Feedforward deep neural network and LSTM surrogate models trained on TRACE thermal-hydraulic simulations of a design-basis loss-of-coolant accident. They forecast the time series of core pressure, break mass flow rate, peak clad temperature and water level as a fast decision-support tool for accident progression.
incurred_insecurity:
A fast DNN/LSTM surrogate trained only on TRACE simulations of a design-basis LOCA is offered as decision support for accident progression. Its main insecurities are confident but unflagged extrapolation outside its training envelope, inherited simulation-only error validated only against TRACE, over-trust by operators and emergency staff, and an opacity and qualification gap. Adversaries can poison or backdoor the simulation-to-model pipeline, manipulate live inputs, extract the model, or deny the tool during an event. Independent safety-grade protection and EOPs bound the severity, so harm needs a human-factors failure or a manipulated model combined with failures of those barriers.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
Feedforward and LSTM regressors return smooth, plausible pressure, flow, PCT and level curves for breaks, ECCS states, sensor faults or beyond-design-basis sequences outside the sampled TRACE scenarios, with no uncertainty or OOD flag. Operators may read a false margin to the clad limit and mistime mitigation, and an adversary could act during exactly such an event, or craft inputs in the brittle regions, relying on the tool's confident wrongness.

Simulation-only provenance and inherited code error -- implicit, exploitable
The surrogate reproduces TRACE's modelling biases (nodalization, critical flow and reflood correlations), and its 92-99% held-out accuracy measures fidelity to the code, not to plant behavior. With no field data for comparison, a subtle adversarial bias is indistinguishable from ordinary simulation error, so the acceptance evidence gives it cover.

Automation over-trust and skill erosion -- implicit, exploitable
A fast, smooth, accurate-looking forecast in a rare, high-stress scenario invites anchoring on it over independent indications and EOP symptoms, and its speed makes cross-checking against TRACE unlikely. An adversary could time a manipulation or denial to periods of peak reliance, relying on the misplaced trust.

Qualification gap, opacity and lifecycle drift -- implicit, exploitable
Opaque, non-deterministic networks lack a conventional V&V path, and plant modifications, uprates, new fuel, TRACE version changes or retraining silently shift behaviour without defined retraining triggers or configuration control. A malicious modification or poisoned retrain is hard to tell from ordinary drift, so weak change control gives insiders cover.

Cascading and fleet propagation -- implicit
Per-variable LSTMs can yield physically inconsistent combinations, and forecast errors feed downstream tools such as dose projection or protective-action recommendations, or replicate across plants reusing the model. No realistic adversary gains much beyond amplifying the other threats.

Training-data, model and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Altered TRACE input decks, parameter-sweep scripts, datasets or weights, including backdoor triggers, can make PCT or level forecasts systematically optimistic or pessimistic in a narrow region while passing aggregate accuracy checks. The defect stays latent until a real event or emergency analysis, leading to underestimated severity or spurious escalation.

Inference-time input manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofed or perturbed plant data on the historian or data link, or physically implausible but in-range values, can steer the forecast toward false reassurance or false alarm, since nothing enforces physical-consistency checks. This can be paired with sabotage timed so the decision-support display looks benign.

Model extraction and reconnaissance -- adversarial
Published architecture and accuracy, plus theft or querying of weights and datasets, let an adversary build a proxy and learn plant-specific design and margin information. The proxy supports offline crafting of adversarial inputs, and cloud or remote hosting widens exposure.

Denial, degradation and host compromise -- adversarial
Taking down or corrupting the serving host or weights mid-event pushes operators onto slower methods and adds cognitive load. The hosting workstation, credentials and serving pipeline also give a foothold into operations-adjacent networks.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is a fast surrogate for a design-basis LOCA, trained entirely on TRACE output. It therefore inherits every TRACE modelling assumption (nodalization, correlations, break spectrum, boundary conditions) and adds interpolation error on top. The main downstream danger is an operator, technical support center or emergency-response staff treating a smooth, fast, 92-99% 'accurate' forecast as ground truth during a real transient. Real accidents involve instrument failures, partial ECCS availability, operator actions and beyond-design-basis conditions that the training envelope probably never covered. Existing practice offers strong barriers: the safety-grade protection system, EOPs and symptom-based procedures, and qualified licensing codes remain the basis for action, and a decision-support surrogate does not actuate anything. Harm therefore needs a human-factors failure (over-trust, or a wrong diagnosis or mitigation priority) or a manipulated input or model combined with failures of those independent barriers. The realistic consequences are degraded situational awareness, delayed or misdirected mitigation, and false reassurance or false alarm. An adversary gets the most leverage by targeting the surrogate's role in drills, training and emergency-planning analyses, where trust builds up.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Out-of-distribution and generalization failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03): the surrogate is trained on a bounded set of simulated LOCA scenarios. A real event with a different break size or location, degraded safety injection, a concurrent loss of offsite power, or sensor faults lies outside the training envelope. The network still returns a confident, smooth forecast of pressure, peak clad temperature (PCT) and level with no inherent uncertainty flag. Consequence: operators may read a false margin to the 1204 C / 2200 F clad limit, or miss an approaching core uncovery, and so mistime mitigation. (2) Simulated-data provenance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203): there is no field LOCA data, so the model reproduces TRACE's modelling errors and validates only against TRACE. Its reported accuracy is fidelity to a code, not to plant behavior. Plant modifications, fuel burnup changes or code updates cause concept drift (OP.C0302.02) and silently invalidate it. (3) Automation trust and human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102): a fast, plausible tool invites over-trust in a rare, high-stress scenario where operators are out of the loop. Consequence: anchoring on the forecast over independent indications or EOP symptoms. (4) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0402): DNN/LSTM opacity, training non-determinism and version changes do not fit conventional software QA or safety-analysis qualification. Its error bounds are not conservative in the licensing sense, since a forecast of PCT or water level can err on the non-conservative side. (5) Cascading propagation (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603): feeding the forecast into other tools, such as dose projection or protective-action recommendations, carries its errors forward. Fleet reuse of the same model across plants (OP.C0602) replicates the error.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data or simulation-input poisoning and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059): altered TRACE decks, input files or model weights could bias the PCT forecast, for example by under-predicting clad temperature for certain break sizes or adding a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004). The pipeline is offline and modest in size, so it is cheap to tamper with and hard to detect with standard V&V, and the defect stays latent until a real event or a high-consequence analysis. (7) Input manipulation at inference (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031): spoofed or perturbed plant data on the historian or data link, or adversarial sensor values, can push the forecast toward false reassurance or a spurious escalation. Consequence: misdirected operator actions or unnecessary emergency declarations. Plant data networks and isolation of safety systems from the support tool are the main defenses. (8) Denial or delay of the tool (AML.T0029): it is not safety-critical, so the main effect is lost situational awareness during an event and loss of trust. (9) Model and IP exfiltration and reconnaissance (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0044): theft of the weights and training set reveals plant-specific design and safety-margin information that helps targeting and crafts better adversarial inputs (AML.T0043.000). Cloud or remote hosting (OP.C0601) widens this exposure. Overall severity is bounded by the independent safety systems and procedures. The worst credible outcomes come from poisoned or unqualified outputs being trusted in emergency-response analysis, training or accident-management decisions.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a surrogate trained entirely on simulated data (OP.C0201.01/.02): TRACE runs of a design-basis LOCA sampled over a parameter grid (break size, location, ECCS availability, etc.). The model inherits every TRACE modelling error and learns only the interpolation manifold of the sampled scenario space. Reported 92-99% accuracy comes from held-out scenarios drawn from the same generator, so it says nothing about extrapolation to beyond-design-basis conditions, multiple failures, instrument faults or degraded ECCS states. In the accident regime the tool is meant for, inputs can easily fall outside the training envelope. Feedforward and LSTM regressors give no built-in out-of-distribution signal, and they produce smooth, plausible-looking trajectories with no epistemic uncertainty. The real exposure is therefore in the pipeline and in how users trust the output, more than in the facility around it. Autoregressive LSTM forecasts also compound error over long horizons, and the 'very large speed-up' invites use as a real-time decision aid, which pushes it beyond the validated scope.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) OOD and generalization failure (OP.C0302, C0302.03, C0403): a surrogate trained on a fixed set of TRACE scenarios silently extrapolates when the real accident differs in break spectrum, ECCS configuration, plant aging or sensor state. It outputs confident but wrong pressure, flow, PCT and level curves, and operators may read a wrong PCT margin as reassurance. (2) Simulation-only provenance and inherited model error (OP.C0201.01, C0201.02, C0203): there is no real LOCA data to validate against, so TRACE's own biases (for example in critical flow and reflood correlations) are baked in and are invisible to the surrogate's test metrics. (3) Qualification and verification gap (OP.C0303, C0501, C0401, C0402): static test-set error does not qualify a dynamic, safety-relevant time-series predictor. The DNN and LSTM are opaque and their training is non-deterministic, so retrained versions may differ. There is no established V&V path for safety-adjacent AI. (4) Lifecycle drift (OP.C0302.01/.02): plant modifications, power uprates, new fuel, or TRACE version and nodalization changes invalidate the training set, and no retraining trigger or configuration control is defined. (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, C0101.03, C0304.03): automation bias under accident stress, and ambiguity about whether the tool is advisory or procedural. Output that omits uncertainty, or forecasts only four variables, may mask other limiting phenomena. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data and pipeline poisoning or supply-chain compromise (AML.T0020, T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0043.004): the simulation datasets, input decks, pretrained weights and ML libraries are the trust anchors. Subtle manipulation of a few scenarios, or a backdoor keyed to particular input patterns, could bias PCT or level forecasts under specific conditions while passing aggregate accuracy checks. This is especially plausible because nobody can compare against real data. (7) Input manipulation at inference (AML.T0015, T0043): if the model is fed live plant signals, spoofed or drifted sensor values, or crafted inputs that are physically implausible but within the numeric range, can steer forecasts. Nothing enforces physical-consistency checks. (8) Model and IP exposure (AML.T0024.002, T0035, T0005): the surrogate can be extracted or cloned, exposing which design-basis behaviours and plant parameters it encodes, and letting an adversary build a proxy for offline crafting of adversarial inputs. (9) Integrity erosion and denial (AML.T0031, T0029, T0076): silent corruption of weights or normalization parameters, or loss of the serving host when the tool is needed, degrades decision support at exactly the moment it is relied on. Adversaries could time an action to coincide with an event, exploiting the implicit over-trust and lack of OOD detection described above.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial lens, this surrogate is an attractive stepping stone because it sits in the accident-response decision loop, where operators and emergency staff under extreme time pressure would rely on a fast, confident-looking forecast of pressure, break flow, peak clad temperature and water level. It is trained only on TRACE simulations of a design-basis LOCA, so it has no field data and only the physics code's assumptions to anchor it. That makes its failures hard for a human to spot in real time. An adversary does not need to cause an accident for this to matter. Corrupting or biasing the surrogate, or simply degrading trust in it, could shape how operators judge accident severity during a real or staged event. The surrogate also has a large speed advantage over TRACE, which makes cross-checking it during an event unlikely and so weakens the human safeguard that would catch errors. Even without an attacker, its non-adversarial weaknesses are exploitable: it could be timed around, or an attacker could exploit the fact that it is poorly calibrated outside its training envelope.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Training-data and model integrity. The training set is a bank of TRACE runs, so the simulation input decks, the parameter-sweep scripts, the stored datasets and the trained weights are all supply-chain artifacts. An insider or a compromised engineering contractor could subtly poison the simulations or modify the trained model (AML.T0010.002, T0020, T0018.000, T0076, T0059). The result would be a surrogate that is accurate on routine test cases but systematically optimistic about peak clad temperature or water level in a particular region of the parameter space, or under a trigger condition (T0043.004). Because reported accuracy of 92-99% on held-out scenarios is the only acceptance evidence, a targeted bias confined to a narrow region could go undetected. Consequence: operators underestimate accident severity and delay or soften mitigating actions, or overestimate it and take unwarranted ones. The second case is a way to cause costly disruption, spurious escalation or public alarm. (2) Input and data-feed manipulation. The surrogate consumes plant measurements or scenario parameters. Spoofed or perturbed inputs (T0043, T0015) could steer the forecast while the plant is actually in a safe state, or mask a real degradation. This could be combined with physical or cyber sabotage timed so that the decision-support display looks benign. (3) Concentration of trust and a stepping-stone role. Where the tool is integrated into emergency-response displays, its hosting workstation or server, credentials and model-serving pipeline become a pathway into operations-adjacent networks (T0012, T0055, T0112). Adversaries may prefer it because qualified safety-related I-and-C is much better defended. (4) Denial or degradation (T0029, T0031). Taking the tool down, or making it erratic, in the middle of an event pushes operators back onto slower methods and adds cognitive load at the worst moment. (5) Reconnaissance from open literature. The architecture, training methodology and accuracy are published (T0000, T0002, T0005), which lets an adversary build a proxy and craft inputs to which the surrogate is brittle. IMPLICIT, exploitable: (a) Extrapolation and out-of-distribution failure (OP.C0302, C0303). A surrogate trained on one design-basis LOCA family can give plausible, confident but wrong trajectories for beyond-design-basis sequences, multiple failures, different break sizes or locations, or degraded equipment. There is no built-in uncertainty signal, and a beyond-design-basis event is exactly when an adversary would act. (b) Simulated-data provenance (OP.C0201.01, C0201.02). It inherits every TRACE modelling error, and its errors look like TRACE's. Agreement with the simulator is mistaken for agreement with reality. (c) Automation trust and out-of-the-loop effects (OP.C0101.04, C0101.01, C0102). A fast, smooth, accurate-looking tool invites over-trust and erodes independent physics-based judgement and skill (C0101.06). Attackers could time an action to periods when this reliance is highest. (d) Opacity and qualification gaps (OP.C0401, C0501, C0504). Neural nets cannot be audited the way safety-grade codes are, so a compromised or drifting model is hard to distinguish from a merely inaccurate one. (e) Model configuration control and retraining (OP.C0502, C0302.01). Changes to the plant, the code version or retraining can silently change behaviour, and weak change control gives insiders cover for malicious modification. The tool's LSTM-per-variable design also allows inconsistency between the four forecast variables (OP.C0603), so an operator might see physically incoherent combinations without any alarm.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on OOD failure, simulation-only provenance, over-trust, the qualification gap, and poisoning, input manipulation, extraction and denial as adversarial threats. I dropped thinly supported items (reconnaissance via open literature codes, OP.C0504, mistake-type codes) and kept the stepping-stone host compromise as part of the denial/host paragraph.

evidence.citation: "Neural-based time series forecasting of loss of coolant accidents in nuclear power plants," Expert Systems with Applications (Elsevier), vol. 160, 113699 (2020)
evidence.note: The authors built deep-learning expert systems on data from many TRACE simulations of a LOCA. The systems predict four key plant responses over time for test scenarios that were not in training. A DNN that fits all outputs and an LSTM for each response were compared. An accompanying OSTI version reports accuracies of roughly 92–99% and a very large speed-up over the physics code..

evidence.citation: Radaideh et al. (2020), "Neural-based Time Series Forecasting of Loss of Coolant Accidents in Nuclear Power Plants," Expert Systems with Applications
evidence.note: Describes this exact system: feedforward DNN and per-output LSTM surrogates trained on TRACE LOCA simulations. They forecast core pressure, break flow, peak clad temperature and water level, with 92–99% accuracy on held-out cases and about 100,000x speedup. The authors propose it as a decision-support tool. The venue name comes from my own recollection, not from the retrieved page.

evidence.citation: OSTI accepted-manuscript version (2020), "Neural-based Time Series Forecasting of Loss of Coolant Accidents in Nuclear Power Plants," OSTI.gov
evidence.note: Full-text version of the same study. It gives the TRACE dataset dimensions and the split into training, validation and test cases, and it frames the DNN/LSTM models as a decision-support system. This supports the point that the training data come only from TRACE runs.

evidence.citation: Interpretable time series forecasting of NPP parameters in accident scenarios (2022), Nuclear Engineering and Design
evidence.note: A follow-on paper that builds on the LSTM LOCA forecasting of core pressure, break flow and peak clad temperature. It shows the approach is being extended by other researchers. Only the abstract and introduction were retrieved. The journal name comes from the ScienceDirect PII and my own recollection.

evidence.citation: Evaluating the reliability of machine-learning-based predictions used in nuclear power plant instrumentation and control systems (2024), Reliability Engineering & System Safety
evidence.note: Nuclear-specific source on the limits of ML surrogates and digital twins. It says operational data rarely match training data, that ML models falter at extrapolation, and that OOD detection is needed to decide when predictions can be trusted. It supports the out-of-distribution extrapolation and simulation-only provenance mechanisms. Journal name is from my recollection of the ScienceDirect PII.

evidence.citation: Out-of-Distribution Data: An Acquaintance of Adversarial Examples – A Survey (2025), ACM Computing Surveys
evidence.note: Peer-reviewed survey stating that deep models tend to give overconfident but wrong predictions on unfamiliar inputs. This is the general mechanism behind unflagged OOD extrapolation and brittle-region input crafting. The survey is about classification and not nuclear. Venue (ACM Computing Surveys) is from my recollection.

evidence.citation: Out-of-Distribution Detection in Computer Vision: A Comprehensive Survey and Research Challenges (2025), ACM
evidence.note: Survey noting that deterministic neural networks can extrapolate with overconfidence on far-OOD inputs, and that predictive uncertainty does not reliably rise outside the training data. It supports the lack of an OOD or uncertainty flag in the surrogate. It is general and not nuclear-specific.

evidence.citation: Cinà et al. (2023), "Wild Patterns Reloaded: A Survey of Machine Learning Security against Training Data Poisoning," ACM Computing Surveys
evidence.note: Peer-reviewed survey of training-data poisoning and trigger-based backdoor attacks. It includes outsourced or altered training sets that implant backdoors. This supports the poisoning threat to the TRACE-generated datasets, scripts and weights. It is not nuclear-specific.

evidence.citation: Li, Jiang, Li and Xia (2020), "Backdoor Learning: A Survey," arXiv:2007.08745 (not peer reviewed in this arXiv form)
evidence.note: Survey of backdoor attacks and defenses. It notes that backdoors are stealthier than classical poisoning and that checking accuracy on a local verification set detects classical poisoning more easily than backdoors. This matches the concern that a poisoned surrogate could pass aggregate accuracy checks.

evidence.citation: Verification strategy for artificial intelligence components in nuclear plant instrumentation and control systems (2023), Nuclear Engineering and Design
evidence.note: Nuclear-specific paper on the qualification gap. It reports regulator and engineer concerns about missing documentation, the lack of a widely accepted way to show dataset adequacy, and existing software guidance that does not fit AI components. It supports the opacity and V&V gap. Journal name is from my recollection of the ScienceDirect PII.

evidence.citation: Reliability verification methods for artificial intelligence components in instrumentation and control systems at nuclear power plants (2025), Nuclear Engineering and Technology
evidence.note: Nuclear-specific paper saying AI components are hard to verify because they are complex, lack formal specifications and behave non-deterministically. It proposes a qualitative and quantitative reliability framework. This supports the opacity and qualification-gap mechanism. Journal name is from my recollection of the ScienceDirect PII.

evidence.citation: Enhancing accident diagnosis in nuclear power plants through knowledge distillation: Bridging the gap between simulation and real-world scenarios (2024), Nuclear Engineering and Design
evidence.note: Nuclear accident-diagnosis paper that addresses the domain gap between simulation-trained models and real-plant deployment. It also lists transparency, uncertainty and adversarial-attack vulnerability as barriers to AI adoption in NPPs. It supports the simulation-only provenance and input-perturbation points. Journal name is from my recollection of the ScienceDirect PII.

evidence.citation: PSAM 17 / ASRAM 2024, "Assessing Cybersecurity Risks in AI-Based Nuclear Power Plant ..." (title truncated in retrieved result)
evidence.note: PSAM conference paper on cybersecurity of AI-based NPP operator-support systems. It includes a signal V&V and recovery module meant to catch faulty or untrained input signals to deep networks. This relates to the inference-time input manipulation and missing data-integrity check concerns. Only a short excerpt was retrieved, so the author list and full title are unconfirmed.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a poisoned or manipulated surrogate, or unflagged OOD extrapolation, producing false reassurance during a LOCA and mistimed mitigation; this could erode safety margin significantly, but independent safety-grade protection and EOPs bound it well short of a guaranteed release, so 4 rather than 5.

reproducibility.why: OOD extrapolation and over-trust reliably occur whenever an event falls outside the training envelope, but the harmful outcome requires a rare accident scenario or a deliberately timed manipulation combined with failures of the other barriers.

exploitability.why: Poisoning the pipeline, spoofing historian data, or compromising the serving host generally requires insider or privileged access to engineering or OT networks, while implicit OOD failure needs no attacker effort but cannot be directly exploited without access.

affected_users.why: Impact centers on control room and emergency staff using one decision-support tool for one plant, but errors can cascade into dose projection and protective-action tools and replicate across plants that reuse the model.

discoverability.why: The architecture, training basis, accuracy and decision-support framing are published in the open literature, and OOD brittleness, poisoning and extraction are well-documented classes for neural surrogates, so an outsider can readily infer the weaknesses even without plant-specific internals.

use_case: Convolutional neural network combined with an iterative reconstruction algorithm to produce cross-sectional images from fast-neutron (14.1 MeV) interrogation of dry storage casks. The images are used to locate missing fuel bundles inside the cask, so safeguards inspectors can verify cask contents without opening it.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places a safeguards conclusion, that no bundle is missing from a sealed dry storage cask, on a CNN-plus-iterative-reconstruction image whose only documented validation is Monte Carlo simulation with a stated detection floor (at least 75% of pins removed). The main risks are silent false assurance from sim-to-real and learned-prior failures, inspector over-trust of an opaque image, and adversaries who use the public detection limits or tamper with the model and data chain to conceal diversion or falsify the record.

Simulation-to-reality gap -- implicit, exploitable
Training and validation use idealised Monte Carlo geometry, source terms and detector response, so real casks (different designs, loading, burnup, scatter, generator and detector drift) fall out of distribution and the CNN fails silently with a missed or spurious missing-bundle finding. An adversary can rely on this unmeasured gap, since a diversion that looks unlike the simulated anomalies yields a clean image.

Learned-prior smoothing below the detection floor -- implicit, exploitable
A CNN prior biased toward a regular lattice can fill in or smooth away partial pin removal, displaced bundles or dummy assemblies, presenting an intact lattice the data do not support. The published 75% threshold is a roadmap for an operator to design a diversion that stays under it.

No real diversion ground truth -- implicit, exploitable
Real missing-bundle cases are essentially absent, so false-negative and false-positive rates rest on synthetic defects and cannot be calibrated in the field. An adversary gains from the resulting uncertainty, because performance claims cannot be challenged against realistic diversion patterns.

Automation over-trust and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Inspectors may treat an authoritative-looking tomogram as verification of a cask that cannot be reopened, while being unable to separate data-supported structure from prior-supplied structure. An adversary can time or design diversion around this reduced corroboration by gamma, neutron, seal and inventory checks.

Qualification, repeatability and drift gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Training non-determinism, retraining, software updates and ageing of the generator and detector can change detection behaviour, and no established safeguards acceptance regime covers ML-reconstructed imagery. Legitimate-looking result variation gives an adversary cover to hide a deliberate change to weights or parameters.

Concealment by physical evasion -- adversarial
An operator who knows the method can use partial removal, dummy or lower-enrichment substitutes, or absorber and moderator material to create projections that the learned reconstructor maps to a normal lattice. The consequence is false confirmation of contents and loss of continuity of knowledge.

Training-data and model poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with Monte Carlo inputs, cross-section and geometry libraries, pretrained weights or the retraining pipeline (vendor, inspectorate or operator insider) could implant a backdoor that reconstructs specific bundle positions or configurations as present. Opacity and the lack of field ground truth make this hard to detect.

Falsified reconstruction evidence -- adversarial
Altering weights, reconstruction parameters or post-processing after qualification, or substituting a fabricated or edited image at the reporting stage, can create a false safeguards record or a false accusation. This is an authentication and chain-of-custody problem, worse where the inspected party runs or supplies the reconstruction.

Open-literature reconnaissance and proxy probing -- adversarial
The architecture and performance limits are published, so an adversary can replicate a proxy model and probe its blind spots offline to design diversion below the detection floor without touching the inspectors' system.

nuclear_engineer.argument: The output here is a safeguards conclusion about cask content, which is continuity-of-knowledge material. It is not a control action, so the threat is a false assurance or false alarm that enters an inspector's verification record, not a plant transient. The documented system is a Monte Carlo simulation study with a stated detection floor (at least 75% of pins removed, scans under two hours). Anything below that threshold, such as partial pin diversion, substitution with dummy or lower-enrichment material, or a bundle shifted rather than removed, sits outside the demonstrated envelope, and a CNN-cleaned image could present that as a plausible intact lattice. The safeguards that would also have to fail are independent verification (gamma or passive neutron measurement, C/S seals, surveillance, declared-inventory reconciliation) and inspector judgment. Automation bias is the main risk to those, because a clean, authoritative-looking tomogram invites over-trust in a cask that cannot be reopened.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: training and validation are Monte Carlo-only, so real casks bring differences the simulation lacks. These include actual burnup and neutron-source distributions, basket and canister tolerances, moisture and corrosion, detector response, generator output drift, scatter and background, and geometry variety across cask designs. The CNN can fail silently and out-of-distribution. The mechanism is model failure; the consequence is a missed or falsely reported missing bundle. (2) Learned-prior hallucination: a CNN prior that expects a regular lattice can fill in or smooth away anomalies, so the image looks intact when the data do not support it. Partial removal below the 75% threshold, substitution with dummies of similar neutron attenuation, or rearrangement becomes the blind spot. Hidden diversion here would be a safeguards failure that may surface much later. (3) Low base-rate and scarcity: real missing-bundle events are essentially absent from the data, so false-negative and false-positive rates cannot be measured in the field. The performance claims depend on simulated defects that may not resemble real diversion. (4) Automation bias and opacity: inspectors may accept a CNN image as evidence without being able to explain it, and the approach is hard to qualify under safeguards authentication and reproducibility norms (for example, differing reconstructions on repeated scans, or retraining changing results). (5) False-positive burden: spurious missing-bundle findings can trigger disputes, unnecessary follow-up, or loss of confidence in the method, which hurts the regulator and the operator. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) A facility operator intent on concealment could exploit the known detection limits, or the model's blind spots, by choosing diversions or substitutions that stay below threshold. The published performance numbers give a roadmap. Because inspection cases are few, adversarial-example or attenuation-mimic substitution is plausible without any access to the model. (7) Tampering with the training or simulation dataset, model weights, reconstruction software, or the scan-to-image pipeline (supply chain, insider or vendor compromise) could bias the output toward always showing a full cask. This would be hard to detect without independent authentication of the software and data chain. (8) Tampering with or spoofing the neutron generator, detector data, or geometry metadata, or inserting a pre-rendered image, could create a false record. Data availability and integrity matter for the audit trail. (9) Sensitive cask design, inventory, and measurement data moving through cloud or vendor analytics raise confidentiality and model-extraction concerns, and could reveal inspection capabilities and limits. Existing practice partly guards against all of this: the image is meant to supplement, not replace, other safeguards measures, and any anomaly should trigger corroboration. The residual risk is that convenience and apparent authority erode that corroboration.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a CNN plus iterative-reconstruction pipeline whose documented evidence base is Monte Carlo simulation only. Its training data is therefore simulated (OP.C0201.01), and its real-world performance (the 75%-pins-removed, under-2-hour result) is untested against the things that dominate real casks: neutron generator output variation, detector gain and dead-time, scatter from the concrete overpack and canister internals, cask-to-cask variation in burnup, enrichment, basket geometry, and loading pattern, and actual spent-fuel source terms. The CNN acts as a learned prior or denoiser on an ill-posed, low-count inverse problem. It will tend to output a plausible, regular fuel-lattice image, which is the exact failure mode that matters for a verification tool, since the question is whether something is missing and the prior is biased towards 'nothing missing'. Verification depends on reconstruction fidelity, and the system cannot be judged from its output alone. A safeguards conclusion would rest on a model whose false-negative behaviour at partial diversion (under 75% pin removal) and out-of-distribution conditions is unmeasured and hard to explain.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT (no adversary needed). (1) Sim-to-real gap / OOD failure (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303): the network is trained and validated on Monte Carlo phantoms with idealised geometry, cross-section libraries, and noise. Real casks differ in design, loading, and hardware, and so the model can fail silently. The consequence is a hallucinated or smoothed reconstruction that shows a full lattice when a bundle is absent (missed diversion or false assurance), or shows an artefact hole when fuel is present (false alarm that wastes inspection resources and erodes trust). (2) Data scarcity and low base rate (OP.C0202, OP.C0701, OP.C0203): real examples with verified missing bundles essentially do not exist, so there is no field ground truth for calibrating detection thresholds, and the performance claim rests on synthetic positives. A fixed 75% pin-removal threshold implies a detection-floor blind spot for partial pin removal, which a knowledgeable adversary could exploit by staying under it. This is an implicit weakness that can be timed or designed around. (3) Learned-prior bias and content fidelity (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403, OP.C0401): hallucinated structure from the CNN and opacity about which features are data-supported versus prior-supplied make inspector interpretation and independent review hard. Combined with automation bias and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06), inspectors may accept a clean image as verification. (4) Repeatability and qualification gaps (OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504): training non-determinism, retraining on new data, and software updates change detection behaviour without a clear regime for re-qualifying it for safeguards or licensing evidence, and no established acceptance criteria exist for ML-reconstructed imagery. (5) Lifecycle drift (OP.C0302.01): generator target ageing, detector degradation, and fuel-type changes shift input statistics over the cask's long storage life.

ADVERSARIAL. (6) Training/data integrity (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004): because training data is simulation-derived, the Monte Carlo inputs, geometry libraries, cross-section data, and pretrained weights form a supply chain. Tampering could bias the network, for example with a backdoor or trigger pattern that reconstructs a missing bundle as present for a particular configuration. The attack is hard to detect given opacity and no field ground truth. (7) Inference-time evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041): an insider or host-state operator with physical access to the cask could alter the interrogation physics, for example by placing moderator or absorber material, changing loading, or shielding, in ways that create structured perturbations in the measured projections. A learned reconstructor may map those to a normal lattice image, so the attack hits the ML component's sensitivity rather than the physics. (8) Pipeline and model tampering or corruption (AML.T0076, AML.T0018, AML.T0031): modifying reconstruction parameters, weights, or post-processing after qualification, or substituting a reconstruction at the reporting stage, could falsify safeguards conclusions. This is a record-integrity and authentication problem for state-provided or shared tooling, and also an inspectorate independence problem if reconstruction is run or supplied by the inspected party (OP.C0505).
