(9) Model and data reconnaissance (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005): because the work is openly published, the architecture and performance limits are public. An adversary can build a proxy model and probe the detection floor offline to design diversion that stays below it.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this system concentrates safeguards trust in one image-derived conclusion, 'no bundle is missing', which substitutes for physically opening a cask. That makes it a high-value target for diversion and concealment. The source is a Monte Carlo study with no field deployment, so the CNN is trained and validated on simulated data. A real cask will differ from the simulations in geometry, loading pattern, burnup, and detector response. A deliberate adversary, such as an operator-state concealing diversion or a proliferator, need not hack anything. They only need to exploit the gap between the simulation and real conditions, or the stated detection floor (at least 75% of pins removed). Partial diversion below that threshold, or diversion from positions where the reconstruction is weakest, would yield a clean image and false assurance. The reconstruction is also opaque, so an inspector has little basis for doubting a plausible-looking image.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Concealment and evasion. A host facility that knows the method and its sensitivity limits can design diversion (partial pin removal, dummy or surrogate assemblies, shielding or neutron-absorbing or moderating substitutes) to stay below the detectability threshold or to look like intact fuel to a CNN trained on a narrow set of simulated anomalies. This is an evasion of the model's learned decision boundary (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003) and a material substitution problem (OP.C0702.01). The safeguards consequence is false confirmation of cask contents, continuity-of-knowledge loss, and a diversion going undetected. (2) Supply-chain and model-integrity compromise. The CNN weights, reconstruction software, simulated training sets and the neutron-generator/detector firmware are trusted artifacts. If poisoned or backdoored (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004), they could be made to ignore specific bundle positions or patterns. The insider pathway is whoever controls retraining, calibration or the data pipeline, whether at the vendor, the inspectorate or the operator. The facility-side dependency is that inspectors rely on the output to verify cask contents without opening it. (3) Authenticity of evidence. Reconstructed images are easy to fabricate or alter after the fact, and a manipulated image could also be used to falsely accuse a state or operator. This raises data-integrity and chain-of-custody needs that a purely physical inspection does not have (OP.C0703, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). (4) Oversight-blind attack timing: an adversary who knows inspectors will rely on the AI (low vigilance) can time a diversion to the period between scans. NON-ADVERSARIAL BUT EXPLOITABLE: (5) Simulation-to-reality gap and data scarcity. Training is on Monte Carlo data, with no real-cask labeled ground truth, because real missing-fuel cases are rare (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0701, OP.C0302.03). Cask type, loading, burnup and dose-field variation could produce silent false negatives, and an adversary can probe for them using a public paper and open-source simulation tools (AML.T0000, AML.T0005). (6) Automation trust and opacity. The 75%-pin-removal figure is a simulation result, but it may be treated as an operational guarantee. Inspectors may over-trust a clean image (OP.C0101.04), cannot easily audit CNN artifacts or hallucinated structure in the reconstruction (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0401), and face qualification gaps for an AI-based verification method (OP.C0501, OP.C0303). Non-repeatability between scans or retrained versions (OP.C0402) undermines the evidentiary standing of a result, which matters when a dispute is being adjudicated. (7) Secondary: data from scans (cask internals and loading maps) is sensitive and could be exfiltrated for targeting or for sensitivity-limit reconnaissance (OP.C0505, AML.T0025). A sophisticated adversary would more probably exploit the detection floor and the simulation gap than attack the software directly, since those are cheap and publicly documented.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, CNN-prior hallucination, the 75% detection floor, data scarcity, automation over-trust and opacity, plus backdoor poisoning and evasion; I merged their overlapping items into single threats. I dropped the false-positive burden, cloud and model-extraction, and scan-data exfiltration items as weakly argued or secondary, and included OP.C0703 and AML.T0076 only for the falsified-evidence threat.

evidence.citation: "Neutron Tomography of Spent Fuel Casks," Journal of Signal Processing Systems (Springer)
evidence.note: This is a Monte Carlo simulation study, not a field deployment. It pairs an iterative reconstruction with a CNN to image the fuel inside a dry storage canister. The authors report that a bundle with at least 75% of its pins removed can be located with a scan time under two hours, using a commercial neutron generator. An arXiv version of the same work exists (2110.08939), but the cited version is the peer-reviewed journal article.

evidence.citation: Liu et al. (2021), "Neutron Tomography of Spent Fuel Casks," arXiv:2110.08939 (preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: This is the source study for the use case. It is a Monte Carlo study that combines an iterative reconstruction with a CNN on 14.1 MeV interrogation of dry casks. It states a detection floor of at least 75% of pins removed and a scan time under two hours. Validation is simulation only.

evidence.citation: Special Issue preface (2022), "Preface to the Special Issue on Signal Processing, Data Acquisition and Front-end Systems for Radiation Detection and Measurements," Journal of Signal Processing Systems (OSTI accepted manuscript)
evidence.note: The journal's editorial summarises the peer-reviewed "Neutron tomography of spent fuel cask" article. That article uses an iterative linear inverse method plus a CNN to find missing pins for safeguards verification. It was validated only by modelling and simulation, which supports the feasibility-only status.

evidence.citation: Genzel, Macdonald & März (2022), "Solving Inverse Problems With Deep Neural Networks – Robustness Included?," IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence
evidence.note: This study examines the robustness of deep-learning reconstruction, including Radon-type tomography measurements. It reports that earlier work found small input distortions could cause severe artifacts. It also says reliability must be verified before safety-critical use. This supports the adversarial-perturbation and instability concerns, although the study itself found standard networks more robust than previously reported.

evidence.citation: Bhadra, Kelkar, Brooks & Anastasio (2020), "On hallucinations in tomographic image reconstruction," arXiv:2012.00646 (preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: Generic (non-nuclear) literature on learned tomographic reconstruction producing hallucinated structure. It matches the learned-prior smoothing and fill-in risk, where an image looks plausible but the data do not support it. I retrieved only a search snippet of the reference list, so this entry rests on the title and the topic.

evidence.citation: Interval Neural Networks as Instability Detectors for Image Reconstructions, arXiv:2003.13471 (preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: It documents that deep-learning reconstruction can be unstable under imperceptible adversarial noise and under out-of-distribution features not seen in training. This supports the sim-to-real and OOD silent-failure mechanism, and the paper proposes uncertainty quantification to detect such failures.

evidence.citation: Scientific Reports (2020), "Alternation of inverse problem approach and deep learning for lens-free microscopy image reconstruction"
evidence.note: It names hallucination, poor generalization to unseen data, and adversarial fragility as limits of CNN image reconstruction. It shows CNN-introduced errors on real data that the later reconstruction step did not fix. This is general imaging evidence, not nuclear-specific, for the failure mechanisms in this entry.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is concealment or falsification of cask contents (diversion hidden behind a false 'intact' image, or a falsified safeguards record), which is a loss of material control and safeguards falsification at the top of the damage scale.

reproducibility.why: The sim-to-real gap, lattice-prior smoothing and the published detection floor reliably yield missed below-threshold anomalies once a diversion is designed beneath the floor, though real-cask performance is unmeasured and outcomes depend on cask and scan conditions.

exploitability.why: Physical evasion and proxy-model probing need only open-literature knowledge and operator-level access to the material, but poisoning or weight tampering and record falsification need insider positions in the vendor, inspectorate or reporting chain, and real diversion from a sealed cask needs substantial resources.

affected_users.why: Impact is confined to the verification of individual casks and the associated safeguards conclusions, though a systematic blind spot or poisoned model would undermine continuity of knowledge across all casks inspected with the method and weaken the wider safeguards regime.

discoverability.why: The architecture, the 75% pin-removal detection floor, the scan time and the simulation-only validation are published in the open literature and preprints, and the general weaknesses of ML reconstruction (sim-to-real gap, prior smoothing) are well documented for this class of system.

use_case: Feedforward neural-network estimator of steam generator water mass inventory, used in closed-loop feedwater control in place of downcomer water-level control. It is meant to avoid shrink-and-swell effects and reduce reactor trips during start-up and low-power operation of a nuclear power plant.
incurred_insecurity:
A feedforward neural-network soft sensor that replaces downcomer level as the controlled variable in steam generator feedwater control gives the plant an inferred, unverifiable quantity driving a safety-significant loop. The documented evidence is simulation only, so the main implicit threats are simulator-to-plant gap and drift, sensor-fault propagation, qualification and opacity limits, and operator over-trust and skill fade. The main adversarial threats are model and training-data tampering and manipulation of the estimator's input signals, which could induce a trip or feedwater upset. Independent hardwired protection channels limit worst-case safety consequences, so the realistic harm is initiating events and loss of availability. That limit holds only while the estimator's inputs stay independent of the protection channels.

Simulator-to-plant gap and out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
The network is trained on thermal-hydraulic simulator labels that embed the code's void and density-closure biases, and it has no native uncertainty estimate. It can therefore return a confident wrong water mass in start-up and low-power regimes, where real data are scarcest and fouling, ageing and plant differences shift the inputs, producing overfill, dryout or a spurious trip. An adversary could time an attack for these windows, when estimator reliability and control margin are lowest, and hide a manipulation inside the expected error.

Sensor-fault propagation into control -- implicit, exploitable
The estimator fuses several transmitter signals, so a stuck, drifting or noisy input is silently mapped to a plausible inventory value and acted on by the feedwater valves. Shared sensors with protection channels would add common-cause exposure, and closed-loop gain interactions can cause instability that open-loop validation misses. An adversary who biases a few inputs within alarm bands could rely on this absence of an independent level cross-check to steer the estimate.

Opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A black-box regressor in a safety-relevant loop has no defined failure envelope, and static validation does not cover closed-loop dynamics, so it is hard to qualify under software and I&C regimes. Training non-determinism and unplanned retraining or fleet reuse without requalification weaken configuration control. This makes a tampered model hard to distinguish from drift, and an adversary could exploit weaker integrity controls on weights than on conventional control logic.

Operator over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A smooth estimate with no direct gauge invites over-trust, loss of familiarity with downcomer level behaviour, and mode errors when switching between estimator and level control. This delays recognition of a quiet bias or real inventory problem. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust so that a slow manipulation is read as a process upset.

Model, weights and training-data tampering -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor can poison simulator or retraining data or modify the small weights file so it passes acceptance tests but misestimates under a chosen operating state, such as low power. The consequence is a covert, hard-to-attribute bias in feedwater control causing a trip, a heat-sink margin loss or moisture carryover.

Input-signal manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofing or biasing transmitter data through the I&C network or maintenance equipment, or crafting plausible-range perturbations, pushes the inventory estimate away from truth while validity checks stay quiet. The result is an induced spurious trip or degraded feedwater control without touching protection systems.

Estimator denial and engineering-path access -- adversarial
Crashing, stalling or corrupting the estimator forces fallback to level control during the very transients it was meant to ease, raising trip likelihood and operator workload at a chosen time. Compromised engineering-workstation credentials on the deployment path give persistent access to the model.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This estimator would sit inside the feedwater control loop of a PWR steam generator and replace downcomer level as the controlled variable, mainly in start-up and low-power operation, where shrink-and-swell is worst and trips are most common. Steam generator level is a safety-significant parameter: low-low level trips the reactor and starts auxiliary feedwater, and high-high level trips the turbine. If the estimate is wrong, the feedwater valves are driven on a false picture of inventory. That risks overfill (moisture carryover to the turbine, water hammer) or dryout and loss of heat sink, or else a spurious trip, which defeats the purpose of the use case. The documented evidence is simulation only and the training data are model-generated, so the estimator has never been tested against real two-phase flow, fouling, sludge, or instrument degradation. The main protection is existing engineering practice: the protection system keeps using independent, hardwired narrow-range and wide-range level channels, so a bad estimate has to coincide with a protection failure or an operator ignoring it to cause real harm. The remaining risk is the control-to-protection boundary. If the estimate is used as the controlled variable and operators lose their familiar level indication, or the neural net's inputs share sensors with the protection channels, independence erodes.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Simulation-to-plant gap and out-of-distribution failure: the network is trained on simulated data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0203). The low-power and start-up regime is where it is most needed and where plant data are scarcest and flow regimes are least well characterized, so it may extrapolate badly there. Ageing, tube fouling, feedwater temperature or power-level differences between plants, and transients absent from training all produce drift or heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, .02, .03). The consequence is a biased inventory estimate and incorrect feedwater demand, producing a trip or overfill/dryout. This would show up first at the moments of greatest operational stress. (2) Qualification and opacity: a black-box estimator in a safety-relevant loop is hard to qualify under software and I&C standards (OP.C0401, OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). No failure envelope has been defined, and static test validation does not cover closed-loop dynamics. (3) Operator factors: operators may over-trust a smooth estimate that avoids swell, or lose a mental model of level behavior (OP.C0101.01, .04, .06). A silent estimator fault, or a mode error when switching between estimator and level control, can delay recognition of a real inventory problem. (4) Fault propagation: input sensor faults such as drifting differential pressure, temperature, or flow transmitters pass directly into the estimate and the control action (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01), and common-cause sensor faults could defeat both control and diversity if the inputs are shared. (5) Fleet and model-update propagation: one trained model reused across units, or retrained without re-qualification, spreads a latent error (OP.C0602, OP.C0502).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. Because the model is a small feedforward net running on I&C hardware, the likely attack surfaces are the supply chain and the data path, not prompts or APIs. (a) Poisoned or tampered training data or simulation models, or a tampered model or weights file in the update or deployment chain (AML.T0010.002, T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0076). The result is a subtle bias or backdoor that behaves normally in testing but misestimates under a specific input pattern or operating state (T0043.004). (b) Manipulation of the input signals (spoofed or falsified transmitter data, or evasion-style perturbations staying inside plausible ranges) so the estimate departs from true inventory while sensor-validity checks stay quiet (AML.T0015, T0043). A cyber-physical attacker could use this to induce a spurious trip, or to degrade feedwater control in a way that stresses the plant. (c) Denial or corruption of the estimator (T0029, T0031), forcing fallback to level control during the transients the estimator was built to handle, which makes trips more likely. The physical consequence depends on the independent protection channels, which should stop an overfill or dryout, so the plausible worst cases are initiating events, operational disruption, and loss of confidence. Adversaries could also time an attack around start-up or low-power windows, when the control margin is smallest and the estimator's training coverage is weakest.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a soft-sensor in a closed control loop: a feedforward NN maps measurable signals (differential pressures, temperatures, flows, level taps, power) to an unmeasurable quantity, steam generator water mass, and that estimate replaces downcomer level as the controlled variable. The documented evidence is simulation-only, so the training set is almost certainly generated by a thermal-hydraulic code or plant simulator. The estimator is then only as valid as the simulator's two-phase flow and density closures, which are the very quantities the authors say are too hard to obtain analytically. The system is most exposed in start-up and low-power transients, where void fraction, flow regime and sensor behaviour are least well characterized, data is sparsest, and the network is most likely to extrapolate. Because the output has no direct ground-truth sensor in operation, errors are hard to detect, and the controller acts on them with full authority.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulator-to-plant gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0203): the training labels (true water mass) exist only in simulation, never in a real SG. Any bias in the code's void and density models is baked into the estimator and cannot be checked against a measured label. A real plant has fouling, tube plugging, aging instruments, and geometry and calibration differences that the training data lacks. (2) OOD and drift (OP.C0302, .01, .03): start-up and low-power are the regimes of most interest, and they are also the least populated and most nonlinear. A feedforward net has no native uncertainty estimate, so extrapolation yields a confident wrong mass. Plant aging, power uprates, feedwater-train changes and sensor drift shift the input distribution, and the model needs retraining and requalification, which is rarely planned (OP.C0303, OP.C0501). (3) Sensor-fault propagation (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01): the network fuses many inputs, and a single degraded transmitter (stuck, drifting, noisy) is silently mapped to a plausible mass. The control loop can then drive feedwater to over- or under-fill, which risks a trip, steam carryover/moisture to the turbine, or loss of heat sink margin. A closed-loop interaction with the network's gain can also produce instability that open-loop validation misses. (4) Opacity and qualification (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0504): a safety-relevant controller built on a black-box regressor is hard to verify, bound, or fit into software qualification and I&C classification regimes. Training-time non-determinism complicates configuration control and repeatability. Operators lose the intuitive downcomer level cue, so mode confusion and skill fade follow (OP.C0101.01, .03, .06), and fallback to level control during estimator failure has to be rehearsed. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Integrity of the estimator as a manipulation surface (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031): an adversary who can bias or spoof a few input channels, whether by compromising I&C data paths, calibration or maintenance, can steer the estimate far more than a simple level loop would allow, because the network's sensitivity is not intuitively bounded. This could cause a trip or an unsafe feedwater state that looks like a process upset. (6) Model and supply-chain tampering (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0020, AML.T0076): the weights, the training data or simulator outputs, the retraining toolchain or the vendor update path could be poisoned or backdoored. Triggers could be tied to particular input regimes, such as start-up conditions, so the compromise lies dormant through normal testing. A fixed weights file is a small, easily modified artifact that is hard to inspect for malicious change. (7) Recon and surrogate building (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0044): the published architecture and approach enable proxy models for crafting inputs or timing attacks, particularly if the plant-specific data or model leaks. An attacker can time actions to low-power transitions, where model reliability is weakest and where operators are most reliant on the estimator.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this estimator is a trusted virtual sensor placed inside a closed-loop control path that governs feedwater to the steam generators. It substitutes for downcomer level, a directly measured and well-understood parameter, with an inferred quantity that operators cannot check against any single instrument. That makes it a high-leverage and quiet target: a small bias in the estimate produces a real inventory error while the control loop sees nothing wrong. An adversary would probably prefer to corrupt the model's inputs or the model artifact over attacking the plant directly, and would look to time any action for start-up or low-power transients. Those are the regimes where the estimator is meant to help, and also where training data is thinnest and operators are least able to tell a drifting estimate from a real transient. The documented evidence is simulation only, so the as-deployed system could carry qualification gaps that an adversary or an ordinary fault could exploit.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or weight tampering by an insider or supply-chain actor: a feedforward network is small and opaque, so a modified weight set or retrained model can pass functional acceptance tests while carrying a bias or a trigger condition that appears only in a chosen operating region, such as low power or a particular temperature and flow combination (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0043.004). The facility function that depends on it is feedwater control, so the consequence is a real over- or under-fill, leading to a trip, a loss of heat sink margin, or moisture carryover and turbine damage, and it could be timed to coincide with another degradation. (2) Input-sensor manipulation: the estimator fuses several signals such as pressures, flows and temperatures. Spoofing or biasing a few of them through the I&C network or maintenance equipment can push the estimate off while each input stays within its alarm band, since there is no redundant level measurement to expose the discrepancy (AML.T0043, AML.T0031). That would be a stepping stone for an attacker who wants a trip or a reliability event without touching protection systems directly. (3) Training and calibration data poisoning during retraining or recalibration, especially if plant data or simulator data are used to tune the model after outages (AML.T0020, AML.T0059). (4) Credential and engineering-workstation access: model deployment tools bridge the engineering network and the control network, creating a new pathway for persistence (AML.T0012, AML.T0055). (5) A denial-of-estimate event, such as crashing or stalling the estimator, forces a fallback to manual or level control during the very transient it was meant to ease, so an adversary can induce operator workload at a chosen time (AML.T0029). IMPLICIT. (6) Qualification gap and simulation-only evidence: the model was validated on simulated data, with possible distribution shift when it meets real flow regimes, fouling, aging and sensor drift, which is exactly the flow-regime information the authors say is hard to obtain (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). Operators and a would-be attacker alike can exploit this unreliability, because it makes real anomalies look like model noise or the reverse. (7) Automation trust and skill fade: a mass-inventory estimate has no direct gauge, so operators may over-trust it, lose familiarity with manual level control, and be slow to catch a quiet bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102). (8) Opacity and the repeatability of retraining make it hard to detect a modified model or to tell tampering from drift (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502). (9) Regulatory-scope drift: a control-path ML component may not fall within existing cyber and software configuration-management regimes for digital I&C, so integrity controls on weights are weaker than for conventional control logic (OP.C0503, OP.C0504). Overall, a nation-state adversary would find direct attacks on this one component less attractive than using it as a covert, hard-to-attribute lever on plant availability, with its safety significance limited by the independence of the protection systems.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on simulation-only evidence and drift, sensor-fault propagation, qualification and opacity, operator trust, weight and data tampering, and input manipulation. I dropped speculative or weakly grounded items (open-literature recon and proxy building, credential theft via T0055, T0059, T0102-style items, and OP.C0102 and OP.C0403 as restatements of other threats), and merged denial and credential access into one adversarial paragraph.

evidence.citation: "Steam Generator control in Nuclear Power Plants by water mass inventory," Nuclear Engineering and Design (Elsevier), vol. 238, no. 4, 2008; record hosted by OSTI/ETDEWEB
evidence.note: The paper proposes controlling steam generator water mass directly, because flow-regime and density information is too hard to get for an analytical estimator. It builds a feedforward neural-network mass estimator for this and reports that theoretical analysis and simulation results show improved operation and safety. The evidence is simulation-based, not a plant deployment. I read the abstract record on OSTI, not the full text.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is tampering or input manipulation that induces a spurious trip, feedwater upset, overfill or dryout, and heat-sink margin loss. Independent hardwired protection channels limit the harm to initiating events and loss of availability, so this is operational disruption with minor safety-margin erosion, not a radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Simulator-to-plant gap, sensor-fault propagation and out-of-distribution errors recur reliably once the plant enters start-up or low-power regimes or an input degrades. Adversarial manipulation depends on access and timing, so the entry as a whole is moderately conditional.

exploitability.why: The credible adversarial paths (insider or supply-chain tampering with weights or data, I&C network spoofing, engineering-workstation compromise) all need privileged or OT-network access, and nothing here is achievable through routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: The estimator drives feedwater control of the steam generator and can cause a plant trip, and fleet reuse without requalification could spread a flaw across units. Independent protection channels and the single-loop scope keep the impact short of facility-wide propagation across coupled systems.

discoverability.why: Soft-sensor drift, sensor-fault propagation and adversarial ML against regressors are well documented in the open literature. The specific deployment, its input set and its training data would have to be inferred from partial information, and the source is a published simulation-only paper.

use_case: Temporal Convolutional Network plus Fourier Neural Operator surrogate for the TRANSURANUS fuel performance code. It maps rod power histories to predicted fuel-rod behaviour, such as centerline temperature and rod internal pressure. It evaluates thousands of fuel rods in milliseconds, so it can support time-critical fuel-behaviour assessment in operating reactors.
incurred_insecurity:
A TCN+FNO surrogate trained on TRANSURANUS output would feed fast fuel-behaviour predictions (centerline temperature, rod internal pressure) into margin-to-limit assessments. Its main exposures are silent out-of-distribution and tail-error failure, inherited simulation bias, a qualification gap with creeping over-trust, and adversarial corruption of the model, its training data or its input power histories. Because the output is a smooth plausible number that is rarely cross-checked, natural error and deliberate manipulation are hard to tell apart, and both erode fuel margin without an alarm.

Out-of-distribution tail error -- implicit, exploitable
The surrogate is trained only on realistic power histories and has no OOD detector or calibrated uncertainty, so ramps, load-follow, high burnup or new fuel and cladding can yield confident, non-conservative under-prediction of temperature or pressure that a few-percent mean error conceals. An adversary could push operations toward those regimes, or hide a targeted bias inside the accepted error band.

Simulation-only provenance and version coupling -- implicit
Labels are TRANSURANUS outputs, not post-irradiation or in-reactor measurements, so errors in fission gas release or gap conductance correlations propagate into the surrogate and appear validated, and the surrogate goes stale when the code is updated. An adversary gains little directly, beyond weak configuration control making tampering harder to notice.

Opacity, qualification gap and over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
An opaque, non-deterministic network has no established licensing path, uncharacterised seed and retraining variability, and static validation that does not match dynamic use. Millisecond answers invite operators to stop running the reference code and let the surrogate drift from screening tool to decision basis. An adversary could rely on that lapsed cross-checking and time manipulation to a ramp, and there is no baseline against which to detect an insider change.

Correlated fleet-wide propagation -- implicit, exploitable
One model bias, or one corrupted upstream feed, affects all thousands of rods and any plants sharing the model at once, while aggregate agreement hides individual outlier rods. An adversary needs only a single upstream or model compromise to reach every rod assessment.

Model, training-data and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with TRANSURANUS-generated training sets, pretrained artifacts, weights or ML dependencies can embed a systematic or triggered under-prediction for specific burnup or power-history signatures while passing average-error validation. The result is eroded fuel-integrity margin, an unanalysed condition, or an unplanned derate.

Power-history input manipulation -- adversarial
Falsified or perturbed power histories from core monitoring or the data historian, exploiting the FNO's sensitivity to frequency content, can steer predictions non-conservatively without touching the model. Output tampering between the surrogate and the consuming assessment tools can similarly mask an approaching limit or force spurious conservative actions.

Model extraction and IP theft, stepping stone -- adversarial
Querying or exfiltrating the model, training data and fuel-vendor power-history data exposes proprietary design information, and the host at the OT/IT boundary gives a foothold toward core-design and vendor networks. Denial of the surrogate mainly removes rapid assessment, a modest safety effect if the qualified code remains the fallback.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations and fuel-performance perspective, this surrogate sits in the core-monitoring and fuel-assessment chain. It would feed predicted centerline temperature and rod internal pressure into margin-to-limit evaluations, which cover fuel melting, cladding stress and rod-internal-pressure criteria. Real harm needs more than a bad prediction: the surrogate would have to be trusted instead of the qualified TRANSURANUS or licensing-basis code, and conservative margins, on-line monitoring, and technical-specification limits would have to fail to catch the error. The main risk is that millisecond speed invites use in screening, operating-envelope or power-maneuver decisions, where a few-percent mean error hides large tail errors in the very high-burnup, power-ramp and transient regimes that set the limiting rods. Surrogate outputs are also easy to alter or replace without anyone noticing, because a plausible smooth number needs no corroboration. Existing engineering practice (qualified codes, conservative uncertainty margins, independent verification) mitigates this only if the surrogate stays advisory and is bounded by an applicability domain.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution failure: the surrogate is trained on TRANSURANUS output for realistic power histories, so it inherits the code's own model error and adds its own. Mean test error does not bound worst-case error. Novel histories such as load-following, extended power ramps, power-uprate, new cladding or fuel types, higher burnup, or accident-tolerant fuel could produce silently wrong centerline temperature or pressure, and nothing flags that the input left the training envelope. Non-conservative under-prediction near limits is the dangerous direction: operators believe margin exists when it does not. (2) Surrogate-of-a-simulation provenance: there is no direct field truth, only simulated data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02). Errors in TRANSURANUS correlations, such as fission gas release and gap conductance, propagate into the surrogate and look validated. (3) Qualification gap: a TCN+FNO network has limited explainability and no established regulatory path (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0504). It risks creeping from a screening tool into a decision basis, and automation trust and over-trust effects (OP.C0101.04) arise once operators and fuel engineers see fast, plausible agreement. Retraining or version changes can alter outputs without re-qualification (OP.C0402, OP.C0303). (4) Fleet or cross-site reuse of one model across different plants, fuel designs or cycles propagates the same bias widely (OP.C0602, OP.C0302.03). Batch evaluation of thousands of rods can also hide individual outlier rods behind aggregate agreement.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Integrity attacks on the model or its supply chain, such as poisoned training data or surrogate weights, a backdoor trigger, or tampering in the pipeline (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0076). These could make the surrogate under-predict temperature or pressure for specific power-history signatures while behaving normally on validation sets. (2) Input manipulation: falsified or perturbed power histories from core simulators or plant computers would shift predictions with no model attack at all (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). (3) Output manipulation between the surrogate and the consuming assessment tools, which would mask an approaching limit or trigger spurious conservative actions that cost availability. (4) Model extraction or proprietary-data theft, which exposes fuel-vendor design and operating data (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025, AML.T0048.004). (5) Denial of the surrogate (AML.T0029), whose consequence is mainly loss of rapid assessment capability, a modest safety effect if the qualified code remains the fallback. Consequences are most serious if an adversary also degrades independent checks, for example the reference code run or in-core monitoring. Physical harm then needs several defeated layers, so the realistic outcomes are eroded fuel margin, undetected degradation, unplanned derates or outages, and loss of licensing confidence.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a regression surrogate trained on outputs of another model (TRANSURANUS), not on measured reactor data. Its ceiling is therefore the fidelity of the physics code, its input deck and its calibration, and it inherits every TRANSURANUS blind spot. A TCN+FNO pair is interpolative: the FNO learns resolution-invariant operators in the frequency domain, and the TCN learns temporal receptive fields. Neither has a mechanism to flag when a power history falls outside the training manifold (rapid ramps, power transients, high burnup, novel cladding or fuel types, new core loading patterns). The reported 'few percent mean test error' is an average over in-distribution, realistic histories. It says little about tail error on exactly the cases that matter for fuel-limit assessment (PCI margin, centerline melt margin, rod internal pressure limits), and the surrogate offers no calibrated uncertainty. The 'thousands of rods in milliseconds' speed encourages integration into real-time or near-real-time loops where there is no time for a human to cross-check against the reference code, so the surrogate's errors can pass straight into operating-limit decisions.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution and drift failure: the surrogate is trained on a bounded set of simulated power histories. Plant operation introduces new fuel designs, extended burnup, load-follow or flexible-operation patterns, and changed core design. Inputs outside that envelope can produce confident but wrong centerline temperature or rod pressure predictions, usually non-conservative in the tails, with no built-in OOD detector. Mean error hides this. (2) Data provenance: the labels are simulation outputs. Any bias, missing physics or stale material-property correlations in TRANSURANUS propagate into the surrogate, and the surrogate adds approximation error on top. The two errors can compound, and in-distribution test error is measured only against the code, not against post-irradiation examination or in-reactor measurements. If the physics code is updated or recalibrated, the surrogate is silently stale, which is a lifecycle and version-coupling problem. (3) Qualification mismatch: a non-deterministic, opaque neural surrogate is hard to fit into licensing and QA frameworks built for validated deterministic codes. Error bounds, training-seed variability, and retraining reproducibility are poorly characterised. (4) Human factors: millisecond answers invite over-trust, and operators may lose the habit of running or checking the reference code. A fleet-wide surrogate produces correlated errors across all rods at once, since a single model bias affects every rod evaluation.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Supply-chain and training-pipeline compromise: tampering with the training dataset, the TRANSURANUS-generated labels, the model weights or the checkpoints, or with the Python and ML framework dependencies, could introduce a systematic non-conservative bias or a triggered backdoor keyed to particular power-history signatures. Outputs would look plausible and pass average-error checks. (b) Input manipulation: the surrogate takes power histories from plant instrumentation and core-monitoring systems, so falsified or perturbed histories could steer predictions toward non-conservative values and mask margin erosion. Crafted adversarial perturbations to smooth time series are plausible because the FNO is sensitive to frequency content. (c) Integrity of the pipeline: if retraining or fine-tuning uses data from operational feeds, poisoning is possible. (d) Model-file and weight integrity matter more than confidentiality here, since the main risk is silent corruption (AML.T0018, AML.T0076) rather than theft.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this surrogate is a poor first-choice target for a nation-state, because it is an advisory analytical tool and not a control or protection path. It does, however, create a new trust-concentration point. Operators who get milliseconds-scale answers for thousands of rods will stop running the slow reference TRANSURANUS calculations, and the surrogate's few-percent mean error then becomes the de facto basis for margin decisions (centerline temperature versus melting limits, rod internal pressure versus cladding-lift-off limits). An insider or supply-chain adversary who can quietly bias outputs, or who just waits for a natural out-of-distribution case, can erode fuel-integrity margins with no alarm, because nothing independent is checking the result. The model is also an attractive stepping stone: the training pipeline, the power-history data and the deployment environment carry integrity and proprietary-data risks, and an adversary could use them to reach better-connected core-design and fuel-vendor networks.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or training-data integrity compromise. A malicious insider, a compromised vendor or research repository, or a tampered pretrained artifact could poison the TCN-FNO weights or the TRANSURANUS-generated training set (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002). The result would be a systematic, subtle underprediction of centerline temperature or rod internal pressure in specific burnup or power-ramp regimes. The facility depends on the surrogate for fast screening of fuel-performance limits, so the consequence is eroded fuel-integrity margins, with possible cladding failure, an unplanned shutdown, or an unanalysed condition. A few-percent average error gives a poisoned model natural cover, since a targeted bias hides inside the accepted error band. (2) Input manipulation. Tampering with the power-history feeds (from core monitoring or the data historian) would produce falsified fuel-behaviour predictions without touching the model (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Because thousands of rods are evaluated at once, one corrupted upstream feed propagates fleet-wide (OP.C0603). (3) Surrogate as stepping stone and IP target. Model extraction or inference of proprietary fuel-vendor TRANSURANUS data, plus access to the OT/IT boundary where the surrogate is hosted, gives a lateral-movement foothold and exposes fuel design information (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0048.004). (4) Timing. An adversary who knows operators have stopped cross-checking could time an attack to a power ramp or an unusual operating regime. IMPLICIT, and exploitable by an adversary. (5) Out-of-distribution blindness. The training set covers 'realistic' power histories only, so novel burnup, load-follow, or off-normal transients fall outside it (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202). The surrogate returns confident numbers with no uncertainty flag, and an adversary only has to push operations toward the edges where it fails. (6) Automation trust failure. Out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity and skill fade follow once the fast surrogate replaces slow code runs and analyst judgement (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). (7) Opacity and qualification gaps. The surrogate is hard to explain, is not qualified like a licensed fuel performance code, and its static validation does not match dynamic use (OP.C0401, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). Silent degradation and model tampering are therefore hard to tell apart, and there is no baseline against which to detect an insider change. (8) Training-data dependence. Synthetic outputs inherit the biases of the physics code, and versions of surrogate and reference code can drift apart, which an adversary could exploit through weak configuration control (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0502).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on OOD tail error, simulation-only provenance, qualification and over-trust gaps, and model/input integrity attacks, so these were merged into single threats. I dropped AML.T0010.002-style detail beyond the supply-chain item and kept extraction and denial as one short combined threat, with the security specialist's timing point folded into the implicit threats.

evidence.citation: "Deep heterogeneous joint architecture: A temporal frequency surrogate model for fuel performance codes," Annals of Nuclear Energy (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The authors built and tested a joint TCN and FNO neural-network surrogate. It was trained on realistic power histories and the matching outputs from the TRANSURANUS fuel performance code. It evaluates many rods almost instantly with a mean test error of a few percent on unseen data.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is silent non-conservative under-prediction of fuel centerline temperature or rod internal pressure, whether from poisoning or from input manipulation, which erodes fuel-integrity margin and could contribute to fuel failure; the entry itself names eroded margin, unanalysed conditions and derates, and a direct radiological release is mediated by other safety barriers, so this is not a 5.

reproducibility.why: OOD tail error and fleet-wide bias propagation occur reliably whenever operation enters under-represented regimes or a shared model or feed is biased, since the surrogate has no OOD detection or uncertainty; triggered poisoning also reproduces once embedded, though it depends on the regime being hit.

exploitability.why: The deliberate threats (poisoning of training data or artifacts, tampering with historian feeds, output tampering) need supply-chain, OT-network or insider access to a nuclear plant's fuel-assessment chain; the implicit failures need no adversary, but exploiting them on purpose still requires influencing operations.

affected_users.why: The correlated fleet-wide propagation threat means one biased model or corrupted feed affects every rod assessment and any plants sharing the model, which is broad impact across coupled assessments, though limited to the fuel-assessment function rather than all facility systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture and its limits are public in the open literature, and OOD brittleness, simulation-label inheritance, poisoning and extraction are well-documented classes for surrogate models, so a capable outsider can readily infer the weaknesses, although deployment specifics remain non-public.

use_case: Three-dimensional convolutional neural network, trained on real PWR plant measurement-derived data, that predicts at assembly level whether a fuel assembly will be affected by crud-induced power shift (CIPS) at a given point in the cycle. It uses Monte Carlo dropout for uncertainty quantification. It replaces computationally expensive physics-based crud codes and supports operational management of CIPS.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory 3D-CNN surrogate for crud-induced power shift (CIPS) sits in cycle and chemistry management beside independent barriers: tech-spec AO/ΔI limits, in-core and ex-core flux monitoring, and licensed physics codes. Its main exposure is therefore slow degradation of decision quality, not direct safety harm. The threats are silent out-of-distribution failure on a small reactor-specific dataset, overconfident Monte Carlo dropout uncertainty, erosion of the physics-code cross-check, a qualification and governance gap, and quiet integrity attacks on training data, weights and inputs. A further threat is aggregation and exfiltration of plant-specific operating data.

Distribution shift on small, low-base-rate data -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on few plants and cycles with rare CIPS positives and labels inferred indirectly from axial offset anomalies, the CNN extrapolates silently under new fuel designs, uprates, chemistry regimes, loading patterns or another unit. The result is missed CIPS (an unplanned axial offset anomaly and eroded shutdown or power-shape margin) or false alarms (needless derates and distorted core design). An adversary could time or disguise a manipulation within periods of operational change, when errors are expected and look like ordinary model error.

Miscalibrated uncertainty and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Monte Carlo dropout understates epistemic uncertainty off-distribution, so tight intervals read as validated confidence bounds, and the opaque CNN cannot be checked against crud or boron-hideout physics. Stochastic inference also makes runs hard to repeat, complicating audit. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust so that a biased output goes unchallenged and tampering is hard to separate from sampling noise.

Loss of the physics cross-check and human skill -- implicit, exploitable
If the cheaper surrogate displaces physics-based crud codes, planners drift into over-trust and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity and lose the skill and tools to challenge a wrong prediction. An adversary who corrupts the model or its data meets a weakened human defense.

Qualification and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
No established qualification path exists for an ML surrogate in a safety-relevant analysis chain, and static validation on historical cycles does not match prospective use. Version control, change control, retraining non-determinism and data provenance checks are under-specified, and the tool may migrate from advisory use into licensing or reload evaluations. An insider could use weak change control to slip in altered weights or data unnoticed.

Fleet or shared-pipeline propagation -- implicit, exploitable
Reusing one trained model or pipeline across units or vendor and research partners spreads any shared bias, whether natural or implanted, to many plants. A single compromise of the shared artifact would then reach all of them.

Training-data and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider, vendor, lab collaborator or compromised pipeline can poison the measurement archive, physics-generated augmentation data, calibration step or weights, so the model systematically under- or over-predicts CIPS for chosen assemblies or cores. Under-prediction masks margin erosion, while over-prediction causes unnecessary derates and outage extension, an economic sabotage that looks like model error.

Inference-input manipulation -- adversarial
Altered burnup, power-history or chemistry inputs from a compromised historian or engineering workstation skew the prediction, and a falsified low-risk output defers mitigation of a developing power shift. This is mainly ordinary data-integrity compromise of the engineering network, not a crafted adversarial perturbation.

Supply-chain and software compromise -- adversarial
Research-grade ML frameworks, pretrained components, containers and dependencies not hardened to security standards can carry tampered code or weights into the engineering-analysis network. They give a foothold for pivoting into engineering or corporate IT.

Data and model exfiltration -- adversarial
Training sets and the calibrated model encode loading patterns, power histories, chemistry and fuel-performance behavior, so theft or model-extraction and inference attacks expose a plant's operating envelope and margins. This is proprietary and useful for reconnaissance but not safeguards-critical.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant operations view, this model sits in the core design and reload/cycle management loop (core monitoring, power-shift/axial offset anomaly management, chemistry and loading-pattern decisions). It is advisory and sits beside strong independent barriers: Technical Specification limits on AO/ΔI, in-core and ex-core flux monitoring, shutdown margin verification, and licensed physics codes (e.g., MAMBA/BOA-class tools) and fuel vendor methods. So a wrong output rarely causes direct safety harm. The realistic consequences are mispositioned operational margin: unnecessary derates or outage-driven loading/chemistry changes if it over-predicts, and unanticipated axial offset anomaly, shutdown margin or flux-tilt surprises, plus lost power or fuel-reliability costs, if it under-predicts and operators or designers relax mitigations. The main vulnerabilities are implicit: a small, reactor-specific, low-base-rate dataset that does not generalize to new fuel designs, chemistry regimes, power uprates or new loading patterns; and trust in MC-dropout uncertainty that is poorly calibrated out of distribution. Adversarial paths exist but are mostly indirect, through poisoned measurement and training data or model tampering that biases the CIPS forecast in a quiet, hard-to-detect way.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift and small-data limits. CIPS events are rare and the training data come from a few plants and cycles with specific fuel, chemistry (pH/boron/zinc), duty and loading-pattern histories. The model's failure mechanism is silent extrapolation when the core moves outside its training envelope (new fuel designs, higher duty, uprates, chemistry changes, a different plant). The affected function is the CIPS risk ranking used for cycle design and operational management. The consequence is an under-predicted crud-induced axial offset anomaly, which means unplanned power maneuvering or derates and eroded margin to AO/shutdown-margin limits. Tech-spec limits and in-core monitoring still bound the physical outcome. (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0201.05.) (2) Uncertainty miscalibration and opacity. MC dropout often under-represents epistemic uncertainty, especially off-distribution, so narrow confidence bands can encourage trust the model has not earned. Because the CNN is opaque and its outputs are not tied to boron-hideout physics, an engineer cannot easily check a prediction against crud mechanisms. (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0402.02.) (3) Qualification gap. Replacing a licensed physics code with an ML surrogate in a safety-relevant analysis chain invites regulatory and QA questions: there is no established qualification path, version control is weak, and retraining can silently change behavior. If the model's output feeds licensing-basis or reload safety evaluations rather than only advisory management, that would be a serious governance failure. (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0502, OP.C0303.) (4) Human factors. Staff may defer to a fast surrogate and lose proficiency with the physics codes (skill fade, out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity). Reactor-specific calibration also needs ongoing data feeds, so a gap in measurement continuity degrades the model unnoticed. (OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0204.) ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training and calibration data poisoning, or tampering with the plant measurement archive (flux maps, chemistry records, core-follow data). A biased input set or backdoored retrained weights could steadily under-predict CIPS for chosen assemblies or cores. The result is bad operating guidance, leading to unnecessary derates (economic sabotage) or masked margin erosion. A subtle bias is harder to catch than an outage. (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0059, AML.T0031.) (6) Input manipulation at inference. Altered core-state inputs (burnup, power history, chemistry) from compromised data historians or engineering workstations could skew predictions. This is not the usual crafted-perturbation attack. It is closer to ordinary data-integrity compromise of the engineering-analysis network. (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0112.001.) (7) Model and data exfiltration. Plant-specific operating data and the calibrated model reveal fuel performance, duty and core design information, which is proprietary and sensitive but not safeguards-critical. (AML.T0024, AML.T0035.) (8) Reduced availability. Denial of the model, or reversion to slow physics codes, delays outage planning at worst. This is a low consequence for safety. Overall, the physical risk is bounded by independent monitoring and tech-spec barriers. The residual concern is slow, undetected degradation of decision quality, plus the qualification and governance questions if the tool migrates from advisory use to licensing support.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a supervised 3D-CNN surrogate for a physics-based crud code (e.g., MAMBA/BOA-class), trained on measurement-derived data from a very small population: a handful of plants and cycles, with CIPS being a low-base-rate event. The core ML fragility is data scarcity and class imbalance. The model is also reactor-specific and calibrated to historical cycles, so any shift in operating conditions can push inference out of distribution. Examples include new fuel designs, uprates, different chemistry or coolant-pH regimes, new loading patterns, and a different plant. Monte Carlo dropout is a weak, poorly calibrated proxy for epistemic uncertainty. It tends to be overconfident on OOD inputs, and the operator may read it as a validated confidence bound. The 'measurement-derived' labels are themselves inferred from axial offset anomalies and core-follow residuals, so the ground truth carries noise, proxy bias and physics-code dependence. The model replaces a physics code, which removes an independent cross-check. Its inputs (core loading maps, power histories, chemistry, thermal-hydraulic data) come from upstream neutronics and monitoring chains whose errors propagate straight into the prediction.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Drift/OOD and operational heterogeneity: the model is trained on a few plants and cycles. New fuel designs, power uprates, chemistry changes, loading-pattern shifts or a transfer to another unit change the input-to-crud relationship (covariate and concept drift). The CNN extrapolates silently, and the failure is a missed or false CIPS prediction. A missed prediction means an unplanned axial offset anomaly and a power-shape or shutdown-margin surprise, with possible derating. A false alarm means unneeded cost and distorted core design. (2) Small-data, low-base-rate problem and label provenance: CIPS positives are rare, and labels are derived from plant measurements and inferred indirectly. This gives high variance, a risk of overfitting to plant-specific artifacts, and a cause-versus-correlation problem when the model learns surrogate signals instead of crud physics. (3) Uncertainty quantification limits: MC dropout under-represents epistemic uncertainty and is miscalibrated off-distribution, so operators may over-trust a tight interval. Automation bias is compounded if the tool displaces the physics code and the staff expertise that goes with it (skill fade). (4) Qualification mismatch: the model is validated statically on held-out historical cycles, but it is used prospectively in changing cycles. No established V&V regime exists for such a surrogate, and its opacity limits diagnosis. Retraining non-determinism hampers repeatability. (5) Fleet propagation: if one model or training pipeline is reused across sites, a shared bias spreads to many plants.

ADVERSARIAL threats. (6) Training-data and pipeline poisoning: plant measurement archives, fuel-cycle databases or the vendor and research data-sharing path could be tampered with so that the model learns biased CIPS susceptibility. The effect is quiet and persistent, and it is hard to separate from natural drift. Poisoning of the physics-code-generated augmentation data works the same way. (7) Input manipulation and evasion: altering core-monitoring or chemistry inputs (sensor or historian tampering) skews the prediction. The CNN's image-like input layout is sensitive to small structured perturbations, and a falsified 'low risk' output can mask a developing power shift or defer mitigation. (8) Model or artifact tampering (weights, container, dependency supply chain) or access to the model via a vendor or cloud workflow. Implicit weaknesses such as OOD blind spots and overconfident UQ give an adversary cover, because a manipulated output looks like ordinary model error. Where the model is part of operational decision support, a compromised prediction affects fuel management and operating-margin decisions, rather than directly affecting protection systems.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is an advisory, off-line predictor of a slow-developing, economically significant phenomenon (CIPS / axial offset anomaly), not a real-time protection function. A sophisticated adversary would be unlikely to go after it directly, because it has no actuation path and the physical consequences of a bad prediction are bounded by technical specifications, core monitoring and operator review. Its real exposure lies elsewhere. First, it concentrates reactor-specific core-physics and chemistry data (loading patterns, power histories, coolant chemistry, measured flux and offset data), which is valuable reconnaissance for anyone studying a plant's fuel performance, operating margins and outage-planning vulnerabilities. Second, it creates a quiet integrity pathway: an insider or a supply-chain actor who can alter training or calibration data, or the model, can bias cycle-management decisions in a way that looks like ordinary model error. Third, uncertainty estimates that look rigorous but are miscalibrated can make planners trust the model more than they should, and a patient adversary could time interference around that trust.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Data and model integrity: the model is trained on real, reactor-specific plant data with reactor-specific calibration. An insider, a vendor or lab collaborator, or a compromised data pipeline could poison or subtly shift the inputs, the calibration step or the weights (AML.T0020, T0010.002/T0010.003, T0018.000, T0031, T0059). The AI failure mechanism would be a systematic under-prediction of CIPS risk, or over-prediction. The facility depends on it for planning power-shape management, chemistry or cleaning decisions, and fuel-reload design. The consequences would be unplanned axial offset or power derates, shutdown-margin or thermal-margin erosion if the physical effect is underestimated and independent checks are weak, and unnecessary mitigation cost and outage extension if it is overestimated. The last of these is an economic-sabotage outcome that is easy to disguise as a modeling error. (2) Information aggregation and exfiltration: the training sets and the trained model encode sensitive operating history and fuel-performance behavior. Exfiltration of the data, or inference or extraction attacks against the model, would leak plant-specific information and expose the plant's operating envelope (AML.T0025, T0035, T0024.000/T0024.002, T0036). Model sharing across research or vendor partners (ORNL, utility, vendor) widens the exposure surface, so access governance matters (OP.C0505, OP.C0602). (3) Supply chain and software hygiene: ML frameworks, pretrained components and research-grade code that is not hardened to security standards are a stepping stone into engineering networks, and a plausible route to the utility's corporate or engineering IT (AML.T0010.001, T0011.000/T0011.001, T0112.001, OP.C0502). Even so, a nation-state would more likely use this as a pivot or an intelligence source than as a sabotage target.

IMPLICIT, EXPLOITABLE OR TIMEABLE. (4) Automation trust and out-of-the-loop effects: if physics-based crud codes are retired because the surrogate is cheaper, staff may lose the skill and tools to cross-check it (OP.C0101.01, C0101.04, C0101.06). That loss weakens the human defense against both natural and malicious errors. (5) Drift and out-of-distribution failure: a model calibrated on historical cycles may fail under new fuel designs, power uprates, changed chemistry regimes or longer cycles (OP.C0302.01/.02/.03, C0303, C0202). Crud events are rare and plant-specific, so data is small and base rates are low. An adversary who understands this could use a period of operational change, when the model is least reliable, as cover for a manipulation. (6) Miscalibrated uncertainty: Monte Carlo dropout is known to understate epistemic uncertainty, so confident-looking intervals may offer false assurance (OP.C0403, C0401, C0402.02). Repeatability is also an issue, because stochastic inference gives different outputs on different runs, which complicates audit and detection of tampering. (7) Governance: there is no established AI qualification route for non-safety-related but operationally important predictors (OP.C0501, C0504). This leaves model versioning, change control, and provenance and integrity checks of training data under-specified, which an insider could exploit.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on drift/small-data, miscalibrated MC-dropout uncertainty, skill fade, the qualification gap and data/model poisoning. I dropped minor items (availability denial, OP.C0204, AML.T0112.001, AML.T0024.000) as low-consequence or weakly argued, and kept supply chain and exfiltration from the security specialist. The sub-technique AML.T0043 was kept as a root code because the engineer called input manipulation more like data-integrity compromise than crafted perturbation.

evidence.citation: "Data-driven prediction and uncertainty quantification of PWR crud-induced power shift using convolutional neural networks," Energy (Elsevier), vol. 316, art. 134447, 2025 (Oak Ridge National Laboratory publication record)
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper (Furlong et al.) builds an ANN with 3D convolution that exploits the image-like layout of core input data. It predicts CIPS at assembly level with reactor-specific calibration built in. The arXiv version (2407.04726, not itself peer reviewed) adds that the model is trained on real PWR measurement data and uses Monte Carlo dropout for uncertainty.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is silent under-prediction of CIPS (from drift or poisoning) that erodes axial power-shape and shutdown margin, or over-prediction that causes unnecessary derates; independent tech-spec AO/ΔI limits and in-core/ex-core monitoring keep this at operational disruption and minor margin erosion, not release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Distribution-shift failures recur reliably whenever fuel designs, uprates or chemistry regimes change, but deliberate poisoning or input manipulation needs specific conditions, and stochastic inference and independent cross-checks make a given outcome less certain.

exploitability.why: Credible adversarial paths (poisoning training data or weights, tampering with a compromised historian, or abusing weak change control) need insider, vendor or engineering-network access, while the implicit drift failures need no attacker effort.

affected_users.why: A single-plant advisory tool mainly affects that unit's core and cycle management, but shared models or pipelines reused across units and partners can spread a bias or compromise to a fleet, so impact is moderate and not facility-wide on safety systems.

discoverability.why: The CNN approach is published in the open literature, and the general weaknesses (small-data drift, MC-dropout overconfidence, supply-chain and poisoning classes) are well documented, though plant-specific data and pipeline details are not public.

use_case: 3D convolutional and recurrent neural networks that unfold the reactor transfer function from simulated in-core neutron-noise detector readings. They classify the type of core perturbation and localise its source in a pressurised water reactor, for on-line core anomaly monitoring.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory neutron-noise classifier and localiser for PWR core monitoring was trained and validated only on simulated data, so its main insecurity is a silent gap between simulation and the real plant. That gap yields confident but wrong diagnoses, which erode operator vigilance and mask or mimic real core degradation. Adversaries can exploit the blind spots, manipulate the detector signal path, or compromise the training and model supply chain. Because the tool sits outside the protection system, direct safety consequences are bounded by defence in depth. The larger losses are degraded early detection of fuel and internals faults, misdirected maintenance, and unnecessary outages.

Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
The networks learned idealised simulated noise and a closed set of perturbation classes, so real detector artefacts, compound or unmodelled perturbations and plant-specific spectra produce confident but wrong classes or source locations. This causes missed fuel assembly or control rod vibration or false alarms. An adversary can rely on these systematic misses to hide a physical or instrumentation interference without knowing the model internals.

Cycle drift and data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Burnup, reloads, boron changes and detector ageing shift the true transfer function, and with few real labelled events there is no ground truth to detect degradation or calibrate false-alarm rates. An adversary could time interference around post-reload or end-of-cycle windows, when model confidence is poorest and operators already discount alerts.

Automation trust and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
A precise but unverifiable localisation such as a named assembly invites anchoring, a usually quiet monitor invites complacency, and noise-analysis skills fade. The model's opacity, non-deterministic training and lack of AI-specific qualification make a manipulated output indistinguishable from model error, and false-alarm fatigue that drives disuse can be induced deliberately. A staged event then meets a less attentive response.

Qualification gap and scope creep -- implicit, exploitable
As a non-safety-classed advisory tool it escapes rigorous verification and cyber scrutiny applied to I&C, and creeping reliance could put an unqualified model into maintenance-relaxation or protection-adjacent decisions. Its bad classifications can also propagate into downstream trending and maintenance planning. An adversary gains from the weaker scrutiny of this layer and from the false assurance it can provide.

Detector-signal evasion -- adversarial
With access to the detector or data-acquisition path, an adversary can inject, replay or shape low-amplitude noise spectra that exploit the model's learned spectral and spatial features, so a real perturbation reads as benign or a false source is raised. The model has no input-integrity check, and range checks would not flag such perturbations.

Training-data and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Shared simulation data, simulator parameters and pretrained weights from research consortia can be altered, or a backdoor trigger keyed to a spectral pattern implanted, creating a persistent blind spot that survives review. If one model is deployed across a fleet, the compromise propagates to many plants.

Insider tampering and monitoring-service denial -- adversarial
An insider with maintenance or data-science privileges can quietly alter thresholds, retrain on altered data or swap weights, producing false assurance during a physical act. Denying or corrupting the monitoring service, or using its plant-network connections as a bridge, can remove a diagnostic layer during another event.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory on-line core-monitoring tool for a PWR. It classifies perturbation type (fuel assembly vibration, control rod vibration, inlet temperature/flow fluctuations, etc.) and localizes the source from in-core neutron-noise detector readings. The key facts are that it was trained and validated only on simulated noise (CORTEX/CORE SIM-type frequency-domain models), and that it sits in the O&M monitoring layer, not in the protection or control system. Plant safety is protected by the reactor protection system, technical specification limits, and conventional vibration, temperature and flux monitoring, so a wrong output will rarely cause a direct safety event. The realistic harms are misdirected maintenance, unnecessary outages or derates, missed early indications of mechanical degradation (for example, fuel assembly or control rod vibration), and erosion of operator trust. The main engineering concern is the gap between simulated and real plant data, because real noise is non-stationary, has uncertain detector and plant parameters, and contains background sources that the simulation did not model. That gap interacts with automation bias and with opacity, since the output names a specific source location that operators cannot easily check independently.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: networks trained on simulated neutron noise, with assumed transfer functions and idealized or Gaussian background noise, face real plants with different detector sets, burnup-dependent cores, measurement noise, ex-core/instrumentation artefacts, and several simultaneous perturbations. Mechanism: out-of-distribution input yields confident but wrong classification or localization. Consequence: false alarms that trigger needless inspection or derates, or false negatives that miss real assembly or rod vibration, leading to fretting wear, fuel damage or a later forced outage. The latter would require the conventional monitoring and periodic inspection to also miss it. (2) Concept and operational drift across the fuel cycle: cross-sections, burnup, boron concentration, and detector aging all alter the true transfer function, so the model degrades silently unless it is recalibrated or revalidated. (3) Automation bias and opacity: operators and engineers may trust a precise localization, such as 'assembly X-Y is vibrating', that has no ground truth in the plant. The consequence is misdirected inspections, or complacency toward the conventional diagnostics. (4) Qualification gap: an advisory tool outside the safety classification sits outside rigorous V&V. Creeping reliance (scope creep toward feeding control or protection decisions, or toward justifying relaxed inspection) would put an unqualified model in a safety role. (5) Data scarcity: real labelled perturbation events are rare, so there is little operational data to validate against and the tool cannot be tested thoroughly. Non-repeatability between retrained versions makes regulatory acceptance hard.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Manipulating detector or data-acquisition signals (evasion, chaff, or injected narrowband noise) can mask a real perturbation or fabricate a false one. The mechanism is that the model has no integrity check on the input, and the outcome is a missed or spurious anomaly diagnosis. A capable adversary would more likely use this to hide a developing mechanical fault, or to delay or time an attack, than to cause harm directly, because the protection system is independent. (7) Training-data or model supply-chain poisoning: the simulation data, the simulation code and the pretrained models come from research consortia and are shared. Altered simulated data or a backdoored model could bias localization or suppress specific classes. This is relevant to the vendor/utility fleet if one model is deployed to many plants (cross-fleet propagation). (8) Compromise of the monitoring network could be used for denial of the monitoring service, or for corruption of the outputs shown to operators. The exposure depends mainly on how well the network is segregated from the safety systems and on whether the tool runs on-premises.

Overall risk is moderate to low in direct safety terms thanks to defence-in-depth, but it is higher for operational reliability and for degraded early detection of fuel and internals degradation. The risk grows if the tool is trusted beyond its validated envelope.

ai_engineer.argument: This system is trained and validated entirely on simulated neutron-noise data (CORTEX-style frequency/time-domain noise simulators with idealised perturbation models), then proposed for on-line monitoring of a real PWR. The core ML fragility is the sim-to-real gap. Real in-core detector signals include detector-specific noise, calibration offsets, dead or degraded channels, plant-specific spectral features, and background vibration and thermal-hydraulic noise that the simulator may not capture. A 3D CNN/RNN that reaches high accuracy on held-out simulated data says little about calibration or behaviour on field data, and the fixed softmax classifier assumes a closed set of perturbation types. Real cores will produce compound perturbations, unmodelled anomalies, and slow burnup-driven changes in the transfer function. These inputs are out of distribution, yet the model will still return a confident class and location. Because labelled real anomalies are rare and sensitive, there is little way to validate, recalibrate, or monitor drift, and the spatial 3D input grid is tightly coupled to detector layout and core loading pattern, which makes retraining per plant and per cycle a lifecycle burden.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real / OOD failure (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03): the training distribution is simulator output with idealised noise, so field inputs may be misclassified or mislocalised with high confidence. The consequence is a missed or misdiagnosed core anomaly (for example, a fuel assembly vibration, flow blockage, or control rod issue misattributed), which delays operator response, or false alarms that erode trust.
