(2) Drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02): burnup, fuel reloads, changes in detector sensitivity, and changing moderator temperature coefficient shift the reactor transfer function over the cycle. A model tied to a fixed simulated core state degrades silently, and no ground truth is available to detect this. (3) Small-data and low base rate (OP.C0202, OP.C0203): real perturbation events are few, so there is no real-anomaly test set, and calibration of detection thresholds and false-alarm rates is largely unverifiable. (4) Qualification and opacity gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0303): a black-box localiser has no accepted qualification path for I&C-adjacent monitoring, training is non-deterministic, and static simulated testing does not match dynamic plant conditions. (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102): a monitoring tool that is usually quiet invites complacency, and a confident localisation can anchor operators on the wrong cause. (6) Closed-set and cascading error (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603): compound or novel faults are forced into known classes, and the output may feed downstream maintenance or trending.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Sensor-level evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041): an adversary with access to the detector signal path or acquisition electronics could inject small, structured perturbations that exploit the model's learned spectral and spatial features. This could suppress a real anomaly's signature or induce a false class and location. The model's smoothness and the simulator-derived features make this a plausible, low-amplitude attack that conventional range checks would not flag. (b) Training and data supply-chain poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003): simulated datasets, simulator parameters, and pretrained weights shared across research consortia are a poisoning surface. A backdoor trigger, such as a particular spectral pattern, could cause misclassification only under attacker-chosen conditions, and the lack of real-data cross-checks would make this hard to detect. (c) Model and data exfiltration (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035): the model and the simulation data encode core design and detector layout information, which is sensitive and could aid reconnaissance. (d) Timing: an adversary could time interference around the known drift windows (post-reload, end of cycle) when model confidence is poorest and operators are already discounting alerts. (e) Integrity of the monitoring integration (AML.T0031, AML.T0029): denial of the inference service or erosion of the model through online retraining or recalibration pipelines would disable or skew monitoring without touching safety-class systems, so it may escape cyber-security scrutiny applied to I&C (OP.C0503, OP.C0502).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is an on-line core anomaly monitor that classifies and localises perturbations (fuel assembly vibration, absorber-of-variable-strength, flow/temperature inhomogeneities) from in-core neutron-noise signals. Its value to an adversary is mostly as a vigilance-shaping and masking layer, not as a direct control target. If operators come to rely on it to say that the core is quiet or that an anomaly is benign, a sophisticated actor can time a mechanical, thermal-hydraulic or instrumentation interference around the model's blind spots. The system was trained and validated only on simulated data, so its real-plant blind spots are poorly characterised. Those gaps are non-adversarial, and they are also exactly what a patient insider or a supply-chain actor could probe and exploit.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Input manipulation or evasion (AML.T0015, T0043, T0031): the model's inputs are in-core detector signals, plus ex-core signals and the digital chain that carries them. An adversary with access to the instrumentation or data-acquisition path could inject, replay or shape noise spectra so a real perturbation is classified as benign, or so a false localisation is raised. Either outcome would delay the response to genuine fuel or core-internals degradation or provoke needless operator action. Neutron-noise features are physically smooth and well characterised in the open literature (AML.T0000), which lowers the cost of crafting plausible spectra. (2) Training-pipeline and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0059): the model is trained on simulated data from open-literature noise simulators and then fine-tuned or retrained. A poisoned simulation dataset, a backdoor trigger keyed to a specific spectral signature (T0043.004), or a tampered pretrained model would give a persistent, near-undetectable blind spot that survives routine review. Vendor, university or consortium hand-offs are the likely injection points. (3) Insider access and trust concentration (AML.T0012, T0018, T0076): someone with maintenance or data-science privileges can alter thresholds, retrain on altered data, or swap model weights quietly. The system could then become a quiet sabotage-enabler, giving false assurance while a physical act is carried out. It could also be used to discredit the monitor and push operators to disuse it. (4) Stepping-stone and IT/OT bridging (AML.T0049, T0025, T0029): an on-line monitor that connects to plant computers, historians or remote vendor support is a new pathway into the plant network. Denial or degradation of the monitor could also be timed to remove a diagnostic layer during another event.

IMPLICIT, WITH ADVERSARIAL EXPLOITABILITY. (5) Simulation-to-plant gap (OP.C0201.01, C0203, C0302, C0302.03): the models have never been validated on real plant noise, and real noise varies between units, cycles and burnup. Missed detections, wrong localisation and false alarms are all likely, and an adversary can exploit the systematic misses without any knowledge of the model internals. (6) Automation trust and complacency (OP.C0101.04, C0102, C0101.06, C0101.01): sustained quiet outputs erode operator and engineer vigilance and the underlying noise-analysis skills, so a staged event meets a less attentive response. Alarm fatigue from false positives drives disuse (C0101.05), which an attacker can induce deliberately. (7) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, C0402, C0501): deep networks are poorly explainable, so it is hard to tell a manipulated output from a model error. Without AI-specific qualification, the lack of independent cross-checks means a compromised or drifting model is unlikely to be caught. (8) Cascading dependence (OP.C0301.01, C0603): the classifier's output could feed downstream diagnostics or maintenance planning, so a bad classification would propagate into those decisions.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, drift, automation trust, qualification gap, signal evasion and supply-chain poisoning. I dropped speculative or weakly grounded codes (exfiltration, T0049 and T0025 IT/OT bridging, T0000, T0059, T0046, T0041, OP.C0503 and OP.C0502) and kept insider tampering and fleet propagation as distinct threats.

evidence.citation: "3D convolutional and recurrent neural networks for reactor perturbation unfolding and anomaly detection," EPJ Nuclear Sciences & Technologies (EDP Sciences)
evidence.note: This paper comes from the Euratom CORTEX project. It describes a deep-learning framework that identifies and localises reactor-core perturbation sources from neutron detector readings in PWRs, in both the time and frequency domains. The networks were built and tested on simulated neutron-noise data, not on plant data.

damage.why: The tool is advisory and sits outside the protection system, so defence in depth bounds direct safety consequences; the credible worst case (supply-chain or evasion attacks hiding a real fuel or internals fault while a physical act proceeds) is degraded early detection, misdirected maintenance and unplanned outages, which is operational disruption and minor safety-margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real gaps, cycle drift and automation over-trust are systematic and recur reliably, and an adversary can rely on the resulting misses; the adversarial paths (signal injection, poisoning) depend on gaining access to the signal path or supply chain.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (detector or DAQ path injection, supply-chain poisoning, insider retraining) need privileged access to plant instrumentation, data or model pipelines, and a successful attack needs a coordinated physical or instrumentation event; the implicit weaknesses are easier to exploit but still need timing and context.

affected_users.why: A single-plant deployment affects the monitoring and maintenance functions of one core, but a fleet-wide pretrained model or shared simulation data could propagate a compromise across many plants, and bad classifications feed downstream trending and maintenance planning.

discoverability.why: Sim-to-real gaps, drift and adversarial evasion are well documented for this class of AI model, and the source paper is public and states that it was trained only on simulated data; specific blind spots would still need system-specific knowledge, but the existence of the weakness class is evident.

use_case: Convolutional and fully connected neural-network analysis of measured M400 CZT handheld gamma spectra from UF6 cylinders and U3O8 samples. The models predict the uranium enrichment, or classify it into discrete values, so that inspectors can check declared enrichment. The framework was benchmarked against the GEM analysis code.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case puts a CNN/FCNN enrichment estimator, trained largely on GADRAS-simulated spectra with a small set of measured ones, at the inspector's declared-versus-measured verification boundary. The main threats are adversarial evasion of the learned model through physical manipulation of the measured spectrum, poisoning or backdooring of the data and model lifecycle, and reconnaissance enabled by published methods. Implicit threats are sim-to-real distribution shift with no uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag, automation over-trust, and the lack of qualification, repeatability and fleet-level control. All of these converge on one consequence: a falsely reassuring 'consistent with declared' result that conceals misdeclaration, diversion or undeclared enrichment.

Spectral evasion of the classifier -- adversarial
An operator who knows the model family, or a proxy built from the published work, can alter the measured spectrum through shielding, wall-thickness or attenuator changes, material mixing or substitution, or added sources. This steers the CNN's predicted enrichment toward the declared value, and the learned model has no physics-consistency check of the kind GEM provides.

Training-data and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with GADRAS-generated sets, measured reference spectra, simulation decks or model weights, or implanting a spectral trigger, can bias predictions in a chosen enrichment band during training or an update. This yields persistent, hard-to-detect false acceptance.

Spectrum and analysis-chain tampering -- adversarial
Altering stored spectra, calibration or gain files, or the handheld-to-analysis software changes the model input or output while the inspector's confidence is preserved. This degrades the integrity of the verification result without touching the model.

Reconnaissance and proxy-model building -- adversarial
Published architecture, data sources, benchmarks and accuracy limits let an adversary train a surrogate and verify evasion spectra offline. This lowers the cost of the evasion above.

Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
Training on simulated spectra plus narrow measured data (few cylinders, limited enrichment points, possible train/test leakage) means the network can learn simulator artifacts. Variations in wall thickness, fill geometry, detector gain or temperature drift, resolution loss, and minor isotopes such as U-234 or U-236 push inputs outside the training envelope, yet it still emits a confident point estimate with no uncertainty. An adversary can place a manipulation inside these poorly covered regions, such as near the declared value or the HEU boundary, where the model is least reliable but most trusted.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A benchmark that beats GEM on UF6 invites inspectors to treat the number as proof and to drop independent spectral sanity checks and physics cross-checks. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, timing a diversion or substitution around reduced scrutiny.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The model is opaque, retraining with different seeds shifts outputs, and no uncertainty budget or AI-specific qualification exists for safeguards use, so a disputed or subtly wrong result is hard to audit or defend. An adversary can exploit this ambiguity to contest legitimate discrepancies or to hide a subtle bias that cannot be traced.

Fleet-wide model propagation -- implicit, exploitable
One model file distributed across inspector devices and sites means a single flaw or compromised release propagates widely. This makes the shared artifact a high-value single point of compromise.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a safeguards verification aid. An inspector uses a handheld CZT spectrum (M400, low resolution) to check declared enrichment of UF6 cylinders and U3O8 at enrichment plants. The AI output is an attribute or number that supports a declared-versus-measured comparison, so the main consequence is a wrong safeguards conclusion, not a physical plant event. A false 'consistent with declared' result could mask diversion, undeclared enrichment, or material substitution. A false discrepancy could trigger unnecessary follow-up, waste inspection effort, or cause a diplomatic dispute. Existing practice is a strong safeguard: handheld NDA is a screening tool, and anomalies or key decisions are backed by independent measurements such as DA/NDA, ULTRA/environmental sampling, and cylinder weighing and seals. The risk therefore rises if the ML number comes to be trusted in place of those layers, or if its uncertainty is not understood.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT WEAKNESSES: (1) Training-data provenance and scarcity (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0701, OP.C0701.01). The models are trained largely on GADRAS-simulated spectra plus a limited set of measured spectra. Real cylinders differ in wall thickness, fill geometry, container attenuation, detector temperature/gain shift, background, 234U/236U content, and the age and daughter ingrowth of the material. This is a sim-to-real gap, so the model may be accurate on the benchmark set and be biased or overconfident on out-of-distribution items (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). A bias is most dangerous when it fails near the declared value, such as 4.95% versus slightly higher, or around the highly enriched uranium boundary for U3O8. The single-point numeric output also gives no calibrated uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag (OP.C0401, OP.C0403). (2) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). A better-than-GEM benchmark on a limited cylinder set could lead to over-reliance, with the number replacing physics-based checks and inspector skill fading. Models in a regulatory use are not repeatable or qualified in the way GEM is (OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504), so results may be hard to defend or reproduce in a dispute. (3) Material substitution and unusual samples (OP.C0702.01): the model may be blind to a deliberately constructed spectrum, such as shielding or mixing, that still gives a plausible enrichment. ADVERSARIAL THREATS: (a) A host-state or insider adversary could craft or shape the spectrum, for example through liner/shielding changes, source or filler placement, or a decoy, so that a CNN reads a lower or declared enrichment. This is evasion of an ML classifier and is more plausible than against GEM because the model's decision boundary is less transparent (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0043.001). Insider knowledge of the model's behavior makes black-box probing practical if repeated measurements are allowed. (b) Poisoned or tampered training data, a trojanned model, or compromised weights, supplied through lab pipelines, shared repositories, or software updates, could cause systematic under- or over-prediction of particular enrichment bands (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0043.004). Fleet-wide distribution to inspectorate devices would propagate the bias (OP.C0602). (c) Tampering with the handheld-to-analysis chain or the stored spectra (calibration files, gain settings, spectrum alteration) could change results while bypassing ML-specific checks (AML.T0031, AML.T0059). (d) Publication of the architecture, data, and benchmarks supports adversary reconnaissance and proxy-model building (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0002). Net consequence: a plausible falsely reassuring result that is mitigated only if independent verification continues and the ML output is treated as screening, not proof.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a regression/classification model on low-resolution CZT spectra (M400, roughly 2-3% FWHM at 662 keV), so the 185.7 keV U-235 region sits on a continuum dominated by detector response, container attenuation, and background. The model is trained largely on GADRAS-simulated spectra, plus a small amount of measured data, so it has a sim-to-real gap and a small-data problem. Reported accuracy comes from a few measured campaigns (U3O8 0.31-93.17%, UF6 0.2-4.95%). That accuracy says little about unseen cylinder wall thicknesses, fill geometries, detector gain drift, temperature, or enrichments between and beyond the benchmark points. Because the output is a number that inspectors compare against a declaration, the real exposure is an unqualified black-box estimator that looks authoritative and is hard to audit, with the CNN/FCNN replacing a physics-based code (GEM) whose failure modes are well understood.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and distribution shift (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). GADRAS-heavy training means the network may learn simulator artifacts. At inference, shifts in gain/calibration, resolution degradation as the CZT ages, temperature, count time, cylinder type, wall thickness, shielding, or the presence of Pu or U-236/minor isotopes can move the input outside the training manifold. The network will still emit a confident point estimate with no native out-of-distribution flag (OP.C0403, OP.C0401). The consequence is a biased enrichment estimate that either misses a real discrepancy or raises a false one, undermining the safeguards conclusion. (2) Small, narrow measured data (OP.C0202, OP.C0701.01). Few real UF6 cylinders and U3O8 samples at limited enrichment values mean validation is probably interpolative, with possible leakage between train and test spectra from the same item or campaign. Reported superiority over GEM may not carry over to other facilities. (3) Qualification mismatch and non-repeatability (OP.C0303, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501). Retraining with different seeds can shift outputs. There is no established uncertainty budget, so inspectors cannot attach a defensible measurement uncertainty, which is central to safeguards statistical conclusions. (4) Automation bias (OP.C0101.04). A fast, accurate-looking number from a handheld invites inspectors to over-trust it, especially if it replaces GEM cross-checks. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Evasion via physical input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0041). An operator who knows the detector class and model family can alter the measured spectrum with shielding, container geometry, or added sources, or exploit adversarial sensitivity of the CNN, so that a non-declared enrichment reads as declared. Spectral-shape perturbations that a physics code would constrain can sway a learned model more easily. Public ORNL papers lower the reconnaissance cost (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0005). (6) Supply-chain and data poisoning (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000). Tampered training spectra, simulation input decks, or model weights, or a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004) keyed to a spectral feature, could bias outputs during deployment or retraining. Because model files live on inspector laptops or tablets and are updated across devices, one poisoned release can propagate across a fleet (OP.C0602). (7) Model extraction and integrity (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0031). Repeated queries could reveal decision sensitivities for evasion planning.

security_specialist.argument: From a safeguards-adversary lens, this tool sits at the verification boundary: an inspector's handheld CZT measurement is one of the few independent checks on a declared enrichment, so anything that shapes the AI's output shapes the inspector's conclusion. A state or insider that wants to hide enrichment above declared values (e.g., a diversion, undeclared HEU production, or a mislabeled cylinder) gains a new target in the model, its training data, and the measurement geometry. This is a stepping stone because spoofing the spectrum is cheaper than defeating the facility's physical protection, and an opaque CNN gives inspectors less ability to notice a subtly manipulated spectrum than a physics-based code like GEM does. The non-adversarial weaknesses (reliance on GADRAS simulated data, narrow measured training sets, container and shielding variation, and drift in detector response) are what a capable adversary would exploit or time an attack around, because they define where the model is least reliable and most trusted.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by spectral manipulation: an adversary with knowledge of the model family or a proxy (from the published paper and simulation tools) could craft or physically produce spectra, using shielding, attenuator or wall-thickness changes, mixed or substituted material, or added sources, that shift the predicted enrichment toward the declared value while the true enrichment differs. The AI mechanism is adversarial or out-of-distribution input sensitivity in a CNN/FCNN with no physics-consistency check. The dependent function is the inspector's declared-versus-measured enrichment check, and the consequence is a false verification that conceals misdeclaration or undeclared enrichment, which is a safeguards failure. (2) Training-data and model supply-chain compromise: poisoning or backdooring the GADRAS-generated sets, the measured reference spectra, or the weights (insider access to the data pipeline or to model updates) could embed a trigger or a bias in a particular enrichment range, giving persistent, hard-to-detect false acceptance. Because the model is trusted across inspections, it concentrates trust in a single artifact that is valuable to compromise. (3) Insider or host-level tampering with the analysis software, the handheld-to-laptop chain or the calibration and reference files, which would leave the inspector's confidence intact while the outputs are altered. (4) Adversary reconnaissance: publication of architecture, data sources, and accuracy limits lets a proxy model be trained and attacks verified offline.

IMPLICIT, EXPLOITABLE. (a) Automation over-trust and skill fade: accurate average performance (better than GEM on UF6) invites inspectors to defer to the number and lose the habit of independent spectral sanity checks, which an adversary could time a diversion around. (b) Narrow, scarce and domain-mismatched data: enrichment-range coverage is uneven, UF6 and U3O8 are limited sets, and simulated-to-measured transfer is imperfect, so detector drift, temperature, geometry, wall thickness and container heterogeneity can cause silent error outside the training distribution. (c) Opacity and non-repeatability: little explainability, plus retraining variability, make it hard to defend or audit a disputed result. (d) Qualification and regulatory gap: no AI-specific qualification for safeguards use, and benchmarking against GEM on a limited sample does not establish robustness. (e) Fleet propagation: if one model is distributed to many inspectors or sites, one flaw or compromise propagates widely. Overall, a nation-state would more likely target the data and model lifecycle or the physical measurement conditions than the tool's operation itself, and the weakest link is human reliance on the output.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on spectral evasion, data/model poisoning, sim-to-real shift, over-trust and fleet propagation. I dropped lower-support or weakly argued items: AML.T0024.002 model extraction (no inference API is evident), AML.T0041, AML.T0012 and AML.T0001, with tampering mapped to T0031/T0059 and the physical-manipulation evasion to T0015/T0043.003 instead.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning framework for predicting uranium enrichments from M400 CZT gamma spectra," Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A (Elsevier), Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Bae & Hu), 2024
evidence.note: The paper builds a deep-learning framework, using FCNN and CNN models trained with GADRAS-generated and measured M400 spectra. It reports tests on measured spectra of U3O8 samples (0.31–93.17% enrichment) and UF6 cylinders (0.2–4.95%). Enrichment predictions were accurate, and on UF6 cylinders the model was more accurate than the GEM code.

damage.why: The worst credible threat is a falsely reassuring 'consistent with declared' enrichment result (via evasion or poisoning) that conceals misdeclaration, diversion or undeclared enrichment, which is a safeguards falsification and loss-of-material-control outcome.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution weaknesses, and the lack of any uncertainty flag, are inherent to this model class and recur reliably once inputs leave the training envelope; poisoning and tampering are more conditional, so this is not a 5.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (poisoning the training or model supply chain, tampering with the analysis chain) need insider or privileged lifecycle access, and effective spectral evasion needs a state-level operator with material and shielding resources and a surrogate model, though a facility operator can physically alter the measured item.

affected_users.why: A single model file distributed across inspector devices and sites means one flawed or compromised release propagates across the fleet, which affects many verification results, though it stays within the safeguards verification function rather than coupling to plant systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, data sources, benchmarks and accuracy limits are published, and sim-to-real, out-of-distribution and adversarial-evasion weaknesses are well documented in the open literature for this class of model, so a capable outsider can readily infer the weaknesses, though specific model internals are not public.

use_case: Single-agent and multi-agent deep reinforcement learning (Proximal Policy Optimization) that rotates control drums to make a nuclear microreactor follow load changes. Each agent controls one drum and shares core-wide information. It is trained and tested on a point-kinetics model with thermal and xenon feedback, and benchmarked against PID control, including with noisy power measurements.
incurred_insecurity:
A learned PPO policy that directly commands control drums, which are reactivity-control actuators, is an opaque, hard-to-qualify controller validated only in a low-fidelity point-kinetics simulator. The main threats are manipulation of the sensor channel feeding the policy, tampering with the policy or its training pipeline, and a set of implicit weaknesses (sim-to-real gap, opacity, qualification gaps, over-trust) that give an adversary cover or leverage. The work is simulation-only, so these are forward-looking risks for any remote or lightly staffed microreactor deployment. Independent protection systems and operators remain the barriers, and their erosion is the real concern.

Sensor-channel manipulation -- adversarial
Biased or structured perturbations of neutron-flux, temperature or xenon-estimate inputs can steer a neural policy off its intended trajectory more subtly than they would a bounded, well-understood PID loop, masking a real power rise or inducing drum swings. In the multi-agent design the shared core-wide state lets one corrupted input bias every drum at once.

Policy and pipeline compromise -- adversarial
Tampered weights, a poisoned simulator, reward function or RL library, or an upstream-compromised training environment can embed a trigger-conditioned behavior that passes nominal benchmarks yet erodes margin or causes oscillation or a trip under a rare load pattern. A single vendor-trained policy shipped across a fleet would propagate one compromise to every site.

Proxy-model reconnaissance -- adversarial
Published architecture, algorithm, hyperparameters and reward structure let an attacker build a proxy policy and optimize perturbations or triggers offline before touching the plant.

Availability degradation -- adversarial
Compromising or stalling the controller node or its inference and sensor pipeline forces fallback to PID or manual control, or a trip, possibly timed to a load or grid event. The fallback path itself needs qualification.

Simulator fidelity and generalization gap -- implicit, exploitable
Training and testing on a reduced-order model with no spatial flux, drum-worth nonlinearity, actuator lag, burnup or sensor dynamics means the policy can issue confident but wrong drum commands out of distribution (post-trip xenon, aged core, unusual load profile), and the 1% result is simulator-versus-simulator evidence. An adversary could push the plant toward regions where the policy is unreliable, or use the resulting anomaly as cover for sabotage.

Narrow noise-robustness validation -- implicit, exploitable
Robustness was shown only for random added noise, not bias, drift, stuck or dropped sensors, or correlated failures, so the policy has no tested response to realistic or structured sensor faults. This creates false assurance that an adversary can exploit with slow bias that stays inside the validated noise envelope.

Opacity, non-repeatability and goal misalignment -- implicit, exploitable
Neural policies lack gain and phase margin analysis, retraining with different seeds yields different behavior, and a reward tuned for load tracking may trade away safety margin. A malicious weight change or abnormal drum motion is therefore hard to distinguish from legitimate learned behavior or retraining.

Multi-agent coupling -- implicit, exploitable
Shared observations and emergent drum-to-drum interaction, such as asymmetric positions causing core tilt that point kinetics cannot show, can amplify one agent's or one sensor's error across all drums. An adversary needs to corrupt only one shared input to gain core-wide leverage.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Strong benchmark results against PID invite over-trust and unattended operation, leaving operators out of the loop, deskilled and slow to spot a degrading policy or an RL versus fallback mode mismatch. An adversary can rely on this reduced scrutiny and on the opacity of the policy to pass malicious actions off as normal behavior.

Qualification and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
No accepted V&V or licensing path exists for a learned controller on reactivity actuators, pushing toward either premature autonomy or ad hoc deployment, and policy updates without rigorous change control create a legitimate-looking channel for inserting altered weights.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is a simulation-only research controller that would command control drums, which are reactivity-control actuators and so sit at the top of the safety hierarchy. Any real consequence therefore depends on whether the RL policy is ever allowed to move drums without independent protection. In practice the reactor protection system (scram, rate and limit trips, drum-speed limits, interlocks) and the operator remain the barriers. The vulnerabilities worth raising are therefore (a) a policy validated on a low-fidelity point-kinetics model that meets conditions it never saw, (b) a sensor or measurement path that an adversary or a fault can manipulate, and (c) erosion of those independent barriers, through qualification gaps or automation trust, as autonomy is increased for remote or unattended microreactor operation.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Model-fidelity and generalization gap (OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0201.01). The policy is trained and tested only on a point-kinetics model with lumped thermal and xenon feedback. It has no spatial flux tilt, drum-worth nonlinearity or interaction between drums, no heat-pipe or thermal-hydraulic dynamics, no burnup or temperature-coefficient drift, and no sensor lag. Out-of-distribution states, such as xenon transients after a trip, end-of-life core conditions or an unusual load profile, can drive the agent to aggressive or oscillatory drum motion. That risks power or temperature excursions, unplanned trips, fuel or moderator thermal stress, and loss of availability. The 1% error on 300-minute runs is a simulator-vs-simulator result and should not be read as evidence about the plant. (2) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0403). Neural policies lack the gain and phase margin analysis that licensing relies on for PID. Training seeds and stochastic action sampling make behavior hard to qualify. Multi-agent coordination adds emergent drum-to-drum interactions, such as asymmetric drum positions causing core tilt, that point-kinetics cannot expose (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). (3) Automation trust (OP.C0101.03, .04, .06). Good benchmark performance against PID invites over-trust. Operators of a remote or lightly staffed microreactor may skill-fade, and may not recognize a degrading policy or a mode mismatch between RL and fallback PID, so they would intervene late. (4) Governance gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). There is no accepted qualification path for an ML controller driving reactivity actuators, which pushes toward either unsafe deployment or indefinite advisory-only use. (5) Noise-robustness claims cover only added Gaussian noise (OP.C0302.01). They do not cover bias, drift, stuck or dropped sensors, or correlated sensor failure.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Sensor and measurement-path manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Slow bias or crafted perturbation of neutron-flux or temperature signals can steer a neural policy more subtly than it would steer a PID loop. A PID controller's response to such perturbation is bounded and well understood, while a learned policy's is not. The consequence is drum motion that is not consistent with true core state, such as masking a real power rise or inducing unnecessary swings. The attacker needs only the I&C data path, not the model. The protection system acts as the independent barrier, but only if it uses separate, diverse sensors. (7) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0076). Poisoned training environments, simulators or RL libraries, or a tampered policy file, could embed a trigger-conditioned behavior that passes benchmarking and activates under a specific load pattern or state. Training and retraining pipelines for a vendor-supplied fleet controller become a high-value target, and a shared policy could propagate across sites (OP.C0602). (8) Denial or degradation (AML.T0029, AML.T0112). Compute or software compromise of the controller node forces a fall-back to manual or PID operation, or a trip at a bad moment, and could be timed to coincide with a load or grid event. Remote update or telemetry links create a cyber-physical attack surface (OP.C0601). The conventional protections are hardware-enforced drum rate and position limits, one-way data diodes, and the independent protection system. Harm from the AI layer should be bounded to availability loss unless those protections are also defeated or bypassed through authorization of wider autonomy.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is a PPO policy trained entirely in a low-fidelity point-kinetics simulator with thermal and xenon feedback, then benchmarked against PID in the same simulator. The pipeline's weakest points are therefore the simulator-to-reality gap and the narrow training distribution (short transients, Gaussian-style noise). The RL policy is effectively a black-box function of the observation vector. Its safe behaviour exists only on the state-action manifold it was trained on, and the paper's own 300-minute generalization result is evidence from one simulator, not a qualification basis. In the multi-agent variant, each per-drum agent consumes shared core-wide information, so one corrupted or biased shared signal propagates to every actuator at once. This makes the data channel a bigger exposure than the network weights.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and model-fidelity gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0303). The policy is trained and tested on the same reduced-order model, which has no spatial effects, drum-worth nonlinearity, actuator backlash or delay, or sensor dynamics. Closed-loop performance parity with PID is thus a property of the simulator, and an unmodeled regime such as a different burnup state, xenon history or fuel temperature coefficient could produce confident but wrong drum commands. Dependent function: reactivity control and load following. Consequence: power or temperature excursions, or unnecessary trips. (2) Out-of-distribution inference (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). Training on short transients and testing on long ones is mild extrapolation. Real operation has component aging, sensor faults, off-nominal initial conditions and unusual load profiles. A PPO policy has no built-in OOD detector or uncertainty estimate, so it fails silently. (3) Noise robustness is narrowly validated. Robustness to simulated noise does not cover bias, drift, stuck-at or dropout faults, which are the realistic sensor failure modes (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0603). (4) Opacity and qualification gaps (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0402.02, OP.C0403, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Stochastic training and seed dependence mean retrained policies differ. Neural-network policies resist the deterministic verification, V&V and licensing evidence that PID gains satisfy. There is no formal guarantee of bounded behaviour, and reward shaping may encode objectives, such as tracking error over safety margin, that are misaligned with safety (OP.C0301). (5) Multi-agent coupling (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). Shared observations and coordination can amplify one agent's error or a single sensor fault across all drums, and emergent miscoordination is hard to test exhaustively. (6) Human factors (OP.C0101.01, .06). An autonomous microreactor operated with minimal staff leaves operators out of the loop, with skill fade and over-trust in a controller that benchmarked well.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Observation-channel manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0041). The small-perturbation sensitivity of deep policies lets an adversary who can alter or spoof power, temperature or xenon-estimate inputs craft inputs that steer the drums, while staying plausible to a simple range check. Time-correlated perturbations that exploit the policy's learned dynamics are more dangerous than random noise, and PID is easier to bound. Shared core-wide inputs make this a single point of leverage across all agents. (b) Supply-chain and model-integrity compromise (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076). The pipeline depends on open-source RL libraries, simulator code and model weight files. Tampered weights, a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004) or a poisoned simulator or reward function could embed unsafe behaviour that only appears under specific states and passes nominal benchmarks. (c) Retraining or online-update poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0031). If operational data is later used for fine-tuning, an adversary can bias it gradually. (d) Reconnaissance and proxy building (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0005, AML.T0013). The paper and any open code reveal architecture, algorithm, hyperparameters and reward structure, which lets an attacker build a faithful proxy model for offline adversarial optimization. (e) Availability (AML.T0029, AML.T0046). Flooding or stalling the inference or sensor pipeline forces fallback to manual or PID control, which is a degradation path that has itself to be qualified.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial lens, an RL policy that directly commands control-drum position is a different class of asset from an advisory tool. It is a learned, opaque actuator-side controller whose behavior is fixed in weights that few people can inspect. Microreactors will probably be remote, lightly staffed or autonomous, and sited with thinner security and operator presence than large plants. Both facts raise the value of compromising the policy, the surrounding training pipeline or the sensor stream feeding it. The documented work is simulation-only, so there is no deployed attack surface yet, but the paper's design choices (point-kinetics training, noise robustness benchmarking, multi-agent shared state) show where an insider or supply-chain adversary would act and where non-adversarial gaps would give cover for an attack.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Policy/model integrity: the weights, reward function and training environment are a new high-value insider target. A subtle backdoor or poisoned policy (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0043.004) could behave well across validation scenarios yet respond to a rare trigger, such as a particular power-demand profile or sensor pattern, by driving drums in a way that erodes margin, causes xenon-driven power oscillation or produces a trip. Because the policy is opaque (OP.C0401), a malicious change is hard to tell from legitimate retraining. Sabotage can be timed to a load-following event or outage. (2) Sensor-channel manipulation: the agent trusts power, temperature and xenon-related measurements. Spoofed or biased inputs (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) can steer the learned policy off the intended trajectory while PID-style plausibility checks are absent. The reported noise robustness covers random noise, not adversarial structured perturbations, so it may give false assurance. In a multi-agent design the shared core-wide state gives one compromised input or agent a path to bias every drum (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). (3) Supply chain and tooling: the RL stack (PPO libraries, simulators, pretrained checkpoints, containers) is typically open-source Python (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.004). Compromise upstream or in the vendor's development environment propagates into a control system far more consequential than ordinary analytics. If a vendor trains one policy and ships it across a fleet of identical microreactors, a single compromise propagates (OP.C0602). (4) Reconnaissance and extraction: published architectures, hyperparameters and open training code let an adversary build a proxy model (AML.T0005, AML.T0000) and develop attacks offline, so the 'security by obscurity' of proprietary control logic is weaker.

IMPLICIT (exploitable or timeable). (a) Sim-to-real and drift gap: training on a low-order point-kinetics model with xenon and thermal feedback omits spatial effects, drum-worth nonlinearity, actuator lag and fuel burnup. Real behavior will go out of distribution (OP.C0302, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0303, OP.C0203), and with no operational data on new-build designs, there is nothing to calibrate against. Extrapolation from short training transients to 300-minute runs shows some generalization but not coverage of off-nominal states. An adversary can push the plant into regions where the policy is unreliable, and an anomalous fault is also a convenient cover for sabotage. (b) Automation trust and skill fade: if the RL controller routinely beats PID, operators and the regulator may drift toward unattended operation, so the people who could spot manipulated behavior or take over are no longer there (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Because of the opacity of the policy, explaining why a drum moved is difficult, so malicious actions can pass as 'learned behavior'. (c) Qualification and regulatory gap: no accepted V&V framework exists for learned safety-relevant control (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402). Retraining or updating policies without rigorous change control creates a legitimate-looking channel for insertion of altered weights. (d) Goal misalignment: a reward tuned for load tracking may trade away margin, wear or conservative behavior near limits (OP.C0301), and an adversary can exploit that tradeoff. Overall, a nation-state is likelier to go after the training pipeline, update process or sensor inputs than to attack the model directly, and the protections should sit there: an independent non-AI protection system, a hard-limited actuation envelope, and signed and audited model artifacts.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sensor-channel manipulation, policy and supply-chain compromise, the sim-to-real gap, opacity and qualification gaps, and automation trust; these were merged into single threats. I kept proxy-model reconnaissance and availability degradation as distinct adversarial threats, but dropped narrower ATLAS codes with weak traceability (AML.T0041, AML.T0046, AML.T0010.004, AML.T0013, AML.T0002) and OP.C0203, since the use case is a simulation study rather than a new-build data problem.

evidence.citation: "Nuclear microreactor transient and load-following control with deep reinforcement learning," Energy Conversion and Management: X (Elsevier), Vol. 27, 101090 (2025); Tunkle, Abdulraheem, Lin, Radaideh (University of Michigan / Idaho National Laboratory)
evidence.note: The paper builds RL controllers, both single-agent and multi-agent, for load-following in a simulated microreactor using a point-kinetics model with thermal and xenon feedback. It compares them with a PID controller. The RL agents matched or beat PID on short transients, stayed within about 1% error on long 300-minute scenarios despite training only on short ones, and held up better under added measurement noise. The work is simulation-only, with no physical deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is policy or pipeline compromise, or sensor manipulation, acting on reactivity-control actuators. This could erode safety margin, cause oscillation or a trip, and mask a real power rise, but independent protection systems remain a barrier, so a radiological release is not the direct outcome.

reproducibility.why: Sensor-channel bias and the sim-to-real gap are reliable once the conditions exist, such as a tampered input or an out-of-distribution state. Trigger-conditioned backdoors and timed availability attacks depend on specific conditions and on the independent protection layers not intervening.

exploitability.why: The worst threats need access to the sensor channel, the training pipeline or supply chain, or the controller node, which means insider, supply-chain or well-resourced capability. Only the proxy-model and reconnaissance steps are achievable externally.

affected_users.why: Multi-agent shared state lets one corrupted input bias every drum and so the whole core. A vendor-trained policy shipped across a fleet propagates one compromise to every site, though the scope is a single microreactor or fleet rather than a broad grid.

discoverability.why: The paper publishes the architecture, algorithm, hyperparameters and reward structure. Adversarial-ML weaknesses such as sensor perturbation, poisoning, sim-to-real gaps and opacity are well documented in the open literature for this class of AI system. Plant-specific integration details would still need to be inferred.

use_case: Swin-Transformer image-restoration network with dynamic cross-attention (Swin-DCIR) that reconstructs transmission attenuation images in tomographic gamma scanning (TGS) of low- and intermediate-level radioactive waste drums. It preserves edge detail and reduces noise compared with algebraic iterative and residual-network reconstructions. The aim is better non-destructive assay of drum contents, because the transmission image is the basis for the later emission-image reconstruction.
incurred_insecurity:
Swin-DCIR is not on a protection path, but it produces the transmission attenuation map that corrects the emission reconstruction, and so it sets the activity and nuclide inventory reported for LLW/ILW drums. Its main threats are implicit: it can hallucinate or erase structure, it fails silently on real waste that differs from its simulated training data, and it cannot be qualified under current frameworks. The adversarial threats are tampering with the model or its data chain and manipulating input projections, which would hide drum contents behind a clean, credible-looking image.

Hallucinated or erased features -- implicit, exploitable
A network optimised for sharp, edge-preserving images can invent or smooth away small dense inclusions, voids or thin shielding, so attenuation correction is wrong while the image looks better. An insider could place or configure drum contents so that a masking feature falls in this blind spot, relying on the output's apparent credibility to hide it.

Sim-to-real distribution shift and data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Training on simulated or limited phantom drums leaves the network outside its envelope on heterogeneous matrices, high densities, abnormal counting statistics, detector aging or geometry changes. It then returns confident but wrong attenuation maps with no uncertainty flag, biasing activity and LLW/ILW or transport classification. An adversary could deliberately choose drum configurations or timing in these regimes, knowing no alarm will trip.

Qualification gap and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
PSNR/SSIM image quality does not establish quantitative assay accuracy, and the model is opaque, with no traceable uncertainty budget and with retraining or version changes that can silently shift bias. The lack of an accepted qualification regime lets a malicious model swap or retrain pass as a routine update.

Automation trust and cascading bias -- implicit, exploitable
Operators who see clean images stop checking raw projections or the iterative baseline, and conventional reconstruction skill fades, while a transmission error propagates unchecked into every emission reconstruction and activity declaration. An insider can rely on this misplaced trust and the lack of independent cross-checks so that a single manipulated step goes unquestioned across many drums.

Model, weights and training-data tampering -- adversarial
A supply-chain or insider compromise of pretrained weights, simulation datasets, software or the deployed model, including a backdoor triggered by a drum signature, can systematically suppress attenuating features. The result is concealed or misdeclared activity, nuclear material or waste category in safeguards, accountancy and transport records, with the change left invisible because outputs remain smooth.

Input perturbation of projection data -- adversarial
An actor with access to the acquisition or processing chain can craft or modify transmission projections or stored reconstructions so the non-robust, unconstrained network restores a benign-looking image. This hides a source or shielding without an obvious anomaly in the output.

Open-literature reconnaissance and proxy modelling -- adversarial
The published architecture lets an adversary build a proxy model to study failure regions and prepare the above attacks offline.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Swin-DCIR sits in the middle of the assay chain for LLW/ILW drums. Its transmission attenuation map is used to correct the later emission (gamma) reconstruction, which gives the activity and nuclide inventory that drives waste-acceptance, transport classification, and safeguards/accountancy declarations. A learned restorer that produces clean, sharp-edged images can look more trustworthy than it is, because it may smooth over or invent structure (dense inclusions, voids, shielding, matrix heterogeneity). The attenuation errors then flow silently into the activity estimate as a systematic bias. This differs from an alarm-type AI. Nothing trips when it is wrong, and the downstream consumers (assay software, waste-acceptance staff, transport classifiers) see only a plausible number. Existing practice does mitigate this: calibration with standard drums, periodic QC checks, dose-rate cross-checks at the drum surface, and conservative uncertainty margins. All of these assume the reconstruction behaves like a characterized, deterministic algorithm, and a neural restorer erodes that assumption.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Content fidelity failure: the network is trained mostly on simulated or phantom drums (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0202). It may hallucinate or erase small high-density features such as hot-particle clusters, lead or shielding inserts, and voids. The reconstruction looks sharper while the attenuation correction is wrong, so activity is under- or over-estimated, and a drum may be misclassified across an LLW/ILW or transport limit, or have its fissile or nuclide content misdeclared (OP.C0304.01/.03). (2) Distribution shift: real drums differ from training data in matrix type, density, fill height, drum geometry, detector aging, and scan-geometry changes. Out-of-distribution inputs give confident but wrong images with no built-in uncertainty flag (OP.C0302, .03, OP.C0401). (3) Qualification mismatch: image-quality metrics such as PSNR/SSIM and edge preservation are not the same as quantitative assay accuracy. Nuclear QA and measurement-uncertainty frameworks (traceable calibration, stated MDA and bias) have no accepted way to qualify a learned reconstructor, and retraining or version changes can silently change the bias (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0402). (4) Automation bias: operators who see clean images stop checking the raw projections or the algebraic baseline (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). Errors in the transmission step also propagate into the emission reconstruction, giving cascading, correlated bias across many drums (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Integrity attack on model weights, training or fine-tuning data, or the software supply chain (AML.T0010, T0018.000, T0020, T0031, T0076). A backdoor or trigger could, for example, make the model suppress an attenuating feature of an adversary's choosing. That would hide diversion, mask misdeclared or higher-category waste, or cause systematic misstatement in safeguards or transport records. It is a stealthy, low-signature route to an insider- or supplier-enabled falsification. (6) Adversarial perturbation or tampering of projection or sinogram data upstream of the network, or of the stored reconstructions (AML.T0043, T0015, T0059). Detector-signal manipulation is amplified by a non-robust network. (7) Denial or degradation of the AI step (AML.T0029) pushes sites back to slower, lower-fidelity methods and creates assay backlogs and storage or transport delays, which is a nuisance rather than a safety issue. Consequence ceiling: consequences are mostly regulatory, accountancy, and transport-compliance harms from a persistent bias, not an immediate criticality or release event. Independent safeguards (surface dose-rate measurement, calibration drums, paired NDA, administrative controls) must also fail for harm to materialize. Severity is highest where TGS results are the sole characterization basis or where an insider can exploit the opacity.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, Swin-DCIR is a learned inverse-problem solver that sits upstream of a physics computation. The transmission image yields attenuation coefficient maps, which are used to correct the emission-image reconstruction and, ultimately, the activity quantification of a waste drum. The central fragility is that a network trained to produce visually clean, edge-preserving images is optimizing perceptual or pixel-wise fidelity, not quantitative attenuation accuracy. It can hallucinate or smooth structure, and the error is then multiplied through the downstream correction, where it is hard to see. Training almost certainly relies on Monte Carlo or simulated TGS data, or on a small set of bench-measured mock drums, because real drums with ground-truth matrix, density and void distributions are scarce. Real waste is heterogeneous (dense inclusions, voids, unusual matrices, hot spots, detector drift, and count-rate and low-statistics regimes), so the inference-time input distribution is likely to fall outside the training distribution. The network gives no calibrated uncertainty, and its failures look like plausible clean images rather than visible artifacts.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). Mechanism: training on simulated or limited phantom drums, with noise models and geometries that differ from real detectors and real waste. When a drum contains an unmodeled dense inclusion, a void, an unusual matrix or abnormal counting statistics, the network emits a confident, smooth reconstruction with wrong attenuation values. Dependency: the emission reconstruction and activity quantification of the drum. Consequence: biased assay results, with possible misclassification of waste category (LLW vs ILW), transport or disposal-limit exceedance, and under- or over-declared inventory that undermines waste-acceptance and safeguards or accountancy records. (2) Content fidelity failure (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03). Mechanism: a restoration network trained on edge sharpness can invent or erase small features, including thin high-Z shielding or a localized absorber that masks a source. The output cannot be told apart from a true reconstruction. (3) Qualification and opacity gaps (OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0403). Mechanism: image-quality metrics such as PSNR and SSIM do not translate into quantitative assay uncertainty. There is no traceable uncertainty budget, the model is opaque, and training and inference non-determinism and framework or version changes undermine reproducibility for regulatory assay methods. (4) Drift and lifecycle (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0204). Mechanism: detector aging, source decay, collimator or geometry changes and new waste streams shift the input distribution, and without monitoring or periodic requalification the error is silent. (5) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). Mechanism: operators see clean images and over-trust them, and skill with conventional iterative reconstruction fades. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data and model poisoning or supply-chain compromise (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). Mechanism: tampered simulation datasets, pretrained Swin weights or libraries, or a backdoor triggered by a specific drum signature that causes systematic attenuation underestimation or masking. Consequence: concealed or misdeclared radioactive content, a safeguards and security concern about diversion or mischaracterization. (7) Inference-time input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031). Mechanism: an insider with access to the acquisition or processing chain perturbs the raw transmission data, or arranges the drum contents or shielding geometry, so that the network's output hides a source, exploiting the network's lack of physics constraints. (8) Model or artifact tampering after deployment (AML.T0076, AML.T0018, OP.C0502). Mechanism: replacement or corruption of weights on a workstation with weak software hygiene or integrity controls. Consequence: silent bias across all assays until detected. The same weakness is reproduced across sites if the model is shared (OP.C0602, OP.C0603).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, Swin-DCIR does not sit on a safety-protection path, but it sits upstream of a safeguards and waste-acceptance number. The transmission attenuation map corrects the emission image, so a deliberately or accidentally biased transmission image propagates into the reported activity and nuclear material content of a drum. A deep restoration network that 'preserves edge detail' by synthesizing plausible structure is an attractive place for an insider or supply-chain adversary to hide a bias, because the output looks cleaner and more credible than the raw reconstruction it replaces. A sophisticated adversary would more likely attack the data and model-update chain than the physics, since the model is a small, opaque artefact that few operators can independently audit, and it concentrates trust in one reconstruction step that downstream steps do not re-check.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Model or weights manipulation and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0010.001, T0076). A tampered or backdoored model, or a poisoned retrain on simulated or bench TGS data (T0020, T0043.004), could systematically bias attenuation in chosen regions or density ranges. For example, it could under-represent a dense or shielding inclusion so that a diversion, mis-declaration or non-compliant waste form is hidden within a drum. Dependent functions are waste acceptance, transport classification, and inventory/safeguards accounting for LLW/ILW drums. Consequences are mis-characterized activity, possible transport or disposal limit breaches, and undetected material substitution (OP.C0702.01). (2) Insider or valid-account pathway (T0012, T0044). Staff who control reconstruction software or the drum scan pipeline can swap the model or tune the pre/post-processing, and the change leaves no obvious trace because the output stays smooth and plausible. An adversary could also craft or modify raw projection data (T0043, T0015) so the network 'restores' a benign-looking image. (3) Cloud or vendor dependency and open-literature reconnaissance (T0000, T0002.001, T0005). Published architectures let adversaries build proxy models and study failure regions, and any off-site model hosting or update channel adds an access path (OP.C0601). IMPLICIT, exploitable by timing: (4) Hallucination or over-smoothing in restoration (OP.C0304.01, C0304.03). Learned priors can invent or erase small high-contrast features, and an adversary could exploit this in drum configurations that fall outside the training distribution. (5) Distribution shift and data scarcity (OP.C0302, C0201.01/.02, C0202). The network is likely trained on simulated or limited drum matrices and so generalizes poorly to heterogeneous, high-density or unusual real waste, and an adversary could pick such drums deliberately. (6) Automation trust and opacity (OP.C0101.04, C0401, C0501). Operators see a cleaner image, trust it, stop checking against iterative baselines, and skill in the older method fades (C0101.06), while no AI-specific qualification regime exists for the model. (7) Error propagation to emission reconstruction (OP.C0603, C0301.01). A transmission error is silently amplified into the assay result with no independent cross-check, so a single compromised or drifted step carries through to the final assay. Overall this is a moderate-value target: nation-state actors would likely prefer simpler routes, but an insider seeking to conceal drum contents would find it a low-visibility, high-credibility manipulation point.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on hallucination/over-smoothing, sim-to-real shift, qualification opacity, automation trust, error propagation, and model/data tampering as the core threats. I merged duplicates, dropped the low-value denial-of-service and cloud-dependency points, and kept recon as a brief distinct item from the security specialist.

evidence.citation: "Swin-DCIR based for transmission image reconstruction of TGS nuclear waste drums," The European Physical Journal Plus (Springer), vol. 140, art. 474 (2025)
evidence.note: The authors propose and test a deep-learning model that combines a Swin Transformer with dynamic cross-attention and a variable-kernel convolution module. It reconstructs TGS transmission images of waste drums, and they present it as an improvement over algebraic iterative and ResNet-based methods. I only retrieved the abstract and bibliographic pages, not the full text.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is tampering or insider masking that causes concealed or misdeclared activity, nuclear material or waste category in safeguards, accountancy and transport records. This is safeguards falsification, but it sits off the protection path and does not directly cause a release, so I score it just below the maximum.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real shift, hallucinated or erased features and silent bias propagation recur reliably whenever drums fall outside the training envelope, and the model gives no uncertainty flag. Backdoor and tampering effects are deterministic once the model is compromised.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (weight or data-chain tampering, manipulating acquisition or processing projections, insider drum configuration) need insider or privileged access to the assay chain and some ML skill, so they are not routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: A transmission error propagates into every emission reconstruction and activity declaration, which affects many drums and downstream waste classification and transport records. It stays within one assay and waste-management function and does not reach facility-wide coupled safety systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture is published in the open literature, and the failure modes (hallucination, sim-to-real shift, lack of qualification) are well documented for deep-learning image reconstruction. An adversary can build a proxy model to probe failure regions offline, but knowing the specific deployment and data chain still needs some insider knowledge.

use_case: Reduced-order hybrid GRU–LSTM recurrent neural network, working in an SVD-derived latent space, to predict long-term spatiotemporal xenon-135 distributions in a PWR core. Its outputs include power peak factor estimates, and it is meant to support reactor stability and operational management without needing precise initial xenon/iodine distributions.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory xenon-135 forecaster is trained and validated only on simulated HPR1000 data and compresses core states through a fixed SVD basis, so its main insecurity is quiet, confident error in peak-factor and xenon-distribution forecasts, not direct control compromise. Implicit threats include simulation-to-plant distribution shift, a truncated-basis blind spot, opacity with weak qualification, and operator over-trust. Adversarial threats centre on poisoning of the training data, basis or weights, manipulation of live inputs, and theft of core-design information. Independent protection and measured limits bound the safety effect, but the tool can erode margin awareness without raising any alarm.

Simulation-to-plant distribution shift -- implicit, exploitable
The network and SVD basis are fitted only to simulated trajectories of one design, so real burnup, rod histories, detector noise and non-standard load-follow fall outside the training envelope and give silently wrong, optimistic peak-factor forecasts. An adversary could time a manipulation to load-follow or post-refuelling periods when accuracy is predictably worst and deviations are easiest to attribute to model error.

Truncated latent-basis blind spot and error accumulation -- implicit
A fixed SVD basis cannot represent rare spatial patterns such as azimuthal or local xenon oscillations, and autoregressive latent errors compound over long horizons, so local peaking can be underestimated while forecasts look smooth. An adversary gains little here beyond what the distribution-shift threat already provides.

Over-trust, skill fade and scope creep -- implicit, exploitable
The claim that no precise initial xenon/iodine state is needed removes a cross-check, so operators may accept fast forecasts over core-follow codes and flux maps, lose manual xenon-management skill, or see the advisory tool drift into decision use. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust so that falsified or biased advisory outputs go unchallenged.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
GRU-LSTM hidden states are hard to explain, training is seed-dependent, and a research prototype has no QA basis, validity envelope, uncertainty bounds or configuration control, so silent corruption or an unverified retrain cannot readily be detected. An adversary could hide tampering with weights or the basis inside this unauditable behaviour, and one flawed version shared across a fleet would become a common-cause planning error.

Training-pipeline and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with simulator outputs, the SVD basis or the checkpoint, including a regime-triggered backdoor, can bias peak-factor forecasts in specific burnup or transient conditions while passing average validation metrics. The consequence is eroded thermal-margin awareness or a mis-timed power maneuver.

Input manipulation on the live data path -- adversarial
Spoofed or biased detector, rod-position or historian inputs, including structured perturbations of the low-dimensional latent state, can steer forecasts toward false reassurance or spurious derates. The paper's noise robustness is benign-noise only and does not show resistance to such attacks.

Model and data extraction -- adversarial
Queries or theft of the weights, SVD basis and training sets can reveal core design and loading-pattern behaviour of a proprietary reactor design. This is a secondary concern, relevant mainly to confidentiality and proliferation sensitivity.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, xenon-135 spatial oscillations are slow (hours), and operators already manage them through axial offset limits, ex-core and in-core detector monitoring, the core monitoring system (e.g., on-line nodal codes), and Technical Specification limits on peaking factors. A reduced-order surrogate used only as an advisory forecast for operational planning is therefore unlikely to cause harm by itself, because several independent safeguards (measured flux maps, protection system trips, LCO margins) would also have to fail. The real concern is quiet erosion of those margins: a model trained purely on simulated HPR1000 data and claiming to work without precise initial xenon/iodine states could give confident but wrong peak-factor estimates under conditions it was never trained for. Operators or fuel/load-follow planners might then trust it over slower and more conservative methods, or use it to justify tighter margins or more aggressive load maneuvers. An adversary or a fault upstream in the data pipeline could exploit this by corrupting the inputs or the model to create believable but wrong forecasts of core behavior.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
1) Simulation-to-plant gap (implicit). The paper's evidence comes from simulated data on a single reactor design. Real cores differ in burnup, fuel loading pattern, control rod histories, detector calibration, and measurement noise. Out-of-distribution behavior (non-standard load-follow, rod-insertion transients, power-maneuver profiles, end-of-cycle conditions, new fuel cycles or designs) can make peak-factor forecasts wrong without warning. The SVD latent basis is fixed at training time, so states outside the span of the training snapshots are projected onto the wrong subspace and the error is silent. Consequence: an optimistic peaking-factor or axial-offset forecast that leads planners toward operating closer to limits than is justified, eroding thermal margin (DNB/linear heat rate) if the independent monitoring and Tech Spec surveillance are weakened or relied on less.

2) Over-trust and automation bias (implicit). The 'no precise initial xenon/iodine needed' claim is attractive because those states are not directly measured, but it also means the model cannot be easily checked against a known state. Operators and reactor engineers who see good average agreement may accept predictions without cross-checking against core-follow code calculations or flux maps, and skills for manual xenon management can fade. RNN outputs offer little physical explainability, so it is hard to recognize when a forecast has gone wrong. The model is advisory, not safety-class, so a reviewer would need to confirm it is never promoted into a decision path (e.g., rod-control guidance, automated load-follow scheduling) without qualification. Mode or scope creep from advisory to decision-driving is the main escalation route to consequential harm.

3) Adversarial or integrity attacks on inputs and model (adversarial). The model depends on historical and online core data (power history, detector readings, rod positions) and a model artifact distributed from a development environment. A supply-chain or insider modification of the weights, the SVD basis, or the training data (poisoning, backdoor trigger on particular operating patterns) could bias peak-factor forecasts subtly enough to pass validation on average metrics. Manipulated sensor or historian data fed to the model could produce misleading forecasts at a chosen moment. Consequence: degraded operational decision quality, unnecessary derates or unplanned maneuvers, or false reassurance, with the safety effect bounded by the fact that the protection system and measured limits remain independent. The model's noise robustness is a benign-noise result, not a demonstration of resistance to adversarially structured perturbations.

4) Qualification and governance gaps (implicit). A research prototype has no software QA basis, no configuration control, no determinism or repeatability guarantee, and no defined validity envelope or uncertainty bounds. Retraining or model updates may change outputs without re-verification. If a utility adopts the model through a vendor or shared tool, a single flawed model version could propagate across a fleet of similar units (cross-site propagation), creating a common-cause error in operational planning at several plants. Regulators would also need to decide how the tool is classified relative to licensed core-monitoring methods.

5) Availability and dependency effects. If operators come to rely on rapid long-horizon predictions, loss of the tool through denial of service, cloud dependency, or data-feed interruption forces a reversion to slower methods at a time when staff familiarity with them has decreased. The consequence is mostly operational delay and workload rather than a direct safety effect.

ai_engineer.argument: From the ML pipeline's perspective, this system is fragile at its foundations. It is trained and validated entirely on simulator-generated xenon fields for one reactor design (HPR1000), and it compresses them through an SVD basis fitted to that same simulated snapshot ensemble. Anything outside the span of that basis, or outside the simulated transient envelope, is either projected away silently or extrapolated by a recurrent net with no guarantee of physical consistency. The claimed benefit, working without precise initial xenon/iodine distributions, is the very place where an unobserved or ill-posed initial state could be hidden by the model's apparent stability under noise. Its outputs (peak factors) also feed a safety-relevant margin decision, so errors in the latent space can propagate directly into operating-limit judgments with little opacity-free way to check them.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulation-to-plant gap: the training data is simulated (OP.C0201.01) and the model was not deployed. Real cores differ from the reference physics model in cross-section uncertainty, burnup and fuel-cycle state, rod and boron histories, detector noise, and xenon oscillation modes. The result is distribution shift (OP.C0302, .01, .03) and a static/dynamic qualification mismatch (OP.C0303), because the network was validated on offline trajectories but would be used for closed-loop long-horizon forecasting. (2) Truncated-basis blind spot: SVD modes learned from nominal trajectories cannot represent unusual spatial patterns such as azimuthal or local xenon oscillations under asymmetric rod insertion or load-follow extremes. The reconstruction error is invisible in latent space, and peak factors can be underestimated exactly when local power peaking matters (OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03). (3) Autoregressive error accumulation over long horizons: small latent errors compound, and non-linear xenon feedback can make the predictions look smooth and confident but physically wrong. The 'intrinsic physics' claim gives no formal guarantee. Noise robustness tested on synthetic perturbations does not cover correlated sensor faults, bias, or missing channels. (4) Opacity and non-repeatability: GRU-LSTM hidden states are hard to explain to a licensing reviewer (OP.C0401), and seed-dependent training (OP.C0402.01) hinders reproducible qualification (OP.C0501). (5) Human factors: operators may trust a fast long-term forecast and neglect the conventional core-monitoring codes (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06), and the 'no initial-state needed' framing can promote over-trust. (6) Lifecycle: retraining after reload, fuel-management changes or design variants is needed but probably not governed (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0502, OP.C0602 if shared across a fleet). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Supply chain and training-data poisoning: tampering with the simulator outputs, SVD basis, or checkpoint (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000) could bias peak-factor predictions in a subtle way that is hard to detect because validation is on the same pipeline. An unnoticed bias would erode margin awareness. (b) Input manipulation on the live data path: crafted or spoofed plant-process or in-core detector inputs (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) could drive the recurrent state to benign-looking forecasts, or force spurious conservative ones that cause unnecessary derates (AML.T0031, AML.T0029). (c) Model extraction or inversion could reveal design-sensitive core physics data embedded in the SVD basis and weights (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0024.001, AML.T0035). The implicit weaknesses above (opacity, lack of OOD detection, trusted-advisor status) are what an adversary would exploit and time an attack around, for example during load follow or after a refueling transition when the model is least validated.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is a soft target that a sophisticated adversary would rarely attack for its own sake. The xenon predictor is an advisory O&M tool, and the plant's independent protection system does not depend on it. The real concern is trust.
