Its outputs (xenon distribution and power peak factor, a proxy for thermal margin) feed operator decisions during load-follow, restart and axial-offset management. A model that is quietly wrong, or quietly manipulated, can shape those decisions without tripping any alarm. The model is trained only on simulated HPR1000 data, and its headline selling point is that it works without precise initial xenon/iodine states. That means it removes a cross-check operators would otherwise have to reconcile, and it may encourage over-trust. An adversary would more plausibly use it as a stepping stone or a timing lever than as the direct target.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-pipeline and supply-chain integrity (AML.T0010.002/.003, T0020, T0018.000, T0043.004): the model is built from simulation outputs, an SVD basis and recurrent weights. A malicious insider or a compromised vendor or code-coupling toolchain could poison the simulated training data or the latent basis, or insert a backdoor trigger. The result is a systematic bias that under-predicts the peak factor or xenon oscillation in specific regimes, such as a particular burnup or load-follow transient, while looking normal in validation. The facility depends on this output for margin awareness and operating strategy. The consequence is eroded thermal-margin awareness or a mis-timed power maneuver, and this is more plausible than any direct control attack. (2) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, T0015, T0031): if the model ingests plant instrumentation or neutron-detector-derived data, tampering with a few inputs or a drifting sensor could steer predictions. The noise robustness shown in the paper is not adversarial robustness, since structured perturbations in a low-dimensional latent space can be far more effective than random noise. (3) Stepping stone and trust concentration (AML.T0012, T0053, T0112): the prediction server and its data feeds are IT/OT-adjacent assets. A foothold there could be used to pivot toward the engineering network, or to falsify advisory outputs and sow doubt during a separate event. (4) Information value (AML.T0024.002, T0035): model weights and training sets reveal core design and loading-pattern behavior for a specific reactor design, which is proprietary and could be proliferation-relevant. This is a secondary concern. IMPLICIT. (a) Sim-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.01/.02, OP.C0303): a model validated only on simulation will drift as fuel burns up, as actual operating patterns depart from training and as instrumentation ages. An adversary could time an action around this predictable loss of accuracy. (b) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102): operators who rely on the predictor lose their own xenon intuition and become less likely to question outputs, and that complacency can be exploited. (c) Opacity (OP.C0401) and qualification gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0504): an uninterpretable latent-space RNN is hard to audit for tampering or silent corruption. A latent-space truncation can omit rare spatial modes (OP.C0304.03), which hides anomalies. (d) Cascading propagation (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01): peak-factor errors can propagate into downstream planning and surveillance tools. Overall the risk is moderate, driven by trust and integrity of the training data rather than by direct attack value, and it rises sharply if the tool is ever connected to operational data feeds or used without independent verification.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-plant gap, over-trust, opacity/qualification and poisoning/input-manipulation threats; I merged the truncated-basis and error-accumulation points from the AI engineer into one implicit threat. I dropped weakly argued items (availability/DoS, stepping-stone pivot via valid accounts/agent codes) as peripheral or not tied to this offline model, and omitted unsupported codes like AML.T0029, AML.T0059 and OP.C0601.

evidence.citation: "Accelerating Long-Term Xenon Dynamics Prediction: A Reduced-Order Hybrid Recurrent Neural Network with Intrinsic Physics," Nuclear Science and Engineering (Taylor & Francis / American Nuclear Society), Vol. 200, No. 2
evidence.note: The paper builds a model that projects reactor data into a low-dimensional space with singular value decomposition, then trains a hybrid GRU-LSTM network there to forecast xenon dynamics. Numerical experiments on the HPR1000 reactor showed better xenon distribution and power peak factor predictions than traditional methods, and the model stayed stable under noise. This is a model built and tested on simulated data, not a deployed plant system.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is training-pipeline poisoning or input manipulation that biases peak-factor forecasts and erodes thermal-margin awareness or mistimes a power maneuver; the tool is advisory and independent protection and measured limits bound the effect, so this is operational disruption or minor margin erosion, not release.

reproducibility.why: Silent distribution-shift error is reliably present whenever plant conditions leave the simulated training envelope (load-follow, burnup, post-refuelling), but deliberate poisoning or input manipulation needs specific conditions or regime triggers.

exploitability.why: Adversarial paths such as tampering with the training pipeline, SVD basis or checkpoint, or spoofing live detector and historian inputs, need privileged internal access to the ML supply chain or the plant data path; the implicit failure modes need no attacker.

affected_users.why: A flawed forecast affects core-wide operational planning and could propagate across a fleet if one model version is shared, but it remains advisory and limited to one function, not coupled control systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, SVD-latent approach and simulation-only validation are public in the literature, and sim-to-real shift and generic poisoning are well-known classes; finding exploitable weaknesses in a specific deployment would still need partial inside knowledge.

use_case: Attention-based CNN–LSTM model that diagnoses the break size of a loss-of-coolant accident in an HPR1000 pressurized water reactor. It uses only the first ~12–15 seconds of plant data after the accident starts, to give operators early, real-time break-size information.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory model gives an early break-size estimate in the first ~15 seconds of a LOCA, when operator time pressure is highest, so a wrong or manipulated number can steer crew diagnosis without actuating anything. The source does not state the training data, but for a new-build HPR1000 it is almost certainly thermal-hydraulic simulation, which makes sim-to-real fragility, opacity and weak qualification the implicit core. Adversaries can attack the input path, training pipeline and deployed weights, or exploit the model's blind spots and the operators' trust in it. Independent protection systems and symptom-based EOPs bound the consequence, provided the tool does not creep into procedure selection.

Sensor-path input manipulation -- adversarial
An adversary with access to the data-acquisition path, historian or signal conditioning could inject small perturbations into the few channels that dominate the attention-weighted output in the short window. This pushes the break-size class across a boundary or masks a real LOCA signature, misdirecting the crew's early response.

Training-pipeline and weight compromise -- adversarial
Poisoned simulator scenario sets, tampered pretrained or deployed weights or normalization constants, or compromised ML toolchains could embed a backdoor that misdiagnoses specific signal patterns while passing validation on the same simulated distribution. A single corrupted model deployed across units becomes a common-cause fault.

Proxy modelling from public literature -- adversarial
The published architecture and description of the simulated training set let an adversary build a proxy model offline and craft transferable adversarial transients. These can then be tried against the deployed model without touching the plant.

Availability denial and network coupling -- adversarial
Denying or degrading the service during an accident forces a degraded-mode transition for crews who have come to rely on it. The new data path from plant instrumentation to an AI host also adds an interface and update route that can serve as a stepping stone into operational networks if segregation is weak.

Simulation-to-reality gap -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on code-generated LOCA runs with a limited scenario grid, the model has no real-event data. It returns confident wrong size bins under sensor noise, dropouts, concurrent faults, unusual break locations or early operator actions, and it has no reject option. An adversary could time or shape a physical or cyber event to fall outside the validated envelope, where the model's error is predictable and its confidence misleading.

Short-window sensitivity and silent drift -- implicit, exploitable
A 12-15 s window is sensitive to sensor latency, sampling and onset-detection misalignment, and instrument recalibration, ageing and plant modifications shift input distributions with no ground-truth LOCA feedback to reveal it. An adversary could hide gradual signal manipulation inside this unmonitored degradation, or misalign timing so inputs go out of distribution.

Opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The attention-based CNN-LSTM cannot be verified like deterministic I&C. It has unproven uncertainty calibration, uncertain seed-to-seed repeatability and no mature regulatory qualification route for a non-safety advisory that can still influence safety actions. Weak configuration control and non-reproducible outputs make unauthorized model changes or backdoors hard to detect.

Operator anchoring and vigilance erosion -- implicit, exploitable
Operators rarely see real LOCAs, so an early number can anchor diagnosis over symptom-based EOPs, with mode confusion about its advisory status, skill fade, and disuse after false alarms. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust by pairing a spoofed or induced misestimate with a real transient when scrutiny is lowest.

Objective misalignment and error propagation -- implicit
Training for bin accuracy weights errors that cross EOP decision thresholds the same as adjacent-bin errors, and a wrong class feeding downstream tools or emergency-response assessments propagates the error. No realistic adversary gains much beyond what the manipulation threats above already give.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations standpoint, this tool sits in the most time-compressed part of the plant response. LOCA break size drives the choice of mitigation strategy (SI actuation, depressurization, accumulator and RHR expectations, and transition among EOPs and SAMGs) and the operators' mental model of how much time they have. The safety-grade protection system and symptom-based EOPs do not depend on break size, so the model should be advisory only. The harm pathway is therefore a wrong or untimely number that anchors crew diagnosis or biases prioritization, and not a direct actuation. The key facility question is what a confident but wrong early estimate does to a crew in the first minutes, and whether the independent EOP and safety-system layers would still catch it.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT WEAKNESSES (no adversary needed). (1) Data provenance and scarcity: no real large-break LOCAs exist in a new-build HPR1000 fleet. Training data must come from thermal-hydraulic code simulation (RELAP/ATHLET-type) or full-scope simulator runs, so the model learns code and simulator behavior, not plant behavior (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). Real transients involve sensor noise, instrument degradation, unmodeled equipment failures, and concurrent faults (loss of offsite power, stuck valves, multiple breaks) that the labelled scenario grid probably does not cover (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). (2) Narrow time window: a 12-15 s window is sensitive to sensor latency, dropouts, sampling rate and signal-conditioning differences, and to accident-onset detection. If the window is misaligned, the model sees out-of-distribution input yet may still return a confident class (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0204). Break-size discretization and break location, which also change early signatures, may be conflated or poorly resolved at the class boundaries. (3) Qualification: attention-based CNN-LSTM models are opaque and hard to qualify for a safety-relevant role. There is no accepted V&V basis and no demonstrated error bounds, and attention weights are not a reliable explanation (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). Out-of-distribution rejection and uncertainty output matter, because a bare point estimate invites over-trust. (4) Human factors: operators who see an early number may anchor on it, which is automation bias and can displace symptom-based diagnosis (OP.C0101.04). Rarely exercised in real events, it also invites out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity and mode confusion about whether it is advisory (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.03). Underestimating the size could delay or discount large-break actions. Overestimating could prompt unnecessary action or a premature severe-accident posture. Disuse after false alarms is the opposite risk (OP.C0101.05). Consequence is bounded where independent protection and EOPs remain primary. Harm is real if the output is integrated into decision aids, crisis-center and emergency-response assessments, or source-term and emergency-classification inputs.

ADVERSARIAL SURFACES. (a) Input manipulation: an adversary with access to the instrumentation or data-acquisition path, or to a historian or data bus feeding the model, could shift a few early signals (pressure, level, flow, temperature) so the break size is misclassified. This is crafted adversarial input, or chaff/noise, and the model is brittle in a short window (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0046). The effect is most credible when timed to coincide with a real transient, or to blur diagnosis during a drill or event. (b) Training and supply chain: poisoning of the simulation datasets, code-generated scenario libraries, pretrained weights, or ML libraries could embed a backdoor or a systematic bias for particular break sizes, and would be hard to detect because validation uses the same simulated distribution (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). (c) Model integrity: tampering with the deployed weights or the preprocessing, normalization or timing pipeline gives quiet corruption (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, AML.T0031). (d) Availability: denying the service during an accident only removes an advisory aid, but that can shift the crew to a degraded workflow. (e) Plant I/O coupling: a new data path from plant instrumentation to an AI server can become a pathway into a safety-relevant or operations network if one-way data diodes and segregation are not maintained (OP.C0502, OP.C0601). Existing practice mitigates much of this: the protection system is independent and deterministic, EOPs are symptom-based, and I&C segregation separates safety from non-safety systems. These defenses must be preserved explicitly, and the tool must not be allowed to creep into automated or procedure-selection roles. Fleet-wide deployment would turn one corrupted model into a common-cause problem across units (OP.C0602).

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is a supervised time-series classifier or regressor for a rare, safety-significant event, and the data behind it is almost certainly simulated. No HPR1000 has a real LOCA record, so the training set must come from thermal-hydraulic code runs (RELAP/MAAP-class) over a swept grid of break sizes, locations and initial conditions. The model therefore inherits the simulator's fidelity limits and the grid's coverage limits. The 12-15 s window is a hard architectural choice: it is the period when signals are most transient, sensor lag and noise matter most, and the break-size signature is least separated from operator actions, ECCS actuation timing and trip logic. High reported accuracy on held-out simulated runs says little about fit to real plant instruments and conditions. Attention adds some interpretability, but attention weights are not a validated explanation, and the model still gives a single point diagnosis that operators may over-trust in a high-stress, time-compressed setting.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and data provenance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0202): training data is simulated, with no operational LOCA examples. Code-model uncertainty in early blowdown, break-flow models, noding, and sensor models that omit noise, dropout, calibration offset and lag will not transfer to the real plant. Test splits are probably random across runs from the same simulator, so they leak and overstate generalization. (2) OOD and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302.01): inputs outside the training manifold include a different fuel cycle or burnup, degraded or failed sensors, a concurrent fault such as SGTR, loss of offsite power, or failed ECCS trains, an unusual break location, or an operator action in the first seconds. The classifier has no reject option, so it will return a confident wrong size bin. Plant ageing and instrument recalibration add slow drift that nobody monitors because no ground-truth LOCA feedback ever arrives. (3) Qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0403, OP.C0401): a learned model cannot be verified like deterministic I&C. Repeatability across training seeds is unclear, and calibration of its uncertainty is unproven. Any retraining after a plant modification triggers requalification. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.03): a wrong early 'small break' diagnosis could bias operators toward a wrong EOP branch or delay escalation, and a wrong 'large break' diagnosis could cause unnecessary actions. Operators are rarely exposed to LOCAs, so skill fade and automation bias are both plausible. (5) Goal misalignment (OP.C0301): the training objective is break-size accuracy, not decision-relevant error cost, so errors that cross EOP thresholds are weighted the same as adjacent-bin errors.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031): a compromised data path, such as the historian or a network tap feeding the model, or a spoofed sensor, could inject small perturbations that move the diagnosis across a size boundary, or mask a real LOCA signature in the 12-15 s window. Short windows and a deterministic model make crafted inputs easier. (7) Supply chain and training pipeline (AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0059): poisoned or altered simulation datasets, tampered model weights, or compromised ML libraries could embed a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004), for example a particular signal pattern that yields a benign size. Simulator input decks are a high-value, low-visibility target. (8) Model exposure (AML.T0044, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005): published architectures and the likely public descriptions of the thermal-hydraulic training sets let an adversary build a proxy model and craft transferable adversarial transients offline. (9) Availability (AML.T0029): denying or degrading the model during an event removes the early advisory, and an operator staff trained to rely on it face a degraded-mode transition at the worst time. The core exposure is that a tool built on simulated data and untestable on real events sits in the operator's decision loop at the moment of highest stress.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this model is a decision-support advisory sitting in the operator's early-accident window (first ~15 s of a LOCA), when time pressure is highest and human cognitive capacity to challenge an output is lowest. That makes it a trust-concentration point: a wrong or manipulated break-size estimate does not need to actuate anything to matter, because it can steer operator prioritization (e.g., which EOP branch, how aggressively to inject, whether to expect core uncovery) at the moment an adversary or a fault would most want confusion. A nation-state would probably not target this model first, since the safety-grade I&C and procedures are the harder and more valuable path, but it is a plausible stepping stone and a cheap deception layer if it shares data feeds or infrastructure with the plant information systems. Its non-adversarial weaknesses, namely training on simulated LOCA data, a short fixed time window, and little explainability, are exactly the ones an adversary could exploit by timing or shaping an event outside the model's validated envelope.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Input manipulation or sensor-channel spoofing. The CNN-LSTM consumes a short multivariate time series of plant parameters. An adversary with access to the data path (a compromised plant-information gateway, a malicious insider, or a maintenance-time tampering of signal conditioning) could inject subtle perturbations that move the break-size class estimate while staying within plausible sensor ranges. Short windows and attention-weighted features mean a few channels may dominate the output, so small manipulations of those channels have outsized leverage (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). The facility dependency is operator situational awareness. The consequence is misdirected early response, delayed correct diagnosis, or loss of operator confidence. (2) Model or training-pipeline compromise. The model is trained largely on simulator-generated accident databases, so poisoning of the scenario set, a backdoor trigger keyed to a particular parameter pattern, or tampering with deployed weights and normalization constants by an insider or through a vendor or toolchain supply chain could produce a model that behaves normally in testing and misdiagnoses specific conditions (AML.T0010, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). Because outputs are not independently reproducible by operators, detection is hard (OP.C0401). (3) Trust-timing and vigilance erosion. If the tool is accurate in routine drills, operators may anchor on its early estimate, and an adversary or a coincident fault can time an event so the diagnosis is wrong when scrutiny is lowest (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102). A coordinated cyber-physical scenario could also pair a spoofed estimate with a real transient. (4) Stepping-stone and availability: the system adds a software component, an interface, and update paths into the operations network, offering lateral-movement and persistence opportunities. Denial of the service (AML.T0029) could degrade the advisory in an emergency and force reliance on a skill base that has faded. IMPLICIT, ADVERSARY-EXPLOITABLE: (5) Training on simulated or transferred data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203). HPR1000 is a new build with little real LOCA data, so the model's behavior under degraded instrumentation, multiple concurrent faults, unusual plant configurations, or break locations and sizes outside the simulated grid is poorly characterized (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). An adversary can aim to induce such out-of-distribution conditions, because the model gives confident class outputs without reliable uncertainty (OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (6) Drift and qualification gap. Plant modifications, instrument recalibration, and aging shift input distributions without triggering retraining (OP.C0302.01), and there is no mature regulatory pathway for qualifying a non-safety AI advisory that can still influence safety actions (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Weak configuration control and software hygiene would make unauthorized model changes hard to detect (OP.C0502). (7) Cascading misdiagnosis. A wrong break-size class feeding downstream tools or procedures propagates the error (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). Overall, the greatest security value to an adversary is not the model itself but its ability to degrade or misdirect human judgment during a short, high-stakes window, so the security case should treat it as an integrity-critical advisory, not a harmless aid.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sensor-path input manipulation, training/weight poisoning with backdoor, the simulation-to-reality gap, opacity/qualification gap and operator over-trust. I kept the AI engineer's proxy-model threat as distinct, folded the nuclear engineer's plant I/O coupling and the security specialist's stepping-stone point into the availability paragraph, and dropped AML.T0012 and the other unsupported codes.

evidence.citation: "An Attention-Based CNN-LSTM Model to Diagnose Break Size in Loss-of-Coolant Accidents," Nuclear Science and Engineering (Taylor & Francis / American Nuclear Society)
evidence.note: The authors built and tested a convolutional neural network–LSTM model with an additive attention mechanism to predict LOCA break size for the Chinese HPR1000 PWR. They report that it reaches high accuracy from short early-accident time series and improves on the baseline model without attention. The abstract does not say what kind of data was used, so I did not state it.

damage.why: Worst credible threat is a backdoored or manipulated break-size estimate, or a common-cause model fault across units, that misdirects crew diagnosis during a LOCA and erodes safety margin; independent protection systems and symptom-based EOPs bound it below a direct radiological release, so it scores 4 rather than 5.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real gaps, out-of-distribution inputs and operator anchoring recur reliably once the conditions exist, but adversarial manipulation needs a real LOCA or a precisely timed event, and the operators' EOPs and independent protection systems limit how consistently the harm follows.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats, such as sensor-path injection, weight or training-pipeline compromise and timing an attack to a real transient, need privileged access to plant data paths or the ML supply chain, which in practice means insider or advanced-actor capability; only proxy modelling from public literature is lightly resourced.

affected_users.why: A single corrupted model deployed across units becomes a common-cause fault, and a wrong class can propagate to downstream tools and emergency-response assessments, affecting the whole control room crew and potentially a fleet, though the tool stays advisory.

discoverability.why: The published architecture, the simulated-data approach and well-documented adversarial ML and sim-to-real weaknesses let a capable outsider infer that the class of weakness exists, but the specific deployment, data paths and validated envelope need partial insider knowledge.

use_case: Three-stage deep-learning accident-management support tool for a pebble-bed high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (Xe-100). An LSTM autoencoder flags anomalies in plant signals. A CNN then characterises the fault type. That result triggers an LSTM-dense network that predicts remaining time before a safety limit, such as reactor outlet temperature, is crossed. The models were trained on transients from a digital twin of the reactor, and the tool tells operators what fault is occurring and how long they have to correct it.
incurred_insecurity:
This tool places a three-stage cascade (anomaly flag, fault class, time-to-limit countdown) inside the accident-management loop, and it was trained and validated only on digital-twin transients for a reactor that has never operated. The main threats are sim-to-real and closed-set failure, error propagation through the chain, operator over-trust, an unsettled qualification basis, and adversarial manipulation of the sensor path, the training pipeline, or the tool's availability. The independent protection system limits direct harm, but the tool can still misdirect operator urgency and action during a rare, confusing event.

Sim-to-real gap and closed-set misdiagnosis -- implicit, exploitable
The models learned simulator physics and noise, so real sensor noise, instrument degradation, compound faults and unmodelled events fall outside their envelope, and the CNN, having no 'unknown' output, forces them into the nearest known fault class. An adversary could stage or coincide an action with an out-of-distribution condition that the tool will confidently misread, with no field data to expose the blind spot.

Cascading error and unreliable time-to-limit -- implicit, exploitable
The anomaly flag gates classification and the fault label conditions the regressor, so a stage-one or stage-two error becomes a precise but wrong countdown, and an optimistic estimate invites operators to delay action while a pessimistic one prompts unnecessary intervention. An adversary needs to corrupt only one early stage to steer the downstream estimate, and the opacity of the chain hides which stage failed.

Operator over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A quantitative countdown encourages anchoring and outsourced diagnosis, while nuisance alarms push crews toward disuse, and opacity prevents cross-checking against procedures. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, or deliberately induce alarm fatigue, so that a manipulated or wrong output is accepted or a real one is ignored.

Qualification, drift and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
The tool is research-stage with no settled safety classification, V&V basis under nuclear software standards, change control for retraining as the plant ages, or perimeter definition for the advisory network and model-update path. An adversary can target the weakly governed update and retraining path as a low-cost foothold.

Sensor and data-path manipulation -- adversarial
Small, plausible perturbations of plant signals through a compromised historian, data link or instrument can push the autoencoder below threshold to suppress a real anomaly, or drive the chain to a wrong fault class and time estimate. The consequence is misdirected or delayed operator response, or cover for a concurrent physical or cyber action.

Digital-twin and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Because all training data comes from a simulator, altering simulator inputs, scenario libraries, labels, retraining sets or model weights can embed latent blind spots, biased time estimates or backdoor triggers that same-simulator validation would not reveal. The simulator becomes a single point of trust for the whole tool.

Alert-credibility erosion and denial of service -- adversarial
Chaff or spoofed noise that triggers false alarms trains operators to discount the tool, and denial of the service at a chosen moment removes decision support during an accident. Both are precursors or enablers for a real attack.

Model and twin exfiltration for attack design -- adversarial
Model artifacts, thresholds, fault taxonomy and the transient library reveal plant dynamics, safety margins and which signatures are detectable. This lets an adversary design manipulations that stay beneath detection.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations lens, this tool sits in the accident-management loop, so its output shapes operator diagnosis and the time they believe they have. It is a cascaded chain: the anomaly flag gates fault classification, and the classification triggers the time-to-limit prediction. An error at stage one or two therefore propagates unchecked and produces a confident, wrong 'what and how long' answer. The models were trained only on SimuPACT digital-twin transients, with no field data from a plant that has never operated, so the simulator's fidelity bounds the tool's validity. Operators trained to the symptom-based emergency operating procedures and protected by the independent reactor protection system, which trips on hard setpoints and not on any AI output, are the main existing safeguard. Real harm needs the AI error to combine with operator over-reliance, a degraded or mis-sequenced procedure, or a protection-system or instrumentation weakness. The most credible risks are wrong guidance during a rare, confusing event and an adversary who exploits that weakness.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and OOD failure: the training data is entirely digital-twin output (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0302). Real sensor noise, calibration drift, fouling, aging, and multi-fault or unmodelled events (for example water ingress with a coincident instrument fault) fall outside the simulator envelope. The CNN would still assign the nearest known fault class, with no 'unknown' output. The facility consequence is a plausible but wrong diagnosis. (2) Overconfident or optimistic time-to-limit: the LSTM-D prediction depends on the correct fault label and on the dynamics the simulator captured. A late or optimistic estimate could lead operators to delay manual action, accept slower recovery, or spend margin before the protection system acts. A pessimistic estimate could prompt unnecessary manual trips or intervention that adds challenge to the plant. This is a goal-misalignment and content-fidelity failure (OP.C0301, OP.C0304.03). (3) Cascade error propagation across the three stages (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). A false negative at the autoencoder means no diagnosis is offered. A false positive could produce a nuisance diagnosis during a benign transient or a surveillance test. (4) Automation trust and human factors: operators may over-trust a precise-looking countdown or ignore it after nuisance alarms (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102). Skill fade follows if diagnosis is outsourced (OP.C0101.06). Opacity makes it hard to cross-check the output against procedures (OP.C0401). (5) Qualification and governance gap: the tool is a research-stage, simulation-only model. Its safety classification, V&V under nuclear software standards, retraining and change control, and the regulatory basis for advisory-versus-credited use are all unsettled (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0303). Model retraining as the plant ages creates concept-drift management problems (OP.C0302.02).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Sensor or data-path manipulation: an adversary with access to plant signals or the historian could craft inputs that evade the autoencoder (suppressing a real anomaly) or trigger false alarms. They could also steer the CNN to a wrong fault class or skew the time prediction. This is adversarial evasion via crafted data (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031). The consequence is misdirected operator action during a real event, or masking of a concurrent sabotage. It matters most as a cover or enabling step alongside a physical or other cyber action, since the protection system remains independent. (7) Supply-chain and model integrity: poisoned or backdoored digital-twin data, retraining sets or model weights could embed triggers or biased time estimates (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). The simulator becomes a single point of trust. (8) Denial or degradation of the tool during an event (AML.T0029, AML.T0046). Operators lose support exactly when the plant is stressed, which matters little if procedures remain primary but a lot if crews have come to rely on it. (9) Information exposure: model and twin artifacts reveal plant dynamics, safety margins and which signals the tool trusts, which helps an adversary design an attack (AML.T0024, AML.T0035, AML.T0037). Possible corrective constraints: keep the tool advisory only and outside the protection system, require independent sensor validation and an 'unknown/OOD' output, show uncertainty bounds, and validate against plant data once it exists.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, the main exposure is in the data and the chaining. The Xe-100 has no operating fleet, so every training transient comes from a simulator (SimuPACT). The models learn the digital twin's physics and noise, not the plant's. At inference they receive real sensor streams with real noise, calibration offsets, sensor failures and pebble-bed burnup and loading heterogeneity, none of which the simulator represents. The three stages are sequentially gated: the autoencoder's anomaly flag triggers the CNN, and the CNN's fault label conditions the time-to-limit regressor. An error at stage 1 or 2 therefore propagates into a confident, quantitative time estimate with no independent check. The fault classes are a closed set, so the CNN will force an unseen or compound fault into the nearest known label, and the regressor will then output a plausible time-to-limit for the wrong event. The demonstration on a single water-ingress case does not establish coverage, calibration or repeatability. Operators are likely to anchor on a numeric countdown during a stressful event, which makes automation bias and mode confusion worse.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Sim-to-real gap and OOD failure: training data is purely simulated, with no field data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). The autoencoder's reconstruction threshold is tuned on clean simulated signals, so it may either false-alarm on real sensor noise or miss real anomalies whose signature differs from the simulator's. (2) Closed-set misclassification and cascading error: the CNN has no 'unknown fault' option, and the time-to-limit LSTM is conditioned on its label, so wrong diagnoses become wrong, precise time estimates (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603, OP.C0403). Calibration and uncertainty bounds on the remaining-time estimate are probably absent, and an optimistic estimate would lead operators to delay action. (3) Opacity and repeatability: black-box LSTM and CNN outputs cannot be tied to physical causal reasoning, which hinders qualification for safety-related decision support (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (4) Drift: as plant configuration, instrumentation, fuel cycle and control setpoints change, the digital twin and the model diverge. Retraining against an updated twin brings its own version-control and requalification burden (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0502). (5) Human factors: a quantitative countdown encourages over-trust and skill fade, and it can crowd out procedure-based diagnosis (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06). Rare-event base rates make the real accident-condition performance essentially unverifiable (OP.C0202).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Sensor or data-stream manipulation: perturbations that stay within plausible ranges can push the autoencoder below its threshold, hiding a real fault, or can raise false alarms and drive the chain to wrong labels and times (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031). Time-series models are especially sensitive to small coordinated perturbations across channels. The consequence is delayed or misdirected operator response. (2) Supply-chain and training-pipeline compromise: because all training data comes from a simulator, poisoning the digital-twin transient library, simulator configuration, or model artifacts would embed systematic bias or a backdoor trigger that no field data would contradict (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). (3) Model and data exfiltration: a model that encodes safety-margin behaviour and a transient library reveal plant dynamics and which fault signatures are detectable. That helps an adversary design attacks that stay beneath detection (AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0013). (4) Denial of the service, or deliberate chaff data, can desensitise operators to the tool through nuisance alarms, so they disuse it or ignore it when a real event occurs (AML.T0029, AML.T0046, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.05). The implicit weaknesses above (closed-set labels, uncalibrated times, a single demonstrated scenario) make any of these attacks cheaper and harder to detect.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view this is a three-stage cascade whose output (fault type plus a time-to-limit countdown) directly shapes operator urgency and choice of corrective action during an accident. That makes it a high-value lever for an adversary. A cyber or insider actor who cannot touch the protection system could instead degrade the advisory layer's credibility or time a physical or cyber action around its blind spots. The model was trained only on digital-twin transients, so its real-plant generalization is unproven. An adversary does not need to attack it to benefit, because a naturally weak model that operators have learned to trust is itself the exploitable condition. The cascade structure compounds this: an upstream error propagates unchallenged into the countdown, and the whole chain is opaque to the operators who must act on it.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity attack on the sensor-to-model pathway. Subtly manipulated plant signals (a compromised historian, data link or instrument) could evade the LSTM autoencoder, suppressing the anomaly flag while a real fault or sabotage develops (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). Alternatively, crafted inputs could drive a wrong fault classification, so operators work the wrong procedure while the actual transient proceeds. Because the stages are chained, one stage's misclassification sets the next stage's prediction. A falsely long time-to-limit estimate is the most dangerous output, because it invites operators to delay action. (2) Supply-chain and insider poisoning of the digital-twin training pipeline (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000). The whole tool depends on simulated transients, so anyone able to alter simulator inputs, scenario sets or labels can embed blind spots or backdoor triggers that stay latent until an attacker chooses the moment. Validation on the same simulator would not reveal this. (3) Alert-credibility erosion. Injecting chaff or spoofed noise to trigger false alarms (AML.T0046, AML.T0031) trains operators to discount the tool, which is a precursor to a real attack. Denial of the service (AML.T0029) at a chosen moment removes decision support during an accident. (4) Reconnaissance value. The model's thresholds and fault taxonomy reveal which signals the plant treats as critical and which transients it recognizes, which supports attack planning (AML.T0024, AML.T0013).

IMPLICIT (exploitable by timing): Sim-to-real gap and out-of-distribution events (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0203). Real sensor noise, degraded instruments, novel or compound faults and multi-fault scenarios fall outside the simulator envelope. There is little real-plant data for a new-build design, and the paper demonstrates only one water-ingress event. An adversary can design an attack as an out-of-distribution scenario that the tool will misread confidently. Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01): operators who rely on a countdown may stop independently diagnosing, so a manipulated or wrong output is accepted. Opacity and cascading errors (OP.C0401, OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603): operators cannot see why a fault was named or a time was given, and they cannot tell which stage failed. Qualification and governance gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0503): no established path exists for qualifying learned models in accident management, and the security perimeter for the advisory network and model update path may be under-specified, which makes a low-cost foothold plausible. A sophisticated adversary would probably target the data feeds and the model update or retraining pipeline rather than the model itself, which makes those the main points to protect.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sim-to-real/OOD failure, cascade propagation, over-trust, qualification gaps, sensor manipulation, twin poisoning, chaff/denial and reconnaissance. I dropped minor codes (OP.C0402.02, AML.T0024 root, AML.T0037) that were weakly argued and kept the specific ones traceable to the text.

evidence.citation: "A system diagnostic and prognostic framework based on deep learning for advanced reactors," Progress in Nuclear Energy (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper describes an LSTM-AE, CNN and LSTM-D chain for anomaly detection, fault characterisation and remaining-time-to-threshold prediction. It was built and tested on SimuPACT digital-twin transient data of the Xe-100 pebble-bed HTGR, and demonstrated on a water-ingress reactivity-insertion event. Because it was tested only on simulated data, it is reported as an implemented model and not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is sensor/data-path manipulation or model poisoning that suppresses a real anomaly or gives an optimistic time-to-limit, misdirecting operator response during an accident (possibly masking concurrent physical action); an independent protection system limits direct harm, so this stops short of a guaranteed radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Closed-set misclassification, cascading error propagation and over-trust occur reliably whenever out-of-distribution conditions or upstream stage errors arise, since these are structural properties of the cascade architecture.

exploitability.why: Manipulating the sensor path, training pipeline or simulator inputs generally requires privileged access to plant data networks or the model development chain, plus domain knowledge of reactor dynamics, though weakly governed update paths lower the barrier somewhat.

affected_users.why: A misled accident-management tool affects the operating crew and the decisions for a whole plant or unit, but it is advisory and independent protection systems bound propagation to other coupled systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture and its simulator-only training basis are published in the open literature, and sim-to-real gaps, adversarial perturbation, poisoning and chaff are well-documented attack classes for such ML systems, though the exact thresholds and plant specifics remain non-public.

use_case: Stacked-regression ensemble learning (ridge regression, random forest, PLS and XGBoost) applied to laser-induced fluorescence and Raman spectra. It simultaneously estimates uranium(VI), samarium and nitric acid concentrations and solution temperature in nitric acid media, for near real-time in-line monitoring of reprocessing-type (PUREX-like) process streams.
incurred_insecurity:
This in-line spectroscopic monitor turns a stacked regression ensemble into a trusted real-time reading of U(VI), Sm, nitric acid and temperature in a reprocessing stream. It was validated only on synthetic D-optimal bench samples, so the main exposures are silent out-of-distribution error, calibration and drift gaps, over-trust, and weak qualification. The adversarial threats are tampering with the model, its data or its spectral inputs to hide a small bias or diversion, and degrading the monitor at a chosen moment.

Silent out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
The regressors were trained on clean U/Sm/HNO3 bench solutions and always return a point estimate, so Pu, Np, Tc, Ru and lanthanide interferents, TBP carryover, radiolysis products and fouled optics give confident but wrong U and acid values with no domain flag. Process-control and material-balance errors follow, and an adversary could introduce or wait for such conditions, hiding a diversion or off-normal chemistry inside the unflagged error.

Instrument drift and calibration transfer -- implicit, exploitable
Laser power, detector response, fiber darkening, window fouling and cross-instrument or cross-site transfer shift the spectrum-to-concentration mapping, and a model pushed fleet-wide carries one common-mode bias. Reference data for recalibration on radioactive samples are scarce, so staleness can persist. An adversary could time a manipulation to the stale, widened error band or deliberately degrade the optics to accelerate it.

Automation over-trust and opaque ensemble -- implicit, exploitable
A fast readout reporting 2-5% RMSEP invites operators and accountancy staff to drop titration, destructive assay or lab cross-checks, and the four-learner stack hides which model dominates. Correlated errors across the four jointly estimated outputs look self-consistent and mask faults. An adversary could rely on this lapse in verification to time a diversion and on opacity to hide a slow bias.

Over-reach of Sm burnup inference and missing qualification -- implicit, exploitable
The model learned concentration regression, not burnup, so using Sm as a burnup or fuel-history proxy misattributes irradiation history, and no AI-specific QA, repeatability or version-control basis exists for crediting it in a process or safeguards role. An adversary could exploit the unchallenged inference to misrepresent material origin or inventory.

Model, data and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor who poisons the training or calibration data, or alters the model files, stacking meta-learner, preprocessing or libraries, can implant a small systematic bias or trigger below the stated RMSEP. The result is an under-read of U(VI) or a skewed Sm estimate that conceals diversion or hold-up.

Spectral input manipulation -- adversarial
An adversary with physical or network access to the probe, fiber or acquisition path can inject or perturb spectra, or alter optical conditions or interferent content, so that readings stay plausible while the true composition differs. The linear ridge and PLS components ease crafting such inputs, and the absence of robust out-of-distribution detection means the ensemble still returns a confident number.

Targeted denial of the monitor -- adversarial
Corrupting or flooding the acquisition stream, or degrading the monitor, forces a fallback to slower manual analysis at a time chosen around a process upset or diversion.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an in-line analytical monitor on a reprocessing stream. Its output (U(VI), Sm, HNO3, temperature) feeds process control, criticality and chemistry limits, and possibly accountancy and burnup inference. The documented evidence is narrow: D-optimal synthetic bench samples with 2-5% RMSEP, tested in a binary U/Sm/HNO3/temperature matrix. A real PUREX stream adds Pu, Np, Tc, Zr, Ru, Nd/Eu/Gd (which quench or overlap lanthanide fluorescence), TBP/diluent degradation products, radiolysis, and fouled optical windows. These can all move spectra off the training distribution, and the ensemble gives no guarantee of flagging that. The main downstream risk is a plausible but wrong concentration reading that operators trust. The physical consequence still depends on independent protections failing: sampling and lab analysis, densitometry, redundant instrumentation, and criticality-safe geometry and limits. In practice those layers make a single wrong reading unlikely to cause harm by itself, but they would not catch a slow bias that fits the expected trend. A subtler safeguards risk is that a systematically biased or manipulated reading, used as in-line accountancy or burnup support, hides diversion or misstates inventory.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution failure (OP.C0302, .01, .03; OP.C0201.01/.02). The model is trained on clean synthetic or bench data. Real streams have interfering fission products and actinides, changing acidity and radiolysis, and window fouling, laser or detector aging and fiber darkening from radiation. Stacked regressors always return a number, so out-of-domain input yields confident, wrong U or acid values. Consequence: process-control or acid-balance errors, wrong extraction and stripping conditions, poor U/Pu partitioning and misdirected product or waste. Criticality or chemistry limits are only threatened if the independent safeguards (lab samples, redundant measurements) also fail or are ignored. (2) Calibration and transfer gaps. Ensemble performance is not validated across instruments, optical paths or sites (OP.C0303, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0602). A model pushed fleet-wide inherits one common-mode bias. (3) Human factors. Reported 2-5% RMSEP encourages over-trust and skill fade in wet-chemistry verification, and the opacity of a four-model stack hampers diagnosis of a drifting reading (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0401, OP.C0402). (4) Qualification gaps. There is no AI-specific QA basis for in-line instrument credit in a safety-significant or safeguards role (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0502). (5) Sm as a burnup proxy rests on assumptions (OP.C0304.03) and creates safeguards inference risk if treated as verification. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training or calibration data poisoning, or model-file tampering via the supply chain or the maintenance workflow (AML.T0020, T0010.003, T0018.000, T0076), which could implant a small, hard-to-detect bias or trigger. Process or accountancy values would then drift within plausible bounds, concealing diversion or off-normal chemistry. (b) Spectral-input manipulation: tampering with the spectrometer, fiber, or data path, or physically altering the optical conditions, to craft adversarial spectra (AML.T0043, T0015, T0041). The aim is falsified readings while real concentrations differ, or masking a real excursion. (c) Denial or degradation of the monitor (AML.T0029, T0046, T0031) at a time chosen around a process upset or diversion, which forces fallback to slower manual analysis. (d) Model and data exfiltration, which exposes process-condition and stream-composition information (AML.T0024, T0025, T0035). The key judgment is that engineering defenses (redundant sensors, sample verification, criticality controls) make catastrophic outcomes require multiple failures. Safeguards-grade accountancy conclusions and slow, bias-type compromise are the more credible harms because they are not caught by gross-limit alarms.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a multi-output stacked regressor (ridge, RF, PLS and XGBoost base learners feeding a meta-learner) trained on a small, D-optimally designed set of lab-prepared synthetic solutions. The ~2-5% RMSEP is an interpolation result inside a designed factor space. It says little about extrapolation into real PUREX streams, which contain Pu, Np, Tc, Zr, Ru, Nd, Eu and Gd, TBP/dodecane carryover, radiolytic degradation products, variable acidity and turbidity. Several of these quench or overlap the U(VI) and Sm3+ emission bands. None of the base learners has a native out-of-distribution detector, and tree-based models in particular clamp to training-range values and fail silently with plausible-looking numbers. The four jointly predicted outputs share one spectral input and one stacked meta-learner, so a single upstream fault such as probe fouling, laser power drift, a wavelength-calibration shift or fiber darkening propagates coherently into all four estimates at once. The use case sits in an operation and maintenance role where the outputs may be trusted as near-real-time process and accountancy information, and the pipeline has weak qualification, provenance and repeatability controls for that role.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift and silent extrapolation (OP.C0302, .01, .03, OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0303). The training data are synthetic bench solutions with a few components, whereas the deployed streams are chemically heterogeneous, radiolytically evolving and temperature-variable. Mechanism: unmodelled interferents, quenching, inner-filter effects and Raman/fluorescence baseline changes move spectra outside the training manifold. The ensemble still returns confident point estimates with no calibrated uncertainty. Consequence: biased U and HNO3 estimates feed process-control decisions, such as extraction or acidity adjustment, or material-balance information, with no flag that the model is outside its domain. (2) Instrument and calibration drift as concept drift (OP.C0302.01/.02, OP.C0204). Laser output, detector response, optical window fouling and cross-instrument transfer all change the input-to-concentration mapping. Retraining needs new reference data, such as ICP-MS or titration on radioactive samples, which are scarce and costly. The model may be silently stale, and retraining on fresh data raises its own qualification questions. (3) Sm3+ burnup inference (OP.C0301, OP.C0403). Sm is a minor, partly non-monotonic burnup indicator. The model learned concentration regression and not burnup, so using it as a burnup or fuel-history proxy over-reaches its training objective. Because Sm isotopic composition is not measured, there is a risk of misattribution. (4) Ensemble opacity and repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). Stacked meta-learners obscure which base learner dominates in which regime. Random-forest and XGBoost training seeds, plus preprocessing choices, yield non-identical models across retrains. Correlated errors across the four outputs create apparent consistency and can mask a fault. (5) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). A smooth, fast in-line readout can displace slower offline analytical verification, which erodes skills and cross-checks. (6) QA gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504). There is no established qualification path for ML analytical models in reprocessing, and the research-grade Python pipeline carries weak version and dependency control.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training and calibration data tampering (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0031). An insider or supply-chain actor who alters the reference concentrations, spectral libraries or retraining sets can introduce a systematic bias, for example a small U or Pu-proxy offset below the stated RMSEP. This is hard to distinguish from drift, and it matters most for accountancy or diversion concealment. (b) Model or pipeline manipulation (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0076). Serialized model files, preprocessing code or ML libraries can be swapped or backdoored. Because the outputs are within-tolerance regressors, the tampering is quiet. (c) Input-level evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). Someone with physical or network access to the spectrometer, fiber or acquisition stream can inject spectra, add optical perturbations or shift the baseline so that readings stay plausible while the true composition differs. The 2-5% error band gives an attacker room to operate unseen. A white-box attacker can optimize against the ridge and PLS components, which are linear and easily differentiated. (d) Availability and spoofing (AML.T0029, AML.T0046). Flooding or corrupting the acquisition stream, or forcing fallback to manual analysis, degrades monitoring at a time chosen by the attacker. (e) Reconnaissance (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0013). Open publications describe the model family, design space and spectral regions, so an adversary could build a proxy model.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this is a measurement-integrity target. A reprocessing facility's safeguards and process-control posture relies on knowing how much uranium is in each stream. An in-line optical monitor whose ML ensemble outputs U(VI), HNO3, Sm (a burnup/fission-product proxy) and temperature becomes a trusted number. A sophisticated adversary, whether an insider diverting material or a state actor concealing a diversion, would not need to hit the plant directly. Nudging or masking a reading, or timing an action around a known blind spot, would do it. The paper's evidence base is also thin: D-optimal synthetic lab samples, 2-5% RMSEP, and no plant-realistic matrices. Real streams have Pu, Np, Tc, Ru, Nd and Eu spectral interferents, radiolysis, and fouled optics. That gap between validation and operation is where silent error lives, and silent error is exactly what an adversary can time a diversion around or hide behind.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Measurement falsification and concealment. An insider or an intruder on the instrument/OT network could tamper with the trained ensemble (poisoned or backdoored model, altered weights, a swapped stacking meta-learner, or modified calibration/preprocessing). Alternatively they could manipulate spectra in transit or at the spectrometer. Four heterogeneous base learners plus a meta-learner give many places to hide a bias, and the ML output is opaque enough that a small, systematic under-read of U(VI) or a skewed Sm/burnup estimate would not be obvious. Consequence: a process-monitoring or safeguards-relevant concentration signal that understates material, so diversion or hold-up goes undetected, or criticality/solvent-extraction control margins are misjudged. The Sm-as-burnup-proxy use adds a second target: falsified burnup inference could misrepresent the origin or irradiation history of the material. (2) Supply chain and artifact compromise. Training data, pretrained libraries (XGBoost, scikit-learn), model files and retraining pipelines are a quiet insertion point, because few staff can inspect the model. Retraining on operational data lets a patient insider poison it gradually. (3) Physical and optical tampering. A laser/Raman probe is physically accessible. Fouling, misalignment, fiber manipulation, or injecting a chosen interferent shifts spectra off-distribution, and a model with no robust OOD detection will still return a confident number. (4) Stepping stone. A vendor-supported analytics workstation bridging the instrument and the control or accountancy network offers a pivot, and remote model updates or cloud-hosted retraining widen that surface. IMPLICIT, and exploitable. (5) Validation gap and OOD blindness (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0501): synthetic, D-optimal lab training does not cover real PUREX matrices (extra ions, radiolysis products, temperature/acidity excursions, organic carryover). Confident but wrong outputs arise on their own, and an adversary can wait for or induce those conditions. (6) Automation trust and complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06): once the real-time monitor looks accurate, operators and accountancy staff may stop cross-checking against destructive assay or titration. This erodes vigilance and creates a window for diversion timing. (7) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0502): the stacked ensemble is hard to audit, so tampering or silent degradation resists detection. Coupled outputs (U, HNO3, temperature, Sm jointly estimated) mean an error in one propagates to the others (OP.C0603), so a single compromised spectral feature can corrupt several process variables at once. Consequence: degraded process control, mis-stated inventories, and weakened safeguards assurance without any alarm.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on out-of-distribution blindness, over-trust, opacity, qualification gaps, and tampering or input manipulation that conceals diversion. I dropped exfiltration, open-literature reconnaissance and the OT-pivot stepping-stone as weakly argued or restating other threats, and kept Sm burnup over-reach as a distinct implicit threat.

evidence.citation: "Simultaneous quantification of uranium(VI), samarium, nitric acid, and temperature with combined ensemble learning, laser fluorescence, and Raman scattering for real-time monitoring," Analyst (Royal Society of Chemistry); Oak Ridge National Laboratory / DOE PAGES
evidence.note: ORNL authors built a stacked ensemble of machine-learning regressors on combined LIFS and Raman spectra and tested it on D-optimally designed synthetic samples. It predicted U(VI), Sm3+, HNO3 and temperature with percent RMSEP of roughly 2–5%. The authors present it for real-time nuclear fuel cycle monitoring and for possibly quantifying fission products such as Sm3+ to inform burnup.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is model or spectral-input tampering, or silent out-of-distribution error, that hides an under-read of U(VI) and conceals diversion or hold-up in a reprocessing stream, which is a safeguards falsification and loss-of-material-control category of harm.

reproducibility.why: Silent out-of-distribution error, drift and over-trust recur reliably once interferents, fouling or stale calibration are present, because the ensemble always returns a confident point estimate; the adversarial tampering paths are more conditional.

exploitability.why: The most damaging adversarial paths (poisoning calibration data, altering model files, injecting spectra at the probe or acquisition path) need insider, supply-chain or physical and network access inside a controlled reprocessing facility, though the implicit drift and interferent routes need little access.

affected_users.why: A biased in-line reading feeds process control and material accountancy for the whole stream, and fleet-wide model propagation and correlated errors across the four jointly estimated outputs spread the bias across coupled systems and sites.

discoverability.why: The method is published in the open literature with its synthetic-only validation and RMSEP, and the general weaknesses (out-of-distribution blindness, drift, linear components, over-trust) are well documented for this class of spectroscopic ML, though facility-specific deployment details are not public.

use_case: Attention-enhanced multimodal deep-learning surrogate for finite-element analysis of nuclear power plant structures. A structural-parameter encoder and a seismic ground-motion encoder are fused by cross-modal attention. A response decoder then generates full acceleration time-histories at multiple floor locations, with uncertainty in the structural parameters propagated through. The aim is fast probabilistic seismic response and safety assessment for critical plant equipment.
incurred_insecurity:
This surrogate sits upstream of floor response spectra, equipment qualification and seismic PRA, so its failures become latent design-basis errors that surface only in an earthquake. The main threats are out-of-distribution and simulated-data fidelity limits hidden behind a flattering average-error figure, overconfident uncertainty bands, erosion of independent FE cross-checks, weak change control and qualification, and adversarial integrity attacks on training data, model artifacts and inputs, plus theft of sensitive structural information.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
Beyond-design-basis, near-field or long-duration motions, soil-structure interaction, nonlinear or aged as-built states fall outside the sampled envelope, yet the attention-fused decoder still returns smooth, plausible time-histories with no OOD warning, so tail floor response and fragility margin are under-estimated. An adversary could steer inputs or scenarios toward these poorly constrained regions, or hide a deliberate bias inside the unreported error band.

Simulated-data fidelity ceiling -- implicit, exploitable
Training labels come from FE models, so damping, boundary-condition and idealisation errors are inherited and then presented with the authority of a validated ML score, while sparse experimental validation and average MAPE mask peak and high-frequency errors that control equipment qualification. An adversary who tampers with the FE model or its parameters gains cover because the surrogate has no independent physical cross-check.

Overconfident uncertainty and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Propagating only input-parameter variance omits epistemic surrogate error, so tight confidence bands overstate margin in probabilistic safety conclusions, and cross-modal attention gives reviewers no way to explain individual responses. This opacity makes a tampered model hard to distinguish from natural error, which an adversary can rely on to stay undetected.

Automation bias and loss of independent checks -- implicit, exploitable
Fast surrogate answers displace routine FE reruns, so analysts lose skill and review independence, particularly if reviewers use the same tool. An insider could exploit this reliance by submitting manipulated inputs or using the model outside its validated envelope, expecting no one to re-run the analysis.

Non-determinism, change control and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
Seed-dependent training, stochastic uncertainty propagation and retraining alter behaviour without requalification, and nuclear software QA assumes deterministic, traceable calculation, so there is no established qualification route for ML surrogates in safety-class structural analysis. An unauthorised model swap or retrain could pass unnoticed and be dismissed as normal run-to-run variation.

Fleet and standard-design propagation -- implicit, exploitable
Reusing one surrogate across sites or structure types copies any bias or error into every plant's design basis as a common-cause weakness. An adversary compromising a single shared model or dataset gains a multi-site effect.

Poisoned data, model and supply chain -- adversarial
Tampered FE training sets or ground-motion libraries, or a backdoored or poisoned pretrained model or ML dependency, can bias floor response non-conservatively in chosen frequency bands or parameter regions while test-set MAPE still looks good. The result is under-designed anchorage and equipment qualification, a design-phase sabotage path that bypasses the operating plant's security perimeter and can be timed with a seismic or physical event.

Input tampering and adversarial perturbation -- adversarial
Structural-parameter and ground-motion inputs are plain numeric tensors in shared engineering stores, so altering them or crafting perturbations that exploit the attention fusion layer produces systematic non-conservative outputs. The tampering is hard to see because no physical cross-check exists.

Model and design-data theft -- adversarial
Extracting or inverting the surrogate, or stealing weights and training corpora, reveals as-built dynamic properties, equipment fragility and which structures are most seismically sensitive, enabling a proxy model for sabotage planning. Weak data-security models for engineering data and cloud training or serving widen the leakage path.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This surrogate sits in design and construction, so its output feeds floor response spectra (FRS) and fragility or seismic PRA inputs for equipment qualification. A wrong output becomes a latent design-basis error, not an immediate transient. The facility is protected by independent FE analysis, code-mandated conservatism, shake-table or in-situ testing, and design review. Those barriers hold only if the surrogate is treated as a screening tool. The realistic danger is a probabilistic screening result, reported with a flattering ~1.4% average maximum MAPE, quietly replacing FE runs. That would happen because of schedule and cost pressure, and nobody would see the error until an earthquake occurs. Because the failure is latent and invisible, a mismatch between the training envelope and the as-built or aged structure matters more than any overt cyber attack.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Out-of-distribution failure. The surrogate is trained on FE-generated and scaled-model data over a bounded range of structural parameters and ground motions. Beyond-design-basis shaking, long-duration or near-field motions, soil-structure interaction, nonlinear or cracked-concrete behaviour, aging, and design changes late in construction all fall outside that envelope. The model can still return smooth, plausible time-histories. Floor response and the equipment fragility margin are then underestimated in the tails, which are exactly where the safety case lives (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202). (2) Surrogate-of-a-simulation provenance. Training data comes from FE models, so any FE modelling error or an uncalibrated model is inherited and hidden behind an apparent validation score. Average error metrics also mask peak and high-frequency errors that control equipment qualification (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). (3) Uncertainty propagation can be overconfident. If the parameter distributions are misspecified, or the network underrepresents epistemic uncertainty, the probabilistic output will give a false sense of margin. Attention-fusion opacity also means a reviewer cannot tell why a given response was produced (OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03). (4) Automation bias and skill fade. Speed invites analysts to skip independent FE checks, and the design review chain stops being independent if reviewers use the same tool (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0501, OP.C0402). (5) Retraining or tool-version changes alter results without requalification, which hurts repeatability for a nuclear quality assurance record (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502). (6) Fleet or standard-design reuse can copy one error across multiple sites (OP.C0602).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. The more plausible vector is integrity attacks on the engineering data pipeline and model artifact, not runtime evasion. Poisoned or tampered FE training sets, altered ground-motion libraries, or a compromised pretrained model or software dependency could bias floor responses non-conservatively in a targeted way (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). Subtle tampering with the design-input parameters or the hazard spectra fed to the encoders has the same effect and is hard to see, because surrogate outputs have no physical cross-check. Supplier or contractor environments for design and construction often have weaker controls. Theft of the model or training data exposes proprietary structural designs, and design vulnerability information is sensitive for physical protection (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025, AML.T0035, AML.T0036). Cloud-based training or inference adds a dependency and a leakage path (OP.C0601, OP.C0505). Consequences are latent. Equipment or structures could be under-designed or under-qualified, which becomes a common-cause vulnerability to an earthquake and could be time-exploited alongside a physical event. Independent FE benchmarking, hold-out testing at the extremes, data and model hash control, and reviewers who do not use the surrogate would all reduce the risk.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a regression surrogate trained almost entirely on simulated data. The inputs are FE-generated floor responses for sampled structural parameters and ground-motion records, and the targets are the same FE model's outputs. That makes the ML pipeline fragile in a specific way: the surrogate can only be as faithful as the FE model, the parameter sampling distribution, and the ground-motion ensemble used to build it. Its reported ~1.4% MAPE is an interpolation metric on peak values inside the training envelope. It says little about behaviour on beyond-design-basis motions, near-field pulses, soil-structure interaction regimes, or as-built or aged structural states that fall outside the sampled parameter space. A cross-modal attention architecture with a time-history decoder is also hard to verify. It offers no guarantee of physical consistency, such as energy, causality, or response-spectrum envelope behaviour. Its results are only marginally reproducible, given training-time non-determinism and the stochastic uncertainty propagation. If this feeds equipment qualification or probabilistic risk assessment, small systematic biases in the tails matter more than average error.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution failure with no warning. Peak-response MAPE is averaged over the training distribution, but fragility and PRA depend on tail and extreme-motion behaviour, where the surrogate is least constrained. Attention-fused networks extrapolate unpredictably, and no built-in OOD detector flags when ground-motion spectral content or structural parameters leave the training support. The consequence is a non-conservative floor-spectrum estimate used for equipment qualification or seismic margin work, with the error hidden by a good headline accuracy figure. (2) Simulated-data provenance and a fidelity ceiling. Because the training labels come from FE models, the surrogate inherits every FE modelling error (damping assumptions, boundary conditions, soil-structure interaction, idealisation) and presents it with the false authority of validated ML. Experimental validation is likely sparse (small-data problem), so model-form error is poorly characterised. (3) Uncertainty miscalibration. Propagating parametric uncertainty through the network captures only the input-parameter variance. It does not capture epistemic surrogate error, so confidence bounds can look tight while being wrong, which distorts the probabilistic safety conclusions. (4) Model lifecycle and static-versus-dynamic qualification mismatch. When the plant is modified, aged, or re-analysed with an updated FE model, the surrogate silently goes stale. Retraining changes the weights and the behaviour, and neither is covered by established nuclear software QA, which assumes deterministic and traceable calculation. (5) Automation bias and skill fade. Fast surrogate answers displace the independent FE runs that served as a cross-check, so analysts lose practice and error detection. (6) Non-determinism, opacity and fleet propagation. Seed-dependent training and non-repeatable inference undermine the reproducibility that licensing reviews require. One surrogate architecture reused across plants or structure types could replicate its bias widely.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (7) Training-data or surrogate poisoning, and AI supply-chain compromise. An insider, a compromised FE-simulation pipeline, a ground-motion record library, or a pretrained model or framework dependency could be subtly altered. A targeted bias or backdoor trigger would make the surrogate under-predict responses for specific frequency content or parameter regions, while ordinary test-set MAPE still looks good. This offers an integrity-degradation route into the design basis. (8) Manipulation of inference inputs. The structural-parameter and ground-motion input files are plain numeric tensors, so tampering with them can cause systematic non-conservatism, and crafted adversarial perturbations can exploit the attention fusion layer. This is plausible in design workflows and shared engineering data stores. (9) Model and design-data exfiltration. Surrogate weights, structural parameter sets and the training corpus encode proprietary and potentially security-sensitive structural vulnerability information. Inverting or extracting the model could reveal which structures or equipment are most seismically sensitive, which is a sensitive-information risk. (10) Compute and infrastructure dependency. Use of cloud training or serving adds exposure to availability and integrity attacks.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this surrogate is not a flashy target, but it is a quiet one. It sits upstream of design-basis decisions (floor response spectra, equipment qualification demands, margin assessments), so a small and plausible-looking bias in its outputs would not be noticed in operations. It would be built into the as-built plant and show up only during an earthquake. A sophisticated adversary or malicious insider would not need to touch the plant.
