Influence over training data, the FE model that generates it, or the surrogate weights could create latent vulnerabilities in safety-related equipment that are timed to a seismic event or simply exploited as a hidden weakness. The reported ~1.4% average maximum MAPE is also the sort of headline figure that breeds trust. It conceals tail behaviour, out-of-distribution failures, and the fact that nobody can easily audit a deep decoder's output against first principles once FE runs are no longer routine.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity compromise of the design-basis pipeline. The AI failure mechanism is a poisoned or backdoored surrogate, or poisoned FE-generated training data. The attacker could be an insider at the vendor, an engineering contractor, or a supplier of the shared model, or could act through the ML toolchain (AML.T0010, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004, T0059, T0076). The facility depends on the surrogate for probabilistic floor-acceleration time-histories used to qualify safety-related equipment. The consequence is systematically non-conservative floor response in particular frequency bands or structural-parameter regions. This yields under-designed anchorage, supports or equipment qualification, a latent weakness that persists for the plant lifetime and is invisible until a real seismic event. It is a design-phase sabotage path that avoids the facility's operational security perimeter, which is why a state-level actor might prefer it to attacking a running plant. (2) Trust concentration and weak human checks. Once the surrogate replaces repeated FE runs, reviewers lose the habit and the capacity to re-run independent analyses. This creates automation bias and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). Insiders could exploit review fatigue by submitting manipulated structural-parameter or ground-motion inputs, or by selectively using the model outside its validated envelope. (3) Information security. The model and its datasets embed sensitive structural parameters, as-built dynamic properties and equipment fragility data. Model extraction or inversion, or theft of weights, could reveal structural vulnerabilities and aid sabotage planning (AML.T0024.001, T0024.002, T0025, T0035). Stolen data would let an adversary build a proxy to find which seismic or structural scenarios the plant is least robust against (AML.T0005). Weak data-security models for engineering data (OP.C0505.01) make this more likely. (4) Supply chain. Pretrained attention modules, ML frameworks, and outsourced training environments are standard dependencies and give an AI-specific route for implants (AML.T0010.001, T0010.003).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable. (a) Out-of-distribution failure. Real ground motions, soil-structure interaction, nonlinearity and as-built parameter ranges outside the training set (beyond-design-basis shaking, ageing, retrofits) can cause unreported accuracy collapse (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). The ~1.4% figure refers to average maximum MAPE in specific validation conditions, so tail errors in peak acceleration, which drive equipment demand, are under-characterised (OP.C0202, OP.C0403). (b) Training data is simulated or surrogate data, so it inherits any FE model-form error (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0603). Errors propagate invisibly into the surrogate and then into downstream fragility and PRA results, which is a cascading and concentrated bias (OP.C0301.01). (c) Opacity and non-determinism. Cross-modal attention and a generative decoder give limited explainability and possible run-to-run variation (OP.C0401, OP.C0402). Both make it harder to distinguish a tampered model from a natural error, which helps an adversary hide. (d) Regulatory and QA gaps. There is no established qualification route for ML surrogates in safety-class structural analysis (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0303). Software hygiene around versioning and model change control can be weak (OP.C0502), so an unauthorized model swap or retraining may pass unnoticed. (e) Uncertainty propagation can create false confidence, because narrow predictive bands from a mis-specified surrogate look rigorous (OP.C0304.03).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on OOD failure, simulated-data fidelity, automation bias, QA gaps and poisoning/supply-chain/theft threats; I merged overlapping items and dropped weakly argued ones (AML.T0015 evasion, AML.T0044, AML.T0076, AML.T0036, and cloud-availability attacks) but kept input tampering as distinct. Codes were limited to those traceable to the retained threats.

evidence.citation: "Predicting seismic floor response for nuclear power plant structures with time-series uncertainty propagation using attention-enhanced multimodal deep learning," Reliability Engineering & System Safety (Elsevier), Vol. 272, 2026, Article 112582
evidence.note: The paper builds and validates a two-encoder, one-decoder deep-learning surrogate that replaces repeated finite-element simulations. It predicts probabilistic floor acceleration time-histories for NPP structures under uncertain structural parameters, and the authors report an average maximum MAPE of about 1.4% in experimental validation.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoned data or models (or input tampering) that bias floor response non-conservatively, producing under-designed anchorage and equipment qualification that fails in an earthquake; this is a latent safety-margin erosion that could contribute to a release, but it is indirect and mediated by other design layers, so it is short of a direct release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: OOD extrapolation with no warning, inherited FE fidelity limits and overconfident bands recur reliably whenever inputs fall outside the sampled envelope, and a poisoned or biased model reliably yields the same bias once deployed.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (tampering with FE training sets, model artifacts or shared engineering stores, or a supply-chain compromise) need privileged or insider access to the design-phase data or model pipeline, although the implicit weaknesses need no special access to be triggered.

affected_users.why: A shared surrogate propagates bias across structures and sites as a common-cause weakness in the design basis (fleet and standard-design propagation), affecting many plants and the equipment qualified from its outputs, though it is limited to design-stage analyses rather than operating systems.

discoverability.why: Surrogate OOD limits, simulated-data fidelity ceilings, overconfident uncertainty and data-poisoning or extraction attacks are well documented in the open literature, and the published paper describes the architecture and validation, though the specific model, data stores and deployment remain non-public.

use_case: One-Class SVM anomaly detection on multi-channel ultrasonic testing signals, trained only on normal fuel rods, to find cladding breakage defects in nuclear fuel assemblies. It screens every rod in an assembly automatically to support fuel integrity inspection and cut manual review time.
incurred_insecurity:
A One-Class SVM trained only on normal rods acts as the screening gate for cladding integrity, so the main risk is that a breached rod is silently passed as normal. Implicit threats include an unvalidated sim-to-real gap, drift and heterogeneity, automation bias, opacity and a qualification gap. Adversarial threats include baseline or model poisoning, evasion through the acquisition chain, supply-chain tampering and inspection-record manipulation. Together they let a real defect, or a deliberate blind spot, hide behind 'the AI passed it'.

Simulation-only validation and unrepresentative defects -- implicit, exploitable
The reported 100% detection and under 3% false positives come from simulated defects, and a one-class boundary flags only what is unlike normal. Real flaws such as tight cracks, pinholes or hydride-related damage may fall inside the learned envelope and pass, risking fission-product release or re-irradiation of a failed rod. An adversary or fault only needs a defect type outside the simulated envelope, and the unproven coverage makes a miss look like a clean result.

Drift and operational heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Transducer wear, couplant, calibration, burnup, oxide or crud state, and fuel design change the signal statistics, which either floods operators with false alarms or quietly erodes sensitivity. A shifted or loosened threshold is easy to rationalise, so an adversary could deliberately degrade calibration or coupling to push operators to raise the threshold, or hide a manipulation within the drift. A model that does not transfer between rigs or fuel types also spreads the problem if it is propagated across sites.

Automation bias and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
The roughly two-thirds cut in manual review means unflagged rods get little human scrutiny, and inspectors lose the practised eye to catch what the model misses. The screen can become the de facto acceptance basis, and an adversary can rely on this misplaced trust because a consistently passing model is least likely to be questioned.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A scalar anomaly score gives no per-channel explanation, retraining with different normal subsets or hyperparameters shifts the boundary, and no accepted POD demonstration or change-control route exists for an ML screen in a qualified UT process. Unreviewed threshold or model edits therefore go unnoticed, which an insider can exploit to change screening behaviour without detection.

Baseline and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or compromised pipeline can slip signatures of marginal or defective rods into the normal training set, or alter the model, scaler or threshold file, widening the boundary around a chosen defect class. The false-positive rate stays low, so a breached rod enters the core undetected.

Signal-level evasion and tampering -- adversarial
An actor with access to the acquisition chain, gain, gating, channel mapping or exposed scores can shape waveforms near the decision boundary so a defective rod scores as an inlier. White-box access to the support vectors, kernel and threshold makes this easier.

Supply chain and vendor update path -- adversarial
Tampered libraries, model artifacts, update packages or vendor retraining and remote-support channels can change screening behaviour without altering the interface, causing systematic under-reporting of defects. Vendor data transfer also exposes fuel-design and inspection-signature IP.

Denial through induced false alarms and record manipulation -- adversarial
Injected noise or shifted calibration can push the false-positive rate up, forcing full manual inspection during an outage or pressuring operators to loosen the threshold. Manipulating pass/fail logs or the reporting layer can conceal damage and could mask assembly substitution where inspection records feed accountancy.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the plant side, this is a screening aid for fuel integrity inspection, normally done in the spent fuel pool during outage or at the fabricator. Its main safety value is catching leaking or breached cladding before fuel is reinserted or moved. The key engineering question is what happens when it misses a defect or is trusted too much, because the claimed time savings come from reduced manual review. Existing practice (qualified UT procedures, Level III oversight, sipping, in-core coolant activity monitoring, and the fact that most rods are never defective) gives defense in depth. That depth erodes if the ML screen quietly becomes the primary basis for acceptance. The one-class design and simulation-based validation make the risk of silent false negatives real, and the 'detected all defects' result rests on an unrepresentative defect population.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Validation gap and false-negative risk: the reported 100% detection and under 3% false positives come from simulation-based tests, so the defect population is synthetic or surrogate. Real cladding breakage varies widely (secondary hydriding, fretting, crud-covered surfaces, small pinholes, tight cracks). A One-Class SVM trained only on normal rods flags what is unlike normal, not what is a defect. It can miss subtle real defects that sit inside the learned boundary, and it can flag benign variation. The consequence is a leaking or degraded rod passing screening, with fission product release, coolant activity increases, or a failed rod being re-irradiated or handled. (2) Drift and heterogeneity: 'normal' depends on rod design, burnup, oxide thickness, crud, water chemistry and temperature, transducer wear, couplant, coupling geometry and calibration. Changes in any of these shift the signals, either raising false positives (which erodes trust and drives disuse) or shifting the boundary toward missed defects. A model trained on one fuel type or one rig does not transfer to others, and in a fleet-wide deployment a single bad model propagates the problem across sites. (3) Automation bias and skill fade: with a roughly two-thirds cut in manual review, inspectors may rubber-stamp the 'normal' outputs, and over time lose the practiced eye needed to catch what the model misses. The anomaly score is hard to explain, and the choice of threshold is a judgment call (tuning for low false positives costs sensitivity), so a bad threshold goes unnoticed. (4) Qualification and regulatory gap: UT of fuel is a qualified NDE process with demonstrated detection thresholds. An ML screen with no accepted qualification route, probability-of-detection demonstration, or change-control for retraining can drift into a de facto acceptance criterion without any formal basis. Non-determinism across retrains and software versions compounds this. (5) Data continuity: real defective-rod data is rare, so there is no means to verify or monitor sensitivity in service, and few ground-truth confirmations (sipping, PIE) feed back into the model. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data poisoning or contamination: if the 'normal' training set is quietly contaminated with signals from marginal or defective rods, or the model or threshold file is altered, the boundary moves to accept defects, which is hard to detect because there is no labeled defect check. A supply chain or insider actor with access to the model, scaler or configuration could achieve a targeted blind spot. (7) Signal and data manipulation: tampering with acquisition parameters, gain, gating, channel mapping, or the data path between the transducer array and the classifier (a cyber-physical integrity attack) could make defects look normal or flood the operators with false alarms, driving them to turn off the aid. Denial of the service during an outage window has schedule consequences. (8) Safeguards-adjacent concern: fuel inspection records also support accountancy and item identity, so falsified or manipulated inspection results could mask rod damage or substitution. The consequence is likely small and depends on whether independent verification (serial reading, visual inspection, sipping) remains, which is usually the case. The main protection is retaining independent human review of a risk-based sample, establishing a validated POD with real defects, locking down the model and data pipeline, and treating the ML as advisory rather than the acceptance basis.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, a One-Class SVM trained only on normal rods is a boundary estimator, not a defect classifier. Everything depends on how well the normal-class manifold is represented, and on a kernel bandwidth and nu setting (the contamination or outlier-fraction prior) tuned without real positives. The headline figures (all defects detected, under 3% false positives) come from simulation-based tests. That makes the data provenance simulated or surrogate, so the reported recall says little about field recall, where coupling variation, probe wear, channel cross-talk, cladding and oxide variation, assembly design differences and burnup-related changes all shift the 'normal' distribution. The decision boundary is also a single scalar threshold on a score. A small shift in that threshold, in the features feeding it, or in the calibration can silently trade missed defects against false alarms, with no per-defect explanation.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and unvalidated recall. Training and test data are simulated or surrogate (OP.C0201.01/.02) and defect data is scarce (OP.C0202). A defect morphology absent from the simulation, such as a tight crack, a pinhole or a hydride-related flaw, may fall inside the learned normal envelope. The system then reports 'normal' with no way to flag its own ignorance, so a breached rod could be passed into service. The cause is a one-class model with no negative-class check. The consequence is possible in-core fuel failure, fission-product release into coolant, and activity excursions. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303). Transducer aging, couplant changes, replaced channels, temperature, different fuel designs or vendors, and firmware or DSP changes alter signal statistics. This produces either a flood of false positives, which erodes trust and pushes operators to loosen the threshold, or a quiet loss of sensitivity. The model has no built-in OOD or calibration monitor, and one-class scores are poorly calibrated across sites (OP.C0602). (3) Automation bias and human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). The tool is justified by a roughly two-thirds cut in manual review, so reviewers are expected to look only at flagged rods and unflagged rods get little or no human review. Reviewer skill fades, and a miss becomes systematic rather than random. (4) Opacity and repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402). An SVM score does not say which channel or waveform feature drove the flag, which makes dispositioning hard. Retraining with different normal-data subsets, hyperparameters or preprocessing shifts the boundary, and this is hard to demonstrate under nuclear QA (OP.C0501, OP.C0303). The unresolved question is how to qualify a model with no positive-class evidence. (5) Contaminated 'normal' training set. If the 'normal' rods include undetected marginal defects, the boundary absorbs them (a concept-drift or label-quality issue).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data or baseline poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031). Because the model learns 'normal' from inspection data, an insider or compromised data pipeline can slip in signatures of defective rods during baseline collection or periodic retraining. This widens the boundary around a chosen defect type. It needs very little data, and it is hard to detect because the false-positive rate stays low. (7) Evasion and signal manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). Someone with access to the acquisition chain, digitiser or preprocessing software could shape the waveform or inject channel noise so a defective rod scores as inlier. White-box access to the SVM (support vectors, kernel, threshold) makes this simple (AML.T0044, AML.T0018, AML.T0076). Tampering with the threshold or the stored model file is a lower-effort variant. (8) Supply chain and software integrity (AML.T0010.001/.003, OP.C0502). The model is embedded in vendor inspection software, so tampered libraries, model artifacts or update packages could change screening behaviour without altering the GUI. The result would be under-reporting of defects, with consequences for safety, safeguards records and fuel-vendor liability. (9) Denial or degradation (AML.T0029, AML.T0046). Injecting chaff or noise that pushes many rods past the threshold forces a fall-back to full manual inspection, which can lengthen outages.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this is a screening gate on fuel cladding integrity. Its value to an adversary is that it sets the decision boundary for what counts as 'normal' and what gets human attention. An insider who can influence the normal-rod training set, the threshold, or the model file can create a blind spot for chosen defect signatures. Alternatively, the same access can flood reviewers with false positives to hide something else or to degrade trust in the tool. Non-adversarial weaknesses make this easier: a one-class model has never seen real defects, the reported results come from simulation, and a roughly two-thirds cut in manual review invites complacency. An adversary or a simple fault can therefore hide behind 'the AI passed it'. A nation-state would more likely pursue easier targets, but the concentration of trust in one screening score, and the inspection data feeding it, make this a plausible stepping stone for integrity or safeguards-relevant record manipulation.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model poisoning by an insider or a compromised vendor or supply chain: if 'normal' baselines are contaminated with marginal or defective-rod signals, or the model, scaler or threshold file is altered, the One-Class SVM silently accepts a defect class. Consequence: a breached or thinning cladding rod passes into the core, which means fission-product release risk, an integrity event, and loss of confidence in fuel records. (2) Evasion through physically or signal-level crafted conditions: someone with access to the inspection hardware, acquisition chain or channel data could shape signals near the decision boundary, or tamper with couplant, calibration or channel gain, so a real defect scores as in-distribution. A single scalar anomaly score is easy to probe if score outputs are exposed to staff or vendors. (3) Denial or erosion of the tool: injecting noise or shifting calibration to push the false-positive rate up forces a return to manual review, or pressures operators into raising the threshold. This erodes integrity and can be timed to an outage window with schedule pressure. (4) Inspection-record integrity: the pipeline's scores and pass/fail logs are a trusted artifact. Manipulating them or the reporting layer conceals problems and could mask diversion or substitution of assemblies if the inspection record is used as part of the accountancy chain. (5) Vendor and remote-support access: model updates, retraining and data transfer to a vendor create an insider-like pathway and intellectual-property exposure on fuel design and inspection signatures.

IMPLICIT, and exploitable or timeable by an adversary. (a) Validation rests on simulation: the 'all defects detected, under 3% false positives' result comes from simulated defects and a limited data regime, so real-world coverage of defect types, locations, orientations and sizes is unproven (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0302). An adversary only needs a defect type outside the simulated envelope. (b) Drift and heterogeneity: transducer wear, couplant variation, rod batches, burnup state, cladding materials and assembly designs shift the 'normal' distribution. Models trained on one population may fail or over-alarm on another, and a threshold tuned to cut false alarms may be loosened over time (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (c) Automation bias and skill fade: a roughly 66% cut in manual review and a 3-minute screen of 264 rods create pressure to accept the model's pass without independent confirmation, so reviewer skill degrades and complacency grows (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). A quiet, always-passing model is exactly when an attack is least likely to be questioned. (d) Opacity and governance: a one-class decision boundary gives little explanation for why a rod passed, and there is no AI-specific qualification regime for NDE software, with weak change control for retraining or threshold edits (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0502). (e) Data governance of the training corpus and inspection signals is likely handled as ordinary plant data rather than as integrity-critical, with no clear control over who may add 'normal' samples (OP.C0505, OP.C0505.01).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on simulation-only validation, drift, automation bias, opacity/qualification gaps, training-data poisoning, evasion and denial. I dropped codes tied to threats not clearly argued or only weakly supported (model extraction AML.T0024.002, valid accounts, AML.T0044 and AML.T0076 as separate items, and the data-governance OP.C0505 codes), and folded the record-integrity and vendor-access points into the adversarial paragraphs.

evidence.citation: "Application of multi-channel ultrasonic and machine learning for defect detection in nuclear fuel assemblies," Nondestructive Testing and Evaluation (Taylor & Francis)
evidence.note: The paper presents a multi-channel ultrasonic inspection system for fuel assembly cladding. A One-Class SVM is trained on normal samples only, because defective samples are scarce. In simulation-based tests it reportedly detected all defects with under 3% false positives, and it screened the 264 rods of an assembly in under 3 minutes, cutting manual review time by about two thirds. I read only the abstract page, not the full text.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a breached fuel rod silently passing screening (via poisoning, evasion, or an unvalidated sim-to-real gap) and being loaded into the core, risking fission-product release; record manipulation could also mask assembly substitution in accountancy, which is a safeguards falsification category of harm.

reproducibility.why: Misses of out-of-envelope defect types and drift-induced sensitivity loss recur reliably once conditions exist, but targeted poisoning or evasion depends on specific access and on the defect lying near the decision boundary.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (training-baseline or model-file alteration, acquisition-chain tampering, vendor update compromise) need insider or privileged access to a controlled inspection environment, though the implicit weaknesses require no attacker effort.

affected_users.why: Impact spans every rod in an assembly and possibly multiple assemblies, and fleet or cross-site model propagation can widen it, but it is bounded to the fuel inspection process rather than coupled plant control systems.

discoverability.why: One-class SVM limits, drift effects, and automation bias are well documented in the open literature and the source paper is public, but locating a specific blind spot or the model and threshold artifacts requires partial insider knowledge of the deployment.

use_case: Deep-learning classification (AlexNet, ResNet and squeeze-and-excitation network) of gamma emission tomography images of spent fuel assemblies. It detects partial defects, meaning missing or substituted fuel rods, for safeguards verification of stored spent nuclear fuel. It was benchmarked against tree-based ensemble models.
incurred_insecurity:
This classifier gives a safeguards verdict on whether stored spent fuel has missing or substituted rods, so it concentrates trust at a point a diverter would want to subvert or satisfy. It is trained on small, mostly simulated 3x3 tomogram sets, so it carries implicit weaknesses: a sim-to-real gap, closed-set overconfidence, opacity, non-repeatability, inspector over-trust and an immature qualification regime. It also faces adversarial threats: evasion by designed diversion, training-data and model tampering, and manipulation of the image path. The main consequence is a silent false 'intact' result that launders a diversion into a clean record and erodes continuity of knowledge.

Evasion by designed diversion -- adversarial
A diverter who knows or approximates the published architectures and simulation literature can build a proxy model and choose rod removal, dummy rods or substitution patterns whose tomograms fall in the classifier's under-sampled 'intact' region. The result is an undetected partial defect, achieved by physical manipulation of what the detector sees, with no digital access.

Training data and model tampering -- adversarial
Poisoned or mislabeled samples in the small curated defect and simulation sets, or backdoored pretrained weights, can implant a trigger that makes a chosen diversion signature classify as intact. The model then looks normal while carrying a persistent, signature-specific blind spot.

Image path and model file integrity -- adversarial
Tomographic reconstructions can be substituted, edited or AI-generated between detector and classifier, and model files corrupted, so a false 'intact' verdict enters the record without touching the model's logic. The detector-to-classifier chain of custody was not designed with ML integrity in mind.

Sim-to-real gap and data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Training on simulated 3x3 assemblies with few real defect examples means the model may fail silently on real 17x17 or 8x8 assemblies with different burnup, cooling time, detector noise and reconstruction artifacts. The gap is unmeasurable for lack of real ground truth, and the model's blind spots show a diverter which patterns it is least likely to flag.

Closed-set overconfidence and no OOD flag -- implicit, exploitable
A classifier trained on enumerated defect patterns gives confident softmax outputs on novel geometries, substitution materials or defect patterns, and cannot say 'I don't know'. A diverter can use a novel substitution outside the label space, knowing the failure will look like a normal confident 'intact' verdict.

Opacity, shortcut learning and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
CNNs may key on reconstruction artifacts or simulation-specific textures instead of rod-level physics, and seed-to-seed variance prevents exact reproduction of a qualified model. This weakens the evidentiary standing of the conclusion, and retraining variance gives cover that makes deliberate tampering hard to tell from ordinary drift.

Automation bias and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Inspectors may defer to a confident score, stop independently reading tomograms, or ignore the tool after false alarms, which weakens the independent review layer. An adversary can time a diversion around this complacency and rely on the AI verdict being accepted as a screening result.

Qualification and regulatory gap -- implicit, exploitable
No established framework qualifies a learned classifier as a safeguards measurement, and benchmark accuracy does not map to detection probability at a fixed false-alarm rate. Retraining after detector or software changes can silently shift the operating point, and an adversary can exploit the weakly controlled update process to introduce a change that passes as routine retraining.

Fleet-wide propagation -- implicit, exploitable
If one model is distributed across sites or inspectorates, a single drift or poisoning flaw becomes a common-mode blind spot. An adversary needs to compromise or learn only one shared model to defeat verification at many facilities.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a safeguards verification aid: an inspector (IAEA/Euratom/state) uses gamma emission tomography (GET) of stored spent fuel to confirm no pin diversion, and the classifier's verdict feeds a continuity-of-knowledge and non-diversion conclusion. The main downstream hazard is a false 'intact' result on a assembly with substituted or missing rods. The physical safeguards that would also have to fail are the inspector's independent review of the tomograms, complementary NDA (Cherenkov, neutron/gamma), the operator's declared records, and the surveillance and seals. Those layers exist, but a trusted high-accuracy classifier tends to erode them through automation bias. The documented system is also trained on limited, largely simulated 3x3 assemblies and benchmarked on small data, so real-world generalization is the weak point an adversary or ordinary variation could exploit. Real spent fuel is much larger (e.g. 17x17 PWR, 8x8 BWR), with varying burnup, cooling time, and detector geometry.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT: (1) Simulation-to-field gap. Training on simulated or surrogate 3x3 tomograms, with few samples, may not transfer to real assemblies, burnup and cooling-time ranges, detector noise, reconstruction artifacts, or different GET instruments. The result is silent false negatives on partial defects, particularly the hard cases of substitution with similar-emitting material or low-fraction (1 rod) defects. Safeguards consequence: a diversion goes undetected, or false positives cause costly re-verification and erode trust. (2) Data scarcity. Few real defect examples, so rare diversion patterns are poorly represented and the reported accuracy comes from narrow test distributions. Different architectures (SENet vs ResNet) perform best at different data sizes, so performance is fragile and model selection can be tuned to the benchmark. (3) Opacity and non-repeatability. CNN decisions are hard to explain to an inspector or a state under verification, and retraining variance gives different results. This is a problem for the evidentiary and legal standing of a safeguards conclusion. (4) Automation bias and skill fade. Inspectors defer to a confident score and lose independent tomogram interpretation skill. Uncertainty is not conveyed, and there is no out-of-distribution flag. (5) Qualification gap. There is no established framework to qualify an ML classifier for safeguards verification or authenticate its software, and the licensing/regulatory use area is not ready for it. ADVERSARIAL: (6) Evasion by a proliferating or diverting operator who knows or approximates the model (published architectures and papers aid proxy models). They arrange substitute rods, dummies, or placement and neutron/gamma source patterns so the tomogram is classified intact, which is physically realizable as a perturbation within the measurement, not just a digital one. (7) Data or model integrity attacks: poisoning of simulated training sets, or tampering with a model, weights or the reconstruction/preprocessing chain, give a backdoor that passes specific defect configurations. Image manipulation after acquisition (AI-generated or edited tomograms) defeats the verification, which is a risk of unauthenticated data path between detector and classifier. (8) Supply-chain and host compromise of the analysis software, or inspector/host-state disputes over a model trained on state-provided data, with possible leakage of sensitive fuel design or burnup information. Existing practice (multiple NDA methods, inspector judgement, seals, declared records) limits any single point of failure, provided the AI output is treated as advisory and not as the sole determinant.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small-data image classifier for a safeguards verification decision (is a spent fuel assembly intact, or are rods missing or substituted?). The published results rest on simulated 3x3 assembly tomograms, not field SPECT/GET data from real storage pools. The data are synthetic, the assemblies are far smaller than real 17x17 PWR or BWR designs, and the defect classes are enumerated in advance. The ML pipeline is fragile at four points: simulation-to-reality transfer, tiny training sets that favor architectures that overfit gracefully, a closed-set label space that cannot represent novel diversion patterns, and a reconstruction front end whose artifacts the CNN may be learning instead of physics. Because the classifier's output feeds an inspector's or regulator's conclusion about continuity of knowledge, both silent generalization failure and an adversary who understands the decision boundary are credible concerns. Neither requires compromising the facility itself.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and data provenance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0701.01). Training and test images come from Monte Carlo or simulated detector responses, with idealized geometry, noise and reconstruction. Real measurements add detector drift, collimator misalignment, cooling-time and burnup variation, water-attenuation effects, and heterogeneous source terms. A model that scores highly on held-out simulated data can degrade sharply on field data, and nobody can measure by how much, because real defective-assembly ground truth is nearly nonexistent (a low base-rate and small-data problem, OP.C0202). Reported SENet or ResNet superiority at small sample sizes may reflect benchmark-specific overfitting, not a robust architecture choice. (2) Closed-set, distribution-shift blindness (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403). The classifier is trained on enumerated missing or substituted rod patterns. Softmax outputs are overconfident on out-of-distribution inputs, such as a different assembly geometry, a different reactor type, a novel substitution material, or a partial defect pattern not in training. The result can be a confident false 'intact' verdict, which is the safeguards-critical error. Without calibrated uncertainty or OOD rejection the system cannot say 'I don't know'. (3) Shortcut learning and opacity (OP.C0401, OP.C0402). CNNs on tomograms may key on reconstruction artifacts, noise textures or simulation-specific features, not rod-level physics. Run-to-run non-determinism across seeds (OP.C0402.01) means a qualified model cannot be exactly reproduced, which matters for a regulatory or inspectorate tool. (4) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0504). No established framework exists for qualifying a learned classifier as a safeguards measurement. Performance metrics such as accuracy on balanced benchmarks do not map to detection probability at a fixed false-alarm rate, which is how safeguards verification is specified. Retraining after a detector or software change can silently alter the operating point. (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05). Inspectors may over-trust a high-confidence classification, or, after false alarms, ignore it. Skill in interpreting raw tomograms can fade (OP.C0101.06). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Evasion by a diverting party (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0043.003). A state or operator who knows the model family and the defect taxonomy can arrange rod removal or substitution, such as dummy rods, rearranged rods, or low-signature surrogates, so that the tomogram falls in an under-sampled region of the decision space. No digital access is needed, only physical manipulation of what the detector sees. Published papers and datasets support proxy-model building (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0002.000). Because the training data are simulated and the tool is public, the adversary can run a white-box or transfer attack offline. (7) Training data and model supply chain (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). Simulated datasets, pretrained ImageNet weights (AlexNet, ResNet, SENet) and open-source libraries are all injection points. A poisoned dataset or backdoored pretrained weights could embed a trigger pattern that makes a specific diversion signature classify as intact. Retraining with new field data is also a poisoning route if labels come from operator-declared inventories. (8) Input tampering and integrity (AML.T0031, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). The reconstruction pipeline and image files between the detector and classifier are an attack surface. Small perturbations or substituted images can be injected, and model files can be corrupted without breaking the pipeline. The chain of custody for tomograms and weights is typically not designed with ML integrity in mind (OP.C0502, OP.C0505.01). (9) Propagation. If a vendor or inspectorate distributes one model across sites, a single drift or poisoning flaw becomes a fleet-wide blind spot (OP.C0602). Combining the two kinds of threat: the implicit sim-to-real and closed-set weaknesses define where an adversary should act, and the lack of calibrated OOD detection means the failure would not be visible.

security_specialist.argument: This classifier verifies that spent fuel in storage is intact, so it is a trust-concentration point in a safeguards chain whose purpose is to catch a deliberate diverter (a state or insider). A host state or insider wants to hide rod removal or substitution, so an AI verdict of 'no partial defect' is an unusually valuable thing to subvert or to learn to satisfy. The model is trained mostly on simulated tomography of small 3x3 assemblies, with limited samples, so its blind spots are both a natural weakness and a guide to which diversion patterns it is least likely to flag. Once inspectors accept the model's output as a screening verdict, their vigilance falls, and an adversary can time a diversion around that complacency. Compared with defeating the physical measurement or the seals, targeting the model is attractive mainly because it can launder a diversion into a clean, auditable-looking result.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by designed diversion: a diverter who knows or approximates the architecture and training distribution (published AlexNet/ResNet/SENet benchmarks, open simulation literature) can choose which rods to remove or substitute, in what pattern and with what dummy material, so the tomogram falls in a region the classifier labels intact (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0005, AML.T0002, AML.T0001, AML.T0000). The AI failure mechanism is a decision boundary fitted to a small, simulated defect set. The dependent facility function is the partial-defect verification of stored fuel. The consequence is a safeguards false negative, meaning undetected diversion or misdeclared inventory, and continuity-of-knowledge loss. (2) Training-data or model tampering by an insider or supply-chain actor. Defect libraries, simulation configurations, pretrained weights and the benchmark pipeline are small and curated, so a few poisoned or mislabeled samples or a backdoor trigger could create a persistent blind spot for a specific defect signature (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0043.004). The consequence is a systematically biased verdict that looks like a normal model. (3) Tampering with the image path: manipulating or substituting tomographic reconstructions between detector and classifier, or feeding AI-generated or manipulated imagery, lets a false 'intact' verdict enter the record without touching the model (OP.C0703, AML.T0031, AML.T0076). (4) Dataset and model confidentiality: assembly geometries, detector responses and defect libraries are safeguards-sensitive, and extraction or inversion of the model reveals what it can and cannot see (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0036).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable. Training data is scarce and largely simulated or surrogate, which creates a sim-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0701, OP.C0701.02). Real casks and assemblies differ from the benchmark in burnup, cooling time, geometry, detector noise and assembly size, so out-of-distribution failure is likely and silent (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). The model gives no calibrated uncertainty, and the deep networks are opaque (OP.C0401). A sophisticated adversary could exploit these gaps without ever touching the AI. Automation bias and skill fade in inspectors, who may defer to a confident label, reduce independent scrutiny exactly where a diversion is hidden (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Qualification and regulatory readiness for AI in a licensing and safeguards role remain immature, and model updates or retraining are poorly controlled, so tampering is hard to separate from drift (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402). Overall, the main concern is not a spectacular cyberattack but a quiet, low-cost loss of detection sensitivity that a determined proliferator could learn about and use. Mitigations include treating the AI as advisory only, with independent non-AI checks, adversarial red-teaming of the defect space, and integrity control of data and weights.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on evasion by designed diversion, the sim-to-real and small-data gap, closed-set overconfidence, human over-trust and the qualification gap. I kept the poisoning and image-path threats as separate adversarial threats and dropped the model extraction and confidentiality threat (raised only by the security specialist) as weakly grounded for this system. I also left out AML.T0059, AML.T0001, AML.T0002 and AML.T0024.002 because no retained threat instantiates them.

evidence.citation: "Development of an AI-Based Image Analysis Model for Verifying Partial Defects in Nuclear Fuel Assemblies," MDPI, Energies 18(3):620
evidence.note: The authors trained and tested neural-network image classifiers on emission tomography images of 3×3 fuel assemblies. They compared these with XGBoost, random forest and LightGBM models for detecting partial defects in spent fuel. ResNet and SENet performed best with limited training data, and SENet did well with the fewest samples.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is evasion, tampering, or image-path substitution producing a silent false 'intact' verdict on spent fuel, which is safeguards falsification and loss of continuity of knowledge over nuclear material.

reproducibility.why: Closed-set overconfidence, the sim-to-real gap and automation bias are structural properties that recur reliably once a novel diversion pattern or tampered input is presented, though success depends on the proxy model matching the real classifier.

exploitability.why: Credible diversion requires state-level or facility-operator insider access to spent fuel, knowledge of the measurement chain, and the ability to build proxy models or tamper with data and model files, which is far from routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: A single fleet-distributed model or shared training set creates a common-mode blind spot across multiple storage sites and inspectorates, which affects verification broadly, though it does not cause a physical facility-wide hazard.

discoverability.why: The architectures, the simulation literature and the general weakness classes (adversarial evasion, OOD overconfidence, poisoning) are publicly documented, but locating specific blind spots needs partial knowledge of the deployed model, its data and its measurement chain.

use_case: Stacking-ensemble machine-learning classifier (logistic regression, decision tree, random forest, gradient boosting and perceptron models combined) on dissolved-gas chromatography time series (H2, CO, C2H4, C2H2) from nuclear power plant power transformers. It detects and diagnoses transformer faults (partial discharge, low-energy discharge, low-temperature overheating) for condition monitoring of ageing transformers.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory transformer-fault classifier sits beside independent protections (Buchholz and differential relays, IEC 60599 ratio methods, lab DGA), so its direct safety consequence is limited. The real exposure is quiet false assurance in maintenance decisions on main and auxiliary power transformers. Main threats are weak evidence on rare faults, silent drift and out-of-class faults, opacity and qualification gaps, over-trust, and adversarial manipulation of the gas data path, retraining data and model artifacts.

Rare-fault and label weakness -- implicit, exploitable
The 0.974 F1 comes from a non-peer-reviewed single-fleet held-out split with few, often rule-assigned labels for partial discharge and low-energy discharge, so recall on rare faults is likely overstated and incipient faults get missed. An adversary can rely on this blind spot, staging a physical or electrical stressor on the transformer where the model is weakest while operators trust a 'normal' call.

Drift and out-of-class faults -- implicit, exploitable
Oil regeneration, sensor recalibration, ageing, different transformer designs and faults outside the three trained classes (arcing, severe thermal) or lacking CH4, C2H6 and CO2 inputs shift the gas patterns, and the model forces them into a known class or 'normal' without any uncertainty signal. An adversary could hide a slow manipulation or real fault inside this degraded detection band, or time an attack around a maintenance event that resets the baseline.

Opacity and qualification gap -- implicit
A five-learner stacked ensemble is harder to explain than Duval or IEC ratios, retraining changes behaviour non-deterministically, and preprint-only evidence gives no AI-specific QA basis for plant use. An adversary gains little directly, beyond making retraining or tampering harder to notice.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A confident single class label and a headline F1 invite reduced manual trend review and Duval analysis, and false alarms can push the opposite error of disuse. An adversary can time a fault, overload or grid disturbance for periods of lowest vigilance and rely on the misplaced trust in a 'healthy' verdict.

Gas data-path tampering -- adversarial
Altering the four DGA channels, timestamps or historian entries, either by small physically plausible shifts across a decision boundary or by slow drift within the learned normal region, can suppress a developing fault or fabricate fault calls. The result is a masked transformer failure with loss of offsite or auxiliary power, or forced outages and eroded operator trust; flooding with spurious alarms has the same trust-eroding effect.

Training-data and model-artifact compromise -- adversarial
Scarce labels push operators to vendor, fleet or published datasets and retraining pipelines, where poisoned labels, a backdoor or a tampered model or ML library can bias the model toward missing a chosen fault class. Cloud-hosted or fleet-shared models spread any compromise across many units at once.

Public architecture and hosted-analytics exposure -- adversarial
The open preprint discloses architecture and features, letting an adversary build a proxy model to craft evasive inputs offline, while vendor or cloud analytics adds a remote access path toward OT-adjacent networks. Denial of the analytics service removes the monitoring aid, mainly consequential where manual practice has been reduced.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view this is an advisory condition-monitoring tool on main/auxiliary power transformers. DGA fault classification sits beside established practice (IEC 60599, IEEE C57.104 gas limits, Duval triangle, offline oil lab analysis, Buchholz/sudden-pressure relays and differential protection), so a wrong output rarely causes harm directly. The real exposure is in maintenance decisions: a missed or late incipient-fault call lets a degrading transformer run toward failure, which can mean a unit trip, loss of offsite or station power, or a transformer fire. A false alarm drives unnecessary outages, oil sampling and de-energisation. The cited F1 of 0.974 comes from a non-peer-reviewed preprint on a held-out split of one fleet's labelled data, and it says little about performance on rare fault classes, other transformer designs or sensor changes. The protection layer would need to fail as well before this becomes a safety event, which limits severity but not the quiet erosion of maintenance quality.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Small-data and low-base-rate weakness: serious faults are rare in labelled DGA records. Classes such as partial discharge and low-energy discharge are thinly represented, and a headline F1 can hide poor recall on the faults that matter most. The model may also be labelled against heterogeneous or lab-assigned ground truth (OP.C0202, OP.C0201, OP.C0701-style scarcity). (2) Drift and OOD behaviour: ageing transformers, oil regeneration or replacement, load-profile changes, different manufacturers and sensor recalibration or replacement all shift gas-evolution patterns. Online chromatographs also have drift, cross-sensitivity and missing-data gaps. The model has no concept of these shifts and fails silently (OP.C0302.01/.02/.03, OP.C0204). (3) Omitted features: the input set (H2, CO, C2H4, C2H2) lacks CH4, C2H6 and CO2, so high-temperature thermal faults and cellulose involvement can be misclassified or ignored. The classifier is also limited to a fixed fault taxonomy (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403). (4) Opacity and qualification: the stacked ensemble is harder to explain than the Duval or IEC ratio methods that engineers trust. It is non-deterministic across retraining, and there is no AI-specific QA or qualification basis for plant use (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501). (5) Automation bias and skill fade: if staff accept the label over rate-of-change trends and oil lab results, a confident 'normal' can defer an inspection, and diagnostic skill atrophies (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). A threshold alarm is an independent safeguard, so the ML output should never replace it.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Data integrity and manipulation: tampering with chromatograph readings or historian data, whether in transit, in storage or at the sensor-to-server link, can suppress or fabricate gas trends (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0046). It could mask a developing fault, or generate false alarms to force outages and degrade grid-support availability or operator trust. The gradual, slow-moving nature of DGA makes slow evasion plausible. (7) Training and retraining poisoning: labels or data fed from fleet databases, vendor datasets or retraining pipelines could be poisoned (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000), biasing the model toward missing a specific fault class. (8) Model and supply-chain compromise: a tampered model artifact or ML library, or cloud-hosted analytics (AML.T0010.001/.003, OP.C0601), could degrade diagnoses. Fleet-wide model propagation would then affect many units at once (OP.C0602). (9) Denial of the analytics service (AML.T0029) would remove the monitoring aid. This is a modest consequence if manual DGA practice is retained, but larger if staffing and procedures have already been reduced around the tool. Overall severity is low to moderate because of the independent protections, but the main concern is a slow loss of maintenance assurance that is hard to detect and could be timed around a stressed grid or outage period.

ai_engineer.argument: From the ML-pipeline lens, this is a classical tabular stacking ensemble (LR, tree, RF, GBM, perceptron) over four DGA gas channels, and its fragility sits in the data, not the architecture. DGA data is sparse in time (oil samples taken days to months apart, or at best slow online monitors), and the fault classes (partial discharge, low-energy discharge, low-temperature overheating) are rare in any single fleet, so labels are scarce, often assigned retrospectively by IEC 60599/Duval-style rules or expert judgement, and may be inconsistent. A 0.974 F1 on a held-out split from an unreviewed preprint most likely reflects within-fleet, within-distribution evaluation: random splits of autocorrelated time series leak across train/test, and class imbalance inflates F1 relative to recall on the rare, safety-relevant faults. Deployed to ageing transformers at other units, the inputs (different oil types, load profiles, degassing/oil-treatment events, sensor calibration, cellulose ageing) shift away from what was trained on, and the model has no native way to say 'I don't know'. The stacked meta-learner also adds opacity and several retraining non-determinism points without evidence of qualification.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT: (1) Label and provenance weakness: ground truth derives from rule-based gas-ratio interpretation or post-mortem inspection, so the model may simply reproduce a legacy diagnostic standard or its biases, and its apparent accuracy is circular. Rare-fault base rates (OP.C0202) and few field-confirmed events make the stated F1 an optimistic estimate; the actual risk is missed incipient faults (false negatives) that progress to transformer failure, loss of offsite/auxiliary power, or a reactor trip/station blackout challenge. (2) Drift and OOD: sensor replacement, oil reclamation, load-regime change, new-build or replaced units with no history, and ageing itself move the gas-generation baseline; slow concept drift will silently degrade a static model, and a fault mode outside the three trained classes (e.g. high-energy arcing, thermal fault >300°C, or a combination) is forced into the nearest known class with confident-looking output (OP.C0302, OP.C0303). (3) Human factors: a single class label with an F1 headline invites automation over-trust or, after false alarms, disuse; operators lose the habit of independent Duval-triangle or trend analysis (OP.C0101). (4) Qualification gap: preprint-only evidence, no repeatability or version control for a multi-model ensemble, and weak explainability make it hard to justify in a plant's I&C/software QA regime (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402). ADVERSARIAL / exploitable: (5) Integrity attacks on the input stream—tampering with online DGA monitor outputs, historian values or lab-result entry—need only small, physically plausible shifts in the four gas channels to push classifications across a decision boundary (evasion, AML.T0015/T0043) or to mask a real developing fault while a sabotage or physical attack on the transformer proceeds. Low-dimensional tabular inputs make black-box probing and crafted perturbations easy. (6) Training-data or retraining-pipeline poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0018.000), including manipulated labels in a vendor or fleet-shared dataset, could bias the model towards under-calling faults; model-file tampering is similar. (7) Denial or degradation of the monitoring feed, or a flood of spurious alarms, erodes trust and masks genuine events (AML.T0029, T0046, T0031). (8) If models or data are vendor-hosted or fleet-shared, one compromised or drifted model propagates across sites (OP.C0601, OP.C0602). Consequences are primarily availability/safety of the plant's electrical power supply rather than direct radiological release, but a transformer fault exacerbated by an undetected degraded monitor can stack onto other grid or plant vulnerabilities.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this is a low-glamour, indirect target. The classifier sits in the condition-monitoring path for main and auxiliary power transformers. Those transformers connect the plant to the grid and feed offsite and onsite power, so the classifier's output shapes maintenance timing and trust in asset health. A sophisticated adversary is unlikely to attack the model itself. The more plausible play is to use it as a stepping stone or a timing instrument. That means corrupting or spoofing the DGA data feed, or exploiting the plant's habit of deferring to a 'healthy' verdict, so that a physical or cyber attack on the transformer or grid connection is hidden or timed to a period of low human vigilance. The non-adversarial weaknesses also matter, because they are exactly what an adversary would exploit: a preprint-only evidence base, a small and imbalanced fault dataset, and a headline F1 that is unlikely to hold up on the data of a different plant.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Data-path integrity: the model trusts four gas-concentration channels (H2, CO, C2H4, C2H2) that come from online monitors or from lab chromatography entered through plant IT. An insider or an intruder who can alter these values or their timestamps can suppress a developing fault, or trigger spurious fault calls that burn outage budget and erode operator confidence. AI failure mechanism: no input-integrity or plausibility check beyond the classifier itself. Dependency: maintenance decisions on safety-relevant offsite and auxiliary power. Consequence: an undetected or mistimed transformer failure, loss of offsite power, and a challenge to safety systems. Relevant ATLAS techniques: AML.T0043 and AML.T0020 (crafted or poisoned data), and AML.T0010.002 if retraining data comes from external sources. (2) Training and retraining pipeline: labelled fault data is scarce, so operators may pull in vendor, fleet or published datasets. This gives an adversary or a careless supplier a route to poison labels or insert a backdoor, quietly shifting decision boundaries (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003). A shared or fleet-wide model would spread any compromise across sites (OP.C0602). (3) Vigilance erosion: a stacked ensemble that reports 0.974 F1 invites reduced manual DGA review and trending. An adversary who knows this can time a stressor, such as an incipient fault, an induced overload or a grid disturbance, for when attention is lowest (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). (4) Evasion by slow drift: gradual manipulation can keep readings inside the learned 'normal' region, and a tree-based ensemble with no explicit uncertainty output gives no warning (AML.T0015, OP.C0401). (5) Reconnaissance and infrastructure: the open arXiv paper reveals the architecture and features, which lets an adversary build a proxy model (AML.T0005, AML.T0000.001). Any cloud-hosted or vendor-hosted analytics adds a remote access path into OT-adjacent networks (OP.C0601, AML.T0012). IMPLICIT. (6) Evidence and generalisation gap: the result is a non-peer-reviewed single-dataset study, likely under-represented in rare faults and on a different transformer population. Performance may drop sharply in service because of operational heterogeneity, oil-type and loading differences, and ageing-driven drift (OP.C0302, OP.C0202, OP.C0501, OP.C0201). The fault classes covered (partial discharge, low-energy discharge, low-temperature overheating) exclude severe thermal faults and arcing, so a miss outside the trained classes looks like 'normal' (OP.C0301, OP.C0403). (7) Opacity and non-repeatability: five stacked learners make it hard to explain why a given call was made, and retraining changes behaviour in ways that are hard to requalify (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01). Taken together, the threat is less a dramatic AI hijack than a quiet false-assurance channel that an adversary could exploit or time an attack around.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on rare-fault label weakness, drift/OOD, over-trust, qualification gaps, input tampering, poisoning and fleet propagation; I merged overlapping items and dropped weakly grounded codes (e.g. AML.T0031, AML.T0059, OP.C0301, OP.C0502) and the low-value OP.C0204 mention. The proxy-model/open-preprint and cloud-access points were kept as one distinct security-specialist threat.

evidence.citation: "Machine Learning Methods for Anomaly Detection in Nuclear Power Plant Power Transformers," arXiv (Katser, Raspopov, Kozitsin, Mezhov; Skolkovo Institute of Science and Technology)
evidence.note: The authors build and test several ML classifiers on labelled dissolved-gas time series from power transformers, and combine the best of them into a stacking ensemble. The ensemble reached an F1 of 0.974 on a held-out test set, and its output class supports both fault detection and fault diagnosis. This is an arXiv preprint and has not been peer reviewed. I did not find a peer-reviewed version.

damage.why: The worst credible case (masked transformer failure causing loss of offsite or auxiliary power, or forced outages) is operational disruption with some safety-margin erosion, not a direct radiological release, because the classifier is advisory and independent protections (Buchholz and differential relays, IEC 60599 ratios, lab DGA) remain.

reproducibility.why: Drift, out-of-class faults, rare-fault blind spots and over-trust are structural properties of this kind of classifier and recur reliably whenever the conditions occur (regeneration, recalibration, unmodelled fault types, reduced manual review).

exploitability.why: The credible adversarial paths (tampering with the DGA data path or historian, poisoning retraining data or model artifacts, or compromising a vendor or cloud service) need OT-adjacent or supply-chain access, though the implicit blind spots need no special tooling.

affected_users.why: Impact is usually limited to the monitored transformers and the power-supply systems they feed, but fleet-shared or cloud-hosted models could propagate a compromise across many units.

discoverability.why: The open preprint discloses architecture and features, and the weaknesses of ML classifiers (drift, evasion, poisoning, low-base-rate labels) are well documented in the public literature, so a capable outsider could readily infer where the blind spots are.

use_case: Faster R-CNN deep-learning object detection (Inception-v2 backbone performed best) on camera images of fuel assembly exterior surfaces to detect and locate scratch defects. It replaces manual visual appearance inspection of fuel assemblies, which depends on the inspector's experience and attention, and supports fuel assembly integrity checks.
incurred_insecurity:
Replacing manual visual inspection of fuel assembly surfaces with a Faster R-CNN scratch detector creates a single, weakly qualified gate on exterior integrity, validated only on a laboratory mock-up with randomly made scratches. The main threats are sim-to-real generalization failure and a mismatch between detecting scratches and assessing integrity, erosion of human inspection capability, and weak AI-specific qualification and change control. Adversarial threats are poisoning or backdooring of the model and its data, physical-domain evasion, and tampering with the image pipeline or inspection records.

Surrogate-data generalization gap -- implicit, exploitable
Training on 18,816 images of a 15x15 mock assembly with random scratches in lab conditions does not cover real fretting, handling gouges, crud or oxide films, reflections, pool lighting or other designs, so missed real defects pass silently and the single TPR/FPR figure hides per-class recall. An adversary could use defect types, textures or conditions outside the training envelope as a blind spot that the model fails to flag without any tampering.

Objective misalignment and low base rate -- implicit, exploitable
Box-level scratch detection says nothing about depth, location or cladding integrity, and a 0.1 FPR at the real, much lower defect prevalence yields mostly false alarms, pushing operators toward overriding alerts or loosening thresholds. An adversary could exploit the learned override habit, or flood the station with nuisance alarms as cover, so a real defect is dismissed.

Automation trust, skill fade and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
With the inspector reduced to a reviewer of the model output, over-trust in no-detection results, skill fade and complacency set in, and the detector gives no severity rationale to challenge a miss. An adversary could time a manipulation to low-vigilance periods and rely on the misplaced trust in the 98% headline figure.

Static qualification, drift and governance gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Camera ageing, lighting or lens changes, new assembly designs, and retraining shift the operating point, while nuclear quality programs lack an AI-specific qualification basis, so a retrained model applied across lines or sites propagates the same blind spot. Weak change control and the treatment of a vision system as ordinary QA software let a deliberate threshold or model change hide among expected variability, with failure indistinguishable from sabotage.

Model and training-data poisoning or backdoor -- adversarial
An insider, labelling contractor or compromised model-zoo source could poison labels, tamper with pretrained backbone weights, or implant a trigger so that defects with a given pattern, location or texture are never flagged while routine acceptance tests still pass. The consequence is damaged assemblies accepted into transport and core loading, and falsified fabrication QA traceability.

Physical-domain evasion -- adversarial
Surface finishes, coatings, marking, lighting changes, glare or camera occlusion can suppress or mask defects, since the assemblies are physically accessible at fabrication and the mock-up's random scratches never exercised adversarial inputs. The result is missed defects or induced false alarms that exhaust inspector attention.

Workstation and record tampering -- adversarial
Compromise of the inspection workstation or image pipeline through valid accounts can alter weights, thresholds or stored images and results, falsifying pass records that support fuel quality assurance and item accountancy. It also opens an IT-to-fuel-handling pathway and possible exfiltration of assembly design data.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the plant and fabrication-line side, this is a surface-appearance screen on cladding and assembly structure. It sits upstream of, and does not replace, the qualified inspections that actually carry safety credit: dimensional checks, ultrasonic and eddy-current weld and cladding tests, and pool-side or receipt inspection. The consequence of a wrong output is therefore bounded only if the AI stays a screening aid. The main risk is procedural: a 0.98 TPR / 0.10 FPR result from a 15x15 mock-up with randomly made scratches gets read as proof of qualified inspection capability, and the inspector's attention is then withdrawn (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). A missed scratch that is a real handling or grid-to-rod fretting precursor, or a mechanical-damage site, could reach the core. It would then matter through cladding breach, fission-product release into coolant, and fuel reliability problems. For a fabricator, a miss is a quality escape into the fleet. The 10% false-positive rate is also not benign, because it drives rework, re-handling, and a tendency to override or tune alerts down.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data and qualification gap: the training data is laboratory mock-up imagery with artificial, random scratches, so it is a surrogate (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.01) and not field data (OP.C0201.05). Real defects (fretting wear, handling gouges, oxide or crud films, discoloration, weld marks, spacer-grid contact marks) differ in morphology, depth and contrast. Real conditions differ too: irradiated or crudded surfaces, pool lighting and water distortion, glare on metallic cladding, different vendor designs and lighting rigs. Expect poor generalization and drift (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0202). Rare critical defects are low base-rate and will be under-represented (OP.C0202). A single reported TPR/FPR hides per-defect-class recall, so the worst misses are invisible. (2) Human factors: the removal of manual inspection brings out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity, skill fade, complacency about a tool that is usually right, and mode errors when the operating point or threshold is changed (OP.C0101.01, .03, .06, OP.C0102). Opacity limits an inspector's ability to challenge a miss (OP.C0401). A scratch is not a safety-significant quantity unless depth, location and cladding integrity are assessed. The AI detects an appearance feature, so the objective is misaligned with 'integrity' (OP.C0301). (3) Governance: there is no AI-specific QA basis in typical nuclear quality programs (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Retraining and model updates need configuration control, and a retrained model used across several lines or sites propagates the same blind spot (OP.C0602). Camera or lighting changes and software hygiene lapses degrade results silently (OP.C0502). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (4) Integrity of the inspection record: poisoning of training or labelling data, or of the supply chain for pretrained backbones (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004), could create a backdoor so that defects with a trigger pattern are never flagged. Because this is an insider-accessible, offline-ish quality system, the realistic actor is an insider or a compromised vendor, acting to conceal damage or sabotage quality. (5) Physical-domain evasion: surface treatments, marking, or lighting changes that defeat the detector (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003) are plausible in fabrication, where components are physically accessible. (6) Tampering with images or results between camera and record (falsified pass records), or denial or degradation of the service to force a fallback to rushed manual inspection (AML.T0029, AML.T0031), has quality-assurance and regulatory-record consequences. Existing practice (independent NDE, sampling audits, traceable records, human review of flagged and passed items) mitigates much of this. That only holds if the AI remains advisory and a periodic blind check against known seeded defects is kept.

ai_engineer.argument: From a pipeline view, this system was trained and validated on 18,816 images of a 15x15 mock assembly with randomly made scratches in lab lighting, so the data is simulated/surrogate (OP.C0201.01/.02), not field data. Real assemblies vary in cladding alloy, oxide or crud films, handling marks, reflections, grid spacers, and camera geometry. Detector performance, reported as 0.98 TPR at 0.1 FPR, is an in-distribution figure from one lab set. A 10% FPR is operationally heavy, and the metric says nothing about scratch severity, which is what matters for integrity. The architecture is a standard open-source Faster R-CNN with Inception-v2 backbone, usually fine-tuned from public pretrained weights, so supply chain and the objective itself (box-level detection, not safety-relevant defect classification) are the fragile points, more than the facility around it.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real generalization and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.02): a model trained on random mock-up scratches meets real assemblies with different surface finish, lighting, camera pose, and defect morphology (fretting, pitting, debris marks, handling damage). Missed detections (false negatives) are silent and show up as passed assemblies with real cladding damage, which is an integrity and fuel-performance risk. (2) Small-data and low base-rate problem (OP.C0202, OP.C0203): real defective assemblies are rare, so the labelled defect distribution is artificial. Calibration at the lab prevalence will not hold at the real, much lower prevalence, and a 0.1 FPR then yields mostly false alarms. That drives either disuse (OP.C0101.05) or threshold loosening that raises misses. (3) Drift and qualification (OP.C0303, OP.C0501): camera aging, lens contamination, lighting changes, new assembly designs or coatings, and retraining on new data all shift the operating point. A static one-time qualification does not cover this. (4) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01): replacing the inspector removes the human baseline. Reviewers then over-trust 'no detection' outputs, while the detector's bounding box has no explainability about severity (OP.C0401). (5) Objective misalignment (OP.C0301): detecting 'a scratch' is not the same as assessing whether it is acceptable under the integrity criterion. Detection without depth or severity can pass or fail the wrong things.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Supply chain compromise (AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0018.000/.002, AML.T0011.000): public pretrained backbones, detection frameworks, and model-zoo checkpoints could carry a backdoor or unsafe serialized artifact, and an inspection station that trusts them has no independent check. (7) Training-data poisoning or label tampering (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059): an insider or compromised annotation pipeline could alter labels or insert trigger patterns so that certain defect types or locations are consistently missed, which is a quality-assurance and possibly sabotage path in fabrication. (8) Evasion at inference (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0041): physical adversarial patterns, surface treatments, reflective or texture artifacts, or trigger markings on an assembly could suppress detection. Camera feed tampering or image-level perturbations in the capture pipeline could do the same, since the input is a raw image stream. (9) Model integrity attacks (AML.T0018, AML.T0031, AML.T0076): tampering with weights, thresholds, or NMS settings on the inspection workstation can quietly lower sensitivity, and no one will notice without ongoing ground-truth checks. (10) Records integrity: inspection pass/fail logs feed traceability and quality records for fuel, so a manipulated model has downstream consequences for assurance of fuel quality.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this detector becomes a single trusted gate on fuel assembly exterior integrity at fabrication and at the reactor site. It replaces an attentive human whose judgment was hard to systematically influence. A deliberate adversary, whether an insider, a supplier, or a state actor with access to the model supply chain, gains a new low-visibility lever: causing damaged assemblies to be passed (or good ones rejected) without any physical intrusion into the fuel area. The evidence base is a lab mock-up with random scratches (18,816 images) and a stated 0.1 false-positive rate, so the system has weak operational qualification, and that gap is where a quiet attack or an ordinary failure can hide. An adversary would probably favor easier targets, but this one matters as a stepping stone: the inspection workstation, image pipeline and training data sit at the junction of IT and fuel-handling, and a backdoored or degraded model erodes the human inspector's skills and vigilance over time.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Model or training-data tampering (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004). An insider or a compromised vendor or labeling contractor could poison the labelled images, or implant a trigger that suppresses detection of a particular defect type, location or texture. The model would still score well on routine acceptance tests. The facility depends on the detector for exterior-damage screening, so the consequence is that damaged assemblies are accepted into transport and core loading. That raises the risk of cladding or grid damage going unnoticed, with downstream fuel-failure, release and quality-assurance integrity consequences. A tampered model also undermines the traceability that fabrication QA records are meant to provide. (2) Physical-domain evasion (AML.T0015, T0043.003, T0041). Defects could be hidden, or made to look benign, through lighting, surface finishing or coatings, camera angle, or camera occlusion. Defects could also be induced in patterns the model never saw. Detection of this kind of evasion depends on the model's training distribution, and the mock-up's random scratches are not adversarial. The consequence is a missed defect, or a flood of false alarms that exhausts inspector attention and is used as cover (AML.T0046, T0029). (3) Image-pipeline and workstation compromise (AML.T0012, T0055, T0076, T0025). Altering stored images or inspection results, or tampering with thresholds, can falsify the integrity record. This creates a new IT-to-fuel-handling pathway and may also be a safeguards concern, because inspection records support item accountancy and tamper-evident verification.
