The same pipeline could carry data exfiltration of geometry and design details. (4) Supply-chain and cloud exposure (AML.T0010.001, OP.C0601). Pretrained backbones from public repositories and outsourced training bring in unvetted artifacts. IMPLICIT, exploitable: (5) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102, C0101.01). Manual inspection skills and attention will fade once the human becomes a rubber-stamp reviewer. An adversary can time an action to periods of low vigilance, and the 98% headline hides who catches the missed 2%. (6) Qualification and drift gaps (OP.C0501, C0302.01, C0302.03, C0303, C0202, C0203). The evidence is a lab mock-up only. Real assemblies vary in design, oxide, crud, reflections, and lighting. Defect types other than scratches, such as dents, fretting and debris marks, are not covered. Model or camera replacement also drifts performance. A 10% false-positive rate means operators will learn to override alerts, and an adversary can exploit that override habit. (7) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, C0402), which make tampering or silent degradation hard to distinguish from normal variability, and (8) scope drift (OP.C0503, C0505), in which a vision system is treated as ordinary QA software rather than as a security-relevant component, so access control, change control and logging are weaker than for safety I&C. Overall, an elite adversary might not choose this target first, but a modest insider could use it cheaply, and its weak qualification means failure may be indistinguishable from sabotage.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on surrogate-data generalization, objective misalignment, automation trust and skill fade, and on model/data poisoning plus physical evasion as the core threats. I dropped weakly argued items (cloud dependency, non-repeatability, data access governance, T0029/T0031/T0055 on thin support) and merged the records-tampering and workstation-compromise pathways into one.

evidence.citation: "Defect detection of nuclear fuel assembly based on deep neural network," Annals of Nuclear Energy (Elsevier), vol. 137, 107078
evidence.note: The authors built a 15x15 mock fuel assembly with randomly made surface scratches and collected and labelled 18,816 images. They compared several CNN detectors (Faster R-CNN with Inception-v2, ResNet-101 and ResNet-50, SSD, R-FCN) and found Faster R-CNN with Inception-v2 worked best, at 0.98 true-positive rate against 0.1 false-positive rate. The source says fuel assemblies can be damaged during production, transport and operation, so the facility domain is not tied to a single stage. I chose fabrication and power generation as a judgement call. The evidence is a laboratory mock-up, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoning/backdoor or record tampering that lets damaged fuel assemblies pass QA into transport and core loading, with falsified fabrication traceability; this is a serious integrity/safety-margin and records-falsification harm, though a surface-scratch gate is not directly a release pathway.

reproducibility.why: The implicit generalization gap, low-base-rate alarm fatigue, and over-trust failures recur reliably once the model is deployed outside its lab-trained envelope, whereas the adversarial paths are more conditional.

exploitability.why: Implicit blind spots and physical-domain evasion need only physical access or routine interaction at fabrication, but poisoning, backdoors, and workstation/record tampering need insider, supply-chain, or valid-account access.

affected_users.why: A blind spot or tampered model propagates across a fuel line, multiple sites, and downstream transport and core loading, but it stays confined to the fuel inspection function and does not span all facility systems.

discoverability.why: Surrogate-data gaps, automation over-trust, and poisoning/evasion of vision models are well documented in open literature, and the published mock-up study with its headline metrics lets a capable outsider infer the training envelope and blind spots.

use_case: Random forest, artificial neural network and Gaussian naive Bayes classifiers that grade the level of internal fuel-assembly damage in a sealed spent-fuel dry storage canister. They use features from the change in vibration frequency response functions (hammer excitation and accelerometer responses) measured only on the canister's exterior, tested on a 2/3-scale canister mock-up. The aim is non-destructive structural-integrity monitoring of stored spent fuel.
incurred_insecurity:
Grading internal fuel damage in sealed dry storage canisters from exterior vibration data, using classifiers validated only on a 2/3-scale mock-up, concentrates integrity assurance in one weakly validated inferential channel. The main threats are adversarial manipulation of the physical measurement, baseline and model, and implicit sim-to-real, drift, out-of-distribution and over-trust failures that an adversary could hide behind. The realistic harms are false assurance of fuel integrity, concealed tampering or diversion, and unnecessary canister handling, not an acute accident, because passive safety margins are high.

Physical-channel evasion -- adversarial
An insider with pad access can change excitation point, sensor coupling or mounting, or add mass or damping, so the difference-FRF features shift and the classifier grades a doctored input as low damage, or fabricates a damage signal. This can conceal real degradation or removal of contents, or serve as a distraction that triggers unneeded handling and dose.

Baseline, training-data and model tampering -- adversarial
Every grade is relative to a stored intact baseline FRF, and the training set is small, so a few altered baseline or training records, shifted labels or a swapped model file move the decision boundary toward reporting intact. With no explainability, operators would not notice the change; public methods and data also let an attacker build a proxy model and tune perturbations offline.

Pipeline compromise and denial -- adversarial
Compromise of the acquisition laptop, analysis workstation or any off-site analytics can falsify results or the audit trail, and denying the service removes monitoring when it is needed. A shared model or baseline across casks or sites would propagate a single compromise or bias.

Sim-to-real and scale gap -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on surrogate assemblies with artificially induced damage in a mock-up, the model faces full-scale canisters with real burnup, loading, overpack coupling and ageing, so its grades may be miscalibrated, with no real-damage ground truth. An adversary needs no exploit, only to act in the regions where the model is unvalidated and rely on its confident false assurance.

Baseline and environmental drift -- implicit, exploitable
Temperature, humidity, overpack condition, mounting and hammer-force variability shift the FRFs over decades, so the grade degrades silently or flags benign change as damage. An adversary could hide a gradual manipulation inside this drift or time an action to when the baseline is stale.

No out-of-distribution rejection and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
RF, ANN and GNB emit a confident class for any input, so rare or unseen damage types are mapped to the nearest known grade, and the ANN in particular cannot be interrogated. An attacker could craft inputs the model confidently calls benign, knowing no rejection mechanism will flag them.

Over-trust and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
Because the canister interior cannot be inspected, a clean AI grade may be used to relax inspection intervals or support licensing without AI-specific QA, and stochastic training makes results hard to reproduce. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust and on operator complacency to time concealment.

Safeguards role overreach -- implicit
Crediting a vibration-based grade with continuity-of-knowledge value would leave fuel substitution or partial removal undetected unless it changes the structural response, and it is no substitute for NDA or containment and surveillance. Adversary gain is covered by the over-trust threat above.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a monitoring/diagnostic use case on sealed dry storage canisters, where the physical hazard is slow and passive and the canister is a robust multi-barrier system. The main downstream risk is therefore not an acute accident. It is wrong inspection or regulatory decisions: missed internal fuel degradation (false negatives), or false alarms that trigger costly canister handling and unneeded unloading, with the added dose and handling risk. The classifier has only been shown on a 2/3-scale mock-up with simulated damage, and it grades damage using a vibration signature that is also affected by temperature, boundary conditions, basket and fuel-loading variation, concrete overpack coupling, and sensor placement. A real canister may sit far outside the training distribution, and about 0.92 accuracy on a mock-up says little about confidence in the field. Existing practice (thermal and surface monitoring, aging-management inspections, periodic visual or camera checks of the exterior, and the canister's design-basis margins) would catch gross failures, so the AI should be seen as a supplementary indicator. The real danger is that a clean AI grade is treated as evidence of integrity or used to justify relaxed inspection intervals.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and scale gap: models trained on mock-up data with induced damage (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03) may not transfer to full-scale canisters with differing fuel burnup, loading patterns, cladding states, thermal gradients, weld and boundary conditions, and decades of aging. Consequence: false assurance that fuel is intact, or spurious alarms. This is compounded by the low base rate of real internal damage (OP.C0202) and the near-absence of labeled real-world damage data (OP.C0204). (2) Concept and operational drift: environmental effects such as temperature cycling, seasonal changes, and overpack or pad condition shift the frequency response functions (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). A baseline FRF recorded years earlier no longer matches, so degradation could be masked, or benign change could be flagged as damage. Sensor-location sensitivity and repeatability of hammer excitation (operator-dependent force and position) add measurement variance (OP.C0402, OP.C0303). (3) Opacity and qualification: the ANN and RF models are hard to explain, and a damage grade with no physical interpretation (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0403) is hard to license or defend to a regulator. Teams may over-trust the output (OP.C0101.04) and use it to justify extending inspection intervals or deferring more rigorous examination, and the same ambiguity makes operators less likely to challenge the grade. (4) Safeguards-adjacent point: if internal-state inference is used to claim continuity of knowledge on sealed content, it is no substitute for NDA or containment-and-surveillance verification. A fuel-diversion or substitution scenario would be undetected unless it changes the vibration response (OP.C0702.01), so the tool must not be credited with a safeguards role it cannot fill. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Data and baseline integrity: an adversary or insider who tampers with stored baseline FRFs, training or calibration data, or the model file (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059, AML.T0031) could bias the classifier to report 'intact' for a degrading canister, or inflate damage grades to force unnecessary operations or generate public and regulatory alarm. (6) Physical-layer evasion: the input is a physical vibration measurement, so anything that changes the structural response, such as added mass or damping at the exterior, altered sensor coupling or placement, or timed measurement conditions, can shift features (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015, AML.T0041). This could mask real damage or fabricate it without any cyber compromise. The mock-up work shows sensitivity to sensor location, which is itself an exploitable dependency. (7) Pipeline and infrastructure: compromise of the data-acquisition laptop, analysis workstation or any off-site or cloud analytics (OP.C0601, OP.C0502, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0012) allows falsification of results or the audit trail, and a denial of service (AML.T0029) removes the monitoring capability when it is needed. Because facility response is human-mediated and the canister has high passive safety margin, severe physical consequences require additional failures: an independent degradation mechanism, plus missed thermal or other inspection signals. The principal realistic harms are misplaced regulatory confidence, unnecessary canister interventions, and erosion of trust in monitoring programs.

ai_engineer.argument: From the ML pipeline side, this system is fragile mainly because of its data. It is trained on hammer-excitation frequency response functions (FRFs) from a 2/3-scale mock-up with surrogate assemblies and artificially induced damage. That is simulated/surrogate data (OP.C0201.01, .02), and the training set is tiny and cleanly labeled. Real canisters differ in several ways: full scale, real irradiated fuel, decay heat, helium fill, concrete overpack coupling, boundary conditions, and years of environmental and thermal cycling. The classifier's ~0.92 accuracy is an in-distribution, lab-condition number with no field ground truth, because there are no labeled examples of real internal damage in sealed canisters and none can be easily obtained (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). The input is a difference feature (damaged minus intact baseline), so the model depends on a baseline FRF captured at a specific time and state. Any shift in temperature, boundary conditions, sensor placement or excitation consistency looks like damage, or masks it. The architecture also has no out-of-distribution rejection: random forest, ANN and GNB all emit a confident class for any input.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and scale gap (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303): the model is qualified on a mock-up, but deployment faces different structural dynamics. Its damage grades may be uncalibrated or meaningless on real canisters. The consequence is false assurance of integrity, or false alarms that trigger unnecessary and costly canister handling or retrieval. (2) Baseline and environmental drift (OP.C0302.01, .02): the diff-FRF features move with temperature, humidity, overpack condition, accelerometer mounting and hammer force variability, all over decades-long storage. Without drift monitoring, baseline re-calibration or retraining, the damage grade degrades silently. Mock-up results where sensor-location changes were tolerated do not cover these conditions. (3) Missing OOD handling and class imbalance (OP.C0403, OP.C0401): real damage is rare and may be of types absent from training, and the classifiers will map it into the nearest known grade. Opacity makes this hard to catch, especially for the ANN. (4) Automation bias (OP.C0101.04) and a qualification gap (OP.C0501): a 'healthy' output may be used to justify reduced inspection or licensing arguments for storage, with no AI-specific QA basis. Training non-determinism (OP.C0402.01) compounds the repeatability problem. The data is also scarce and hard to refresh (OP.C0204). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Evasion via the physical channel (AML.T0015, T0041, T0043.003): with access to the exterior, an adversary can alter the measured FRFs by changing coupling, adding mass, shifting sensor mounts or varying the excitation. This could mask real damage or fabricate a damage signal. Insider tampering with the baseline measurement is the simplest route, since every later classification is relative to it. (6) Poisoning and integrity attack (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0018.000, T0031): the training set is small, so a few corrupted FRF records, mislabeled damage grades or a swapped model file would shift the decision boundary. Public availability of the methods and mock-up data (T0000, T0002.000) lets an adversary build a proxy model (T0005) and optimize perturbations offline. (7) Data-pipeline compromise (AML.T0112, T0029): tampering with or denying the acquisition and classification chain could suppress alerts. Absent a trustworthy alternative, this creates a safeguards and safety blind spot, in which a degraded or diverted fuel state could go unrecognized or unverifiable by non-intrusive means.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this use case turns a sealed, deliberately opaque canister into something whose integrity state is asserted by a small set of classifiers fed by exterior hammer-and-accelerometer data. That concentrates trust in a single inferential channel. If a diversion, substitution or degradation event (or an adversary's wish to conceal one) matters, the classifier's "intact" grade is exactly what an insider or remote actor would want to control. It is also a low-cost target compared with the canister itself: the measurement chain is physically reachable by anyone with cask-pad access, and the model sits on ordinary IT. Implicit weaknesses make it more exploitable: it was validated only on a 2/3-scale mock-up with ~0.92 accuracy, so there is no real-canister ground truth, and an adversary can hide behind the model's honest uncertainty.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Measurement-chain manipulation and evasion: an insider with pad access could alter excitation point, sensor coupling, mounting, or add mass or damping, or swap or recalibrate accelerometers, so the frequency response function differences shift. A baseline/"intact" reference could also be replaced or poisoned. The AI failure is a classifier that grades a doctored input as low damage; the dependency is a monitoring and integrity-assurance decision for stored spent fuel; the consequence is concealed fuel degradation, or concealed tampering or partial removal of contents (a safeguards continuity-of-knowledge concern), plus false confidence in storage integrity. A small low-capacity model (RF, GNB, ANN) is easy to proxy and probe offline with public literature (the paper is public), so crafted perturbations are cheap (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0005). (2) Reverse flow: false-positive injection, in which spoofed or noisy data cause a high-damage grade, triggers unnecessary inspection, cask handling or transfer, raising worker dose, operational disruption and reputational harm, and can serve as a distraction or timing cover for another action (AML.T0031, AML.T0046, AML.T0029). (3) Model or baseline tampering and supply chain: retraining pipelines, thresholds and stored baseline FRFs are high-value, low-visibility files; changes would be invisible to operators with no explainability (AML.T0018, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0012). IMPLICIT, exploitable. (4) Qualification and generalisation gap: 2/3-scale mock-up, simulated or lab damage, and sensor-location robustness shown only in a narrow range mean real canisters (different fill, temperature, concrete overpack, ageing, boundary conditions, environmental noise) fall out of distribution, and the classifier may fail silently (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0202, OP.C0303). The adversary needs no exploit, only to act where the model is weak. (5) Automation trust and skill fade: because the inside cannot be inspected, operators will tend to over-trust a convenient grade, with no independent check and eroding vigilance. An attacker can time activity to periods of complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0401). (6) Non-repeatability and weak governance: stochastic training, absent AI-specific QA and unclear regulatory scope for monitoring data (OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0505). (7) Fleet and cloud propagation: if one model or baseline is shared across casks or sites, or hosted off-premises, a single compromise or bias propagates across many canisters (OP.C0602, OP.C0601, OP.C0603). Overall, a nation-state is unlikely to target the classifier itself, but it is an attractive enabler and cover mechanism for concealment, and its unvalidated blind spots are the easiest thing to exploit.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the physical-channel evasion, baseline/model tampering, sim-to-real gap, drift and over-trust threats; I merged near-duplicate implicit points and dropped codes that only restated them. I omitted weakly supported items such as spamming with chaff data and governance-only codes not tied to a distinct threat.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning-aided damage identification of mock-up spent nuclear fuel assemblies in a sealed dry storage canister," Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence, vol. 128, 107484 (Elsevier), 2024
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed article trains RF, ANN and GNB classifiers on features from the difference between frequency response functions of an intact and a damaged canister mock-up, and grades damage levels. Random forest performed best (about 0.92 accuracy), including when the sensor locations were changed. The URL is a ResearchGate abstract page for the journal paper (DOI 10.1016/j.engappai.2023.107484). The ScienceDirect page for the same article was also returned by search.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is concealed fuel degradation, removal or substitution hidden behind false assurance of integrity (a safeguards falsification category). The entry itself notes there is no acute accident, so this stays below radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Implicit failures such as sim-to-real gap, drift and the lack of out-of-distribution rejection occur reliably. Deliberate manipulation of the baseline or the physical channel depends on specific conditions and on the insider position.

exploitability.why: Most credible exploitation needs insider pad access or compromise of the baseline, model or acquisition pipeline, and the implicit weaknesses still need an adversary with insider access to act on them.

affected_users.why: Impact is per canister, but a shared model or baseline could propagate bias or compromise across casks and sites. It remains a monitoring and assurance function, not a facility-wide process.

discoverability.why: The methods and data are published, and the weaknesses of this class of ML (no OOD rejection, drift, scale gap) are well known. Exploiting them still requires site-specific knowledge of baselines and procedures.

use_case: Artificial neural-network models that combine plant measurements with system physics to estimate steam generator feedwater flow rate in PWRs on-line, so venturi meter fouling is caught before it causes needless power derating. The same approach estimates the thermal efficiency of feedwater heaters in the balance of plant.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory feedwater-flow and heater-efficiency estimator sits upstream of the secondary calorimetric heat balance that sets the thermal power indication, so its errors become power-measurement errors rather than harmless reporting errors. The main threats are silent estimation error from label circularity, drift and common-cause coupling; misplaced operator trust and weak qualification of the non-safety tool; and adversarial manipulation of the model, its training data or its inputs. Harm requires a human or procedural step acting on a wrong estimate, and the licensed calorimetric, nuclear-instrumentation cross-checks and technical specification limits bound the consequences, so the realistic outcomes are regulatory power-limit exceedance, hidden instrument faults, lost margin and needless derates, not acute accident initiation.

Label circularity and sparse fouling data -- implicit, exploitable
If training labels come from the fouled venturi or from a heat balance that uses it, the network learns the fouling bias as normal and reports a confident but wrong flow into the thermal power determination. Fouling episodes are also rare and episodic, so validation is weakest where it matters. An adversary could rely on the model's inability to flag a biased baseline to hide a real flow anomaly or a small manipulation inside the learned bias.

Drift and operating-regime failure -- implicit, exploitable
Feedwater heater tube plugging, power uprates, sensor recalibration or replacement, heater outages and transients move the operating point outside the training envelope, so the network returns plausible but wrong flow and heater-efficiency values with no extrapolation flag. An adversary could time interference for post-outage or post-uprate periods, when staff expect discrepancies and the model is least trustworthy.

Common-cause coupling and fault masking -- implicit, exploitable
The flow and heater estimators use the same temperatures, pressures and valve states that feed the calorimetric, so a single drifting RTD or transmitter biases both estimate and reference, and the network smooths the drift into a plausible output. This undermines the independence of the cross-check and lets instrument degradation propagate unseen. An adversary could exploit this by making small coordinated shifts in a few inputs that the fused estimate absorbs and the reference reproduces.

Over-trust, skill fade and alarm complacency -- implicit, exploitable
Staff trained to prefer the model over a fouled venturi may defer venturi cleaning, rescale the calorimetric constant or stop independent ultrasonic or manual heat-balance checks, while false alarms can push others to ignore it. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust so that a biased estimate is accepted as authoritative and the independent verification that would catch it has eroded.

Opacity and qualification gaps -- implicit, exploitable
The network cannot explain why an estimate changed, training non-determinism can yield different models from the same data, and non-safety status invites weak change control and no defined requalification after plant changes. A deliberate manipulation therefore looks like legitimate drift, which gives an adversary cover.

Model and training-data tampering -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor who poisons historian extracts used for retraining, alters stored weights, or compromises ML libraries or model artifacts can embed a bias of a few percent that hides real fouling or fabricates a derate justification. The result is a skewed calorimetric power indication, either eroded margin to a licensed limit or lost output.

Input falsification -- adversarial
An adversary with access to the historian or instrument network can make small coordinated falsifications of several fused process signals, staying inside the physics-consistent envelope, to steer the estimate. The output shifts the inferred feedwater flow and thermal power while every individual sensor still reads plausible.

Data-path pivot and fleet propagation -- adversarial
The analytics host needs a feed from plant process systems, often with vendor remote support, creating an IT/OT connection that can serve as a pivot into plant data networks. Vendor-hosted retraining or one model propagated across a fleet could carry a single flawed or compromised build into several units, and the performance data and model sensitivities also reveal which instruments the power estimate depends on.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Feedwater flow is the dominant input to the secondary-side calorimetric heat balance, which sets the licensed thermal power indication. A hybrid physics-plus-ANN estimator sits directly in that chain, so its error is a power-measurement error, not a harmless reporting error. This is an advisory O&M tool meant to separate venturi fouling from real flow changes, and plant practice already guards against its errors: the licensed power calorimetric, the nuclear instrumentation cross-calibration, and technical specification limits. Harm therefore needs a human or procedural step to act on a wrong estimate, for example by recalibrating the flow measurement, rescaling the calorimetric, or declining to correct real fouling. The credible harms are quiet ones: a regulatory power-limit exceedance, a hidden instrument fault, or a lost margin to a limit. They are not acute accident initiators, and the engineering controls that bound them should be credited.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Drift and operating-regime generalization (OP.C0302, .01, .03). The ANN is trained on a given plant's historical data. Changes such as fouling progression, feedwater heater tube plugging, power uprates, a different fuel cycle, sensor replacement or recalibration, and unusual transients all move the operating point away from the training distribution. The model can then return a plausible but wrong flow. (2) Ground-truth circularity (OP.C0201, OP.C0204). Reference flow is rarely independently known. If training labels come from the same fouled venturi, or from a heat balance that uses it, the model learns the fouling bias and certifies it as normal. Scarcity of labeled fouling episodes also gives a small-data, low-base-rate problem (OP.C0202). (3) Common-cause coupling (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). The estimator uses the same plant measurements (temperatures, pressures, steam flow) that feed the calorimetric. A single drifting RTD or pressure transmitter can bias both the estimate and the reference, so the 'independent cross-check' is not independent and the error propagates unseen. (4) Over-trust and mode confusion (OP.C0101.03, .04, OP.C0102). Operators or performance engineers may use the estimate to justify not repairing or cleaning the venturi, or to adjust the power calorimetric constant. Alternatively, they may ignore it after false alarms (disuse). The sensitivity analysis in the source supports the method's performance, but I could not confirm its scope or how well it covers the cases above. (5) Qualification and opacity gaps (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). It is unclear how a non-safety ANN estimate would be verified, versioned and requalified after plant changes. This is an AI-specific QA gap, and the model cannot readily explain why a given estimate changed. Feedwater heater efficiency estimates carry a similar but lower-consequence risk, mainly misdirected maintenance and lost economic performance.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Integrity manipulation of the inputs or model (AML.T0043, T0020, T0018, T0010). A capable adversary with access to plant historian or data-network feeds, to retraining data, or to model files in the supply chain could shift the estimate slowly. The aim would be to mask real venturi fouling or a real flow anomaly, to push an apparent derate, or to cause operators to scale the calorimetric incorrectly. Slow, bounded bias is the hardest to detect, and the main exposure is a non-safety-to-operations data path, such as a historian or performance-monitoring server, that bridges into the IT network. (7) Availability and trust erosion (AML.T0029, T0031). Spoofed alarms or degraded model service could cause needless derates or erode confidence in the tool, with economic effect and little safety effect. (8) Supply chain and off-site dependencies (OP.C0601, OP.C0602). If a vendor retrains or hosts the model, or the same model is propagated across a fleet, one compromised or flawed build could bias several units. The existing safeguards still bound consequences: redundant safety-grade instrumentation, calorimetric procedures, independent calibration checks, and protection systems do not rely on this estimate. The main risks are therefore regulatory non-compliance, undetected degradation of instruments, and economic loss, provided the tool stays advisory and is not wired into automated power or setpoint adjustments.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a physics-informed virtual sensor for feedwater flow, a quantity that sets the calorimetric reactor thermal power calculation. That makes the ML pipeline's weak points the training labels, the feature set, and the cross-validation target, more than the network architecture. The key problem is circularity. A feedwater flow model trained on plant data inherits whatever bias the fouled venturi had during the training window. If the labels are venturi readings or a heat balance built on them, the model learns the fouled instrument and cannot serve as an independent check. If the labels come from a different reference, such as ultrasonic flow meters, tracer tests or a heat balance, the training set is small and episodic. Early-1990s networks were also trained on limited operating envelopes, so inference is fragile at power ramps, transients, feedwater heater outages, and after a retrofit or uprate. The risk is that the model reports plausible numbers outside its training distribution and nothing flags the extrapolation.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Label and provenance circularity: if the model is trained on or calibrated against the fouled venturi or the plant computer's derived flow, it hides fouling or reproduces it. The consequence is a confident but wrong flow estimate feeding thermal power determination, with possible over-power (a licensed-limit and safety-margin issue) or under-power (economic loss). (2) Drift and out-of-distribution failure: the training data span a limited set of operating states. Feedwater heater fouling, sensor aging, a heater out of service, power uprates, and component replacement shift the input-output mapping (data drift and concept drift). Without a retraining or revalidation schedule or an input-envelope monitor, errors grow silently. (3) Fault-masking and cascading propagation: the same inputs (temperatures, pressures, pump or valve states) feed both the flow and heater-efficiency estimators. A single faulty sensor, or a sensor drifting in a correlated way, can skew both outputs together and look like consistent corroboration. A network also tends to absorb input drift into a smooth, plausible output, which suppresses the signal an operator would use to detect a failing instrument. (4) Opacity and qualification gap: a trained network has no traceable relation to the physics the operator must justify, which makes qualification for any role beyond advisory difficult. Training non-determinism (random seeds, initialization) can yield different models from the same data. (5) Automation trust: if operators start using the estimate to defer venturi cleaning or to justify power recovery, the plant may rely on an unvalidated virtual sensor, and skill in the manual heat-balance check may fade.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Integrity attack on inputs: because the model is a deterministic function of plant measurements, an adversary with access to the data historian or instrument network can make small coordinated manipulations of feature inputs to steer the estimate while staying inside plausible ranges (evade model, craft adversarial data). Physics-informed constraints help only if they are enforced as hard checks. (7) Training-data and model tampering: poisoning the historian extracts or altering stored weights during retraining could embed a bias that hides real fouling or fabricates a derating justification (poison training data, manipulate model, erode model integrity). (8) Supply chain: modern reimplementations use third-party ML libraries, pretrained surrogates and container images that can be compromised. (9) Sensitive insight: the model and its sensitivity analysis reveal which instruments the thermal power estimate depends on, and so which are worth targeting. Hence insecurity here is mostly silent degradation of an advisory metric that could slide into a de facto control or licensing input, plus an adversarial route that exploits that slide.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this is not a high-value direct target, because it is an advisory, on-line estimator in the balance of plant and not a protection or safety-actuation function. It is still worth modeling for one reason: feedwater flow is the input to the secondary calorimetric heat balance, which sets the reactor thermal power indication. An estimator that corrects for venturi fouling therefore sits close to the number that decides how hard the plant is allowed to run. Any adversary able to bias that estimate, whether an insider with write access to the model or its inputs, or a supply-chain actor, gets a quiet way to shift a power-related indication while keeping every individual sensor in range. The more relevant concern is a slow, stealthy attack that exploits the operator trust the tool is designed to build. The tool's purpose is to tell operators the venturi is wrong and the real flow is different, so staff are being trained to prefer the model over the instrument. An adversary would favor timing and plausible-looking deviation over any dramatic compromise. A nation-state would more likely use this as a stepping stone into the plant data network than as a sabotage target.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or training-data integrity: the model learns the relation between plant measurements, physics terms and flow, so poisoned or tampered historian data, or a manipulated retrained model, can shift the estimate by a few percent. That shifts the inferred feedwater flow and hence the calorimetric thermal power, giving either hidden over-power margin erosion or false derating that costs revenue. An insider with historian or engineering-workstation access is the realistic actor (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0031). (2) Input spoofing: the model fuses many process signals (temperatures, pressures, valve positions), so coordinated small falsifications of a few instruments, perhaps through an already-compromised I&C or data-diode-adjacent network, can move the output while each input stays plausible. A fused estimator masks a single-sensor tamper because it smooths it, and the attacker needs only to stay inside the physics-consistent envelope (AML.T0043, T0015). (3) Stepping-stone and concentration of trust: the estimator needs a data path from plant process systems to an analytics host, often with vendor remote support, which creates a new IT/OT connection and a pivot point (AML.T0010.001, T0012, T0025). The ANN output may be handed to the performance-monitoring team as an authoritative reference, so it becomes a high-leverage thing to corrupt. (4) Model-data theft yields little, but plant performance data carries operating-margin information that has intelligence value (AML.T0024, T0037).

IMPLICIT, AND EXPLOITABLE BY TIMING. (a) Automation trust and skill fade: once staff accept the model over a fouled venturi, they stop cross-checking with ultrasonic flow measurement or tracer methods, which erodes the independent check that would catch a biased model (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (b) Drift and generalization: after feedwater heater maintenance, power uprates, instrument recalibration or new fouling regimes, the ANN may be out of distribution. Because it is trained on historical operating data, it can encode past instrument biases, including the fouling it is meant to detect, as truth (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0201.05). An adversary could time interference for known post-outage periods, when the model is least trustworthy and staff expect discrepancies. (c) Opacity and qualification gap: ANN estimates cannot be readily explained, so a manipulation looks the same as legitimate drift. Nuclear QA frameworks for safety-related software do not cover retraining, and the tool's non-safety status can lead to weak change control and configuration management (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0503). (d) Sparse data for abnormal states (rare fouling or fault conditions) leaves validation weak where it matters most, and the sensitivity analysis in the source covers statistical behavior, not deliberate input manipulation (OP.C0202, OP.C0304.03). The main consequence is erosion of the independent verification of reactor power and a hidden channel into plant data networks, not a direct safety-system compromise.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on label circularity, drift, common-cause input coupling, over-trust, opacity/qualification gaps, and slow integrity manipulation of data or model; I merged these into single threats and kept the stepping-stone and fleet-propagation concerns as one adversarial paragraph. I dropped weak or tangential codes (AML.T0029 and AML.T0024/T0037 data theft, AML.T0059, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0503) as not clearly instantiated or adding little.

evidence.citation: "Monitoring Feedwater Flow Rate and Component Thermal Performance of Pressurized Water Reactors by Means of Artificial Neural Networks," Nuclear Technology (American Nuclear Society / Taylor & Francis), Vol. 107, No. 1
evidence.note: The journal article builds neural-network models for on-line prediction of PWR steam generator feedwater flow and feedwater heater thermal efficiency. These address venturi-meter fouling and the resulting unnecessary derating. The authors also developed a statistical sensitivity analysis to assess how well the method performs. I could only read the abstract in the search result, not the full text.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a skewed calorimetric power indication from model/data tampering or input falsification, but licensed calorimetric, NI cross-checks and tech spec limits bound it to regulatory power-limit exceedance, eroded margin, hidden instrument faults or derates, not radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Implicit failures (label circularity, drift after outages or uprates, common-cause sensor bias) recur reliably once conditions exist, but harm needs a human or procedural step to act on the wrong estimate, and adversarial manipulation needs particular timing and access.

exploitability.why: Adversarial paths (poisoning historian retraining data, altering weights, coordinated falsification of fused signals inside the physics envelope) need insider, supply-chain, or OT-network access plus process knowledge; the implicit weaknesses are easy to exploit once known, but the adversarial ones are not routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: The most severe credible case, a single flawed model build propagated across a fleet or a common-cause bias entering the thermal power determination, reaches unit-wide or multi-unit scope, while a typical instance affects one unit's secondary-side power measurement.

discoverability.why: The general weaknesses of ML-based virtual sensors (drift, circularity, common-cause coupling, over-trust) are well documented in open literature and the published method is public, but learning which instruments the power estimate depends on and how to exploit that takes partial system knowledge.

use_case: Self-supervised one-class prototypical networks for detecting pipe leaks in nuclear power plants. The networks train only on normal-state acoustic signals from piping, with no labelled leak data. Augmented normal data serve as pseudo-leak samples. The model adapts to new plant environments from a few support samples, so operators can detect leaks early.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case is an advisory acoustic leak detector trained only on normal-state signals, with augmented normal data standing in for leaks and a few-shot support set defining the plant's 'normal'. Its main insecurities are control of the baseline (support-set and prototype poisoning), evasion by acoustic masking or false-alarm flooding, tampering with the model or sensor chain, and silent-miss failures from an unvalidated simulation-only performance claim. These are compounded by drift, operator over-trust and weak qualification, so the quiet channel can mask a real leak or sabotage. Defence-in-depth leak indications bound the severity only if the AI stays independent of them.

Support-set and prototype poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or an attacker with historian, edge or commissioning access can seed the few-shot support samples or normal-data streams with a leak signature or shifted baseline, so the prototype absorbs a real leak as in-distribution. Because the system holds no leak-labelled data, nothing exposes the manipulation, and the result is a delayed or missed primary or secondary pipe leak.

Acoustic masking and chaff evasion -- adversarial
An actor with physical or cyber access to the sensors or DAQ stream can add broadband or band-limited noise, or replay or attenuate the signal, to hold leak embeddings inside the normal radius during a real breach or sabotage. The same access can flood the detector with false alarms so operators loosen thresholds or switch it off before the real event.

Model, artifact and sensor-chain tampering -- adversarial
A tampered pretrained backbone, augmentation library, prototype or threshold file, or edge deployment can carry a backdoor that maps a trigger signature to 'normal' or silently shifts thresholds. Such a backdoor is invisible to AUC testing on simulated data and opens a new IT/OT path from the acoustic monitoring network into plant data systems.

Publication-enabled reconnaissance -- adversarial
The published architecture, Grad-CAM-identified leak-relevant frequency bands and augmentation strategy tell an adversary which spectral features the detector depends on, narrowing the search for effective masking.

Proxy-task and sim-to-real mismatch -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained to separate augmented normal data from normal data, not real leaks, and the 0.994 AUC comes from simulated plants. Small, low-flow or incipient leaks, the early-detection goal, may fall inside the learned normal manifold, and the false-negative rate cannot be measured without leak labels. An adversary can rely on this unmeasured blind spot and on operators' trust in the headline AUC, timing a leak or sabotage to stay below detection.

Drift and re-adaptation absorbing degradation -- implicit, exploitable
Pump and valve line-ups, power level, sensor aging, insulation work and seasonal change shift the acoustic baseline, producing nuisance alarms or, when the prototype is re-fit, silently normalising slow-developing leaks. An adversary could deliberately time a gradual degradation, or a re-adaptation window, so the drift is absorbed as normal.

Automation complacency and alarm fatigue -- implicit, exploitable
A quiet detector invites reduced walkdowns and discounting of other indications, while chronic false alarms drive desensitisation and threshold relaxation, eroding manual inspection skill. An adversary can induce nuisance alarms or act during quiet periods of misplaced trust to hide a leak or sabotage action.

Opacity, non-determinism and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
Grad-CAM saliency is weak evidence of causal leak sensitivity, and stochastic augmentation seeds and support selection reduce repeatability, so a non-safety-classed learned monitor is hard to qualify and its re-adaptation is easy to perform and hard to audit. An adversary can exploit weak change control to slip in an unreviewed re-adaptation or model change, and scope creep toward safety-significant reliance widens the consequence of any silent miss.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is an advisory monitoring aid for O&M that sits alongside existing leak-detection layers (sump level, humidity, radiation, inventory balance, operator rounds), so one bad output rarely causes harm alone. The main downstream risks are false reassurance (a missed leak while operators trust a 0.994 AUC) and alarm fatigue or nuisance trips (false positives that erode trust or prompt unnecessary outages or isolation). The reported performance comes from simulated plant environments with augmented normal data standing in for leaks. Real plant acoustics are noisy and non-stationary (pump and valve line-ups, flow changes, outage work), so the performance claim may not transfer. Because the model is trained only on 'normal' and adapts from a few support samples, the definition of normal is the attack surface and the weak point: whoever controls or contaminates the support set controls what counts as healthy.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Support-set or baseline poisoning. The few-shot adaptation step builds the 'normal' prototype from a handful of samples. If those are captured during an existing degraded condition, during masking noise, or are deliberately manipulated by an insider, contractor or compromised data pipeline, the prototype can absorb a leak signature or a sensor-tampered baseline as normal. A real leak is then scored as in-distribution. Consequence: a delayed or missed detection of a primary or secondary pipe leak, with escalation to loss-of-coolant or loss of function only if the independent layers (inventory balance, sump, radiation monitors, walkdowns) also fail or are discounted. (2) Evasion by acoustic masking or sensor manipulation: a physical or cyber actor injecting broadband noise, or spoofing, replaying, or attenuating the acoustic sensor or DAQ stream, could hold the embedding inside the normal prototype radius. The same access allows inducing false alarms to cause nuisance outages, to desensitize operators, or to time an attack around a degraded detector. (3) Model or pipeline supply-chain tampering (the trained weights, augmentation code, threshold or prototype files, edge or cloud deployment), including silent threshold shifts. This is a new IT/OT attack surface where the acoustic monitoring network bridges to plant data systems. IMPLICIT: (4) Sim-to-real and OOD gap. Training and testing on simulated environments with augmentations as pseudo-leaks means that real small or incipient leaks (the early-detection claim) may look nothing like augmented normal data. AUC-ROC also hides operating-point behaviour: the false-alarm rate at the chosen threshold, which matters under very low leak base rates. (5) Drift: aging, flow regime, maintenance, insulation, and seasonal changes shift 'normal' (concept and data drift), and few-shot re-adaptation can silently absorb slow-developing degradation, so a leak that grows gradually is normalized. (6) Automation bias and complacency: operators may reduce walkdowns or discount other indications when the AI is quiet, or ignore it after nuisance alarms. Grad-CAM explanations are weak evidence of causal reasoning and could give false confidence. (7) Qualification and governance gap: a non-deterministic learned model with no leak-labelled validation is hard to qualify, so it is likely limited to non-safety-class use. Risk comes from scope creep, where an advisory tool is gradually relied on for safety-significant decisions without qualification, change control, or retraining and version management. Existing mitigation: defence in depth and diverse leak-detection methods bound the severity, but only if the AI is kept independent and not used to downgrade the other indicators.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a one-class prototypical network that never sees a real leak: the decision boundary is defined by a prototype built from normal acoustic embeddings, with augmentations of normal data standing in for 'pseudo-leaks'. The pipeline's central assumption is that augmentation-induced distortion resembles the spectral and temporal signature of real leaks, and that a handful of support samples from a new plant is representative of that plant's normal state. The reported AUC-ROC of 0.994 comes from simulated plant environments, so it is evidence of separability under simulator assumptions, not of field performance. The real exposure sits in the prototype and support-set mechanism, the augmentation proxy, and the absence of any leak ground truth for validation. These make the system fragile to anything that shifts, contaminates or imitates the 'normal' reference.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Proxy-task mismatch (OP.C0301, OP.C0403, OP.C0201.01/.02): the model is trained to detect augmented normal data, not leaks. Real leaks vary with pipe geometry, fluid phase, pressure, crack morphology and sensor coupling, and may sit below ambient noise, so low-flow or early leaks (the stated goal) can fall inside the learned normal manifold. Simulated or transferred data produce optimistic AUC, and with no leak labels the false-negative rate is essentially unmeasurable. This is a silent-miss failure, not a loud one. (2) Drift and OOD (OP.C0302.01/.02/.03, OP.C0303): plant acoustics change with power level, pump speed, valve line-ups, outage vs. operation, sensor aging, mounting changes and insulation work. A one-class detector treats such changes as anomalies (alarm floods, then desensitisation or threshold loosening, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.05) or, if the prototype is re-fit, absorbs them as normal. Few-shot adaptation also means quality hinges on a tiny support set: if it is captured during an unrecognised slow leak, a noisy transient or an atypical mode, the prototype is mis-centred and the leak becomes the baseline (OP.C0202, OP.C0204). Non-stationary operating states are poorly covered by the simulated environments. (3) Opacity and verification (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504): Grad-CAM saliency on frequency bands does not verify causal sensitivity to leaks, and it can give false assurance. Embedding and few-shot stochasticity (augmentation seeds, support selection) reduce repeatability and complicate qualification of a monitoring function whose failure is a missed degradation. (4) Human factors: operators may read a quiet detector as proof of integrity, with automation complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06) and reduced walkdowns/inspections.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Support-set/prototype poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059, AML.T0031): the few-shot adaptation path is a low-cost, high-leverage data-ingestion point. An insider or an attacker with historian or edge access can seed support samples or normal-data streams to shift the prototype so a real leak, or a sabotage-induced one, stays 'normal'. Because the system learns only from normal data, there is no labelled leak set to expose the manipulation. (6) Evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0043.003): an adversary with knowledge of the sensor placement, preprocessing and embedding (from published papers, AML.T0000/T0002) could craft acoustic masking, such as injecting broadband or band-limited noise near sensors, or shaping process noise, to push leak embeddings toward the prototype or flood the system with false alarms (AML.T0046, AML.T0029) to degrade trust or hide a real event. (7) Supply chain and artefact integrity (AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0018, AML.T0076): pretrained backbones, augmentation libraries and the edge deployment pipeline can be tampered with. A backdoored embedding that maps a trigger signature to 'normal' would be invisible to AUC testing on simulation. (8) Fleet propagation (OP.C0602): a shared base model or adaptation recipe reused across units or sites spreads any systematic blind spot or compromise. The core insecurity is a detector that fails silently and whose notion of normal is cheap to redefine.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this is a monitoring-and-assurance function, not a control function, so a nation-state is unlikely to target it directly. It matters as an enabler. An acoustic leak detector that is trained only on 'normal' and adapts from a few support samples has an intrinsic weakness: whoever supplies or influences what counts as normal defines the blind spot. Once operators trust a 0.994 AUC-ROC result, an insider or intruder could time a leak, a steam or coolant loss, or a physical sabotage action around the detector's weakened vigilance or contaminated baseline, and could use the quiet alarm channel to hide the activity. The reported performance comes from simulated plants, so the real-world false-alarm and miss rates are unknown. That gap pushes operators toward either over-trusting or silencing the system, and both responses are exploitable.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Support-set and baseline poisoning. The few-shot adaptation step is a small, low-volume, high-leverage data pathway. An insider with access to commissioning or recalibration can submit support samples that already contain a slow leak signature, or ones that shift the 'normal' prototype so a real leak embeds inside the normal class. Facility dependence: leak and early-warning monitoring of piping. Consequence: a masked leak, delayed response, and loss of the defense-in-depth monitoring layer. Because the system is one-class, there is no leak-labelled data to expose the poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059). (2) Evasion by acoustic mimicry or masking. An adversary with physical access, or a nuisance-noise source, can add broadband or band-limited sound that suppresses the anomaly score during a real breach or sabotage. Alternatively they can flood the detector with chaff to cause false alarms, so operators raise thresholds or switch it off before the real event (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0046, AML.T0029, AML.T0041). (3) Sensor-chain and model-artifact compromise: tampering with acoustic sensors, signal conditioning, or model and prototype files, or a compromised vendor or open-source pretrained backbone and augmentation pipeline, could install a backdoor trigger. A leak that carries the trigger would then be classed as normal (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0076). (4) Recon through publication: the paper discloses the architecture, the Grad-CAM-identified leak-relevant frequency bands, and the augmentation strategy, which tells an adversary which spectral features the detector depends on (AML.T0000, AML.T0013, AML.T0063). IMPLICIT, and exploitable by timing: (5) Unvalidated generalization. The AUC-ROC comes from simulated plants, with simulated or surrogate leaks and no field base rate. Real plants have pumps, valves, flow transients and seasonal noise, so drift and heterogeneity will cause misses or nuisance alarms (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202). Pseudo-leaks made by augmenting normal data may not resemble real leak physics, so small or distant leaks could be missed (OP.C0301, OP.C0403). (6) Alarm fatigue and automation trust. Chronic false alarms lead to desensitization and threshold relaxation. Quiet periods produce complacency and skill fade in manual walkdowns and acoustic inspection, a window an adversary can target (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). (7) Qualification and governance gaps: a non-safety-classed analytic with weak change control, little retraining oversight, and Grad-CAM as the only explainability evidence. Re-adaptation is easy to perform and hard to audit (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0401, OP.C0505).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on support-set/baseline poisoning, acoustic masking or chaff evasion, supply-chain tampering, sim-to-real/drift silent misses, and automation complacency. I kept the security specialist's publication-reconnaissance threat as distinct and omitted weakly supported codes (e.g. AML.T0010.002, OP.C0505, OP.C0602, OP.C0204) that no retained threat clearly instantiates.

evidence.citation: "Self-Supervised One-Class Prototypical Networks for Nuclear Power Plant Pipe Leak Detection," IEEE (IEEE Xplore)
evidence.note: The paper builds a deep-learning leak detector that learns from normal-state data across several domains. It adds a self-supervised step that treats augmented normal data as pseudo-leaks. It was tested in several simulated nuclear power plant environments, including unseen ones, with an average AUC-ROC of 0.994. A Grad-CAM analysis checked that the model focuses on leak-relevant frequency bands. I could not confirm the journal or conference name from the search result, and the IEEE Xplore page is not a listed priority category, so I marked it 'other'.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a masked or missed pipe leak, or sabotage hidden by a poisoned baseline, which could delay detection of a primary or secondary leak; defence-in-depth indications and the advisory role keep this below a direct radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Once the trigger conditions exist, the class is reliable: a poisoned support set is absorbed by the prototype, the proxy-task blind spot is structural, and drift and re-adaptation predictably normalise slow degradation.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (support-set poisoning, sensor or DAQ access, artifact tampering) generally need insider, commissioning, or OT/edge access in a protected plant, though some implicit weaknesses need no special access.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly confined to the monitored piping and its acoustic detection channel, but a backdoor or IT/OT pivot, or over-trust that erodes other indications, could spread it to several systems.

discoverability.why: The published architecture, Grad-CAM frequency bands, augmentation strategy and headline AUC are public, and one-class and few-shot detector weaknesses are well documented, so a capable outsider can infer the class of weakness without insider knowledge.

use_case: Gaussian-process, support-vector-machine and neural-network regression models that predict the decay heat of discharged PWR and BWR spent fuel assemblies. Inputs are assembly-averaged enrichment, assembly-averaged burnup, initial heavy-metal mass and cooling time. The models are trained on calorimetric decay-heat measurements, augmented with synthetic data, and include uncertainty analysis. They are intended for spent fuel thermal characterisation in storage.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case is a small-data decay-heat surrogate (91 PWR and 171 BWR calorimetry points, padded with synthetic data) whose outputs feed spent-fuel thermal characterisation, heat-load limits and cask loading. It is offline and sits behind bounding calculations and monitoring, so harm needs compounding failures. The main insecurities are silent out-of-envelope extrapolation, circular synthetic data and over-tight uncertainty, over-trust and missing qualification, and data, model and input tampering that hides inside normal model uncertainty. Safeguards-relevant false corroboration of declared fuel properties is also a concern.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
The regressors see only four assembly-averaged inputs and a few US and Swedish campaigns, so high-burnup, MOX, new-cladding or unusual-history assemblies get confident but wrong decay-heat values, which underestimates heat load and erodes cladding temperature margin in storage and transport. An adversary could select or declare assemblies in the poorly validated region so that a deliberate error looks like ordinary model uncertainty.

Synthetic-data circularity and false uncertainty -- implicit, exploitable
Synthetic augmentation probably inherits the biases of the depletion codes the model complements, so validation overstates accuracy and the reported intervals are too tight. Anyone able to alter the synthetic generator or the calibration could hide a bias within the claimed error band.

Qualification gap and repeatability limits -- implicit, exploitable
No established qualification route exists for ML in heat-load licensing bases, neural-network training is not strictly reproducible and its internals are opaque, so a drifted or wrong model is hard to detect before it is embedded in long loading campaigns. Run-to-run variability also weakens forensic separation of tampering from normal variation, which an adversary can rely on.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A tidy point value with an uncertainty band invites use in place of conservative bounding calculations, especially as skills in the detailed methods fade, and loading may be optimised close to limits. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust so that a small biased prediction goes unchallenged.

Fleet-wide bias propagation -- implicit
One model reused across pools, campaigns and sites spreads the same bias to many canisters at once, defeating independence between units. A realistic adversary gains little beyond what data or model tampering already offers.

Training and synthetic data poisoning -- adversarial
With only a few hundred records, a handful of altered calorimetry or synthetic entries, or a tampered public dataset, can bias predictions in a sparse burnup region while staying inside the stated uncertainty. The result is under-predicted decay heat that relaxes thermal limits or masks discrepancies in declared assemblies.

Model and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
Altered weights, kernel hyperparameters, scalers, ML library dependencies or uncertainty-calibration code can subtly shift outputs or shrink reported bands, and regression tests on held-out cases are the only likely detection.

Input record manipulation and false corroboration -- adversarial
Falsified burnup, enrichment, mass or cooling-time records flow through the model into plausible predictions, which lend false independent confirmation of declared inventories and could mislead a safeguards comparison of measured and predicted heat.

Model and dataset leakage and reconnaissance -- adversarial
The public method and dataset, or an exfiltrated model and operator data, let an adversary build a proxy model, locate where uncertainty is understated, and infer operator-specific assembly properties.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a small-data regression surrogate (91 PWR and 171 BWR calorimetry points, padded with synthetic data) that would feed spent-fuel thermal characterisation for pool and dry storage and for transport: heat-load limits, cask loading patterns, cladding temperature margins and time-to-boil. Operationally, decay heat is a slowly evolving quantity, and cask and pool designs already carry conservative bounding calculations (ORIGEN/SCALE-type depletion and decay codes with margins), surface or pool temperature monitoring, and licensed heat-load limits. A wrong prediction therefore rarely causes harm alone. It matters when someone substitutes it for the bounding calculation, when loading is optimised close to the limit, or when it is trusted for assemblies outside its narrow training envelope. There is also a safeguards angle: decay heat tied to declared burnup and cooling time is a verification signature, so a model that is biased or manipulated could mask discrepancies in declared assembly properties.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Out-of-distribution failure. Training data come from a limited set of US and Swedish measured assemblies. Assembly-averaged inputs omit axial and radial burnup profiles, power history, and the pre-discharge irradiation history that sets short-lived and long-lived nuclide inventories. Assemblies with high burnup, new fuel and cladding designs, MOX, unusual enrichment, very short or very long cooling times, or unusual operating histories lie outside the data. GP, SVM and NN regressors extrapolate poorly and can return confident, physically implausible values, such as non-monotonic decay with cooling time. The consequence is underestimated heat load. That can mean cask or canister loading patterns with higher-than-analysed cladding temperatures, an overestimated time-to-boil in pool loss-of-cooling planning, or transport heat-load declarations that are wrong. (2) Synthetic-data circularity. Augmenting with simulated or surrogate data (probably from depletion codes) imports the biases of the codes the model is meant to complement. Validation against that data overstates accuracy, and a systematic error is passed on as an apparent independent confirmation. (3) Uncertainty quantification is not trustworthy under scarcity. Intervals are conditional on the model class and on a sample that is small and unevenly spread, and they are typically uncalibrated outside the data. Run-to-run variability from NN initialisation and training splits also hurts repeatability, which matters in a licensing setting. (4) Automation bias and qualification gap. The tool is faster and cheaper than detailed calculations. Staff may use point predictions to optimise loading or shorten cooling-time decisions without a conservative bound, especially as skills in the detailed methods fade. No established NQA-1-style qualification or regulatory acceptance path exists for ML in heat-load licensing bases. Opacity, especially in the NN, limits independent verification. (5) Common-cause propagation. One model reused across a fleet, several pools, or successive loading campaigns spreads the same bias across many canisters at once, which defeats independence between units. Physical safeguards (monitoring, margins, bounding analyses) still limit consequences, but only if they are not eroded on the strength of the model.

ADVERSARIAL threats. (a) Poisoning or tampering with the training and calibration data, or with model files and the pipeline. With only a few hundred records, a handful of altered calorimetry or synthetic entries carry large leverage, and small biases can stay inside the claimed uncertainty. The model could be biased low to relax thermal limits or biased to hide discrepancies. (b) Manipulation of the inputs. Burnup, enrichment, mass and cooling time come from operator records and burnup codes. Falsified or erroneous declarations would flow straight into plausible-looking predictions, and the model would then add false confidence that a declared inventory is consistent. A safeguards inspector or regulator comparing measured to predicted heat could be misled, for example about substituted or partially removed assemblies, if the predictor is biased or its error bars are too wide to flag them. (c) Confidentiality. The queryable model and the measured dataset can leak operator-specific burnup and inventory data, or allow inference of declared fuel properties. (d) Availability. Denial or corruption of the tool pushes users back to slower methods, which is a minor consequence provided fallbacks are retained. Because margins and independent monitoring exist, the credible safety harm requires several compounding failures. The more serious class of harm is erosion of conservatism and of independent verification.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small-data tabular regression problem. 91 PWR and 171 BWR calorimetric points from two national campaigns (US and Swedish) are used to fit GP, SVM and NN models on only four assembly-averaged features. The ML-pipeline fragility sits in data provenance and coverage. The measured set is tiny and clustered around older fuel designs, burnups, cooling times and enrichments, while the intended use (storage thermal characterisation) will meet modern high-burnup, MOX, advanced-cladding and long-cooled assemblies. Assembly-averaged inputs drop axial and radial burnup profiles, power history, and fuel-type and irradiation-history information, so the model has an irreducible blind spot that no training fix removes. Synthetic augmentation is probably generated from physics codes such as ORIGEN, or from the model's own fit, so its biases and the model's can be baked together. This inflates apparent accuracy and shrinks the reported uncertainty, and the uncertainty is itself only valid in-distribution. The architecture is small and easy to audit, so the exposure is less in the model's internals than in data lineage, validity-envelope enforcement, and trust in the outputs.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution extrapolation (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). GP, SVM and NN models degrade without warning outside the training hull of burnup, enrichment and cooling time. NNs and RBF-kernel SVMs can extrapolate confidently and wrongly. GP variance can also collapse to the prior or be misread. Mechanism: the input falls outside the training distribution and the model still returns a point value. Dependency: cask loading, pool-rack placement and thermal limits that use the predicted decay heat. Consequence: underestimated heat load, with cladding temperature margin eroded in dry storage or transport, or overestimated heat causing needless cost and extra handling. (2) Data provenance and synthetic contamination (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0202, OP.C0204). Synthetic augmentation of a 262-point set can leak test information, circularly validate against the same physics codes, and mask poor coverage. Calorimetric measurements from different facilities and eras have different systematic errors that are not captured as features. Uncertainty from the model is therefore not the same as total uncertainty. Consequence: a licensing or safety case that cites over-tight confidence bounds. (3) Feature insufficiency and concept shift (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0301). Assembly-averaged inputs omit the axial profile, power history and fuel-design details that drive decay heat. A new fuel design, or a shift in operating practice such as extended cycles, makes the learned mapping invalid. The model is retrained rarely and has no new ground-truth source, because calorimetry is scarce and expensive, so drift cannot be detected from feedback. (4) Qualification and repeatability (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0401). Nuclear thermal analysis expects qualified codes with bounding uncertainty, but ML retrained from random seeds or synthetic draws gives non-reproducible predictions. There is no established qualification route for such a surrogate, and NNs are opaque. Consequence: regulators are asked to accept a model they cannot verify, or it is used informally without proper qualification. (5) Automation bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). A tidy output with an uncertainty band invites unchecked use by analysts who never see the training envelope. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data and synthetic-data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0031). With only about 260 points, a handful of altered calorimetric or synthetic records, or a tampered public dataset, can bias the fit, notably in the high-burnup region where data are sparse. The result is a systematic under-prediction that an adversary or an insider could time to coincide with high-density loading. (7) Model and pipeline tampering (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076). Altered model weights, kernel hyperparameters, preprocessing scalers or Python library dependencies would shift outputs subtly, and the shift would be hard to detect without regression tests on held-out cases. (8) Input manipulation (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015). Changing declared burnup, enrichment or cooling time in the assembly records that feed the model skews the predicted heat and hides it behind plausible inputs. This is a weakness of record integrity that the AI model extends: a precise model amplifies any error in its inputs and gives it a numerical stamp of authority. (9) Open-literature reconnaissance (AML.T0000, AML.T0002.000, AML.T0005). The dataset and method are public, so an adversary can build a proxy model and learn where the model is weakest and where uncertainty is understated.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view this is a low-glamour target: a small-data surrogate that sits in offline thermal characterisation of storage and transport, not in a real-time protection path. Its security significance is as a trust-concentrating number that feeds cask loading plans, thermal limits, and cooling-time decisions. It also feeds, indirectly, burnup and decay-heat consistency checks that safeguards inspectors rely on. A sophisticated adversary would more likely use it as a quiet way to bias a downstream decision, or as a stepping stone into the engineering data pipeline, than as a direct sabotage target. The more realistic concern is that its non-adversarial weaknesses (about 260 training points, synthetic augmentation, extrapolation to unmeasured fuel types) create a plausible-deniability space in which a deliberate error would look like normal model uncertainty.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and synthetic-augmentation integrity: with only 91 PWR and 171 BWR calorimetry points, a few tampered or fabricated records, or a manipulated synthetic-data generator, can shift predictions in a particular burnup/enrichment region (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000). The facility depends on these predictions for cask thermal loading and storage-pool/cask heat-load limits. Consequence: systematically underpredicted decay heat could lead to over-dense loading, cladding temperature margin erosion, or degraded cask performance, while a systematic overprediction could drive unnecessary cost or mask a discrepancy between declared and actual fuel. Because the real measurements are so few, an insider with data-curation access has outsized leverage and little statistical cross-checking exists. (2) Input manipulation by an insider: the model takes only four assembly-averaged inputs (enrichment, burnup, HM mass, cooling time) from fuel-records systems. Falsified or inconsistent burnup/cooling-time records, whether from record tampering or a diversion-concealment effort, would flow through a model that cannot detect them. Its smooth outputs could even lend false corroboration to altered declarations (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0031). This creates a safeguards-relevant stepping-stone: the model's agreement with a record is treated as independent verification when it is not. (3) Model artifact and supply-chain tampering: weights, scikit-style or custom ML libraries, and uncertainty-calibration code could be modified (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018, AML.T0076). The change could be subtle, for example shrinking the reported uncertainty bands, so as to evade review and remain within credible error. (4) Model-as-reconnaissance: an exfiltrated model or dataset reveals fuel inventory characteristics and thermal behaviour, and can be used to infer assembly properties (AML.T0024.001, AML.T0035). Sensitivity is modest but nonzero for safeguards and proliferation-relevant information. IMPLICIT. (5) Small-data and extrapolation failure (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.02): the US and Swedish calorimetry set does not cover newer high-burnup, MOX, or advanced-cladding assemblies, and synthetic data may encode the assumptions of the code that produced it. Predictions outside the training domain may look confident, and an adversary or an error-prone operator can exploit this gap by choosing assemblies where the model is least validated. (6) Automation trust and uncertainty misuse (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501): a decay-heat figure with an uncertainty band is easy to treat as a validated licensing input, displacing conservative lookup-based methods and calorimetry, with skill fade in the established calculation route. Opacity of the neural network and the lack of a qualification pathway for ML-derived thermal inputs mean that a drifted, wrong, or tampered model is hard to detect before it is embedded in loading campaigns that run for years.
