(7) Non-repeatability across training runs (OP.C0402.01): because multiple runs and synthetic data are used, results are not strictly reproducible, which weakens forensic ability to tell tampering from normal variation. Overall risk is moderate: low attractiveness to a nation-state as a direct target, but meaningful as a quiet bias or false-corroboration vector, and the main mitigation is retaining independent conservative calculation and measurement checks and strict provenance control over the calorimetry and synthetic datasets.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on out-of-envelope extrapolation, synthetic-data circularity, over-trust with a qualification gap, and data, model and input tampering; the security specialist's framing of the implicit weaknesses as cover for deliberate error shaped the exploitability statements. I dropped the weakly argued candidates (AML.T0015, AML.T0048.002, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0701) and kept reconnaissance and leakage as one distinct adversarial threat.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning of LWR spent nuclear fuel assembly decay heat measurements," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Elsevier / Korean Nuclear Society), vol. 53, issue 11, pp. 3563-3579, 2021
evidence.note: The paper trains three ML regressors (Gaussian process, SVM, neural network) on 91 PWR and 171 BWR measured assembly decay-heat values from US and Swedish calorimetry. Because the dataset is small, it uses multiple runs and synthetic data, and it also quantifies model uncertainty. The abstract does not state the downstream storage decision, so that purpose is my own framing.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is the biased under-prediction of decay heat that erodes cladding thermal margin in storage and transport, together with false corroboration of declared fuel properties in a safeguards comparison. This gives a safeguards-falsification category of harm. A release would need compounding failures because bounding calculations and monitoring sit behind the model, so the score stops short of 5.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-envelope extrapolation and small-data bias reliably occur once an assembly falls outside the sparse training region, but harm requires the model output to be used without bounding checks and the bias to stay inside the uncertainty band, so it is conditional.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (training or synthetic data poisoning, pipeline tampering, record falsification) need insider access to data, model artifacts or operator records. Only the public-dataset and out-of-envelope declaration routes are less demanding, and both still need a position in the fuel data chain.

affected_users.why: A single reused model spreads the same bias across many canisters, pools and campaigns, defeating independence between units, so the impact is broad across a storage inventory. It is not tightly coupled to reactor operation, so the score stays below 5.

discoverability.why: The method, the small dataset and the general weaknesses of small-data ML surrogates (extrapolation, synthetic-data circularity, uncertainty miscalibration) are publicly documented, so an outsider can readily infer where the model is weak. Operator-specific pipeline details are not public.

use_case: LSTM network with a multi-input multi-output multi-step strategy that predicts future trends of plant parameters after operator device actions in emergency situations. It was trained on emergency-operation data from a nuclear power plant simulator. Operators could use it to catch human errors early and to help diagnose accidents.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory LSTM forecaster, trained only on simulator emergency data, is consulted when operator stress and trust are highest, so a plausible but wrong forecast can steer diagnosis or action. The main implicit threats are simulator-to-plant out-of-distribution failure, compounding multi-step error, rare-event data scarcity, over-trust with skill fade, and the lack of a qualification path. The main adversarial threats are manipulation of live inputs, poisoning or backdoor of training data and model weights, model and data theft, and use of the tool as an IT/OT stepping stone or a denial target.

Simulator-to-plant gap -- implicit, exploitable
The LSTM learns the simulator's thermal-hydraulic approximations and scripted scenarios, so real sensor noise, ageing, plant modifications and multi-fault sequences fall outside its training support. It extrapolates smoothly with no uncertainty signal, producing confident wrong trajectories. An adversary could time an attack for such an off-nominal state, where tool error is expected and sabotage is easily mistaken for model error.

Multi-step error accumulation and counterfactual invalidity -- implicit, exploitable
Forecast error compounds over the horizon, and the model predicts the effect of actions from scripted correlations rather than causal guarantees. A false 'action worked' or 'action is safe' forecast can mask a human error or push a wrong diagnosis, defeating the tool's purpose. An adversary could rely on operators trusting such forecasts to make a harmful action look benign.

Rare-event data scarcity and aggregate-accuracy blind spot -- implicit, exploitable
Severe and erroneous action sequences are thinly represented, and the 95.4% 'mostly accurate' figure hides whether the roughly 5% misses cluster in the severe states that matter most. An adversary could steer the plant toward the scenarios where the tool is least reliable.

Over-trust, skill fade and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Under stress, operators may over-trust the forecast or drop it after a visible miss, and reliance erodes manual diagnostic skill. Opacity prevents telling a tampered forecast from an honest error. An adversary could exploit this misplaced trust and blurred attribution, or induce false alerts to desensitise operators before a real or staged event.

Qualification and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
No established qualification path exists for a non-deterministic, opaque advisory network, and retraining after plant changes risks silent regression or de facto reliance without verification. Weak configuration and data-access control over retraining supplies the missing integrity controls an attacker would depend on.

Live input manipulation -- adversarial
An adversary with a foothold on the plant data path, or spoofed sensor or historian feeds, can craft perturbations that make the LSTM forecast a benign trend during a real transient or a spurious divergence during a normal one. The result is hidden faults, induced unnecessary actions, or lost operator confidence.

Training data and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor altering simulator datasets, the retraining pipeline or the weights can embed a bias or a backdoor keyed to a parameter pattern, so a harmful action is endorsed or a correct one flagged. Held-out simulator validation would still look good, so detection is unlikely.

Model and data theft -- adversarial
Extracting the model or its simulator-derived data reveals plant-specific response dynamics and operating-procedure information. That helps an adversary plan sabotage and choose when the advisory tool will mislead.

IT/OT stepping stone and denial of advisory -- adversarial
The tool's link to the process network and MLOps infrastructure offers a path across the IT/OT boundary and a lower-hardened foothold than safety-classified I&C. Denial or degradation of the tool removes the aid at the moment operators need it, pushing them back to manual diagnosis under stress.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory predictor for control-room operators during emergencies. It forecasts how plant parameters will evolve after a device action, so it is consulted when time pressure is highest and operator stress is greatest. In practice it would sit beside the safety-classified I&C and the symptom-based EOPs, so the failure to worry about is a plausible-looking wrong forecast that shapes an operator's decision or diagnosis. It is not a direct actuation failure. The documented system was trained and tested only on simulator data, and its best reported result is 95.4% 'mostly accurate'. That leaves roughly 5% of predictions off, and the paper does not say whether those misses cluster in the rare, severe, off-nominal states where the tool matters most.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Simulator-to-plant gap: the LSTM learns the simulator's thermal-hydraulic model, not the real plant. Real plant response, with instrument noise, sensor degradation, ageing and unmodeled equipment states, can differ from it, especially in beyond-design-basis or multi-fault sequences that were never simulated. The output looks smooth and confident but is out-of-distribution, and the model gives no warning that it is extrapolating (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0401). The plant would also need a retraining or revalidation process after plant modifications, setpoint changes or simulator updates, or the model drifts from the facility (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). (2) Multi-step error accumulation: a multi-step forecast degrades with horizon, and a misleading trend can look reassuring or alarming. Operators might wrongly 'confirm' that an action worked, or abandon a correct action. They might also diagnose from a forecast that fits the wrong accident class. Possible consequences are delayed or inappropriate mitigation, or a spurious action that worsens the transient. The tool is meant to catch human error, but a wrong forecast could introduce one (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.02, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0402.02). (3) Low base rate: severe accidents are rare in the training data, and the tool is built around operator actions in emergencies, so action-conditioned data for unusual or erroneous action sequences is thin (OP.C0202, OP.C0204). Aggregate accuracy hides this. (4) Qualification and governance: this is not a safety-class function, but if it is used for diagnosis it could drift into de facto reliance without qualification, V&V or EOP integration (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Operator training may erode manual diagnostic skill (OP.C0101.06).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Input integrity: the model consumes live plant-parameter streams. A cyber adversary who spoofs or biases sensor or historian data feeding the predictor, or who evades the model with crafted input patterns, could make it forecast a benign trend during a real transient or a spurious divergence during a normal one. The aim would be to induce incorrect operator actions or distrust, or to time an attack so that the tool misleads while a separate degradation is under way (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031, AML.T0046). (6) Supply chain and model integrity: tampering with the trained weights, the training data or the simulator-derived datasets could implant a backdoor that triggers on specific parameter states. Because the model is opaque, the tampering would be hard to detect (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0076). (7) Availability: denial of the tool, or erosion of operator trust through induced false forecasts, removes the decision aid when it is most needed (AML.T0029). A crucial mitigation is network isolation and one-way data flow from safety systems, which keeps this to a degraded-advisory failure. Independent EOP verification and the shift technical advisor role remain the barriers that would also have to fail for real harm to occur.

ai_engineer.argument: From a pipeline view, this is a multi-step LSTM surrogate trained entirely on simulator-generated emergency transients, then proposed as a real-time advisor that conditions on operator actions. Its fragility is mostly structural. The training distribution is a finite set of simulated scenarios and action sequences, so the reported 95.4% 'mostly accurate' figure measures interpolation within the simulator's scenario space, not generalization to real plant sensor behavior, unmodeled faults, multi-failure sequences, or off-script operator actions. Both data provenance (simulator, not plant) and the action-conditioned input design make out-of-distribution inference the default state during exactly the rare, novel emergencies where operators would lean on it. Because the model is a black-box regressor with no physics constraint, nothing at inference time tells the user when a trajectory has become implausible.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulator-to-plant gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302): the model learns the simulator's thermal-hydraulic approximations, fixed noise-free or synthetic sensor behavior, and scripted scenario library. Real plants have instrument degradation, calibration offsets, plant-specific configuration, and aging, so forecasts can be confidently wrong in a systematic way. The consequence is a plausible but incorrect trajectory shown to operators during an accident. (2) OOD and low base rate (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03): real emergencies are rare and heterogeneous, so there is little field data to validate or retrain on. Combined multi-fault or beyond-design-basis events fall outside training support. The LSTM extrapolates smoothly and gives no calibrated uncertainty, so errors look the same as correct outputs. (3) Multi-step error accumulation and counterfactual validity (OP.C0403, OP.C0301.01): multi-step outputs compound error over the horizon, and the model predicts effects of operator actions without causal guarantees; it learns correlations in the scripted action-response data. A wrong 'this action looks safe' forecast could mask a human error, which defeats the purpose of early error catching. Wrong forecasts could also mislead diagnosis. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05, OP.C0101.03): operators under stress may over-trust the tool, or discard it after a visible miss. Operators may also be unsure whether a prediction assumes the action was already taken. (5) Qualification and explainability gaps (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0303, OP.C0501): there is no established qualification path for a non-deterministic, opaque network in an operator-support role. Retraining or recalibration for plant modifications, or for plant-specific adaptation, risks silent regression.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0046): the model consumes live plant parameters and operator-action signals. An attacker with access to the data path, or to compromised sensors or historian feeds, could craft small perturbations that bend the forecast, either hiding a developing fault or inducing a false alarm or an unnecessary action. LSTM regressors are known to be sensitive to this, and the forecast is also a feedback signal operators use to judge their own actions. (6) Training-pipeline compromise (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059): simulator datasets, scenario libraries, and model files are the key assets. Poisoning, or a backdoor keyed to a particular parameter pattern, would be hard to detect, since validation on held-out simulator runs would still look good. (7) Model and data theft (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035): a surrogate of plant response, plus the simulator data behind it, leaks plant-specific dynamics and operating-procedure information that helps an adversary plan sabotage or time an attack for when the advisory tool is least reliable. (8) The tool opens an IT/OT data-flow path that must be read-only; an integrity or availability attack on it (AML.T0029) pushes operators back to manual diagnosis at high-stress moments.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this tool sits in the control room at the worst possible moment: an emergency, when operators are under stress and most inclined to trust a forecast of how plant parameters will respond to their actions. That concentrates trust in a component whose output a deliberate adversary, or an insider with model or data access, could shape to push operators toward a wrong action or to suppress an alarm they would otherwise act on. It is a hard direct target for a nation-state, but it is attractive as a stepping stone. It is an advisory ML component that is likely to be less hardened than safety-classified I&C, and it bridges simulator data, training pipelines and operator displays. Its non-adversarial weaknesses (simulator-only training, a reported ~95% accuracy that leaves a 5% tail, opacity) are exactly what an adversary would time an attack around, because they give a fault plausible deniability and blur the line between a model error and sabotage.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data or model integrity compromise: the model learns from simulator emergency-operation data, so an insider or supply-chain actor who can alter the simulator datasets, the retraining pipeline or the model weights could embed a subtle bias or trigger. The model would predict benign trends after a specific harmful operator action, or flag a correct action as an error. Facility dependence: operators use it to catch errors and diagnose accidents. Consequence: a latent wrong-action endorsement or a false reassurance during a real transient, which is hard to detect because the model looks accurate on average (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0031). (2) Input and data-path manipulation: the model consumes live plant parameters plus operator action signals. An adversary with a foothold on the plant data network could spoof or perturb those inputs, so forecasts diverge from the real plant state. This could mislead diagnosis, or desensitize operators through repeated false alerts so that a later real or staged event is dismissed (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0029, AML.T0046). (3) Stepping-stone and trust-concentration risk: a tool connected to the process-information network and to training or MLOps infrastructure could give an adversary a path across the IT/OT boundary, or a cheap way to degrade operator confidence in both the tool and the real instrumentation (AML.T0012, AML.T0018.002, AML.T0025). (4) Model theft or reconnaissance: because the model captures plant response dynamics, extracting it or its training data would aid an adversary in planning how the plant reacts to given actions (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035).

IMPLICIT (exploitable or timeable). (1) Simulator-to-plant gap: training on simulator data only means real-plant noise, sensor faults, degraded equipment and unseen multi-fault scenarios are out of distribution, so a failure can pass for an ordinary prediction error (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (2) Automation trust failure: over-trust at the moment of highest stress, and operator skill fade in manual diagnosis, mean a failure or manipulation has an outsized effect. An adversary can time an attack for an emergency or choose a scenario the tool handles poorly (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (3) Opacity and the ~5% inaccurate tail: an LSTM's reasoning cannot be inspected, so operators cannot tell a tampered forecast from an honest miss. That blurs attribution and slows incident detection (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0402.02). (4) Governance gaps: no established qualification path for an advisory ML tool in operations, plus weak configuration control and data-access governance over retraining, leave the integrity controls an attacker would rely on missing (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0505, OP.C0504).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulator-to-plant gap, error accumulation, input manipulation and poisoning/backdoor threats. The security specialist's stepping-stone and trust-concentration point was kept as distinct, while the detailed model-theft and denial points were merged from the AI engineer and nuclear engineer.

evidence.citation: "Real-time prediction of nuclear power plant parameter trends following operator actions," Expert Systems with Applications (Elsevier), vol. 186, 115848 (2021)
evidence.note: The authors compared nine candidate models. These paired a multilayer perceptron, a vanilla RNN or an LSTM with different multi-step prediction strategies, and all were trained on emergency-operation simulator data. The multi-input multi-output LSTM worked best across several emergency scenarios, with the best model reported at 95.4% 'mostly accurate' predictions. The paper reports a model built and tested on simulator data, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a false 'action is safe' or benign-trend forecast during an emergency, whether from poisoning, input manipulation or OOD failure. It could mask a human error or steer a wrong diagnosis in a power-reactor emergency and erode safety margins. Because the tool is advisory and operators and safety-classified I&C remain independent barriers, a direct radiological release is less likely, so this stops short of 5.

reproducibility.why: Simulator-to-plant OOD failure and compounding multi-step error occur reliably whenever off-nominal or multi-fault states arise. Adversarial manipulation or poisoning needs specific conditions, such as a data-path foothold or pipeline access, and a confident wrong forecast must coincide with an operator acting on it.

exploitability.why: The credible adversarial paths (a foothold on the plant data path, insider or supply-chain access to the retraining pipeline or weights, or crossing the IT/OT boundary) need substantial access and resourcing. The implicit weaknesses need no attacker access, but exploiting them deliberately by timing or steering plant states is hard.

affected_users.why: Impact centers on the control-room operating crew and the plant state they are managing during an emergency. A misleading forecast could affect decisions across coupled plant systems, but the tool is advisory, single-plant and not in the safety-classified control path, so it is not facility-wide by default.

discoverability.why: Simulator-to-plant gap, OOD extrapolation, error accumulation, over-trust and data-poisoning are well documented in open literature for LSTM forecasters. The paper is public and discloses the architecture, the training source and the accuracy figure. Plant-specific weak points would still need insider knowledge.

use_case: Neural-network regression of spinel liquidus temperature in high-level nuclear waste glasses, to support glass formulation for waste vitrification. The network is trained with an l1-norm censored-data loss that uses slack variables. This lets it learn from left-, right- and non-constrained (inequality-bounded) liquidus measurements that are normally discarded. It was validated on synthetic data and on nuclear waste glass data.
incurred_insecurity:
This is an offline, advisory neural-network regressor whose spinel liquidus predictions set waste loading and melt-temperature limits in HLW vitrification. Its main exposures are silent non-conservative bias, from out-of-distribution extrapolation, inconsistent censored-bound labelling and synthetic-data validation, and quiet erosion of confirmatory testing. Adversarially, the most plausible route is insider or pipeline tampering with the cheap-to-alter inequality records or the model artifacts, producing slow-burn sabotage that is hard to attribute. Together these could cause spinel accumulation, melter or discharge-riser fouling and out-of-spec waste forms, but only if laboratory confirmation and margin controls are weakened.

Censored-record poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or compromised data pipeline could flip the direction or shift the threshold of left- or right-censored liquidus records, which carry no point value to cross-check and are rarely scrutinised. Under the l1 slack-variable loss this biases the learned liquidus surface optimistically in a chosen composition region, yielding non-conservative T_L predictions that surface only after crystallization.

Model and toolchain tampering -- adversarial
Altering network weights, scaler or normalisation parameters, training code or ML library dependencies could subtly bias formulation recommendations. Aggregate R2 and MAE checks would not reveal this, and ordinary retraining non-determinism gives it cover.

Input and feed-composition manipulation -- adversarial
Altered upstream waste-characterisation records or formulation inputs could be crafted to land in poorly modelled regions and yield a falsely safe T_L. Since the model and data are openly published, an adversary can study the method and build proxy models to find such compositions.

Waste-composition information exposure -- adversarial
The training set and formulation-space maps could reveal composition and loading strategies of legacy defence-related waste streams if the database or model is collected or probed. The consequence is an information-security concern rather than a direct safety one.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
The network gives confident scalar T_L values with no calibrated uncertainty for new tank wastes or unusual Cr, Ni, Fe, Mn and Al contents outside the lab-quenched training envelope, and averaged R2 and MAE hide local errors. An adversary could target formulations or feed changes at poorly covered regions, relying on users not noticing the extrapolation.

Synthetic-data validation and bound-label inconsistency -- implicit, exploitable
Validation on synthetic data tests the loss mechanics rather than real measurement noise, and censored bounds from different labs, hold times and detection methods mean inconsistent things, so the l1 slack fit can bias point predictions. Inconsistent bound semantics give an adversary cover to hide altered records among ordinary heterogeneity.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
As the model outperforms its baseline, engineers may adopt single-number T_L outputs and cut confirmatory crucible melts and isothermal holds, and an optimizer pushing toward the liquidus boundary will exploit model errors. An adversary could time a bias injection to this window of reduced verification.

Opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
Seed-dependent retraining and opaque NN behaviour make results hard to reproduce or audit, so a deliberately induced shift looks like normal retraining variation. This lets sabotage evade attribution.

Qualification and change-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
The research artifact has no AI-specific QA basis, versioning, or governance for data admission and retraining before it feeds a waste-form compliance chain, and reuse across sites could propagate shared bias. An adversary could exploit the absent change control to slip in modified data or models and rely on fleet-wide reuse to spread the effect.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a process-safety view, this model is an advisory formulation-screening tool, not a control function. Its output (spinel liquidus temperature, T_L) sets how much waste can be loaded into a glass and how hot the melter and canister pour can run. The real hazard is a non-conservative T_L prediction that is acted on without margin. Spinel crystals can settle and accumulate on the melter floor, block the discharge riser, and reduce throughput. In the worst case this forces a melter outage or replacement, with a recovery burden and a possible waste-form quality excursion. The existing layers are strong. Formulations go through composition-property models, laboratory confirmation (crucible melts, isothermal holds, quench-and-XRD), and the Waste Form Qualification/Product Consistency programs, and operating limits carry margin such as a T_L limit relative to melt temperature. So a single wrong prediction is unlikely to cause harm alone. The real risks are quiet erosion of those safeguards and the gradual loss of conservatism.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Censored-data training uses inequality-bounded measurements, so the model is only as good as the labeling of those bounds, such as 'T_L above the highest tested temperature' or 'no spinel at the lowest tested temperature'. Mislabeled or inconsistently reported censoring, or a slack-variable l1 loss that lets the fit absorb bounds in a biased way, could give systematically under-predicted T_L in sparse, high-spinel-risk compositions. A point-prediction regressor does not give calibrated uncertainty, so a non-conservative error looks as confident as a good one (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03). (2) Out-of-distribution use is the main operational exposure. Sites differ in waste chemistry (high Fe, Cr, Ni, Al, and Mn-rich legacy streams) and in redox control and melter conditions. The training data are laboratory-quenched, isothermal-hold measurements, not melter-scale behavior, and some of the data may derive from legacy defence waste. Formulators could extrapolate beyond the validated composition envelope, especially as waste-loading optimization pushes toward the liquidus boundary (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0202, OP.C0303). Validation on synthetic data adds provenance risk if the synthetic generator's assumptions are mistaken for physical truth (OP.C0201.02). (3) Automation bias and skill fade. If the model's accuracy gains lead to reduced confirmatory testing, or if it is used inside an optimizer that searches for formulations at the edge of its competence, the optimizer will find the model's errors and exploit them (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0301). (4) Qualification gap: there is no AI-specific QA basis for a regression model feeding a waste-form compliance chain, and retraining non-determinism makes results hard to reproduce (OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01). Reproducibility matters when a formulation is later audited.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. These need a different threat model, since the model has no public inference surface and runs offline in R&D or flowsheet teams. (a) Poisoning of the measurement database, or of the curated censored and inequality-labelled records, could shift T_L predictions low in a target region. Insider or supply-chain access to shared glass property databases is the plausible route (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0018.000). (b) Tampering with model weights or the training or optimization code (AML.T0018, AML.T0010.001) could bias formulation recommendations. A subtle bias is hard to detect with only aggregate R² and MAE checks. (c) Confidentiality: the training set and formulation-space maps could reveal waste composition for defence-related streams (AML.T0024.000, AML.T0025). The consequence is an information-security concern rather than a safety one.

Consequence chain: the AI fault produces an under-predicted T_L, which allows an over-aggressive waste-loading or melt-temperature choice, leading to spinel accumulation and a melter or discharge-riser blockage, an unplanned outage, a waste-form quality issue and a schedule or cost impact. This requires the lab confirmation, margin and sampling controls to fail or be bypassed. Radiological release consequences are indirect and low-likelihood. The main takeaway is to keep the model strictly advisory, report conservative and uncertainty-aware bounds, enforce a validated-domain check, and retain mandatory experimental confirmation.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a tabular regression NN (composition to T_L) whose novelty is the l1 censored loss with slack variables, which lets inequality-bounded liquidus observations (e.g., 'T_L below 950 C', 'spinel present at 1050 C') enter training. Its fragility sits in the data pipeline. Censored points are far more numerous than exact ones, they are heterogeneous in method and lab, and they sit close to the boundary that matters for formulation, so label quality and interpretation of each bound directly shape the learned surface. The loss also gives a cheap, flat penalty for violating a bound, so a mislabeled or adversarially flipped inequality (left vs right censoring) shifts the fit without any large residual that would flag it. Validation on synthetic data plus a limited waste-glass set says little about extrapolation: HLW glass compositions for new tank wastes, or legacy defence waste with unusual Al/Fe/Cr/Ni/Mn content, can fall outside the training convex hull, and an NN regressor gives a confident scalar there with no native uncertainty. The use case is advisory (formulation support, not a protection function), but its output is turned into an operating envelope for a melter, where an underpredicted liquidus can lead to spinel crystal accumulation and melter or discharge-riser fouling.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution extrapolation: waste compositions change with tank retrievals, new-build or new-site feeds, and legacy defence streams. Spinel liquidus is non-monotonic and sensitive to a few species (Cr, Ni, Fe, Mn, Al, Mg). The NN may be locally accurate yet silently wrong in unseen composition corners, and the reported R²/MAE are averages that hide it (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). (2) Synthetic-data validation and surrogate provenance: synthetic data tests the loss mechanics, not real-world measurement noise, so the censored-loss gains may not transfer. Mixed lab/bench and operational measurement provenance, with differing hold times, spinel detection methods and thermal histories, makes the meaning of a 'bound' inconsistent (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0303). (3) Censored-loss behaviour: l1 slack formulations can make the model trade exact-point fit against bound satisfaction, so a high volume of bound data can bias point predictions or compress predicted variance. There are no calibrated intervals, and results depend on seeds and initialisation, which weakens repeatability and qualification (OP.C0403, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0401). (4) Automation bias: a single-number T_L from a published model can be adopted as a margin-to-limit input by formulation engineers who have little visibility into training coverage or bound handling, and engineers may under-test with confirmatory crucible melts (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (5) Fidelity of reuse: the model is a research artifact with no stated QA, versioning or retraining governance, and it risks being reused across sites or waste classes, with shared bias propagating across the fleet (OP.C0502, OP.C0602). Drift also arises as waste chemistry shifts and the dataset is not refreshed (OP.C0204).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training-data poisoning or integrity erosion: because inequality records are cheap to alter and are weakly checked, an insider or a compromised data pipeline or shared database could flip or shift bounds, or inject a few low-T_L-bound compositions in a target region. This skews predictions toward optimistic liquidus in a chosen compositional area without obvious outliers (AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031). (b) Model or weights tampering and supply chain: altering weights, scaler or normalisation parameters, or ML library dependencies in the formulation toolchain (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076). (c) Input manipulation: altered feed-composition inputs from upstream waste characterisation records lead to a falsely safe T_L. Waste characterisation data is itself an input trust boundary (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015). (d) Reconnaissance and inversion: the open publication and published datasets give an adversary full knowledge of architecture, loss and data, which supports white-box crafting of compositions that are misjudged and proxy-model building (AML.T0000.000, AML.T0002.000, AML.T0005, AML.T0044). Consequence in each case is degraded vitrification: crystal formation, melter or canister quality nonconformance, and disruption or delay of the storage and disposal chain. Exposure of waste composition data from legacy defence streams is a secondary confidentiality concern. Because the tool is advisory and has experimental backstops, severity is moderate, but silent bias is the main way it fails.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team lens, a liquidus-temperature regressor is a poor direct target. It is an offline formulation-support tool that sits behind human review, melter operating limits and waste-form qualification, and no one would pick it to cause an immediate release. It matters as a quiet integrity target and a trust-concentration point. If it is used to push glass formulations toward higher waste loading, a small, hard-to-detect bias in its predictions could erode the margin against spinel crystallization. Crystal accumulation can clog the melter discharge or degrade the product, and that damage would show up months later, well after any anomalous input could be traced. The inequality-bounded measurements are a distinctive new surface: they are inexpensive to alter, since a bound has no point value to check against, and they are rarely scrutinized because they were previously discarded as unusable.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data integrity. The method's selling point is admitting censored records that used to be thrown away. An insider or compromised lab-data pipeline could add or relabel left- or right-censored entries, for example flipping a bound's direction or shifting its threshold. With an l1 slack-variable loss, such entries can shift the learned liquidus surface in a composition region of interest. The mechanism is that bound records carry no point measurement to cross-check. The dependency is that glass formulation limits and waste-loading decisions rely on the predicted liquidus. The consequence is non-conservative predictions that go undetected until crystallization occurs, which means melter or canister quality problems, throughput loss, and out-of-spec waste forms that complicate storage and transport acceptance. Model weights and the composition/property database are also a concentrated target. Subtle model tampering would be slow to surface and hard to attribute because of ordinary NN non-determinism (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059, AML.T0031). (2) Information value. Compositions, liquidus data and model behavior may reveal waste stream composition and loading strategies, including for legacy defence waste, so the model and its dataset are a reconnaissance and data-aggregation target (AML.T0035, AML.T0036, AML.T0024.001). (3) Supply chain and academic provenance. The tool originates in open academic code and data, with possible third-party libraries and public datasets. That raises the risk of poisoned pre-trained artifacts or dependencies, and it exposes the method to adversary study (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0000, AML.T0002.000).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable or timeable. (a) Validation was on synthetic and one family of waste-glass data, so out-of-distribution or new-composition behavior is poorly characterized. Extrapolation to new waste streams (OP.C0302, OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01) is plausible and invisible to users, and an adversary could aim formulations at poorly covered regions. (b) Automation trust grows as the model beats the baseline, so engineers may reduce confirmatory crucible or isothermal-hold testing, which creates a window where a bias goes uncaught (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). (c) Opacity and non-repeatability make a deliberately induced shift look like normal retraining variation (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01). (d) There is no AI-specific qualification regime or change control for retraining and data admission (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0505). The practical mitigation is to keep the model advisory, retain mandatory experimental verification, and control provenance of censored records. Threat realism is low to moderate, because this would be a slow-burn sabotage or attribution-confusing option for a sophisticated insider, not a first-choice target.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on censored-record/data poisoning, weight tampering, out-of-distribution extrapolation, automation trust, and the qualification gap; I merged these. I dropped weakly supported codes (e.g. AML.T0024.x model inference, AML.T0044, AML.T0076, OP.C0204, OP.C0203, OP.C0504) since there is no inference API or clear mechanism, and kept input manipulation and reconnaissance as distinct adversarial threats.

evidence.citation: "Leveraging Inequality-Constrained Data for Enhanced Liquidus Temperature Prediction in Nuclear Waste Glass Melts," International Journal of Applied Ceramic Technology (Wiley), authors from Brigham Young University and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed article, published July 2026, builds and tests a neural network that predicts spinel liquidus temperature in high-level waste glasses. It adds a censored-data regression method so inequality-constrained data can be used in training. It reports better accuracy (R² and MAE) than a baseline network. Waste-glass vitrification is the closest fit to the waste_storage_transport domain, and the glass data may relate partly to legacy defence waste rather than purely civil waste.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is silent non-conservative liquidus bias (from censored-record poisoning or model tampering) causing spinel accumulation, melter or riser fouling and out-of-spec waste forms; this is operational disruption and waste-form quality erosion, not a direct radiological release, and it requires confirmatory testing and margin controls to be weakened.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution extrapolation and bound-label inconsistency reliably yield biased predictions once feed compositions leave the training envelope, but a harmful outcome also depends on lab confirmation being skipped and on the composition region actually being used.

exploitability.why: The credible adversarial routes (altering censored records, model artifacts, or the training pipeline) need insider or pipeline access, while the externally reachable route (manipulating feed-composition records) also needs access to upstream characterisation data.

affected_users.why: The effect is scoped to a vitrification formulation chain, which is a single process; cross-site reuse of the shared model could spread a bias, but the model is offline and advisory, which limits coupling across systems.

discoverability.why: The method, data and model are openly published and the weaknesses (OOD extrapolation, aggregate-metric blindness, reliance on synthetic validation, no calibrated uncertainty) are well documented for this class of neural-network model, so an outsider can readily infer the exposures; the specific site pipeline remains unknown.

use_case: Feedforward artificial neural network (Keras, hyperparameters tuned with Talos) trained on a Dakota-MARS thermal-hydraulic uncertainty-propagation database. It predicts peak cladding temperature in a large-break loss-of-coolant accident from the 9 to 11 most influential uncertain input parameters. The parameters are drawn from a phenomena identification and ranking table (PIRT). It serves as a fast surrogate for uncertainty quantification in bounding accident safety analysis.
incurred_insecurity:
This surrogate is an offline design-stage tool, not a control asset, so its main insecurity is to the integrity of safety-case evidence: a fast ANN trained on MARS/Dakota output stands in for expensive code runs in the 95/95 peak cladding temperature statement against the 1204 C limit. The main threats are adversarial tampering with its data, weights and dependencies, plus implicit tail and extrapolation error, inherited simulation bias, weak AI QA and repeatability, and automation trust that erodes code confirmation. Physical consequence needs several failures together (a non-conservative result, no independent MARS check, and review that misses it), so this is a low-likelihood, high-consequence design-integrity risk.

Lifecycle integrity compromise -- adversarial
An insider or supplier could poison the Dakota-MARS database, the PIRT ranges or sampling, or the saved weights, scalers and Keras/Talos dependencies, so the surrogate under-predicts tail PCT. Because R2 of about 0.9 leaves room to hide a systematic shift, the result reads as ordinary regression error and yields hidden design non-conservatism or unjustified margin recovery.

Input and parameter manipulation -- adversarial
Altered upstream input values, distributions or PIRT parameter definitions fed to the unmodified surrogate can steer its PCT output low without any attack on the model itself. The result is a plausible but non-conservative margin figure in a safety-analysis deliverable.

Model-exchange leakage and stepping-stone -- adversarial
Model files, notebooks and databases pass between analysts, vendors and regulators, so they can carry malware or be exfiltrated or replicated. They also reveal which parameters dominate PCT and where margins sit, often under weaker information-security rules than the plant data itself.

Tail and out-of-distribution error -- implicit, exploitable
A feedforward ANN trained on MSE with sparse high-PCT samples is least accurate near cliff-edge phenomena such as reflood onset and cladding burst, and it returns confident values for inputs outside the sampled hypercube (new fuel, uprates, other plants, design-extension or severe-accident regimes). An adversary could place a manipulation in the poorly constrained tail or out-of-range region, where it passes as model error.

Inherited simulation bias and scope mismatch -- implicit
The labels are MARS output with no experimental anchor, so code model-form error is baked in and the surrogate's approximation error is added on top, which makes combined uncertainty look tighter than the evidence supports. Changes to the MARS version, nodalization, fuel or PIRT silently invalidate the training basis, and the reduced 9-11 parameter set cannot report omitted parameters. A realistic adversary gains little directly beyond hiding behind this ambiguity.

Repeatability and AI QA gap -- implicit, exploitable
Talos search and seed non-determinism, library-version dependence and the absence of an AI-specific qualification regime mean retraining gives different weights and tail behavior, and the model is opaque and cannot be checked against monotonic physics. An adversary could hide a malicious model change inside accepted retraining variance.

Automation trust and verification erosion -- implicit, exploitable
A cheap surrogate invites analysts to sweep designs without rerunning MARS, so skill and independent code confirmation fade, especially under schedule pressure. An adversary gains a long window in which a tampered or drifted model is trusted because its output looks like a code result.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-safety viewpoint the real question is whether a surrogate's PCT distribution ever substitutes for the MARS runs that underpin the 95/95 statement against the 1204 C (2200 F) limit in a large-break LOCA. The ANN is trained on one code, one plant model, one nodalization and one PIRT-derived parameter set. An R² of about 0.9 is weak where the acceptance criterion sits in the upper tail: average fit says little about error at the high-PCT tail, which is what the licensing-relevant margin depends on. Existing practice (code-based best-estimate-plus-uncertainty methods, regulatory review, independent verification) is a strong backstop only if the surrogate stays advisory. The danger is gradual: a fast and convenient tool used in design iteration, reload or fuel-design screening, or design-extension and severe-accident studies, where its output is trusted and the full code is rarely rerun. Humans act on bad output at the design-decision stage, and the guardrail is a code-based confirmatory analysis that schedule pressure may erode.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Tail under-prediction and extrapolation. The surrogate is fit to a sampled input hypercube and can silently under-predict PCT near cliff-edge phenomena (reflood onset, cladding burst and ballooning, rapid quench changes). It also gives plausible numbers when inputs fall outside the training range. A non-conservative error then enters the margin-to-limit assessment, and a 95/95 statistic computed from the surrogate may not be the code's 95/95 (OP.C0302, OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (2) Fidelity inheritance and scope mismatch. The ANN carries the MARS model's own biases and omissions: it is simulated and surrogate data with no experimental anchor. Changed fuel (high burnup, accident-tolerant fuel), uprates, different core loading or a different plant invalidate the training distribution. The reduced 9-11 parameter set drops parameters that matter in the new configuration, and the surrogate cannot report that omission (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0304.03). (3) Automation trust and scope creep. The authors suggest use for design-extension and severe-accident decisions, which are regimes outside the training basis and where code runs are fewest. Automation bias, no quantified surrogate error budget and under-used code confirmation could lead to margin being credited, or hardware and procedure changes being justified, on surrogate output (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (4) Reproducibility and QA. Keras and Talos retraining is non-deterministic, hyperparameter search can overfit, and library versions can shift results. Software-hygiene and model-version control under a nuclear quality-assurance program (10 CFR 50 Appendix B style) is rarely mature for ML artifacts (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502, OP.C0501). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Integrity of the training database or model file. Poisoned Dakota-MARS samples, altered model weights, or a compromised ML dependency or supply chain could bias PCT low in a way that looks like ordinary regression error, since R² of 0.9 leaves room to hide a systematic shift. The consequence is erosion of calculated margin in a safety-analysis deliverable, long before operations; the plausible harm is hidden design non-conservatism or unjustified margin recovery, not an immediate physical event (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0031, AML.T0076). (6) Input manipulation. Altered input ranges, distributions or PIRT parameter definitions fed to the surrogate can steer results while leaving the model untouched. Exposure of the surrogate or the underlying design data also leaks sensitive plant design and safety-margin information (AML.T0043, AML.T0024, AML.T0025). Physical consequence requires several failures together: a non-conservative result, no independent code verification, and regulatory or design review that fails to catch it. That makes this a low-likelihood, high-consequence design-integrity risk, mitigated mainly by keeping the tool explicitly non-credited and by requiring confirmatory code runs near the limit.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a classic simulation-trained surrogate: the entire training distribution is MARS output sampled by Dakota over PIRT-derived parameter ranges, so the model learns the code's behavior (including its closure-model errors) and not the physical plant. Its validity region is therefore the sampled hypercube of 9 to 11 inputs. Anything outside it is extrapolation: a different plant, fuel burnup or cycle state, a modified nodalization, an updated MARS version, or a PIRT revision that adds or removes parameters. An R² of about 0.9 is a mean-fit statistic. In bounding safety analysis the quantity that matters is the upper tail of PCT (the 95/95 value), and a feedforward ANN trained on MSE with a thin tail, near cliff-edge phenomena such as reflood onset or cladding burst, is least reliable exactly where the regulatory number is read off. The pipeline also has weak lifecycle controls. Talos hyperparameter search, random seeds and Keras/TensorFlow version dependence create repeatability and qualification gaps, and the model is opaque, so a reviewer cannot confirm that it respects monotonic physics such as higher decay heat producing higher PCT.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT: (1) Out-of-distribution and extrapolation failure. The surrogate returns a confident scalar for inputs outside the Dakota sample space, with no native uncertainty or applicability-domain flag. Examples are a changed plant configuration, new fuel, or a PIRT-driven parameter outside the sampled bounds. The consequence is an under-predicted PCT margin in a bounding analysis (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403). (2) Inherited simulation bias. The code's model-form error is baked into the labels, and the surrogate adds approximation error on top, so the combined uncertainty is rarely propagated. UQ results can look tighter than the evidence supports (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02). (3) Tail and low-base-rate weakness. High-PCT cases near the 1204 °C or 10 CFR 50.46 limits are sparse, so tail error is large relative to R² (OP.C0202). (4) Concept drift when MARS versions, nodalization, correlations or the PIRT change, which silently invalidates the training database (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303). (5) Repeatability and qualification gaps from Talos search non-determinism, framework and library versions, and no established AI QA regime for use in a licensing-grade analysis (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504). (6) Automation bias, where analysts prefer cheap surrogate sweeps over code runs and verification against MARS erodes (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401). Stated extension to design-extension and severe-accident conditions is a particular risk, because the training physics does not cover those regimes.

ADVERSARIAL: (a) Training-data or database poisoning. An insider or a compromised Dakota/MARS pipeline could subtly bias labels or input sampling, for example by trimming the parameter ranges or perturbing high-PCT runs. The surrogate then systematically understates PCT while still validating at R² of about 0.9 on a test split drawn from the same poisoned database (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059). (b) Model or artifact tampering. The weights file, the input scaler or normalization constants, or the Python/Keras dependency chain could be modified, with a backdoor trigger in a narrow input region, so the manipulation is invisible on typical validation (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076). (c) Input manipulation. Because the 9 to 11 inputs are hand- or script-supplied, altered upstream values from design databases or PIRT ranking inputs shift the output without a model attack (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0031). (d) Public-literature reconnaissance. Published architecture, inputs and ranges allow an adversary to build a proxy and understand which parameters drive the result (AML.T0000, AML.T0005). The security consequence is mainly integrity of safety-case evidence, meaning corrupted design-basis margins, rather than direct plant control.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this surrogate is not a real-time control asset, so a nation-state would have little reason to attack it directly. Its value to an adversary is as a quiet integrity target upstream of licensing and design-margin decisions. A small, trusted, easily retrained ANN stands in for hundreds of expensive MARS/Dakota runs. Few people can independently re-verify its output, and reviewers will tend to trust a figure that looks like a code result. A single insider, or a compromised supply chain (Keras/Talos dependencies, training database, saved model file), could bias the 95/95 peak cladding temperature estimate in the non-conservative direction. That could erode real safety margin or hide a design weakness, and it would leave little forensic trace. A reported R² of about 0.9 also leaves a lot of unexplained variance for a bias to hide in, and the authors' suggestion of extending use to design-extension and severe-accident conditions invites the model to be used outside the range it was trained on.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity attack on the surrogate's lifecycle. An insider or supplier alters the Dakota-MARS training database, the PIRT parameter ranges or sampling, the Talos tuning outputs, or the serialized model weights. The surrogate then systematically under-predicts peak cladding temperature in the tail region that governs the licensing limit. The facility depends on it for the margin-to-limit statement in bounding accident analysis, so the consequence is a non-conservative safety case, hidden design weakness, and later erosion of defense-in-depth. The attack is attractive because the output looks plausible and a small model file is easy to swap (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0031, AML.T0076). (2) Trusted-intermediary and stepping-stone risk. Model files, notebooks and databases move between analysts, vendors and regulators, so they can carry malware, or the exchange can be used for reconnaissance. Reference models of this kind also reveal which parameters are treated as most influential and where the margins sit. That information is useful to an adversary planning sabotage and is often handled under weaker information-security rules than the underlying plant data (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0011.000, AML.T0018.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002; OP.C0505.01).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable or timeable by an adversary: (3) Automation trust and verification erosion. Once analysts rely on a fast surrogate, MARS re-runs and independent verification become rare. The loss of skill and the reduced review give an adversary a long window in which a tampered or drifted model goes unchallenged (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (4) Accuracy and extrapolation limits. R² of about 0.9 is weak for a tail-sensitive safety metric. Using the model outside its training envelope (new fuel, uprates, different plant models, design-extension or severe-accident conditions) leads to out-of-distribution error that is not flagged, and the model is opaque so the error is hard to detect (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (5) Provenance and qualification gap. The training data are simulated and code-dependent, so any MARS model error or bias is inherited and hidden behind a neural-network veneer. There is no AI-specific QA basis for the surrogate in a regulatory submission, and no reproducibility control, since retraining can give different weights and different tail behavior. This makes it hard to tell a malicious change from normal retraining variance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504, OP.C0601).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on lifecycle integrity poisoning, tail/extrapolation error, inherited simulation bias, QA/repeatability gaps and automation trust. I dropped low-value or speculative codes (reconnaissance/proxy, backdoor trigger, spearphishing-style malware, cloud dependency) and kept the model-exchange leakage threat as a distinct but secondary item.

evidence.citation: "Using Machine Learning to Predict the Fuel Peak Cladding Temperature for a Large Break Loss of Coolant Accident," Frontiers in Energy Research (Frontiers Media)
evidence.note: The paper builds and validates an ANN that replaces repeated thermal-hydraulic code runs in uncertainty quantification of peak cladding temperature for a large-break LOCA. It was trained on a database generated by propagating PIRT-derived uncertain parameters through a MARS model, and it reached about R² 0.9. The authors suggest it could support decisions for design-extension conditions and severe accidents. I did not retrieve the paper's full text, so the choice of use area (Design and Construction rather than Licensing and Regulation) is my judgement. It also overlaps somewhat with existing LOCA surrogate entries, though it targets uncertainty quantification of peak cladding temperature rather than transient time-series forecasting.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is lifecycle integrity compromise (poisoned data or weights) that yields non-conservative 95/95 PCT evidence and hidden design non-conservatism, which erodes safety margin in a safety case. It is an offline design tool and needs several coincident failures (no independent code check, review misses it), so it falls short of a direct release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Tail and out-of-distribution error and retraining non-determinism recur reliably once inputs fall in sparse or out-of-range regions, but a deliberate tampering that survives review depends on the surrogate being used without independent MARS confirmation and on the R2 ~0.9 error masking a shift.

exploitability.why: The most credible adversarial paths (poisoning the training database, PIRT ranges or saved weights, or supplier dependencies) need insider or supply-chain access to the analysis workflow, while the implicit weaknesses need no special access but yield little targeted control.

affected_users.why: A biased surrogate would propagate into safety-analysis deliverables and design decisions for a plant or fleet of similar designs, so it has broad analytic reach, but it is confined to design-stage evidence rather than coupled operating systems.

discoverability.why: The surrogate class and its weaknesses (tail error, extrapolation, inherited code bias, nondeterminism) are well documented in open literature, and the source paper is public and reveals the architecture and parameter set. Knowing where a specific tampering would go unnoticed still needs some inference about the workflow.

use_case: Deep neural-network surrogate for PWR fuel depletion in a fuel cycle simulator. Trained on a spent-fuel assembly database, it predicts used-fuel isotopic composition, decay heat and activity from initial enrichment and burnup. It is embedded as a reactor model in the Cyclus agent-based fuel cycle simulator for rapid, medium-fidelity depletion calculations and used-fuel inventory projections, including batches with assemblies of varying burnup.
incurred_insecurity:
This planning-stage depletion surrogate is not a protection or control function, so its main insecurity is the quiet corruption of used-fuel inventory, decay heat and activity projections. Those projections feed spent-fuel pool, cask, transport and repository planning and safeguards-relevant material expectations. The main threats are silent out-of-envelope extrapolation, circular and aggregate-only validation, a qualification and over-trust gap, error propagation through Cyclus, and tampering with the weights, data or simulator supply chain that hides inside accepted model error.

Silent out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
The network is trained on historical US PWR assemblies and takes only enrichment and burnup, so high-burnup, high-enrichment, accident-tolerant, MOX or new-design inputs, and mixed-burnup batches that average away hot assemblies, return confident but wrong inventories and decay heat with no uncertainty flag. An adversary could steer scenario inputs into these regimes to get non-conservative storage or inventory numbers that appear to come from a validated tool.

Simulation-derived data and circular validation -- implicit, exploitable
The training database holds ORIGEN-type calculated values rather than measurements, and the under-5% error was checked against the same database and an aggregate inventory profile. This hides larger tail errors in minor actinides, Pu isotopes and decay heat at specific burnups or cooling times. An adversary who alters a narrow region could stay inside the headline tolerance, because no independent reference exists to expose it.

Opacity and qualification gap with over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
A non-qualified, opaque network with no AI-specific QA, no versioned link to a specific SCALE/ORIGEN and nuclear-data release, and possibly non-repeatable retraining is used because it is far faster than ORIGEN. That speed erodes independent re-calculation and analyst skill, so qualified codes stop being the controlling basis for thermal and inventory inputs. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust so that a biased output is accepted without cross-checking.

Error cascade through the simulator and shared use -- implicit, exploitable
Surrogate errors propagate through Cyclus agent mass flows into storage, reprocessing and repository sizing, and a model reused across studies or organisations spreads one bias widely. An adversary needs to corrupt only one shared artifact to degrade many downstream analyses.

Weights, data and plug-in tampering -- adversarial
A compromised upstream contributor, insider or supply-chain actor could alter the model weights, the training database or the open-source Cyclus plug-in and dependencies, for example by unsafe model-file deserialization. A small plausible bias in decay heat or Pu content would then undersize cooling or storage margins or mask diversion-relevant inventory discrepancies, while passing the self-referential validation.

Input manipulation and proxy reconnaissance -- adversarial
Public papers, data and model files let an adversary build a proxy to find the regions where the surrogate is weakest, then craft out-of-range or burnup-specific inputs, for example in batch-generation scripts, to force confident wrong outputs. This degrades planning results without any live inference interface being attacked.

Inventory information leakage -- adversarial
If the surrogate is tuned on restricted assembly-level records, model inversion or extraction could expose burnup, enrichment or inventory details and reveal how facility inventory estimates are derived. This is a lesser concern while the training data remain public.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a design-phase planning surrogate, not a protection or control function, so no single wrong output moves directly to a physical event. The real risk is that bad used-fuel inventory, decay heat and activity projections quietly feed decisions on spent-fuel pool and dry-cask capacity, cask loading and thermal limits, transport and repository planning, and fuel-cycle scenario studies. Existing practice mitigates this: licensing-basis thermal and shielding analyses use qualified ORIGEN/SCALE-type codes with margins, and cask loading relies on assembly-specific records. The exposure arises when a fast, convenient surrogate with a headline 'under 5% error' is used outside its validated envelope, or by people who have forgotten what it was trained on. It is also a safeguards-adjacent concern, because isotopic predictions (Pu, minor actinides) can feed material accountancy expectations and diversion-detection baselines.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution and qualification mismatch (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303): the network is trained on a spent-fuel database of historical US PWR assemblies, so it is only valid for the enrichment, burnup, assembly design, power history and cooling-time ranges in that data. Applying it to high-burnup or high-enrichment fuel, accident-tolerant or advanced fuels, MOX, or new-build cores extrapolates silently, with no built-in uncertainty flag. (2) Data provenance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203): the database holds code-calculated (ORIGEN-type) rather than measured values, so the surrogate inherits the biases of the simulation and adds its own error. Validation against the same database is circular, and a global '<5%' figure can hide larger errors in specific isotopes, minor actinides, or the tails of the burnup distribution. (3) Inputs of only enrichment and burnup (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403): the model omits power history, moderator conditions and cycle-specific effects, so it flattens real heterogeneity inside batches of mixed-burnup assemblies and averages away hot assemblies. That error is non-conservative for thermal and criticality-relevant limits. (4) Opacity and over-trust (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04): the speed advantage over ORIGEN invites its use for numbers that should come from qualified codes, and single-nuclide errors are hard to trace. (5) Software hygiene and propagation (OP.C0502, OP.C0603, OP.C0602): the model is embedded in Cyclus, so errors cascade through agent-to-agent mass flows into storage, reprocessing and repository sizing. Retraining or version changes may not be repeatable (OP.C0402.01). The same model reused across studies or sites propagates one bias widely.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Supply-chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0076): a tampered weights file, a poisoned training database (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002) or a compromised Cyclus archetype could bias decay heat or Pu inventory by small, plausible amounts. The effects would be undersized cooling or storage margins, distorted cost and proliferation-resistance comparisons, or skewed inventory baselines. Open-source tooling and public data make such changes easy to hide and hard to detect (AML.T0000, AML.T0002.001). (7) Input manipulation (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0031): out-of-range or crafted burnup/enrichment inputs can force confident but wrong outputs, for example inside a batch-generation script. (8) Information value: a model that is validated or tuned on restricted assembly-level data could leak design or operating details (AML.T0024.001, OP.C0505). Overall consequence: no direct physical failure, but erosion of safety and safeguards margins in planning, which is only caught if independent qualified calculations and assembly-level records remain the controlling basis.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a tabular regression surrogate (enrichment, burnup -> isotopics, decay heat, activity) trained on UNF-ST&DARDS, which is itself the output of ORIGEN/SCALE depletion runs on a finite set of historical US PWR assemblies. It is therefore a surrogate of a simulation, not of reality (OP.C0201.01/.02), and it inherits the physics approximations, nuclear data library versions and assembly-design coverage of that database. The architecture offers no hard guarantee of physical consistency: nothing enforces mass or nuclide-chain conservation, monotonic burnup trends, or decay-heat/activity consistency with the predicted isotopics. The main fragility sits at inference. Cyclus calls the model with whatever enrichment/burnup pairs a scenario generates, including future advanced fuels, extended burnup, high-assay or accident-tolerant fuels, and mixed-burnup batches. These can fall outside the training envelope, where a DNN extrapolates silently with no uncertainty output. The reported under-5% error was validated against an aggregate inventory profile, which can hide compensating errors at assembly or nuclide level. It was also validated against the same database it was trained on, not against independent measured data.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution extrapolation (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03): a design or planning scenario uses fuel types, burnups, enrichments or power histories not represented in the database, and the surrogate returns confident but physically wrong inventories, decay heat or activity. Downstream, this could undersize cooling, storage, cask loading or repository-capacity estimates, and distort actinide and fissile inventory projections used for proliferation or safeguards-relevant material accounting. (2) Aggregate-metric masking: the average error is low, but tail errors in minor actinides (Pu-239/241, Am-241, Cm-244) or in decay heat at specific cooling times can be large. Since heat and activity are dominated by few nuclides, small isotopic errors compound. Mixed-burnup batch handling, such as averaging, adds a second approximation layer (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0603). (3) Qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401): the surrogate is non-qualified and opaque, yet its outputs can propagate into design-stage decisions. Its error is not traceable to specific physics, retraining may change results non-reproducibly (OP.C0402.01), and there is no versioned linkage to a particular SCALE/ORIGEN and nuclear-data release (OP.C0502). Silent drift can also arise when the underlying database is updated or when new reactor designs make the training population obsolete (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0204). (4) Automation bias: the speed advantage over ORIGEN encourages using it for many scenarios without spot-checking against high-fidelity runs (OP.C0101.04). Errors then cascade through the fuel cycle simulator into dependent facility agents (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. The attack surface is mainly the supply chain and data pipeline rather than a live inference API. (a) Poisoning or tampering with the training database, the model weights, or the Cyclus plugin or model files (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076) could bias a narrow region, for example specific burnup ranges. This would understate decay heat or plutonium content in a way that evades aggregate validation. (b) Pre-trained weights or the open-source simulator repository (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0011.000) could be backdoored, for example via unsafe model-file deserialization. (c) Public availability of the paper, database and model (AML.T0000, AML.T0002.000/.001, AML.T0005) lets an adversary build a white-box proxy, learn where the surrogate is weakest, and time or shape scenario inputs (AML.T0043) to exploit it. The consequence is manipulated or degraded planning outputs, such as spent-fuel inventory and material-quantity projections, that downstream analysts trust. The risk is less a direct plant-safety effect than corrupted design-basis, storage-planning and safeguards-relevant inventory estimates.

security_specialist.argument: This is a design-and-planning surrogate, not a real-time control function, so a nation-state would rarely attack it directly. The security interest lies in what it feeds: used-fuel inventory, isotopic and decay-heat projections that inform storage, transport, repository and fuel-cycle strategy, and potentially safeguards-relevant material accounting assumptions. A quiet, plausible-looking bias in a fast, opaque surrogate is hard to detect because few people re-run ORIGEN once the surrogate is trusted, and that makes it a good low-effort target for an insider or a supply-chain actor. Because the surrogate is a small, easily copied artifact trained on a public database and embedded in an open-source simulator, the barriers to tampering are low and the barriers to detection are high. Its reach is also broad, since any study or fleet-level scenario that imports the model inherits its errors.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or training-data tampering, plus supply-chain compromise of the surrogate weights, the Cyclus plug-in or the open-source dependencies (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.001). An insider or upstream contributor could subtly bias isotopic, decay-heat or activity outputs, for example by underpredicting decay heat or fissile content at certain burnups. Dependents are cooling-time, storage-loading, cask and transport planning and repository-capacity studies. The consequence is non-conservative thermal or inventory margins in design and licensing inputs, or distorted material-quantity projections that could mask diversion-relevant discrepancies. The error stays inside the stated 5% tolerance, so it would not trip review. (2) Compromised calibration and validation. The only documented check compares the predicted inventory profile with the database it was trained on, so an adversary who alters both the data and the check leaves no independent reference to expose the change (AML.T0059, OP.C0201.03). (3) Information leakage and reconnaissance. A surrogate trained on spent-fuel records can expose proprietary or sensitive burnup, enrichment and assembly-level inventory information through inversion or extraction (AML.T0024.001, AML.T0024.002). The model is also a cheap proxy for learning how facility inventory estimates are derived (AML.T0005.001). (4) Stepping stone. The simulator environment and shared model files are a path into planning networks or into data that links to operator records (AML.T0012, AML.T0025). IMPLICIT. (5) Out-of-distribution extrapolation: the model is built on historical US PWR data and will degrade for new fuel types, high burnup, accident-tolerant fuels, mixed-enrichment batches or other reactor designs (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). Beyond the training range, errors are silent and no uncertainty is reported, which an adversary could exploit by steering studies toward such regimes. (6) Automation trust and skill fade: speed encourages replacing ORIGEN, so independent verification atrophies and a corrupted surrogate would go unnoticed (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). (7) Opacity and the qualification gap: a deep network offers no mechanistic traceability, and there is no AI-specific QA basis for using it in safety-adjacent inventory or decay-heat inputs (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0502). (8) Error propagation across studies and sites: a shared model reused across scenarios or organizations carries one bias into many analyses (OP.C0602, OP.C0603, OP.C0304.03). Together these make the surrogate a low-cost, low-visibility way to degrade decision quality or to hide a tampering event inside accepted model error.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on out-of-distribution extrapolation, simulation-derived circular validation, the qualification and over-trust gap, error propagation, and supply-chain or weights tampering; I kept those and folded the overlapping items together. I dropped weakly supported codes (AML.T0012, AML.T0025, AML.T0059, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0204, OP.C0302.01) and kept inversion/extraction leakage as a minor threat tied to restricted data.

evidence.citation: "Deep learning approach to nuclear fuel transmutation in a fuel cycle simulator," Annals of Nuclear Energy, Vol. 139, 107230 (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The authors trained a neural network on the UNF-ST&DARDS Unified Database to predict PWR used-fuel composition, decay heat and activity from initial enrichment and burnup. They validated it by comparing its predicted U.S. used-fuel inventory profile with the database's profile, then implemented it in the Cyclus simulator. The paper reports under 5% error for assembly decay heat and activity, and the model runs much faster than ORIGEN depletion calculations.

damage.why: Most severe credible threat is silent tampering or bias in decay heat and Pu inventory projections that undersizes storage and cooling margins or masks diversion-relevant discrepancies; because the tool is planning-stage and not a protection or control function, harm is mostly operational disruption and margin erosion, with only an indirect route to safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution extrapolation with no uncertainty flag and circular validation reliably produce confident wrong outputs whenever inputs fall outside the training envelope, which is deterministic behavior of the model class.

exploitability.why: Steering scenario inputs or building a proxy from public artifacts needs only modest access, but the tampering threats (weights, data, plug-in supply chain) need contributor, insider or supply-chain positioning.
