affected_users.why: Errors cascade through Cyclus mass flows into storage, reprocessing and repository sizing, and a shared model spreads bias across studies and organizations, though the impact stays in planning analyses rather than in a single facility's operating systems.

discoverability.why: The paper, training database and model approach are public, and OOD extrapolation, surrogate-validation gaps and model-file supply-chain risks are well documented for this class of AI system, so an adversary can readily learn where the weaknesses lie.

use_case: Ensemble of Bayesian neural networks that predicts irradiation hardening (embrittlement) of light-water-reactor pressure vessel steels. The inputs are alloy composition and irradiation conditions such as flux, fluence and temperature. The model is built to extrapolate to low-flux, high-fluence, extended-life conditions and so support vessel integrity assessment for licence extension beyond 60 years.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case feeds a Bayesian neural network ensemble into reactor pressure vessel integrity assessment for licence extension beyond 60 years. The vessel is the one non-replaceable barrier, and the model is asked to extrapolate to low-flux, high-fluence conditions where no matching power-reactor data exist. The main threats are non-conservative extrapolation, data scarcity and provenance gaps, over-trust in ensemble uncertainty, qualification and repeatability gaps, and adversarial corruption of the data, model or inputs that would bias a decades-long safety case without visible anomaly.

Extrapolation and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on accelerated-flux test-reactor data and validated on one intermediate-flux ATR-2 campaign, the ensemble can confidently under-predict hardening where low-flux dose-rate effects and late-blooming Ni-Mn-Si phases are unrepresented. This inflates margin in the reference-temperature shift and pressurised thermal shock screening. An adversary could place a bias in the poorly validated tail, where in-distribution checks cannot see it, and time it to a licence-renewal submission.

Test-reactor to power-reactor data gap -- implicit, exploitable
A small, heterogeneous, transferred dataset with differences in spectrum, flux, temperature control and unrecorded segregation or product-form variables introduces systematic, direction-unknown bias. It also adds a hardening-to-shift conversion proxy step. Few high-fluence points give any altered record outsized leverage, so a handful of changes could pass as natural scatter.

Uncertainty miscalibration and automation trust -- implicit, exploitable
Ensemble credible intervals are overconfident off-manifold, and a smooth, published, probabilistic output invites staff and reviewers to treat it as validated margin, thinning surveillance-capsule checks and physics-based bounding. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust, biasing the bands or inputs so that a non-conservative result looks well-calibrated and draws less scrutiny.

Qualification, opacity and repeatability gap -- implicit, exploitable
No accepted pathway qualifies neural-network ensembles under the RPV integrity rules, and seed non-determinism, retraining on new surveillance data and silent preprocessing changes undermine traceability and reproduction of a licensing prediction. A tampered or swapped model or dataset version could be waved through because change control cannot show that outputs changed.

Training-data and database poisoning -- adversarial
Altering or mis-curating a few high-fluence or low-flux irradiation or surveillance records, or the composition and condition metadata, biases the extrapolated hardening trend non-conservatively while in-distribution validation stays intact. The result appears independently corroborated and erodes defence-in-depth against brittle fracture and thermal shock over decades.

Model and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
An insider or third-party collaborator could poison or swap ensemble weights, a pretrained artefact or ML dependencies, or insert a backdoor keyed to specific composition-flux combinations that random hold-out validation will not catch. This lowers predicted embrittlement for chosen vessels without detection.

Input manipulation in the assessment pipeline -- adversarial
Falsified or mis-transcribed alloy chemistry or irradiation-condition fields entered by materials or surveillance staff can skew an individual vessel's prediction, and the model's narrow credible interval makes the skew look legitimate.

Proprietary data leakage and model extraction -- adversarial
Weakly controlled academic, vendor and laboratory collaborators handling alloy chemistry, irradiation histories and vessel-specific margins could leak them, or the model could be replicated as a proxy. This reveals which vessels are most vulnerable and where the model is least certain, which helps an attacker choose where a bias will stay invisible.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant engineering view, this model feeds RPV integrity assessment for operation beyond 60 years, where the vessel is the one non-replaceable barrier. The assessment normally sits inside a conservative regulatory framework: surveillance capsule data, Charpy and fracture-toughness measurements, 10 CFR 50.61a/Reg Guide 1.99 trend curves, margins, and pressurized thermal shock screening. Wrong output therefore usually causes harm indirectly. An optimistic (under-predicted) hardening value could be used to justify relaxed surveillance schedules, less conservative P-T limits, or acceptance of extended-life operation. A pessimistic one gives unnecessary derating or premature shutdown. The key weakness is that the model is built to extrapolate to low-flux, high-fluence conditions where there is essentially no matching power-reactor data. It is trained on test-reactor data (IVAR, BR2, ATR) with flux far above service conditions, and validated on a single ATR-2 campaign. That leaves a validation gap exactly where the decision matters, and an ensemble's uncertainty bands are not a safe substitute for physical validation.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and out-of-distribution failure (OP.C0302, C0302.03, C0303): the model covers flux, fluence and composition ranges with sparse data. Late-blooming phases (Ni/Mn/Si-rich clusters), flux effects, and the hardening-to-embrittlement (ΔT41J / RT_NDT shift) conversion may be mis-extrapolated. Bayesian ensembles can still be confidently wrong off-manifold, because epistemic uncertainty from a small ensemble and approximate priors is poorly calibrated far from the data (OP.C0403, C0401). (2) Data scarcity and provenance (OP.C0202, C0203, C0201.03/.04/.05): test-reactor accelerated-flux data are transferred to power-reactor service. Small datasets, heterogeneous alloy chemistries, and unrecorded variables (e.g. Cu/P/Ni segregation, product form, temperature history) mean that hidden confounders bias the output in a systematically optimistic or pessimistic direction. (3) Automation trust and anchoring (OP.C0101.04, C0101.03, C0102): a smooth, probabilistic, publication-backed prediction can anchor licensing staff, who may treat narrow credible intervals as validated margin. This risk grows if it replaces or delays surveillance capsule withdrawal. Existing practice (conservative bounding, surveillance, regulator review) mitigates this, but only if the ML result is used as a supplementary trend check and not as the primary basis. (4) Qualification and regulatory gaps (OP.C0501, C0504, C0402): there is no accepted pathway for qualifying ML under the RPV integrity rules, and non-repeatable retraining and version drift could undermine traceability in a licence basis.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training-data poisoning or integrity erosion (AML.T0020, T0059, T0010.002): if irradiation databases or surveillance records are altered or mis-curated, the model learns a biased hardening trend. Test data that is quietly altered could produce an optimistic extended-life prediction that appears independently corroborated. (6) Model or artifact tampering (AML.T0018, T0010.003, T0076) and manipulation of inputs such as composition or fluence in the assessment pipeline (AML.T0043.003) could lower predicted embrittlement for a specific vessel. Consequence: reduced margin acceptance without detection, which is a slow safety-erosion mode that physical safeguards (capsule testing, in-service inspection) would need to catch. (7) Model extraction or leakage of proprietary alloy and surveillance data (AML.T0024, T0025) is a lesser, confidentiality-type concern. Overall, the main downstream risk is a latent, hard-to-detect error in a long-lived safety case, not an abrupt event. The principal safeguards are independent physical surveillance data and regulator conservatism, and they should remain mandatory cross-checks.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a tabular regression ensemble (Bayesian NN) trained on a small, heterogeneous, mostly test-reactor dataset (IVAR, BR2, ATR-1), and it is intended to be used exactly where no training data exist: low flux, high fluence, and beyond-60-year life. Its main exposure is in the pipeline and the model's statistical limits, not in any single component. Flux-effect and late-blooming phase physics (Ni-Mn-Si precipitates) are poorly sampled, so the model's covariate shift is also a concept shift. The ATR-2 hold-out is only an intermediate-flux test and does not demonstrate validity at true power-reactor flux. Bayesian ensembles give epistemic uncertainty estimates, but those are known to be overconfident far from the data, and they are only as good as the priors and ensemble diversity. A regulator or utility could read a narrow credible interval as qualification evidence.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and OOD failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403): the model learns correlations among composition, flux, fluence and temperature from accelerated test-reactor conditions. Mechanisms at low flux (dose-rate effects, late-blooming phases, saturation or softening) may not be represented in the training data. The AI failure is a confident under-prediction of hardening at the extended-life tail. Vessel integrity margins, such as the reference-temperature shift and pressurised thermal shock screening, depend on that output. The consequence is non-conservative embrittlement estimates that are used to justify licence extension. (2) Data provenance and scarcity (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0204): test-reactor data are transferred or virtual relative to power-reactor field data. They carry spectrum, flux, temperature-control and measurement-protocol differences, and the compositions are a narrow set of alloys. Surveillance-capsule data are sparse, proprietary and inconsistently curated. Training/test leakage across correlated irradiation campaigns can inflate reported accuracy. Hardening-to-ΔT41J conversion adds a further proxy step that is not in the training data. (3) Uncertainty miscalibration and opacity (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04): an ensemble variance that looks authoritative is mistaken for validated uncertainty. Analysts over-trust it and abandon conservative physics-based bounding, which is a form of automation bias. (4) Qualification gap (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402.01): there is no accepted pathway for qualifying a data-driven model against regulatory guides on embrittlement trend curves. Retraining with new surveillance data changes outputs, and seed and ensemble non-determinism makes results hard to reproduce for a licensing basis. Concept drift occurs as new data arrive from different alloys and fabrication routes. (5) Governance: the model is tied to a specific dataset version, and silent updates to inputs or preprocessing break traceability (OP.C0502).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. Because the model is trained on a small curated dataset, the main attack classes are data and supply-chain integrity attacks, and they are cheap to carry out. Poisoning or subtle alteration of the training database, surveillance records or preprocessed feature tables (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059) can bias predictions at the extrapolation tail while leaving in-distribution validation intact. Compromised model weights, a poisoned pretrained package, or ML library dependencies (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018.000) are further routes. A backdoor trigger on specific composition-flux combinations is unlikely to be caught by random hold-out validation (AML.T0043.004). Input manipulation of the composition or condition fields (for example, falsified or mis-transcribed alloy chemistry) can skew an individual assessment (AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Because the published paper and the data are open (AML.T0000, AML.T0002.000), an adversary can build a proxy model and learn where the model is least certain, so an insider or a vendor could choose where the bias will be invisible. Consequence: degraded vessel integrity margins and a compromised safety case, with an attacker able to time the manipulation to licence-renewal submissions.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view this is an offline, advisory, low-cadence analytical tool. It has no actuation path, so a nation-state would not choose it as a direct target. Its value to an adversary lies in what it does to the licensing basis. A long-lived, authoritative-looking prediction of RPV hardening supports a 60-to-80-year licence-extension case, and that case is an integrity decision whose consequences play out over decades. The attack surface is the training and test data, the model artefacts and the people who interpret the outputs. A small corruption there would be cheap, would stay hidden for years, and would be hard to attribute. Even without an adversary, the model is asked to extrapolate beyond its data (low flux, high fluence, long life) with few test-reactor points and limited validation. That is the situation in which an adversary can hide a subtle bias, or in which automation trust can let a non-adversarial error stand in for a conservative margin.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model integrity. The curated database of test-reactor and surveillance hardening data is small, hand-assembled and shared across institutions. Whoever can alter a handful of high-fluence or low-flux records, or the composition and condition metadata, can shift the extrapolation in the non-conservative direction without any visible anomaly. A model-weight or ensemble tampering insider (poisoning, backdoor, or swapping a pre-trained artefact in the supply chain) could do the same. The consequence is under-predicted embrittlement feeding vessel integrity assessment, so the licensee or regulator might accept a reduced safety margin for an extended-life case. This would erode defence-in-depth against pressurised thermal shock and brittle fracture long after the manipulation. (2) Concentrated trust. Because the model's output beats legacy correlations and carries a Bayesian uncertainty estimate, it can become the favoured basis for the case. An adversary does not need to cause an event. They only need to bias the uncertainty bands or the input pipeline (alloy composition entered by surveillance or materials staff) so that a non-conservative result looks well-calibrated. (3) Insider and third-party pathways. Academic, vendor and national-laboratory collaborators handle both the data and the code. These are weakly controlled relative to plant systems, so they are an easier stepping stone than the plant. They could also leak proprietary alloy chemistry, irradiation histories and vessel-specific embrittlement margins, which would reveal where individual vessels are most vulnerable. IMPLICIT (exploitable or timeable). (4) Extrapolation and drift: the model is validated on a small test-reactor set (IVAR, BR2, ATR-1/2). Flux effects, late-blooming phases and composition ranges outside training coverage may be mispredicted, and the surveillance-capsule and test-reactor data used differ in provenance from real vessel conditions. The result is a systematic non-conservative bias that is hard to detect. (5) Opacity and non-repeatability: ensembles of neural networks are hard to explain and to qualify under existing nuclear QA. Training non-determinism and retraining on new data can change a licensing prediction without clear change control, and a regulator may not be able to reproduce it. That governance gap is where a bad or tampered result would be waved through. (6) Automation trust and skill fade: as materials engineers rely on the model, independent checks against mechanistic models and surveillance data may thin out. An adversary or a plain error then meets less scrutiny. (7) Small-data and scarcity limits: with few high-fluence points, a few corrupted or unrepresentative records have disproportionate leverage.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on extrapolation failure, test-reactor data scarcity, over-trust in ensemble uncertainty, the qualification gap, and training-data and model integrity attacks. I dropped weakly supported or generic codes (AML.T0012, AML.T0035, AML.T0002.000 reconnaissance, AML.T0015 evasion, OP.C0301) and kept leakage and extraction as a lesser distinct threat.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning predictions of irradiation embrittlement in reactor pressure vessel steels," npj Computational Materials (Nature Portfolio)
evidence.note: The paper trains machine-learning models on test-reactor irradiation data (IVAR, BR2 and ATR-1). It then tests them on high-fluence, intermediate-flux ATR-2 irradiations, where the predictions beat extrapolations of existing hardening models. The models are ensembles of Bayesian neural networks, and the work is aimed at extended-life vessel conditions.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is non-conservative bias in RPV embrittlement predictions feeding a licence-extension safety case, which erodes margin against brittle fracture and pressurised thermal shock on a non-replaceable barrier. The effect is a decades-long erosion of safety margin rather than a direct release, and independent surveillance and physics-based checks partly bound it.

reproducibility.why: Overconfident extrapolation error in the poorly validated low-flux, high-fluence region is systematic and recurs once the model is used there. Deliberate poisoning or tampering is conditional on insider or collaborator access and on how the bias lands relative to the true behaviour.

exploitability.why: Credible adversarial paths such as poisoning the data, swapping the model or backdooring it need insider, collaborator or supply-chain access plus domain knowledge to keep the bias plausible. The implicit extrapolation weakness needs no attacker effort, but exploiting it deliberately still requires placing a bias and timing it to a submission.

affected_users.why: A bias would affect the integrity assessment of one or more vessels, or a fleet if a shared model or database is corrupted, and so erodes the safety case for the whole plant. It does not propagate across coupled operational systems, so impact stays within the structural-integrity function.

discoverability.why: Open literature documents the extrapolation limits, dose-rate effects, data scarcity and ML poisoning and supply-chain risks for this class of model. The ensemble's uncertain regions can be inferred from published validation. Vessel-specific data and margins are less visible.

use_case: Federated, privacy-preserving temporal digital-twin network (Edge Temporal Digital Twin Network). It uses a graph-neural-network temporal-attention mechanism on time-series sensor data from nuclear power units. Each unit trains locally and shares only model parameters with a cloud server. It is used for sensor-driven fault detection and predictive maintenance when plant data cannot be shared between units.
incurred_insecurity:
This federated digital twin gives each unit's fault-detection and predictive-maintenance analytics a shared cloud aggregation node that links 17 otherwise isolated plants. The main threats are fleet-wide poisoning or tampering through the parameter channel, leakage of plant state despite the privacy label, evasion by manipulated sensor streams, and several implicit weaknesses (heterogeneity and drift, scarce fault data, opacity, over-trust, and a missing qualification basis) that degrade or mask detection. The tool is advisory and sits outside the protection path, so consequences are mainly missed or mistimed maintenance and reduced scrutiny, unless independent surveillance and alarms also fail.

Federated poisoning and backdoor -- adversarial
A compromised unit, edge node, insider or someone with access to a historian or sensor feed submits manipulated local updates or trains on falsified data, giving the global model a blind spot or trigger-activated backdoor for a chosen degradation signature. Because raw data never leaves the site, the aggregator cannot inspect training data, and non-IID heterogeneity makes anomalous updates look benign, so missed early warnings and deferred maintenance spread across all units.

Aggregator and supply-chain compromise -- adversarial
The cloud server, model registry or edge software stack is a single integrity and availability node; tampered global weights pushed to every unit create correlated false negatives or false-alarm floods, and credential or supply-chain compromise also opens an IT-to-OT pivot through the edge-to-cloud channel. Denial of the aggregator freezes retraining, leaving a stale model that operators still trust.

Parameter and gradient leakage -- adversarial
Inversion, membership inference or model extraction against shared parameters can reveal operating regimes, outage history, sensor topology and fault records of individual units. This is sensitive reconnaissance for timing an attack and for an IP or physical-security exposure the 'privacy-preserving' label understates.

Sensor-stream evasion -- adversarial
Spoofed or slowly ramped time-series inputs can be shaped to stay inside the graph-temporal-attention model's normal envelope, or to trigger false alarms. Sabotage or process manipulation is then hidden from a tool that operators trust over manual cross-checks.

Heterogeneity, drift and data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Non-IID differences across reactor designs and vintages, concept and data drift after outages, sensor replacement or uprates, and few labelled faults mean the global model can silently miss faults at individual units or on novel fault types, and federated retraining rounds can add unnoticed regressions. An adversary could pass manipulation off as model noise or time an action to a post-outage or post-update window when detection is weakest.

Fault propagation across the sensor graph -- implicit, exploitable
A single faulty or manipulated sensor corrupts graph-based reasoning and spreads bias across channels, and the same flawed model is reused fleet-wide. An adversary could compromise one sensor or unit to degrade detection broadly.

Opacity, over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Attention weights are a weak explanation, so engineers cannot readily challenge an alert or a non-alert, and strong benchmark results on 17 units invite over-trust, reduced trend review and walkdowns, and diagnostic skill fade. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust and low false-alarm rate to hide manipulation or time actions around it.

Qualification, governance and cloud-dependence gap -- implicit, exploitable
Continuously retrained, non-deterministic models have no clear qualification, version-control or change-management basis, cyber-zone classification of a cloud-connected O&M tool is unsettled, and parameters shared under a privacy label may get less security scrutiny than raw data. An adversary could exploit weak update provenance and incident-response ambiguity, or time an attack to a connectivity loss that leaves models stale.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an O&M advisory tool for fault detection and predictive maintenance. It is not in the protection or control path, so a wrong output normally lands on a maintenance planner or condition-monitoring engineer rather than on a safety actuation. The real exposure is in what the workforce comes to rely on and in the federated architecture. Several 'no-sharing' units are tied to one cloud aggregator, so a failure or manipulation there can reach many units at once. Existing practice (technical specifications, surveillance testing, independent safety I&C, operator alarms) still bounds the consequence, but only if the twin does not displace those functions.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Federated poisoning: a compromised or spoofed edge client, or someone with access to a unit's historian or sensor feed, can send manipulated parameter updates or train on falsified data. Result: the global model gets a backdoor or a blind spot, so a specific degradation signature (e.g. pump bearing wear or sensor drift) is classed as normal across the fleet. Consequence: deferred maintenance and a missed early warning. Escalation to a safety event would also need independent surveillance and alarms to fail. (2) Aggregator compromise: the cloud server is a single point of integrity and availability. Tampered global weights distributed to all 17+ units give correlated false negatives or a flood of false positives. Denial of service of the aggregator degrades model updates, and a stale model is then trusted. (3) Privacy claims are overstated: shared gradients and parameters can leak operating-regime or plant-state information through inversion or membership inference. That is a sensitive-information and physical-security concern, not just an IP one. It also opens an IT/OT egress path from the plant to the cloud, which needs a data diode or an equivalent segregation argument. (4) Sensor-level evasion: an adversary with access to the instrument or network layer can shape slow drifts below the model's attention sensitivity, hiding sabotage or degradation from a tool operators have learned to trust. IMPLICIT. (5) Non-IID heterogeneity across reactor designs, vintages and operating modes means the global model can be wrong for an individual unit. Low base rates of real faults and few labelled failures make validation weak, and the paper's results from historical datasets may not hold in service. (6) Concept and data drift after outages, sensor replacement, uprates or fuel-cycle changes can silently invalidate the twin. (7) Opacity of graph temporal attention makes it hard for engineers to challenge an alert or a non-alert. Over-trust and skill fade follow, and routine trend review and walkdowns get reduced. (8) Fault propagation: a single bad sensor corrupts the graph-based reasoning and spreads the bias across channels. (9) Governance: there is no clear qualification path for continuously retraining models. Version control, change management and cyber-security classification for a cloud-connected O&M tool are unsettled, and off-site cloud dependence can conflict with the plant's cyber requirements. An adversary could time an attack around outages or model updates when scrutiny is lowest.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this system is fragile in three places: the federated aggregation channel, the data each unit trains on, and the lack of a qualification basis for its outputs. Federated learning moves the trust boundary from the data to the parameter updates. A central cloud server then becomes a single point through which a poisoned or biased global model can reach every unit. Each unit's local data is non-IID and mostly normal operation, with few labeled faults, so the model's fault-detection ability rests on thin, heterogeneous, weakly labeled data. At inference time, a unit whose sensors, calibration, load regime or fuel cycle differ from the other 16 may fall outside what the global representation module learned. The model can then fail silently, with no calibrated out-of-distribution signal, while an operator treats the digital twin as ground truth for maintenance decisions.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Federated poisoning and backdoors: a compromised unit, edge node or insider submits manipulated local updates (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). The aim is a global model that systematically under-reports a specific fault signature or sensor pattern, or that carries a trigger-activated blind spot. Because raw data never leaves the site, the server cannot inspect training data, which makes poisoning hard to detect. The dependent function is fault detection and predictive maintenance. The consequence is missed degradation, and the same flawed model propagates to many units (OP.C0602). (2) Aggregation and cloud compromise: the cloud server or its model registry could be attacked through supply chain or credential routes (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0012, AML.T0018). This allows a tampered global model to be distributed to every plant at once, creating a fleet-wide common-cause failure and a new IT-to-OT pathway through the parameter channel. Denial of the cloud service (AML.T0029) stalls retraining and model updates. (3) Privacy leakage that federated learning does not prevent: gradient or parameter inversion and membership inference (AML.T0024.000, AML.T0024.001) can reveal operating regimes, outage history or fault records of individual units. That is sensitive operational information, and it can help an adversary time an attack. (4) Sensor-level evasion: manipulated or spoofed time-series inputs (AML.T0015, AML.T0043) can keep a fault inside the model's normal envelope or trigger false alarms. Proxy models built from published architectures and datasets (AML.T0005, AML.T0000) make these attacks easier.

IMPLICIT. (1) Non-IID heterogeneity and drift: the unit-to-unit differences the architecture is designed to handle also cause concept and data drift from sensor aging, recalibration, power uprates and maintenance changes (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03). Retraining by federated rounds can itself introduce unnoticed regressions at some units. (2) Label and fault scarcity: real faults are rare, so detection performance is dominated by normal data (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.05). Reported gains on 17 units may not carry over to new faults, new reactor types or new builds (OP.C0203). (3) Qualification mismatch: a continuously retrained, non-deterministic, attention-based model has no clear qualification basis for safety-adjacent maintenance use (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0402, OP.C0401). Attention weights are a weak explanation, so operators cannot easily check why a fault was or was not flagged. (4) Human factors: a twin that outperforms baselines invites over-trust, and skill fade in diagnosis (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Missed detections are then treated as plant health. (5) Dependency and data continuity: reliance on off-site cloud aggregation and on stable sensor feeds (OP.C0601, OP.C0204) means connectivity or governance changes can freeze models in a stale state. An adversary can time an attack for that window. Cross-unit sharing of parameters under a privacy label may also receive less security scrutiny than raw data would (OP.C0505.01).

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, the federated design shifts the threat surface rather than shrinking it. 'Privacy-preserving' parameter sharing creates a cloud aggregation server that is a concentrated trust node connecting 17 otherwise isolated units. That node gives an adversary a one-to-many pathway (poisoning, backdoor insertion, or reconnaissance) that would not exist if each unit's analytics stayed local, and it quietly dissolves segmentation that plants deliberately maintain between sites. The use case is advisory (fault detection and predictive maintenance), so a nation-state would probably not choose it as the primary target. It is attractive as a stepping stone, as a way to blind or mistime maintenance, and as an information-leak source on fleet health. The most dangerous exploitation is slow degradation of detection sensitivity that operators come to trust, because it can be timed around a physical or cyber action elsewhere.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Poisoned or backdoored federated updates: a compromised unit, insider, or edge node submits crafted local parameters or a triggered backdoor (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0043.004, T0010.002, T0031). The aggregator folds these into the global model that every unit consumes. The AI failure is a global model that is silent on chosen fault signatures or sensor patterns. Plant reliance is on early fault detection and condition-based maintenance. The consequence is missed degradation, an unplanned trip, or a cover window for sabotage, and it propagates fleet-wide (OP.C0602). Non-IID heterogeneity across units makes anomalous updates look benign, so Byzantine-robust aggregation is hard to verify. (2) Cloud/aggregator compromise and supply chain: the cloud server, model registry, or edge software stack is a single high-value node (AML.T0010.001/.003, T0012, T0044, T0018, T0025, OP.C0601). Subverting it enables model replacement, an OT-adjacent pivot into plant networks through the edge-to-cloud channel, and denial of service (T0029) that removes monitoring at all sites at once. (3) Information leakage despite 'privacy': gradients and parameters can leak operating-regime information through inversion or membership inference (AML.T0024.000/.001, T0024.002 model extraction). An adversary or curious participant can learn fleet operating profiles, outage patterns, sensor topology, or fault history. That is valuable reconnaissance for timing an attack. This is a false sense of data security (OP.C0505.01). (4) Sensor-level evasion: an attacker who can manipulate sensor streams (spoofing, slow ramps) can craft inputs that evade the graph-temporal-attention detector (AML.T0015, T0043). If the twin is trusted over manual cross-checks, process manipulation can be hidden or mimic a benign drift. IMPLICIT, exploitable. (5) Automation trust and complacency: a 'validated on 17 real units' result breeds over-trust, skill fade, and reduced manual trending (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102). A low false-alarm rate is something an adversary can time actions around. (6) Drift and heterogeneity: unit-specific ageing, refits, and sensor replacement cause data and concept drift and non-IID mismatch (OP.C0302.01/.02/.03). Fault data are rare, so detection is weak on novel faults (OP.C0202), and the opaque attention-based output is hard to challenge (OP.C0401). A natural performance gap can mask malicious activity as 'model noise.' (7) Governance gap: federated learning is not covered by existing I&C software qualification or cybersecurity-zone assumptions (OP.C0501, C0503, C0504). Cross-unit and cross-operator data flows blur ownership, accountability, and incident response when a poisoned update is suspected. Update provenance and versioning are weak (OP.C0502).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on federated poisoning, aggregator compromise, gradient leakage, sensor evasion, drift/heterogeneity, over-trust and qualification gaps, so these were merged into single threats. I dropped weakly supported codes (e.g. AML.T0073, AML.T0059, AML.T0005, AML.T0044, AML.T0031) because the text does not describe those mechanisms distinctly, and I kept T0025 only for the edge-to-cloud pivot and exfiltration path.

evidence.citation: "Edge Temporal Digital Twin Network for Sensor-Driven Fault Detection in Nuclear Power Systems," Sensors (MDPI), 2025, 25(24), 7510
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests a cloud–edge federated digital-twin model. It combines a continuous-time representation of sensor series with a global representation module for non-IID data and graph-based temporal attention. It was tested on real operating datasets from 17 independent nuclear power units and outperformed existing methods without any data sharing.

damage.why: The tool is advisory and outside the protection path, so the most severe credible threat, fleet-wide poisoning or tampered global weights that cause correlated missed or mistimed maintenance and mask sabotage, mainly means operational disruption and eroded safety margin. A radiological release would also require independent surveillance and alarms to fail.

reproducibility.why: Model poisoning and aggregator tampering work reliably once a foothold exists, and drift and heterogeneity degrade detection routinely. Success still depends on the attacker having a compromised node, a credential, or sensor access, and on robust aggregation or independent checks not intervening.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (poisoning, backdoors, aggregator or supply-chain compromise) need a compromised unit, insider access, or privileged access to the cloud and edge stack, plus ML expertise. Sensor-stream evasion and leakage inference are somewhat easier, but they still need access to the data path or the shared parameters.

affected_users.why: The shared cloud aggregator pushes one global model to all 17 coupled units, so poisoning or tampered weights propagate fleet-wide, and a single sensor can bias graph-based reasoning across channels.

discoverability.why: The architecture is published in the open literature, and poisoning, inversion and evasion against federated learning are well documented as a class. An outsider would still have to infer the deployment details, such as aggregator placement, the update channel, and which units participate, from partial information.

use_case: Passive, non-destructive convolutional neural network that takes detector-count data from around a nuclear waste cask and reconstructs the inhomogeneous radioactivity distribution of activation-product nuclides (e.g. Co-60, Cs-137, Eu-152) inside cement-solidified PWR nuclear power plant waste. It is trained on a Geant4-simulated 'Radiation Distribution Detector Count' dataset and is used to characterise waste cask contents and to optimise detector placement.
incurred_insecurity:
This CNN turns boundary detector counts from a sealed waste cask into an inferred nuclide activity map, trained only on Geant4 simulation with no real-cask validation. The main insecurity is an unquantified sim-to-real gap on an ill-posed inverse problem. It yields confident but possibly wrong characterizations that feed waste acceptance, transport classification and inventory records, and it creates a convenient place for an adversary to bias or hide what is inside a cask. Input tampering, physical evasion, pipeline poisoning and layout disclosure are the adversarial threats; automation over-trust, opacity and qualification gaps are the implicit ones.

Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
Real casks have voids, matrix density gradients, unmodelled nuclides, detector gain drift and background that the idealized simulation lacks. The CNN returns plausible maps with no uncertainty flag, so Co-60, Cs-137 or Eu-152 hotspots can be under-estimated and packages mis-categorized for dose, shielding and transport. An adversary could hide a diversion or under-declaration behind this unquantified error, passing it off as model uncertainty or a reconstruction artifact.

Ill-posedness, opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
Many different activity distributions produce near-identical surface counts, so the CNN resolves the ambiguity with priors learned from the simulation, and retraining variance and weak explainability make the result hard to reproduce or defend in a licensing or waste-acceptance record. An adversary can rely on this non-uniqueness, placing material so that a benign reconstruction is equally consistent with the counts.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Tomography-like output invites acceptance without independent gamma scanning, dose-rate surveys or sampling, and conventional characterization skills erode, which removes the independent check. An adversary can time tampering to periods of routine reliance, when doubt falls on the person who challenges the map.

Detector-placement optimization bias -- implicit
Layouts optimized on the simulator can lock in blind spots, leaving real measurements insensitive to the regions that matter, and the bias carries into every later campaign. An adversary gains little from it directly, except through knowledge of those blind spots (see layout disclosure).

Qualification gap and fleet propagation -- implicit, exploitable
No AI-specific qualification regime governs a safety- and records-relevant ML tool, and uncontrolled retraining or reuse across casks or sites spreads one systematic bias or compromise across the inventory. An adversary who compromises one shared model or update gains systematic mischaracterization that passes routine checks.

Detector-input manipulation and physical evasion -- adversarial
Tampering with counts, calibration or gain files, or placing shielding or sources near the cask, produces out-of-distribution inputs that the unstable inverse mapping reconstructs as benign. The consequence is a hidden hotspot, diversion or non-conforming package behind a falsified activity record.

Training-pipeline and supply-chain compromise -- adversarial
Poisoning the simulated dataset, Geant4 source, geometry or material configuration, or the model weights can embed a systematic bias or a count-pattern backdoor that suppresses a nuclide or location. This yields mischaracterization that is hard to detect without independent measurement, and unmanaged model files and third-party toolchains also give a foothold into the records network.

Model, output and layout disclosure -- adversarial
The model, its outputs and the detector-placement recommendations reveal sensitivity gaps and blind spots, and allow a proxy model to be built to craft evasive count patterns offline. This turns the optimization function into reconnaissance for later concealment.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a waste-storage and transport lens, this CNN produces an inferred activity map (nuclide, location, magnitude) that could feed cask characterization, waste-acceptance and transport-classification decisions, dose and shielding assumptions, and the detector layouts used for later measurements. Its only evidence is Geant4-simulated data with no real-cask validation, so the main risk is an unquantified sim-to-real gap, not an attack. Real cement-solidified waste has density voids, moisture, matrix heterogeneity, unmodeled nuclides, detector gain drift, background variation and geometry tolerances that simulation idealizes. The inverse problem is also ill-posed, since many activity distributions yield similar surface counts, and a CNN will return a confident, plausible-looking map regardless. Existing practice (gamma scanning with calibrated segmented-scanning or tomographic gamma scanning, dose-rate surveys, scaling factors from sampled waste streams, and process knowledge) would normally act as an independent check. That protection erodes if the AI map becomes the accepted characterization, particularly if it reduces sampling or destructive assay, and the harm would then be latent and discovered late.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure: the model is trained on idealized Geant4 data, so real casks with different matrix density, voids, nuclide mixes, detector efficiency drift or geometry offsets can yield wrong hotspot location or magnitude with no uncertainty flag. The consequence is under-estimated Co-60, Cs-137 or Eu-152 inventory or hotspots, which affects dose-rate and shielding assumptions, transport and disposal classification, and worker exposure in handling. It is mitigated if independent dose-rate and gamma-scan checks are retained. (2) Ill-posedness, opacity and non-repeatability: the CNN gives one plausible solution among many. Retraining variance and weak explainability make it hard to qualify or reproduce for a licensing or waste-acceptance record. (3) Automation bias and skill fade: if outputs look like tomography, operators and waste-acceptance staff may over-trust them, reduce conventional sampling, or lose the skills to challenge them. (4) Detector-placement optimization: layouts optimized on the simulated model can bake in its blind spots, leaving real measurements insensitive to the regions that matter. (5) Data scarcity and provenance: there is no real labeled ground truth for destructive-assay comparison, so validation is hard and drift cannot be detected. (6) Fleet propagation: one model reused across casks or sites spreads a systematic bias widely.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Manipulation of detector inputs, by tampering with counts, calibration files, gain settings, or placing local shielding or sources near the cask, could steer the reconstruction to hide a hotspot or mask a nuclide. Material diversion or misdeclaration, or concealment of a higher-activity or non-conforming package, is the transport and security consequence. The adversarial input crafting here is physical or data-level and is hard to detect when the CNN is opaque. (b) Training-data or model supply-chain compromise (poisoned simulation dataset, altered Geant4 configuration or weights, backdoor triggered by a count pattern) would give systematic mischaracterization that passes routine checks. (c) Denial or degradation of the tool, or of its data pipeline, would delay characterization and shipment. This is low consequence if conventional methods remain available. (d) Leakage of waste inventory and detector geometry from the model or its data is a modest confidentiality and security risk. Overall severity depends on whether the output is advisory or becomes a sole basis for classification. For a simulation-only research system it is currently moderate, but it rises sharply if deployed without independent verification.

ai_engineer.argument: This is an ill-posed inverse problem (reconstructing a 3D source distribution from a few boundary detector counts) solved by a CNN trained only on Geant4 simulation. Its fragility sits in the data pipeline, not the architecture. The training distribution is whatever the simulation authors assumed: source geometries, cement matrix density and homogeneity, nuclide mix, detector response, and cask geometry. A real cask has voids, density gradients, container deformation, unlisted nuclides, shielding or self-absorption variation, detector gain drift and background. Any of these puts inference out of distribution, and a standard CNN regressor gives no native signal of that; it simply returns a plausible-looking distribution map. Because the problem is under-determined, many different true distributions produce near-identical counts, so the network resolves the ambiguity with priors learned from the simulated set. The output therefore looks precise but may carry hidden bias, and no field ground truth exists to check it against because the cask is closed and destructive assay is exactly what this method avoids.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: the evidence is simulation-only, so the model is unvalidated against real detector physics (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). Mechanism: unmodelled geometry, matrix inhomogeneity, detector response, background and nuclide inventory shift the inputs away from the training manifold. The model outputs confident but wrong activity maps. Dependence: waste characterisation for acceptance, transport and storage (activity limits, criticality-adjacent and dose/heat assumptions, hot-spot location). Consequence: under-reported hot spots or misattributed nuclide activity could lead to a mis-categorised package, with safety and regulatory-compliance exposure and wrongly declared inventories. (2) Ill-posedness and ML-theoretic limits (OP.C0403, OP.C0401): non-unique solutions, opaque priors, and no uncertainty quantification, so a reviewer cannot tell data-supported structure from learned prior. Small-data and base-rate issues (OP.C0202): rare extreme hot-spot configurations are probably under-sampled in the simulated set. (3) Detector-placement optimisation (OP.C0301): the model is used to choose where to put detectors. If that optimisation is tuned to the simulator, it can lock in a geometry that is blind to real-world features, and the bias then propagates into every later campaign (OP.C0603, OP.C0602 if the model or layout is reused fleet-wide). (4) Human factors: a tidy reconstruction image invites automation over-trust, and skill fade in conventional gamma scanning or NDA (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). Stale models after changes in waste stream, cement recipe or detector hardware cause concept and data drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). Training non-determinism and the absence of an AI qualification regime make results hard to reproduce for a licensing or regulatory dossier (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Input manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043, T0043.003): the model is passive and unauthenticated on its input, so an insider or someone with access to the acquisition chain could shift counts, or place or shield material, so that the reconstruction hides a localised source or diverted material. This is a safeguards and security concern, since the network may be treated as evidence of content. Low-amplitude perturbations exploit the network's sensitivity because the inverse mapping is unstable. (6) Training-pipeline and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.002, T0010.003, T0020, T0018.000, T0043.004): the simulation datasets, Geant4 configurations, cross-section libraries, and pretrained weights are the single source of truth. A poisoned or backdoored dataset, or a tampered simulation parameter, can embed a systematic bias or a trigger pattern that suppresses one nuclide or location, and it is difficult to detect without independent measurement. (7) Reconnaissance and model extraction (AML.T0000, T0002, T0024.002, T0005): published architecture and dataset let an adversary build a proxy model and craft evasive count patterns offline. Overall, the exposure is the unverifiable simulator-to-reality assumption, which both honest drift and a deliberate attacker can exploit.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this CNN sits where waste-cask content characterization feeds waste acceptance, transport classification, inventory declarations, and safeguards or accountancy-adjacent records. Whoever can bias its output can change what the facility believes is inside a cask without touching the cask. The model is trained only on Geant4 simulation with no field validation, so its errors are unbounded and unseen. That makes it a convenient place to hide a diversion, an under-declaration, or a mis-classification behind 'model uncertainty'. A nation-state would more likely target the simulation and training pipeline, the detector data path, or the trust placed in the output than the neural network itself. The most realistic insider risk is a quiet shift in accepted characterization, and it matters more than any dramatic attack.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity attack on the characterization output. Mechanism: poisoning or backdooring the model, simulated training data or Geant4 source/geometry/material configs, or tampering with the detector-count stream (AML.T0010.002, T0018.000, T0020, T0043, T0043.004, T0031). Dependence: waste acceptance, dose and transport classification, and inventory records rely on the reconstructed activity map. Consequence: hot spots or specific nuclides are hidden or smeared, so decay-heat, shielding, and criticality-adjacent assumptions are wrong, and records are falsified. Material substitution or removal inside a cement matrix could be masked as a 'reconstruction artifact' (OP.C0702.01). (2) Evasion by physical shielding or source arrangement. Mechanism: because the inverse problem is ill-posed and the model is trained only on simulated distributions, an insider who can place shielding, spacers, or sources, or who knows the detector layout, can craft out-of-distribution configurations that the CNN reconstructs as benign (AML.T0015, T0041, T0043.003). Consequence: undetected diversion or concealment. (3) Detector-layout disclosure. The 'optimise detector placement' function produces knowledge of blind spots and sensitivity gaps. Models, outputs, and layout recommendations are therefore reconnaissance assets (AML.T0035, T0024.002, T0013, T0007, OP.C0505). (4) Supply chain and software hygiene. Pretrained frameworks, third-party simulation toolchains, and unmanaged model files are stepping stones into the waste-storage and records network (AML.T0010.001, T0010.003, OP.C0502). IMPLICIT, and exploitable by timing. (5) Sim-to-real gap. The model has never seen real casks, with their sensor noise, geometry tolerances, density variation, or nuclide mixes outside Co-60/Cs-137/Eu-152, so errors are silent and unquantified (OP.C0201.01, C0302, C0302.03, C0203, C0202). Consequence: false confidence, or a cover story for anomalies. (6) Automation trust and opacity. Operators may accept smooth, plausible activity maps without independent gamma-scan cross-checks. Skill fade in manual characterization, and the CNN's opacity, shift the burden of proof onto the human who raises doubt (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0401, C0403, C0304.03). An adversary can time a tampering action to periods of routine reliance. (7) Qualification gap. Nothing exists to qualify an ML tool for a safety-relevant, records-bearing role, and retraining or updating creates uncontrolled change (OP.C0501, C0303, C0402, C0504). (8) Fleet propagation. If one model is reused across sites or casks, a single compromise or a single bias becomes systematic across the inventory (OP.C0602, C0603).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, automation trust, qualification gaps, fleet propagation, input manipulation and pipeline poisoning. I folded the nuclear engineer's and AI engineer's overlapping items into single threats, kept layout disclosure as distinct, and dropped denial of service and weak-evidence codes such as reconnaissance of public papers and OP.C0702.01.

evidence.citation: "Neural-network-based reconstruction of spent-fuel radioactive distribution in nuclear waste cask," Annals of Nuclear Energy (Elsevier), Vol. 197, Article 110259, March 2024
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests a CNN on a simulated (Geant4) detector-count dataset. The CNN identifies nuclides and reconstructs their non-uniform radioactivity distribution in PWR-derived solidified waste casks. It also proposes using the results to optimise how detectors are arranged. The evidence comes from simulated data only, with no real-cask deployment reported.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is detector-input manipulation or pipeline poisoning that hides a hotspot, diversion or under-declaration behind a falsified activity record, which erodes material accountability and waste classification for transport and acceptance; this falls just short of a direct radiological release.

reproducibility.why: The ill-posed inverse mapping and the sim-to-real gap reliably produce plausible but wrong maps whenever real casks depart from the idealized simulation, and non-uniqueness lets benign reconstructions persist, though a targeted bias needs specific conditions.

exploitability.why: Deliberate concealment generally needs insider or physical access to the cask, the detector chain, calibration files or the training pipeline, and a compromised dataset or model needs privileged access, although exploiting the implicit sim-to-real error needs little.

affected_users.why: Impact is mainly per-cask, but a shared model or update, or reuse across casks and sites, can propagate one systematic bias across the waste inventory and the records, transport and acceptance decisions that depend on it.

discoverability.why: The class is well documented in open literature (simulation-only training, ill-posed inversion, adversarial and poisoning risks) and the source paper is public, but locating specific blind spots or exploitable count patterns needs partial system knowledge such as layout or model outputs.

use_case: Layered 'composite classifier' of three binary machine-learning classifiers for cybersecurity monitoring of a digital reactor. It uses operational-technology and information-technology data streams to separate normal from abnormal states and cyber events (false data injection, denial of service) from non-cyber anomalies. It also identifies the type of cyber event. It was tested on a live, fully digital research reactor, PUR-1.
incurred_insecurity:
A layered ML classifier that decides whether a digital reactor's OT/IT data show normal operation, a non-cyber anomaly, or a cyber event (false data injection, denial of service) becomes the arbiter of what defenders escalate as cyber. The panel converged on four main threats: adversarial evasion and misattribution, corruption of the training and model pipeline, a new OT/IT attack surface with reconnaissance help from public documentation, and implicit weaknesses from a narrow single-reactor evidence base that breed false assurance. Harm arrives through operators and incident response acting on its verdict, with diverse safety-system trips bounding the direct physical consequence.

Evasion by crafted data -- adversarial
False data injection or DoS activity shaped to resemble normal operation or a benign process transient is classed as normal or non-cyber. Because the three binary classifiers cascade, defeating an early gate also hides the attack from the event-type stage, so a compromise gets troubleshot as an equipment fault instead of isolated.

Misattribution induced to misdirect response -- adversarial
An adversary can induce cyber-like symptoms during a genuine process fault, or disguise a cyber attack as a sensor or mechanical anomaly. The wrong verdict delays the security or the safety response and absorbs staff attention while a second action proceeds.

Poisoning of training data and model -- adversarial
Retraining on operational logs the attacker has touched, or a compromised data, labeling or model-update path, can shift the decision boundary or embed a backdoor trigger that keeps one signature invisible. Operators then see silence during an attack or a raised false-alarm rate.

Monitor as OT/IT pivot and chaff target -- adversarial
The classifier needs both OT and IT feeds, so its host, credentials and data pipeline bridge the networks and can serve as a lateral-movement and reconnaissance point. Flooding or malforming its input streams can blind it or bury a real attack in alert fatigue.

Public disclosure enabling proxy rehearsal -- adversarial
The NRC letter report and arXiv preprint publish the architecture, features, attack types and performance. This lets an attacker build a proxy model and rehearse evasion offline.

Narrow data provenance and low base rate -- implicit, exploitable
Training rests on attacks and faults staged on one small research reactor, so real adversary behavior and rare transients are under-represented and reported accuracy overstates field performance. An adversary can use novel or low-and-slow tradecraft outside the staged attack set, which the model will not recognise.

Transfer and drift failure -- implicit, exploitable
A model tuned to PUR-1's simple, fully digital I&C degrades on a commercial plant's hybrid architecture and different dynamics, and further through recalibration, software updates and operating-mode changes. An adversary can wait for or induce the drift and act inside the degraded detection band.

Cascade error propagation -- implicit, exploitable
A first- or second-stage miss silently propagates into the event-type label, so operators receive a confident but wrong classification. An adversary can aim for the gate whose error is most likely to cascade.

Over-trust, opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
Operators may defer to a 'normal' or 'non-cyber' verdict, let independent network monitoring and manual vigilance fade, and be unable to challenge opaque decisions or reproduce them after retraining. An adversary can time action around that complacency or around alert-fatigue disuse after false positives.

Qualification and evidence gap -- implicit
No accepted QA or regulatory pathway exists for a retrainable ML security monitor, and the evidence is a non-peer-reviewed preprint plus a regulator letter report. No realistic adversary gains directly from this beyond the false assurance already described.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the plant side, this is a monitoring and decision-support layer on OT/IT data, not a protection function, so a wrong output does not directly move rods or trip the reactor. Harm would arrive through operators, SOC staff and incident-response procedures acting (or failing to act) on its classification. The main downstream questions are whether a missed cyber event (false negative) delays detection of false data injection that is also degrading operator situational awareness, and whether a false cyber alarm or a mislabelled non-cyber anomaly triggers unnecessary isolation, manual operation or a shutdown. Existing practice, including hardwired and diverse analog or safety-system trips, defense-in-depth, and technical-specification-driven operator actions, limits the physical consequence. Even so, the classifier sits where an adversary would want to blind the defenders, and the evidence base is a single small, fully digital research reactor that may not carry over to a commercial power plant with a hybrid analog/digital I&C architecture.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Evasion by crafted data (AML.T0015, T0043, T0043.001/.003). An adversary who knows the process and the feature set can shape false data injection or DoS traffic to look like a benign non-cyber anomaly or normal state, so the layered classifier routes it to 'not cyber'. The facility then treats a cyber compromise as an equipment or process fault and troubleshoots it instead of isolating. Safety-system diversity still bounds the physical result, but the monitoring blind spot is the harm. (2) Poisoning and integrity erosion (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0031, T0059, T0010.002/.003). Retraining or tuning on plant data that an attacker has already touched, or a compromised model or data supply chain, can embed blind spots or raise the false-alarm rate. Operators then see either silence during an attack or alarm fatigue. (3) The monitor as an attack surface. It ingests both OT and IT streams, so it needs data-diode or tap paths into the control network. Its host, credentials and data pipeline become a pivot into the OT/IT boundary (AML.T0012, T0049). Sensor-feed denial or chaff (AML.T0029, T0046) can blind it or flood it with alerts at the moment an attack is under way. (4) Reconnaissance: the public NRC report and arXiv preprint disclose features, attack types, architecture and performance (AML.T0000, T0001, T0002), which supports building proxy models and tuning evasion (AML.T0005). IMPLICIT: (5) Data scarcity and provenance. Training data come from one live research reactor, probably with a limited set of staged attack and anomaly scenarios (OP.C0201.01, C0202, C0203). Real attacks are rare and varied, so the low base rate and the novelty of real attacks mean unseen attack types are likely misclassified. Reported accuracy is unlikely to hold up (OP.C0302, C0302.03). (6) Transfer and drift. A model tuned to PUR-1's small, simple, fully digital I&C and its operating regime may not generalise to a commercial plant with different dynamics, hybrid I&C, power maneuvers, or seasonal and maintenance-driven changes. Instrument recalibration, software updates and operating-mode changes cause data and concept drift that quietly erode performance (OP.C0302.01/.02, C0303, C0602 if the model is replicated across a fleet). (7) Human factors. A cyber/non-cyber verdict and an attack-type label invite over-trust, with operators deferring to 'non-cyber' and skipping independent cross-checks (OP.C0101.04, C0102). Opaque layered decisions are hard to audit during an incident (OP.C0401). A composite of three classifiers adds error propagation between layers, so a first-stage miss silently cascades (OP.C0603, C0301.01). (8) Qualification and regulatory gap. There are no established QA or qualification criteria for AI-based cyber monitors, and the evidence is a non-peer-reviewed preprint plus a regulator letter report (OP.C0501, C0504, C0503). Non-repeatability across retrains complicates change control (OP.C0402.01). The key safeguard is that this should remain advisory, with independent network IDS, diverse protection systems and procedural fallbacks that do not depend on the classifier.

ai_engineer.argument: From the ML pipeline side, this is a supervised, layered classifier (normal vs. abnormal, cyber vs. non-cyber, cyber-event type) trained on data from one small, fully digital research reactor (PUR-1). The labels for the cyber classes almost certainly come from attacks the researchers injected themselves (FDI, DoS), and the non-cyber anomalies from a narrow set of induced faults. So the model learns the signatures of a specific attack generator and a specific plant. Three cascaded binary classifiers also multiply error: a mistake at layer 1 or 2 propagates into layer 3 and into the label an operator sees. The cascade also gives an adversary a conditional structure to probe and evade. The real exposure is the gap between the narrow, lab-style training distribution and the open-ended operational and adversarial distribution a power-generation deployment would face. The only evidence is a regulator letter report and a non-peer-reviewed preprint.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion (AML.T0015, T0043, T0043.001/.003): an attacker who knows or infers the feature set (OT/IT telemetry, signal statistics) can craft FDI that is slow, low-amplitude, or physically consistent, or that mimics a benign process transient. The classifier then reads it as normal or non-cyber. Because the cascade is layered, evading the first or second gate is enough to hide the attack from the type classifier. This leaves the monitoring layer giving false assurance, and the defenders' own sensing is the weakest link. (2) Training and data poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0018.000, T0043.004): if retraining or tuning uses operational logs that include attacker-influenced traffic, the attacker can shift the decision boundary or insert a backdoor trigger. The same risk applies to historian and data-pipeline compromise. (3) Model/artifact access and recon (AML.T0007, T0013, T0044, T0005): theft of the model or of the open preprint's architecture and features lets an attacker build a proxy and optimize attacks offline. (4) Availability and chaff (AML.T0029, T0046): flooding the IT/OT streams with benign-looking noise or malformed packets degrades the classifier, creates alert fatigue, or pushes inputs out of distribution, which can be used to cover a real attack. (5) New attack surface: the monitor needs IT and OT data feeds, so its integration (taps, data diodes, an analytics host) can itself become a pivot into the control network.

IMPLICIT. (a) Narrow data provenance and low base rate (OP.C0201.01/.05, OP.C0202, OP.C0203): training uses injected or simulated attacks on one research reactor, so real adversary behavior and rare non-cyber transients are under-represented. Reported accuracy probably overstates field performance, and class imbalance will make false positives or false negatives dominate in a power plant. (b) Transfer and generalization failure (OP.C0302, .01, .03, OP.C0303): PUR-1 is a low-power, fully digital research reactor, unlike a commercial plant with different dynamics, network architecture, and legacy analog/digital mixes. Moving to power generation without requalification is an out-of-distribution deployment, and plant aging, modifications, and new attack tradecraft cause drift and concept drift. (c) Cascade error propagation (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603): errors compound across the three binary layers, and a misclassified event type can misdirect the response, for example treating a cyber event as a sensor fault. (d) Opacity and qualification (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402.01): there is no accepted way to qualify a learned classifier for a safety-adjacent monitoring role, and retraining non-determinism makes the verified artifact hard to pin down. (e) Human factors (OP.C0101.04/.05, OP.C0102): over-trust in a 'normal' output, or disuse after false alarms. An adversary can time an attack for when operator trust is lowest or highest. (f) Evidence quality: the sources are a regulator letter report and a non-peer-reviewed preprint, so claims have not been independently reproduced.

security_specialist.argument: A cyber-monitoring classifier is a security control, so an adversary treats it as something to blind, steer or exploit rather than as a target in itself. Its value to an attacker is that it is the arbiter between 'cyber event' and 'non-cyber anomaly', and operators will act on that verdict. An adversary who understands the model's features (OT/IT data streams) can craft false data injection or DoS activity that looks like a benign anomaly or normal state, or can manufacture cyber-looking signatures to trigger alarms during a real physical event. The use case was demonstrated on one small, fully digital research reactor with a limited, mostly lab-generated attack set, so the gap between that evidence and a power-generation environment is exactly what a capable adversary would exploit. A sophisticated adversary would more likely attack the data pipeline, the labels, or the operators' trust in the classifier than the model weights themselves.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by mimicry: the classifier separates only a few known event types (false data injection, DoS), so novel or low-and-slow attacks, or injected data statistically close to normal operation, can be classed as normal or non-cyber. The AI failure is a misclassification driven by crafted inputs; the facility depends on it for timely cyber detection and incident response; the consequence is undetected manipulation of instrumentation or control data, or a misdirected response. The layered binary structure also offers an attacker a decision path to probe: evading the first 'normal vs abnormal' stage defeats the downstream attribution stages. (2) Misattribution as a weapon: an adversary can induce cyber-like symptoms during a genuine process fault, or disguise a cyber attack as a mechanical or sensor anomaly. Because the classifier decides what gets escalated as cyber, this can delay either the safety response or the security response, or consume staff attention while a second action proceeds. (3) Data and model integrity: training and retraining data come from OT/IT telemetry and from attack runs that were simulated or injected. An insider or supply-chain actor with access to the data collection, labeling, or model update path can poison labels or insert a backdoor trigger that keeps one signature invisible. The monitor sits on both OT and IT networks, so it also bridges them. A compromised classifier host, its feeds, or its credentials becomes a lateral-movement and reconnaissance point and a map of what the defenders can and cannot see. (4) Concentration of trust: operators who come to rely on the classifier's 'normal' verdict may let independent network monitoring and manual vigilance fade, and an attacker can time action around that fade or around known alert fatigue from false positives. Exposure of the model's features, thresholds and performance (the arXiv preprint and the NRC report are public) lets an attacker build a proxy model and rehearse evasion offline.

IMPLICIT. (5) Generalization gap: validation on one small digital research reactor with narrow operating regimes and a limited attack set does not carry over to a power reactor's plant states, transients, maintenance modes, and network architecture. Drift from plant modifications, software updates, or seasonal and load-following changes will raise false negatives or false-alarm rates, and an adversary can wait for or induce the drift. (6) Low base rate and label scarcity: real cyber events at reactors are essentially absent, so performance rests on synthetic or injected attacks and cannot be assumed to represent real adversary behavior. Performance metrics are likely overstated, and the opacity of the classifier makes it hard for operators to challenge a wrong verdict. (7) Qualification gap: no established regulatory or QA pathway exists for an ML security monitor whose retraining changes behavior, and inference or training non-determinism makes the verdict hard to reproduce for forensics. The overall consequence is a false sense of cyber assurance for plant security and safety staff.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on evasion by crafted data, poisoning, monitor-as-pivot, chaff, public-document reconnaissance, and the single-reactor generalization gap; I merged overlapping items and kept misattribution as distinct because it targets response rather than detection. I dropped lower-support ATLAS codes (e.g., T0007, T0013, T0044) and the fleet-propagation OP code as not clearly instantiated.

evidence.citation: "Letter Report TLR RES/DE-2024-003 (AI/ML characterization of cyber events and abnormal states in the PUR-1 research reactor)," U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC ADAMS), Office of Nuclear Regulatory Research
evidence.note: The NRC report describes an AI/ML use case implemented on Purdue's digital research reactor PUR-1. Several algorithms were evaluated on the collected data, and a composite classifier made of three binary classifiers with different objectives was built. The same team also posted this work as an arXiv preprint (2509.00076), which is not peer reviewed. This NRC report is a regulator technical letter report and is not a journal paper.

damage.why: The worst credible threat is evasion or misattribution that hides a cyber compromise (FDI/DoS) and delays response, which could erode safety margins or disrupt operations; diverse safety-system trips bound direct physical consequence, so it falls short of release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Evasion, drift and cascade-error failures recur reliably once conditions exist (cascading gates, narrow training data, published architecture), but poisoning and pivot threats are conditional on pipeline access or specific deployment choices.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (poisoning the training or update path, pivoting through the OT/IT bridge, crafting evasive data against the plant's feeds) generally require insider or privileged access to OT/IT data paths and substantial adversary resourcing, though proxy-model rehearsal lowers the barrier somewhat.

affected_users.why: A blinded or misdirected monitor degrades the cyber-versus-fault verdict for the whole monitored digital I&C and the staff responding to it, but impact is bounded to monitoring and response and independent safety systems limit propagation across coupled systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, features, attack types and performance are public in an NRC letter report and an arXiv preprint, and adversarial ML evasion, poisoning and drift are well documented in open literature, so a capable outsider can readily infer the weaknesses; only plant-specific details remain hidden.

use_case: Autoencoder neural network combined with ARIMA time-series forecasting to estimate the health condition and remaining useful life of Class II nuclear power plant piping that is subject to flow-accelerated corrosion. The model is trained on synthetic wall-thinning data from a finite-element digital replica of the piping.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case incurs mostly implicit insecurity, because an autoencoder-plus-ARIMA remaining-useful-life (RUL) estimate trained only on finite-element-simulated flow-accelerated corrosion (FAC) thinning can look authoritative while being unvalidated against plant reality. The main threats are a sim-to-real and drift gap, over-trust that erodes inspection coverage, opacity and qualification gaps, and adversarial tampering with the replica, training data, model or sensor feed. Because the output is a smooth trend rather than an alarm, both faults and manipulation are hard to detect, and the system is a stealthy way to bias lifetime-extension and inspection decisions.

Sim-to-real gap and out-of-distribution blindness -- implicit, exploitable
The model learns the replica's assumed wear law, geometry and clean noise rather than real localized FAC, and ARIMA cannot represent step changes from chemistry excursions, uprates or component replacement, so RUL is falsely narrow and non-conservative with no out-of-distribution warning. An adversary could hide a manipulation or a real degradation event inside this unquantified uncertainty, since a novel degraded state may map to a benign latent region.

Synthetic data scarcity and circular validation -- implicit, exploitable
No run-to-failure field data exists to validate the rare event the model predicts, so replica errors are baked in as ground truth and testing against the same simulation cannot expose them. An adversary who alters replica parameters would pass all validation, relying on this circularity.

Over-trust and erosion of inspection vigilance -- implicit, exploitable
A single scalar RUL invites inspection intervals to be stretched and weakens the FAC inspection skill base, undermining defense-in-depth and risking undetected wall loss below minimum thickness in a leak or rupture. An adversary could time tampering or a real failure to this reduced scrutiny, relying on the misplaced trust.

Opacity, non-determinism and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The latent health indicator has no physical interpretation, retraining can shift RUL, and no accepted qualification path exists for an ML model that deprioritizes ultrasonic inspection, so operators and regulators cannot reconcile it with thickness measurements. Weak change control lets silent tampering or unreviewed retraining pass as ordinary variation.

Poisoning of replica, training data and model -- adversarial
An insider or compromised supplier or toolchain can alter the replica's wear parameters, the simulated training set or the autoencoder weights, producing systematically optimistic RUL that defers inspections and corrupts lifetime-extension licensing evidence. A pessimistic bias instead forces needless outages.

Evasion and falsification of the monitoring feed -- adversarial
