Low-amplitude manipulation of sensor or historian data crafted to reconstruct well keeps the reconstruction-error-based health indicator in the normal range while ARIMA forecasts a longer life than reality. It can be timed to a maintenance cycle or licensing submission.

Supply chain, shared-model propagation and design-data leakage -- adversarial
Compromised third-party finite-element tools, ML libraries or model files, and a replica reused across segments or plants, give common-cause reach for a single flaw or compromise. The replica and model files also expose piping geometry and weak points useful for sabotage targeting, and a poorly segmented model host offers a foothold into plant data networks.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, FAC is a slow, well-characterized degradation mechanism already managed through programmatic controls: CHECWORKS-type predictive codes, UT/ECT thickness inspection, ASME Section XI and code minimum wall requirements. The main danger of this tool is therefore not a sudden failure. It is that a smooth, quantitative RUL number trained on synthetic data gets used to justify deferring inspections or extending service life for Class II piping. The model learns from a finite-element replica, not from plant-measured wall loss. FAC in reality depends on local geometry, water chemistry (pH, oxygen, hydrazine), temperature, flow velocity, and alloy chromium content, and it is notoriously localized, so a replica can miss the worst-case spot. A wrong RUL only becomes a leak or rupture if inspection scheduling, code-minimum-wall margins and operator judgment also fail, but that is exactly the erosion of defense-in-depth the tool invites if its number is trusted.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: the autoencoder's health indicator and the ARIMA forecast reflect only what the FE replica represents. Unmodeled chemistry excursions, weld or elbow geometry, flow-regime changes, repairs and replacements, and plant-specific heterogeneity produce out-of-distribution inputs. ARIMA assumes smooth, stationary-after-differencing trends, so step changes (chemistry upset, power uprate, operating-mode change) and the accelerating late-life thinning that matters most are extrapolated poorly. The result is a non-conservative, falsely narrow RUL (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). (2) Consequence: the tool is used to support lifetime extension and predictive-monitoring decisions. If the RUL is optimistic, inspection intervals may be stretched or wall-loss locations deprioritized. The loss of coverage is then discovered late, as a through-wall leak or pipe break on secondary-side or Class II systems. The physical consequences include steam or feedwater loss, a transient or trip, and personnel injury, as at Surry 1986 and Mihama 2004. Existing UT inspection, minimum-wall calculations and regulatory acceptance should catch this, but only if the model stays advisory and is not allowed to substitute for them (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (3) Opacity: a compressed single health indicator hides which sensor or feature drives the score. Operators and regulators cannot easily reconcile it with UT readings or judge its uncertainty, and a single scalar can mask a localized fault (OP.C0401, OP.C0402). (4) Data scarcity: real end-of-life, run-to-failure FAC data is very scarce, so validation against truth is weak (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Sensor drift, gaps or recalibration also break the ARIMA continuity (OP.C0204). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Integrity manipulation: an adversary who compromises the FE replica inputs or parameters, the training pipeline, or the live sensor and inspection feed can poison the model or bias the health indicator slowly. The trend then looks healthy while the pipe thins (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031, AML.T0043). This is a stealthy sabotage precursor, since a physical failure would be timed with other events, and it would also corrupt life-extension licensing evidence. A false-alarm variant forces unnecessary outages or inspections, with an economic and availability impact. (6) Supply chain and software hygiene: third-party FE tools, ML libraries and model files carry compromise risk (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, OP.C0502). Replica geometry and thinning data are also sensitive design and vulnerability information, which could leak and show where the plant's weakest piping is (AML.T0025, AML.T0037, OP.C0505). Mitigations from existing practice: keep the tool advisory only, validate it against UT/ECT thickness measurements, apply conservative bounding margins, run independent inspection programs, and require model-change control.

ai_engineer.argument: The pipeline has three stacked fragilities. (1) Training data is entirely simulated from a finite-element digital replica, so the model learns the FE model's assumptions about FAC (a fixed wear law, idealized geometry, clean sensor noise, smooth monotonic thinning), not plant reality. (2) The autoencoder collapses multivariate input to one health indicator whose relationship to wall thickness and failure margin is never calibrated against ground truth, and ARIMA then extrapolates that scalar by assuming stationarity after differencing and a stable trend. FAC is in fact a threshold- and chemistry-sensitive process (pH, oxygen, temperature, flow, material Cr content), so real degradation can show regime shifts, localized pitting-like acceleration and step changes that neither component can represent. (3) The output feeds lifetime-extension and inspection-interval decisions, so a smooth, confident-looking RUL curve is exactly the kind of artefact that invites over-trust, and the model has no native way to say 'this input is outside what I was trained on'.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (a) Sim-to-real gap / synthetic provenance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0202): no failure-labelled field data exist for a well-maintained Class II line, so the model cannot be validated on the rare event it exists to predict. Errors in the FE replica (wrong wear coefficient, wrong flow field, ignored weld/elbow geometry) are baked in as ground truth and are invisible to the autoencoder's reconstruction metric. Consequence: non-conservative RUL, with pipe wall dropping below minimum allowable thickness between inspections; this is a safety-margin and licensing issue for lifetime extension. (b) Drift and OOD (OP.C0302.01, .02, .03): water chemistry excursions, power uprates, component replacement, or a changed operating regime move the sensor distribution away from the simulated one. An autoencoder trained only on simulated degradation trajectories reconstructs poorly on OOD input, but that error can be confused with 'unhealthy', or worse, a degraded-but-novel state can map to a benign latent region. ARIMA's refit on a short, noisy health-indicator history gives wide, unstable forecasts or falsely tight ones, and it is blind to structural breaks (OP.C0403). (c) Qualification mismatch and opacity (OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01): the latent health indicator has no physical interpretation, and training non-determinism or the choice of latent dimension can shift RUL between retrainings; no established qualification path exists for an ML model that substitutes for or deprioritizes ultrasonic thickness inspection. (d) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102): a single scalar plus a RUL number encourages over-trust and may reduce inspection frequency, so the model's blind spots become the facility's blind spots. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (e) Integrity attacks on the monitoring data stream (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031): slow, low-amplitude manipulation of historian or sensor values can be crafted to stay inside the autoencoder's reconstruction-error tolerance while shifting the health indicator trend, so ARIMA forecasts a longer life than reality. This is a stealthy way to delay maintenance, and it could be timed with a real degradation event. Because the model is a low-dimensional compressor, its latent space is easy to probe and manipulate in a white-box setting. (f) Supply-chain and artefact tampering (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059): the FE-simulated training set, FE input decks, and trained weights are attack surfaces; a poisoned wear-rate parameter or a backdoored model yields systematically optimistic RUL while passing all testing against the same tampered simulation, which is a circular verification problem. (g) Model/data confidentiality (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0036): the digital replica and RUL outputs reveal piping geometry, degradation state and weak points, which has value for sabotage targeting. Mitigation directions at pipeline level: anchor the model to UT inspection ground truth, report out-of-distribution scores and forecast uncertainty alongside RUL, treat the model as advisory only with conservative bounds, and hash and version simulation inputs, training data and weights.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is not a high-value direct target. It is a decision-support tool for slow-moving degradation in Class II piping, so an adversary gets little from attacking it head-on. The real concern is that it can lower the human inspection vigilance that currently guards a safety-relevant degradation mechanism. Its credibility also rests on a synthetic digital replica, and that replica is a single point of trust. Whoever can quietly shift the replica's parameters, the training data or the health-indicator baseline can bias remaining-useful-life (RUL) estimates in either direction without ever touching the plant's control systems. An insider with write access to model files or inspection data, or a supplier in the model-development chain, is the credible actor. A nation-state would more plausibly use this as a stepping stone or an integrity-erosion path than as a primary objective.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Manipulation of the model or the synthetic training pipeline. The FE digital replica, its corrosion-rate and flow assumptions, and the trained autoencoder weights are the trust anchor. If they are poisoned or subtly altered by an insider or a compromised supplier or toolchain, the health indicator and the ARIMA forecast can be biased. Optimistic bias would defer ultrasonic thickness inspections and extend piping life beyond its safe margin. Pessimistic bias would trigger unnecessary outages or replacements, which is an economic or availability harm. The result is a wall-thinning failure (leak or rupture) in a Class II line, or an unjustified lifetime-extension case. Because the output is a smooth, plausible trend and not an alarm, tampering is hard to detect. (2) Manipulation of inputs. Sensor or inspection data feeding the autoencoder could be falsified to hold the health indicator in the normal range, or to generate false degradation. A reconstruction-error-based health indicator is vulnerable to evasion by inputs crafted to reconstruct well, and adversarial examples against the autoencoder are plausible. (3) Stepping stone and cover. Interference with RUL outputs could be timed to a maintenance-planning cycle or lifetime-extension licensing submission, which would turn the tool into a way to shape regulatory or maintenance decisions. The data pipeline, the model host and any engineering workstation connected to it also give a lateral-movement foothold into plant data networks if they are poorly segmented. If the vendor or an analytics service is cloud-hosted, there is an additional exposure channel. Model files and the replica also contain design and geometry information about piping, which makes them useful reconnaissance material.

IMPLICIT, and exploitable by timing. (4) Synthetic-to-real gap. The model is trained only on simulated thinning and has little or no validated field data for it. Real flow-accelerated corrosion (FAC) is heterogeneous: it depends on water chemistry, local geometry, temperature and material chromium content. Out-of-distribution behaviour, and drift in operating conditions, can therefore make RUL estimates overconfident without any warning. An adversary or a simple fault can hide inside this unquantified uncertainty. (5) Automation trust and skill fade. A single scalar health indicator with an RUL number invites over-trust, reduces inspection frequency and erodes the human FAC-inspection skill base. An adversary could time an attack, or a degradation event, to a period of reduced human scrutiny. (6) Opacity and qualification gaps. An autoencoder's compressed health indicator is hard to explain physically, ARIMA assumes stationary or simple trends that can break under step changes (a chemistry excursion, a flow change), and there is no accepted qualification path for this kind of model in safety-related lifetime-extension decisions. Weak change control and model versioning make silent tampering or unreviewed retraining harder to catch. (7) Model-fidelity propagation. Errors in the shared FE replica propagate to every piping segment and every plant that reuses the model, which means a single flaw or compromise has common-cause reach.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, over-trust eroding inspections, opacity/qualification gaps, and poisoning or input manipulation producing optimistic RUL; I merged the overlapping variants into single threats. I dropped AML.T0024.002, AML.T0036 and AML.T0012 as weakly argued (model extraction and valid accounts were only asserted) and kept confidentiality under data-leakage codes AML.T0025/AML.T0037.

evidence.citation: "Hybrid neural network and statistical forecasting methodology for predictive monitoring and residual useful life estimation in nuclear power plant components," Elsevier (Nuclear Engineering and Design)
evidence.note: The paper builds a finite-element digital replica of a Class II piping to simulate progressive thinning from flow-accelerated corrosion, and uses the synthetic data to train an autoencoder. The autoencoder compresses multivariate data into a single health indicator, and ARIMA forecasts that indicator to estimate remaining useful life. This supports lifetime-extension and predictive-monitoring decisions.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a systematically optimistic RUL (from poisoning, feed falsification, or sim-to-real error) that defers inspections and lets wall loss go below minimum thickness, risking a Class II piping leak or rupture and corrupting lifetime-extension licensing evidence; this is a serious safety-margin and defense-in-depth erosion, but it falls short of a direct radiological release or loss of material control.

reproducibility.why: The implicit sim-to-real gap, ARIMA's inability to represent step changes, and circular validation recur reliably whenever the model is deployed on real plant data, while deliberate tampering also reliably yields biased RUL once access exists.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (altering replica parameters, training data or model weights, or crafting low-amplitude falsification of historian or sensor feeds) generally need insider, supplier, or toolchain access and plant-specific knowledge, though the implicit failure modes need no attacker at all.

affected_users.why: Impact is mainly on a piping segment or system and its inspection and licensing decisions, but shared replicas and models reused across segments or plants (common-cause propagation) can widen reach to multiple systems or sites.

discoverability.why: Sim-to-real gaps, synthetic-data circularity, over-trust, and poisoning and evasion of ML-based condition monitoring are well documented in open literature, and the methodology is published, so a capable outsider can readily infer where the weaknesses lie, though plant-specific details remain internal.

use_case: Custom convolutional neural network, followed by a deterministic post-processor, that detects flaws in ultrasonic testing (UT) scans of CANDU reactor pressure tubes. It finds flaw regions despite mechanical chatter noise in the scans. It automates the manual outage inspection of fuel-channel pressure tubes and cuts false positives.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places a custom CNN and a deterministic post-processor as the first-pass screening filter for CANDU pressure-tube UT scans. A missed flaw is never sized, so the tube stays in service unassessed. The main threats are silent false negatives from scarce, label-biased data, drift, and a false-positive-reduction objective; erosion of independent analyst review; an unresolved qualification gap; and adversarial tampering with data, model or post-processor that the filter's opacity and apparent legitimacy would conceal.

Rare-flaw false negatives -- implicit, exploitable
Flaws such as hydride blisters and cracks are rare and labels come from past analyst calls, so the CNN can miss rare, atypical or low-amplitude flaws, especially those resembling chatter. Tuning for fewer false positives pushes the operating point toward misses and leaves the miss rate on safety-significant flaws poorly characterised. An adversary could place a manipulation inside this known blind spot and present the resulting sensitivity loss as an apparent improvement.

Drift and fleet-wide propagation -- implicit, exploitable
Changes in probe, couplant, calibration, scan settings, tube ageing or chatter signature move inputs out of distribution, and the CNN gives no reliable warning while the post-processor thresholds stay tuned to old data. A blind spot in a tool reused across units also repeats fleet-wide. An adversary could hide a gradual signal manipulation within this degraded detection band or time an attack to a campaign after a hardware change.

Automation bias and partial-detection anchoring -- implicit, exploitable
The tool only needs to locate part of each flaw, so analysts reviewing only flagged regions may skip adjacent indications and under-size extent. Their independent detection skill also fades under outage schedule pressure. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust, timing tampering to high-volume outages when independent review is thinnest.

Opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A custom CNN has opaque decision logic and retraining non-determinism, and there is no accepted qualification route under codified NDE procedures. A proof-of-concept result could therefore become a de facto screening filter without assurance. An adversary or weak change process could slip unvalidated model or threshold updates past review.

Training-data and label poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor could tamper with archived scans, annotations or retraining inputs to implant a blind spot or backdoor for specific flaw signatures. Opacity and the small dataset make this hard to detect, and the missed flaws persist undetected across operating cycles.

Model, post-processor and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
Altered weights, a compromised model update, or changed deterministic post-processor thresholds and preprocessing could silently suppress chosen flaw morphologies while headline metrics look fine. The post-processor is an easily overlooked tamper point and the false-positive-reduction goal gives cover.

Scan-data manipulation and evasion -- adversarial
Scan files or the chatter-noise preprocessing upstream of the model could be altered, or perturbations resembling chatter injected, so a real flaw reads as noise. Chaff could also flood analysts with false positives, delaying the outage and eroding trust in the tool.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, the pressure tube is a primary pressure boundary and fitness-for-service component, so a missed flaw is the dominant consequence. The AI sits at the front of the disposition chain: it finds flaw candidates, and analysts then size and characterise them. That makes it a screening filter. If the filter is wrong, the analyst may never see the indication, and the sizing step cannot recover it. Existing practice offers real defences: qualified UT procedures, certified analysts, periodic inspection programmes, leak-before-break assessment, and leak detection. These defences weaken sharply if analysts shift from independent review to confirming what the AI highlights, or if the tool is used to cut analyst scrutiny and outage time. The tool's key claim is that it cuts false positives while tolerating chatter noise, and that claim is the one a quiet failure would undermine.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Missed-flaw false negatives: the training set is small and imbalanced, because real flaws such as debris fret, crevice corrosion and bearing-pad fretting are rare, and critical ones like hydride blisters or cracks are rarer still. The CNN may therefore handle common benign or well-represented flaws well and miss rare, novel or low-amplitude flaws. Because the tool is tuned to cut false positives, the operating threshold trades sensitivity for specificity, and the miss rate on rare, safety-significant flaws may be poorly characterised. Consequence: an undetected flaw leaves an unassessed tube in service, eroding margin against fitness-for-service criteria and eventually raising the risk of tube failure or leak. (2) Partial-detection design: the system aims to locate at least part of each flaw. The deterministic post-processor then defines the region, and flaw extent can be under-bounded. Analyst sizing anchored on the AI region may under-size length or depth. (3) Drift and generalisation: changes in probe, scanning-head, fixture, couplant, calibration, tube condition, the aging fleet, or chatter signatures between stations or campaigns can shift the input distribution. The performance validated on the original data would then not transfer, and the tool would degrade silently. Tools used for one unit or vendor may be reused fleet-wide, so the same blind spot propagates. (4) Automation bias and skill fade: analysts see fewer raw flaws and confirm AI outputs, and outage schedule pressure rewards trusting the tool. Independent detection capability and the cross-check on AI output both decay. (5) Qualification gap: pressure-tube inspection is performed under codified, qualified procedures. A CNN has opaque decision logic, may not be repeatable across retraining, and has no accepted qualification route. Using a proof-of-concept result in production would be a regulatory and QA gap. (6) Chatter-noise suppression may also suppress genuine low-amplitude signals that resemble noise. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (7) Training or validation data poisoning, or tampering with the model, by an insider or a supply-chain actor (a vendor, a contractor's analysis workstation, or a model update), could create a backdoor that hides a specific flaw signature or amplitude pattern. This is hard to detect given the opacity and small data. (8) Manipulation of scan data between acquisition and analysis, or an adversarial perturbation resembling chatter, could suppress detection or flood the analysts with false positives to delay the outage and erode trust, so they disable the tool. (9) Corruption of the post-processor's deterministic thresholds or configuration. (10) Denial or delay of analysis on the outage critical path. Physical harm would still require a real flaw to exist and the independent safeguards (periodic inspection, leak detection, sizing review) to fail, so the more likely harm is an economic and regulatory consequence. The main concern is a degraded, trusted filter in a long-lived safety-relevant inspection programme.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a supervised CNN-plus-deterministic-post-processor for flaw detection on UT scans, and its fragility sits in the data and the qualification story rather than in exotic architecture. Flaw classes such as debris fret, crevice corrosion and bearing-pad fretting are rare, and labels come from past analyst calls, so the model inherits human labelling bias and low base-rate imbalance. The 'cuts false positives' objective trades directly against recall, and the dangerous failure is the silent false negative on a scan the model was never trained to see. Scans come from specific probes, acquisition systems, tube conditions and chatter regimes, so any change to hardware, calibration, scan settings, noise profile or fleet unit pushes inputs out of distribution with no built-in signal that confidence is no longer meaningful. Because the system gates a safety-relevant fitness-for-service inspection, the structural exposure is that a proof-of-concept detector gets de facto trusted as a screening filter before it has a qualification basis suited to a non-deterministic learned component.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Training-data scarcity and label provenance (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0302): rare flaw types and few examples mean the model may detect only common morphologies, while novel or atypical flaws, such as ones overlapping chatter, go unflagged. Labels derived from earlier manual analysis also embed analyst misses, so the model's ceiling is the labeller's blind spots. Mechanism: sparse, biased ground truth. Dependency: outage inspection of pressure-tube integrity. Consequence: missed degradation and an eroded safety margin. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303): changes in probe, couplant, scan speed, acquisition software, tube aging or chatter character shift the input distribution. The CNN gives no reliable out-of-distribution warning, and the deterministic post-processor's thresholds, tuned on old data, can mask degraded detection. Qualification done on a static dataset does not cover this dynamic input space. (3) False-positive suppression objective (OP.C0301): tuning for fewer false alarms moves the operating point toward missed flaws, and the reduced analyst workload invites automation bias and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). If analysts review only flagged regions, nothing independently catches misses, and the instruction that analysts do sizing only on detected flaws creates a single point of omission. (4) Opacity and repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0403): retraining non-determinism, saliency that is hard to justify, and no AI-specific QA basis make acceptance by regulators and code authorities difficult, and results are hard to reproduce for audit.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training-data and label integrity (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059): tampering with archived scans or annotations, or injecting crafted scans during retraining, can create blind spots or backdoors for specific flaw signatures. An insider or compromised data store is the plausible route. (6) Model and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076): altered weights, post-processor thresholds or preprocessing libraries can silently reduce sensitivity while headline metrics look fine. The deterministic post-processor is an easily overlooked tamper point. (7) Evasion and input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0046): UT data are acquired and transferred as digital files, so perturbations or injected noise patterns resembling chatter could hide real flaws, or chaff could overwhelm analysts. (8) Exploiting known weaknesses: an adversary who knows the system is trusted as a first-pass filter can time tampering to an outage campaign, exploiting reduced independent review. Consequence class: degraded inspection integrity affecting pressure-tube fitness-for-service decisions, with the AI as a new, low-visibility attack surface on an otherwise manual, independently reviewed process.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, the CNN is a trust-concentration point. Pressure-tube fitness-for-service decisions, including the decision to keep a channel in service for another operating cycle, depend on whether a flaw is flagged. If an adversary, or a quiet natural failure, causes the detector to miss a flaw class, the harm shows up later as an in-service tube integrity problem, not as an immediate alarm. The system is only a detector, and analysts still size and characterise flaws. That is a real mitigation. But the stated goal of replacing manual scan review, together with the pressure to cut false positives, erodes the human review that serves as the independent check. An adversary or an insider could time a manipulation to an outage window, when scan volume is high, schedules are tight and analysts lean hardest on the tool. A nation-state would more likely reach this through the supply chain, the training data or the post-processor than through the model weights.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity attack on the detector: an insider or a compromised vendor/tooling supply chain could poison the training or labelling data, tamper with model weights, or change the deterministic post-processor thresholds so that particular flaw morphologies, locations or amplitudes are suppressed (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0031, AML.T0076). The facility depends on this output to find debris fretting, crevice corrosion and bearing-pad fretting. The consequence is a missed flaw that is not sized, which is a safety consequence for tube integrity that can persist undetected across cycles. The false-positive-reduction objective gives cover, because tuned-down sensitivity looks like a legitimate improvement. (2) Data-path tampering: the scan files or the chatter-noise preprocessing sit upstream of the model, so a crafted perturbation or modified scan data could make a flaw look like noise (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0059). A plain scan-integrity compromise would give the same result without any AI-specific skill, so the AI path is not necessarily the easiest target. Its value to an adversary lies in how well the manipulation hides behind the model's opacity. (3) Confidentiality: the inspection dataset and model show flaw distributions and detection limits, which would let an adversary learn the blind spots, so exfiltration is a reconnaissance step (AML.T0035, AML.T0025, AML.T0024.002).

IMPLICIT, AND EXPLOITABLE BY TIMING. (4) Automation trust and skill fade: as analysts shift from first-pass detection to reviewing machine-proposed regions, they become less likely to search outside the regions the tool highlights, and it is easy to anchor on them. The tool only needs to find part of each flaw, so analysts can be steered to the region it flags while a missed adjacent flaw goes unnoticed (OP.C0101, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (5) Small-data and drift problems: serious flaws are rare, labels come from historical manual analysis, and a proof-of-concept model may not generalise to new probes, tubes, vendors or noise conditions (OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). The result is silent loss of sensitivity for rare or atypical flaws, with no alarm. (6) Opacity and qualification gap: a custom CNN is hard to qualify under inspection-qualification regimes for NDE, which creates a regulatory and assurance gap (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). An adversary or a weak process could exploit that gap to keep unvalidated model updates from being caught. (7) Governance: version control and change management of weights and post-processor parameters, and access to retraining, must be treated as safety-significant configuration items (OP.C0502, OP.C0505). Otherwise an insider has a low-visibility way to change inspection outcomes.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on missed-flaw false negatives, drift, automation bias, the qualification gap, and poisoning/tampering of data, model and post-processor. I dropped the confidentiality/exfiltration and denial-of-service items, which were raised by only one panelist each and were thinly argued, and I merged the governance point into the tampering and qualification threats.

evidence.citation: "Using Deep Learning to Automate the Detection of Flaws in Nuclear Fuel Channel UT Scans," IEEE Transactions on Ultrasonics, Ferroelectrics, and Frequency Control
evidence.note: The paper describes a proof-of-concept deep-learning system built and tested on CANDU pressure-tube UT scans. It aims to replace the manual analysis of scans during plant outages by locating at least part of each flaw (e.g. debris fret, crevice corrosion, bearing-pad fretting) while keeping false positives low. Analysts then do the sizing and characterisation.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is silent false negatives or tampering that leave a flawed pressure tube in service unassessed, eroding structural safety margins on a primary-coolant boundary component and potentially leading to a loss-of-coolant event; this falls just short of a direct radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: The implicit failure modes (rare-flaw misses at a false-positive-tuned operating point, drift after hardware or calibration changes, analyst over-trust) recur reliably whenever the stated conditions hold, while the adversarial paths depend on obtaining the relevant access.

exploitability.why: The most credible adversarial paths (poisoning archived scans or labels, altering model weights or post-processor thresholds, tampering with scan files) need insider or supply-chain access to inspection data and analysis pipelines, though the implicit weaknesses need no special capability to be triggered.

affected_users.why: A blind spot in a tool reused across fuel channels and units repeats fleet-wide, and missed flaws persist across operating cycles, but the effect stays within the inspection and fuel-channel integrity function rather than propagating through all coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The general weaknesses of CNN-based flaw detection (small-data bias, drift, over-trust, opacity) are well documented in the open literature and the proof-of-concept is published, but locating a specific blind spot or tamper point needs knowledge of the deployed model, thresholds and data pipeline.

use_case: Hybrid native-transformer plus LSTM deep-learning detector of anomalous Modbus TCP traffic (IP-layer and application-layer features). It flags cyber-attacks on the air-gapped industrial control system of a nuclear power plant safety-shutdown system. It runs outside the ICS network, behind a one-way data diode, and was validated on an ICS testbed that replicates safety-shutdown components.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places a learned transformer+LSTM anomaly detector, validated only on a replica testbed, as the evidence that a nuclear safety-shutdown ICS network is free of cyber-attack. The one-way diode keeps a wrong output from actuating the safety system, but it protects nothing about the monitor's own data, model files, update path, alert channel or readers. The main threats are mimicry evasion, poisoning of baselines and models, blinding or flooding of the monitor, and theft of the monitor's plant-revealing data. They are compounded by the testbed-to-plant gap, drift, opacity, over-trust and narrow protocol scope, which together turn a quiet dashboard into false assurance.

Mimicry evasion -- adversarial
Because the architecture and Modbus feature set are published, an adversary can build a proxy model and craft protocol-valid function codes, register writes and polling cadence that score as normal, or move slowly. A malicious command set can then be staged against the shutdown logic while the detector reports a clean network.

Baseline, retraining and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
An adversary present while the 'normal' baseline is collected or the model is retrained, or one who tampers with training data, pretrained components or model files on the IT-side or vendor path, can teach the detector to treat their traffic as benign. A backdoor trigger in traffic fields could blind it to one attacker's pattern, and the one-way flow means the ICS never has to be touched.

Monitor flooding, feed tampering and alert suppression -- adversarial
Chaff or noisy traffic, or a spoofed or flooded mirror/tap feed, can saturate inference or the alert queue and push staff to loosen thresholds. The same degradation can mask a concurrent attack, and tampering with the alert path or thresholds blinds operators without touching the model.

Monitor data as reconnaissance source -- adversarial
The monitoring host, its captured traffic, logs and model artifacts reveal ICS topology, device addressing, polling cycles and safety-system behaviour. They are likely held under a lower security classification than the ICS itself, so they are an easier collection and exfiltration target.

Testbed-to-plant gap and attack-data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Training on scripted attacks and a narrow benign testbed baseline, with almost no real safety-system attack data, leaves outage, commissioning, maintenance and firmware-change traffic out of distribution. This yields false-positive floods or missed novel attacks, and benchmark scores cover only the attacks the authors simulated. An adversary could time actions to maintenance or outage windows, when anomalies are tolerated and detection is weakest.

Drift and retraining burden -- implicit, exploitable
Plant modifications, new engineering workstations and changed scan rates shift the benign baseline, while retraining needs labelled attack data that does not exist in the field and becomes a configuration-control and qualification problem. An adversary could hide a gradual manipulation in this drift, or exploit each retraining window to normalise malicious traffic.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A hybrid deep model gives poor explanations and varies across training runs, so alerts are hard to triage, misses are hard to trace, and no mature qualification path exists for AI cyber-monitoring of safety-related systems. The detector may be unqualified yet informally relied on, so an adversary gains from the weak forensic attribution and the unjustified trust.

Automation bias and alert complacency -- implicit, exploitable
A rarely alarming detector is read as proof of a clean network, while a noisy one is ignored or desensitised, eroding independent integrity checks, configuration audits and engineering-change controls. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, or deliberately induce alert fatigue before acting.

Protocol and channel scope gap -- implicit, exploitable
A Modbus TCP detector gives no coverage of other protocols, removable media, maintenance laptops or implanted logic, which are the realistic paths into an air-gapped system. An adversary can simply route around the monitor while its presence suggests the network is covered.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is a passive, out-of-band monitor behind a one-way diode, so a wrong output cannot directly actuate the safety-shutdown system. That is a real engineering safeguard and it limits the worst physical consequence. The harm is mostly indirect: a false-negative detector gives security staff and shift management false assurance that the safety-system network is clean, and a noisy false-positive detector can drive unnecessary investigations, procedural responses or operator distrust. The system was validated on a testbed that replicates the shutdown components, not on a live plant, and Modbus TCP is a simple, well-structured protocol. Real traffic, commissioning and outage states, and a patient adversary who mimics normal polling can all sit outside what the testbed taught the model.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Testbed-to-plant gap: the model is trained and validated on simulated or testbed traffic and attacks (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302.03). Real plants differ in polling cadence, device firmware, maintenance laptops, calibration and test traffic, and refuelling-outage modes. This causes either false alarms that wear down trust (OP.C0102, OP.C0101.05) or missed attacks. (2) Small-data and low base-rate problem: genuine attacks on safety-system ICS are almost nonexistent in field data, so detection claims rest on synthetic attack injections (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Reported accuracy may not reflect novel attack classes. (3) Drift after plant modifications, such as firmware updates, I&C upgrades, new engineering workstations and changed test schedules, shifts the benign baseline (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). Retraining then becomes a configuration-control and qualification problem (OP.C0303, OP.C0501). (4) Opacity and non-repeatability of a hybrid deep model make it hard to justify an alert to a cyber-security or regulatory review, or to trace why traffic was missed (OP.C0401, OP.C0402). (5) Automation bias: a quiet dashboard can displace defense-in-depth practices such as periodic integrity checks, key-switch and procedural controls, and independent surveillance testing (OP.C0101.04). 

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Evasion: an adversary with knowledge of the Modbus function codes, timing and register patterns of the plant, possibly from public papers or a proxy model, crafts low-and-slow or protocol-compliant malicious commands that stay inside the learned distribution (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0005, AML.T0000). (2) Poisoning during any retraining or baseline-learning window, for example malicious traffic injected while the 'normal' baseline is collected, or tampered training data and model artifacts in the supply chain (AML.T0020, AML.T0018, AML.T0010). This hides the attacker's own activity and is the most serious route to a blind monitor. (3) Diode and monitoring-host weaknesses: the diode protects the ICS from the monitor but does not stop attacks on the monitor's own IT-side host, model files or alert pipeline. Suppressing or flooding alerts, or denying the AI service, could mask a parallel attack (AML.T0029, AML.T0046, AML.T0031). Model updates carried across the boundary by removable media or vendor channels are also a path in. (4) Spoofed or flooded mirror and span feeds could blind or confuse the detector without touching the ICS. 

The consequence chain therefore needs several failures together. The detector must miss or be blinded, other cyber and physical defenses must fail, and the attacker must reach safety-system logic. That chain could result in degraded or spuriously disabled shutdown capability, or in unnecessary spurious trips and outages if alerts are over-trusted into response actions. Existing practice in the form of hardwired trip logic, diverse and independent safety channels, and one-way architecture already limits this, provided the detector is treated as advisory and not as a safety function.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this detector is only as good as the testbed traffic it was trained and validated on. A hybrid transformer+LSTM on Modbus TCP IP-layer and application-layer features is a learned model of what 'normal' and 'attack' looked like in a replica, and the replica's attacks were chosen and generated by the researchers. The three weak points are the provenance and representativeness of that data (OP.C0201.01/.02/.03, OP.C0202), the model's behaviour on real plant traffic that was never in training (OP.C0302), and the fact that it is a learned classifier on a feature space an attacker can shape. The one-way diode and out-of-network placement limit the AI's own attack surface, but they also mean the model cannot be corrected, queried or retrained in the loop. The pipeline around it (taps, feature extraction, model update path, alert handling) therefore carries most of the exposure.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Testbed-to-plant transfer gap: training and validation data come from a replica with synthetic or scripted attacks and a small, clean set of normal Modbus patterns. A real safety-shutdown ICS has different polling cadences, vendor function-code usage, maintenance and outage traffic, and firmware changes. Inference on out-of-distribution traffic can produce false-positive floods or false negatives. Operators then either tune the detector into insensitivity or ignore it, and the plant is left with an assumption of cyber monitoring it does not really have (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.05). (2) Drift and concept drift: ICS traffic is highly regular, so the model may overfit to that regularity, and any legitimate change (a new engineering workstation, a changed scan rate, a plant modification, a new attack tradecraft not in the training set) shifts the distribution. Retraining requires fresh labelled attack data that does not exist in the field, so the lifecycle is under-specified (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0204, OP.C0503). (3) Qualification and opacity: a transformer+LSTM hybrid is hard to explain, its non-determinism across training runs and its threshold choices are hard to qualify for a safety-adjacent monitoring role, and the benchmark metrics (accuracy/F1 on a testbed) say little about detection of low-and-slow or protocol-compliant malicious commands (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0403, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). (4) Automation bias and false assurance: a 'detector is in place' claim can reduce other defence-in-depth effort, and a quiet detector is read as a clean system (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Evasion: an adversary who knows or can infer the feature set (the Modbus IP and application fields are standard, and the paper is public, so ATLAS T0000/T0013/T0014 recon is cheap) can craft traffic that is semantically malicious but statistically in-distribution, such as valid function codes at normal rates, mimicry of the polling cadence, or slow changes to setpoints. The aim is to stay below the anomaly score (AML.T0015, T0043.000-.003, T0005 proxy model from the public paper and public Modbus datasets). (b) Training and validation data poisoning: if baseline 'normal' traffic is collected from a live or possibly already-compromised network, or if retraining is on captured data, an attacker present during collection can normalise malicious behaviour (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0059). Backdoor triggers in traffic fields are also conceivable (T0043.004). (c) AI supply-chain: pretrained transformer components, ML frameworks, containers and model files imported into the monitoring host carry the usual risk (AML.T0010.001/.003/.004, T0011.000). Because the host sits outside the ICS but ingests diode traffic, it is a plausible pivot or an intelligence-collection target, since a model plus its logs reveals the plant's network topology and protocol behaviour (AML.T0025, T0035, T0037). (d) Chaff and denial: flooding the monitored segment with benign-looking noise can saturate the inference pipeline or alert queue and mask a concurrent real attack, or drive alert fatigue (AML.T0046, T0029, T0031). (e) Alert-channel manipulation: the diode removes the feedback path to the ICS, but alerts reach humans via other networks, so tampering with the alert output or thresholds is a way to blind operators without touching the model (AML.T0081-style config modification, T0076). A diode also does not stop an attacker who controls the sensor tap or mirrored-port feed, so the data integrity of the input to the model is itself an unverified trust point.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this detector matters less as a target in itself than as a trust anchor and a source of blind spots. Its output is the evidence on which operators and cyber staff will base the claim that the safety-shutdown ICS network is clean. An adversary, including a patient nation-state actor with a supply-chain or insider foothold, would not need to defeat the air gap or the diode to benefit. They would only need to shape traffic so it falls inside the learned envelope, or to degrade the detector's credibility so alerts get discounted. The diode is a real strength, but it only protects the ICS from the monitor. It does nothing for the monitor's integrity, its training pipeline, or the humans who read its output.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by mimicry (AML.T0015, T0043): Modbus TCP is simple and deterministic, so an attacker who knows or can approximate the learned traffic profile can craft malicious function codes, register writes and timing that stay inside the learned distribution. Slow, low-and-slow manipulation, or attacks that reuse legitimate engineering-workstation behavior, are the classic gap for learned detectors. Reconnaissance on model class and features is easy because the architecture and features are published (AML.T0000, T0013, T0014, T0005), so a proxy model can be built offline. The consequence is a false assurance of integrity on the safety-shutdown system while a malicious command set is staged. (2) Training and update pipeline compromise (AML.T0010.002/.003, T0018, T0020, T0059): the detector sits outside the ICS, so its baselines, retraining data, model files and tooling are handled on a less-protected IT-side or vendor path. That makes it the easier stepping stone, and the one-way data flow means the model can be poisoned without ever touching the ICS. A poisoned baseline or a backdoor trigger (T0043.004) could blind the detector to a specific attacker's traffic pattern. Insiders with access to labeling, thresholds or retraining are the highest-leverage actors here. (3) Denial or degradation of monitoring (AML.T0029, T0046): chaff or benign-but-noisy traffic that raises false positives pushes operators to loosen thresholds or disable alerts, which an attacker can time around. Because the diode blocks feedback, only the detector side can be saturated, which makes this cheap. (4) Information value of the detector (T0025, T0036, T0024): captured traffic, alert logs and model weights reveal the plant's ICS topology, device addressing, polling cycles and safety-system behavior. They are valuable reconnaissance and are likely to be held under lower security classification than the ICS itself (OP.C0505.01). IMPLICIT, AND EXPLOITABLE. (5) Testbed-to-plant gap (OP.C0201.01, C0302.03, C0303): validation on a replica testbed gives clean, labeled, synthetic attacks and a narrow benign baseline. Real plant traffic varies across outages, maintenance, calibration and firmware changes, so drift or false-positive floods are likely and attackers can time actions to maintenance windows when anomalies are tolerated. Scarcity of real attack data (OP.C0202) means detection claims cover only the attacks the authors simulated, with unknown coverage of novel ones. (6) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, C0102, C0101.05): low alert rates breed complacency, while high rates breed disuse. Either way, a 'the AI watches the network' belief can erode independent procedural checks, configuration audits and engineering-change controls, and that erosion is a vigilance gap an adversary can use. (7) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, C0402, C0501): a hybrid transformer-LSTM gives poor explanations for alerts, which makes triage and forensic attribution hard, and there is no mature qualification path for AI in cyber monitoring of safety-related systems, so the detector may be treated as unqualified yet still relied on informally. (8) Scope drift (OP.C0503): a detector built for Modbus TCP gives no coverage of other protocols, out-of-band channels such as removable media and maintenance laptops, or supply-chain-implanted logic, which are the pathways a sophisticated adversary would actually use against an air-gapped system. Overall, a competent adversary would more likely attack the monitor's data and humans, or bypass it altogether, than defeat it head-on.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on mimicry evasion, baseline/supply-chain poisoning, chaff/denial, the testbed-to-plant gap, opacity and automation bias; I merged the AI engineer's alert-channel and feed-tampering points into the flooding threat. I kept the monitor-as-reconnaissance-source and protocol-scope threats as distinct, and left out T0036, T0024 and T0081 as weakly grounded, since no data repository, inference API or agent configuration is documented in this use case.

evidence.citation: "Anomaly Detection in Air-Gapped Industrial Control Systems of Nuclear Power Plants," IEEE (2024 Cyber Awareness and Research Symposium, CARS; DOI 10.1109/CARS61786.2024.10778886), page hosted on ResearchGate
evidence.note: The paper combines two neural networks, a transformer and an LSTM, to detect cyber-threat anomalies in the ICS of a nuclear power plant's safety-shutdown system. It builds a testbed that replicates the shutdown components and uses it to validate the model. I read only the abstract and excerpts shown on the ResearchGate page, not the full text.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is mimicry evasion or baseline poisoning that hides a malicious command set staged against safety-shutdown logic behind false assurance, which could contribute to loss of a safety function and a potential release. The monitor itself is isolated by the diode and does not actuate, so the harm is indirect and the score stays below 5.

reproducibility.why: Evasion by a proxy-model approach, alert flooding and automation bias are fairly reliable once an adversary has the needed position. Poisoning requires being present during baseline collection or retraining, and the testbed-to-plant gap and drift weaknesses are present continuously, so reliability is moderate overall.

exploitability.why: Reaching a safety-shutdown ICS segment, its mirrored traffic feed, or the vendor and IT-side model supply path generally requires substantial resourcing, such as a capable or state-level actor. A few weaknesses, such as over-trust and routing around Modbus-only scope, need little additional specialist tooling once such access exists.

affected_users.why: A blinded or falsely reassuring monitor undermines assurance across the whole safety-shutdown ICS network and the operators and engineering controls that rely on it. It does not by itself propagate into other coupled plant systems, so the impact falls short of facility-wide.

discoverability.why: The architecture, feature set and general weaknesses of ML anomaly detectors (evasion, poisoning, drift, testbed gap, narrow protocol scope) are published and well documented in the open literature. Learning that a particular plant deploys such a detector would still take some outside inference.

use_case: Generative design of a PWR (SMR-type) 17×17 fuel-assembly layout with a small language model (Gemma 3 270M). The model is fine-tuned in stages on Monte Carlo data, with parameter-efficient adaptation and Direct Preference Optimization. Each lattice is serialised as a 289-token sequence of fuel, control and burnable-absorber (Gd) pin types. The model proposes candidate layouts in a single forward pass, and OpenMC transport simulations check them against power-peaking and other neutronic limits.
incurred_insecurity:
A small generative model proposes PWR assembly layouts that are screened only by OpenMC power-peaking and related neutronic checks, so the insecurity lies mainly in the trust placed in that narrow verifier and in the provenance of the generator's training data. The main threats are poisoning or tampering with the training corpus, preference pairs and model artifacts; compromise of the verification loop; theft of proprietary design knowledge; and implicit proxy-objective misalignment, simulation-only data, qualification gaps and reviewer over-trust. Physical harm would still need the downstream licensing analyses and independent review to fail, but a subtle defect would sit in the design basis with long latency.

Poisoned data, preference pairs or adapters -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor who alters Monte Carlo labels, DPO preference pairs, LoRA adapters or base weights can shift the generator toward layouts that pass the nominal OpenMC check but degrade margins it does not test, such as burnup-dependent peaking, Gd depletion or shutdown margin. A trigger-conditioned backdoor in the lattice sequence is also possible. The shift is distributional, so no single output looks wrong, and a weakened design basis enters shortlisting.

Verification-loop compromise -- adversarial
Tampering with OpenMC inputs, cross-section libraries, geometry templates, tally post-processing or acceptance thresholds turns the one independent check into a rubber stamp for marginal layouts. The AI output then appears credible because it is labelled verified, so compromising the verifier is worth more than compromising the generator.

Design-IP extraction and model-artifact exposure -- adversarial
Fine-tuned weights, the layout corpus and inference queries encode proprietary assembly designs (enrichment, Gd placement, margins), which could be extracted or stolen from design workstations or shared checkpoints. Export-controlled design data used in fine-tuning adds a data-governance exposure.

Manipulated conditioning inputs -- adversarial
If the model is conditioned on constraints or prompts, altered constraint specifications could steer it toward off-nominal layouts that still satisfy the screening check.

Proxy-objective misalignment -- implicit, exploitable
The DPO reward and acceptance test cover only power peaking and k-eff, so the model optimises toward the edge of that proxy and neglects manufacturability, transients, thermal-hydraulics, xenon and Gd burnout, leaving little margin for simulator or cross-section error. An adversary could target the unchecked criteria, knowing the generator and verifier will not flag a weakness there.

Simulation-only data and out-of-distribution generalisation -- implicit
Training data is OpenMC output tied to one nuclear data library, lattice and enrichment menu, so changed enrichments, boundary conditions or pin types fall outside the training envelope. The single-pass generator gives no uncertainty signal and emits plausible layouts regardless. No realistic adversary gains much beyond what the misalignment threat above already offers.

Automation bias and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Novel asymmetric layouts framed as showing emergent physical reasoning and marked as simulation-passing invite over-trust and a narrower reviewer scrutiny, with design intuition eroding over time. An adversary can rely on this reduced vigilance to hide a subtle defect in an unusual layout.

Non-determinism, opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
Sampling variability, training non-determinism and the lack of any rationale make layout lineage hard to reproduce, and no QA basis exists for a generative model in design work from an unreviewed preprint. This lets a tampered output be indistinguishable from ordinary variation in later audit or licensing review.

Fleet propagation of a flawed checkpoint -- implicit, exploitable
A shared checkpoint reused across projects or SMR designs spreads any systematic bias or planted weakness. An adversary who compromises one checkpoint gains reach across several designs.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a design-stage tool: a 270M-parameter model proposes 289-token pin layouts, and OpenMC checks each one. Existing practice already guards against a bad layout reaching the core. Candidates must pass a neutronics check, then licensed reload and safety analysis (coupled thermal-hydraulics, CHF/DNBR, transient and accident analysis, LOCA, shutdown margin, reactivity coefficients) with independent review before fabrication. The residual risk is therefore less a direct physical hazard than a process-integrity one. The AI shifts which designs get examined, and a verifier built on a single code, a small set of conditions and a small set of metrics defines the whole feasibility envelope. The tool could produce plausible but weakly vetted asymmetric layouts that pass the screening neutronics yet carry unmodelled penalties, and designers could over-trust them or under-scrutinise them because they are novel. An adversary, or plain drift, could erode the chain by corrupting the verifier or its data. Harm would need the downstream licensing analyses and independent review to fail as well.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Verifier-scope and objective misalignment: the DPO preference signal and the acceptance test are the OpenMC power-peaking and k-eff limits. The model learns to satisfy the proxy, not the full set of design criteria. Fabrication tolerances, burnup-dependent peaking, Gd depletion and residual reactivity penalty, xenon transients, temperature feedback, local void and thermal-hydraulic limits, fuel-cycle economics and manufacturability can all be left out. A layout that is optimal against the proxy sits at the edge of the margin, so any error in the proxy or in cross-section data leaves little cushion. The preprint is not peer reviewed, and the claim of 'emergent physical reasoning' invites over-trust (OP.C0301, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0304.03). (2) Data provenance and OOD: training data is Monte Carlo simulation output, with no field or measured data. Statistical noise, nuclear-data library version, and a single geometry or enrichment family are baked in. Generalisation to other SMR designs, enrichments, burnable poison types or boundary conditions is unvalidated, and 'hallucinated' layouts can look plausible (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0203, OP.C0304.01). (3) Qualification and repeatability: stochastic sampling means the same query yields different layouts, and the model gives no explanation of why a layout works. The tool has no QA basis for use in safety-related design, which raises a regulatory readiness gap, and reproducing the design basis (provenance of the layout) is harder (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (4) Automation bias in the loop: engineers can anchor on the AI's asymmetric layouts and then run a narrower review, so skill fade and loss of design intuition follow over time (OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01). Simulation-passing becomes a stand-in for qualification. 

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Poisoned training or preference data, or a tampered fine-tuned or adapter checkpoint (a supply-chain compromise of a public base model, LoRA weights or datasets), could bias the generator toward layouts with a subtle weakness: a hot-spot that appears only under a condition the verifier does not test, degraded shutdown margin, or a proprietary-layout leak. The bias can be introduced stealthily because it only needs to shift the distribution, not break any single output (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0019, AML.T0058). (6) The more serious attack surface is the verification pipeline rather than the model: modified OpenMC inputs, cross-section libraries or tally post-processing could let marginal layouts pass. The model could also be steered by crafted prompts or conditioning inputs toward a design the attacker wants (AML.T0043, AML.T0051). (7) Information risk: proprietary assembly designs and optimisation results could be extracted from the model through inference queries or from model weights, and fine-tuning on export-controlled design data creates a data-governance problem (AML.T0024.000, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0057, OP.C0505). The model is small and likely runs on-premises, which limits cloud exposure, but shared checkpoints can propagate a flaw across projects (OP.C0602). 

The consequence is an erosion of design margin, schedule and cost, or an undetected latent flaw. It becomes a safety issue only if the independent analysis, review and licensing steps also miss the problem, so independent re-verification with different codes and data is the key compensating control.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, ReactorFold is a 270M-parameter autoregressive model fine-tuned in stages (SFT on Monte Carlo data, LoRA-style adaptation, then DPO) to emit 289 discrete tokens. It has no physics in its weights, only statistical regularities of whatever OpenMC-labelled layouts it saw. The safeguard is the OpenMC verification loop, so the main exposure is whether that loop is truly independent and complete, and whether the training and preference data are representative. The 'emergent physical reasoning' framing invites over-trust in an unreviewed preprint-grade method. The generator also sits upstream of design choices that propagate into core loading, licensing and fuel procurement.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data provenance and fidelity: all training and preference labels come from OpenMC on a single assembly-level configuration. That means lattice-level, simplified boundary conditions, a specific nuclear data library and limited burnup/thermal-hydraulic coupling. The model inherits simulator biases and can learn to exploit them, so the DPO reward is a proxy and the optimiser pushes into regions where the simulator is least validated. Candidates that pass OpenMC may then fail under coupled depletion, xenon, TH feedback, transient or accident conditions (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0301, OP.C0303). (2) Narrow verification: the check covers power peaking and a few neutronic limits. It does not cover manufacturability, fuel-performance, shutdown margin, reactivity coefficients, Gd burnout, or mechanical and thermal limits. 'Verified' is read as 'acceptable', which is a goal-misalignment and automation-trust risk (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0301). (3) OOD and generalisation: the model is trained on one lattice size and one enrichment/Gd menu. Changes to enrichment, SMR core boundary conditions, symmetry assumptions or new pin types are out of distribution, and a single-pass generator has no uncertainty signal, so it will emit plausible token strings regardless (OP.C0302, OP.C0403). Drift arises when the nuclear data library, OpenMC version or design basis changes and the model is not retrained. (4) Repeatability and qualification: sampling non-determinism, training non-determinism under LoRA/DPO, and no standard for qualifying a generative model in design give a weak QA basis. Reproducing an exact design lineage for licensing is difficult (OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). The preprint is not peer reviewed. (5) Opacity and low base rate: the model cannot explain why a layout works, so designers cannot tell a physics-driven asymmetric layout from a simulator artefact (OP.C0401, OP.C0202).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Supply chain: the base model weights, LoRA adapters, tokenizer, dataset and OpenMC/nuclear data libraries are all external artefacts. Poisoned or backdoored weights or adapters, or tampered cross-section data, could bias outputs toward layouts that look fine in the checker but carry a hidden weakness, or that pass only because the checker is compromised (AML.T0010.001/.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0059). (7) Preference-data and reward manipulation: DPO pairs are an attractive poisoning point. Subtly mislabelled preferences can shift the model's notion of 'good' without being visible in headline metrics (AML.T0020, AML.T0031). (8) Verifier-side attacks: compromise of the OpenMC pipeline, tolerances or limit definitions turns the independent check into a rubber stamp (AML.T0076, OP.C0502). (9) Design-IP exposure: fine-tuned weights and the layout corpus encode proprietary core-design knowledge, so model extraction or training-data inversion could leak it (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0048.004). (10) Fleet propagation: one compromised or flawed model reused across SMR designs or vendors spreads a systematic bias (OP.C0602, OP.C0603).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modelling view, this is an upstream design-phase tool. An adversary would not attack it directly; they would use it to shape what reaches the licensing and fabrication pipeline. Its appeal is that a small model (270M parameters) can run on a laptop, is fine-tuned in stages from public base weights, and uses a Monte Carlo corpus and preference data with no obvious chain of custody. That makes insider tampering with training data, adapter weights or preference labels cheap and hard to attribute. The OpenMC check is the key control. It is only as strong as its inputs, cross-section libraries, tally definitions, and the limits it tests against. A generator that learns to satisfy a verifier concentrates trust in that verifier, and a subtle compromise of the verifier is worth far more than compromise of the generator. The tool also produces unusual asymmetric layouts that humans may not read closely, which erodes reviewer vigilance and gives cover for a subtle defect.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Poisoning of the Monte Carlo corpus, the DPO preference pairs, or the PEFT adapters. Mechanism: an insider or supply-chain actor biases the generator toward layouts that pass the nominal check while degrading margins the check does not cover, such as burnup-dependent peaking, transient or accident reactivity coefficients, Gd depletion behaviour, or a trigger-conditioned backdoor in the lattice sequence. The facility depends on the generator to shortlist designs; the consequence is a weakened safety margin or a hidden defect embedded in the core design basis, with long latency. (2) Compromise of the verification loop, not the AI itself. Tampering with OpenMC inputs, nuclear data libraries, geometry templates or acceptance thresholds lets bad layouts pass, and the AI's output looks credible because it was 'verified'. (3) Model-artifact and supply-chain exposure: public base weights, third-party fine-tuning scripts and hosted notebooks give a path into design workstations that hold proprietary core-design data. Stolen or extracted designs and fine-tuning data (fuel loading, enrichment, Gd placement) are valuable IP and reveal design margins. (4) Evasion and adversarial inputs: if the model is conditioned on constraints or prompts, manipulated constraint specifications could steer it toward off-nominal designs.

IMPLICIT, and exploitable by timing: (a) Automation bias and skill fade among reactor physicists reviewing novel asymmetric layouts that nominally satisfy constraints, which reduces independent scrutiny. (b) Goal misalignment, in that the model optimises the proxy of passing power-peaking limits and may exploit gaps in the verifier (Goodhart effect) rather than satisfy the underlying safety intent. (c) Data scarcity and a synthetic-data provenance gap: training data is simulated, with little operational or benchmark validation, and the work is an unreviewed preprint, so no AI-specific QA or qualification basis exists. (d) Non-determinism and opacity: sampling variability and the absence of a rationale make candidate provenance hard to reproduce or audit, so a later investigation cannot tell a tampered output from an ordinary one. (e) Limited reach: single-pass generation over 289 tokens covers only one neutronic slice, so thermal-hydraulics, fuel-performance and fabrication constraints are unchecked, and a sophisticated adversary would target those gaps.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on poisoning and supply chain, verifier compromise, proxy-objective misalignment, simulation-only data, automation trust and qualification gaps; I merged overlapping items and dropped weakly argued codes (e.g., AML.T0012, AML.T0031, AML.T0059, AML.T0043 root, AML.T0019/T0058, AML.T0057, AML.T0024.000), keeping AML.T0051 for conditioning-input steering only as a modest fit.

evidence.citation: "ReactorFold: Generative discovery of nuclear reactor cores via emergent physical reasoning," arXiv (Y. Lee)
evidence.note: The preprint builds and tests a language-model generator that treats fuel-assembly layout design as sequence modelling. Its candidate layouts are verified with OpenMC, and the model adjusts the gadolinium rod count and finds asymmetric configurations that meet power-peaking constraints. This is an arXiv preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

damage.why: The worst credible threat is a poisoned generator or compromised verification loop that lets a marginal fuel-assembly layout enter the design basis with long latency; physical harm would still need licensing analyses and independent review to fail, so this stays below a direct radiological release or safeguards falsification (5).

reproducibility.why: Distributional poisoning or verifier tampering would reliably shift outputs once access exists, and the implicit proxy-misalignment and over-trust weaknesses recur by construction, but the effect on a real design still depends on downstream reviews missing the defect.

exploitability.why: The most severe threats (poisoning training data, preference pairs or adapters, or tampering with the OpenMC verification loop) need insider or supply-chain access to design workstations and pipelines, though shared checkpoints and conditioning inputs offer somewhat easier routes.

affected_users.why: A flawed or compromised checkpoint could propagate across several SMR projects and designs, but the impact is concentrated in the design basis of fuel assemblies and is not facility-wide operational coupling.

discoverability.why: Poisoning, verifier over-trust, proxy-objective gaps and fine-tuned model theft are well documented in the open literature for this class of AI system, and the source is a public preprint describing the OpenMC screening and the narrow acceptance criteria, though specific internals are not public.

use_case: Large-language-model agent with retrieval-augmented access to plant documentation, function calling and a predictive module. It helps operators respond to a boron concentration anomaly in a nuclear reactor simulator. It can also draft a new operating procedure that parallels a provided manual, without extra model training.
incurred_insecurity:
This LLM agent combines retrieval over plant documentation, function calling, a predictive boron module and procedure drafting, demonstrated only on a simulator. It puts one trusted advisory component between operators and a reactivity-relevant event. The main threats are corruption of the knowledge and tool layer, over-broad tool authority, supply-chain and leakage exposure, denial during an anomaly, and implicit weaknesses (hallucination, simulator-to-plant gap, non-repeatability, over-trust, governance gaps) that degrade operator judgment and mask tampering.

Retrieval corpus poisoning and indirect injection -- adversarial
The agent treats whatever the RAG index or ingested logs and notes return as trusted fact or instruction. Forged, superseded or altered documents, or embedded instructions, can steer boration and dilution advice, which reaches a stressed operator with cited, authoritative-looking presentation.

Function-calling over-reach -- adversarial
A prompt-injected, hallucinated or poisoned tool call can turn advice into unauthorized action, data exfiltration or tampering with predictor inputs, and tool credentials and definitions are themselves targets. If tool permissions extend beyond read-only access, this bridges the documentation domain toward the control domain and defeats the separation between information systems and operational functions.

Predictive-module input manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofed or adversarially crafted boron, flow or rod-position inputs can push the surrogate to a wrong diagnosis or forecast, which the LLM then narrates fluently. The error propagates into the narrative output and gets compounded.

Model and supply-chain compromise -- adversarial
The opaque foundation model, embedding model, orchestration framework, plugins and any hosted API can be tampered with or silently updated, changing advice with no change control. Hosted dependencies also expose sensitive design documentation through prompts and responses.

Denial of decision support -- adversarial
Resource-intensive queries or chaff can degrade or remove the agent during an anomaly. Operators who have come to rely on it face slower diagnosis when it is most needed.

Documentation and configuration leakage -- adversarial
The aggregated plant documentation, system prompt and tool definitions are concentrated reconnaissance material that retrieval or model outputs can leak. This lowers an insider's or outsider's cost of learning plant structure, procedures and response logic.

Simulator-to-plant gap -- implicit, exploitable
The predictive module and agent were shown only on idealized simulator dynamics, so sensor faults, calibration drift, cycle-dependent boron behavior and rare anomalies are out of distribution with no qualification basis. An adversary could hide manipulated inputs inside the resulting unvalidated, noisy error band.

Content fidelity failure and procedure drafting -- implicit, exploitable
The LLM can invent steps, drop cautions or Technical Specification limits, misread units or merge superseded revisions, and a new procedure drafted by analogy carries the form and authority of a validated manual without its engineering basis. An adversary can rely on cursory review of the well-formed draft to get a subtly altered step or omitted precondition into the controlled procedure stream.

Non-repeatability and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
The same anomaly can yield different advice across runs or model versions, and explanations are post-hoc, so there is no reproducible evidence for qualification or incident review. An adversary gains cover because tampering is indistinguishable from normal variability and forensics cannot separate error from attack.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Fluent, cited and usually correct answers breed automation bias, out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity, diagnostic skill fade and confusion between advisory text and executed tool actions. An adversary can time a poisoned recommendation for a high-workload atypical anomaly when independent cross-checks are weakest.

Qualification, governance and index drift -- implicit, exploitable
There is no accepted QA or safety-classification path for a probabilistic operator aid, and the retrieval index and hosted model drift out of sync with controlled-document revisions and plant modifications. An adversary can wait for a stale index or upstream model update, or exploit informal use outside Appendix B-type controls, to turn ordinary AI error into consequential error.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation
Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, a boron concentration anomaly is a reactivity-management event, so it belongs to a safety-significant evolution governed by technical specifications, approved abnormal/emergency operating procedures, and licensed operator authority. An LLM agent that retrieves procedure text, calls functions, and drafts new procedures sits in the advisory path for that evolution, and the main danger is wrong or manipulated content that a stressed operator trusts.
