Existing engineering practice (independent reactivity monitoring, shift technical advisor review, procedure verification and validation, interlocks, and trip/ESFAS protection that does not depend on the agent) would stop most single failures from reaching the core. The residual risks are the ones that erode those defenses: degraded operator judgment, an unverified procedure entering the controlled-document stream, and an agent whose function-calling reach extends beyond read-only advice. The evidence so far comes from a simulator only, so the field behavior of this system is untested.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Poisoning of the retrieval corpus or of function-call outputs (AML.T0070, T0071, T0066, T0051.001, T0099, T0110). Altered or injected content in plant documentation, a spoofed manual revision, or a tampered predictive-module output could cause the agent to recommend wrong boration or dilution actions, wrong setpoints or sequencing, or to cite superseded procedure revisions. Consequence: a plausible, authoritative-looking but wrong reactivity recommendation reaches the operator. Harm needs the operator to act on it and independent checks (boron sampling, nuclear instrumentation, rod position, shift supervisor cross-check) to miss it. (2) Function-calling as a new attack surface (AML.T0053, T0101, T0112.000, T0083). If tool permissions reach beyond read/query, for example to the plant computer, simulator-to-plant interfaces, or chemical and volume control setpoints, a prompt injection or compromised tool could turn advice into action. Consequence: a path from the IT or documentation domain toward the control domain, which breaks the one-way data-diode and defense-in-depth model. (3) Procedure drafting as a laundering path (AML.T0067, T0051, T0054). A subtly altered draft that parallels the manual can pass cursory review, and the fluent format lends it false legitimacy. Consequence: an unsafe step or omitted precondition enters the procedure library if V&V is shortened because the document looks well formed. (4) Denial or delay of the agent (AML.T0029, T0046, T0034). Time-critical dependence during an anomaly could degrade response if operators have come to rely on it. Consequence: slower diagnosis and skill-fade effects. (5) Leakage of plant documentation, which is sensitive design and security information, through retrieval or a cloud-hosted model (AML.T0057, T0085.000, T0024; OP.C0601).

IMPLICIT. (1) Hallucination, omission, or misattribution in the procedure and retrieval answers (OP.C0304.01, C0304.03, C0304.02). The agent could invent a step, drop a caution or limit, or misapply a procedure from a different plant or unit. Consequence: wrong boration or dilution quantities, or missed technical-specification action statements. (2) Automation over-trust and out-of-the-loop effects (OP.C0101.04, C0101.01, C0101.06, C0102). The agent will be right in the many routine cases, which breeds complacency, and operators may defer to it exactly when the anomaly is atypical. Consequence: erosion of the operator's reactivity-control judgment and a weaker independent check. (3) Simulator-to-plant gap (OP.C0201.01, C0302, C0302.03, C0303, C0203). The predictive module and the agent were demonstrated on a simulator's idealized dynamics, with clean data and no sensor faults, plant-specific cycle effects, or noisy conditions. Consequence: unvalidated accuracy in a real boron or reactivity anomaly, and no basis for claiming the agent has been qualified. (4) Non-determinism and opacity (OP.C0402.02, C0401). The same anomaly can yield different recommendations, which cannot be verified or reproduced for a licensing or incident-review audit. (5) Qualification and governance gaps (OP.C0501, C0504, C0502). There is no accepted software QA basis for a probabilistic agent in an operator-aid role, and its safety classification is unclear. Consequence: ambiguity over whether it falls under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B-type controls, which invites informal use. (6) Document-control drift (OP.C0204, C0603). If the retrieval index is not synchronized with revisions of controlled documents, the agent cites stale procedures, and an error in the predictive module propagates into the narrative output and compounds. Adversaries could time an attack to these weaknesses.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a composite architecture: a general-purpose foundation LLM, a RAG index over plant documentation, a function-calling layer, and a separate predictive module for boron concentration. Each component adds its own failure mode, and none of them is qualified for I&C-adjacent use. The system was validated only on a simulator with no extra training, so its apparent competence comes from in-context learning over retrieved text. That competence is brittle, non-deterministic, and untested against real plant data distributions. The main ML-pipeline exposure is in the retrieval corpus, the tool-call boundary, the predictive module's training provenance, and the lack of any way to bound inference-time behavior. It is not in the facility around the model.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Retrieval corpus integrity: the agent's truth is whatever the RAG index returns. If an adversary or a careless insider alters, adds or supersedes documents (a stale revision, a falsified setpoint table, a forged procedure), the agent will confidently ground its boron-response advice in them (AML.T0070, T0071, T0066, T0010.002). The operator sees a cited answer, and citation presentation itself lends credibility (T0067.000). (2) Indirect prompt injection: documentation, logs, or free-text alarm and shift-note fields that the agent ingests can carry instructions that steer the reasoning or tool calls (T0051.001, T0093, T0080). (3) Function-calling surface: the LLM translates natural language into tool invocations. If tools can reach the simulator or plant data interfaces or the predictive module, an injected or hallucinated call becomes an unauthorized action, an exfiltration path, or manipulated input to the predictor (T0053, T0086, T0101, T0010.005). Credentials and configuration stored in the agent are an additional target (T0083, T0084). (4) Predictive module manipulation: adversarial or spoofed sensor inputs (boron, flow, rod position) can push the surrogate to a wrong diagnosis or forecast, and the LLM will narrate it fluently (T0043, T0015, T0020, T0018.000). (5) Supply chain: the foundation model, embedding model, vector store, orchestration framework and any hosted API are opaque, frequently updated dependencies (T0010.001, T0010.003, T0109). A silent upstream model change alters behavior with no change control. (6) Denial or degradation of the agent during an anomaly, through resource-intensive queries or chaff, removes decision support when it is most needed (T0029, T0046, T0034.001). (7) Information leakage: the aggregated plant documentation, system prompts and tool definitions are concentrated, high-value reconnaissance material (T0057, T0056, T0085.000).

IMPLICIT. (a) Simulator-to-plant gap: the predictive module likely trained on simulated or surrogate data, and the agent was demonstrated only in simulation. Real plant noise, sensor faults, instrument calibration drift, fuel-cycle-dependent boron behavior and plant-specific configuration are out-of-distribution (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). Rare anomalies give a low base rate and little validation evidence (OP.C0202). (b) Content fidelity: the LLM can hallucinate procedure steps, misread units or setpoints, omit conditional branches or Technical Specification limits, and merge superseded revisions (OP.C0304.01/.03, OP.C0304.02). Such errors are plausible-looking and hard to catch. (c) New-procedure drafting by analogy to a manual is the riskiest mode: the output imitates the form of a validated procedure without its engineering basis, hazard analysis or verification. It can embed subtle unsafe sequencing and then carry the authority of the template (OP.C0301, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0501). (d) Non-determinism: the same query can yield different guidance across runs, model versions or temperature settings, so there is no repeatable evidence for qualification, and explanations are post-hoc and unfaithful (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02). (e) Human factors: fluent, cited answers invite over-trust and automation bias during a stressful anomaly, skill fade in diagnostic reasoning, and mode confusion between advisory text and executed tool actions (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.03, OP.C0102). (f) Lifecycle and governance: document revisions, plant modifications and RAG re-indexing are untracked drift sources. There is no accepted AI qualification path for operator-support software, and hosted LLMs add cloud dependency and data-governance mismatch (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504, OP.C0601, OP.C0505.01). (g) Adversary timing: an attacker can wait for known weak points, such as a stale index after a plant modification, an upstream model update, or an anomaly in which the agent is most relied on, and use them to turn an ordinary AI error into a consequential one.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this agent changes the facility's threat surface because it gives a single trusted component three things at once: read access to the plant's documentation corpus, function-calling authority that reaches plant or simulator data and a predictive module, and the ability to author procedure text that humans may treat as authoritative. Boron concentration anomalies are reactivity-relevant, so an operator who is stressed and time-pressured and who comes to rely on the agent is a good moment for an adversary to time an attack around. Even a simulator-only demonstration shows the pattern: if this moves toward training or decision support, the documentation store, tool definitions and procedure-drafting path become high-value, low-visibility targets. A sophisticated adversary would probably prefer to corrupt the knowledge and tool layer, or the human's trust in it, rather than attack the reactor controls directly, because that route is cheaper and harder to attribute.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Retrieval and document poisoning: an insider or supply-chain actor who can edit or add to the indexed plant documentation, or inject content into retrieved text, can steer the agent's diagnosis or recommended boron-related actions toward plausible but wrong guidance (AML.T0070, T0071, T0066, T0051.001, T0099). The AI failure is that retrieved text is treated as trusted instruction or fact. The facility depends on it for anomaly response guidance, and the consequence is misdirected operator action on reactivity management or degraded response during a real event. Because the documents look legitimate, the manipulation resists detection. (2) Tool/function-calling abuse: the agent's tool definitions, credentials and call chains form a new privileged pathway between a language interface and plant data or simulation or control-adjacent functions (AML.T0053, T0110, T0084.001, T0083, T0098, T0010.005). The failure mechanism is over-broad agent authority combined with prompt-injection susceptibility. The consequence could range from data exfiltration or tampering with predictive-module inputs to unauthorized actions, and it bypasses the traditional separation between information systems and operational functions. (3) Procedure-drafting as a stepping stone: the ability to generate a new procedure that parallels a manual, with no extra training, makes the drafted text a vector for subtle, adversary-induced or hallucinated deviations (for example altered setpoints, steps or sequencing) that a reviewer reading a familiar-looking document may miss (AML.T0031, T0067, T0018, T0043.004). The consequence is a flawed procedure entering the approved baseline, or one that persists long after the intrusion. (4) Model and supply-chain compromise: a hosted or third-party foundation model, plugins or an external API create a dependency and exposure route, including leakage of sensitive design or operational documentation via prompts and responses (AML.T0010.003, T0057, T0085.000, T0024, T0036, OP.C0601). (5) Social-engineering and insider leverage: the agent can be used to learn which documents exist, how procedures are structured and how the plant responds, thereby lowering the reconnaissance cost for an insider (AML.T0064, T0069, T0084). IMPLICIT, adversary-exploitable. Hallucination, oversimplification and mis-citation by the LLM (OP.C0304.01, .03) and its inference-time non-repeatability (OP.C0402.02) mean the same anomaly can yield different advice, which hides the signal of tampering from the noise of normal variability. Automation trust and out-of-the-loop effects (OP.C0101.04, .01, .06, OP.C0102) can degrade operator diagnosis skills and vigilance, so a poisoned or incorrect recommendation is accepted unchallenged, and an adversary can time an attack for a moment of high workload. Evidence from a simulator is not qualification for plant use, and the model was not trained on plant-specific anomalies (OP.C0303, OP.C0302, OP.C0501, OP.C0401), so the only barrier against subtle errors is human review that is itself being eroded. Limited explainability makes post-event forensics ambiguous between error and attack. Finally, cross-use of the same agent for diagnosis and procedure authoring concentrates trust: one compromise propagates across several functions (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on retrieval poisoning, tool-calling over-reach, the simulator-to-plant gap, hallucination, over-trust and non-repeatability; I merged these and dropped weakly argued codes (e.g. T0031, T0018, T0043.004 for drafting, T0064, T0024) that restated other threats or did not clearly apply. Procedure drafting was treated as an implicit fidelity and governance weakness that an adversary exploits through misplaced trust, rather than as a separate ATLAS technique.

evidence.citation: "Large language model agent for nuclear reactor operation assistance," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Elsevier), Vol. 57, Issue 12, 103842, December 2025
evidence.note: The authors built an LLM agent architecture that combines plant documentation, callable functions and other modules, and tested it on a nuclear reactor simulator. They ran two experiments: handling a boron concentration anomaly with a predictive module plus documentation, and generating a new procedure from a provided manual. The tests were on a simulator, not a deployed plant.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoned or hallucinated boration/dilution advice, or over-broad tool authority, reaching operators during a reactivity-relevant anomaly. That erodes safety margins and could contribute to a reactivity event, but the agent is advisory and operators and independent safeguards sit between it and any release, so it falls short of the 5 reserved for direct release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Retrieval poisoning, indirect injection, and LLM content-fidelity failures are well-documented and reliably produce wrong outputs once the agent ingests tainted content or the conditions occur. Non-repeatable LLM output adds some variability to any individual trigger.

exploitability.why: Some threats, such as chaff, resource-intensive queries, and injection through ingested logs or notes, need little access. Corpus poisoning of controlled documents, tool-layer tampering, and supply-chain compromise need privileged or insider access, and plant operational networks are typically segregated, so the overall requirement is moderate.

affected_users.why: The agent is a single advisory layer used by the control room team. If tool permissions bridge into control functions, or a poisoned procedure enters the controlled stream, the effects could propagate across coupled systems. As demonstrated, the impact is confined to one operator-aid component.

discoverability.why: RAG poisoning, prompt injection, agent tool over-reach, hallucination, and automation over-trust are heavily documented in the open literature, and the source paper is public. Plant-specific index contents and tool configuration would still need insider knowledge.

use_case: Artificial neural network (two hidden layers, compared against logistic regression and Bayesian networks) that predicts human error probabilities for operator actions in nuclear reactor probabilistic risk assessment. It is trained on classified operator-performance and event-report data held in the APPROP human-reliability repository, where each record is categorised by cognitive function failure, error mode, error cause and context. Its predictions are meant to replicate the qualitative human reliability analysis.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline ANN estimates human error probabilities for PRA from a small, classified, analyst-coded repository, so its outputs feed fault and event trees, core damage frequency and risk-informed decisions without touching plant control. The main threats are covert tampering with the training data or model so that human-error risk is quietly understated, leakage of classified operator-performance patterns through the model, and a set of implicit weaknesses (label circularity, rare-event data scarcity, distribution shift, opacity, over-trust, governance gaps) that make an unreliable HEP look validated and hard to challenge.

Training-data and label poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or compromised curator account could subtly relabel, add or delete records (error cause, mode, context) in the small APPROP corpus, systematically lowering predicted HEPs for chosen action classes. The result is an optimistic CDF and relaxed technical-specification, procedure or training decisions, and because validation uses the same data the bias is hard to detect.

Model and toolchain tampering -- adversarial
A modified ML library, serialised weights or notebook in the analyst environment could shift outputs only for particular context combinations (backdoor trigger) without any visible data change. This produces a quiet bias in a licensing-relevant analysis with no operational alarm, and the workstation could also serve as a foothold toward the classified repository.

Classified data leakage via model and outputs -- adversarial
Membership inference, inversion or collection of the model, its outputs and associated artefacts could expose which operator actions, procedures and plant states are most error-prone. That is a map of human-factor weaknesses usable for insider-assisted sabotage or attack timing, and a classified dataset moved into an ML workflow may escape the controls built for the original repository.

Label circularity and goal misalignment -- implicit, exploitable
Because the model is trained to replicate qualitative HRA, it reproduces analyst coding conventions and biases rather than true error likelihood, giving systematic errors a veneer of validation. An adversary can rely on the resulting misplaced credibility to have a tampered or biased HEP accepted as a data-driven confirmation of expert judgement.

Small-data, rare-event and distribution-shift failure -- implicit, exploitable
Severe errors are rare, and data come from one fleet and repository, so a headline F1 of about 0.876 hides poor calibration in the high-consequence tail and for other designs, new digital interfaces, new builds or procedure changes. Concept drift while the model stays frozen worsens this, and an adversary could time action around tasks the model rates as low-risk or hide manipulation inside the unreliable regions.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A two-hidden-layer ANN point estimate with no uncertainty treatment, seed-dependent retraining and no established qualification route for ML-derived HEPs is hard to trace or defend in regulatory review. Weak versioning, change control and provenance checks make silent drift or data manipulation harder to attribute, conditions an insider would favour.

Analyst over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Analysts may anchor on the ANN's category or HEP as an objective baseline and elicit less expert judgement, with errors propagating across many PRA basic events. This weakens the independent review that would otherwise catch poisoned or drifted outputs, so an adversary benefits from the misplaced trust.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline PRA/HRA support tool. It does not touch plant control, so the downstream pathway is slow and runs through risk-informed decisions: HEP values feed fault/event trees, which feed core damage frequency (CDF) estimates, technical specification and allowed-outage-time decisions, procedure and training priorities, and the licensing basis. A wrong HEP does not cause a physical event on its own. It biases the plant's picture of where risk lives, and that can steer maintenance, staffing, procedure and modification resources away from real vulnerabilities. Existing practice (expert elicitation, HRA method review, PRA peer review, sensitivity and uncertainty analysis) is a strong barrier, but it weakens if the ANN output is treated as a data-driven 'answer' that reviewers accept because it replicates the qualitative HRA. The main exposures are a small, classified, hard-to-audit training corpus, an opaque model standing in for analyst judgement, and an unusual insider/data-confidentiality profile.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity of the APPROP repository and the training pipeline. An insider or someone with compromised credentials could mislabel or alter event records (cognitive function failure, error mode, cause, context), or inject or delete records. Subtle label shifts would systematically lower HEPs for particular action classes. Failure mechanism: poisoned training data or a tampered model. Facility dependence: PRA inputs for operator actions. Consequence: optimistic CDF, wrongly relaxed risk-informed decisions, and under-prioritised procedures or training. Stealth is high because the corpus is classified and small, so few people can cross-check it, and model validation uses the same data. (2) Confidentiality. Classified operator-performance and event data can leak through the model (membership inference, inversion) or through model artefacts and outputs moving to less-controlled analysis environments. This exposes operator behaviour weaknesses and event vulnerabilities that would help an adversary plan insider-aided sabotage or time an attack around known human-performance gaps. (3) Supply chain and software integrity of the ML toolchain and model files, where a modified model could shift outputs only for chosen context combinations (backdoor). Consequence: a quiet bias in a licensing-relevant safety analysis, with no operational alarm to expose it.

IMPLICIT: (4) Data scarcity and low base rate. Severe-error events are rare, so the model learns mostly benign or routine cases. F1 of about 0.876 on one screening target says little about calibration of rare high-consequence HEPs, and class imbalance and small samples inflate apparent skill. (5) Distribution shift and generalisation. The data come from one national fleet and repository, and the reactor type and features are unconfirmed. Applying the model to different designs, new builds, digital control rooms, new procedures or beyond-design-basis and severe accident contexts is out of distribution, and plant-specific performance shaping factors differ. (6) Goal misalignment: replicating the qualitative HRA reproduces existing analyst biases and classifications rather than true error likelihood, so the model can look validated while carrying forward systematic errors. (7) Opacity and non-repeatability. A two-hidden-layer ANN gives poor explainability, and retraining non-determinism can change HEPs between versions, which is hard to defend in a regulatory review that expects traceable methods. (8) Automation bias and skill fade among HRA analysts, who may rely on the screening output instead of eliciting judgement. (9) QA and regulatory gap. There is no established qualification route for ML-derived HEPs in PRA, and weak configuration control, versioning and data governance make silent drift or tampering harder to detect. Mitigations such as independent expert review, bounding sensitivity studies and keeping the ANN advisory only substantially reduce the physical consequence, so the real risk is credibility erosion and slow-burn analytical bias rather than an immediate safety event.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small, tabular, supervised classifier (two-hidden-layer ANN against logistic regression and a Bayesian network) whose labels are themselves outputs of a qualitative HRA process. The model therefore learns to reproduce analyst judgment, not ground-truth operator failure, and its main exposure lies in the data pipeline and qualification of its outputs rather than in the architecture. Event-report corpora are sparse, skewed to the few events that were reported, and heavily dependent on how analysts coded cognitive function failure, error mode, cause and context. An F1 of 0.876 on a held-out split from the same repository says little about performance on a new plant, new procedures, a new control-room interface or a rare high-consequence scenario. The result is then fed into PRA, where a bad human error probability (HEP) propagates quietly into core damage frequency and risk-informed decisions, so the AI's influence is both high-leverage and hard to see.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Label circularity and data provenance: the training targets are analyst-coded categories and screening HEPs from a single organisational repository (APPROP, BARC). The model encodes that team's coding conventions, historical biases and plant-specific context. Applied to a different reactor design, operating regime or procedure set, it gives confident but unvalidated HEPs. This is OP.C0201.05, OP.C0302.03 and OP.C0302. (2) Small-data and low-base-rate problem: severe errors, such as those in beyond-design-basis or rare accident sequences, are underrepresented, and classifier metrics like F1 hide poor minority-class performance. Outputs would be biased toward frequent, benign error modes and may underestimate risk in the tail, which is the part PRA cares about most. This is OP.C0202 and OP.C0203. (3) Drift and concept drift: procedures, training, digital HMI upgrades, staffing and safety culture change over time, so the mapping from context to error probability shifts while the model stays frozen. This is OP.C0302.01 and OP.C0302.02. (4) Qualification and explainability gap: a neural network in a safety-significant PRA input chain is hard to justify to a regulator. Two-hidden-layer networks are non-deterministic across training seeds, and the paper compares models without a documented uncertainty or confidence treatment. HRA is itself defined by uncertainty bounds, and a point-estimate classifier discards them. This is OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0403, OP.C0501 and OP.C0504. (5) Automation trust and anchoring: analysts may accept the ANN's category or HEP as an objective baseline, which reduces scrutiny of the qualitative HRA. Skill fade in the analyst community follows, and an error is then propagated across many PRA basic events. This is OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01 and OP.C0603. (6) Goal misalignment: 'replicating the qualitative HRA' optimises agreement with past analysis, not accuracy of real human performance, so systematic analyst errors are reproduced and given a veneer of validation. This is OP.C0301.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (7) Training-data poisoning or label tampering in the classified repository, by an insider or through compromise of the data-curation workflow. Small, subtly relabelled sets of records (shifting error cause or context categories) would be enough to shift predicted HEPs downward for particular tasks. Because the data is small and curation is manual, a few altered records have outsized effect, and the change would be hard to spot. The consequence is understated human-error risk in a PRA, which could support relaxed procedures, surveillance intervals or safety-case claims. This is AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059 and AML.T0031. (8) Model or artifact tampering and supply-chain risk in the training environment, such as ML libraries, serialised weights and notebooks, which would alter outputs without any visible data change. This is AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018.000 and AML.T0076. (9) Data exfiltration and inference: the model and its outputs are derived from classified operator-performance and event data, so access to the model or its predictions could leak membership or sensitive operator-error patterns. Those patterns reveal which procedures or tasks are most error-prone, which is useful targeting intelligence for an insider-assisted or cyber-physical adversary. This is AML.T0024.000, AML.T0024.001, AML.T0025 and OP.C0505. (10) Adversary exploitation of implicit weaknesses: knowing that the model is trained on a narrow, aging dataset, an adversary could time an attack or exploit a task the model rates as low-risk, or push inputs (context categories) to land in a region the model treats as safe. This is AML.T0043 and AML.T0015.

security_specialist.argument: This model is an offline analytical tool rather than a control-path component, so a nation-state adversary would not target it for direct plant effects. The real exposure is indirect: it concentrates trust in a number that feeds the PRA, which in turn informs risk-informed decisions such as technical-specification relaxations, maintenance scheduling, procedure changes and staffing. It is also trained on a classified repository of operator-performance and event data, which makes it a collection and aggregation target and a way to pierce a security boundary. From an insider and security-culture view, the question is who can alter the training records, features or labels, and whether anyone would notice, given that the output is a plausible, opaque probability that is hard to audit and is meant to replicate expert judgement.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data poisoning and label manipulation by an insider or a compromised analyst account (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0012). The AI failure mechanism is a subtly biased model, for example one that systematically under-predicts human error probability for particular cognitive-function failures or error modes. The facility depends on the PRA to justify risk-informed decisions, so the consequence is a quietly understated human-error contribution to core damage frequency. That could mask a real operational weakness, or weaken the safety case for decisions that favour an adversary, and the bias would be hard to attribute because the model is opaque and small-data. (2) Model and data exfiltration through the model itself (AML.T0024.000/.001, AML.T0035, AML.T0036). Inversion or membership inference against a model trained on classified operator-performance and event records could leak crew-level weaknesses, vulnerable procedures and error-prone plant states. An adversary planning sabotage or social engineering could use this as a targeting aid: it shows which operator actions are least reliable under which contexts, which is a map of human-factor vulnerabilities. The model, its training set and the repository are all attractive aggregation points, and a classified dataset moved into an ML workflow may escape the data-handling controls built for the original repository (OP.C0505.01). (3) Supply-chain and tooling compromise (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018, AML.T0076). A tampered ML library or model file in an analyst workstation environment could alter outputs without any visible malfunction. The workstation may also be a stepping stone into a network that holds the classified repository.

IMPLICIT, but exploitable. (4) Small-data and low-base-rate limits (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03). Real human errors are rare, and records come from one repository with a specific plant and cultural context. The model can look accurate (F1 about 0.876) while generalising poorly to other plants or new designs, and an adversary could exploit or time actions around the unreliable regions. (5) Automation trust and opacity (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501). Analysts may defer to a model that appears to reproduce the qualitative HRA, so the independent expert review weakens (OP.C0101.06 skill fade). This reduces the chance that an insider's data manipulation or a drifted output is caught, and it concentrates trust in a single plausible-looking number. (6) Fidelity and governance gaps (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0402, OP.C0503). The model replicates the labels but not the reasoning behind them. It may omit context factors, give non-repeatable outputs across retraining, and fall outside regulatory and security scope as a non-safety offline tool, so it gets little change control, little provenance checking and little access auditing. Those are the conditions an insider would prefer.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on data/label poisoning, classified-data leakage via inference, toolchain tampering, and the implicit data-scarcity, drift, opacity, goal-misalignment and over-trust cluster. I dropped speculative adversarial evasion (AML.T0043/T0015) and the weakly argued OP.C0503/OP.C0304.03 and merged duplicates; AML.T0025 and AML.T0018 root were omitted as not specifically traceable.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning based predictive model to enhance human reliability analysis for risk assessment of nuclear reactors," International Journal of System Assurance Engineering and Management (Springer)
evidence.note: The paper builds and compares logistic regression, Bayesian network and ANN models that predict human error probability from operator-performance data stored in the APPROP repository, which was developed at Bhabha Atomic Research Centre. It reports that the ANN models can replicate the qualitative human reliability analysis in their predictions, and gives an F1 score of 0.876 for the ANN that estimates the overall screening human error probability. I could only see parts of the paper in the search results, so the exact reactor type and the full input features are not confirmed.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is covert poisoning or backdoor tampering that understates human-error risk, which feeds core damage frequency and risk-informed licensing decisions and erodes safety margins. It does not touch plant control, so a direct release is indirect and not the 5 category, while the classified-data leakage that could support sabotage timing adds to the harm.

reproducibility.why: Once an insider or compromised account has write access, a biased relabel or model change reliably shifts the HEP output in a small corpus. The implicit weaknesses (rare-event scarcity, drift, circularity) are always present. The effect depends on which action classes and contexts are affected, and on whether analysts adopt the output.

exploitability.why: Poisoning, model tampering, and extraction of classified data all require insider access or a compromised curator account or analyst workstation, in an access-controlled environment. This is well above routine external interaction, though the small corpus and weak change control lower the effort once access exists.

affected_users.why: A biased HEP propagates across many PRA basic events, fault and event trees, and risk-informed decisions for a plant or fleet. The model is offline and does not couple to control systems, so the impact stays in the analysis and decision domain rather than being facility-wide in operation.

discoverability.why: The approach, the dataset family, and the F1 score are in the published literature. The general classes of ML poisoning, membership inference, and over-trust are well documented. The specific repository contents, access paths, and toolchain are internal, so a capable outsider can infer the weakness but not locate its details.

use_case: Radial basis function neural networks reconstruct temperatures at control-rod positions that have no thermocouple. They work from the readings of the thermocouples that are installed, taken at the moment of an accidental control rod drop in a PWR core. The rod that dropped is then identified as the fuel assembly position with the lowest reconstructed temperature, which supports on-line control rod monitoring.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory rod-drop localiser interpolates core temperatures from sparse thermocouples with an RBF network and names the dropped rod by taking the lowest reconstructed temperature. Independent rod position indication, excore flux and protection limit direct harm, so the main risks are operator misdiagnosis and misplaced trust. The threats are a simulation-to-plant gap, a brittle argmin decision rule, automation over-trust, weak qualification, and adversarial manipulation of thermocouple inputs or of the model and its training artifacts.

Simulated training data and sim-to-real gap -- implicit, exploitable
Real rod drops are almost nonexistent, so the network learns simulator physics from a small simulated set, and validation on simulated cases hides localized errors in the real core. An adversary could hide a tampered weight or training-data change behind this absence of real ground truth, because aggregate validation would not expose it.

Drift and operational heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Burnup, xenon, reload patterns, power level and thermocouple degradation move inputs outside the training envelope, and RBF extrapolation fails silently with a biased reconstruction. An adversary could use this degraded band to hide a small thermocouple bias or to time an action when the tool is least reliable.

Argmin decision fragility without uncertainty -- implicit, exploitable
The lowest-temperature rule always returns one confident-looking assembly even when the gap between neighbours is below interpolation error, or when a misaligned rod, partial insertion, multiple rods or a flow anomaly create similar cold spots. An adversary could stage a decoy or a masked event that the rule reports as a clean single-rod answer.

Operator over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Operators who almost never see real drops may accept the highlighted assembly under transient stress, neglect cross-checks against rod position indication and excore flux, and lose manual diagnostic skill. An adversary could time a disturbance or an alarm flood so that the unverified answer misdirects the response.

Qualification and lifecycle gap -- implicit
A non-safety advisory tool can become de facto relied upon without ML-specific V&V, and retraining per core reload and non-deterministic RBF centre and width selection go unqualified. A fleet-wide model copy would repeat the same error across units; an adversary gains little directly from this beyond the tampering cover noted above.

Thermocouple input manipulation -- adversarial
Falsified, biased or spoofed readings on a few channels, injected through the instrumentation or data-acquisition path, shift the argmin to the wrong assembly or mask the true cold spot, which misleads diagnosis or hides a real anomaly. The small low-dimensional input space makes such perturbations easy to optimise offline.

Model and training-data tampering -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor with maintenance access could poison the simulation training set, RBF centres or weights to create position-specific blind spots or a trigger response that is invisible in routine operation. Few reviewers inspect these small artifacts.

Denial of the monitoring aid -- adversarial
Corrupting or flooding the thermocouple feeds or the service at the moment of a transient removes the diagnostic aid when it is needed and pushes operators to slower diagnosis. The effect is bounded by independent rod position indication and procedures.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory on-line monitoring aid that localizes a dropped rod. It does so by interpolating core exit temperatures at uninstrumented positions from sparse thermocouples and picking the position with the lowest reconstructed temperature. Existing practice limits the harm from a wrong answer. Rod drop is already detected by rod position indication, excore flux tilt and power-range negative flux rate trips, and reactor protection acts without the AI. The residual risk is therefore mostly about operator diagnosis and response (misidentifying the rod, delayed recovery decisions, wrong power-distribution or restart assumptions) and about eroded confidence in monitoring. It is not about direct loss of protection. The main weaknesses are that the model is trained and validated on simulated transients, that argmin-of-interpolation is a brittle decision rule with a small margin between neighbouring positions, and that the thermocouple inputs can be degraded by faults or manipulation without the model signalling it.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT: (1) Training data is almost certainly simulated (neutronic/thermal-hydraulic code) because real rod-drop events are extremely rare. This gives simulated-to-real and small-data gaps (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0302). Real cores differ from the simulations through burnup, xenon, fuel-loading patterns, cycle-to-cycle changes, thermocouple calibration offsets, failed or drifting thermocouples, flow mixing and crossflow. The reconstruction can then be systematically biased, and the argmin can pick the wrong assembly, especially for rods near the periphery, near each other, or in a symmetric region (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (2) The lowest-temperature rule always returns an answer. It gives no uncertainty, no check that a drop actually occurred, and no handling of other events (rod misalignment, partial insertion, a flow anomaly, multiple rods) that produce similar cold spots. That risks misattribution, and RBF interpolation outside its training envelope degrades without warning (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0401, OP.C0403). (3) Operators may over-trust the highlighted position (OP.C0101.04, automation bias) and so under-use rod position indication. Consequences could be a wrong rod being inspected or recovered, delayed realignment, or a wrong assumption about power peaking and shutdown margin. The model also gets little real-world use, so operators have little experience of it (OP.C0101.01). (4) Model changes per core reload, retraining and non-determinism in RBF center/width selection need qualification. A software-hygiene or fleet-wide propagation gap would repeat the same error across units (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0602). 

ADVERSARIAL: (5) Manipulating thermocouple data or the plant data path feeding the model is the most credible vector (AML.T0043, AML.T0015 in a data-path sense, AML.T0031). Spoofed or biased readings, or a small perturbation of a few channels, can move the argmin to a different assembly or mask the cold spot. This would be most damaging when combined with a real or concealed rod-position anomaly, a stuck-rod condition or an insider action, and it would mislead operators about which rod is affected. (6) Supply chain or maintenance-time tampering with the trained weights, the training simulation data, or the retraining pipeline (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020) can create a bias that is invisible under normal operation. (7) Denial or delay of the service at the moment of the transient (AML.T0029) removes the diagnostic aid when it is most needed, but this is bounded by the independent rod position indication and procedures. (8) If the tool sits in an on-line monitoring network linked to plant systems, it adds an IT/OT attack surface and a data-governance question (OP.C0505) even though it is advisory. The safeguard that would have to fail for serious harm is independent confirmation by RPI, excore detectors and procedures, so severity is low to moderate unless the operators' trust in the tool displaces those checks.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small RBF interpolator that fills in spatial temperature values from a sparse thermocouple array, then applies an argmin to name the dropped rod. The ML fragility sits in the training data and in the final decision rule. A rod-drop transient is a rare event, so the training set is almost certainly simulated (neutronics/thermal-hydraulics code output), not field data. Inference-time inputs from a real core will differ from that: sensor noise, failed thermocouples, burnup and cycle-dependent power shapes, xenon transients and different rod configurations. The argmin step has no calibrated uncertainty, so when interpolation error exceeds the temperature gap between neighbouring assemblies, the model still returns a confident-looking single answer. Reported success on an abstract-level validation says little about out-of-distribution robustness or qualification for an operations-support role.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulated or surrogate training data (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0202, OP.C0203): true rod-drop data from operating PWRs is almost nonexistent, so the network learns the simulator's physics, not the plant's. The mechanism is a sim-to-real gap. The facility dependency is on-line rod monitoring that operators may consult during an upset. The consequence is a misidentified or missed dropped rod, which leads to wrong power-distribution and peaking-factor assessments and wrong recovery actions, a safety-margin concern. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303): the network is trained on a fixed core loading, burnup state and power level. Fuel cycle progression, reload patterns, power maneuvers, and thermocouple degradation or drift move the input distribution. RBF networks extrapolate poorly beyond their basis-function centres, so errors are silent. Retraining needs new simulations per cycle, and the static training versus dynamic plant mismatch is a qualification gap. (3) Argmin decision fragility (OP.C0403, OP.C0401): the output is a hard identification from small temperature differences, with no confidence measure. Multiple simultaneous events (a partial insertion, a misaligned rod, thermocouple failure) fall outside the single-drop assumption and yield a plausible but false identification. (4) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102): operators who rarely see real drops may over-trust the highlighted assembly or dismiss it when it conflicts with other indications, and may lose the manual diagnostic skill. (5) Qualification and hygiene gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504): a non-safety-classified advisory tool can become de facto relied upon, with no V&V regime for ML-based interpolation or for retraining after changes to the core. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0041): the model's inputs are a small number of thermocouple signals. An adversary with access to the instrumentation or data path who falsifies a few readings could shift the lowest-temperature assembly, causing a false rod-drop identification or masking a real one. This is an evasion attack on a low-dimensional interpolator, and the small input space makes it easy to optimise offline if the training simulations or architecture are known (AML.T0005, AML.T0002, AML.T0000 from published literature). (7) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020): poisoned or altered simulation data, or tampered network weights and centres, could create localised errors at specific assembly positions that pass aggregate validation, because the validation set is also simulated. (8) Denial of the monitoring function (AML.T0029, AML.T0031): corrupting or flooding the thermocouple feeds degrades the tool at the moment it is needed, pushing operators back to slower diagnosis. The consequence of the adversarial cases is erosion of confidence in core-monitoring information or deception about core state during a transient, not direct actuation, because the tool is advisory. The risk grows if its output is later wired into automatic protective logic.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this is an unattractive direct target but an interesting stepping stone: an RBF interpolator over in-core thermocouple readings is a small, cheap, on-line diagnostic, and a rod-drop event is already a transient the operator is under pressure to diagnose. The question is whether the tool's existence adds an insider-accessible pathway or a trust point. A rod-drop identifier that outputs a single 'lowest-temperature position' invites operators to accept it quickly during a stressful transient. An adversary who can influence its inputs, or time actions around when operators defer to it, could misdirect the response or mask a different event. The more serious non-adversarial weaknesses are an interpolator trained on simulated drop transients, a very low base rate of real drops, and a single-argmin decision rule that has no confidence output. Those are exactly the weaknesses a patient adversary would exploit or time an attack around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Input integrity: the model depends entirely on the thermocouple signals reaching it. An insider or a compromised data-acquisition or historian path could bias or replace a few channels, or spoof a drop-like pattern, so the argmin points to the wrong assembly. The mechanism is evasion/adversarial data (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) or integrity erosion (AML.T0031). The facility consequence is a misidentified rod during monitoring. That could mean a wrong diagnosis, an unnecessary or poorly targeted power maneuver, delayed recognition of a real misalignment, or a decoy event that distracts operators while something else is going on. Because the tool is advisory, the harm is mainly to operator decisions, not direct actuation. (2) Model and training-data tampering: weights, RBF centers and the simulation-derived training set are small, rarely reviewed artifacts. An insider with maintenance or engineering access could subtly poison or modify them (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0076). Examples include a blind spot at particular positions, or a backdoor-like response to a specific input pattern. Such a change would be hard to detect because real drops are almost never seen in operation, so there is no routine ground truth to expose it. (3) Trust-timing: if operators come to rely on the tool, a deliberate disturbance, or an alarm-flood scenario, could be timed so that the confident-looking single answer is accepted without cross-checking against rod-position indication and ex-core flux. This is an attack on vigilance, not on the model itself. (4) Stepping stone: the tool sits on a network segment between instrumentation and the monitoring layer, so it is a possible foothold or lateral-movement point with software-supply-chain exposure through ML libraries and the toolchain (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0012).

IMPLICIT. The training data is probably simulated or surrogate transients, not field data, and real rod drops are extremely rare (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0203). The model may fail on different burnup states, power levels, xenon distributions, failed or drifting thermocouples and other plants (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03), and it may be static while the core evolves each cycle. The argmin rule gives no uncertainty estimate and little explainability (OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03), so ambiguous cases look as confident as clear ones. Over-trust and skill fade in the manual rod-drop diagnosis (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102) and the lack of AI-specific qualification for a function near safety (OP.C0501, OP.C0303) are the gaps an adversary would rely on. Overall, direct targeting has low value, but the missing validation and provenance controls make quiet tampering and the timing of trust exploitation plausible for a patient insider.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, the argmin fragility, over-trust, and input and model tampering. I dropped the IT/OT stepping-stone and valid-accounts items (AML.T0012, AML.T0010.001) as generic rather than specific to this model, and left out AML.T0041, AML.T0005 and AML.T0076 as weakly argued.

evidence.citation: "Identification model of an accidental drop of a control rod in PWR reactors using thermocouple readings and radial basis function neural networks," Annals of Nuclear Energy (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests an identification model. RBF neural networks interpolate core temperatures at control-rod positions from the available thermocouple measurements. It reports that the predicted temperatures were good enough to pinpoint the dropped rod. I read only the abstract and highlights, not the full text.

damage.why: The worst credible threat is operator misdiagnosis or a masked anomaly from a manipulated advisory tool, but independent rod position indication, excore flux and protection systems bound the harm to rework or delayed diagnosis rather than release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: The argmin fragility and sim-to-real gap produce wrong or overconfident answers whenever inputs leave the training envelope, but a wrong answer that actually misleads operators requires a rare real rod-drop event plus a coincident condition.

exploitability.why: Manipulating thermocouple data or model artifacts needs access to the instrumentation or data-acquisition path or insider and supply-chain maintenance access to a plant network, so routine external interaction is not enough.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly confined to one unit's advisory diagnosis for a single event, and fleet-wide model copying could repeat the error across units, but the tool is non-safety and independent indications limit propagation.

discoverability.why: The RBF and argmin approach is published in open literature and generic weaknesses such as sim-to-real gaps and adversarial inputs are well known, but finding exploitable specifics needs plant-specific knowledge of thermocouple layout and deployment.

use_case: Gradient-boosting regression model that predicts the sintered density of MOX fast-reactor fuel pellets. Inputs are 18 production-process variables, such as raw-material type and sintering temperature, taken from a database of Japanese MOX pellet production records. It supports control of pellet density, a key fuel specification, during fuel fabrication.
incurred_insecurity:
This gradient-boosting model advises on sintered density, a key MOX fuel specification, using 18 process variables from a small historical Japanese production database. Independent density measurement limits direct harm, so the main insecurity is a confident-looking model that fails silently, is over-trusted, and sits on integrity and confidentiality attack surfaces. The main threats are out-of-distribution failure, evaluation optimism and data scarcity, over-trust that erodes independent checks, qualification gaps, data and model integrity attacks, input manipulation, and exposure of process know-how.

Out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
Tree ensembles cannot extrapolate and return confident point densities for new powders, Pu or Am content, furnace ageing or recipes, so operators tune sintering to a wrong target, producing out-of-spec or scrapped Pu-bearing pellets. An adversary could present or induce inputs in this unvalidated region, where a manipulated or wrong prediction looks plausible and draws no suspicion.

Evaluation optimism and data scarcity -- implicit
An R^2 near 0.996 on a small, clustered, few-line dataset likely reflects in-distribution or leaky validation, with rare out-of-spec batches underrepresented, so the model's reliability is overstated. No realistic adversary gains much beyond what the out-of-distribution threat already provides.

Over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
High apparent accuracy invites operators to rely on the prediction, reduce density sampling and lose the engineering judgement to question it. An adversary could time a model or input manipulation to this reduced vigilance, knowing an error will not be caught until a late measurement or in-reactor discrepancy.

Opacity and qualification gaps -- implicit, exploitable
An academic research model with partly interpretable feature importances, non-deterministic retraining and no AI-specific QA, version control or change management has no integrity baseline. Tampering or silent drift would therefore go undetected, and an adversary could hide a change among routine retraining.

Training data and model integrity attack -- adversarial
An insider or compromised pipeline can alter production records, retraining data, or the serialized model or libraries to bias predicted density, possibly only for a specific material type or temperature band. The result is pellets drifting to the specification edge, or false rejections that disrupt supply, with the sabotage resembling natural model error.

Process-input manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofing the 18 inputs, such as temperature logs or material-type codes in the MES or historian, steers the prediction or masks a real process excursion, and a tree model is easily probed in black-box fashion. This can pass out-of-spec product through a soft gate.

Process-data and model exposure -- adversarial
The consolidated MOX production database and queryable model encode recipe-to-density relationships and material information for plutonium fuel. Theft, model extraction or inversion yields proliferation-sensitive process knowledge, especially if the tool is governed under a weaker security model than process control or safeguards data.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a fuel fabrication standpoint, this is an advisory regression model for a process-control parameter. Sintered density is verified by measurement on every lot (immersion density, ceramography, QA hold points), so a wrong prediction does not directly put a defective pellet in a reactor. The real risks are subtler. Operators adjust sintering temperature, atmosphere, or blend recipe based on the prediction. A biased model can steer the process toward out-of-spec product, cause rework and scrap of plutonium-bearing material, and raise worker dose and waste volumes. It can also erode attention to the independent measurement. The reported R^2 of about 0.996 is likely an in-distribution fit to a historical Japanese production database. It says little about performance on new feed powders, new furnaces, new Pu content or americium content, or a new campaign, and the data are small and tied to specific lines. The safeguards-relevant angle is that the model's inputs and outputs form a record of process behaviour and material type, which is sensitive information.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift and generalization failure: the model is trained on historical Japanese MOX records, with a small and heterogeneous sample, few lots per recipe, and a narrow range of raw-material types. New powder characteristics (MIMAS vs. other routes, Am-241 ingrowth in aged Pu, different O/M control atmosphere), furnace aging, or a new facility could push the model out of distribution while it still returns confident point predictions. The consequence is that operators tune sintering to a wrong target. Pellets then miss the density spec, causing scrap and rework of Pu-bearing material (dose, waste, criticality-control loading), or marginal pellets reach the fuel pin line if downstream sampling is thin. Existing practice (100% or statistical density verification, pellet acceptance specs) limits the harm, so the AI would need to fail alongside a lapse in measurement discipline. (2) Automation bias and skill fade: a model with R^2 near 1 invites over-trust, and the pressure to reduce destructive sampling or measurement frequency would defeat the independent check. (3) Opacity and qualification gaps: gradient-boosting feature importances are only partly interpretable, and there is no AI-specific QA basis. Retraining and version changes alter behaviour without a requalification step, and the model is not within the existing nuclear QA scope. (4) Data quality and provenance: the production database may contain mis-entered records, lab-to-line measurement inconsistencies, and survivorship bias. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training-data or input manipulation, via a corrupted historical database, a compromised MES/LIMS feed, or falsified process-variable entries. A subtle bias could shift recommended temperature or recipe so that density drifts toward the spec edge, or it could mask a real process fault. The target would be product quality and economics, or fuel performance reliability over the long term, and the attack leaves little trace. (6) Supply chain and model tampering of the model file, libraries, or retraining pipeline, which gives persistence and silent drift. (7) Information exposure: the model and its data encode proprietary recipe-to-density relationships and material type and quantity information for plutonium processing. Extraction or inversion would support recon on process parameters and also touches safeguards and proliferation-sensitivity concerns. (8) Safeguards interplay: process-model predictions used as a cross-check for material accounting or for material-unaccounted-for (MUF) explanations could be gamed, so predicted-vs-measured discrepancies should not be allowed to explain away anomalies. Mitigations are to keep the model advisory, require independent measurement acceptance, monitor for drift and out-of-range inputs, and place the model in a controlled, isolated environment with versioned retraining.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view this is a small-to-medium tabular regression on a historical Japanese MOX production database. The reported R^2 of about 0.996 is a warning sign, not reassurance. It points to a random split over correlated batch records, leakage through near-duplicate lots, or a narrow process envelope where the model interpolates between near-identical campaigns. Gradient-boosted trees cannot extrapolate beyond the training range. The cases where fuel fabrication most needs a prediction are new feedstock, new powder lots, new furnace conditions, and fast-reactor MOX with a different Pu content or recipe, and these are the cases where the model is least reliable. The data is also scarce, heterogeneous, and tightly held. Its provenance (which line, furnace, era, and measurement method) determines whether the model generalizes, and the abstract does not say how this was validated. An adversary or a plain process change can therefore degrade the model without being noticed, because a tree ensemble returns a confident point estimate with no native uncertainty.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution failure and drift (OP.C0302, .01, .03). Furnace aging, a change in powder supplier or specification, an atmosphere change, and measurement recalibration are all covariate or concept shifts. Trees saturate silently at the edge of the training range, so the model can output plausible densities for inputs it has never seen. Consequence: operators relax sampling or adjust sintering set-points on a wrong density estimate, and pellets go out of specification (too low in density or too high), which matters for fuel performance and for criticality or inventory accounting. (2) Evaluation optimism and data scarcity (OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0403). The near-perfect R^2 probably comes from in-distribution testing. Without temporal or leave-one-campaign-out validation, qualification rests on a number that overstates how far the model can be trusted. Records from a small number of production lines mean low diversity, and the rare out-of-spec batches the model most needs to catch are underrepresented. (3) Qualification and governance gaps (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0402). Fabrication quality assurance expects controlled, repeatable methods. Retraining nondeterminism, version changes, and the lack of an AI-specific qualification path let the model's behavior change between runs and releases. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). Over-trust in a model that reproduces past data to within 0.4% erodes confidence in physical measurement and lowers vigilance over time. Weak explainability (OP.C0401) makes it hard for operators to see why a prediction is off.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training data poisoning or integrity erosion (AML.T0020, T0059, T0010.002). The production database and the retraining pipeline are the main attack surface. Small, targeted shifts in recorded densities or process variables, or label-feature correlations inserted into the retraining data, would steer predictions in a particular direction. Because the model seems highly accurate, the tampering would be hard to see. Consequence: systematic bias that passes QA until a destructive-test or in-reactor discrepancy appears. (6) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, T0015). An insider or someone who has compromised the MES or historian can alter the 18 inputs, such as temperature logs or material-type codes, to produce a desired prediction and mask a real process excursion. A tree model is easy to probe in black-box fashion. (7) Model or artifact tampering and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0018, T0010.001/.003, T0076). Serialized model files and ML libraries (scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM) can be swapped or backdoored, with a trigger on rare input combinations. (8) Information-security exposure (AML.T0024.001/.002, T0035, T0036, OP.C0505, OP.C0201.05). The model and database encode proprietary MOX process recipes, so extracting or inverting the model leaks fabrication know-how, which has sensitivity for proliferation and commercial reasons. Data-access rules designed for ordinary plant data may be misapplied (OP.C0505.01).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is a small tabular regression model, not a safety-system controller, so a nation-state would more likely go after fabrication data, process recipes or the QA records themselves than the model. Its real significance is where it sits: it advises on a key fuel specification (sintered density) and is backed by a consolidated database of MOX production records. That database is a concentrated, high-value dataset, because it reveals process parameters for plutonium-bearing fuel and so has proliferation-sensitivity and commercial value. An insider with write access to that data or to the model artifact could quietly bias density predictions. The result would be out-of-spec pellets passing a soft gate, or good lots being rejected to disrupt production, and an R^2 of about 0.996 would make operators trust the output and relax independent checks. The implicit weaknesses matter just as much: a small, heterogeneous, mostly historical dataset with few off-normal samples, plus a reported fit that may not reflect extrapolation to new recipes. These give an adversary, or simple drift, a window in which wrong predictions look authoritative.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: (1) Integrity attack on training data or model (insider, or a compromised data pipeline). AI failure mechanism: poisoned or silently altered production records, or a tampered model file, shift predicted density in a chosen direction or only for particular input regions, such as one raw-material type or a sintering temperature band. Facility dependence: fabrication process control and release decisions that use the prediction to tune sintering or to reduce destructive or measured density checks. Consequence: pellets outside the density specification reach fuel pins, with possible effects on fuel performance, or a false-reject campaign that disrupts supply. The sabotage is hard to attribute because it looks like a natural model error. This is plausible for an insider but, relative to other targets, lower in priority for a sophisticated external actor. (2) Confidentiality and proliferation-relevant aggregation. Mechanism: the consolidated MOX production database, trained model and feature set encode process know-how and operating windows for plutonium fuel. Facility dependence: data governance and information security for fabrication. Consequence: the aggregated dataset and model become a single, attractive theft or exfiltration target. A model that can be queried also leaks process sensitivities through its input-output behavior, which supports model extraction or inference of recipes. Treating it as a mere analytics tool under a weaker security model than process control or safeguards data would be a gap. (3) Implicit automation-trust and vigilance erosion that an adversary can time an attack around. Mechanism: very high reported accuracy encourages over-trust and skill fade in density engineering and QA, and reduces independent measurement. Consequence: when the model is wrong, whether through drift, new raw materials, new process setpoints or a deliberate perturbation, nobody notices until the density measurement or later in-reactor behavior reveals it. An adversary needs only to wait for reduced human checking. (4) Implicit data and generalization weaknesses. Mechanism: a small, domain-specific dataset from Japanese production, with few failures or edge cases, strongly clustered by material and campaign. Gradient boosting cannot extrapolate beyond training ranges, and the model is opaque to operators. Consequence: out-of-distribution inputs, such as new feedstock, new equipment or changed fabrication lines, give confident but unsupported predictions. These are the same conditions in which an adversary could slip in manipulated inputs (sensor or record spoofing of the 18 process variables) and have them pass as plausible. (5) Qualification and lifecycle gaps. Mechanism: an academic research model with no AI-specific QA, version control, change management or monitoring for retraining. Consequence: unverifiable model provenance when moved into operations, and no integrity baseline to detect tampering or drift.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on drift/out-of-distribution failure, over-trust, small-data limits, qualification gaps, data/model integrity attack and process-data exposure, which I merged into single threats. I dropped AML.T0012 (valid accounts) and the MUF safeguards-gaming point as insufficiently grounded in this advisory process model, and dropped OP.C0303 and OP.C0102, which restated other threats..

evidence.citation: "Machine Learning Sintering Density Prediction Model for MOX Fuel Pellet," Transactions of the Atomic Energy Society of Japan (Atomic Energy Society of Japan), Vol. 22, No. 2, pp. 51-58 (2023)
evidence.note: The authors built a database of MOX pellet production results from Japan and chose 18 input variables from the production process. A gradient boosting regressor trained on it reproduced measured sintered densities with R^2 of about 0.996. I only retrieved the abstract and bibliographic record, not the full text.

damage.why: Independent density measurement limits direct harm, so the credible worst case is out-of-spec or scrapped Pu-bearing pellets, supply disruption, and erosion of fuel-quality margin (operational disruption); the proliferation-sensitive process-knowledge exposure threat is real but does not amount to loss of material control or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Tree-ensemble extrapolation failure and over-trust occur reliably whenever inputs fall outside the training distribution or operators relax sampling, and data or input tampering reliably biases outputs once the pipeline is reached.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (training-data or model tampering, spoofing MES/historian inputs, extracting the model or database) generally need insider or privileged access to a controlled plutonium fuel-fabrication environment, though the implicit out-of-distribution and over-trust failures need no attacker.

affected_users.why: Impact is limited to a single fabrication-line advisory function for pellet density, with downstream effects on pellet batches; it is not coupled to plant-wide control or safety systems.

discoverability.why: Tree-model extrapolation limits, data poisoning and model extraction are well documented in the open literature for this class of AI system, and the published paper reveals the model type and inputs, but the specific deployment, data pipelines and governance gaps need insider knowledge.

use_case: Deep reinforcement learning (PPO, compared with A2C) that picks control-drum positions for a heat-pipe microreactor. It is trained on surrogate models of Serpent Monte Carlo simulations. The goal is to reach criticality and keep the power evenly spread across the six core sectors (hextant power tilt) at different burnup states.
incurred_insecurity:
A deep RL agent that commands the control drums, the primary reactivity actuators of a heat-pipe microreactor, is trained only on surrogates of Serpent simulations and has never seen the real plant. It therefore incurs implicit risk from the sim-to-real gap, narrow burnup coverage, a thin reward, opacity and weak qualification, and operator over-trust. It also incurs adversarial risk through poisoning of the data and model pipeline, manipulation of the state inputs, theft of model artifacts, fleet-wide update compromise, and denial of the agent. Consequences range from unplanned reactivity or power-tilt excursions and fuel or heat-pipe stress to a degraded, deskilled fallback to manual control. Severity is bounded only if independent deterministic protection sits between the agent and the drums.

Surrogate fidelity and sim-to-real gap -- implicit, exploitable
The PPO policy is optimised against an emulator of Monte Carlo output, so it can exploit surrogate errors and act confidently and wrongly on real drum worth, xenon and temperature feedback, heat-pipe degradation or as-built geometry, for which no operating data exist. The result is a criticality offset or tilt larger than the reported ~10 pcm and 1.002 suggest, with no warning. An adversary could use the headline performance as cover, or steer the plant into such out-of-distribution states and blame the resulting drum motion on model error.

Burnup and operating-state coverage -- implicit, exploitable
The policy is trained at only three discrete burnup states, so interpolated burnups, load-following, restarts and irradiation-driven drift in cross sections and drum worth fall outside what it has seen, and the policy may behave unpredictably there. An adversary could time an attack for these poorly covered regimes, where anomalous behaviour looks like ordinary drift.

Objective misalignment -- implicit
The reward covers only criticality and hextant tilt, not reactivity insertion rate, shutdown margin, drum wear or peak fuel and heat-pipe temperature. A reward-optimal policy can therefore take aggressive multistep trajectories that erode safety margin. An adversary gains little from this directly beyond what the other threats already offer.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A stochastic, seed-dependent neural policy cannot be statically verified, and no accepted qualification route or regulatory basis exists for a learned controller in a reactivity-control path; the evidence is a non-peer-reviewed preprint on a single design. Because a tampered retrain cannot be told apart from a normal one, an adversary could rely on this to hide a modified policy.

Automation trust and operator skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Strong surrogate results invite over-trust, and operators of a remote or lightly staffed site lose criticality-approach skill, vigilance for slow tilt drift and clarity about AI versus manual mode. An adversary could use a long benign record as cover for latent sabotage, or force a handoff to manual control when operators are unpracticed.

Pipeline and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Poisoning the Serpent-derived data, the surrogate, the reward or the policy checkpoint, including inserting a backdoor trigger, can yield a policy that passes the keff and tilt validation yet commands unsafe drum setpoints in a chosen regime. The result is power peaking, reduced thermal margin or heat-pipe stress concentrated where verification is thin.

Sensor and state manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofed or perturbed flux, temperature, power-sector or burnup inputs can push the differentiable policy out of distribution and drive harmful drum moves, a false critical state, or masked real tilt. The policy has no learned robustness to adversarial states, so only the independent protection layer limits the damage.

Model theft and offline staging -- adversarial
Exfiltrating policy weights or surrogates leaks proprietary core physics and gives an adversary a proxy model for crafting adversarial states offline and transferring them to the plant. Public preprint details of the eVinci-like design further lower the cost of building such a proxy.

Fleet propagation and remote update path -- adversarial
A flawed or compromised policy pushed through remote retraining or redeployment to many standardized microreactors becomes a common-cause failure with cross-site consequences. A weakly controlled update path makes this a very efficient attack vector.

Denial or corruption of the agent -- adversarial
Denying inference or corrupting weights forces fallback to manual drum control, which can be timed around a physical or cyber attack or used to induce operator error during the transition.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations lens, this agent sets control-drum positions, which are the primary reactivity control on a heat-pipe microreactor. The policy is trained wholly on surrogates of Serpent Monte Carlo runs, so every physical claim (10 pcm criticality, 1.002 tilt) is a claim about the surrogate and not the plant. The plant differs from the training world in ways that matter: drum worth and calibration, temperature and xenon feedback, heat-pipe failures, instrumentation noise and burnup history. The consequence of a bad output would be an unplanned reactivity change or a power tilt that stresses fuel and heat pipes. That consequence is bounded only if independent safeguards sit between the agent and the drums: rate limits, a hardware-based scram and tilt/power interlocks, and operator authority. This has to be established by design and qualification. The main exposures are therefore qualification gaps and automation bias that erode those barriers, plus a new attack surface into the drum-command path.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and surrogate fidelity gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0203). A microreactor of this type has almost no operating history, so no field data exist to validate the surrogate, and the policy is tuned to the surrogate's errors. Real drum worth, as-built geometry, temperature and xenon dynamics, heat-pipe degradation and sensor bias can all place the plant outside the training distribution.
