The failure mode is a confident but wrong drum move, with a criticality offset or tilt that exceeds what the simulation suggested. (2) Burnup coverage. Training at only three discrete burnup states means interpolation between them, and off-nominal histories such as load-following or restarts are untested (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). (3) Objective misalignment (OP.C0301). The reward targets criticality and tilt only. It ignores rate of reactivity insertion, margin to limits, drum wear, peak fuel and heat-pipe temperature, and shutdown margin. A reward-optimal policy could take aggressive or non-physical multistep trajectories. (4) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0403, OP.C0501). Neural policies are hard to verify against nuclear software qualification and deterministic-behavior expectations, and a stochastic PPO policy may give different actions for the same state. Preprint-level evidence (not peer reviewed) with reliance on one reactor design adds to the regulatory readiness gap (OP.C0504). (5) Human factors (OP.C0101, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). Good performance on a surrogate invites over-trust, operator skill fade in manual criticality approach, and mode confusion between AI and manual control. This matters most for a remotely or lightly staffed microreactor. Existing practice (rod/drum worth measurements, approach-to-critical procedures, independent protection systems) mitigates this only if the AI is kept advisory or tightly bounded. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Sensor and state manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Spoofed or biased flux, temperature or drum-position inputs could drive the policy to move drums in a harmful direction. The policy has no learned robustness to adversarial states, and it acts on one trusted data channel. This is a false-data attack with a physical effect whose damage is limited only by the independent protection system. (7) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, OP.C0502). Poisoned surrogate training data, a tampered surrogate or policy, or a backdoored checkpoint could produce a policy that behaves normally in the usual regime and fails in a trigger regime. Surrogates and weights are a new asset class with little integrity control. (8) Fleet propagation (OP.C0602). One compromised or flawed policy deployed across many standardized microreactors gives a common-cause failure. (9) Availability and cloud dependence (AML.T0029, OP.C0601, OP.C0204). Loss of the agent forces fallback to manual operation, and skill fade makes that harder. (10) Model and design leakage (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025). Surrogates and policies encode proprietary reactor physics and design data. Overall severity depends on keeping the AI outside the protection function and on rate-limited, hardware-bounded drum authority. Without those, a single bad output can start a reactivity or tilt transient.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, the main fragility is that the policy is never trained on the reactor. It is trained in a surrogate-of-a-simulator: Serpent Monte Carlo results are distilled into a fast emulator, and PPO optimizes against that emulator. Every reported result, including ~10 pcm criticality control and a tilt ratio of ~1.002, is therefore a statement about the surrogate's fidelity rather than the plant. The policy will exploit any surrogate error that pays reward, which is a standard RL pathology. Training data is also inherently scarce for a new-build microreactor (no operating history), covers only three discrete burnup states, and carries Monte Carlo statistical noise, nuclear-data uncertainty and geometry idealization. At deployment, drum-bank asymmetries, heat-pipe failures, temperature feedback, xenon transients, sensor bias or burnup between the trained points are all out-of-distribution inputs, and a DRL policy gives no guaranteed graceful degradation there. Finally, the source is a non-peer-reviewed preprint with stochastic training (PPO beats A2C, so results depend on seed and hyperparameters), and no qualification basis exists for a learned controller in a reactivity-control path.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Sim-to-real and surrogate-fidelity gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0302): the policy is optimal for the surrogate, not the reactor. Reward hacking of surrogate artifacts can produce drum configurations that look good in the emulator but are wrong in the real core, leading to unexpected reactivity or power-tilt excursions and local fuel or heat-pipe thermal stress. Because the policy may produce a confident output outside the training manifold, the failure is silent. (2) Burnup and operating-state coverage (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03): the policy was trained at three burnup points and so interpolates or extrapolates between or beyond them. Concept drift occurs as cross sections, drum worth and heat-pipe performance change with irradiation, and the surrogate is never retrained against real data. (3) Qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402): a stochastic, opaque neural policy trained with seed-dependent PPO has no static V&V basis. Repeatability across retrainings is poor, and no formal envelope exists for what actions it might choose. Over-trust of the 10 pcm headline figure (OP.C0101.04) and out-of-the-loop operators (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06) would erode manual criticality-search skills in a design intended for remote or autonomous operation. (4) Objective misalignment (OP.C0301): the reward covers criticality and tilt only, not drum-rate limits, margin to scram, thermal limits or xenon effects, so a policy that scores well can still be operationally unsafe.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Sensor and state-input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043): the policy consumes flux, power-sector and burnup estimates. Small crafted or spoofed perturbations to those measurements can push it into out-of-distribution regions, causing mis-positioned drums, induced tilt or a false 'critical' state. Because the policy is a differentiable function of its input, it is more brittle to such perturbations than a conventional PI or rule-based controller. (6) Supply chain and training-pipeline integrity (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020): the Serpent-derived datasets, surrogate model, RL libraries and checkpoint files are all injection points. A poisoned or backdoored surrogate (for example, one that is subtly wrong in a specific burnup regime) or a policy with a trigger condition would pass nominal validation yet misbehave in a chosen state. Surrogate data generated by third parties or shared across a fleet (OP.C0602) propagates the compromise. (7) Reconnaissance and proxy attacks (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0005): the preprint and open eVinci-like geometry make it easy to build a proxy surrogate and craft adversarial states offline, then transfer them. (8) Integrity of the control path (AML.T0029, AML.T0076): denial of inference or corruption of model weights forces fallback to manual control at a moment when operators are unpracticed. Together, the implicit weaknesses (silent OOD behavior, unvalidated surrogate, deskilling) give an adversary a window and a plausible-deniability cover, since anomalous drum motion can be blamed on 'AI drift'.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, a policy that sets control-drum positions on a heat-pipe microreactor is a high-value target. The drums are the main reactivity actuators, and the system is likely to be deployed at remote or lightly staffed sites, where autonomy is the selling point. The system is built on surrogate models of Serpent simulations, so the real attack surface is the whole pipeline: simulation inputs, surrogate training, reward design, policy artifacts, and the point where the policy's output reaches the drum actuators. A nation-state would probably go after the training and supply chain, or the operator's trust in a policy that appears to work, before it tried to attack the policy in real time. The policy's strong benchmark results (about 10 pcm, tilt around 1.002) also build trust that an adversary could exploit. The reported results come from a non-peer-reviewed preprint of surrogate-only training, so none of that performance has been demonstrated against real plant behavior.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Pipeline and supply-chain poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0059). The surrogate is trained on Serpent-derived data, and the reward is built from criticality and tilt targets. An insider or upstream compromise could bias the surrogate in a narrow region, such as a particular burnup state or drum configuration. It could also embed a backdoor trigger (T0043.004) in the policy, or tilt the reward subtly. The policy would still pass nominal validation, because the validation metrics (keff error, tilt ratio) are exactly what the poisoner leaves intact. The consequence is safe-looking drum setpoints that produce unsafe power peaking, reduced thermal margin, or localized heat-pipe stress, concentrated where verification is thin. (2) Sensor and observation manipulation (T0015, T0043). A DRL policy reacts to its state inputs. Falsified or perturbed in-core or ex-core measurements, such as power, temperature, or burnup estimates, could steer the policy into drum moves that are hazardous or that mask a real tilt. An adversary does not need to break the control system if it can fool the policy's picture of the state. (3) Model theft and insider access (T0024.002, T0035, T0044, T0012). Policy weights and surrogate models encode design-sensitive core physics. Exfiltrating them gives a proxy model (T0005) for staging attacks offline and may leak proprietary reactor characteristics. (4) Remote operation and updates (OP.C0601, OP.C0602). Retraining, redeployment, or fleet-wide model propagation across many microreactors is a single point of compromise with cross-site consequences. A signed, controlled update path is essential, and a weak one is a very efficient attack surface. (5) Denial and degradation (T0029, T0031). Forcing the system to hand off to manual control could be used to time a physical or cyber attack around the loss of the optimizer, or to induce operator error during the transition. IMPLICIT, exploitable by an adversary. (a) Sim-to-real and distribution gap (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). There is no operating fleet data for a new-build design. Surrogate error, burnup dynamics, drum-worth changes, xenon and temperature feedbacks, and as-built deviations all create out-of-distribution states in which the policy behaves unpredictably. The adversary can wait for or induce those states. (b) Opacity and non-determinism (OP.C0401, C0402.01, C0402.02). A neural policy cannot be inspected for hidden triggers or tamper, so the usual configuration-control and review practices cannot confirm integrity. Training-time randomness also makes it hard to distinguish a tampered retrain from a normal one. (c) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.01, C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102). Operators who defer to a policy with an excellent track record gradually lose the skill and vigilance needed to catch slow tilt drift. A long run of benign behavior is the best cover for a latent sabotage. (d) Governance gaps (OP.C0501, C0503, C0504). There is no accepted qualification route for a DRL controller in a safety-significant role, and security regulations were not written with learned controllers in mind. In the worst case the policy could be treated as an optimization aid without the cyber-security rigor of an I&C system. The main mitigations are keeping the policy advisory or bounded by an independent, deterministic, non-AI protection and interlock layer (so even a compromised policy cannot command unsafe drum positions), plus provenance control for the training data and artifacts, and runtime out-of-distribution monitoring.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the surrogate sim-to-real gap, pipeline poisoning, sensor manipulation, opacity/qualification gaps and operator deskilling. I kept the distinct threats of model theft, fleet update propagation and denial of the agent, and dropped speculative or weakly supported codes (cloud dependence beyond the update path, AML.T0031, AML.T0012, AML.T0044, AML.T0025).

evidence.citation: "Multistep Criticality Search and Power Shaping in Microreactors with Reinforcement Learning," arXiv (preprint by Radaideh et al.; the authors later published a version in Nuclear Science and Engineering, 2025)
evidence.note: This arXiv version has not been peer reviewed. The authors built surrogate models of high-fidelity Serpent simulations for a Westinghouse eVinci-motivated heat-pipe microreactor. They used the surrogates to train PPO and A2C policies that set drum positions at three burnup levels. PPO held criticality within about 10 pcm and kept the hextant power tilt ratio near 1.002, while A2C performed only modestly.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoning or a compromised fleet update, or a spoofed-state attack, that drives harmful control-drum moves (reactivity or power-tilt excursions, fuel and heat-pipe stress); independent deterministic protection should bound this below a radiological release, so it falls just short of the top score.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real gaps and out-of-distribution failures of a surrogate-trained policy are likely to recur once the plant is in poorly covered regimes, but the adversarial paths (backdoors, update compromise) depend on specific pipeline conditions, and independent protection may mask the effect.

exploitability.why: The most damaging adversarial paths need privileged access to the training pipeline, the model supply chain, the remote update channel, or plant sensor inputs, which generally calls for an insider position or well-resourced actor; only denial and some input perturbation need less.

affected_users.why: A compromised or flawed policy pushed through the remote update path to standardized microreactors is a common-cause, cross-site failure, and even a single plant's drum commands affect the whole core and coupled systems.

discoverability.why: Sim-to-real gaps, adversarial-state fragility, poisoning and model extraction are well documented for this class of AI system, and the public preprint on an eVinci-like design reveals the approach, the training regime (three burnup states) and the reward structure; only system-specific internals remain hidden.

use_case: Physics-informed convolutional neural network (using a Kirchhoff-Helmholtz integral constraint) that reconstructs the temperature field in the solid region of a prismatic high-temperature gas reactor fuel assembly. It uses readings from sensors in only a few cooling channels, and it can also detect blockage in a cooling channel that has no sensor. The aim is non-invasive monitoring of hot spots where thermocouples are unreliable.
incurred_insecurity:
This physics-informed CNN reconstructs solid-region temperatures and infers blockage in unsensed channels from a handful of cooling-channel sensors, in the places where thermocouples are unreliable. It therefore creates a hard-to-cross-check virtual sensor whose main threats are manipulation of its sparse inputs, tampering with its weights and simulation-derived training pipeline, and silent, confident error from the sim-to-real gap, drift, and ambiguous blockage inference. Operator over-trust and a missing qualification route turn these into undetected hot spots or spurious derates if the tool moves from advisory use toward margin or inspection decisions.

Sparse-sensor input manipulation -- adversarial
Because the network extrapolates a whole field from a few channel readings, small coordinated spoofing, biasing or replay of those signals moves the reconstruction in a smooth, self-consistent and credible way. The result is a masked real hot spot or blockage, or a fabricated blockage alarm that triggers needless derates or inspections.

Model and training-pipeline tampering -- adversarial
Poisoned simulation or surrogate data, altered weights or constraint kernels, or a trigger-conditioned backdoor can suppress hot-spot indication in a localized region or cooling regime. It would pass aggregate validation because no ground truth exists at the hot spot, and it could lie dormant until timed around an outage or transient.

Design leakage and monitoring-path foothold -- adversarial
Theft of the weights or training data exposes the assembly geometry, sensor layout and thermal behaviour, which lets an adversary build a proxy and tune input perturbations offline. A monitoring server that ingests plant instrumentation data is also a new OT/IT pathway for access to plant-data networks or for denial of the monitoring layer.

Sim-to-real gap and drift -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained and validated on simulated or surrogate data with no real prismatic-core hot-spot or blockage examples, so irradiation-changed graphite conductivity, bypass flow, geometry tolerances, burnup power shapes and new cooling regimes push it out of distribution. It then returns a smooth but biased field that understates peak fuel temperature, and no ground-truth channel exists to reveal the error. An adversary could hide real degradation or a manipulation as ordinary model error, or time actions to post-refuelling or new-regime windows when error is largest.

Blockage-inference ambiguity and rarity -- implicit, exploitable
Inverse non-uniqueness and the rarity of real blockages mean that sensor drift, conductivity change, partial blockages or power-shape shifts can mimic or mask a blockage signature. This gives uncharacterized false negatives on a safety-relevant fault and false alarms that erode trust. An adversary could craft or exploit conditions that look like benign confounders to conceal a real blockage, or provoke false alarms to desensitize operators.

Over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A clean, physics-branded full-field map invites operators to treat it as ground truth. The advisory tool can drift into a de facto margin input and erode thermocouple and core-physics cross-checks. An adversary can rely on that misplaced trust and lowered vigilance to make a manipulated output go unchallenged.

Opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The soft physics constraint gives no guarantee and little documented uncertainty quantification, regulators have no established route for NN inference in monitoring roles, and retraining and non-deterministic training complicate configuration control. Malicious or benign model changes can therefore escape change management, so an adversary could slip in a tampered model version that looks like routine retraining.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an O&M monitoring tool that infers solid-region temperatures, including hot spots in prismatic HTGR fuel, from a handful of coolant-channel sensors and flags blockage in unsensed channels. The main downstream hazard is a false-negative or falsely smooth reconstruction. Operators or a fuel-performance and margin-to-limit process might then rely on a field they cannot independently check, because thermocouples in those locations are unreliable by premise. Real harm needs several things to fail together: the reconstruction is wrong, the independent protection system (core outlet temperature, power and flow trips, neutron flux) does not catch it, and operators or the surveillance program accept the output as a margin assessment. Existing practice mitigates this if the tool stays advisory, but the key engineering concern is that the 'unreliable ground truth' rationale removes the usual cross-check. Validation is also based on simulation-derived data and a published heated-channel case, so the gap between demonstration and qualified use is large.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Generalization and data scarcity: no operating prismatic HTGR fleet gives abundant labelled field data, so training and validation rest on simulated or surrogate data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203). The physics-informed constraint, a Kirchhoff-Helmholtz integral formulation, assumes boundary conditions, material properties and a heat-transfer model. Irradiation-driven graphite conductivity change, gap and contact resistance, bypass flow, fuel-block cracking or bowing, and sensor placement not seen in training violate those assumptions. The result is a smooth, plausible but biased field that understates peak fuel temperature (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (2) Blockage detection from sparse sensors has a low base rate and an ambiguity problem. Few real blockages exist to test against (OP.C0202). Other causes, such as sensor drift, conductivity change or power-shape shifts, can mimic or mask a blockage signature, giving false negatives for a safety-relevant condition or false alarms that erode trust (OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102). (3) Human factors: operators may over-rely on a clean, physics-branded temperature map, or an advisory tool may gradually become a de facto margin input (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0301). The physics constraint can also give false confidence that the output is 'guaranteed' (OP.C0401, OP.C0403). Uncertainty quantification is not documented. (4) Qualification gap: regulators have no established route for NN-based inference feeding monitoring or margin decisions (OP.C0501, OP.C0504), and retraining or model updates complicate configuration control (OP.C0502, OP.C0402).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Sensor-input manipulation or spoofing: because the network extrapolates from few channels, small coordinated perturbations or chaff to those readings can move the reconstructed field a lot (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0046). An attacker could mask a real blockage or hot spot, or raise a spurious blockage alarm to trigger unnecessary derates or inspections (AML.T0031, AML.T0048). The sparse-sensor design makes this high-leverage. (b) Supply-chain or model tampering of weights, training and simulation datasets, or physics-constraint code, including a backdoor that suppresses hot-spot indication under a trigger condition (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0076). Poisoned simulation or surrogate data is hard to detect because no ground truth exists at the hot spot. (c) The monitoring and data path between plant instrumentation and the model is a new IT/OT attack surface. Denial of the service (AML.T0029) removes a monitoring layer, and compromise could provide lateral movement into plant-data networks (AML.T0012). (d) Model and design leakage: weights and the training data reveal fuel-assembly geometry, sensor layout and thermal behaviour, informing where an attacker should perturb (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0037). Consequence class: undetected local overheating, with fuel or graphite degradation and reduced safety margin, and a degraded ability to find coolant-flow anomalies. Defence in depth (independent trips, conservative limits, periodic inspection) should limit direct physical consequence if the tool stays advisory. The exposure is greatest where it is used to justify relaxed margins or reduced inspection.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is a sparse-sensor field-reconstruction (inverse) problem where a CNN with a Kirchhoff-Helmholtz integral constraint is trained almost certainly on simulated data (CFD/conduction solutions of an idealized prismatic assembly) and validated against a simulated MLP baseline. The physics constraint buys interpolation accuracy, but the architecture is only as good as the assumed boundary conditions, material properties (graphite conductivity changes with irradiation, temperature, and annealing), and the sensor-to-grid mapping. Since there is essentially no operational HTGR hot-spot ground truth (the reason thermocouples are being replaced), the model cannot be validated in the very regime it is meant to serve. The blockage-detection function is an under-determined inference: the network must infer a fault in an unsensed channel from indirect, smooth thermal signatures, so the output depends on priors baked into synthetic training and could be confidently wrong. The exposure sits in the model, its simulated provenance and the sensor input channel, not in the plant around it.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and provenance gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0202): training and validation use simulated fields and idealized heated-channel cases, with no blockage or hot-spot examples from real prismatic cores. The failure mechanism is that the model performs well in-distribution but misreconstructs under real geometry tolerances, bypass flow, and non-modeled heat sources. The dependent function is hot-spot monitoring and the margin/limit decisions based on it. The consequence is under-estimated peak fuel/graphite temperatures, with fuel-integrity safety implications. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302, .01, .02, .03): burnup-dependent power shapes, graphite conductivity change under irradiation, control-rod positions, and new cooling regimes are not covered by training, so the physics residual is evaluated against stale material and boundary assumptions. The model drifts silently because there is no ground-truth channel to detect it. (3) Blockage-detection limits (OP.C0403, OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03): inverse non-uniqueness means different blockage locations, partial blockages, or conduction-path changes can give similar sparse readings. This yields false negatives, which is a safety problem, and false positives, which cause unnecessary outages. The soft physics constraint also gives little uncertainty quantification, which hampers qualification (OP.C0501, OP.C0303). (4) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102): a smooth full-field map looks authoritative, which encourages over-trust and can erode retained thermocouple/core-physics cross-checks (skill fade). (5) Training non-determinism and repeatability (OP.C0402.01) complicate regulatory qualification (OP.C0504).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Sensor-channel manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031): because the network is trained on only a few channel readings, an adversary who can tamper with those few sensor feeds, or a compromised acquisition layer, can craft small perturbations. A physics-constrained network interpolates smoothly, so false hot spots are suppressed or a spurious blockage is reported, concealing a real fault or provoking a trip. The dependency is the sparse-sensor input integrity; the consequence is a masked thermal excursion or a spurious shutdown. Sparsity amplifies leverage per sensor. (b) Supply-chain and model-integrity compromise (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0076): poisoned simulation datasets, tampered physics-solver or ML libraries, or altered weights or constraint kernels could bias reconstructions in a localized region while passing aggregate validation, because few real checks exist. (c) Model/data exfiltration and reconnaissance (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0007, AML.T0000): published architecture and the reactor design data behind training could help an adversary build a proxy (AML.T0005) to tune sensor-spoofing attacks offline, and reveal design-sensitive thermal characteristics. (d) Implicit weaknesses an attacker could time around: unmonitored drift windows after refueling or new regimes, when the model's error is largest and operators are least able to detect a discrepancy.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is a virtual-sensor layer that fills in temperatures where physical instruments are unreliable, so operators will gradually treat its output as ground truth for hot spots and blockage in unmonitored channels. That concentrates trust in a single, hard-to-audit inference path. An adversary, insider or external, does not need to damage the reactor. They only need to make the reconstruction look nominal while a real hot spot or blockage develops, or to make it cry blockage and trigger needless derates. The few sparse sensor inputs are the whole attack surface, and an inferred field is much harder to cross-check than a direct thermocouple reading. Whether a nation-state would bother depends on the architecture. If the output only advises, it is a low-priority target. If it displaces thermocouple verification or feeds protection or operating-limit decisions, it becomes a quiet, deniable way to hide degradation or to time other actions.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Input manipulation: the CNN extrapolates a whole solid-region field from a handful of cooling-channel sensors. Spoofing, biasing or replaying those few signals (by an insider with I&C access, through a compromised data historian, or via a supply-chain compromise of sensor or acquisition firmware) shifts the reconstruction in a physically plausible way. Because the physics-informed constraint makes outputs look self-consistent, tampered inputs yield smooth, credible fields rather than obvious garbage. The blockage-detection function adds a second lever: forged inputs can mask a real blockage in an unsensored channel or fabricate one. The consequence is undetected local overheating and fuel or graphite degradation, or unnecessary shutdowns and loss of confidence. (2) Model and pipeline integrity: the trained weights, boundary-condition and material-property configuration, and the training-data pipeline (simulation-derived data) are insider-accessible artifacts. Subtle poisoning or a backdoor trigger, for example under a specific cooling regime, would be invisible in routine validation and could be dormant until an adversary times it around a maintenance outage or transient. Supply-chain compromise of the ML framework or a vendor-delivered model is also plausible. (3) Stepping stone: a monitoring server that ingests plant sensor data creates a new network pathway between OT data and IT or analytics environments, especially if it is cloud-hosted or vendor-maintained. The model also exposes its design basis, since the geometry and thermal-hydraulic parameters are sensitive. Model-extraction or data-theft risk is modest, but it supports reconnaissance of the plant's monitoring blind spots. IMPLICIT, and exploitable by an adversary. (4) Automation trust and skill fade: as operators rely on the virtual sensor where thermocouples are unreliable, the independent check that would reveal manipulation or error erodes. Attackers can time actions to when vigilance is lowest. (5) Generalization and drift: the model is trained and validated on simulated cooling regimes. Real plants have aging, irradiation-changed conductivity, bypass flow, asymmetric loading and sensor degradation, and all of these push it out of distribution. Reconstruction error can then be silent and confident, giving an adversary cover to hide a real degradation as model error. Blockage detection is a rare-event problem with little real operational data, so false negatives and false positives are poorly characterized. (6) Qualification and opacity gaps: there is no established regulatory pathway for a learned model in a monitoring role, limited explainability, and weak change control for retraining, so model modifications, malicious or benign, may escape configuration management and detection.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sparse-input manipulation, model/data poisoning, the sim-to-real gap, over-trust, and the qualification gap. I dropped unsupported or weakly grounded codes (cloud dependency, chaff data, direct data-from-local-system, OP.C0301 goal misalignment, OP.C0101.05 disuse) and merged overlapping drift, scarcity and blockage-ambiguity items.

evidence.citation: "Application of a Physics-Informed Convolutional Neural Network for Monitoring the Temperature Fields in High-Temperature Gas Reactors," Nuclear Science and Engineering (Taylor & Francis / American Nuclear Society), 2025; record hosted by DOE OSTI
evidence.note: The journal article builds a physics-informed CNN and tests it against a purely data-driven multilayer perceptron on a heated-channel case, where the CNN cuts errors by orders of magnitude. It then shows the CNN reconstructing HTGR fuel-assembly temperature fields across several cooling regimes and detecting blockage in a cooling channel with no sensor.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is tampering or input manipulation that masks a real hot spot or blockage in a high-temperature reactor core, which erodes fuel-temperature margin and could contribute to fuel damage; it is advisory, so the harm is indirect and stops short of a certain radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real drift and sparse-sensor extrapolation error recur reliably once the model is out of distribution, but deliberate masking of a hot spot depends on specific conditions such as a localized region, a cooling regime, or timing.

exploitability.why: Manipulating sensor inputs, poisoning the training pipeline, or altering weights generally requires OT/IT foothold, insider or supply-chain access, and some knowledge of the model, which is well beyond routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: A misleading virtual sensor affects hot-spot monitoring and derate or inspection decisions across a whole fuel assembly or core region, but it is an advisory layer and does not directly propagate across coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability classes (adversarial inputs, poisoning, sim-to-real gap, over-trust) are well documented in the open literature, and the published paper reveals the architecture and sensing approach, but a capable outsider would still need partial knowledge of the specific deployment's sensor layout and configuration.

use_case: U-Net convolutional autoencoder that denoises noisy sinograms and fills in incomplete ones from passive gamma emission tomography (PGET) measurements of spent fuel assemblies. It also speeds up Monte Carlo simulation of PGET data. The aim is to give safeguards inspectors complete, usable sinograms for verifying that no fuel pins are missing or substituted in stored spent fuel.
incurred_insecurity:
A U-Net that denoises and inpaints PGET sinograms sits directly in the evidence chain for concluding that no spent-fuel pins are missing or substituted. Because it is trained to emit complete, plausible-looking assemblies, it can turn 'not measured' into 'looks normal'. The main threats are anomaly-suppressing hallucination, input evasion that exploits the learned prior, training-data or model poisoning, output tampering, sim-to-real data weakness, surrogate circularity, and unqualified over-trust.

Hallucinated or smoothed-over anomalies -- implicit, exploitable
The autoencoder fills gaps with a prior learned from intact assemblies, so it can render a missing or low-intensity substitute pin as normal or fabricate spurious features, because it is rewarded for image similarity rather than for missing-pin detection sensitivity. The result is a false negative on diversion or substitution, or a false alarm, in an output that looks like a complete measurement. An adversary can rely on this bias by arranging which regions go unmeasured, knowing the gaps will be completed as normal.

Evasion through crafted input -- adversarial
A host state or operator who knows the model class, possibly via a proxy built from published architectures and papers, can shape source geometry, shielding, scan gaps or noise so that the inpainting prior reconstructs a diversion as an intact pin pattern. The anomaly then disappears from the output without any attack on the detector itself.

Training-data and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor who influences the mostly simulated training corpus, the surrogate, or the weights could plant a bias or backdoor trigger that makes specific missing-pin or substituted-pin signatures reconstruct as normal. The opaque network makes this indistinguishable from ordinary denoising, so a safeguards conclusion would rest on compromised evidence.

Output and data-chain tampering -- adversarial
Altering raw or reconstructed sinograms, swapping the model file, or presenting a falsified reconstruction as authenticated inspector output undermines the verification record, because measured and synthesised pixels are not marked or distinguishable. Injected noise could also force false alarms and erode confidence in the verification regime.

Sim-to-real gap and data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Training leans on Monte Carlo data with little real PGET data and almost no verified diversion cases, so the model is unvalidated on real detector response, dead channels, fuel types, burnup and cooling-time ranges, and rare substitution patterns, and out-of-distribution inputs fail silently. An adversary could choose configurations outside the training envelope, or act around retraining and version changes, where the model's behaviour is least characterised.

Surrogate circularity -- implicit, exploitable
The same fast network accelerates Monte Carlo generation and can feed training or calibration data back into itself or into other tools, so bias compounds and validation by image similarity diverges from the safeguards objective. A single compromised or biased surrogate could propagate skewed reference data into other verification tools' qualification.

Automation trust and missing qualification -- implicit, exploitable
Millisecond, clean-looking output with no per-pixel uncertainty, no provenance marking and no detection-probability or false-alarm characterisation invites inspectors to skip raw-data review, and retraining can shift behaviour silently. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust and on periods of heavy workload to get an anomaly past review.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a safeguards-engineering view, PGET is an independent verification tool, so a U-Net that denoises and inpaints sinograms sits directly in the evidence chain for a diversion or substitution conclusion. The inspector acts on the reconstructed image, and a learned prior that fills missing sinogram regions with plausible fuel-pin patterns can synthesize the pin-by-pin evidence that was never measured. Bad output has two directions. A missing or substituted pin could be hidden (false negative), or a spurious anomaly could trigger a false-alarm investigation. The physical safeguards that must also fail are the inspector's skepticism, raw-data review, complementary measurements (Cherenkov viewing, gamma spectrometry, declared operator records), and the IAEA's authentication and evaluation procedures. Those are strong in principle, but a clean-looking image invites automation bias, especially under time pressure in a pool or cask-loading campaign.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Hallucinated or over-smoothed content (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03): inpainting fills gaps with training-set statistics, so a missing pin or low-intensity substitute (dummy rod, older or cooler pin) can be rendered as a normal pin, or noise can be rendered as an anomaly. The U-Net is trained to produce complete sinograms, so it is biased toward 'looks like a complete assembly'. This is a goal misalignment (OP.C0301): visual plausibility is rewarded, not safeguards detection sensitivity. (2) Data scarcity and provenance (OP.C0202, OP.C0701, OP.C0201.01/.02): real PGET data on spent fuel with known diversions barely exist, so training leans on Monte Carlo simulation, and the same network accelerates that simulation. Simulation-to-reality gaps and a circular loop (a surrogate trained on simulation, then generating more training data) leave a model that is unvalidated on real substitution cases, new fuel types, burnup/cooling-time ranges, detector geometries, or rare diversion patterns. (3) Drift and heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01/.03): different assemblies, detector collimators, count times, and facilities change the noise and attenuation statistics, and out-of-distribution inputs fail silently. (4) Opacity and qualification (OP.C0401, OP.C0303, OP.C0501): no uncertainty quantification or detection-probability characterisation exists for the inpainted regions, and this does not fit conventional safeguards instrument qualification, which requires known false-alarm and non-detection rates. (5) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102): inspectors see a clean image and stop checking the raw data. Machine-learned reconstruction of this kind also gets used for other evidence workflows with no established detection-limit statements. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) A State or operator adversary with knowledge of the public model class can exploit the inpainting prior. They could shape which pins or regions are shielded, placed, or measured with gaps so that the network completes them as normal (evasion by crafting inputs, AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031), using proxy models trained on public papers (AML.T0000, AML.T0005). (7) Poisoned training or simulation data, a tampered model, or a compromised software toolchain could embed a backdoor that makes specific substitution signatures vanish (AML.T0020, AML.T0018, AML.T0010, AML.T0043.004). This is especially dangerous because the reviewer cannot tell it from normal denoising. (8) Injected noise or tampered sinograms before the model (AML.T0046, AML.T0059) could also force false alarms and erode confidence in the verification regime. Consequences: undetected diversion or substitution at spent-fuel storage (a safeguards-conclusion failure), or false-positive anomalies that waste inspection resources and create diplomatic or licensing disputes. Mitigations in existing practice (retained raw data, independent instruments, authenticated chains of custody, inspector judgment) work only if the AI output is treated as an aid and never as the sole evidence.

ai_engineer.argument: This is an image-to-image U-Net trained mostly on Monte Carlo-simulated sinograms, with a small amount of real PGET data, and it is used to produce the evidence from which inspectors conclude that no pins are missing or substituted. A generative inpainting model optimizes for plausible, statistically typical reconstructions, so it tends to fill missing or noisy regions with whatever looks like an intact assembly. The failure it is least able to tolerate is therefore the one the inspector most needs to see: a real anomaly such as a removed or substituted pin, which is rare in training data and is exactly what the prior smooths away. Fragility sits at the sim-to-real gap, the rarity of diversion-like examples, the lack of per-pixel uncertainty or provenance marking, and the fact that the same fast surrogate serves both inference and simulation, so any bias is reinforced across both uses.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Hallucinated or smoothed-over anomalies (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403). The AI failure is that the autoencoder inpaints missing sinogram regions with a learned prior of intact assemblies and can suppress or fabricate pin-level features. The safeguards verification of pin presence depends on this. The consequence is a false-negative on diversion or substitution, or false positives that erode confidence, with the output looking like a complete measurement. (2) Sim-to-real and distribution shift (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). Training is dominated by simulated data, so the model may not cover real detector response, dead or misaligned collimator channels, fuel types, burnup and cooling-time spectra, water attenuation, or pin-lattice geometries. Inference on out-of-distribution assemblies yields confident but wrong reconstructions. Because real data and verified-diversion data are scarce, the evaluation cannot show that the model preserves the weak signatures it exists to protect (OP.C0202, OP.C0701, OP.C0701.02). (3) Surrogate simulation circularity (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). If the same networks speed up Monte Carlo generation and are then trained or validated on that output, errors compound, and the validation metric (image similarity) differs from the safeguards objective (detecting a missing pin) (OP.C0301). (4) Automation trust and qualification (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). Millisecond, clean-looking output encourages over-trust, and opacity prevents inspectors from knowing which pixels were measured and which were generated. There is no established AI qualification route for authenticating evidence in a licensing or safeguards context, so the evidence's standing could be challenged either way. (5) Retraining and repeatability (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0302.01). Retraining after detector or campaign changes can silently shift behavior.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data or model poisoning and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003). An adversary with access to the simulation corpus, the surrogate, or the weights could bias the model to normalize missing-pin signatures or embed a trigger, which would be hard to detect given the opacity. (7) Evasion through crafted input (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0043.004). A host state could shape the physical source geometry or the incomplete-data pattern, for example by exploiting known gaps or detector dropouts, so that the autoencoder reconstructs the diversion as normal. The mechanism targets the model's prior rather than the detector. (8) Tampering with the inspection data chain (AML.T0031, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). Manipulated raw or reconstructed sinograms, or a swapped model file, would undermine the integrity of the verification record. (9) Model and data reconnaissance (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0013). Published architectures and data make it easier to build a proxy and tune attacks (AML.T0005, AML.T0043.002), which supports the evasion threat above.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this tool sits directly between raw detector data and the inspector's verification judgment on whether pins are missing or substituted in spent fuel. That makes it a high-value place to concentrate trust. An inpainting autoencoder is built to produce plausible, complete-looking output where data is absent, so it can hide the very anomaly (a diverted or dummy pin) that the inspector is looking for. A diverting state or insider does not need to defeat the safeguards system outright. They only need to degrade, bias or time-exploit a step that reconstructs what the physics did not measure. The easier route is probably not a nation-state attack on the model itself. It is exploiting the ordinary habit of trusting clean images, and the opacity of a learned prior, to explain away or smooth over an anomaly.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data or model tampering (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004): the training set is mostly Monte Carlo-simulated sinograms plus a few real measurements. An insider or supply-chain actor who influences the simulation set, or who plants a backdoor trigger, could make the network learn to reconstruct a particular missing-pin or substituted-pin signature as normal. Inspectors and the inspected party share this pipeline, so the question of who controls the training data and weights is a safeguards question, not just an IT one. (2) Evasion through the input (AML.T0015, T0043): an adversary who knows the denoiser's behaviour could shape the measurement, for example through partial shielding, incomplete scans or an engineered noise pattern. The model would then fill gaps with a plausible full-assembly picture, so the anomaly vanishes from the output. Inpainting turns 'we could not measure this' into 'looks fine', which is a fail-safe-to-fail-silent inversion. (3) Output integrity (AML.T0031, T0076, T0073): in-memory or file tampering, or presenting a falsified reconstruction as authenticated inspector output, would exploit the fact that a human cannot easily distinguish measured from synthesised pixels. Without provenance marking, the reconstructed sinogram can be mistaken for evidence. (4) Acceleration of Monte Carlo simulation is a secondary vector: a compromised surrogate could produce biased reference data used to qualify or calibrate other verification tools (OP.C0603, OP.C0201.02).

IMPLICIT (adversary can time around them). Hallucinated fine structure or erased real features (OP.C0304.01, C0304.03) are inherent to autoencoders trained on mostly simulated data (OP.C0201.01, C0302.01), so real-world drift in detector, fuel type, burnup, cooling time or geometry (OP.C0302.03) is expected. Real diversion cases are essentially absent from training data (OP.C0701, C0202), so the model has never seen the rare event that matters, and its validation says little about it. Automation trust and complacency (OP.C0101.04, C0102, C0101.06) matter here: millisecond clean output encourages inspectors to skip the raw sinogram, and skills for reading degraded data fade. Opacity and weak qualification regimes (OP.C0401, C0501, C0504, C0303) mean there is no agreed basis to say the reconstruction is safeguards-grade. An adversary can wait for a version change or retraining, or for a period of heavy workload, when scrutiny is lowest. Data and software governance for what is partly proprietary, facility-sensitive measurement data (OP.C0505, C0502) adds exposure to exfiltration of assembly signatures (AML.T0025, T0024.001), which gives an adversary a map of what the inspector's tooling can and cannot see.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on inpainting-driven anomaly suppression, input evasion, poisoning/backdoor, output integrity, sim-to-real scarcity and automation trust. I dropped the security specialist's lone exfiltration of assembly signatures (AML.T0025, AML.T0024.001) as weakly argued and peripheral to the use case, and kept the reconnaissance/proxy pathway only as an enabler of evasion.

evidence.citation: "Enhancing passive gamma emission tomography data with deep learning," Annals of Nuclear Energy (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper trains CNNs to map incomplete or noisy PGET sinograms to their full versions. It tests them on both simulated and real measurements, covering sinogram denoising and inpainting, with execution times on the order of milliseconds. An earlier INMM conference version describes the same work as a U-Net autoencoder (https://resources.inmm.org/sites/default/files/2023-07/finalpaper_167_0426105910.pdf).

damage.why: The worst credible threat (anomaly-suppressing reconstruction or poisoning that makes a pin diversion or substitution look intact) amounts to safeguards falsification and loss of assurance on material control in spent fuel.

reproducibility.why: Inpainting bias toward 'normal' and silent out-of-distribution failure are inherent to the model class and recur reliably once gaps or atypical configurations are present, though the specific outcome depends on the geometry and the training envelope.

exploitability.why: Credible exploitation needs a host state or operator with control over the measurement setup, or an insider or supply-chain position for poisoning and tampering, plus enough modeling capability (e.g. a proxy model) to shape inputs; this is not routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Impact spans every assembly verification that relies on the tool and can propagate through surrogate-generated data into other verification tools' qualification, but it remains confined to the safeguards verification chain for stored spent fuel rather than facility-wide operations.

discoverability.why: The architecture, the inpainting and denoising approach and its simulation-heavy training are published in open literature, and hallucination and out-of-distribution weaknesses of autoencoders are well documented for this class, so a capable outsider can infer the weakness readily.

use_case: Bidirectional LSTM sequence-classification network trained on historical Integrated Dry Route (IDR) process batch data from UF6-to-UO2 conversion. It predicts whether a batch's UO2 output will meet the fluorine-content quality specification faster than the current off-line factory test. It is proposed as a step toward a digital twin and on-line kiln feedback for responsive fuel-feedstock manufacturing.
incurred_insecurity:
A Bi-LSTM classifier that predicts fluorine-in-UO2 batch quality from 1685 historical IDR batches would, once trusted, become the quiet gate on feedstock release and a stepping stone toward on-line kiln feedback. Its weaknesses are mostly implicit: thin, imbalanced single-site data, drift, a retrospective-to-closed-loop qualification gap, opacity, and erosion of the independent off-line test. The adversarial threats are integrity attacks on data and model, evasion through manipulated process inputs, and a new IT/OT and exfiltration surface from the digital-twin link.

Data and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor who alters historian records, assay labels, operator-derived features, retraining sets or model weights can implant a bias or a backdoor-style trigger that makes off-spec fluorine batches classify as satisfactory. The opaque Bi-LSTM makes such a trigger hard to detect, and out-of-spec UO2 would then move on to pelleting and sintering.

Sensor-input evasion -- adversarial
Falsified or biased temperature, flow or gas-composition streams can hold the input sequence inside the 'good' region while the real chemistry is off-spec, or trigger false rejections that deny production. If the prediction becomes the quality record, the same manipulation also hides deliberate off-spec production and confuses traceability.

Digital-twin IT/OT bridge and data theft -- adversarial
Linking OT kiln data to analytics or ML tooling, possibly cloud- or vendor-hosted, creates a pivot path toward process networks. If outputs ever drive kiln setpoints, a compromised model or host becomes an indirect actuator on a UF6/HF process. Denying the AI service at a critical time can stall release decisions, and the model and process data expose proprietary conversion know-how.

Small-data and low base-rate blindness -- implicit, exploitable
With few defective batches, headline accuracy hides poor and unstable recall on the defects that matter, so false 'pass' calls go unmeasured for long periods. An adversary can hide a slow manipulation among rare, statistically invisible failures.

Drift and single-site generalisation failure -- implicit, exploitable
Kiln refractory wear, UF6 feed impurity changes, recalibration, recipe changes and maintenance shift the process away from the single historical window the model was trained on, so it degrades silently and does not transfer to other lines. An adversary can time tampering around known changes, or dress it up as drift, since the degradation is easy to blame.

Retrospective-to-closed-loop qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained on complete, cleaned, post-hoc batch records with a bidirectional architecture that needs the full sequence. Streaming, partial or noisy on-line inference and feedback into setpoints are therefore not covered by the validation, and a wrong call could push the kiln into regimes absent from training. An attacker can exploit a model qualified only as a passive classifier once it is quietly promoted to feedback, steering the process through its blind spots.

Label latency and noise -- implicit
Off-line assay error, sampling variance and delayed labels corrupt training and retraining, and if model predictions later decide which batches are tested, selection bias contaminates the next dataset. No realistic adversary gains much beyond what the poisoning threat already gives.

Opacity and non-repeatable training -- implicit, exploitable
Without calibrated uncertainty or causal explanation, and with seed-dependent retraining, engineers cannot tell whether a bad call came from drift, error or sabotage. This lets deliberate corruption of a retrained model pass as ordinary variation.

Erosion of the independent off-line check -- implicit, exploitable
Fast, usually correct predictions invite reduced sampling of the off-line fluorine test and skill fade among QA staff, turning the model into a single point of failure for product quality. An adversary can time tampering for when the lab check has been de-emphasised, relying on the complacency built by long runs of correct output.

nuclear_engineer.argument: As scoped, this is an advisory quality predictor for fluorine content in UO2 from an IDR kiln, and it sits next to a robust, independent barrier: the off-line factory test and the product specification still decide batch release. The main downstream risk is therefore gradual erosion of that barrier, not an immediate physical event. If the model is trusted to shorten or replace the off-line test, or later drives on-line kiln feedback (the stated digital-twin direction), a wrong 'satisfactory' call lets out-of-spec UO2 move on to pelleting and sintering. A wrong 'defective' call causes needless rework or scrap and wastes throughput. The consequence is mostly a quality, economic and fuel-performance problem (fluoride-related corrosion and sintering behaviour), plus possible criticality-control and material-accountancy side effects if batches are held, reworked or re-blended on model advice. The data are only 1685 batches from one route, and defective batches are likely rare, so the classifier's validity is narrow and fragile. Adversaries are not needed for it to fail, but they could exploit or time an attack around that fragility.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Small-data and low base-rate: with few defective batches, headline accuracy hides poor recall on the defects that matter, and the false-negative rate is unknown. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity: kiln refractory wear, feed UF6 or steam/hydrogen supply changes, instrument recalibration, recipe changes and maintenance cycles shift the process distribution. The model, trained on one historical window and one site's route, degrades silently, and it does not transfer to other lines or sites. (3) Concept and qualification mismatch: the training labels come from off-line test results, with their own measurement noise and sampling error. Offline retrospective validation does not show closed-loop behaviour, so a model qualified as a passive classifier could be quietly promoted to on-line feedback without safety-case rework. (4) Automation trust and skill fade: operators and QA staff who see fast, usually correct predictions may relax sampling frequency or skip confirmatory tests. This becomes a single point of failure for product quality once the independent check is thinned. (5) Opacity: a Bi-LSTM over raw process sequences gives little causal explanation, so engineers cannot tell whether a call rests on process physics or on spurious correlates such as operator-added features and batch ordering. Non-determinism across retraining makes requalification hard. (6) Cascading effects: feedback into kiln setpoints could push the process towards regimes absent from training, with possible effects on off-gas/HF handling, powder properties and moderator/hydrogen-related criticality controls.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Process-historian or sensor-data manipulation (evasion or chaff): falsified or biased temperature, flow or gas-composition streams can make a defective batch look satisfactory, or trigger false rejections that deny production. The same applies to the training pipeline (data poisoning, label tampering in the lab database) and to the model artifact or supply chain (backdoor trigger, poisoned retraining). A poisoned model could pass a defect class only under a specific process signature, which would be hard to detect given the opacity. (b) Quality-record integrity: the model's output could become the record of conformance, so manipulation could hide deliberate off-spec production or confuse batch accountancy and traceability. (c) New attack surface: a digital-twin link between OT kiln data and IT/ML tooling, possibly cloud-hosted or vendor-supported, opens a path from the corporate or ML environment toward process networks, and a denial-of-AI-service attack at a critical time could stall release decisions. (d) Information exposure: the data and model encode proprietary process know-how and possibly throughput indicators for a fuel-cycle facility. Mitigation largely rests on keeping the model advisory, keeping the off-line test as a statistically sampled independent check, drift monitoring, data-integrity controls, and a formal change process before any closed-loop use.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline standpoint, this is a small-data, imbalanced-label sequence classifier. It has about 1685 valid batches, and defective batches are presumably a small minority. The labels come from a slow off-line fluorine assay, so label provenance, latency and noise (assay variance, sampling location, batch-to-label alignment) are the core data issues. The 'valid batch' filtering and the operator-informed feature engineering embed human choices that may not hold on-line. The step from a retrospective batch classifier to on-line kiln feedback is a large qualification jump. Training data was complete, cleaned, post-hoc batch records, but inference would be on streaming, partial, possibly missing or noisy sensor data under changing equipment, feedstock and setpoints. The model gives no calibrated uncertainty and little explainability, and a Bi-LSTM is bidirectional, which means it needs the full sequence. Its use as a real-time or feedback predictor is therefore architecturally questionable, because future context cannot be available causally. The exposure is mainly in the data and lifecycle layers, with adversarial opportunities arising wherever the model is wired into the process historian and quality release.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Small-data/low-base-rate: few defective batches means unstable recall on the minority class, inflated headline accuracy and overfitting to batch-specific artefacts. The consequence is false 'pass' predictions, so off-spec UO2 (excess fluorine) could proceed downstream to pellet and fuel fabrication, which is a fuel-quality and safety-margin concern, or false 'fail' predictions that cause rework and throughput loss (OP.C0202, OP.C0302). (2) Drift/OOD: kiln refractory and wear, feedstock UF6 impurity variation, sensor recalibration, setpoint policy changes and seasonal effects shift the input distribution, and concept drift changes the relation between process signals and fluorine content. A single-site training set (Springfields) generalises poorly to other lines or sites (OP.C0302.01, .02, .03, OP.C0602). (3) Training/inference mismatch: the bidirectional architecture and batch-level feature engineering, which uses entire completed batch records, do not transfer to causal on-line feedback. This is a static versus dynamic qualification mismatch (OP.C0303). (4) Label latency and noise: fluorine assay error and delayed labels corrupt training and retraining, and if the model's own predictions later gate which batches get tested, selection bias contaminates the next dataset (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0301). (5) Opacity and non-repeatability: seed-dependent training and no uncertainty estimates make independent verification and licensing evidence hard, and encourage over-trust once the model is faster than the lab (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0501). Closed-loop kiln control would also add cascading fault propagation, where a wrong prediction changes process conditions, which creates further off-distribution inputs (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Data poisoning or integrity erosion of the historian, labels or retraining set, such as subtle bias in logged sensor values or assay results. Poisoning could create blind spots or a backdoor-like trigger pattern so off-spec batches are classified satisfactory (AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). (b) Evasion through manipulated live sensor or PLC inputs that keep the feature sequence in the 'good' region while the real chemistry is off-spec; this would also hide process sabotage from a monitor that operators have begun to trust (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). (c) Supply-chain or model-artifact tampering of weights, preprocessing code or ML libraries in the digital-twin toolchain (AML.T0010, AML.T0076). (d) Exfiltration of the model, features or process data, which exposes proprietary conversion know-how and the process-to-quality relationship (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035). (e) Connecting the on-line model to kiln feedback creates a new IT/OT attack path, where compromising the AI service could mean denial of the prediction (AML.T0029) or steering of process setpoints. Drift and thin data make it easy for an attacker to hide an attack inside normal model uncertainty, and attacks can be timed to when the model is known to be weakest, such as after a maintenance change or feedstock switch.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this classifier is an attractive stepping stone and a trust-concentration point, more than a direct target. It sits between process data and the release decision for UO2 feedstock. Once it is trusted to replace or shorten the slow off-line fluorine test, it becomes the quiet gate on product quality, and the lab test that was an independent check erodes. A nation-state or insider would more plausibly corrupt the data, the historian feed or the retraining pipeline than attack the model directly. The easier route to harm is to make the model confident and wrong at a chosen time, or to use its on-line feedback path as a bridge into kiln control. The non-adversarial weaknesses are also exploitable: a small, single-site dataset of 1685 batches, a low defect base rate, and the feasibility-study maturity level.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
1) Integrity attack on the data and model (adversarial; ATLAS AML.T0020, T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0043, T0031, T0059). An insider or supply-chain actor who can alter historian records, operator-derived features, or retraining sets could bias the classifier toward false 'satisfactory' calls. The model need not be hacked directly. Because the features include operator domain knowledge and raw process signals, small, plausible-looking shifts in sensor or label data could pass unnoticed. The dependent function is quality release of UO2 feedstock. The consequence is out-of-spec fluorine material entering fuel fabrication, which means product quality, downstream corrosion or chemistry problems, and possible loss of regulator confidence. Backdoor-style triggers (T0043.004) tied to particular process conditions would be hard to detect given the model's opacity (OP.C0401).

2) Erosion of independent verification and vigilance (implicit; OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102, C0101.01). Faster predictions invite reducing the off-line test sampling. Operators and QA staff lose practice with manual fluorine-trend interpretation. An adversary could time tampering for when the lab check has been de-emphasised, or for the long stretches of correct predictions that breed complacency. A low defect base rate (OP.C0202) makes silent failures statistically invisible for a long time.

3) Digital-twin and on-line feedback pathway as a new attack surface (OP.C0303, AML.T0053/T0112, T0012, T0091). The stated roadmap moves the model from advisory to kiln feedback. This creates a data path from IT/analytics into process control. If the model output ever drives setpoints, a compromised model or its host becomes an indirect actuator on a chemical process involving hazardous UF6/HF. Even in advisory mode, the analytics server and the data replication feeding it are a new IT-OT bridge and a pivot point for lateral movement, and they hold commercially sensitive process recipes. That also invites exfiltration of process IP (AML.T0025, T0035, T0048.004).

4) Implicit weaknesses an adversary could time around (OP.C0302.01/.02/.03, C0203, C0501, C0502, C0402). Drift from feed-quality changes, kiln wear, maintenance or recipe changes, or a new campaign will degrade a model trained on a single historical route. Tampering that mimics drift is then easy to explain away. Retraining without strong provenance, versioning or qualification, together with non-repeatable training, makes it hard to prove whether a bad prediction came from drift, error or sabotage. A feasibility-grade model has no AI-specific QA basis for safety-relevant use, so there is little baseline against which an anomaly would be flagged.

5) Realistic targeting. Direct attack on this use case is probably not worth a sophisticated actor's effort at present, because it is advisory and low-consequence. Its main risk is as a precedent. The architecture, data access and trust habits it establishes will carry over to higher-consequence models and to enrichment-adjacent or safeguards-relevant analytics, so security controls need to be designed in now.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on data/model integrity attacks, drift and small-data weakness, the advisory-to-closed-loop qualification gap, and erosion of the off-line test. I dropped the security specialist's 'precedent' point and pure-IT lateral-movement and credential codes (T0012, T0091, T0053, T0112) as not directly instantiated by this advisory classifier, and kept supply-chain, exfiltration and denial codes that were consistently raised.

evidence.citation: "A responsive integrated dry route for uranium hexafluoride conversion using machine intelligence," Elsevier (Energy Conversion and Management: X, Vol. 28, Article 101230, Oct 2025)
evidence.note: The authors built and tested a five-layer Bi-LSTM classifier on real industrial data from 1685 valid IDR batches at the Springfields UO2 production route. The model flags defective versus satisfactory batches by fluorine content, using features from raw process data and operator domain knowledge. They present it as a feasibility study for a responsive IDR digital twin, not as a full plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is data/model poisoning or sensor-input evasion that lets off-spec UO2 pass as satisfactory and hides deliberate off-spec production, with possible indirect actuation of a UF6/HF process if the model drives setpoints. That means quality-record falsification and a chemical process upset, but it stops short of a direct radiological release because downstream pelleting and sintering add further checks.

reproducibility.why: Silent drift, low base-rate blindness and the qualification gap occur reliably once the model is trusted or promoted to feedback. Targeted poisoning or evasion success depends on the attacker's access and on how much the model leans on the off-line check, so overall reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: The credible adversarial paths (altering historian records, labels or retraining sets, tampering with model weights, falsifying process sensor streams, pivoting through the IT/OT bridge) need insider or supply-chain access or a substantial OT intrusion. Routine external interaction is not enough.

affected_users.why: A compromised quality gate affects every batch released from the conversion line and the downstream fuel-fabrication steps, and traceability is confused. It is largely confined to one line or site, though, unless the digital-twin link propagates the compromise into coupled process systems.

discoverability.why: The class is well documented in the open literature (poisoning, drift, small-data blindness), and the published feasibility study reveals the model type and use case. Finding that a specific deployment is exposed or gating release needs partial inference from vendor, procurement or operational information.

use_case: Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) acting as a real-time virtual sensor in a nuclear digital twin. It maps operating inputs to spatially distributed thermal-hydraulic fields, such as pressure and turbulence, in the hot leg of a pressurized water reactor. It is trained on CFD simulation data. It stands in for physical sensors in hard-to-reach locations and supports condition monitoring for degradation such as erosion-corrosion.
incurred_insecurity:
A DeepONet virtual sensor trained only on CFD stands in for physical measurement at hard-to-reach PWR hot-leg locations and feeds condition monitoring for erosion-corrosion. It is advisory and not a protection input, so the main danger is a quiet, unverifiable single point of trust upstream of inspection and maintenance decisions on primary-system components. The main threats are a CFD-to-plant fidelity gap, proxy-versus-target mismatch, opacity and qualification gaps, over-trust, input-channel manipulation, training-data and model tampering, the twin's IT/OT pathway, and denial of the service.

CFD-only training and sim-to-real gap -- implicit, exploitable
The surrogate reproduces the CFD solver's turbulence closure, mesh, boundary conditions and idealized geometry, so real geometry change, fouling, transients and off-design operation fall out of distribution and still yield smooth, confident, wrong fields with no uncertainty flag, so erosion-corrosion hot spots can be missed or mislocated. An adversary could time a manipulation or sabotage to these known blind spots (transients, post-maintenance configurations), where the twin cannot expose the anomaly.

Proxy-versus-target mismatch and frozen physics -- implicit
The model predicts pressure and turbulence fields rather than wall thinning, and it stays fixed at training-time physics while the plant changes through repair, replacement or new operating regimes. Over-reading these proxies as wall-condition evidence compounds error into wall-thinning trending and remaining-life analytics. An adversary gains nothing directly from this beyond the general blind-spot effect.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A data-driven substitute for a measurement has no accepted QA or validation basis, offers little explanation, and can change outputs between retrained versions, while ground truth at the deployed locations is unmeasured by design. Weak configuration and cyber-scope control of weights and training data lets a malicious change pass as routine retraining.

Over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Speed (about 1400 times faster than CFD) and low reported error against held-out CFD invite reduced inspection frequency, deferred or uncalibrated physical sensors, and out-of-the-loop engineering staff. An adversary can rely on this weakened human cross-checking, so that a manipulated or denied twin goes unchallenged.

Input-channel manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofed, replayed or subtly biased operating inputs (flow, temperature, pressure boundary values) make the surrogate output an internally consistent but false field, hiding a real excursion or fabricating one to force outages. With no co-located physical sensor to disagree, the twin cannot reveal the manipulation.

Training-data and model tampering -- adversarial
Poisoning the CFD dataset or solver configuration, backdooring a checkpoint, or altering stored weights through supply chain, insider or credentialed access biases outputs at chosen locations or regimes while validation stays clean, since validation comes from the same pipeline. The result is deferred or misdirected inspection, and one tampered artifact propagates to every site if the model is shared across a fleet.

Digital-twin IT/OT pathway and model extraction -- adversarial
The twin links plant data to modeling, analytics and possibly vendor or cloud hosting, widening the IT/OT bridge and offering a route to operational data or a pivot if connectivity is not one-way. Extracting or proxying the surrogate also reveals thermal-hydraulic behavior and lets an attacker craft inputs that evade monitoring.

Denial or degradation of the twin -- adversarial
Flooding or corrupting inputs, or taking the twin offline, removes the monitoring layer at hard-to-reach locations once it is no longer redundant. The safety impact is bounded by remaining instrumentation and NDE, but it can be timed around an inspection deferral.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, the hot-leg virtual sensor is an advisory condition-monitoring tool, not a protection-system input. A wrong output therefore does not directly trip, fail to trip, or mis-position anything. The real exposure is slower and quieter. Maintenance and inspection decisions for erosion-corrosion and flow-accelerated degradation could drift onto a surrogate that was trained only on CFD, with no measured field data in the loop. Existing practice limits the damage: ISI/NDE programs, wall-thinning trending, and RTD, pressure and flow instrumentation all stay in place, and the paper itself says it does not model degradation. The harm path is credible only if the virtual sensor's smooth, low-error fields are trusted to defer or replace inspection or physical instrumentation, or if a manipulated twin hides a real excursion from operators and engineers.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) CFD-only training and sim-to-real gap. The DeepONet reproduces the CFD solver's turbulence model and boundary-condition assumptions, not the plant. Actual geometry (weld offsets, wall thinning, fouling, roughness), transients, off-nominal power, and sensor-fed inputs that differ from the training envelope can push it out of distribution. It will still return plausible smooth fields with no native uncertainty flag. Consequence: erosion-corrosion hot spots are missed or mislocated, and wall-thinning trending is non-conservative. (2) Qualification and verification gap. A surrogate that replaces a physical sensor has no accepted software-QA or validation basis. It is hard to explain, and nondeterminism or retraining can change outputs between versions. It is also hard to benchmark against ground truth, because the locations are hard to reach and so unmeasured. That is the very reason it is deployed. (3) Automation bias and skill fade. A fast, low-error virtual sensor invites reduced inspection frequency and less attention to anchoring measurements. Operators and engineers then become out of the loop on thermal-hydraulic behavior. (4) Indirect degradation inference. Pressure and turbulence are proxies for degradation, not measurements of it. Over-reading them as wall-condition evidence is a goal-misalignment risk. (5) Fault propagation. Errors in the upstream instrument inputs feed the model and the twin's downstream analytics, such as remaining-life or maintenance scheduling. These can be confidently amplified with no independent cross-check.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Input manipulation. Spoofed or biased operating-parameter feeds, or adversarial perturbations within the sensors' plausible range, can make the twin show healthy fields while real conditions deviate, or raise false alarms that cause unnecessary outages.
