This is a class of integrity attack on the data feeding the twin. It matters mainly if the twin is trusted over physical instruments. (7) Model or training-data supply-chain tampering. Poisoned CFD datasets, a backdoored checkpoint, or altered weights in the twin pipeline can bias outputs at chosen operating points. This is hard to detect given the opacity and the lack of ground truth. (8) Twin-IT/OT boundary. A digital twin that ingests plant data and publishes results to engineering staff opens a data-flow path and attack surface. Operational data may leak through it, and it is a potential pivot if connectivity is not one-way. Cloud or off-site hosting adds exposure. (9) Denial or degradation of the service. This is low safety impact, since physical monitoring remains, but it removes the monitoring benefit and could be timed around an inspection deferral or maintenance decision. Overall safety consequence is bounded, because independent instrumentation, NDE and the protection system must also fail for harm to occur. The significant concern is erosion of defense-in-depth margin through gradual substitution of unvalidated virtual measurements.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this DeepONet is a surrogate trained entirely on CFD output (OP.C0201.01/.02), so its ground truth is a model of the plant, not the plant. It is then deployed to replace physical sensors in locations where no ground truth exists to check it. The reported low error is measured against held-out CFD, not field data, so the model's fidelity is bounded by the turbulence closure, mesh, boundary conditions and idealized geometry used to generate the training set. Hot-leg operating states outside the sampled CFD design-of-experiments (transients, off-nominal flow, pipe wall roughening or wall thinning from erosion-corrosion, instrument drift in the input channels) are out-of-distribution (OP.C0302), and a DeepONet will still return a smooth, plausible-looking field with no native uncertainty signal. The paper states it does not simulate material degradation, so the system monitors thermal-hydraulic proxies at degradation-prone locations. That creates a gap between what is measured and what is claimed (condition monitoring of degradation). The most important exposure is therefore the training-data and verification chain plus the inference-time trust placed in an unverifiable virtual sensor, more than the network architecture itself.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Sim-to-real gap and unvalidated ground truth: the training data are CFD only, with fixed geometry and boundary conditions. Real hot-leg conditions differ through aging, deposits, changed roughness, power uprates and transients. The model reports confident fields that are systematically wrong, and nothing physical at that location contradicts it (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). Consequence: undetected degradation progression or false reassurance in condition monitoring, and possible missed or mistimed inspection and maintenance decisions. (2) Concept drift in the digital twin: the plant changes (component replacement, geometry change after repair, new operating regime), while the surrogate stays frozen at its training-time physics (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303). Static qualification of the surrogate does not match the dynamic plant. (3) Proxy-versus-target mismatch: the system predicts pressure and turbulence fields, but the decision-relevant quantity is wall thinning or erosion-corrosion rate. Mapping the first to the second happens downstream through human judgment or additional models, and error in either step is compounded (OP.C0301, OP.C0603). (4) Opacity and no calibrated uncertainty: a DeepONet gives point estimates with weak OOD detection, so operators can't tell interpolation from extrapolation (OP.C0401, OP.C0403). Combined with a 1400x speed advantage that invites continuous reliance, this raises over-trust and skill fade in sensor-based diagnostics, and the loss of redundant physical measurement (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (5) Qualification and regulatory gap: there is no established route to credit a data-driven virtual sensor as a replacement for a measurement in safety-relevant monitoring (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Retraining or retuning versions create reproducibility issues (OP.C0402.01).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Input-channel manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015): the model is driven by operating inputs from plant instrumentation or the historian. Spoofed or subtly biased inputs yield an internally consistent but false field, and the surrogate would mask a real anomaly, or fabricate one to trigger unnecessary outages or interventions. Because the virtual sensor has no independent physical cross-check, the twin cannot expose the manipulation. (2) Training-data and model supply chain (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004): the CFD dataset, solver configuration, pretrained weights or ML libraries could be tampered with, including a backdoor or a systematic bias in specific flow regimes or at specific locations. This is hard to detect because the validation set is generated by the same pipeline. (3) Model and twin integrity at deployment (AML.T0076, AML.T0031, AML.T0018): weight or configuration alteration on the edge or twin host, or in the retraining loop, quietly shifts outputs. The digital twin's connectivity and data flows to OT/IT networks also make it a new attack surface into plant data (OP.C0601, OP.C0602 if models are shared across a fleet, in which case one poisoned artifact propagates). (4) Reconnaissance and extraction (AML.T0000, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005): the published architecture and training approach help attackers build a proxy model to craft inputs that evade monitoring. (5) Denial of service (AML.T0029, AML.T0046): flooding or corrupting inputs, or taking the twin offline, removes the only monitoring at hard-to-reach sites. Attackers could time actions around known OOD blind spots such as transients or post-maintenance configuration changes.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, a DeepONet virtual sensor in a PWR hot leg is an attractive stepping stone, not a primary target. It replaces physical measurement in hard-to-reach locations with a model output that nobody can independently check, and it feeds a digital twin that supports condition monitoring and maintenance decisions. That concentrates trust in a single artifact (trained weights, CFD training set, input data feed) whose compromise would be silent, because there is no co-located physical sensor to disagree with it. The risk is also non-adversarial: the model is trained only on CFD simulation data, the paper itself does not simulate degradation, and the model reports low error only inside the distribution it was trained on. An adversary, or an insider, could time an action around the model's blind spots, or around the operator vigilance the model has eroded, so that a real anomaly goes unseen.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model integrity: the model is trained on CFD runs, so the simulation pipeline, mesh and boundary-condition files, and the stored weights are the assets worth attacking. A supply-chain, insider or credentialed-access actor could poison the CFD dataset or alter the weights, so that outputs stay plausible and low-error on the validation set but are biased at specific locations such as pipe bends (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0012). The facility depends on these outputs for erosion-corrosion monitoring and inspection planning, so the consequence is deferred or misdirected inspection and undetected wall thinning in a primary-system component. There is no independent sensor to catch the discrepancy. (2) Input-channel manipulation: the virtual sensor is only as honest as the operating inputs (flow, temperature, pressure boundary values) that drive it. Tampering with, spoofing or replaying those upstream signals shifts the inferred fields while every other system sees nominal values (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). The result is a false picture of a safety-relevant location, and possibly masking of real degradation that an adversary or insider wants hidden. (3) Digital-twin pathway: the twin links OT data to modeling, analytics and possibly vendor or cloud environments. The AI component widens the IT/OT bridge and the data flows through it, which gives an adversary a new route toward plant data and a stepping stone to operational systems (AML.T0025, AML.T0036, AML.T0044, OP.C0601). Model extraction or access to the surrogate also reveals thermal-hydraulic behavior and sensor-placement logic that would aid sabotage planning (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035). (4) Timing around lost vigilance: once operators and engineers rely on the twin, physical sensors in hard-to-reach locations may be removed, deferred or left uncalibrated. An adversary can then exploit this weaker human cross-checking, and denial of the AI service (AML.T0029) or quiet degradation of it removes a monitoring layer that is no longer redundant.

IMPLICIT. (5) Fidelity and generalization gap: the model learns CFD, not the plant. Mesh and turbulence-model error, real geometry changes from erosion, fouling and weld wear, and off-design transients all produce out-of-distribution inputs on which the DeepONet can return confident, wrong fields without any signal that it is wrong (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). The paper explicitly does not model degradation, so a monitoring claim for erosion-corrosion rests on an inferred link between turbulence and pressure and material loss. Any adversary who understands this gap can time an action to the conditions where the model is weakest. (6) Opacity and over-trust: speed (about 1400 times faster than CFD) and low reported error encourage reliance and skill fade among thermal-hydraulics staff, while the neural operator offers little explanation that would let a human challenge an output (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102, OP.C0401). (7) Governance: qualification of a data-driven virtual sensor as a substitute for measurement lacks an established regime. Retraining, versioning and configuration control of weights and training data may not fall under the plant's cyber and configuration-management scope, so a malicious or careless change is hard to detect (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0503, OP.C0504). If the same model is replicated across a fleet, one compromise or one bias propagates to every site (OP.C0602). Overall, the main concern is a single, hard-to-audit trust point that sits upstream of inspection and maintenance decisions on primary-system components.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the CFD-only fidelity gap, over-trust, qualification gap, input manipulation and training-data/model tampering; I merged their overlapping lists into single threats. I dropped weakly supported or unargued codes (e.g. AML.T0012, AML.T0036, AML.T0044, AML.T0076, AML.T0000, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0059, AML.T0035) because they were not distinct threats in the text, and kept the model-extraction and proxy-model pathway as a single threat.

evidence.citation: "Virtual sensing-enabled digital twin framework for real-time monitoring of nuclear systems leveraging deep neural operators," npj Materials Degradation (Nature Portfolio)
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper builds and tests a DeepONet surrogate as a virtual sensor for thermal-hydraulic parameters in a PWR hot leg. It reports low prediction error and speeds about 1400 times faster than CFD. The authors say the study does not simulate material degradation directly. Instead, it monitors turbulence and pressure in locations prone to degradation, such as pipe bends.

damage.why: The twin is advisory and not a protection input, so the worst credible harm (a tampered or out-of-distribution surrogate hiding erosion-corrosion and causing deferred or misdirected inspection of primary-system components) erodes safety margin and disrupts operations, but it is bounded by remaining instrumentation and NDE and does not directly cause a release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: The CFD-to-plant fidelity gap is a structural property that reliably yields confident but wrong outputs whenever operation goes off-distribution, and input manipulation or model tampering produces consistent biased fields once the access condition is met.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible adversarial paths (training-data or checkpoint tampering, or crossing the IT/OT bridge to spoof plant inputs) need insider, supply-chain or credentialed access and some domain knowledge of the plant, though the implicit blind spots need no special effort.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly the monitored hot-leg locations and the downstream inspection and remaining-life decisions, but a tampered model shared across a fleet could propagate to multiple sites, which raises it above a single component without making it facility-wide in the coupled-system sense.

discoverability.why: The open literature documents CFD-trained surrogate limits, sim-to-real gaps, and ML poisoning, evasion and extraction as general classes, and the cited paper publicly describes the approach and its scope, so a capable outsider can readily infer the weaknesses even though system-specific details would take deeper knowledge.

use_case: Back-propagation neural network that predicts human error probability for nuclear power plant operators. Its inputs are eye-response indices, subjective workload ratings and situation-awareness levels collected from operators. It is meant for evaluating and predicting operator reliability.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory back-propagation network turns eye-tracking, workload and situation-awareness data on named operators into a predicted human error probability that may shape staffing, fitness-for-duty perceptions, training and HRA/PRA inputs. It has no direct control authority, so the main exposure is indirect: poorly validated outputs trusted beyond their evidence, and an adversary or insider manipulating the score, its data or the operator profiles. The main threats are weak ground truth and generalisation, opacity and non-repeatability, automation trust failure, integrity manipulation, input gaming, and exposure of sensitive operator data.

Small-data and proxy-label circularity -- implicit, exploitable
The network is trained on a few simulator or experiment cohorts, with HEP labels derived from task scoring or HRA methods (THERP, SPAR-H). It therefore reproduces another model's assumptions, and the high R² (0.93-0.97), probably inflated by subject or session leakage, gives false precision for rare, high-consequence errors. An adversary can hide manipulation or a real impairment inside this unquantified error band, because a bad score looks like ordinary model inaccuracy.

Drift and simulator-to-plant generalisation failure -- implicit, exploitable
Eye-response indices, self-rated workload and SA scores shift with tracker hardware, HMI changes such as digital I&C upgrades, fatigue, crew and scenario, and the network extrapolates unpredictably with no out-of-distribution flag. Silently miscalibrated outputs let an adversary operate in conditions where the score is unreliable, or time an action when the model is known to be unreliable.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A back-propagation network gives no auditable link between inputs and HEP, and different random seeds can change individual predictions. No AI-specific qualification regime exists for such tools, so a tampered weight file or retrained model is indistinguishable from legitimate variation and cannot be readily defended in nuclear QA or regulatory review.

Automation trust failure in personnel decisions -- implicit, exploitable
Managers may treat a low predicted HEP as clearance and reduce oversight, or ignore the tool after a visible miss, and operators who know the score feeds evaluation may suppress honest ratings. An insider can time an act to a period of high model-assigned confidence or reduced supervision, or exploit the predictable shift in human vigilance.

Cross-system propagation of biased HEP -- implicit, exploitable
A biased or drifted HEP feeding PRA/HRA studies, staffing or training decisions, or a model reused across a fleet, spreads the same error into risk-informed decisions at several sites. An adversary who biases one shared version gets that bias propagated everywhere.

Poisoning and tampering of data and model -- adversarial
Corrupting training or retraining records, labels or stored weights, or compromising the eye-tracker firmware, feature-extraction software or model files in the supply chain, systematically biases HEP. Under-prediction gives false assurance about an impaired or compromised operator and lowers scrutiny of a targeted shift. Over-prediction removes competent staff or creates staffing gaps. With no ground truth in daily operations, detection is unlikely.

Input manipulation by operators or insiders -- adversarial
The feature set is low-dimensional and easy to infer, so an insider can alter gaze behaviour, tamper with eye-tracker or questionnaire data, or misreport workload and SA ratings to keep predicted HEP low and conceal impairment, or to push a colleague's HEP high and sideline them. This degrades fitness-for-duty and reliability screening.

Exfiltration and inference of operator profiles -- adversarial
Gaining access to the biometric and performance datasets, or inferring them from the model by membership inference or inversion, reveals which operators or shifts are fatigued or error-prone. That supports coercion, recruitment, social engineering and attack timing. The data is usually governed as research or HR data, so the security model is mismatched to its sensitivity.

Weakly hygienic stepping-stone systems -- adversarial
Eye-tracking hardware, analytics software and any vendor or cloud processing link operator-monitoring systems to networks adjacent to the plant, with weaker hygiene than safety systems. They offer an easier foothold for lateral entry into plant IT and personnel-security systems and for intelligence gathering.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is an advisory human-reliability tool, not a control or protection function. It sits well outside the safety-system chain, so a wrong output cannot directly move a rod, trip a pump or defeat an interlock. The real exposure is indirect: managers, training staff and HRA analysts may rely on a predicted human error probability (HEP) for crew staffing, fitness-for-duty screening, procedure design or PRA inputs. The model was trained on experimental or simulator data from small operator cohorts, with R² of about 0.93-0.97 reported on a sample probably drawn from the same population. That suggests weak generalisation to real crews, real shift conditions and real emergencies. The harm would come from bad human-performance decisions made with unjustified confidence, from the tool being quietly weaponised against individual operators, or from corrupted risk inputs. It would need to defeat independent defence-in-depth, operator procedures and regulatory-accepted HRA methods (THERP, SPAR-H, CREAM) to cause real harm, so the consequence is mostly degraded risk-informed decision quality and personnel-security issues rather than an accident.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT: (1) Small-data and ground-truth problem (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01/.05). True HEP is a very low-base-rate quantity. Labels are likely derived from simulator error counts or from expert-judgement HRA values, so the network learns to reproduce another model's assumptions. High R² on train, validation and test splits hides this circularity and does not show predictive validity for rare, high-consequence errors. (2) Generalisation and drift (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303). Eye-tracking indices, NASA-TLX-type workload ratings and SA scores vary with operator, interface design (analogue vs digital HMI), fatigue, tracker hardware and scenario type. A model fitted to one simulator study may be miscalibrated for a different control room or crew, or after a digital I&C upgrade. Simulator-to-real-plant transfer is untested. (3) Opacity and repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01). A back-propagation network gives no auditable link between the inputs and the HEP. Training with different random seeds can change individual predictions, which weakens qualification and regulatory acceptance (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (4) Automation trust failure (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05). Over-trust could lead to low-HEP operators or shifts being given less oversight. Under-trust could lead to the tool being ignored after a visible miss. Subjective inputs such as self-rated workload and SA can also be gamed, and the model is unlikely to be tested against that. (5) Operator privacy and labour issues. Biometric and eye-response data are sensitive personnel data (OP.C0505, OP.C0505.01). Using HEP scores for individual fitness or retention decisions creates insider-trust, discrimination and reporting-culture problems, such as operators suppressing honest workload ratings. ADVERSARIAL: (6) Poisoning or tampering with training data, calibration data or stored model weights (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031) could bias HEP downward or upward. A downward bias would hide a stressed crew or justify reduced staffing. An upward bias would unjustly sideline qualified operators, which is a way to degrade operations through the workforce. Because the model is a niche research artifact with little QA (OP.C0502), such tampering would likely go unnoticed, and the plausible actor is an insider or someone who compromises an engineering workstation. (7) Adversarial or perturbed sensor inputs (AML.T0043, AML.T0015), including manipulated eye-tracker or questionnaire data, could skew predictions in real time. (8) Exfiltration of operator biometric and performance profiles (AML.T0025, AML.T0024.000) could support targeting, coercion or social engineering of identified weak-performing operators. (9) HEP outputs feeding PRA or HRA studies (OP.C0603) could propagate a bias into risk-informed licensing or training decisions. Existing practice mitigates much of this: the tool is advisory, human review of HRA is standard, and safety systems are independent. The residual risk is therefore quiet, systematic degradation of human-performance management rather than an acute event.

ai_engineer.argument: From the ML pipeline view, this is a small tabular regression model (a BP-NN over a handful of physiological and self-report features) whose reported R² of about 0.93-0.97 comes from data that is almost certainly simulator or experimental-participant data, with a small number of subjects and a very low base rate of real errors. The target variable, human error probability, is not directly observed. It is a label derived from task-performance scoring or from HRA methods such as THERP or SPAR-H, so the model learns to reproduce another model's or an annotator's judgment rather than ground-truth operator failure. Strong in-sample and test fit on a split that likely shares subjects, scenarios and sessions can hide leakage and poor generalization to new operators, crews, plants, shifts or real transients. The fragility sits in the data and label provenance and the qualification gap, and the architecture adds little: it is opaque, non-deterministic across seeds, and has no uncertainty output. Its inputs are also intimate biometric and subjective signals that an operator or an adversary can shape, which creates a new attack surface.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data provenance and small-data failure (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Training data come from simulator or lab experiments with few participants, and real-plant error events are rare. The model is therefore fitted to a narrow population, scenario set and sensor setup. Mechanism: subject or session leakage between train, validation and test sets inflates R². Consequence: overconfident HEP estimates that could feed staffing, shift or procedure decisions, or HRA inputs to probabilistic safety assessment, with the plant exposed to unrecognized operator-reliability risk. (2) Label and objective misalignment (OP.C0301). The model predicts a proxy HEP, not actual error. Mechanism: it inherits the biases and uncertainty of the labeling method. Consequence: the model gives false precision and may be treated as validated evidence in safety cases. (3) Out-of-distribution and drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03). Eye-tracking indices depend on hardware, lighting, control-room layout, HMI changes (for example analog to digital upgrades) and operator fatigue or experience. Self-reported workload and SA ratings, such as NASA-TLX or SAGAT-like instruments, shift with culture, rating habits and the knowledge that they feed an evaluation. Mechanism: covariate and concept drift, and a BP-NN that extrapolates unpredictably outside its training range. Consequence: silently wrong predictions with no OOD flag. (4) Static versus dynamic qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501). Experiments are performed in controlled simulator runs, while use would be continuous or online, with different operator states under real stress. (5) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01). Different initializations give different weights, and the model offers no causal explanation of which feature drives risk. This is hard to defend under nuclear QA expectations. (6) Human-AI interaction (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05). Managers may over-trust a high-R² score, or operators may distrust it. If HEP scores are used for individual evaluation, automation trust failure and a punitive reporting culture follow, and operators begin to game the inputs. (7) Data governance (OP.C0505, OP.C0505.01). Biometric and gaze data about named operators are sensitive personnel data, and standard plant OT security models do not cover them.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Input manipulation or evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003). An insider or an operator who knows the features can alter gaze behavior or give biased self-ratings so that predicted HEP stays low (to hide impairment) or goes high (to remove a colleague from duty). Mechanism: the feature set is low-dimensional and easy to reverse-engineer. Consequence: degraded fitness-for-duty and reliability screening. (b) Data poisoning and training-set tampering (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059). Retraining on newly collected plant data, or on pooled data from other sites, can be skewed by corrupting a few records or labels, which shifts the model's reliability estimates. Consequence: a systematic bias in HRA-supporting numbers. (c) Sensor or supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.000, AML.T0010.001). The eye-tracker firmware, feature-extraction software or model files could be tampered with. Consequence: corrupted indices, or model weights altered to suppress high-risk outputs. (d) Confidentiality (AML.T0024.000, AML.T0024.001, AML.T0037, AML.T0036). Model inversion, exfiltration of the biometric and performance dataset, or access to the model outputs lets an adversary learn which operators or shifts are weakest and time social engineering, insider recruitment or physical or cyber action around those windows. (e) Cross-site propagation (OP.C0602, AML.T0018). If the model is reused across a fleet, one compromised or drifted version propagates the same bias everywhere.

security_specialist.argument: From a security-culture and insider-threat lens, this model is dangerous less as a safety-critical controller than as a trusted, personnel-facing reliability metric. It turns biometric (eye-tracking) and self-reported data about named operators into a score that may influence staffing, shift assignment, fitness-for-duty perceptions and training decisions. That makes it a lever for an adversary or a malicious insider: manipulating inputs or outputs can shape who is on console and how much supervisors trust them, and the operators' subjective inputs are themselves gameable. A sophisticated adversary would probably not target the model itself first. It would use the model, its data store, or the operator-behavior profile as reconnaissance and timing information, or as a way to erode vigilance. Non-adversarial weaknesses, such as small cohorts, simulator-derived data and opaque back-propagation behavior, give an attacker cover because a bad output looks like normal model error.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
1) Personnel-reliability data as an intelligence and targeting asset (ATLAS AML.T0036, T0037, T0025, T0024.000/.001; OP.C0505, OP.C0505.01). Eye-response, workload and situation-awareness records tied to individual operators are sensitive human-performance and biometric profiles. If exfiltrated or inferred from the model (membership inference or inversion), they reveal which operators are fatigued, overloaded or error-prone, and when. That lets an adversary choose targets for coercion or recruitment, or time a sabotage or social-engineering action to a low-reliability shift. The data is usually governed as research or HR data rather than as security-relevant plant information, which is a mismatch in the security model. Consequence: insider-targeting and attack-timing information, plus privacy and labor-relations harm.

2) Integrity manipulation of the score (T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0031, T0043, T0015, T0059). Poisoned or biased training data, a tampered model file, or inputs gamed by a malicious operator or insider could systematically under- or over-predict error probability. Under-prediction gives false assurance that a compromised or impaired operator is reliable. It would also lower scrutiny of a shift an adversary intends to exploit. Over-prediction could be used to remove competent staff, create staffing gaps, or generate false grounds against particular individuals. Because the output is a soft, probabilistic number with no ground truth in daily operations, tampering is hard to detect. Consequence: degraded operational safety margins and corrupted personnel-reliability decisions, not direct plant control loss.

3) Implicit weaknesses that an adversary can exploit or time around (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0304.03). The reported R² of about 0.93–0.97 likely comes from small, simulator-based, homogeneous operator cohorts with human error probability labels from other models or expert estimates. It would not generalize across crews, plants, stress regimes or eye-tracker hardware, so it is vulnerable to drift and out-of-distribution failure. Subjective workload and situation-awareness inputs can be strategically misreported. The model is opaque, so no one can say why a score changed, which hides manipulation. No AI-specific qualification regime exists for such tools. These gaps make an attacker's interference indistinguishable from ordinary model error.

4) Automation bias and concentration of trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). If managers treat a low predicted error probability as clearance, supervisory vigilance drops, and an adversary could time an insider act to a period of high model-assigned confidence. Conversely, repeated false alarms lead to disuse, which also leaves a window. Consequence: shifts in human oversight that an adversary can predict and exploit.

5) Stepping-stone and supply-chain exposure (T0010, T0012, T0049, T0052, OP.C0601, OP.C0502). Eye-tracking hardware, analytics software and any cloud or vendor processing connect operator-monitoring systems to networks that sit near, but not in, the control environment. These systems are likely to have weaker hygiene than safety systems, so they are an easier foothold than the plant itself. A nation-state would more plausibly use this as access and information gathering than as a sabotage target. Consequence: lateral entry into plant IT and personnel-security systems.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on weak ground truth and generalisation, opacity and qualification gaps, trust failure, integrity manipulation, input gaming and operator-data exfiltration. Narrow extras were kept only where they described a distinct pathway (stepping-stone systems, fleet propagation). T0049, T0052 and OP.C0304.03 were dropped for lack of a specific mechanism, and the AI engineer's T0043.003 and T0015 were retained for input gaming.

evidence.citation: "Constructing Neural Network Model to Evaluate and Predict Human Error Probability in Nuclear Power Plants Based on Eye Response, Workload Rating, and Situation Awareness," Nuclear Technology (American Nuclear Society / Taylor & Francis)
evidence.note: The paper reports a back-propagation neural network built to predict human error probability from eye-response indices, subjective workload ratings and situation-awareness levels. The authors first showed these measures correlate with human error probability. They then reported prediction accuracy on training, validation and test sets (R² about 0.93–0.97). I read only the abstract page, not the full text.

damage.why: The tool is advisory with no control authority, so the worst credible harm is false assurance about an impaired or compromised operator, or biased HEP feeding PRA/HRA and staffing decisions, which erodes safety margin and operations but does not directly cause a release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Weak labels, drift, non-repeatability and trust failures occur reliably whenever the model is deployed, and input gaming or data tampering works consistently once an insider or data-path foothold exists.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (insider gaming of gaze or ratings, tampering with data or weights) need insider or data-pipeline access, but the low-dimensional inputs and weakly hygienic research/HR systems keep the barrier moderate.

affected_users.why: Impact is mainly on individual operators, shifts and crews, but biased HEP propagating into PRA/HRA studies or a fleet-shared model can spread across sites, giving moderate-to-broad reach.

discoverability.why: The general weaknesses of small-data neural networks and operator-monitoring data are well documented in the open literature, and the model class and inputs are published, but how a particular deployment uses scores and what its data pipeline looks like needs partial insider knowledge.

use_case: Automated end-face inspection of PWR nuclear fuel pellets during fuel fabrication. Structured-light imaging is paired with two lightweight deep semantic-segmentation networks. Defect-ENet segments surface defects such as missing material, and Crack-SegNet segments tiny cracks. The system gives high-throughput, per-pellet quality inspection.
incurred_insecurity:
This automated end-face inspection gate concentrates pellet acceptance in two lightweight segmentation networks that nobody can re-verify at line speed. The main threats are quiet integrity compromise of the models or their configuration, physical-channel evasion of the structured-light input, and a set of implicit weaknesses (rare-crack data scarcity, drift, qualification gaps, over-trust) that hide misses and give an adversary predictable blind spots. The consequence is a latent fuel-quality problem, such as cracked or chipped pellets reaching cladding with a clean inspection record, rather than an immediate accident.

Model, data and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or vendor who poisons or label-flips training data, backdoors pretrained weights or the retraining pipeline, or swaps weights, thresholds or post-processing rules can make specific crack morphologies or trigger signatures pass as acceptable. Defective pellets then enter fuel rods with a valid pass record, and the opacity of the networks makes the change look like ordinary drift.

Physical-input evasion and line flooding -- adversarial
An actor with line access can alter pellet surface finish, illumination, fixturing, optical cleanliness or calibration so that real cracks fall below the segmentation threshold without changing the pellet's fitness. Flooding the line with false rejects or degrading throughput can also push operators toward bypassing or relaxing the AI gate.

Inspection record tampering and update-channel propagation -- adversarial
The AI station's results database and its vendor or remote update channel are an easier foothold than process controls. Falsifying pass/fail, reject or scrap records can hide substitution or diversion at the margin, and a compromised model update can propagate across lines or sites.

Rare-crack data scarcity and misaligned objective -- implicit, exploitable
Real cracks are rare, class-imbalanced and often lab-staged or augmented, and Dice/IoU losses barely penalise thin cracks, so the headline 98% accuracy hides poor recall on tiny cracks, the safety-relevant false negative. An adversary can craft or induce defect morphologies that sit in this known blind spot, relying on the weakness to look like a natural miss.

Drift and operational heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Changes in pellet design, gadolinium-bearing or enrichment variants, powder or sintering lots, lighting, projector aging or lens contamination shift the image distribution and silently degrade masks, with no on-line ground truth and no out-of-distribution warning. An adversary can hide a deliberate manipulation inside this degradation band or time it around a lot or hardware change.

Qualification gap, opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
A paper-level benchmark gives no probability-of-detection versus flaw-size curves, no requalification path for retraining, and little explainability or repeatability across hardware or software versions. A malicious model or threshold swap is then indistinguishable from a routine update.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Sub-second throughput and a headline accuracy figure invite reduced manual sampling, rubber-stamp reject review and decay of inspector skill, removing the independent layer. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust to let a slow-onset degradation or an update-timed attack go unnoticed.

Two-network cascade bias -- implicit
Bias or error in the defect network, such as a surface-defect mask occluding a crack, propagates to the crack network and compounds misses. An adversary gains little from this beyond what the other blind spots already offer.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a fuel-fabrication operations lens, this system is a quality-control screen for pellet end-face defects (chips, missing material, fine cracks) before pellets are loaded into cladding. A false accept sends a marginal pellet toward rod loading. The credible downstream harm is a latent fuel-quality problem, such as pellet-cladding interaction sensitivity, a localized hot spot, or a fuel failure that shows up later in-reactor. It is not an immediate accident. Existing practice already limits this: the pellet process has sampling, dimensional and density checks, metallography, rod-level controls, and often human visual inspection, so an AI miss has to coincide with failures in those layers to matter. The real risk is that high throughput and a reported 98%+ accuracy lead to a quiet reduction of those layers, or to the AI being treated as the sole acceptance authority, without qualification for rare, critical defects. That 98% is an aggregate figure and says little about recall on tiny cracks.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT: (1) Small-data and low-base-rate problem. Real cracks and defects are rare and varied, so training data is likely small, partly lab-curated or augmented, and tuned to one pellet design and imaging setup. Aggregate accuracy can hide poor recall on the rare, small cracks that matter most. A false negative is the safety-relevant error, and class imbalance biases the models toward 'good'. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity. Changes in pellet surface finish, lubricant or powder lot, enrichment or gadolinium-bearing pellets, lighting and projector aging, camera or optics contamination (dust, powder), vibration, and sintering-line changes shift the image distribution. Performance degrades silently, with no ground truth available on the line to reveal it. (3) Qualification and opacity gaps. Lightweight segmentation networks are hard to explain, and segmentation thresholds that map pixels to accept/reject are a tuning decision with no standard acceptance basis. A paper-level validation is not nuclear QA (the OP.C0501 gap). Retraining or model updates without requalification, and non-repeatable behavior across hardware or software versions, undermine traceability. (4) Automation bias and skill fade. Operators and QA staff stop looking at pellets, so human inspection skills decay and reject-review becomes a rubber stamp, removing the independent layer. (5) Throughput pressure. Sub-second inspection invites replacing sampling-based checks with AI-only acceptance. ADVERSARIAL / exploitable: (6) Integrity manipulation. Poisoned training or update data, a tampered model or weights, or a compromised vendor software supply chain could bias the system to pass specific defect types or to misclassify at a chosen time. This is a plausible insider or supply-chain sabotage path that degrades fuel quality without any visible event. (7) Input-level evasion, such as physical changes to the imaging environment, lighting or surface condition, or tampering with calibration or thresholds, could make defects invisible to the model while remaining within normal-looking operation. (8) Denial or false-reject flooding could halt the line, hurting supply and production, though this is a lower-consequence nuisance. (9) Quality and inspection records, including defect images and pass/fail data, are commercially sensitive and also reveal detection limits. Their exfiltration helps an adversary shape evasion. Safeguards relevance is minor, though inspection-linked pellet counts and rejects feed material accounting, so manipulated reject or scrap records could mask diversion at the margin. Overall severity is moderate and delayed. The main mitigations are keeping independent sampling, metallographic and rod-level checks, monitoring per-defect-class recall with seeded or reference defect pellets, and controlling model and configuration changes.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a supervised semantic-segmentation pipeline (ENet and SegNet variants) trained on labeled end-face images from a structured-light rig. Its fragility sits in the data and the label definition, not in the facility around it. Defects and cracks are rare, small, and class-imbalanced. Pixel-level labels are subjective at the threshold between acceptable and rejectable. A headline figure like '>98% accuracy' is typically pixel- or image-level on a curated set, and says little about recall on tiny cracks, which is the safety-relevant tail. Inference quality depends on a narrow imaging distribution (lighting, fringe projection, pellet surface finish, dish/chamfer geometry, powder lot, grinding wear). Anything outside that distribution produces confidently wrong masks, with no built-in out-of-distribution signal. Because the system acts as the gate for pellets entering fuel rods, a silent false negative becomes a latent fuel-integrity issue downstream.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Small-data and low base-rate problem: real cracks and missing-material defects are scarce, so training sets are small, augmented, or lab-staged, and crack-class recall is poorly characterized with wide uncertainty (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.04/.02). Possible provenance mismatch: bench or seeded-defect pellets differ from naturally occurring production defects. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity: a new pellet design or enrichment/gadolinium-bearing variant, a powder or sintering-recipe change, a different line, camera or projector aging, lens contamination, and ambient light or fixture changes all shift the input distribution. This degrades segmentation silently (OP.C0302.01/.03). Concept drift also arises when acceptance criteria are revised but the labels are not (OP.C0302.02). (3) Qualification mismatch: a fuel-fabrication QA regime expects a qualified, repeatable inspection method with a known probability of detection. A frozen offline benchmark does not give POD-vs-flaw-size curves or a defined retraining and requalification path (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0402). (4) Opacity and objective misalignment: the segmentation loss (Dice/IoU) optimizes pixel overlap, not 'never miss a through-crack'. Thin cracks contribute little to pixel-weighted loss, so the model is tuned to look good while under-detecting the critical class (OP.C0301, OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (5) Automation trust: high throughput (<1 s/pellet) with 98% headline accuracy encourages over-trust, reduced manual sampling, and skill fade among human inspectors (OP.C0101.04/.06, OP.C0102). (6) Two-network cascade: errors or bias in one model (for example, a surface-defect mask that occludes a crack) propagate to the other (OP.C0603).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Training-data and label poisoning, or supply-chain compromise of pretrained weights, frameworks, or the labeling and retraining pipeline: a backdoor or label-flip could make a specific crack morphology or a trigger pattern pass as acceptable (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). This is plausible for a quiet insider or vendor, and is very hard to see given the opacity. (2) Evasion through the physical channel: structured-light inputs can be perturbed through pellet surface treatment, contamination, or fixture, illumination or projector manipulation, so that real defects are suppressed without altering the pellet's fitness record (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). The same effect can arise from accidental drift, so an attacker can hide inside it. (3) Model or configuration tampering at deployment, such as swapping weights, thresholds, or post-processing rules that decide pass/fail, or corrupting the model (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, AML.T0081, AML.T0112.001). Failures would look like ordinary drift, giving plausible deniability. (4) Denial or degradation of inspection (AML.T0029) forces fallback to slower manual inspection, which can create pressure to relax controls. (5) Proprietary pellet geometry, defect statistics, and trained models are commercially sensitive, so exfiltration or extraction is an IP and process-knowledge exposure (AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025). The consequence chain is: undetected cracked or chipped pellets enter fuel rods, with potential cladding-interaction and fuel-performance impact in service; or falsified inspection records undermine quality assurance and traceability.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this system is an automated quality gate sitting between fabrication and fuel loading. A deliberate adversary, including an insider, would not need to attack the reactor. They only need pellets with latent defects (cracks, chips, density or surface anomalies) to pass inspection, so that cladding or in-core performance degrades later and the cause is hard to trace. Once the network's accept/reject decision replaces per-pellet human review at under one second per pellet, trust is concentrated in two lightweight segmentation models. Nobody can realistically re-verify their output at that throughput, and the only audit is sampling. The security-relevant risk is therefore mostly quiet integrity degradation of an accept/reject authority, not a visible outage. Non-adversarial weaknesses (small crack data, drift, over-trust) also give an attacker predictable blind spots to time an attack around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or pipeline integrity compromise by an insider or supply chain: an actor with access to training data, labels, model weights, preprocessing code or the threshold and config files could poison or backdoor the models, or quietly shift segmentation thresholds. The result would be that specific defect types, or defects with a particular trigger signature, are systematically under-segmented. The facility depends on the output as the per-pellet acceptance record, so the consequence is defective fuel entering the supply chain with a clean inspection record. Candidate techniques: poisoning training data and models (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.003), data supply chain (T0010.002), valid accounts (T0012), model corruption for defense evasion (T0076). (2) Physical-input evasion: structured-light imaging depends on surface condition, lighting and fixturing, so an insider with line access could alter surface finish, lighting, optical cleanliness or calibration to push real cracks below the segmentation threshold, or flood the line with false rejects to degrade throughput and push operators toward bypass (T0015, T0041, T0043.003, T0046, T0029). (3) Trust-concentration and record falsification: inspection results feed quality records used for regulatory and customer assurance, and possibly safeguards-adjacent item accounting. Tampering with the results database, or masking pellet identity or count discrepancies, could hide diversion or substitution. This is a stepping stone, because the AI inspection station is likely an easier IT/OT foothold than the process controls it is networked to (T0112, T0031, T0059). (4) Cloud or vendor dependency and model update channels: remote retraining or vendor-supplied updates create a persistence path and a way to propagate a compromised model across fabrication lines or sites (OP.C0601, OP.C0602).

IMPLICIT. (a) Tiny-crack scarcity: real cracks are rare and class-imbalanced, and training often relies on lab or augmented samples. This creates a predictable detection blind spot for novel crack morphologies, and an adversary or a natural process shift can exploit it (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.03). (b) The headline >98% accuracy is a pixel- or sample-level figure on one dataset, not a measured miss rate for safety-significant defects. It does not cover drift in pellet lots, powder or sintering changes, or camera aging (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303). (c) Automation over-trust and skill fade: at line speed, human inspectors become sampling auditors, so their vigilance erodes. This lets a slow-onset degradation, or an attack timed to a model update, go unnoticed (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (d) Opacity and weak AI-specific QA: lightweight segmentation networks give little explanation, and the change-control and requalification regime for retrained models is likely immature, so a malicious or erroneous model swap may be indistinguishable from routine updates (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0502). A sophisticated state actor would probably find simpler routes to fuel sabotage. For an insider or a supply-chain adversary seeking deniable quality degradation, however, this gate is an attractive, low-visibility target.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on poisoning/tampering of the accept/reject authority, physical-channel evasion, and the same implicit weaknesses (small data, drift, qualification gap, over-trust). I dropped the exfiltration/IP-theft threat as low-consequence and weakly tied to safety, and kept record falsification as a distinct threat from the security specialist.

evidence.citation: "An automatic defects detection system for nuclear fuel pellets end face based on deep learning and structured light," Journal of Nuclear Science and Technology (Taylor & Francis)
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests an inspection system that combines a structured-light imaging device with two segmentation networks, Defect-ENet for defects and Crack-SegNet for fine cracks, on PWR fuel pellet end faces. The authors report over 98% defect recognition accuracy and under 1 second per pellet, and present it as feasible for high-throughput inspection in fuel fabrication.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is record tampering or model compromise that hides defective or substituted pellets, so latent fuel-quality defects reach cladding and could erode fuel safety margins and, in the worst case, falsify material accounting. The entry itself says the result is a latent quality problem and not an immediate release, so this stops short of 5.

reproducibility.why: The implicit weaknesses (low recall on thin cracks, drift, no out-of-distribution warning) recur reliably once conditions exist. The adversarial poisoning and tampering paths depend on gaining a foothold and on the model's particular blind spots, so overall reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: The most damaging threats (training-data poisoning, weight or threshold swaps, update-channel compromise, results-database falsification) need insider, vendor or privileged access in a controlled fabrication facility. Physical-input evasion needs line access, which is also restricted.

affected_users.why: A compromised model update or shared pipeline could propagate across lines or sites, affecting all pellets inspected and downstream fuel rods and assemblies. Impact still stays within the fuel-fabrication quality chain and does not reach coupled plant control systems.

discoverability.why: Weaknesses of this class (class imbalance, thin-crack under-detection, drift, adversarial evasion, supply-chain poisoning) are well documented in the open literature, and the published paper describes the architecture and the benchmark accuracy. Learning facility-specific configuration still needs insider knowledge, which keeps this below 5.

use_case: Cascade-forward neural network combined with a decision tree that classifies the degree of PWR fuel cladding failure from fission-product specific activities measured in the primary coolant. It is designed to separate an intact fuel rod from one with a small defect, as an alternative to isotopic-ratio methods for on-line fuel failure detection.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory classifier turns coolant fission-product activities into a one-hot fuel-failure degree, and its hardest call, intact versus small defect, is where it is least reliable. The main threats are manipulation of the coolant-activity data path, tampering with or poisoning of the model and its training data, silent sim-to-plant and drift failure, and misplaced operator trust or skill fade. Independent Technical Specification limits and isotopic-ratio methods cap direct safety consequences, but a degraded or manipulable fuel-integrity signal can still conceal or counterfeit fuel failure.

Coolant activity data manipulation -- adversarial
An adversary or insider with access to the historian, lab information system or spectrometry software could alter, delay or replay specific-activity values so the classifier stays below the defect threshold, or fabricate a failure call. The result is delayed detection of a progressing defect with higher coolant activity and worker dose, or an unwarranted power reduction, outage or report.

Model, training-data and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
The network weights, tree thresholds, preprocessing code, retraining data or simulation inputs are small artifacts that could be poisoned or modified to embed a small-defect blind spot or a trigger pattern. Opaque one-hot outputs and absent regression tests make a tampered model look like a legitimate retrain, and a shared model would carry the bias across sites.

Proxy-model evasion from public design -- adversarial
The published architecture and input features let an attacker build a proxy classifier and learn which activity patterns evade detection. Exposure is limited because inputs are measured physics rather than an open inference API, so this mainly aids an insider crafting evasive input patterns.

Simulation-trained, data-scarce classifier -- implicit, exploitable
Real defect events with known defect size are rare, so training likely rests on simulated or surrogate release models, and the network learns the simulator's mapping rather than plant behaviour, so the intact versus small-defect boundary is unreliable. An adversary could act in this poorly validated region, where manipulation or a real defect is indistinguishable from model error.

Drift and confounded inputs -- implicit, exploitable
Power transients, iodine spiking, tramp uranium, purification changes, burnup and plant or fuel heterogeneity shift activities independent of cladding state, yet the model returns a confident class with no out-of-distribution or abstention mechanism, causing missed small defects or false alarms. An adversary could time or hide input perturbations within these ambiguous conditions, for example after an outage.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The network cannot show which isotopes drove a class, retraining gives non-identical classifiers, hard labels hide uncertainty, and no accepted qualification, version or change control regime exists for this tool. An adversary can rely on this to make a modified model or biased output indistinguishable from legitimate retraining, and the tool risks creeping into compliance roles unqualified.

Over-trust, disuse and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A confident 'intact' output may lead staff to deprioritise isotopic-ratio and sipping follow-up and let manual iodine-spike interpretation skills fade, while repeated false positives breed disuse. An adversary could time manipulation to periods of high trust to suppress follow-up.

Measurement-chain and propagation faults -- implicit
Errors in gamma spectrometry, sampling timing, decay correction or calibration enter as plausible inputs, and the classifier cannot distinguish instrument faults from physical change; stacking a tree on the network adds error propagation. An adversary gains little beyond what the deliberate input manipulation already provides.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory, on-line diagnostic for fuel cladding integrity in a PWR. It ingests coolant fission-product specific activities (iodines, noble gases, Cs) and outputs a one-hot failure-degree class. Downstream, chemistry, reactor engineering and fuel-reliability staff use it to decide on power maneuvering, coolant cleanup, sipping and outage fuel inspection scope, and whether Technical Specification coolant activity limits are approached. Existing practice is a strong backstop: Tech Spec limits on dose-equivalent I-131 and gross activity, the isotopic-ratio methods, and routine chemistry sampling are independent of the AI, so a wrong output has to coincide with those being ignored or deprioritized before real harm occurs. The main consequences are therefore degraded fuel-reliability decisions (late detection or false alarms causing unneeded shutdowns or inspection costs) and erosion of defect-trend records, not a direct safety-system challenge. The AI-specific issue is that the model is a small-data, simulation-trained classifier whose most valuable discrimination (intact vs. small defect) is exactly where signal is weak and confounded.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data scarcity and provenance: real defect events with known defect size are rare, so training likely relies on simulated or surrogate source-term and release models (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Sim-to-plant transfer is uncertain. Clean-run and defect-run labels from real plants are sparse and rarely have ground truth, such as post-irradiation examination. (2) Drift and out-of-distribution behavior (OP.C0302.01/.03): coolant activity depends on power level, power transients, burnup, tramp uranium contamination on the cladding surface, letdown and purification flow, coolant chemistry, plant-specific RCS volume, and fuel type and cycle design. The model may misclassify tramp-uranium background or post-transient iodine spiking as a defect, or miss a small defect masked by background. Different plants or new fuel designs will shift the distribution. (3) Automation trust and masking effects (OP.C0101.04/.05, OP.C0102): a confident 'intact' output could cause staff to deprioritize isotopic-ratio or sipping follow-up, delaying detection of a progressing defect (secondary hydriding or fuel washout) and raising coolant activity, worker dose, and the extent of fuel damage. Repeated false positives lead to under-trust and disuse. (4) Opacity and qualification gaps (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303): the network cannot readily show which isotopes drove its class, and the decision-tree cascade can have discontinuous class boundaries. There is no accepted qualification route for AI in fuel-failure monitoring, and the model must not drift into a role feeding Tech Spec compliance decisions without qualification. Hard class labels without uncertainty further hide ambiguity. (5) Measurement-chain dependence (OP.C0204, OP.C0603): errors in gamma spectrometry, sampling timing, decay correction, or calibration propagate into the model as plausible-looking inputs, and the model cannot distinguish instrument faults from physical changes. Sampling-frequency gaps make time-dependent iodine features unreliable.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Manipulation of the input chain (AML.T0043, AML.T0031, AML.T0010.002): an adversary with access to the chemistry data historian, the lab information system, or the spectrometry software could alter or bias activity values, or time changes to mimic a defect or hide one. This is a data-integrity attack on the plant data pipeline, with the AI as an amplifier or a weak link, and it can trigger a false alarm that drives an unwarranted power reduction or outage, or suppress a true one. The plausible impact is largely economic or reliability-related, since independent sampling and Tech Spec surveillance would still catch severe release. (7) Model or training-data poisoning, or supply-chain compromise (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003): a tampered model, a vendor or research-code update, or poisoned training/simulation data could embed a bias such as a blind spot for small defects, and staff would not notice because of the opacity. If the model is shared across a fleet or by a fuel vendor service, a single compromise could propagate (OP.C0602, OP.C0601). (8) Evasion and reconnaissance (AML.T0015, AML.T0000): the published architecture and the input features are public, which helps in crafting inputs. Practical exposure is low because the plant's inputs come from measured physics, and the realistic concern is insider or network access to the analysis workstation rather than public inference APIs. Overall severity is moderate-to-low for safety because of independent defense in depth, but meaningful for fuel-reliability, outage planning, and dose management, and it grows if the tool is later promoted into automated or compliance roles.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, the main fragility is the training data. Fission-product coolant activities with labelled failure degrees are almost never available from real PWR operation, because defect size and count are rarely known with ground truth. The training set is therefore very likely generated by a source-term or release-model code (diffusion/escape-rate coefficients, assumed burnup, power history, coolant cleanup rates), which makes this simulated or surrogate data (OP.C0201.01/.02) with a low base-rate of real failures (OP.C0202). A cascade-forward net with a decision tree learns the simulator's mapping, not plant reality, and one-hot degree-of-failure labels impose hard class boundaries on what is a continuum of defect size, location and burnup. At inference, specific activities are affected by confounders absent from the training distribution: coolant purification and letdown changes, power transients and shutdown iodine spikes, tramp uranium contamination, multiple simultaneous defects, sampling and gamma-spectrometry uncertainty, and plant-to-plant or cycle-to-cycle differences. Under these conditions the classifier will still return a confident class, because it has no out-of-distribution or abstention mechanism.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Sim-to-real and distribution-shift failure (OP.C0302, .01, .03; OP.C0201.01/.02; OP.C0303): a model trained on simulated release data misclassifies real coolant activity profiles, with silent false negatives, where a small defect is called intact and slow degradation goes undetected, or false positives that prompt unnecessary power reduction or outage. Because the tool is pitched as an alternative to isotopic ratios, a mismatch between the two methods could either erode trust or, worse, lead operators to defer to the more opaque one. (2) Small-data and label problems (OP.C0202, OP.C0203): too few real failure events exist to validate or recalibrate, and plant, cycle and fuel-design heterogeneity makes a model tuned on one reactor poorly transferable. Reuse across a fleet could replicate one bias everywhere (OP.C0602). (3) Opacity and brittleness (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0402.01): neural network weights vary with initialization, so retraining after new data gives non-identical classifiers, and a tree on top stacks error propagation (OP.C0603). The degree-of-failure output has no uncertainty estimate. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04/.05, OP.C0102): operators may over-trust a clean 'intact' reading or ignore alarms after repeated false positives. (5) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0504): no established route to qualify a non-deterministic classifier for an on-line fuel-integrity monitor.

ADVERSARIAL threats. The inputs are sensor and lab-chain values, so the attack surface is the data path, not the model API. (a) Manipulating or spoofing coolant activity data upstream of the model, or in the sampling, spectrometry or historian chain (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031), could hold the classifier below the failure threshold, masking real fuel degradation, or manufacture false failure signals to force outages. Low-amplitude drift-like manipulation is hard to distinguish from the model's natural brittleness and would be hard to catch. (b) Poisoning the retraining or recalibration data, or the simulation inputs used for synthetic training sets (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000), could shift decision boundaries or create trigger-like blind spots. (c) Compromise of model files or software dependencies (AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0076) would be a persistent way to bias outputs. (d) Knowledge of the published architecture and input features (AML.T0000, AML.T0013, AML.T0005) lets an attacker build a proxy model and find which activity patterns evade detection. The consequence is concealed fuel failure: delayed response, increased coolant contamination and worker dose, and degraded confidence in fuel-integrity monitoring.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this classifier is a low-value direct target but a useful way to blind or time-shift an adversary's actions. It sits between the coolant radiochemistry data stream (specific activities of fission products) and the operators' and fuel-reliability engineers' picture of cladding integrity. A sophisticated adversary, or a malicious insider, would not need to damage fuel. They would only need to shape what the classifier says about it: hold a developing defect at "intact" or "small defect", or flood operators with spurious escalations. The more the 'small defect vs. intact' boundary, the hardest and most consequential one, is handed to a model that was trained mostly on simulated or scarce data and is opaque to operators, the more a quiet bias, drift or tampering looks like normal plant behaviour. The use case also creates a new pathway: the data historian, the sampling and analysis chain, and the model artifact all become things to compromise, and none of them has historically been treated as security-relevant.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Input integrity: the model consumes coolant specific-activity values from sampling, gamma spectrometry or on-line monitors, and an adversary or insider with access to the lab information system, historian or analysis software could alter, delay or replay the activity data (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Because the model outputs a graded 'failure degree' from a small number of isotopes, small coordinated perturbations could keep the output below the decision-tree threshold. The consequence is delayed detection of a real defect, with later fuel degradation, elevated coolant activity, unplanned outage or a release-related event that an adversary can time around. The same manipulation could also create a false failure call that forces an outage or a regulatory report (an economic or reputational attack through AML.T0048). (2) Model and supply-chain integrity: the network weights, decision-tree thresholds and preprocessing or normalisation code are small, easily altered artifacts. If they are modified (AML.T0018, AML.T0010, AML.T0076) or a backdoor trigger is inserted for a particular activity pattern (AML.T0043.004), the manipulation is unlikely to be noticed because there is no independent regression test and the one-hot output hides confidence. Vendor, university or open-source tooling and the published paper's architecture (AML.T0000, AML.T0002) also give adversaries reconnaissance on how the classifier behaves and where its boundary lies (AML.T0005). (3) Trust concentration and a vigilance gap: if the classifier is accepted as an alternative to isotopic-ratio methods, the chemistry staff's skill in manual iodine-spiking and ratio interpretation may fade, and an operator may defer to a confident categorical output (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). An adversary could time action around a period of high trust, or after an outage when conditions differ from the training set. IMPLICIT, exploitable weaknesses. (4) Data scarcity and provenance: real defective-fuel data is rare, and most training sets are simulated or from a few plants and cycles (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203). The small-defect vs. intact boundary is therefore the least reliable region of the model, and an adversary would exploit it by operating where it is least trustworthy. (5) Drift and heterogeneity: coolant chemistry, power history, tramp uranium, burnup, coolant-cleanup performance, load-follow transients and iodine spiking all shift fission-product activities independently of cladding state (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). A model not recalibrated for these will produce false or missed calls, and attackers can hide behind that ambiguity. (6) Opacity and qualification: there is no explanation of which isotope drives the class, and no AI-specific QA or software-hygiene regime for an O&M-support tool (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0505). Tamper detection, version control and change control are therefore likely to be missing, and a modified model would be indistinguishable from a legitimately retrained one. Overall the realistic worst case is not a direct accident but a degraded, insider-manipulable fuel-integrity signal that cheaply conceals or counterfeits fuel failure, so the facility should keep independent isotopic-ratio cross-checks and treat the model and its data path as security-relevant.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on input-chain manipulation, model/training poisoning, sim-to-real data scarcity, drift, opacity and over-trust as the core threats. I dropped weakly supported codes (AML.T0002, AML.T0013, OP.C0505, OP.C0504, OP.C0403) and folded the engineer's separate fleet-propagation point into the tampering threat.

evidence.citation: "An Improved Method for PWR Fuel Failure Detection Using Cascade-forward Neural Network With Decision Tree," Frontiers in Energy Research (Frontiers Media)
evidence.note: The paper proposes a cascade-forward neural network with a decision tree for PWR fuel failure detection. Its input is the specific activity of fission products measured in the coolant, and its output is a one-hot-encoded degree of fuel failure. The authors report that it classifies failure degree well, including telling intact rods from rods with small defects.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is manipulation or tampering that conceals a progressing cladding defect (or fakes one), which leads to higher coolant activity, worker dose, or unwarranted outages; independent Technical Specification limits and isotopic-ratio methods cap this at operational disruption and some safety-margin erosion, not a radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Drift, confounded inputs, and weak small-defect discrimination reliably degrade the classifier whenever transients, iodine spiking, or sim-to-plant mismatch occur, but a deliberate manipulation or poisoning attack depends on specific access and conditions.

exploitability.why: Altering the data path or model artifacts takes insider or privileged access to the historian, lab systems, or the model pipeline, and there is no open inference interface for routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Impact falls on one plant's fuel-integrity monitoring, coolant activity and dose, and operational decisions, but a shared or propagated model could carry bias across sites, and the advisory role limits coupling to other systems.

discoverability.why: The published architecture, inputs, and well-known classes of drift, poisoning, and over-trust are inferable by a capable outsider, but finding actual exploitable weak spots needs plant-specific data and pipeline knowledge.

use_case: Multilayer-perceptron and convolutional neural networks that use accelerometer vibration responses from nuclear equipment-piping systems to locate degradation (non-uniform wall-thickness loss at elbows) and classify its severity as minor, moderate or severe. The networks were trained on a digital twin and tested on data from a lab piping rig driven by pump-like harmonic excitation, for condition monitoring of safety-system piping.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory condition-monitoring use case, in which MLP and CNN models trained on a digital twin classify elbow wall-thinning in safety-system piping, incurs mainly implicit risk. The models have never been shown to work on real plant data, and the main danger is a silent false negative that is trusted enough to defer UT/FAC inspection. Adversaries could exploit that blind spot through sensor-level evasion, poisoning of the twin and training pipeline, or compromise of the analytics host.

Sim-to-real and rig-to-plant gap -- implicit, exploitable
The networks learn the digital twin's idealised physics and are validated on one lab rig with clean harmonic drive. Broadband flow noise, varying pump states, temperature, support changes, sensor re-mounting and different thinning geometry are out of distribution, so the model can miss severe elbow thinning or misattribute operating changes to degradation. An adversary could time physical sabotage or pipe degradation around this known blind spot, or rely on operators trusting a monitor that stays quiet.

Scarce real degraded-pipe data and coarse severity classes -- implicit, exploitable
Real severe wall-loss examples are rare, so the minor/moderate/severe bins come from the twin's discretisation and may not map to minimum-wall or remaining-life criteria. Severity labels near the decision threshold are therefore poorly calibrated, and an adversary could hide thinning inside the mislabelled band.

Opacity, overconfidence and automation over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
Softmax outputs from the MLP and CNN show high confidence on out-of-distribution input and give no calibrated uncertainty, so staff may defer UT or FAC inspection on a quiet dashboard. After false alarms they may instead discount the system. An adversary could exploit the resulting inspection window, or induce nuisance alarms to push operators into discounting or disabling the monitor.

Ageing drift, retraining and qualification gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Healthy baseline stiffness and damping shift with ageing, repairs and support changes, and retraining with seed-dependent behaviour has no AI-specific qualification or change-control path for a safety-system monitoring role. A drifted or quietly altered model could stay in service unnoticed, which gives a tampered model cover.

Sensor-level evasion and chaff -- adversarial
Someone with physical or network access to the accelerometer path can alter mounting, replay healthy-baseline vibration, or inject crafted or narrowband signals so real thinning falls inside the learned healthy response. Crafted perturbations of low-dimensional signals are cheap, and chaff can flood operators with false alarms.

Twin and training-pipeline poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or vendor/supply-chain actor who tampers with FE model parameters, simulation data or model weights can embed blind spots, such as classifying severe thinning at chosen elbows as minor. This undermines maintenance planning for safety-system piping and is the cheaper route for a capable adversary than the sensors.

Monitoring host compromise and denial -- adversarial
A compromised analytics workstation holding model artifacts and vibration data gives a foothold, reconnaissance on piping condition and design knowledge, and a way to extract the model. Denial or delay of monitoring, or a new IT/OT path from plant sensors into analytics, can also create blind periods.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view this is an advisory condition-monitoring tool for flow-accelerated corrosion and erosion at elbows in safety-related piping. Its value and its risk both depend on how far maintenance and inspection decisions lean on it. The system is trained on a digital twin and validated on a single lab rig with pump-like harmonic excitation, so the main weakness is the gap between that data and a real plant. Real plants have broadband flow-induced vibration, multiple pumps and supports, temperature and pressure effects, changing boundary conditions, sensor aging, and degradation geometry that differs from the rig's. Existing practice (ASME Section XI, FAC programs such as CHECWORKS, UT wall-thickness inspection, leak detection, and in-service inspection intervals) already guards against a single wrong output. Harm needs the AI to be trusted enough to defer or replace those measures, or to fail without anyone noticing.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and rig-to-plant gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). The networks learn the digital twin's idealised physics, and the validation is on one rig with clean harmonic drive. In a plant, operating-state changes, fouling, support or snubber changes, a different pipe class, or non-uniform thinning geometry would be out of distribution. A missed severe elbow (false negative) is the dangerous failure.
