It could let thinning go unchecked, deferring UT or FAC inspection and raising the risk of rupture or loss of a safety-system function. False positives cause unnecessary outages, ALARA dose and wasted inspection. (2) Scarcity of real degraded-pipe data (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Severe, real wall-loss cases are rare and cannot be produced at scale on operating plant, so severity classes are poorly calibrated. The coarse minor/moderate/severe bins also hide where decisions actually matter, near the minimum wall thickness. (3) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0401). Opaque CNN outputs, confident labels and a quiet dashboard can breed complacency among monitoring staff or in a risk-informed inspection program. They give no uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag. Localisation errors could send inspectors to the wrong elbow. (4) Qualification and repeatability (OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0302.01). Safety-system monitoring needs a qualified method, and retrained models may behave differently. Sensor drift or a loosened accelerometer mount would look like degradation or mask it.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. These matter less than the implicit ones, but an adversary could time an attack around the implicit weaknesses. (a) Tampering with sensor data or acquisition (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0046): injecting or shaping vibration signals, or physically changing accelerometer placement or coupling, could hide real thinning or fabricate alarms. Because the model is brittle off-distribution, small perturbations may flip the severity class. This could support sabotage or an outage-inducing nuisance campaign. A change in actual pipe excitation (for example the pump operating condition) could do the same. (b) Training pipeline and digital-twin integrity (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003): poisoning the simulation parameters, synthetic data or retrained weights could build in blind spots for particular elbows or severities. Vendor or third-party twin supply chains and model updates are the likely entry points (OP.C0502, OP.C0602 if the model is propagated across a fleet). (c) Denial or delay (AML.T0029, OP.C0601, OP.C0204): loss of monitoring or cloud analytics at a critical time degrades condition awareness. A bigger concern is a new IT/OT network path from plant sensors into analytics (AML.T0049, AML.T0012).

Safety consequence needs coincident failure of independent barriers (UT inspections, leak detection, pressure testing, FAC programs). So the realistic worst case is erosion of defence-in-depth through deferred inspection, not direct loss of safety function. Because the use case is advisory and in O&M, it is not a protection-system function. The main concern is credit-taking creep into inspection-interval decisions.

ai_engineer.argument: The central fragility is the sim-to-real gap. The MLP and CNN models are trained on finite-element digital-twin vibration data and then tested on a single lab rig with pump-like harmonic excitation. A plant has very different boundary conditions, supports, fluid loading, temperature, flow-induced broadband noise, sensor mounting and ageing. The twin's fidelity fixes what the model learns, so any twin simplification (idealised wall-loss geometry, damping, supports) becomes a baked-in bias that field data cannot easily correct. The label space is also coarse (location plus minor/moderate/severe), and degradation at real elbows (erosion-corrosion, FAC) is rarely a clean graded scenario. Real labelled degraded data is close to nonexistent, so the models cannot be validated on the failure modes that matter, and a softmax output can show high confidence on out-of-distribution input. Because the monitored piping serves safety systems, a confident 'no or minor degradation' output under drift is more dangerous than a false alarm, and the system gives operators no reliable way to tell when it is out of its envelope.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real / transferred-data failure (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). The model is trained on synthetic twin data and validated on one rig with one excitation type. Real plants have operational heterogeneity: varying pump speeds, transients, multi-source excitation, temperature and fluid-state changes, sensor degradation and re-mounting, and support or hanger relaxation. These shift vibration signatures independently of wall thinning. The model may therefore misattribute operating-condition changes to degradation (false positives that erode trust) or miss real thinning (false negatives that let wall loss progress toward leak or rupture in a safety-system line). (2) Data scarcity and a low base rate (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Severe, real, labelled thinning examples barely exist, and the severity classes are tied to the twin's discretisation rather than to code-based minimum wall or remaining-life criteria. Class boundaries may not map to any regulatory or engineering threshold. (3) Concept drift and ageing (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). Baseline stiffness and damping change with ageing, repairs, insulation and support changes, so the healthy reference moves. This needs retraining or recalibration, which in turn needs a qualification path for the updated model (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0402.01). (4) Opacity and overconfidence (OP.C0401, OP.C0403). Neither CNN nor MLP gives calibrated uncertainty or an out-of-distribution flag, and the location outputs are hard to cross-check against ultrasonic thickness measurement. This encourages automation over-trust or, after false alarms, under-trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102). If predictions replace or defer inspection intervals, latent wall loss goes unseen. (5) Training non-determinism: seed-dependent results complicate reproducibility for qualification (OP.C0402.01).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Integrity attacks on the data path. Accelerometer streams reach the model over plant or monitoring networks. Spoofing or replaying healthy-baseline vibration, injecting small perturbations, or adding narrowband excitation that mimics or masks thinning signatures could evade the model (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031). Because the input is low-dimensional physical signal data, adversarial examples are cheap to craft, and a black-box proxy trained on a public twin or published paper could transfer (AML.T0005, AML.T0043.002, AML.T0000). An adversary who also does physical sabotage or accelerates degradation could hide it from condition monitoring. (7) Twin and training-data supply chain. A poisoned or tampered FE model, simulation dataset, pretrained weights or vendor-supplied model could embed a blind spot or backdoor, for example for a particular elbow location or frequency band (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). (8) Model and twin exfiltration give design-level knowledge of piping geometry and sensitivity (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035). (9) Availability: chaff or noise injection and denial of the monitoring service force false alarms or blind periods (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). (10) Unvalidated ML software and library stacks fall under AI-specific QA and software-hygiene gaps (OP.C0502, OP.C0504).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this is a passive, read-only condition-monitoring aid on safety-system piping, so it is a poor direct target for a sophisticated adversary. Its main value is as an enabler: it could hide real degradation, or it could erode the vigilance and inspection cadence that would otherwise catch it. The weakest points are the training pipeline and its heavy reliance on a digital twin, plus a lab-to-plant gap that the system's own failure modes already widen. An adversary, or just bad luck, could time pipe degradation or a pipe-integrity event around a monitor that is quietly blind or over-trusted. The security concern is concentrated trust in a model that was never shown to work on real plant data.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Poisoning or manipulating the digital twin, its simulation parameters, or the training data and model weights (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059). Mechanism: an insider or supply-chain actor with access to the FE model or the training pipeline biases the networks so that severe elbow thinning at particular locations is classified as minor, or never flagged. Dependency: maintenance and inspection planning for safety-system piping. Consequence: undetected wall loss, and possible loss of piping integrity at a time of the adversary's choosing. The cheaper route for a capable adversary is the data and model pipeline, not the sensors. (2) Evasion at the sensor level (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). Mechanism: someone with physical access can alter accelerometer mounting, cabling or excitation, or inject a crafted vibration signature, so that real degradation falls inside the learned 'healthy' response. Consequence: a masked defect, or a flood of false alarms (AML.T0046) that pushes operators to disable or discount the system. This takes only plant-level access and no AI expertise. (3) The monitor as a stepping stone. Mechanism: a compromised monitoring or analytics workstation that holds model artifacts and plant vibration data gives the adversary a foothold and a reconnaissance picture of piping condition (AML.T0035, AML.T0036, AML.T0025). Piping vulnerability data is itself sensitive.

IMPLICIT. (4) Sim-to-real gap and drift (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0203). The networks were trained on a twin and tested on a clean lab rig, not on in-service plant data. Real pipes have operating noise, varying flow, temperature, supports and corrosion shapes that differ from the training data. Accuracy on the bench therefore says little about performance in the plant, and the monitor may stay silent or classify wrongly in ways an adversary could count on. (5) Severity classification is coarse and its base rate is low (OP.C0202, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0401). Real severe degradation is rare, and the model's opacity makes silent failure hard to notice. (6) Automation trust, skill fade and alarm complacency (OP.C0101.04/.06, OP.C0102). Once the monitor is trusted, ultrasonic and radiographic inspection may be reduced, which creates a window in which degradation can progress unobserved. (7) Qualification and governance gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0303). There is no AI-specific qualification for a safety-system monitoring role, and nothing requires periodic re-validation or change control on the twin and model. A drifted or tampered model could therefore stay in service unnoticed. Overall, the highest-consequence path is a quiet false-negative on a safety-system pipe, whether from tampering or from ordinary generalization failure.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, data scarcity, over-trust and a false-negative worst case, with the same adversarial pathways (sensor evasion, twin/pipeline poisoning); I merged these. I dropped the speculative, weakly supported codes (OP.C0601, OP.C0602, AML.T0049, AML.T0012, AML.T0005, AML.T0000, AML.T0043.004) and kept the exfiltration and foothold threat from the AI and security panelists as a single compromised-host threat.

evidence.citation: "Deep learning application for monitoring degradation in nuclear safety systems," European Journal of Environmental and Civil Engineering (Taylor & Francis), Vol 28, No 13, 2024
evidence.note: The paper experimentally tests an AI-based monitoring framework for nuclear piping. It uses an instrumented piping rig with graded wall-thinning, plus its digital twin. MLP and CNN models detect where the degradation is and how severe it is. The authors compare results from experimental data with results from simulated data. Only the abstract was retrieved, so this note rests on the abstract.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a silent false negative on elbow wall-thinning in safety-system piping that defers UT/FAC inspection, eroding safety margin and potentially leading to a pipe failure or loss-of-coolant-type event. The monitor is advisory and inspection layers remain, so a direct radiological release is less likely than serious safety-margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real distribution shift, ageing drift and overconfident softmax outputs on out-of-distribution input are systematic properties of models trained on a digital twin, so missed detections recur reliably once plant conditions differ from the lab rig. Targeted adversarial outcomes are more conditional, but the implicit failure is dependable.

exploitability.why: The adversarial routes (physical or network access to the accelerometer path, insider or supply-chain tampering with twin parameters or model weights, compromise of the analytics host) generally need privileged or insider access and some domain knowledge of piping dynamics. The implicit blind spot needs no access, but exploiting it for sabotage still needs capability and timing.

affected_users.why: Impact spans multiple elbows and monitored safety-system piping, and a poisoned or drifted model or a compromised host could affect every monitored location and inform maintenance planning plant-wide. It stays within the condition-monitoring function and is not tightly coupled to other control systems, so it falls short of facility-wide propagation.

discoverability.why: Sim-to-real gaps, softmax overconfidence, drift and the vulnerability of low-dimensional sensor signals to evasion are all well documented in the open literature, and the study is published. Learning specific blind spots or the deployment details of a given plant would need more knowledge, but the class itself is readily evident.

use_case: Domain adaptation of the BERT transformer language model on the text of 10 CFR Parts 1-199, so that NRC staff have a model that understands regulatory language. It was explored as a way to support efficient completeness and intake reviews of licensing submittals, which can run to hundreds of pages.
incurred_insecurity:
A domain-adapted BERT encoder used to screen hundreds-page licensing submittals for completeness controls no plant component, so its danger is quiet erosion of regulatory assurance: deficient submittals passing intake and the screening filter itself becoming a manipulation point. The main threats are applicant-side evasion of the screen, tampering with the model or its data, leakage of sensitive submittal content, and implicit weaknesses (automation trust, mismatch between training text and real submittals, drift, opacity, no qualification regime) that an adversary can time around.

Crafted-submittal evasion -- adversarial
The model learned regulatory phrasing, not technical sufficiency, so an applicant or a party posing as one can use lexical mimicry, formatting, padding or buried or hidden content to make missing or weak material score as satisfied. Deficient or obfuscated safety, security-plan or safeguards content then enters detailed review without the flag it should have raised.

Model and training-data tampering -- adversarial
A backdoored public BERT checkpoint, unsafe serialized artifacts, or altered adaptation corpus and downstream fine-tuning labels could carry a trigger that suppresses flags on chosen phrasing or topics. Because the model is trusted as regulation-aware and the effect is persistent and low-visibility, systematic review bias would be hard to detect without a stable benchmark.

Sensitive submittal leakage -- adversarial
Submittals and any fine-tuning data derived from prior reviews hold proprietary, security-related and safeguards-sensitive information. Staging it in ML pipelines, logs or externally hosted services creates an aggregation target, and extraction or inversion of the adapted model could leak it.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A tool pitched for efficiency invites reviewers to skim whatever the model did not flag, and intake skills decay under workload pressure, so false 'complete' calls go unchallenged. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, timing or structuring a submission to ride the unexamined pass.

Training-to-deployment distribution mismatch -- implicit, exploitable
A masked-language encoder trained on terse CFR text with a 512-token window cannot hold cross-references, applicability logic or absences across hundreds of pages, nor handle tables, figures, guidance or novel non-LWR designs. An adversary can place deficiencies where chunking and truncation hide them, or file novel-design material far from the training distribution.

Regulatory drift and silent staleness -- implicit, exploitable
Amendments and new frameworks such as Part 53 change what 'complete' means, while a frozen model lags without versioned retraining and requalification. An adversary can time a submission just after a rule change to exploit the stale criteria.

Opacity, non-repeatability and missing qualification -- implicit
Embedding-based flags are hard to explain, vary with seed and version, and have no established AI QA regime or measured false-'complete' rate, so informal use can creep into real intake with unclear accountability and weak audit trails. No distinct adversary gain beyond the blind spots already described.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a regulator-side, non-real-time tool: a domain-adapted BERT (an encoder, not a generator) for completeness and intake screening of hundreds-page licensing submittals. No reactor or fuel-cycle component is controlled by it, so the physical consequence path is long and runs through the licensing decision. A wrong output would have to be missed by the staff technical review, the safety evaluation, ACRS/hearing process, inspection and the licensee's own QA before it becomes a plant-safety issue. The real exposure is quiet erosion of review rigor, which is hard to see because intake screening is an upstream filter whose misses are rarely visible. A secondary issue is that a regulator-trusted model, or its training and retrieval corpus, becomes an attractive manipulation target for an applicant or a hostile actor. Existing practice (human reviewers, acceptance review checklists, later detailed review) limits the damage, but only if the tool stays advisory and its error rates are known.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Automation bias and complacency at intake: if staff treat a model's 'complete / no gaps' signal as sufficient, incomplete or deficient submittals (missing analyses, absent commitments, gaps against specific Part 50/52/53/70/72/73 requirements) pass acceptance review. The consequence is that deficiencies surface late, or are never found, which delays or degrades the safety finding. Skill fade among junior reviewers compounds this (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (2) Fidelity and scope limits: a BERT encoder trained on regulation text alone sees no guidance (Reg Guides, NUREGs, SRP), precedent, or applicant-specific technical content. It can match language without checking whether a technical basis is adequate, so it favors form over substance. Long documents exceed the context window and are chunked, so cross-references and omissions (what is absent) are structurally hard for it to detect (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (3) Corpus drift and qualification gaps: 10 CFR is amended, and new frameworks such as Part 53 and risk-informed guidance change what 'complete' means. A frozen model goes stale silently, and novel reactor designs and non-LWR submittals are out of distribution relative to historical patterns (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0503). No established QA regime exists for validating such a screening tool, and the error rate for false 'complete' calls is unmeasured (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402). (4) Sensitive-data governance: submittals contain proprietary, export-controlled and security-related information (SUNSI/SGI). Hosting, fine-tuning on or logging them on a poorly scoped or cloud platform creates leakage paths (OP.C0505, OP.C0601). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Applicant-side evasion: a submitter who knows or infers that an NLP screen is used can craft formatting, phrasing or boilerplate that satisfies the model's learned notion of compliance while thin on substance, or hide gaps in places the model underweights (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0063). This is most plausible as deliberate gaming or low-quality submittals rather than sabotage, and it is bounded by human review but could degrade the effective filtering of high-volume submissions. (6) Supply-chain and model/data integrity: a tampered pre-trained BERT checkpoint, fine-tuning data, or downstream classification head and labeled sets could systematically bias which requirements are flagged or missed. This is a low-visibility, persistent effect that would be hard to detect without a stable benchmark (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0031). (7) Information exposure: reconnaissance on staff tooling, or model inversion and extraction of submittal-derived data, reveals review priorities or proprietary content (AML.T0024, AML.T0036). Overall consequence class: degraded regulatory assurance and fairness/defensibility of licensing decisions, not an immediate physical hazard. The severity rises only if outputs are treated as authoritative or the tool is extended beyond intake into safety-significant determinations.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a masked-language-model continued-pretraining job on a small, static, highly structured corpus (10 CFR 1-199, a few tens of MB of text). The artifact is an encoder that produces embeddings; it is not a classifier. The risk therefore sits in the downstream heads, thresholds and retrieval layers that would be fine-tuned on it for completeness or intake screening, and that is where labelled data are scarce. The base model is almost certainly a public BERT checkpoint pulled from a hub, so pretrained-weight provenance matters. The adaptation corpus is public and authoritative, which makes the training data easy to reproduce but also easy to target for poisoning or recon. The deployment risk is that a model that 'understands regulatory language' will be trusted to judge completeness of 100s-page submittals that are unlike its training text (tables, scanned figures, vendor-proprietary content, guidance such as Regulatory Guides and NUREGs, not just the CFR).
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Supply chain: the base BERT checkpoint, tokenizer, and Python/transformers dependencies come from public hubs. A tampered or backdoored base model (AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0058, AML.T0011.000 via unsafe pickle artifacts) would carry into the domain-adapted encoder and into every downstream head. Consequence: a latent trigger could cause specific submittal phrasing to be scored as 'complete' or 'not relevant', degrading review integrity without any visible fault. (2) Applicant-side evasion: submittal text is authored by parties with an interest in passing intake. Once an applicant can infer or probe how the screener behaves (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0013/T0063 via the staff-facing outputs or published results), they can shape wording, section ordering, padding or formatting so that required content is judged present when it is only superficially similar. Embedding similarity is exploitable by lexical mimicry of regulatory phrases. Consequence: incomplete or deficient applications pass intake, with the deficiency surfacing late or never. (3) Data/training-corpus integrity: the corpus is scraped or exported CFR text, with versioning and amendments. Tampering with or silently substituting the corpus, or any later fine-tuning labels (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0059), would shift the model's notion of requirements. Fine-tuning data derived from past staff reviews also encode sensitive or proprietary content; an adapted model could leak it (AML.T0024.000, T0057). (4) New attack surface: if the tool ingests applicant documents, malicious files (PDF parsers, embedded text, hidden text/white-on-white content) become an input channel into the pipeline, and any LLM-style extension (summarisation, Q&A) adds prompt injection (AML.T0051.001) from the submittal itself. IMPLICIT: (a) Mismatch between pretraining objective and task: masked-token adaptation does not teach legal obligation logic, cross-references (e.g. 50.34 pointing to Appendix B), applicability conditions, or negation; completeness is a checklist-satisfaction problem that BERT's 512-token window cannot hold over hundreds of pages, so chunking will fragment context and drop cross-section requirements (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403, OP.C0302). (b) Distribution shift: the CFR text is terse, normative language, while submittals are technical, tabular, figure-heavy, and vendor-specific; novel reactor designs (advanced, non-LWR) use vocabulary and frameworks not in training (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). (c) Concept drift: rule changes, new Parts (e.g. Part 53), guidance, and licensing-basis precedent change what 'complete' means; a frozen model silently lags unless there is a versioned retraining and requalification process (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303, OP.C0503). (d) Label and evaluation scarcity: few ground-truth completeness determinations, low base rate of specific deficiency types, and risk of test leakage from public data make performance claims weak (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.05). (e) Opacity and non-repeatability: embedding-based flags are hard to explain to staff or in legal challenge, and seed/version variation changes outputs (OP.C0401, OP.C0402). (f) Human factors: a tool pitched for efficiency invites automation bias, with reviewers skimming what the model did not flag and skills fading in intake review (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). An adversary can time submissions to exploit these weaknesses, e.g. just after a rule change or with a novel design. (g) Governance gaps: there is no established AI QA regime for licensing-support software and an unclear status of the model as safety-relevant or not (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0502). Overall consequence is mainly regulatory-process integrity: erroneous intake decisions, inconsistent treatment of applicants, and potential downstream safety-review gaps, rather than direct plant impact.

security_specialist.argument: This is a regulator-side, advisory NLP tool, so a nation-state would not attack it for direct physical effect. It matters as a stepping stone and as a trust-concentration point. If it screens completeness and intake of hundreds-page licensing submittals, then whoever shapes what the model flags or passes can shape where human reviewers spend limited attention. That makes it an indirect route to a licensing, security-plan or safeguards-relevant deficiency getting through, and a quieter route than defeating a physical protection system. The non-adversarial weaknesses are what an adversary would time around. Reviewer complacency, a model fine-tuned only on regulation text that may never have seen real submittals, and opacity about why a section was judged complete all create predictable blind spots. The easier targets are still the submittal documents, the applicant-to-regulator pipeline and the staff, not the model. The AI's main contribution to the threat surface is a new, lightly scrutinized, trust-bearing component in the review chain.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by crafted submittals: an applicant or a hostile party posing as one (or a compromised vendor or document preparer) formats, structures or words content so the domain-adapted BERT classifier or completeness check rates missing, weak or buried material as satisfied. Mechanism: the model learned regulatory language patterns, not technical sufficiency, so it can be steered by surface features. Dependence: intake and completeness screening that decides which submittals get deeper human attention. Consequence: a deficient, or deliberately obfuscated, submittal enters detailed review without the flag it should have raised, which weakens regulatory assurance on safety, security-plan or safeguards content. (2) Model or pipeline integrity compromise: an insider or supply-chain actor tampers with the pretrained BERT weights, the fine-tuning corpus (which should be public CFR text, but the later mix of internal guidance and prior submittals may not be), the checkpoint or the inference service. A trigger-based backdoor could suppress flags on particular phrasing or topics. Because the model is trusted for being 'regulation-aware,' tampering would be hard to detect. (3) Information-pathway risk: submittals can contain proprietary, security-related or safeguards-sensitive information. Staging that content in an ML pipeline, logs or an external or cloud-hosted service expands who can reach it and creates an aggregation target. Extraction or inversion attacks on a model fine-tuned on sensitive documents could leak content. (4) Reconnaissance value: knowing the screening criteria and the model's blind spots tells an adversarial applicant how to shape filings. IMPLICIT. (5) Automation bias and reviewer deskilling: over-reliance on 'passed' results reduces the vigilance of staff under workload pressure, and an adversary can time a submission to this. (6) Domain and distribution mismatch: training on 10 CFR text is not training on the structure, quality or length of real hundreds-page submittals, so the model generalizes poorly to unfamiliar formats, tables, figures and long documents that exceed the context window. Truncation and omission can hide missing content. (7) Regulatory drift: rule changes make the model stale and give inconsistent determinations over time. (8) Opacity and non-repeatability give weak audit trails and make it hard to defend or reconstruct a flagged or unflagged decision. (9) Qualification gap: the tool was explored in research and has no AI-specific QA, so informal use could creep into real intake without controls, with the accountability chain left unclear.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on applicant-side evasion, model/data tampering, automation bias, the training-versus-submittal mismatch, drift and the qualification gap; I merged the near-duplicate points and dropped weakly argued codes (e.g. AML.T0012, AML.T0036, AML.T0051.001, AML.T0058) that were not clearly instantiated by the documented use.

evidence.citation: "Application of Natural Language Processing to NRC Regulatory Documents Future Focused Research (FFR) Project Closeout," U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (ADAMS ML24345A023)
evidence.note: This NRC research-project closeout memo reports that the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model was trained on 10 CFR Parts 1-199. It was one of three NLP tasks, and the aim was to help staff do regulatory reviews more efficiently and to build knowledge on how such language models are trained. The NER task in the memo is matching-based, so I did not use it as the AI use case. The memo is an NRC ADAMS document and not a peer-reviewed paper.

damage.why: The worst credible threat is crafted-submittal evasion or model backdoor letting deficient safety, security-plan or safeguards content pass intake; this erodes regulatory assurance, but it controls no plant component and detailed technical review remains a downstream barrier, so it is a minor safety-margin erosion rather than a direct release.

reproducibility.why: Evasion of a lexical encoder screen and exploiting automation trust, truncation, or staleness are fairly reliable once the model is in real intake use, but outcomes depend on how the tool is deployed and on human review practices, and tampering requires specific conditions.

exploitability.why: Applicant-side evasion needs only the ability to submit documents, which is routine external interaction, but knowing how the screen behaves and tampering with checkpoints or training data require more insight or supply-chain access.

affected_users.why: A systematically biased or stale intake screen could affect many licensing submittals and review outcomes across the regulator, but the impact stays in the licensing process and does not propagate to coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: Adversarial evasion and backdoor risks for BERT-class encoders are well documented in open literature, but an outsider would need to infer that and how the NRC uses such a screen, which is only partly public (a closeout memo describes exploratory use).

use_case: Intelligent Drawing Query (IDQ) system that uses cloud AI optical character recognition (Azure OCR and Azure Document Intelligence), with multimodal GPT-4 tested for extra detection tasks, to read equipment tags in scanned engineering drawings of a CANDU station (Darlington). It automates equipment identification for plant maintenance and design-information lookup.
incurred_insecurity:
The Intelligent Drawing Query system routes scanned CANDU engineering drawings through closed, third-party cloud OCR and multimodal GPT-4 services whose output becomes an index key for maintenance and design lookup. It incurs an information-aggregation and confidentiality risk, a quiet integrity risk that is hard to tell from ordinary OCR error, and several implicit risks: plausible-but-wrong tag reads, silent vendor-side change, erosion of human cross-checking and an unclear qualification status. It is not a control or protection function, so harm runs through people acting on a wrong tag, and independent verification and tagout practice bound the severity.

Cloud exfiltration and design-information aggregation -- adversarial
Bulk upload of drawings to a commercial cloud tenant, and the structured tag-to-equipment-to-drawing index derived from it, expose security-sensitive design information to compromise through valid accounts, tenant misconfiguration, stolen API keys, vendor retention or insiders. The aggregated index of safety systems, redundancy and common-mode dependencies supports later sabotage target selection.

Drawing, image and index manipulation -- adversarial
An insider or an attacker with write access to the drawing repository, scan intake or extracted-tag store can alter drawings, perturb characters or embed hidden instruction-like text so that tags are misread, omitted or mapped to the wrong equipment, including through indirect prompt injection of the multimodal GPT-4 path. Corrupted extractions persist in the lookup database as authoritative metadata and look like normal OCR error, giving deniable wrong-component isolation or work-package references.

Supply-chain and service-availability attack -- adversarial
A compromised vendor component, SDK, API credential or malicious model-version change can alter extraction behaviour outside facility change control, and denial or flooding of the cloud service can force staff back to slow manual methods. An adversary could time such degradation to an outage window when schedule pressure favours shortcuts.

Confusable-character and hallucinated tag reads -- implicit, exploitable
OCR on aged, skewed, annotated or dense scans confuses characters (0/O, 1/I, 5/S), truncates tags, and lets fuzzy matching or GPT-4 hallucination substitute a similar component, such as a redundant-train valve or a connection that does not exist. An adversary could hide deliberate image or index tampering within this expected error band, relying on the output being dismissed as OCR noise.

Silent vendor drift and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
Managed OCR and GPT-4 endpoints update without notice and sample non-deterministically, and accuracy shown on one station's curated drawings may not transfer to other vintages, revisions, drawing types or CANDU units, so validated performance degrades with no frozen artifact to requalify. An adversary could use a vendor update or the unmonitored drift to mask a manipulation or to time an attack.

Automation bias and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
As the tool replaces slow manual lookup, planners and engineers stop cross-checking against the controlled drawing, so errors become correlated across the workforce and the tool becomes the de facto source of truth. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust so that a manipulated or erroneous tag passes unchallenged.

Qualification, data-governance and revision-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
There is no AI-specific QA basis for a non-safety-class cloud tool whose output can feed safety-related work, no clear status for that output in configuration management, and a security model built for plant networks is applied to hyperscale cloud tenancy. The tool may also index superseded or uncontrolled scans, and an adversary could exploit the unclear drawing-of-record status and the lack of integrity checks to introduce altered or stale drawings.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, IDQ is an information-retrieval aid in O&M and design lookup, not a control or protection function, so a wrong output does not directly move a plant parameter. The harm path runs through people: a planner, work-control authority or engineer acts on a mis-read equipment tag, or on a drawing the tool wrongly matched or missed. That can mean work on the wrong component, a wrong isolation or tagout boundary, a wrong design-basis lookup, or a missed interface during a modification. Existing practice already guards against much of this: field verification of tags, independent verification, work-order and clearance and tagout processes, and design-authority review of controlled drawings. The residual risk is erosion of those defenses through automation bias, schedule pressure and OCR output treated as authoritative. A second risk is cloud exposure of sensitive station drawings.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Content fidelity failure: OCR on scanned legacy P&IDs, electrical and instrument drawings makes confusable-character errors (0/O, 1/I, 5/S, B/8) and drops or garbles tags in dense, skewed, low-resolution or annotated areas, producing a plausible but wrong tag. Fuzzy matching to a tag database can then silently substitute a similar component, for example a redundant-train or similarly numbered valve. GPT-4 multimodal detection can hallucinate symbols or connections. The consequence is wrong-component identification feeding work planning, isolation boundaries or design lookups, and it matters most for safety-related, seismically qualified and redundant-train equipment. Bad output turns into harm only if field walkdown, independent verification and tagout practice also fail. (2) Automation bias and skill fade: as the tool replaces slow manual lookup, users stop cross-checking against the controlled drawing, and errors become correlated across the workforce. (3) Drift and heterogeneity: accuracy was demonstrated on one station's drawing conventions. Different vintages, revisions, drawing types and scan quality, or a vendor model update, can change performance without notice. Cloud model versions change, giving non-repeatability and a qualification gap, because these tools are not covered by software QA norms for safety use. (4) Drawing revision control: the tool may index superseded or uncontrolled scans, so a user acts on an out-of-date configuration. (5) Cloud and availability dependence: loss of the Azure service or connectivity delays outage-critical work and pushes staff back to slow manual methods they may have lost skill in. (6) Evaluation limits: a small, curated test set may overstate real-world accuracy, and rare tags are underrepresented.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Confidentiality: station P&IDs, layouts and safety-system drawings are security-sensitive. Sending them to a commercial cloud OCR or LLM service creates exposure through the vendor, tenant misconfiguration, credentials, API-key theft or data retention, and aggregated tag and layout data supports sabotage target selection. This is a data-governance and sensitive-information security issue. (b) Integrity: tampering with the drawing corpus, the scan pipeline or the tag-to-equipment index, or insider or supply-chain manipulation of the service or its model version, could cause systematic misidentification that looks like ordinary OCR error and defeats detection. Adversarially altered drawing images or embedded text could mislead the multimodal model or inject instructions (indirect prompt injection) into the GPT-4 path. (c) Availability: denial of the AI service, or flooding it, at a time such as an outage window, causes schedule pressure that favors shortcuts. Overall severity is moderate and bounded by independent verification; the main systemic risk is that the tool gradually becomes the de facto source of truth.

ai_engineer.argument: IDQ is not a model the facility trains. It is a pipeline of third-party, closed, cloud-hosted foundation services (Azure OCR, Document Intelligence, GPT-4 multimodal) that the utility cannot version-pin, inspect, retrain, or qualify in the usual sense. The ML fragility sits in the input domain: scanned legacy P&IDs, logic and electrical drawings with degraded scan quality, stamps, revision clouds, handwritten markups, dense symbology, and tag conventions (CANDU system-device-number formats) that are almost certainly absent from the vendors' training corpora. Results are therefore probabilistic, unevenly distributed across drawing types, and can change silently when the vendor updates the backend. The output is a tag string that becomes an index key into maintenance and design-information lookup. A confidently wrong or fluent-but-wrong read (O/0, 1/I, 5/S, dropped suffixes, a neighbouring tag merged in, a hallucinated tag from GPT-4) therefore looks like a valid identifier and leads to the wrong component being linked to a work package or design basis. Meanwhile, the benchmark-style evaluation reported on a curated set of drawings does not establish operational error rates across the whole drawing corpus.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Silent vendor-side model drift and non-repeatability: managed OCR/GPT-4 endpoints update without notice, so tag extraction accuracy and output formatting can change after validation. There is no frozen artifact to requalify, so the static/dynamic qualification mismatch and the repeatability gap are structural, and GPT-4 sampling adds inference-time non-determinism. (2) Out-of-distribution input and long-tail error: degraded scans, rotated or skewed text, overlapping lines, non-standard drawing templates and older revisions fall outside what the services were built for. Errors are structured (character confusions, truncation, wrong tag association to a symbol) and cluster on exactly the hard drawings. Confidence scores from OCR engines are poorly calibrated for domain tags. (3) Content fidelity: multimodal GPT-4 used for extra detection tasks (symbol or equipment-type recognition, relationships between items) can hallucinate or oversimplify connectivity and attribute it to the drawing, which is then trusted as ground truth. (4) Automation bias and skill fade: once manual identification is replaced, verification effort shrinks. Plausible-looking wrong tags propagate into maintenance planning, isolation and clearance preparation, or design-change impact checks, and the error can persist because downstream systems store the extracted tag as authoritative metadata. (5) Ground-truth and data provenance weakness: evaluation depends on manually labeled drawings from one station. Generalization to other CANDU units, revision histories, or other sites is untested, and tag coverage is sparse for rare equipment classes. (6) Governance gap: there is no clear AI-specific QA basis for a non-safety-class tool whose output can feed safety-related work, so classification decisions may understate its role in the maintenance chain.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Supply chain and cloud dependency: engineering drawings (sensitive design information, potentially export-controlled or security-sensitive) are sent to a hosted API. Exposure comes through tenant misconfiguration, credential theft, logging or retention of submitted documents, and data-residency issues. The same pipeline is a collection target, because an aggregated index of equipment tags and locations is a high-value reconnaissance asset. The cloud path also creates an availability dependency (denial of AI service, vendor outage) that can degrade the maintenance workflow. (2) Input manipulation: an insider or an attacker with write access to the drawing repository or scan intake could alter or inject drawings, or craft adversarial artifacts (perturbed characters, near-invisible text, embedded instruction-like text for the multimodal LLM, indirect prompt injection) so that tags are misread, omitted or mapped to the wrong equipment. This works as a low-signature integrity attack because the output still looks normal. (3) Result store and index poisoning: corrupted extractions written to the lookup database persist beyond the original input and are hard to trace back to a cause. (4) Model or service-side compromise (API key abuse, a malicious wrapper or SDK, pipeline code) can alter outputs selectively. Cross-cutting: because there is no local model to hash or validate, integrity assurance has to be built around the outputs (cross-checking against the equipment master list, format validators, sampled human review) rather than the model.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, IDQ is mainly an information-aggregation and trust-concentration target, and secondarily an integrity target. It sends scanned CANDU engineering drawings (piping/instrumentation, electrical, layout, with equipment tags) to commercial cloud OCR and multimodal LLM services, so the facility's most structured design-information corpus now sits outside the protected area, under a data-security model built for plant networks, not hyperscale cloud tenancy. A sophisticated adversary would more likely use the cloud pipeline for reconnaissance, a convenient index of safety-significant equipment, than try to sabotage OCR output. The integrity risk is quieter: maintenance and design staff who trust automated tag lookup stop cross-checking drawings, and that complacency is something an adversary, or a plain OCR error, can exploit or time around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Sensitive design-information exfiltration and aggregation: drawings and extracted tag databases are bulk-uploaded to Azure services, and the structured output (tag-to-equipment-to-drawing mappings) is a ready-made targeting index of safety systems, redundancy, and common-mode dependencies. Consequence: a security-sensitive information compromise via the cloud tenant, a compromised insider or valid account (AML.T0012, T0025, T0036, T0085), or the supply chain, enabling later physical or cyber sabotage planning. Retention, training-use, and jurisdictional handling by the vendor are outside the facility's control (OP.C0601, OP.C0505.01). (2) Supply-chain and service dependency: a silent change to a vendor's model or API, or a compromised vendor component (AML.T0010, T0109), changes extraction behaviour without the facility's change control, and the facility cannot freeze or re-qualify it. Denial of the service (AML.T0029) degrades maintenance lookup and pushes staff back to slow manual methods during an outage, when an adversary could want that friction. (3) Data and drawing manipulation by an insider: altering or substituting a scanned drawing, or injecting text or markings into an image (AML.T0043.003, T0051.001 for the multimodal GPT-4 path), could make a tag misread or map to the wrong equipment. The result is a wrong isolation, work-package or modification reference, which is a safety-relevant mistake with deniable attribution because it looks like an OCR error. Multimodal GPT-4 adds prompt-injection exposure from text embedded in drawings if it is ever connected to workflows or tools. (4) The system becomes a trusted-intermediary stepping stone: network paths from the plant or corporate network to cloud APIs, plus stored API keys and service credentials, create a new egress and credential-theft channel (AML.T0055, T0083).

IMPLICIT, EXPLOITABLE. (5) OCR error modes on aged, scanned, low-quality and handwritten-annotated drawings: confusable characters in tags (0/O, 1/I, 5/S), dense layouts, and rotated or overlapping text produce plausible but wrong tags. These errors are not random in effect, because similar tags in redundant trains can be swapped. Consequence: wrong-equipment identification during maintenance, with a risk of train or unit mix-up (OP.C0304.01, C0304.03, C0302.03). (6) Automation trust failure: staff who see good average accuracy lose the habit of verifying against the controlled drawing, and skill and cross-checking fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102). An adversary or a latent error need only time an action around the lapse in vigilance. (7) Governance gaps: there is no qualification basis for a commercial cloud AI tool whose version and behaviour are opaque and non-repeatable, and no clear status for its output in configuration management and records, so drawing-of-record integrity is unclear (OP.C0501, C0402.02, C0401, C0503). Evaluation on a single station's drawing set may not transfer to other drawing conventions, which matters if the tool is replicated across fleets (OP.C0602).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on cloud exfiltration of drawings, OCR and hallucination wrong-tag errors, automation bias, vendor drift and non-qualifiability, and input or index manipulation, so these were merged. Single-panelist ATLAS codes with weak fit (AML.T0015, AML.T0031) and weakly traced OP codes (OP.C0702, OP.C0602, OP.C0503) were dropped, and AML.T0043 was narrowed to the specific manual-modification sub-technique.

evidence.citation: "Automating equipment identification in nuclear engineering drawings," Nuclear Engineering and Design (Elsevier), Vol. 436, 114002, 2025
evidence.note: The paper presents design methods for the IDQ system. It compares how well Azure OCR and Azure Document Intelligence extract equipment tags from Darlington Nuclear Generating Station drawings, sets out best practices to raise extraction efficiency, and explores GPT-4's multimodal ability for further detection tasks. It replaces slow, error-prone manual identification of equipment in drawings.

damage.why: Most severe credible threat is manipulated or erroneous tag mapping leading to wrong-component isolation or work-package references, plus design-information aggregation that supports sabotage target selection; the tool is not a control or protection function and independent verification and tagout bound severity, so harm is operational disruption or safety-margin erosion rather than direct release.

reproducibility.why: Confusable-character and hallucinated reads, drift and automation bias occur reliably in the class, but a harmful outcome (wrong-component action) needs a persistent error to coincide with a skipped cross-check, and deliberate manipulation needs write access.

exploitability.why: Deliberate attack paths need valid accounts, repository or intake write access, vendor compromise or insider position, while the implicit failures need no attacker but only exist to be exploited by someone with that access.

affected_users.why: A shared index and a cloud tenant spanning many drawings, planners and engineers can propagate correlated errors across a station's maintenance and design workflows, but the effect stays within information-lookup functions and does not couple to protection systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, cloud OCR and GPT-4 use, and error modes such as character confusion, vendor drift, prompt injection and automation bias are documented in a public paper and the open literature, so an outsider can readily infer the weakness class.

use_case: Open-set fault diagnosis of reactor coolant pump shaft and bearing faults using class-specific semantic reconstruction (VDI-CSSR). The model takes RCP vibration-monitoring-system signals converted into multi-channel orbit-plot and recurrence-plot images. It uses per-class reconstruction errors to separate known fault modes from previously unseen ones, even when labelled fault data are scarce.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory open-set diagnostic for reactor coolant pump shaft and bearing faults is validated only on simulation and a journal-bearing testbed, so its known/unknown decision boundary is unqualified for real plant conditions. Its main insecurities are a sim-to-real and threshold-calibration gap, drift of the reconstruction-error baseline, analyst over-reliance, and adversarial manipulation of input signals, thresholds and the retraining loop. Because plant protection and conventional vibration alarms are independent, harm requires a co-failing safeguard, but the tool can quietly mask or mimic degradation of a safety-significant component.

Sim-to-real threshold miscalibration -- implicit, exploitable
Class-specific reconstruction thresholds tuned on simulated and testbed signals can fail silently on real RCP variation in speed, load, seals, flow excitation and sensors. This yields false 'unknown' floods or a novel fault reconstructing well under a benign class, delaying maintenance on a degrading bearing or shaft. An adversary could time a real degradation or sabotage around these known blind spots, or rely on the tool's unvalidated 'healthy' verdict.

Open-set limits and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Rejecting unseen faults by reconstruction error is theoretically unguaranteed, the real unknown space (new faults, sensor faults, transients) is unbounded, and rare faults leave no basis to validate the false-negative rate. An adversary could craft a fault signature that reconstructs under one class decoder, relying on the opaque score to escape scrutiny.

Drift and static qualification mismatch -- implicit, exploitable
Bearing wear, rebalancing, sensor replacement, outage baselines and image-preprocessing changes shift the normal and known-fault manifolds, so qualified thresholds go stale without labels to reveal it. An adversary could hide a slow manipulation within this drift band or exploit post-maintenance periods when the baseline is least trusted.

Automation bias, alarm fatigue and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A tidy 'known fault' or 'healthy' label can anchor analysts away from the true mechanism, while frequent uninformative 'unknown' flags drive disuse and erode vibration-analyst skill. An adversary could deliberately induce nuisance flags until the tool is ignored, then act during that disuse.

Qualification and fleet-propagation gaps -- implicit, exploitable
No AI-specific V&V path exists for an ML advisory in a safety-related monitoring chain, training non-determinism undermines threshold stability across retrains, and one model replicated across units copies any bias or compromise everywhere. An adversary could compromise one shared model or retrain to propagate a blind spot across a fleet.

Evasion of open-set rejection -- adversarial
An insider or compromised signal path can shape vibration signals or derived orbit and recurrence images so a real fault, or tampering-induced damage, reconstructs under a healthy or benign class, or injects false 'unknown' flags to force an outage. The consequence is delayed detection of progressive damage on a core-cooling pump or an unnecessary shutdown.

Poisoning and supply-chain contamination of models and data -- adversarial
Because labelled faults are scarce, a few crafted or mislabelled samples, tainted simulated datasets, vendor models, or self-labelled unknowns folded back into retraining can disproportionately shift per-class decoders and implant persistent blind spots.

Threshold and configuration tampering -- adversarial
The reconstruction-error threshold is a single tunable parameter, so silent modification by someone with configuration access widens the 'known' region and shifts the open-set boundary with no visible failure.

Chaff and denial of diagnostic value -- adversarial
Injected out-of-distribution noise or induced operating excursions can drive the unknown rate up or make the tool unavailable, eroding operator trust so it is disabled while another degradation is paired with it.

Pipeline data exposure -- adversarial
Vendor- or cloud-hosted analytics links to the vibration monitoring system could leak RCP fault signatures and maintenance state or serve as a lateral path, though safety impact is lower.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is an advisory condition-monitoring tool on the RCP vibration channels. It is not a protection function. The RCP trip setpoints, vibration protection and operator procedures are independent, so a wrong output usually means a missed or delayed maintenance call, or an unnecessary outage, not an immediate safety event. The real exposure is that the evidence is simulation and RK4 journal-bearing testbed data, not plant data. The 'unknown fault' decision rests on reconstruction-error thresholds that are fragile under real operating variation, and a plant would plausibly lean on it as a screening layer that quietly erodes vibration-analyst attention. Harm needs a co-failing safeguard: a missed shaft or bearing degradation would also have to slip past conventional vibration alarms, trending and analyst review, and the risk grows if the tool is used to relax those practices.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203): the model is validated on simulated and testbed data. Real RCPs vary with speed, load, temperature, seal and flow conditions, sensor placement and plant-specific rotordynamics. Reconstruction thresholds may therefore be miscalibrated, producing false 'unknown' alarms that cause nuisance outages and alarm fatigue, or false 'known/normal' classifications that miss real degradation. (2) Open-set limits (OP.C0403, OP.C0202, OP.C0401): detecting unseen faults is not guaranteed, and a novel fault that reconstructs well under a known class is silently misclassified. A reconstruction-error score is also hard to justify to a reliability engineer. Rare-fault scarcity means there is little basis for validating the false-negative rate. (3) Drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303): aging, maintenance, rebalancing, sensor replacement and refurbished bearings shift the signal distribution. The image pipeline (orbit and recurrence plots) is sensitive to preprocessing, scaling and sampling, so static qualification may not hold dynamically. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102): automation bias and skill fade may lead analysts to defer to 'known fault, low severity' labels, and a confident misclassification may drive the wrong maintenance action. (5) Governance (OP.C0501, OP.C0504): there is no qualification path for an ML advisory in a safety-related component's monitoring chain, and its classification is not clear.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Manipulation of vibration or condition-monitoring data in transit or at the data historian (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0020, AML.T0059): a perturbation of orbit or recurrence images, or subtle signal modification, can push a real fault toward a 'normal' or known-benign reconstruction and mask developing shaft or bearing damage. The same mechanism can inject false 'unknown fault' flags to force an outage. The consequence is delayed intervention on a primary-circuit component or an unplanned shutdown, with plant-protection and conventional vibration alarms as the backstop. (2) Poisoning at retraining or supply chain (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0070): contaminated fault libraries or vendor-supplied models with per-class decoders create persistent blind spots. Retraining on operational data labelled by the system itself is an especially quiet route. (3) Model and threshold tampering (AML.T0076, AML.T0031): changing the reconstruction-error thresholds subtly shifts the open-set boundary without any visible failure. (4) Denial or timing (AML.T0029): an attacker can pair a degraded or unavailable diagnostic with other degradation, relying on the plant leaning on it. (5) Data leakage (AML.T0025, AML.T0024): RCP fault signatures and plant dynamics are operationally sensitive, although the safety impact is lower. Overall severity is bounded by independent protection, but the vulnerability is the quiet degradation of predictive maintenance for a critical component.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, VDI-CSSR's central fragility is that its evidence base is simulation plus an RK4 journal-bearing testbed, not field RCP data. Per-class reconstruction errors and the known/unknown rejection threshold are calibrated on that synthetic distribution (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203). Real RCP vibration includes seal and flow-induced excitation, speed and load transients, sensor and cable degradation, and plant-to-plant variation. These shift the reconstruction-error distributions, so the open-set boundary can fail silently in either direction (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). Open-set recognition is also ML-theoretically hard. Rejecting 'unknown' depends on a threshold tuned on the few unknowns used at validation, and the real unknown space (new fault modes, sensor faults, transient operating states) is unbounded (OP.C0403, OP.C0202). The image encoding (orbit and recurrence plots) adds preprocessing parameters such as embedding, windowing, scaling and channel pairing. Small changes in these shift the input distribution without any change to the model. The system is a decision-support layer on a safety-relevant asset, so a reliable unknown flag matters more than closed-set accuracy.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and threshold miscalibration. Class-specific autoencoders trained on simulated and testbed signals may reconstruct real-plant signals poorly. This produces a flood of false 'unknown' alerts that cause alarm fatigue and disuse (OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102). Alternatively, a generative decoder that is too flexible may reconstruct unseen faults well and mislabel them as a known benign class (a confident false negative that delays maintenance on a degrading bearing or shaft). (2) Drift. Bearing wear, rotor-balance changes, sensor replacement, outage-induced baseline shifts, and seasonal or load-following changes move the 'normal' and 'known fault' manifolds (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). Per-class reconstruction thresholds go stale with no ground-truth labels to detect it, because faults are rare (OP.C0202). (3) Qualification and repeatability gaps. Training-time non-determinism of the reconstruction networks and a lack of any AI-specific V&V regime for CBM models make it hard to show that a threshold is stable across retrains (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). Opaque reconstruction-error scores also give operators little to explain an 'unknown' verdict (OP.C0401). (4) Automation bias in both directions. A tidy 'known fault class X' label can anchor diagnosis away from the real mechanism, while an uninformative 'unknown' verdict gives no actionable guidance (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Evasion at the input boundary. An adversary who can alter data between the vibration-monitoring system and the model, or who manipulates the sensors or signal conditioning, could shape orbit and recurrence images so that a real fault reconstructs under a benign class or is rejected as noise (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). Open-set detectors based on reconstruction error are generally evadable because the attacker only needs to reduce the error under one class decoder. (6) Poisoning of the retraining loop. Because labelled faults are scarce, operators will be tempted to fold newly flagged 'unknowns' and pseudo-labelled data back into training. This opens a path for poisoning or mislabelled data to shift thresholds or implant a blind spot (AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0031). Supply-chain risk comes from pretrained backbones, simulation toolchains, and shared datasets (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003). (7) Low-and-slow denial of diagnostic value. Deliberate chaff, such as injected spurious vibration patterns or induced operating-point excursions, could drive the unknown rate up until operators disable or ignore the tool (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). Model theft or reconnaissance through published papers and open data would help an adversary build a proxy to craft evasions (AML.T0000, AML.T0005). The main consequence is degraded or misleading condition monitoring of a safety-significant RCP. That erodes the defense-in-depth role of vibration monitoring and can mask a developing fault, leading to unplanned trips or, in the worst case, loss of a coolant pump. It is not a direct control path, so the risk comes mainly from trust, calibration and data integrity rather than actuation.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this is a condition-monitoring advisory tool for RCP shaft and bearing health. A direct attack on it is probably not the easiest route for a sophisticated adversary, but it creates three things worth modelling. First, it is a trust-concentrating decision filter: its 'known fault / unknown fault / healthy' output shapes maintenance and trip-or-continue judgments on a safety-significant component. Second, it adds an AI/ML data and model pipeline (vibration data historian, training sets, model weights, image-conversion code) that sits adjacent to plant networks. Third, its documented evidence base is only simulation and a journal-bearing testbed, so its real-plant behaviour is unqualified, and an adversary or a natural process could exploit that gap. The most plausible role for an adversary is to use it as a stepping stone or a timing instrument, for example by degrading analysts' trust or masking a real mechanical or sabotage-induced degradation, rather than as the final target.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Evasion by masking. The model reconstructs orbit/recurrence images per class and flags an unknown fault when reconstruction error is high for every known class. A deliberate insider or a compromised signal path could shape vibration signals or the derived images so that a real unknown fault, or tampering-induced bearing or shaft damage, reconstructs well under the 'healthy' or a benign known class. The AI failure mechanism is evasion of the open-set rejection threshold (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). What depends on it is early warning of bearing or shaft degradation on a pump that is critical to core cooling. The consequence is delayed detection of progressive damage, with possible forced outage or loss of a coolant-flow margin. Reconstruction-error thresholds are a single tunable parameter, so an adversary or insider with access to configuration can silently widen the 'known' region (AML.T0081, AML.T0018). (2) Poisoning and integrity erosion. Scarce labelled fault data means a few mislabelled or crafted samples could shift class-specific reconstructors disproportionately (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031). Simulated and synthetic training data from outside vendors or research groups is an additional supply-chain entry point (AML.T0010.003). (3) Nuisance-alarm attack. Injecting out-of-distribution noise or chaff could drive false 'unknown fault' flags (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). This would erode operator trust and cause the tool to be disabled or ignored. An adversary can then time a real action around that disuse (OP.C0101.05). (4) Stepping-stone and exfiltration. The pipeline links the vibration monitoring system to analytics hosts, possibly vendor-hosted or cloud-hosted, which could provide a lateral path or leak operational signature data that reveals plant condition and maintenance state (AML.T0025, AML.T0036, OP.C0601, OP.C0505.01). IMPLICIT: (5) Qualification and generalization gap. Results come from simulation and a testbed, not plant data. Real RCPs vary with load, speed, seals, process noise and sensor degradation, so false normal or false unknown results are likely, and these are exactly what an adversary could time around (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). (6) Automation trust and skill fade. An 'unknown fault' verdict has no label or explanation, so analysts get little diagnostic guidance. Over-reliance on a 'known/healthy' verdict can dull vigilance (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0401). (7) Drift and sensor-change effects. Aging, maintenance or sensor replacement shifts the image distributions and silently moves the open-set threshold, with no clear drift monitoring (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). (8) Fleet propagation. If one model is replicated across units or sites, one compromise or one bias is replicated everywhere (OP.C0602). Overall the risk is moderate. Advisory use, plant-independent protection systems and the low probability that a nation-state would pick this target all limit it, but a concealed or insider-assisted degradation of a critical pump could be hidden by this tool at a time of the adversary's choosing.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, drift, open-set limits, human factors, and input evasion, poisoning and chaff as the core threats. I dropped speculative codes (AML.T0005, AML.T0000, AML.T0070, AML.T0076, AML.T0036, AML.T0024, OP.C0504) as weakly grounded or redundant, and kept the security specialist's configuration tampering, fleet propagation and exfiltration points as distinct.

evidence.citation: "Towards Open-Set Fault Diagnosis for Reactor Coolant Pumps under Unknown Fault Conditions," Prognostics and Health Management Society (Asia Pacific Conference of the PHM Society 2025 proceedings)
evidence.note: The paper proposes an open-set recognition framework based on class-specific semantic reconstruction. It is applied to orbit-plot and recurrence-plot images derived from RCP vibration-monitoring signals. The authors report it was tested on simulation data and RK4 journal-bearing testbed data, where it kept competitive closed-set accuracy and detected unknown faults better than baselines. These are simulated and testbed results, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is evasion or threshold tampering that masks progressive bearing or shaft degradation on a core-cooling pump; because the tool is advisory and plant protection and conventional vibration alarms are independent, harm needs a co-failing safeguard, so the credible outcome is operational disruption or delayed maintenance and minor safety-margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real miscalibration, drift and over-reliance recur reliably once the tool is deployed on real plant signals, but adversarial evasion, poisoning and tampering need specific conditions such as signal-path or configuration access, or retraining loops that ingest the tampered data.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (shaping signals within a compromised signal path, tampering with thresholds or configuration, poisoning retraining data or vendor models) require insider or privileged access to an OT-adjacent monitoring chain, though the implicit weaknesses can be exploited by timing around them without special tooling.

affected_users.why: Impact is mainly the monitored RCPs and the analysts who rely on the tool, but fleet-wide model replication across units can propagate a shared blind spot or compromise across a site or fleet; the advisory role limits coupling to protection systems.

discoverability.why: Open-set reconstruction limits, sim-to-real gaps, drift and adversarial evasion and poisoning of ML classifiers are well documented in the open literature, and the source paper itself publishes the method and its simulation and testbed-only validation, so a capable outsider can readily infer where the weaknesses lie.

use_case: Artificial-neural-network surrogate of the OFFBEAT multi-dimensional (2-D/3-D) fuel performance code. It emulates steady-state fuel thermo-mechanics, including fuel centreline temperature, with released fission gases, swelling, densification and creep given as inputs. It lets Monte Carlo-based uncertainty quantification and data assimilation run quickly, and was tested on a data-assimilation case based on the first ramp of the IFA-432 instrumented fuel assemblies.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline design-stage surrogate has no actuation path, so its main exposure is to the integrity of the fuel-performance evidence behind design margins and licensing submissions. The main threats are silent extrapolation and simulated-data inheritance, thin validation and qualification, erosion of independent verification, and adversarial poisoning or tampering with the surrogate, its training data or its assimilation inputs. A lower-severity exposure is theft of proprietary fuel-behaviour knowledge.

Out-of-envelope extrapolation in the UQ loop -- implicit, exploitable
Monte Carlo and assimilation samplers push the ANN into the tails of the input space, or into physically inconsistent combinations of fission gas release, swelling, densification and creep, where it returns smooth but wrong centreline temperatures with no warning. This produces over-narrow posteriors and optimistic fuel-melt and PCI margins, and an adversary could place a subtle bias in the poorly validated region and pass it off as ordinary extrapolation error.

Simulated-data inheritance and thin validation -- implicit, exploitable
Every training label is OFFBEAT output, so the surrogate reproduces OFFBEAT's model-form error, and validation on two IFA-432 pins from one ramp gives little evidence of generalisation. Close agreement with OFFBEAT is easily read as agreement with reality, which makes the evidence look tighter than it is. An adversary could rely on that misplaced trust to leave a manipulated surrogate or biased calibration unchallenged.

Qualification gap and verification erosion -- implicit, exploitable
No accepted QA or error-bound method exists for ANN emulators in safety-related analysis, and training non-determinism and opacity prevent independent reproduction. Because the surrogate exists to avoid full-code reruns, convenience and over-trust erode cross-checking against OFFBEAT and against measurements. An adversary could hide tampering inside normal retraining variation and count on no reviewer rerunning the full code.

Version drift and cross-site propagation -- implicit, exploitable
The surrogate is tied to a specific OFFBEAT version, mesh and set of correlations, and goes silently stale when these change. A surrogate shared across designs or organisations propagates the same bias widely. An adversary could exploit weak version control to substitute an artifact, which would then spread through every user of the shared model.

Training-data, weights and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or a compromised dataset, library or weights file could make the surrogate accurate nearly everywhere but biased in a chosen regime, such as high burnup, power ramps or conditions near centreline-melt and PCI limits, while still passing benchmark checks. The result is non-conservative margins entering the design or licensing basis, with little chance of detection because the full code is rarely rerun.

Assimilation input and measurement manipulation -- adversarial
Falsified or selectively chosen instrumented-assembly measurements, or manipulated priors and inputs, steer the calibrated posterior through the fast emulator toward wrong fission-gas-release and swelling parameters. The speed of the surrogate makes this cheap to iterate, and the outcome is hidden margin erosion presented as a quantified uncertainty result.

Model and training-set theft -- adversarial
The weights and the OFFBEAT-generated database encode proprietary fuel-performance behaviour and possibly vendor or irradiation-test data, which could be exfiltrated or extracted by query. This is mainly an IP and commercial-sensitivity loss rather than a safety loss.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline design-and-licensing analysis tool, not a control or protection function. Nothing in the plant acts on it in real time, and the paper itself calls it a preliminary investigation. The consequence of failure therefore runs through engineering decisions: fuel rod design, margin to centreline-melt and PCI limits, and uncertainty bounds in a safety case. The credible harm is a surrogate that looks faithful to OFFBEAT but is wrong outside its sampled region. It could then give optimistic centreline temperatures or too-narrow posterior uncertainties, and those could carry into a licensing submission or a fuel-performance basis. Existing practice already provides strong backstops. OFFBEAT can be rerun at the final design point, there are separate licensed codes, benchmark data from IFA-432 and similar experiments, and conservative regulatory margins, so a surrogate error would have to pass several independent checks before it became physical harm. The main risk is that these checks erode through convenience, because the surrogate makes the Bayesian workflow cheap enough that nobody reruns the full code.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Out-of-distribution and extrapolation failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). The surrogate is trained on a bounded input envelope covering fission gas release, swelling, densification and creep. Burnup, power history, geometry or material variants outside that envelope, such as new cladding, new fuel types or higher burnup, can produce confident but wrong centreline temperatures with no warning. Data assimilation then pulls calibrated parameters toward values that compensate for surrogate error. (2) Surrogate-induced bias in UQ and data assimilation (OP.C0603, OP.C0304.03). Small emulator error is amplified in posterior distributions, giving over-narrow uncertainty and biased calibration of fission gas release and swelling models. The consequence is understated margin to fuel melt or PCI limits in a design or licensing basis. (3) Data provenance and scarcity (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). Training data are simulated OFFBEAT output, so the surrogate inherits OFFBEAT's model-form errors. Validation rests on a few IFA-432 pins, which gives little evidence for generalisation. Agreement with OFFBEAT is easily mistaken for agreement with reality. (4) Qualification and verification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01). Neural-network emulators have no established QA path under nuclear software and licensing frameworks. Retraining non-determinism, opacity and no error bound complicate acceptance. Treating a research result as design-grade evidence is the main human-factors route to harm (OP.C0101.04). (5) Software and version drift (OP.C0502, OP.C0302.02). The surrogate is tied to a specific OFFBEAT version and set of correlations. Updates to OFFBEAT can silently invalidate it. If surrogates are reused across a fleet or across designs, the same bias propagates everywhere (OP.C0602). ADVERSARIAL THREATS.
