Insider or supply-chain tampering with the training dataset, the model weights or the pretrained artifact (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0076) could bias outputs in a region the validation does not probe. A backdoor-style bias could shift predicted centreline temperatures or posteriors a few percent in a chosen operating regime while passing benchmark checks. The motive could be commercial or reputational: favouring a design, undermining a vendor, or inflating margin. Corrupted shared design-analysis repositories or datasets (AML.T0059, AML.T0010.001) are an equivalent route. Model-extraction or data theft (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025) would mostly leak proprietary fuel design data and code behaviour, which is an IP and export-control issue more than a safety one. The safety consequence is limited because the output is advisory and gets independent review, but a quiet error that enters the licensing basis could surface only after operating experience or an inspection finding. The most plausible systemic failure is erosion of independent verification, with the surrogate becoming the only thing exercised in the UQ chain.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a classic simulation-trained surrogate. Every training label comes from OFFBEAT, not from reality, so the ANN inherits all of OFFBEAT's model-form error, and it adds approximation error that is only validated over the sampled input hypercube. Its main job is as an inner-loop likelihood or forward model for Monte Carlo UQ and Bayesian data assimilation. That makes it fragile in a specific way: samplers and optimisers actively seek the edges of the input space, where a neural net extrapolates unreliably and gives no warning. The experimental anchor is a single ramp on two IFA-432 pins, so the evidence for generalisation to other burnups, geometries, power histories and designs is thin. The 'agrees closely with OFFBEAT' result shows emulator fidelity, not predictive validity of the fuel-performance estimate, and downstream users may confuse the two.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulated-data provenance and model-form inheritance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02). The surrogate's agreement with OFFBEAT can mask OFFBEAT's own bias. Because the surrogate is used for data assimilation, calibrated parameters, posterior uncertainty bands and margin estimates can look statistically tight and still be wrong. The consequence is design-stage or licensing-support fuel temperature and gap-conductance margins that are too optimistic. (2) Out-of-distribution failure inside the UQ loop (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403). Monte Carlo and assimilation samplers draw from priors and posteriors whose tails go beyond the training design. Inputs such as fission gas release, swelling, densification and creep are supplied to the net as given, so physically inconsistent combinations can occur that OFFBEAT's coupled physics would never produce. The ANN returns smooth but wrong centreline temperatures, which corrupt posterior distributions and hide tail risk, and these are exactly the quantities that matter for safety margins. (3) Small-data and new-build scarcity (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Validation rests on a preliminary case with two instrumented pins from a single ramp, and a new design will have even less data. Sparse instrumented data can also make assimilation ill-posed, and the surrogate can overfit to it. (4) Qualification and lifecycle gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01). The surrogate is tied to a particular OFFBEAT version, mesh, and set of material models. When OFFBEAT is updated or correlations are revised, the surrogate silently goes stale unless it is retrained and re-verified. Training non-determinism, opacity, and the lack of any accepted error-bound methodology for ANN surrogates in safety-related analysis make it hard to show that the emulator's error is bounded and negligible against the uncertainty being quantified. (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04). Fast, convenient, high-sample-count UQ can encourage over-trust and erode the habit of spot-checking against full OFFBEAT runs. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Supply chain and artifact integrity (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020). Tampering with the OFFBEAT-generated training dataset, the trained weights, or the ML libraries and containers could bias the surrogate in a targeted way, for example by under-predicting temperature in one region of input space. Because the results feed design and licensing evidence, such tampering is hard to detect and nothing downstream forces re-verification. (7) Evidence manipulation (AML.T0031, AML.T0059). An insider or intruder who alters the experimental data fed to assimilation, or the input priors, can steer calibrated parameters through the fast emulator. The effect is hidden margin erosion presented as a quantified uncertainty result. (8) Model and IP exposure (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035). Surrogate weights and training sets encode proprietary fuel behaviour and possibly vendor or irradiation-test data, and could be exfiltrated or extracted by query. Overall, the main exposure lies in the validation and provenance chain, not in operational control, because the system's output is a trusted number inside a larger safety argument.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial standpoint this is a low-value direct target. It is an offline, design-stage analysis tool with no actuation path, and a nation-state would find easier routes to plant or reactor systems. Its threat relevance comes from what it quietly changes: it concentrates trust in a fast emulator that stands in for the qualified code (OFFBEAT) in uncertainty quantification and data-assimilation workflows. Those workflows produce margin, calibration and uncertainty-bound arguments that feed fuel design and licensing submissions. An insider or supply-chain adversary who can alter the surrogate, its training set or its inputs gets a subtle, hard-to-attribute way to bias design margins. Nobody re-runs the thousands of full-physics cases the surrogate was built to avoid, so the bias is unlikely to be caught. The most plausible exploit is therefore a long-dwell integrity attack on the safety-case evidence, not a disruptive one. The same non-adversarial weaknesses (limited validation, extrapolation error, opacity) are also the cover an adversary would use for deniability.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data or model poisoning and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0059, T0031). The surrogate is trained on OFFBEAT-generated samples and then reused for Monte Carlo UQ and Bayesian data assimilation. A malicious insider, a compromised dataset or a tampered weights file could produce a surrogate that is accurate nearly everywhere but biased in a region that matters, such as high-burnup or power-ramp conditions, or in centreline temperature near fuel-melt or PCI margins. The facility dependency is the design and licensing evidence for fuel temperature margins and uncertainty bounds. The consequence is non-conservative margins that enter the safety case unnoticed, since the reason for the surrogate is to avoid re-running the full code. (2) Input and measurement manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015). Data assimilation tunes model parameters against instrumented-assembly measurements (the IFA-432 ramp case). Falsified or selectively chosen measurement data, or adversarially chosen inputs such as fission gas release, swelling and densification, would steer the calibrated posterior toward the wrong parameters. The fast surrogate makes this cheap to iterate and test (AML.T0042, T0005). (3) Model theft and reconnaissance (AML.T0024.002, T0035, T0013). The surrogate and its training database encode proprietary fuel-performance behaviour and vendor-sensitive correlations, which is an IP and commercial-sensitivity exposure rather than a safety one. (4) Cross-site propagation (OP.C0602). If the surrogate is shared across designers, vendors or regulators, one compromised artifact spreads the bias widely.

IMPLICIT. (a) Validation is thin: the paper calls it preliminary, and it was tested on two pins from one experiment. The surrogate is likely to be applied outside its training domain (new cladding, burnup or geometry, other reactor types), with silent extrapolation error (OP.C0302, C0302.03, C0403, C0201.01). Because the training data are simulated, the surrogate inherits OFFBEAT's own model-form errors, and these are hidden by a close surrogate-to-code match (OP.C0201.01, C0201.02). (b) Over-trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0101.01). Fast UQ makes the surrogate the default. Analysts lose the habit of cross-checking against the full code or against measurements, and reviewers get an appearance of rigorous UQ with no AI-specific qualification (OP.C0501, C0504, C0303). (c) Opacity and repeatability. Neural-network training non-determinism and limited explainability make independent reproduction and audit hard (OP.C0401, C0402.01), so a tampered or degraded model would be hard to distinguish from normal variation. This gives an adversary deniability. (d) Weak software hygiene and version control of surrogate artifacts and training sets (OP.C0502, C0505) would enable silent substitution of a model version in a design-stage environment where security culture is typically lax.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on extrapolation, simulated-data inheritance, qualification and verification erosion, and poisoning of the training data or weights as the core threats, so these were merged into single entries. I dropped input-side ATLAS codes the panel only loosely supported (T0015, T0005, T0013) and kept T0043 and T0042 for the manipulated-input pathway; I kept model theft as a separate low-severity threat.

evidence.citation: "Artificial Neural Networks as Surrogate Models for Uncertainty Quantification and Data Assimilation in 2-D/3-D Fuel Performance Studies," Journal of Nuclear Engineering (MDPI), EPFL Laboratory for Reactor Physics and System Behaviour
evidence.note: The paper trains ANN surrogates of the steady-state thermo-mechanical behaviour of nuclear fuel computed by OFFBEAT. The goal is to avoid the thousands of expensive 2-D/3-D runs needed for sampling-based uncertainty quantification and data assimilation. The trained network is applied to a data-assimilation study on two pins from IFA-432, where it agrees closely with OFFBEAT itself. The authors describe this as a preliminary investigation.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is training-data/weights poisoning (or biased extrapolation) that silently yields non-conservative fuel-melt and PCI margins in the design or licensing basis; this erodes safety margins and could contribute to a radiological release path, but it has no direct actuation and relies on downstream review failing, so it falls just short of 5.

reproducibility.why: Silent extrapolation, simulated-data inheritance and verification erosion occur reliably whenever samplers leave the validated envelope or the surrogate replaces full-code reruns, while a deliberately planted regime-specific bias would persist and pass benchmarks consistently.

exploitability.why: Deliberate exploitation (poisoning training data or weights, supply-chain compromise, falsifying assimilation inputs) generally needs insider or privileged access to the design workflow, although the implicit extrapolation failure needs no special access.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly confined to a design or licensing analysis for a fuel design, but shared surrogates and version-drift propagation can spread bias across designs and organisations without reaching facility-wide coupled-system effects.

discoverability.why: The weaknesses of ANN surrogates (extrapolation, inherited model-form error, lack of QA standards, opacity) are well documented in the open literature and the source paper is public, though finding a specific weak regime in a particular surrogate requires some insight.

use_case: Recurrent neural network (Keras) digital-twin predictor of multi-time-series, location-dependent inside- and outside-wall temperatures in PWR reactor coolant system pressure-boundary components such as the hot leg and surge-line nozzles. It is trained on finite-element transient heat-transfer data under design-basis and grid-load-following loading cycles. Its predictions feed real-time structural-state and environmental fatigue-life estimation, so the finite-element model does not have to run online.
incurred_insecurity:
The RNN surrogate sits between plant instrumentation and the environmental fatigue-life estimate for RCS pressure-boundary nozzles, and the finite-element model is deliberately not run online to check it. Because fatigue is slow and cumulative, the main exposure is quiet integrity corruption of the aging-management record, not an acute event. The threats are a surrogate trained on simulated data and weakly validated, extrapolation outside its training envelope, error amplification into fatigue usage, loss of human cross-checking, and adversarial tampering with the model, its training data or its input streams.

Simulated-data provenance and weak validation -- implicit, exploitable
The RNN learns the finite-element model's assumptions and errors (film coefficients, idealized transients) and is validated only on two lab fatigue datasets, so non-conservative bias in plant-component temperatures and usage factors can go undetected. An adversary can hide a deliberate bias inside this uncertainty, since discrepancies would be attributed to model limitations.

Out-of-envelope extrapolation and drift -- implicit, exploitable
Off-normal events (surge-line stratification, valve leakage, trips, sensor faults), new load-following patterns, uprates and nozzle-to-nozzle geometry differences fall outside the training cycles, and the RNN still returns confident, smooth temperature traces with no out-of-envelope flag. An adversary could exploit this by pushing inputs into the unvalidated region, where small plausible perturbations have outsized effects.

Error propagation into fatigue life -- implicit
RNN error accumulates over long sequences and flows through stress and Fen multiplier calculations, where nonlinear strain-amplitude dependence amplifies it, with no formal uncertainty bound in the chain. No distinct adversary gain beyond what the other threats already provide.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
RNN opacity, Keras/TensorFlow training and inference non-determinism, library-version retraining shifts and the lack of an ML qualification pathway for structural-integrity work undermine the licensing-grade audit trail. An adversary gains cover because tampering cannot be distinguished from benign run-to-run variation, which weakens forensics.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Once the twin becomes the routine basis for fatigue reports and inspection scheduling, analysts stop cross-checking against finite-element or thermocouple data and fail to notice drift. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust and time a manipulation around reduced vigilance or a life-extension decision.

Input-stream manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofed or subtly biased temperature, pressure or flow signals, or a compromised historian, can keep predicted loading benign while real loading is severe, or inflate it to force outages. Because the model is not physics-constrained, the result is a stealthy misstatement of accumulated damage that defers inspections or distorts license-renewal arguments.

Model, training-data and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor who poisons the finite-element input decks or training set, substitutes or backdoors the saved weights, or compromises the Keras/TensorFlow stack can embed a systematic or trigger-conditioned bias that passes the narrow lab benchmarks. With no online independent check, the corrupted fatigue record erodes structural margin or inspection prioritization.

IT/OT bridge and data exposure -- adversarial
The analytics environment links plant data historians with vendor, laboratory and corporate networks and holds sensitive component-geometry, material and operating-cycle data. This gives a path for exfiltration, reconnaissance and stepping-stone access, and raises data-access governance questions.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This RNN is a surrogate for a finite-element thermal model. It supplies the temperature histories that drive structural-state and environmental fatigue (Fen) usage-factor estimates for RCS pressure-boundary nozzles. Fatigue is a slow, cumulative, margin-bearing damage mechanism, so a single bad prediction is unlikely to cause an immediate event. The real risk is quiet bias: the model drifts or is miscalibrated, cumulative usage factors are under-reported, and inspection intervals, license-renewal (subsequent license renewal) arguments or load-following operating regimes are accepted on false confidence. Existing practice (ASME Section III/XI fatigue monitoring, ISI/NDE, thermocouple-based monitoring, conservative design margins) bounds the immediate consequence. Those same safeguards erode if the digital twin is allowed to replace them, or if operators defer to its output because it is 'validated'.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Training-domain and qualification gap: the RNN is trained only on FE-simulated transients (design-basis and load-following cycles) and validated on lab fatigue tests (in-air and PWR-water loop), not on in-plant instrumented nozzle data. Real plants have off-normal events such as thermal stratification in the surge line, valve leakage, unplanned trips, and sensor faults. These fall outside the training envelope, so the RNN may extrapolate smoothly and confidently. The result is under-predicted thermal gradients and strain ranges, and non-conservative Fen usage factors. The failure is slow and silent. (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). (2) Error propagation: temperature error feeds stress, then fatigue-life, then Fen multiplier calculations, and the nonlinear fatigue-life dependence on strain amplitude amplifies small thermal errors. The RNN's accumulated error over long multi-time-series sequences is hard to bound, and there is no formal uncertainty quantification in the chain. (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603, OP.C0401, OP.C0403). (3) Automation trust and deskilling: if the twin's outputs become the routine basis for fatigue-monitoring reports and inspection scheduling, engineers may stop cross-checking against FE or thermocouple data. Out-of-the-loop staff would then miss a drifting model, for example after a power-uprate or operating-mode change, or after a plant-specific geometry or material differs from the training set. (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102, OP.C0302.01). (4) Non-repeatability: Keras training and inference non-determinism, plus version changes in the libraries, can shift predictions between retrainings, which undermines a licensing-grade audit trail. (OP.C0402, OP.C0502). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Integrity of the input stream: if live plant temperature, pressure or flow inputs drive the RNN, spoofed or subtly biased signals, or a compromised data historian, can keep predicted loading benign while real loading is severe. Because the model has no physics-based sanity check, the result is a stealthy under-estimate of accumulated damage that could defer inspections. Conversely, inflated predictions could force costly outages or derating. Neither path is directly safety-system-related, but each corrupts a safety-relevant aging-management record. (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). (6) Model and training-data tampering: poisoning of the FE training sets or the saved model weights, or supply-chain compromise of the Keras/TensorFlow stack or pretrained artifacts, could embed a systematic non-conservative bias that passes validation on the narrow lab benchmark datasets. (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076). (7) Cyber-pathway consideration: an analytics server connected to plant data creates a new network path between the plant data network and corporate or vendor environments. It also raises data-access governance questions around proprietary design and transient data. (AML.T0025, OP.C0505). Overall, consequences are more a long-term integrity-of-structures and regulatory-trust problem than an acute safety event, provided that fatigue monitoring retains independent, conservative checks.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a surrogate model trained entirely on simulated finite-element (FE) transient data. It is then asked to stand in for the FE solver online, upstream of a fatigue-life calculation. Its fragility sits in the pipeline rather than the facility. The model can only be as good as the FE model's boundary conditions, material properties and transient library. It has been validated against only two lab datasets (an in-air rig and a PWR-water loop), which are not the plant. At inference the RNN receives plant instrument streams (thermocouples, flow, pressure) that are noisier, drift-prone and often outside the envelope of the idealized design-basis and load-following cycles it saw in training. Because a recurrent model's error compounds across time steps and its output is integrated into cumulative fatigue usage, small biases are not self-correcting. They accumulate into a systematically wrong remaining-life estimate that looks plausible and is hard to audit.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulated and surrogate data provenance (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0201.03). The RNN learns the FE model's physics and its errors, such as film-coefficient assumptions, idealized transient shapes and mesh limits. It inherits those errors and has no independent ground-truth correction. Lab validation on two small-scale tests is transferred to plant components, so the real-world validity of the surrogate is under-demonstrated. The consequence is a non-conservative fatigue-usage estimate, which can erode margin on a pressure-boundary component. (2) Out-of-distribution and drift (OP.C0302, .01, .03). Real operation includes off-normal transients, flow stratification, sensor faults, power-uprate or load-following patterns different from the training cycles, and component aging that changes heat transfer. The RNN will still output a confident temperature trace with no native out-of-envelope flag, so fatigue calculations run on extrapolated values. Location-dependent outputs add heterogeneity across nozzles and plants, so a model trained on one geometry may not transfer (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0602). (3) Qualification gaps (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402). Static FE-trained models are used for a dynamic, time-integrated safety-relevant quantity. Training-time non-determinism (random seeds, Keras and TensorFlow versions) and the opacity of an RNN make repeatability and regulatory justification hard, and retraining after a library or version update can silently change predictions. (4) Error propagation into fatigue life (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). Temperature errors feed stress and cumulative usage factor calculations, so the downstream estimate inherits and amplifies them, with automation bias (OP.C0101.04) hiding the problem once engineers trust the digital twin to replace the FE run. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Input manipulation at inference (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Spoofed or subtly biased sensor or historian streams, or crafted boundary-condition inputs, shift predicted temperatures. This could hide real thermal-fatigue accumulation or trigger spurious inspections or life-extension decisions, and it is not visible as an obvious alarm. (6) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076). The Keras and TensorFlow dependencies, serialized model weights and FE-generated training sets are all tamperable. A poisoned FE training database (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002) or a backdoored model file (AML.T0043.004) could bias fatigue life in a way that survives routine testing, especially since few independent plant data exist to cross-check it. (7) Integrity of the monitoring chain. Altering results between the RNN and the fatigue module attacks the integrity of the structural health record rather than the plant's control, and this can be timed around a licensing or life-extension decision. Overall, the exposure is long-lived integrity corruption of an advisory fatigue record, not an acute control-system compromise.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling lens, this surrogate sits in a quiet but valuable position. It is a trusted intermediary between plant instrumentation (thermocouples, operating-history inputs) and a structural-integrity and fatigue-life estimate for pressure-boundary components, and that estimate can drive inspection intervals, life-extension arguments and operating margin. An adversary would not need to cause a transient. Quietly biasing the surrogate's temperature predictions, or the data and model artifacts behind them, could make cumulative usage factor look healthier or worse than reality, with no alarm and no immediate physical signature. Such a degraded estimate would be believed because it comes from a validated-looking digital twin and replaces an offline FE model that people can no longer check online. Nation-state-level actors would more plausibly use this as a long-dwell integrity or credibility attack on the safety case than as a direct route to physical damage, and the non-adversarial weaknesses (a surrogate trained on simulated data, limited validation, opacity) are exactly what would let such tampering go unnoticed.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model integrity: the model is trained on FE transient heat-transfer data. An insider or supply-chain actor who can alter the FE input decks, the generated training set, or the Keras model weights and artifacts (poisoning, backdoor, or silent substitution of the model file) can introduce a systematic, location-specific temperature bias, or a trigger behavior under particular load-follow patterns. The consequence is a mis-stated fatigue usage factor: non-conservative error would erode real structural margin or defeat inspection prioritization, while conservative error could force unnecessary outages or inspections and cause financial or credibility harm. There is no independent online check, since the FE model is deliberately not run online. (2) Input-side manipulation: spoofing or drifting the plant temperature or transient-history signals that feed the RNN. Because the model is learned rather than physics-constrained, it can extrapolate unpredictably on out-of-envelope inputs, so small crafted perturbations may have outsized effects while looking plausible. (3) Trust concentration and stepping-stone risk: the twin ties together plant data historians, ML tooling and engineering analysis networks, and may be hosted or developed by external labs or vendors. This creates an IT/OT bridge, a model supply chain (Python/Keras packages, pretrained artifacts, shared datasets), and a source of sensitive component-geometry, material-property and operating-cycle information that is valuable for reconnaissance. (4) Timing risk: once staff rely on the twin, field verification and manual fatigue tracking degrade, and an adversary can time a physical or cyber action around reduced vigilance.

IMPLICIT (exploitable). (a) Surrogate trained only on simulated FE data and validated on two lab fatigue-test datasets (in-air and PWR-water loop) is weakly validated for real plant conditions: sensor-versus-model mismatch, geometry differences, thermal stratification and unmodeled transients are out-of-distribution, so errors would be silent and plausibly blamed on noise. (b) Design-basis and load-following training cycles may not cover real or novel operating patterns, such as grid-driven cycling changes, giving drift and generalization failure. (c) Recurrent-network opacity and training or inference non-repeatability make it hard to show that a deviation is a fault rather than tampering, which weakens forensic detection and regulatory acceptance. (d) Automation trust and skill fade: fatigue analysts may stop cross-checking with the FE model, and the lack of a qualification pathway for ML in structural-integrity work leaves a governance gap that an adversary can exploit and that could contaminate downstream license-renewal or life-extension arguments.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulated-data and validation gap, out-of-envelope extrapolation, error propagation, trust and deskilling, and input and model/supply-chain tampering. I dropped speculative codes (AML.T0035, AML.T0012, AML.T0048) that were not clearly instantiated and merged the overlapping threats on the monitoring chain and the timing risk into the tampering and trust paragraphs.

evidence.citation: "Development of Digital Twin Predictive Model for PWR Components: Updates on Multi Times Series Temperature Prediction Using Recurrent Neural Network, DMW Fatigue Tests, System Level Thermal-Mechanical-Stress Analysis (ANL/LWRS-21/02)," Argonne National Laboratory (DOE LWRS Program)
evidence.note: This Argonne report describes a digital-twin framework for real-time environmental fatigue prediction of reactor components. In it, an RNN is trained on data from system-level finite-element thermal analyses to predict temperatures over time and location. The report says the RNN was validated against two laboratory fatigue-test datasets, one from an in-air system and one from a PWR-water loop. The report is a national-lab technical report, not a journal article.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat, tampering or bias in the fatigue-life record (model/training-data tampering and input-stream manipulation), erodes structural margin and defers inspections of RCS pressure-boundary components, but the process is slow and cumulative, so it is a safety-margin and aging-management integrity issue and not a direct acute release.

reproducibility.why: Implicit failures such as out-of-envelope extrapolation, simulated-data bias and error accumulation occur reliably once off-normal or novel conditions arise, but a deliberate stealthy manipulation depends on specific access and timing, so reliability is conditional.

exploitability.why: Effective exploitation (poisoning the finite-element decks or training set, swapping weights, compromising the historian or the ML stack, or spoofing plant signals) generally requires insider or supply-chain position or a footprint inside the OT/IT bridge, which is well beyond routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Impact spans multiple RCS nozzle components and the plant's fatigue-usage reports, inspection scheduling and license-renewal basis, but it stays confined to one analytics chain and is not facility-wide coupled-system propagation.

discoverability.why: The weaknesses (surrogate trained on simulated data, no out-of-envelope flag, non-determinism, lack of an ML qualification pathway, automation over-trust) are well documented in open literature and in the public national-lab report, so a capable outsider can readily infer the class; specific system internals remain non-public.

use_case: Feed-forward neural network model of the separative performance of an experimental uranium gas centrifuge. It is trained on experimental centrifuge test data (product and waste mass flows, line pressures and related operating variables) and is used to find optimal operating conditions for uranium isotope separation. The optimum was confirmed in a follow-up experiment.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline, advisory surrogate model of one experimental uranium gas centrifuge is not in a control loop, and hardware limits and a confirmatory experiment bound direct safety harm. The dominant insecurity is proliferation-sensitive: the weights, test data and optimum operating point form a compact, portable performance map of an enrichment machine. Secondary threats are integrity attacks that quietly misdirect R&D, and implicit fragilities (narrow validity, optimizer extrapolation, drift, over-trust, opacity, weak governance) that an adversary could use as cover.

Model and data exfiltration -- adversarial
The trained weights, the test dataset (mass flows, pressures, operating variables) and the optimum are easy to copy from workstations, removable media or the network, and a model with query access can be probed or extracted to reveal the optimum, sensitivities and stable-region edges. The consequence is transfer of enrichment-relevant separative knowledge and a ready proxy for an adversary's own machine, an export-control and safeguards concern rather than a plant-safety one.

Data and model tampering -- adversarial
An insider or compromised toolchain that biases flow, pressure or calibration records, or alters weights or normalization constants, can steer the recommended set-point toward degraded separation, shortened machine life or rotor stress. The result looks like ordinary experimental scatter, and the single confirmatory run is a trust anchor that can lend a poisoned optimum unearned acceptance.

Weak-security research toolchain -- adversarial
ML workstations, Python environments and shared notebooks sit under a research-grade security model, not an enrichment-sensitive one, and offer a foothold toward more sensitive enrichment networks. Compromise of these accounts and software dependencies also exposes the data and model directly.

Optimizer-driven extrapolation and single-machine validity -- implicit, exploitable
The optimizer seeks the edges of a small training set where the uncertainty-free feed-forward network is least reliable, and the source states validity only for the one centrifuge, so reuse on another rotor, a worn machine or a different cascade position gives confident but unsupported set-points near mechanical or UF6 limits. An adversary could rely on the absence of envelope checks to slip a manipulated or off-nominal recommendation past review as a plausible surrogate artifact.

Drift, over-trust and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Wear, calibration shift and instrument degradation silently move the input-output mapping, while a sub-1% confirmation and an opaque network encourage operators to accept stale optima without re-verification and erode independent baselines. An adversary could hide gradual or induced degradation in this unmonitored drift band and rely on the misplaced trust.

Small-data and governance gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Sparse, single-machine laboratory data and the absence of AI-specific qualification, configuration control and retraining governance leave the model fragile and make tampering hard to detect. Data-handling rules written for ordinary R&D data also ease the theft path described above.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline, advisory surrogate model for an experimental centrifuge. It is not in a control loop, and its output is checked in a follow-up experiment, as it was in the source (under 1% deviation). That makes direct safety consequences small. Process safety is carried by hardware and procedure: UF6 pressure and temperature limits, rotor speed and vibration trips, and cascade interlocks. A wrong optimum would have to defeat all of these to cause harm. The real exposure is proliferation sensitivity. The trained model and the test data encode enrichment-relevant separative performance, so the risks are confidentiality and integrity of that knowledge, plus quiet misdirection of R&D. The source states the model is valid only for the one centrifuge it was built on, so the main implicit risk is misuse outside that domain.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL (1) Theft of the model or training data. An adversary who gets the weights, the test dataset or the optimum operating point (AML.T0035, T0025, T0037, T0044, T0024.002) gains a compact, validated map of operating conditions for a specific machine. This is the dominant consequence, and it is a proliferation and export-control concern, not a plant-safety one. Surrogate models also make this knowledge easier to move and query than raw test logs. The same applies to inversion or extraction through any inference interface (T0024.001, T0040). (2) Poisoning or tampering with test data or the model (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002, T0031). Biased flow or pressure records, or a modified network, could steer R&D toward a suboptimal or off-nominal operating region and waste experimental campaigns. Safety harm would also require an engineer to adopt the point without the confirmatory run and to defeat the machine's protective limits, so this is a low-probability, schedule and capability-degradation consequence. A sophisticated actor could still use it to hide a real performance gain or to induce rotor stress during tests.

IMPLICIT (3) Narrow validity and extrapolation. The model is fitted to one machine over a limited experimental envelope (OP.C0302, C0302.03, C0202, C0203). An optimizer will tend to push toward the edge of the training data or beyond it, where a feed-forward network gives confident but unsupported predictions. Applying it to another machine, a different rotor condition or an aged machine (drift from wear, OP.C0302.01) could produce misleading set points. (4) Automation bias and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0401). The weights are opaque, and an optimum that was confirmed once may be trusted without re-verification after the machine, instrumentation calibration or feed conditions change. (5) Instrument and data quality (OP.C0201.04, C0204). Sensor calibration errors in test data propagate into the model and then into the optimum. (6) Governance. Weak QA and configuration control of the model (OP.C0501, C0502), and data-handling rules built for ordinary R&D data rather than sensitive enrichment data (OP.C0505.01), make the theft path easier. Overall, the existing process-safety practice of hardware limits and confirmatory experiments makes physical harm unlikely. Information security and sensitive-technology controls are the weak point.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small, tabular, feed-forward regression surrogate trained on a limited set of experimental runs from one centrifuge, then used as an objective function for an optimizer. From an ML-pipeline view the main fragility is that optimization actively seeks the edges of the training distribution, where a surrogate with no uncertainty estimate is least reliable. A <1% confirmation at one follow-up point shows local accuracy, not global validity. The source itself says the model is valid only for that machine, so any transfer to other machines, rotors, or aging hardware is out-of-distribution by construction. The data (flows, pressures, operating variables) and the learned response surface are also highly proliferation-sensitive artifacts. The model is therefore both a fragile predictor and a compact, portable store of enrichment performance knowledge.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Optimizer-driven extrapolation: gradient or search-based optimization over a small-sample NN surrogate exploits regions where the model overfits or extrapolates, so the 'optimum' may be a surrogate artifact. The single confirmation experiment does not cover the operating envelope. The consequence is that operators run the machine at conditions nearer to mechanical, thermal, or UF6 phase and pressure limits than the data supports, risking rotor stress, process upsets, or off-spec product/tails (OP.C0302, OP.C0202, OP.C0403, OP.C0303). (2) Machine-specific validity and drift: the model encodes one centrifuge's geometry and condition. Wear, rotor aging, vacuum degradation, instrument calibration drift, or replacement of the machine silently shifts the input-output mapping (data and concept drift). Without drift monitoring, stale optima persist, and an unnoticed degradation could also mask real anomalies (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03). (3) Data provenance and instrumentation: training data depends on flow and pressure sensor calibration and on laboratory-versus-cascade conditions. A lab single-machine surrogate misapplied to cascade operation (OP.C0201.04 versus .05) is a transfer failure. (4) Opacity and qualification gap: the NN gives no physics-based bounds or confidence, and there is no AI-specific qualification or retraining governance for a model that sets operating points (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01). (5) Automation trust: a model validated at <1% invites over-trust and skill fade in operators and process engineers (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training-data or sensor-data poisoning or tampering (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0059): subtle bias in historical test records or in the retraining feed shifts the recommended optimum toward degraded separation, hidden wear, or unsafe conditions while still passing a coarse acceptance check. (b) Model theft and inversion (AML.T0035, T0037, T0025, T0024.001, T0048.004): the weights and training set are a compact, high-value encoding of centrifuge separative performance, so exfiltration yields proliferation-relevant knowledge and a ready proxy for an adversary's own machine (AML.T0005). Because the net is tiny, it is easy to copy and hard to detect. (c) Model or artifact manipulation (AML.T0018.000, T0076, T0010.003): tampering with the weights or normalization constants in the deployment pipeline silently moves the setpoint recommendations. (d) Sensor-input manipulation at inference (AML.T0015, T0043): falsified pressure or flow readings drive the optimizer to wrong settings. Safeguards-relevant concern: an optimized, hidden operating regime could change throughput or enrichment behavior in ways that complicate declared-capacity verification (OP.C0701).

security_specialist.argument: From a security lens, the main issue is not whether the network predicts well. The model and its training data together encode the optimal operating envelope of a uranium gas centrifuge, which is proliferation-sensitive design and performance knowledge in compact, portable, queryable form. That makes the model, the dataset and the optimisation results valuable espionage and insider-exfiltration targets, because the model is far easier to steal than a hardware design. The use case also adds an optimisation-driven path to operating points that sit closer to mechanical or process limits, and an insider or supply-chain adversary could use that path to degrade or damage machines without touching safety systems. A nation-state would more likely go after the data and the model, or the engineering workstation, than attack the AI function itself.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Sensitive-knowledge concentration and exfiltration. The training set (mass flows, pressures, operating variables) and the trained weights make up a compact performance map of a centrifuge, and they can be removed on removable media or over the network. A model also leaks more than its authors intend: anyone with query access can probe it for the optimum, for sensitivity to the operating variables and for the edges of the stable region, which amounts to model extraction or inversion (AML.T0024.001, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0037, AML.T0025). The data is routinely shared with an AI/ML toolchain, notebooks and collaborators, so it is typically held under a security model suited to research data rather than enrichment-sensitive data (OP.C0505.01). (2) Integrity attack on the model or data. An insider or a compromised toolchain who poisons experimental records, sensor calibration or the model file (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0031, AML.T0059) can steer the 'optimal' set-point toward operation that degrades separative performance, shortens machine life or causes a crash. This leads to sabotage or an unexplained loss of output that looks like ordinary experimental scatter, and it does not require any attack on a safety system. The follow-up experiment that confirmed the optimum is itself a trust anchor an adversary could exploit, since the result is then accepted with reduced scrutiny. (3) Stepping stone. Because the work blends enrichment data with ML tooling, the workstations, Python environments and data pipelines have a weaker security posture and could provide a route into a more sensitive enrichment network (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0012). 

IMPLICIT. (a) The model is valid only for the specific machine tested. Reusing it on a different rotor, a worn machine or another cascade position invites out-of-distribution extrapolation and silent error (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). An adversary can time an action around the fact that no one checks these limits. (b) A reported prediction error below 1% encourages operators to over-trust the optimiser without bounds on the training range (OP.C0101.04). It can also hide drift as the machine ages (OP.C0302.01), so gradual or induced degradation goes unnoticed. (c) Small data, narrow experimental coverage and non-extensive validation (OP.C0202, OP.C0501) make the optimum fragile and tamper-evidence weak, because there is no independent baseline for detecting subtle poisoning. (d) Opacity of the network (OP.C0401) prevents reviewers from checking why a given operating point was selected. (e) The proliferation relevance is the central point: an optimisation study accelerates a state's or non-state actor's own centrifuge development, so the work and its outputs need export-control and safeguards-aware handling. Governance for the threat landscape (OP.C0503) and for data access (OP.C0505) is likely to lag the AI tooling.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on exfiltration of the model and data as the dominant threat, data/model tampering, and implicit narrow-validity/extrapolation and drift with over-trust. I dropped speculative inference-time sensor spoofing, proxy-model staging and the safeguards-capacity point as weakly argued or restating other threats, and kept the toolchain stepping stone as a distinct security-specialist contribution.

evidence.citation: "Analysis and optimization of gas-centrifugal separation of uranium isotopes by neural networks," Brazilian Journal of Chemical Engineering, 19(3), 299-306 (2002)
evidence.note: The authors built a feed-forward neural network on new experimental data from ultracentrifuge tests (CTMSP and IPEN, Brazil). It predicted the centrifuge's separative behaviour in good agreement with the data. They then used it for an optimisation study, and a new experiment at the predicted optimum differed from the prediction by less than 1%. The source notes the model is valid only for the specific centrifuge used in the experiments.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is exfiltration of a portable enrichment performance map, which is a proliferation and export-control harm (loss of sensitive enrichment knowledge) short of a radiological release, while direct safety harm is bounded by hardware limits and the confirmatory experiment.

reproducibility.why: Copying weights and data from research-grade workstations, and biasing records or optimizer extrapolation, work reliably once access exists; model drift and out-of-distribution failures also recur predictably.

exploitability.why: Exfiltration and tampering need a foothold on a research network or insider access, but the weak research-grade security model and commodity ML tooling mean no nation-state resourcing is required.

affected_users.why: The model covers a single experimental centrifuge in an advisory role outside any control loop, so direct impact is narrow, though a research toolchain foothold could extend toward more sensitive enrichment networks.

discoverability.why: The approach is published in open literature, and weak research-toolchain security, small-data fragility and surrogate-model extrapolation are well-documented for this class of AI system, so an adversary can readily infer that the weaknesses exist.

use_case: Machine-learning regression (multilayer perceptron and random forest, among other models) that predicts the equilibrium nitric acid concentration in the TBP organic phase of the PUREX solvent-extraction process. Inputs are initial aqueous acid concentration, TBP concentration and diluent type. The training data are compiled from published literature on HNO3 extraction by TBP. It is a proof-of-concept in-silico aid for understanding and controlling PUREX extraction behaviour in used-fuel reprocessing, and for designing experiments.
incurred_insecurity:
This proof-of-concept regressor predicts organic-phase HNO3 equilibrium in PUREX from three inputs, trained on heterogeneous literature data. It has no direct actuation path, so its exposure comes from how far its outputs are trusted and where it may be extended. The main threats are out-of-distribution and omitted-physics error, trust and scope creep toward control without qualification, poor repeatability and configuration control, and data and model integrity attacks that the weak provenance would make hard to detect.

Literature-data heterogeneity and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
The training data mix temperature, purity, method and diluent conditions that are not model inputs. Accuracy is already inconsistent across diluents, and the model returns confident values with no applicability-domain flag for degraded, irradiated, actinide-loaded or novel-diluent solvent. An adversary who knows these weak regions could place a manipulation, or steer conditions, where wrong acid-loading estimates would be trusted and would mis-set extraction, scrub or third-phase margins.

Omitted physics and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
The three-input model leaves out temperature, metal loading, nitrate effects and DBP/MBP degradation products, and it cannot explain when it is invalid. A plausible but wrong number can therefore hide a missing-variable error, and an adversary could rely on that opacity to let a tampered or biased output pass as ordinary model error.

Automation trust and scope creep -- implicit, exploitable
The paper's 'prediction and control' framing invites movement from experiment design into advisory or flowsheet use without AI-specific qualification or hot-plant validation. Smooth predictions can also discourage direct equilibrium measurement and weaken chemists' own checks. An adversary could exploit this misplaced trust, and the lack of independent verification, to push a poisoned or swapped model's output into operating decisions.

Non-repeatability and weak configuration control -- implicit, exploitable
MLP seed and hyperparameter sensitivity, plus research-grade workflows without formal versioning, mean the same inputs can yield different predictions and a legitimate retrain cannot be told from a tampered one. An insider or intruder could substitute or quietly retrain a model without detection.

Training-data and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
The compiled literature dataset, preprocessing scripts, ML libraries and model files can be altered, and a few corrupted entries in a small dataset can bias organic-phase acid predictions in a targeted diluent or acidity regime. The result is subtly mis-set experiments or flowsheet parameters that erode criticality, partitioning or solvent-degradation margins, with little independent checking to catch them.

Research-environment foothold and insider tampering -- adversarial
The tool likely runs on ad hoc workstations or notebooks with loosely managed Python dependencies and model files, outside the cyber regime protecting safety and safeguards systems. Malicious packages, valid-account abuse or insider model substitution could use it as a low-scrutiny foothold into the reprocessing site's engineering network.

Model extraction of plant-tuned versions -- adversarial
The public model reveals little, but a version fine-tuned on proprietary facility measurements would aggregate process data worth extracting or inverting. This is a future concern that grows if the model is operationalised.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a proof-of-concept regressor that predicts equilibrium HNO3 in the TBP phase from only three inputs (aqueous acid, TBP concentration, diluent type), trained on literature data. A bad prediction does not act on the plant directly. It reaches the facility through a process engineer or experiment designer who uses it to set acid feed/scrub/strip conditions or to choose experiments. In PUREX, organic-phase acid affects Pu/U/Zr/Tc distribution, third-phase formation, and the acid-dependent degradation chemistry of TBP and diluent (red oil/runaway-reaction precursors). Many safeguards sit between a wrong number and harm: measured acid by titration or inline probes, flowsheet codes, hot-cell and criticality controls, and operating-envelope limits. The realistic risk is therefore degraded engineering judgement and wasted or misdirected experiments, rather than an uncontrolled release. That risk grows if the tool later moves toward 'control' without being qualified.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats (no adversary needed):
(1) Generalization and data-scarcity failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0201.04). The data are heterogeneous literature values measured by different labs, methods, temperatures and diluent purities, and the authors report inconsistent accuracy across diluents. Plant solvents differ from the training set: they carry dissolved actinides and fission products, degradation products (DBP/MBP), irradiated or recycled solvent, higher temperature and ionic strength, and different diluent blends. The model may extrapolate confidently outside its envelope and return no uncertainty. Consequence: acid-loading or stripping behaviour is mis-estimated, which feeds into wrong extraction/scrub design, wrong assumptions about third-phase margins, and wrong guidance on thermal-hazard (nitrated-organic) conditions. These errors are caught only if measurement or flowsheet-code cross-checks are kept.
(2) Omitted physics and oversimplification (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0301, OP.C0401). The three-input model omits temperature, metal loading, and nitrate/salt effects, and it is opaque. A correct-looking number can hide a missing-variable error. Engineers may not know when it is invalid.
(3) Automation bias and scope creep (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). A published 'prediction and control' framing invites later use in decision support or advisory control without AI-specific qualification or validation against hot-plant data. Consequence: the model becomes a de facto basis for operating limits without a safety-case or QA basis.
(4) Non-repeatability and software hygiene (OP.C0402, OP.C0502). Different MLP seeds or retrained versions give different predictions for the same inputs, which undermines procedure traceability.

ADVERSARIAL threats:
(5) Data and model integrity (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059, AML.T0031). The literature corpus is public, so a supply-chain or training-data adversary could seed or alter compiled values, or tamper with a retrained model or surrogate. This could bias predictions in a targeted region, for example toward under-predicting organic acid near a hazardous regime. Consequence: subtle misdirection of design or experiments, or erosion of confidence in the tool. The effect is small if outputs are cross-checked.
(6) Crafted-input manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015). The input space is tiny and well-understood, so crafted-input attacks add little beyond the data and model tampering already described.
(7) Reconnaissance and information value (AML.T0000, AML.T0024.002). Open publication and public data reveal little beyond known chemistry. Any value to an adversary lies in deployed, plant-tuned versions trained on proprietary data, and that is a future concern, not a present one.

Overall: low direct hazard at proof-of-concept. The main exposure is unvalidated drift from research aid to operational reliance, plus integrity of the training data. Existing practice (measurement, flowsheet codes, operating envelopes) is the effective barrier, so the key controls are keeping those independent checks and limiting the model to advisory use.

ai_engineer.argument: From a pipeline view this is a small tabular regression model (3 features, MLP and random forest) trained on literature-compiled HNO3/TBP equilibrium data. Its main fragility is data provenance. The training set is a heterogeneous aggregate of published measurements taken at different temperatures, ionic strengths, TBP purities, diluent grades and analytical methods, and none of these are model inputs. The inputs are also too sparse to capture the real PUREX chemistry: no temperature, no dissolved U/Pu/Zr/Tc, no radiolytic or degraded TBP (DBP/MBP), no third-phase boundary. The paper itself reports inconsistent accuracy across diluents, which is a direct sign of operational heterogeneity and low coverage in the training distribution. Because it is a proof-of-concept in-silico aid, the exposure is in how it might be extended or trusted, not in its present role. Random forests cannot extrapolate beyond the training range, and an MLP extrapolates unpredictably, so out-of-range inputs yield plausible but wrong outputs with no built-in uncertainty or applicability-domain flag.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data provenance and heterogeneity: literature data with unrecorded conditions and uncurated measurement error, plus possible duplicated or non-independent points across papers causing leakage and optimistic validation. Cause: unrepresentative, noisy training data. Dependency: experiment design and any future control logic. Consequence: biased acid-uptake predictions that misguide experiment planning or flowsheet setpoints, affecting extraction/scrub/strip acidity and so U/Pu partitioning, criticality margin and process-loss behaviour. (2) Out-of-distribution and diluent-specific failure: sparse coverage for some diluents (dodecane vs. kerosene-type or novel diluents) gives uneven error. An aggregate metric hides the weak regions, and categorical diluent encoding cannot generalise to unseen diluents. (3) Qualification and scope mismatch: the model is equilibrium and static, while real PUREX runs under dynamic, multicomponent, radiolytically aged conditions, so a proof-of-concept could be over-trusted as it moves toward 'control' (automation bias, scope creep). There is no uncertainty quantification, and non-determinism in MLP training and seed/hyperparameter sensitivity limit repeatability. It is a poor candidate for a safety-relevant role without an applicability-domain check and thermodynamic-model benchmarking. (4) Cascading propagation: if its outputs feed a larger digital twin or a mixer-settler/flowsheet model, bias propagates to downstream predictions of distribution ratios. ADVERSARIAL THREATS (lower probability, tied to the pipeline). (a) Training-data poisoning or supply-chain tampering: the literature-scraped, publicly sourced dataset and ML library or model-file dependencies could be quietly altered. A small number of corrupted entries in a small dataset has outsized effect and is hard to spot, creating a subtle bias toward unsafe acidity predictions (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000). (b) Model or dataset integrity erosion after deployment, e.g. tampering with stored weights or the compiled dataset during retraining (AML.T0031, AML.T0059). (c) Reconnaissance value: published model, features and data let an adversary build a proxy and learn what the operator relies on for acid control, though the chemistry is largely public (AML.T0000, AML.T0002.000, AML.T0005). The adversarial exposure is modest today but rises sharply if the model is wired into live process monitoring or control.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is a low-value direct target. It is an offline, proof-of-concept regression model on public literature data with three inputs, and it has no actuation path. The concern is its trajectory and the trust it accumulates. If it migrates from experiment design into process-control advice for a reprocessing line, it becomes a quiet channel through which a poisoned dataset, a swapped model file, or a subtly biased prediction could shift operator or flowsheet decisions. Its known weakness (accuracy that varies by diluent) is exactly what a patient adversary or an unlucky drift could exploit. The main threat here is erosion of verification discipline and scientific provenance, not a dramatic cyber-physical attack.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Training-data and supply-chain integrity. The model is built from compiled open literature and probably public ML libraries, so a determined actor could poison or bias the compiled dataset, the preprocessing scripts, or a distributed model artifact (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). A small bias in predicted organic-phase acid in specific diluent or TBP regimes would be hard to detect because few independent checks exist. The facility dependency is acid-extraction behaviour. That behaviour affects Pu/U partitioning, third-phase and solvent degradation margins, and acid-balance in flowsheet design. The consequence would be mis-set experiments or flowsheet parameters, with possible criticality-relevant or material-accountancy margins eroded downstream. (2) Stepping-stone and insider pathway. A research-grade tool run on ad hoc workstations or notebooks, with loosely managed model files and Python dependencies, offers a low-scrutiny foothold into a reprocessing site's engineering network (AML.T0011.001, AML.T0018.002, AML.T0012, AML.T0025). Such environments sit outside the rigorous cyber regime that protects safety and safeguards systems (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0503, OP.C0502). An insider could also quietly retrain or substitute a model, with no formal configuration control to catch it (AML.T0076, OP.C0501). (3) Information value. Fine-tuning on facility-specific measurements would turn the model into an aggregate of proprietary process data that is worth exfiltrating, via model extraction or inversion (AML.T0024.001/.002, AML.T0035).

IMPLICIT, TIMEABLE BY AN ADVERSARY: (a) Inconsistent accuracy across diluents is a known out-of-distribution weakness. It will be worse for novel diluents, high acid concentrations, or irradiated or degraded solvent conditions that the literature data do not cover (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0201.04). Literature data from heterogeneous labs also carry hidden measurement and temperature inconsistencies (OP.C0201). An adversary who understands where the model is weak knows where its errors will be trusted but wrong. (b) Automation trust and skill fade. Smooth predictions can discourage direct equilibrium measurement and weaken chemists' mental models, so credibility rests on the tool rather than on verification (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0401). That is a window for sabotage or an error to pass unchallenged. (c) Non-determinism across random-forest and MLP training runs, with no pedigree, makes it hard to tell a legitimate retrain from a tampered one (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501). (d) Scope creep from a proof of concept to control or design use without qualification (OP.C0303, OP.C0504). Overall rating: low direct attractiveness, moderate as a trust-concentration and foothold risk if it is ever operationalized without provenance controls, independent validation against measurements, and bounded-use limits.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on literature-data heterogeneity and out-of-distribution failure, trust and scope creep, and training-data and supply-chain poisoning as the core threats. I dropped crafted-input evasion and open-source reconnaissance as low-value for a three-input offline model, and kept the foothold and extraction threats as distinct but secondary adversarial pathways. I also omitted lower-confidence or loosely traceable codes (AML.T0018.002, AML.T0025, AML.T0035, AML.T0005 and cascading-propagation codes) because the text does not instantiate them directly.

evidence.citation: "Machine Learning Prediction of Nitric Acid Extraction Behavior in PUREX Process," ACS Omega (American Chemical Society); related PNNL publication
evidence.note: The authors compiled literature data on nitric acid extraction by TBP across several diluents and trained ML models (an MLP and a random forest performed best) to predict organic-phase acid equilibrium concentration. The paper presents this as a first, proof-of-concept step toward ML-based prediction and control of PUREX solvent extraction. It also notes that accuracy was inconsistent across diluents.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoned or out-of-distribution acid-loading predictions mis-setting extraction, scrub or third-phase margins, which erodes criticality and partitioning margins; with no actuation path and with chemist checks and hot-plant validation still in place, this is operational disruption or minor safety-margin erosion, not a release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution and omitted-physics errors recur reliably whenever inputs fall outside the training domain, but a harmful outcome also needs the output to be trusted operationally, and targeted poisoning needs specific conditions to hold.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (dataset or model poisoning, supply-chain compromise, insider substitution, valid-account abuse) need access to the research environment, data pipeline or model files, which is beyond routine external interaction, though the loosely managed workstations lower the bar somewhat.

affected_users.why: As a proof-of-concept aid for experiment design, impact is mostly confined to one process-chemistry workflow and its flowsheet parameters, and would spread across coupled systems only if the model were operationalised.

discoverability.why: The model, its three-input design, its data sources and its inconsistent per-diluent accuracy are published in the open literature, and the weaknesses of small-data ML regressors, such as poisoning, drift and missing variables, are well documented, though plant-specific deployment details are not public.

use_case: Random Forest and AdaBoost regression (scikit-learn) that predicts the bias (simulated minus experimental keff) of MCNP6 criticality calculations. Inputs are nuclide-wise keff sensitivity profiles, with or without energy dependence, and optionally the simulated keff, taken from more than 1000 benchmark experiments in the Whisper package. The model is meant to complement criticality-safety code validation and to flag the nuclides and reactions that drive bias.
incurred_insecurity:
This model sits inside criticality-safety code validation, where predicted bias feeds the upper subcritical limit and subcritical margin for fissile operations. Its main exposures are silent integrity compromise of the benchmark and sensitivity data or the model artifact, extrapolation failure of tree ensembles outside the ~1000-benchmark coverage, and the promotion of an advisory estimate to licensing evidence. The harm is mostly slow erosion of margin that existing independent review would have to catch, rather than sudden failure.

Training-data and benchmark poisoning -- adversarial
Altering a few benchmark records, experimental keff values or Whisper sensitivity files (by an insider, compromised workstation or tampered shared dataset) can bias tree-ensemble predictions toward optimistic bias in a chosen nuclide or spectrum region while aggregate cross-validation metrics stay good. The result is a non-conservative subcritical margin that looks defensible in a validation report, and the large benchmark scatter hides the change.

Model artifact tampering and unsafe deserialization -- adversarial
A swapped or retrained pickled scikit-learn model, or a compromised package version, can silently alter bias outputs or the feature-importance ranking that points reviewers to bias-driving nuclides and reactions, hiding a real driver such as a faulty cross-section library. Unsafe pickle/joblib loading also gives code execution on an analyst workstation holding criticality models and facility process data.

Input manipulation of sensitivity profiles or simulated keff -- adversarial
Anyone able to alter MCNP outputs, sensitivity files or the optional simulated-keff feature, or an applicant tuning the submitted nuclide mix or energy binning, can steer the predicted bias toward a favourable value. Black-box queries to a small, interpretable model would be enough to find such inputs.

Extrapolation and applicability failure -- implicit, exploitable
Random Forest and AdaBoost cannot extrapolate and give no novelty signal, so configurations with new fuel forms (HALEU, accident-tolerant fuel), unusual reflectors or moderators, or advanced-reactor spectra return bounded, plausible biases that understate the true bias where benchmarks are sparse. An adversary can pick or frame an application in these thinly covered regions, relying on the model's confident output to pass review.

Label noise, correlated benchmarks and leaky validation -- implicit
The target (simulated minus experimental keff) carries benchmark uncertainty comparable to the signal, and related benchmark series leak across random splits, so reported skill overstates generalization and the model may fit evaluation noise. No realistic adversary gains much from this beyond the general over-confidence covered below.

Nuclear-data library and code drift -- implicit, exploitable
Sensitivities and bias labels are tied to a specific MCNP version and ENDF library, so an update silently invalidates the trained model and yields confident but wrong predictions. An adversary could time a data or library change around this window, or hide a manipulation inside the resulting prediction shift.

Circular, correlational attribution -- implicit, exploitable
Sensitivities come from the same code and data whose bias is being predicted, so feature importances reflect correlation among sensitivities and existing nuclear-data errors rather than cause, and can misdirect data-improvement effort or mask compensating errors. An adversary hiding a real driver can lean on reviewers' trust in the ranking.

Automation trust and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A smooth ML bias estimate with good cross-validation scores can be over-trusted and used to shrink validation margins or extend areas of applicability, with no accepted nuclear QA path or regulator readiness for ML-augmented validation. Seed, version and hyperparameter non-repeatability, and absent hashed data and model lineage, make tampering hard to tell from retraining variation, so the lowered vigilance is where an undetected change would sit.

Information exposure from facility-specific use -- adversarial
If applied to facility-specific configurations, stored inputs and query history reveal fissile process parameters and margins. The benchmark data are largely public, so model theft is a low concern.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This model sits in criticality-safety code validation, where the bias and its uncertainty set the subcritical margin (USLs) for fissile operations such as storage, handling, transport and processing. The facility-side question is who acts on a predicted bias. If an analyst or reviewer uses a smooth ML estimate to shrink a validation margin, extend an area of applicability, or reduce conservatism, a wrong prediction removes margin that the licensing basis assumed. Existing practice is a strong guard: ANSI/ANS-8.1 and NUREG/CR-6698 style validation, administrative margins, independent review and double-contingency control. Real harm therefore needs both an AI error and a human or procedural failure to accept it uncritically, and the main risk is slow erosion of rigor rather than a sudden failure. The main danger comes from advisory output being quietly promoted to evidence in a licensing submission.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and applicability failure: the training set is more than 1000 benchmarks, clustered around well-studied configurations (HEU/LEU/Pu, thermal and fast, solution and metal). Real applications with unusual moderators, reflectors, mixed fuels, new fuel forms (HALEU, accident-tolerant fuel) or advanced reactor spectra fall outside it. Tree ensembles cannot extrapolate, so predictions regress toward the training mean and understate large biases exactly where validation data are sparse. This is a drift/OOD problem (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03) combined with small-data and low base-rate issues (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). (2) Benchmark data quality: bias is simulated minus experimental keff, so benchmark uncertainties, evaluation errors, and nuclear-data library versions (ENDF/B-VII vs VIII) get baked into the labels. A model trained on one library may not carry over after a library update (OP.C0303, OP.C0201.01). (3) Circularity and objective misalignment: predicting the bias of a code from sensitivities that come from the same code and data risks learning correlations that merely mirror existing nuclear-data errors, with no independent check on them (OP.C0301, OP.C0401). Feature-importance output that flags nuclides and reactions is correlational and can mislead data-improvement priorities or mask compensating errors. (4) Automation bias in licensing review: a low predicted bias with a good cross-validation score can be over-trusted by an analyst or regulator and used in place of conservative USL margins (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Cross-validation on random splits also overstates skill if related benchmark series leak across the split. (5) Non-repeatability across scikit-learn versions, seeds and hyperparameters hurts QA reproducibility (OP.C0402, OP.C0502). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. Poisoning of the benchmark database or sensitivity files, such as altered ICSBEP-derived entries or Whisper inputs (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059), could shift predicted biases in a chosen direction. The result would be less conservatism in a safety basis, and it would be hard to detect because errors are within benchmark uncertainty. Model or pipeline tampering (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076) and manipulation of the sensitivity inputs for a specific application model (AML.T0043) are other routes. The need for subtle changes is itself a barrier, and independent MCNP calculations and peer review limit impact. Model theft is a low concern because the data are largely public, though export-controlled or proprietary application models are a confidentiality issue (AML.T0035).

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small-tabular-data regression problem (~1000 rows, very high-dimensional sensitivity features, especially energy-resolved) with a target that is a difference of two noisy quantities, simulated keff minus experimental keff. Experimental keff carries benchmark uncertainty comparable to the bias signal, so the model may largely fit noise or the evaluated-benchmark-handbook curation choices. Tree ensembles (Random Forest, AdaBoost) cannot extrapolate: for an application whose sensitivity profile lies outside the benchmark convex hull, the prediction collapses to a value within the range of training biases and looks plausible rather than flagging that the case is uncovered. This is the very situation that code validation exists to detect, namely areas of applicability. The model's value in licensing rests on trust in its coverage, which the architecture cannot self-report, so the main exposure lies in the pipeline and its qualification rather than in the facility.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution and extrapolation failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0403): tree ensembles return bounded, confident-looking bias estimates for novel configurations, such as new fuel forms, reflectors, or moderators, or for advanced reactor and HALEU systems, which have no benchmark coverage. Mechanism: no native uncertainty or novelty signal. Dependency: the criticality-safety validation and upper subcritical limit (USL) margin. Consequence: an under-predicted bias becomes an optimistic subcritical margin in a licensing basis. (2) Data provenance and label quality (OP.C0201, OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03): the target is a derived quantity whose experimental side includes benchmark uncertainty, evaluation-specific model simplifications, and correlated experiments from the same series. Random train/test splits leak between correlated benchmarks, so reported accuracy overstates generalization. Sensitivities are themselves computed with a specific MCNP version and nuclear data library, so a library or code update (ENDF/B revision, MCNP release) shifts both features and the bias target and silently invalidates the trained model (data/concept drift, OP.C0302.01/.02, OP.C0303). (3) Opacity and interpretability (OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03): feature importances used to flag bias-driving nuclides and reactions reflect correlation among sensitivities, not causation, so they can misdirect cross-section evaluation or validation effort; this is a human-factor risk in which the model's attribution is over-trusted (OP.C0101.04). (4) Qualification and repeatability gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502): scikit-learn ensembles depend on random seeds, library versions, and hyperparameter tuning, and no accepted nuclear QA (e.g., NQA-1-style) path exists for ML augmenting validation; regulators may lack readiness to review it (OP.C0504). (5) Automation bias in licensing (OP.C0101): a model-derived bias estimate used to shrink conservatism or to substitute for missing benchmarks erodes the independent-evidence principle of validation. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data or benchmark poisoning and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0018.000): a small number of altered benchmark records, sensitivity files, or experimental keff values in the Whisper package or in the internal data pipeline would shift learned bias in targeted regions of the feature space. Tabular data of this kind has no inherent integrity checks, and the effect is hard to see because the bias target already carries large scatter. Consequence: a systematically non-conservative bias for specific materials or configurations, which could enable an unsafe licensing margin to pass review. (7) Model or artifact tampering (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, AML.T0010.001): pickled scikit-learn models are executable artifacts, and a tampered file or compromised package version could alter outputs or execute code on a licensing workstation. (8) Input manipulation by an applicant (AML.T0043, AML.T0015): where the model screens an applicant's submitted sensitivity profile, a party could tune the submitted inputs, for example by choosing the nuclide mix or energy binning, to land in a region with favorable predicted bias. Black-box queries would suffice given a small, interpretable model (AML.T0040, AML.T0005).
