(9) Reconnaissance: public LANL papers and open benchmark data (AML.T0000, AML.T0002.000) let an adversary build a proxy model and learn where coverage is thin.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this model sits inside the criticality-safety validation chain, where the output (predicted bias, and so the upper subcritical limit and margin) can end up justifying fissile handling limits in licensing submissions. That makes it a trust-concentration point. An adversary, or a motivated insider, does not need to touch the reactor or the plant. Quietly shifting a bias prediction or the 'drivers of bias' ranking is enough to erode margin or steer attention away from a problematic nuclide or reaction, and a slow, plausible-looking error is much harder to catch than a crash. The most plausible targets are the benchmark and sensitivity data pipeline and the model artifact. Realistically a nation-state would find this a low-priority direct target, but it is cheap leverage for degrading safety margins or undermining regulatory confidence. The non-adversarial weaknesses (small data, applicability gaps, automation bias) are the ones an adversary would time an attack around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity attack on the training data or model. The inputs are sensitivity profiles from the Whisper/ICSBEP-derived benchmark set, produced by MCNP runs and stored as files. Anyone with write access (insider, compromised workstation, or tampered shared package/dataset) could poison a few benchmarks or retrain or swap the pickled scikit-learn model (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0059, T0031). Tree ensembles are easy to bias locally, for example toward optimistic bias for a specific nuclide or spectrum region, while aggregate cross-validation metrics stay good. Consequence: understated bias, eroded subcritical margin, and a licensing or validation basis that looks defensible but is not, a criticality-safety rather than a security-of-material outcome. (2) Manipulated 'flagging' output. The feature-importance ranking that points reviewers to bias-driving nuclides and reactions can be nudged so that real drivers (for example a compromised cross-section library or a deliberate benchmark misrepresentation) are hidden, which is a defense-evasion route for a separate attack on nuclear data or validation. (3) Input manipulation. If the optional simulated keff is a feature, anyone able to alter MCNP outputs or sensitivity files can steer the prediction (AML.T0043.003). Unsafe pickle or joblib deserialization of model files is also a code-execution foothold on an analyst network that holds sensitive criticality models and facility process data (AML.T0011.000, T0018.002). (4) Information exposure. A model trained on benchmark data may be benign, but if applied to facility-specific configurations, the query history and inputs reveal fissile process parameters and margins (AML.T0024, T0036). IMPLICIT, usable by an adversary: (a) Small data and poor coverage (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03). Only about 1000 benchmarks cover some fissile forms, spectra, and reflectors thinly, so the model is out-of-distribution for novel applications. Analysts may still use it as supporting evidence, creating a predictable blind spot. (b) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). A tool that appears to quantify bias can substitute for expert judgment on applicability and become the unexamined basis of a validation report, reducing vigilance in exactly the place an adversary or undetected error would exploit. (c) Opacity and qualification gap (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0502). Ensemble models are not qualified under nuclear QA frameworks, and non-deterministic training makes tampering hard to distinguish from retraining variation (OP.C0402.01). Without versioned, hashed data and model lineage, poisoning or drift cannot be detected. (d) Data drift (OP.C0302.01). Library updates (new ENDF/MCNP versions) change the bias landscape, so a stale model gives confident but wrong predictions. Overall the risk is moderate: low as a direct target, but it lets silent integrity compromise reach a safety-significant licensing decision unless human review and independent conventional validation remain mandatory.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on poisoning of benchmark/sensitivity data or the pickled model, tree-ensemble extrapolation failure, library drift, and automation over-trust in licensing; I kept these as single threats. I dropped weakly supported or restated items (reconnaissance and proxy-model building, model theft, AML.T0035, AML.T0024) and merged the unique correlational-attribution and input-manipulation points, noting model-artifact code execution from the security view.

evidence.citation: "Using Machine Learning Methods to Predict Bias in Nuclear Criticality Safety Simulations (LA-UR-17-27855)," Los Alamos National Laboratory (prepared for the 25th International Conference on Transport Theory)
evidence.note: The LANL report describes training ML models on a large set of criticality benchmark experiments to predict the bias in MCNP6 criticality calculations, which is the key quantity in code validation for criticality safety. A related journal version, also by LANL authors, reports that AdaBoost with energy-integrated sensitivities plus simulated keff gave the best predictions.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoning or tampering that produces non-conservative bias predictions feeding the upper subcritical limit for fissile operations, which could erode criticality safety margin and enable an inadvertent criticality; independent review and conservative margins make this a slow erosion of margin rather than a direct release, so 4 rather than 5.

reproducibility.why: Tree ensembles reliably return bounded, plausible outputs outside their benchmark coverage, and a poisoned dataset or swapped model artifact reliably yields shifted predictions once the access condition is met.

exploitability.why: Poisoning and artifact tampering need insider or workstation-level access, but an applicant framing a configuration in thinly covered regions, or steering inputs, needs only routine interaction, so the overall requirement is moderate.

affected_users.why: Impact spans every fissile operation or licensing case whose validation relies on the model's bias estimates, and a corrupted validation basis could propagate to multiple applications, but it stays confined to the criticality-safety validation workflow rather than coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: Tree-ensemble extrapolation limits, pickle deserialization risks, and dataset poisoning are well documented in open literature, and the LANL report and benchmark data are public, though knowing which regions are thinly covered or how the model is used in a specific process needs more knowledge.

use_case: Ensemble-stacking machine-learning regression, combining ANN, CHAID decision-tree and linear-regression models, that predicts the external soil corrosion rate of carbon-steel spent nuclear fuel canisters. It takes soil and environmental variables as inputs, and temperature and chloride turned out to be the most influential. The prediction supports choosing protection and integrity-management measures for buried or underground canister storage.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory regression stack (ANN, CHAID tree, linear model) sits upstream of long-horizon integrity decisions for buried carbon-steel spent-fuel canisters. It is not in a protection path, so its main insecurity is a quiet, systematic under-prediction of corrosion that is trusted and defers inspection or mitigation until confinement degrades years later. The main threats are an unrepresentative data basis and extrapolation, blindness to localized corrosion, over-trust of an opaque model without qualification, and adversarial corruption of data, inputs or model artifacts, plus information exposure.

Training-data provenance and transfer mismatch -- implicit, exploitable
The model is probably fit on small, pooled lab, literature or analogue buried-steel datasets rather than long-term field data from heat-generating canisters with welds and coatings. Its tree and linear components cannot extrapolate and the ANN extrapolates unpredictably, so it returns confident, typically optimistic rates outside its validity domain with no uncertainty bound. An adversary could rely on this unvalidated, hard-to-check output to hide a small bias, or alter site conditions (e.g. chloride from de-icing salt, drainage) knowing the model will not flag the shift.

Blindness to localized corrosion and drift -- implicit, exploitable
With few real failures to learn from, the model captures mean uniform corrosion and misses pitting, SCC, crevice and microbiologically influenced attack, while changing soil chemistry, moisture and decay-heat decline drift away from the static training snapshot. Because temperature and chloride dominate, an adversary could steer or mask change in those few inputs, relying on drift being read as ordinary soil variability.

Opacity, non-repeatability and over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
A stacked ANN/CHAID/linear ensemble with seed-dependent training and unstable feature importances is hard to explain, reproduce or qualify, yet its high headline accuracy invites managers to relax margins, inspection intervals or monitoring. An adversary could exploit this misplaced trust, since a manipulated prediction would replace independent checks and go unchallenged.

Qualification and regulatory gap -- implicit, exploitable
There is no accepted qualification route for ML in long-term storage safety cases, so an advisory screening aid can drift into safety-case evidence without commensurate V&V. An adversary benefits because a weakly verified model offers a deniable lever whose corrupted conclusions would face little scrutiny.

Fleet-wide model reuse -- implicit, exploitable
If one model is reused across sites or canister populations, a single flaw or bias propagates to every site. An adversary could compromise the shared model or dataset once to degrade integrity assurance across the fleet.

Data and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or compromised pipeline could bias chloride, temperature or moisture records, retraining data, or the stacked-model artifact toward under-prediction, and a small dataset makes a few altered records disproportionately influential. The result is deferred intervention and eventual wall breach with attribution nearly impossible, or conversely over-prediction driving needless retrieval, cost and dose.

Runtime sensor and input tampering -- adversarial
Tampering with soil, temperature or chloride feeds or input records pulls predictions into a favorable range at inference time, exploiting the model's steep sensitivity to those inputs. The false reassurance suppresses inspection or mitigation while real degradation proceeds.

Model and pipeline supply-chain compromise -- adversarial
Unversioned model files, notebooks, shared corrosion databases or statistics tooling could be altered to backdoor or corrupt the ensemble with no integrity checks or regression tests to detect it. The analytics workstation and data-collection path are also softer IT/OT-adjacent footholds toward wider waste-storage networks.

Model and data information exposure -- adversarial
Published feature importances, trained models and datasets reveal which conditions drive canister degradation and may reveal design, material, burial depth and margins. This aids adversary planning and is a security information-control concern.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a waste-storage engineering view, this is a decision-support regression model for long-horizon integrity management of buried or underground carbon-steel canisters. It does not sit in a trip or protection path. The consequence of a wrong prediction is therefore slow and mediated by inspection, monitoring and maintenance decisions, not an immediate accident. The real risk is a quiet, systematic under-prediction of corrosion that is believed because the model is accurate, which defers inspection or mitigation (cathodic protection, backfill control, drainage, canister repositioning) until a through-wall failure or confinement degradation shows up late. That failure would be hard to detect and costly to retrieve, and it depends on in-situ monitoring, periodic inspection and conservative corrosion allowances also failing or being relaxed. The model's data basis and qualification are the weak points, because the stored-fuel environment (decay-heat temperature fields, chloride accumulation, wetting-drying cycles, microbial and stray-current effects, welds and heat-affected zones) is poorly represented by generic soil-corrosion datasets.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data provenance and extrapolation: the model is likely trained on lab, literature or analogue buried-steel corrosion data (pipelines, coupons) and not on field data from actual canister sites. It then transfers to decades-long exposure, canister-specific metallurgy and weld conditions, and heat-generating thermal histories that are out of distribution. Consequence: biased, typically optimistic, corrosion rates that look precise but are not valid for the actual site (OP.C0201.02/.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). (2) Small-data and low base-rate problem: there are very few real canister failures or localized-attack events, so the model captures mean uniform corrosion and is blind to pitting, SCC, crevice and microbiologically influenced corrosion, which are the modes that actually breach confinement (OP.C0202, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403). (3) Static versus dynamic mismatch and drift: soil chemistry, moisture, temperature and chloride change over time (road salt, groundwater, climate, decay-heat decline). A model fit on static snapshots drifts silently, and a few dominant features (temperature, chloride) mean small sensor errors or unmeasured confounders shift the predictions heavily (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303). (4) Opacity and automation bias: an ANN/CHAID/linear stack gives limited mechanistic explanation, and high headline accuracy invites over-trust. Managers may then substitute the prediction for conservative design margins or inspection intervals, or justify life extension and relaxed monitoring (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501). Non-repeatability from ANN training and ensemble construction complicates licensing-grade reproducibility (OP.C0402.01). (5) Regulatory readiness: there is no accepted qualification route for ML in long-term storage safety cases, so use could drift from advisory to safety-case evidence without commensurate V&V (OP.C0501, OP.C0504).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. Corrupting the model or its inputs is the realistic attack class. Training-data or model poisoning, or supply-chain compromise of a shared corrosion database or model artifact, could bias predictions downward (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059, AML.T0031). Tampering with soil or temperature/chloride sensor feeds or lab-sample records could suppress or inflate predictions at run time (AML.T0043, AML.T0015). Under-prediction defers maintenance and sets up a delayed integrity or release problem. Over-prediction could drive unnecessary retrieval or repackaging, with cost, worker dose and public-confidence effects. Adversary leverage is limited by the long timescale, by independent inspection and monitoring, and by the fact that the model is advisory. The most plausible exploit is therefore a subtle, hard-to-attribute bias that erodes margins and is exposed only on the next inspection, not an acute event. Where records support safeguards or inventory-linked decision making, falsified model-supported conclusions could also undermine confidence in the storage safety case, as an integrity-assurance problem and not a diversion pathway. Mitigating practice is to treat the model as a screening aid, bound it with conservative mechanistic and empirical corrosion allowances, validate against field inspection and coupon data, version-control and hash datasets and models, and keep sensor integrity checks independent of the model.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a tabular regression stack (ANN, CHAID tree and linear regression combined by a meta-learner) trained on a small, heterogeneous corpus of soil-corrosion measurements. That corpus is most likely pooled from literature, lab coupon tests and legacy buried-pipeline or steel-structure studies, not from spent-fuel canisters in service. The structural weakness is a mismatch between what the model learned and what it is used for. It learned short-duration, mostly lab or analogue corrosion rates and is asked to guide decades-long integrity management for a safety-significant, hard-to-inspect asset. Stacking raises benchmark accuracy but adds layers of opacity, and the stacked accuracy figure only reflects interpolation within the training envelope. The fragility is therefore in data provenance, extrapolation behavior and qualification, not in the facility around the model.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Provenance and transfer mismatch (OP.C0201.03, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0202, OP.C0204): the training data are probably lab or analogue-structure measurements, with few or no long-term field data from canisters that have heat load, welds, coatings, cathodic protection or backfill. The model's apparent accuracy is then a cross-validation artifact on a small, possibly autocorrelated dataset, with leakage between folds from repeated measurements at the same site. Mechanism: weak validity for the real target. Dependency: protection and monitoring decisions for buried or underground canisters. Consequence: under-predicted corrosion, inadequate protection, delayed inspection, and later through-wall or stress-corrosion degradation of the confinement barrier. (2) Out-of-distribution and drift (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403): tree and linear components cannot extrapolate beyond the training range, and the ANN extrapolates unpredictably. Temperature and chloride come out as dominant features, but a canister's thermal history, chloride ingress over decades, wetting and drying cycles, microbial activity and climate change move inputs outside the training distribution. The learned correlations may also not be causal (OP.C0302.02). The model returns confident point estimates with no uncertainty bound, so nobody can tell when it has left its validity domain. (3) Qualification gap (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402): a static offline benchmark stands in for a lifetime-scale validation that cannot be done. Ensemble stacking and ANN training are non-deterministic across seeds, and the model is hard to explain, so it is hard to justify in a safety case. The feature-importance ranking can also be unstable under correlated inputs such as temperature, moisture and chloride. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04): a numerically precise corrosion rate invites over-trust and displaces conservative engineering margins, physics-based models and direct inspection. Because the burial itself limits inspection, the model has no ground-truth feedback loop to expose its errors.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Data poisoning and integrity erosion (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0031): the model depends on soil-survey, sensor and literature datasets. Quiet manipulation of site chloride or temperature records, or of retraining data, could shift predicted rates downward and cause under-protection, or upward and cause wasted resources. Small-data regimes make a few altered records disproportionately influential. The same manipulation can be timed to hide real degradation. (6) Evasion by input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043): tampering with the soil or environmental sensor feed or the input spreadsheet can pull predictions into a favorable range, and the steep feature sensitivity to temperature and chloride shows which inputs matter most. (7) Model and pipeline supply chain (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018, AML.T0076, OP.C0502): unversioned model files, notebooks and commercial statistics software (CHAID-style tools) could be altered to backdoor or corrupt the stacked model, with no integrity checks or regression tests to detect it. (8) Information exposure (AML.T0000, AML.T0024): the published model and feature importances disclose which environmental conditions drive corrosion, so an adversary could infer where canister integrity is most vulnerable or how site decisions respond to inputs. The main exposure is unmanaged dependence on the model, not a direct operational control path.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this is an advisory model that sits upstream of long-horizon integrity decisions for buried spent-fuel canisters. It is not a real-time control, so a sophisticated adversary would rarely bother attacking it directly. Its security significance is different. Corrosion predictions can justify deferring inspection, excavation or remediation, and the consequences surface years later, after the people and logs that could attribute a cause are gone. The model also gives insiders and supply-chain actors a quiet, deniable lever. A small bias in the inputs, training data or model artifact looks like ordinary soil variability, and no alarm fires. The more serious risk is therefore mostly non-adversarial: a published, well-fitted model built on limited data gets over-trusted, and an adversary exploits that over-trust and the long detection lag.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL (1) Integrity manipulation of the data or model. The model depends on soil chemistry and temperature inputs, plus corrosion training data from lab, analogue or field sources. An insider, a contractor or a compromised data pipeline could bias the chloride, temperature or moisture records, or the stacked-model artifact, toward under-prediction. The AI failure mechanism is silent poisoning or corruption of a model whose outputs are never validated against ground truth in the short term. The facility then relies on it to set inspection intervals, cathodic-protection or coating choices and monitoring density. The consequence is deferred intervention and eventual canister wall breach, with radiological, safety and regulatory-confidence effects, and attribution is nearly impossible because the effects appear decades later. (2) Concentrated trust in a published methodology. Because the approach is public, an adversary can study which variables dominate (temperature, chloride). Knowing this lets them target the few sensor streams or site-characterization datasets that most move the prediction, or influence the environment itself, for example de-icing salt or drainage changes near a storage area. The model's high sensitivity to a couple of inputs makes it easy to steer. (3) Sensor and data-supply pathway as stepping stone. Environmental data collection and the analytics workstation or cloud tooling are lower-hardened IT or OT-adjacent systems. They offer a foothold toward wider waste-storage networks, and an external ML-service or library dependency adds supply-chain exposure (AML.T0010, T0018, T0020, T0059, T0031). (4) Exposure of sensitive information. Trained models and datasets reveal canister design, material, burial depth and degradation margins. That helps adversary planning and is a safeguards and security information-control issue (AML.T0024, T0035). IMPLICIT (5) Extrapolation and data scarcity. The training data likely comes from limited, heterogeneous soil sites and accelerated or analogue tests. Real storage conditions over decades, including changed groundwater chemistry, microbial effects, coating failure and thermal history, are out of distribution. The model is confidently wrong in exactly the regimes that matter and is hard to validate on a decades-long timescale (OP.C0302, OP.C0202, OP.C0201). (6) Opaque ensemble and automation trust. The ANN stack is hard to explain or qualify, and the strong headline accuracy invites over-trust, so inspection frequency or conservatism may be reduced. An adversary can exploit this complacency, because the prediction replaces independent monitoring (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). (7) Fleet-wide propagation. If one model is reused across sites or canister populations, a single flaw or manipulation propagates everywhere (OP.C0602, OP.C0603).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the data-provenance/extrapolation, over-trust/opacity, qualification and data-poisoning threats; I merged their overlapping phrasing and kept fleet propagation, supply chain and information exposure as distinct threats. I dropped the weakly argued reconnaissance code AML.T0000, and the minor sensor-pathway stepping-stone point was folded into the supply-chain paragraph.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning modeling of predictive external corrosion rates of spent nuclear fuel carbon steel canister in soil," Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio), via PubMed Central
evidence.note: The authors built and compared several ML models (boosted and bagged ANNs, CHAID decision trees, linear regression and a stacked ensemble) to predict soil corrosion rates of spent-fuel carbon-steel canisters. The ensemble-stacking model had the highest accuracy, and a feature-importance analysis found corrosion rate most sensitive to temperature and chloride.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is quiet under-prediction (or poisoning) that defers inspection or mitigation until canister confinement degrades and a breach occurs. The model is advisory and long-horizon, so the harm falls short of a direct release but is a serious integrity and confinement concern, and it may also erode safeguards assurance.

reproducibility.why: Extrapolation failure, blindness to localized corrosion, and drift away from a static training snapshot occur reliably whenever inputs fall outside the training domain. Over-trust and the lack of uncertainty bounds make the failure repeatable, though it depends on the site and data conditions.

exploitability.why: The most credible adversarial routes (poisoning data or model artifacts, tampering with sensor feeds, supply-chain compromise) require insider access or a compromised pipeline. A few implicit weaknesses need no access, but turning them into harm still requires manipulating site conditions or data.

affected_users.why: Fleet-wide model reuse means one bias or compromise propagates across all sites and canister populations that rely on the model, so the impact reaches a whole storage inventory rather than a single component. It does not propagate to coupled operating plant systems.

discoverability.why: The study is published openly, including the model types and the dominant features (temperature and chloride). The limits of ML on small data, extrapolation, and the blind spot for localized corrosion are well documented for this class of model. Outsiders can infer the weaknesses without insider knowledge of any specific system.

use_case: Deep reinforcement learning (Proximal Policy Optimization) that searches for PWR core reload loading patterns. The agent places fuel assemblies one at a time to minimise fuel cycle cost under design constraints. Its performance was benchmarked against genetic algorithm, parallel simulated annealing, tabu search and an ensemble evolutionary/swarm method in core-design optimisation scenarios.
incurred_insecurity:
A PPO core-reload optimiser sits upstream of the licensed reload safety analysis, so a single bad pattern is unlikely to cause direct physical harm. Its insecurity is the silent erosion of design margin and trust: the agent optimises whatever its evaluator computes, and it is opaque, non-repeatable and benchmarked as better than legacy methods. The main threats are tampering with the optimisation pipeline, backdoored policies, exfiltration of proprietary core-design data, and several implicit weaknesses (reward hacking, surrogate fidelity gaps, generalisation failure, non-repeatability, over-trust and weak qualification) that make tampering easier to hide.

Pipeline and reward tampering -- adversarial
An insider or poisoned dependency (RL library, pretrained policy, simulator wrapper, cross-section data, reward or constraint penalties) can make the agent converge on patterns that pass the surrogate's checks but carry hidden erosion of peaking-factor, shutdown-margin or MTC margin. Because the attack sits upstream of the independent verification meant to catch it, it is low-visibility sabotage of the design basis.

Backdoored or triggered policy -- adversarial
A poisoned policy can behave normally on benchmark cases yet misbehave on a specific fuel inventory or burnable-absorber configuration. This lets sabotage be timed to a particular reload while evading acceptance testing.

Design data and model exfiltration -- adversarial
Trained policies, search histories, cost models and core-design inputs reveal fuel management strategy and plant-specific neutronic margins. Theft or extraction of these artifacts leaks commercially and proliferation-relevant information and gives quiet reconnaissance for later attacks.

Optimiser availability denial -- adversarial
Denying or degrading the optimisation compute service during outage planning can push designers toward hurried, less-reviewed manual decisions. The scenario is modest, because manual methods remain available.

Reward hacking and surrogate fidelity gap -- implicit, exploitable
Single-objective cost minimisation with penalty-based constraints lets PPO exploit errors in a fast core simulator or surrogate, producing patterns that under-predict peaking or trade unencoded margins (burnable-absorber placement, fretting, power history) for cost. An adversary who subtly perturbs the evaluator or penalty weights can hide inside this already-tolerated fidelity gap, since the resulting bias looks like ordinary optimiser behaviour.

Out-of-distribution generalisation -- implicit, exploitable
Policies trained per core geometry, enrichment set, cross-section library and cycle length emit plausible but poor or infeasible patterns, with no signal, when fuel design or limits change. An adversary could change such inputs or exploit the missing out-of-distribution warning to induce degraded patterns.

Opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
Stochastic training and sampling make results seed-dependent, and the sequential placement policy yields no readable rationale. A tampered output is therefore hard to distinguish from normal run-to-run variation, and attribution of manipulation is difficult.

Over-trust, skill fade and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
Benchmark superiority over GA, SA and tabu search encourages over-trust, and reload engineers' pattern-making intuition fades, while no AI-specific QA path or model-version and provenance control exists for safety-related design software. An adversary can rely on this complacency and weak provenance control, timing a manipulation to pass cursory review.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a core-design standpoint, an RL loading-pattern optimiser sits upstream of the licensed reload safety analysis. Its output is a candidate pattern, not a decision, and it is then checked by the qualified neutronics/thermal-hydraulics codes, the reload safety evaluation, and technical specification limits (peaking factors, shutdown margin, MTC, boron letdown). That layered review makes direct physical harm from a single bad pattern unlikely. The real risks are the ones that slip through those layers: a pattern that satisfies the constraints the optimiser was given but exploits fidelity gaps in its surrogate or fast core simulator, a constraint set that is incomplete, or optimisation pressure that drives the design to the edge of margin. There is also a security dimension: the loading pattern, cycle economics and core-physics inputs are sensitive design information, and an optimiser that is quietly manipulated could bias design toward degraded margin or economics in ways that are hard to spot by inspection.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Tampering with the evaluation environment, the reward function or constraint penalties, the cross-section/depletion data, or the trained policy (supply chain or insider; ATLAS T0010, T0018, T0020, T0076). The agent then reliably converges on patterns that look optimal but carry hidden margin erosion, such as hot-spot peaking, reduced shutdown margin or a worse burnup distribution. A patient adversary would aim for a pattern that passes the standard checks but degrades margin, fuel reliability or economics. The physical downstream hazard is limited because independent reload safety analysis and plant surveillance would have to fail too, but the cost is credibility and added fuel-failure or cycle-length risk. (2) Exfiltration or inference of proprietary core design, fuel inventory and cost models through the optimiser's inputs, outputs and trained weights (T0024, T0025, T0035, T0036). The result is design-information leakage from the vendor or utility, which is also relevant to safeguards. (3) Supply-chain compromise of RL libraries, simulators or pre-trained policies used in the design workflow (T0010.001, T0010.003, T0011.000).

IMPLICIT: (1) Reward hacking and objective misalignment (OP.C0301): the single-objective cost minimisation can trade away margins or constraints not fully encoded, such as burnable-absorber placement, power-history effects, vibration or grid-to-rod fretting, and operational flexibility. Penalty-based constraint handling can leave marginal violations. (2) Fidelity and generalization gaps (OP.C0302, C0303, C0201.01/.02): the agent is trained and benchmarked on simulated data from a fast core model, which can diverge from the licensed code system, especially for new fuel designs, plant-specific features, or end-of-cycle and extended-burnup states. (3) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, C0402): the policy cannot be explained, results vary by seed, and the optimum is not provable, so designers may over-trust a pattern that merely beats legacy heuristics (OP.C0101.04). (4) Skill fade and out-of-loop effects (OP.C0101.01/.06): reload engineers' intuition for pattern-making erodes, which weakens their ability to catch implausible patterns. (5) Governance gaps (OP.C0501, C0504): there is no established qualification path for AI-generated designs under 10 CFR 50 Appendix B-type QA. The adversarial and implicit failures compound: an attacker can time or hide tampering behind the normal run-to-run variability and opacity that reviewers already tolerate.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a PPO agent whose reward comes from a core physics surrogate or simulator (nodal diffusion code) that scores each candidate loading pattern for cycle cost and design constraints. The ML fragility sits in three places. First, the reward function is the model, so any bias in the simulator or surrogate gets amplified by the optimiser. Second, PPO policies are trained per problem instance, so they generalise poorly to a different core size, enrichment set, burnable absorber scheme or cycle length. Third, a learned search heuristic is hard to qualify, because the only trusted output is the candidate pattern, and that must be re-verified by qualified codes. In a design-phase use the risks are mostly latent. A subtly wrong pattern can enter the licensing basis, or an adversary or error could skew what the optimiser finds attractive. Benchmarks against GA, SA and tabu were done on specific scenarios and may not transfer.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Reward and surrogate fidelity: the agent optimises whatever the evaluator computes. If it uses a reduced-order or surrogate physics model, or a coarse-mesh nodal solver, PPO will exploit its errors, for example by finding patterns where the surrogate under-predicts peaking factors or the power-peaking margin. The result is optimised-for-the-evaluator loadings that sit close to real safety limits (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0301 objective misalignment). Cost is the stated objective and constraints are handled as penalties or masks, so a mis-weighted penalty can trade margin for cost. (2) Generalisation and drift: policies are trained on particular core geometries, depletion histories and cross-section libraries. A change in fuel design, cross-section data, plant licensing limits or cycle strategy makes the policy out-of-distribution, and it may emit plausible but poor or infeasible patterns without any signal that this has happened (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203 for new-build scarcity). (3) Non-determinism: stochastic training, random seeds and stochastic sampling at inference mean the same problem can give different patterns, which complicates verification and reproducibility for the design record (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0402.02). (4) Opacity and automation bias: engineers may over-trust a pattern because the method 'beat legacy optimisers' in a benchmark, and may not do independent checking of the margins. A policy that places assemblies sequentially gives no readable rationale (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0501 AI-specific QA gap, OP.C0303). (5) Benchmark overfit: claims of superiority rest on specific scenarios and tuned hyperparameters, so the confidence is not transferable (OP.C0403).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Supply chain and artifact integrity: tampering with the trained policy weights, the RL framework, the simulator wrapper or the cross-section and reactor model inputs (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076). A backdoored policy, or a perturbed evaluator, could steer designs toward patterns with hidden margin erosion, such as unfavourable peaking or reduced shutdown margin, that nominal checks might not flag; the consequence is a degraded safety case or a fuel performance problem later. (b) Data and reward poisoning: manipulating the training scenarios, constraint definitions or cost parameters (AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0031) shifts what the optimiser considers optimal. (c) Information exposure: the model, training scenarios and optimised patterns encode proprietary core design and fuel management strategy, so exfiltration (AML.T0025, AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002) is an IP and potentially a security risk. (d) The AI adds a modest new attack surface through GPU/cloud compute and ML dependencies for a design environment that was previously isolated (OP.C0601, OP.C0502). Because the pattern is later verified by licensed physics codes, the main danger is a silent bias that passes that verification, or a verification step skipped under schedule pressure.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, a PPO loading-pattern optimiser is a poor direct target for a nation-state, because a bad pattern still has to pass the licensee's independent neutronics and thermal-hydraulic verification and the regulatory reload safety evaluation. Its significance is as an integrity-of-design-basis stepping stone and as a trust-concentration point. If it becomes the default generator of candidates, an insider or supply-chain actor who can bias its reward, constraint handling or surrogate physics can steer the whole candidate pool toward patterns that look optimal but have thin, hidden margins. The same actor can also nudge fuel-cycle economics or exploit reviewer complacency. The optimiser is non-deterministic and opaque, so reviewers see only the final pattern, not the search path or the reasons for rejected alternatives. That makes subtle manipulation hard to attribute and lets review fatigue set in when the AI keeps outperforming legacy methods. The policy, reward code and the core-design and fuel-cost data it consumes also hold commercially and proliferation-relevant information about fuel design and core physics.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity compromise of the optimisation pipeline: a malicious insider or a poisoned dependency (RL libraries, pretrained policies, checkpoints, the physics-solver wrapper) could alter the reward function, constraint penalties or the reactor-physics surrogate or simulator the agent trains against. The agent would then systematically favour patterns that satisfy the surrogate's checks but sit closer to real limits (peaking factors, shutdown margin, moderator temperature coefficient) than the downstream licensing codes would accept without scrutiny. The consequence is a degraded safety margin that passes screening, or a pattern that is deliberately uneconomic or hard to license, causing outage delay. This is a low-visibility sabotage route, because the optimiser output is a design proposal and the attack sits upstream of the independent verification meant to catch it. (2) Trigger-based or backdoored policies: a poisoned model could behave normally on benchmark cases but misbehave on rare inputs, such as a particular fuel inventory or burnable-poison configuration, so the sabotage can be timed to a specific reload. (3) Data and IP exfiltration: core-design inputs, cost models, trained policies and search histories reveal fuel management strategy and plant-specific neutronic margins, and model extraction or theft of the artifacts is a quiet reconnaissance gain. (4) Availability: denial of the optimisation service, or tampering with compute, could pressure outage schedules into hurried manual or less-reviewed decisions.

IMPLICIT. Benchmark superiority over GA, simulated annealing and tabu search encourages OP.C0101.04 over-trust and skill fade in the experienced core designers who could spot an implausible pattern, and an adversary could time a manipulation to that complacency. Because the optimiser is stochastic, results are non-repeatable (OP.C0402), so a tampered output cannot easily be told apart from ordinary run-to-run variation. Opacity (OP.C0401) hides why a pattern was chosen. The agent is trained on one plant's core and cycle data and may not generalise to new fuel types, enrichments or cycle-length regimes (OP.C0302), and any mismatch between its surrogate physics and the licensing-grade codes (OP.C0303) can produce patterns that exploit the surrogate's errors, which is reward hacking or goal misalignment (OP.C0301). Weak AI-specific qualification and software hygiene (OP.C0501, OP.C0502) mean model versions and training provenance may not be controlled to the standard applied to safety-related design software, which is what makes the adversarial paths above credible.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on pipeline/reward tampering, backdoored policy and exfiltration as adversarial threats, and on reward hacking, surrogate fidelity, opacity, over-trust and qualification gaps as implicit threats. I dropped weakly argued items (T0012, T0036, T0059, T0031, OP.C0203 new-build scarcity, OP.C0403, cloud dependency) as restatements or poor fits for a design-phase optimiser.

evidence.citation: "Surpassing Legacy Approaches to PWR Core Reload Optimization with Single-Objective Reinforcement Learning," Nuclear Science and Engineering (Taylor & Francis / American Nuclear Society)
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed article applies PPO-based deep RL to PWR core loading pattern optimisation. It compares the method with the stochastic optimisers most commonly used for this problem (genetic algorithm, parallel simulated annealing with mixing of states, tabu search) and with an ensemble method (PESA). The authors report that PPO can act as both a global and a local search method, which is how it improves on the legacy approaches.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is pipeline/reward tampering (or a backdoored policy) that silently erodes peaking-factor, shutdown or MTC margin upstream of the licensed reload analysis; independent verification limits the chance of direct release, so this is minor safety-margin erosion, and the exfiltration of proliferation-relevant design data stays below the safeguards-falsification level.

reproducibility.why: Reward hacking, surrogate-fidelity gaps and out-of-distribution failures recur reliably once the optimiser is in use, but a deliberate tamper must evade downstream independent verification and stochastic variation, so success is conditional.

exploitability.why: Tampering with training pipelines, evaluators, cross-section data or policies generally needs insider access or a supply-chain foothold in a controlled design environment; only the implicit weaknesses need no special access.

affected_users.why: A compromised optimiser would affect a whole reload cycle design for a plant or fleet using the same tool, and corrupted margins propagate into core operation, but it stays confined to the design function and is bounded by the downstream safety review.

discoverability.why: The method, benchmark results and the general classes (reward hacking, surrogate gaps, poisoning, supply chain) are public in the open literature, but locating where a specific deployment's pipeline, data and evaluators sit requires partial insider or vendor knowledge.

use_case: CatBoost gradient-boosting regression, with post-hoc calibrated uncertainty estimates and SHAP explainability, that predicts intergranular stress corrosion crack growth rate in austenitic stainless steels under BWR and PWR coolant conditions. It is trained on a curated experimental crack-growth database (material, environment and stress-intensity inputs) and supports ageing-degradation and structural-integrity assessment of light-water-reactor components.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory CatBoost crack-growth-rate model has no actuator authority, but its output feeds inspection intervals, flaw-evaluation margins and life-extension cases for austenitic stainless steel components. The main threats are silent non-conservative predictions outside a small lab-derived data envelope, over-read calibration and SHAP outputs, ungoverned model use, and adversarial tampering with the curated database, model artefacts or calibration layer. The likely consequence is eroded structural-integrity margin and wrongly deferred inspection, not direct plant upset, because bounding curves and NDE remain as independent safeguards.

Out-of-distribution flat extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
Tree ensembles clamp predictions to leaf values outside the training hull, so irradiated, cold-worked, weld-HAZ, unusual-heat or chemistry-transient conditions yield confident, non-conservative crack-growth rates with no warning. An adversary could time a degradation event, or deliberately steer analysis inputs toward these thinly covered regimes, so that a low prediction supports deferred inspection.

Calibration and validation overstatement -- implicit
Post-hoc calibrated intervals assume exchangeability and give only marginal coverage, which fails for small, clustered, repeated-measurement crack-growth data, especially in the rare high-growth region. Errors on the log-rate scale can also hide order-of-magnitude misses. No realistic adversary gains from this beyond what the out-of-distribution threat already offers.

Lab-to-plant data provenance gap -- implicit
The database mixes laboratories, specimen geometries, K-validity criteria, measurement conventions and imputed inputs such as ECP, so the model may learn lab artefacts that are never validated against plant-flaw data. Undocumented curation choices make a subtle record edit hard to distinguish from ordinary heterogeneity, which would help conceal a poisoning attempt.

Explainability and automation over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
SHAP shows correlational attribution inside the model, not physical mechanism, yet tidy plots and tight intervals invite engineers to treat a single precise number as qualified evidence and let mechanistic assessment skills fade. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, so that a biased prediction, with plausible attributions, passes without independent challenge.

Qualification, version and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
No recognised pathway qualifies an ML crack-growth predictor against disposition-curve methodology, so it can influence judgement informally while seeds, retrains and database updates go uncontrolled and SHAP rankings shift between versions. Weak version control and provenance let silent change pass unnoticed, and the research database may be handled as non-sensitive even though it encodes component susceptibility.

Training-data and database poisoning -- adversarial
A few altered, mislabelled or deleted records in the small, manually curated database (insider, shared repository or tampered published dataset) can bias the learned dependence on sensitization, ECP or chemistry, and shift predictions non-conservatively in a targeted regime. Aggregate metrics and tree-model opacity make this difficult to detect, and it persists through retraining.

Model, calibration and software tampering -- adversarial
Unsigned model files, unpinned open-source dependencies or a modified calibration stage can alter point predictions or narrow reported uncertainty while the outputs still look credible. Compromised artefacts could also carry malicious code into an engineering workstation near plant-sensitive data.

Input manipulation and model or data exfiltration -- adversarial
Falsified or mis-keyed chemistry, ECP, K or material descriptors move predictions without touching the model, and the explainability layer can lend them credibility. Theft of the database or model has low direct impact but reveals which components and conditions the operator treats as life-limiting.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a structural-integrity standpoint this model sits upstream of ageing-management decisions: inspection intervals, flaw-evaluation crack-growth rate (CGR) assumptions, and component life or repair/replace calls for austenitic stainless steel internals and piping. The real hazard is a plausible-looking but non-conservative CGR prediction. Lab CGR data are sparse, heterogeneous, and concentrated in certain heats, sensitization levels, irradiation conditions and water chemistries, so the model is likely to extrapolate poorly exactly where plant risk is highest (high fluence, unusual chemistry transients, weld residual stress fields). Existing practice already guards against this: NRC and BWRVIP/MRP disposition curves, conservative bounding crack-growth laws, ASME Section XI inspection, and NDE. The AI does not replace those, so harm needs a second failure, such as the ML output being used to justify relaxing inspection scope or interval, or being trusted over the bounding curve. The main exposures are therefore human and organizational (over-trust, SHAP narratives treated as mechanistic proof, calibrated intervals read as qualified margins) and data integrity, rather than direct plant control.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution and data-scarcity failure: the curated experimental database is small and biased toward lab-tested heats, with limited neutron-irradiated, cold-worked, or weld-HAZ data and few long-duration low-CGR tests. Predictions for plant conditions outside that envelope may be confidently wrong, and CatBoost's tree-based structure extrapolates flat rather than flagging a limit. This is the non-conservative direction that matters for flaw evaluation. (2) Calibration mismatch: post-hoc calibrated intervals are valid only for the calibration distribution. Plant components differ in heat, residual stress and chemistry history, so the stated coverage may overstate confidence and be read as a qualified margin. (3) Lab-to-field transfer and data provenance: the database mixes labs, specimen geometries, K-validity criteria, and measurement conventions; the model may learn lab artifacts, and field operational data may not match. (4) Explainability overreach: SHAP shows correlational attribution within the model and is not physical causation. BWR-versus-PWR comparisons could be mistaken for mechanism, or anchor engineering judgment on spurious feature interactions. (5) Qualification and regulatory gap: no recognized path exists for qualifying an ML CGR predictor against disposition-curve methodology, so it would be used informally, and model versions and retraining may be undocumented or non-repeatable. (6) Automation bias and skill fade, where analysts defer to an apparently precise number over bounding curves, which is more serious when the output supports extended operation or inspection-interval extension.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Training-data or database poisoning (supply chain, curated-data tampering, or insider edits) that subtly biases CGR predictions low for specific material/environment regions. It is hard to detect because tree models are opaque to review and the data are expert-curated. (2) Model or pipeline tampering, or manipulation of input parameters (water chemistry, ECP, K, material descriptors) in an analysis workflow, to produce non-conservative results that justify deferring inspection or repair. Another goal could be repeatedly undermining confidence (denial of trust) to disrupt outage planning. (3) Exfiltration of the database or model, which is low direct risk but reveals component susceptibility and degradation margins, informing target selection. The consequence requires defeat of the independent safeguards (conservative codes, regulator review, NDE), so the likely outcome is degraded safety margin, erroneous deferral of inspection, or economic and outage impact, and not a rapid physical failure. Detection of such manipulation is also weak where a single analyst's workflow is the only verification.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a tabular gradient-boosting regressor trained on a small, curated lab crack-growth database, and the ML pipeline is fragile in exactly the places where structural-integrity use is most sensitive. Tree ensembles cannot extrapolate: predictions outside the training envelope (new heats, irradiated or highly sensitized material, unusual water chemistry, ECP or hydrogen transients, low-K or high-K regimes) are clamped to leaf values and look confident. Post-hoc calibration (conformal or isotonic) assumes exchangeability between calibration and deployment data, and that assumption fails for the small, clustered, heavily autocorrelated data typical of crack-growth testing. SHAP attributions explain the model's learned correlations, not the physical mechanism, so they can lend a false sense of mechanistic validation. A model of this kind is a tempting input to inspection intervals and flaw-evaluation margins, and the main exposure is silent mis-prediction or a corrupted dataset, not a dramatic attack.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution failure with deceptive confidence. The training data is a compiled, heterogeneous literature or lab database whose test-to-test variability (heat chemistry, cold work, sensitization, ECP, conductivity, loading waveform) is large and unevenly sampled. A CatBoost model flat-extrapolates beyond the data hull. Plant conditions such as transients, impurity excursions, new water-chemistry regimes (e.g. hydrogen water chemistry or noble-metal additions) and welds or heat-affected zones are likely under-represented. The result is non-conservative crack-growth predictions, which feed ageing-management and flaw-evaluation decisions and could erode safety margin. (2) Calibration and validation weaknesses. Random train/test splits on a database of repeated measurements from the same specimen or lab leak information and overstate performance. Calibrated intervals are marginal, not conditional, so coverage can fail in exactly the high-consequence, rare, high-growth-rate region. This is a small-data, low-base-rate problem. Because the target is a log-scale rate, errors of an order of magnitude can be hidden. (3) Data provenance and label noise. The curated database mixes lab-measured data with different measurement protocols and unreported or inferred inputs (ECP, K-validity, crack-length criteria). Curation choices, imputations and outlier removal are undocumented model-defining decisions. Lab-to-plant transfer is unqualified, and the model is neither fitted to nor validated against plant-flaw data. (4) Concept drift and qualification mismatch. The physics knowledge base (susceptibility, regulatory disposition curves) evolves, and no mechanism exists to retrain or retire the model. Static lab-derived relationships are applied to dynamic plant operation. Non-deterministic training (seeds, categorical encoding, hyperparameter search) can shift predictions and SHAP rankings between retrains, which makes reproducibility and QA under nuclear software standards difficult. (5) Human factors. Single-number outputs with uncertainty bands and tidy SHAP plots invite automation bias and over-trust by non-ML engineers. Conversely, one visibly wrong prediction may lead to disuse. A BWR/PWR SHAP comparison can be over-read as causal evidence.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data poisoning and dataset integrity. The database is small and manually curated, so a few altered, added or removed records (an insider, a compromised shared spreadsheet or repository, a tampered published dataset) can bias the learned dependence on a variable such as ECP or sensitization. This can shift predicted rates in a targeted regime, or hide a susceptibility from the model, and the change would be hard to see in aggregate metrics. (7) Supply chain and artifact tampering. Model files (pickles or CatBoost binaries), Python dependencies, notebooks and calibration code are an unsigned-artifact attack surface. A swapped model or a modified calibration layer could shrink the reported uncertainty, and the tampering would be invisible downstream. (8) Input manipulation. If the model is fed from plant chemistry or operating-condition records, falsified or drifting sensor and chemistry inputs, or a mis-keyed material descriptor, move predictions without any model attack. The explainability layer could also be manipulated to mask this. (9) Model and IP exfiltration through repeated queries could reveal proprietary materials-performance data, although this is lower risk. Overall, the dominant exposure is quiet integrity erosion of an advisory model that informs safety-significant margin decisions.

security_specialist.argument: This is an offline, advisory regression model with no actuator authority, so a direct nation-state attack on it is unlikely when easier targets exist. The real exposure is indirect: the model's output feeds ageing-management and structural-integrity judgements, such as inspection intervals, flaw-evaluation margins and life-extension cases. A subtly biased crack-growth prediction would erode the conservatism in those judgements while looking technically credible, and it would be accompanied by calibrated uncertainty bands and SHAP plots that make it look rigorous. The value to an adversary is in quietly shifting a safety-relevant engineering decision, or in an insider timing a degradation event around a period when inspections have been deferred on the model's say-so. Non-adversarial weaknesses make this easier to hide: a small, curated lab database, extrapolation to untested plant conditions, and a human tendency to over-trust a model that quantifies its own uncertainty.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and database poisoning. The curated experimental crack-growth database is the single trust anchor. It is small, assembled from literature and lab sources, and curated by a few people. A subtle insider or supply-chain edit, such as shifting a few high-sensitivity points, mislabelling a material or environment condition (sensitisation, dissolved oxygen/hydrogen, conductivity) or dropping fast-growth records, would bias predictions in the non-conservative direction. Because the model is tabular and low-dimensional, the edit is hard to see in review and would survive retraining (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0018.000). (2) Post-hoc tampering with the calibration layer. If the calibration stage is altered, the uncertainty bands are narrowed while the point predictions stay unchanged. Reviewers who treat tight intervals as evidence of reliability are then misled (AML.T0031, AML.T0076). (3) SHAP-based explanation as a trust-laundering channel. Plausible attributions can lend credibility to a biased prediction and discourage independent challenge, which is a way of turning explainability into an attack aid (AML.T0067). (4) Model and software supply chain. Open-source gradient-boosting and calibration libraries, pickled model files and unpinned dependencies can carry compromise into an engineering workstation that sits near plant-sensitive data (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0011.000). (5) Reconnaissance and information value. Published models, databases and plant-specific input parameters tell an adversary which components and conditions the operator considers life-limiting (AML.T0000, AML.T0002.001, AML.T0035).

IMPLICIT, AND EXPLOITABLE BY TIMING. (6) Out-of-distribution extrapolation. Plant-specific conditions such as irradiation, cold work, water-chemistry transients, unusual heats and weld regions are sparse in lab data. Tree ensembles also cannot extrapolate beyond the training range, and they flatten predictions there without any warning, so non-conservative results appear exactly where the data are thinnest (OP.C0302, OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.04). Lab-to-plant transfer is a data-provenance gap that an adversary or an unlucky transient can exploit (OP.C0201.03). (7) Automation trust and complacency. Calibrated uncertainty and SHAP plots encourage over-trust and skill fade in mechanistic crack-growth assessment. Inspection scope may be reduced on the model's say-so, and the resulting window is one an attacker or a degradation process could use (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (8) Qualification and governance gaps. There is no established regulatory pathway for ML-derived crack-growth rates in code-based flaw evaluation. The model is not qualified, but it can still influence judgement informally. Retraining versions and database updates may also not be controlled, which makes silent change possible (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0502, OP.C0402.01). (9) Opacity and misapplied data security. The crack-growth database and models may be treated as non-sensitive research artefacts, even though they encode plant ageing vulnerabilities (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0401). The overall consequence is erosion of structural-integrity margin and degraded ageing-management decisions, with an indirect pathway to a loss of primary-boundary integrity. The model's tamper-evident provenance and version control matter more than its average accuracy.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on out-of-distribution flat extrapolation, calibration and SHAP over-trust, qualification gaps, and database poisoning plus artefact tampering; I merged these and kept distinct provenance, input-manipulation and exfiltration threats briefly. I dropped speculative codes with weak grounding (e.g. AML.T0000 reconnaissance, AML.T0048.002, OP.C0102) and generic adversarial-data codes only partly traceable to the text.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning for modeling intergranular stress corrosion cracking of stainless steels in light water reactors with uncertainty quantification and explainability," npj Materials Degradation (Nature Portfolio)
evidence.note: The paper builds a curated crack-growth-rate database for BWR and PWR environments and trains CatBoost on it. CatBoost outperformed NGBoost, Gaussian process regression and TabNet. The authors calibrate its uncertainty with post-hoc methods and use SHAP to compare BWR and PWR crack-growth behaviour. The work is a model built and tested on experimental data, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is non-conservative predictions or database poisoning that lead to deferred inspection and eroded structural-integrity margin on safety-relevant components; bounding curves and NDE remain independent safeguards, so this stays below a direct radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Tree-ensemble flat extrapolation outside the training envelope is a deterministic, reliable behavior whenever inputs fall in thinly covered regimes, and tampering or input errors reliably shift outputs once the access conditions are met.

exploitability.why: Targeted poisoning, artefact tampering or steering of analysis inputs needs insider or supply-chain access to a specialist engineering workflow, though the implicit out-of-distribution and over-trust weaknesses need no special tooling.

affected_users.why: A biased model can propagate across inspection intervals, flaw evaluations and life-extension cases for many austenitic stainless steel components at a plant or fleet, but it is advisory with no actuator authority and does not couple across plant control systems.

discoverability.why: Tree-model extrapolation limits, the lack of calibration guarantees for small clustered data, and the paper, database and open-source tooling are all publicly documented, so a capable outsider can readily infer where the weaknesses lie; exact plant usage is less visible.

use_case: Function-calling large-language-model interface for retrieving operational data from legacy nuclear power plant databases. The LLM maps a user's natural-language request onto a library of pre-approved, expert-validated query functions. It does not generate free-form SQL. This is meant to make retrieval of plant operating data more accurate, transparent and maintainable for plant staff. The paper also uses NL-to-SQL tools to draft the function code, which experts then validate.
incurred_insecurity:
A function-calling LLM front end over legacy plant databases removes free-form SQL generation, but it moves trust onto two unqualified points: the router that picks a function and fills its arguments, and the function library, whose code is drafted by NL-to-SQL tools and expert-reviewed. The main threats are silent wrong-but-valid answers, drift and governance gaps in the library, erosion of human verification, compromise of the library or routing artifacts, prompt manipulation of routing, and over-broad data access that eases reconnaissance. Safety impact is bounded because the use is read-only and sits outside protection and control systems. The real exposure is the integrity and confidentiality of the information that maintenance, surveillance and investigation decisions rest on.

Routing and parameter mis-binding -- implicit, exploitable
The LLM maps an ambiguous request (similar tags, unit A vs B, time window, engineering units) to a near-neighbour approved function or wrong argument. It returns a well-formed, validated result that looks authoritative, and it can drop data-quality flags or caveats, so engineers may trend or plan on the wrong data and a degrading component goes unnoticed. An adversary could rely on this lack of any visible failure signal, steering or timing a subtle wrong-data result so it passes as ordinary router error.

Library drift, coverage gaps and unqualified routing -- implicit, exploitable
Schema changes, tag renaming, instrument replacement, or a silently updated vendor model can make a once-validated function or routing behaviour return wrong data without error, and the routing layer has no AI-specific qualification or regression testing. Results are non-repeatable across versions, out-of-vocabulary plant jargon is forced onto a best-match function instead of rejected, and coverage gaps push users to ungoverned ad hoc tools. An adversary could hide manipulation inside this accepted noise or exploit the shadow workarounds.

Human-factors erosion and thin evidence -- implicit, exploitable
Staff who stop writing or inspecting queries lose schema familiarity and skill, and they stop sanity-checking outputs, while accuracy claims rest on a limited preprint benchmark of one utility's data. An adversary could time a subtle data or function manipulation around this reduced vigilance and the misplaced trust in the 'pre-approved' label.

NL-to-SQL drafting review weakness -- implicit, exploitable
Functions drafted by NL-to-SQL tools can embed subtle errors in joins, null handling, units or time windows that survive reviewer fatigue and rubber-stamping, then are trusted at scale. An adversary controlling or poisoning the drafting tool, or an insider, could exploit reviewers checking plausibility rather than adversarially auditing.

Cloud and data-governance exposure -- implicit, exploitable
A vendor-hosted LLM, or a security model designed for direct database users rather than an LLM intermediary, can cause availability loss and let operational data leave the facility boundary through prompts or logs. An adversary could exploit the provider or logging path, or the service account's broader rights, for collection or to degrade the aid at a chosen moment.

Function library and routing artifact compromise -- adversarial
Poisoned or tampered function bodies, function descriptions, routing prompts or the drafting-tool supply chain can silently redirect routing or cause over-retrieval, which the facility then treats as pre-approved. The consequence is systematically misleading maintenance, trending or surveillance data.

Prompt manipulation of function selection -- adversarial
Crafted requests, or instructions hidden in work-order notes, logs and database free text re-ingested by the LLM, can steer function choice and arguments, or push it toward bulk or unauthorized retrieval. Authorization enforced only by the LLM's choices is weak, so confidentiality or integrity is breached inside the approved function envelope.

Over-broad access and reconnaissance -- adversarial
A service account with wider database rights than the user, plus a natural-language front end with weaker audit trails, lets an insider or compromised account enumerate and aggregate outage, equipment-health and configuration data. The result is target development for sabotage planning, and exposed tool definitions reveal data structures.

Denial or degradation of the interface -- adversarial
Resource-intensive or excessive queries, or biasing the interface to fail, degrade the legacy database or service when quick retrieval matters, such as during outages or event response. Staff fall back to slower manual retrieval at a time the adversary can choose.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations lens this is a read-only retrieval aid, and its design (a closed library of expert-validated query functions instead of free-form SQL) removes the worst failure class, because the LLM cannot invent a query against a legacy historian or maintenance database. The remaining danger is a wrong answer that looks authoritative: the LLM picks the wrong function, fills the wrong parameters (unit, tag, time window, units of measure), or the function silently returns something other than what the engineer thought they asked for. Staff then use that data in surveillance trending, work-planning, operability or condition-based maintenance decisions, outage prep, or event investigation. Existing practice helps here, since safety-significant decisions run through procedures, independent verification and the plant's own control-room indications rather than an ad hoc database query, and the LLM sits outside the protection and control systems. The real exposure is gradual: quiet erosion of data-verification habits, a function library that goes stale or is poorly governed, and an adversary exploiting the assistant's trusted position in engineering workflows.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Function misrouting or parameter mis-binding: the LLM maps an ambiguous request (similar tag names, redundant channels, unit A vs B, as-found vs as-left, calendar vs outage time windows, engineering units) to a plausible but wrong approved function or argument. Output is well-formed and from a validated query, so it looks trustworthy. Consequence: engineers trend or compare the wrong data, which can mask a degrading component, produce a bad surveillance or reliability assessment, or misdirect maintenance and event-investigation work. Harm needs a human to act on it and independent checks (procedures, redundant indications, peer review) to also miss it. (OP.C0101.04 over-trust, OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0402.02 inference non-repeatability: same question yielding different function choices.) (2) Silent omission and oversimplification: the natural-language summary or framing drops data-quality flags, sensor-bad status, gaps, or calibration caveats that the raw query exposes; this is the transparency claim failing in practice. (3) Function library governance and drift: validated functions encode assumptions about schema, tags and units of the legacy DB. Schema changes, instrument replacements, tag renaming, plant modifications or database migration can make a once-validated function return wrong data without any error. Added to this, functions drafted by NL-to-SQL tools and then expert-reviewed carry reviewer-fatigue and rubber-stamping risk, as well as subtly wrong joins, filters or aggregation. Coverage gaps push users toward unsupported queries or toward workarounds with unvalidated tools (shadow use). (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0401.) (4) Human-factors erosion: skill fade in direct database use and loss of familiarity with data lineage; staff stop sanity-checking results. (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102.) (5) Reliability and benchmark limits: accuracy results come from a limited test set on one utility's data, which may not generalize to other sites or to the long tail of real requests (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202). The source is a preprint/conference paper, so independent validation is thin. (6) Cloud or vendor-hosted LLM dependency could create availability loss or data-exposure concerns for operational data (OP.C0601, OP.C0505).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (7) Prompt injection, direct or indirect: instructions hidden in free-text fields, work-order narratives, or documents the interface ingests can steer function selection or parameters (AML.T0051, T0051.001), or make the LLM return crafted data. Consequence: manipulation of what an engineer sees, data exfiltration of sensitive operating or configuration data by repeated queries, or reconnaissance of plant state. (8) Function-calling as attack surface: if the function layer has overly broad DB credentials, parameters aren't sanitized, or tool definitions can be modified, the 'safe' library becomes an injection or privilege-escalation path into legacy systems that were never designed to be exposed (AML.T0053, T0081, T0084.001, T0110, T0099, T0010.005). Legacy DBs often have weak authentication and flat network trust, so an IT-side compromise via the LLM service could bridge toward OT-adjacent data. (9) Data confidentiality: aggregation of operational data through a natural-language front end eases insider or compromised-account collection of sensitive information (security-relevant plant vulnerabilities, staffing and outage schedules), and may leak through logs or the LLM provider (AML.T0057, T0036, T0085, T0012, OP.C0505.01). (10) Integrity attacks on the underlying data or function code (supply chain of NL-to-SQL drafting tools, tampered function definitions), which the LLM would then present with unwarranted credibility (AML.T0010, T0018, T0031). (11) Denial of service or cost harvesting that degrades the aid during outages or event response, when quick retrieval matters most (AML.T0029, T0034). Overall severity is bounded: read-only, outside protection and control systems, and with human review. The worst plausible outcomes are misinformed engineering and maintenance decisions, subtle data manipulation that evades casual checks, and information-security exposure; direct physical consequence would require several independent safeguards to fail.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this architecture is a classifier-plus-argument-extractor: the LLM does intent routing over a closed function library and fills parameters (tag names, units, date ranges, aggregation windows). That is a much smaller attack and failure surface than free-form SQL generation, but the risk shifts rather than disappears. The model's job becomes selecting the right function and binding the right arguments, and errors there are silent. A well-formed, validated query that answers a different question than the user asked looks authoritative, and nothing in the pipeline flags it. The 'pre-approved' guarantee covers the function body only, not the routing decision or parameter binding, and it relies on experts validating NL-to-SQL-drafted code in a process whose rigor is undocumented. The evidence is also thin: the reported accuracy comes from a conference paper/preprint benchmark of unclear size and distribution, which says little about real staff phrasing, plant jargon, or a shifting function catalogue.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Routing and parameter-binding errors: the LLM may pick a near-neighbour function or mis-bind arguments (wrong unit, channel, time zone, sample vs. average, similar tag IDs across units). The query is valid, so the result looks trustworthy. Operations and maintenance staff may then base trend assessments, surveillance results, or work-planning decisions on the wrong data. Mapped to OP.C0304 (content fidelity, including mistranslation, omission and misattribution), OP.C0101.04 (over-trust), and OP.C0401 (opacity of why a function was chosen). (2) Out-of-distribution input and heterogeneity: plant slang, abbreviations, bilingual phrasing, requests that fit no function, or multi-step questions requiring composition. Closed-set routers tend to force a best match instead of abstaining unless explicitly calibrated for rejection. This is OP.C0302 and OP.C0302.03. (3) Catalogue and model drift: the function library, database schema, tag naming and model version (especially if a vendor-hosted LLM is silently updated) all change independently. Regression tests may not be re-run, producing OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303, OP.C0402.02 (non-repeatable routing at temperature or across versions), and OP.C0502/OP.C0501 (no AI-specific QA for the routing layer). (4) Code-drafting provenance: NL-to-SQL-drafted functions that experts review can embed subtle logic errors (join semantics, null handling, units, off-by-one time windows) that survive review through automation bias. Once approved, they become trusted and are used at scale. This falls under OP.C0101.04, OP.C0304.03 and OP.C0502. (5) Legacy-data quality: the LLM sits over databases of uneven provenance, with calibration offsets, sensor substitutions and gaps, and will present them without caveats (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0204). (6) Cloud/off-premises LLM dependency, if used, creates availability and data-governance exposure (OP.C0601, OP.C0505.01).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Prompt injection, direct or indirect: free-text fields in the databases (work-order notes, operator logs, comments) that are returned to the LLM and re-ingested can steer subsequent function calls or summaries (AML.T0051.000, AML.T0051.001, AML.T0093).
