The closed function set limits the impact to over-broad retrieval or misleading answers, but parameters can still be pushed toward bulk or sensitive data. (b) Excessive agency and access scope: the LLM service account often has broader database read rights than the individual user. Natural-language requests become a path around row/role-level access control, enabling aggregation of sensitive operational data (AML.T0036, AML.T0053, AML.T0057, OP.C0505). (c) Supply-chain and tampering: the function library, routing prompt, function-schema descriptions and embedding index are high-leverage artifacts. A modified function description or poisoned function body redirects routing silently (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018, AML.T0081, AML.T0110, AML.T0099). The NL-to-SQL drafting tool is a further upstream dependency (AML.T0010.005). (d) Evasion and integrity attack: crafted phrasing that makes the router select a benign-looking but incorrect function, or timed to hide anomalous data (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003). (e) Recon and denial: the exposed function catalogue and system prompt reveal data structures (AML.T0056, AML.T0084.001), and resource-intensive queries can degrade legacy databases or the service (AML.T0029, AML.T0034.001). Overall, the architecture is genuinely safer than free-form SQL, but its security claim depends on the integrity and governance of the function library and on routing behaviour that is not itself qualified.

security_specialist.argument: The design is deliberately conservative: a closed library of expert-validated query functions removes the free-form SQL injection and hallucinated-query surface, so a sophisticated adversary would see little value in attacking the LLM directly. My concern is that the interface changes the threat surface in other ways. It becomes a natural-language front door to legacy operational databases that were previously reachable only by trained users, and it concentrates trust in two places: the function library and the router that selects among its functions. It also lets staff stop looking at the underlying data. For a nation-state or insider, the realistic targets are the function library's change-control path, the NL-to-SQL drafting step, the router's selection behavior, and the retrieval of aggregated operational data for reconnaissance. A quiet, subtly wrong answer to a routine query is more valuable to them than any dramatic exploit.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Function-library and drafting-pipeline compromise. The paper uses NL-to-SQL tools to draft function code that experts then validate. A poisoned or compromised drafting tool, or an insider with commit rights, could introduce a function with a subtle logic flaw (wrong time window, wrong unit or tag mapping, dropped rows, excess scope) that passes review because the reviewer is checking plausibility rather than adversarially auditing. The facility depends on 'pre-approved' meaning trustworthy, so the approval step becomes a high-value trust anchor. The consequence is systematically misleading operational data feeding maintenance, trending or surveillance decisions, or a function that over-retrieves. Relevant techniques: AML.T0010 supply chain, AML.T0010.005 agent tool, AML.T0110 and AML.T0099 tool poisoning, AML.T0109 rug pull. (2) Prompt manipulation of routing. Function-calling does not eliminate prompt injection. Crafted requests, or injected content in any text the LLM ingests, could steer function selection or argument values (plant, unit, date range, parameter), which would still pull data the requester should not see or return a wrong but valid result. The consequence is a confidentiality or integrity breach inside the 'approved' envelope, and an authorization model enforced only by the LLM's choices is weak. Relevant techniques: AML.T0051, AML.T0053, AML.T0054, AML.T0068. (3) Reconnaissance and data aggregation. Natural-language access lowers the skill barrier for an insider or a compromised account to enumerate and aggregate sensitive operating data (configurations, outage history, equipment health, vulnerabilities), and it may leave weaker audit trails than direct DB access. The consequence is insider-enabled target development for sabotage planning. Relevant techniques: AML.T0012, AML.T0036, AML.T0057, AML.T0085, AML.T0084.001, which also covers discovery of tool definitions. (4) Availability and degradation. Denial of the interface, or biasing it to fail, pushes staff back onto manual retrieval at a time an adversary could choose, such as during an outage or a coincident cyber event. Relevant techniques: AML.T0029, AML.T0031.

IMPLICIT, exploitable by an adversary. (5) Automation trust and skill fade. Staff who no longer write or inspect queries lose familiarity with the schema and the data's quirks, so wrong-but-plausible outputs go unchallenged (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). An adversary can time subtle data manipulation around this reduced vigilance. (6) Router errors. Ambiguous natural-language requests can map to the wrong function or parameters, such as the wrong unit or unit-of-measure. The result is an answer that looks authoritative and has no visible failure signal (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0402.02, OP.C0401). (7) Library drift and coverage limits. When the legacy schema, tag naming or plant configuration changes, functions go stale silently, and users may fall back to ungoverned NL-to-SQL or ad hoc routes (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0501, OP.C0502). (8) Governance gaps. A data-security model designed for DB users may not fit an LLM intermediary, and if the LLM is cloud-hosted, operational data leaves the boundary (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0601, OP.C0503). The safety impact is bounded because the use is read-only and administrative. The greater risk is to the integrity of the information that human decisions rest on, and to confidentiality.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on silent router/parameter errors, library drift and governance, trust erosion, supply-chain compromise of the function library, prompt injection, and data aggregation. I dropped weakly supported ATLAS candidates (jailbreak, obfuscation, evasion, rug pull, system-prompt extraction) and kept the closely related OP.C0302.01/OP.C0302.03 plus the data-provenance codes only where traceable to the text.

evidence.citation: "Enhancing Accuracy and Maintainability in Nuclear Plant Data Retrieval: A Function-Calling LLM Approach Over NL-to-SQL," Canadian Nuclear Society, 44th Annual CNS Conference (Toronto, June 2025); also posted on arXiv
evidence.note: This conference paper, written by OPG and Dalhousie authors, argues that having an LLM generate SQL directly is risky for legacy nuclear plant databases. It proposes calling pre-approved functions that wrap validated SQL, and it compares this against direct NL-to-SQL generation, reporting better accuracy and maintainability. I only retrieved the abstract and the arXiv listing. The arXiv copy is a preprint posting, and I could not confirm the conference's review process from the search results.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is silently wrong-but-valid data, or compromised function and routing artifacts, corrupting the information behind maintenance, surveillance and investigation decisions. The interface is read-only and outside protection and control systems, so the harm is operational disruption and erosion of safety margin, not a direct radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Routing mis-binding on ambiguous requests, library drift after schema changes, and reviewer fatigue are recurring properties of LLM routing over legacy databases that appear reliably once the conditions exist. Deliberate compromise of artifacts or prompt steering needs further preconditions, such as write access or injectable free text.

exploitability.why: Prompt manipulation, including indirect injection through free-text fields, and over-broad service-account access can be reached by an insider or a user of the interface. Tampering with the function library, routing artifacts or the drafting-tool supply chain needs privileged or supply-chain access, so the overall requirement is moderate.

affected_users.why: A shared interface and function library serve many plant staff and feed maintenance, trending and surveillance decisions across systems. It stays a read-only information aid and does not couple to control systems, so impact is broad within the information layer but not facility-wide in a physical sense.

discoverability.why: Prompt injection, tool poisoning, LLM routing errors and over-privileged service accounts are well documented in the open literature for function-calling agents. The approach itself is described in a public paper, so an outsider can infer the weakness class. Details of a specific deployment's library and data stay internal.

use_case: Ultrasonic acoustic sensing combined with probabilistic CNN models (an ensemble of 1-D and 2-D CNNs, plus MLP, decision-tree and logistic-regression classifiers) to detect and quantify low-level impurity gases (argon, air) in the helium backfill of sealed spent nuclear fuel dry-storage canisters. The goal is non-invasive monitoring of the canister's internal condition.
incurred_insecurity:
Using an ultrasonic-plus-CNN ensemble as a non-invasive indicator of helium backfill purity in sealed dry-storage canisters concentrates trust in one channel that was validated only on a bench simulator at 0-1.2% argon/air. The main insecurities are silent sim-to-field failure, narrow-ontology and drift blindness, misplaced trust in uncertainty outputs, a missing qualification basis, and adversarial manipulation of the sensing chain, the model supply chain and the monitoring records. In a passive, rarely inspected storage setting, a failure or manipulation is hard to discover and recovery means inspecting a loaded canister.

Sim-to-field generalisation failure -- implicit, exploitable
The CNNs were trained on a bench rig and can learn rig-specific features, so decay-heat gradients, wall and basket geometry, pressure and coupling on a real canister fall out of distribution and yield confident wrong concentration estimates or a false 'pure helium' call. An adversary could time or shape a concealment or leak around this blind spot, since a shift in temperature or coupling would be indistinguishable from the model's ordinary field error.

Narrow contaminant ontology and label scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Only argon and air at 0-1.2% were modelled, with no field ground truth for rare events, so moisture, hydrogen, krypton/xenon fission gas from cladding breach or helium loss may be mapped onto the nearest known class and cannot be validated or recalibrated. An adversary could introduce or exploit an unmodelled gas or degradation signature that the model is structurally unable to flag.

Long-term sensor and environmental drift -- implicit, exploitable
Transducer ageing, coupling degradation, radiation effects and falling decay heat shift the signal over decades, and the model can confuse sensor drift with gas change or the reverse. An adversary could hide a slow manipulation of the signal or the gas inside this expected drift band.

Miscalibrated uncertainty and automation trust -- implicit, exploitable
Dropout and ensemble uncertainty are not reliable off-distribution, yet they lend rigour to a 'nominal' reading that operators on a sparse surveillance schedule may accept, deferring independent inspection and letting verification skills fade. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, tuning inputs to stay within confident 'clean' outputs, while false alarms could be used to desensitise operators or provoke unnecessary handling and dose.

Qualification, repeatability and governance gaps -- implicit, exploitable
The prototype has non-deterministic training, a heterogeneous ensemble of model families, opaque decisions and no established QA or regulatory path for ML-based canister condition monitoring, so degradation or tampering of the model is hard to prove or defend. Any retraining, update or remote analytics path also risks adding connectivity into otherwise isolated storage-site monitoring, which an adversary could use as an entry route.

Sensing-channel evasion -- adversarial
Someone with physical or signal-chain access can alter acoustic coupling or temperature, or inject ultrasonic or electrical interference or spoofed waveforms, so the classifier reads clean helium during real degradation or floods operators with spurious alarms. Small waveform perturbations can flip the output, concealing a leak or air ingress or masking activity at the canister.

Model and training-data poisoning or backdoor -- adversarial
Tampered pretrained weights, calibration datasets, vendor pipelines or scarce field retraining data can bias quantification or implant a trigger signature that always reports nominal. The consequence is undetected backfill degradation and false assurance that lowers inspection frequency.

Monitoring record and baseline integrity -- adversarial
Altered, deleted or falsified stored baselines, trends and results can hide a developing leak or deliberate degradation from regulators and safeguards inspectors, or erode confidence in monitoring so that it is withdrawn. Condition data on canister contents are also sensitive, and their exfiltration would reveal inventory or condition.

Reconnaissance and proxy-model crafting -- adversarial
The published architecture, concentration range and sensing method let an adversary build a proxy model and craft inputs that stay inside confident 'clean' outputs. This lowers the cost of the evasion attack above.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a dry-storage operations view, helium backfill purity matters because it governs convective heat transfer, cladding temperature, corrosion and stress-corrosion cracking, and leak-tightness inference. A non-invasive acoustic monitor would feed a long-lived, low-frequency surveillance and aging-management decision: whether a canister is healthy, needs inspection, or needs remediation. The model is trained on a bench simulator at 0-1.2% argon/air, not on loaded canisters with real decay heat, thermal gradients, wall geometry, shielding and field noise. So the main risk is a confident but wrong output, either a false 'pure helium' or a false 'contaminated' call, that is trusted because it comes with uncertainty estimates. Existing practice limits the consequence: canisters are welded, backfill is verified at loading, and temperature and dose surveillance, inspections and thermal analyses provide margin. Harm therefore needs a coincident real degradation mechanism that the monitoring misses, or an unnecessary intervention that carries its own dose and handling risk.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Sim-to-field generalization failure: the ultrasonic signature depends on temperature, pressure, canister geometry, wall coupling, fuel-basket structure and ambient noise, and the lab platform does not reproduce these. A model that is accurate on the bench can be biased or badly miscalibrated on a hot, loaded canister (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (2) Narrow training envelope and limited data: only argon and air at 0-1.2% were tested, so other degradation products (water vapor, fission gas such as krypton/xenon from a cladding breach, hydrogen, helium leakage with pressure loss) are out of distribution and may be silently mapped onto the nearest known class. Fission gas from failed fuel is a safety-relevant case the model was never trained on (OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0403). (3) Drift over decades: sensor coupling, transducer aging, and changing temperature as decay heat falls shift the input distribution, while there are essentially no long-term field labels to detect the drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0204). (4) Automation trust failure: probabilistic uncertainty outputs from an ensemble can look rigorous, but dropout and ensemble uncertainty are not guaranteed to be calibrated off-distribution. Operators on a sparse surveillance schedule may over-trust a 'nominal' reading and defer inspection, or over-react to a false alarm, which means unnecessary dose and handling (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02). (5) Qualification gap: no established QA or regulatory path exists for ML-based canister condition monitoring, and many classifiers with different failure behaviours complicate validation and change control (OP.C0501, OP.C0504).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Manipulating the sensing channel (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0041): physical access to the canister exterior or the sensor mount, or injected acoustic or electrical noise, could suppress or fake the signature. This could hide a real change in the gas or cause nuisance alarms. The attacker needs site access, and access to dry-storage pads is controlled, but remote or lightly staffed ISFSI sites make tampering plausible. (b) Poisoned or tampered training data or model artifacts in the vendor, lab or supply chain (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020), for example a backdoor that reports nominal for a particular signature. (c) Data and model integrity in the monitoring pipeline, including stored baselines and results (AML.T0031, AML.T0059). Falsified trending could cover up deliberate degradation of the backfill or a leak, or erode confidence in monitoring (denial of service, AML.T0029). (d) Safeguards and security angle: acoustic data on canister contents and condition is sensitive, and exfiltration could reveal inventory or condition (AML.T0025). The more important consequence is a monitoring blind spot being used to time a physical attack or concealment. Overall consequence severity is moderate because passive safety margins and independent surveillance exist, but the failure is silent and hard to discover, and recovery means opening or inspecting a loaded canister.

ai_engineer.argument: The model is trained entirely on bench data from a simulated canister platform covering argon and air in helium at 0-1.2%. A real loaded dry-storage canister differs from that bench in decay heat gradients, wall and basket geometry, pressure, temperature, radiation-induced sensor effects, and acoustic coupling to a thick steel shell. Ultrasonic velocity and attenuation in a binary gas mix depend heavily on temperature, pressure, and path geometry, so the CNN can easily learn rig-specific features, and the 0-1.2% range plus the two impurity species are narrow assumptions. The ensemble and probabilistic outputs (dropout, max-likelihood) give uncertainty estimates, but those are calibrated in-distribution and are least reliable exactly when the input is out-of-distribution. There is also essentially no field ground truth: leaks and degradation events are rare, and the true internal gas composition of a sealed canister cannot be verified, so label scarcity, validation, and retraining are structurally hard. The architecture is a small-data, tabular and waveform ensemble, so the exposure lies in provenance, domain transfer, and how the output is trusted, not in model scale.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real transfer failure (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03): the model was trained on a bench-simulated canister, so a real canister's thermal state, geometry, wall coupling, and sensor mounting fall outside the training distribution. The AI failure is a confident but wrong concentration estimate, or a false 'pure helium' classification. The facility depends on this to assess backfill integrity, and the consequence is that a real leak or air ingress goes undetected, with degraded heat removal, cladding oxidation and corrosion risk, and an inaccurate safety-case record. A false alarm is also costly, since it could trigger unnecessary canister handling and dose. (2) Low base-rate and no field labels (OP.C0202, OP.C0204, OP.C0701): real impurity events are rare and not independently verifiable, so the model cannot be validated, recalibrated, or detected as drifting against ground truth. (3) Slow environmental and sensor drift (OP.C0302.01/.02): transducer aging, coupling-agent degradation, radiation damage and temperature decay over decades of storage shift the signal distribution. This is slow and monotonic, so it looks like a gradual change in impurity level, and the model can mistake sensor drift for gas change or vice versa. (4) Miscalibrated uncertainty and opacity (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0101.04): operators may treat the probabilistic output as validated confidence, even though it is unreliable under distribution shift. Automation bias then shifts inspection effort away from a canister the model labels clean, and inspection skills decay (OP.C0101.06). (5) Qualification and software-hygiene gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0402, OP.C0303): a research prototype with non-deterministic training, an ensemble of heterogeneous model families, and no AI-specific QA basis for a safety-relevant monitoring claim. (6) Narrow ontology: any unmodeled contaminant, such as moisture, hydrogen, fission gas from cladding failure, or different gas ratios, may be forced onto the argon/air axes.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Evasion by physical or signal manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043.003, T0041): an adversary with proximity to the sensor or its signal chain could alter the acoustic coupling, temperature, or injected ultrasonic noise so the CNN reads 'clean helium' during real degradation, or generate spurious detections to cause alarm fatigue. Because the model is sensitive to subtle waveform features, small perturbations may flip the output. (b) Training-data and model-lifecycle poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0031): during any retraining or recalibration on scarce field data, a few poisoned or mislabeled waveforms, or a tampered pretrained or ensemble artifact, can bias the quantification systematically, or insert a backdoor trigger on a specific signal pattern (T0043.004). (c) Integrity of the data path (AML.T0010.000, T0112): the sensor, digitizer, and analysis software are a new IT/OT attack surface on the waste-storage safety monitoring chain. Spoofed or replayed waveforms can hide real conditions, and the model's output may feed records used for regulatory assurance and safeguards. (d) Reconnaissance and proxy models (AML.T0000, T0005, T0013): published architecture, concentration range, and sensing method allow an adversary to build a proxy and craft inputs that defeat the detector. The compounding vulnerability is that the implicit weaknesses (no field validation, drift confused with signal, trust in uncertainty estimates) mean a successful manipulation would be hard to distinguish from normal variation.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, the main issue is that this system would become a trusted, non-invasive indicator of canister integrity: a 'helium pure, no ingress' reading could replace or reduce intrusive inspection, so it concentrates trust in a single acoustic-plus-ML channel. Dry-cask storage is a passive, low-staffing environment where inspection is infrequent and long-lived. That makes any quiet degradation of the sensing chain (a tampered sensor, a poisoned or swapped model, a falsified reading) valuable to an adversary because nobody is watching continuously. A nation-state would probably find it easier to attack physical access or the records than to subvert this AI, but the AI could serve as a stepping stone or as cover. It could mask real in-leakage or help conceal activities around a canister, with safeguards and containment-verification consequences. The documented work is lab-only, on a simulated platform with 0-1.2% argon/air, so many weaknesses come from the gap between that and real casks, and an adversary could time an action around those gaps.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or data integrity compromise: the model sits in a supply chain of third-party training code and weights, calibration datasets, and a vendor-run inference pipeline. Poisoning or backdoor-triggering (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004) could make specific acoustic signatures, such as a particular gas mixture or a crafted signal, read as 'pure helium'. The facility depends on this to judge canister confinement, so the consequence is undetected backfill degradation or leakage, or a false assurance that lowers inspection frequency. (2) Sensor-level evasion: an insider with physical access, or someone who modifies the transducer coupling or injects ultrasonic interference, could craft inputs that push the classifier toward 'clean' or flood it with false alarms (AML.T0015, T0043, T0041, T0046). The ML response is that acoustic velocity or attenuation shifts caused by temperature, pressure or coupling changes can be confused with, or deliberately used to hide, impurity signatures. False alarms could also be used to desensitise operators or create diversion. (3) Records and trending integrity: monitoring results feed the long-term canister condition record, and altered or deleted data (AML.T0059, T0031) could hide trends from regulators or safeguards inspectors. (4) Uncertainty outputs can be manipulated or misread: the probabilistic confidence values give an air of rigour, and an adversary who knows how the model reports uncertainty could tune an attack to stay inside 'confident' ranges (AML.T0063, T0013, T0005 for proxy models built from the open paper). Public publication of the architecture and ranges makes reconnaissance and proxy-model construction easy (AML.T0000, T0001). IMPLICIT. (5) Lab-to-field generalisation: training data come from a simulated platform with narrow concentration ranges and few canister geometries, wall thicknesses, temperatures, or decay-heat conditions, and thermal gradients and radiation differ in the field (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). The model can silently fail out of distribution or drift as sensors age, and an adversary only has to wait for those conditions or encourage them. (6) Automation trust and skill fade: a non-invasive 'green' indicator on a passive system produces complacency and reduces independent verification (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06), so ensemble disagreement or a wide uncertainty band may be ignored. (7) Opacity and qualification gaps: an ensemble of CNNs, MLP and tree models is hard to explain, and there is no established qualification path for AI in spent-fuel monitoring (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Tampering or degradation is therefore hard to prove, and its output could be hard to defend to regulators or inspectors. (8) Maintenance and cloud dependencies: retraining, updates or remote analytics could add network connectivity into otherwise air-gapped storage-site monitoring (OP.C0601, OP.C0502, OP.C0505), which opens a new route into site networks and safeguards-relevant data.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sim-to-field failure, drift, narrow training envelope, uncertainty over-trust and the qualification gap, plus sensor evasion, poisoning and record integrity as adversarial threats. I dropped weakly argued or speculative codes (T0029, T0112, T0010.000, T0063, T0001, OP.C0701 which concerns safeguards imagery/NDA scarcity) and kept the cloud and connectivity concern only as part of the governance threat.

evidence.citation: "Impurity gas detection for SNF canisters using probabilistic deep learning and acoustic sensing," Measurement Science and Technology (IOP Publishing), vol. 35, no. 12, article 126005, 2024
evidence.note: The authors built an experimental platform that simulates canister conditions and collected ultrasonic data on argon and air in helium at 0–1.2% concentrations. They trained classifiers to tell pure helium from contaminated helium. They also trained CNN models, including dropout and maximum-likelihood variants and an ensemble of 1-D and 2-D CNNs, to quantify impurity concentrations with uncertainty. This is a laboratory-tested model, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is concealment of backfill degradation or leak (false 'pure helium' call, poisoned model, or falsified monitoring records), which erodes safeguards and condition assurance for spent fuel and could delay response to cladding breach or air ingress. This falls just short of direct release, because the canister confinement boundary and other controls remain.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution failure on a real canister and drift-masking are fairly reliable once field conditions differ from the bench rig, but deliberate evasion, poisoning, or record falsification each depend on specific preconditions and on real degradation being present.

exploitability.why: Exploiting the sensing chain, model supply chain, or stored records generally requires physical or signal-chain access at a controlled storage site or a position in the vendor pipeline, and a meaningful concealment needs a capable, well-resourced adversary; the implicit sim-to-field failures need no attacker action.

affected_users.why: The impact is limited to canisters using this monitoring channel, but a systematic model flaw or poisoned weights would apply across all monitored canisters at a site or fleet, and false assurance lowers inspection frequency widely, though it does not propagate to coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, concentration range, and sensing method are published in the open literature, and the general weaknesses (bench-only validation, narrow ontology, drift, adversarial fragility of CNNs) are well-known for this class of AI system, so a capable outsider can readily infer the blind spots.

use_case: Residual neural network (ResNet) detection of corrosion (iron-oxide discoloration, pitting, stress corrosion cracking) in camera images of stainless-steel dry storage canisters holding used nuclear fuel. Canister images are cropped into small tiles, and a ResNet classifies each tile. An image is labelled corroded or intact from the count of corroded tiles. The aim is to automate and speed up remote canister inspection and reduce radiation dose to personnel.
incurred_insecurity:
A ResNet tile classifier that screens dry storage canister images for corrosion becomes the de facto gate on whether a canister receives human attention, so its failures erode the aging-management inspection basis for a spent-fuel confinement boundary. The main threats are a silent false 'intact' verdict from unrepresentative data and a fragile tile-count rule, loss of human vigilance, an unqualified AI inspection method, and adversarial manipulation of images, training data, model weights or inspection records, with a single model reused across sites spreading any compromise.

Training-data scarcity and surrogate imagery -- implicit, exploitable
Real in-service chloride-induced SCC imagery is rare, so training relies on small lab, coupon or surrogate sets, and headline accuracy (inflated further by possible tile leakage across splits) overstates field recall on early SCC. An adversary can hide real degradation or tampering in the resulting blind spots, which no one knows to look for because the tool appears validated.

Field distribution shift and heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Variation in canister vendor, weld seams, salt and dust deposits, heat tint, lighting, camera and crawler geometry, plus slow morphological change in corrosion, pushes inputs out of distribution. A plain ResNet gives no reliable uncertainty signal, so degraded images produce false 'intact' verdicts or nuisance alarms without warning. An attacker can pick coatings, lighting or surface conditions that fall in this unflagged band to make corrosion read as intact.

Tile-count aggregation and objective misalignment -- implicit, exploitable
Labelling an image from a count of corroded tiles means a single crack or small pitting cluster can fall below the threshold, and tiling discards crack continuity. The threshold is tuned for accuracy rather than rare-event recall and can be changed silently. An adversary who learns the rule needs to keep only enough tiles below the count, and the opacity of tile-level decisions makes the result hard to challenge.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
If inspectors are cut to realise the dose and cost savings, reviewers lose practice and defer to 'intact' labels, and false positives can instead cause alarm fatigue and disuse. An adversary can time tampering or exploit real degradation for when human review has become cursory.

AI qualification and change-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
There is no accepted way to qualify a CNN as equivalent to NDE, no probability-of-detection curve, and no procedure for retraining, version or threshold control, or revalidation after a camera change. Retraining is non-deterministic, and research-grade code adds dependency exposure. A quiet retrain or model swap leaves no trace, so an adversary can introduce a blind spot without detection.

Input image manipulation and tampering -- adversarial
Physical changes at the canister (cleaning, coatings, surface marks, lighting) or tampering with images between camera, archive and classifier can keep corroded tiles under the count threshold, or generate false positives that waste dose and disrupt operations. The result is deferred repair or relocation of a canister with developing SCC.

Training-data, model and supply-chain compromise -- adversarial
Poisoning the small curated tile set, backdooring a pretrained ImageNet ResNet or retrained checkpoint, or training from an edited image archive can implant a trigger or blind spot that reads specific corrosion types or canisters as intact. Open architecture and weights also let an attacker build a proxy model to craft evasions offline and transfer them to the deployed model.

Fleet-wide propagation of a single model -- implicit, exploitable
Reusing one model, or any cloud inference service, across sites replicates any bias, drift or compromise into every site's inspection record. An adversary needs to compromise only one shared model or update channel to get the same blind spot everywhere.

Inspection record integrity and pipeline abuse -- adversarial
Image sets and classifier outputs form the evidentiary record for regulators, so altering, deleting or inserting synthetic images conceals degradation history. The camera, archive and workstation chain is also a lateral-movement path into the wider waste-storage network, and its archives reveal canister condition and inspection coverage.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Seen from the ISFSI/dry cask storage pad, this tool screens camera images of stainless-steel canisters for chloride-induced SCC, pitting and discoloration. It is an aging-management aid, and its main downstream actors are the inspection engineer and the aging-management program owner. A missed detection is not a quick physical hazard, because SCC through-wall penetration develops over years and is bounded by defense in depth: the overpack, monitoring of helium or temperature or radiation, and periodic inspection. The real consequence is erosion of the inspection basis. A false 'intact' result could defer a repair, a canister relocation or a regulator-notifiable finding. It could also let a developing through-wall crack reach a point where fuel can no longer be transferred or retrieved under the licensing basis. A false 'corroded' result adds dose and cost from unnecessary follow-up, which defeats the tool's stated purpose of dose reduction. A tile-count image label also adds distinctive weaknesses: the model never sees fine cracks in context, and the threshold is a policy choice that is easy to set wrongly or change silently.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data scarcity and provenance. Real SCC on in-service canisters is extremely rare and mostly seen in lab specimens or a few field examples. Training sets are therefore small, often mock-up, lab or surrogate imagery (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01-.04). A tool that scores well on this data can fail on field images and still look validated. (2) Distribution shift and heterogeneity. Canister surfaces vary with weld seams, dust and salt deposits, lighting, camera and robot differences, vent-screen shadows, paint and markings, and different vendor designs and sites. These can be mistaken for rust (false positives) or can mask a real indication (false negatives) (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). A crack-like tile classifier is especially prone to missing hairline SCC against textured steel. (3) Aggregation and objective misalignment. Labelling an image 'corroded' from a tile count creates a fragile decision rule. A threshold tuned for accuracy on a balanced dataset is wrong for a rare-event safety screen, where recall on the worst cases matters most, and a single critical crack may occupy fewer tiles than the threshold requires (OP.C0301, OP.C0403). (4) Automation trust. If inspectors are reassigned to reduce dose, reviewers get less practice and become unfamiliar with how corrosion looks, and they come to trust 'intact' labels, especially if the tool is marketed on cost and dose savings (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06). Opacity and lack of per-tile explanation make it harder to challenge a result (OP.C0401). (5) Qualification gap. Software used in aging-management and inspection records is not qualified for AI. This leaves retraining, version and threshold control, and revalidation after a camera or lighting change without a procedure (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0402.01).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Manipulation of image inputs. An adversary or insider with access to the acquisition chain, or to physical conditions at the canister such as lighting, coatings or surface marks, could craft inputs that make real corrosion read as intact. The same access could instead trigger false alarms that waste dose, disrupt operations and damage public confidence (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0041, AML.T0031). Because the scene is physically controlled, pixel-level attacks matter less than tampering with images in storage or transit (AML.T0010.002). (b) Training-data or model poisoning and supply-chain compromise. Poisoning the small curated training set, or substituting a pretrained ResNet or a retrained checkpoint, could implant a blind spot for particular corrosion types or canister designs (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003). Compromised results would then be propagated across a fleet if one model serves many sites (OP.C0602). (c) Integrity of the inspection record. Image sets and classification outputs become the evidentiary record for regulators. Altering or deleting them hides degradation history, and AI-generated or synthetic images could be inserted into the record (OP.C0703, AML.T0059). (d) Denial of service or delay of the inspection pipeline would push back inspections but is low safety consequence given the inspection intervals.

Compensating engineering practice. Human review of flagged and sampled images, independent visual and eddy-current or ultrasonic follow-up, canister and overpack monitoring, and regulator-approved aging-management intervals all limit harm. Their effectiveness is lost if the AI output becomes the sole basis for deferral, or if sampling by humans is stopped as the tool proves 'accurate'. The tool should therefore be positioned as a screening aid with conservative thresholds, recall-focused acceptance testing on field data, controlled model and threshold versions, and signed image provenance.

ai_engineer.argument: From a pipeline perspective this is a small, tile-level image classifier whose headline accuracy rests on data that probably does not represent the deployment distribution. Real corroded dry-storage canisters are rare and heterogeneous, so training imagery is likely lab-made or surrogate: coupons, accelerated-corrosion specimens, or stainless-steel photos from other settings. That is OP.C0201.02/.04 and OP.C0202, and it makes the reported accuracy a poor guide to field performance. Tile-wise labelling and a count-threshold image decision add further fragility: tile-level labels are noisy, tiles from one image or canister leak across train/test splits and inflate metrics, and the image-level threshold is a tuned hyperparameter with no calibrated link to inspection-relevant severity. In deployment the camera, lighting, surface finish, weld geometry, deposits (salt, dust, rust-colored non-corrosion stains) and vent-path or crevice access conditions will differ from training, so the model faces OOD inputs it cannot flag, because a plain ResNet softmax gives no reliable uncertainty. Because the system is meant to replace dose-incurring human inspection, the main exposure is a silent false negative that people trust, not a loud failure.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data provenance and scarcity (OP.C0201.02, .04, OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0204): there are few labelled images of real chloride-induced stress corrosion cracking on in-service canisters, so SCC, the most safety-relevant mode, is likely under-represented or represented only by lab surrogates. The class imbalance and the small, hard-to-see crack signatures mean tile-level recall for SCC can be far lower than the aggregate accuracy suggests. A missed early-stage SCC finding would delay corrective action on a confinement boundary. (2) Distribution shift (OP.C0302, .01, .03): each site, canister vendor, camera and robot crawler, illumination, and the narrow-annulus or overhead-vent access geometry produces a different image distribution. Surface contamination, discoloration from heat tint, welds and dust produce false positives (alarm fatigue, disuse, OP.C0101.05) or, worse, mask real corrosion. Concept drift occurs as corrosion progresses morphologically over decades while the model stays frozen. (3) Aggregation logic: the image-level label comes from counting corroded tiles against a threshold, so small localized pitting or a single crack may not reach the count, creating a structural blind spot that is independent of tile accuracy (OP.C0301, OP.C0403). Tile cropping also discards spatial context such as crack continuity. (4) Qualification and assurance gaps (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402): there is no established way to qualify a CNN as an inspection method equivalent to NDE procedures, there is no probability-of-detection curve, retraining is non-deterministic, and saliency explanations are weak, so the model is hard to audit. Automation bias (OP.C0101.04) and skill fade (OP.C0101.06) follow if human reviewers are removed to realize the dose and cost savings. A 'corroded' flag on fuel storage could also drive unnecessary and dose-intensive interventions. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043): physical or digital perturbations, such as surface coatings, patterned stains, lighting changes, or tampering with images in transit, could push tiles below the threshold. Any access to the imaging pipeline could also alter or replace images to hide degradation. Because the tile-count rule is simple, an adversary who learned it (AML.T0013, AML.T0063) could shape just enough tiles. (6) Supply-chain and data integrity (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059): pretrained ImageNet ResNet weights, public repositories such as the arXiv-linked code, and shared inspection image sets can be backdoored or poisoned (AML.T0043.004, a trigger pattern yielding 'intact'). Retraining on field data from an edited archive could erode model integrity (AML.T0031). Because the architecture and weights are open (AML.T0002.001, AML.T0000), a proxy model (AML.T0005) allows offline white-box attack crafting, with transfer to deployed variants. (7) Fleet propagation (OP.C0602, OP.C0603): one model reused across sites means a single poisoned or biased model replicates the same blind spot everywhere. The consequence in each case is undetected degradation of a confinement barrier, with possible effects on safety and on the integrity of inspection records used for regulators and safeguards.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, the direct target value is modest but real. A ResNet tile classifier on canister camera images is an advisory screening tool whose main purpose is to lower inspection effort and dose, and that is exactly what makes it a useful tool for an adversary. The risk is that it becomes the de facto gate on whether a canister gets human attention. An insider or supply-chain attacker who suppresses or shifts the corrosion verdict could hide chloride-induced SCC progression on a canister, or flood the system with false positives to cause unnecessary retrievals or operational disruption. The more insidious path is slow erosion of human vigilance: once the tool produces clean results for a long time, inspectors review fewer images, which gives an adversary a window to time physical tampering or to exploit genuine degradation. A nation-state would probably pick easier targets, but a patient insider, or a vendor-side model or data compromise, is a plausible route because this process is low-visibility and its outputs are rarely re-audited.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Model or data integrity attack. Poisoning or backdooring the training tiles or weights (AML.T0020, AML.T0018, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0043.004) could make specific visual patterns, or specific canisters, read as intact. The facility depends on this verdict for the inspection and aging-management record, and the consequence is undetected SCC on spent-fuel confinement barriers, which is a safety, security and regulatory-compliance problem. (2) Input-side evasion and tampering. Physical or digital manipulation of images (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041), such as cleaning, coating or lighting changes, or tampering in the camera-to-classifier chain, can defeat tile-level detection. The count-threshold aggregation also gives an attacker a clear target: keep corroded tiles below the threshold. (3) Verdict denial or flooding. Chaff or adversarial images (AML.T0046, AML.T0029, AML.T0031) could generate false alarms or break trust in the tool, leading operators to disable it or revert to manual inspection at higher dose. (4) Concentrated-trust and stepping-stone risk. An inspection pipeline linking cameras, image archives and analysis workstations is a lateral-movement path into the wider waste-storage network (AML.T0012, AML.T0052). Image archives also reveal canister condition, location and inspection coverage, which is useful for reconnaissance (AML.T0036, AML.T0037).

IMPLICIT (adversary can time or exploit): (a) Automation complacency and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Over time, inspectors defer to the classifier, and an adversary can time an attack or tampering for when review has become cursory. (b) Data scarcity and domain shift (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.03). Real corrosion, especially early SCC, is rare, so training relies on limited, lab-generated or surrogate imagery. Variation in canister surface, lighting, dust, weld features or camera hardware can degrade performance in ways no one notices, and an adversary can exploit those blind spots. (c) Tile-count aggregation (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0401). A few small cracks can be lost in the count threshold, and tile-level opacity makes the verdict hard to audit. (d) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0502). There is no AI-specific V&V or change control for model updates, so a quiet retrain or swap leaves no trace. Research-grade code and dependencies add supply-chain exposure. (e) Cross-site model reuse (OP.C0602) and any cloud inference (OP.C0601) would spread a single compromise or drift across multiple sites' inspection records. Consequence: a false sense of confidence in canister integrity, plus potential safeguards and security records that cannot be trusted.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on data scarcity, distribution shift, tile-count aggregation blind spots, automation complacency, the qualification gap, input evasion, poisoning/supply chain and fleet propagation; I merged them and dropped weakly argued items (denial of service, phishing-based lateral movement, chaff, and AML.T0013/T0063 discovery steps). I kept the record-integrity and archive-access threat from the nuclear engineer and security specialist, and the proxy-model path from the AI engineer, as distinct.}

evidence.citation: "Automated detection of corrosion in used nuclear fuel dry storage canisters using residual neural networks," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Korean Nuclear Society / Elsevier); Oak Ridge National Laboratory-led authors
evidence.note: This peer-reviewed ORNL-led paper trains ResNets on tiles cropped from canister images and flags whole images as corroded or intact from the per-image count of corroded tiles. It reports high accuracy and presents the method as a way to automate canister inspections, cut costs and reduce personnel dose. A preprint version is on arXiv (2003.03241), but the journal version is the one cited.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a silent false 'intact' verdict or concealed inspection records that defer detection of stress corrosion cracking on a spent-fuel confinement boundary, eroding aging-management safety margins; a release is possible only over a long chain of further failures, so this falls just short of the maximum.

reproducibility.why: Distribution shift, thresholded tile-count blind spots, skill fade and fleet-wide model reuse recur reliably once the conditions exist, while poisoning and backdoor threats are more conditional.

exploitability.why: Physical surface or lighting changes and exploiting an unflagged blind spot need modest access, but tampering with data, weights or archives requires insider or supply-chain access, so the overall requirement is moderate.

affected_users.why: A single shared model or update channel replicates the blind spot into every site's inspection record, and the archive/workstation chain is a lateral path into the wider waste-storage network, though the effect stays within the inspection function rather than coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The method is published in an open peer-reviewed paper with a public preprint, and ResNet evasion, poisoning and proxy-model transfer are well documented in the open literature, so a capable outsider can readily infer the weaknesses even without facility specifics.

use_case: Two-stage text-mining pipeline that screens US nuclear power plant operating-experience event reports, such as licensee event reports. A knowledge-informed binary classifier, built on 44 shutdown-initiating-event keyword/phrase patterns, first screens out non-shutdown events. A fine-tuned BERT language model then sorts the remaining events into four shutdown initiating event types. The output supports building shutdown probabilistic risk assessment (PRA), replacing manual analyst review of event reports.
incurred_insecurity:
This text-mining pipeline sits upstream of shutdown PRA and has no actuation authority. The danger is quiet, hard-to-trace bias in initiating-event frequencies and type splits, which then informs outage risk management and risk-informed licensing. The main threats are a silent keyword-gate recall failure, rare-class and drift degradation, loss of human review, opacity and qualification gaps, and adversarial manipulation of the corpus, models, keyword list or report wording.

Stage-1 keyword gate false negatives -- implicit, exploitable
The 44-pattern prescreen is a hard, unaudited gate, so true shutdown events written in novel, abbreviated or legacy phrasing are dropped before BERT sees them, biasing rare initiating-event frequencies low (a non-conservative error). Because the rule logic is transparent and deterministic, an adversary or an incentivised licensee could word reports to fall below the gate, knowing the loss is invisible to the reported 97% exclusion figure.

Rare-class and small-data masking -- implicit, exploitable
About 95% average accuracy on 10,928 imbalanced, analyst-labelled events hides poor recall on the rare shutdown initiator types that dominate PRA frequency sensitivity, and four-class forcing drops multi-cause or mode-of-operation context. An adversary could place manipulations or precursor patterns in these poorly performing classes, where the error is attributed to ordinary model weakness.

Drift and heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Changes to LER format and reporting rules, terminology, and new-build or advanced-reactor designs push inputs outside the training distribution, while the frozen keyword list and static test set give no warning. An adversary could time manipulation to a period of degraded accuracy so that it is read as drift.

Automation bias and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
The tool is meant to replace manual review, so analysts stop reading raw reports, lose edge-case skill, and treat labels as ground truth. This removes the independent check, so a corrupted or evaded classification can pass into PRA inputs unnoticed.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
Fine-tuned BERT lacks calibrated confidence and explainability, retraining can flip borderline events, and PRA and QA frameworks have no accepted qualification route for an ML component. An adversary benefits because tampering cannot readily be distinguished from ordinary model error in the audit trail.

Error propagation into PRA inputs -- implicit, exploitable
Misclassifications are aggregated into numerical frequencies that are consumed downstream, so a systematic error is laundered into the risk basis with no per-event trace. An adversary can rely on this laundering to make a small, deniable bias persist.

Training data, label and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor can alter the training corpus, annotations, pretrained BERT base, fine-tuned weights or the keyword list, including with trigger phrasings, so chosen event types or plants are systematically under-classified. The result is an understated shutdown risk, such as a hidden loss-of-shutdown-cooling trend, that is hard to attribute.

Evasion through report wording -- adversarial
Licensee-authored LER text is the input, so an incentivised insider can phrase events to avoid the keyword patterns or land in a benign class. This reduces the visibility of risk-significant precursors in the PRA record.

Event database and artifact tampering or exposure -- adversarial
Falsified LER or OPE records, or altered model files, pattern lists and post-processing, feed corrupted inputs into the pipeline, and a research-lab environment may have weaker cyber controls than plant systems. Exfiltrating weights or rules adds little direct value but enables probing the prescreen for evasion.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant and PRA perspective, this tool does not touch the plant. It sits in the licensing and risk-analysis chain, where it turns LER text into shutdown initiating event frequencies and type splits. Those numbers feed shutdown PRA, which informs outage risk management, technical specification and risk-informed licensing decisions, and operating-experience feedback. A wrong output rarely does direct physical harm. It biases the risk model quietly, and that bias is hard to see later. Existing practice offers some protection: PRA peer review, NRC and ASME/ANS standards, and conservative treatment of uncertainty. These protections assume the event counts are right, and they were not designed to catch systematic classification error from an automated screen that analysts have stopped checking.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Stage-1 false negatives. The keyword prescreen is a hard gate. About 3% of non-shutdown events pass, but the more serious case is a true shutdown-initiating event written in non-standard vocabulary, such as a novel failure mode, an older LER format, or a different licensee's phrasing. That event is dropped before BERT ever sees it. The result is an undercount of rare initiating events in the frequency estimates. Shutdown PRA is a low-base-rate problem, so the tails matter most, and 95% average accuracy can hide poor performance on rare classes (OP.C0202, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403). (2) Drift and heterogeneity. LER reporting rules, terminology, plant designs (new builds, SMRs, advanced reactors), and outage practices change. A model trained on 10,928 historical events can silently degrade, and the fixed 44-pattern list will age (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). (3) Automation bias and skill fade. The tool is meant to replace manual analyst review. Analysts lose familiarity with raw events, stop auditing the outputs, and treat the labels as ground truth. A mislabelled event then flows into PRA inputs without anyone seeing it (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01). (4) Opacity and qualification. BERT classifications are not explainable at the level needed for regulatory submissions. Fine-tuning is non-deterministic, so retraining can shift classifications. PRA and software QA frameworks such as NQA-1 and the ASME/ANS PRA standard have no accepted route for qualifying an ML component (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (5) Hallucination or oversimplification. Forcing events into four types loses context, such as multi-cause events and events that straddle categories (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03). These errors carry through to every downstream consumer of the labels (OP.C0603). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Poisoned or manipulated data. An insider or supply-chain actor could alter the training corpus, the fine-tuned weights, or the keyword list so that particular event types or plants are systematically under-classified. The result is a PRA that understates a vulnerability, for example by hiding a precursor pattern or a loss-of-shutdown-cooling trend (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059). (7) Evasion through wording. Licensee-authored LER text is the input. A licensee, or anyone who can influence report text, could phrase events to avoid the 44 patterns or to land in a benign class. This is mainly a regulatory-integrity concern, because it could reduce the visibility of risk-significant events, and the keyword gate is easy to probe if it is public (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015, AML.T0013). (8) Data integrity of the event database. Tampering with the LER or OPE repositories feeds the pipeline falsified inputs (AML.T0059, AML.T0031). Sensitive or security-related event content could also leak if the tool is run on external or cloud infrastructure (OP.C0601, OP.C0505). CONSEQUENCE AND MITIGATION. The consequence is a biased shutdown PRA that understates risk and could feed into outage planning and regulatory risk-informed decisions. For that to cause real harm, PRA peer review, NRC inspection, and the plant's own outage defence-in-depth would all also have to miss the error. Those layers make acute harm unlikely, but they are slow and weak at catching a quiet systematic bias. Sensible controls are sampled human audit of Stage-1 rejects, per-class recall reporting, versioned and checksummed models and keyword lists, and drift monitoring against the LER corpus.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline lens, this is a cascaded text classifier whose real exposure is the interaction between a hand-built 44-pattern keyword gate and a fine-tuned BERT head trained on a small, imbalanced, historically bounded corpus (about 10.9k LER-style events, with shutdown events a small minority and four-class labels produced by a few analysts). Stage 1 is a hard, non-probabilistic filter: any shutdown event that does not match a pattern is dropped permanently and never reaches BERT, so recall errors there are silent, unaudited, and structurally uncorrectable downstream. Stage 2 reports roughly 95% average accuracy, but averaging hides per-class performance on rare initiating event types. Those rare types are exactly what shutdown PRA frequency estimates are most sensitive to, because a rare-event frequency is count divided by exposure time and a handful of misclassified events moves it by large factors. The inputs are free-text narratives whose style, vocabulary, and reporting rules change over time (LER format changes, new plant designs, new licensee writing conventions, 10 CFR 50.73 revisions), so drift and out-of-distribution failure are expected, not exceptional. The output is an aggregate count feeding a risk model, not a per-event decision, so errors are laundered into numerical PRA inputs where they are hard to trace back to the classifier.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Cascaded-filter recall blindness: the keyword gate silently removes true shutdown events that use novel, abbreviated, or non-standard phrasing, such as new-reactor terminology, so the BERT stage never sees them. The result is biased-low initiating-event frequencies in shutdown PRA, a systematic non-conservative error that the reported 97% exclusion figure does not reveal (OP.C0302, OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). (2) Small-data and base-rate problems: rare shutdown initiating event types have few labeled examples, so aggregate accuracy overstates reliability on the classes that drive risk, and a small label error rate can swamp rare-event estimates (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.05). (3) Label provenance and concept drift: ground truth is analyst-assigned, and the taxonomy and report conventions evolve, so the model degrades quietly and the benchmark does not track future reports (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303). (4) Fine-tuning non-determinism and opacity: seed-dependent BERT heads and no calibrated confidence mean borderline events flip across retrainings, and analysts cannot easily see why an event was classified as it was (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0403). (5) Automation bias: a pipeline built to replace manual review removes the independent check, and analysts lose the skill to audit edge cases (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0501). (6) Content fidelity: narrative summarization-like behavior may drop qualifying context, such as the mode of operation at event time, which determines whether an event counts as shutdown-relevant (OP.C0304.03).

ADVERSARIAL threats. (1) Training-data or label poisoning through the corpus, annotation, or fine-tuning supply chain, including pretrained BERT weights from public hubs, could shift class boundaries so specific event types are systematically under- or over-counted (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002). (2) Because the keyword patterns are a transparent, deterministic filter, an actor who learns them, from the open publication or by observing outputs, could craft or influence report phrasing so that real events evade the screen, or could flood the pipeline with chaff that dilutes counts (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0046, AML.T0000). The exposure is modest because reports are authored by licensees and reviewed under regulatory processes, but an insider-licensee with an incentive to understate shutdown-relevant events is the realistic actor. (3) Tampering with model files, the pattern list, or the post-processing that turns classifications into PRA inputs would be hard to detect without integrity-controlled artifacts and regression test sets (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, OP.C0502). The net consequence is a regulatory risk model that is quietly biased in the optimistic direction, with the bias hard to attribute to the AI component.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view this is an unattractive direct target. It is an offline analytic aid that sits upstream of shutdown PRA and has no actuation authority, so a capable adversary would go after plant control systems or physical security before it. The concern is slow, deniable integrity degradation of risk knowledge. If the classifier replaces analyst review of LERs, its errors and any manipulation become the de facto record of which shutdown initiators matter. The pipeline also concentrates trust in a fixed keyword list and a single fine-tuned model, and it removes the human readers who would notice odd or missing events. An adversary, or a plain failure, can therefore shift PRA inputs with little chance of detection.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Data and model integrity: the training corpus, the 44-pattern list, the fine-tuning checkpoint and the pretrained BERT base are supply-chain and insider-accessible artifacts. Poisoning or backdoor-triggering them (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004) could make certain event phrasings, or a class of initiator, systematically fall into 'non-shutdown' or the wrong type. Mechanism: label or keyword manipulation. Dependency: shutdown PRA initiating-event frequencies and the licensing and risk-informed decisions built on them. Consequence: understated or misallocated shutdown risk, hard to trace back. (2) Evasion at the source: report text is written by licensees, and in principle by anyone who influences the wording of event reports. Phrasing that avoids the keyword prescreen (AML.T0015, T0043.003) could hide event precursors from the PRA record. This is a low-effort, plausible insider or negligent path, because the prescreen's rule-based nature makes its logic easy to infer. (3) Model and artifact access: weights, rules and data exfiltration (AML.T0035, T0025) give little direct value, but they enable crafting inputs against the prescreen, and the repositories may sit in a research-lab environment with weaker cyber controls than plant systems (OP.C0505.01). 

IMPLICIT, exploitable or timeable. (4) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102): about 95% average accuracy invites analysts to stop reading the reports. The residual errors then fall on rare shutdown types, where small-data, low base-rate effects (OP.C0202) make performance worst, and those are exactly the events that matter most for risk. Average accuracy hides class-level failure. (5) The 97% prescreen exclusion rate has an unmeasured false-negative tail. Anything the prescreen drops is never seen by BERT or a human, so a silent single point of failure (OP.C0603, C0304.03). (6) Drift: reporting language, LER format rules, and plant designs and operating practice change (OP.C0302.01, C0302.02, C0503). A frozen keyword list and model will degrade quietly, and the static test set gives no warning (OP.C0303). (7) Opacity and non-repeatability of the fine-tuned BERT (OP.C0401, C0402.01) weaken the audit trail needed in a regulated PRA context, so an anomaly cannot readily be attributed to tampering as opposed to ordinary model error (OP.C0501, C0504). Overall the facility consequence is degraded integrity of the risk basis rather than any immediate safety event. An adversary's best use is as a low-visibility stepping stone for corrupting the evidence base.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on keyword-gate false negatives, rare-class masking, drift, automation bias, opacity, and data/model poisoning plus wording evasion. I dropped speculative or weakly grounded codes (cloud dependency, AML.T0046 chaff, AML.T0013, hallucination as a distinct threat) and kept the exfiltration codes only as an enabler of evasion.

evidence.citation: "A knowledge-informed large language model framework for U.S. nuclear power plant shutdown initiating event classification for probabilistic risk assessment," Proceedings of the Institution of Mechanical Engineers, Part O: Journal of Risk and Reliability (Idaho National Laboratory / University of Idaho; OSTI record)
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper, which has an INL report version, describes a prescreening classifier plus a fine-tuned BERT classifier. It was evaluated on a dataset of 10,928 events. The prescreening stage excluded more than 97% of non-shutdown events, and the BERT stage reached about 95% average accuracy in the published version.

damage.why: The pipeline has no actuation authority, so the worst credible harm (e.g., the poisoning threat that hides a loss-of-shutdown-cooling trend) is a silent, non-conservative bias in shutdown PRA inputs, which erodes safety margin and risk-informed decisions but does not itself cause a release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Keyword-gate recall loss, rare-class masking, drift and error propagation occur reliably once the described conditions exist (a deterministic gate, imbalanced data, evolving report language), though a deliberate manipulation needs specific conditions.

exploitability.why: The most severe adversarial paths (training-data, label or model poisoning, and tampering with event databases or artifacts) need insider or supply-chain access, while wording evasion needs only licensee-author access and so is more accessible but still limited to insiders.

affected_users.why: A systematic bias flows into shutdown PRA frequencies and so into outage risk management and licensing across plants and the fleet-level risk basis, but it stays within the analytic and regulatory domain and does not propagate across coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The approach, keyword-gate design and BERT classifier are published in the open literature, and keyword gating, class imbalance, drift and poisoning are well-documented weakness classes, though the specific 44 patterns and weights would require more detailed knowledge.

use_case: Multi-agent large-language-model framework that automates reactor core design and analysis workflows by driving a deterministic PWR core-analysis code (CORCA-3D, in its educational version CORCA-sim) on an HPR1000-based model. The agents run under state-machine-constrained coordination, and each stage advances only after the required intermediate files are generated and verified. The framework was evaluated with four LLM backbones on nine tasks. It was demonstrated on critical boron search, distributed power analysis, control rod worth, reactivity coefficients and operational-domain assessment.
incurred_insecurity:
Placing an LLM multi-agent layer between engineers and a deterministic core-analysis code creates a new, high-trust pathway that writes input decks, runs the solver and reports design parameters such as critical boron, rod worth, reactivity coefficients and operating-domain margins. The state-machine gate checks that files exist and are well-formed, not that the modelled case is the intended one, so both honest agent errors and deliberate manipulation can pass as clean runs. Main threats are silent wrong-but-valid inputs, adversarial steering of the agents or their supply chain, false assurance from the gating and the 84-96% success figure, loss of reproducibility and qualification basis, and exposure of proprietary design data.

Semantically wrong but valid decks -- implicit, exploitable
The LLM hallucinates, mistranslates or omits parameters (burnup step, rod bank position, cross-section library, units, boundary conditions), and the solver runs cleanly because the gate tests form rather than physics. A non-conservative shutdown margin, rod worth, coefficient or operating-domain limit can enter the design basis, and an adversary can hide a deliberate deck alteration among these plausible errors; agents sharing one backbone also make cross-checks non-independent.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
High reported success rates and fluent auto-formatted reports induce over-trust, and designers who stop hand-building decks lose the feel for implausible boron or peaking values. An adversary can time subtle tampering to routine high-volume campaigns, relying on reviewers not recomputing.

Non-repeatability and missing qualification basis -- implicit, exploitable
Temperature and phrasing sensitivity means the same request can yield different decks, and the reasoning trace is not a faithful explanation, so design-of-record QA, traceability and forensic comparison fail; the qualified solver lends unearned credibility to an unqualified LLM wrapper. Adversarial deviations can pass as ordinary run-to-run variability, and the lack of a reproducible baseline weakens detection.

Out-of-distribution transfer and backbone drift -- implicit, exploitable
Validation on an educational code, one HPR1000-based model and nine tasks does not cover proprietary cores, novel loadings or off-nominal states, and silently updated or deprecated API-hosted backbones invalidate the reported success rates. An adversary could exploit unannounced behaviour changes or a swapped backbone, which occur without change control, to mask altered behaviour.

Cloud and governance gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Commercial hosted backbones move proprietary design data off-premises, and existing security and QA regimes treat design software as deterministic and do not cover agent privileges, prompt and configuration integrity or model provenance. These gaps give an adversary an unmonitored exfiltration channel and a change-control blind spot.

Prompt injection and retrieval or tool poisoning -- adversarial
Instructions or biased content planted in manuals, prior-case files, templates, tool outputs or intermediate files can steer agents to change a library, tolerance, rod position or acceptance criterion, or to misreport solver results or declare a stage verified. The effect is a non-conservative design or licensing basis that passes the file-existence gate and may surface only years later.

Supply-chain and backdoor compromise -- adversarial
A compromised or swapped model, agent framework, tool wrapper or solver input/library file, or a backbone rug pull, can systematically bias outputs or fire a backdoor trigger on specific design conditions. Because deterministic output is presumed trustworthy, this insider-style integrity attack on the design chain is very hard to detect.

Agent privilege abuse and configuration tampering -- adversarial
Agents with file-system and code-execution rights can, if hijacked or if their memory or state-machine configuration is altered, overwrite or delete verified decks and results, weaken the verification gates, or harvest stored credentials for lateral movement toward more sensitive networks. LLM-attributed actions also blur audit trails and let a malicious insider hide edits.

Design-data exfiltration -- adversarial
Core loading patterns, neutronics models and margins concentrated in agent context, logs, RAG stores and provider APIs can be leaked through LLM data leakage or agent tool invocation. This is chiefly an espionage and export-control consequence; the public educational CORCA-sim also gives adversaries a proxy to tune attacks offline.

Service denial and schedule pressure -- adversarial
Attacks on the model service or resource-exhausting agent loops can stall design work. Safety consequence is low at design stage, but schedule pressure can push teams toward unreviewed shortcuts.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Data Destruction via AI Agent Tool Invocation
Exfiltration via AI Agent Tool Invocation

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a design-stage tool: LLM agents write input decks for a deterministic core-analysis code (CORCA-3D/sim), run it, and report critical boron, power distribution, rod worth, reactivity coefficients and operating-domain margins. The deterministic solver and the state-machine gating check that files exist and are well-formed, but they do not check that the case modelled is the case intended. An agent that silently mis-specifies a burnup state, rod bank position, boron concentration, cross-section library, or thermal-hydraulic boundary condition gets a clean run and a plausible number. The downstream hazard is a wrong design or licensing-basis input (peaking factors, shutdown margin, moderator temperature coefficient sign, operational-domain limits) that a reviewer accepts because the workflow shows 84-96% 'success'. Independent verification and validation, the design-review chain and later commissioning physics tests are real backstops, but they weaken if the tool is trusted to the point that reviewers stop checking inputs. The 4-16% failure rate is itself a hazard: success is defined as workflow completion, and failures that look like successes are the dangerous ones.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Semantically wrong but syntactically valid runs. The AI failure is hallucinated, mistranslated or omitted input parameters, such as wrong units, wrong rod bank or burnup step, or a defaulted library. The facility dependency is the safety-analysis inputs: shutdown margin, rod worth, reactivity coefficients and DNB/peaking-limited operating domain. The consequence is a non-conservative design basis if reviewers skip independent recomputation. The state machine verifies that files were generated, not that physics intent was met (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0401). (2) Automation bias and skill fade. Fluent, auto-formatted reports invite over-trust, and junior designers lose the feel for expected magnitudes, so they no longer catch implausible critical boron or Fq values (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01). (3) Non-repeatability. Temperature and prompt-phrasing sensitivity means the same request can produce different decks, which undermines QA traceability and reproducibility of design calculations (OP.C0402.02, OP.C0501). (4) Qualification and transfer gap. It was demonstrated on an educational version (CORCA-sim) and a single HPR1000-based model with nine tasks. Industrial use, with different cores, fuel designs, transients or code versions, is out of distribution, and the benchmark does not cover rare edge cases such as off-nominal configurations (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0202, OP.C0203). (5) Cloud/vendor dependency. Commercial LLM backbones may involve off-premises processing of proprietary design data, and silent model updates change behaviour (OP.C0601, OP.C0502, OP.C0302.02).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Indirect prompt injection and RAG/tool poisoning through documents, code manuals, templates or intermediate files the agents ingest. This could bias parameter choices or the interpretation of results, for example by quietly changing a library, tolerance or acceptance criterion, while the output still passes file-existence gates (AML.T0051.001, AML.T0070, AML.T0099, AML.T0110, AML.T0080). (7) Supply-chain compromise of the model, agent tools, code wrappers, or the solver input/library files, which gives insider-style manipulation of design results that is hard to see because deterministic output is assumed to be trustworthy (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.005, AML.T0018). (8) Exfiltration of proprietary design data, such as core loading patterns, neutronics models and margins, through LLM data leakage or agent tool invocation, which is a security and export-control concern more than a safety one (AML.T0057, AML.T0086, AML.T0025). (9) Agent tool abuse, because file-system and code-execution privileges let a hijacked agent alter or delete deck and result files, or reach the engineering network (AML.T0053, AML.T0101, AML.T0050). (10) Denial or degradation (AML.T0029, AML.T0034) is low consequence at design stage, but could be used to schedule-pressure teams into shortcuts.
