Overall severity is bounded by human design review and later commissioning tests, but those safeguards erode if the tool becomes an unquestioned step in the licensing-basis chain.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is not a trained-model-in-the-loop system: it is a general-purpose LLM used zero- or few-shot as a planner and code/input-deck generator around a deterministic solver. The fragility therefore sits in the prompt/orchestration layer, the LLM backbone lifecycle, and the interface between free-text generation and a physics code that accepts syntactically valid but physically wrong inputs. The reported 84-96% success rates across four backbones imply a 4-16% failure tail, and the state-machine gate 'intermediate files generated and verified' checks artifact existence and format rather than physical correctness. The evaluation used an educational code (CORCA-sim) and a single HPR1000-based model, so nothing is known about behavior on proprietary, plant-specific, or as-built data. Nothing here has a qualification basis, since the stochastic LLM is entering a design-basis analysis chain that was built on deterministic, validated tools.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Silent plausible-but-wrong inputs (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0603): the LLM hallucinates or misattributes a cross-section library, a burnup state, a control-rod bank map, or boundary-condition units. The deterministic solver runs, the file-existence gate passes, and the result looks authoritative. Consequence: an erroneous critical boron concentration, rod worth, reactivity coefficient or operating-domain margin enters design documentation, and a non-conservative error could affect safety-case margins. Verification gates that check form but not physics are a core architectural weakness, as is correlated error across agents sharing one backbone, because multi-agent cross-checking is not independent. (2) Non-repeatability and qualification mismatch (OP.C0402.02, OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401): temperature and semantic-perturbation sensitivity means the same request may yield different decks. The generated reasoning trace is not a faithful explanation, and there is no AI-specific QA basis for design-of-record use. (3) Backbone drift and lifecycle (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0601, OP.C0204): API-hosted LLMs are silently updated or deprecated, which invalidates the benchmark success rates; a cloud dependency also creates availability and design-data confidentiality exposure. (4) Data provenance and out-of-distribution (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0302.03): validation on a simulated or educational code and a reference-type model does not transfer to real plant data, novel core loadings, or edge-of-envelope states, where LLM and solver-manual knowledge is thin. (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06): a 90%-plus success rate drives over-trust and skill fade in core-design engineers, who then lose the ability to catch the failing minority. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Indirect prompt injection and retrieval poisoning (AML.T0051.001, AML.T0070, AML.T0066, AML.T0099): manipulated solver manuals, prior-case files, tool documentation or engineering notes read by agents can steer parameter choices or the workflow. This is a subtle integrity attack on design outputs and would be hard to detect because outputs look valid. (7) Supply chain (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.005, AML.T0109): a compromised or swapped model, agent framework, or tool wrapper, or a backbone rug pull, can alter outputs systematically or introduce backdoor triggers (AML.T0043.004) that fire on specific design conditions. (8) Agent tool invocation (AML.T0053, AML.T0050, AML.T0101, AML.T0086): agents that write files and execute a solver have a code-execution surface; compromised context could lead to deleted or overwritten verified intermediates, or exfiltration of proprietary design data. (9) Context and configuration tampering (AML.T0080, AML.T0081, AML.T0084): altering agent memory or the state-machine configuration could weaken the verification gates themselves. (10) Information exposure (AML.T0057, AML.T0085.000): leakage of proprietary core design parameters via the LLM provider or RAG store. Adversaries can also time attacks around known failure tails, hiding malicious deviations within the already accepted 4-16% run-to-run variability.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this framework puts an LLM-driven agent layer between engineers and a qualified deterministic core-analysis code. That creates a new, high-trust, scriptable pathway that can read and write input decks, generate intermediate files, and report core design parameters such as boron concentration, rod worth, reactivity coefficients and operational margins. The state-machine gating checks that files exist and are well-formed, not that the physics is right. So an insider or supply-chain adversary does not need to attack the validated solver. Subtly altering what the agents feed it or how they summarize the results is easier and likely to go unnoticed. The reported 84-96% success rate also means 4-16% of runs fail or deviate. That noise masks deliberate tampering and conditions users to rubber-stamp whatever the pipeline produces. A nation-state would probably prefer other targets for direct sabotage, but design-basis data, proprietary core models and a poisoned design-analysis chain are valuable for espionage and long-dwell integrity attacks.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity attack on the design chain: through prompt injection (direct, or indirect via documents, tool outputs or retrieved reference material), poisoned agent tools or configurations, or a compromised model or supply-chain component, an adversary can steer agents into modifying input decks, such as cross sections, rod positions, boron settings or limits. They can also make agents misreport solver outputs or declare a stage verified when it is not. The facility dependency is the design and safety-analysis basis. The consequence is non-conservative margins, wrong operational-domain or rod-worth conclusions, or eroded confidence in licensing submissions, and it may surface only years later. Because state-machine checks test file presence and format rather than physical validity, the verification gate gives false assurance. (2) Insider pathway: agents hold broad file and execution privileges and abstract away individual actions, so a malicious or coerced insider can hide edits behind plausible LLM-attributed behavior, and attribution and audit trails weaken. Credentials in agent configurations, tool access tokens and an agent's ability to execute code on analysis workstations are lateral-movement opportunities from a lower-security design network toward more sensitive systems. (3) Information exfiltration: agent context, logs and generated files concentrate proprietary reactor design data. If a cloud-hosted LLM backbone is used, which is typical for the four backbones tested, core models and results leave the facility boundary. Data leakage through model APIs, RAG stores or chat history is a real espionage target. (4) Denial or degradation: attacks on the model service or resource-exhausting agent loops can stall design schedules, and a swapped or silently updated backbone can change behavior with no change control. (5) Stepping stone: the educational CORCA-sim and HPR1000-based model give adversaries a public proxy to develop and tune attacks offline before applying them to the production tool chain.

IMPLICIT, exploitable or timeable. (a) Automation trust and skill fade: as engineers stop hand-building decks, they lose the intuition to catch a subtly wrong boron value or power shape. An adversary can time tampering to routine, high-volume campaigns. (b) Non-determinism: inference-time variability, plus sensitivity to temperature and semantic perturbation, means failures look like normal noise and results cannot be reproduced for forensic comparison. (c) Hallucination or omission in summarizing and interpreting results can pass fabricated or oversimplified conclusions downstream. (d) Qualification gap: the deterministic code may be qualified while the LLM wrapper is not, so the whole chain borrows credibility it has not earned, and validation on a simulator or educational version may not transfer to the production code and plant data. (e) Backbone version drift and vendor updates silently change behavior. (f) Governance: current security and QA regimes treat design software as a deterministic tool and may not cover agent privileges, prompt and config integrity, or model provenance.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on silent plausible-but-wrong decks passing a form-only gate, automation trust, non-repeatability, qualification gap, cloud/backbone drift, and the injection, supply-chain, tool-abuse and exfiltration adversarial set. I excluded weakly supported codes (e.g., AML.T0067, OP.C0505, OP.C0102, AML.T0066, AML.T0084) and kept the rest where the text traces to them.

evidence.citation: "Exploring a multi-agent framework with large language models for nuclear design automation," Elsevier (ScienceDirect)
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests a simulator-grounded LLM multi-agent workflow coupled to an industrial core-analysis code for an HPR1000 reactor model. It reports workflow success rates of about 84–96% across four LLM backbones, plus robustness tests against model temperature and semantic perturbation. Details come from the abstract and visible sections of the search result; I did not read the full paper. I also did not confirm the journal title.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is silent wrong-but-valid or tampered decks (including supply-chain or prompt-injection steering) that put non-conservative shutdown margin, rod worth or operating-domain limits into the design or licensing basis; this erodes safety margins and could falsify design assurance, but it is a design-stage integrity harm with downstream review layers rather than a direct release, so it scores just below 5.

reproducibility.why: Wrong-but-valid decks pass a gate that checks form rather than physics, and LLM errors, over-trust, non-repeatability and backbone drift are recurring properties of the architecture, so the class triggers reliably once such a pipeline is deployed; targeted injection or backdoor variants are more conditional.

exploitability.why: Indirect prompt injection or poisoning of manuals, templates and intermediate files needs only modest access to content the agents ingest, while supply-chain compromise, configuration tampering and insider-style edits need deeper access, so the overall requirement is moderate.

affected_users.why: The impact spreads across the design chain, covering every analysis the framework produces, the design-of-record and the licensing basis, plus proprietary data exposure, but it stays within the design and analysis function rather than propagating through coupled operating plant systems.

discoverability.why: Prompt injection, tool and RAG poisoning, supply-chain and hallucination weaknesses are well documented in the open literature for LLM agents, and the public paper and the educational CORCA-sim give outsiders an offline proxy to learn how the workflow behaves, though specifics of a deployed proprietary pipeline remain less visible.

use_case: Deep-neural-network critical heat flux (CHF) models, one purely data-driven and two hybrid bias-correction models that learn residuals of the Bowring correlation or the Groeneveld lookup table. They were trained on tube CHF data and implemented in the CTF subchannel code. They predict the location and magnitude of CHF in a PWR-type 5x5 rod-bundle test series, to support thermal-hydraulic safety analysis and fuel design margins.
incurred_insecurity:
A tube-trained DNN and hybrid residual CHF models embedded in CTF set DNBR margins and fuel design limits through a quiet, design-phase path. No plant sensor or alarm is touched, so errors surface late if at all. The main threats are an unflagged tube-to-bundle generalization gap that hides non-conservative tails, opacity and qualification gaps, over-trust in an apparently validated hybrid model, and adversarial tampering with training data, weights or the software chain. Design-tool integrity sits outside operational cyber-security scope, which makes the adversarial paths harder to detect.

Training-data or weight poisoning -- adversarial
A few manipulated records in the small, expensive tube CHF dataset, or a tampered weights file, can make the DNN or its residual correction over-predict CHF in a narrow pressure, flux or quality regime while still passing mean-accuracy benchmarks. The result is a non-conservative DNBR limit that erodes real margin and is found only by an unusual test or event.

Supply-chain and integration compromise -- adversarial
Tampered ML libraries, serialized model files or the CTF coupling layer that loads weights can alter CHF output or give a foothold on engineering workstations holding proprietary fuel and licensing data. Weights are loaded as opaque files with little change control, so swapped or corrupted weights are hard to detect.

Tube-to-bundle domain shift and tail masking -- implicit, exploitable
A model trained on tube data has never seen spacer grids, mixing vanes, cross-flow or non-uniform axial power, and CTF's own coupled inputs lie outside its training distribution. Confident, unflagged and non-conservative errors can hide behind an average-accuracy win on one bundle series, and the hybrid residual may degrade its Bowring or Groeneveld baseline outside the training envelope. An adversary could hide an engineered bias in this tail, with natural extrapolation error giving plausible deniability.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
An opaque DNN with no calibrated uncertainty and training-run non-determinism cannot support a 95/95 DNBR justification, and there is no accepted AI-specific QA route. Retraining or CTF updates can silently shift the design basis. These same limits stop reviewers from using physical reasoning to spot tampering, so an adversary benefits from the misplaced confidence.

Over-trust and skill fade in CHF review -- implicit, exploitable
A model that beats W-3, Bowring and Groeneveld on average invites analysts to treat it as a validated drop-in replacement and lets classical CHF cross-checking atrophy. An adversary relying on that trust faces a weaker human check on a manipulated output.

Fault propagation through CTF and shared artifacts -- implicit, exploitable
Non-physical DNN trends can destabilize CTF's iterative coupled solve and inject artifacts into the subchannel solution. If one model artifact is reused across vendors or analyses, one bias or compromise spreads across all of them, which gives an adversary a broad blast radius from a single tampered file.

Data scarcity and weak configuration control -- implicit, exploitable
Sparse proprietary bundle CHF data, unclear versioning and possible train/test leakage inflate confidence and make independent verification difficult. Weights and normalization constants outside configuration control could be applied to the wrong geometry or units unnoticed, and an adversary could hide changes in that gap.

Proxy-model reconnaissance -- adversarial
Published architecture and open tube CHF datasets let an adversary build a proxy model to find poorly calibrated regions. That knowledge could target poisoning or shape inputs that exploit out-of-distribution behavior. Model extraction to leak proprietary vendor correlations is a minor confidentiality concern.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a thermal-hydraulics and fuel-design standpoint, CHF prediction sets the DNBR limit and therefore operating margin, so a wrong prediction means a non-conservative limit that nobody sees. The failure is quiet: a DNN in CTF returns a smooth, plausible CHF number, with no alarm or trip tied to it. Existing practice partly guards against this. Licensing-grade CHF correlations are qualified against bundle data with a 95/95 DNBR limit, and vendors use proprietary bundle correlations. A research model trained on tube data and validated on one 5x5 test series would not be accepted into a safety analysis without that qualification. The real risk is that an 'on average more accurate' result gets read as 'conservative' and gets used in preliminary design or scoping. A tail error, such as an unconservative CHF overprediction at one pressure, flow or flux-shape condition, then propagates into margin claims, and independent review has to catch it.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Tube-to-bundle transfer gap. Training on tube data and testing on a 5x5 bundle means the model has never seen spacer grids, mixing vanes, cold-wall effects, non-uniform axial power or subchannel cross-flow. It can be accurate on one test series and unconservative elsewhere. Mean-error improvement hides tail behavior, and the safety-relevant quantity is the unconservative tail. Out-of-distribution inputs, such as high-burnup or novel fuel geometries, new grid designs, transients, or low-flow and high-pressure corners, give no warning because the DNN has no calibrated uncertainty. (2) Hybrid residual models can make the baseline worse outside the training domain. The ML correction can add error to a correlation whose behavior is well understood and bounded, and the combined model's validity range is harder to state than that of Bowring or the Groeneveld table. (3) Qualification and licensing mismatch. Opacity makes a 95/95 DNBR limit difficult to justify, and there is no accepted AI-specific QA route. Retraining, solver changes or CTF version updates change the numbers without any physical-basis review. Non-determinism across training runs and library versions makes reproducibility of the design basis uncertain. (4) Automation and benchmark bias. Reviewers may over-trust a code-integrated ML model that beat W-3 and Bowring, and a single test series (small-data, one facility) invites overfitting to its conditions. Public data scarcity for bundle CHF makes independent verification hard. (5) Software hygiene. Embedding a DNN in CTF adds a dependency, and weights and normalization constants that are not under configuration control could be applied to the wrong geometry or units without detection. ADVERSARIAL THREATS (lower likelihood, higher consequence). (6) Poisoning or tampering with the training CHF dataset, the weights file or the ML library in the supply chain so that CHF is overpredicted in a narrow regime. The result is quiet, unconservative margin that passes a mean-accuracy check but erodes the DNBR limit. An adversary would need to be able to time this with a design or reload analysis. (7) Integrity attacks on shared model artifacts, if the model is distributed across fleet or vendor analyses. A single compromised artifact then propagates the same bias across multiple analyses (cross-fleet propagation). (8) Confidentiality is minor, because proprietary CHF data and fuel-vendor correlations could leak through model extraction or inversion. Consequence chain: bad CHF output, then a non-conservative design margin, then reduced real DNB margin. Harm still requires independent code verification, vendor-licensed correlations, the conservatism built into the licensing methodology and regulatory review all to fail, so near-term severity is limited to design-phase and research use.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, the central fragility is a train/deploy domain mismatch. The models learn from tube CHF data (uniform geometry, no spacer grids, no cross-flow, no mixing vanes, no non-uniform axial or radial power) and are then run as closure models inside CTF to predict location and magnitude of CHF in a 5x5 bundle. CTF supplies local subchannel conditions (quality, mass flux, pressure) that are themselves model outputs, so the DNN receives inputs from a distribution it never saw: they are coupled, uncertain and shaped by CTF's own closures. The hybrid residual architecture inherits Bowring or Groeneveld's validity envelope and adds a learned correction that has no physical constraint outside the tube-data hull. It can extrapolate confidently and wrongly with no built-in out-of-distribution flag. The evidence offered is average accuracy on a single bundle test series from one vendor, a small and possibly non-independent validation set. That is thin support for a tool meant to set safety margins, where the tail errors (non-conservative under-prediction of CHF) matter more than the mean.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Domain shift and extrapolation (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.03): tube-to-bundle transfer, plus operating conditions outside the training envelope (low pressure, low flow, transients, grid-spacer effects, axial power shapes), can yield non-conservative CHF predictions. The AI failure is silent OOD generalization. The dependent artifact is the DNB/CHF margin used in safety analysis and fuel design limits. The consequence is overstated margin and potentially unsafe core or fuel limits. (2) Average-metric masking (OP.C0403, OP.C0402): a mean-error win over W-3, Bowring and Groeneveld hides the error tails, and a pointwise DNN has no guaranteed monotonicity or smoothness. Non-physical trends can destabilize CTF's iterative coupled solve, so the surrogate injects numerical artifacts that propagate through the subchannel solution (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). (3) Qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401): the opaque DNN lacks a validated uncertainty quantification pathway and cannot easily meet regulatory code-qualification and verification requirements built for correlations with documented validity ranges. Training-time non-determinism means that retraining may change licensing-basis behavior (OP.C0402.01). (4) Data provenance and scarcity (OP.C0202, OP.C0204): proprietary CHF databases (tube and bundle) are limited, with heterogeneous measurement uncertainty and unclear versioning. Hidden train/test leakage, or tuning on the same bundle data used to claim performance, would inflate confidence. (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04): analysts may treat the low-error hybrid model as a validated drop-in replacement and let it set margins.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training data and supply chain poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000): small, curated CHF datasets are especially sensitive to a few manipulated records. Tampering with the dataset, the trained weights, or the CTF integration artifact could bias predictions non-conservatively in a targeted regime while still passing average-accuracy benchmarks. (7) Model or code integrity (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, OP.C0502): weights embedded in a Fortran or C++ solver are loaded as opaque files, so there is little change control and swapped or corrupted weights would be hard to detect. (8) Misconduct-style erosion of margin: an actor with access to the validation set could hide a localized non-conservative region, since the model's behavior is not interpretable (OP.C0401). The common problem is that the safety conclusion rests on an AI component whose failure is silent, small in average terms, and propagated by a trusted simulation workflow into design and licensing decisions.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, a DNN-based CHF model embedded in CTF is a low-glamour but high-leverage target: CHF predictions set departure-from-nucleate-boiling margins that feed fuel design limits and licensing analyses, so a quiet bias in the model propagates into approved margins without any plant-side sensor or control being touched. The attack surface is the model lifecycle (training tube data, residual-learning pipeline, weights file, code integration into CTF), not an operating-plant interface, which means a patient insider or supply-chain adversary can act months or years before any consequence and with very low detectability. The hybrid architecture is the concerning part: because the network learns only a residual on Bowring or Groeneveld, a small, targeted perturbation hides inside a plausible-looking correction and the baseline correlation gives false reassurance that the output is 'anchored'. Non-adversarial weaknesses (tube-to-bundle extrapolation, sparse data, opacity) are what an adversary would exploit, since they supply plausible deniability for any engineered error.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Poisoning or manipulation of the training data or trained weights (tube CHF database, residual targets, or the stored model file) so that CHF is over-predicted in a specific parameter region (pressure/mass flux/quality ranges relevant to a given fuel design). Mechanism: AI model integrity compromise; dependency: fuel design margins and safety-analysis acceptance; consequence: non-conservative DNBR limits, eroded safety margin, discovered only by an unusual test or an event. Because CHF data are sparse and expensive, few independent datapoints exist to catch a localized bias, and an insider who curates or merges datasets is well placed. (2) Software supply-chain and integration compromise: ML libraries, model-serialization formats, or the CTF coupling layer (loading of weights, Fortran/Python interface) could carry tampered artifacts, also giving a foothold in an engineering workstation network that holds proprietary fuel and licensing data. The CHF model is thus a stepping stone as much as a target. (3) Adversary reconnaissance and model extraction: published architecture and training approach, plus the open nature of CHF tube datasets, let an adversary build a proxy and learn where the model is weak or poorly calibrated, informing either targeted poisoning or the crafting of submitted test/design inputs that exploit out-of-distribution behavior. (4) Concentration of trust: if the model is reused across vendors, sites, or licensing submittals (fleet propagation), a single compromised artifact has a broad blast radius, and a regulator's reliance on an apparently validated 'hybrid' result raises its value as a target. IMPLICIT (exploitable or timeable): (5) Tube-trained models applied to rod bundles involve transferred/virtual data and distribution shift (spacer grids, nonuniform axial/radial power, geometry), so errors in unseen conditions are plausible and hard to distinguish from sabotage; an adversary gains deniability. Average-accuracy gains on one bundle series can mask poor tails where margin matters most. (6) Opacity and non-repeatability of DNNs reduce an analyst's ability to detect tampering via physical reasoning, and an improvement-over-correlation narrative encourages over-trust and skill fade in classical CHF assessment, weakening the human cross-check that would otherwise catch a manipulated output. (7) Governance gaps: no established qualification path for ML CHF models in licensing codes, weak configuration control and provenance for training data/weights, and no AI-specific security requirements for design-phase analysis tools (which are often outside cyber-security programs scoped to operational systems) leave the tool in a low-protection zone. Overall, the credible consequence is not an immediate event but silently degraded design margins, with a sophisticated adversary more likely to exploit the weak controls around design-tool integrity than to attack an operating-plant system directly.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on tube-to-bundle domain shift, mean-accuracy masking, qualification and opacity gaps, over-trust, and poisoning or supply-chain tampering of data and weights. I kept proxy-model reconnaissance from the security specialist and CTF solver propagation from the AI engineer as distinct, and dropped AML.T0012, AML.T0044, AML.T0059 and AML.T0076 as unsupported or redundant with the retained codes.

evidence.citation: "Prediction of Critical Heat Flux in Rod Bundles Using Tube-Based Hybrid Machine Learning Models in CTF," Oak Ridge National Laboratory / Transactions of the American Nuclear Society, vol. 134 (2026)
evidence.note: This peer-reviewed ANS Transactions conference paper (ORNL record) covers the work. The method details above come from the authors' arXiv version of the same paper (arxiv.org/html/2602.03805), which is a preprint and not itself peer reviewed. The authors put tube-trained DNN and hybrid residual-correction CHF models into the CTF subchannel code. They then compared the models with the W-3 correlation, the Bowring correlation and the Groeneveld lookup table on the Combustion Engineering 5x5 bundle CHF tests. All three ML approaches were more accurate on average, and the hybrid lookup-table model did best.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is non-conservative DNBR/CHF margin from poisoned or shifted models, which erodes real safety margin in fuel design and could in the worst case contribute to fuel damage. It sits upstream of operation and is buffered by regulatory review, so it falls short of a direct radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Tube-to-bundle domain shift and tail masking are reliably present whenever a tube-trained model is applied outside its training envelope, and a tampered weights file reproducibly yields the same biased output once loaded.

exploitability.why: Deliberate manipulation needs access to training data, weight files, or the software supply chain of a design tool, which means insider or supply-chain positioning and some domain knowledge. The implicit weaknesses, however, need no attacker effort.

affected_users.why: A shared model artifact reused across vendors or analyses, and coupled into CTF's solve, can spread one bias across many design analyses and licensing bases, though it stays within the design-phase domain rather than reaching every plant system.

discoverability.why: The architecture, open tube CHF datasets, and the generalization and opacity limits of ML CHF models are published in the open literature, so an outsider can readily infer where weaknesses lie, although specific weight handling and configuration control remain internal.

use_case: Artificial neural network and k-nearest-neighbour regression surrogates of a detailed fuel matrix degradation (FMD) process model. They predict the UO2 spent-fuel dissolution (degradation) rate from fuel cask temperature, dose rate and the local concentrations of carbonate, O2, Fe2+ and H2. The surrogates are embedded in a deep geologic repository performance-assessment simulation, where they capture local and temporal environmental effects on degradation after waste packages breach.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline surrogate sits between the fuel matrix degradation (FMD) process model and the source-term, release and dose numbers of a repository safety case, so it incurs mainly integrity and assurance risk rather than a direct physical-release pathway. The main threats are silent out-of-envelope extrapolation, inherited and hidden process-model error, error compounding in the coupled simulation, opacity and qualification gaps with reviewer over-trust, and adversarial tampering with the training data, weights or code that would bias the dissolution rate in a favourable direction.

Training-data and surrogate tampering -- adversarial
Poisoning the FMD-generated training set, or altering the ANN weights or kNN reference table (where the data is the model), can embed a region-specific bias in predicted UO2 dissolution rate. The bias would pass routine in-range validation and silently skew source term and dose margins in a siting, design or licensing case.

Software and model supply chain -- adversarial
A compromised ML library, unsafe serialised model file or tampered PA code in a shared laboratory or contractor pipeline can substitute or corrupt the surrogate during integration. The same path reaches HPC environments that share credentials and data with other repository analyses.

Reconnaissance and input manipulation -- adversarial
Published architectures, input ranges and error behaviour show where the surrogate is blind, enabling targeted perturbation of upstream temperature or chemistry inputs, or a campaign to discredit the safety case. Impact is limited to credibility and decision integrity, and needs prior access to the simulation chain.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
PA realizations over 10^4 to 10^6 years can drive high H2, low carbonate or extreme temperature-dose combinations beyond the training design, where the ANN extrapolates confidently and kNN saturates at its nearest neighbour, giving unflagged non-conservative rates and a low-biased source term. An adversary could place a manipulation in these unflagged regions, or steer inputs into them, knowing the output will look like a legitimate result.

Simulated-only provenance and false validation -- implicit, exploitable
The surrogate is trained and validated against the FMD model, not measurements, so process-model kinetic and radiolysis errors are inherited and masked by a good surrogate fit. This unwarranted confidence is what an adversary would rely on to keep a tampered or biased rate from being questioned.

Coupled-system error propagation -- implicit
The surrogate is called at every cell and timestep, so small biases or non-smooth ANN behaviour feed back into local H2, Fe2+ and carbonate concentrations and compound into system-level release estimates. No realistic adversary gains beyond what other threats here already offer.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
ANN opacity, non-deterministic training and the lack of a qualification regime for learned components in safety-case software make results hard to reproduce, audit or version-control. This weak audit trail gives an insider a quiet path to tamper without detection and makes any change hard to attribute.

Reviewer over-trust and lifecycle staleness -- implicit, exploitable
A fast surrogate that matches the process model in range invites reviewers to stop spot-checking against the full model, and it silently goes stale when the process model, host rock, canister or fuel type changes. An adversary or sloppy contractor can rely on this complacency and on reuse across sites to carry a manipulated or outdated surrogate through review.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This surrogate sits inside a repository performance-assessment (PA) code that feeds a safety case and licensing decisions, so the main risk is a quiet bias in the source term. There is no plant operator and no real-time actuation. A wrong dissolution rate becomes a wrong radionuclide release estimate, a wrong dose-to-public margin and, eventually, a wrong siting or design decision. The surrogate is validated against the process model and not against measurements. It is only reliable inside its training envelope, while PA samples very wide, long-duration environmental ranges (temperature, dose, carbonate, O2, Fe2+, H2) after package breach. Existing practice (probabilistic sensitivity analysis, conservative bounding, independent review) is a real defence, but it assumes the community can see the model's behaviour. An opaque, locally accurate surrogate can hide errors from that review.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT. (1) Extrapolation and out-of-distribution failure. Monte Carlo PA realizations, coupled with evolving repository chemistry over 10^4 to 10^6 years, can push inputs (high H2 from corrosion, low-O2 reducing conditions, temperature-dose combinations) outside the FMD training set. ANN output is unconstrained there. kNN saturates at the nearest training neighbours. Either way the rate may be non-conservative, which biases the source term low and erodes safety margin without any visible flag. (2) Surrogate-of-a-model provenance. The training data are simulated output of the FMD model, so any FMD error (kinetics from limited lab data on UO2, no field analogue for millennia of degradation) is inherited and can look validated by the surrogate's good fit. This makes the output a model-of-a-model with compounded, untraceable uncertainty (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0303). (3) Error propagation and coupling. The surrogate is called at every cell and timestep, so small biases or non-smooth ANN behaviour can feed back into the chemistry and transport coupling. Positive feedback on the local H2, Fe2+ and carbonate concentrations can cascade into system-level release estimates (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). (4) Opacity and repeatability. ANN explainability is limited, training is non-deterministic, and retraining or hyperparameter changes can shift results, which complicates QA, reproducibility and regulatory review (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Reviewers may over-trust the speed-up and the headline agreement metrics (OP.C0101.04).

ADVERSARIAL. The attack surface is the model and data supply chain, not an operational interface. (a) Poisoning or tampering with the FMD training set or the surrogate weights (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0031). A subtle, region-specific underestimate of the rate could make a poor site or design appear compliant. This is hard to detect because the surrogate is only spot-checked against the full model. (b) A tampered PA code or model file in a shared national-laboratory or contractor pipeline (AML.T0010.001). (c) Reconnaissance on published surrogate architectures and training ranges (AML.T0000.000), which tells an adversary where a surrogate is blind. The consequence is the integrity of the licensing evidence, with public and regulatory trust at stake (AML.T0048.002). There is no direct physical release pathway, because the waste is not affected by the analysis. Harm comes only if the corrupted result drives a siting, design or acceptance decision, and independent re-computation with the full process model and peer review are the safeguards that must also fail. Mitigations are therefore to enforce training-envelope checks with fallback to the full FMD model, keep conservative bounding runs, and control model version and integrity.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a regression surrogate trained on outputs of another model (the FMD process model), not on measurements. So the data is simulated/surrogate in provenance, and the surrogate can at best inherit the process model's errors, plus its own interpolation error. The core ML fragility is that the surrogate is validated only inside its training envelope (temperature, dose rate, and carbonate/O2/Fe2+/H2 concentrations), yet it is embedded in a coupled, time-stepping PA simulation. There, the inputs are generated by other models (geochemical transport, canister corrosion, hydrology) and can drift into corners of input space the training design never sampled. ANN and kNN fail differently: the ANN extrapolates smoothly and confidently, and kNN saturates at the nearest training neighbour. Neither raises an out-of-domain flag unless one is engineered in. Because the output is a source term feeding long-horizon dose and risk estimates used in a safety case, small biases or unflagged extrapolation can propagate through the coupled system and be buried in aggregate probabilistic results.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution inference inside a coupled simulation (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). The surrogate is called with local, time-varying environmental state produced by upstream models. Under breach scenarios, rare combinations such as high H2 with low carbonate, or extreme temperature and dose, may lie outside the sampled design. The surrogate returns plausible but wrong dissolution rates without any signal. Dependence: the source term and radionuclide release in the repository PA. Consequence: biased dose/risk estimates that look credible and enter the safety case, in either direction. (2) Error stacking and false validation (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). Agreement is measured against the process model, not against experiment. Process-model structural error, such as limited experimental calibration of radiolysis and H2 effects at repository timescales, is inherited and hidden by good surrogate-vs-model fit. Static regression accuracy does not establish accuracy under dynamic, path-dependent coupling, where small errors accumulate over 10^5-10^6 year time steps. Consequence: unwarranted confidence in regulatory-facing performance margins. (3) Qualification and repeatability gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01). Training randomness (ANN initialisation, hyperparameters, kNN k and distance metric) means different retrainings give different surrogates. Opacity limits review of why a rate was predicted. Existing QA regimes for PA software were not written for learned components. Consequence: results that are hard to reproduce, audit or defend before a regulator. (4) Automation bias (OP.C0101.04). A fast surrogate that matches the process model within range invites reviewers to treat it as the process model and stop checking spot comparisons. (5) Lifecycle drift (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0502). When the process model is updated or the repository concept changes (host rock, canister design, fuel type), the surrogate silently becomes stale unless retrained and requalified. Version and artifact control are weak points.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data and model integrity (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076, AML.T0031). The training set is a generated database of process-model runs, stored as files, plus serialised ANN weights or kNN reference tables. Tampering with the dataset, the generation scripts, or the saved model, for example by shifting dissolution rates in a narrow region or embedding a backdoor-like bias at specific input combinations, would be hard to detect. kNN is especially exposed because the training data is the model. Consequence: a covertly biased source term that understates or overstates release, undermining integrity of the licensing or safety case (a safety-assurance and credibility harm, not an operational one). (7) Supply chain (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0011.000). ML libraries and unsafe model deserialisation formats are a path into HPC or PA environments that hold sensitive site and design data. (8) Reconnaissance and model extraction (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0024.002). The paper is public and the surrogate is cheap and low-dimensional, so a third party could replicate it and learn which inputs drive the source term. Low severity on its own, but it helps target adversarial input manipulation or challenge the safety case. (9) Input manipulation upstream (AML.T0043, AML.T0015). Perturbing upstream geochemical or temperature inputs to push the surrogate into a poorly fit region is realistic, but it requires prior access to the simulation chain. This is mainly a way to exploit threat 1.

security_specialist.argument: This is not an operating-plant control system. It is an offline analytical tool whose output feeds a safety case, so the adversarial prize is long-term: shift a regulatory conclusion about repository performance, or erode confidence in it, rather than cause a near-term physical event. From a threat-surface view, the surrogate adds a small, opaque, hard-to-audit component between the process-model science and the dose/release numbers a licensing decision relies on. Anyone with access to the training set, the surrogate weights, or the embedding code could bias the degradation rate in a favourable direction, and the shift would be slow, plausible and hard to attribute. A sophisticated adversary would probably find easier targets such as the physical site or operational plants. But an insider, a supply-chain actor, or someone seeking to discredit a repository programme could use this one quietly. The implicit failure modes matter most here, because extrapolation outside the training envelope looks just like a legitimate result.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity of the surrogate and its training data: an insider or compromised collaborator could poison the FMD-generated training set, alter the ANN weights or kNN reference set, or swap the surrogate during integration into the performance-assessment code (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0076). The mechanism is a systematic bias in predicted UO2 dissolution rate. The safety case depends on that rate for source-term, release and dose estimates, so the consequence is a non-conservative or over-conservative safety case, which is either a latent safety or a licensing-credibility problem. Because the surrogate is accepted on agreement with the process model within the training range, a bias placed in sparsely sampled regions or in coupled-variable corners (high H2, Fe2+, low carbonate) could pass routine validation. (2) Trust concentration and weak audit: reviewers see only a fast, cheap function in place of a mechanistic model, and ANN opacity makes malicious or accidental tampering hard to detect by inspection (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0502). Model files, versioning and provenance are typically handled as research software rather than safety-graded software, so an insider has a quiet pathway to tamper with a result that is not re-run against the full model. (3) Reconnaissance and disinformation: the published methodology, input ranges and error behaviour tell an adversary or a litigant exactly where the surrogate is weakest (AML.T0000, AML.T0043). Bias can be introduced, or a model-credibility campaign mounted, against a safety case, which is a reputational and societal-harm vector (AML.T0048.001/.002). (4) Stepping-stone risk is low but real: the model sits in a simulation workflow that may share infrastructure, compute and credentials with other repository or safeguards-relevant analysis (AML.T0012, AML.T0010.001).

IMPLICIT, exploitable without an attacker. (a) Out-of-distribution extrapolation: after waste-package breach the real environment (temperature, dose-rate decay, evolving chemistry over very long times, different host rocks, different fuel types) may fall outside the training envelope. The surrogate then returns confident but wrong rates with no uncertainty flag (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0403). A full-scale shale reference case does not validate other geologies or inventories, and reuse across sites would propagate the same error (OP.C0602). (b) Simulated-only provenance: training data come from a process model, not from measurements, so the surrogate inherits and hides the process model's own errors and uncertainty, with no independent check on millennial timescales (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0202). (c) Coupled-system error propagation: surrogate errors feed local concentrations of the species it depends on, so an error can compound through the time-stepping simulation (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). (d) Human factors: a fast, close-agreeing surrogate invites reviewers and regulators to stop checking against the full model (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). That complacency is what an adversary or a sloppy contractor would rely on. (e) Governance: there is no settled regulatory framework for qualifying ML surrogates inside safety-case computations, and non-deterministic retraining weakens repeatability and independent verification (OP.C0504, OP.C0402.01).

I dropped speculative codes (e.g. AML.T0012, AML.T0024.002, OP.C0203) that were not clearly traceable to the synthesized text.

evidence.citation: "Machine Learning Surrogates of a Fuel Matrix Degradation Process Model for Performance Assessment of a Nuclear Waste Repository," Nuclear Technology (Taylor & Francis on behalf of the American Nuclear Society); Sandia National Laboratories authors
evidence.note: The Sandia-authored paper builds ANN and kNN regression surrogates that stand in for a computationally expensive FMD process model. They show good agreement with the process model within the training range. A full-scale shale repository reference-case simulation demonstrates the surrogates while keeping computational cost low. Its use_area (Licensing and Regulation) is my judgement: the source frames it as repository performance assessment, i.e. safety-case analysis, not licensing as such.

damage.why: The worst credible threat is tampering or non-conservative extrapolation that biases the dissolution rate low and understates source term and dose in a repository safety case, which is a safeguards- or safety-case falsification harm (not a direct release) with long-term public-safety and licensing-decision consequences, so just under the maximum.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution extrapolation reliably produces unflagged non-conservative outputs whenever PA realizations enter those regions, but tampering and poisoning outcomes depend on gaining access to the pipeline and on region-specific conditions.

exploitability.why: Credible adversarial paths (poisoning training data, altering weights, compromising the supply chain or HPC pipeline) need insider or privileged access to a laboratory or contractor simulation chain, though the implicit extrapolation and over-trust weaknesses need no special access.

affected_users.why: A biased surrogate propagates through every cell and timestep into system-level source term and dose estimates and can be reused across sites, but it affects one repository safety case's analysis rather than operating facility systems.

discoverability.why: Published architectures, input ranges, error behavior and well-documented surrogate-extrapolation and over-trust failure classes in open technical literature let a capable outsider infer where the surrogate is blind, though specific tampering points need pipeline knowledge.

use_case: Deep neural network classification of motorized rotating pancake coil (MRPC) eddy-current signals from steam generator tubes. It discriminates axial from circumferential defects, and the pipeline includes signal preprocessing and data augmentation. It supports automated analysis during time-limited in-service inspection of nuclear power plant steam generator tubing.
incurred_insecurity:
A deep neural network that classifies MRPC eddy-current signals as axial or circumferential sits on the steam generator tube integrity decision path, so any quiet error in it can leave a degraded pressure-boundary tube in service. Its main threats are an implicit surrogate-to-field generalization gap, drift and heterogeneity, automation bias under outage pressure, opacity and qualification gaps, and adversarial poisoning, supply-chain compromise and insider or acquisition-side tampering. The common failure is a silent false negative or wrong-orientation call that looks like honest model error and surfaces only at a later outage or a tube leak.

Specimen-to-field generalization gap -- implicit, exploitable
The model was trained and demonstrated on small sets of specimens with deliberately introduced defects, which lack the morphology and noise of real stress-corrosion cracking, fretting or mixed-mode flaws (deposits, dents, support plates, probe wobble). A closed-set classifier with no abstention will confidently label such signals, often axial when the flaw is circumferential or benign, and so misdirect plugging and repair decisions. An adversary could rely on this blind spot so that a manipulation or an induced flaw is indistinguishable from honest model error, which also weakens attribution.

Drift across plants and campaigns -- implicit, exploitable
New probes, acquisition firmware, calibration standards, tube materials, steam generator designs and preprocessing settings shift the input distribution, and accuracy degrades with no alarm unless performance is monitored routinely. An adversary could hide gradual changes to acquisition or preprocessing inside this expected drift, or exploit a model reused across units to affect many plants at once.

Automation bias under outage pressure -- implicit, exploitable
Time-limited outage inspection encourages analysts to accept the classifier's call as the second independent opinion. This erodes the dual-analyst independence and rare-flaw recognition skill that the qualification regime assumes. An adversary could time any compromise or data manipulation to the outage window, relying on the rubber-stamping to carry it through unchallenged.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A DNN with augmentation artifacts, training-time non-determinism and retraining does not map onto performance-demonstration qualification of analysts and techniques. This leaves no stable baseline and no explanation for individual calls. An adversary gains cover because tampering cannot be separated from honest error, and forensic detection of quiet degradation is weak.

Training-data poisoning and model supply-chain backdoor -- adversarial
Poisoned or relabeled training and augmentation data, or a backdoored pretrained model delivered through the vendor or software chain, could make a specific signal signature classify as benign or as the wrong orientation. Because the corpus is small, a few corrupted samples have outsized influence, producing a systematic false negative on a pressure-boundary flaw.

Insider and acquisition-side tampering with data or model -- adversarial
An insider, or an adversary with access to the acquisition-to-model pipeline, could alter eddy-current files, preprocessing parameters or model weights so real indications fall outside the decision boundary while appearing plausible to the reviewer. Perturbed or hardware-manipulated signals could likewise evade the classifier. The effect is concealed degradation of the pressure boundary that accumulates across outage cycles.

Inspection data and model exfiltration -- adversarial
Theft of inspection data or the model would reveal detection limits and show an adversary what degradation would escape classification. This is a lesser concern that lowers the cost of crafting evasive signals.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the plant side, this is an inspection-decision aid: its output feeds the steam generator tube integrity assessment, which determines plugging, repair and operational-assessment conclusions. Steam generator tubes are the reactor coolant pressure boundary, so a missed or misclassified flaw (especially a circumferential one, which has different structural significance than axial) could erode defense-in-depth against tube rupture or leakage, including SGTR and bypass of containment. The documented system was trained and demonstrated on specimens with deliberately introduced defects, not on real service-induced degradation, and the outage time pressure it is meant to relieve is also what encourages over-trust. Existing practice (qualified analyst/data-analysis procedures, EPRI ISI guidelines, site-specific performance demonstration, dual independent analysis, and a downstream human lead analyst) is a strong barrier only if the AI stays advisory and does not displace independent analysis or silently reduce analyst scrutiny.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Training-data provenance and generalization gap: notch/EDM or artificially seeded defects in lab specimens do not have the signal morphology of real stress-corrosion cracking, intergranular attack, or fretting wear, and real signals add noise from deposits, dents, support plates, tube-sheet transitions, and probe wobble. A classifier that looks accurate on specimens can misclassify or confidently mislabel real service-induced flaws, with the worst case being a circumferential or mixed-mode crack called axial or called benign. The low base rate of real flaws also gives poor calibration of rare-defect performance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). (2) Drift across plants and campaigns: different SG designs, tube materials, probe models, instrument vendors, frequencies, calibration standards, and signal-chain settings shift the input distribution. Silent degradation of accuracy would not be noticed unless there is routine performance monitoring (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303, OP.C0602). (3) Automation bias and skill fade under outage schedule pressure: analysts may accept the AI call as the second 'independent' opinion, which would compromise the independence of the dual-analyst process and degrade skill in rare-flaw recognition (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (4) Opacity and qualification: a DNN is hard to qualify under the performance-demonstration regime that qualifies analysts and techniques. Augmentation artifacts, non-repeatable training and a lack of explainability make it hard to justify the output to a regulator or in a tube integrity assessment (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Axial/circumferential discrimination alone is also an incomplete task: it ignores sizing, depth, and detection of flaws that are absent from the training taxonomy. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Data poisoning or supply-chain tampering of training/augmentation data, pretrained models, or the retraining pipeline, which could embed a backdoor or bias that suppresses flagging of one class of flaw, for example via a trigger-like signal feature (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0043.004). (6) Integrity manipulation of the eddy-current data stream or the analysis software between acquisition and review, such as subtle adversarial perturbations or file tampering that lowers flaw detectability while looking normal to the analyst (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). The consequence is a concealed degradation of the pressure boundary that accumulates unnoticed across outage cycles, which makes the attack attractive to a patient actor or an insider and difficult to attribute. (7) Availability: denial of service or delayed analysis during a time-limited outage causes schedule slippage and pressure to shortcut review (AML.T0029). Mitigation relies on keeping the AI advisory, preserving independent human analysis, using real-flaw performance demonstrations, integrity-controlling the data chain and model versions, and monitoring for drift.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline perspective, this system is fragile at the data layer first. The documented model was trained on MRPC signals from tube specimens with deliberately introduced defects (EDM notches, machined flaws, possibly lab-grown cracks), which is a surrogate/bench distribution. Real service-induced defects such as SCC, PWSCC, ODSCC, fretting and pitting have different morphology, branching, and noise from deposits, denting, support plates, and probe wobble. Real axial-vs-circumferential discrimination is also a low-base-rate, small-data problem: genuine flaws are rare, and labels come from human analysts or destructive pull-tube validation, so ground truth is noisy and scarce. Augmentation (shifts, noise, scaling, rotation) can create synthetic samples that violate eddy-current physics, such as phase-angle/amplitude relationships, which inflates validation performance when augmented copies leak across splits. A closed-set classifier with no abstention or out-of-distribution (OOD) detection will confidently label anything, including volumetric indications, mixed-mode flaws, and signals from a new probe or a new tube material, as axial or circumferential. Time-limited outage inspection pushes users to accept the model's output, which compounds the automation-bias risk.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Surrogate-to-field generalization gap: the model learns specimen-specific signatures (OP.C0201.01/.02/.04, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). Mechanism: the training distribution misses real degradation, geometry, and noise. Dependence: the dispositioning of tubes (plug, repair, or leave in service). Consequence: a misclassified or missed flaw orientation, which matters because circumferential cracking has different structural and burst-margin significance than axial cracking, so an error can leave a degraded tube in service and compromise the integrity of the primary pressure boundary. (2) Drift and heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303): probe wear, a new acquisition system or firmware, differing calibration standards, different SG designs and tube materials, and changing degradation mechanisms across outages all shift the inputs. Preprocessing (filtering, normalization, calibration mixing) is a hidden dependency that can silently change the input statistics. (3) Small-data, label-noise and leakage problems (OP.C0202, OP.C0403): inflated accuracy claims, poorly calibrated confidences, and no rare-class coverage. Non-determinism in training and augmentation seeds (OP.C0402.01) hinders requalification after retraining. (4) Opacity and automation bias (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102): analysts under outage schedule pressure rubber-stamp the model, and skill fade erodes the independent double-analysis that qualification regimes (for example, EPRI-style analyst qualification) assume. A static, qualified-once model also fits poorly with regulatory expectations for NDE procedure qualification (OP.C0501, OP.C0504).

ADVERSARIAL threats. (5) Supply-chain and data integrity compromise of the training corpus, augmentation scripts, or pretrained weights (AML.T0010.002/.003, T0020, T0018.000, T0059): poisoned or relabeled data, or a backdoor trigger (T0043.004), could cause specific signal patterns to be classified as benign or to take the wrong orientation. The corpus is small, so a few corrupted samples have outsized influence. (6) Tampering at the acquisition-to-model interface (T0015, T0043.003, T0031, T0076): an insider or an adversary with access to the data pipeline could alter raw signals or preprocessing parameters so that real indications fall below or outside the decision boundary, which is hard to see in an opaque DNN. An adversary can also time this around outages, because the verification window is short. (7) Model extraction or theft, or reconnaissance on the published architecture (T0000, T0002, T0024.002), is a lesser concern but lowers the cost of crafting adversarial signals. Overall, the exposure is mostly in the data and qualification pipeline, with a quiet failure mode that looks like normal operation.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this classifier sits on a safety-significant decision path: steam generator tubes are a primary-to-secondary pressure boundary, so a missed or misclassified flaw is a latent integrity and radiological-release precursor. Its documented purpose is to ease analyst workload during time-limited outage inspections, which is where trust concentrates and human vigilance erodes. The model was demonstrated on tube specimens with deliberately introduced defects, so the gap to real operational degradation (field data, noise, probe wear, deposits, denting) is the implicit weakness an adversary could exploit or time an attack around. A nation-state adversary is unlikely to attack the model for its own sake. It is more plausible that they compromise the data, model or analysis-software supply chain as one component of a broader effort to degrade boundary integrity quietly, or that they exploit an insider who already has legitimate access to inspection data. Because the output is a quiet false negative that surfaces only at the next outage, or at a tube leak, the attack is hard to attribute and may be indistinguishable from honest model error.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Training-data and augmentation-pipeline poisoning, or a backdoored model delivered via the vendor or software supply chain (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0043.004). A trigger-style backdoor could make a specific signal signature, such as a particular axial or circumferential crack morphology, classify as benign or as the wrong orientation. The model and its dependencies are small and cheap to tamper with, and the effect is a systematic false negative on a pressure-boundary flaw that is hard to detect. (2) Insider tampering with eddy-current data files, preprocessing parameters or model weights after acquisition (AML.T0012, AML.T0031, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). An insider with legitimate account access could shift a threshold or alter stored signals so that defect calls drift, with the change looking like routine reprocessing. (3) Adversarial or crafted inputs (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) are less likely, because the signals come from a physical probe, but a hardware or acquisition-side manipulation could produce signals that evade the classifier while a human reviewer sees only plausible data. (4) Model or data exfiltration (AML.T0025, AML.T0035) would reveal inspection sensitivity and defect-detection limits, which tells an adversary what degradation would escape detection. IMPLICIT, AND EXPLOITABLE BY TIMING: (5) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Under outage time pressure, analysts may rubber-stamp classifier output, so any compromise or silent error propagates unchallenged, and an adversary can time action to the outage window. (6) The gap between specimen data and field data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0203). Training on small, artificially flawed specimens, with augmentation standing in for real variability, means rare real flaw types, noisy signals, new probes or different plant geometries are out-of-distribution. The classifier will still return confident labels, and the resulting misclassifications are indistinguishable from an attack. (7) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402) make it hard to tell tampering from honest error, which weakens forensic detection. (8) Qualification gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0502): inspection techniques are normally qualified under a performance-demonstration regime, which a DNN with retraining and drift does not map onto cleanly. This leaves no clear baseline against which to detect quiet degradation. (9) Model reuse across units or fleets (OP.C0602) would spread a single poisoned or biased model to many plants at once, which makes it a higher-value target. Overall, the threat is less a direct attack on the AI than a degradation of the inspection barrier's reliability, with human-in-the-loop checks the key control that both the AI and the schedule pressure erode.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the specimen-to-field gap, drift, automation bias, opacity/qualification and poisoning/tampering threats. I dropped the denial-of-service and model-extraction items as marginal, and kept exfiltration as a short threat because it reveals detection limits.

evidence.citation: "MRPC eddy current flaw classification in tubes using deep neural networks," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Elsevier; Korean Nuclear Society), Vol. 51, Issue 7, pp. 1784-1790, 2019
evidence.note: The paper builds and demonstrates a deep neural network pipeline on MRPC eddy-current data from tube specimens with deliberately introduced defects. The steps are data acquisition, preprocessing, augmentation, training and demonstration. It reports that the network separates axial from circumferential defects, which would ease the heavy signal-analysis load in steam generator tube inspections.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a silent false negative or wrong-orientation call on a pressure-boundary flaw, which can leave a degraded steam generator tube in service and risk a tube leak or rupture with possible radiological consequences; this is a serious safety-margin erosion but sits behind dual-analyst review and defense-in-depth, so it falls short of a direct release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: The specimen-to-field generalization gap and drift are reliably present whenever the closed-set classifier sees out-of-distribution signals, and over-trust under outage pressure recurs every campaign, although the adversarial poisoning and tampering paths depend on specific access conditions.

exploitability.why: The deliberate adversarial paths (training-data poisoning, supply-chain backdoor, insider tampering with the acquisition-to-model pipeline) need privileged insider or vendor-chain access plus domain knowledge of eddy-current signals, even though the implicit weaknesses need no special access.

affected_users.why: Impact centers on steam generator tube integrity at one plant, but a model reused across units or campaigns could propagate the error across multiple plants and tubes, which is broader than a single component yet short of facility-wide coupled-system effects.

discoverability.why: The approach is described in open literature, and the generalization gap, drift and automation-bias weaknesses are well-documented for this class of ML system, so a capable outsider can readily infer that they exist, although finding the specific deployed pipeline and its detection limits requires more knowledge.

use_case: Deep-learning pipeline (RWB-Net) for automated weld bead inspection of radioactive pipelines in nuclear reprocessing plants. A light-robust denoising network cleans the inspection images. An attention U-Net refined with hidden-Markov-model optimisation then locates the weld beads. Finally, multi-domain adversarial fusion of handcrafted descriptors with deep features classifies each weld bead, supporting structural-integrity checks in low-contrast, noisy, hard-to-access piping.
incurred_insecurity:
RWB-Net sits in a trusted accept/reject position for weld integrity on radioactive reprocessing pipework, where re-inspection is costly and dose-intensive, so its output risks becoming the de facto integrity record. The main exposures are silent false accepts of real defects caused by data scarcity, drift and stage-to-stage error compounding, unqualified use of a hard-to-explain model, and adversarial manipulation of the image path, model artifacts or supply chain to hide a degraded weld. Any resulting undetected weld degradation could lead to a leak or loss of confinement and corrupt the safety-case evidence base.

Rare-defect data scarcity and provenance mismatch -- implicit, exploitable
Real defective welds are rare, so training likely leans on augmented, simulated or surrogate imagery, and the ~94% accuracy (with unknown false-accept versus false-reject asymmetry) is dominated by the majority acceptable class. A structurally significant weld can then be passed as sound; an adversary could target the poorly covered rare defect signatures, knowing the test set cannot reveal the blind spot.

Drift and out-of-distribution degradation -- implicit, exploitable
Changes in camera, illumination, crawler pose, radiation-induced pixel noise, surface oxidation or deposits move the inputs outside the denoiser's and segmenter's training envelope with no uncertainty signal, so performance falls silently. An adversary could hide gradual tampering within this unflagged degradation or time an action to when drift is greatest.

Denoiser content-fidelity failure and cascading errors -- implicit, exploitable
The denoiser can hallucinate or smooth away fine cracks and lack-of-fusion cues, and a mislocalised bead from the attention U-Net/HMM stage feeds the classifier the wrong region, so downstream stages are confident on altered evidence. An adversary gains a high-value single point to suppress a defect before segmentation and classification, and the compounding errors mask the manipulation.

Automation bias, skill fade and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Fast 0.41 s outputs, hard-to-access piping and a hybrid handcrafted/deep/HMM/adversarial-fusion architecture encourage bulk acceptance, erode manual inspection skill and make disagreement hard to adjudicate or forensically investigate. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust and lapsed human check to pass a manipulated or sabotaged weld.

Qualification, change-control and non-determinism gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Academic validation is not nuclear-grade performance demonstration, and retraining or updates with training-time non-determinism can silently change acceptance behaviour outside any validated envelope. Absent change control, an adversary can slip a modified model through as a routine drift-motivated update.

Evasion of the inspection image path -- adversarial
Adversarial perturbation, tampering with capture, storage or denoising, or physical surface coatings, markings and grinding patterns exploiting low-contrast noise sensitivity can cause a defective weld to be classified acceptable, or a good weld flagged to force dose-incurring rework. This most plausibly needs insider, maintenance-window or fabrication access.

Poisoning, backdoors and supply chain compromise -- adversarial
Poisoned fine-tuning data, a trojaned pretrained backbone, library or model file, or altered weights can implant a trigger or targeted blind spot that hides specific defect signatures and still passes a small acceptance test set. The multi-model fusion makes such a compromise hard to attribute or regress-test.

Model extraction and proxy-based attack preparation -- adversarial
The published architecture and datasets, plus model extraction from the inspection workstation, let an adversary build a proxy model to craft transferable evasion inputs aimed at the conditions where RWB-Net is least reliable. Extracted imagery also leaks weld geometry and piping layout.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, RWB-Net sits in the inspection chain for weld integrity on radioactive process piping, where a missed defect or misclassified bead can lead to a leak of highly active liquor or a loss of confinement. The consequence depends on how the output is used. If it only triages images for a qualified Level II/III inspector, existing practice (ASME/RCC-M-style acceptance criteria, independent review, hydrotest, periodic re-inspection) gives defence in depth. If hard-to-access, high-dose piping means humans seldom look at the raw images, the AI output becomes the de facto record and the main barrier. About 94% accuracy is not a safety-grade figure: the 6% error is not characterised by defect type, and the base rate of critical defects is very low. Several stages are chained (denoise, segment, classify), so errors can compound without anyone seeing them, and the pipeline's behaviour on out-of-distribution conditions (new alloys, radiation-induced sensor noise, corrosion or deposits) is the main implicit risk.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Missed or under-classified defects (false negatives) driven by the low base rate of real defects, small and unrepresentative training data from a few plants, and the shift between published test imagery and in-situ conditions (drift in camera, illumination, radiation noise, surface condition, weld procedure or material). The facility consequence is a degraded weld passing integrity checks and a later leak or contamination event, which is bounded only if independent NDE (UT, RT, hydrotest) and human review still exist. (2) The denoiser can hallucinate or smooth away fine features such as cracks and lack-of-fusion indications. It may do so before segmentation, so the downstream models are 'confident' on altered images. This is a content-fidelity failure that is hard to see in the output. (3) Automation bias and skill fade: with remote, low-dose-driven inspection, inspectors lose the habit of looking at raw images. The 0.41 s speed encourages bulk acceptance, and a hybrid handcrafted/deep/HMM/adversarial-fusion architecture is hard to explain, so disagreement is hard to adjudicate. (4) Qualification gap: AI inspection tools rarely have an established procedure-qualification route equivalent to a qualified NDE technique with performance demonstration (POD), so the tool may be used outside any validated envelope. Non-determinism after retraining or software updates can silently change acceptance behaviour. (5) Record integrity: the AI classification becomes the structural-integrity record used for life-extension and licensing arguments, so systematic bias propagates into safety-case evidence.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Manipulating the image or data path (adversarial perturbation or evasion, or tampering with the capture, storage or denoising stage) so a defective weld is classified as acceptable, or a good weld is flagged to cause unnecessary shutdown and dose-incurring rework. A physical-world variant is surface coating or marking on the pipe. The adversary needs access to the inspection data chain or the physical site, which is usually restricted, so this would more likely be an insider or supply-chain scenario. (7) Poisoning of training or fine-tuning data, or a backdoored pretrained model or library, which would produce a targeted blind spot that passes acceptance testing because the test set is small. (8) Compromise of the inspection workstation or robot platform pulling in the model, or tampering with the model files, which breaks the integrity of the inspection record. Timing an attack around outages or maintenance campaigns, when inspection reliance peaks, is a further consideration. Sabotage of a weld that is then passed would need a coordinated physical act, so the AI is an enabler rather than the sole cause. Mitigations are keeping the tool advisory, retaining independent NDE and a human reviewer on raw images, running a POD-style qualification, controlling model and data configuration, and monitoring input drift.

ai_engineer.argument: RWB-Net is a three-stage cascade (denoise, then segment/localise with attention U-Net plus HMM, then classify via fused handcrafted and deep features), so the main exposure lies in the pipeline's data and stage coupling rather than in the plant around it. Real defective welds in reprocessing pipework are rare, access-limited and imaged under heterogeneous conditions (radiation-induced sensor noise, low contrast, varied cameras, borescopes and crawlers). The training set is therefore probably a small, class-imbalanced mix of lab, simulated or augmented imagery plus a limited field sample. A reported ~94% accuracy, measured on a curated or in-distribution test split, says little about the rare defect class that matters for integrity, nor about behaviour on out-of-distribution inputs such as new pipe geometries, a different sensor, accumulated lens or sensor degradation, or a changed illumination rig. Each stage assumes its predecessor's output distribution. A denoiser that over-smooths can erase fine cracks or lack-of-fusion cues before the classifier ever sees them, and a segmentation or HMM localisation error silently mislocates the ROI, so errors cascade without any stage flagging them. The model's confident, fast output (0.41 s/image) invites automation bias in a setting where manual re-inspection is difficult.

Result: false-negative rates on real flaws are unquantified, so a structurally significant weld can be passed as sound. (2) Drift and OOD failure (OP.C0302, .01, .03): changes in camera, lighting, crawler pose, radiation-induced pixel noise, surface oxidation or contamination shift the input distribution. The denoiser's 'light-robust' training envelope may not cover these shifts, so there is no uncertainty signal and the failure is silent.
