(3) Cascading fault propagation (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603): the denoiser can hallucinate or remove flaw texture, and a mislocalised bead from the attention U-Net/HMM stage feeds the classifier with the wrong region. Errors compound without per-stage confidence checks or independent verification. Content-fidelity failure in the denoiser (OP.C0304.01/.03) is a particular concern because it alters the evidence itself. (4) Qualification and opacity gaps (OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0501): the fusion of handcrafted and adversarially aligned deep features is hard to explain or validate against code-based NDE acceptance criteria. Static benchmark accuracy does not establish dynamic in-plant performance, and training-time non-determinism (OP.C0402.01) complicates re-qualification after retraining. (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, .06, OP.C0102): trust in a fast classifier and fading manual-inspection skill, in an environment where re-inspection is costly and dose-intensive, reduce the chance that a bad output is challenged. ADVERSARIAL: (6) Integrity attack on inputs or pipeline: adversarial perturbation or physical patterns that cause missed defect detection (AML.T0015, T0043), or tampering with the inspection image stream so flawed welds look clean. This is plausible because the denoiser and fusion stages add attack surface and because handcrafted features may be reverse-engineered. Adversarial training of the 'multi-domain adversarial' fusion targets domain alignment, not attack robustness, so it should not be mistaken for it. (7) Supply chain and artifact compromise (AML.T0010.001/.003/.004, T0018.000, T0020, T0059): poisoned or backdoored weights, pretrained backbones or retraining data, which could be a trigger tuned to hide flaws. These can be timed around retraining, a drift-motivated update that is also an opportunity. (8) Model and data theft or reconnaissance (AML.T0024.002, T0000, T0002, T0007): the published architecture and datasets ease construction of proxy models for black-box transfer attacks (AML.T0005, T0043.002). Combined with the implicit weakness of an in-distribution-only validation, an adversary can aim at precisely the conditions where the model is least reliable. Consequence class: undetected weld degradation in radioactive piping, with leak or containment-integrity and radiological safety implications, and potentially a degraded evidence base for safeguards or integrity records.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, RWB-Net matters because it sits in a trusted accept/reject position on weld integrity in high-radiation reprocessing piping, where humans seldom re-inspect and access is costly. That makes it a low-visibility place to hide a degraded weld, or to build a latent condition for a later sabotage or release scenario. The pipeline has several attackable stages (denoiser, segmenter, fused handcrafted and deep classifier) and a multi-stage supply chain (published architecture, training data, vendor tooling). Even without an adversary, the claimed ~94% accuracy means roughly 6% of classifications are wrong, with unknown error asymmetry. In a low-contrast, noisy domain with scarce defect data, that gap is what an insider or sophisticated actor would exploit or time around. A nation-state would probably prefer easier targets such as the plant's IT/OT or the inspection robot, so the realistic risk is the AI quietly becoming the single point of trust for integrity assurance, not a headline attack.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity attacks on images or the model. An insider with access to the inspection data store, the robot/camera chain, or the model files could poison training data, plant a backdoor trigger, or alter weights so that specific defect signatures (for example certain crack or lack-of-fusion patterns) are denoised away or classified 'acceptable'. The denoiser is a particularly attractive point: it can suppress a defect before segmentation and classification ever see it, and a defect hidden at that stage evades both the HMM-refined localisation and the classifier. The resulting consequence is an undetected structural weakness in radioactive process piping, with a possible leak, loss of containment, or later exploitation by a second-stage sabotage action. (2) Supply chain compromise. A published research architecture, pretrained components, handcrafted-feature libraries, and framework dependencies could carry trojaned models or malicious packages into the plant's qualification environment. Because the pipeline combines several models and fusion logic, a compromise is hard to attribute and regress-test. (3) Evasion through physical or surface manipulation. Someone with access during maintenance or fabrication could apply surface treatments, coatings, or grinding patterns that exploit known weaknesses of low-contrast, noise-sensitive models, so a defective weld is passed. (4) Stepping stone: the inspection workstation and robot data path are a potential IT/OT foothold if they are connected to model-update or data-export channels. Model extraction or inversion of inspection imagery would also leak weld geometry and piping layout, which are sensitive facility information. IMPLICIT, adversary-exploitable: (a) Automation bias and skill fade (OP.C0101, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). With 0.41 s per image and hard-to-access piping, human reviewers will defer to the output, and an adversary can time an act of sabotage to periods when the human check has lapsed. (b) Data scarcity and low base rate (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.02). Real defects in reprocessing welds are rare, so training probably relies on augmented or surrogate data, and the 94% figure may not reflect rare, safety-significant defect classes. Error asymmetry (false accepts versus false rejects) is the key unknown, and a false accept is the dangerous direction. (c) Drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). Radiation-induced noise, camera degradation, lighting, and weld-geometry changes shift the input distribution, so the denoiser and segmenter degrade silently. Gradual drift also gives an adversary cover for tampering. (d) Opacity (OP.C0401). The attention, HMM, and adversarial-fusion layers make it hard to explain why a weld passed, which weakens forensic detection of manipulation. (e) Qualification gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0303). Academic validation does not equal nuclear-grade qualification, and absent change control (OP.C0502) any retraining or update becomes an unreviewed integrity pathway. (f) Concentration of trust in a single pipeline (OP.C0603): errors in the denoiser propagate to every downstream stage, which makes compromise of this one stage disproportionately valuable.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on rare-defect data scarcity, drift, denoiser-driven cascading errors, automation bias, qualification gaps, and evasion/poisoning/supply-chain attacks; I merged these into single threats. I dropped generic or weakly supported codes (e.g. T0031, T0059, T0012, T0112 and the speculative IT/OT stepping stone) and kept model extraction/proxy attack as a distinct, well-argued adversarial threat.

evidence.citation: "RWB-Net: A deep learning framework for automated weld bead segmentation and classification in nuclear reprocessing plants," Elsevier (ScienceDirect)
evidence.note: The journal article describes a model that was built and evaluated on weld-bead inspection images from nuclear reprocessing-plant pipelines. It combines a denoising network, an attention U-Net with HMM optimisation for localisation, and adversarial feature fusion for classification. The abstract reports about 94% classification accuracy and 0.41 s inference per image. I could not confirm the journal's exact name from the search result, so the publisher is given as Elsevier/ScienceDirect.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a silent false accept of a structurally significant weld defect (via evasion, poisoning, or implicit drift) on radioactive reprocessing pipework, which could lead to leak or loss of confinement and corrupt safety-case evidence; this is serious but indirect and mediated by other integrity controls, so just short of a direct release.

reproducibility.why: The implicit failure modes (rare-defect blind spots, drift, denoiser smoothing of fine cracks, automation bias) recur reliably whenever the stated conditions occur, though adversarial variants depend on access and conditions.

exploitability.why: Adversarial paths (tampering with image capture, poisoned fine-tuning data, trojaned model artifacts, supply chain) most plausibly need insider, maintenance-window, or fabrication access in a controlled nuclear facility, although the implicit weaknesses need no special access to occur.

affected_users.why: Impact spans all welds inspected by the pipeline and the safety-case record for the affected pipework, with errors cascading through coupled stages, but it is limited to the inspection function of one plant area rather than facility-wide systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, datasets, and accuracy are published, and the weaknesses (data scarcity, drift sensitivity, adversarial vulnerability of image models, transfer attacks) are well documented in the open literature for this class of AI system, so a capable outsider can readily infer them.

use_case: Facial-recognition-derived (principal-component-analysis-based) image classification that screens each fuel-rod sub-image from Digital Cerenkov Viewing Device images and gamma emission tomography reconstructions of spent fuel assemblies. It flags missing or substituted rods, and fusing the two data types raises single-missing-rod detection well above either alone. It supports safeguards partial-defect verification of stored spent fuel, runs in near real time, and keeps an information barrier between the measurement and the output.
incurred_insecurity:
This PCA-based rod classifier sits at a trust-concentration point in spent-fuel partial-defect verification, where a 'no defect' output substitutes for rod-level inspection of plutonium-bearing material. The main threats are evasion or tampering by a diverting operator or host state, poisoning of the reference gallery and software chain, a barrier that hides the evidence needed to detect either, and optimistic performance claims drawn from scarce, largely simulated data. The common consequence is false assurance about continuity of knowledge, not a radiological hazard, since the tool is advisory.

Signature-matched rod substitution -- adversarial
A dummy or modified rod whose Cerenkov and gamma appearance projects inside the low-dimensional, published PCA 'present rod' subspace passes as intact, and the 3% miss rate and 50-70% single-modality rates leave a patient adversary an exploitable margin. The operator's physical access to the assemblies and pool, and the ability to rehearse against a proxy built from the open literature, make this a realistic path to an undetected diversion.

Reference gallery and software-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with the baseline images of declared intact assemblies, the eigenbasis, thresholds, reconstruction or calibration software, or the fusion stage shifts the decision boundary so a chosen substitution pattern passes while known test cases still pass. A backdoored or trojaned classifier or barrier could return benign outputs that the inspector cannot cross-check.

Information barrier as concealment -- adversarial
The barrier hides raw measurements from the inspector, so a quietly corrupted or spoofed pass/fail output is hard to detect or independently reproduce. The barrier software also becomes its own authentication and supply-chain attack surface, with a possible hidden channel or falsified verdict.

Sensor degradation and alarm manipulation -- adversarial
Degrading or spoofing one modality, for example through water clarity, lighting or geometry affecting DCVD, pulls the fused score toward 'normal' or leaves only the weak single-modality rates. Induced false alarms or a denied sensor can also desensitise inspectors or cause the tool to be set aside just before a real diversion.

Scarce simulated training data and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
Few real diversion examples exist, so training and validation rest on simulated or surrogate defects and a handful of measured assemblies, and the 97% figure may not transfer across burnup, cooling time, assembly design, detector geometry or reconstruction artifacts. Eigenface-style methods are brittle to intensity, registration and pose shifts, producing silent misses or false alarms, and an adversary can choose assembly conditions that fall in the untested weak zone, such as low-contrast rods in highly cooled fuel.

Fusion fragility -- implicit, exploitable
The fusion gain depends on co-registered modalities and a fixed rule, so a degraded channel can make the fused result worse than either input without any visible fault. An adversary could deliberately degrade one channel to exploit this.

Over-trust, skill fade and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
A fast, headline-97% pass/fail verdict with opaque eigen-feature thresholds encourages inspectors to defer to it, erodes independent DCVD/GET interpretation skill, and treats a policy threshold as a technical fact. An adversary can time a diversion around this complacency and rely on the trust the barrier output creates.

Qualification and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
There is no AI-specific qualification regime or accepted authentication standard for ML verification software, and no formal revalidation when the reference library, calibration, reconstruction pipeline or fuel type changes. Updates could therefore pass unreviewed, giving an adversary a window to slip in changed models or data.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a safeguards-operations view, this is a partial-defect verification aid for stored spent fuel. An inspector uses it to decide whether an assembly still holds all its rods, or whether rods were diverted or substituted with dummies. The real hazard is a false negative that leads to a 'no defect' conclusion on an assembly that has been tampered with. That would give false assurance about continuity of knowledge over fissile material (plutonium-bearing spent fuel). The ~97% single-rod figure comes from a limited, largely simulated or lab-scale dataset. It is not a field-qualified detection probability, and the individual-instrument rates (50% DCVD, 70% GET) show how fragile detection is when one input degrades. Existing practice reduces the risk: inspectors still use the conventional DCVD and GET analysis, the tool is not the sole basis for a verdict, and IAEA safeguards conclusions rest on several measures. Even so, a quiet false-negative bias would let an inspector gain unearned confidence, and a diverter who understands the classifier's blind spots could exploit it.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Evasion by the diverting party or host state. The PCA/eigenface-style classifier is a linear, low-dimensional, well-understood method, so a rod substitute with the right Cerenkov/gamma signature (or a partial-length or low-burnup-mimicking dummy, or loading/cooling-time choices that shape the image) can land inside the 'present rod' subspace. The facility consequence is an undetected diversion judged as nominal. A facility operator being inspected is also an interested party with physical access to the assemblies, the pool conditions and possibly the instrument. This is a natural attack setting. Applicable codes: AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041. (2) Tampering with the image chain: manipulating reconstructions, the reference/training 'gallery' of intact-rod images, or the fusion stage so that one modality overrides the other. A poisoned or substituted reference set would shift every later verdict, and the information barrier can hide this from the inspector because they cannot see the underlying measurement. Applicable codes: AML.T0020, AML.T0018, AML.T0010, AML.T0070. (3) Information-barrier tradeoff: the barrier protects host-state sensitive data but also hides the classifier's inputs and reasoning from the inspector, so tampering or a fault is harder to detect. Authentication of the barrier and its software is a separate attack surface. Applicable codes: OP.C0401, AML.T0074. IMPLICIT: (4) Data scarcity and provenance. There are few real diverted-rod examples, so training and tests rely on simulated or surrogate defects. The 97% figure may not transfer to real assemblies with different burnup, cooling time, enrichment, assembly design, water clarity or camera geometry, and this is a heterogeneity and out-of-distribution failure. Applicable codes: OP.C0701, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202. (5) Residual error rates, especially false negatives for single-rod defects (3%) and for substitutions that mimic real rods. In addition, a detection rate that is not tied to a known false-alarm rate gives no usable confidence in partial-defect verification. A high headline number encourages automation over-trust and a decline in manual analysis skill. Applicable codes: OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0403. (6) Qualification and governance gaps: no AI-specific QA, no formal revalidation when the reference library, instrument calibration or fuel type changes, and no accepted IAEA authentication standard for ML-based verification software. Applicable codes: OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0303. (7) Availability and continuity: DCVD is limited to certain fuel cooling times and conditions, and the benefit from fusion depends on both data streams, so a degraded or missing sensor or a denial of service can leave the inspector with only the weak single-modality rates. Applicable codes: OP.C0204, AML.T0029. Overall consequence: a safeguards conclusion that diversion has not occurred when it has, or conversely false alarms that waste inspection resources or strain host-state relations. No direct radiological or criticality hazard follows, because the system is advisory, so the main harm is to the integrity of nonproliferation assurance.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a classical PCA/eigenface-style subspace classifier, so the main fragility is the data it learns from and the assumption that real measurements resemble it. Cerenkov and GET images of spent fuel are scarce, access-controlled and mostly simulated or taken from a few lab or field campaigns. The reported ~97% single-rod detection (versus ~50% DCVD and ~70% GET alone) comes from a narrow, controlled evaluation. It says little about performance across burnup, cooling time, enrichment, assembly design, pool water clarity, detector geometry, or reconstruction artifacts. Eigenface-style methods are also known to be brittle to illumination, pose and registration shifts, which map directly onto Cerenkov intensity decay, assembly misalignment and tomographic reconstruction variation. The information barrier keeps the measurement hidden, but the inspector must trust a pass/fail output that cannot easily be explained or independently checked.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT: (1) Data provenance and scarcity. Training and validation rely heavily on simulated or surrogate images and a handful of measured assemblies. Few real diversion or substitution examples exist, so the low base rate and the unrepresentative defect types give optimistic detection figures (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0202, OP.C0701, OP.C0701.02). (2) Drift and out-of-distribution failure. Cerenkov brightness falls as the fuel cools, and the PCA basis is fitted to a particular range of fuel and geometry. New assembly types, damaged or partial rods, different detectors, or a changed reconstruction pipeline shift the input off the learned subspace. Reconstruction error or distance thresholds then become miscalibrated, producing false alarms that erode trust, or silent misses (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303). (3) Fusion fragility. The gain from combining DCVD and GET depends on the two modalities being co-registered and on a fixed fusion rule. If one channel degrades (for example, a poor DCVD view), the fused score can be worse than either channel alone and the failure is not obvious (OP.C0603, OP.C0403). (4) Opacity and the information barrier. Hiding the raw measurement limits independent verification and reproducibility. Operator and inspector reliance on a binary result invites over-trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501). The partial-defect threshold is also a policy choice presented as a technical one.

ADVERSARIAL: (1) Evasion by a state operator who knows the method is PCA-based and published. They could substitute dummy rods or proxy material whose Cerenkov/gamma appearance projects close to the legitimate reference subspace. They could also exploit the fact that a single missing rod is the weakest case in single-modality tests (ATLAS AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0001, AML.T0000, AML.T0013, OP.C0702.01). (2) Poisoning or tampering with the reference or training set, the eigenvector basis, or the declared-assembly template (simulated or from operator declarations). This shifts the decision boundary so that a particular substitution pattern passes (AML.T0020, AML.T0018, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031). (3) Manipulation of the inputs before the classifier, such as tomographic reconstruction parameters, detector calibration, or image-pipeline software, which would corrupt both modalities consistently and bypass the fusion benefit (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0076, OP.C0502). (4) Model or threshold extraction through repeated inspections or leaked software, to tune a diversion (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0044). (5) Barrier compromise. The information barrier is itself software, so a hidden channel or trojaned barrier could leak sensitive fuel data or falsify the outcome. Pass/fail data from an AI model that is not independently authenticated could also be spoofed (AML.T0112, AML.T0073).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this classifier is a trust-concentration point in the safeguards verification chain for spent fuel. A pass result substitutes for human inspection of rod-level diversion, and diversion of spent fuel is the very outcome partial-defect verification is meant to deter. A state-level insider adversary (a facility operator, or a state hiding diversion from inspectors) does not have to defeat the physics. It is enough to shape the inputs, the reference library or the model so that a rod substitution looks like a normal assembly. The information barrier makes this worse, because it deliberately hides the measurement from the inspector. That makes a quietly wrong output hard to detect, and it limits independent checking of the model's behaviour.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by crafted or substituted content (AML.T0015, T0043.003). A PCA/eigen-image classifier is a low-dimensional linear model whose behaviour is well understood and can be replicated from published papers (T0000, T0005.001, T0043.000). An operator who controls the assembly could place dummy rods, or rods with modified emission or Cerenkov signatures, so that the projection falls inside the accepted subspace. The facility depends on the flag for partial-defect detection. A missed substitution leaves the inspector with false assurance and undermines the safeguards conclusion. The stated 97% figure is for a single missing rod, not for deliberate, signature-matched substitution. A 3% miss rate, plus the 50-70% single-modality rates when one sensor is degraded, gives a patient adversary an exploitable margin. (2) Manipulation of the reference or training data and the model (T0020, T0010.002, T0018.000, T0031). The classifier is only as trustworthy as the baseline images of declared intact assemblies. A host-state-supplied or operator-supplied reference set could embed the diversion in the baseline. A tampered eigenspace or threshold would also pass every test on known cases. (3) Information barrier as an attack surface. The barrier hides the raw data, so a compromised or backdoored classifier (T0018, T0043.004, T0010.001) could return a benign output with no inspector able to see the discrepancy. Software-supply-chain trust in the barrier and in the platform becomes the central assumption. Barrier authentication and certification may also lag behind AI-specific tampering. (4) Sensor-level and fusion attacks. Degrading or spoofing one of the two modalities (DCVD is sensitive to water clarity, lighting and geometry) could pull fusion output toward 'normal'. The adversary could also trigger false alarms (T0046, T0029) to desensitise inspectors, or to cause disuse of the tool just before a real diversion. (5) Reconnaissance and extraction from the open literature, which describes the method, sensors and performance (T0000.000, T0001), makes it easy to build a proxy model for evasion rehearsal. IMPLICIT, adversary-exploitable. (6) Over-trust and skill fade. A fast near-real-time automated verdict encourages inspectors to defer to it and lose independent interpretation skills (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Adversaries can time an attempt around that complacency. (7) Data scarcity and unrepresentative training data. There are few real diversion or missing-rod examples, so validation relies on simulated or surrogate defects (OP.C0701, OP.C0701.02, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202). Performance in the field across burnup, cooling time, assembly design and detector conditions is untested (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). Low-contrast rods in highly cooled assemblies are the weak points. (8) Opacity and qualification gaps. Eigen-feature thresholds are poorly explained to inspectors, and there is no AI-specific qualification regime for safeguards instrumentation (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0303). Model updates or recalibrations could pass without independent re-authentication. Overall, a sophisticated adversary would consider this use case worthwhile mainly as a way to defeat a deterrent. A state-level actor with insider access would find tampering with the reference data or the physical rod content easier than attacking the algorithm directly.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on signature-matched evasion, reference or model poisoning, the information barrier hiding tampering, scarce simulated data, and over-trust, so these were merged. I dropped speculative ATLAS codes with weak traceability (model extraction, T0112, T0076, T0070, T0024.002, T0001) and the sensor spoofing claims were kept as one adversarial threat.

evidence.citation: "Automated Defect Detection in Spent Nuclear Fuel Using Combined Cerenkov Radiation and Gamma Emission Tomography Data," Nuclear Technology (American Nuclear Society / Taylor & Francis), Vol. 204, No. 3
evidence.note: The paper reports classification algorithms adapted from facial recognition and applied to DCVD and gamma emission tomography images of spent fuel. It reports about 97% detection of a single missing rod with the two data types combined, against roughly 50% (DCVD) and 70% (GET) alone. The abstract does not name PCA. I took that detail from the accepted-manuscript version of the same work at OSTI (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1440901).

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is signature-matched rod substitution or gallery/software poisoning that yields undetected diversion of plutonium-bearing spent fuel, which is a loss of material control and safeguards falsification, even though there is no direct radiological hazard.

reproducibility.why: Once an adversary has operator-level access, evasion by in-subspace substitution and exploitation of out-of-distribution weak zones is fairly repeatable, but success depends on the specific assembly conditions, the sensor setup and the adversary's ability to build a good proxy.

exploitability.why: The credible severe paths need operator or host-state physical access to the assemblies and pool, or insider access to the reference gallery and software chain, and a patient adversary with state-level resources; routine external interaction is not enough.

affected_users.why: A compromised classifier or gallery would undermine continuity-of-knowledge assurance across all assemblies and inspections that use the tool, which is broad for safeguards verification, but it is confined to one verification function and does not propagate across coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The method, the PCA-based approach, the performance figures (97% fused, 50-70% single-modality) and the limits of the data are all in the open literature, so a capable outsider can infer the weak margins and the lack of qualification regime, though facility-specific configuration stays hidden.

use_case: Deep-learning (convolutional neural network) classification and regression of uranium enrichment from handheld M400 CZT gamma spectra of U3O8 samples and UF6 cylinders. It is intended to replace manual spectrum analysis by safeguards inspectors when verifying declared enrichments at enrichment and fuel-cycle facilities. It was trained and tested on measured spectra, and outperformed the GEM analysis code on UF6 cylinders.
incurred_insecurity:
A CNN that converts handheld M400 CZT spectra into an enrichment value, replacing manual inspector analysis, puts a safeguards conclusion on an opaque, narrowly trained model. The main threats are physical-presentation evasion by the inspected party, training-data and model-integrity compromise, and several implicit weaknesses: distribution shift, circular declared-value labels, missing uncertainty, inspector over-trust, and qualification gaps. The consequence is a false assurance, or a false alarm, about declared enrichment. It does not threaten plant safety. That false assurance could hide misdeclared or undeclared enrichment.

Physical evasion of the classifier -- adversarial
An operator controlling cylinder preparation, wall deposits, shielding, filler or measurement conditions can present items whose spectra push the non-physics-constrained CNN toward the declared enrichment, while a physics code or a human reading the spectrum would see an anomaly. The result is an undetected enrichment discrepancy recorded as a clean verification.

Training-data and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Poisoned or mislabeled GADRAS or measured training spectra, tampered weights, or a compromised update path could implant a spectral trigger that maps to a chosen enrichment, and average-case accuracy testing would not reveal it. Because the same model runs on every instrument, one compromise becomes a fleet-wide single point of trust.

Spectrum-path and device integrity -- adversarial
Tampering with spectrum files, preprocessing or the inference layer on the handheld or laptop can skew results without touching the detector. The same foothold can serve as a stepping stone into inspectorate systems.

Model extraction for offline evasion -- adversarial
A proxy model built from queries, leaked weights, or the published paper and open GADRAS material lets an adversary refine presentations offline and test them before an inspection. This also exposes safeguards-sensitive spectral signatures.

Simulation gap and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
Training on GADRAS-simulated spectra and a limited set of measured cylinders, wall thicknesses, detector units and enrichments leaves the CNN open to shortcut learning on geometry and gain. It also has no out-of-distribution flag, so it snaps intermediate or unseen enrichments to the nearest class or returns a confident biased value. An operator can steer samples toward these blind spots.

Circular labels and detector drift -- implicit, exploitable
Labels and test targets are operator-declared enrichments, so performance such as 0.03% error on UF6 cylinders measures agreement with declarations, not independent truth. CZT gain, temperature and aging drift with no monitoring or retraining pipeline further erode validity. An adversary can exploit the unmonitored degradation or a declaration-consistent bias to mask a deviation.

Over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
With manual analysis replaced and a low average error advertised, inspectors lose the habit of checking spectra against physical expectations and over-trust the number, even though tail errors matter more than the mean. An adversary can time or design a deception around this reduced scrutiny and the institutional authority the output carries.

Qualification, opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
An opaque, seed- and version-dependent CNN is hard to fit into safeguards authentication and certification, and inspectors cannot explain anomalous outputs. A deceptive state can exploit the resulting ambiguity to contest findings in a dispute.

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a safeguards-minded nuclear engineer, I see this as an independent verification tool: the inspector's CZT enrichment estimate is meant to confirm or challenge an operator's declaration at an enrichment plant. The danger is therefore not a physical accident but a false assurance that the declaration is correct, or a false alarm that wastes inspection resources. A CNN that replaces manual analysis removes the inspector's visual check of the spectrum, which today catches gross anomalies such as wrong peaks, shielding, or unusual matrices. The training data mix (GADRAS simulation plus measured spectra from a limited set of cylinders, wall thicknesses, and detector units) and the 'outperformed GEM' claim both leave a gap between lab or test-campaign performance and real field conditions. The consequences are in safeguards conclusions (diversion, undeclared enrichment, material substitution) rather than plant safety.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT WEAKNESSES. (1) Distribution shift and generalization: real cylinders vary in wall thickness, deposit and heel, temperature, detector gain drift and unit-to-unit variation, background, and shielding. Simulated GADRAS spectra and a finite measured set may not cover these (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202). The model could return a confident, plausible enrichment that is biased (for example, a low-enriched declaration 'confirmed' when the cylinder is not). (2) Discrete-class and regression overconfidence: a classifier trained on a fixed set of enrichments will snap an unseen or intermediate enrichment to the nearest class, and there is no native out-of-distribution flag (OP.C0401, OP.C0403). (3) Automation bias and skill fade: if the tool replaces manual analysis, inspectors lose the habit of cross-checking spectra against physical expectations (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). A 0.03% average error invites trust even though tail errors matter more for safeguards than the mean. (4) Qualification gap: safeguards instruments undergo formal authentication and certification, and an opaque, retrained CNN is hard to fit into that regime or to reproduce across versions (OP.C0501, OP.C0402, OP.C0303). (5) Material substitution and unusual matrices: the model verifies the spectrum, not the material's provenance, so mixtures, depleted/natural blends, or other uranium forms outside the training set may produce misleading output (OP.C0702.01, OP.C0701.01).

ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by a cheating operator or state: because the model is a black box with a known data basis (published paper), a diverter could craft sample presentation, such as added shielding, attenuating layers, internal liner or heel configurations, or masking sources, that pushes the CNN toward the declared enrichment while a human analyst would see an anomaly (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0001). Physical perturbation is the realistic attack surface, not digital perturbation. (2) Supply chain and model integrity: poisoned training data, a tampered model file, or a compromised update pipeline for handheld units could bias outputs in a way the inspectorate cannot see (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002). (3) Spectrum data injection or tampering between detector and analysis software, or by facility-supplied reference spectra used for calibration, could shift results (AML.T0043, AML.T0031). (4) Inspectorate-side impact: a manufactured discrepancy, such as a spoofed 'mismatch', can trigger false alarms, reputational harm, and diplomatic or contractual disputes (AML.T0048.001, AML.T0048.002). Existing practice that mitigates: the tool is typically one input among others (NDA, DA, sealing, mass balance, destructive sampling), so one bad estimate should not alone close a safeguards conclusion, provided inspectors keep the model advisory and retain a manual-analysis fallback and a periodic check against known standards.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a small-data, narrow-domain spectral regressor whose labels are declared enrichments rather than independently assayed ground truth, and whose training mixes GADRAS-simulated spectra with a limited set of measured M400 spectra. A CNN learns whatever correlates with the label in that corpus, which includes detector-unit response, cylinder wall and geometry, container and shielding, count time, temperature/gain drift and background. These nuisance factors are confounded with enrichment in a small campaign. The 0.03% average error on UF6 cylinders is an in-distribution figure, and nothing in the description says how the model behaves on out-of-distribution inputs such as new detector units, different cylinder types, matrix/age/impurity effects, or deliberately altered items. Used to replace manual analysis in a verification role, the model has no physics-based fallback and no calibrated uncertainty or OOD flag, so it is both implicitly brittle and an attractive target for an adversary who can influence the input.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Label and provenance weakness: training and test labels are operator-declared enrichments, so any bias in the declarations is baked into the model and is validated only against the same declarations. A model that agrees with declarations is not verified as independent. Simulated GADRAS spectra mixed with measured spectra add a sim-to-real gap and the risk that the network keys on simulation artefacts (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0201.05). (2) Small, homogeneous data and shortcut learning: a limited set of enrichments, cylinder types, detector units and sites means the CNN can latch onto geometry, wall thickness, gain or background features instead of the 185.7 keV and related line physics, which reduces generalisation to unseen facilities or enrichment values between the discrete classes (OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0701.01). (3) Drift and qualification mismatch: handheld CZT gain and resolution shift with temperature, aging and firmware or recalibration, and no retraining or monitoring pipeline is described. A static, offline evaluation does not qualify the model for field use under varying conditions (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). (4) Opacity and overconfidence: a point-estimate regressor without calibrated uncertainty produces a confident number for any spectrum, including nonsensical ones. Inspectors facing 0.03% accuracy claims may over-trust it or, once the replaced manual skills fade, be unable to second-guess it (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0403). (5) Non-repeatability: seed-dependent training and version changes can shift outputs on borderline cases, which is awkward for evidentiary safeguards conclusions (OP.C0402.01).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Evasion at inference: a facility operator or proxy who knows or can approximate the model class, via published papers and open GADRAS-based material, can craft physical or data-level perturbations, such as shielding, positioning, mixing or masking sources, or spectrum-file manipulation, so that a non-declared enrichment is read as the declared value. Because the CNN is not physics-constrained, it can be fooled by perturbations that a physicist would find implausible (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0043.002, AML.T0000, AML.T0005). (b) Training-data and supply-chain poisoning: if the model is retrained with inspection data, simulated data, or imported weights or libraries, a backdoor or label bias could be inserted that makes a specific spectral trigger map to a chosen enrichment (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). (c) Integrity of the deployed artefact and data path: tampering with the model file, preprocessing or spectrum files on the inspector's laptop or handheld could silently skew results (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, AML.T0031). (d) Model theft and extraction of the safeguards-sensitive spectral signatures and thresholds (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035). The consequence is a false-negative or false-positive safeguards finding on declared enrichment, which can mask undeclared enrichment or cause unwarranted escalation, and can erode confidence in IAEA-style verification.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view this tool sits at the verification boundary: it converts a handheld CZT spectrum into the enrichment number an inspector records against the operator's declaration. If it replaces manual analysis, the inspector's independent judgment (the main defense against a deceptive operator) is replaced by an opaque model whose output carries institutional authority. A state-level proliferator or a facility-level diverter would not need to defeat the inspectorate's physics. It would only need to shape what the instrument sees, or what the model learned, so that a non-declared enrichment reads as declared. Even without an adversary, a narrow model trained on a limited set of geometries, cylinder types and enrichments, with partly simulated training data, has blind spots that a deceptive operator could learn to sit in. This is a high-value, low-cost target compared with attacking the plant itself, because it attacks the trust in the verification conclusion rather than the material.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion of the model by the inspected party (AML.T0015, T0043, T0041). The operator controls the sample presentation, cylinder preparation, wall deposits, shielding or filler, and the measurement environment. A CNN is sensitive to spectral features that a physics-based code like GEM treats explicitly (attenuation, peak ratios). An operator who can probe how the model responds to its own samples could find presentations that move the output toward the declared value. The failure mechanism is non-robustness of a learned classifier to input perturbation outside its training manifold. What depends on it is the declared-versus-measured comparison. The consequence is an undetected enrichment discrepancy, which is a safeguards failure (misdeclared or diverted material, or undeclared HEU production) that looks like a clean verification. (2) Training-data and model supply-chain compromise (T0010.002/.003, T0018, T0020, T0059, T0043.004). The model is trained on GADRAS-simulated and measured spectra. Poisoned or mislabeled data, or a backdoor keyed to a specific spectral feature, would let the model report a chosen enrichment on trigger. This is a stealthy insider or supplier pathway, and the backdoor is hard to find through accuracy testing on the average case. It would exist across every instrument carrying the same model, which is a fleet-wide single point of trust (OP.C0602). (3) Handheld device and software integrity (T0010.000/.001, T0112, T0025). The M400 and its laptop or tablet software become a new attack surface. Tampering at the spectrum file, preprocessing or inference layer could alter results without touching the detector, and it could also be a stepping stone into inspectorate networks. (4) Model extraction and reconnaissance (T0024.002, T0005, T0063). A proxy model built from repeated queries or leaked weights lets an adversary optimize evasion offline (T0043.000/.002) and test it before an inspection. Published papers and open GADRAS data help here (T0000, T0002). IMPLICIT, EXPLOITABLE. (5) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102). If the tool is meant to reduce inspector burden, manual analysis atrophies, and inspectors lose the ability to spot implausible outputs. A 0.03% average error invites over-trust, and an adversary can time a deception around that reduced scrutiny. The consequence is misplaced confidence in a conclusion that carries political weight. (6) Narrow-distribution and qualification gaps (OP.C0302, C0302.03, C0201.01/.02, C0202, C0701.01, C0303, C0501). Enrichment values, cylinder types, wall thickness, temperature, detector aging and detector-to-detector variation outside the trained range may degrade results silently. Accuracy reported against declared enrichments is circular if the declarations were wrong. Benchmarking against GEM on UF6 cylinders does not establish performance on adversarially presented items. Unrepresentative simulation data can also create exploitable gaps. (7) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, C0402). Inspectors cannot explain an anomalous output, which undermines its evidentiary value in a dispute with the state, and a deceptive party can exploit that ambiguity to contest findings. Mitigation direction: keep a physics-based code and inspector review as independent cross-checks, use the model as a screening flag rather than the sole determination, run out-of-distribution detection, protect data and model provenance, and combine with other verification methods such as NDA and destructive assay.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on physical-presentation evasion, training/supply-chain poisoning, and the implicit cluster of distribution shift, over-trust and qualification gaps. I merged overlapping items and dropped weakly grounded codes (reputational-harm ATLAS codes, T0059, T0112, T0025, T0000/T0001 and OP.C0702.01) because the text does not clearly instantiate them.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning framework for predicting uranium enrichments from M400 CZT gamma spectra," Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A (Oak Ridge National Laboratory; J.W. Bae and J. Hu)
evidence.note: ORNL authors built a deep-learning framework, using GADRAS-generated and measured M400 spectra, that classifies discrete enrichments and regresses enrichment values for U3O8 samples and UF6 cylinders. It was tested against declared enrichments, with about 0.03% average absolute error on UF6 cylinders, and compared favourably with the GEM code. The paper presents it as a way to reduce the burden on safeguards inspectors.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is physical-presentation evasion or model/training-data compromise producing false assurance about declared enrichment, which is a safeguards falsification and could hide misdeclared or undeclared enrichment (no plant-safety impact, but the safeguards category is maximal).

reproducibility.why: Non-physics-constrained CNNs reliably show shortcut learning and OOD blind spots once presentation or distribution conditions are met, but a specific evasion or poisoning outcome depends on the operator's knowledge of the model and the inspection conditions.

exploitability.why: The most credible evasion needs control over item preparation, which the inspected state has, plus meaningful knowledge of the model's behavior. Supply-chain poisoning or device tampering requires insider or state-level resources, so the class is generally difficult to exploit.

affected_users.why: The same model runs across all handheld instruments and inspections, so a model-level compromise or systematic bias becomes a fleet-wide single point of trust affecting safeguards conclusions across facilities, though it remains confined to enrichment verification.

discoverability.why: The paper, open GADRAS material and the general literature on adversarial and OOD weaknesses of CNNs make the vulnerability class and its likely blind spots inferable by a capable outsider, though system-specific details remain non-public.

use_case: Multitask 3D convolutional neural network that unfolds neutron noise recorded by a sparse set of in-core neutron detectors (48 positions). It classifies the type of in-core anomaly (an absorber of variable strength, axially travelling coolant-temperature perturbations, fuel assembly vibrations, control rod vibrations, core barrel vibrations) and localizes it, for on-line core diagnostics and monitoring of a reactor. The network was trained and validated on frequency-domain neutron noise simulated with the CORE SIM+ two-group diffusion core simulator.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory neutron-noise diagnostic classifies and localizes in-core anomalies using a 3D CNN trained and validated only on CORE SIM+ simulation. Its main threats are a sim-to-real and closed-set failure that yields confident but wrong diagnoses, silent drift, opacity and qualification gaps, and operator over-trust. Adversarially, the main threats are manipulation of the detector-to-model data path and compromise of the model or training pipeline. Because independent protection and monitoring layers cap direct consequences, the realistic harm is misdirected or delayed maintenance and inspection decisions, and gradual erosion of those layers if the tool becomes the trusted primary diagnostic.

Sim-to-real and closed-set failure -- implicit, exploitable
The 0.11% classification and ~4 cm localization errors measure inversion of an idealized diffusion simulator, not performance on real noise, compound anomalies or unseen events such as loose parts, flow blockage or instrument faults. With no abstain class, such inputs are forced into one of five labels with a plausible location, so real fuel, control-rod or barrel degradation can be misdiagnosed or missed. An adversary could time or shape a physical off-nominal vibration source to fall into a class the model reads as benign, relying on its false confidence.

Drift and detector degradation -- implicit, exploitable
Burnup, cycle and loading changes, xenon transients and detector aging or failure across only 48 channels shift the perturbation-to-noise transfer function, so accuracy degrades silently without a recalibration regime. An adversary could hide a gradual signal manipulation, or a failed or spoofed channel, inside this degraded and poorly characterized input band.

Opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The CNN gives no attribution to detectors or physics, is non-deterministic across training, and has no AI-specific qualification basis, with a likely non-safety classification and thinner cyber controls. Operators cannot judge whether a localization is credible, and retraining or model changes are hard to audit, so an insider or attacker alteration of the model or thresholds would be hard to detect.

Over-trust, skill fade and alarm fatigue -- implicit, exploitable
Clean class-and-location labels invite deference and let conventional noise-analysis expertise lapse, while frequent spurious calls on real data push staff toward ignoring or disabling the tool. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust to make a physical fault go uncross-checked, or induce false alarms to open a window of reduced vigilance.

Detector-path input manipulation -- adversarial
An attacker with access to detector signal conditioning, the acquisition and FFT pipeline or the model inputs could add small structured perturbations to the noise spectra that flip class or shift localization, for example reading a control-rod or core-barrel vibration as a benign absorber or fabricating a vibration diagnosis. No adversarial robustness or input-integrity checks exist, and each channel has high leverage in the sparse 48-position array.

Model, training-data and supply-chain compromise -- adversarial
Poisoned simulated training sets, tampered simulator parameters, weights or software dependencies could embed trigger-conditioned blind spots, such as a fault never reported at certain locations. Simulation is the only ground truth and no plant data exist to cross-check it, so tampering is hard to detect, and reuse of one trained model across sites could propagate a compromise.

Proxy-model and false-alarm abuse -- adversarial
The published architecture and the open CORTEX/CORE SIM+ literature let an adversary build a proxy model offline and craft transferable adversarial inputs. Repeated injected or induced spurious anomalies could force needless inspections or outages and erode confidence in the diagnostic.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory on-line diagnostic: it does not trip the reactor or move control rods, so a wrong output does not directly cause harm. The harm path runs through operator and engineering decisions. A false 'fuel assembly vibration' or 'core barrel vibration' call could trigger unnecessary investigation or a power reduction, and a missed or misclassified real anomaly could delay inspection while mechanical degradation continues. The core-protection system, the in-core instrumentation limits, and the existing vibration-monitoring and surveillance practice (conventional noise analysis, ex-core detectors, accelerometers, chemistry and thermal-hydraulic trends) are independent barriers, which caps near-term consequences. The main weakness is that the 0.11% classification error and ~4 cm localization error come from CORE SIM+ two-group diffusion simulations. They say little about measured plant noise, which includes instrument noise, unmodelled physics, and operating states that differ from the simulation. The system is also hard to qualify, with a small sparse detector set, five fixed classes, and no 'unknown' class.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: the model was trained and validated only on frequency-domain noise from a two-group diffusion simulator, so measurement artifacts, detector degradation or failure, cycle burnup, xenon transients, and plant-specific transfer functions are all out of distribution. Reported accuracy is therefore not evidence of field performance, and the result could be confidently wrong, with silent drift across cycles and fuel loadings (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). (2) Closed-set and low base rate: real anomalies are rare, can occur together, or fall outside the five classes (for example loose parts, flow blockage, or an instrument fault). The softmax-style output forces a plausible label and location for any input, so spurious or merged anomalies are misdiagnosed (OP.C0202, OP.C0403, OP.C0301). (3) Opacity and qualification: a 3D CNN gives no physics-based explanation, and an operator cannot judge whether a localization is credible. Model changes and retraining sit awkwardly under I&C software qualification, even for a non-safety diagnostic, and the model may be reused across plants (OP.C0401, OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0602). (4) Automation bias and skill fade: when the tool is usually right, as in the benign cases, staff may defer to it or let conventional noise-analysis expertise lapse. The opposite failure is disuse after false alarms (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (5) Detector dependency: with only 48 positions, failed or drifting detectors change the input pattern, and a degraded input could look like an anomaly or mask one (OP.C0204).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. Because the system is advisory, the realistic goal for an adversary is to erode trust or steer maintenance decisions, not to damage the core directly. Manipulating detector signals or the acquisition and data pipeline, or applying adversarial perturbations to the noise spectra, could suppress a real mechanical-degradation indication or fabricate a vibration or absorber diagnosis (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Tampering with the model, training data, or simulated training sets, or supply-chain compromise of the model, simulator outputs, or software dependencies, could plant a backdoor that misclassifies specific spectra (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0043.004). Repeated false alarms could force unneeded outages or inspections, or cause staff to disable the tool (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). These attacks matter most when combined with an independent physical degradation, a cyber intrusion that also hides conventional indications, or an accident timed around a maintenance or outage decision. The existing independent protection and monitoring layers make a standalone consequence unlikely. The residual risk comes from gradual erosion of those layers if the tool becomes the primary, trusted diagnostic, or from the economic cost of false actions.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, the central fragility is that this model has only ever seen CORE SIM+ two-group diffusion output in the frequency domain, with perturbations injected as clean, idealized point or line sources into a known, fixed core model. The 0.11% classification error and ~4 cm localization error measure how well the CNN inverts the simulator. They say nothing about performance on real plant signals. Real detector data carry non-Gaussian measurement noise, detector sensitivity drift and failures, ex-core and thermal-hydraulic noise sources, multiple simultaneous perturbations, burnup- and cycle-dependent cross-sections, and an unknown real-world anomaly base rate. The multitask architecture over a sparse 48-position input is a heavily underdetermined inverse problem that the network has implicitly regularized to the simulator's perturbation priors, so inputs outside those priors will still produce confident, in-vocabulary outputs. Because there is no 'none of the above' class, the classifier cannot flag novelty.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Sim-to-real gap and OOD failure. The training data are purely simulated, with no field or lab-measured data, so the model is untested against real noise spectra, simultaneous or compound anomalies, detector dropouts and fuel-cycle evolution. Out-of-distribution inputs get forced into one of five anomaly classes with a plausible location. Consequences are false positives that cause unnecessary investigation or outages, and false negatives or misclassification that mask a real fuel, control-rod or barrel degradation mechanism. (2) Drift and concept change. Cross-sections, burnup, loading patterns and detector aging shift the transfer function between perturbation and noise. Without a recalibration and retraining regime, or a requalified simulator, accuracy degrades silently, and the simulated 0.11% error gives operators false precision. (3) Closed-set classification and a missing calibrated uncertainty or abstain option. Operators may over-trust the outputs (automation bias), especially since the network is opaque (no attribution to which detectors drove the call). The simulator-derived error figures are likely to be quoted as operational accuracy. (4) Qualification and repeatability gap. Training non-determinism, no established validation basis for a diagnostic that feeds O&M decisions, and weak provenance for the simulated training corpus (model version, parameters, perturbation ranges). Per-plant reactor-specific simulators make the model non-transferable, and there is a risk of fleet-wide reuse of a model tuned to one core geometry.

ADVERSARIAL threats. (5) Input manipulation. An adversary with access to detector signal chains or the data acquisition network could craft or inject low-amplitude noise patterns that steer the classification or localization, hiding a real anomaly or fabricating one. The 3D CNN has no adversarial robustness testing, and frequency-domain inputs are easy to perturb in a structured way. A compromised or spoofed detector channel is especially effective in a sparse 48-sensor array, where each channel has high leverage. (6) Training pipeline and supply chain. Poisoning or backdoor insertion in the simulated training set, the simulator configuration, or pretrained weights and framework dependencies could embed trigger-conditioned blind spots, such as a class that is never reported at certain locations. Because the training data are simulated, tampering with the simulator inputs is hard to detect afterwards. (7) Model and data exposure. The published architecture, the open CORTEX/CORE SIM+ literature and the simulation parameters make it easy to build a proxy model and craft transferable adversarial inputs offline. They also reveal the simulator's assumptions about the core, so the model itself leaks core-design information. (8) Evasion by timing. An adversary or a fault that falls into the model's blind spots (compound or low-amplitude anomalies) can exploit the system's reliance on its trained taxonomy for the duration of a cycle.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this is a read-only diagnostic advisor, so a nation-state would not target it for direct reactor effect; the real concern is that it concentrates diagnostic trust in a channel that is easy to bypass and hard to audit. It was trained and validated only on CORE SIM+ frequency-domain simulation, so its behavior on real plant noise (instrument noise, unmodeled perturbations, plant-specific heterogeneity) is unqualified. The reported 0.11% classification error therefore says nothing about field reliability, and an adversary or ordinary insider could exploit that gap. Its most plausible adversarial uses are as a stepping stone or a deception tool: shaping what operators believe about core state, masking a mechanical fault or sabotage as a benign anomaly class, or inducing false alarms that waste outage time and erode vigilance. Just as relevant is the non-adversarial failure that an adversary could time an action around, namely a confident but out-of-distribution misclassification that operators over-trust.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: (1) Evasion or manipulation of the detector-to-model data path (adversarial). Anyone with write access to detector signal conditioning, the noise acquisition and FFT pipeline, or the model's input features could shape the spectra. Because the 3D CNN is a learned mapping, small structured perturbations could flip the class or shift the localization (for example, labeling a control-rod or core-barrel vibration as a benign absorber, or the reverse) without tripping conventional limits. The AI failure mechanism is adversarial-input sensitivity plus the absence of input-integrity checks. What depends on it is on-line core diagnostics that inform maintenance and operating decisions. The consequence is delayed detection or misdiagnosis of a real mechanical degradation, or a fabricated anomaly that drives unnecessary shutdowns or inspections. The sparse 48-detector input makes spoofing a handful of channels more consequential. (2) Supply chain and model integrity (adversarial). The model, the training pipeline and the simulator (CORE SIM+) are research-grade artifacts from a collaborative project. Poisoned training data or simulation parameters, or a tampered model file, would be hard to detect because the simulated-data ground truth is the only reference and no plant data exists to cross-check. Fleet or site reuse of the trained model could propagate one compromise widely. (3) Insider and trust concentration. A diagnostic that outputs a clean class and location label invites operators to defer to it. An insider who can alter or time model updates, thresholds or the retraining set can steer attention away from a location or fault type. The opacity of a CNN makes post-hoc audit of such changes difficult. (4) Implicit sim-to-real gap (no adversary required, but exploitable). The model is trained only on simulation, which brings simulated-data provenance limits, a static versus dynamic qualification mismatch, and likely drift as fuel burnup, core loading and detector degradation change the noise. It was not trained on multiple simultaneous anomalies or on unseen anomaly types, so a closed-set classifier will force novel events into one of five labels with false confidence. Over-trust and skill fade in manual noise analysis mean that humans may stop cross-checking. An adversary who understands these blind spots could time a physical action (for example, an off-nominal vibration source) to fall into a class the model reads as benign. (5) Alarm-fatigue exploitation. A system that produces frequent spurious classifications on real data will be tuned down or ignored, which opens a window for an attacker. (6) Governance. There is no AI-specific qualification regime, and the model's security classification is likely treated as non-safety, so it may sit with weaker cyber controls than the reactor protection systems it informs. Connecting it to plant networks creates a new pathway for lateral movement even if the model itself is a low-value target.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real/closed-set gap, input manipulation of the detector path, training/supply-chain compromise, over-trust and qualification gaps; I merged overlapping items and kept the AI engineer's proxy-model threat and the security specialist's alarm-fatigue point as distinct. I dropped AML.T0012 and AML.T0029 as insufficiently tied to a specific mechanism, and the generic OP.C0301 and OP.C0504 as restating other threats.

evidence.citation: "Neutron Noise-Based Anomaly Classification and Localization Using Machine Learning," EPJ Web of Conferences (EDP Sciences), 2021, doi:10.1051/EPJCONF/202124721004; link is an academia.edu copy
evidence.note: The paper proposes a 3D CNN that takes in-core neutron-detector noise and identifies the type of reactor-core perturbation and where it is. It was tested only on simulated data, with a reported classification error of at most 0.11% and a localization error of under about 4 cm. It was developed under the Euratom CORTEX project, and the authors said at the time that tests on real plant data would follow.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a misdiagnosis or backdoored model that causes a real fuel, control-rod or barrel degradation to be missed or misdirected; independent protection layers cap direct consequences, so the harm is delayed or misdirected maintenance and minor safety-margin erosion rather than a release.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real and closed-set misclassification of unseen or compound anomalies and silent drift occur fairly reliably once the model is run on real plant data, but targeted adversarial or poisoning outcomes depend on specific conditions and access.

exploitability.why: Adversarial paths need access to the detector signal chain, the acquisition pipeline, or the model and training pipeline, which means insider or privileged position; only the false-alarm and proxy-model aspects need less, and physical off-nominal sources are hard to shape.

affected_users.why: The tool is an advisory diagnostic across the whole core's detector array, and a reused model could propagate a compromise across sites, but independent protection layers limit the coupled-system impact.

discoverability.why: The architecture, the simulator and the sim-only validation are published in open literature (CORTEX/CORE SIM+), and sim-to-real, drift and adversarial-example weaknesses are well documented for this class of CNN, though system-specific data-path details remain non-public.

use_case: Weighted-ensemble regression CNN that localizes damage (stress-corrosion-crack-type acoustic sources) on stainless-steel spent fuel storage canisters from single-sensor acoustic emission signals. Waveform, FFT spectrum and spectral-entropy data are fused, and CWT and STFT coefficients are fed to the network. It outputs the damage coordinates, to support long-term structural health monitoring of dry storage canisters with a minimal number of sensors.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places a single-sensor, learned acoustic-emission localizer in the role of primary evidence that a spent fuel canister's confinement boundary is healthy. It incurs implicit risk from lab-to-field generalization failure, decades-long drift, a regressor that cannot reject unfamiliar inputs, and weak qualification. It also incurs adversarial risk from manipulation of the one signal chain, poisoning of the model or its data, and chaff-driven denial or alarm fatigue. Harm requires the output to displace independent inspection, but the concentration of trust in one low-redundancy channel is what makes each threat consequential.

Lab-to-field generalization failure -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained on bench-scale plate data (simulated or pencil-lead-type sources), while real welded, curved canisters in ventilated overpacks have different geometry, dispersion, reflections and attenuation, and labeled SCC events are rare. Coordinates can therefore be confidently wrong, either misdirecting inspection or leaving a real flaw unlocalized. An adversary can rely on this unvalidated gap, treating the monitoring as non-credible and acting where its output is least trustworthy.

Long-term drift and data continuity -- implicit, exploitable
Couplant aging, sensor re-mounting, thermal cycling, surface deposits, changing noise, and library or hardware changes over decades shift the waveform, CWT and STFT feature statistics, so predictions degrade silently with little ground truth to detect it. An adversary could hide gradual tampering with the signal, baselines or retraining data inside this expected degradation, since it is indistinguishable from ordinary drift.

No uncertainty or rejection capability -- implicit, exploitable
The regression head returns a plausible point coordinate for any input, including thermal cracking, flow noise, vibration or crafted signals, and has no 'not a crack' class or calibrated uncertainty. This yields false localizations and alarm fatigue, and 'no damage localized' may be read as 'no damage'. An adversary can inject benign-looking transients to desensitize operators, or rely on the misplaced trust to slip a real event through.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The weighted ensemble, multi-feature fusion, and stochastic training make results hard to explain, reproduce or qualify, and plate-level accuracy is not an accepted basis for aging-management or regulatory decisions. Over-trust and skill fade in a lightly staffed site may reduce manual NDE follow-up. A tampered model or pipeline change would be hard to distinguish from legitimate retraining or update.

Single-sensor input manipulation -- adversarial
With one sensor and no cross-channel consistency check, an adversary with physical or cable-level access can inject or replay crafted acoustic or electrical waveforms, or perturb the CWT and STFT inputs, to shift predicted coordinates, mask a genuine crack, or fabricate phantom damage. The consequence is a false negative or misplaced SCC indication on a confinement barrier, delaying inspection and breaking continuity of knowledge.

Model, data and pipeline poisoning -- adversarial
Poisoned or backdoored training and calibration data, pretrained components, a tampered ensemble, or a compromised vendor update to the preprocessing code can embed a blind spot at particular coordinates or frequencies. Scarce ground truth and CNN opacity let this persist undetected for years, and tampering with stored baselines or the monitoring record can erode integrity gradually.

Chaff flooding and denial of monitoring -- adversarial
Noise or chaff injection, or compromise of remote or cloud analytics, can saturate the model with spurious localizations or interrupt monitoring in a way that mimics sensor failure. This can be timed to cover a physical action at the cask while operators are desensitized.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the facility side, this is a monitoring-and-advisory tool for dry cask storage canisters, which are passive, heavily shielded and hard to inspect. SCC detection and localization therefore directly drives inspection scheduling, repair or overpack decisions, and the licensee's aging-management case. The authors state that adaptation to real canisters is still needed, so the main implicit risk is a model trained on plate-level lab data (likely pencil-lead breaks or simulated sources) being trusted on real welded, curved canisters with different geometry, wave modes, attenuation, coupling, temperature and background noise. Consequences are asymmetric. A false localization or false negative can give false assurance that the canister is sound while SCC progresses, or it can send inspection effort to the wrong location. A false positive causes costly, dose-bearing inspection. Safeguards already exist, including periodic visual or ultrasonic and eddy-current inspection, temperature and leak monitoring, and a conservative aging-management program, so a single wrong output rarely causes a release by itself. Harm would require the AI to displace, defer or de-prioritize those independent measures through automation bias or budget pressure.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT: (1) Sim-to-real and geometry generalization failure. Training on flat plates with artificial sources does not transfer to curved, welded canister shells with heat-affected zones, stiffeners, or a concrete overpack or vent environment. A single sensor localizing from waveform features is highly sensitive to propagation path, dispersion and reflections, so coordinate errors can be large and confidently stated. (2) Drift: sensor coupling degradation, thermal cycling, aging of adhesives or waveguides, and changing environmental noise (wind, rain, ventilation, electronics) shift signal statistics over decades, while true SCC events are rare. This creates a low base rate, little field-validated ground truth and little way to detect silent degradation. (3) Regression models output a point coordinate with no calibrated uncertainty and no way to flag out-of-distribution inputs. Operators may over-trust it, and a 'no damage localized' result may be read as 'no damage'. Opacity of the CNN limits defensibility in a regulatory aging-management submission. (4) Qualification gap: no established framework for qualifying ML-based AE localization as a monitoring basis for a canister, and ensemble weights or retraining add change-control burdens. ADVERSARIAL: (5) Integrity attack on the AE data stream, where an adversary with access to the sensor, cabling or acquisition system injects or replays crafted waveforms or noise. Adversarial perturbations to the CWT/STFT inputs could suppress real crack signatures or fabricate events at chosen coordinates, hiding degradation or triggering unnecessary intervention. Physical injection of acoustic noise near the sensor is an alternative path. (6) Supply-chain or training-data poisoning of the model or its calibration data by a vendor or contractor, which biases localization in particular regions, for example near welds, and is hard to detect because ground truth is scarce. (7) Denial or degradation of the monitoring service through chaff or noise flooding or compromise of remote or cloud analytics, which causes a loss of monitoring continuity that mimics sensor failure. Safeguards consequence is limited: spent-fuel monitoring is not a material-accountancy function, but it could undermine confidence, inspection scheduling and public or regulatory trust. Mitigation: use the AI as an advisory layer only, keep independent inspection intervals, require periodic in-situ calibration against known sources, apply OOD and uncertainty flags, and use data-diode or isolated acquisition.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a regression CNN trained on bench-scale AE data (pencil-lead breaks, simulated sources, or lab-induced events on a stainless plate) and meant to run for decades on real dry-storage canisters. The model learns a mapping from single-sensor waveform to coordinates that depends on plate geometry, thickness, boundary reflections, sensor coupling, temperature and the wave-propagation environment. None of these are the same on a welded, curved canister inside a ventilated overpack, so the main exposure is a large lab-to-field distribution shift. The authors themselves say it needs adapting to real canisters. A single sensor also gives no redundancy or physical cross-check, because localization comes entirely from learned multipath signatures. A regression head always returns a plausible coordinate, even for inputs it has never seen, and the output carries no native uncertainty or rejection mechanism. Adversaries and ordinary environmental change therefore both act on a fragile, opaque mapping with very little data to validate it against.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Lab-to-field generalization failure and data provenance. Training data is simulated or bench-measured (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0203), while real SCC events on aged canisters are rare, slow, and not available as labeled ground truth (OP.C0202). Without labeled field events the model cannot be validated for its actual task, and a confident but wrong coordinate can send inspection to the wrong place or hide a real flaw location. (2) Drift over a decades-long service life (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03). Sensor couplant aging, sensor replacement or re-mounting, temperature cycling, changing surface condition and deposits, and differences between canister designs all shift waveform, spectral and CWT/STFT features. The model's predictions then degrade silently, and retraining needs ground truth that is hard to obtain. (3) Background noise and non-damage acoustic sources such as thermal cracking, convective flow and mechanical vibration were probably not in training. A regressor has no 'not a crack' class, so any transient is mapped to a coordinate, which produces false localizations and alarm fatigue (OP.C0102, OP.C0403). (4) Weak verification. The weighted ensemble, the fusion of several feature types, and stochastic training and inference make results hard to reproduce or qualify (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). Coordinate accuracy on a plate is not a qualified basis for structural-integrity or regulatory decisions, and over-trust by operators who have little ground truth is likely (OP.C0101.04). A localization error that is merely unvalidated can also lead operators to dismiss a true signal (OP.C0101.05). (5) Data continuity and software hygiene. The system needs years of consistent sensor data and a pinned preprocessing pipeline (OP.C0204, OP.C0502). Changes to the CWT/STFT libraries or acquisition hardware alter inputs without any visible fault.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Input-level evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). An adversary with physical or cable-level access to the sensor or its signal chain can inject or replay crafted waveforms, whether acoustic or electrical. These can shift the predicted coordinates away from a real defect, mask a genuine event, or create phantom damage. Gradient-based perturbations are likely to transfer, because the CWT/STFT inputs are low-dimensional and the architecture is a standard CNN (AML.T0043.002, AML.T0005).
