A single sensor with no redundancy makes this much easier. (2) Training-data and model supply chain (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000). Public datasets, pretrained backbones, or contractor-supplied training and calibration data could be poisoned or backdoored, for example with a trigger waveform signature that suppresses detection. Because ground truth is scarce, such tampering could go undetected for years. (3) Integrity of the monitoring record (AML.T0031, AML.T0059). Tampering with stored baselines, calibration sets or retraining data erodes model integrity gradually and in a way that looks like ordinary drift. (4) Denial of the AI service (AML.T0029, AML.T0046). Chaff or noise injection can swamp the model with spurious localizations, and this can be timed to cover a physical or safeguards-relevant activity at the cask. Together, these failures degrade the integrity of the monitoring evidence for the canister, and they could also erode confidence in aging-management and containment assurance.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view this is a low-value direct target but a meaningful enabler of timing and concealment. Dry storage canisters are long-lived, sealed, hard-to-inspect assets. If single-sensor AE localization becomes the primary SCC monitoring channel with few sensors, its output becomes the main evidence that the confinement boundary is healthy. That concentrates trust in one inexpensive, low-redundancy signal chain. An adversary with insider or supply-chain access does not need to breach the canister. They only need the monitoring to say 'no damage' or 'damage is elsewhere', or to flood it with false localizations that erode operator vigilance before a real event. The authors state the method still needs adapting to real canisters, so a gap exists between the lab-plate validation and the field deployment. Both an adversary and a natural failure can exploit that gap.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Sensor-channel manipulation. The model relies on a single AE sensor, so there is no cross-sensor consistency check. Injected or masked acoustic energy, coupling changes, or tampering with the acquisition chain can shift predicted coordinates or suppress detection (AML.T0043 / T0015 / T0041). A physical-access insider could also mimic benign signatures. The consequence is a false-negative or misplaced SCC indication on a confinement barrier, which delays inspection and undermines safety and safeguards continuity-of-knowledge. (2) Chaff and alarm-fatigue timing (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). Spurious localizations or saturated output desensitize operators, and an adversary or saboteur can time an action around the resulting complacency (OP.C0102). (3) Supply-chain and model integrity. Poisoned training data, a tampered weighted-ensemble model or preprocessing code (CWT/STFT/fusion pipelines), or a compromised vendor update (AML.T0010, T0018, T0020, T0031) could embed a blind spot at particular coordinates or frequencies, which is hard to detect given CNN opacity. (4) Insider falsification of the monitoring record. Long-term SHM data is a trusted record, and manipulating it could hide degradation or support a false narrative about canister condition. Remote or cloud analytics would widen the attack surface (OP.C0601). Dry storage sites are often lightly staffed, which raises the value of this channel to an attacker.

IMPLICIT, and exploitable. (a) Lab-to-field gap. The model was trained and tested on plate data with simulated or pencil-lead-style sources, while real canisters have curved geometry, welds, heat-affected zones, thermal gradients, ventilation noise, and decades of aging. This produces out-of-distribution and drift failure (OP.C0302, C0201.01, C0203, C0202) and possibly confident but wrong coordinates, because regression CNNs give a point estimate with no inherent uncertainty (OP.C0401, C0403). Real SCC events are rare, which means little real-event data and an inability to validate. (b) Automation trust. Teams with few sensors may treat the coordinate output as ground truth and reduce manual or NDE follow-up, producing skill fade and over-trust (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06). (c) Long lifecycle. Storage periods outlast software, hardware and vendor support, raising model-maintenance, requalification and data-continuity problems (OP.C0204, C0501, C0502, C0303). An adversary can wait for these weaknesses to widen and strike when the monitoring is least credible.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on lab-to-field shift, drift, missing uncertainty/OOD rejection, over-trust, and single-sensor manipulation, poisoning and chaff as adversarial paths. I merged overlapping items and dropped weakly argued codes (e.g., AML.T0005 and T0043.002 as speculative, and OP.C0201.02 and OP.C0301 as lacking support in the documented system)..

evidence.citation: "Localizing damage on stainless steel structures using acoustic emission signals and weighted ensemble regression-based convolutional neural network," Measurement (Elsevier), vol. 211, 112659, 2023
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper builds and tests a CNN regression model that estimates where damage is on a stainless-steel canister plate using only one acoustic emission sensor. It uses data fusion and time-frequency transforms of the AE signals. The motivation is monitoring spent-fuel storage canisters while keeping sensor numbers low because of cost and environmental limits. The authors say the method still needs adapting to real canisters.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a masked or misplaced stress-corrosion crack on a spent fuel canister's confinement boundary, which breaks continuity of knowledge and delays inspection and mitigation; harm is indirect because it requires the output to displace independent inspection, so it falls just short of a direct release.

reproducibility.why: Lab-to-field generalization failure, drift and the lack of a reject option are reliably present as properties of the system, but turning them into consequential harm requires the output to replace independent inspection and a real flaw to be present, so reliability is conditional.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (physical or cable-level sensor access, poisoning of training data or vendor updates, tampering with stored baselines) generally require site access, supply-chain position or insider capability; only the implicit weaknesses can be relied on with little effort.

affected_users.why: Impact is confined to the monitored canister or cask population at a storage site and does not propagate to coupled operating systems, though a shared model or vendor update could affect multiple canisters.

discoverability.why: The paper is public and states it needs adaptation to real canisters. The weaknesses of single-sensor learned acoustic monitoring (domain gap, drift, no uncertainty, adversarial input) are well documented for this class of AI system, so a capable outsider can infer them readily.

use_case: Random-forest and deep-neural-network surrogates of a numerical triple-layer surface complexation model of uranium sorption on oxide minerals. They predict surface charge densities, electrostatic potentials and surface-species concentrations. They were trained on more than one million simulated data points and are intended for incorporation into contaminant-migration models used in the safety assessment of geological spent fuel repositories after a canister leak.
incurred_insecurity:
This surrogate sits upstream of a repository licensing decision, so its main insecurity is a quietly wrong, non-conservative retardation and dose estimate that a regulator accepts and that cannot be revisited after closure. The panel converged on implicit threats from simulator-only training, out-of-distribution failure, error propagation in coupled transport and the absence of any qualification regime for ML surrogates, and on adversarial threats from tampering with the surrogate, its data or its inputs. The model is a low-value direct target but a high-value place to hide a bias.

Simulator-circular training data -- implicit, exploitable
All 1M+ training points come from the surface complexation model, so the surrogate reproduces that model's structural error with high apparent precision, and the reported accuracy measures agreement with the simulator, not real uranium retention. An adversary could rely on the resulting false sense of validation to slip a biased surrogate or manipulated inputs past reviewers who only check surrogate-to-model agreement.

Out-of-distribution and convergence-gap failure -- implicit, exploitable
Training is biased toward chemistry where the solver converges, so in extreme regimes (high carbonate, cement-leachate pH, radiolysis) random forests flat-line and DNNs extrapolate smoothly and wrongly with no applicability-domain flag. The loss of solver convergence failure as an implicit sanity check also lets an adversary steer or manipulate site-chemistry inputs into a poorly fit region without any visible alarm.

Error accumulation in coupled transport -- implicit
The surrogate is called millions of times inside reactive-transport codes, so small per-call biases and non-physical outputs (charge-balance violations, non-monotonic isotherms) compound and shift plume fronts and dose estimates in a way that is hard to trace. No realistic adversary gains much beyond what the other threats already offer.

Qualification, opacity and non-repeatability gap -- implicit, exploitable
No established regulatory pathway exists for qualifying ML surrogates in a 10^5 to 10^6 year safety case, and DNN opacity, training-time non-determinism and weak version control leave no routine control to catch a drifted or swapped model. An adversary could exploit research-grade configuration control to alter the artifact undetected, or cite the lack of qualification to discredit a licence.

Reviewer over-trust and skill loss -- implicit, exploitable
Speed gains encourage wide Monte Carlo sweeps that create false confidence in narrow uncertainty bands, while reviewers stop re-running the original solver and lose the ability to interpret it. An adversary could time a submission or an alteration around this complacency.

Surrogate, data and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
An insider or a compromised dataset, generator script, library or released weight file could introduce a small non-conservative sorption bias or a localized backdoor-like error in borderline pH, carbonate or ionic-strength regimes that passes aggregate accuracy checks. The consequence is a systematically optimistic release and dose estimate underpinning licensing, and one tampered open-source artifact could propagate into several assessments.

Upstream parameter and input manipulation -- adversarial
Altering the thermodynamic database, SCM parameters or site-characterization chemistry inputs corrupts training data or surrogate inputs without triggering any convergence failure. The corrupted results flow silently into the safety case.

Public-method reconnaissance and proxy probing -- adversarial
Published architecture, training ranges and open artifacts let an adversary build a proxy surrogate and locate regions where it diverges from the SCM. They could then craft inputs that land in a favorable error region or use the divergences to discredit an assessment.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This surrogate sits upstream of a licensing decision: it feeds sorption (retardation) behavior into contaminant-migration models that support a repository safety case. Nothing on a plant floor reacts to it. The harm is a quietly wrong or non-conservative dose and release estimate that a regulator accepts, which then shapes siting, canister design, and buffer or backfill choices that cannot be revisited once the repository is closed. Existing practice does provide some protection, namely independent reviewers, conservative Kd bounding, sensitivity analysis, and comparison with the original numerical model. But the surrogate was trained on simulated output from a single model that often fails to converge, so it inherits that model's structural error and can hide its own failures. Any safeguard that leans on 'the surrogate matches the SCM' is therefore circular, and it only holds if someone actually checks against experimental sorption data and against the full solver at the edge of the training domain.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulated-data circularity and fidelity. All of the 1M+ training points come from the SCM, not from measurement. The surrogate can therefore reproduce SCM error and structural bias (wrong surface-species set, wrong site densities, wrong constants) with great apparent precision. The headline accuracy figure is about agreement with the SCM, not truth about uranium retention. Downstream, retardation is overestimated, peak dose is underestimated, and the safety case looks more favorable than reality. (2) Out-of-distribution failure. The training sweep may not cover real repository geochemistry, such as high carbonate, elevated temperature, radiolysis near the canister, cement-leachate pH, mixed or altered mineral assemblages, or colloids. Random forests flatten and cannot extrapolate. DNNs can extrapolate smoothly and wrongly with no warning. The conditions where the SCM fails to converge are likely the chemically extreme ones, so they are probably underrepresented in the training set, and those are the conditions that matter for a leak scenario. (3) Coupled-transport error propagation. The surrogate is called repeatedly inside reactive-transport codes over long time spans, so small biases or non-physical outputs (charge-balance violations, non-monotonic isotherms, discontinuities) accumulate, can destabilize the solver, or can shift the plume front. Safety margins are then misjudged in a way that is hard to trace. (4) Qualification gap. There is no established regulatory pathway for qualifying ML surrogates in a safety case that must stand for 10^5 to 10^6 years. Model versioning, retraining reproducibility, random-seed non-determinism, opacity of the DNN, and validation against the SCM versus experiments are all weak points. Reviewers may defer to a Nature-family publication as de facto qualification. (5) Automation and credibility bias. Large speedups invite a shift to much wider Monte Carlo and uncertainty sweeps, creating false confidence in narrow uncertainty bands while the dominant uncertainty, conceptual model error, goes unexamined. Staff may lose the ability to run or interpret the original SCM, and the convergence-failure knowledge may be lost. (6) Dependency and lifecycle. Version drift between the surrogate, the SCM, and the thermodynamic database can leave stale constants embedded in an apparently frozen model.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. These are lower-likelihood but high-consequence, because the target is the credibility of the safety case, not an operating system. (a) Supply-chain or model-artifact tampering (a poisoned or swapped model file, a modified training set, a compromised surrogate library) could bias sorption in a non-conservative direction in a way that is subtle and passes SCM spot checks. (b) Manipulation of the upstream SCM parameters or thermodynamic database, which then propagates into the training data without anyone noticing. (c) Because the surrogate is a smooth function with open publication, an actor who wants to challenge or undermine a repository licence, whether an opponent, a developer, or a state-linked influence operation, can probe the published method to find input regions where it diverges from the SCM and use them to discredit or to slip in favorable assessments. Impact is mainly on regulatory integrity, public trust, and long-term radiological protection, not an immediate release. The main safeguard is independent re-computation with the full SCM and experimental benchmarking on a sample of cases, with configuration control over the surrogate artifact. Without that, nothing downstream would catch a wrong answer.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a surrogate-of-a-simulator pipeline. Every training label is an output of the numerical triple-layer surface complexation model (TLM), so the surrogate inherits all of the TLM's structural error, parameter uncertainty and convergence-region bias, and its reported "very close reproduction" is fidelity to the simulator, not to real uranium sorption on real repository minerals. Because the TLM often fails to converge, the training set is probably biased toward easy, well-behaved chemistry. The hard regimes (high ionic strength, carbonate-rich, near-neutral pH, strongly coupled speciation) are the ones where a surrogate returns a smooth, confident answer and the original solver would have failed or flagged an error. Once embedded in a reactive-transport or contaminant-migration code, the surrogate is called millions of times across spatial and temporal gradients and with evolving chemistry after a canister leak. That makes out-of-distribution inputs, error accumulation and non-conservation of mass and charge likely, and none of these is visible to a regulator reviewing only R² or RMSE on a held-out split. The ML-specific risks are therefore interpolation or extrapolation silently outside the training envelope, no uncertainty or applicability-domain flag, and a licensing evidence chain that is hard to qualify.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution and extrapolation failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03): the training grid of pH, ionic strength, carbonate, uranium concentration, site density and mineral type is finite and synthetic. Future repository porewater (glaciation, cement leachate plumes, corrosion products, radiolysis) can leave it. DNN and RF fail differently here: RF saturates to the nearest leaf values and so flat-lines, while the DNN extrapolates unpredictably. Either can produce a Kd or sorption estimate that is non-conservative, and the regulator sees a clean number. (2) Simulated-data provenance and circularity (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02): the surrogate has no independent validation against experimental or field data. Training and test data share the same model structure and parameter sets, so test accuracy overstates real-world validity. Selection bias from non-converged runs creates a hidden gap in the data. (3) Static/dynamic and qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401): safety-case tooling needs traceability and reproducibility, but there are no established qualification standards for ML geochemical surrogates, and DNN internals are opaque. Training non-determinism (OP.C0402.01) means a retrained model gives different outputs, which complicates configuration control over a safety assessment that spans decades. (4) Error propagation (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01): small per-call biases in surface charge or speciation compound through coupled transport and shift breakthrough curves and dose estimates. Small errors near sharp sorption edges are amplified. (5) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04): the speed gain encourages wide parameter sweeps and probabilistic assessments, and reviewers may trust the output without asking for the original solver on a spot-check subset. ADVERSARIAL OR EXPLOITABLE THREATS. (6) Training-data and pipeline poisoning or supply-chain compromise (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000): the dataset of over one million points, the generator scripts, the open-source libraries and the released weights are all manipulable. A subtle bias in the sorption regime, such as slightly overpredicted retention in a narrow chemistry window, or a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004) keyed to particular input combinations, would pass aggregate accuracy checks. A state or insider with a stake in a repository siting or licensing decision could use this to favor or sink a safety case. (7) Model or artifact tampering after qualification (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, AML.T0031): if the surrogate is shipped as weights inside a larger transport code, a weight swap or silent version change alters assessment results with no obvious provenance break. Weak hashing and version control are an OP.C0502 hygiene issue. (8) Public-literature reconnaissance (AML.T0000, AML.T0002): published architecture, training ranges and open artifacts let an adversary build a proxy (AML.T0005) and learn the blind spots to target, or to craft inputs, such as manipulated site-characterization chemistry data, that land in a poorly fit region (AML.T0043). (9) Upstream data manipulation (AML.T0059): tampered or erroneous groundwater chemistry, mineral and site-density inputs move the assessment through the surrogate with no solver convergence failure to signal the anomaly. That failure was an implicit sanity check which the surrogate removes. Consequence class: an overly optimistic or non-conservative long-term release and dose assessment that underpins a repository licensing decision, with errors that surface only decades later or under adversarial scrutiny of the safety case.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is a low-value direct target but a high-value place to hide an error. Uranium sorption sets retardation in the contaminant-migration calculation, and that calculation feeds a licensing safety case that is reviewed rarely, relies on a few specialist modelers, and has a very long time horizon. An adversary, or a plain compounding error, does not need to cause an event. A small, systematic bias in predicted sorption could shift a dose or release estimate toward a favorable licensing outcome and stay buried in a surrogate that reviewers cannot easily inspect. The surrogates were trained entirely on simulated output from the very model they replace, so there is no independent empirical anchor to expose a subtle compromise. They also exist because the numerical model often fails to converge, so the original is a weak cross-check precisely where the surrogate is most needed.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity compromise of the surrogate or its training pipeline (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0031, AML.T0076). Mechanism: an insider, a contractor, or a compromised public or pretrained artifact in the modeling toolchain introduces a small bias or a localized backdoor-like error in sensitive regions of geochemical space, such as particular pH, carbonate or ionic-strength regimes where sorption is borderline. Dependency: the repository safety assessment and the licensing decision built on it. Consequence: systematically non-conservative retardation estimates that look plausible, understate long-term release or dose, and undermine the safety case's credibility. Discovery would be late, possibly decades later, and could prompt reputational and regulatory crises. A nation-state or advocacy adversary would find manipulating or discrediting a safety case a cheap, high-leverage objective, and this is much easier than attacking physical safeguards. (2) Provenance and trust concentration (AML.T0010, AML.T0059, OP.C0502). Surrogates are shared as open-source artifacts and incorporated into larger transport codes, so one tampered model could propagate into several assessments (OP.C0602, OP.C0603). The same openness also lets an adversary study the surrogate offline to find where it extrapolates badly (AML.T0005, AML.T0043). That knowledge could be used to argue after the fact that a safety case is unreliable, or to shape inputs so the error lands in a favorable direction. IMPLICIT, and exploitable. (3) Because the training data is simulated and not field-measured (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02), the surrogate inherits every structural flaw of the surface complexation model and gives a false sense of validation. It can fail silently outside its training envelope when geochemistry, mineral phases or radionuclide speciation differ from what was sampled (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). Reviewers may over-trust a good surrogate-to-model agreement figure (OP.C0101.04) and may not re-run the original, especially since that model often does not converge. This is the same complacency an adversary could time a submission or an alteration around. (4) Opacity of the DNN (OP.C0401), the absence of AI-specific qualification regimes for licensing evidence (OP.C0501, OP.C0504), and the mismatch between static validation and the dynamic coupled-code use (OP.C0303) leave no routine control that would catch a tampered or drifted surrogate. Security culture around safety-case modeling tools often treats them as research code, not as safety-significant software (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0503), so access control, version integrity and change management are weak. Consequence: either undetected non-conservatism in the licensing basis or, if discovered, loss of regulator and public trust.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on simulator-circular data, OOD failure, error propagation, the qualification gap and tampering of the surrogate or its pipeline. I merged overlapping items, and kept the reconnaissance and upstream-input threats because they are distinct pathways. I dropped the secondary lifecycle point on version drift into the hygiene and tampering threats.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning surrogates for surface complexation model of uranium sorption to oxides," Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio), vol. 14, article 6603, 2024
evidence.note: The authors built and tested two ML surrogates, a multioutput random-forest ensemble and a deep neural network. They replace a computationally costly surface complexation model that often fails to converge. They report that the DNN reproduces the numerical model's outputs very closely, and they position the surrogates for use in spent-fuel repository safety assessment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a quietly non-conservative sorption/dose estimate (from tampering or silent OOD error) underpinning an irreversible geological repository licensing decision, which means potential long-term release and safeguards-adjacent assurance failure, though it is indirect and mediated by other safety-case layers, so not a full 5.

reproducibility.why: Simulator-circular training, OOD extrapolation failure and error accumulation in coupled transport occur reliably whenever the surrogate is used outside the well-converged chemistry regime or called at scale, and tampering persists once introduced.

exploitability.why: Artifact/dataset tampering and upstream parameter manipulation need insider or supply-chain access to research-grade pipelines, while exploiting OOD gaps or public artifacts for proxy probing needs only moderate capability, giving a mid-range requirement.

affected_users.why: A biased surrogate propagates across millions of calls in coupled reactive-transport codes and potentially across multiple assessments if an open-source artifact is shared, affecting the whole safety case and several licensing reviews, though confined to the repository waste domain.

discoverability.why: The method, architecture, training ranges and artifacts are published in the open literature, and simulator-only training and OOD limits are well-documented ML weaknesses, so a capable outsider can readily infer where weaknesses lie without insider knowledge.

use_case: LSTM recurrent neural network, with feature variables ranked by recursive feature elimination using a random-forest regressor. During a severe accident it reconstructs lost or corrupted plant signals and estimates key accident-management parameters from the remaining intact signals. It was trained and tested on multiple MELCOR simulations of the Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3 accident, and is meant to help operators diagnose severe-accident progression.
incurred_insecurity:
This LSTM reconstructs lost or corrupted severe-accident signals and key accident-management parameters from the surviving channels, but it was trained and tested only on MELCOR simulations of Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3. Its outputs are therefore surrogate estimates of a code's predictions, not measurements, and they are used when no independent ground truth exists and operators are under heavy load. The main threats are simulation-only distribution shift, error propagation from corrupted inputs, operator over-trust, manipulation of the input signals, and tampering with the training data or model.

Simulator-to-reality gap and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
Training and testing on a small set of MELCOR scenarios for one unit means the model inherits MELCOR's errors and extrapolates confidently, without an uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag, on unmodelled behaviour such as hydrogen events, containment leakage or real sensor failure modes. This can yield plausible but wrong drywell pressure, level or core-state estimates that misdirect venting, injection or depressurization decisions. An adversary could time an attack to a transient that pushes the plant outside the training envelope, or rely on the model's confident smoothing to hide a manipulation.

Corrupted-input propagation and masked sensor faults -- implicit, exploitable
The model is built for clean dropout, but drifting, saturated or stuck-at inputs feed through the recurrent state into several mutually consistent estimates, and the RFE-selected feature set may depend on only a few variables. Reconstruction can therefore hide a sensor fault instead of exposing it, and reused models could spread a Unit-3-specific bias to other plants. An adversary could induce or exploit an instrument failure so that the reconstructed picture becomes the operators' main view.

Opacity, non-repeatability and automation bias -- implicit, exploitable
LSTM outputs give little explanation, training is non-deterministic (the paper's own sensitivity to training/test combinations and neuron count shows this), and sensitivity studies do not amount to qualification for a safety role. Operators may over-trust a smooth time series that fills a gap in their picture, and skill fade or loss of independent diagnosis weakens cross-checking. An adversary can rely on that trust, degrading real indications so the AI estimate becomes the main source of truth.

Input-signal manipulation -- adversarial
Because the model infers lost values from the surviving channels, an intruder or insider who spoofs or biases a few sensor feeds or data-path signals can steer the reconstructed parameters in a chosen direction while the output remains internally consistent. The result is a misdiagnosed accident state and mistimed mitigation, at the moment when independent verification is weakest.

Training-data and model tampering -- adversarial
Poisoned MELCOR decks or simulation datasets, a tampered feature-selection or training pipeline, or backdoored weights could embed bias that appears only under specific accident signatures. With no real accident data to validate against and an opaque LSTM, such a latent bias could persist undetected until it matters.

Model and data exposure, and availability -- adversarial
Published architecture, scenarios and feature rankings, or stolen model artifacts, reveal which signals the diagnosis depends on and ease proxy-model building and adversarial-input crafting. Denial of the tool or its data feeds during an accident removes an advisory aid, with limited consequence if operators can still proceed without it.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This tool is meant to help operators in the worst moment of a plant's life: instrumentation is degraded, procedures (SAMGs) depend on a few key parameters, and the crew is under heavy cognitive load. The LSTM is trained only on MELCOR simulations of one plant (Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3), so every 'reconstructed' signal is really a surrogate-model estimate of a code's prediction, and not a measurement. It inherits MELCOR's modelling uncertainty, and it is only valid inside the simulated scenario envelope. Real accidents involve instrument failure modes (saturation, drift, harsh-environment errors, ex-vessel phenomena) that were never in the training set. An estimate that looks authoritative could then drive a wrong diagnosis, and it will often be least reliable exactly when the input signals are most corrupted. Existing practice (SAMG trigger parameters, redundant instruments, TSC analysis with MAAP/MELCOR, conservative decision-making) limits the harm only if operators treat the output as advisory. The main safeguard that has to fail is human cross-checking, and automation bias under stress is the likeliest way for it to fail.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Distribution shift and a qualification mismatch. The training data is simulation-only and covers one unit and a narrow set of boundary conditions (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0303). A real accident with different timing, different failure sequences, hydrogen events, unmodelled core-melt or containment-failure behaviour, or a different plant type can produce confident but wrong reconstructions of drywell pressure, water level or core temperature. The consequence is a misread of accident progression and a mistimed or misdirected action such as venting, injection or evacuation advice. This cannot be separated from MELCOR's own errors, because the network reproduces them. (2) Compounding input error. The model reconstructs signals from the remaining ones, but those are the signals most likely to be corrupted. A bad input, such as a drifting or failed sensor, is fed through the recurrent state and spreads into several estimates, so errors propagate and look mutually consistent (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). Feature selection by recursive feature elimination can also leave the model dependent on a few variables, and loss of one of them degrades it sharply. (3) Human factors. Operators or the TSC may over-trust a smooth, plausible time series, especially when it fills a gap in their picture and nothing independent contradicts it (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01). Opacity makes it hard to tell when the estimate is unreliable (OP.C0401), and the paper's own sensitivity to training/test combinations and neuron count points to unstable behaviour (OP.C0402.01). A tool with no uncertainty indicator invites misuse. Harm requires an operator action based on the estimate and a failure to cross-check against independent indications. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (4) Sensor or data-path manipulation. An adversary who can spoof or alter the plant signals that feed the model (a cyber intrusion into data historians or the plant-computer/SPDS network, or an insider) can steer the reconstruction and make the 'corrected' parameter look benign or alarming during a crisis (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Because the model is trained to fill in missing signals, it will quietly smooth over tampering and mask an inconsistency that a human would otherwise notice. Even without a physical event, an attacker could time such manipulation around an exercise or real transient to degrade diagnosis. (5) Model and supply-chain integrity. Poisoned training simulations, a tampered MELCOR input deck or dataset, or a backdoored model file or library could bias specific estimates (AML.T0020, AML.T0018, AML.T0010, AML.T0076). Retraining on new data without configuration control opens a second path (OP.C0502, OP.C0501). Subtle bias would be hard to detect before an accident, since no real data exists to validate against. (6) Availability. Denial or degradation of the tool, or of the data feeds it needs, during an accident (AML.T0029) mainly removes an advisory aid. The consequence is bounded if operators are trained to proceed without it, but skill fade from reliance on the tool (OP.C0101.06) would make that fallback weaker. (7) Model or training-data theft is of modest consequence, though it reveals plant-specific accident-progression data and instrumentation dependencies (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025, OP.C0505). Overall the consequence is a degraded or misled accident-management decision. The residual safeguards are redundant instruments, SAMG conservatism and independent TSC analysis, so the use case is only as safe as the discipline that keeps it advisory and checked.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a signal-reconstruction (imputation/virtual-sensor) model trained only on MELCOR output for one plant and one accident family (Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3). It will be used in the one regime where no real labeled data exists and where inputs are least like any training distribution. The weaknesses are structural: simulator-only provenance, a tiny scenario set, feature selection (RFE with a random forest) that bakes simulator correlations into the input set, and an LSTM whose temporal state makes it sensitive to corrupted or missing history. The same reconstruction function that makes it useful also makes it dangerous, because it manufactures plausible values for exactly the channels operators can no longer trust, and it does so when instrumentation is degraded, adversarial manipulation is hardest to spot, and no independent ground truth is available to check it.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulator-to-reality gap and data provenance: training and test data both come from MELCOR runs, so the test split measures interpolation within the simulator's own physics and modelling assumptions, not fidelity to a real accident. The real accident had unmodelled behaviors, such as leakage paths, hydrogen combustion, and instrument failure modes (e.g., thermocouple or level-sensor reading errors in high temperature and radiation), and the model has never seen them. A model that reproduces MELCOR's errors has an error that is invisible to its own validation (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0303). (2) Small-data and OOD failure: a few scenarios varied across a narrow parameter set means real plant states can fall outside the support of the training data. An LSTM will extrapolate confidently with no native uncertainty signal and no OOD flag, producing a smooth, plausible trajectory that is wrong (OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403). Transfer to other units or plants is also unvalidated, and fleet reuse would propagate a Unit-3-specific bias (OP.C0602). (3) Corrupted-input handling: the model is trained for 'lost' signals, but real failure is often corrupted, drifting, or stuck-at signals rather than clean dropout. Corrupted inputs propagate through recurrent state and across all reconstructed outputs, and reconstruction can mask a sensor fault instead of exposing it (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). The chosen feature set may also lack redundancy, so loss of a few key signals could silently degrade accuracy. (4) Opacity, repeatability and automation bias: LSTM outputs offer little explanation, training is non-deterministic, and operators under stress with no ground truth may over-trust the estimates for diagnosis and accident-management decisions (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0501). Post-hoc sensitivity studies on neurons and features do not amount to qualification for a safety-relevant role. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Input manipulation at inference time: because the model infers lost values from remaining ones, an adversary able to tamper with a small set of upstream signals, through the data link or sensor spoofing, can steer the reconstructed parameters in a predictable direction. Reconstruction is a force multiplier, and this evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043) could mislead operators about core damage state or containment pressure at a moment when verification is weakest. (6) Supply chain and training-data/model integrity: MELCOR input decks, simulation datasets, RFE-selected features, and model weights pass through research-grade toolchains. Poisoning or backdoor-trigger insertion (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004) could embed a subtle bias that appears only in specific accident regimes and would be undetectable with such a limited test set. Public publication of the architecture and scenarios also eases proxy-model building and crafting of adversarial inputs (AML.T0000, AML.T0002, AML.T0005, AML.T0043.002). (7) Availability: if the model is deployed as a decision-support tool, denial or corruption of its service (AML.T0029) or retraining pressure after recalibration (OP.C0503) would remove or degrade an aid that operators have come to rely on, leaving skill fade (OP.C0101.06) and unfamiliarity (OP.C0101.01) when they most need independent diagnosis.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this tool is attractive mainly as a stepping stone and a timing instrument, not as a direct target. It sits in the most trust-sensitive moment in the plant, a severe accident with degraded or lost instrumentation. In that moment operators have little ground truth to cross-check an AI-reconstructed drywell pressure or core-state estimate. An adversary who can corrupt a few inputs, or exploit the model's blind spots, gets leverage over diagnosis exactly when the tool is most relied on and least verifiable. A second concern is that the model is trained purely on MELCOR simulations of one unit's accident, so its non-adversarial failure modes (out-of-distribution behavior, simulation-to-reality gap) are things an adversary could exploit or time an attack around. Plant states outside the training envelope would produce confident but wrong reconstructions that look plausible to a stressed operator.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Input-signal manipulation. The LSTM infers lost signals from the surviving ones, so its output is only as trustworthy as the intact channels. An insider or a cyber-intruder who spoofs or biases a few sensor feeds, or who exploits a real instrument failure, can steer the reconstructed parameters (e.g., drywell pressure, water level, core temperature proxies) while the output still looks internally consistent. This is adversarial-data crafting and evasion (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). The facility dependency is operator diagnosis and accident-management decisions such as venting, injection and depressurization. The consequence is a misdiagnosed accident state, delayed or mistimed mitigation, and possibly a larger release. This is much more valuable to an adversary who has already degraded the plant than to one acting alone. (2) Model and pipeline tampering. The model comes from simulation data, a feature-selection stage (random-forest RFE) and a training pipeline. These give supply-chain and insider access points for poisoning the training data, altering the weights, or adding a backdoor trigger that activates only under specific accident signatures (AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). Because the tool is rarely exercised outside rare events, a latent backdoor or silent degradation could persist undetected for years, and the opacity of an LSTM makes tampering hard to spot. (3) Trust concentration and erosion of vigilance. If operators are trained to lean on reconstructed values when instruments are lost, an adversary can time an attack so that real sensors are lost or spoofed and the reconstruction becomes the main picture. Over-trust and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity are the exploitable behavioral weaknesses (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102). (4) Information exposure. Model artifacts, MELCOR input decks and the feature-importance rankings expose which signals matter most and how the plant's accident behavior is characterized. That helps an adversary choose which instruments to attack or sabotage (AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0007).

IMPLICIT (exploitable without an attacker). (a) Simulation-only training on a single unit (Fukushima Unit 3 MELCOR) means a data-provenance gap and poor generalization to other plant designs, to accident paths not modeled, and to real instrument-failure patterns, including noise and sensor faults that MELCOR does not capture (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). Any transfer to other sites invites fleet-wide propagation of the same blind spot (OP.C0602). (b) MELCOR model uncertainty is inherited, and the LSTM can present it as precise values with no uncertainty bounds, so there is a content-fidelity and qualification-mismatch risk (OP.C0304, OP.C0303, OP.C0401). (c) Severe-accident conditions are rare and the system cannot be validated against real events, so qualification is hard to establish (OP.C0501, OP.C0202). (d) Reconstructed signals may feed other systems or displays, so an error propagates downstream (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). A realistic adversary would probably find easier targets, such as the instrumentation itself or plant networks, so the main exposure is as an amplifier and a deception layer rather than a primary target.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on simulation-only distribution shift, error propagation, over-trust, input manipulation and training/model tampering. I dropped speculative or weakly tied codes (AML.T0025, AML.T0076, AML.T0035, AML.T0007, OP.C0503, OP.C0505, OP.C0502, OP.C0102) and merged availability and exposure into one lower-consequence paragraph.

evidence.citation: "A machine learning informed prediction of severe accident progressions in nuclear power plants," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Elsevier), Vol. 56, Issue 6, June 2024
evidence.note: The paper builds an LSTM platform and tests it on MELCOR-simulated Fukushima Daiichi Unit 3 accident scenarios. The platform predicts lost signals, such as drywell pressure, and key accident-management parameters from the remaining available plant variables. It also runs sensitivity studies on target variables, training/test data combinations, number of features and number of neurons.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a confidently wrong reconstruction of the accident state (from simulator-to-reality gap, masked sensor faults, or manipulated inputs) that misdirects venting, injection or depressurization during a severe accident. That could worsen a radiological release, though the tool is advisory and not a direct control path, so it falls just short of 5.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution failure and masked sensor faults recur reliably whenever a severe-accident transient falls outside the MELCOR training envelope. Targeted manipulation or poisoning that produces a chosen bias depends on specific signal and accident conditions, and severe accidents are rare.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (spoofing a few sensor feeds, tampering with the training pipeline, backdooring weights) need insider or privileged access to plant data paths or the ML supply chain. Implicit failures need no attacker, but an adversary timing an attack to a transient still needs a position to induce it.

affected_users.why: The reconstructed parameters feed operators' whole accident-diagnosis picture, so errors propagate through several mutually consistent estimates and into mitigation decisions across the unit. Reuse of the model could spread bias to other plants, though it is deployed per unit, which keeps it below facility-plus-fleet maximum.

discoverability.why: The paper, architecture, scenarios and feature rankings are public, and the weaknesses of simulation-trained surrogate models, adversarial inputs and automation bias are well documented in the open literature. Learning how a specific deployed system depends on its signals still takes some inference, so it falls short of 5.

use_case: On-line intelligent core controller for load-following operation of a nuclear power plant. A recurrent neural network core model, trained on a 3-D reactor core dynamics code and updated with plant data, predicts core behaviour. A fuzzy-system critic built on operator knowledge then selects the optimum control-rod-group manoeuvre and overlap strategy. The aim is to limit xenon-induced oscillations and local power peaking.
incurred_insecurity:
This controller sits in the reactivity-control path, choosing control-rod-group manoeuvres and overlap during load-following, and rests on an RNN surrogate trained on a 3-D core code and updated online with plant data. The main threats are sim-to-plant and drift failure of the surrogate, an unqualified self-updating model, objective misalignment in the fuzzy critic, operator over-trust and skill fade, and adversarial manipulation of the sensor/data path, the update loop, the model and rule-base integrity, and the IT/OT boundary. The independent protections (rod insertion limits, RPS trips, Tech Specs, operator oversight) bound the realistic outcome to margin erosion, trips and Tech Spec excursions rather than fuel damage, unless those protections are also defeated.

Sim-to-plant gap and drift -- implicit, exploitable
The RNN learns from code-generated trajectories, so burnup, reload patterns, detector aging, rod-worth error and off-nominal xenon states outside its envelope produce confident but wrong xenon and power-peaking forecasts, and the critic then selects manoeuvres that erode peaking and axial-offset margin. Because the same 3-D code serves as training source and test plant, published performance is circular, and an adversary could hide a slow manipulation inside this natural prediction error, which looks like ordinary drift.

Online-update and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
Continuous updating on plant data creates a moving, unqualified target: faulty or abnormal-period data can be learned as normal, and behaviour after retraining is non-repeatable, which defeats a licensing basis built on a fixed verified software baseline. An adversary could rely on the missing change control and re-qualification to slip a bias into the model unnoticed.

Critic objective misalignment and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
The fuzzy critic encodes static operator heuristics such as smoothness or rod wear that can trade away unmodelled margin to limits and fail in rare states like post-trip xenon, while the recurrent network's opacity prevents operators from seeing why a manoeuvre was chosen. This opacity makes sabotage hard to distinguish from natural error, giving an adversary cover.

Operator over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A controller that is usually right trains operators to stop watching xenon and peaking margins and erodes their manual load-following skill, so they are slow to notice or take over from a degrading controller. An adversary could time an attack or denial of the controller around this lost vigilance.

Sensor and data-path manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofed or biased detector, temperature, power or rod-position inputs push the RNN's state estimate off truth, and recurrence accumulates a small persistent bias so the controller recommends harmful manoeuvres while appearing normal. The consequence is margin erosion, a trip or a power-limit violation.

Poisoning of the update loop and training data -- adversarial
Altering plant or historian data, the retraining pipeline, or the 3-D code training corpus can slowly bias the surrogate or embed a backdoor that activates only in specific load-ramp transients. The result is subtle margin erosion that resembles operational variation and is hard to attribute.

Model, rule-base and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
A compromised core code, stored model weights or the small, editable fuzzy rule base and membership functions let a supply-chain actor or privileged insider change rod-movement behaviour without touching conventional control logic and with little forensic trace.

IT/OT bridge and denial of controller -- adversarial
The controller needs a plant-data link and a write path to rod control, creating a possible bridge from analytics networks toward safety-relevant I&C, and denying or degrading it forces manual load-following at an awkward grid-demand moment.

Model reconnaissance and proxy building -- adversarial
Published architecture details allow an adversary to build a proxy surrogate and test perturbations offline before applying them to the real data path.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the plant side, this controller proposes control-rod-group manoeuvres and overlap in a PWR-type core during load-following, which is exactly where xenon oscillations, axial offset and local power peaking (FΔH, Fq) margins are most easily eroded. The literature describes a simulation-only design in which a 3-D core code stands in for the plant. Everything that matters in real operation (instrumentation noise, detector and calibration drift, fuel burnup state, rod-worth uncertainty, operator-set constraints) is untested. Existing practice limits the damage: rod insertion limits, shutdown-margin and axial-offset technical specifications, the reactor protection system (RPS) with its overpower/DNB trips, and operator oversight. These are independent of the AI and would all have to be bypassed or fail for the harm to become a fuel-integrity event. The realistic consequence of bad output is therefore more likely eroded operating margin, spurious power manoeuvres, trips or Tech Spec violations than core damage. Closed-loop authority, or advisory output with high operator trust, would weaken that defence in depth.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Sim-to-plant gap and drift: the RNN is trained on a 3-D core code and 'updated with plant data'. Its predictions of xenon transients and power distribution depend on burnup, fuel-cycle changes, reload patterns, rod-worth and detector calibration, none of which the training reflects. Under-predicted xenon or axial offset would lead the fuzzy critic to select manoeuvres that worsen oscillations or local peaking (OP.C0302, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0203). (2) Online updating on plant data adds concept drift and silent degradation of the model. Sensor faults or off-nominal states could be learned as normal, and a model update would need re-qualification (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0501). (3) The fuzzy critic encodes operator heuristics that may mis-weight objectives, for example prioritising manoeuvre smoothness over peaking margin, or may fail in rare states such as unusual rod configurations or xenon after a trip. Opaque RNN dynamics make it hard for operators to see why a manoeuvre was chosen (OP.C0301, OP.C0401, OP.C0403). (4) Human factors: operators who rely on the controller for routine load-following may suffer skill fade and mode-confusion, and may be slow to take over when it degrades (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.03, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). (5) Qualification: neural-network software in a control function has no established licensing basis, and non-repeatable behaviour after retraining makes V&V and safety classification difficult (OP.C0501, OP.C0402, OP.C0504).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Manipulation of the model's inputs: spoofed or biased ex-core/in-core detector, temperature or xenon-estimate signals fed through the plant-data path could lead the controller to infer a wrong core state and command inappropriate rod motion. This is evasion of the model in effect, an input-integrity attack on a control function (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). (b) Poisoning of the online-update pipeline or of the 3-D code training set could embed a bias or trigger that only shows under certain load-following transients (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031). (c) Supply-chain compromise of the model or the core code, or tampering with the fuzzy rule base, could produce persistent, subtle degradation of margin that looks like operational variation (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076). (d) The controller adds a new path from IT/analytics networks to rod-control commands, so access to the compute node could be turned into a means of manoeuvre manipulation, or into denial of the controller (AML.T0029) that forces manual load-following at an awkward time. The key point for defenders is that harm requires the adversary to also get past rod-insertion limits, RPS and operator checks. The practical risk is therefore economic loss, trips or Tech Spec excursions, with fuel-integrity harm only if the independent protections are compromised too. The consequence is greater if the controller output is trusted without an independent validator or hard-wired manoeuvre limiter.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a closed-loop, model-predictive-style controller whose entire value depends on an RNN surrogate staying faithful to real core physics. The surrogate is trained on a 3-D core dynamics code and only 'updated with plant data'. That sets up a sim-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01 / OP.C0201.03), and the critical regimes (xenon transients, local power peaking near thermal limits) are exactly where operational data is scarce and the surrogate is least validated (OP.C0202, OP.C0302). The published evidence is simulation-only, with the same 3-D code serving as both training source and 'plant', so the reported performance is circular and says little about out-of-distribution behaviour, burnup/cycle drift, instrument error or off-nominal rod configurations. The fuzzy critic encodes operator heuristics that are static, so they will not track core aging or fuel-loading changes. Together, the pipeline has a likely failure surface at the surrogate's boundaries, and that is where an adversary or a plain drift event would bite.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Surrogate drift and OOD failure: the RNN is trained on code-generated trajectories, then updated on-line with plant data. Burnup progression, fuel reload patterns, detector degradation and xenon states outside the training envelope cause silent prediction error (OP.C0302.01/.02/.03). The mechanism is a confident but wrong core-state forecast. The facility dependence is rod-group selection and overlap, and the consequence is under-predicted power peaking or xenon oscillation, eroding thermal margins (safety). (2) On-line learning risk: continuous updating from plant data creates a moving, unqualified target (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0402). Learning from noisy, faulty or abnormal-period data degrades the model without notice, and non-repeatable behaviour defeats a licensing basis built on a fixed, verified software baseline. (3) Optimizer/critic misalignment (OP.C0301): the fuzzy critic optimizes operator-derived 'optimum' criteria such as smoothness or rod wear, which can trade away margin to limits, and it has no formal guarantee of respecting limiting conditions. Opacity of the RNN (OP.C0401) makes review hard, and operators can over-trust or lose skill in manual load-following (OP.C0101.04/.06, OP.C0101.01). (4) Sim-to-real mismatch (OP.C0201.01/.03): code-generated training data carries the physics assumptions and cross-section errors of the code itself. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Sensor and data-path manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015): crafted or spoofed in-core detector, power or rod-position inputs, or plain false data injection, push the RNN's state estimate off truth. Because recurrence carries error forward, a small persistent bias accumulates, and the controller then recommends harmful manoeuvres while looking normal. The consequence is margin erosion, or a trip or power-limit violation that disrupts generation. (6) Poisoning of the on-line update loop (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059): the plant-data update channel is a standing, low-visibility route to model corruption. Slow poisoning can embed a backdoor or bias that triggers under specific load-ramp conditions (AML.T0043.004). (7) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0076): tampering with the training simulator, its datasets, or the stored model weights and fuzzy rule base changes controller behaviour without touching conventional control logic. (8) Reconnaissance and extraction (AML.T0000, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005): published architecture details allow a proxy model to be built and perturbations to be tested offline before use. Overall, the exposure sits in the data update path and the surrogate's validity envelope, not in the rod hardware, and mitigation needs bounded authority, an independent physics-based limit check, and frozen or qualified model versions.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team lens, this use case is unusual because it sits in the reactivity-control path: it picks control-rod-group manoeuvres and overlap strategy, not just advice. That makes it a possible target for an insider or a supply-chain adversary, even though a sophisticated state actor would probably find the plant's existing I&C and the safety-system boundary easier or more valuable. The more realistic danger is a quieter one. A controller that is usually right trains operators to stop watching xenon and power-peaking margins, and an adversary (or a coincident natural fault) could time an action around that lost vigilance. The core model is a surrogate trained on a 3-D code and updated with plant data, so both the training pipeline and the online update loop are trust-concentration points with few independent checks. Because the source is a simulation-only design, the gap between simulated and real plants is itself the weakness an adversary would exploit.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity of the online-update path: the RNN is updated with plant data, so anyone who can alter sensor or historian data, or the retraining pipeline (insider or compromised engineering workstation), can slowly bias the core model. The model then mispredicts xenon distribution and power peaking, and the fuzzy critic chooses manoeuvres that look optimal but erode margin toward local power-peaking and fuel-limit conditions. Slow poisoning of this kind looks like ordinary drift and is hard to attribute. (2) Tampering with the fuzzy critic's rule base and membership functions. These encode operator knowledge and are small, human-readable and editable, so a privileged insider can change them with little forensic trace, which gives the insider a new low-skill pathway to influence rod movement. (3) Supply chain and qualification of the surrogate: the model is trained on a 3-D core code and its datasets, so a poisoned or backdoored model, or a corrupted training corpus, could carry a trigger that activates only in specific load-follow transients. (4) Stepping-stone risk: an on-line controller needs a data link from plant instrumentation and a write path to rod-control systems, which is a possible bridge between IT and OT zones and a route for a cyber actor to reach the safety-relevant I&C boundary. (5) Denial or degradation of the controller during a grid-demand transient can force manual load-following at a stressful moment, which an adversary could time around.

IMPLICIT, exploitable or timeable. (a) Automation trust and skill fade: operators lose practice at manual xenon management, so they are less able to notice or counter a bad manoeuvre, and a window opens for a concurrent attack. (b) Sim-to-real and drift: the model is trained on simulated data, and fuel burnup, core reload changes and instrument aging push it out of distribution, so the model may be confidently wrong in states it was never trained on. (c) Opacity of a recurrent network combined with a fuzzy critic makes it hard to tell a natural error from sabotage. (d) Qualification gap: the controller is a simulation-tested design with no established qualification path for adaptive, self-updating software in a safety-related function, and online updating changes the validated configuration without formal change control. (e) Optimization against a goal of limiting oscillations and peaking can trade away margins not represented in the objective (cascading fault propagation).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sim-to-real drift, unqualified online updating, critic misalignment, operator over-trust, and poisoning/supply-chain/sensor-spoofing adversarial paths; the security specialist's IT/OT bridge and insider rule-base tampering were kept as distinct. I dropped weakly supported codes (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0049-style exploitation, OP.C0502, OP.C0403, OP.C0101.03) because the text did not clearly support them, and kept AML.T0005/T0000 from the AI engineer for the published-architecture recon point only.}

evidence.citation: "An intelligent nuclear reactor core controller for load following operations, using recurrent neural networks and fuzzy systems," Elsevier (Annals of Nuclear Energy)
evidence.note: The paper builds a controller from a recurrent-neural-network core model, a control-rod-group manoeuvre generator, a fuzzy critic and an optimum-manoeuvre finder. In simulation, with a 3-D core code standing in for the real plant, the controller handled load-following with optimum rod-group manoeuvres and variable overlap. The record is an abstract page, so the journal name comes from the ScienceDirect article identifier and the Elsevier listing. It is a simulation-tested design, not a reported plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is sensor/data-path or update-loop manipulation, or a drifted surrogate, driving rod manoeuvres that erode peaking and axial-offset margin and cause trips or Tech Spec excursions; independent protections (rod limits, RPS, operator oversight) bound this below radiological release, so it is operational disruption and minor margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-plant drift and out-of-envelope states recur reliably once the model is outside its training range, but a deliberate attack such as a backdoor or slow bias depends on specific transients, access and conditions, so reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (tampering with the data pipeline, model weights, rule base or retraining loop, or bridging IT/OT into rod control) generally need privileged, supply-chain or insider access, or a foothold in plant networks that is hard to obtain, though the implicit drift weaknesses need no access.

affected_users.why: The controller acts on core-wide reactivity and power distribution during load-following, so effects span the whole core and unit, and operators lose skill and vigilance. It is a single unit's control function, however, and independent protection layers limit propagation to other systems.

discoverability.why: Surrogate drift, online-learning qualification gaps and operator over-trust are well documented in the open literature for this class of AI controller, and the published architecture allows a capable outsider to infer weaknesses. Confirming specific plant exposure still needs partial system knowledge.

use_case: Explainable graph-neural-network accident diagnosis for nuclear power plants (Concept-Constrained Physical Graph). Multivariate transient signals are grouped into 12 operator-readable physical plant-function nodes, such as core power, primary loops, steam generators and containment. The model extracts node-wise temporal features and propagates them over a mechanism-guided graph. A concept bottleneck with prototype learning then predicts the accident class and produces a reviewable evidence package of concepts, affected nodes and stage order. It supports operator and safety-engineer accident diagnosis.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory accident-diagnosis aid concentrates operator trust in a polished evidence package (concepts, affected nodes, stage order) from a model validated only on simulated five-class NPPAD data and never deployed. Its main threats are a simulation-to-plant gap with closed-set misdiagnosis, persuasive but unfaithful explanations that drive over-trust, graph-propagated sensor faults, a qualification gap, and adversarial manipulation of input data, training pipeline, and the evidence presentation. Safety-system actuation and symptom-based procedures remain the backstop, so harm mostly arises through misled operator situational awareness during a transient.

Simulation-to-plant gap and closed-set misdiagnosis -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on simulator transients with near-ceiling benchmark accuracy, the closed-set classifier forces real noise, instrument drift, compound faults, and beyond-design-basis events into one of five known classes, attaching a confident, coherent mechanism story and delaying recognition of the real event. An adversary could time a sabotage or deception action around these known blind spots, so that the resulting misdiagnosis looks like ordinary out-of-distribution error.

Plausible but unfaithful explanations -- implicit, exploitable
The concept bottleneck, prototypes, and hand-built mechanism graph can yield post-hoc, simulator-correlated narratives that look like verified physics, encouraging automation over-trust, skill fade, and reduced cross-checking against independent indications. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, so a manipulated or merely wrong diagnosis goes unchallenged, or a false alarm campaign can induce operator disuse of a correct output.

Graph propagation of faulty channels -- implicit, exploitable
Features propagate across the 12 physical-function nodes, so one failed, stuck, or biased sensor group skews the whole diagnosis in a way that is hard to trace. An adversary with a foothold in one instrument or data path gains amplified influence over the overall diagnosis from a small perturbation.

Qualification, drift, and classification gap -- implicit, exploitable
No established qualification path exists for a learned diagnostic aid, and plant modifications, setpoint changes, instrument replacement, and non-deterministic retraining shift the signal-to-concept mapping, while an 'advisory' label may leave it in a laxer cyber zone or beyond its validated envelope. An adversary could exploit the weaker protection of this trusted tool and hide manipulation inside post-outage or post-modification drift windows; fleet or vendor model reuse would multiply a single compromise.

Sensor and data-path input manipulation -- adversarial
An actor on the historian, gateway, maintenance laptop, or sensor path can craft physically plausible perturbations or spoofed streams that flip the predicted class or flagged node while the evidence package stays self-consistent, masking a real transient or provoking an unnecessary response. This is most dangerous when timed with an actual transient or a separate attack.

Training and supply-chain poisoning or backdoor -- adversarial
Poisoning simulator-generated training sets, prototype and concept definitions, pretrained components, or weights during training, retraining, or vendor delivery can install a trigger that misclassifies a specific accident, such as a loss-of-coolant accident, as benign while passing benchmark validation. Human-readable prototypes lend the tampering a plausible justification that evades review.

Evidence-package tampering and model probing -- adversarial
Forging or altering the concept and stage-order presentation lends credibility to a false narrative without touching the model, or undermines trust in a correct diagnosis. Query access to outputs can also reveal which signal combinations separate accident classes, letting an adversary learn to evade or mimic a different transient.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the operations side, this is an advisory diagnostic aid for operators and safety engineers during transients. Its main risk is not a direct actuation path but a wrong or over-trusted diagnosis that shapes operator situational awareness during a high-stress, time-compressed event. Plants already have symptom-based emergency operating procedures, safety-system automatic actuation and independent shift technical advisor oversight, so bad output would normally need to coincide with operator deviation from the procedures to cause harm. The explainable evidence package, with its concepts, nodes and stage order, is the part I worry about most. It looks like physical reasoning, so it earns more trust than it has been qualified for, and it can be internally coherent while wrong. The system was validated only on a five-class simulated benchmark with near-ceiling accuracy and has never been deployed, so its performance on real plant data, on multiple concurrent faults, and on sensor degradation is unknown.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulation-to-plant gap and closed-set limits. The model is trained and tested on simulator data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203). Real transients differ from the simulator in sensor noise, instrument drift, plant-specific configuration, and operator actions that alter trajectories. Unseen events, such as multi-fault, beyond-design-basis or novel sequences, will be forced into one of the five known classes. The result is a confident, mislabeled diagnosis with a plausible-looking evidence package, so the consequence is delayed or misdirected recognition of the actual event. Safety-system actuation and EOPs are the backstop. (2) Persuasive but unfaithful explanations (OP.C0304, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04). The concept bottleneck and the mechanism-guided graph give a false sense of verifiability. Concept activations can reflect correlation artifacts of the simulator, not causal physics, and a coherent evidence path can raise automation bias, especially for less experienced operators. Skill fade and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06) also matter if the tool becomes the primary diagnostic reference. Disuse after false alarms is the opposite failure (OP.C0101.05). (3) Qualification and I&C-classification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0303, OP.C0402). There is no established path for qualifying a learned diagnostic aid in the control room. Questions remain about its safety classification, its separation from safety-class I&C, its human-factors validation and its repeatability across retraining. Using the tool as a quasi-safety function without that qualification is a governance risk. (4) Instrument and data-integrity dependence (OP.C0204, OP.C0603). The graph propagates features across nodes, so one failed, stuck or biased sensor group can skew the whole diagnosis, and the effect is hard to trace. Predictions also degrade when channels are lost or mapped differently across plants (OP.C0602 if a model is reused across a fleet). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). An adversary who can alter the data feed, for example through a compromised historian, data diode or gateway, or a compromised sensor network, could inject small perturbations or spoof signals. These would flip the diagnosis or suppress the correct class while the evidence package stays consistent, which would mislead operators during a real event or provoke unnecessary response during a benign one. This is most dangerous when timed with another attack or an actual transient, and the main safeguard is that the safety-class protection system stays independent. (6) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). Poisoning or backdooring during training, retraining or vendor delivery could embed trigger-based misclassification. Because the explanations are plausible, the tampering would be hard to detect. (7) Availability and IT/OT bridging (AML.T0029, OP.C0601). If the tool depends on shared compute or off-site retraining, it opens a new pathway into the OT network, and denial of service removes the aid when it is most needed. Since it is advisory, the consequence is mostly a loss of decision support and added operator workload, not a direct safety-function loss.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this system's headline strength, high accuracy with an operator-readable evidence package, rests on a fragile base. It was trained and validated only on simulated NPPAD transients, a five-class closed-set benchmark, and has never seen field data. The 12-node physical graph and the concept bottleneck inject expert priors, so the 'explanations' are partly by construction. They show what the architecture is built to emit, not necessarily what drove the prediction. At inference time a real plant will supply sensor noise, calibration drift, failed or missing channels, multiple simultaneous faults, unseen accident types and operating states, and a closed-set softmax head with prototype similarity will still output a confident, tidy mechanism story. The real exposure is therefore a plausible-looking but wrong diagnosis in a safety-relevant decision loop, and that exposure is both implicit and exploitable.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and OOD failure (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203): training uses code-generated simulator data from one plant model. Real instrumentation has noise, bias, sensor dropout, differing plant states and ageing, and no labeled real accidents exist to calibrate against. Accuracy near 100% on a benchmark mostly shows separable simulated classes. A closed-set classifier forced to choose among five accident labels will map beyond-design-basis, compound or novel transients onto the nearest known class and attach convincing concept and node evidence. The consequence is misdiagnosis during real events, with the operator steered toward the wrong procedure or toward delayed recognition. (2) Explanation fidelity and automation bias (OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01): concept bottlenecks and prototypes can be shortcut-leaky, and the stage-order and affected-node 'evidence' may be coherent post-hoc narratives rather than causal attribution. Reviewable evidence raises operator trust, so errors become harder to challenge under stress and operators lose skill over time. Wrong-but-explained outputs are worse than wrong-but-opaque ones. (3) Drift and qualification (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402): plant modifications, setpoint changes, instrument replacement and fuel-cycle effects shift the signal-to-concept mapping. A model trained on static simulated transients has no qualification path for dynamic, real-time use, and retraining non-determinism makes revalidation hard. Gaps in AI-specific QA and regulatory readiness let it be used beyond its validated envelope. (4) Graph-prior brittleness (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01): a hand-defined mechanism graph propagates a single corrupted or failed node's features to its neighbours, so one bad sensor group biases the diagnosis of the whole plant. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031): an adversary with access to the sensor, historian or data-acquisition path could perturb a few signals, or exploit the 12-node grouping, to push the class or suppress the concept evidence, for example to mask a real transient as benign or induce a false diagnosis and an unnecessary trip. Plausible, physics-consistent perturbations of simulated-like signals may evade any plausibility checks. Fixed concept definitions and prototypes make the decision surface easier to learn through model extraction or proxy training (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0005). (6) Supply chain and training pipeline (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004): public benchmark data, pretrained components, and simulator-generated retraining corpora are poisoning surfaces. A backdoor keyed to a specific signal pattern could cause deliberate misclassification at a chosen time while passing benchmark validation.
