(7) Evidence-package trust (AML.T0067, AML.T0031): because humans rely on the concept and stage-order report, tampering with the presentation layer lets an attacker lend credibility to a false narrative without changing the model. Timing an attack around known drift windows, such as after outages or modifications, compounds all of these.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, an accident-diagnosis aid that emits a polished, operator-readable 'evidence package' (concepts, affected nodes, stage order) is a trust-concentration point. An adversary does not need to break the reactor protection system. They only need to shape what a stressed operator believes in the first minutes of a transient. The explanation layer is the persuasive part: a fluent, mechanism-consistent rationale lowers the operator's urge to cross-check against independent indications, and that is the vigilance erosion an attacker could time around. The system was validated only on simulated NPPAD data with near-ceiling accuracy and has never been tested in a plant. So its real-world failure modes are unknown, and an insider or supply-chain adversary can hide inside that uncertainty because a wrong or manipulated diagnosis would look like ordinary out-of-distribution error. A nation-state would more likely target the data path and the model supply chain than the model's math. A cheaper route may be to ignore the AI entirely, but a diagnosis aid that is trusted and advisory is a good force multiplier for a deception or sabotage scenario.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Input and signal manipulation: the model ingests multivariate transient signals grouped into 12 plant-function nodes. An actor with access to the instrumentation or data-historian path (an insider, a compromised maintenance laptop, a compromised data gateway) could craft subtle perturbations or spoofed sensor streams that shift the predicted class, or flip which node is flagged, while staying inside plausible physical ranges (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). The mechanism-guided graph and concept bottleneck do not make this robust; a few poisoned node features could propagate along the graph edges and produce a coherent but wrong evidence path. The consequence is misdiagnosis during a real or staged transient, delayed or misdirected operator response, and, in the worst case, a safety-significant mistake. (2) Supply chain, training-data and model integrity: training depends on simulator-generated transient sets, so poisoning or backdooring the simulation data, the concept/prototype definitions or the model weights (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004) could install a trigger that misclassifies one accident type, for example making a loss-of-coolant accident look like a benign class. Because prototypes and concepts are human-readable, a tampered prototype library could carry a plausible justification and so evade review. Retraining and update workflows are a persistent insider pathway. (3) Explanation as an attack surface: the evidence package can be manipulated or forged (AML.T0067, AML.T0074) to give false assurance, or to make operators distrust a correct diagnosis (inducing disuse). An adversary could also use outputs for reconnaissance (AML.T0024, AML.T0063): query access reveals which signal combinations separate accident classes, which tells them how to evade detection or time a cyber-physical action to look like a different transient.

IMPLICIT, exploitable without an attacker. (a) Sim-to-real gap: validation only on simulated NPPAD data gives unquantified performance under real noise, sensor faults, degraded instruments or plant-specific configurations (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0203). An adversary could time action around known blind spots such as compound or novel events outside the five classes. A closed-set classifier forced into the nearest accident class is dangerous when the true event is outside its training set (OP.C0403). (b) Automation trust and out-of-the-loop effects: neat explanations can encourage over-trust, skill fade and alarm or monitoring complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Explanations may also be post-hoc rationalizations of a wrong class (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0401). (c) Governance: no qualification pathway exists for ML in this safety-adjacent advisory role, and the cybersecurity classification of an 'advisory' tool is likely to be too lax, so it may sit on a less protected network zone yet influence operator decisions (OP.C0501, OP.C0503, OP.C0505.01). Model updates and fleet-wide propagation of one model across sites would multiply the impact of a single compromise (OP.C0602). Any dependence on cloud hosting or vendor retraining adds external exposure (OP.C0601).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sim-to-real closed-set failure, unfaithful persuasive explanations, input manipulation, and training/supply-chain poisoning; I merged these. I dropped denial-of-service and cloud dependency (OP.C0601, AML.T0029) as weakly argued for an advisory tool, and kept model extraction and reconnaissance only as a brief probing threat, mapping to AML.T0024.002 and AML.T0063 and omitting the broader AML.T0005 and AML.T0024 roots.

evidence.citation: "Mechanism-Aligned Nuclear Power Plant Accident Diagnosis via Physically Guided Concepts and Evidence Paths," Applied Sciences (MDPI)
evidence.note: The paper proposes and tests a graph-based, concept-bottleneck neural framework. It was evaluated on the simulated NPPAD five-class accident benchmark and reached very high classification accuracy. Unlike a plain accident label, it outputs mechanism-aligned evidence that operators can review. It was tested only on simulated data, not deployed in a plant.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a backdoor or input manipulation that masks a real transient (e.g., a loss-of-coolant accident classified as benign) and misleads operator situational awareness; because safety-system actuation and symptom-based procedures remain the backstop, this falls just short of direct radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Closed-set misdiagnosis and over-trust occur reliably whenever an out-of-distribution event arises, but targeted manipulation or backdoor outcomes depend on timing with a real transient and on a foothold, so reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (historian, gateway or sensor-path foothold, training or supply-chain poisoning, evidence-package forgery) need privileged access to OT networks or the vendor pipeline, and timing with a real transient adds sophistication, though the implicit weaknesses need no special effort.

affected_users.why: Graph propagation across the 12 plant-function nodes lets one faulty channel skew the whole diagnosis, and fleet or vendor model reuse could multiply a single compromise across sites, though the tool is advisory and scoped to operator diagnosis.

discoverability.why: The open-literature paper, public NPPAD benchmark, and well-documented ML weaknesses (simulation-to-plant gap, closed-set limits, adversarial examples, backdoors, explanation unfaithfulness) make the vulnerability class widely known, though exploiting it for a specific plant would still need system knowledge.

use_case: Fine-tuned open-weight multimodal LLM (Gemma 4 31B-IT) with supervised fine-tuning on distilled chain-of-thought rationales, optionally combined with BM25 retrieval over the DOE Fundamentals Handbooks. It answers questions from the NRC Reactor Operator Generic Fundamentals Examination (PWR and BWR papers) and is scored against the 80% human passing criterion. The aim is to test whether a domain-adapted LLM can handle reactor operator knowledge and licensing-exam content for operator training and qualification.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case is a teaching-and-learning benchmark with no control function, so the physical pathway to harm is long and passes through instructor review, simulator assessment and NRC-administered exams. The insecurity lies in quiet erosion of operator competence and of the safeguards that protect it. The main threats are misplaced trust in a model that passed only 8 of 14 papers, confidently wrong generated rationales, a weak and possibly contaminated benchmark, poisoning of the model, rationale data or retrieval corpus, and weak governance of a tool outside the safety-classified estate.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A score near the 80% human pass mark invites trainers and trainees to treat the model as an authoritative tutor, and heavy use weakens trainees' independent derivation and instructors' review. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust to pass off a tampered tutor, or time an action against a cohort whose competence is lower than its records show.

Content fidelity failure in rationales -- implicit, exploitable
Distilled chain-of-thought rationales from a teacher LLM are synthetic and unverified. The fluent output can therefore carry hallucinated or misattributed handbook content, omitted caveats, sign or unit errors, PWR/BWR confusion and misread figures, with nothing marking which answers fall in the roughly 20% error band. An adversary could hide deliberately planted wrong physics inside this expected error rate, where it looks like ordinary model fallibility.

Benchmark validity, contamination and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
The 2015-2021 exam papers and the handbooks are probably in pretraining data. With a small 14-paper test set, non-deterministic inference and an unreviewed preprint, the pass result may reflect memorisation, not reasoning, and cannot support claims of qualification. No AI-specific QA basis exists for training tools, and the opaque rationales cannot be checked against the computation. This false confidence lets a degraded or compromised model be accepted into a qualification pipeline without challenge.

Retrieval limits and distribution shift -- implicit
BM25 over fixed-size chunks of generic DOE handbooks can split or drop limits, units, tables and figures. Plant-specific content, revised handbooks and changed exam formats fall outside the training distribution, so answers may conflict with plant procedures or technical specifications. An adversary gains little beyond some cover for tampering.

Weak governance of a low-tier tool -- implicit, exploitable
Because the tool is academic and not safety-classified, it is likely to get weak change control, provenance checks and access governance over its models, data and serving hosts. An adversary could use these gaps as an easy foothold or an unnoticed route to alter training content.

Model and training-data supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Open-weight base models, adapters, the distilled rationale set and community tooling are unvetted inputs. A poisoned model or tampered rationale set, possibly with a backdoor trigger on specific question phrasing, could embed subtly wrong reactivity-feedback, shutdown-margin or setpoint reasoning. Miseducated operators would result, and the effect would be latent and hard to trace to its source.

Retrieval corpus tampering and injection -- adversarial
The handbook corpus and BM25 index are simple, editable stores. One altered chunk, or a false entry added from an instructor or vendor document, can shift answers on targeted topics while aggregate exam scores stay unchanged. If the corpus is extended, embedded instructions can also act as indirect prompt injection.

Exam-integrity abuse -- adversarial
A capable exam-answering model lets candidates or insiders defeat knowledge assessment in unproctored settings. This would push under-prepared people into licensing pipelines and weaken the human qualification barrier.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a teaching-and-learning benchmark, not a control or safety function, so the direct physical pathway is long: a wrong answer has to be believed by a trainee or instructor, survive simulator and OJT training, the licensing exam, and the shift-crew verification culture, and then coincide with a plant transient before it matters. The real downstream risk is quiet degradation of operator knowledge. Trainees or training departments may treat an LLM that scores near or above 80% as an authoritative tutor, and its confident, fluent chain-of-thought rationales can embed wrong physics, wrong sign conventions or wrong PWR/BWR distinctions. The weak evidence base makes this worse. The system passed only 8 of 14 papers, the work is a non-peer-reviewed preprint, and 2015-2021 exam content is likely public and may be contaminated in the training data. A benchmark score therefore says little about reliable instruction, yet it invites over-trust. The existing safeguards are strong (instructor review, simulator-based assessment, NRC-administered exams, and plant-specific licensed-operator training), so the main concern is erosion of those safeguards through automation bias and misplaced reliance, not a single failure.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Over-trust and skill fade: if the tool is used for self-study or exam prep, fluent distilled rationales can propagate plausible but wrong reasoning (hallucinated or misattributed handbook content, omitted caveats, unit or sign errors, PWR/BWR confusion). Nothing in the output flags which answers are in the roughly 20% error band. Heavy use could also weaken trainees' own derivation skills, and instructors may relax review. Consequence: latent knowledge gaps that surface only during off-normal events, mitigated by simulator training and crew cross-checking. (2) Validity of the benchmark: contamination from public exam papers, a small test set of 14 papers, an exam score that is not a competence measure, and a pass criterion that is borrowed from human licensing. Together these can produce false confidence that the model is qualified for training use. The preprint is unreviewed and non-deterministic inference makes results hard to repeat. (3) Retrieval limits: BM25 over fixed chunks of the DOE Handbooks can miss figures, tables and context, and the handbooks are generic and not plant-specific, so answers may conflict with plant procedures or technical specifications. Multimodal figure interpretation is a particular weak point. Content fidelity failure here is a training-quality problem. (4) Drift and qualification: handbook or exam-format updates, along with plant-specific content, are out of distribution, and there is no AI-specific QA basis for using the tool in a qualification pipeline. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Supply chain and poisoning: an open-weight model, a fine-tuning dataset of distilled rationales, and a retrieval corpus are all points where a subtle poisoned model, tampered handbook index or altered rationale could inject systematically wrong physics or safety-relevant misconceptions. Tampering is hard to detect because outputs look authoritative, and the damage accumulates across a training cohort or fleet if a shared tool is deployed widely. (6) Indirect prompt injection or false RAG entries if the corpus is extended with instructor or vendor documents. (7) Exam integrity: the same capability could be misused for cheating or credential fraud in remote or unproctored settings, which would put under-prepared people into licensing pipelines. (8) Low-severity items: leakage of training material and denial of service, which only inconvenience training. Overall severity is low to moderate and depends on how far the tool moves from experiment to trusted instructional authority.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline standpoint, this system is fragile in its evaluation design before it is fragile in any facility sense. It is fine-tuned on distilled chain-of-thought rationales, which come from a teacher LLM and so are synthetic and unverified. It is benchmarked on 14 public exam papers from 2015-2021 that are likely in the base model's pretraining corpus and may overlap with the fine-tuning and retrieval material. The pass result is therefore weak evidence of generalization: it is a small test set, only one of eight configurations passed, and it passed on 8 of 14 papers. Meanwhile, BM25 over a static handbook corpus plus an open-weight multimodal model creates a supply-chain, retrieval-integrity and non-determinism surface that is unqualified for operator training and qualification, where a confidently wrong rationale is learned as fact.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Contamination and inflated validity: the public exams, and the handbooks they derive from, are probably in pretraining data. The 80% criterion may measure memorization or retrieval of leaked items rather than reasoning, and a fine-tune-plus-retrieval configuration that crosses the line on only 8 of 14 papers is high-variance (OP.C0202, OP.C0403, OP.C0302). The distilled-CoT data is synthetic, so teacher errors and plausible-but-wrong physics rationales are baked into the weights (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0304.01). (2) Distribution shift: exam style, plant-specific content, figures, tables and curve-reading, and revisions to the exam bank or handbooks all fall outside the training distribution. Multimodal input handling for graphs and P&IDs is likely weakest exactly where operator reasoning needs it, and BM25 chunking can split or omit procedure limits, units and conditions, giving oversimplified or truncated answers (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0304.03). PWR and BWR cross-contamination is a specific confusion mode (OP.C0302.03). (3) Verification gaps: sampling non-determinism means the same question can pass or fail across runs, rationales are not faithful explanations of the computation, and there is no AI-specific qualification regime for training tools (OP.C0402.02, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Trainee over-trust and skill fade follow from a tool scored against a human pass mark, and a passing score invites it to be treated as equivalent to qualified instruction (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0301).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Supply chain: open-weight base models, adapters, quantized checkpoints and fine-tuning dependencies pulled from public hubs can carry poisoned weights, backdoor triggers or unsafe serialization (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0058, AML.T0011.000). (2) Data and retrieval poisoning: tampering with the distilled rationale set, the handbook corpus or the BM25 index can plant subtly wrong values, setpoints or procedure logic that trainees absorb as authoritative, which degrades operator competence over time without any alarm (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0070, AML.T0071, AML.T0059, AML.T0031). (3) Multimodal inputs and indirect injection: images or documents ingested into the pipeline can carry adversarial perturbations or embedded instructions (AML.T0043, AML.T0051.001). (4) Reconnaissance and extraction: the model, prompts and benchmark results are public, so an adversary can learn exactly which failure modes to target (AML.T0000, AML.T0002.001). The insider and exam-integrity angle is that a model that drives a leaked or compromised answer key could be used to cheat or to game qualification. Although the stated scope is training, a compromised model also becomes a trust anchor that could later be reused for operations support (OP.C0602).

security_specialist.argument: Seen as a threat surface, this is a low-value direct target but a credible stepping stone and an erosion-of-vigilance risk. The model answers licensing-exam knowledge questions and does not touch plant control, so a nation-state would not bother attacking the AI itself. Its realistic danger is cultural and pathway-based. Operators and trainers could come to trust a system that only reached the 80% pass mark on 8 of 14 papers. An insider or supply-chain adversary could poison the fine-tuning rationales, the BM25 corpus or the open-weight artifact, and the error would reach the qualification pipeline for the people who will later hold the control-room license. Because the system is small, academic and not safety-classified, it will probably get weak change control, access governance and provenance checks, and that makes it an easy foothold or a quiet channel for influencing operator competence.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Training-pipeline and supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0019, T0058). Open-weight base models, distilled chain-of-thought rationales generated by another LLM, and community retrieval tooling are all unvetted inputs. A poisoned rationale set or corrupted handbook index could embed subtly wrong physics or procedural reasoning, such as reactivity feedback signs, shutdown margin logic or setpoint relationships, or a backdoor trigger on particular question phrasing. The AI failure is a confident, well-explained wrong answer. Training and qualification content depends on it. The consequence is miseducated operators, which is a latent safety effect that appears years later and is hard to attribute to the source. Insiders who maintain training materials have unusually direct access to this lever. (2) RAG and corpus tampering (AML.T0070, T0071, T0066, T0099). A BM25 index over handbooks is a simple, editable corpus, so one altered chunk could shift answers on targeted topics while aggregate exam scores look unchanged. (3) Stepping-stone and information risks. Training environments often sit near corporate networks, and unmanaged GPU hosts, credentials and model-serving endpoints are an easy foothold (AML.T0012, T0055, T0083). Fine-tuning on exam-derived data may also leak proprietary or exam-controlled content (AML.T0024, T0057), which is an exam-integrity and compromise risk. (4) Cheating and credential-integrity abuse. A capable exam-answering model lets candidates or insiders defeat knowledge assessment, which weakens the human qualification barrier that other security and safety arguments rely on. IMPLICIT: (5) Automation over-trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102). A headline accuracy figure measured on 2015-2021 exams invites trainers to use the tool as an authoritative tutor or answer key. Learners then disengage from independent reasoning, and an adversary could time an attack on an operator or procedure when the cohort's competence is lower than records suggest. (6) Benchmark validity and contamination. Past exams and handbooks are likely in pretraining data, so passing scores overstate real capability (OP.C0302.03, C0403, C0304.01). Pass rates are inconsistent (8 of 14 papers), the work is a non-peer-reviewed preprint, and no AI-specific QA exists for training tools (OP.C0501, C0504, C0402.02, C0401). PWR and BWR differences, multimodal diagram misreading and plausible hallucinated rationales are residual weaknesses. Weak oversight of this lower-tier use is itself the gap an adversary would use.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on over-trust and skill fade, benchmark contamination and weak validity, hallucinated rationales, the missing AI-specific QA basis, and supply-chain and RAG poisoning as the dominant adversarial pathway. I dropped low-severity items (denial of service, data leakage, reconnaissance) and the speculative T0012/T0055 credential codes, and I did not assign an ATLAS code to the cheating threat because no ATLAS technique matches it.

evidence.citation: "Benchmarking Fine-tuning and Retrieval Strategies for a Multimodal Language Model on the NRC Reactor Operator Licensing Examination," arXiv (Hwang, Lee and Alam)
evidence.note: The authors built and tested eight configurations (base model, supervised fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation and retrieval-augmented fine-tuning) on 14 NRC Generic Fundamentals Examination papers from 2015-2021. Only the fine-tuned model with fixed-size-chunk retrieval met the passing criterion, on 8 of the 14 papers. This is an arXiv preprint and has not been peer reviewed.

damage.why: Worst credible threat is supply-chain or corpus poisoning that embeds subtly wrong reactivity, shutdown-margin or setpoint reasoning, which erodes operator competence and safety margins; the tool has no control function and passes through instructor review, simulator assessment and NRC exams, so harm is indirect and stops short of a radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Over-trust, hallucinated rationales and non-repeatable inference occur reliably, but a poisoning or backdoor effect depends on a tampered artifact being adopted and on the right trigger phrasing, so reliability varies by threat.

exploitability.why: Open-weight models, editable BM25 corpora and weakly governed academic hosts need only moderate access, but placing tampered artifacts into a specific training pipeline requires some supply-chain or insider foothold.

affected_users.why: A poisoned tutor or corpus can affect a whole training cohort or program and its qualification records, but the impact is limited to the training population and does not propagate across coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: Poisoning of open-weight models, RAG corpora and supply chains, plus LLM hallucination and benchmark contamination, are well documented in the open literature, and the preprint openly reports the 8-of-14 result and the method, so an outsider can readily infer the weakness class.

use_case: LSTM-based autoencoder normal-behaviour model of control rod drive mechanism (CRDM) coil current signals in nuclear power plants, with an XGBoost classifier that flags outliers in the reconstruction residuals. It detects timing-sequence anomalies in CRDM operation for real-time condition-based maintenance.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory CRDM coil-current anomaly detector sits outside the protection chain, so its direct safety consequence is bounded, but it incurs insecurity by defining 'normal' for a safety-relevant mechanism from limited, partly simulated data and by shaping maintenance vigilance. Its main threats are poisoning of the normal baseline, evasion through the data path, supply-chain and fleet-wide compromise, and alert flooding. Implicit threats are the data-scarcity blind spots, drift and baseline creep, over-trust, and weak qualification, each of which an adversary can use to hide a fault or a manipulation.

Baseline poisoning at training or retraining -- adversarial
An insider, vendor or compromised historian can bias the cleaned 'normal' coil-current set, or tamper with the model, thresholds or labels, so that a degraded or tampered timing profile is learned as normal. A developing CRDM fault or sabotage of rod-motion timing then goes unflagged, and the periodic recalibration lets the route recur unnoticed.

Residual-threshold evasion and data-path manipulation -- adversarial
An adversary with access to the acquisition chain or historian can replay, smooth or slowly drift coil-current traces, or shape perturbations to the autoencoder's reconstruction strengths, so residuals stay under the XGBoost decision boundary. A real mechanical or electrical fault, or a hidden manipulation, then passes as healthy while staff rely on the flag in place of manual inspection.

Supply-chain and fleet propagation -- adversarial
Third-party ML libraries, pretrained weights or vendor-distributed models can carry tampering or embedded code, and the monitor's position at the IT/OT boundary gives it value as a pivot. A single compromised or flawed model pushed across several units becomes a common-mode blind spot.

Alert flooding and denial -- adversarial
Injected chaff or noise can drive false positives, or the monitor can be disabled, causing alarm fatigue so that operators loosen thresholds or switch the detector off. An action can then be timed for after the desensitisation.

Simulated-label and rare-fault blind spots -- implicit, exploitable
The classifier is likely trained on injected or simulated anomalies, and real faults are rare, so novel degradation such as insulation ageing, latch wear or gradual timing creep may reconstruct as normal. An adversary can hide a manipulation inside these uncovered fault regions, which are indistinguishable from natural degradation.

Drift, heterogeneity and baseline creep -- implicit, exploitable
Temperature, supply voltage, ageing, refurbishment and unit-to-unit differences shift the residual distribution, causing false alarms or threshold retuning that widens the normal envelope. Retraining on recent data absorbs slow degradation, and an adversary can ride this drift to normalise a gradual manipulation.

Two-stage coupling and non-repeatability -- implicit
The XGBoost stage is calibrated to the residual statistics of one autoencoder version, so retraining stage one silently invalidates stage two, and training non-determinism makes revalidation hard. An adversary gains little directly from this, beyond the weak change control it implies.

Over-trust, opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A quiet dashboard may lead staff to lengthen inspection intervals or let manual trending and skills lapse, while opaque residual flags give no causal explanation. A non-safety classification may leave the retraining pipeline without AI-specific QA, change control or cyber review. An adversary can time an action for when vigilance is lowest and use the unqualified retraining path as the weakest entry point for poisoning.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory condition-monitoring tool on CRDM coil current. The CRDM is not the trip function, because rod insertion on trip is by gravity after coil de-energization, and the reactor protection system is independent. Credible harm is therefore mostly indirect, through maintenance decisions, and it is bounded by existing practice such as surveillance testing, rod-drop time tests, technical-specification limits and periodic CRDM inspection. The real downstream risks are a missed or late degradation call (a false negative) that lets a latent mechanism fault go unnoticed between surveillances, or false positives that cause unnecessary rod exercising, outages or tests. Each of these needs the conventional safeguards to also fail or be relaxed before it affects safety, and the main way that happens is if the tool's output is trusted enough to replace or defer those safeguards. Each concern is below, with its cause and consequence kept distinct.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Training-data and label problems. The autoencoder learns from 'cleaned' normal data, and real CRDM faults are rare. The XGBoost stage depends on labelled or simulated anomalies, so it may recognise only the anomaly types seeded in the paper. Novel degradation modes, such as coil insulation ageing, latch wear or a gradual timing shift, may then sit inside the learned normal envelope. The consequence is a missed degradation signature that stays latent until a surveillance test or an in-service failure such as a stuck or slipped rod. Simulated or injected anomalies also give optimistic test performance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0302). (2) Drift and heterogeneity. Coil current depends on temperature, supply voltage, power-supply and cabling changes, fuel cycle, rod position, and differences between rods and between plants. Normal drift gives false alarms, which lead to alarm fatigue and disuse. Slow real degradation can instead be absorbed if the model is retrained on recent data, so a gradual fault is normalised. A model transferred between units or plants, or retrained after maintenance, can fail silently (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0602). (3) Human factors. Maintenance staff may treat a quiet dashboard as evidence of health and lengthen inspection intervals, or may spend effort chasing opaque flags. Opaque residual-to-fault mapping limits root-cause diagnosis (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0401). (4) Qualification and governance. Tools of this kind usually sit outside safety classification, so software QA, change control and revalidation after retraining may be thin. Any later use for surveillance credit or interval extension needs a qualification basis that the research-grade model does not have (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0504). Non-repeatable training adds to the problem (OP.C0402.01).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Data-integrity attack on the monitoring path. An adversary with access to the plant data historian or the data-acquisition network could alter, replay or smooth coil-current streams to hide a real fault or to induce false alarms (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0031, AML.T0046). The consequence is a masked mechanism fault, or wasted outages and operator attention. This is an attack on the data pipeline rather than on the model, but the AI amplifies it because staff rely on automated flagging. Physical manipulation of sensing or a slow low-amplitude drift engineered to stay under the residual threshold are evasion variants (AML.T0015). (6) Poisoning at retraining. If the 'normal' training window is refreshed from operational data, a patient adversary or a latent fault can contaminate the baseline (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002). The consequence is a model that treats fault behaviour as normal. Threshold, config or model-file tampering has the same effect (AML.T0076). (7) Supply chain and connectivity. Third-party Python/ML libraries, pretrained artifacts, or an off-site vendor analytics link create IT-to-OT pathways and a route for exfiltrating operational data (AML.T0010.001, OP.C0601). Reconnaissance on CRDM health data would also reveal degradation timing, which is of marginal value to an adversary. (8) Denial of service. Alert flooding or disabling the monitor mainly removes a convenience layer, so safety consequences are small but cumulative if maintenance has come to depend on it (AML.T0029).

Overall, the severity is low-to-moderate and is governed by whether the tool stays advisory. The defence-in-depth barriers are trip logic independence, rod-drop and exercise surveillance, and technical specifications. The main risk is erosion of these through over-reliance, and the main security concern is data-pipeline integrity rather than model attack.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a two-stage pipeline: an LSTM autoencoder trained only on cleaned normal coil-current traces, then an XGBoost classifier on the reconstruction residuals. The first stage defines 'normal' purely from what was in the training set. The second stage needs labelled anomalies, which in a real plant barely exist, so they are almost certainly injected or simulated. The fragility sits in the interface between the two. The classifier learns the residual signature of synthetic faults, while the autoencoder's residual distribution shifts with every aging, temperature, supply-voltage or sensor-calibration change. Reported accuracy comes from a clean, curated dataset, and nothing in the paper shows it holds on field data with drift, rare fault modes, or deliberately shaped inputs. CRDM current traces are also low-dimensional, highly stereotyped timing signals. That makes them easy to model, but it also makes it easy to craft or replay input that reconstructs well.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data provenance and scarcity: real CRDM failures are rare, so the XGBoost anomaly labels are likely simulated or injected, and 'normal' data is cleaned by a human or heuristic filter. The detector therefore only recognises the anomaly types the authors imagined, and it may silently reconstruct novel real degradation (coil insulation aging, latch wear, gradual timing creep) as normal. Residuals stay low, and the maintenance team is told nothing is wrong. (2) Drift and heterogeneity: the model is trained on one plant, one CRDM population and one operating regime. Fuel cycle changes, coil temperature, power supply replacement, sensor or ADC changes, and unit-to-unit variation shift the residual distribution. Either false alarms erode trust, or the threshold is retuned until real anomalies are hidden. Slow degradation is also absorbed if the model is retrained on recent 'normal' data (concept drift and baseline creep). (3) Two-stage coupling: the classifier is calibrated to residual statistics from one autoencoder version, so any retraining of stage one invalidates stage two. Together with training non-determinism, this makes qualification and repeatability hard. (4) Human factors and qualification gap: a CBM advisory tool is likely to be over-trusted and used to defer inspections of a safety-relevant mechanism, and it is hard to justify under I&C software qualification regimes. Opacity of LSTM residuals also makes operators unable to tell which timing feature triggered an alert. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Evasion: an adversary with access to the plant data network or the current acquisition chain could shape or replay coil-current traces, or do slow low-amplitude manipulation, to stay under residual thresholds while a real mechanical or electrical fault develops. Alternatively, they could inject chaff to cause false alarms and unnecessary outages. The model's narrow input domain makes surrogate modelling feasible from published architectures and similar public data. (6) Training-data and pipeline poisoning: an insider or compromised historian can bias the 'normal' set during cleaning, or tamper with labels, so that a particular fault signature becomes the learned baseline (a backdoor-like blind spot). Model files, thresholds and preprocessing code are further integrity targets. (7) Supply chain and fleet propagation: the same open-source LSTM and XGBoost libraries, pretrained weights, or vendor-distributed models deployed across a fleet turn one poisoned or flawed model into a common-mode blind spot across many units. CONSEQUENCES. These range from undetected CRDM degradation affecting rod insertion timing margin (safety), to unnecessary outages from induced false positives (economic and operational), to degraded confidence in the integrity of plant monitoring data. Because the tool is advisory and sits outside the protection system, direct safety impact depends on how heavily maintenance decisions rely on it.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is a condition-monitoring model sitting on the signal path of the CRDM, the mechanism that actuates reactivity control and scram insertion. It is advisory and not in the protection chain, so a nation-state would probably not choose it as the direct target. It matters as a stepping stone and as a vigilance-shaping tool. Maintenance staff will learn to trust its 'normal' verdict, and a model that defines normal can be taught, by someone with data or model access, to accept a degraded or tampered coil-current profile as normal. That would mask real mechanical or electrical degradation, or hide tampering with the drive's timing sequence, while an adversary sets up a separate action. The most credible adversary is an insider or a vendor/integrator with access to training data, model artifacts or the historian feed, not an outsider.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and baseline poisoning. The 'normal' model is trained on cleaned historical coil current. Someone with access to the data pipeline, to the cleaning step or to retraining could slowly shift the baseline so that a developing fault or an intentionally introduced timing deviation falls inside the learned envelope (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). The facility depends on the model for condition-based maintenance and for deferring or scheduling CRDM work. The consequence is suppressed detection of degrading drives, or a covert window in which sabotage of rod motion timing is not flagged, which is a safety and availability consequence. Because the model is retrained or recalibrated as the plant ages, the poisoning route recurs without anyone noticing. (2) Evasion of the two-stage detector. The XGBoost classifier on residuals is a small, learnable decision surface. An insider who knows the residual features and thresholds can craft signal perturbations that keep residuals low, for example slow drift or anomalies shaped to the model's reconstruction strengths (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0044). The facility relies on the outlier flag as a substitute for periodic manual inspection, so a successful evasion converts into a missed fault or a hidden manipulation. (3) Supply-chain and integrity compromise. The model is a pipeline of third-party ML libraries, trained weights and a data connection to plant I/O (AML.T0010, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.002). Its position in an OT/IT boundary zone gives it value as a pivot toward the CRDM control or monitoring network, even though the model itself is advisory. A data diode or one-way path is assumed, but integrations tend to erode it over time. (4) Alert flooding and denial. Injecting chaff or noise to trigger false positives (AML.T0046, AML.T0029) causes alarm fatigue, or prompts operators to disable or loosen the detector. An adversary can then time an action for after the desensitisation. (5) Reconnaissance. Publication of the architecture, data characteristics and reported anomaly classes (AML.T0000, AML.T0002) lowers the cost of building a proxy model (AML.T0005).

IMPLICIT, exploitable by an adversary. (1) Automation complacency: if the detector rarely alarms, staff may relax manual trending and walk-down inspection, and skills fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Adversaries can time an action for when vigilance is lowest. (2) Scarcity of real fault data and a low base rate. Training on normal data only means that the anomaly classes seen in testing are probably injected or simulated, so real-world coverage is unknown (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02). Gaps in coverage are exactly where an adversary or a natural fault can hide. (3) Drift and operational heterogeneity. Coil current changes with ageing, temperature, power supply changes, refurbishment and between plants. Unmonitored drift either floods operators with false alarms or silently widens the normal envelope, which masks real degradation (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). (4) Opacity and qualification gaps. Residual-based flags give no causal explanation, and a non-safety classification may leave the model without AI-specific QA, change control or cyber-security review (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0503). An unqualified retraining pipeline is the weakest point from which poisoning could be introduced. (5) Cross-fleet propagation. If a vendor pushes the same model or baseline to several units or sites, one compromise or one bad update will propagate (OP.C0602).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on baseline poisoning, evasion below residual thresholds, scarcity of real fault data, drift, over-trust and the qualification gap, and these were merged into single threats. I dropped weakly argued items (reconnaissance and proxy-model building, the off-site cloud link, AML.T0041, AML.T0044, and the generic AML.T0043 and OP.C0503/C0603 codes) because their pathways were marginal or are covered by more specific codes already assigned.

evidence.citation: "Anomaly detection of control rod drive mechanism using long short-term memory-based autoencoder and extreme gradient boosting," Nuclear Science and Techniques (Springer)
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests an anomaly detector on CRDM coil-current data. An LSTM autoencoder is trained on normal (cleaned) operating current to model normal behaviour. XGBoost then classifies the reconstruction residuals to pick out anomalies. The authors report that it detects several kinds of timing-sequence anomalies and forecasts the coil current more accurately than comparison methods.

damage.why: The detector is advisory and outside the protection chain, so the worst credible harm (a missed developing CRDM fault or hidden manipulation of rod-motion timing, plus fleet-wide common-mode blind spots) is eroded safety margin and maintenance vigilance, not a direct radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Drift, baseline creep, simulated-label blind spots and over-trust arise reliably in this class of model, but adversarial poisoning or evasion needs specific access and conditions, so overall reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (baseline poisoning, data-path manipulation, supply-chain compromise) need insider, vendor, historian or acquisition-chain access, which is well beyond routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Impact is typically a single CRDM monitoring function, but a compromised or flawed model pushed across units becomes a multi-unit common-mode blind spot, still bounded to the advisory maintenance layer.

discoverability.why: The architecture is published and the weakness classes (poisoning, evasion of reconstruction residuals, drift, supply chain) are well documented in the open literature, but learning a specific deployment's thresholds, data path and retraining cadence needs partial insider information.

use_case: Three-stage deep-learning diagnostic and prognostic framework for a pebble-bed high-temperature gas reactor (Xe-100 type). An LSTM autoencoder detects anomalies in plant transient signals. A CNN then characterises which transient is occurring. An LSTM-dense network predicts remaining useful life, meaning the time until a safety limit such as reactor outlet temperature is exceeded. The models were trained on transients from a SimuPACT digital twin and tested on a water-ingress reactivity-insertion event. The framework is meant to support operators in accident management and in reducing forced shutdowns.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory detect-classify-predict chain for a pebble-bed HTGR is trained only on SimuPACT digital-twin transients and tested on one water-ingress case. Its main exposures are an unvalidated sim-to-real gap, closed-set misclassification feeding a falsely authoritative time-to-limit, operator over-trust or disuse, and a lack of qualification basis. Adversaries can corrupt the data and model pipeline, evade or spoof the detector through input manipulation, or time actions around its predictable blind spots. The tool is not in the protection path, so harm depends on operators crediting the advice.

Sim-to-real gap and data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Training solely on idealised simulated transients for a new-build design with no operating history leaves real sensor noise, degradation, pebble-flow and burnup heterogeneity outside the learned distribution, so the autoencoder misses real precursors or raises false alarms. An adversary could study published methods to locate these blind spots and time a physical or cyber action inside them.

Closed-set misclassification and cascading error -- implicit, exploitable
The CNN must assign a known transient label to novel, compound or sensor-fault conditions, and the RUL regressor then extrapolates a confident time-to-limit along the wrong trajectory with no calibrated uncertainty, so upstream misses compound silently. An adversary could trigger or coincide with a condition outside the closed set so that operators receive a plausible but wrong diagnosis and margin.

Operator over-trust, disuse and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A precise countdown to a safety limit invites anchoring during high-workload accident management, while rarely used tools erode manual diagnosis skill and frequent false alarms breed disuse. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust by skewing the countdown to buy time for concurrent sabotage, or cultivate alarm fatigue with nuisance alerts before a real event.

Qualification, opacity and repeatability gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Opaque LSTM and CNN features, non-deterministic training, single-case static testing and no AI-specific QA or licensing basis mean outputs cannot be justified in a safety case, and retraining can silently change behaviour. An adversary could hide subtle poisoning or tampering inside what looks like ordinary retraining drift, since forensics cannot separate the two, and exploit a lower-assurance advisory path adjacent to protected I&C.

Training-data, twin and model tampering -- adversarial
Poisoning simulation inputs, transient libraries, the retraining pipeline or model weights can implant a backdoor trigger or systematic blind spot, such as a transient signature labelled benign or an inflated RUL, that passes simulation-only validation. The result is silently delayed or misdirected accident-management response that persists across model versions.

Input evasion and spoofing -- adversarial
An adversary with access to sensor or historian paths can craft slow, low-amplitude perturbations that stay within the autoencoder's reconstruction tolerance, or mimic one transient while causing another, hiding a developing event. The same access can inject chaff or spoofed anomalies to force unnecessary shutdowns and erode trust.

Proxy-model reconnaissance and theft -- adversarial
Published architectures and open Xe-100-type data let an adversary build a proxy model offline, learn detection thresholds and failure regions, and extract model artefacts that encode proprietary reactor behaviour. This supports tuned evasion and timing of actions around the detector.

Service denial and IT-OT exposure -- adversarial
Disrupting or delaying the inference path, or compromising the IT/OT bridge, update channel or vendor remote access hosting the analytics, removes accident-management support operators have come to rely on and may push a conservative shutdown. It also gives a foothold toward plant data networks.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is an advisory diagnostic and prognostic chain (detect, classify, predict time-to-limit) that sits beside the protection system, not in it. Real harm therefore needs a human or procedural layer to fail as well. The risks are operators leaning on a wrong classification or a wrong time-to-limit estimate during an upset, and the framework triggering unnecessary shutdowns or false confidence. The system is trained entirely on SimuPACT digital-twin transients and tested on one water-ingress/reactivity event for a design with little or no operating history, so it is never qualified against real plant behaviour, and its errors are hard to see until a real transient exposes them. The chain is also serial, so a miss or misclassification at stage 1 or 2 propagates into the RUL estimate, and the final number looks authoritative while resting on compounding uncertainty.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and new-build data scarcity. Training and test data come from a digital twin of a design with no fleet history. Real sensor noise, instrument degradation, fouling, calibration offsets, pebble-flow and burnup heterogeneity, and operating modes the twin does not model all fall outside the training distribution. The consequence is missed or delayed anomaly detection, or false alarms. Missed detection delays accident-management actions. False alarms drive unneeded trips or erode operator trust, so the tool is ignored when it is right (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (2) Narrow validation. One reactivity-insertion test case says little about the many other transient classes, concurrent faults, or sensor-fault cases. The CNN is forced to pick from a closed set of known transients, so a novel or compound event gets a confident but wrong label. The RUL net then extrapolates time-to-limit along the wrong trajectory (OP.C0202, OP.C0403, OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). (3) Human factors. A precise-looking countdown to a safety limit invites anchoring and over-trust during a high-stress event. Operators with little hands-on HTGR experience may defer to it, or may follow a misdiagnosis that contradicts their procedures. Over time the tool may also cause skill fade and alarm complacency. Mitigations already exist: emergency operating procedures, symptom-based response, and the independent protection system. The residual risk is delayed or misdirected operator action in the gap before those layers engage (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102, OP.C0401). (4) Qualification and repeatability. Training non-determinism, opaque features, and no AI-specific QA or licensing basis for use in accident management mean the outputs cannot be justified in a safety case. Retraining or updating the model after twin revisions, or after real data arrive, can silently change its behaviour (OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0502). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Integrity attacks on the input signals or the twin-derived data. Subtle manipulation of plant-signal streams, historian data, or retraining data could suppress anomaly flags, induce a wrong transient classification, or skew the time-to-limit estimate. The effect is false reassurance during a real event, or nuisance shutdowns that cost availability. The adversary does not need to touch protection systems. Success needs only operators to credit the advisory output. An adversary could also time this around a real or induced transient (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0010.002). (6) Model or pipeline tampering. A compromised model file, training pipeline, or simulator dependency could embed a backdoor trigger or degrade accuracy while leaving test metrics apparently normal. Because validation is simulation-only, hidden degradation is hard to spot (AML.T0018, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0031). (7) Denial or degradation of the service. If operators rely on the tool, DoS or latency on the inference path degrades accident-management support and may push a conservative shutdown (AML.T0029). It also adds an IT-to-OT attack surface if the analytics are connected to plant data networks (OP.C0601, OP.C0505).

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, the main fragility is that all three stages are trained purely on SimuPACT digital-twin output for a reactor type with essentially no operating fleet. There is no field data to calibrate against, so sim-to-real gap, sensor noise and fault models, and the physics fidelity of rare events like water ingress are all unvalidated. The pipeline is also cascaded: the autoencoder gates the CNN, and the CNN's transient label conditions the RUL regressor. A miss or misclassification at stage 1 or 2 therefore propagates silently into a confident time-to-limit estimate. The stages also have closed-set assumptions (the CNN can only name transients it was trained on, and the RUL net only extrapolates within the simulated trajectory manifold), so novel, compound or sensor-fault conditions produce plausible but wrong outputs, exactly when operators need accident-management support. Testing on one reactivity-insertion case leaves coverage, calibration and uncertainty quantification largely unestablished.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and data provenance: training exclusively on simulated transients, with a new-build design that has no operational data, means the learned signal-to-fault mapping reflects the twin's assumptions (nodalisation, noise-free or idealised sensors, modelled fault set). On real plant data the autoencoder reconstruction threshold may produce false alarms (eroding trust and driving disuse) or miss real precursors. This is OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0203 and OP.C0302. (2) Out-of-distribution and closed-set failure: the CNN classifier will assign a known label to novel, concurrent or instrument-fault conditions, and the RUL regressor will output a confident time-to-limit number with no calibrated uncertainty. Operators may act on a wrong accident diagnosis or wrong time margin (OP.C0302, OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (3) Cascading architecture: stage-to-stage dependence means one upstream error biases all downstream outputs (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603), and the final RUL gives an appearance of quantitative authority. (4) Qualification mismatch: a static test on one water-ingress case does not qualify a dynamic, safety-relevant advisory tool. Non-deterministic training, no explainability and no defined retraining or revalidation path make it hard to qualify under I&C software regimes (OP.C0303, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Automation bias and skill fade are likely if operators lean on the RUL during accident management (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Data and model supply chain: the twin outputs, training sets, weights and retraining pipeline are high-value integrity targets. Poisoning the simulation inputs or the model (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004) could implant blind spots or backdoor triggers, such as a signature pattern that suppresses anomaly flags or a skewed RUL. Because there is little field data, such tampering would be hard to detect against a ground truth. (6) Input manipulation at inference: an attacker with access to plant data networks or sensor channels could craft or inject small perturbations (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) so the autoencoder reconstructs a developing transient as normal, or the CNN mislabels it, delaying detection or inflating the time-to-limit estimate. Alternatively, spoofed anomalies or chaff (AML.T0046) could trigger false alarms and unnecessary forced shutdowns, which is an availability and economic attack. Recent knowledge of the published architecture and open Xe-100-type data eases proxy-model construction (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0002). (7) Timing exploitation of implicit weaknesses: an adversary who understands the model's closed-set limits and calibration gaps could time manipulation to coincide with a real off-nominal condition, where the model is least reliable and operator reliance highest. The consequence is degraded accident management and possible shutdown margin misjudgement; the system is advisory, so the consequence depends on how far operators come to rely on it.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this three-stage pipeline sits between raw plant signals and operator situational awareness during off-normal events. That is exactly when an adversary would want operators to hold a wrong picture: a missed anomaly, a wrong transient label, or an inflated time-to-limit. The chain is serial, so a single compromised or biased stage (the training pipeline, the digital-twin data feeding it, or the input signal path) propagates to both the diagnosis and the countdown the operator relies on. Even without an adversary, the system is trained purely on simulated SimuPACT transients and validated on one water-ingress case. Its blind spots are therefore large, predictable and discoverable, and a patient adversary could time a physical, cyber or insider action around them, or exploit operator trust in the tool. The model's most valuable role as an adversary's stepping stone is as a trusted advisory layer that can be steered (a quiet bias rather than a loud failure), not as a direct actuator.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and digital-twin integrity: the models are only as trustworthy as the simulator transients they learn from. An insider or supply-chain actor who alters simulation inputs, transient libraries, or the retraining pipeline could embed a backdoor or a systematic blind spot (e.g., a particular transient signature classified as benign or as a different event). The AI failure is silent corrupted learning. The facility dependence is that operators use the anomaly flag and transient label for accident management. The consequence is delayed or misdirected response, and it persists across model versions (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004, OP.C0201.01). (2) Evasion and input manipulation: an adversary with access to sensor or data-historian paths could craft slow, low-amplitude signal changes that stay inside the autoencoder's reconstruction tolerance, or that mimic one transient while causing another. The CNN classifier and the RUL regressor are brittle outside the simulated distribution. This lets an attack be masked as a benign state, or, in the opposite direction, trigger false alarms and forced shutdowns (an economic and trust-erosion attack) (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031, AML.T0046). (3) Model theft and reconnaissance: published methods and architectures let a motivated adversary build a proxy model and learn its detection thresholds and failure regions offline, then time actions around them (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0044, AML.T0024.002). The model artefacts and the digital twin also encode sensitive design and behaviour data for a proprietary reactor (AML.T0035, AML.T0025). (4) Concentrated trust and vigilance erosion: a prognostic countdown to a safety limit is an authoritative-looking number. If operators defer to it, an adversary who skews it (e.g., overestimating time-to-limit) buys time for a concurrent sabotage or lengthens the window for harm, and may do this in parallel with a conventional attack that the tool fails to flag. Compromise of the IT/OT bridge that hosts the model, an update channel, or a vendor remote-access path is the likelier route than attacking the model mathematically (AML.T0012, AML.T0018, AML.T0010.001).

IMPLICIT. (5) Sim-to-real gap and thin validation: training on a single digital twin with no operational data for a first-of-a-kind design, and testing on one reactivity-insertion event, gives no assurance on sensor noise, degradation, novel transients, or concurrent faults. Out-of-distribution inputs yield confident but wrong labels and RUL. An adversary does not need to attack the model if it already fails predictably, and could pick a scenario where it is known to be weak (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0301.01). (6) Cascading error through the three stages: a missed or late anomaly detection means no classification and no prognosis, while a misclassification feeds a wrongly-conditioned RUL. Errors compound rather than being independently checked (OP.C0603, OP.C0304.03). (7) Human factors: reliance on the advisory output during high-workload accident conditions invites over-trust, and unfamiliarity from rarely-used tools erodes skills for manual diagnosis. Frequent false alarms push the opposite way, toward disuse, which an adversary can deliberately cultivate over time before a real event (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.05). (8) Opacity and repeatability: black-box LSTM and CNN outputs cannot easily be audited by operators or investigators, and retraining non-determinism makes tampering hard to distinguish from drift, which weakens forensic detection of a subtle poisoning (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0502). (9) Governance: advisory tools that are not safety-classified may skip the cyber and QA rigour applied to I&C, even though operators treat them as decision-critical, leaving a lower-assurance pathway adjacent to protected systems (OP.C0501, OP.C0503, OP.C0504).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, cascaded closed-set error, human over-trust, qualification gaps, data/model poisoning and input evasion; I merged these and dropped weakly supported codes (AML.T0044, AML.T0025, AML.T0059, AML.T0002, OP.C0304.03) that restated other threats or lacked a clear mechanism in the text.

evidence.citation: "A system diagnostic and prognostic framework based on deep learning for advanced reactors," Progress in Nuclear Energy (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests an LSTM-autoencoder, CNN and LSTM-dense pipeline on simulated Xe-100 pebble-bed HTGR digital-twin transient data. It reports anomaly-detection delay, transient-characterisation accuracy and time-to-threshold prediction error on a reactivity-insertion test case.

damage.why: The tool is advisory and outside the protection path, so the most severe credible threat (poisoned or evaded diagnosis delaying accident-management response, possibly timed with concurrent sabotage) mostly erodes safety margin or causes spurious shutdowns; a release would need additional independent failures.

reproducibility.why: Closed-set misclassification, sim-to-real gaps, and over-trust reliably occur once off-distribution conditions or operator reliance exist, but adversarial evasion or poisoning outcomes depend on access, model specifics, and operator behavior.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (poisoning the retraining pipeline or weights, or manipulating sensor or historian paths) need privileged OT/IT or supply-chain access, though proxy-model reconnaissance from open literature needs little.

affected_users.why: A compromised diagnostic and prognostic chain misleads operator decisions across the plant's accident-management function and persists across model versions, but it stays advisory and does not directly act on coupled systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture and training approach are published, open Xe-100-type data exist, and the weaknesses (sim-only training, closed-set classification, single-case testing) are well documented for this class of AI system, so a capable outsider can infer them.

use_case: Deep-learning surrogate models (BPNN, PSO-optimised BPNN, CNN and RBFNN) trained on a high-fidelity 3D CFD database of fouled PWR steam generators. They rapidly predict the fouling-layer thermal resistance from operating parameters, and their noise robustness was tested. The aim is to support fouling monitoring and cleaning decisions during steam generator maintenance.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory fouling-resistance surrogate (BPNN, PSO-BPNN, CNN, RBFNN) is trained only on simulated CFD data at a few discrete fouling levels and feeds fouling monitoring and cleaning decisions. It is not a protection function, so the main exposure is quiet mis-scheduling of maintenance rather than an acute event. The main threats are a sim-to-real and out-of-distribution gap, drift and non-repeatability, over-trust, and governance gaps (all implicit), plus adversarial input manipulation, training-data and model tampering, and model or CFD-database theft.

Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
The surrogates learned idealised, uniform CFD fouling and give point estimates with no uncertainty, so they can be confidently wrong on patchy deposits, partial tube-support-plate blockage, sensor bias or new SG designs. Under-prediction defers cleaning and erodes thermal margin and tube integrity, while over-prediction forces unnecessary outages and cleaning-chemistry exposure. An adversary could time a chemistry excursion or sensor tampering for operating regions where the model is least reliable, and could rely on the unflagged error to hide the effect.

Concept drift and fleet propagation -- implicit, exploitable
As the SG ages, chemistry changes, power is uprated or cleaning resets the baseline, the static model becomes unrepresentative with no recalibration trigger, and one copy reused across units repeats the same bias. An adversary could slowly shift plant conditions or the historian baseline so that the drift looks natural and the divergence is attributed to ageing.

Training non-repeatability and opacity -- implicit
PSO and random weight initialisation produce different models and different R_f values on each retraining, and the opaque networks give no basis to challenge outputs. This undermines qualification and comparison of results across outages, and an adversary gains little directly from it.

Over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A fast, smooth R_f value can displace eddy-current inspection, delta-P trending and first-principles judgement, leaving fewer independent checks on the model. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust so that a biased estimate goes unchallenged.

Qualification and change-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
A maintenance-support tool is easily left outside AI-specific V&V, change control and cybersecurity scope, so it can migrate toward safety-relevant use and its retraining or weight swaps go unreviewed. This is the unreviewed change path an insider or compromised vendor would use to alter the model.

Input manipulation -- adversarial
Small, structured bias in the pressure, flow and temperature inputs, via spoofed sensors or a tampered historian, can drive R_f falsely low or high and delay or force cleaning without tripping any alarm. The paper's synthetic random-noise test says nothing about crafted perturbations.

Training-data and model tampering -- adversarial
An insider or compromised CFD, ML-library or vendor supply chain could poison the CFD database, retraining data or weight files, or erode integrity through retraining on manipulated historian data. The result is a systematically optimistic or pessimistic model that passes spot checks and skews maintenance timing.

Model and CFD-database theft -- adversarial
The surrogate and its CFD database encode proprietary SG geometry and thermal-hydraulic characteristics, and the model can be extracted through its interface or exfiltrated by cyber means. Vendor or academic collaboration channels, and any cloud hosting, widen the leak path.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory surrogate for steam generator fouling monitoring and cleaning scheduling. It is not a protection-system function, so the plausible failures are slow degradation rather than an acute event. The surrogate learned a simulated world (3D CFD at a handful of fouling levels), not a measured one, and it is fed noisy plant instrumentation (SG pressure, flow, temperature, power). Wrong output matters through two routes. Fouling is under-predicted, so cleaning is deferred and the plant accumulates thermal-performance loss, tube support plate (TSP) blockage, water-level instability, and corrosion or tube degradation. Alternatively fouling is over-predicted, which causes unnecessary outages, chemical cleaning and tube-wall exposure to cleaning chemistry. Existing practice already guards against this: inspection (eddy current, visual), secondary chemistry control, delta-P and level trending, and engineer sign-off on cleaning. Harm therefore needs those independent checks to be skipped, or the model to quietly take over as the trending basis.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT. (1) Sim-to-real gap: training data is CFD at discrete fouling levels with idealised geometry, deposit morphology and uniform fouling. Real deposits are patchy, change with chemistry (magnetite, copper, TSP deposits), and vary by SG design and plant. The model may extrapolate or interpolate badly off-grid, and the paper's 'noise robustness' test uses synthetic noise, not real sensor bias, drift or fouled-instrument error. This is OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0203 and OP.C0303. Output can look precise (a smooth R_f value) while having no validated uncertainty, which invites over-trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401). (2) Non-repeatability: PSO-BPNN depends on random initialisation and swarm search, so retraining gives different models and different R_f values (OP.C0402.01), which complicates qualification and trend comparison across outages (OP.C0501). (3) Concept drift as the SG ages, chemistry changes, power is uprated, or cleaning alters the baseline. The model silently becomes unrepresentative without a recalibration trigger (OP.C0302.02). A fleet-wide copy of the model would repeat the same bias across units (OP.C0602). (4) Goal misalignment: fouling resistance is a proxy for the actual concerns of tube integrity, TSP blockage and stability, so a good R_f can mask localised blockage (OP.C0301, OP.C0304.03).

ADVERSARIAL, and mostly low consequence given the advisory role. (a) Input manipulation or sensor spoofing, or tampering with historian data feeding the model (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0059), could bias R_f downward to delay cleaning or upward to force an outage. This is a quiet way to degrade performance or economics without tripping any alarm. (b) Poisoning or tampering with the CFD database, the training pipeline or the weights, including an insider, vendor or supply-chain compromise of the ML tooling (AML.T0010, AML.T0020, AML.T0018, AML.T0031), would produce a systematically optimistic model that passes spot checks. (c) Theft of the model or the CFD database exposes proprietary SG geometry and operating data (AML.T0024, AML.T0025), and in a cloud or vendor-hosted setup this is a data-governance concern (OP.C0601, OP.C0505). Mitigations are independent measurement, such as inspection results and plant thermal-performance calculations, model versioning with integrity checks, and periodic validation against as-found outage data. The residual risk is complacency, where the surrogate gradually replaces inspection-based judgement (OP.C0101.06).

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a surrogate trained entirely on simulated data: a 3D CFD database of fouled PWR steam generators at a handful of discrete fouling levels, with no evident field-measured ground truth. The model therefore inherits every CFD assumption (idealized fouling geometry and roughness, uniform deposit properties, fixed boundary conditions) and has no mechanism to detect when real SG behaviour departs from them. The small, sparse, low-dimensional input space is ideal for BPNN/RBFNN interpolation but fragile at inference. Real plants have non-uniform deposits, tube-support-plate blockage, sensor bias and transients that were likely never sampled, and PSO-tuned hyperparameters may be overfit to a narrow database. Noise robustness was tested only against synthetic noise, which says little about structured, correlated or adversarial perturbations to the instrument inputs. The deeper exposure is that a point-estimate regressor with no uncertainty output sits behind a maintenance decision and looks authoritative.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and OOD failure: CFD-only training data means the surrogate predicts confidently on inputs outside the simulated fouling regimes (different deposit morphology, partial tube plugging, new SG designs, power uprates, water chemistry changes). Cause: simulated provenance and discrete fouling levels. Dependency: fouling-monitoring and cleaning-schedule decisions. Consequence: under-estimated thermal resistance leads to deferred cleaning, tube degradation, reduced heat-removal margin and corrosion-related integrity risk. Over-estimated resistance leads to unnecessary outages, chemical-cleaning exposure and cost. (2) Drift and transferability: fouling evolves with chemistry, materials and operating history (concept drift). Surrogates are static, with no recalibration against plant data, and transferring one model across units or SG designs is unqualified. (3) Explainability and uncertainty gaps: BPNN, CNN and RBFNN regressors give point estimates without calibrated intervals. Different architectures can disagree, and PSO and weight-initialisation stochasticity cause training non-repeatability, which makes qualification and reproducing an audited result hard. (4) Automation bias and skill fade: a fast, plausible number can displace inspection and eddy-current evidence. (5) Qualification and QA gap: no established V&V path for ML surrogates in non-safety O&M decision support, so a model can quietly migrate toward safety-relevant use.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Input manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043): the surrogate consumes operating parameters such as temperatures, flows and pressures. Spoofed or biased sensor or historian data makes the model emit a falsely benign fouling estimate and delay maintenance. Because the models are small and simple, black-box probing or proxy-model construction would be cheap, and the paper's synthetic-noise robustness does not address crafted perturbations. (b) Training-data and model integrity (AML.T0020, T0010.002/T0010.003, T0018.000): tampering with the CFD database, retraining sets or the PSO-tuned weight files, or compromised ML libraries, could bias predictions systematically in a way that is hard to notice without independent ground truth. (c) Calibration-baseline poisoning (AML.T0059, T0031): if plant data later feeds retraining, slow manipulation of the historian erodes model integrity. (d) Model and IP exposure (AML.T0024.002, T0035): the CFD database and surrogate encode proprietary SG geometry and design information. Pipeline-level mitigations include out-of-distribution detectors, ensemble disagreement as an uncertainty signal, field-data validation, signed model artifacts, and sensor-integrity cross-checks.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view this is a low-value direct target: a surrogate that estimates fouling thermal resistance sits on the advisory side of maintenance planning, and a nation-state would not spend effort on it for sabotage. Its interest lies in what it changes about trust and timing. If cleaning schedules and fouling monitoring come to rely on a fast, opaque estimate, then whoever can bias that estimate (a training-set insider, a compromised CFD toolchain, a manipulated sensor feed) can steer maintenance timing and shape the steam generator's thermal-hydraulic condition without touching any safety-classified system. The reported noise-robustness testing covers random noise, not structured or adversarial perturbation, and that gap is exactly what a deliberate adversary would use. Its main role in an attack is as a stepping stone or a source of misplaced confidence, not as the target itself.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model integrity: the CFD database and the trained weights (BPNN, PSO-BPNN, CNN, RBFNN) are small, high-value artifacts that an insider or a compromised simulation/ML supply chain could poison or backdoor (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0043.004). A subtle bias makes fouling look lower than reality, so cleaning is deferred and degradation goes unnoticed. Or it makes fouling look higher, which triggers unneeded outages, extra worker dose and downtime. The consequence is eroded steam generator performance and tube-integrity margin, or economic harm, with no obvious alarm. (2) Input manipulation: the models take operating parameters (temperatures, flows, pressures) from plant instrumentation. Coordinated, small, structured deviations in those inputs could evade the model (AML.T0015, T0043), and robustness to random noise says little about this. This matters most if an adversary already has footholds in the data historian or the IT/OT boundary, and the surrogate gives them a way to shape decisions indirectly. (3) Model and data exfiltration: the surrogate and its CFD database encode steam generator geometry and thermal-hydraulic characteristics, which are proprietary and potentially sensitive design information (AML.T0024.002, T0035, T0025). Vendor or academic collaboration channels widen the leak path (OP.C0505.01).

IMPLICIT, TIMEABLE BY AN ADVERSARY. (4) The model is trained on simulated CFD at a few discrete fouling levels, so it is only valid within that envelope.
