Real fouling is non-uniform and changes in composition, and there is no field validation (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0303). The surrogate can be confidently wrong out of distribution. An adversary who understands this can time an action, such as a chemistry excursion or sensor tampering, for when the model is least reliable. (5) Automation trust: a fast PSO-BPNN readout invites over-trust and skill fade in the staff who would otherwise judge fouling from first principles, from inspection, and from secondary-side trends (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Opacity limits challenge (OP.C0401). A single shared model could also propagate one bias across a fleet of units (OP.C0602). (6) Governance: a maintenance-support tool is easy to leave outside AI-specific qualification, change control and cybersecurity scope (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0503). Retraining or swapping weights is then an unreviewed change path, which is the access an insider needs.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sim-to-real/OOD failure, drift, over-trust, input manipulation, training/model tampering and model theft; I merged the overlapping statements and kept governance and non-repeatability as distinct threats. I dropped speculative codes (e.g. T0012, T0043.004, goal misalignment, cloud dependency) that were not clearly instantiated by the documented system.

evidence.citation: "A machine learning and CFD based approach for fouling rapid prediction in shell-and-tube heat exchanger," Nuclear Engineering and Design (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper builds CFD simulations of steam generator fouling at several fouling levels and trains four neural networks on them to predict fouling thermal resistance quickly. It compares their accuracy, speed and anti-noise performance, and finds PSO-BPNN gives the best balance of speed and accuracy. I could only read the abstract and introduction snippet in the search results, not the full paper.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is biased fouling estimates that silently mis-schedule cleaning (deferred cleaning eroding thermal margin and tube integrity, or forced unnecessary outages); this is operational disruption with minor safety-margin erosion, since the tool is advisory and not a protection function.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real and OOD gaps, unflagged point estimates, and static-model drift recur reliably whenever operating conditions leave the idealised CFD training envelope, and a poisoned or biased model yields consistent systematic error.

exploitability.why: Natural OOD and drift errors need no access, but deliberately steering outputs through input manipulation, data or model tampering requires access to sensors, the historian, or the vendor supply chain and some domain knowledge.

affected_users.why: Impact is mainly on one steam generator's maintenance decisions, but a single model copy reused across units propagates the same bias fleet-wide, though it stays confined to maintenance planning rather than coupled safety systems.

discoverability.why: Sim-to-real gaps, drift, over-trust and adversarial-input and poisoning weaknesses of neural surrogates are well documented in the open literature, and the paper itself discloses its simulation-only training and synthetic-noise-only robustness test.

use_case: Transformer-based reconstruction anomaly detection for reactor coolant pump condition monitoring in nuclear power plants. Each sensor's observations are treated as a token, and attention learns the correlations between channels. The model trains only on normal-condition historical operating data. Large reconstruction errors on the input signals flag early-stage deterioration, before it develops into unplanned shutdowns or reactor trips.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory reconstruction-error monitor for reactor coolant pump sensors sits outside the protection path, so its main danger is lost early warning and misplaced confidence, not direct harm. Its definition of 'normal' comes entirely from historical data, and validation rests on one labelled anomaly, so missed-detection rates are unknown. Main threats are baseline poisoning, sensor-level evasion, model and pipeline tampering, alarm flooding, drift, evidence and opacity limits, operator complacency, and weak governance.

Baseline and training-data poisoning -- adversarial
Because the model trains only on 'normal' history, an insider or compromised historian pipeline can insert degraded or manipulated periods into the training set or a retraining window, so a real seal, bearing or shaft fault later reconstructs with low error. The result is a persistent, low-visibility blind spot and delayed warning of pump deterioration ahead of trips.

Sensor-level evasion and induced false alarms -- adversarial
An adversary with spoofing or write access to sensor, acquisition or historian data can make slow, correlation-preserving changes that cross-channel attention reconstructs well, hiding real degradation or sabotage precursors. The same access can inflate error to provoke needless derating, outages or loss of trust.

Model, threshold and toolchain tampering -- adversarial
Altering weights, thresholds, normalization constants, or compromised ML libraries and containers can silently desensitize the detector. Because the output is a continuous score rather than a discrete safety signal, such tampering is hard to notice.

Alarm flooding and denial -- adversarial
Injecting chaff or noisy channels, or denying the service, triggers nuisance flags that push operators to disable the tool or loosen thresholds. This can be timed ahead of a real action to remove the monitoring layer.

Model and residual reconnaissance -- adversarial
The architecture, features and benchmarks are public, and weights, residuals and thresholds reveal which channels matter and how sensitive the detector is. An adversary can build a proxy model to craft perturbations that stay below detection.

Operating-regime drift and re-baselining -- implicit, exploitable
Power changes, sensor recalibration or replacement, pump refurbishment, fuel-cycle and seasonal effects shift what is normal, causing false-alarm floods or silent loss of sensitivity, and retraining on history already containing early deterioration absorbs slow faults into the baseline. An adversary could wait for post-outage or retraining windows when the model is least reliable, or induce the shift deliberately.

Thin validation and data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
RCP failures are rare and validation used one labelled anomaly, with no fault library for seal, bearing, impeller or shaft faults, so false-negative rates and threshold choices are essentially unvalidated. An adversary can rely on this unmeasured blind-spot profile when choosing fault or manipulation types.

Opacity and over-generalization -- implicit, exploitable
Reconstruction error does not localize or diagnose a fault, attention weights are unreliable explanations, and cross-channel attention can reconstruct a degrading channel from healthy correlated ones. A deliberate fault could be dismissed as a sensor glitch, an ambiguity an adversary can depend on.

Operator complacency and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Treating 'no anomaly' as a health assurance relaxes manual vibration trending and walk-downs, while alert fatigue produces disuse and fading interpretive skill. An adversary can time a mechanical or cyber-physical action around the weakened independent vigilance.

Qualification and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
As non-safety monitoring software, the tool likely escapes configuration control, change management, retraining control and cybersecurity scrutiny, and non-deterministic training hampers baseline reproducibility. Weak change control makes tampering with models or thresholds harder to detect, and creep toward use in maintenance-deferral decisions would be unqualified.

Fleet template propagation -- implicit
Reusing a model or threshold template across pumps or units imports one unit's definition of normal into another. No distinct adversary pathway beyond poisoning the shared template.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory O&M condition-monitoring tool on a non-safety-classified path. The reactor protection system, pump vibration/temperature trips and seal-injection and leakoff alarms remain independent, so a wrong output is unlikely to cause direct harm. The real exposure is degraded defense-in-depth: a missed early-stage seal, bearing or shaft deterioration is a missed warning, and a flood of false positives erodes operator and maintenance-planner trust. Because the model trains only on normal data and was validated on a single labelled historical anomaly, the evidence for its detection performance and false-alarm rate is thin. It is also exposed to anything that changes what counts as normal (operating regime, instrument replacement, retraining on contaminated history). Consequences depend on the human and procedural layer: the maintenance decisions, outage scheduling and pump-trip judgments made on the strength of this tool.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift: the model learns normal as the history it saw. Power level changes, coolant temperature and chemistry changes, fuel cycle effects, sensor recalibration or replacement, pump refurbishment and seasonal heat-sink changes can cause either false-alarm floods or silent loss of sensitivity. Slow degradation can also be absorbed into the baseline if the model is periodically retrained on history that already contains early-stage deterioration, so the fault becomes normal. (2) Evidence gap: one labelled anomaly, with no systematic fault library for seal failure, bearing wear, impeller damage or shaft bow, gives no basis for estimating missed-detection rates. Reconstruction error also gives no fault localization or diagnosis, and attention weights are not a reliable explanation, so staff cannot readily judge an alert. Failures to flag are invisible by nature. Threshold selection is a hidden judgment that sets the balance between nuisance alarms and missed detections. (3) Human factors: over-trust leads to relaxed manual vibration trending or walk-downs. Alert fatigue leads to disuse. Staff skill in interpreting pump data fades. A model that reconstructs a faulty sensor channel too well may mask sensor faults, or flag an instrument fault as a pump fault. (4) Governance: the tool is typically outside safety-classified software QA, so configuration management, retraining control and change control may be weak. Any later promotion toward operator action or an automated trip or setback input would be unqualified.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Integrity attack on input data or historian: slowly biasing or spoofing sensor values, or tampering with the data pipeline, can suppress reconstruction error while a real fault develops, or inflate it to prompt unnecessary derating or outages. Because the model is trained only on normal history, it is vulnerable to poisoning of that history (so that a fault signature becomes baseline), to model or threshold tampering, and to supply-chain compromise of the ML software or pretrained artifacts. (b) Concealment: an adversary or insider who also damages the pump, or exploits a coincident degradation, could use the monitor's silence as a cover and delay detection of mechanical or process faults. (c) Availability and trust: denial of the service or deliberately induced false positives drives operators to turn it off, which is a way to erode attention. Spoofing outputs that reach a maintenance planning system could also mislead outage decisions. (d) Data and IP exposure: operating data and the model reveal pump performance and plant state, and an IT/OT boundary connection or cloud or vendor retraining pipeline creates a path into plant networks. Harm still requires failure of independent protection and operator vigilance, so the realistic consequences are unplanned outages, economic loss, a missed degradation window and, in a compound scenario, a reduced safety margin.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a one-class reconstruction model: it learns what 'normal' looks like from historical RCP sensor data and treats high reconstruction error as deterioration. Its weaknesses sit in the definition of 'normal' and in the thresholding step, not in the attention architecture. 'Normal-only' training sets are rarely clean. They contain unlabelled slow degradation, and they cover only the operating regimes (power level, startup/shutdown, seal injection and cooling configurations, seasonal heat-sink temperature, post-outage states) that were seen. The published validation is also thin. It rests on historical data with one labelled anomaly and benchmarks against LSTM-VAE, TranAD and others, so true-positive rate, false-alarm rate, and lead time across fault modes are essentially unknown. Reconstruction models can also over-generalize through cross-channel attention, so a degrading channel is 'explained' by correlated healthy channels and the fault is reconstructed away. Finally, the detector is only as trustworthy as the sensor and historian pipeline feeding it, and that pipeline is a path for both accidental and adversarial manipulation.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Drift and regime shift (OP.C0302, .01, .03). Normal changes after maintenance, sensor replacement or recalibration, fuel cycle, seal or impeller replacement, setpoint changes, or ageing. The model then either floods operators with false alarms, which leads to alarm fatigue and disuse (OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102), or silently re-baselines when retrained on drifting data. Retraining on recent 'normal' data lets a slow fault become the new normal, which is a concept-drift and self-poisoning loop (OP.C0302.02). (2) Contaminated or scarce data (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0202, OP.C0204). Real RCP failures are rare, so the anomaly class cannot be validated. Threshold selection and the claimed early-detection advantage rest on very few events. Missing data, sensor dropouts and historian compression or resampling change signal statistics relative to training. (3) Blind spots and opacity (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0303). Reconstruction error does not say which component or failure mode is responsible, and attention maps are not reliable explanations. Faults that change correlated channels coherently, or that appear only in untokenized variables such as vibration spectra, are missed. Static offline benchmarking does not match dynamic plant-transient behaviour. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, .01). Operators may treat 'no anomaly' as assurance and relax diverse manual checks and vibration-analyst reviews, or may be unable to act on an unexplained alert. (5) Qualification and governance gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0502). It is probably advisory and non-safety-classified, but there is no accepted process for qualifying a retrainable model, versioning it, and controlling thresholds. Its output could drift toward being used in maintenance-deferral decisions without that rigour. Non-deterministic training (OP.C0402.01) also hampers reproducibility of the baseline. (6) Fleet propagation (OP.C0602). A model or threshold template reused across pumps or units imports one unit's definition of normal into another.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Training-data poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0059). An adversary or insider with write access to the historian or training set injects subtly degraded or manipulated 'normal' data so that a later real fault falls inside the learned envelope. This is a persistent, low-visibility backdoor. (2) Evasion through sensor-level manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043, T0043.004). An attacker who can alter field signals or the data path, for example by spoofing or slowly biasing a few channels, can keep reconstruction error low while physical degradation or sabotage proceeds. Since attention couples channels, a small coordinated perturbation can be absorbed. The same access can do the reverse and induce false alarms to provoke unnecessary derating or trips, or to erode trust (AML.T0031, T0046). (3) Model and pipeline integrity (AML.T0018, T0010.001/.003, T0076). Tampering with weights, thresholds, preprocessing or normalization constants, or compromised ML libraries and containers, can silence or distort detection without leaving an obvious trace. (4) Timing around implicit weaknesses. An adversary who knows the model is blind after an outage or sensor change, or is in a retraining window, can time an action to that period. (5) Reconnaissance and extraction (AML.T0000, T0002, T0005, T0024.002). The architecture, features and benchmark data are public, so an attacker can build a proxy model to craft undetectable perturbations. Consequence: loss of early warning on a critical primary-system component and possible masking of sabotage or equipment-damage activity, or unwarranted trips and operational disruption, as a result of compromised or misleading monitoring output.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling lens, a reconstruction-error detector on reactor coolant pump (RCP) sensors is a monitoring and advisory layer, not a control path, so a nation-state would probably not target it first. Its value to an adversary is as a blinding or timing tool. The model is trained only on 'normal' history, so whatever was in that history defines what counts as normal. An adversary or insider who can influence the training window, the retraining baseline, or the thresholds can teach the model that a deterioration pattern is normal. Alternatively, an attacker can make slow, physically plausible, correlated sensor changes that the attention mechanism reconstructs well, so a real degradation (or a sabotage-induced one) never raises an alarm. A second concern is vigilance erosion: once operators trust 'no anomaly flagged', their independent trending of vibration, seal and temperature data weakens. That creates a window an adversary could time a mechanical or cyber-physical action around. The paper's evidence is thin for this role, being one historical anomaly detected at the labelled onset, so the unknown false-negative profile is itself something an adversary could exploit.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and baseline poisoning (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002, T0059): the 'normal-only' paradigm makes the historian extract and every retraining cycle a trust anchor. An insider or compromised data pipeline can slip degraded or manipulated periods into the baseline, so that later real deterioration reconstructs with low error. The facility depends on the model to give early warning ahead of trips, so the consequence is delayed detection of pump or seal degradation, with safety and availability impact. (2) Evasion through plausible sensor manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043, T0031): the model detects violations of inter-channel correlation. An adversary with write or spoofing access to the sensor, data-acquisition or historian layer could craft changes that preserve the learned correlations, or stay below the threshold with gradual drift. This hides real degradation or masks a sabotage precursor. Anyone able to craft such changes would already be deep inside the OT/IT boundary, so the AI is more a force-multiplier for concealment than the primary target. (3) Model, threshold and pipeline tampering (AML.T0076, T0018, T0010.001/.003, T0012): a modified threshold, a swapped model file, or a compromised ML library or toolchain can silently desensitize the detector. Because the output is a continuous score rather than a discrete safety signal, such tampering is hard to notice. (4) Alarm-flooding or denial (AML.T0046, T0029): injecting noisy or chaff channels triggers nuisance flags, driving operators to disuse the tool or raise thresholds, and this can be timed ahead of a real attack. (5) Sensor and plant-state reconnaissance: model weights, reconstruction residuals and thresholds reveal which channels are most informative and how sensitive the system is (AML.T0024.002, T0063). IMPLICIT, exploitable by an adversary. (6) Automation complacency and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102): 'no flag' becomes a proxy for health, which reduces manual trending and creates a window for timed action. (7) Drift and operating heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, C0302.03, C0303): load changes, maintenance, pump replacement or sensor recalibration shift the normal envelope, and an adversary can wait for the post-outage period when the model is least trustworthy. (8) Data scarcity and unlabelled faults (OP.C0202, C0201.05): RCP failures are rare, so false-negative performance is practically unvalidated, and a single-event benchmark offers little assurance. (9) Opacity (OP.C0401): a reconstruction-error spike gives no root cause, and attribution via attention is unreliable, so a deliberate fault could be dismissed as a sensor glitch, with an attacker depending on this ambiguity. (10) Governance gaps (OP.C0501, C0502, C0505): the model is likely classed as non-safety monitoring and therefore escapes the configuration control, change management and cybersecurity scrutiny that its operational influence deserves. Overall priority: moderate. It is a stepping stone and a concealment layer that needs prior access, but poisoning of the baseline and complacency are the most credible routes.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on baseline poisoning, sensor-level evasion, drift, thin validation, complacency and governance gaps. I merged overlapping model/pipeline tampering items and dropped weakly supported ones (cloud dependency, IP exposure, generic external harms). I did not assign ATLAS codes to the implicit threats themselves.

evidence.citation: "A Novel Transformer-Based Anomaly Detection Model for the Reactor Coolant Pump in Nuclear Power Plants," Science and Technology of Nuclear Installations (Wiley/Hindawi), 2024
evidence.note: The paper proposes an attention-based transformer model for reactor coolant pump condition monitoring. It is trained on normal historical operating data and flags anomalies from signal reconstruction error. It was tested on historical pump data containing an anomaly, where it detected the anomaly's onset at the same point as the labelled start and compared favourably with LSTM-VAE, TranAD, DAGMM, PCA and USAD.

damage.why: The monitor is advisory and outside the protection path, so the worst credible outcome (the baseline-poisoning and tampering threats) is lost early warning of pump degradation, causing operational disruption such as trips or unplanned outages and some erosion of safety margin, but not a direct radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Drift, thin validation and complacency occur reliably as implicit conditions, but adversarial poisoning, evasion and tampering depend on specific preconditions such as a retraining window or write access to the data pipeline.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (poisoning the historian or training pipeline, spoofing sensors, altering model artifacts) need insider or privileged access to plant OT/IT data paths, which is a high bar, though the weak governance of non-safety software lowers it somewhat.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly confined to the monitored reactor coolant pumps and the operators relying on the tool; fleet template propagation could extend it across pumps or units, but it stays in an advisory monitoring layer rather than coupled safety systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, features, benchmarks and the general weaknesses of reconstruction-based anomaly detectors (poisoning, evasion, drift, thin validation) are well documented in the open literature, so an outsider can readily infer the vulnerability class, though specific thresholds and pipelines remain internal.

use_case: Artificial-neural-network metamodel for seismic fragility analysis of nuclear power plant equipment. It maps selected seismic intensity measures of ground motion to structural response, replacing repeated costly structural calculations when computing fragility curves for seismic probabilistic risk assessment. The most relevant intensity measures are chosen by forward selection on semi-partial correlation coefficients. The ANN's prediction uncertainty, aleatory plus epistemic, is quantified with the delta method and its effect on the fragility curves is assessed.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline ANN metamodel produces the fragility curves that feed seismic PRA, so its errors flow into seismic risk numbers, margin assessments and qualification or retrofit decisions. The main threats are implicit: tail extrapolation and reuse outside the training envelope, inheritance of simulator bias, brittle intensity-measure selection, understated uncertainty, and over-trust with no AI-specific qualification regime. The adversarial threats are integrity tampering with data, model or workflow, and loss of sensitive equipment-vulnerability information. Both are cheap and hard to detect because the opaque surrogate replaces the independent calculations that would reveal them.

Training pipeline and model tampering -- adversarial
An insider, compromised contractor workstation or poisoned shared library or pretrained component can alter the finite-element-derived training set, ground-motion records, intensity-measure selection or trained weights. The result is fragility curves and HCLPF-type capacities skewed optimistic or pessimistic, which corrupt the licensing and design basis and are hard to spot because nobody recomputes the full analyses.

Supply-chain compromise of ML tooling -- adversarial
Compromised ML libraries, notebooks or pretrained checkpoints in the analysis environment can embed a bias toward unconservative tail responses, or corrupt a model file undetected. This gives a persistent, latent degradation of the seismic risk basis.

Exfiltration of vulnerability information -- adversarial
Theft of the trained model, datasets or per-equipment fragility results from analyst workstations, collaborator systems or shared and cloud repositories can reveal which equipment fails first and at what ground-motion level. This is a ranked weakness map useful for sabotage planning or timing, and such environments often sit under weaker data-security regimes than plant networks.

Tail extrapolation and out-of-distribution reuse -- implicit, exploitable
The ANN is trained on a finite suite of simulated ground motions and equipment models, so it can silently underpredict response in the rare, strong, nonlinear tail that drives PRA, or when reused after a design change, new site or hazard update. An adversary could hide deliberate bias inside this plausible-looking error, or rely on the unflagged weak region.

Simulator-bias laundering and staleness -- implicit, exploitable
The metamodel reproduces the finite-element model, not the physical equipment, so boundary-condition, nonlinearity and degradation errors appear validated, and the surrogate goes stale when the as-built plant or model changes. An adversary gains cover for tampering because manipulated outputs are indistinguishable from ordinary simulator error.

Intensity-measure selection blind spots -- implicit, exploitable
Forward selection on semi-partial correlations is linear and order-dependent, so it can drop nonlinearly or modally relevant measures or keep collinear ones, leaving the model blind to some ground-motion features. Because this step is a small, high-leverage point, an adversary could silently drop a relevant measure and the change would look like normal parsimony.

Uncertainty understatement and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
Delta-method uncertainty rests on local linearization and a well-specified model, so it under-covers with sparse data, model-form error and seed or architecture variation, producing narrow bands that give false assurance in PRA. Non-deterministic retraining and weak version control also let an adversary substitute or alter a model without a forensic trail.

Over-trust and missing qualification regime -- implicit, exploitable
Analysts and reviewers may over-trust the fast, smooth, statistically sophisticated outputs and let full structural spot-checks atrophy, while no established QA route exists for ML surrogates in safety-related analysis. An adversary relies on this lost independent baseline so that tampered or degraded curves pass review.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline design-and-analysis surrogate that feeds seismic PRA, not a real-time control function, so the consequence path is slow and runs through engineering judgment. A wrong fragility curve can understate or overstate the high-confidence-low-probability-of-failure (HCLPF) capacity of safety-related equipment. That biases seismic core damage frequency, margin assessments, and decisions on anchorage, qualification and retrofit. The safeguards that would also have to fail are the independent review of the PRA, conservative design margins, seismic walkdowns, shake-table or code-based qualification, and regulator scrutiny. These make a sudden physical failure unlikely. The credible harm is a quietly optimistic risk model that survives review because the ANN is opaque and its uncertainty treatment looks rigorous. Adversarial exposure is mainly integrity of data, model and workflow rather than live attack surface.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Extrapolation and OOD failure: the ANN is trained on a finite set of finite-element runs and ground-motion records. Fragility curves need the tail, meaning rare, strong or non-stationary motions and nonlinear equipment behaviour such as sliding, impact and anchor yield. A surrogate that is accurate in the bulk can mislead exactly where PRA is most sensitive (OP.C0302, OP.C0202, OP.C0403). It is also tied to one equipment model, boundary conditions and site hazard. Reusing it after a design change, a new site, or a change in floor-response spectra is an unqualified generalization (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (2) Data provenance: the training responses are simulated or synthetic, so the metamodel inherits the biases of the structural model and any record-selection bias, and it adds approximation error on top (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02). The cause is the training data and model. The consequence is fragility curves that look validated but only reproduce the simulator. (3) Intensity-measure selection: forward selection on semi-partial correlation captures linear association only. It can drop a measure that matters for nonlinear or multi-mode response, or keep collinear ones, giving a reduced input set that is blind to certain ground-motion features (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403). (4) Uncertainty understatement: the delta method relies on local linearization and asymptotic assumptions. It is poorly suited to small training sets, to training non-convergence, or to epistemic uncertainty from model form and the choice of network. Narrow confidence bands then give false assurance and lead to less conservatism in the PRA (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01). Training-time non-determinism makes results sensitive to seeds and architecture, which is a repeatability and QA problem (OP.C0402, OP.C0501). (5) Human factors: analysts and reviewers may over-trust the speed and apparent statistical sophistication, and may skip spot-checks against full structural runs (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0502). The use case has no explicit qualification route in nuclear QA programmes for ML surrogates, which is a regulatory readiness gap (OP.C0504). ADVERSARIAL THREATS (lower likelihood, but they exploit those weaknesses). (6) Training-data or simulation-input tampering, such as altered ground-motion records, finite-element models, or material or damping parameters, and corruption of the trained model file, via a compromised engineering workstation, a third-party design contractor, or shared analysis repositories (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). The aim would be to shift fragility curves subtly toward optimistic or pessimistic results. Optimistic bias degrades safety-margin decisions, and pessimistic bias drives cost, delay, or unneeded modification. Because outputs are smooth curves and review rarely re-derives them, tampering is hard to detect. (7) Supply-chain exposure through ML libraries, pre-trained components or notebooks used in the analysis (AML.T0010.001). (8) Information exposure: fragility curves, equipment capacities and PRA inputs are sensitive security information, because they reveal which structures and equipment are seismically weakest. Surrogate models and datasets stored in shared or cloud environments could leak it (AML.T0025, AML.T0035, OP.C0505, OP.C0601). Overall, the main downstream consequence is a biased seismic risk basis that persists across licensing and design decisions, and it is mitigated only if independent verification and benchmarking against full-model runs are mandatory.

ai_engineer.argument: This is an offline design-stage surrogate: a small feed-forward ANN trained on outputs of expensive finite-element time-history runs, not on field data. Its fragility is therefore concentrated in the training set, because the data are simulated or synthetic (OP.C0201.01, .02). They cover a limited ground-motion suite, and the tail region that drives seismic PRA is sparsely sampled (OP.C0202). Fragility curves and the resulting core-damage frequency depend on extrapolating into that tail, where an ANN has no guarantees (OP.C0403, OP.C0302). The delta-method uncertainty is a local linearization around the fitted weights. It is known to under-cover when the data are sparse, the model is misspecified, or the input is out of distribution, so it can create false confidence in the very region that matters. The forward-selection step on semi-partial correlations is a second pipeline stage that assumes linear, additive relevance. It can drop intensity measures that matter nonlinearly or for particular failure modes, and the metamodel then inherits that blind spot silently.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution and tail extrapolation: the metamodel is trained on a finite set of ground motions and structural-model variants. Real hazard-consistent motions (long-duration, near-field, site-specific spectra, new hazard updates) or a changed equipment configuration can fall outside that envelope, so the surrogate underpredicts response with no warning (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403). Consequence: fragility curves are biased unconservatively, seismic risk is understated, and design margins or seismic-qualification decisions are wrong. (2) Surrogate-fidelity and concept drift: the ANN reproduces the FE model, not the physical equipment. Model errors in that FE model (boundary conditions, nonlinearity, degradation, retrofits) are laundered into a fast tool that looks validated, and when the FE model or as-built plant is updated the surrogate goes stale unless it is retrained and requalified (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303). (3) Uncertainty quantification weakness: the delta method relies on local linearity, Hessian conditioning and Gaussian assumptions. Epistemic uncertainty from a different seed, architecture or training subset is underrepresented. Training non-determinism means the same pipeline can yield different fragility curves (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0401). Consequence: overly narrow confidence bands are carried into PRA and regulatory submissions. (4) Feature-selection brittleness: forward selection on semi-partial correlations is order-dependent and linear, and it can omit interacting intensity measures. A reviewer sees a clean, parsimonious model and misses the omission (OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (5) Automation and qualification gap: ML surrogates in safety-related analysis lack established verification standards. Analysts may trust smooth curves, reduce direct FE spot-checks (OP.C0101.04), and an undocumented pipeline (OP.C0502, OP.C0501, OP.C0504) is hard to audit. (6) Error propagation: fragility outputs feed event trees and risk-informed decisions, so a surrogate bias spreads into plant-wide risk metrics and into any other plants or sites that reuse the model (OP.C0603, OP.C0602).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. The attack surface is the engineering data and software supply chain rather than a live inference endpoint. (a) Training-data or simulation-input tampering, such as altered ground-motion records, FE model parameters, or surrogate training sets, can shift fragility curves in a chosen direction with little visible trace, because the outputs are plausible and few people recompute them (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059). (b) Model or weight manipulation, or compromised ML libraries and pretrained checkpoints in the analysis environment, can embed a bias toward unconservative results in the tail (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076). Consequence: understated seismic risk can enter licensing or design basis, a latent safety degradation that an adversary could later exploit, or that simply remains undetected. (c) Reconnaissance on published methodology and intensity-measure choices lets an adversary anticipate where the surrogate is weak (AML.T0000, AML.T0001). Impact is limited unless integrity of the analysis chain is compromised, so integrity controls on data lineage and independent FE validation are the key defenses.

security_specialist.argument: This is an offline design-and-analysis surrogate with no actuation path, so a sophisticated adversary would not use it as a direct target. It still deserves attention as a trust-concentration point. Its output, fragility curves feeding seismic PRA, sets the seismic capacity and risk-significance numbers that drive design margins, equipment qualification, retrofit decisions and licensing arguments. A small number of analysts and a few files (training set, selected intensity measures, trained weights, uncertainty estimates) can therefore quietly shift safety-case numbers, and the change can survive for decades. Insider or supply-chain manipulation is cheap and low-visibility, and the damage is latent: it surfaces only in a real earthquake, or in an adversary's choice of timing and physical-attack planning. The non-adversarial weaknesses, namely extrapolation beyond the training data, small and simulated training sets, and an uncertainty method that understates epistemic error, are the same ones that make tampering hard to tell from ordinary model error.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity attack on the metamodel pipeline. The failure mechanism is manipulation of the finite-element-derived training set, the intensity-measure selection step, or the trained weights (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0059, AML.T0031), through insider access, a compromised contractor workstation, or a poisoned pretrained or shared tool. The facility depends on the metamodel for fragility curves and HCLPF-type capacities in seismic PRA. The consequence is a fragility curve biased toward 'robust' (or toward a falsely fragile result that diverts resources). That means understated seismic risk, misdirected upgrades, and a licensing basis resting on corrupted evidence. Because the ANN is opaque and replaces the expensive full calculations, nobody has a cheap independent check, so the tampering is hard to detect. The consequence is a latent safety and security weakness that an informed adversary could later exploit if they learn which components are really weaker than documented. (2) Information value and reconnaissance. The failure mechanism is exfiltration or inversion of the model, its data, or the per-equipment fragility results (AML.T0025, AML.T0035, AML.T0024.001/.002, AML.T0037, OP.C0505). The facility depends on keeping equipment-specific seismic vulnerability information, which is sensitive, from reaching an adversary. The consequence is a ranked map of which equipment fails first and at what ground-motion level. That is useful for sabotage planning, or for choosing when to act during a seismic event. Analyst workstations and academic or vendor collaborators typically sit under weaker data-security regimes than plant networks (OP.C0505.01). (3) Trust concentration and reduced vigilance. The failure mechanism is over-trust in a fast, smooth surrogate that returns tight confidence bands (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0101.06). The facility depends on engineers continuing to run, or at least spot-check, full structural analyses. As those calculations atrophy, reviewers and regulators lose the ability to notice manipulated or degraded outputs. The consequence is an adversary or an error that slips past review because the review no longer has an independent baseline.

IMPLICIT, and exploitable or timeable by an adversary. (4) Extrapolation and distribution shift. The failure mechanism is use outside the training domain: new equipment configurations, ground-motion types or modifications, ageing-related stiffness changes, or a different site (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0203). The consequence is confidently wrong fragility estimates with no error flag. Sound-looking but wrong numbers also provide cover for deliberate bias. (5) Uncertainty understatement. The failure mechanism is that delta-method uncertainty is local and assumes a well-specified model, so it can omit model-form error and training-set sparsity (OP.C0403, OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0304.03). The facility depends on the epistemic-uncertainty term for margin decisions. The consequence is overly narrow bounds and thin real margin. (6) Qualification and reproducibility gaps. The failure mechanism is no AI-specific QA regime for a model whose output enters a safety-related analysis (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0504). Retraining non-determinism and weak version control make it hard to prove a given curve came from a given trusted model. That leaves room to substitute or alter models without a forensic trail.

An intensity-measure selection step is also a small, high-leverage tampering point, because dropping one relevant measure silently changes what the model sees. Overall priority is moderate. The use case is unlikely to be a nation-state primary target, but it is a cheap, quiet way to degrade a safety argument and is worth integrity controls and independent verification sampling.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on tail extrapolation, simulated-data inheritance, delta-method uncertainty understatement and data/model integrity tampering. I dropped weakly supported items (reconnaissance on published methods, model inversion/extraction of a non-API model, cross-site propagation) and kept exfiltration as a distinct threat raised by the nuclear engineer and security specialist.

evidence.citation: "Seismic fragility analysis with artificial neural networks: Application to nuclear power plant equipment," Engineering Structures (Elsevier), vol. 162, pp. 213-225, 2018
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper builds an ANN to speed up the structural-response calculations behind fragility curves for NPP equipment in seismic PRA. It also presents an intensity-measure selection algorithm and a decomposition of the ANN's prediction uncertainty. I read only the abstract and highlights, so details of the specific equipment case study are not reported here.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is tampering with the training data, model, or workflow, which skews fragility curves and HCLPF capacities and erodes safety margins and the design and licensing basis. The harm is indirect, passing through PRA and review rather than causing a release directly, so it falls short of 5. The exfiltrated weakness map adds a sabotage-enabling dimension.

reproducibility.why: The implicit failures (tail extrapolation, simulator bias, understated delta-method uncertainty, over-trust) occur reliably whenever the model is used outside its training envelope or without independent checks. Tampering also persists once it is introduced and is rarely caught.

exploitability.why: Tampering with the training set, weights, or selection step needs insider access, a compromised analyst or contractor workstation, or a successful supply-chain compromise. Exfiltration from weaker-security collaborator or cloud environments is easier, but the integrity attacks need privileged position.

affected_users.why: Corrupted fragility curves propagate into seismic PRA, margin assessments, and qualification or retrofit decisions across many equipment items and plant-level risk numbers. The impact is confined to the analysis and design basis rather than coupled operating systems, and it is offline.

discoverability.why: Surrogate extrapolation limits, simulator-bias inheritance, delta-method under-coverage, and ML supply-chain risks are well documented in the open literature. The paper is public, so an outsider can infer the general weak points, though details of a specific workflow still require insider knowledge.

use_case: Deep metric learning for identifying individual TRISO-fueled pebbles in pebble-bed reactors with on-line refuelling. A convolutional neural network trained with triplet loss maps X-ray radiographs of each pebble to a compact embedding space. The mapping uses the unique, manufacturing-imprinted distribution of TRISO particles in each pebble as a fingerprint. Distances between embeddings are used to re-identify and track pebbles as they enter and leave the core, supporting nuclear material accountancy and safeguards.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case makes a CNN embedding match the only item-level evidence of identity for bulk-handled TRISO pebbles in material accountancy and safeguards, yet it was validated only on 1,250 simulated radiographs. The main threats are implicit: sim-to-real and scale failure, open-set threshold fragility, drift and retraining incompatibility, and misplaced trust with no qualification basis. Adversarial threats are corruption of the reference gallery or training chain, evasion through the imaging path, and service degradation, and an adversary can also hide inside the model's known error rate.

Sim-to-real and small-data gap -- implicit, exploitable
Training on 1,250 MCNP images with no real detector noise, scatter, rotation, wear or irradiation history gives no assurance of embedding stability on real pebbles, and the blur-driven accuracy jump suggests sensitivity to image artifacts that differ between simulation and hardware. The resulting false matches and non-matches corrupt the pebble inventory record, and an adversary could write off a diverted pebble as an ordinary misidentification inside this quantifiable residual error rate.

Open-set and scale fragility -- implicit, exploitable
A distance threshold validated on about 1,250 identities has no demonstrated ability to reject never-enrolled, dummy or substituted pebbles among hundreds of thousands, and collision rates rise with gallery size. Because the threshold is the de facto safeguards decision, an adversary could present a substitute that falls inside the match region, or exploit threshold changes that silently trade false-accept for false-reject.

Drift, irradiation change and retraining incompatibility -- implicit, exploitable
Source or detector ageing, new fuel batches, and in-core swelling or surface change of the same pebble shift the identity signal, while non-deterministic retraining yields embedding spaces incompatible with the enrolled gallery. Forced re-enrolment after such changes creates a legitimate-looking window for an insider to alter identity records and breaks continuity of knowledge.

Automation trust, opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
Inspectors may treat a reported accuracy measured on simulated data as proof of identity, let independent bulk verification and conventional accountancy skills lapse, and cannot explain individual matches or rely on any qualification route for ML item identification. An adversary can rely on this deference and on unowned threshold and gallery change control to get a false match or an unreviewed change accepted.

Gallery, training-data and model tampering -- adversarial
An insider who alters enrolled embeddings or radiographs, the simulation inputs or the model weights can create ghost identities or let a diverted or substituted pebble inherit a legitimate identity, or implant a trigger-conditioned backdoor. The accountancy ledger then shows self-consistent continuity of knowledge where none exists, concealing diversion.

Evasion and manipulated radiographs -- adversarial
An operator who controls the imaging chain can craft, replay, inject or filter radiographs, or alter preprocessing, to push a diverted pebble's embedding into a declared pebble's match region or to generate false non-matches. The model's robustness to small image changes is unproven, so the result is false safeguards assurance.

Service degradation and alarm flooding -- adversarial
Flooding or corrupting inputs to force false non-matches can stall identification or normalise alarm dismissal, and no alternative item-level method exists for pebbles. A diversion can then be timed inside the degraded or distrusted window.

Model extraction from open literature -- adversarial
The published architecture and simulation setup let an adversary build a proxy model and search offline for embedding collisions or perturbations that transfer to the deployed system. This lowers the cost of a later evasion attempt.

Fingerprint data sensitivity -- implicit, exploitable
Per-pebble radiographs and embeddings reveal particle-level fuel design and manufacturing detail that is proprietary and possibly safeguards-sensitive, and storage, sharing or off-premises processing under a mismatched data security model makes the database an exfiltration target. An adversary gains fuel design knowledge and a template for fabricating matching pebbles.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a safeguards and material-accountancy view, this system is meant to replace item-level tagging that pebble-bed reactors do not have. If it misidentifies or fails to re-identify a pebble, the facility's book inventory of fissile material drifts from physical reality, and the inspector's continuity-of-knowledge claim rests on a fingerprint the model may not reproduce. The reported 93.5% (98.7% after blur) accuracy comes from 1,250 MCNP-simulated radiographs, not real pebbles, so the sim-to-real gap, the small dataset, and the lack of any qualification basis are the central weaknesses. Existing practice offers some backstop: burn-up measurement by gamma spectrometry, core-discharge counts, and fresh-fuel batch records. But those are bulk or statistical controls. The AI is the only item-level layer, so quiet failures would go unnoticed, and a diversion or substitution scenario could hide inside the model's error rate.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and data-scarcity failure: the model is trained on 1,250 simulated radiographs, with no manufacturing variability, detector noise, scatter, pebble rotation, or cumulative irradiation and wear of real pebbles over many core passes. Embeddings that separate pebbles in simulation may not stay stable across real recirculation cycles, so identification errors rise in the field. The gain from Gaussian blur suggests sensitivity to image-level artifacts. Consequence: false non-matches create apparent 'missing' pebbles, and false matches create apparent 'present' ones. Either way the accountancy record is wrong and inspectors lose confidence. (2) Closed-set versus open-set mismatch and base rate: the system must reject a pebble that was never enrolled, whether foreign, substituted, or a dummy. Metric learning with a distance threshold has no built-in guarantee of this, and the threshold is hard to calibrate without real impostor data. Real fleets hold hundreds of thousands of pebbles, far beyond the tested population, so the false-match rate rises with gallery size. (3) Drift and qualification gap: changes in X-ray source, detector ageing, geometry, or fuel-batch manufacturing process shift the input distribution. Retraining changes the embedding space, which invalidates the existing enrolment gallery or forces re-enrolment. There is no regulatory qualification route for a non-deterministic, opaque identifier in a safeguards role. (4) Automation bias: inspectors and operators may treat 'matched' as proof of identity and stop applying independent bulk verification, and skills for conventional accountancy may fade. (5) Opacity: it is hard to explain to an inspector or regulator why two pebbles matched, which weakens evidentiary standing in licensing and safeguards conclusions. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Substitution or spoofing by an insider or state operator: fabricating or altering pebbles to produce a matching radiographic fingerprint, or crafting inputs near the decision boundary, so that a diverted pebble is accepted as the original or a substitute passes as enrolled. This is an evasion attack on the model, which the model's accuracy statistics cannot rule out. (7) Tampering with the enrolment gallery, embeddings database, or radiograph stream, such as poisoning during enrolment, replacing the model weights, or manipulating the imaging chain. This corrupts the reference record itself, so any later comparison appears to agree. Consequences are hidden diversion, falsified accountancy, or a nuisance flood of false anomalies that erodes trust and hurts availability. (8) Denial or degradation of the identification service, which stalls refuelling throughput or forces fallback to manual verification, a possible pressure point against a power-generation facility. (9) Data security: the radiograph fingerprints and enrolled embeddings reveal the particle-level fuel design and manufacturing detail, which are proprietary and may be safeguards-sensitive. Mitigating factors: pebble-bed fuel is low-enriched (HALEU in some designs), strong physical controls and burn-up measurement exist, and the tool is not in the safety-critical protection path. The main exposure is therefore safeguards integrity and licensing credibility, not accident initiation.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this system's main fragility is a train/deploy data gap. The documented model was trained and tested on only 1,250 MCNP-simulated radiographs of unique pebbles. Simulated radiographs lack real detector noise, scatter, beam hardening, geometric jitter, pebble rotation and handling-induced surface wear, and the reported jump from ~93.5% to ~98.7% after Gaussian blur suggests the embedding is sensitive to high-frequency content that differs between simulation and hardware. Metric learning also has an open-set, scaling problem. Accuracy on ~1,250 identities says little about discriminating among hundreds of thousands of pebbles circulating in a real core, where embedding collisions grow with population and the match threshold becomes the de facto safeguards decision. Because the output feeds accountancy and safeguards conclusions (continuity of knowledge, diversion detection), a silent mis-association is worse than an obvious failure.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap and small data: training on MCNP-simulated images only (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0302). The first real scanner, detector replacement or recalibration, X-ray source ageing, or a new pebble-manufacturing batch with a different particle-packing distribution shifts the input distribution (OP.C0302.01, .03). Embeddings drift, genuine re-identifications fall below threshold, and the system either raises false alarms or, if thresholds are loosened, accepts wrong matches. The consequence is degraded nuclear material accountancy, with unreliable pebble inventory and burn-up history. (2) Open-set and threshold fragility: there is no ground truth for 'unknown pebble' in training, and verification of the nearest-neighbour threshold across a growing gallery is not demonstrated (OP.C0403, OP.C0303). The same pebble re-imaged after in-core irradiation, with possible swelling, fission-product and dimensional changes, may look different from its pre-irradiation enrolment image. This is concept drift in the identity signal itself (OP.C0302.02), which could break re-identification at exactly the moment it matters. (3) Non-repeatability and opacity: training-time non-determinism means two retrained models yield different embedding spaces, and gallery embeddings are tied to a specific model version (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0401). Retraining or a patch forces re-enrolment or risks incompatible comparisons, which hurts safeguards continuity of knowledge. (4) Human factors: inspectors may over-trust a high reported accuracy figure (OP.C0101.04) that was measured on simulated data, and regulators lack a qualification basis for ML-based item identification (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Evasion at inference (AML.T0015, AML.T0043): an insider or operator with access to the imaging chain could craft or induce perturbations, such as altered blur, filtering, or a physical marker or shielding feature, that move a diverted pebble's embedding into the match region of a declared pebble. This is a substitution or diversion masking attack whose consequence is a safeguards false assurance. Because the system is a learned metric model, its robustness to small changes in the radiograph is not guaranteed, and the blur finding shows the preprocessing step materially affects results. (6) Data and model integrity (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059): tampering with the enrolment gallery, with the simulated training set or MCNP input decks, or with the weights could implant backdoor triggers or quietly shift identities. Since training is simulation-based, the simulation toolchain becomes a supply-chain asset, and a poisoned gallery would make the whole accountancy ledger self-consistently wrong. (7) Operator-controlled data path: the imaging operator is often the party being safeguarded, so the inspectorate's trust in images and embeddings depends on authentication of the acquisition and storage chain (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0703 analogues for synthetic or manipulated radiographs). Injection of generated or replayed radiographs would defeat re-identification entirely. (8) Denial or degradation (AML.T0029, AML.T0046): flooding or corrupting images forces fallback to manual methods that do not exist for pebbles, since the paper states no current tagging method exists, so there is no independent check on the ML output.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team lens, this system matters because it becomes the evidentiary basis for item-level accountancy of a bulk-handled, high-throughput material stream, where manual verification is impossible. That makes it a concentration of trust: if the embedding match says 'same pebble, accounted for', inspectors and operators will stop asking whether it was actually the same pebble. The documented evidence is thin: 1,250 simulated MCNP radiographs, about 93.5% accuracy, and improvement after Gaussian blur. That is a gap between demonstrated and operational performance that an adversary, or just a motivated operator, can hide in, since real pebbles, real imaging noise, and a population of hundreds of thousands are far outside the validated regime. A sophisticated adversary would more likely go after the surrounding pipeline (radiograph acquisition, the reference embedding database, the match-threshold configuration) than the CNN itself, and a state-level diverter would value any ability to make a removed pebble look accounted for.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Reference-gallery or training-data integrity. The embedding database is the ground truth for 'identity'. An insider who can add, replace or alter enrolled embeddings or radiographs (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0070-like integrity attacks on the gallery) could create 'ghost' identities or let a diverted or substituted pebble inherit a legitimate identity. Consequence: a safeguards-relevant material-accountancy record that shows continuity of knowledge when none exists, i.e. concealed diversion or substitution (OP.C0702.01 material substitution, OP.C0703 manipulated verification imagery). (2) Evasion and manipulated imagery. Inputs are images, so tampering anywhere between detector and model (replay, injection, or modified radiographs) can cause false matches or false non-matches (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0088). Since the model's embedding is compact and its decision rests on a distance threshold, a small tweak to the threshold or to preprocessing, such as the blur step that lifted accuracy, silently trades false-accept for false-reject (AML.T0081, AML.T0018). An adversary can also deliberately flood the operator with false non-matches (AML.T0046, AML.T0029) to force manual fallback or to normalise alarm dismissal, then time a diversion in that window. (3) Model or supply-chain compromise: a backdoored or poisoned model or weights from a third-party or research code base could behave normally except for a trigger pattern (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). (4) Reconnaissance and model extraction: open literature fully discloses architecture, approach and simulation setup, which lets an adversary build a proxy model and probe for collisions offline (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0024.002). IMPLICIT, exploitable by timing: (5) Simulation-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302): training on simulated radiographs with 1,250 unique pebbles gives no assurance for operational noise, detector ageing, pebble wear or surface changes in the core, or populations in the hundreds of thousands, where collision rates in embedding space will grow. Because the ~93.5% accuracy is far below what accountancy needs, a known and quantifiable residual error rate becomes a masking cover for deliberate diversion: a missing pebble can be written off as a 'misidentification'. (6) Automation trust and complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06): inspectors lose independent capacity to verify items and defer to the match score, while operators learn that most mismatches are benign. (7) Opacity and threshold governance (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0503): embeddings cannot be explained, there is no regulatory qualification pathway for ML-based item identification, and who owns the thresholds, retraining and gallery changes is undefined, which weakens change control and creates insider opportunity. (8) Drift and retraining (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303): any retraining or re-enrolment after hardware change gives a legitimate-looking route for altering identity records. (9) Data governance and dual-use (OP.C0505): the database of per-pebble fingerprints and fuel-geometry radiographs is sensitive proliferation and design information, so its storage, sharing with inspectorates, or cloud processing (OP.C0601) adds an exfiltration target. Overall, a nation-state would not need to defeat the CNN; corrupting the gallery or exploiting its known error rate is the cheaper path, so security needs to be assessed at pipeline and process level.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sim-to-real/small-data, open-set scaling, drift/retraining, automation trust, and gallery/evasion tampering as core threats; I merged overlapping phrasings and kept the security specialist's unique extraction and error-rate masking points. I dropped weakly supported codes such as AML.T0024.001, AML.T0035, AML.T0073, AML.T0081 and AML.T0070, and the cloud-dependency code, since the text gives no basis for them.

evidence.citation: "Tracking of individual TRISO-fueled pebbles through the application of X-ray imaging with deep metric learning," Elsevier (Annals of Nuclear Energy)
evidence.note: The paper builds a deep CNN trained with triplet loss to recognise individual TRISO pebbles from radiographic images. It was trained and tested on 1,250 MCNP-simulated radiographs of unique pebbles. Reported accuracy was about 93.5%, rising to about 98.7% after Gaussian-blur transformation of the dataset. The motivation given is that no method currently exists to tag and track pebbles for accountancy and safeguards.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is gallery or model tampering, or evasion, that lets a diverted or substituted pebble inherit a legitimate identity. This falsifies safeguards records and conceals diversion of nuclear material, which is the top-tier harm category.

reproducibility.why: Implicit failures such as sim-to-real gap, threshold fragility at scale and drift should reliably occur once real deployment conditions exist. Adversarial outcomes depend on access and on the model's unproven robustness, so reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: The most damaging paths (gallery, training-chain or model tampering, control of the imaging chain) need insider or operator-level access, and diversion of pebbles needs significant resources. Only proxy-model building from open literature is achievable externally, and it is a preparatory step.

affected_users.why: Because the embedding match is the only item-level identity evidence, a compromised or degraded system undermines accountancy and continuity of knowledge across the whole pebble inventory and the safeguards regime for the facility. It does not propagate to coupled physical plant systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, simulation setup, reported accuracies and the stated absence of any alternative method are published in the open literature. Generic weaknesses of metric-learning identification (open-set thresholds, drift, adversarial perturbation) are well documented, though deployment-specific details remain non-public.

use_case: Neural-network surrogate of Monte Carlo keff calculations, combined with a genetic algorithm, to optimise how used nuclear fuel assemblies are assigned to geological-disposal canisters. The method was demonstrated on 212 representative assemblies loaded four to a canister. It minimises the number of canisters within decay-heat and keff limits and evens out decay heat and keff across canisters.
incurred_insecurity:
A neural-network keff surrogate driven by a genetic algorithm sits between assembly burnup and isotopic records and a sealed-canister loading plan whose errors surface decades later. The main threats are the optimiser exploiting the surrogate's own error, limited and non-representative training data, missing qualification, over-trust of the optimised plan, and adversarial tampering with the surrogate, its training data or the input records.

Optimiser exploitation of surrogate error -- implicit, exploitable
The genetic algorithm searches for configurations the network scores as efficient, which concentrates canisters in tail regions where it under-predicts keff or decay heat, even though average test error looks acceptable. The result is a plan that looks compliant but has eroded subcriticality or thermal margin. An adversary could hide a deliberate bias inside this expected optimistic error, because it is indistinguishable from natural model error.

Small-data and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
The surrogate is trained on SERPENT outputs for about 212 assemblies loaded four to a canister, and it has no out-of-domain detection. Different reactor types, burnup or axial profiles, cooling times or canister designs give confident but unvalidated keff values. An adversary could present assemblies or loading patterns in the unflagged gap between the demonstrated and operational envelope.

Qualification and opacity gap -- implicit, exploitable
A stochastic, opaque, retrain-dependent network plus a stochastic optimiser has no benchmarked bias-and-uncertainty route, so results are not repeatable across seeds or retraining and reviewers cannot see why a loading is acceptable. An adversary benefits because tampering with the model or its outputs is hard to attribute or detect.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A minimum-canister plan that is optimal by construction invites acceptance without re-running independent Monte Carlo on each canister, while criticality analysts lose hands-on bias-evaluation skill. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust so that one biased surrogate or plan propagates across many canisters unchecked.

Objective misalignment toward limits -- implicit
Minimising canister count and equalising heat and keff rewards operating near the limits, trading away conservatism that the safety case implicitly depends on. An adversary gains nothing distinct here beyond what the optimiser-exploitation threat already offers.

Surrogate and training-data poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or compromised supply chain could poison the SERPENT-generated training data, the weights or the ML software stack so keff or decay heat is slightly under-predicted for chosen assembly types or features. The optimiser then packs those assemblies into canisters that look compliant but carry reduced margin that is found late or never.

Falsified assembly records and input manipulation -- adversarial
Altered burnup, enrichment, cooling-time or isotopic declarations pass through the surrogate as plausible inputs, giving a skewed loading plan and false internal consistency. This could mask misdeclaration or substitution of fissile content, a safeguards concern, and gives wrong keff with no check.

Compromised accounts and loading-plan exfiltration -- adversarial
A compromised operator or model-maintainer account could alter the model, objective function or limits, and the surrogate, loading rules and inventory data could be stolen. This reveals margin policy and inventory composition and helps an adversary craft inputs the optimiser accepts.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a waste-packaging and criticality-safety view, the danger is that a neural-network keff estimate stands in for a validated Monte Carlo/depletion calculation in a loading plan, and the genetic algorithm actively pushes canisters toward the edge of the keff and decay-heat limits. That is the region where surrogate error matters most. The study covers 212 assemblies loaded four to a canister, so a real fleet with different burnup, enrichment, cooling time and canister design would be out of distribution. If a bad loading plan were accepted, harm would still require several independent barriers to fail: licensed criticality safety analysis with margin, burnup-credit verification, independent re-calculation of the final loading, and fuel-characterisation records. Real engineering practice should catch this, but only if the surrogate is treated as a screening tool and not as the safety basis. The risk is that its speed and the optimiser's apparent rigour encourage over-trust, and that bad assembly inputs go undetected.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT. (1) Optimiser exploitation of surrogate error. The GA searches for configurations where the NN under-predicts keff or decay heat, so it concentrates canisters near limits, where small, systematic and non-conservative errors erase margin. Typical regression error looks acceptable on average but is not bounded in the tails. The consequence is a loading plan that appears compliant yet has a real keff above the limit or an unaccounted decay-heat peak. The result is either caught in independent verification (rework, schedule loss) or, if it is not, a reduced criticality margin in a disposal package. (2) Out-of-distribution generalisation. Training on a small, representative set of 212 assemblies means a different reactor type, burnup range, axial or radial burnup profile, or cooling time can fall outside the surrogate's validity. Validity is unlikely to be flagged by the surrogate itself. (3) Input data quality. Declared burnup, enrichment and cooling-time records are often calculated rather than measured. Errors or falsified values propagate through the NN with no check, producing a confident but wrong keff. This is also a safeguards concern, because assembly identity and material accountancy are tied to the loading plan. (4) Qualification and traceability gap. A stochastic, opaque, retrain-dependent surrogate does not fit conventional validated-code requirements (benchmarked codes, bias and uncertainty). Without a defined qualification route, results may be used outside their intended screening role. (5) Automation bias and skill fade. Planners who see an optimised, minimum-canister result may reduce independent checking, and criticality analysts may lose hands-on familiarity with Monte Carlo bias evaluation. ADVERSARIAL. (6) Poisoning or tampering with training data, surrogate weights, or the SERPENT-generated ground truth (ATLAS AML.T0020, T0018, T0010.002/.003) could create a hidden non-conservative bias in a region the attacker knows the plan will occupy. The effect is subtle and easily mistaken for normal model error. (7) Manipulating assembly input records, or the objective function and limits in the optimiser configuration, could skew loading or hide diversion-relevant assembly substitution. Existing practice (independent final Monte Carlo verification of every canister, margin, and physical fuel verification) mitigates both, so the main residual risk is organisational: skipping the verification step because the surrogate is trusted.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a classic surrogate-in-the-loop optimiser. A neural network trained on a limited set of SERPENT runs stands in for the physics, and a genetic algorithm searches the input space for configurations the surrogate scores as best. The pipeline is fragile at one point: the GA is an adversarial optimiser against its own surrogate. It actively seeks regions where the network underestimates keff or decay heat, because those regions look like efficient packing. Those are exactly the out-of-distribution, extrapolation-error regions where a small training set (a few hundred assemblies, four per canister) offers no coverage guarantee. The surrogate's error is therefore biased optimistic in the places the optimiser favours, which is not the average-case error validation would report. Provenance matters as well. Inputs such as burnup, enrichment, cooling time and the depletion-derived isotopic inventory come from operator declarations or code-computed values, not from measurement of each assembly. Errors or manipulation in that data propagate straight into the loading plan.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Optimiser exploitation of surrogate error (OP.C0403, OP.C0302): the GA converges on assembly combinations where the NN underestimates keff, which is a safety-relevant non-conservative bias. Aggregate test RMSE hides this, so the loaded canisters could nominally breach criticality margins in the long-term disposal geometry, including with water ingress and burnup-credit assumptions. (2) Training-data scarcity and representativeness (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01/02): the surrogate is trained on SERPENT simulations of a small assembly population. Different fuel types, burnup ranges, canister designs or four-per-canister assumptions cause distribution shift (OP.C0302.03) with no built-in out-of-domain detection. (3) Qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501): a neural surrogate is not a qualified criticality code, and no validation framework treats a stochastic, retrained NN plus a stochastic GA as part of the safety basis. Non-repeatability across GA seeds and NN training (OP.C0402) hurts reproducibility and regulatory defensibility. Opacity (OP.C0401) leaves reviewers unable to check why a loading is acceptable. (4) Automation bias (OP.C0101.04): a plan that is optimal by construction invites acceptance without independent Monte Carlo verification, and skill fade in manual loading-plan analysis erodes the backstop. (5) Objective misalignment (OP.C0301): minimising canister count and equalising heat and keff pushes margins toward their limits, trading away conservatism. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Poisoning of training data or the SERPENT-generated library (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003): a tampered surrogate, or a backdoor triggered by particular assembly features, can bias keff or heat predictions for chosen assemblies. (7) Manipulating the declared assembly inventory (burnup, cooling time, isotopics) that the surrogate takes as input. This is an input-integrity and safeguards problem, since a skewed loading plan could also hide diversion or misdeclaration of fissile content because the model is trusted as a proxy for the records (AML.T0043, AML.T0031). (8) Model or plan tampering through unqualified software supply chains (Python ML stacks, AML.T0010.001), and loss of the loading-plan data as a sensitive-information target (AML.T0025, AML.T0035). Combined consequence: criticality-safety margin erosion and thermal-limit exceedance in a repository that is hard to correct once canisters are sealed.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modelling view, this tool does not touch the reactor or the physical protection system, but it sits between assembly burnup and isotopic records and the final canister loading plan, so it becomes a trust-concentration point for a long-lived criticality safety and safeguards case. A nation-state or insider would not use it to cause an immediate event. They would use it to bias a decision whose consequences surface decades later, in a sealed repository, where nobody can check them. The surrogate replaces independent Monte Carlo evaluation, so the genetic algorithm will actively seek out whatever regions the surrogate under-predicts keff. That makes ordinary surrogate error systematic and exploitable, whether or not anyone intended it. The 212-assembly demonstration is small and not a plant deployment, so a gap between demonstrated and operational conditions is built in, and an adversary could time a manipulation around it.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity attack on the surrogate or its training data (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0010.002, T0059). The surrogate is trained on SERPENT outputs and assembly inputs such as burnup, enrichment, cooling time and decay heat. An insider or a compromised supply chain could poison those data or the weights so that keff is slightly under-predicted for particular assembly types or loading patterns. The optimiser then concentrates those assemblies in canisters that look compliant but carry less margin. The facility depends on this for the criticality safety demonstration and for packing density. The consequence is eroded subcriticality margin in sealed canisters, found late or never. (2) Manipulation of inputs and records (AML.T0043, T0031, T0015). Falsified or altered assembly declarations such as burnup, initial enrichment or history would pass through the optimiser as plausible inputs. This could hide material diversion or substitution, because the loading plan makes the records look internally consistent (OP.C0702.01).
