It is a safeguards concern: the optimised plan lends false credibility to bad declarations. (3) Concentration of trust. A fast optimiser that outputs a single plan invites the plan to be adopted without re-running Monte Carlo on every canister, so one compromised tool or one compromised operator account (AML.T0012) can bias many canisters. If the model is shared across sites, errors and tampering propagate together (OP.C0602). (4) Reconnaissance and knowledge theft (AML.T0000, T0024.002, T0035). The loading rules, limits and the surrogate itself reveal inventory composition and margin policy. They are worth exfiltrating for adversary planning and could be used to craft inputs the optimiser accepts. NON-ADVERSARIAL WEAKNESSES AN ADVERSARY COULD EXPLOIT: (5) Surrogate-optimiser mismatch (OP.C0301, OP.C0302, OP.C0403). The genetic algorithm exploits surrogate errors by driving loadings toward the edge of the training distribution and toward the keff limit, so the optimiser itself selects the worst-predicted cases. Natural error is turned into a bias that is hard to distinguish from sabotage. (6) Small and non-representative data (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.03). Training on about 212 assemblies, with surrogate data generated from simulation rather than measurement, leaves other fuel types, burnup ranges or nuclide-credit assumptions out of distribution. Nuclear data and depletion-code uncertainties stay hidden behind the surrogate. (7) Automation trust and verification gaps (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). Opacity, no AI-specific qualification, and skill fade in Monte Carlo analysts mean that nobody independently checks the outputs. A sophisticated adversary would favour this over attacking a hardened system, because the long time horizon and weak verification mean tampering is hard to attribute and may never be noticed. The practical mitigations are independent Monte Carlo verification of every final canister, provenance controls on training data and model files, and separation of duties between those who build the model and those who approve plans.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on optimiser exploitation of surrogate error, small-data distribution shift, qualification and over-trust gaps, and training-data and input-record tampering. I dropped weakly supported codes (OP.C0602 and OP.C0702.01 for a single-study demonstration, AML.T0000 and AML.T0015 as poor fits) and kept the speculative account-compromise and exfiltration pathway as one brief threat.

evidence.citation: "Optimisation of used nuclear fuel canister loading using a neural network and genetic algorithm," Springer (Neural Computing and Applications, vol. 33, 2021; Solans, Rochman, Brazell, Vasiliev, Ferroukhi, Pautz)
evidence.note: The paper trains an artificial neural network as a fast stand-in for time-consuming SERPENT transport and depletion runs when evaluating canister keff. A genetic algorithm then uses that network to optimise canister loading against decay-heat and criticality safety parameters. The study is a worked case on a set of representative spent-fuel assemblies, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a biased or poisoned surrogate, or falsified assembly records, producing sealed-canister loading plans with eroded subcriticality or thermal margin that surface decades later, and potentially masking fissile misdeclaration (a safeguards falsification concern); this is serious but not an immediate release and sits behind independent licensing checks.

reproducibility.why: Optimiser exploitation of surrogate error and out-of-distribution extrapolation occur reliably whenever a genetic algorithm searches over an unvalidated surrogate with no OOD detection, so the class is highly repeatable once the described conditions hold.

exploitability.why: Deliberate exploitation (poisoning training data or weights, altering records, using compromised accounts) generally requires insider or privileged access to the model pipeline or declaration data, though the implicit failure modes need no attacker at all.

affected_users.why: A single biased surrogate or plan propagates across many canisters in a disposal campaign, and the error is systematic across the inventory, though it is limited to the waste-loading workflow rather than coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: Surrogate-optimiser exploitation, small-data limits and OOD failure are well documented in the open ML literature, and the source paper is published, but finding a specific exploitable gap in the operational envelope or margin policy requires partial knowledge of the actual deployment.

use_case: Cascaded fuzzy neural network, made of serially connected fuzzy neural network modules, that predicts hydrogen concentration inside the containment of an OPR1000 PWR during severe accidents. It was developed and tested on MAAP4 severe-accident simulation data. The goal is to give operators an early forecast, so they can act to prevent hydrogen combustion or explosion.
incurred_insecurity:
This hydrogen forecaster is an advisory model trained and validated only on MAAP4 simulation output, so it incurs mainly implicit insecurity: a simulator-to-reality gap, unflagged degraded inputs, cascade error compounding, and operator over-trust in a rarely exercised regime. Adversarial threats (input spoofing, data and model poisoning, proxy-model reconnaissance) matter chiefly as ways to exploit or time around those weaknesses during a real event. Independent hydrogen monitoring, igniters, recombiners and the SAMGs limit direct physical harm, so the main consequence is distorted decisions in the emergency response organisation.

Simulation-only training and validation -- implicit, exploitable
The model learns MAAP4's modelling assumptions (hydrogen generation, stratification, recombiner and igniter behaviour), and its sub-5% RMS error measures agreement with the simulator, not with a real accident. It can therefore under-forecast hydrogen build-up in unmodelled or compound scenarios, delaying venting, spray or igniter actions and risking a combustion challenge to containment. An adversary could induce or time an off-nominal accident state outside the training envelope and rely on operators trusting the overstated accuracy figure.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation without uncertainty signal -- implicit, exploitable
The training set is a finite grid of initiating events, break sizes and equipment states, and a fuzzy neural network extrapolates unpredictably beyond it while reporting no uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag. An adversary could probe, using a proxy model built from the published architecture, for input regions where forecasts degrade, and steer conditions into them.

Cascade error propagation and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Serially connected modules pass upstream error into later stages with no independent check, and the final output hides which stage failed, limiting fault attribution and V&V. An adversary could hide a small manipulation in an early stage, where it compounds into a plausible but wrong final forecast.

Degraded severe-accident instrumentation -- implicit, exploitable
Containment pressure, temperature, hydrogen and radiation sensors may drift, saturate or fail under accident conditions, while the model was trained on clean simulator signals and has no demonstrated robustness to missing or biased channels. An adversary could hide spoofed or perturbed inputs inside this expected degradation, where they are indistinguishable from real instrument faults.

Operator over-trust and miscalibration -- implicit, exploitable
Severe accidents are almost never practised, so operators cannot calibrate trust in a numeric forecast with a low headline error, risking over-trust, confusion with measured hydrogen readings and SAMG guidance, or abrupt dismissal after a false alarm. An adversary could time an attack to coincide with this reliance, steering decisions when other information is scarce.

Qualification and lifecycle gap -- implicit, exploitable
Advisory software in a post-core-damage regime has no clear safety classification, V&V basis or defined cybersecurity class, and later MAAP versions, plant modifications or retraining on regenerated data cause drift and repeatability questions. An adversary could use the weaker assurance and likely less-protected network placement as a foothold or as cover for undetected model changes.

Runtime input manipulation -- adversarial
Spoofed, tampered or perturbed containment sensor or plant-computer data feeding the network can push the forecast low to suppress warning, or high to provoke unnecessary venting or other actions that release radioactivity. The attack exists only because the AI is consuming the signal, and is hard to tell from genuine instrument degradation.

Training data and model poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with the MAAP scenario corpus, parameter files, fuzzy membership parameters or model weights, via vendor, researcher or insider access, can introduce a dormant bias or backdoor that underpredicts hydrogen in a targeted regime. Aggregate RMS acceptance on simulated test data would not reveal it, so it could stay latent until a real accident.

Proxy-model reconnaissance -- adversarial
The published architecture and reliance on MAAP4 data let an adversary replicate a proxy model and search it for blind spots before timing an intervention. This produces no direct harm but enables the input-manipulation and out-of-envelope attacks above.

Availability loss during emergency response -- adversarial
Denying or delaying the forecast service while operators have come to depend on it adds burden at a critical moment. Independent instrumentation and procedures limit the consequence.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory forecaster for a severe-accident regime, which is rare, high-stress, and instrumented in degraded ways. It is trained wholly on MAAP4 simulation output because there is no real severe-accident data for OPR1000. The facility-level risk therefore has little to do with the model being attacked. It comes from operators or technical support centre staff trusting a forecast whose training distribution is a simulator's idealization of the accident. Engineering practice already guards against this: SAMGs, passive autocatalytic recombiners, igniters, containment hydrogen monitors and the TSC all operate independently of the model. Harm needs the model to be wrong and the human or procedural layer to defer to it, or to be diverted by it, during a time-critical decision window.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulation-only training (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). The model learns MAAP4's models of core degradation, zirconium oxidation, molten-corium-concrete interaction, and steam/hydrogen stratification. The simulator's modelling uncertainties, such as lumped-parameter containment nodalization and uncertain oxidation and ex-vessel hydrogen generation, are baked into the model and then hidden behind a low RMS figure. That figure is measured against the same simulator, so it says nothing about error against reality. Real accidents, Fukushima-type events with unanticipated pathways, would be out of distribution. In those cases the model may confidently under-forecast hydrogen build-up or its timing (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). The consequence is false reassurance, with delayed or mis-prioritized mitigation (igniter or spray actuation, venting decisions) and a possible deflagration or detonation challenge to containment. (2) Degraded inputs (OP.C0204, OP.C0304.03). In a severe accident the sensors that feed the model (containment pressure, temperature, hydrogen, radiation, water level) may be failed, drifting, or reading outside their qualified range. In a cascaded structure, error in an upstream module propagates into later stages (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). Missing or biased inputs may produce plausible but wrong outputs with no flag, and the fuzzy rule structure does not guarantee graceful degradation. (3) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.03). Severe accidents are very rarely practised, so operators have little basis for calibrating trust. A forecast that conflicts with the hydrogen monitor, or with SAMG guidance, could be over-trusted or abruptly dismissed. A forecast without uncertainty bounds invites over-trust, and mode confusion between 'prediction' and 'measurement' is possible. (4) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0401). Advisory software in a post-core-damage regime has no clear safety classification or V&V basis. Interpretability of the serial fuzzy-NN stack is limited, so it is difficult to demonstrate behaviour across the accident space or to justify reliance during licensing.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Integrity of inputs and outputs. An adversary does not need to attack the model. Falsified or spoofed containment instrument data, or tampering with the display or data path (AML.T0043, AML.T0031, AML.T0015), could steer the forecast low during a real event, or high to trigger unnecessary venting or other actions that release radioactivity. This matters most as a coordinated or timed attack alongside a real transient. Corrupted data are indistinguishable from real degraded-instrument behaviour, which makes detection harder. (6) Supply chain and lifecycle. The training pipeline, MAAP4 scenario databases, and model files are potential targets for poisoning or backdoors (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059). A subtly skewed training set, or one that omits scenarios, would be hard to detect given the opacity and the absence of real-world validation data, and could create a latent failure in a rarely exercised regime. Because validation is also simulator-based, tampering could go undetected until a real accident. (7) Denial or delay (AML.T0029). If the tool is part of the emergency response workflow, loss of availability while operators depend on it would add burden at a critical moment, though the independent layers described above limit the consequence.

Overall, the dominant risk is implicit: sim-to-real gap, unflagged input degradation and over-trust, with adversarial manipulation chiefly an amplifier timed to a real event. Existing defence-in-depth limits direct physical harm. The residual concern is decision distortion in the emergency response organisation.

ai_engineer.argument: From a pipeline standpoint, this model is trained and validated entirely on MAAP4 output, so it is a surrogate of a code, not of the plant. No real severe-accident data exists to anchor it, and the sub-5% RMS error is an in-distribution fit to the simulator's own physics and its assumptions about hydrogen generation, steam inerting, recombiner and igniter behavior, and break and injection scenarios. A cascaded architecture makes this worse: each fuzzy neural module's output feeds the next, so errors compound and the first module's mistakes are laundered into later stages with no independent check. At inference time the model would see degraded, failed or out-of-range instrumentation in the very scenario it targets, which is far from the clean simulator inputs it was trained on. The real exposure is a confident hydrogen forecast that operators trust during a high-stress severe accident, when the model has never been tested against reality.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulation-to-reality gap and untestable validity. The model learns MAAP4's modeling choices, including known uncertainties in hydrogen sources, mixing and stratification in a lumped-parameter containment, and recombiner/igniter performance. Reported error therefore measures agreement with MAAP4, not with a real accident. Real severe accidents (TMI-2, Fukushima) fall outside any validation set, and no field data exists to reveal a systematic bias. The consequence is an underpredicted hydrogen peak, which delays venting, spray or igniter actions and risks deflagration or detonation and containment challenge. (2) Scenario coverage and OOD failure. The training set is a finite grid of initiating events, break sizes, injection timings and equipment-availability states. Accidents with unmodeled combinations, such as multiple failures, operator deviations or novel injection paths, lie outside it, and a fuzzy neural network extrapolates unpredictably with no native OOD flag. (3) Cascade error compounding. Serial modules propagate and amplify upstream error, and the final output hides which stage failed, which limits explainability and fault attribution. (4) Input degradation. Severe-accident conditions of high radiation, temperature and humidity can leave hydrogen, pressure and temperature sensors drifting, failed or saturated, while the model was trained on noise-free simulator signals. It has no demonstrated robustness to missing, stuck or biased channels. (5) Human factors. A numeric early forecast with a low headline error invites over-trust, and operators have little experience with it. It also risks mode confusion with the Severe Accident Management Guidelines and the plant's own hydrogen instrumentation, and with disagreement between the AI and the instruments. (6) Lifecycle. Updates to MAAP versions, plant modifications such as new recombiners, and fuel or core changes cause concept drift between the model and the plant. Retraining on regenerated simulation data raises qualification and repeatability questions for safety-relevant use, and nothing in the paper suggests an established V&V basis. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (7) Data and model integrity. The training data are simulator runs that are generated, stored and shared as files. Poisoning or tampering with the simulation corpus, the weights or the fuzzy membership parameters could introduce a subtle bias, for example underpredicting hydrogen in a targeted regime, that passes aggregate-RMS acceptance testing. Supply-chain exposure arises through the MAAP toolchain, ML libraries and third-party research code. (8) Runtime input manipulation. If the forecast consumes plant-computer or sensor data, spoofed or perturbed inputs could steer the forecast away from the true hydrogen trajectory, either suppressing warning or triggering unnecessary mitigation actions. This is an inference-time evasion path that only exists because of the AI. (9) Reconnaissance. The published architecture and its reliance on MAAP4 simulation data help an adversary build a proxy model, find its blind spots and time an intervention around them. The main exposure is a trusted advisory output whose accuracy cannot be checked against real events and which can be silently degraded.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this is not a high-value direct target, since it is advisory, runs only in severe-accident conditions, and a nation-state would get more from attacking plant protection or instrumentation directly. Its threat relevance is as a trust-concentration and timing tool. If operators come to rely on a forecast of a safety-critical parameter (hydrogen, which drives combustion and explosion risk) during the worst hours of an accident, then corrupting or degrading that forecast, or exploiting its blind spots, could steer operator action when other information is scarce and stress is high. The model was trained only on MAAP4 simulation, never on real severe-accident data, so its blind spots are large and can't be bounded. An adversary who understands this could design accident conditions, or manipulate sensor inputs, that fall outside the training envelope and so produce confident but wrong forecasts. The most plausible adversary-relevant weaknesses are therefore the implicit ones: simulation-only provenance, opacity, and over-trust at the moment of crisis. Supply-chain and insider pathways to the model and training data come second.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
1) Implicit weakness that an adversary can exploit (simulation-to-reality gap): The model learned only from MAAP4 scenarios of one plant design, so its behavior under real accident progressions, degraded instrumentation, unmodeled phenomena (recombiner or igniter performance, unusual break locations, operator actions) and compound events is unvalidated. The failure mechanism is out-of-distribution extrapolation with no uncertainty signal. Operators rely on the forecast to decide on mitigation such as venting, spray or igniter use. The consequence is a missed or false hydrogen-risk forecast during a beyond-design-basis event, potentially leading to a delayed mitigation or an unnecessary action that worsens containment conditions. A deliberate adversary, particularly one combining a physical or cyber attack that creates an off-nominal accident state with a forecast operators trust, can exploit this because the 'RMS error below 5%' figure overstates real-world reliability.

2) Adversarial input manipulation: The network consumes containment sensor and plant-state signals. Corrupted, spoofed or drifting inputs (sensor tampering, a compromised data link, or degradation from accident conditions an adversary can induce or time around) produce plausible but wrong forecasts. A cascaded structure makes this worse, because an error in an early module propagates and compounds in later ones with no independent check. The result is a quiet, credible misdirection of operators rather than an obvious alarm, which is more dangerous than a denial of service.

3) Model and data integrity, supply chain and insider: Training data come from simulation runs and a model file that few staff can audit. A poisoned training set, a tampered MAAP parameter file or a backdoored model, introduced by a vendor, researcher or insider, would be hard to detect because fuzzy-neural weights and rules are poorly explainable and the validation set is also simulated. Such a backdoor could stay dormant until an accident, when the model is actually consulted. The standard test-set error would show nothing because the backdoor would sit outside the tested scenarios.

4) Human-factors and security-culture effects: A forecast that is almost never used in real conditions invites out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity and miscalibrated trust. Operators have no experience of when it fails, and the first real use is the worst moment to learn. Over-trust can displace independent hydrogen monitoring and accident-management guidance, whereas under-trust after a false alarm can mean the tool is ignored when correct. An adversary who can predict this behavior can time an attack around it.

5) Lower-priority exposures: Outputs and design details are published in the open literature, so an adversary can build a proxy model and probe for the input regions where forecasts degrade. The use case also lacks defined qualification and cybersecurity classification, since it is advisory and non-safety-class, so it may sit on a less-protected network segment. That would make it a stepping stone into operator-facing or plant-information systems. Overall criticality is moderate, driven mostly by exploitation of implicit weaknesses, and compensating controls would be independent instrumentation cross-checks, input-plausibility checks, uncertainty reporting, and integrity control of the model.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulation-to-reality gap, cascade error propagation, degraded inputs and over-trust as the dominant implicit threats, with adversarial manipulation as an amplifier timed to a real event. I kept poisoning, input spoofing, proxy-model reconnaissance and denial as separate adversarial threats and dropped weaker codes (OP.C0504, OP.C0503, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0304.03, AML.T0010.003) that restated other threats or lacked a clear mechanism.

evidence.citation: "Prediction of hydrogen concentration in nuclear power plant containment under severe accidents using cascaded fuzzy neural networks," Nuclear Engineering and Design (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper builds a cascaded fuzzy neural network model for forecasting containment hydrogen concentration. It trains the model on MAAP4-simulated OPR1000 severe-accident scenarios, because real severe-accident data are not available. It reports a prediction RMS error below about 5% and says the model could help operators avoid hydrogen explosions.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is runtime input manipulation or a latent poisoned bias that distorts hydrogen forecasts during a severe accident, which could delay mitigation (risking a combustion challenge to containment) or provoke unnecessary venting that releases radioactivity; independent hydrogen monitoring, igniters, recombiners and SAMGs limit direct harm, so this stops short of 5.

reproducibility.why: The implicit weaknesses (simulator gap, out-of-distribution extrapolation, degraded sensors) reliably produce forecast error whenever the accident state leaves the training envelope, but a deliberate attack needs a rare severe-accident window and specific conditions to have effect.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible attacks (poisoning the MAAP corpus or weights, or tampering with plant-computer or sensor data feeding the model) require vendor, insider or privileged OT-network access, and timing them to a real severe accident is demanding; only proxy-model reconnaissance is achievable externally.

affected_users.why: A misleading containment hydrogen forecast distorts decisions across the emergency response organisation and the single-unit response, but it is an advisory output for one plant and does not propagate across coupled control systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, the MAAP4 training basis and the headline RMS error are published in the open literature, and simulator-trained models in general are known to have OOD and sensor-degradation weaknesses, so a capable outsider can infer them; finding actual blind spots or deployment details needs more knowledge.

use_case: Deep neural-network surrogate (a U-Net encoder-decoder with a multigroup attention pooling layer) trained on OpenMC-calculated keff sensitivity vectors for grid-based critical-experiment geometries. Gradient-based optimisation through the surrogate designs critical-experiment geometries that maximise the neutronic similarity coefficient c_k to a target system. The method was applied to the TN-LC transportation cask loaded with HALEU fuel. It supports criticality-safety validation where existing benchmark experiments cover the cask poorly.
incurred_insecurity:
This surrogate sits upstream of the criticality-safety validation basis for a HALEU transport cask, so its main insecurity is quiet erosion of the claimed subcritical margin rather than any operational disruption. The principal threats are optimiser exploitation of surrogate error, shared simulation error behind a thin benchmark base, an unqualified and opaque method that invites over-trust, proxy-objective misalignment, and integrity compromise or steering of the data, model or objective by a patient insider or supply-chain actor. Information aggregation around the cask and HALEU loading is a secondary concern.

Optimiser exploitation of surrogate error -- implicit, exploitable
Gradient ascent on c_k drives inputs into regions outside the training distribution where the U-Net over-predicts similarity, so designed experiments look neutronically close to the cask while their true sensitivity vectors differ, overstating validation coverage and understating keff bias and uncertainty. An adversary who knows this can lean on the failure mode, and a deliberately crafted objective or input would be indistinguishable from natural error.

Simulated-only labels and shared simulation error -- implicit, exploitable
Training labels come from one transport code and one nuclear-data library on grid geometries, so cross-section, covariance and statistical errors for HALEU and cask materials propagate into the similarity measure with no independent ground truth, exactly where benchmarks are scarce. An adversary could hide a biased dataset or library change inside this unobservable systematic error.

Unqualified, opaque method and over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
A non-peer-reviewed surrogate with attention pooling offers no explanation of why a geometry scores well, has no accepted AI qualification path, and yields non-repeatable designs across seeds, so reviewers may treat a high c_k as evidence and skip the independent Monte Carlo and sensitivity recalculation. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust and weak auditability to get a manipulated result through review.

Proxy objective and design-space drift -- implicit
Maximising c_k is a proxy that can select geometries that are impractical to build, omit spectral or reaction sensitivities relevant to damaged or accident configurations, and become invalid when the cask, enrichment or nuclear data change while the model stays fixed to its grid parameterisation. No distinct adversarial gain beyond the steering threats below.

Training-data, model and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
Poisoned OpenMC sensitivity datasets, altered cross-section or covariance libraries, a tampered checkpoint, or a compromised ML or transport-code dependency can bias the surrogate to systematically over-score similarity or under-represent sensitivity in particular nuclides, energy groups or regions. The consequence is a validation set that looks adequate while real keff bias stays unconstrained.

Objective and constraint steering -- adversarial
An insider or applicant who can edit the target definition, bounds, acceptance thresholds or objective can make the optimiser faithfully produce a favourable but non-representative experiment set, and cherry-picking among runs is hard to audit. This needs no ML expertise.

Design-information aggregation -- adversarial
The cask model, HALEU loading, sensitivity profiles and optimal layouts form an aggregated sensitive dataset that could be collected or partly inverted from the surrogate, and the public preprint on a named cask eases reconnaissance.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This surrogate sits upstream of criticality-safety validation for a HALEU transport cask. It designs experiments whose neutronic similarity (c_k) to the cask is meant to justify the bias and uncertainty applied to keff in the safety case. If the surrogate is wrong, nobody sees a plant transient. The harm is a quietly eroded subcritical margin that shows up years later, as a loaded package or array with less margin than the licensing basis claims. Existing practice is a real defence: the ANSI/ANS-8.24 and NUREG/CR-6698 validation framework, independent Monte Carlo and sensitivity/uncertainty (TSUNAMI-type) recalculation of the final design, and actual physical experiments with reviewed benchmark evaluations. These all sit between the surrogate and the license. They only help if the surrogate is treated as a design aid and not as evidence, and the source is an unreviewed preprint with a small number of demonstrated cases.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT. (1) Surrogate fidelity and out-of-distribution failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03): the network is trained on OpenMC sensitivity vectors for grid-based geometries. Gradient optimisation actively searches for inputs where the surrogate over-predicts similarity, which is adversarial-example behaviour arising on its own. The resulting designs can look highly similar to the cask (high c_k) while the true sensitivity profile is not, so the validation basis overstates coverage. The consequence is an understated bias or uncertainty and eroded margin. A physical safeguard would be an independent forward Monte Carlo/S-U check of every candidate, and the harm requires that check to be skipped or run with the same code and data. (2) Shared-error and data provenance (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0603): the training labels are simulated, from one transport code and one nuclear data library. Errors in cross-section data (HALEU, high-enrichment, and cask materials such as the neutron absorber and the polyethylene or resin) propagate into the 'similarity' measure and are never independently exposed. The method can show the experiment resembles the cask in the model's view, not in reality. HALEU benchmark scarcity (OP.C0203) is the very reason the tool is needed, so the check against reality is the thinnest where the tool is used. (3) Qualification and regulatory gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0401): there is no accepted qualification path for ML-designed validation experiments, the model is opaque, and the preprint has had no peer review. An applicant or reviewer could over-trust a c_k number (OP.C0101.04) and treat it as defensible evidence, or a regulator could lack the tools to challenge it. (4) Goal misalignment (OP.C0301): c_k maximisation is a proxy. It may select geometries that are impractical to build, fall outside measurement capability, or leave out sensitivity to reactions or spectral regions that matter for accident or damaged-package configurations. The proxy then substitutes for a full area-of-applicability analysis. ADVERSARIAL (secondary, because the tool is offline and used by analysts). (5) Supply chain and tampering (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0031): poisoned training data, a tampered pre-trained checkpoint, or a modified optimisation script could bias designs toward geometries that look similar but systematically understate cask sensitivity, for example to ease a licensing outcome or hide non-conservatism. Such bias would be hard to detect given the opacity and nonrepeatability of gradient search and training (OP.C0402). (6) Insider or applicant manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0031): the optimiser's freedom to choose objectives, bounds and acceptance thresholds lets an applicant tune the inputs until a favourable c_k comes out, which makes cherry-picking hard to audit. The compensating control is regulator-side reproduction of the results with independent tools. Overall severity is moderate and delayed, and it is bounded by independent Monte Carlo recalculation and physical experiment. The real exposure is cultural and procedural: treating surrogate output as validation evidence in an area where benchmarks are already sparse.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is a surrogate-in-the-loop inverse design system. The surrogate is trained entirely on OpenMC-simulated keff sensitivity vectors for grid-based geometries, and gradient ascent on c_k then pushes the design toward whatever region of input space the surrogate is least reliable in. Optimisation against a learned model is effectively an adversarial-example search run by the designer. It tends to find off-manifold geometries where the surrogate over-predicts similarity, and nothing in the described pipeline guarantees that the output sensitivity vectors match what transport code would compute for that layout. The training data is 100% simulated (OP.C0201.01), there is no operational data for HALEU casks, and the target system is exactly where the benchmark data is thin (OP.C0203, OP.C0202). The output feeds a licensing and criticality-safety validation argument, so a fidelity error in the surrogate can become an unconservative bias in the claimed validation coverage.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Optimiser exploitation of surrogate error: gradient-based design drives inputs out of the training distribution (OP.C0302, OP.C0403). The surrogate reports a high c_k, but the real sensitivity vectors of the proposed experiment differ. If the designed experiment is built or cited on the surrogate's c_k alone, the cask's validation basis is overstated, which is an unconservative criticality-safety margin. Mitigation requires re-running OpenMC on every final design, and the process must make that step mandatory. (2) Error inherited from the simulation: nuclear-data library uncertainty, OpenMC statistical noise in the sensitivity estimates, and the grid discretisation all enter the training labels. The surrogate cannot see its own systematic bias, and the HALEU energy regime may sit outside where cross-section covariance data is well characterised (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0304.03). (3) Qualification gap: this is a non-peer-reviewed preprint with no established V&V regime for a neural surrogate in licensing (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0401). Opaque attention pooling gives no explanation of why a geometry scores well, and training non-determinism means different seeds may yield different 'optimal' designs (OP.C0402.01). Automation bias is also a risk: a high c_k number looks authoritative to reviewers (OP.C0101.04). (4) Drift: any change to the cask design, fuel enrichment or loading, or to nuclear data libraries, requires retraining, but the surrogate is fixed to a grid parameterisation (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Poisoning of the simulation data or training pipeline: tampered OpenMC inputs, cross-section libraries, or generated sensitivity datasets (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000) could bias the surrogate so that certain unsafe configurations are scored as well-covered. Such a bias would be hard to detect because the labels are synthetic and there is no independent ground truth. (6) Model or weight tampering and software supply-chain compromise of the PyTorch or OpenMC stack (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076) could cause a falsely high c_k at the final design step. (7) Adversarial steering of the optimisation: someone who can alter the target definition, constraints, or objective could steer the design toward a non-representative experiment while appearing to follow the method (AML.T0043, AML.T0031). (8) Information exposure: sensitivity profiles and HALEU cask designs may be export-controlled or proprietary, and the surrogate or its dataset could leak design detail (AML.T0024.001, AML.T0035).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this tool is not a plant-control system, so a nation-state would rarely bother attacking it directly. It matters because it sits upstream of a licensing safety argument. It helps decide which critical experiments get built and then cited as evidence that keff for a HALEU transport cask is adequately validated. That concentrates trust in a single, opaque, non-peer-reviewed surrogate, and compromise or quiet error there would propagate into the validation basis, with effects that appear years later and across many shipments. The attack class is therefore integrity of the safety case, not disruption of operations, and it favours a patient insider, a supply-chain actor or a plain mistake over a loud intrusion. A malicious party who wanted an under-validated cask configuration to look well-covered would have a quiet route.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity compromise of the surrogate or its training data: poisoned or subtly biased OpenMC sensitivity datasets, a tampered model or weights, or a compromised pretrained or open-source ML dependency (AML.T0010, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). The mechanism is that the surrogate systematically over-estimates c_k, or under-represents sensitivity in particular nuclide, energy-group or geometry regions. The facility dependency is that the licensing validation basis relies on the designed experiments being neutronically similar to the cask. The consequence is a validation set that looks adequate but leaves real keff bias or uncertainty unconstrained, which erodes criticality-safety margin for transport of HALEU, a safeguards-relevant and higher-enrichment material. An insider who can edit the target-system definition, the cross-section or covariance libraries, or the optimisation constraints could steer the design the same way with no ML expertise, because the gradient optimiser will faithfully exploit whatever objective it is given. (2) Adversarial exploitation of the optimiser: gradient optimisation through a surrogate can find inputs that score high c_k on the surrogate while being poor in the true transport calculation. This is the same property as adversarial-example crafting (AML.T0043.000, AML.T0015). It is a natural failure, and also a lever for anyone who controls or can see the model. (3) Information-security side: the c_k-optimal experiment layouts, the cask model and the HALEU loading specifications form an aggregated, sensitive dataset (AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0036). Cask design details and sensitivity profiles could support targeting or sabotage analysis, and a public arXiv preprint about a named cask and HALEU also eases reconnaissance (AML.T0000.001). IMPLICIT, and exploitable. (4) The method is unreviewed and unqualified, so there is no established AI-specific QA or regulatory pathway for surrogate-driven experiment design (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0401). The surrogate is opaque, and the final physics check is a manual OpenMC rerun that a time-pressed team may skip, which is a classic automation-trust path (OP.C0101.04). (5) Simulated-only training data, with no real experimental ground truth, means the model inherits OpenMC and nuclear-data errors, and may generalise poorly to HALEU geometries outside the grid-based design space (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0403). Attackers need not create these gaps; they only need to rely on the reviewers being unlikely to catch them. (6) Stochastic training and optimisation give non-repeatable designs, which weakens auditability (OP.C0402). Overall risk is moderate in likelihood and high in consequence if the output is adopted uncritically, because the effect is silent, delayed and hard to attribute.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on optimiser exploitation of surrogate error, simulated-only provenance, the qualification gap and over-trust, and poisoning/tampering of the data and model; I merged these and kept steering and information aggregation as distinct. I dropped AML.T0015, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0036 and the AML.T0043.000 sub-technique as weakly supported, since the model is offline and no white-box or evasion pathway is documented.

evidence.citation: "Inverse Critical Experiment Design via Gradient Optimization and a Multigroup Attention-Based Neural Network Architecture," arXiv (MIT Department of Nuclear Science and Engineering authors: Savage, Burnett, Price)
evidence.note: The authors train a deep neural-network surrogate on simulated sensitivity profiles and use gradient optimisation to generate critical-experiment layouts. They apply it to the TN-LC HALEU transport-cask validation case and report c_k scores for three configurations. This is an arXiv preprint submitted June 2026. It has not been peer reviewed, and I found no peer-reviewed version.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is quiet erosion of the claimed subcritical margin in a HALEU transport cask validation basis (via tampering, steering, or over-trust), which could allow an inadequately bounded keff bias to pass review; this is a serious criticality-safety consequence but indirect and mediated by independent review, so just short of a direct release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Optimiser exploitation of out-of-distribution surrogate error and proxy-objective misalignment recur reliably whenever gradient ascent is run against a fixed surrogate, and objective steering is deterministic once the editor has access.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (poisoning datasets or libraries, tampering with checkpoints, editing objectives or thresholds) require insider or supply-chain position within a licensing or applicant workflow, though steering needs no ML expertise.

affected_users.why: Impact concentrates on one cask design's validation basis and the licensing decisions that rely on it, but it could propagate to the transport and storage campaigns and other HALEU applications using the same method, not facility-wide coupled systems.

discoverability.why: Surrogate extrapolation failure, simulation-only labels, and opacity are well documented for this class of AI system, and a public preprint names the cask, method and architecture, so an outsider can readily infer where weaknesses lie.

use_case: Keras artificial neural network metamodel, tuned with Talos, that predicts fuel peak cladding temperature in an APR1400 large-break LOCA from 9–11 key uncertain input parameters. The training database comes from MARS-KS best-estimate thermal-hydraulic runs, with PIRT-derived uncertain parameters sampled through the Dakota-MARS uncertainty quantification framework. It acts as a fast surrogate for uncertainty quantification in safety analysis.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline LBLOCA peak-cladding-temperature surrogate has no actuation path, so its main insecurity is corrupted or overtrusted safety-margin evidence rather than a direct plant transient. The implicit threats are non-conservative error in the sparse high-PCT tail, inherited MARS-KS and PIRT fidelity limits, silent out-of-envelope use, automation over-trust, and qualification and reproducibility gaps. The adversarial threats are integrity tampering with the training data, model file or toolchain, and theft of the plant-response knowledge the surrogate encodes.

Tail underprediction masked by aggregate metrics -- implicit, exploitable
With R2 of about 0.9 and an MSE averaged over a bulk-sampled database, the ANN can underpredict the rare high-PCT cases that set the 95/95 value against the 1204 C limit, giving non-conservative margin that aggregate metrics never reveal. An adversary could place a deliberate bias inside this poorly characterised band, where it looks like ordinary ML error and is unlikely to be challenged.

Simulated-data fidelity ceiling -- implicit
The surrogate learns MARS-KS output rather than experiment, so code model-form error, nodalization choices and PIRT omissions or truncated ranges are inherited invisibly and validity is measured only against the code. Because the data is purely simulated and the 9-11 parameters are frozen, an adversary gains little here beyond what a data-integrity attack already gives.

Silent out-of-envelope extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
A Keras MLP gives no out-of-distribution flag, so reuse after a core or fuel change, power uprate, different plant, or the proposed extension to DNBR yields confident but arbitrary PCT values without requalification. An adversary could rely on this by steering analysis toward unvalidated regions, or by letting scope creep carry a flawed result through review.

Automation over-trust and erosion of code-based checks -- implicit, exploitable
Speed encourages many more sweeps and fewer MARS-KS confirmation runs at the extremes, so analyst familiarity with code behaviour fades and the surrogate becomes the working basis of margin claims. An adversary could exploit this misplaced trust by swapping or biasing the surrogate, knowing few reviewers will regenerate the full database to check.

Qualification, reproducibility and configuration gap -- implicit, exploitable
Talos hyperparameter search and random seeds make training non-deterministic, the network is opaque about dropped physical regimes such as reflood or ballooning, and no established regulatory route (RG 1.203 EMDAP) covers an ML emulator in the statistical argument. Weak version control lets a quietly modified or retrained model pass undetected, which an adversary can use to hide a manipulation.

Surrogate and training-pipeline integrity compromise -- adversarial
An insider, vendor or supply-chain actor can poison or alter the Dakota input decks, MARS-KS results, parameter distributions, scalers or saved weights, or the Keras/Talos dependencies, to bias PCT downward in a narrow input region while aggregate metrics still pass. The result is a design or licensing basis that appears conservative but is not.

Unsafe model-file loading and toolchain compromise -- adversarial
Third-party Python packages and serialized model files (pickle or HDF5) can execute code when loaded, giving an initial-access route onto engineering workstations that hold design-basis analysis data. A malicious package or model artifact could also embed malware in the surrogate.

Surrogate and database exfiltration for vulnerability reconnaissance -- adversarial
The trained model, the LOCA database and the PIRT sensitivity rankings encode which plant parameters and combinations drive cladding damage, and a copied surrogate can be queried offline and cheaply to explore that response surface. This gives sabotage-planning leverage and proprietary-information loss, though it is not a direct physical risk.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline design/licensing-support surrogate for LBLOCA PCT uncertainty quantification, not a real-time protection function, so its failures show up as bad safety-analysis margin evidence rather than direct plant transients. The consequences are downstream: analysts or reviewers trust a fast metamodel's PCT distribution (especially the 95/95 upper tail against the 1204 °C / 10 CFR 50.46-type limit) and approve design, fuel loading, or operating-limit decisions with less margin than believed. The safeguards that would also have to fail are independent code-based verification (MARS-KS reruns, bounding calculations), regulator review, and conservative licensing practice. These are real barriers, but they erode if the cheap surrogate becomes the working basis for iteration and the full-code runs are skipped. The metamodel's R² of ~0.9 is weakest exactly where it matters, in the sparse high-PCT tail, and an adversary or ordinary error can hide there.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Tail inaccuracy and low base rate: PCT exceedance cases are rare in the sampled database, so an ANN with a good average MSE and R² can underpredict the upper tail that drives 95/95 statements. Aggregate fit metrics mask this, and the consequence is non-conservative margin (OP.C0202, OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03). (2) Surrogate-of-a-surrogate fidelity: the training data are MARS-KS outputs, not experiments. Code model-form error, nodalization choices, and the PIRT-selected 9–11 parameters (omitted phenomena, truncated ranges, assumed distributions) are inherited and hidden, which could give false confidence (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0304.03). (3) Out-of-distribution use: the metamodel is valid only inside its sampled envelope. Reuse after a core redesign, new fuel type, power uprate, burnup change, or a different plant or break spec (including the proposed extension to DNBR) can silently extrapolate with no OOD flag (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0602). (4) Automation trust and process erosion: speed encourages many more parametric studies and less scrutiny, and analysts lose familiarity with code behaviour. This is a path to misuse or over-trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). (5) Qualification gap: ANN surrogates fall outside the NRC RG 1.203 EMDAP / 10 CFR 50 App. B framework. Training non-determinism (Talos hyperparameter search, random seeds), opacity, and unversioned models hurt repeatability and reviewability (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502, OP.C0504).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Integrity attacks on the pipeline: tampering with Dakota input decks, MARS-KS result files, parameter ranges and distributions, the trained model file, or the Keras/Talos toolchain and dependencies (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). A small bias in the tail, or a backdoor-like region of underprediction, could make a marginal design look compliant. Given the licensing stakes, the plausible actors are insiders, vendors, or supply-chain compromise, and the harm is a latent safety-margin error that passes review because it looks like ordinary ML error. (7) Confidentiality: the plant model, the sampled database, and the design margin are proprietary and sensitive. Extracting them through model or data theft (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025, AML.T0035) gives an adversary a fast tool for finding vulnerable accident sequences, though this is a modest concern since the results are not directly actionable. (8) Availability and cloud/shared compute dependence mostly cause schedule delay, not safety harm (AML.T0029, OP.C0601). Existing practice (independent code reruns for the limiting cases, regulatory audit, conservative bounding) is the main defence, so the recommendation is to keep the surrogate screening-only, with full-code confirmation of tail cases, a documented validity envelope, and configuration control of the data and model.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a regression surrogate trained entirely on simulated data. The data is MARS-KS best-estimate runs, with inputs sampled by Dakota from PIRT-derived distributions, so the metamodel's fidelity is capped by the code, the nodalization, and the PIRT. It inherits every code bias and every missing phenomenon, and the pipeline contains no field or experimental ground truth to expose them. The reported R² of about 0.9 means roughly 10% of the variance is unexplained. That residual is concentrated in the tail, where regulatory decisions are made: the 95/95 PCT against the 1204 °C (2200 °F) limit. A mean-squared-error metric over a bulk-sampled database can hide poor accuracy exactly there. The 9–11 inputs also assume a fixed, frozen PIRT-selected parameter space and a fixed plant model. A design change, a different fuel type, burnup, a different power uprate, or a revised PIRT puts inference outside the training support, and a Keras MLP gives no native out-of-distribution signal when that happens. Because the surrogate acts as a quantitative stand-in for the thermal-hydraulic code in safety analysis, errors in it become licensing-margin errors without anyone noticing.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Simulated-data fidelity ceiling and tail inaccuracy (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0403): the surrogate learns MARS-KS, not physics. Code model-form error, nodalization choices, and PIRT omissions are baked in invisibly. An MLP trained on a Latin-hypercube or random sample is usually weakest at the extreme high-PCT tail, which is the region that decides compliance. Aggregate MSE or R² can mask that, so the surrogate could under-predict PCT near the limit and give a falsely non-conservative margin. (2) Out-of-distribution extrapolation (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03): inputs outside the sampled ranges, or combinations the training design did not cover, produce confident but arbitrary outputs. This is likely when the surrogate is reused for a different plant state, a new fuel design, or a reshaped uncertainty distribution, and when the proposed extension to DNBR or other figures of merit is made without retraining. (3) Qualification and V&V gap (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01): Talos hyperparameter search and random weight initialisation make training non-deterministic, so the 'same' surrogate cannot easily be reproduced. Framework, version, and seed drift further undermine configuration control. No established regulatory acceptance route (e.g. under 10 CFR 50.46 or Korean equivalents or in codes such as RG 1.203) covers an ML emulator replacing a qualified code in the statistical (GRS/Wilks) argument. The opacity of the network also makes it hard to demonstrate monotonic or physically plausible sensitivity, so errors in surrogate response may go undetected. (4) Automation over-trust (OP.C0101.04): a fast surrogate invites running far more samples and design sweeps. Analysts may then rely on its output without cross-checking against MARS-KS at the extremes, and the bounding case may never be verified with the actual code.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training-data and artifact tampering (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059): the MARS-KS run database, the Dakota input decks, and the saved Keras model file are the whole attack surface. Because the training data is simulation output stored in ordinary files, a subtle integrity attack is plausible: biasing a small region of the input-output space, altering sampling distributions, or modifying the model weights. This could shift predicted PCT downward in a narrow region to make a non-conservative design or an inadequate margin appear acceptable. A targeted shift is hard to detect from R² or MSE and could also be timed to a licensing submission. (6) Supply-chain and deserialization risk (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0011.000, AML.T0018.002): the Keras/TensorFlow/Talos/Dakota Python stack depends on third-party packages, and pickled or HDF5 model files can execute code when loaded. This gives an initial-access route into engineering workstations that hold design-basis analysis data. (7) Model and data exfiltration (AML.T0035, AML.T0025, AML.T0024.002): trained surrogates and the underlying LOCA databases encode proprietary, safety-significant knowledge about plant response and margins, which could be of use to an adversary studying vulnerabilities and sensitivity of the design. (8) Adversarial input crafting is less relevant at inference, because inputs are sampled parameter vectors from a controlled analysis environment rather than an exposed interface. The main exposure is integrity of the analysis chain rather than evasion at run time, and the main weakness is the lack of independent verification that would catch a tampered or drifted surrogate.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial standpoint this is an unattractive direct target: it is an offline design-phase surrogate with no actuation path, so no one would attack it to cause a physical event. It matters as a stepping stone to a licensing or safety-margin outcome. A surrogate for LBLOCA peak cladding temperature (PCT) is trusted because it is fast, and it stands in for slow MARS-KS/Dakota runs that few people can reproduce. That concentrates trust in a small artifact (training database, scaler, weights, Talos hyperparameter logs) that an insider, a vendor or a supply-chain actor could quietly bias. The more serious risk is non-adversarial and sits in the gap between what the model is validated for and how it gets used. An R² of about 0.9 is weakest in the tail, and the tail (the 95/95 upper bound on PCT near the 1204 °C limit) is exactly what regulators care about. A deliberate or careless actor could exploit that gap, and the 'extend to DNBR and other parameters' proposal widens it.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity compromise of the surrogate or its pipeline: poisoning or altering the MARS-KS/Dakota-generated training database, scalers or weights, or hyperparameter-search artifacts (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/T0010.003, T0059, T0076). The AI failure mechanism is a surrogate that systematically under-predicts PCT in a narrow region of input space, for example a particular break size, ECCS availability or gap-conductance combination, while matching on aggregate metrics. The dependent function is the safety-analysis UQ used to demonstrate PCT margin. The consequence is a licensing or design basis that looks conservative but is not. This is a stealthy, low-cost insider or supplier manipulation, because the artifacts are small files and Keras/Talos/Python dependencies are open-source supply-chain exposure (AML.T0010.001). Few reviewers regenerate the full MARS-KS database to check. (2) Reconnaissance value: the PIRT parameter ranges, sensitivity rankings and PCT response surface are themselves sensitive. They reveal which plant parameters and failure combinations drive cladding damage, and a queryable surrogate lets someone explore that response surface offline and cheaply (AML.T0024.001/T0024.002, T0035, T0037). This is information-security and sabotage-planning leverage, not direct physical risk. (3) Trust-concentration and timing: once the surrogate is accepted, human vigilance over the underlying MARS-KS runs erodes. A swap or drift can then go unnoticed for a long time (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06).

IMPLICIT. (a) Extrapolation and tail inaccuracy: the model is trained on a sampled parameter envelope, so out-of-range inputs, a design change, or a different plant or fuel type produces confident but wrong PCT, with no built-in out-of-distribution flag (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403). Applying it to DNBR or other parameters requires re-qualification, and the gap here is the same kind. (b) Training-data provenance: the data is simulated code output and carries MARS-KS model-form error and its own uncertainties, so the surrogate inherits and hides them (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02). Validity is measured against the code, not against experiment. (c) Qualification and governance: there is no established regulatory pathway for ML surrogates in safety analysis, and weak version control, retraining governance and non-deterministic training make results hard to reproduce and audit (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502, OP.C0401). An adversary could exploit this by shifting the model quietly, since nothing detects it. (d) Opacity: a black-box metamodel cannot show whether a physical mechanism has been dropped, such as a reflood or ballooning regime change (OP.C0303, OP.C0304.03).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on tail inaccuracy, simulated-data fidelity, out-of-envelope use, over-trust, qualification gaps, and pipeline integrity tampering; I merged them and dropped availability/cloud (schedule-only harm) and inference-time adversarial input crafting (no exposed interface). I kept the deserialization/supply-chain and exfiltration threats as distinct adversarial items, and omitted codes for the dropped threats (AML.T0029, OP.C0601) and the weakly argued OP.C0602 and OP.C0302.01.

evidence.citation: "Using Machine Learning to Predict the Fuel Peak Cladding Temperature for a Large Break Loss of Coolant Accident," Frontiers in Energy Research (Frontiers Media), vol. 9, article 755638, 2021
evidence.note: The authors built and tested an ANN on a database generated by propagating PIRT-derived uncertainties through a MARS-KS model of an APR1400 LBLOCA. After training and validation it predicted peak cladding temperature with an MSE of about 0.002 and R² of about 0.9. They propose extending the same framework to other safety parameters such as DNBR.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is integrity tampering or non-conservative tail underprediction, which yields a falsified safety-margin basis (a licensing/design-basis erosion) with no direct actuation path; this is close to safeguards-falsification-type harm but indirect and requires downstream review failure, so it scores 4 rather than 5.

reproducibility.why: Tail underprediction, out-of-envelope extrapolation and unversioned model modification recur reliably once the surrogate is used beyond its validated scope or with weak configuration control; a deliberate tail bias also persists once embedded.

exploitability.why: The most severe adversarial threats (poisoning the training pipeline, or altering model files or toolchain) need insider, vendor or supply-chain access to offline design-analysis environments, though the implicit over-trust and scope-creep weaknesses need no special access.

affected_users.why: A biased surrogate can propagate into the safety analysis and licensing basis of the plant design, and potentially of other designs if reused, but it stays confined to analysis products with no coupled-system propagation.

discoverability.why: The approach is published in open literature, and ANN-surrogate limits (tail error, no OOD flag, unsafe pickle/HDF5 loading, supply-chain risk) are well documented for this class, though locating specific tamper points needs some inside knowledge.

use_case: Acoustic-emission monitoring of internal leakage in high-temperature nuclear power plant valves. High-temperature piezoelectric AE sensors capture the signals. A convolutional neural network with a Convolutional Block Attention Module (channel and spatial attention) classifies the AE spectrum data into valve leakage states, to support valve condition assessment.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory AE-spectrum classifier supports valve condition assessment and maintenance prioritisation rather than protection logic, so its harm is mainly masked internal leakage across isolation or containment-boundary valves, or spurious leak calls that force needless outages and dose. The main threats are a bench-to-plant generalisation gap with drift and opacity, human over-trust that erodes independent checks, a missing AI qualification path, adversarial manipulation of the sensor signal, the training data or the model, and the monitoring workstation as a foothold into OT networks.

Bench-to-plant domain shift -- implicit, exploitable
A CNN+CBAM classifier trained on rig AE spectra with induced leaks, fixed pressures and temperatures, few valve types and rare leak labels can latch onto rig-specific resonances and fail on plant background noise, valve designs and coupling. The closed-set softmax gives confident wrong classes (missed leaks or false alarms) with no out-of-distribution flag. An adversary could rely on these predictable blind spots, or hide a real leak or manipulation inside the misclassification band, without attacking the model.

Sensor ageing and spectral drift -- implicit, exploitable
High-temperature piezoelectric sensitivity, couplant or waveguide condition, thermal cycling and sensor or valve replacement shift the input spectra silently, degrading accuracy with no drift alarm. An adversary could time an action to a period of accumulated drift or exploit it to mask deliberate signal tampering as ordinary ageing.

Automation trust and attention-map opacity -- implicit, exploitable
CBAM heatmaps look like explanations but are not validated causal evidence, so staff may over-trust a 'no leak' output and skip leak-off temperature, downstream temperature and walkdown checks, and skills fade. An adversary could rely on this complacency and the resulting reduced vigilance, as a quiet window for masking leakage or following a flood of false alarms.

AI qualification and model-change gap -- implicit, exploitable
No established V&V path exists for a CNN in a valve-diagnostic role, and training non-determinism makes version-to-version behaviour hard to demonstrate or bound. A malicious or careless model update or retraining could therefore pass review unnoticed, which an insider could exploit.

Sensor-signal evasion or spoofing -- adversarial
An adversary with physical or cabling access can inject acoustic or electrical noise, or alter coupling, to push the low-dimensional AE spectrum across class boundaries, suppressing a real leak signature or fabricating one. The effect is most serious when combined with a real degraded valve or a maintenance window.

Training-data and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Tampered rig labels, pretrained weights or vendor retraining and updates can implant a backdoor trigger mapping to 'no leakage' or a blind spot for particular valve types. With a small dataset, a few poisoned samples have large effect, and a shared model would repeat the blind spot across a fleet.

Data-path integrity, availability and chaff -- adversarial
Tampering with stored spectra, preprocessing or condition records, or flooding the system with noise or denying the service, can erode trend history, mask progressive degradation and cause alarm fatigue.

Workstation foothold and information leakage -- adversarial
Condition-monitoring workstations and vendor analytics sit in lower-assurance zones with remote vendor access, offering a pivot into OT networks. Exfiltrated spectra, model and valve-condition data reveal degradation state and weak points for attack planning.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is an advisory condition-monitoring tool. Its output feeds maintenance planning and valve condition assessment, not protection logic, and it sits behind existing independent measures such as leak-off temperature, downstream pressure and temperature, inventory balances, ISI/leak-rate tests and technical-specification limits. The realistic harm is therefore degraded maintenance decisions, not a direct transient. A missed leak lets seat degradation go on to a through-seat leak that may defeat isolation (for example, steam, drain or vent valves in safety-related or containment-isolation roles) and may be found late. A false alarm triggers unnecessary outages, valve disassembly, dose and schedule cost. Over time, trust in the classifier could erode those other diverse indications. The paper's validation is likely bench-scale and I read only the abstract, so a gap between lab data and field conditions is the main implicit weakness, and an adversary could exploit or time an attack around it.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Lab-to-plant generalization failure. The model was probably trained on a test rig with artificial leaks, fixed pressures and temperatures, and a limited set of valve types and leak geometries. Real plants have pump, flow and steam-noise background, different valve designs, wear, waveguide and coupling variation, sensor aging at high temperature, and fluid-phase changes. The CNN's learned spectral features may fail to transfer, so it could give false negatives on real leaks or false positives from background noise (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.04 versus OP.C0201.05, OP.C0303, OP.C0202). Real leaks are rare and labeled field data is scarce, so class imbalance and weak per-class confidence are likely (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). (2) Drift. Piezoelectric sensor sensitivity, couplant or waveguide condition and thermal cycling all change signal amplitude and spectrum over time, which shifts the input distribution without any alarm (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). Replacing a sensor or valve invalidates the calibration. (3) Opacity and confidence. The attention maps in CBAM look explainable but do not guarantee physical validity. Operators cannot readily tell whether the model keyed on a leak signature or an artifact, and the classifier may emit confident output on out-of-distribution input (OP.C0401, OP.C0403). (4) Automation bias and complacency. Maintenance staff may defer or skip the independent checks (leak-off temperature, downstream temperature, rate-of-change trends) when the AI reports 'no leak', and may over-trust or under-trust it when it conflicts with other indications (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.05). (5) Qualification gap. There is no established framework for qualifying ML classifiers for safety-related valve diagnostics, and the output is non-linear and cannot be easily bounded (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Sensor-signal manipulation. An adversary with physical or cabling access could inject or mask acoustic or electrical signals, for example a broadband source or spoofed spectrum near the sensor or on the signal chain. This could induce misclassification, whether suppressing a real leak signature or fabricating a leak to force an outage, and the effect is most serious if it coincides with a real degraded valve (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). Existing practice helps because the AE chain is usually non-safety and the plant has diverse indications, but a coordinated attack combined with a real leak, or timed to a maintenance window, could delay discovery. (b) Supply-chain or data poisoning. Compromised training data, pretrained weights, or a vendor-supplied model or update could embed a blind spot for particular leak signatures, or a backdoor trigger (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). Vendor model updates that are not re-validated against plant data are the realistic path. (c) Availability and integrity of the data path. Denial of the monitoring service, chaff data, or tampering with stored spectra or condition-assessment records could degrade trend history and mask progressive degradation (AML.T0029, AML.T0046, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). (d) Information leakage. Leak-state data, valve inventory and the model could reveal plant condition or weak points to a reconnaissance adversary (AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002, OP.C0505). Consequences of any of these are bounded by independent leak detection and ISI, but they can erode defense in depth and degrade maintenance prioritization. If one model were propagated across a fleet, a shared blind spot would repeat across sites (OP.C0602).

ai_engineer.argument: This is a supervised spectrum classifier (CNN + CBAM) trained on AE data from a purpose-built test rig, so its main fragility is the gap between bench-generated labels and in-plant reality. Leakage-state labels come from controlled, artificially induced leak conditions (known orifice sizes, pressures, temperatures). Real plant valves differ in seat wear, fluid, differential pressure, line geometry, sensor mounting and coupling, and background flow and pump noise. Attention modules like CBAM tend to latch onto discriminative frequency bands that may be rig-specific artifacts (resonances, waveguide or mounting response), which sharpens the out-of-distribution risk. The model is trained on a closed set of leakage classes, so it has no native way to say 'none of the above', and softmax outputs give confident labels on unfamiliar input. Because it outputs a condition class that feeds maintenance and condition-assessment decisions, errors are silent unless the output is cross-checked against independent indicators such as downstream temperature, tail-pipe temperature or flow.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Bench-to-plant domain shift (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303). The mechanism is a model trained on lab AE spectra at set temperatures and leak rates that sees different transfer functions, noise floors and valve types in service, which gives false negatives (missed internal leakage, with consequences for reliability, efficiency, loss of isolation integrity and possibly safety-related isolation function) or false positives (needless outages, maintenance dose). (2) Small, imbalanced data (OP.C0202). Real leaking-valve events are rare and the labelled severity classes are few, so reported accuracy from a random split of one rig likely overstates field performance, since adjacent samples are highly correlated (leakage). (3) Sensor and aging drift (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). High-temperature piezoelectric sensor sensitivity, couplant or bonding and cabling change with thermal cycling and radiation, shifting spectra without any change in valve state. A model with no recalibration or drift detection will degrade gradually. (4) Opacity and attention-map overtrust (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04). CBAM heatmaps look like explanations but are not validated causal evidence, which invites automation bias. (5) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01). There is no established V&V path for a CNN in a monitoring role, and retraining non-determinism makes version-to-version behaviour hard to demonstrate. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Sensor-level evasion or spoofing (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). An adversary with physical or near-field access can inject acoustic or electrical noise, or change the coupling, to push spectra across class boundaries and mask a real leak or fabricate one. The input is a low-dimensional spectrum from a known sensor type, so crafting is relatively cheap, and the fixed-class model is easily evaded in the absence of anomaly gating. (7) Training-data and supply-chain poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000). Labelled rig data, pretrained weights, or the vendor's retraining pipeline can be tampered with to implant a backdoor, for example a spectral trigger that maps to 'no leakage', or to bias the model against certain valve types. Given the small dataset, even a few poisoned samples have large effect. (8) Model integrity and IT/OT exposure (AML.T0018, AML.T0076, AML.T0031). Altered weights or preprocessing (FFT window, normalisation) on an edge or analytics server silently degrades classification, and the AI path becomes a new route into monitoring networks and dashboards. Overall, the exposure lies in the data and pipeline (labels, preprocessing, drift) more than in the architecture, and the combination of implicit drift with an unmonitored, closed-set classifier gives an adversary a quiet window for masking leakage.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view this is a low-glamour target: it is an advisory condition-monitoring classifier, probably not safety-class, and a nation-state would more likely go after protection systems or the plant network directly. Its security significance is as a stepping stone and as a quiet enabler of other actions. A valve-leakage classifier that is trusted to reduce manual inspection can mask real internal leakage (isolation, relief, or containment-boundary valves) or generate false alarms, and an insider or intruder could time an action around that blind spot or around the human complacency it builds. The AE sensor chain, the training and spectrum data, and the model artifact give an insider a new, non-obvious, low-visibility integrity pathway because this equipment is rarely under the same security controls as I&C. The abstract suggests lab or bench-trained data with a small number of real leak states, so the model's non-adversarial generalization weakness is itself something an adversary could exploit without needing to attack the model.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity attack on the signal or model path. Someone with access to the sensor, DAQ, or analysis workstation, or who can alter training data or model weights, could cause leakage to be classified as normal (masking real degradation) or cause spurious leak calls (driving unnecessary outages, maintenance dose, and valve work). The AI failure mechanism is a misclassified AE spectrum, either via poisoned or backdoored training data and models (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.003, T0043.004), through supply-chain model or software compromise, or via adversarial perturbation or injected acoustic or electrical noise at the sensor (AML.T0015, T0043, T0041). What depends on it is valve condition assessment and maintenance prioritisation. The consequence is undetected leakage across a pressure, isolation or containment boundary, or an economic and availability impact; the risk is higher if the output feeds an automated work-order or trending system. (2) Stepping stone and trust concentration. Condition-monitoring workstations and vendor analytics typically sit in lower-assurance zones with remote vendor access, which is a pivot into OT networks (AML.T0012, T0052, T0025, OP.C0601, OP.C0505.01). Model or data exfiltration gives an adversary knowledge of valve condition, plant layout and degradation state useful for planning (AML.T0024.002, T0035). (3) Denial or chaff: flooding the system with noise to cause alarm fatigue, then timing action around desensitised operators (AML.T0046, T0029, OP.C0102). IMPLICIT, exploitable by an adversary: (4) Sparse, lab or simulated leak data on a small number of valve types and temperatures, so the model generalizes poorly to different valves, flow noise, background plant acoustics, sensor ageing or coupling changes (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0202, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03).
