Silent drift or out-of-distribution input yields confident but wrong classes, which an adversary can predict and use. (5) Automation trust and skill fade: once the classifier replaces walkdowns, thermography or manual checks, human vigilance erodes and a quiet window exists (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01). (6) Opacity of attention-based CNN and non-repeatable training make tampering or retraining changes hard to detect, and the lack of AI-specific qualification and model-change control means a malicious or careless model update can pass review (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0502). Overall severity is moderate, driven mostly by a masked-degradation consequence and its value as an under-defended foothold rather than as a primary target.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on bench-to-plant generalisation, drift, opacity and automation complacency as implicit threats, and on sensor evasion, poisoning and supply-chain compromise as adversarial threats. I merged overlapping items, kept the security specialist's workstation-pivot point as distinct, and dropped marginal codes (e.g. T0076, T0054) that no threat clearly instantiates.

evidence.citation: "Identification method of internal leakage in nuclear power plants valves using convolutional block attention module," Nuclear Engineering and Design (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper builds an acoustic-emission monitoring device for detecting internal leakage in valves at high temperature. It then trains and tests a CNN with a CBAM attention module that identifies leakage conditions from the AE spectrum data. I read only the abstract and search snippet, not the full paper.

damage.why: The classifier is advisory for condition assessment, so the most severe credible threat is masked internal leakage across isolation or containment-boundary valves (via drift, poisoning or signal evasion), which erodes safety margin and causes needless outages or dose, but the entry does not describe a direct path to radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Bench-to-plant domain shift, sensor ageing drift and over-trust arise reliably once the described conditions exist (rig-trained closed-set softmax model, no drift or OOD alarm), though adversarial variants such as poisoning or spoofing depend on specific access.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible adversarial paths (physical or cabling access to sensors, supply-chain or model-update tampering, insider or vendor access, OT pivot) generally need insider position or significant resourcing, although the implicit weaknesses need no attack at all.

affected_users.why: A given valve's misclassification affects a single component, but a poisoned shared model or common drift can repeat the blind spot across many valves and a fleet, and an OT foothold could reach coupled systems, so impact is broader than one sensor but usually not facility-wide.

discoverability.why: Generalisation gaps, drift, over-trust, adversarial-example and poisoning weaknesses of CNN classifiers are well documented in open literature, and the published rig-trained approach lets a capable outsider infer the blind spots without deep insider knowledge.

use_case: Fast-neutron interrogation of spent fuel dry storage casks, with an iterative tomographic reconstruction combined with a convolutional neural network. The CNN produces a cross-sectional image of the fuel assemblies inside the cask. Safeguards inspectors can then verify the cask contents and detect removed fuel pins without opening the cask. The method was tested on Monte Carlo-simulated back-scattered neutron signatures.
incurred_insecurity:
A CNN-reconstructed cross-section of a sealed dry storage cask becomes the basis for a safeguards conclusion that fuel is intact, yet the only documented validation is Monte Carlo simulation with a coarse detection floor (about 75% pin removal in a bundle). The insecurity is a false-assurance risk: undetected partial diversion, or a disputed false alarm, resting on an image that looks like direct evidence but is a learned inference. The main threats are sim-to-real failure, prior-driven hallucination, scarcity of diversion ground truth, over-trust and qualification gaps, and adversarial evasion, poisoning, tampering and exfiltration aimed at the cheap parts of the pipeline rather than the seal.

Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
The CNN is trained and tested only on simulated back-scatter signatures, so real basket and canister geometry, burnup and enrichment heterogeneity, (alpha,n) background, detector response and drift can push inputs outside its envelope and yield confident but wrong images with no calibrated uncertainty. A diverter can plan around this unvalidated regime, relying on cask-specific conditions that the model has never seen to conceal a removal.

Prior-driven hallucination of intact fuel -- implicit, exploitable
In an ill-posed tomographic reconstruction the CNN can fill gaps with learned fuel-lattice structure, rendering an assembly with missing or substituted pins as intact, or inventing anomalies that trigger a disputed inspection. An adversary can rely on this smoothing, using partial removal or dummy pins with similar scattering so that the reconstruction hides the change.

Small-diversion blind spot and diversion-data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
No real casks with known removed pins exist, so the diversion scenarios are modeller-chosen, thresholds and false-alarm rates cannot be empirically calibrated, and the 75% sensitivity floor is untested against real noise. A state that knows or infers the detection limit can divert just below it or substitute material with a similar neutron-scattering signature.

Over-trust, opacity and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A clean tomogram invites automation bias, while opacity, stochastic training and inference non-repeatability make it hard to explain, reproduce or defend the result, and no AI-specific qualification regime exists for safeguards use. An adversary benefits from inspectors treating one image as authoritative over layered methods, or from the same weakness being used to dispute a true positive.

Model drift and uncontrolled retraining -- implicit
Detector ageing, calibration shifts and new cask types, combined with retraining on new simulations, can silently change sensitivity between inspections. This degrades comparability and credibility; a realistic adversary gains little beyond what the other threats already offer.

Fleet-wide propagation of a shared model -- implicit, exploitable
If one model or reconstruction pipeline is reused across sites or inspection regimes, a single bias or compromise reproduces the same blind spot in every verification. An adversary who corrupts one shared artifact gains broad, uniform concealment.

Evasion by structured shielding or substitution -- adversarial
A host-state operator who understands the beam geometry and learned priors can arrange reflector or shielding material, or dummy pins, so that the back-scatter signature reconstructs as nominal. The consequence is undetected pin diversion with continuity of knowledge appearing intact.

Training-data, model and supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Whoever controls the simulation inputs, geometry libraries, cross-section sets, pretrained weights or reconstruction code can implant a bias or backdoor trigger that renders specific missing-pin configurations as intact. Because the training data is simulated, the systematic blind spot is hard to detect and biases every inspection while looking normal.

Tampering with the acquisition and results chain -- adversarial
An insider or intruder can alter or replay raw detector data, reconstruction parameters, reference baselines or stored images to produce a clean verification record or a fabricated alarm. The result is false assurance or a diplomatic dispute, with trust concentrated in a pipeline few can audit independently.

Model and reference-data exfiltration -- adversarial
Theft or extraction of the model, sensitivity curves and cask-inventory images reveals the detection limit and design details. This lets an adversary tune a sub-threshold diversion and build a proxy model for rehearsal.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This tool would let safeguards inspectors confirm cask contents and detect pin diversion without opening the cask, so its output feeds a continuity-of-knowledge and non-diversion conclusion. The consequence of a wrong image is a safeguards failure, either a false assurance that fuel is intact or a false alarm that triggers a costly investigation. It is not a plant safety event. The documented evidence is Monte Carlo simulation only, and the reported detectability is coarse (a clear signal drop at about 75% pin removal in a bundle). Partial diversion of a few pins, which is the real concern, is not demonstrated. The CNN can also produce plausible images by learning priors, so a clean-looking reconstruction can overstate what the physics supports. Existing practice (seals, surveillance, item counting, Cherenkov viewing, gamma and neutron measurements, declared inventory and burnup records) is layered, so a single image should not carry the verdict. The danger is that the image gets treated as authoritative once it exists.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT WEAKNESSES. (1) Simulation-to-reality gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0303): the CNN is trained and tested on Monte Carlo back-scatter data. Real casks differ in basket and canister geometry, shielding, fuel burnup and enrichment variation, moisture, detector response, background and neutron source drift. Out-of-distribution input may give confident but wrong images, and the method's sensitivity to small diversions in real casks is unknown. (2) Small-diversion blind spot and low base rate (OP.C0202, OP.C0701): diversion examples are essentially nonexistent in real data, so the training set is synthetic and the diverted-fuel scenarios are chosen by the modellers. An adversary who knows the detection threshold can divert fewer pins than the system reliably sees, or substitute dummy pins or other material with similar scattering (OP.C0702.01). (3) Hallucination and opacity (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03, OP.C0401, OP.C0402): the CNN can smooth over or invent structure, and the image looks like direct evidence of pin presence when it is an inference. Inspectors can't easily explain or reproduce the result, which weakens its standing in the safeguards conclusion. (4) Automation bias and qualification gaps (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0501, OP.C0504): a clean tomogram invites over-trust, while no AI-specific qualification or acceptance regime exists for IAEA or state-regulator use. This undermines both the credibility and the independent verifiability of the result.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Manipulating the interrogation input or the model (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020): the operator or a supply-chain actor could shape the signature, for example with shielding or reflector material placed near the cask or on the canister, or poison the training data or model weights, so that diverted configurations reconstruct as intact. Because the CNN is trained on simulated data, anyone who controls or influences the simulation toolchain, geometry libraries or training sets can introduce a systematic blind spot that is hard to detect. (6) Tampering with the acquisition chain and results (AML.T0031, AML.T0059, OP.C0502): altering detector data or reconstruction software, or replacing images, can produce false assurance. It could also produce a false alarm that erodes confidence in the inspection regime or triggers a diplomatic dispute. (7) Data and model confidentiality (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025, OP.C0505): cask design, fuel inventory and detection-limit information is sensitive, and exfiltrating the model or its sensitivity curves would help an adversary tune a diversion below detection. (8) Denial or delay (AML.T0029): loss of the analysis capability at an inspection would delay verification and weaken continuity of knowledge, but this is only a minor consequence since conventional methods can substitute.

Bottom line: the safeguards consequence is a false negative that goes undetected, and it requires a deliberate diverter plus the failure of other layers such as seals, surveillance and records to be serious. The use case should therefore be framed as supplementary evidence until it is validated on real or physical-mockup casks.

ai_engineer.argument: This is an image-reconstruction CNN whose only documented validation is on Monte Carlo-simulated back-scattered neutron signatures. The pipeline's weakest point is therefore the sim-to-real gap, not the network architecture. Real casks have heterogeneous burnup and enrichment, differing basket and canister geometries, neutron-source terms from (alpha,n) and spontaneous fission, detector response and noise, moisture and backfill variation, and corrosion or deformation. A CNN trained on simulation can learn the simulator's priors, and in a reconstruction setting it can produce plausible, clean images of intact fuel that are not backed by measured physics. The one reported result, that a clear signal drop appears only when 75% or more of the pins are removed, implies a low-sensitivity regime. Partial diversion, which is the safeguards-relevant case, may sit below what the learned prior can resolve. The system is also hard to qualify, because there is no field ground truth for sealed casks and removing fuel to obtain one defeats the purpose. That leaves its failure modes unverifiable and gives an adversary or an unlucky distribution shift room to hide.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and OOD failure. Training and test data are Monte Carlo-simulated, so the data provenance is simulated with no field or bench anchor. Cask designs, burnup profiles, detector geometry and background all shift at deployment, and the CNN's output has no calibrated uncertainty when inputs fall outside its training distribution. (2) Prior-driven hallucination. The CNN can fill ill-posed tomographic gaps with learned fuel-lattice structure, so it can output an apparently intact assembly image when pins are missing, or invent anomalies. This is a content-fidelity failure. A false negative means undetected diversion and a false positive means a disputed inspection. The consequence is a safeguards-conclusion error that inspectors may take as independent verification. (3) Scarcity and low base rate. Real removed-pin casks essentially do not exist, so detection thresholds and false-alarm rates cannot be empirically calibrated, and the 75% pin-removal sensitivity floor is untested against real noise. (4) Opacity and repeatability. A hybrid iterative-plus-CNN pipeline has stochastic training, and its initialisation and hyperparameters affect the reconstructions. The combination makes qualification, inspector explanation and dispute resolution difficult. Inspectors may also over-trust a clean image (automation bias) or discount it after a visible artefact (disuse). (5) Lifecycle drift. Detector ageing, calibration changes and new cask types cause drift, and retraining on new simulations may silently change behaviour. Model versions need to be controlled for safeguards credibility.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Evasion by a facility operator or state who knows the system. The operator could arrange diversion so that it stays below the sensitivity floor, for example partial pin removal or substituting dummy pins or surrogate material with a similar scattering signature. They could also exploit the CNN's learned priors with structured modifications that reconstruct as nominal (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). The adversary may not need model access, because the method is published and a proxy can be built from open literature and simulation (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0002). (b) Training-data or model poisoning and supply chain compromise. Simulation datasets, Monte Carlo configurations, pretrained weights and the reconstruction software are shared artefacts. A backdoor that suppresses specific missing-pin patterns, or a corrupted library or cross-section set, would bias every inspection while looking normal (AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). (c) Tampering with the measurement chain. Detector signal manipulation, spoofed or replayed back-scatter data, and altered reconstruction outputs or reports would attack the inspector's trust in the image. (d) Reference data leakage. Cask-specific models and as-declared fuel inventories are sensitive, and model inversion or extraction could reveal design or inventory details (AML.T0024). (e) Fleet propagation. A single compromised or biased model shared across inspection sites or regimes would spread one error widely (OP.C0602).

security_specialist.argument: This tool concentrates safeguards trust in a single image: a CNN-reconstructed cross-section becomes the basis for concluding that a sealed cask still holds all its fuel, which is exactly the diversion-concealment question a state or insider adversary cares about. The published evidence is Monte Carlo simulation only, with a reported detection threshold of roughly 75% pin removal. That is a coarse sensitivity, and an adversary who knows it could remove or substitute fewer pins and stay below the visible threshold. A sophisticated actor would more likely attack the cheap parts (training data, reconstruction software, the acquisition-to-image pipeline, or the operator's trust in a clean-looking image) than defeat a physical cask seal. Even a non-adversarial gap, such as sim-to-real mismatch, is something a diverter can plan around once it is known.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data or model poisoning and supply-chain compromise: the CNN is trained on simulated signatures, so whoever controls the simulation inputs, the pretrained weights or the reconstruction code can implant a bias or backdoor trigger that renders particular missing-pin or substituted-fuel configurations as 'nominal'. The AI failure mechanism is a corrupted learned prior. The facility and safeguards regime depend on the image for item-level verification of sealed casks. The consequence is false assurance of continuity of knowledge and undetected diversion of fissile material. (2) Evasion by adversarial or structured shielding: a host-state operator with knowledge of the beam geometry could place or arrange materials, or substitute dummy pins, so that the back-scatter signature looks consistent with a full assembly. A CNN can hallucinate plausible fuel structure under iterative reconstruction priors, which masks the anomaly. This is the safeguards-specific form of crafting adversarial data, and a state-level actor would likely find it easier than breaking the seal. (3) Insider or inspector-side manipulation of the data chain: tampering with raw detector data, reconstruction parameters or stored reference images, or swapping a reference baseline, lets a single insider produce a clean verification record. Trust is concentrated in an opaque pipeline that few people can audit independently. (4) Model and reference-data exfiltration: stolen model, sensitivity thresholds and cask-inventory images help adversaries learn the detection limit and plan sub-threshold diversion. IMPLICIT. (5) Sim-to-real gap and data scarcity: no field data from real casks with known removals exists, so concrete heterogeneity, cask-design variation, burnup and neutron-background drift are poorly covered. Performance in real conditions is unknown, and an adversary can exploit that uncertainty. (6) Automation bias and opacity: inspectors may accept a clean, high-quality image as proof, and may not be able to separate real structure from reconstruction artifact or CNN hallucination. This lowers vigilance and cuts the use of independent verification such as other NDA methods. (7) Qualification and repeatability gaps: there is no AI-specific qualification regime for safeguards use, retraining or model updates could silently change sensitivity, and inference results may not be repeatable. These make verification findings hard to defend and give a state a basis to dispute true positives.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sim-to-real gap, hallucination of intact fuel, sub-threshold diversion and poisoning/evasion, which were merged as single threats. I dropped the minor denial-of-service point and treated tampering as an adversarial threat mapped through integrity-erosion codes, and I kept fleet propagation and drift as brief distinct items.

evidence.citation: "Neutron Tomography of Spent Fuel Casks," Springer (Journal of Signal Processing Systems)
evidence.note: The paper reports a Monte Carlo simulation study of fast-neutron interrogation of dry storage casks. A CNN is paired with an iterative reconstruction algorithm to image the fuel inside the cask. The paper also reports that a bundle with at least 75% of its pins removed shows a clear drop in back-scattered signal. I worked from the search-result abstract, not the full text.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is undetected partial diversion of spent fuel (or poisoned/tampered reconstruction producing a clean verification record), which amounts to safeguards falsification and loss of material control.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real failure, hallucination of intact structure, and sub-threshold diversion are structural and recur reliably once the model is deployed, but exploiting them depends on cask-specific conditions and on knowledge of the detection limit.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (host-state evasion, supply-chain poisoning, tampering with the acquisition chain) need state-level resources or privileged insider access to the inspection pipeline, though the implicit weaknesses need no special tooling.

affected_users.why: A shared model or pipeline reused across sites and inspection regimes reproduces the same blind spot in every verification, so the impact reaches many casks and across the safeguards regime, short of coupled physical systems.

discoverability.why: The general weaknesses of simulation-only CNN reconstruction and the published detection floor (about 75% pin removal) are inferable from open literature, but cask-specific blind spots and pipeline internals need partial insider knowledge.

use_case: Bagged random-forest and other tree-based machine-learning regression that predicts static and dynamic leaching (dissolution) of borosilicate glass used to vitrify high-level waste from spent-fuel reprocessing. It is trained on unstructured multi-source data: UK vitrification campaign data, literature data and laboratory leaching experiments. Inputs are glass composition, pH and leaching-test conditions. The model predicts element releases (e.g. B, Na, Si, Al), fills in missing data and forecasts release over time, to assess long-term waste-form durability before geological disposal.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline design-and-assessment model feeds waste-form durability claims and, through them, the disposal safety case for vitrified high-level waste. It is not a control system, so the harm is slow, latent and decision-shaping, and it becomes practically irreversible once canisters are filled and sealed. The main threats are unsupported extrapolation to geological timescales, weakly provenanced and imputed multi-source data, over-trust in an opaque model, absent AI-specific qualification, and adversarial corruption or exploitation of the data, model and inputs that exploits those same blind spots.

Extrapolation beyond the training envelope -- implicit, exploitable
Bagged tree ensembles saturate at values seen in days-to-years laboratory tests, so predictions for long-term release (residual rate, secondary phases, resumption of alteration) and for novel compositions or chemistries look confident but are unbounded by physics and understate high-release regimes. An adversary or an interested party could steer a formulation or safety-case argument into these under-predicted regions, relying on the apparently narrow ensemble variance as false assurance.

Heterogeneous data and imputation artefacts -- implicit, exploitable
Literature, campaign and laboratory data with inconsistent protocols, SA/V ratios and leachants, non-active simulant glass that may not transfer to real active waste glass, and few long-duration results for rare behaviours bias the model. Imputed values that resemble measurements and may be recycled as training labels fabricate plausible data where experiments are missing. This sparse, inconsistent corpus gives poisoned or falsified records a natural place to hide as ordinary scatter.

Over-trust and shortcut learning -- implicit, exploitable
High accuracy even with pH or composition omitted suggests the model learns study or protocol proxies rather than mechanisms, and random cross-validation hides this. The result is over-trust that displaces confirmatory long-duration experiments and gives assessors no mechanistic basis for confidence. An adversary can rely on this reduced scrutiny to get a manipulated or non-conservative prediction accepted as evidence.

AI-specific qualification and reproducibility gap -- implicit, exploitable
Unversioned bagging seeds, library versions, curation and imputation steps mean a safety-case figure may not be reproducible, and there is no established nuclear QA or regulatory route for ML-derived waste-form evidence. This weak provenance and audit trail lowers the chance that tampering or poisoning is detected or attributed.

Training-data and literature poisoning -- adversarial
An actor altering published datasets, laboratory records or campaign data, or selectively omitting records, can exploit tree ensembles' sensitivity to high-leverage points in sparse composition regions. This biases predicted release downward for chosen compositions or conditions and produces a non-conservative qualification basis that surfaces only decades later.

Model and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
An insider or a compromised ML library, notebook or serialised model file can subtly alter the imputation step, retraining or model artefact in ways that pass aggregate-accuracy checks. Outputs stay numerically plausible, so a corrupted safety-case input is trusted, and shared research infrastructure can also become a stepping stone toward wider site networks.

Input optimisation against the model -- adversarial
A party wanting a cheaper or more convenient glass formulation can query the model and tune composition and test-condition inputs to find regions where release is under-predicted. The resulting formulation then appears validated by the model despite worse real durability.

Sensitive data and model leakage -- adversarial
Compiled composition, campaign and leaching data, and a model encoding the durability envelope of the UK vitrified product, reveal waste-form properties and inventory knowledge useful for reconnaissance. This is a lesser concern than integrity loss, but it needs access governance matched to its sensitivity.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a waste-form and disposal-safety lens, this is an advisory, offline design-and-assessment tool, not a control system. Its output feeds waste-form qualification, glass formulation choices and long-term durability arguments in a disposal safety case, so the realistic harm is slow, latent and decision-shaping, not an acute event. Wrong predictions would have to survive the independent safeguards that already exist: laboratory leaching tests (MCC-1/PCT/SPFT), natural and archaeological analogue evidence, mechanistic geochemical codes (e.g. GRAAL, PHREEQC-based), conservative bounding assumptions, and regulator review of the safety case. The main concern is quiet erosion of those independent lines through over-reliance, extrapolation beyond the data, or corrupted training data, so that an optimistic durability estimate becomes embedded in formulation or disposal decisions that are practically irreversible once canisters are filled and sealed.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and data-regime failure: the training data is heterogeneous (UK campaign data, literature, lab experiments) and dominated by short-duration tests at lab temperatures and pH. Tree-based regressors cannot extrapolate beyond the training range; they plateau. Predictions of release over geological timescales, of late-stage behaviour (residual rate, alteration-phase formation, resumption of alteration), or for novel compositions (e.g. new waste streams, Mg- or Zn-bearing or high-Al glasses, different Cs/Mo loadings) will look confident but are unsupported. Consequence: an optimistic durability estimate that is not physically bounded. This is OP.C0302, OP.C0303 and OP.C0403. (2) Data provenance and quality: mixing literature and lab data with inconsistent test protocols, surface-area-to-volume ratios, leachants and reporting conventions introduces hidden bias. Model-imputed missing values could then be fed back as training data, which compounds bias (OP.C0201, OP.C0202, OP.C0603). Non-radioactive simulant glass data may not transfer to real active HLW glass with radiation damage, decay heat and actinide content (OP.C0201.03). (3) Automation trust: good headline accuracy, such as the finding that the model works even with pH or composition omitted, can reduce scrutiny of the underlying mechanism. That invites using the model as a substitute for new experiments or for mechanistic modelling, rather than as a screening tool. Black-box output also gives a regulator or assessor little mechanistic basis for confidence (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Non-repeatability across retraining adds to this (OP.C0402.01). (4) Imputation and fill-in of missing data can fabricate plausible values for the exact conditions where experiments are lacking, such as low-pH or high-pH extremes and early-stage dynamics (OP.C0304.01, OP.C0304.03).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training-data poisoning or integrity erosion: an actor who can alter shared literature datasets, lab spreadsheets or campaign records could subtly bias release predictions downward for particular compositions or conditions. The change is hard to detect in unstructured multi-source data, and it would push a formulation or safety-case argument toward acceptance (AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000). The facility consequence is a flawed qualification basis for waste forms, with delayed discovery. It would take failure of the independent experimental verification and peer review to turn this into real harm, which is why the harm potential is moderate and slow. (6) Model or artifact tampering, or a supply-chain compromise of the ML library or trained model, with similar effects (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018, AML.T0076). (7) Confidentiality: compiled composition and performance data for vitrified HLW is commercially and regulatorily sensitive, and inference or exfiltration of it via the model or its data repositories is a lesser concern (AML.T0025, AML.T0024.000, OP.C0505). Overall the safety case is robust to isolated model error, but the vulnerabilities cluster around undetected bias and over-reliance on the model in long-term safety arguments.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is a tabular tree-ensemble regressor trained on a heterogeneous, unstructured corpus (UK campaign data, literature extraction, bespoke lab leaching runs) and then asked to extrapolate to the thing that matters most: multi-millennial durability under repository conditions. That is the central fragility. The training data covers days to years of laboratory dissolution, while the decision it informs concerns timescales and chemistries (Stage III behaviour, secondary phase precipitation, resumption of alteration, corrosion of canister or host-rock interfaces) that are sparse or absent in the data. Tree ensembles cannot extrapolate beyond the training range; they return piecewise-constant predictions bounded by seen values, so they tend to underestimate novel high-release regimes without any warning. Second, the documented finding that the model performs well even when pH or composition is omitted signals that it may be learning proxies, such as study or lab identity, test protocol, or correlated composition families, rather than mechanistic dependence. Such shortcut learning is hard to detect from random cross-validation, and the training data is full of leakage. Third, the dynamic model's use of a species dissolution rate as an input makes it partly autoregressive on measured quantities, so errors or inconsistencies in those inputs propagate directly. Together these make the system's credibility rest on data provenance and validation design, not on architecture.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and OOD failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403): new glass formulations (different waste streams, higher waste loadings, Mg/Ca/Zn-bearing or alternative frits), unusual pH/Eh, temperature, or groundwater/cement chemistry fall outside the training envelope. A bagged forest silently saturates at seen values and gives apparently confident, narrow-looking ensemble variance that does not reflect true epistemic uncertainty. The result is optimistic durability estimates feeding the waste-form safety case or acceptance criteria. (2) Data provenance and heterogeneity (OP.C0201, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0202, OP.C0204): literature data come with inconsistent units, surface-area normalisation, leachant volume, SA/V ratios, durations and undocumented glass compositions. Extraction and imputation of missing values (the model also fills in gaps) can bake in artifacts, and imputed values may then be reused as training labels, creating circular validation. Campaign data represent a narrow composition space with high replication, while rare adverse behaviours are underrepresented (low base-rate of accelerated alteration). (3) Shortcut learning and leakage (OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03): non-mechanistic proxies such as study-specific protocol fingerprints let the model score well on random splits yet fail on new labs or compositions; leave-one-study-out or composition-grouped validation is needed to expose this. (4) Static/dynamic qualification mismatch (OP.C0303): short-term lab tests are mapped onto geological timescales, and the dynamic model is validated only against the same kind of short data, so no ground truth exists for the use it serves. (5) Reproducibility and lifecycle (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504): stochastic bagging seeds, library versions and data curation steps may not be versioned, so a qualified safety-case figure may not be reproducible; there is no established nuclear QA route for ML in a waste-form safety argument. (6) Human factors (OP.C0101.04): a high R² on literature-derived data invites over-trust or use as a screening shortcut that displaces expensive long-duration experiments, causing the experimental database to stagnate (OP.C0204) and the model to drift away from reality as formulations change (OP.C0302.01). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (7) Training-data poisoning or integrity erosion (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0031): because the corpus is assembled from public literature, shared spreadsheets and multi-lab contributions with little cryptographic provenance, a malicious or careless actor could alter, inject or selectively omit records. Tree ensembles are sensitive to a few high-leverage points in sparse regions of composition space. The consequence is a subtle bias toward under-predicted release for a particular formulation, which could affect acceptance or licensing decisions and be difficult to distinguish from ordinary scatter. (8) Model and pipeline tampering (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0076): compromised Python/ML libraries, notebooks or serialised model files (pickle) could alter outputs or execute code on research or design networks that connect to waste-management data. (9) Information-security aspects (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0024.000, OP.C0505): a model trained on proprietary campaign data and queried for composition-to-durability relationships encodes the performance envelope of the UK vitrified product, which is relevant to sensitive process and waste inventory knowledge, so access governance must reflect that. (10) Evasion by design input (AML.T0043, AML.T0015): a party seeking to justify a cheaper or more convenient glass formulation can tune composition and test-condition inputs to find regions where the model under-predicts release, using the model as an optimiser target; the result looks like a validated formulation. Overall, the exposure is mostly in the data and validation pipeline, and an adversary mainly needs to exploit the system's existing blind spots, not break the model.

security_specialist.argument: A direct attack on this model is unattractive to a capable adversary: it is an offline design-and-assessment tool, it sits nowhere in an operational control loop, and sabotaging a vitrified waste form would be far easier by physical or conventional means. The real exposure is indirect. The model's outputs feed durability arguments for waste-form acceptance and, ultimately, for the geological disposal safety case, so a slow, hard-to-attribute corruption of the data or model can quietly bias a decision that will not be tested for decades. The data are unstructured and multi-source (campaign records, literature, lab experiments, imputed gaps), with weak provenance and no independent ground truth over repository timescales, so an insider, a supplier or a published-literature poisoner has a plausible and low-visibility route. The use case also invites reduced vigilance: a fast, apparently validated regression that imputes missing data and extrapolates release over time encourages less experimental confirmation and less scrutiny of the inputs.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and literature poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0019, AML.T0059). Mechanism: altered leaching measurements, composition records or published datasets shift the learned composition-to-release relationship, or add a trigger region in composition/pH space where predicted release is understated. The facility depends on this model for waste-form durability claims and for screening candidate glass compositions. The consequence is a non-conservative durability assessment that could affect acceptance or disposal-readiness decisions, with the error surfacing only decades later. (2) Insider model or pipeline manipulation (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0012, AML.T0076). Mechanism: someone with access to the imputation step, the retraining pipeline or the model artefacts makes subtle changes that pass aggregate-accuracy checks. This is an attractive route because the bagged-ensemble outputs are numerically plausible and opaque, so tampering is hard to see; the consequence is trust in a compromised safety-case input. (3) Intellectual property and sensitive-information leakage (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025, AML.T0035). The glass formulations, campaign data and leaching behaviour are sensitive. They tell an adversary about waste-form properties and the inventory, which is useful for reconnaissance and for making a stored waste form degrade faster than expected. (4) Stepping stone: shared research and data infrastructure (collaborating institutions, cloud notebooks) can serve as an entry route to wider site networks (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0012).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable or timeable. (a) Extrapolation and drift: the model is trained on limited compositions and short-duration experiments and then forecasts long-term release (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303, OP.C0403). Real-world conditions in the repository, such as groundwater chemistry, temperature, and altered-layer or secondary-phase effects, lie outside the training distribution. Underprediction is therefore a plausible natural failure that no one would notice. (b) Data scarcity and heterogeneity (OP.C0202, OP.C0201, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0204): the data are sparse, and few long-duration leaching results exist for unusual compositions. This hides poisoned or erroneous points and makes imputation unreliable, because imputed values are accepted as if they were measurements. (c) Over-trust and automation bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0401): accurate-looking predictions that remain accurate even when inputs such as pH or composition are omitted can lead reviewers to skip experimental confirmation and to treat the model as evidence rather than screening. (d) Governance gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0505): no AI-specific qualification, version control or data-provenance regime exists for what is effectively safety-case evidence, so an adversary who exploits any of the above faces little chance of detection or attribution. Overall this is a low-probability but high-consequence, slow-onset threat to the integrity of evidence, not to operations.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on extrapolation failure, poor data provenance with imputation, over-trust, and data poisoning/model tampering as the core threats; I merged overlapping phrasings and kept the AI engineer's input-optimisation evasion as a distinct, well-argued adversarial threat. I dropped weakly supported codes (e.g. T0024.000, T0031, OP.C0102, OP.C0302.01/.02, OP.C0304.03) that restated other threats or did not clearly fit.

evidence.citation: "Predicting radioactive waste glass dissolution with machine learning," Journal of Non-Crystalline Solids 533 (2020), University of Cambridge / National Nuclear Laboratory (Lillington, Goût, Harrison, Farnan); Cambridge repository record
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper applies machine learning to large, diverse leaching datasets. It reports that tree-based methods, especially bagged random forest, predict static glass leaching well, even when pH or glass composition is left out as an input. It also tests dynamic leaching, where replacing final pH with a species dissolution rate as an input improves accuracy. Another source gives the UK context: the glass is vitrified high-level waste from reprocessing, stored at Sellafield.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoned or non-conservative durability evidence entering the disposal safety case for vitrified HLW, which erodes long-term containment margins and is effectively irreversible once canisters are sealed; harm is latent and indirect, since other evidence and regulatory review sit between the model and any release, so it falls just short of 5.

reproducibility.why: Extrapolation saturation and shortcut learning in tree ensembles occur reliably for out-of-envelope or sparse-region inputs, and data-poisoning leverage in sparse composition regions is a consistent property of the class, though adversarial success depends on the outputs being used in a safety-case argument.

exploitability.why: Input optimisation against the model and altering public literature need only modest access, but tampering with campaign data, pipelines or serialised models needs insider or supply-chain position, and getting a manipulated result accepted into a regulated safety case takes sustained effort.

affected_users.why: A biased durability model could propagate through the waste-form qualification basis across many canisters and the disposal safety case for a national vitrified inventory, but it is an offline assessment tool not coupled to operating plant systems, so impact is broad in the waste-form domain and not facility-wide in the operational sense.

discoverability.why: Tree-ensemble extrapolation limits, data heterogeneity, poisoning susceptibility and the absence of ML qualification routes are well documented in the open literature, and the underlying model and datasets are published, so a capable outsider can readily infer where the weaknesses lie.

use_case: Hybrid unsupervised-plus-supervised anomaly detection on circulating water system data from a pressurized heavy-water reactor. Matrix profile and DBSCAN clustering first separate normal from anomalous operating data. The DBSCAN cluster labels then train a support vector machine, which flags new data points as normal or anomalous in real time. The aim is fault detection as a step toward condition-based maintenance.
incurred_insecurity:
This hybrid DBSCAN-to-SVM detector on a non-safety circulating water system incurs mostly implicit risk: it learns from unverified pseudo-labels, and its quiet output can be mistaken for assurance. Its main threats are circular labelling and validation, drift and retraining contamination, trust-driven erosion of independent inspection, and qualification and scope gaps. The adversarial surface is the historian-to-ML data path, where poisoning, evasion, chaff and artifact tampering could blind the tool, mainly to mask a timed action or an adjacent degradation rather than to defeat safety systems.

Circular labelling and validation -- implicit, exploitable
The SVM learns DBSCAN cluster assignments rather than confirmed fault labels, so reported accuracy only measures agreement with the clustering. Rare real faults (fouling, pump wear, intake blockage) and slow degradation folded into the dominant cluster stay invisible. An adversary can rely on the resulting trust in a 'validated' detector, knowing that whatever the first clustering called normal, including a planted baseline, is treated as ground truth.

Drift and retraining contamination -- implicit, exploitable
Seasonal water temperature, biofouling, load following, outages and sensor recalibration move data away from the training window, so the frozen SVM gives confident labels with no out-of-distribution signal, producing false alarms or silent misses. Retraining on data containing incipient degradation normalizes the fault, and an adversary could time a gradual manipulation to these shifts or exploit the retraining step as an entry point.

Historian data quality -- implicit, exploitable
Sensor faults, gaps and interpolation get clustered as process anomalies or hidden within 'normal', so the model cannot separate instrument failure from equipment failure and may misdirect technicians. An adversary could hide sensor tampering inside this ambiguity.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
If 'no anomaly' is used to extend maintenance intervals, time-based inspections and operator rounds erode, and an opaque SVM boundary gives no component-level explanation to challenge a flag. An adversary could time sabotage or degradation of cooling-water assets to this lowered vigilance.

Qualification, scope and fleet propagation gaps -- implicit, exploitable
As a non-safety tool it attracts little AI-specific QA, cyber or configuration control, so model, scaler or threshold changes are weakly audited and the tool can creep from advisory to decision-driving or be reused on other units without revalidation. An insider's modification would leave little trace, and one flawed or poisoned template reused across units would propagate widely.

Training-data and label poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or intruder on the historian or export path can inject or slowly shift data during the clustering window so a degraded or attack-induced state is learned as normal, and the pseudo-labels carry it into the real-time classifier. Real condenser, pump or intake faults then go unflagged, giving a blind spot for a timed intervention.

Evasion and chaff -- adversarial
Spoofed or slowly drifting sensor values held inside the SVM's normal region keep tampering or equipment damage looking normal. Conversely, injected noise that triggers mass false positives drains maintenance resources, builds alarm fatigue and diverts staff at a chosen moment.

Model, pipeline and data-path compromise -- adversarial
Tampering with the serialized SVM, scalers or research-grade open-source libraries, or a compromise of the ML workstation or shared lab infrastructure, can silently alter detection behaviour. The same foothold offers a stepping stone toward historian and OT networks and exfiltration of plant operating data.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations lens, the circulating water (condenser cooling) system is a balance-of-plant, non-safety-class system. Its main consequences are derating, forced outages, condenser vacuum loss, and fouling or intake problems. A wrong classifier output would most likely produce wasted maintenance or a missed degradation. It would not directly produce a nuclear safety event, because condenser cooling loss is handled by trip logic, protection systems, and operator procedures that do not depend on this tool. The main weaknesses are implicit. The SVM is trained on labels from unsupervised DBSCAN clustering, so 'anomalous' means 'statistically unusual', not 'a verified fault'. The 'high accuracy' figure is measured against those same pseudo-labels, with very few confirmed faults and no maintenance ground truth. The adversarial surface is narrow but real. It sits in the historian/OT-to-IT data path feeding a condition-based maintenance (CBM) decision, where manipulation or poisoning could shift maintenance priorities or hide real degradation. It could also support a staged attack in which the CBM tool is blinded while a physical or cyber action proceeds.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Implicit threats. (1) Label circularity and goal misalignment: SVM labels come from DBSCAN/matrix-profile output with no fault-confirmed ground truth. Reported accuracy therefore measures agreement with the clustering, not fault-detection capability. Rare real faults are poorly represented (small-data and low base-rate problem). The facility consequence is that operators and maintenance planners may trust a 'validated' detector that misses real degradation such as fouling, pump wear, or intake blockage, or floods them with false alarms. This leads either to deferred maintenance on a degrading component, with eventual derate or forced outage, or to alarm fatigue and disuse. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity: circulating water data depend on seasonal lake or sea temperature, biofouling cycles, load following, outages, instrument recalibration, and equipment replacement. A static SVM trained on a window of data will see normal seasonal change as anomalous, or will absorb slow degradation as 'normal' (concept drift). Retraining on newly flagged data can silently normalize a developing fault. (3) Data quality: sensor faults, historian gaps, and interpolation can be clustered as anomalies or hidden inside 'normal'. The model cannot tell instrument failure from process failure, so it may misdirect technicians. (4) Automation bias and skill fade: if CBM extends maintenance intervals based on 'no anomaly', time-based inspection and operator rounds may be relaxed. Because of the limited explainability of SVM boundaries over DBSCAN-derived clusters, a flag does not explain which component or mechanism is involved. (5) Qualification gap: this is a non-safety application, so there is little pressure for AI-specific QA, and the tool can creep from advisory into decision-driving use or be extended to other plant systems without re-validation. Reusing the model across units or sites would carry over local operating assumptions (fleet propagation). Adversarial or adversary-exploitable threats. (6) Data-path integrity: an adversary with access to historian or OT data feeds could inject slow, plausible drift or chaff so the clusters and the boundary learn a degraded state as normal (training-data poisoning or model-integrity erosion). They could also craft inputs that stay inside the normal region, evading the model, or trigger floods of false positives to degrade trust and consume maintenance resources. (7) Model and pipeline tampering: altering the trained SVM, scaling parameters, or thresholds through the software supply chain or a compromised engineering workstation. (8) Concealment role: a blinded or noisy CBM tool is a low-cost way to delay detection of sabotage or degradation of cooling-water assets while another action proceeds. It does not by itself defeat safety systems, which are independent. Overall severity is low to moderate, mainly economic and availability-related. It becomes important if the tool is later cited in maintenance-deferral justifications or connected to automated actions, or if the same architecture is reused for safety-significant systems. Mitigations: keep the tool strictly advisory and one-way (data diode), confirm flags against maintenance work orders, track drift, and keep periodic inspections independent of the model.

ai_engineer.argument: The pipeline's fragility starts with its label source: the SVM is trained on DBSCAN cluster assignments, not on ground-truth fault labels, so it can only reproduce whatever density structure the clustering found in historical circulating water (CW) data. The 'high accuracy' reported on unseen data measures agreement with the clustering, not detection of real faults. That is circular validation, and it says little about recall on rare, safety- or economically relevant degradation modes such as condenser fouling, pump bearing wear, or intake blockage. CW data is strongly non-stationary: lake or sea temperature, seasonal biofouling, load following, outages, and instrument recalibration all shift the 'normal' manifold. DBSCAN's eps/minPts and the matrix profile window length are sensitive hyperparameters, and a frozen SVM will degrade, or flag seasonal change as faults, unless there is a retraining and relabeling policy. That policy in turn creates a feedback risk, because retraining on data that already contains slow degradation absorbs the fault into 'normal'. Because the system is plant-specific and trained on one unit's history, it also has no cross-unit generalization evidence.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Circular labeling and validation: unsupervised pseudo-labels propagate into the supervised model, so unlabeled fault classes, including slow drift that DBSCAN folds into the dominant cluster, are structurally invisible. Reported accuracy overstates fault-detection capability (OP.C0403, OP.C0301, OP.C0202). (2) Drift and OOD: seasonal, load and maintenance-induced regime changes, sensor replacement or recalibration, and post-outage configuration changes move inputs away from the training distribution. The SVM returns a confident normal/anomalous label with no native out-of-distribution signal, producing false alarms (alert fatigue, disuse) or silent misses (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (3) Retraining contamination: periodic refits on operational data that includes incipient degradation normalize the fault and quietly shift the baseline. (4) Condition-based maintenance risk: maintenance intervals extended on the strength of a quiet detector would turn a missed detection into a physical consequence, mainly a reliability or heat-sink availability problem for a non-safety-class but plant-critical system. This invites automation trust failure (OP.C0101.04) and, over time, skill fade. (5) Data provenance and continuity: historian data quality, gaps, sensor faults and compression artifacts become model inputs. The 'normal' training window may itself contain undetected faults (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0204). (6) Qualification and opacity: DBSCAN-derived labels with SVM kernel boundaries are hard to explain and hard to qualify, hyperparameter choices are hard to reproduce, and there is no established AI QA path for even non-safety monitoring tools (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training-data or historian poisoning: an adversary with access to the historian or ML data pipeline can inject or alter data in the training window so that a particular degradation signature is learned as normal, a form of dataset integrity erosion that persists across retrains (AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0031). (b) Evasion at inference: an adversary or compromised sensor or gateway can shape sensor streams to stay inside the SVM's normal region, or slowly drift readings below the decision boundary, so that tampering or genuine equipment damage goes unflagged. A low-and-slow approach exploits the fixed boundary (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). The detector can also be used as an oracle if its outputs leak to a wider network (AML.T0063). (c) Chaff and denial: flooding or corrupting inputs to trigger mass anomaly flags degrades operator trust and masks a concurrent real event (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). (d) Supply chain and artifact integrity: tampering with the serialized SVM, scalers, or open-source libraries used in the pipeline, which are often research-grade code moved into plant IT (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076, OP.C0502). (e) Attack-surface expansion: connecting the OT historian to an analytics environment, possibly external or cloud-hosted, adds a data path into or out of the plant network (OP.C0601, OP.C0505.01).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, the circulating water system is a non-safety, balance-of-plant system, so a nation-state is unlikely to target this model directly. It matters as a stepping stone and as a timing opportunity. A condition-monitoring pipeline that ingests plant historian data creates a new path from the OT/historian layer into an ML environment, concentrates maintenance trust in a model that few staff can inspect, and teaches operators to treat 'normal' flags as assurance. The labels come from unsupervised clustering and are never independently verified, so whatever the first DBSCAN pass called 'normal' is the model's ground truth. That is a quiet integrity weakness an insider or a patient adversary could exploit without touching any safety system.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and label poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0059, T0018.000). An insider or an intruder on the historian or data-export path could slowly shift sensor baselines during the period used to build the DBSCAN clusters, or inject plausible data. The pipeline then learns degraded or attack-induced behaviour as 'normal'. Because SVM labels are derived from DBSCAN with no human-verified ground truth, the poisoning propagates into the real-time classifier and is hard to detect. The consequence is that real condensers, pumps, or intake faults go unflagged. That is mainly an availability and economic harm. Its larger value to an adversary is as a blind-spot generator or a masking tool for a timed intervention on this or an adjacent system. (2) Evasion and low-and-slow manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043). Sensor spoofing or gradual drift injected below the SVM decision boundary could keep a developing fault or tampering looking normal. An adversary would also exploit the opposite: forcing false positives (AML.T0046) to trigger unnecessary maintenance, create alarm fatigue, or pull staff away at a chosen moment. (3) Stepping-stone access. The ML workstation, model artifacts, and data pipeline (AML.T0012, T0010.001, T0035, T0112) are a softer IT-adjacent foothold to pivot toward historian and OT networks, especially if the work is done on research or lab-shared infrastructure or with external collaborators such as national-lab partners (OP.C0601, OP.C0505). Data exfiltration of plant operating data gives reconnaissance on a CANDU/PHWR design's behaviour (AML.T0036, T0025).

IMPLICIT, exploitable by an adversary. (a) Automation trust and complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). If 'normal' becomes the default expectation, vigilance on walkdowns and trend review erodes, and an adversary can time action to that gap. (b) Drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, .03). Seasonal lake or river temperature, biofouling, load-following, outages, and sensor replacement shift the data distribution. A static SVM trained on a limited window will either misclassify or be retrained. Retraining is itself a new attack surface and a governance gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0502). (c) Low base rate of true faults, and unvalidated labels (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0401). 'High accuracy' on unseen data from the same period says little about rare real faults. Unsupervised cluster labels are conflated with real fault states, and opacity limits independent challenge. (d) Qualification and scope gaps (OP.C0503, OP.C0504). Treating it as a non-safety tool may leave it outside cyber and configuration control, so changes to the model or data are weakly audited, and an insider's modification would leave little trace. (e) If the approach is replicated across sister units or a fleet, one poisoned or flawed model template propagates widely (OP.C0602).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on circular pseudo-label validation, drift/retraining contamination, trust-driven complacency, and historian-path poisoning/evasion. I dropped speculative or weakly grounded codes (AML.T0029, AML.T0063, AML.T0076, AML.T0112, OP.C0303, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0403, OP.C0503, OP.C0504) because the text does not clearly instantiate them.

evidence.citation: "Machine Learning–Based Condition Monitoring of a Circulating Water System of a Canadian Nuclear Plant," Nuclear Technology (journal article, 2026), hosted on OSTI (U.S. DOE; INL-affiliated authors)
evidence.note: I read only the abstract on OSTI, not the full paper. It applies matrix profile and DBSCAN to circulating water system data from a pressurized heavy-water reactor to separate normal from anomalous data. It then trains an SVM on the DBSCAN clusters and tests it on unseen data as a real-time classifier, and reports high accuracy.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a blinded detector masking cooling-water degradation or tampering. Because this is a non-safety circulating water system, the likely harm is equipment damage, maintenance misdirection or operational disruption, with only indirect and unlikely links to radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Circular pseudo-labelling, drift-driven silent misses and retraining contamination are structural properties of this detector design and recur reliably once the pipeline is deployed, though a deliberate poisoning attack also needs suitable timing.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (poisoning, evasion, artifact tampering) need insider or intruder access to the historian, export path or ML workstation, plus knowledge of process data. This is well beyond routine external interaction, but not nation-state level.

affected_users.why: Impact centers on a single non-safety circulating water system and its maintenance decisions. Fleet-wide propagation through template reuse is possible but conditional and still confined to non-safety balance-of-plant monitoring.

discoverability.why: The method class is published in the open literature (abstract-level detail), and the weaknesses of pseudo-labelled SVMs, drift and data poisoning are well documented for this class of AI system, so an adversary can readily infer where the weaknesses lie. Plant-specific data paths remain non-public.

use_case: Generative-AI (LLM-based) document-generation tool connected to a digital thread. It retrieves and synthesises authoritative engineering design data from a single source of truth to draft a Documented Safety Analysis (DSA) chapter, a nuclear safety-basis and licensing document. It was applied as a pilot case study for the DOME microreactor test facility within NRIC's digital ecosystem.
incurred_insecurity:
A generative-AI drafting tool wired to a digital thread places an LLM between the single source of design truth and the Documented Safety Analysis that defines the safety basis for a first-of-a-kind microreactor test facility. It incurs implicit risks of content fidelity failure, retrieval and configuration errors, reviewer over-trust, non-repeatability and unqualified QA, and novel-design domain shift. It also incurs adversarial risks of poisoned source data or retrieval content, indirect prompt injection, sensitive-data aggregation and leakage, and supply-chain or model tampering. Harm is mostly latent: a degraded or falsified safety basis that is credited in licensing and later operation.

Content fidelity failure -- implicit, exploitable
Generation not constrained by retrieved data lets the LLM hallucinate, misattribute, mis-convert or drop limiting conditions and oversimplify accident sequences while the prose still reads as authoritative, so omissions and wrong values can become credited assumptions, TSR values or safety-class designations. An adversary could rely on this fluent-but-unreliable output to hide a deliberate non-conservative edit among ordinary-looking drafting errors.

Reviewer over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
As drafts prove mostly correct, reviewers sample or check formatting and citation presence rather than verify substance, and analysts lose the ability to write a DSA unaided, so independent technical review degrades into confirmation. An adversary or negligent insider could time a subtle change around reviewer fatigue and licensing-milestone pressure, relying on the aura of traceability to the single source of truth.

Retrieval and digital-thread data quality -- implicit, exploitable
The retriever can return superseded or unapproved design revisions, miss linked parameters or mishandle units, so the DSA describes the wrong design and one stale thread artifact propagates into every generated section. An adversary could exploit weak version control to slip a stale or altered record into the draft without it appearing as an AI fault.

Non-repeatability, opacity and QA gap -- implicit, exploitable
Inference-time variation means the same query yields different text, and regeneration after a design change may silently alter unrelated passages, breaking configuration control and audit trail, with no accepted qualification basis for AI-authored safety-basis content. An adversary could hide a manipulation inside this regeneration noise, since changes cannot be baselined and the regulator has no means to detect tampering or regression.

Novel-design domain shift -- implicit
The foundation model's priors come from LWR-era text, and a microreactor with different hazards, source terms and passive features has little precedent corpus, so generic language is silently imported where it does not apply. A realistic adversary gains little directly from this beyond the general masking effect already described.

Source-of-truth and retrieval poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or intruder who alters design records, metadata or indexed documents, or plants content the retriever ranks highly, gets the LLM to amplify the change into authoritative narrative that understates a hazard, drops a control or misstates a bounding assumption, with provenance obscured. A low-privilege edit to one record thus gains leverage out of proportion to access, and the resulting latent flaw in the licensing basis could later be exploited physically.

Indirect prompt injection -- adversarial
Instructions embedded in ingested vendor submittals, comments or documents can steer the drafter or its tool calls to omit, reframe or misstate content, or to fabricate supporting citations that reviewers take as trustworthy. The altered draft carries the apparent credibility of the source data.

Sensitive-data aggregation and leakage -- adversarial
The DSA, accident scenarios and security-relevant design details are aggregated in one retrievable corpus, and over-broad connector permissions, model outputs, logs or vendor-hosted inference can leak CUI, export-controlled or vulnerability information, or bypass need-to-know compartmentalization. This gives a state or insider actor a convenient reconnaissance channel on a novel design.

Supply-chain and model tampering -- adversarial
A third-party or hosted base model, plugin or connector can be compromised, or silently updated or swapped without requalification, changing behaviour across all drafts. Because pilot success sets precedent for reuse, one compromise could scale across multiple new-build licensees sharing templates and prompts.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a facility-operations and licensing view, the DSA chapter is the document that defines the safety basis: hazard analysis, accident sequences, controls, TSRs and the assumptions behind them. An LLM drafting tool wired to a digital thread makes the single source of truth both the AI's input and a high-value target. If the tool silently omits, misattributes or mis-synthesises a design parameter, the error can become a credited assumption, and that is a latent fault. It would not trip an alarm or fail in real time. It would surface later as a mis-specified control, an unanalysed accident sequence, or a flawed licensing decision. Existing practice (independent technical review, verification and validation, regulator review, configuration management) is a strong backstop only if reviewers do not defer to fluent, well-formatted AI prose and the review is scoped to catch omissions as well as wrong statements.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Content fidelity failure. The LLM can hallucinate, misattribute, round or unit-convert incorrectly, drop a limiting condition, or oversimplify a hazard or accident sequence while the text still reads as authoritative (OP.C0304, .01, .03). The AI failure mechanism is generation unconstrained by the retrieved data. What depends on it is the safety basis: accident analysis inputs, safety-class SSC designation, TSR/LCO values. The consequence is a latent flaw in the licensing basis that persists into operation, and for a first-of-a-kind microreactor test bed there is little operating experience to expose it. Omissions are the hardest class to catch because reviewers check what is written, not what is missing. (2) Automation trust failure. Reviewers who see mostly correct drafts will sample rather than verify, and independent review degrades into confirmation (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). Skill fade among safety analysts reduces the ability to catch deep errors over time. (3) Retrieval and digital-thread dependency. Stale or unapproved design revisions, an inconsistent data model, or a design change not propagated to the thread lead to a DSA that describes the wrong design. This is a configuration management failure presented as AI output (OP.C0204, OP.C0603, OP.C0201). (4) Non-repeatability and opacity. Different runs yield different text, which complicates QA, traceability and demonstration to the regulator that a section was produced from controlled inputs (OP.C0402.02, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Because the output only supports a document that later undergoes human approval, safety-significant harm needs a second failure in that approval step. Even so, the tool can create a systematic common-cause weakness across many documents. (5) Domain terminology and novel-design gaps. Microreactor and DOME-specific concepts have few public analogues, and the model may default to LWR-style language or assumptions (OP.C0702, OP.C0203, OP.C0302.03).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Integrity attack on the single source of truth. A malicious or insider edit to design data, or poisoning of documents the retrieval layer indexes, flows into the DSA with the credibility of authoritative data (AML.T0070, AML.T0071, AML.T0066, AML.T0099, AML.T0010.002). The aim could be to hide a vulnerability, weaken a physical protection or safeguards-relevant assumption, or insert a subtle non-conservatism. Because the text is AI-generated, a human may not trace the change to its source. (7) Indirect prompt injection through ingested documents, vendor submittals or comments carrying embedded instructions that alter drafted content (AML.T0051.001, AML.T0051.002, AML.T0067). (8) Confidentiality. The DSA, with its accident scenarios, vulnerabilities, and security-relevant design details (often CUI or SUNSI), is aggregated in one retrievable corpus. LLM leakage, over-broad retrieval permissions, or a cloud-hosted model enable extraction or aggregation of sensitive design information (AML.T0057, AML.T0085.000, AML.T0024, OP.C0601, OP.C0505, OP.C0505.01). (9) Supply chain and model integrity: a tampered or silently updated model or tool changes behavior across all drafts without notice (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018, AML.T0109, OP.C0602, OP.C0502). (10) Denial or delay of the tool, which only slows licensing schedules, an operational rather than safety effect, unless the schedule pressure pushes reviewers to accept drafts with less scrutiny (AML.T0029). Overall, the consequence is mostly delayed and latent rather than immediate: a degraded safety basis, wrongly credited controls, regulatory credibility loss, or exposure of sensitive design information.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline layered over a digital thread, so the model itself is probably a general-purpose foundation LLM that was never trained on the DOME design. The real fragility sits in three places: what the retriever pulls from the single source of truth, how faithfully the generator turns that into licensing prose, and how a human reviewer is expected to check the output. The single source of truth is both the strength and the single point of failure. If a design record is stale, mis-versioned, poisoned or mis-linked, the LLM will faithfully launder it into authoritative-sounding safety-basis text. A microreactor test facility has little operating history and a design that is still changing, so there is almost no precedent corpus to check the draft against, and the model will fill gaps with plausible content from generic large-reactor DSA patterns in its pretraining data. I could only see excerpts of the report, so none of this rests on confirmed architecture details.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Content fidelity failure (OP.C0304, .01, .03): the LLM may hallucinate or misattribute values, invent hazard or accident-analysis references, omit limiting conditions, or flatten qualified engineering statements into confident prose. The consequence is a licensing safety-basis document whose claims do not trace to the design, and reviewers may not notice. (2) Domain-shift and new-build scarcity (OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03): the model's priors come from conventional LWR-era text, but a DOME-type microreactor has different hazards, source terms and passive features. Generic phrasing can be silently imported where it does not apply, a form of OOD generalization failure that is hard to see in fluent output. (3) Retrieval and digital-thread data quality (OP.C0201, OP.C0204, OP.C0603): retrieval can return superseded revisions, miss linked parameters, or fail on units and context. Errors in one thread artifact then propagate into every generated section. Chunking and ranking behavior is itself an unqualified component. (4) Non-repeatability and opacity (OP.C0402.02, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303): the same query can produce different drafts, with no accepted QA basis for AI-authored safety-basis content. Regeneration after a design change may silently alter unrelated passages, which breaks configuration control and the audit trail. (5) Automation bias and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, .06, OP.C0102): fluent, well-cited drafts invite reviewers to check formatting rather than substance. Over time, fewer analysts will be able to write a DSA from scratch. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Poisoning the source of truth or the retrieval index (AML.T0010.002, T0020, T0070, T0071, T0099, T0066): an adversary or insider who alters design records, metadata or indexed documents gets a high-leverage route, because the LLM amplifies the change into licensing text and gives it an appearance of provenance. This could hide a safety margin shortfall or skew the accident analysis. (7) Indirect prompt injection (AML.T0051.001, T0093): instructions embedded in ingested documents, vendor submittals or comments could steer the drafter or its tool calls, and could cause it to omit or reframe content. (8) Supply chain and model changes (AML.T0010.001, T0010.003, T0109, OP.C0502, OP.C0601): a hosted or third-party foundation model can be updated, swapped or compromised without notice, changing behavior with no requalification. Sending sensitive design and safety-basis data to an external service also creates a leakage path (AML.T0057, T0085.000, OP.C0505.01). (9) Credential and agent-tool exposure (AML.T0053, T0083, T0098): connectors to the digital thread carry broad read privileges and could be abused to pull export-controlled or security-sensitive design data. The overall exposure is a trusted-looking licensing artifact whose integrity depends on an unqualified retrieval-and-generation chain.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial lens, this tool's value to an attacker is not in the draft itself but in its position: it sits between the single source of truth (the digital thread) and the safety-basis document that a regulator and facility reviewers will treat as the authoritative statement of hazards, controls and accident analysis. Whoever can influence what the LLM retrieves, or how it phrases the synthesis, can shape what reviewers believe is the design and safety envelope, without touching a plant system. This is a pathway for an insider or supply-chain actor that leaves no operational footprint and would only be noticed if reviewers independently trace claims back to source. The non-adversarial weaknesses (fluent but subtly wrong synthesis, omissions, reviewer complacency as drafts get better) are exactly what a patient adversary would time a manipulation around, because they lower the odds of detection.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: 1) Integrity of the safety basis through the retrieval/synthesis path (adversarial). Mechanism: the LLM pulls from the digital thread and RAG-style indexes; poisoned or subtly altered entries in the thread, retrieval index or tool connectors, or injected instructions in ingested documents (indirect prompt injection), cause the draft to understate a hazard, drop a control, misstate a bounding assumption, or cite a source that does not support the claim. Dependency: the DSA is the basis for licensing/authorization decisions and for operating limits and controls. Consequence: a licensing decision or operating envelope rests on a falsified or degraded safety case, which is a latent safety vulnerability that an adversary could later exploit physically, or that simply never gets caught. A low-skill insider with edit rights to one data record gets leverage out of proportion to their access, since the AI propagates the change into narrative prose where it is less visible than a changed number. 2) Concentration of trust in the single source of truth and the generator.
