The digital thread is a high-value target (a single point of compromise for design data, including sensitive design information and potentially security-relevant details such as vital area, protection and response info), and the LLM tool aggregates and summarizes it, creating a convenient exfiltration or data-leakage channel (via model outputs, prompts, logs, vendor-hosted inference, or overbroad retrieval permissions that bypass need-to-know compartmentalization). Consequence: loss of controlled unclassified/export-controlled/proprietary information and of sensitive design-vulnerability knowledge for a novel microreactor design, which is also of interest for reconnaissance by a state actor. 3) Human-factor erosion that can be timed around (implicit). Automation bias and skill fade among safety analysts and reviewers, plus fluent output that masks omissions or hallucinated or misattributed citations, reduce independent scrutiny of the draft; opacity and inference-time non-repeatability mean the same query can yield different text, so review-by-regeneration cannot establish a baseline and changes are hard to audit. An adversary or a negligent insider can exploit reviewer fatigue, schedule pressure in licensing milestones, or the aura of provenance given by 'traceable to the single source of truth' to slip changes through. Reviewers may check that citations exist rather than that they say what the text claims. 4) Supply-chain and qualification gaps. The base model, hosting, plugins and connectors are external dependencies outside nuclear QA; model updates can shift behaviour silently (a rug-pull or ordinary version drift), and there is no established AI-specific qualification regime for safety-basis authoring, so the regulator and licensee may lack a way to detect tampering or regression. A pilot's early success creates precedent that moves the tool toward routine use for other facilities, so a compromise would scale across a fleet of new-build licensees with shared templates and prompts. Realistically, a sophisticated adversary would more likely go after the thread's data and access controls than the LLM itself, so the AI's main contribution is amplification and obscuring of an upstream compromise, and the main controls are provenance, access-controlled retrieval, version-pinned models, logged prompts/outputs, and mandatory independent human verification against source.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on content fidelity failure, reviewer over-trust, retrieval poisoning, indirect prompt injection, leakage and supply-chain risk; I merged these and dropped weakly argued or speculative codes (denial of service, credential harvesting, valid accounts, agent tool invocation, erode integrity) because they were not developed into distinct threats in the text.

evidence.citation: "Evaluation of AI-Enabled Digital Documented Safety Analysis: A Case Study – Generative AI for Nuclear Safety Basis Document Generation within NRIC's Digital Ecosystem (INL/RPT-26-90824)," Idaho National Laboratory (National Reactor Innovation Center)
evidence.note: This INL report is a case study of AI-assisted drafting of a DSA chapter. It says the structured generative-AI document tool was integrated with the NRIC digital thread, which let it retrieve and synthesise engineering data from a single source of truth. A companion INL methodology report (INL/RPT-25-87369) names DOME as the pilot facility. I read only search-result excerpts, not the full report, so I could not confirm further technical details such as the exact model or quantitative results.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is source-of-truth/retrieval poisoning or a non-conservative edit that yields a degraded or falsified safety basis (understated hazards, dropped controls, altered TSR values) credited in licensing; this is a latent safety-margin and licensing-integrity harm that could enable later physical exploitation, though it is mediated by human review and not a direct release.

reproducibility.why: Content fidelity failures, stale retrieval, and non-repeatability recur reliably given the described setup, and poisoned records or injected content are amplified consistently by the LLM, though a specific deliberate falsification must survive review.

exploitability.why: Poisoning the source of truth or retrieval corpus needs insider or privileged-intruder access to design records, but only low-privilege edits are said to be needed, and indirect injection via ingested vendor documents needs only routine external content submission; implicit failures need no attacker.

affected_users.why: One stale or poisoned thread artifact propagates into every generated section of the safety basis, and a supply-chain or model compromise could scale across multiple licensees sharing templates, though impact is concentrated in the licensing documentation rather than live plant systems.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability classes (RAG poisoning, indirect prompt injection, hallucination, over-trust, model supply chain) are well documented in open literature, and the pilot is publicly reported, so a capable outsider can readily infer that these weaknesses exist, though system-specific details remain internal.

use_case: Multivariate time-series meta-model for forecasting the transient response of a PWR during a steam generator tube rupture (SGTR) accident. It compares LSTM, GRU and hybrid CNN-LSTM recurrent networks. A Bayesian neural network adds uncertainty estimates to the predicted plant-parameter trajectories. It is meant as a fast data-driven predictor to support operator accident response.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places a data-driven SGTR trajectory forecaster, with Bayesian uncertainty bands, in front of operators during a rare, fast, release-relevant accident. The main implicit threats are a simulator-to-plant gap with out-of-distribution failure, unreliable uncertainty estimates, degraded-input dependence, and a missing qualification basis with operator over-trust. The main adversarial threats are training-data and model tampering, live input manipulation, denial of the tool at a critical moment, and extraction of plant-response knowledge. Because the tool is advisory and non-actuating, harm runs through operator judgment rather than direct control.

Simulator-to-plant gap and OOD failure -- implicit, exploitable
The meta-model is almost certainly trained on thermal-hydraulic code runs of a generic PWR, so compound faults (multiple ruptures, stuck valves, loss of offsite power), plant-specific differences and unmodeled operator actions fall outside its envelope, and autoregressive rollouts compound error into smooth but wrong trajectories of SG level or primary pressure. The result is mistimed isolation, cooldown or depressurization and larger secondary-side release. An adversary could stage or wait for such an off-envelope condition so that the forecast misleads operators without any model tampering.

Overconfident Bayesian uncertainty -- implicit, exploitable
BNN intervals reflect only in-distribution epistemic uncertainty and stay narrow under shift, giving false assurance on margin to overfill, while visibly wide or missed bands push operators to discard the tool. An adversary can rely on this misplaced confidence, since a manipulated or off-envelope forecast still looks authoritative and a data-integrity attack looks credible rather than like an instrument fault.

Degraded-sensor input dependence -- implicit, exploitable
The forecaster needs a clean, complete multivariate stream, so harsh-environment sensor drift, missing channels or frozen signals push inputs off-distribution with no validity flag. An adversary could cause or exploit such degradation, or time an action to it, because the resulting forecast errors would be attributed to the accident rather than to interference.

Qualification gap, opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
No accepted qualification path exists for an ML predictor in an accident-response role, recurrent networks are opaque, and training seed and inference variability mean forecasts differ across runs and across the LSTM, GRU and CNN-LSTM variants, while weak version control lets model changes pass unreviewed. An insider or supply-chain actor could slip in a modified model, relying on acceptance testing that checks only average simulator error.

Operator over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
In a rare, high-stress event, operators unfamiliar with the tool may defer to a polished forecast over EOP indications, or may mix up predicted, measured and simulated values on one display. An adversary could time a physical, cyber or insider action around this reduced independent diagnosis.

Training-data and model tampering -- adversarial
Poisoned simulation scenarios, tampered pretrained checkpoints or a compromised ML toolchain can embed a bias or trigger-conditioned error, such as optimistic SG-level or pressure trajectories for a given break-size band. It would pass validation drawn from the same simulator and would skew operator timing during a real SGTR.

Live input manipulation -- adversarial
An adversary on the historian, gateway or plant-computer data path can inject temporally coherent perturbations or spoofed and frozen sensor values that evade range checks and steer the forecast, ideally timed to a real or staged transient. This turns the forecaster into a channel for misleading operators toward harmful or unnecessary actions.

Denial or corruption of the tool -- adversarial
Resource exhaustion or corruption of the model artifact removes the decision aid just when operators have come to rely on it, causing confusion or delay during an emergency.

Model and data exposure -- adversarial
The trained surrogate and its scenario database encode plant-specific response behavior and margins, so extraction or leakage supports attack planning and lets an adversary build a proxy model to craft evasion inputs offline.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, an SGTR is a rare, fast-moving event with a primary-to-secondary leak, risk of steam generator overfill, radiological release through the secondary side, and a tightly proceduralized response (EOPs, symptom-based, with safety parameter display). A surrogate forecaster is only useful if operators trust its trajectories during the first minutes, which is exactly when mis-forecasts are most costly and when no real plant data exist. Such a meta-model is almost certainly trained on thermal-hydraulic code simulations (e.g., RELAP/MARS-type runs) of a 'typical' PWR, not field data, so its fidelity is bounded by the simulator and by the sampled range of break sizes, locations, equipment failures and operator actions. Existing practice (EOPs, qualified simulators, independent safety-parameter monitoring, I&C protection that does not depend on this tool) means a wrong forecast should not directly actuate anything, but it can bias operator timing, prioritization, and confidence if it is presented as decision support. The real hazard is therefore advisory contamination of operator judgment during a degraded, high-stress event, plus a quiet qualification gap, rather than direct loss of a safety function.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Simulated/surrogate training data and OOD failure: the model learns code-generated SGTR transients for a generic PWR; real events with multiple tube ruptures, concurrent failures (stuck-open SG safety/relief valve, failed HPSI, loss of offsite power), unusual operator actions, sensor faults, or plant-specific differences fall outside the training envelope. The network may still output smooth, plausible trajectories, so operators could see a confident-looking forecast of SG level, primary pressure or subcooling margin that is wrong, e.g. underestimating time to SG overfill or to reach the termination criteria for RCS cooldown/depressurization. Consequence: delayed or mistimed isolation/cooldown decisions, greater secondary-side release; harm would require operators to defer to it over EOP indications and the shift technical advisor. (2) Bayesian uncertainty is itself unreliable: BNN intervals are calibrated on in-distribution simulation and are typically overconfident under shift, so narrow bands can create false assurance (automation trust failure, over-trust), while wide bands may lead to disuse. (3) Input dependence on instrumentation: the forecaster consumes plant-parameter time series; faulty, drifting or degraded sensors during an accident (harsh environment, loss of power) feed garbage-in forecasts with no obvious flag. (4) Non-repeatability, opacity and qualification: stochastic inference and training-time variability make forecasts differ across runs; recurrent networks are opaque, no deterministic V&V basis exists for a non-safety-classified advisory tool, and the LSTM/GRU/CNN-LSTM comparison offers no assurance on which model governs in a real event. Operators in a rare-event setting have little experience with the tool (skill fade, out-of-the-loop). Latency and mode confusion (forecast vs. measured vs. simulated values on one display) may blur the line between prediction and plant state.

ADVERSARIAL threats. (1) Manipulation of training/simulation data or model weights through the supply chain (poisoned simulation datasets, tampered pre-trained checkpoints, compromised ML toolchain) could embed a bias, for instance systematically optimistic SG-level or pressure trajectories for a specific break-size band, or a trigger-conditioned error; it would be invisible in normal validation if the test set is drawn from the same simulator. (2) Runtime input tampering: an adversary with access to the data path (historian, gateway, plant-computer feed) could shift or spoof inputs to steer forecasts, or time a cyber action to coincide with a real or staged transient to degrade operator confidence or induce a harmful action; the AI becomes an extra channel to mislead operators when they most need reliable info. (3) Denial or degradation of the tool (DoS, resource exhaustion, model corruption) removes the decision aid and may itself cause confusion if operators had come to rely on it. (4) Information exposure: model and training data encode plant-specific thermal-hydraulic response and could aid an adversary in identifying vulnerable transient conditions, if plant-specific. Mitigating engineering context: tool should be isolated one-way from safety I&C, kept non-actuating, displayed with explicit OOD/validity flags, and subordinated to EOPs; harm scenarios need coincident operator over-reliance plus a real initiating event, which bounds likelihood but not the consequence of a mis-timed response in a rare event.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this meta-model is almost certainly trained on simulated transients (thermal-hydraulic code runs such as RELAP5/MELCOR-class, with the training source unconfirmed). That makes it a surrogate of a simulator, not of the plant, so its ceiling is simulator fidelity and the coverage of the sampled scenario space (break size, location, timing, operator actions, equipment failures). SGTR is a rare, low-base-rate event with essentially no real field data, so the model can never be validated against operational reality, only against the same simulator that produced its training data. Recurrent architectures (LSTM, GRU, CNN-LSTM) forecasting autoregressively accumulate error over the horizon and degrade sharply when the inputs leave the sampled envelope, such as compound failures, sensor faults or unmodeled operator interventions. The Bayesian network's uncertainty estimates only capture epistemic uncertainty within the training distribution and are typically overconfident out-of-distribution. In an accident-response role, a confident but wrong trajectory is the worst failure mode.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulation-to-reality gap: the model is trained on simulated or surrogate data, so it inherits code biases and a limited scenario design space. Mechanism: distribution shift between simulator output and real plant signals (noise, sensor bias, calibration drift, plant-specific configuration). Dependency: operators using forecasts to anticipate parameters such as pressurizer level, primary-secondary pressure and SG level, and to time actions such as cooldown and isolation. Consequence: mistimed or misdirected mitigation, or false confidence about margin to overfill or core uncovery. (2) Out-of-distribution and compound accidents: a 'typical PWR' meta-model does not generalize to different plants, burnup states, partial equipment failures, or SGTR combined with other faults (e.g., loss of offsite power, stuck valves). Recurrent rollouts compound errors, and BNN uncertainty bands can stay narrow while being wrong. Consequence: overconfident incorrect forecasts during the very scenarios where decision support matters most. (3) Qualification and verification gap: there is no accepted qualification path for a data-driven predictor in an accident-response role, and the black-box dynamics are poorly explainable. Choosing among LSTM, GRU and CNN-LSTM by a single benchmark can also hide training non-determinism and seed sensitivity. (4) Human factors: operators facing a rare, high-stress event may over-trust a fast, visually polished forecast with uncertainty bands (automation bias), or discount it after a visible miss. Skill fade and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity compound this, because the tool is almost never exercised in real use. (5) Input integrity dependence: the model needs a clean, complete multivariate stream, so sensor failures, missing channels or instrument degradation during the accident push inputs off-distribution. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Input manipulation: an adversary with access to the instrumentation/data path can craft small, plausible perturbations (evasion/adversarial data) that shift forecast trajectories, steering operators toward harmful actions or inducing unnecessary ones. Recurrent forecasters are sensitive to temporally coherent perturbations that evade simple range checks. The implicit OOD fragility makes this easier, and an attacker could time it to an actual transient. (7) Supply chain and training-data poisoning: the simulation datasets, pretrained weights, ML libraries and the retraining pipeline are attack surfaces. A backdoor or poisoned scenario subset could bias forecasts only under specific trigger conditions (e.g., particular break sizes), and could pass aggregate validation metrics unnoticed. (8) Model and data confidentiality: because the model reproduces plant-response behaviour, extraction or leakage of the model or its training data could reveal plant design and safety-margin information, and a proxy model would help an adversary craft evasion inputs offline. (9) Availability: if the tool becomes a relied-upon aid, denial of the service or corruption of the model artefact degrades operator support exactly during an emergency.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, a fast SGTR trajectory forecaster used during an accident is a trust-concentrating advisory tool at the worst possible moment: it matters most during a radiological-release-relevant event, when operators are under stress and have little time to cross-check. A sophisticated adversary would probably not target the model directly, because it is advisory and does not actuate anything. It is a more plausible stepping stone or timing aid, for example by degrading or biasing the forecast during a separately engineered event, or by exploiting the confidence operators place in it. The more realistic danger is a cheap implicit weakness: a surrogate trained on simulator data that behaves unpredictably outside its training envelope (such as multiple concurrent faults, degraded instrumentation or atypical plant states) and shows narrow, falsely reassuring uncertainty bands. An insider or supply-chain actor could exploit that weakness, or simply wait for it to appear.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Training-data and model integrity. The meta-model is almost certainly trained on thermal-hydraulic code simulations, so whoever controls the simulation scenarios, the preprocessing scripts or the model artifacts (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020) can embed subtle biases or backdoor-style triggers. Examples are slightly optimistic predicted pressurizer level or primary-to-secondary leak-rate trajectories under specific input patterns. These are hard to detect because the network is opaque and acceptance testing normally checks average error, not adversarial corners. The consequence is a mis-calibrated forecast that shapes operator timing for isolation, cooldown and depressurization, with downstream effects on release magnitude and defense-in-depth margin. (2) Input manipulation. The forecaster consumes live multivariate plant signals, so spoofed, drifted or frozen sensor feeds, or a compromised data historian or gateway, could steer predictions (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). Because the tool presents a coherent, uncertainty-annotated trajectory, it lends false credibility to a data-integrity attack that would otherwise look like an inconsistent instrument. This creates a new, plausible link between IT and OT data paths and operator decision-making. (3) Timing and vigilance erosion. Once operators routinely lean on rapid forecasts, an adversary could time a physical, cyber or insider action around reduced independent diagnosis (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Denial or degradation of the tool at a critical moment (AML.T0029) could also induce confusion or delay if procedures lean on it. (4) Model and data exposure. A trained SGTR surrogate and its scenario database reveal plant-response behavior, margins and instrumentation relationships that support attack planning (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0005). They are a lower-value target than control systems, but an accessible one. IMPLICIT: (5) Out-of-distribution failure. The model is trained on simulated SGTR scenarios for a 'typical' PWR, so it generalizes poorly to a specific plant, to rare multi-fault cases, or to real instrument noise and failures (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). This produces confident but wrong trajectories, and an adversary could engineer exactly such conditions. (6) Misleading uncertainty. Bayesian neural network uncertainty is approximate and tends to be overconfident off-distribution, so narrow bands give operators false assurance (OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (7) Qualification and governance gaps. There is no established qualification path for safety-adjacent ML advisory tools, version control and retraining are weak, and the approved status of the model is ambiguous. Changes to a model could therefore slip in without review, which is also where an insider would act (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0402, OP.C0504). Overall severity is moderate and driven by trust concentration and advisory influence, not by direct control authority.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on simulator-trained OOD failure, overconfident BNN bands, qualification and opacity gaps, operator over-trust, and the same four adversarial classes (poisoning/supply chain, input manipulation, denial, extraction). I dropped codes that were weakly traceable, such as AML.T0031, AML.T0048, AML.T0059, AML.T0035, AML.T0044 and OP.C0603, and kept AML.T0005 only for the proxy-model pathway.

evidence.citation: "Using machine learning to forecast and assess the uncertainty in the response of a typical PWR undergoing a steam generator tube rupture accident," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Elsevier / Korean Nuclear Society)
evidence.note: The paper builds a multivariate time-series machine-learning meta-model that predicts how a typical PWR responds to an SGTR. It uses LSTM, GRU and CNN-LSTM recurrent networks, and a Bayesian neural network to quantify prediction uncertainty. I read only the abstract and search snippet, not the full paper, so details such as the training data source are unconfirmed. Some entries in the taxonomy list were hidden from me, so I could not check for overlap with them.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a misleading SGTR forecast (from OOD failure, tampering, or input manipulation) that skews operator isolation, cooldown or depressurization timing and enlarges secondary-side release; because the tool is advisory and EOP indications act as a backstop, this stops short of a guaranteed radiological release.

reproducibility.why: OOD failure, overconfident uncertainty bands and sensor-degradation sensitivity recur reliably once an off-envelope or degraded-input condition arises, but the adversarial paths depend on a rare SGTR event, precise timing, and operators actually relying on the forecast.

exploitability.why: Credible adversarial paths such as training-data or checkpoint poisoning, tampering on the historian or plant-computer data path, and insider or supply-chain model substitution require privileged or deep access to plant networks or the ML pipeline, though the implicit OOD and degraded-sensor weaknesses need no special access.

affected_users.why: Impact centers on the operating crew and on plant response decisions for one unit during an accident, which can affect the whole plant's accident response, but the tool is advisory and non-actuating and is not coupled across systems.

discoverability.why: Simulator-to-plant gaps, BNN overconfidence under shift, sensor-drift sensitivity and opacity of recurrent networks are well documented in the open literature, and the model class is published, although plant-specific data paths and deployment details would need insider or partial knowledge.

use_case: Full-spectrum machine-learning regression (multilayer perceptron, convolutional neural network and transformer models) that predicts the burnup of individual TRISO fuel pebbles from high-purity germanium gamma-ray spectra. It is meant for quick, short-cooling-time on-line burnup measurement in pebble bed reactors. The models were trained on spectra simulated with Serpent and GADRAS. Their predictions support the decision to discharge or reload each pebble, and also material control and accountancy.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case puts an opaque, simulation-trained burnup regressor on the discharge/recirculate decision for every pebble and on the material accountancy record at once. Its main threats are an unverified sim-to-real gap with silent out-of-distribution failure, weak AI qualification and change control, automation over-trust, and a correlated dual-use error path into safeguards. Adversarial exposure comes from model or data poisoning, physical or data-path spectrum manipulation, proxy-model reconnaissance, and denial of the measurement chain.

Sim-to-real gap -- implicit, exploitable
The MLP, CNN and transformer models were trained and validated only on Serpent/GADRAS spectra, so real HPGe effects (pile-up, dead time, gain drift, geometry, detector aging) can bias burnup systematically, underestimating it so over-irradiated pebbles are recirculated, or overestimating it so pebbles are discharged early. The resulting standing error floor gives an adversary plausible deniability, so a deliberate bias could hide inside it.

Silent out-of-distribution failure and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Whole-spectrum regressors extrapolate without abstention or calibrated uncertainty, returning plausible burnups for unusual, damaged, dummy or different-enrichment pebbles or for a drifting detector chain, using diffuse features no physicist can review. An adversary could push spectra into this blind region and rely on the absence of any peak-level sanity check to avoid detection.

Qualification and repeatability gap -- implicit, exploitable
There is no established nuclear-grade QA or regulatory standard for validating regression models that drive fuel discharge or safeguards, and retraining or non-deterministic updates can shift predictions without change control. An adversary could slip a tampered model version through update windows that lack independent reverification.

Automation trust and lapsed cross-checks -- implicit, exploitable
The claim that the model beats Cs-137 photopeak regression, combined with high per-pebble throughput, invites over-trust and skill fade, so the photopeak cross-check and independent burnup-code reconciliation may lapse. An adversary could time a subtle manipulation to when those checks have been dropped, relying on the trust the narrative creates.

Dual-use common-cause error in accountancy -- implicit, exploitable
One model feeds both operations and MC&A, so any bias becomes a correlated inventory-difference or MUF error that can mask or mimic diversion, while scarce destructive-assay-verified anchor data and blurred ownership of the data security model make it hard to tell which. An adversary could use this ambiguity to conceal diverted or misdeclared pebbles.

Model and training-data poisoning -- adversarial
Poisoning of the simulation datasets, simulator inputs, or pretrained weights in development, vendor hand-off or update could embed a backdoor trigger or small in-tolerance bias that misreads selected pebbles or burnup bands. Simulation-on-simulation validation would not expose it, and it would falsify discharge decisions and the MC&A record.

Spectrum and data-path manipulation -- adversarial
An insider with physical access could alter shielding, add a small source or change detector settings, or tamper with calibration files and spectral channels, to craft inputs that push the network to misread burnup where a peak-based method would flag an anomaly. The aim would be to understate or overstate burnup for chosen pebbles.

Proxy-model reconnaissance -- adversarial
The published architectures and openly available Serpent/GADRAS pipelines let an adversary build a proxy model and tune perturbations offline that transfer to the deployed regressor. This lowers the cost of the evasion attacks above.

Measurement-chain denial -- adversarial
Disrupting the inference or acquisition service forces fallback to slower manual methods during continuous refueling, cutting throughput and inviting manual errors.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this model sits on the discharge/recirculate decision for every pebble in a continuously refueled core, and also feeds nuclear material accountancy. That makes both a systematic bias and a transient outage consequential. The models are trained and validated only on Serpent/GADRAS-simulated spectra, so no one has shown they transfer to real HPGe detectors, real pebble-to-pebble geometry, real dead-time and pile-up, or real fuel and operating-history variability. Existing engineering practice does give some defence in depth: the core physics code tracks pebble residence and passes, discharge criteria carry margin, and the conventional Cs-137 photopeak method is available as a cross-check. Those defences erode if operators come to trust a more accurate-looking whole-spectrum regressor and stop checking it. The central question is therefore which independent check remains when the ML burnup value drives discharge and accountancy at the same time.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: the models learned the simulator, not the plant (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0303). Detector resolution drift, gain shift, temperature effects, pile-up at short cooling times, collimator or geometry misalignment, pebble position, and fuel or enrichment variations missing from the training set can all shift spectra out of distribution. A whole-spectrum CNN or transformer can fail silently, because it uses features (continuum, minor peaks) that no physicist reviews, whereas a photopeak method fails in an interpretable way (OP.C0401, OP.C0403). Consequence: systematic burnup bias. Underestimated burnup means over-irradiated pebbles are recirculated, eroding fuel-integrity margin (fission-product release under accident temperatures, higher decay heat in the core, a conservative-limit shortfall). Overestimated burnup means premature discharge, lost economics, and spent-fuel accounting distortion. Bias is correlated across pebbles, so it acts as a common-cause error that statistical sampling checks may miss (OP.C0603). (2) Calibration and qualification: AI-specific QA is not established under nuclear-grade software practice, and there is no standard for validating regression models used for fuel discharge or safeguards (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402, OP.C0502). Retraining or model updates change behaviour without a corresponding change control, and inference non-repeatability complicates inspection. (3) Automation trust: operators or safeguards staff who come to rely on faster, more accurate-seeming output may drop the Cs-137 cross-check and independent burnup-code reconciliation (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Outliers such as damaged pebbles, dummy/graphite pebbles, or mixed-in different fuel types may be forced to a plausible burnup value rather than flagged (OP.C0702.01). (4) Accountancy: pebble bed items are numerous and hard to item-count, so burnup-derived fissile inventory is a key accountancy quantity. A biased model would produce persistent material unaccounted for (MUF) or inventory-difference errors that mask or mimic diversion, and inspectors cannot easily tell which (OP.C0701). Data scarcity of real, destructive-assay-verified pebbles limits validation. AVAILABILITY: model or detector-chain downtime during continuous refueling forces fallback to slower methods; throughput loss and manual-process errors follow (OP.C0204, OP.C0601 if cloud-hosted). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training-data and model integrity: poisoning of the simulation datasets, simulator configuration (cross sections, GADRAS response templates), or pretrained weights during development or vendor hand-off can embed a subtle bias or trigger that goes undetected because validation is simulation-on-simulation (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004). Consequence: targeted misreading of specific pebbles or burnup bands. This is a safeguards-relevant insider or supply-chain route to hide diverted or under-burned material. (6) Evasion by physical spectrum manipulation: an insider or adversary with physical access to the measurement station could alter shielding, add a small gamma source, or exploit detector gain to push a spectrum into a region where the network misreads while conventional peak analysis would flag an anomaly (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). The black-box regressor offers no peak-level sanity check. (7) Data-path tampering: spoofing or replaying spectra or burnup outputs between the HPGe acquisition system and the discharge/accountancy records (AML.T0031, AML.T0059). (8) Model theft or probing: query or artifact access lets an adversary learn which spectral features drive predictions, which lets them craft evasion (AML.T0024, AML.T0044, AML.T0007). Overall the severity is moderated by core-physics tracking and discharge margins, but the common-cause bias and the dual use for safeguards make unvalidated deployment a real concern.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, the main fragility is that the whole stack is trained and validated on Serpent/GADRAS simulated spectra and has never been qualified against measured HPGe data from real TRISO pebbles. Whole-spectrum regression with MLP, CNN and transformer models can exploit every channel, including simulator-specific features such as idealized detector response, perfect energy calibration, clean geometry and an assumed nuclide inventory. The apparent gain over Cs-137 photopeak regression may therefore be a simulation-to-reality gap or shortcut learning rather than better physics. Inference takes place in a high-count-rate, short-cooling-time environment with pile-up, dead time, gain drift, scattering from the pebble-handling hardware, mixed-burnup neighbours and detector aging. None of these are likely to be represented in the training distribution, and the models offer no calibrated uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag. Burnup feeds two safety- and safeguards-relevant decisions, discharge/reload and MC&A, so a confident but wrong scalar flows directly into fuel-cycle control and nuclear material accounting.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and data provenance failure: all training data is simulated, so unmodelled physics (detector degradation, calibration drift, pile-up, geometry and temperature effects, and the uncertain pebble-bed fuel and cooling histories behind the simulation inputs) produces systematic bias that only shows up in operation. Without measured HPGe data for qualification, the headline accuracy claim is unverified (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303). (2) Out-of-distribution blindness: regression networks extrapolate silently. Spectra from unusual fuel (different enrichment, new-build fuel with no operating history, damaged or contaminated pebbles) or from a drifting detector chain give plausible but wrong burnups with no abstention. Premature discharge wastes fuel. Late discharge or over-irradiation means a pebble exceeds its burnup limit, with consequences for fuel integrity and fission-product retention margins (OP.C0302, OP.C0203, OP.C0403). (3) Opacity and repeatability: transformer and CNN models rely on diffuse spectral features, which is hard to defend to a regulator against a physics-based photopeak method. Training non-determinism and retraining on new simulation batches can shift predictions between model versions (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0501). (4) Human factors: per-pebble automation at high throughput encourages automation bias, and operators lose the ability to verify burnup by hand (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). (5) Safeguards dependence: if the ML burnup estimate feeds MC&A, a systematic bias becomes a material-accounting error that could mask diversion or inflate inventory difference, with scarce destructive-assay anchoring data to detect it (OP.C0701.01, OP.C0603).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Supply-chain and model integrity: the model weights, preprocessing code, and Serpent/GADRAS pipelines and nuclear data libraries are open or widely shared software. Tampering or poisoning of the training data or weights (AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0076) could introduce a backdoor or a small systematic bias that stays inside plausible error bounds and so stays undetected. (b) Input manipulation at the spectrum or data layer: the model consumes one-dimensional spectra over a digital chain. An insider or someone with network access could alter calibration files, spectral channels or metadata. Alternatively, someone with physical access could add a shielded or spiked source near the detector to craft adversarial spectral perturbations (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0041). The aim would be to understate or overstate burnup for specific pebbles, hiding diversion or forcing wrongful discharge decisions. (c) Reconnaissance: the published papers describe the architectures and simulation setup, enabling proxy-model construction and black-box optimization (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0002.001, AML.T0043.002). (d) Availability: denial or corruption of the inference or acquisition service stalls pebble-handling throughput (AML.T0029). The core exposure is that an unqualified, simulation-trained, uncertainty-free regressor sits as a trusted single point of judgment for both operational and safeguards decisions.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this model sits at a dual-use junction: the same per-pebble burnup number drives an operational decision (discharge or recirculate) and a safeguards/MC&A record. Anyone who can influence the number, whether by tampering with the model, the spectra, or the calibration chain, can shift both the reactor's fuel cycle and the facility's declared material balance without touching the plant's protection systems. An insider who wants to hide diversion of pebbles, or to bias discharge decisions, would find a trusted, opaque regression on a spectrum much easier to nudge than a physical measurement chain with independent cross-checks. The models were trained only on Serpent/GADRAS simulations, so they have a built-in, non-adversarial weakness (sim-to-real gap) that gives an adversary or insider plausible deniability for any anomalous output. High-throughput online pebble flow also lets the model quietly replace the human's analytical vigilance, and an adversary could time a subtle manipulation to that complacency.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Model or pipeline integrity compromise. A trained MLP/CNN/transformer is an opaque artifact; a poisoned or backdoored model (or one altered in the supply chain or at update time) could return a trigger-conditioned or systematically biased burnup for selected pebbles. The consequences are a pebble wrongly discharged or retained (fuel-cycle and economic effects, possible reactivity and power-distribution misperception) and a falsified MC&A record that masks diversion or misdeclared material, which is a safeguards harm. Because the output is a single scalar with no physical audit trail, the tampering is hard to see (ATLAS T0010.003, T0018, T0020, T0043.004, T0076). (2) Input manipulation. An insider with physical access near the HPGe detector could alter the spectrum (shielding, adding a small source, perturbing detector settings) so that the full-spectrum model, which uses features the conventional photopeak method does not, is pushed out of distribution in ways a human review would not catch (T0041, T0043, T0015). Full-spectrum models are more sensitive to subtle, non-photopeak spectral changes than a Cs-137 ratio is. (3) Reconnaissance and stepping stone. The method is published openly, and simulated-data pipelines (Serpent/GADRAS inputs, training sets) are widely available, so an adversary could build a proxy model to learn what perturbation yields what burnup shift (T0000, T0005, T0002). The model's host and data network may also be a convenient route toward the MC&A database or plant data systems (T0012, T0049). Burnup-based accountancy data is also sensitive information about fuel composition and operating history (T0024, T0025). (4) Credibility-based deception: an adversary can exploit trust in an 'AI is better than the photopeak method' narrative to displace independent verification. IMPLICIT, and exploitable: (a) Sim-to-real gap and qualification mismatch. The models were trained and tested on simulated spectra only, so real HPGe effects (dead time, pile-up at high pebble flow, gain drift, geometry and detector aging, background, peak shifts, pebble-to-pebble heterogeneity) can produce unquantified errors. This creates a standing noise floor in which deliberate bias hides (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). (b) Opacity and non-determinism. Without explainability, operators cannot tell a plausible from an anomalous prediction, and retraining non-determinism hampers reproducible verification for inspectors (OP.C0401, OP.C0402). (c) Automation trust. Per-pebble decisions at high throughput encourage over-trust and skill fade in spectral analysts, so an adversary can time a manipulation to when cross-checks lapse (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (d) Dual-use governance. Using one model for operations and for safeguards blurs ownership of the data security model, change control, and the independence expected from inspectors, so a single compromise yields correlated errors in both (OP.C0505, OP.C0505.01, OP.C0603, OP.C0502, OP.C0701). (e) Drift as cover. Operational drift and fuel-design or cooling-time changes outside the training range could degrade accuracy silently (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03), and a trusted but wrong estimate may only be discovered after burnup limits or inventory discrepancies arise.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, opacity, weak qualification, automation trust, dual-use MC&A bias, poisoning, and physical spectrum evasion; I merged these. I dropped panel-proposed codes that did not trace to a distinct threat (e.g., T0031/T0059 data-path tampering folded into input manipulation, T0012/T0049/T0025 stepping-stone speculation, T0024/T0044 model probing, OP.C0601 cloud dependency, OP.C0702.01 material substitution).

evidence.citation: "A Better Method to Calculate Fuel Burnup in Pebble Bed Reactors Using Machine Learning," Nuclear Technology (Taylor & Francis / American Nuclear Society), Vol. 209, No. 9; Brookhaven National Laboratory authors
evidence.note: The paper reports that machine-learning models trained on whole gamma spectra predict pebble burnup far better than the conventional photopeak (e.g. Cs-137) linear regression. This held across the measurement and cooling-time conditions tested, including operational-like ones. The models were trained and tested on simulated spectra, not measured reactor data. Related BNL/INMM reports on the same work (BNL-222105-2021-FORE, INMM 2021) describe the MLP, CNN and transformer comparison.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is the dual-use common-cause error or poisoning: a biased burnup regressor can falsify the MC&A record, mask diversion or misdeclared pebbles, and drive wrong discharge/recirculate decisions, which is a safeguards-falsification category harm. It falls just short of a direct radiological release because discharge errors are bounded by downstream checks.

reproducibility.why: The sim-to-real bias and silent out-of-distribution extrapolation are standing properties of simulation-trained whole-spectrum regressors and recur reliably whenever real detector effects or unusual pebbles are present; targeted poisoning or manipulation depends on additional conditions.

exploitability.why: The most damaging credible threats (poisoning of datasets, weights or updates, physical or data-path tampering, timing around lapsed cross-checks) need insider or supply-chain position and domain knowledge; only proxy-model reconnaissance and some denial paths are achievable externally.

affected_users.why: One model feeds every pebble's discharge decision and the facility's accountancy record, so a bias propagates across the fuel-handling chain and the safeguards inventory, though it stays within the fuel measurement and accountancy domain rather than affecting every plant system.

discoverability.why: The architectures, Serpent/GADRAS pipelines and the sim-only training basis are openly published, and sim-to-real gaps and out-of-distribution blind spots are well documented for this class of AI system, so a capable outsider can readily infer the weaknesses; exploiting them still requires facility-specific knowledge.

use_case: Modified VGG-19 deep convolutional neural network that takes a gamma spectrum from a radioactive waste drum and identifies which radionuclides are present. It is a multi-label classifier over the ten radionuclides most common in a radioactive waste management department (Am-241, Ba-133, Cd-109, Co-57, Co-60, Cs-137, Eu-152, Mn-54, and others). It is trained on simulated drum spectra with data augmentation. It is meant to automate waste-drum characterization with fewer detector calibration cycles.
incurred_insecurity:
A VGG-19 gamma-spectrum classifier trained only on simulated drum spectra sits upstream of waste acceptance, transport classification, and the declared inventory used for regulatory and safeguards records. It incurs mainly implicit risk: silent misidentification from the simulation-to-real gap, closed-set blindness, and erosion of calibration and human verification. Adversarial threats are spectral evasion by someone with physical access and poisoning or backdoors in the model or data pipeline. Each implicit weakness widens the room for an insider to misdeclare drum contents unnoticed.

Simulation-to-real gap -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained and tested only on simulated spectra, so real matrix attenuation, self-shielding, pile-up, detector resolution and background push inputs outside its training distribution. Nuclides are then missed or falsely reported, and drums are mis-categorised for storage or transport. An insider can choose geometries, shielding or masking sources that fall in this poorly covered region and rely on the model failing silently.

Closed ten-class label set -- implicit, exploitable
With no reject or unknown class, the multi-label output forces unlisted nuclides (Pu, U and Th series, Cs-134, Eu-154, and weak-gamma or beta and alpha emitters) into the nearest known class or drops them. Overlapping low-energy peaks and rare nuclides add false negatives, and the inventory looks clean when it is incomplete. An adversary can pick material outside the label set so the classifier reports a confident, benign answer.

Calibration erosion and automation trust -- implicit, exploitable
The goal of fewer calibration cycles removes the check that catches gain and energy-scale drift, while opaque CNN outputs, with no peak-level traceability, encourage over-trust and skill fade in manual spectrum analysis. Bias accumulates unseen until a downstream audit, and any common model reused across detectors or sites replicates it. An adversary can induce or wait for drift and time a misdeclaration for after analysts' vigilance has lapsed.

Lack of AI qualification and repeatability -- implicit
No AI-specific QA regime against standards-based methods is described, and retraining is non-deterministic, so a misidentification cannot easily be reproduced or explained for audit. This chiefly weakens investigation and accountability; it gives an adversary little direct pathway beyond the trust it already supports.

Spectral evasion by physical manipulation -- adversarial
An insider with access to the drum or detector can add decoy or masking sources, shield, or change geometry or the spectrum file so that a nuclide is suppressed or a decoy promoted. CNNs on spectra are sensitive to small perturbations, and a public architecture and label set ease building a proxy for transfer attacks. The result is a falsified waste declaration and possible concealment of regulated or special nuclear material.

Model and data-pipeline poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with the simulation data, augmentation scripts, retraining sets, or the pretrained VGG-19 weights can embed a backdoor, such as a spectral feature that suppresses a given nuclide, that passes validation because of model opacity. Because retraining is expected as detectors change, this exposure recurs.

Acquisition-path and record tampering -- adversarial
Altering spectra, preprocessing, binning or normalization between the analyser and the model, or corrupting its outputs, degrades the classifier without any model change and corrupts the waste inventory database. Loss of the tool forces a fall-back to manual characterization after skills have faded.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a waste-operations view, this classifier sits upstream of decisions that matter: drum characterization feeds waste acceptance criteria, transport classification, activity limits, dose-rate and package labeling, and the declared inventory kept for safeguards and regulatory records. The system is trained and tested only on simulated drum spectra, and the authors admit real sources, drums and standards are still untested. So the main risk is silent, systematic misidentification under real-world conditions (matrix attenuation, self-shielding, density heterogeneity, source geometry, detector resolution and gain drift, pile-up, and nuclides outside the ten classes). The stated goal of fewer calibration cycles weakens the very check that would reveal that drift. Existing practice offers protection: dose-rate surveys, scaling factors, NDA cross-checks, and acceptance sampling, but these only help if operators keep them independent and do not let a fast ML label replace them.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: simulated-only training (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303) means a model that scores well in-sim can fail on real drums, with errors in the matrix, geometry, shielding, and energy calibration. The consequence is missed or false nuclide calls, wrong activity or waste class, and wrong transport or storage category. A physical harm needs further failures: an inaccurate declaration that passes review, plus a dose-rate or surveillance check that misses the problem. (2) Closed-set limitation: only ten classes, so an unlisted nuclide (e.g. Pu, Sr-90 with no gamma signature, Ni-63, H-3, C-14, Cs-134, Eu-154, U or Th series) can be force-fit into the nearest class or ignored (OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03). Hard-to-detect beta and alpha emitters, plus shielded or low-energy emitters, are exactly where inventory error matters for safeguards and disposal. Multi-label thresholding of low-activity or overlapping peaks (Co-57/Ba-133/Am-241 in the low-energy region, Eu-152 complex lines) risks false positives and negatives, and a low base rate for rare nuclides adds to this (OP.C0202). (3) Calibration erosion: the 'fewer calibration cycles' rationale invites gain and resolution drift to go uncorrected (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Operators come to trust an opaque (OP.C0401) CNN output, and checks against standards or source checks lapse, so drift masks bias until a downstream audit. Deployment needs a QA regime for the AI (OP.C0501, OP.C0504); none is described. (4) Calibration across detectors: if one model is replicated to several detectors or sites, a common bias propagates (OP.C0602). Inference is deterministic but retraining is not (OP.C0402.01). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Evasion and manipulation of spectra (AML.T0015, T0043, T0043.003, T0041): an insider or adversary with physical access to the drum or detector could add small sources, shield the drum, or manipulate the spectrum or acquisition file so a nuclide is suppressed or a decoy is promoted. CNNs on spectral 'images' are sensitive to small perturbations. The consequence is a falsified waste declaration or a hidden diversion or mislabeling of material. This matters most where the model is the sole accepted characterization, and the safeguards concern is lower for waste than for fuel but real for Pu and Am-bearing waste. (6) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0059, OP.C0502): poisoning the simulation data, augmentation pipeline, or weights (backdoor triggered by a spectral feature) could produce targeted misses that pass validation. Public pre-trained VGG-19 weights are a supply-chain surface. (7) Integrity and availability of the records pipeline (AML.T0029, T0031): corruption of the output or the data feed leaves the waste inventory database inaccurate, and loss of the tool forces a fallback to manual characterization after calibration skills have faded (OP.C0101.06). Overall severity is moderate and indirect, because dose-rate checks and independent measurements exist; the risk is chiefly regulatory-inventory and transport-classification error that persists unnoticed.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a VGG-19 image-style CNN adapted to 1-D gamma spectra and trained and validated only on simulated drum spectra plus augmentation. The authors themselves say real sources, drums and standards are still untested. The central fragility is the simulation-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302). Simulated spectra (Monte Carlo-style) rarely capture detector-specific resolution, gain drift, dead time, pile-up, scattering and self-absorption in heterogeneous drum matrices, or ambient background. The pitch is fewer calibration cycles, which removes the very correction step that anchors real spectra to the training distribution. A multi-label softmax or sigmoid model over a closed set of ten nuclides has no principled way to say 'none of the above', so out-of-distribution inputs yield confident but wrong labels. Both the data provenance and the architecture's closed-world assumption are therefore weak points. Neither depends on an adversary, though an adversary could exploit both.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and calibration-drift failure (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). Energy-scale shifts, resolution changes, temperature effects and detector-to-detector heterogeneity are exactly what calibration cycles absorb. Removing them lets input drift past what the augmentation covered, and the model silently misclassifies. Consequence: a drum is wrongly characterized and may be routed to the wrong storage or transport category, with a nuclide missed or falsely reported. Waste-acceptance and transport-limit decisions depend on these labels. (2) Closed-world and low-base-rate blind spots (OP.C0403, OP.C0202, OP.C0701). Only ten classes are modelled. Unlisted nuclides, such as pure beta or alpha emitters seen only via weak gammas, shielded or low-activity sources, and heavily overlapping peaks like Eu-152 versus Co-60 or Am-241 versus Cd-109 at low energy, can be absorbed into the nearest known class. Rare isotopes and low-activity minority labels are underrepresented, and the multi-label calibration is unvalidated. Neither a confidence score nor a threshold is shown to be reliable. This is a content-fidelity and omission failure (OP.C0304.03). (3) Automation trust and qualification gaps (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0402). A CNN's per-label outputs are opaque, with no peak-level traceability to a gamma line a spectroscopist can verify. Retraining non-determinism and a lack of AI-specific qualification against standards-based methods encourage over-trust, and gradual skill fade in manual spectral analysis follows. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (4) Evasion by spectral manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). Someone with physical access can change the drum's presented spectrum, for example with shielding, source placement, or a masking or decoy source. The aim is to push the classifier below detection or to the wrong label, which would cause concealment or misdeclaration of waste contents, a safeguards-relevant outcome for fissile or special nuclear material in waste streams. A fixed, public architecture (VGG-19) and a published closed label set make a proxy model easy to build for black-box transfer attacks (AML.T0005, AML.T0043.002, AML.T0001). (5) Supply-chain and data integrity (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000). The pipeline depends on ImageNet-pretrained weights, simulation code and cross-section libraries, and augmentation scripts. A poisoned pretrained model, a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004), or a tampered simulation or retraining set could embed a blind spot for a specific signature, or a trigger peak that suppresses reporting. Because retraining is expected as detectors change, this is a recurring exposure. (6) Spectrum or software tampering upstream (AML.T0031, AML.T0076, OP.C0602). Changes to preprocessing, binning or normalization between the MCA and the model corrupt inputs with no model change at all. If one model is pushed across sites or detectors, a single flaw propagates fleet-wide, with correlated misclassification and no independent cross-check.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this classifier is a trust-concentration point in the waste-characterization chain. Its output feeds declarations of what is in a drum, and those declarations drive storage category, transport classification, shielding, accountancy and any safeguards or diversion-detection reasoning. The model is trained only on simulated spectra, with real sources, drums and standards still untested, so it has a built-in out-of-distribution weakness. An adversary, or an insider with a motive to hide or misdeclare material, gains from that weakness without ever touching the model. The stated goal of fewer calibration cycles is itself a security concern, because it removes a routine human checkpoint where detector drift, tampering or source substitution would otherwise be noticed. A nation-state would probably not target this directly, but an insider or a waste-stream smuggler could use it as a cheap way to launder what a drum contains.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by spectral manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043.003, T0043.001). An insider with physical access could place or shield small sources, add masking sources, or alter geometry so the drum spectrum falls outside the simulated training distribution. A CNN trained on idealized simulations can fail silently on these inputs, so a nuclide is missed or mislabeled. The dependent process is drum characterization for storage, transport and accountancy. The consequence is a false declaration, which means a transport or storage misclassification, and a possible concealment or diversion pathway for special nuclear or other regulated material that sits outside the ten-class label set. (2) Closed label set. Anything outside the ten nuclides (U, Pu, Np, fission and activation products) has no output class, so an adversary can exploit the model's blindness by choice of material. The classifier gives a clean-looking answer where it should flag an unknown. (3) Supply-chain and model integrity attacks (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004). A poisoned simulation dataset, a modified pre-trained VGG-19 weights file, or a backdoor trigger (a specific spectral feature that suppresses a nuclide) would be hard to see because of opacity. Simulated-data pipelines are a quiet, rarely audited insertion point. (4) Detector-side and data-path tampering (AML.T0031, T0059). Because the system is meant to reduce calibration, an adversary can induce gain or energy-scale drift, or alter spectra in the acquisition path, with less chance of human detection.

IMPLICIT, and timeable by an adversary. (a) Sim-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0501): the model is unvalidated on real drums, matrix attenuation, summing, and the real detector response. Misclassification rates will be higher in just the hard cases an adversary would choose. (b) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102): analysts who stop doing manual spectrum inspection lose the ability to spot anomalies, and an adversary can time a diversion for after complacency sets in. (c) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402): a misidentification can't be explained or reproduced for audit or investigation. (d) Overconfident output with no uncertainty (OP.C0403): multi-label thresholds give no calibrated unknown or reject class. (e) Small-data and low base-rate problem (OP.C0202, OP.C0701): rare-event nuclides are underrepresented.

Overall the exposure is moderate: the greatest risk is insider-enabled misdeclaration and erosion of manual verification rather than a sophisticated attack on the model itself.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulation-to-real gap, the closed ten-class set, calibration erosion with skill fade, and spectral evasion plus supply-chain poisoning. I dropped speculative codes (AML.T0029, AML.T0076, AML.T0001 and the public-weights reconnaissance angle) as weakly grounded, and kept the minor QA and repeatability point as implicit-only.

evidence.citation: "Applying Deep Learning in gamma-spectroscopy for radionuclide identification," Brazilian Journal of Radiation Sciences (BJRS)
evidence.note: The paper adapts the VGG-19 image-classification network to classify gamma spectra non-exclusively into ten radionuclide classes for radioactive waste management at IPEN (Brazil). It was built and tested on simulated spectra, and the authors say further tests with real sources, drums and standards are still needed. I read the abstract and the retrieved text of the article.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a falsified or incomplete waste declaration that conceals regulated or special nuclear material and mis-categorises drums for storage or transport, which is a safeguards-falsification and material-control category harm, though a single misidentification does not by itself cause a radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Simulation-to-real gap and closed-set blindness are structural, so out-of-distribution or unlisted nuclides reliably produce silent misclassification once real drums or off-label material are presented.

exploitability.why: The most credible exploitation (physical masking, shielding, off-label material, or pipeline tampering) requires insider or physical access to drums, detectors or the data pipeline, but no deep AI tooling because the implicit weaknesses do most of the work.

affected_users.why: Impact spans waste acceptance, transport classification and inventory records across a waste management department, and a shared model reused across detectors or sites can replicate bias, but it is mostly limited to the waste characterization chain rather than coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, label set and simulation-only training are published in the open literature, which also states that real-drum testing is still pending, and the sim-to-real gap, closed-set limits and CNN fragility are well-documented for this class of AI system.

use_case: Bidirectional LSTM anomaly detection on Asherah nuclear power plant simulator data. The model is trained only on normal operating data and flags abnormal behaviour caused by simulated cyberattacks on three different plant systems. Explainable AI is then used to show which signals drive each detection.
incurred_insecurity:
This simulator-trained, normal-only Bi-LSTM cyber-anomaly detector sits in the O&M monitoring path as an advisory, detect-only layer, so its main harm is false assurance and misdirected incident response rather than direct plant actuation. Its evidence of effectiveness is simulator-bound and rests on three author-chosen attacks. The main threats are sim-to-plant distribution failure, narrow validation, unreliable explanations, retraining and qualification gaps, and adversarial evasion, baseline poisoning, alarm-channel manipulation, model and pipeline tampering, and use of the explanations as reconnaissance.

Simulator-to-plant distribution gap -- implicit, exploitable
The model learned the 'normal' envelope of a simplified, noise-free simulator, so real load-following, outages, sensor ageing and calibration drift fall outside it. This produces either false-alarm floods and operator disuse, or loosened thresholds that let real attacks pass; an adversary can time an attack around the resulting alarm fatigue or threshold loosening, or disguise it as a legitimate transient.

Narrow validation and unknown coverage -- implicit, exploitable
Detection claims rest on three self-designed attacks, with thresholds tuned against known cases and no recall estimate for slow, low-amplitude, multi-channel or unseen attack classes. The 'detected before the protection system responded' result can create false confidence and reduce investment in conventional I&C and network security, which an adversary can rely on by choosing attack classes outside the tested set.

Explanation fidelity and operator over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
Feature attributions on a recurrent model are unstable and spread credit across correlated signals, so they may point at a downstream symptom rather than the attacked component. Operators who accept plausible rankings as root cause misdiagnose which system is compromised, and an adversary who can shape correlated signals can steer response toward the wrong subsystem.

Drift, retraining and qualification gaps -- implicit, exploitable
A non-deterministic learned component has no defined V&V path, versioning or drift governance, and its baseline goes stale after plant modifications, setpoint changes or sensor replacement. Retraining on recent 'normal' can quietly absorb a slow compromise, and an adversary can time an attack to the staleness or retraining window; if the tool later moves beyond advisory use, its lack of qualification and independence becomes a safety issue.

Detector evasion -- adversarial
An adversary or insider who knows or approximates the detection approach can craft slow, low-amplitude or process-plausible manipulations, or mimic legitimate transients, that stay under the anomaly threshold. The compromised plant then looks normal while operators trust the monitor.

Baseline and training-data poisoning -- adversarial
Seeding the historian or retraining data with attack-like behaviour, or drifting it gradually, teaches the model that attack signatures are normal. Because training is unlabeled and one-class, nothing cross-checks the baseline, and a backdoor trigger could also be planted.

Sensor and data-path spoofing -- adversarial
Replaying or falsifying the signals the model ingests lets the real process be manipulated while the detector sees normal data, and the same spoofing can distort the attributions shown to operators. The detector sits downstream of a compromised trust boundary.

Alarm flooding and denial of detection -- adversarial
Induced benign anomalies or chaff create alarm floods that push staff to desensitise, retune thresholds or disable the tool before the real attack, while denial of the monitoring service removes detection at the critical moment.

Model, threshold and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
Weights, scalers, thresholds, ML libraries and data stores are small, high-value targets with weaker controls than safety-class I&C, and a quiet change to a scaler or threshold blinds the detector. A tampered monitor can suppress alerts and give attackers a trusted channel.

Explanation output as reconnaissance -- adversarial
Attribution outputs and the simulator attack dataset reveal which signal channels drive detection and which are weakly weighted. If shared widely, they give an adversary a map for designing attacks that avoid the heavily weighted channels.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a simulator-trained, detect-only monitor for the O&M and cyber-defence layer, so a wrong output does not directly move rods or valves. The harm path is through operators and cyber/security staff who act on, or stop acting on, its alerts. The Asherah simulator is a simplified, noise-free generic PWR model. Normal-only training and three scripted attacks say little about real-plant data, which has load-following, outages, sensor degradation and calibration drift. For the model to contribute to real harm, the plant protection system, operator procedures and independent I&C defence-in-depth would also have to fail or be bypassed. The realistic risks are therefore false assurance, alarm fatigue, and an adversary who knows the detector exists and works around it.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT (no adversary needed). (1) Sim-to-real and distribution gap: normal-only training on clean simulator data means real operational transients (power maneuvers, startup/shutdown, maintenance lineups, instrument aging) fall outside the learned 'normal' distribution. The likely result is a high false-positive rate and alarm fatigue, leading operators to disuse or discount the tool. The facility consequence is that a true detection is ignored or delayed, even though the protection system is unaffected. (2) Narrow validation: three attack types on three systems give almost no coverage of the attack space, such as slow stealthy manipulations, attacks that mimic plausible process dynamics, or sensor-spoofing coordinated across channels. Detection before the protection system acted could be an artifact of the simulator and of attack parameters chosen by the authors. A false sense of coverage could reduce investment in conventional network/I&C security. (3) XAI fidelity: feature-attribution explanations on a Bi-LSTM can be unstable or misleading. Operators or analysts may over-trust a plausible-looking signal ranking and misdiagnose which system is compromised versus which has a genuine fault. That can send response effort to the wrong subsystem or lead to a wrong plant-state judgment during an incident. Explanations are also hard to qualify under nuclear QA. (4) Qualification and governance gap: an LSTM is not deterministic in the way safety-classified software must be. Retraining, versioning and drift monitoring are undefined, and there are no clear criteria for how the tool relates to safety-class I&C. If it is later integrated beyond advisory use, the lack of independence and qualification becomes a safety issue. ADVERSARIAL. (5) Evasion: an adversary with knowledge of the model or of the detection approach can craft low-and-slow or in-distribution manipulations, or replay-style sensor injections, so the anomaly score stays under threshold (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). A compromised plant can then look 'normal' to the detector while operators trust it. (6) Training-data or baseline poisoning: if the 'normal' data used for periodic retraining or recalibration is gathered from a plant already compromised, or manipulated gradually, the attack becomes part of the baseline (AML.T0020, AML.T0031). (7) Alert-channel manipulation: spamming chaff or inducing benign-looking perturbations can create alarm floods or desensitize staff ahead of a real attack, while a denial of the monitoring service removes detection at the critical moment (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). (8) New attack surface: the monitor ingests plant data and sits on the OT/IT boundary. Its servers, data pipeline and model artifacts become targets for supply-chain or model tampering (AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0076). A tampered monitor can suppress alerts or give attackers a trusted channel. Existing defence-in-depth, the hardwired protection system and operator training limit direct physical consequence, so the main exposure is degraded cyber situational awareness and delayed or misdirected incident response.

ai_engineer.argument: From the ML pipeline view, this system is a one-class (normal-only) Bi-LSTM reconstruction/forecast detector trained and evaluated entirely on Asherah simulator data, with attacks that the authors themselves designed and injected. Its fragility lies in three things: the simulator-to-plant data gap (the 'normal' manifold is a simplified physics model, not a real plant's noisy sensors, ageing and transients), the evaluation design (three known attack scenarios, so reported detection-before-protection-system results say little about unseen attack classes or adaptive adversaries), and the XAI layer, which adds a second model-dependent output that operators may trust more than it deserves. A Bi-LSTM also uses a window with future context, so it is not natively causal. Real-time latency claims, such as 'detected before the plant protection system responded', depend on windowing and buffering choices that are not guaranteed to hold in deployment. The architecture sits in the O&M monitoring path, so both its false negatives and its false positives matter.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulator-to-plant transfer and OOD failure: the model learns the simulator's normal operating envelope. On real plant data, sensor noise, calibration drift, fuel-cycle ageing, maintenance configurations, load-following and legitimate transients fall outside that envelope. The result is either a flood of false alarms leading to alarm fatigue and disuse, or a threshold loosened until real attacks pass unflagged (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (2) Normal-only training with a small, author-chosen attack set: the detection claim rests on three simulated attacks, so there is no basis for estimating recall on novel, slow, low-amplitude or multi-system attacks, and thresholds are tuned post hoc against known attacks (OP.C0202, OP.C0403). (3) Concept and operational drift: after a retrain, a plant modification, a setpoint change or a sensor replacement, the learned baseline goes stale. Retraining on 'recent normal' data can silently absorb a slow-moving compromise into the baseline (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0501). (4) Explainability limits: attribution methods such as SHAP or gradient-based ones on recurrent models are unstable, correlated signals share credit, and the explanation can point at a downstream symptom rather than the attacked component. This misdirects operator diagnosis, and operators may treat plausible-looking attributions as validated root cause (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0402.02). (5) Qualification gap: the model is a non-deterministic learned component with no established V&V path for I&C-adjacent use, and its training is not reproducible bit-for-bit (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0504).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Evasion by an adversary who knows or approximates the detector: low-and-slow manipulation, or crafting perturbations that stay within the reconstruction-error threshold, especially if the signal set and architecture can be inferred from publications or plant documentation. An attacker can also stage an attack to mimic legitimate transients (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0005, AML.T0001, AML.T0000). (b) Poisoning of the 'normal' training or retraining data. An adversary already inside the historian or data pipeline can seed the baseline with attack-like behaviour so that it is later classified as normal. Because the model is trained only on normal data and there are no labels, nothing in the pipeline cross-checks the data (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059, AML.T0018.000). (c) Integrity attack on the sensor and data path feeding the model. Spoofing the same signals the model relies on defeats detection and can also mislead the XAI output, which could be used to steer operators toward the wrong component (AML.T0031, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0067). (d) Model and artifact supply chain: the weights, preprocessing scalers, thresholds and ML libraries are all targets, since a small change to a threshold or scaler silently blinds the detector (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018, AML.T0076). (e) Deliberate alarm-flooding or chaff to cause false-positive fatigue before the real attack, or to push operators into disabling the monitor (AML.T0046, AML.T0029, OP.C0102). (f) Disclosure of model behaviour or the simulator-derived attack dataset, which provides a map of what is and is not detected (AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002). Overall the dominant exposure is that the evidence of effectiveness is simulator-bound, so the real risk is unknown coverage rather than a known defect, and an adversary can time an attack around the model's baseline staleness.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, a cyber-anomaly detector for O&M changes the threat surface in three ways: it concentrates operator trust in a detection layer worth compromising or evading, it adds a data and model pipeline that an insider can reach, and its XAI output hands an adversary a map of which signals the defender watches. The documented result is simulator-only, trained on normal data, and tested against three attacks the researchers chose themselves.
