Detecting those attacks before the plant protection system reacts shows the approach is promising, but it says little about an adaptive adversary who knows the detector exists. A capable adversary would probably not attack the LSTM directly. It would shape its actions to stay inside the learned normal envelope, or exploit the false-alarm and complacency dynamics the model creates.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by a knowledgeable or insider adversary (AML.T0015, T0043). A normal-only model learns a boundary around observed behaviour. An attacker who understands the process, such as an insider with operator or I&C knowledge, can make slow, low-amplitude or process-plausible manipulations that stay within learned normal variance, or can mimic legitimate transients. Result: an attack on plant systems goes undetected while operators believe a detector covers it, so false assurance is the real consequence. (2) Explainability as reconnaissance (AML.T0024, T0063, T0013). Feature-attribution output shows which sensor and signal channels drive detection, and therefore which channels the model is blind to or weakly weights. If this reaches broad audiences, vendors or shared dashboards, it helps an adversary design attacks that avoid the heavily weighted signals. (3) Integrity of training data and the model (AML.T0020, T0018, T0010, T0031). 'Normal' baselines are collected from plant or simulator data and retrained as the plant changes. An insider or supply-chain actor who poisons the baseline during a retraining window can teach the model that attack signatures are normal, or can plant a backdoor trigger. The model artifact and its data store are small, high-value targets with weaker controls than safety-classified systems. (4) Sensor-layer spoofing (AML.T0043.003). If the attacker controls the data feed, the detector can be fed replayed or falsified normal-looking data while the real process is manipulated. The detector then sits downstream of a compromised trust boundary. (5) Denial or degradation of detection (AML.T0029, T0046). Chaff or induced benign anomalies can cause alarm floods, which are then used to push operators or management to desensitise, retune thresholds or disable the tool, and to time the real attack around that. (6) Insider access to thresholds and configuration. Detection thresholds are a single tunable parameter, and a quiet change of that value would pass unnoticed. IMPLICIT, exploitable. (a) Simulator-to-plant gap (OP.C0201.01, C0302, C0303). Training and testing on Asherah simulator data with three authored attacks gives no field evidence on real noise, sensor faults, maintenance states, fuel-cycle drift or unseen attack types. Detection coverage is narrow and unknown outside the tested attacks, while the headline claim of beating the protection system may suggest more than has been shown. (b) False positives and alarm fatigue (OP.C0102, C0101). A normal-only model flags every novel but benign condition such as outages, calibration and power manoeuvres. Operators learn to dismiss alerts, which an adversary can time an attack around. The opposite also holds: the detector's silence may suppress human vigilance (OP.C0101.04). (c) XAI fidelity (OP.C0401, C0304). Attribution outputs can be unstable or misleading, and may rationalise a detection for operators with a spurious but plausible story, which misdirects incident response toward the wrong system. (d) Concept drift and retraining governance (OP.C0302.01, C0501, C0502). Retraining on drifting 'normal' without strong QA creates the poisoning window described above. Regulatory scope for non-safety cyber monitoring AI is unclear (OP.C0503, C0504), so controls are weaker than for safety systems. A nation-state would likely prefer simpler paths (supply chain, IT/OT foothold) and treat the detector as an obstacle to blind, not a target to defeat, so its main risk is the false assurance it creates.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-plant gap, narrow three-attack validation, XAI fidelity, retraining and qualification gaps, and on evasion, baseline poisoning, alarm flooding and artifact tampering. I kept the security specialist's explanation-as-reconnaissance threat as distinct, and dropped weakly supported codes such as AML.T0005, AML.T0001, AML.T0000, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0012, AML.T0067 and OP.C0503 because no synthesized threat concretely instantiates them.

evidence.citation: "Anomaly Detection and Analysis in Nuclear Power Plants," MDPI (Electronics, vol. 13, no. 22)
evidence.note: The authors launched three cyberattacks against different systems of the Asherah NPP simulator and collected the resulting data. They trained a Bi-LSTM on normal data. It detected the attacks before the plant protection system responded. They then applied XAI to explain how individual features contribute to the anomaly detections.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is detector evasion or blinding (via sensor spoofing, baseline poisoning, or tampering) that gives false assurance while a cyber manipulation of plant systems proceeds. Because the tool is advisory and detect-only, it does not directly cause a release; the harm is eroded safety margin and misdirected response, which can contribute to serious consequences but stops short of a direct release.

reproducibility.why: The implicit failures (sim-to-plant gap, drift, narrow coverage) occur reliably once the model is deployed on real plant data. The adversarial threats (evasion, poisoning, tampering) depend on conditions such as knowledge of the approach, access to the data path, or a retraining window.

exploitability.why: The most credible adversarial paths (poisoning the historian, tampering with weights or thresholds, spoofing the sensor data path) need privileged OT or insider access and process knowledge. Only the alarm-fatigue timing and reconnaissance paths need less access.

affected_users.why: A blinded or misleading monitor degrades cyber-detection across the plant systems it covers and misdirects the whole response team. It remains an advisory layer without direct actuation, which limits propagation to coupled control systems.

discoverability.why: Sim-to-plant gaps, one-class detector limitations, adversarial evasion, poisoning, and attribution instability are well documented in the open literature for this class of AI system. The source paper is public and states its attack set and the XAI-identified signal channels, though the weaknesses of a specific deployment would still require partial inference.

use_case: Multilayer-perceptron deep neural network that predicts the thermal conductivity of neutron-irradiated uranium-molybdenum (U-Mo) low-enriched nuclear fuel. It is trained on historic Advanced Test Reactor irradiation-test and post-irradiation-examination data. Inputs include Mo concentration, depletion, fission density, fission power, heat flux, neutron flux and temperature. It lets researchers probe how thermal conductivity depends on irradiation conditions without prior knowledge of the microstructure, and so supports fuel performance modelling and experiment planning.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline, research-grade MLP surrogate for irradiated U-Mo thermal conductivity sits upstream of fuel performance codes, irradiation-test design and fuel qualification evidence, not in any control or protection path. Its main insecurity is quiet corruption of design inputs: implicitly through extrapolation, confounded learning, weak data provenance and over-trust of an unqualified model, and adversarially through tampering with the small training dataset or the model artifacts. Credible harm is a biased conductivity baseline that understates fuel temperature margin in the qualification record, not a direct safety-system failure.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation and confounding -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on a few correlated ATR campaigns with no microstructural inputs, the MLP returns smooth but unsupported conductivities at high burnup, in transients, or for other reactors and geometries. It can also learn spurious dependencies among collinear inputs (power, flux, depletion, fission density), so planners read correlation as physics. An adversary could place a subtle bias in a region the model cannot validate, where it would pass as ordinary model error.

Data provenance and measurement uncertainty -- implicit, exploitable
Labels come from PIE and temperature-inferred conductivities with uncertainty, manually compiled historic records and possibly modelled inputs, and these errors are baked in without propagation to the output. Retraining depends on scarce new irradiation data. The weak lineage and manual curation give an insider an opportunity to alter a few records unnoticed.

Opacity, over-trust and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The MLP gives no mechanistic explanation or calibrated uncertainty, has no nuclear-QA qualification path, and has seed-dependent training with weak versioning. Researchers may over-trust its curves and embed it in fuel performance codes or safety-case arguments without confirming experiments. An adversary can rely on that misplaced trust and on the poor reproducibility to hide tampering or drift among normal variation.

Cascading propagation through downstream codes -- implicit, exploitable
A shared model or toolchain feeding multiple fuel performance codes and labs spreads any bias silently into temperature, swelling and margin calculations. An adversary needs to compromise only one widely used artifact to affect many analyses.

Data and model integrity tampering -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor could alter PIE records, preprocessing scripts, the checkpoint or ML dependencies so the learned conductivity surface is non-conservative in a targeted regime, for example high burnup. With so small a dataset the shift is hard to detect, can be timed to a qualification submission or test-planning milestone, and would later be attributed to natural scatter.

Reconnaissance and data or model extraction -- adversarial
The open preprint and journal paper disclose inputs, ATR data origin and qualification data gaps, and theft of the PIE data or model, or model inversion, could expose U-Mo performance characteristics relevant to a sensitive LEU conversion programme. This is an information-security and IP concern rather than a direct hazard, since the fuel is LEU and the inputs are physical parameters under engineer control, not an exposed API.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline, research-grade surrogate for U-Mo thermal conductivity. It sits in design and experiment planning and is not in any real-time control or protection path. Harm therefore comes from a wrong number propagating into fuel performance codes (e.g., BISON/MOOSE-type temperature and swelling calculations), irradiation-test design, or licensing-support arguments. Several independent safeguards would also have to fail before it caused real harm: code-to-experiment benchmarking, conservative design margins, in-pile thermocouple monitoring, PIE, and regulator review of the fuel qualification basis. The dominant risks are implicit: a small, narrow, ATR-specific dataset, extrapolation, and a black-box model that gets treated as physics. An adversary would mostly matter by quietly corrupting the data or model so that a subtly optimistic conductivity enters the qualification record.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
1) Out-of-distribution extrapolation (implicit). The training data come from a limited set of ATR irradiations covering a narrow range of Mo content, fission density, power and temperature. Because the model takes no microstructural input, it cannot represent phenomena such as interaction-layer growth, fission-gas bubble interconnection, recrystallization or swelling breakaway. It may also give smooth but wrong values at high burnup, in transients, or for new geometries and different reactors. Downstream, experiment planning or fuel performance models could take an overestimated conductivity and under-predict centerline temperature, or the reverse, and over-conservatism could waste irradiation slots. The inputs are also correlated (heat flux, power, flux, depletion), so the network can learn spurious dependencies. Reasonable-looking sensitivity studies would then give false physical insight. (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03)

2) Data provenance and quality (implicit, and exploitable). The labels derive from PIE measurements and from temperature-inferred conductivities that carry measurement uncertainty, and the temperature inputs may be modeled rather than measured. Historic records may have inconsistent reconstruction or unclear provenance. Any error in the compiled dataset is baked into the model invisibly, and it is a tempting place for an insider or supply-chain actor to tamper in a way that survives review. The result is a biased conductivity baseline in the qualification evidence. (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0204, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059)

3) Opacity and qualification gap (implicit). An MLP gives no mechanistic explanation and often no calibrated uncertainty. It also has no established QA path comparable to a validated correlation under nuclear QA programmes. Researchers may use it beyond its research purpose, for example by embedding it in a fuel performance code or citing it in a safety-case argument. Automation bias is likely because the predictions look more accurate than the physics-based models they replace. Retraining non-determinism and version drift can also make results hard to reproduce. (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502, OP.C0303)

4) Adversarial surface (lower likelihood, but plausible). Direct manipulation of the model weights, training pipeline or distributed model files (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076) could bias outputs in a particular regime. Adversarial inputs matter little here because the inputs are physical parameters under operator control. The main concerns are integrity attacks on stored artifacts and on the dataset. The model and the data could also be proprietary or export-sensitive, so extraction or theft of the data (AML.T0025, AML.T0024.002) is an IP and nonproliferation-adjacent concern, though the fuel is LEU. A shared model or toolchain propagating across labs and codes would spread any corruption widely (OP.C0602, OP.C0603).

5) Consequence framing. Credible harm is a degraded fuel qualification or design basis: unexpected fuel temperatures, reduced margin, failed or inconclusive irradiation tests, and eroded confidence in test results. It is not a direct safety-system failure. Mitigations include treating the model as a screening tool, benchmarking it against physics-based correlations, reporting uncertainty and applicability bounds, and controlling data and model integrity.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline standpoint this is a small-tabular-data regression surrogate (an MLP over 7 features) trained on a narrow, expensive, and non-iid dataset: a limited number of ATR irradiation campaigns, with many correlated PIE measurements per sample or capsule. The main fragility is data-driven, not architectural. The model is trained and validated on historic ATR conditions (a particular flux spectrum, geometry, Mo range, and burnup envelope), but it is explicitly pitched as a way to explore dependence on irradiation conditions 'without microstructure'. That invites extrapolation beyond the training envelope, where an MLP has no inherent physics constraints and no calibrated uncertainty. The MLP can encode confounded correlations between the inputs (fission density, depletion, power and temperature move together). Researchers may therefore read spurious sensitivities as causal ones when planning experiments or calibrating fuel performance codes. The use sits in design and R&D rather than real-time control, but its outputs feed into fuel performance models and qualification evidence, so errors propagate quietly into downstream codes and licensing-relevant material property correlations.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Small-data and OOD generalization failure (OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03): few irradiation campaigns, correlated samples, and train/test splits that leak across the same capsule or campaign inflate apparent accuracy. Inference outside the ATR spectrum, burnup, Mo content, or temperature range, for example a different reactor, fuel geometry, or accident-like transient, silently yields confident but unsupported conductivity values. Nothing in a plain MLP flags this. (2) Data provenance and measurement issues (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0204): the PIE and in-pile data carry measurement uncertainty, inferred rather than measured conductivities, and historical record gaps. Those errors are baked in and not propagated to the output, and retraining depends on scarce, slow new irradiation data. (3) Physics-opacity and confounding (OP.C0401, OP.C0403): with no microstructural inputs, the model cannot represent phenomena such as swelling, porosity, interaction layers, or recrystallization that actually drive conductivity. Learned sensitivities are therefore correlational, and researchers may over-trust them (OP.C0101.04). (4) Qualification and repeatability gaps (OP.C0303, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501, OP.C0502): the model is a research artifact with seed-dependent training, no formal QA or software-engineering pipeline, and no versioning. If it is used to feed fuel performance codes or experiment design, the unqualified predictions become embedded in the licensing-relevant evidence chain. Cascading error into downstream codes (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01) means a biased conductivity could understate fuel centerline temperatures and erode safety margins in the design basis.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS (lower likelihood, but real for a data-centric R&D artifact). (a) Training data or dataset poisoning and integrity erosion (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059): the small dataset means a handful of altered PIE records, or an altered preprocessing or normalization script, can shift the learned conductivity surface in a targeted region, for example making high-burnup fuel look more conductive. At this scale the change would be hard to detect and could be timed to a fuel qualification or experiment-planning decision. (b) Model or weights tampering and supply chain compromise (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003): public preprint and journal code or weights, and reliance on common ML libraries, give an attack path. A modified checkpoint or dependency could be passed around among researchers and fuel performance groups. (c) Reconnaissance and proprietary data exposure (AML.T0000, AML.T0024.001, AML.T0037): the published method signals which operating conditions are available, and model inversion or the underlying PIE data can reveal U-Mo fuel performance characteristics, which is relevant to a sensitive LEU conversion program. (d) Adversarial inputs matter less here, since inputs come from engineers rather than an exposed API. The more realistic input manipulation is on the upstream simulation or experimental parameters feeding the model (AML.T0043.003), which would shape the 'what-if' conclusions that experiment planners draw.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view this is a low-value direct target. It is an offline, research-grade surrogate model that sits in design and experiment planning, with no actuation path to a running plant. The threat surface it does create is indirect: it sits upstream of fuel performance codes, fuel qualification evidence and test-matrix decisions. A patient adversary, or an insider with write access to the training data or model file, could bias thermal conductivity predictions in a way that is hard to see and that persists quietly into design margins, licensing submissions and irradiation experiment choices. Because the model is opaque, small in data terms (a limited set of ATR campaigns), and published openly with a preprint and a journal paper, it is also useful for reconnaissance. It reveals the inputs and data lineage of LEU research-reactor fuel qualification, and it invites trust beyond its validated domain.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity attack on data or model. The training set is small, curated and historic, and PIE data are manually compiled. An insider, or someone who compromises the supply chain for the data, the model file or the ML software stack, could introduce subtle label or feature bias, or a backdoored or modified model. The AI failure mechanism is a systematic bias in the predicted conductivity. The facility dependency is the fuel performance models, thermal margin calculations and experiment design that consume it. The consequence is non-conservative fuel temperature predictions and understated centreline temperature margin, which affect safety analysis and fuel qualification credibility. The effect would surface late, perhaps only in a later irradiation test or an anomaly review, and the result would be attributed to natural scatter. (2) Concentration of trust. If the surrogate is embedded in multi-physics workflows or used to screen experiments, a single compromised artifact propagates silently through downstream codes (OP.C0603, OP.C0602). (3) Reconnaissance value. Published model inputs, data origin (ATR) and trained-model behaviour disclose fuel design sensitivities and qualification data gaps, and a model inversion or extraction attempt could add to that. This is mostly an information-security and proliferation-sensitivity concern, not a direct hazard, and its level depends on whether the data are export-controlled or sensitive (OP.C0505, OP.C0505.01). (4) Targeted exploitation of decision timing. An adversary could time data tampering to coincide with a qualification submission or an experiment-planning milestone.

IMPLICIT (exploitable): (a) Small-data and low base-rate problem with limited coverage of burnup, temperature and Mo-content space. Extrapolation outside the training distribution gives confident but wrong values, and nothing in the model flags this (OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). (b) Opacity. Without microstructural inputs, the MLP cannot show whether a prediction is physically plausible, so tampering or drift cannot easily be told from real physics (OP.C0401, OP.C0301). (c) Automation trust. Researchers who 'probe' trends may over-trust smooth model curves and skip confirming experiments, which erodes vigilance (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101). (d) Qualification and hygiene gaps. A research model used for design lacks AI-specific QA, version control and data lineage, which makes unauthorized changes hard to detect (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0201.05). (e) Non-repeatability from training randomness, which complicates integrity verification (OP.C0402.01). Overall risk is modest, with the main concern being quiet integrity corruption of design inputs, not dramatic compromise.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on small-data OOD extrapolation, provenance, opacity/over-trust, qualification gaps and quiet integrity tampering of data or model. I dropped weakly argued codes (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0037, AML.T0025, AML.T0031, AML.T0076, OP.C0505, OP.C0505.01) because the inputs are not exposed to adversaries and no direct text-supported mechanism was shown, and I treated downstream propagation as a distinct implicit threat.

evidence.citation: "A machine learning approach to thermal conductivity modeling: A case study on irradiated uranium-molybdenum nuclear fuels," Computational Materials Science (Elsevier), authored at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory and Idaho National Laboratory, record hosted by OSTI/DOE
evidence.note: The paper builds and validates a multilayer perceptron on historic U-Mo irradiation-test and post-irradiation-examination data. The model predicts irradiated-fuel thermal conductivity as a function of reactor operating and material conditions, and does not need microstructural inputs. A preprint (arXiv 1901.00722) of the same work exists, but the peer-reviewed journal version is cited here.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is quiet corruption of design and qualification inputs (a non-conservative conductivity baseline that erodes fuel temperature margin in the safety case), which is a minor safety-margin erosion rather than a direct release or safeguards falsification, since the model is offline and outside any control or protection path.

reproducibility.why: Extrapolation and confounding failures occur reliably whenever the model is used outside its narrow training envelope, but a targeted tampering effect depends on the model being adopted into a qualification or planning workflow and on timing.

exploitability.why: Adversarial manipulation needs insider or supply-chain access to curated PIE records, preprocessing scripts or checkpoints, since the model has no exposed API, though the implicit failures need no attacker at all.

affected_users.why: A biased artifact shared across several fuel performance codes and labs could propagate into temperature and margin calculations (the cascading-propagation threat), but it stays confined to research and qualification analyses for one fuel type rather than facility-wide operations.

discoverability.why: The open paper and preprint disclose inputs, data origin and data gaps, and the weaknesses of small-data MLP surrogates (extrapolation, opacity, poisoning) are well documented in the literature, although finding the actual data and artifacts to tamper with needs more specific knowledge.

use_case: Convolutional neural network that reads ultrasonic testing (UT) scans of CANDU reactor fuel channel pressure tubes during outage inspection. It takes grouped ultrasonic waveforms as a multi-channel input and classifies each scan point as flaw or no flaw. A post-processor then uses estimated depth to cut false positives. Analysts do the final sizing and typing of each flaw. It is built as a proof of concept to shorten outages and reduce the cost of manual scan analysis.
incurred_insecurity:
A CNN plus depth-based post-processor decides which UT scan points of CANDU pressure tubes analysts examine, so its main insecurity is a silent missed flaw that no downstream step re-checks. Implicit threats are false-negative bias, label and data limits, drift, post-processor coupling, automation complacency and a qualification gap. Adversarial threats are integrity attacks on training data, model, thresholds or scan data, evasion through the acquisition path, supply-chain compromise and reconnaissance via the published work. The common consequence is an undetected pressure-tube flaw and eroded fitness-for-service margin that looks like ordinary model error.

Detection-gate integrity attack -- adversarial
Poisoning historical scans or labels, tampering with CNN weights or backdoor-triggering waveform patterns, or altering post-processor thresholds, creates a blind spot for chosen flaw morphologies, depths or tube locations. Flaws in those regions are never flagged for analyst review, and the miss is attributable to normal AI limits.

Insider and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
An insider or valid-account holder with write access to scan files, the depth filter or the flagged-flaw list can suppress indications without touching the model, and the missed flaw can be blamed on model limitations. Supply-chain compromise of ML frameworks, pretrained components or vendor software offers the same effect.

Evasion via acquisition data path -- adversarial
A compromised acquisition system or probe-data path could inject small waveform perturbations that exploit the CNN's brittleness so a real flaw reads as no-flaw, while a human reviewer would still see it. This is an offline tool, so the pathway is narrower.

Reconnaissance and proxy replication -- adversarial
The published architecture and dataset description let an adversary build a proxy model and learn its blind spots, for example how the depth filter suppresses shallow flaws, to prepare evasion or poisoning.

Automation bias and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Analysts reviewing only flagged points under outage-schedule pressure drift from independent analysis to confirmation and lose the ability to catch misses, while the low false-positive rate builds unearned trust. An adversary could time tampering for when attention is lowest and rely on the missing independent full-data check.

False-positive tuning versus sensitivity -- implicit, exploitable
Tuning the CNN and depth post-processor to cut false positives trades off against recall, the safety-critical property, and a depth misestimate discards true small or shallow flaws before any analyst sees them. Errors compound between the two stages, and an adversary could hide manipulation inside the filter's already-suppressed band.

Label quality and rare-flaw scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Ground truth is prior analyst calls rather than metallurgical truth, and safety-significant flaws are rare and heterogeneous, so recall on them is poorly estimated and aggregate metrics hide it. An adversary could target the underrepresented flaw types, knowing the model is weakest there and that training data are small enough to be poisoned cheaply.

Drift and novel degradation -- implicit, exploitable
Probe, couplant, calibration, tooling, tube-age and new degradation-mode shifts move waveforms outside the training envelope, and a fixed CNN gives no drift signal, so recall degrades silently. An adversary could hide gradual waveform manipulation inside that degradation band, where anomalies are expected.

Qualification, opacity and scope creep -- implicit, exploitable
There is no established qualification path, POD evidence or explainability for a deep-learning waveform classifier, and retraining invalidates prior evidence. A proof of concept can slide from advisory to de facto gate, and an adversary could rely on the lack of verifiability to keep tampering undetectable.

Inspection data exposure via ML environment -- implicit, exploitable
Copying inspection history and flaw maps into ML training and storage environments, possibly off-site, widens the access surface to sensitive pressure-tube condition data. An adversary could use it for sabotage planning or to craft targeted manipulation.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view this is a screening aid on a pressure-boundary inspection: the CNN triages UT scan points, a depth-based post-processor suppresses false positives, and analysts still do final sizing and typing. That human-in-the-loop design is a real safeguard, but the AI's most damaging failure is a missed flaw (a false negative). A false negative never reaches the analyst's attention, so the analyst cannot catch it. Over time, analyst attention shifts toward AI-flagged regions, and the AI's apparent low false-positive rate builds trust, which makes this failure mode silent. The downstream consequence is a pressure tube with an undetected flaw, such as a hydride blister, crack-like flaw, or fretting or debris mark, staying in service. This erodes fitness-for-service margins and fuel channel integrity assurance. The system is also a proof of concept trained on historical scans, so the main risks are qualification, data representativeness and automation-bias gaps. Adversarial exposure exists but is narrower: tampering with scan data, training data, or the post-processor thresholds.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Missed-flaw false negatives and automation bias. The CNN and the depth post-processor are tuned to cut false positives, which pushes the operating point toward missed detections. Analysts who see only flagged points may stop reviewing the full scan, so skill fades and reliance grows. Any real flaw the model misses is then unlikely to be caught by the human step. Safeguard that must also fail: independent full-data review, or a qualified procedure that requires it. (2) Training data limits. Historical scans and recorded inspection results carry the labeling errors, sizing uncertainty and bias of past analysts. Real service-induced flaws are rare, so the data are small and imbalanced. Some flaw types or tube conditions may be underrepresented, which hides weak performance on exactly the cases that matter most. (3) Drift and out-of-distribution input. Probe or tooling changes, couplant or calibration differences, scan-head wear, different tubes or stations, and ageing-driven changes in tube condition (e.g. hydrogen equivalent concentration, new flaw morphology) can shift the waveforms. A fixed CNN has no built-in way to show it has drifted. The depth post-processor adds a second hard-coded layer. Its depth estimate error can wrongly discard true small or shallow flaws, so errors cascade between the CNN and the post-processor. (4) Qualification gap. Inspection qualification for pressure tubes (e.g. CSA N285.4 and CSA N285.5-style performance demonstration of the technique, equipment and personnel) was written for conventional techniques. A non-explainable CNN with a trained threshold has no established equivalent. If it were used beyond proof of concept, an unqualified tool could influence fitness-for-service and licensing decisions. Retraining or model changes would also invalidate prior qualification evidence. (5) Outage schedule pressure. The aim of shortening outages and cutting cost creates an incentive to widen the AI's role and shrink analyst review. This interacts with the automation-bias problem. ADVERSARIAL THREATS (narrower). (6) Integrity attack on the data pipeline. Someone with access to the scan files, the labeled training set or the model weights could poison or modify them, or alter the post-processor thresholds, so that flaws in chosen locations are not flagged. This is subtle, may be unnoticed, and could hide safety-significant degradation or support later sabotage. Insider risk is the most plausible vector, and supply-chain compromise of the ML tooling is another. (7) Delay or denial. Corrupting or taking down the analysis workstation during an outage costs schedule, but the manual analysis fallback limits the consequence. (8) Confidentiality of inspection data. Pressure-tube condition and flaw maps are sensitive for security and commercial reasons, and the ML environment widens where they are stored and copied. Existing engineering practice (manual analysis, independent verification, and fitness-for-service evaluation with margins) bounds the consequence if the AI remains advisory with full-data analyst review retained.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a supervised CNN trained on historical CANDU pressure-tube UT scans, with labels taken from past analyst inspection records, so its ceiling is the quality of those labels and the coverage of that archive. Flaws that matter for pressure-tube integrity (e.g., hydrogen-related features, fretting, debris marks, crack-like indications) are rare and heterogeneous, so the positive class is small and skewed towards historically seen, benign-ish types. The system is a detector for historically recorded flaws, not a general anomaly detector. Its fragility is at the data boundary: new probe or instrument hardware, calibration changes, couplant and surface conditions, tube-to-tube and reactor-age variation, and newly emerging degradation modes all produce inputs the model never saw. The architecture (multi-channel waveform CNN plus a depth-based false-positive post-processor) adds a second, hand-tuned stage that can suppress true flaws when depth estimates are wrong. Even with analysts doing final sizing and typing, the model decides which scan points they see, so a missed detection is never examined and is invisible downstream.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Label and provenance limits: ground truth is prior analyst calls, not independently verified destructive or metallurgical truth. Analyst biases, missed flaws and inconsistent historical criteria are baked in as 'truth', and the model reproduces them with confidence (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0202). Few positive examples of safety-significant flaws means recall on rare types is poorly estimated, and aggregate low-false-positive metrics hide this. (2) Distribution shift: scans from different campaigns, probe generations, acquisition electronics, calibration settings, noise floors and aging tubes differ from the training set. Silent degradation of recall without any obvious error signal (OP.C0302, .01, .03, OP.C0303). Novel degradation mechanisms are structurally undetectable, since the classifier only knows the flaw/no-flaw boundary learned from past data. (3) Post-processor coupling: the depth-based false-positive filter is a second model whose errors compound with the CNN's. A flaw misestimated as too shallow or out of the depth window is discarded before any analyst sees it (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01, OP.C0301 for the false-positive-reduction objective trading off against missed-flaw risk). (4) Automation bias and skill fade: analysts reviewing only machine-flagged regions, under outage-schedule pressure (the stated purpose is shorter outages), shift from independent analysis to confirmation, and lose the ability to catch what the model misses (OP.C0101.04, .06, OP.C0102). Partial-region detection ('finds at least part of each flaw') can bias sizing anchoring. (5) Qualification gap: a PoC has no established regulatory qualification path for AI in inspection. Detection performance (POD) curves, repeatability across retrains, and explainability for deep-learning waveform features are not established (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0504). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training or archive data poisoning or label tampering by an insider or via a compromised data-management pipeline, including selective relabeling or injecting scans to desensitize the model to a specific flaw signature (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059). (7) Model or weights tampering, or a backdoor trigger in the waveform pattern, that makes selected indications read as no-flaw (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076). (8) Evasion by manipulating acquisition data, e.g., altered scan files, injected waveform perturbations, or modified depth outputs between the acquisition system and the model, which exploit the model's brittleness to small waveform changes (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). (9) Supply-chain exposure through third-party DL frameworks, pretrained components or vendor analysis software (AML.T0010.001). The shared consequence is an undetected pressure-tube flaw (reduced integrity margin, potential loss of coolant) or a false assurance that is hard to discover later, since the outage window and the AI-filtered review make errors unlikely to be rechecked.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, the CNN is a poor primary target but a credible stepping stone. It sits in the data path between raw UT acquisition and the analyst who signs off on pressure-tube integrity. A flaw-or-no-flaw classifier plus a depth-based false-positive filter becomes a pre-screening gate that quietly sets what analysts look at. Every efficiency gain it delivers (shorter outages, less manual review) weakens the independent human check that is the real security control, and that is what an adversary would exploit. Insiders who touch the training data, model files, scan archive, or post-processor thresholds gain a low-visibility way to suppress or shape detections. The adversary wins by making a real flaw not get reviewed, not by making the AI fail visibly. Public peer-reviewed and preprint literature also lowers reconnaissance cost.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity of the detection gate. Poisoning of the historical-scan training set or labels, or tampering with model weights or the depth post-processor (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.003, T0076), could create a blind spot for particular flaw morphologies, depths or tube locations. The facility depends on this output to decide which scan points analysts examine closely. The consequence is a missed or under-called pressure-tube flaw (e.g., crack-like or hydride-related indications), which is a safety-significant integrity risk and a regulatory-compliance risk, and one that looks like normal AI error. (2) Insider and valid-account abuse (AML.T0012): a person with write access to the inspection pipeline, rather than to the model itself, can alter the waveform data, thresholds or the filtered flaw list. The attribution problem is severe, because a missed flaw can be blamed on model limits. (3) Adversarial or crafted inputs (AML.T0043, T0015): this is less likely in an offline outage tool, but a compromised acquisition system or probe-data path could shape waveforms that evade a CNN even though a human would catch them. (4) Reconnaissance and model replication (AML.T0000, T0002, T0005): the published architecture and dataset description let an adversary build a proxy model and learn its blind spots, for example how the depth filter suppresses shallow flaws. (5) Supply-chain risk (AML.T0010): third-party inspection vendors, ML frameworks and pre-trained components. Stepping-stone risk: a compromised analysis workstation or data store also exposes plant-wide inspection history and fitness-for-service margins, which have value for sabotage planning.

IMPLICIT (exploitable or timeable by an adversary): (a) Automation complacency and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102, C0101.01): a low false-positive rate builds trust, analysts review less closely, and outage schedule pressure adds to that. An adversary can time tampering for the point when attention is lowest. (b) Low base rate and data scarcity (OP.C0202, C0201.05): real flaws are rare, so the model has few examples of unusual flaw types, and rare high-consequence cases are the ones most likely to be missed. (c) Drift and heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, C0302.03): probe wear, couplant changes, different tooling or vendors, or tube-condition changes degrade performance silently, and the depth post-processor can hide this by reducing visible false positives. (d) Opacity and qualification gap (OP.C0401, C0501, C0303): a proof of concept without qualification to inspection-code standards cannot show that it is free of tampering. Over time its status can slide from advisory to de facto gate (OP.C0503). (e) Goal misalignment (OP.C0301): the tuning that minimizes false positives trades off against sensitivity, which is the safety-critical property. (f) Possible cloud or off-site training and storage (OP.C0601, C0505) widen the access surface to inspection data.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on missed-flaw false negatives, automation bias, data scarcity, drift, the post-processor cascade, the qualification gap, and tampering with the data, model or thresholds; I merged these and kept distinct only the evasion, reconnaissance and data-exposure threats. I dropped denial of service as low-consequence given the manual fallback, and omitted weakly supported codes such as OP.C0101.01 and OP.C0403.

evidence.citation: "Using Deep Learning to Automate the Detection of Flaws in Nuclear Fuel Channel UT Scans," IEEE Transactions on Ultrasonics, Ferroelectrics, and Frequency Control (Vol. 69, Issue 1, 2022)
evidence.note: The authors built a proof-of-concept CNN. It was trained on a dataset made from historical CANDU pressure-tube UT scans and their recorded inspection results. It finds at least part of each flaw region while keeping false positives low. IEEE Xplore is a peer-reviewed journal, which should fall in the preferred tier. The tier field is set to 'other' only because the instructions' label options may not fit it exactly, so please check this entry. A preprint of the same work is on arXiv (2102.13635).

damage.why: The worst credible threat (Detection-gate integrity attack / silent missed flaw) lets a pressure-tube flaw go undetected and erodes fitness-for-service margin, which could contribute to tube failure and a radiological release; the harm is indirect because analysts still size flagged flaws and other defense-in-depth layers exist, so this is not a 5.

reproducibility.why: Implicit failure modes (false-negative bias, drift, rare-flaw scarcity, automation complacency) recur reliably once the tool gates analyst review, while deliberate tampering depends on access and on the tool being used as a gate, so reliability is moderately high but conditional.

exploitability.why: The most severe adversarial paths (poisoning, weight or threshold tampering, pipeline write access, supply-chain compromise) need insider or privileged access or significant resources, and the acquisition-path evasion is narrower because the tool runs offline; the implicit weaknesses need no attacker effort.

affected_users.why: Impact is concentrated on a single inspection function (pressure-tube flaw detection) but can span many tubes and the fleet inspection program, and it feeds fitness-for-service decisions; it does not propagate across coupled plant control systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, dataset description and false-positive/depth-filter approach are published in a peer-reviewed journal and an arXiv preprint, and the failure classes (false-negative bias, drift, poisoning, evasion) are well documented in the open literature, though system-specific blind spots need a proxy model or insider knowledge.

use_case: Unsupervised generative-adversarial-network anomaly detection that compares automatically recorded plant sensor data with manually collected surveillance (operator round) data from a nuclear power plant balance of plant. It flags mismatches that can be attributed to human error in day-to-day operation and maintenance. It was benchmarked against one-class SVM and isolation forest.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory balance-of-plant GAN cross-checks automated sensor records against manual operator-round readings, so it becomes a trust-concentration point for plant data integrity while being weakly validated. Its main threats are poisoning of the learned baseline, evasion by an informed insider, alarm flooding, pipeline tampering and data exposure, together with implicit weaknesses: scarce unlabelled error data, drift, opaque attribution, non-repeatable training, misplaced trust and governance gaps. Direct safety consequence is bounded, but masked equipment degradation and concealed tampering of surveillance records are the realistic outcomes.

Baseline poisoning via retraining -- adversarial
An insider or anyone with historian or round-sheet access can gradually shift manual entries or inject mismatch patterns during unsupervised retraining, so a class of discrepancy is learned as normal. Real errors, falsified surveillance readings or degraded equipment then pass unflagged, and the lack of labels means the corruption cannot be detected.

Evasion within learned tolerance -- adversarial
An actor who knows both data streams can infer from repeated flag and no-flag outcomes what the detector tolerates, and keep falsified readings or sensor values inside that envelope. Agreement between streams is treated as evidence of integrity, so a coordinated falsification of both, or a cyber-manipulated sensor stream, yields false assurance.

Alert flooding and desensitisation -- adversarial
Injected chaff or noisy manual entries create false mismatches that drive alarm fatigue, threshold loosening or disabling of the tool. This opens a window for concealing real degradation or an insider act.

Model and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
A compromised ML library, pretrained component or privileged account can silently raise thresholds, corrupt the discriminator or implant a trigger that suppresses flags for chosen patterns. Because the output is only a score, little forensic trace remains.

Operational data aggregation and exposure -- adversarial
The paired sensor and round dataset reveals operating routines, instrument coverage and where manual checks are thin, and may hold personnel-linked records. Exfiltration from the analytics environment, especially if cloud or vendor hosted, supports reconnaissance for later physical or cyber action.

Scarce unlabelled error data and weak validation -- implicit, exploitable
Human errors are rare and unlabelled, and validation used one plant plus an external testbed that may be simulated or transferred, so thresholds rest on unverifiable assumptions and habitual errors may be learned as normal. A patient insider can probe these blind spots and place deliberate errors in them, relying on benchmark-derived confidence.

Drift and operational heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Outages, power manoeuvres, instrument replacement and revised round sheets shift the sensor-to-manual relationship, causing false-alarm floods or silent loss of sensitivity, and limiting transfer between units. An adversary can time actions around these periods, or exploit the documented threshold retuning that follows to weaken the detector quietly.

Opaque attribution and non-repeatable training -- implicit
A reconstruction or discriminator score cannot distinguish operator error from sensor fault, tampering or real process change, and stochastic GAN training means retrained versions flag different events. This misdirects diagnosis and blame and complicates qualification and audit. No distinct adversary gain beyond the blind spots already described.

Automation trust and skill erosion -- implicit, exploitable
Over-trust treats no flag as verification, so rounds become more casual and independent cross-checking atrophies, while chronic false alarms push toward disuse. An adversary can rely on the predictable weak vigilance this creates, or deliberately induce alarm fatigue.

Qualification and security-model gaps -- implicit, exploitable
As a non-safety BOP tool it may receive weaker AI-specific QA, change control, access control, logging and insider vetting than its role as a surveillance-integrity check warrants, and could be extended to safety-relevant uses without requalification. An adversary benefits from lax retraining controls and weak auditing when tampering with the model or its data.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory, balance-of-plant (BOP) O&M tool that cross-checks automatic sensor records against operator round readings, so it sits well outside the reactor protection and safety-related I/C boundary. The credible downstream harm therefore comes from degraded detection, not from direct actuation. Missed mismatches let real instrument drift, miscalibration, a stuck transmitter, or a mis-transcribed reading persist. False alarms erode operator trust and add review burden. Existing practice (technical-specification surveillance, redundant channels, independent verification, calibration programs, peer checks) already limits harm, so a wrong output needs a real equipment degradation and a failed independent check to matter. The more subtle risk is that the tool shifts attention and credibility: operators and QA staff may treat the absence of a flag as verification, or an adversary may exploit that.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Unsupervised training on a small, single-plant dataset with no labeled error base rate (OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0201.05). Human errors are rare and varied, so the model may learn 'normal' that already includes habitual rounding, transcription, or unit errors and then never flag them. Benchmarking against one-class SVM and isolation forest says little about real-world detection rates for specific error types, and the external testbed is not field data (OP.C0201.02). (2) Drift and heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). Outages, power maneuvers, instrument replacement, procedure revisions, round-sheet changes, and seasonal BOP behavior all shift the sensor and manual-data relationship. Model thresholds then give either false-alarm floods or silent loss of sensitivity, and a model tuned at one unit may not transfer to another (OP.C0602). (3) Ambiguous attribution. A GAN reconstruction or discriminator score does not say whether the mismatch is human error, sensor fault, or real process change (OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03). Mislabeling a genuine process or instrument anomaly as 'operator error', or the reverse, delays correct diagnosis and corrective action. (4) Automation trust and blame (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102). Over-trust gives 'no flag, so verified'. Under-trust after alarm fatigue leads to ignored flags. There is also a human-performance and organizational risk: the tool could shift culture toward blame, discourage honest reporting, or push operators to adjust their entries so they match sensor data, which defeats the independent-check value of manual rounds. (5) GAN training instability and non-repeatability (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0403) complicate qualification, change control, and regulatory acceptance (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Data continuity depends on digitized round records, which many plants lack (OP.C0204).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Data integrity attack on the two inputs. Because the tool compares two sources, an adversary who can alter historian data or manual-entry or round-sheet systems could selectively mask a real discrepancy or fabricate mismatches (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0020, AML.T0031, AML.T0059). Consistent tampering of both streams would pass the check, so the tool offers no protection against coordinated falsification. Gradual poisoning through the retraining pipeline would shift the learned baseline slowly enough to avoid notice (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002). (b) Flood-and-desensitize. Injected false mismatches or chaff data cause alarm fatigue or prompt operators to raise thresholds, creating a window for concealing a real degradation or insider action (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). (c) Insider evasion. An insider who knows the model's behavior could make deliberate errors or sabotage that stay within learned normal variation, or exploit the tool's blind spots (AML.T0013, AML.T0063). (d) New attack surface. Pulling plant-historian data across the IT/OT boundary into an analytics environment, possibly cloud-hosted, adds a path for exfiltrating operational data and for compromise of the IT/OT boundary (OP.C0601, AML.T0025, AML.T0036, OP.C0505). Model and software supply-chain compromise also applies (AML.T0010, OP.C0502). Because the tool is BOP-only and advisory, direct safety consequence is bounded. The main impacts are masked degradation, wasted maintenance effort, degraded operational awareness, and weakened insider-threat detection.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is an unsupervised GAN trained on paired automated-sensor and manual-round records, so it learns what normal agreement between the two looks like, with no labelled human-error ground truth. Its fragility starts with the label problem: human error is rare, mostly unlabelled, and mixed in with sensor faults, calibration drift, transcription or format differences, and legitimate process transients. Training instability and mode collapse are known GAN failure modes. The discriminator or reconstruction score has no calibrated link to 'human error', so the system cannot say why a pair mismatches. The reported benchmark rests on one operating-plant dataset and one external testbed against two classical baselines. That says little about generalization across plants, units, seasons, or procedure changes, or about robustness at inference. Both input streams are trust anchors the model cannot verify, so the architecture is exposed to anyone or anything that can shape either stream.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Label and ground-truth scarcity (OP.C0202, OP.C0302): the model is tuned on few real human-error events, so thresholds are set on unverifiable assumptions. Mismatches caused by sensor drift, instrument faults, or plant-state changes get attributed to people, and real errors that mimic normal variance are missed. The consequence is erosion of trust in the tool, or blame misdirected onto operators while a real instrument degradation goes uninvestigated. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01, .02, .03): outages, refuelling, power maneuvers, instrument replacement, and revised round sheets or units all shift the joint distribution. The model sees these as out-of-distribution and either floods operators with false alarms or learns to ignore them. (3) Data-provenance and fidelity mismatch (OP.C0201.05, OP.C0201.03): manual rounds are sparse, low-frequency, and noisy in time alignment and rounding, whereas sensor data is dense. Alignment and preprocessing choices become hidden model parameters. Results from the testbed (possibly simulated or transferred) may not transfer to a real BoP. (4) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0402.02): GAN training is stochastic, so retrained versions can flag different events, which complicates qualification and audit. Explaining a flagged record to a maintenance supervisor is hard. (5) Human-AI interaction (OP.C0101.04, .05, OP.C0102): alert fatigue produces disuse, while over-trust in a 'no flag' result can reduce independent verification of rounds. There is also a goal-misalignment risk (OP.C0301): scoring individual operators on flags would reward gaming the manual entries. Because the tool is BoP and advisory, direct safety impact is modest, but it may later be extended toward safety-relevant systems without requalification (OP.C0303, OP.C0501).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Poisoning or integrity erosion of training and retraining data (AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0010.002): an insider or someone with access to historian or surveillance records can inject gradual shifts during unsupervised retraining, so a particular type of discrepancy becomes 'normal'. This conceals real errors, sabotage, or tampered readings, and retraining on unlabelled data cannot detect it. (2) Evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043): an actor who can alter sensor values or manual entries within the learned envelope could keep an inconsistency from being flagged. The tool then offers false assurance that rounds and sensors agree, which could mask a cyber-manipulated sensor stream, since agreement is exactly what it treats as evidence of integrity. (3) Chaff or alert flooding (AML.T0046, AML.T0029): injecting benign-looking mismatches drives alarm fatigue and can lead to the tool being disabled. (4) Model and pipeline supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000): ML library or pretrained-component tampering, or a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004) that suppresses flags for chosen patterns. (5) Data exposure (AML.T0025, AML.T0037): the aggregated paired sensor and round dataset reveals operating practices, instrument coverage, and blind spots useful for reconnaissance, and it may also hold personnel-linked records. It is likely governed under an inappropriate data security model (OP.C0505.01), especially if analytics are moved to cloud or vendor environments (OP.C0601). The overall exposure is that an anomaly detector becomes a trusted integrity check on plant records while being weakly validated and manipulable.

security_specialist.argument: This system sits at the junction of two data streams that plant staff treat as mutually corroborating: automated sensor records and manual operator-round readings. It is therefore a trust-concentration point. If operators or maintenance supervisors come to rely on the GAN to catch round errors, an insider can exploit that reliance. They could falsify or degrade a manual reading in a way the model has learned to treat as normal, or time a deviation around a period when vigilance is low. The system is also advisory and sits in balance of plant, so a state-level adversary would probably not target it directly. It is better viewed as a stepping stone: a route to manipulating surveillance records, hiding insider tampering, or eroding confidence in the plant's data integrity. The non-adversarial weaknesses are the more important ones here: an unsupervised model with no ground-truth labels, trained on small and heterogeneous data, with a opaque notion of 'mismatch'. These produce blind spots that a patient insider could learn and exploit.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data poisoning and baseline manipulation (AML.T0020, T0059, T0010.002, T0018.000). The model learns 'normal' from historical sensor and operator-round pairs. An insider with round-sheet or historian access could slowly shift manual entries, or insert a plausible pattern of mismatches, until a class of discrepancy is learned as normal. The AI failure mechanism is a corrupted baseline. The facility depends on the model to catch human-error or tampering signals in surveillance. The consequence is that real errors, or deliberate falsification of surveillance data, pass unflagged, which can mask degraded equipment or concealed sabotage preparation. (2) Evasion by an informed insider (AML.T0015, T0043.003, T0063). Operators know both data streams. Over repeated flag and no-flag outcomes they can infer what the detector tolerates and keep a falsified reading inside that tolerance. Nothing in the use case suggests the output is access-controlled or audited. (3) Model or pipeline tampering (AML.T0018, T0010.001/.003, T0076, T0031). If the GAN is integrated into maintenance software or a data-science toolchain, a supply-chain or privileged-account compromise could silently raise thresholds or corrupt the discriminator. This suppresses alerts selectively and leaves little forensic trace, because the output is only a score. (4) Alert flooding (AML.T0046, T0029). Injecting chaff or noisy manual entries produces false positives, leading staff to ignore or disable the tool just before a real event or insider act. (5) Data aggregation (AML.T0036, T0025). Paired sensor and round data reveal operational routines, equipment condition, and where manual checks are thin, which is useful for planning physical or cyber action. IMPLICIT. (6) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, C0101.05, C0101.06, C0102). If the tool is over-trusted, rounds may be done more casually and independent cross-checking atrophies, which gives an adversary a predictable weak window. Chronic false alarms push the opposite way, toward disuse. (7) Unsupervised, unlabeled and scarce human-error data (OP.C0202, C0701, C0201.05, C0201.03). Real human errors are rare and unlabeled, and testing was on one plant plus an external testbed. Performance may not carry over to other plants or to novel error types, and cannot be tested against subtle deliberate falsification. A GAN can also mode-collapse or train non-deterministically (OP.C0402.01, C0403). (8) Drift and heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01/.03, C0302.02). Procedure changes, outages, instrument recalibration or sensor replacement shift the baseline. Staff then retune or suppress thresholds, which creates a documented opportunity for quiet weakening of the detector. (9) Opacity and qualification gaps (OP.C0401, C0501, C0502, C0303). A mismatch score does not explain why a reading was flagged, which makes it hard to tell human error from sensor fault or tampering. Without AI-specific QA and change control for retraining, the model's integrity is hard to demonstrate. (10) Governance and security-model mismatch (OP.C0505.01, C0503). The system may be treated as non-safety balance-of-plant IT, so it receives weaker access control, logging and insider-threat vetting than its role as a surveillance-integrity check warrants. If it is hosted off-site (OP.C0601), operational data exposure and a remote compromise path are added.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on baseline poisoning, in-envelope evasion, chaff flooding, supply-chain tampering, data exposure, and the implicit set of label scarcity, drift, opacity and automation trust. I merged overlapping items and dropped peripheral codes (e.g. OP.C0701, OP.C0204, AML.T0013, AML.T0014) that were weakly tied to the specific mechanisms.

evidence.citation: "Using artificial intelligence to detect human errors in nuclear power plants: A case in operation and maintenance," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Elsevier); also available via OSTI/INL
evidence.note: The authors built a GAN trained to detect mismatches between sensor records and manually collected surveillance data. They tested it on a real operating-plant dataset and on an external testbed dataset, where it outperformed one-class SVM and isolation forest. The model is intended to support future AI-based human-error detection systems.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is concealed tampering with surveillance records or masked equipment degradation (baseline poisoning or evasion), which could cause operational disruption and erode safety margins; the tool is advisory, non-safety BOP, so a direct radiological release is unlikely, though falsified surveillance integrity is a safeguards-adjacent concern.

reproducibility.why: Poisoning during unsupervised retraining and drift-timed actions work reliably once an actor has data access and retraining occurs, but outcomes depend on the retraining cadence, the specific model and the insider's knowledge of both data streams.

exploitability.why: The most credible threats (baseline poisoning, evasion across both data streams, pipeline tampering) require insider or privileged access to the historian, round sheets or ML pipeline, plus knowledge of both streams; only alarm flooding and some exposure paths are less demanding.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly confined to one plant's BOP surveillance-integrity function and its operations staff; it could extend across units or fleet if the model were propagated or reused, but it does not propagate into safety systems.

discoverability.why: Poisoning, evasion, chaff and drift are well documented for anomaly-detection ML in open literature, and the published GAN approach reveals the architecture class, but the deployment, data access paths and tolerance envelope would need insider or partial knowledge to learn.

use_case: Artificial-neural-network model of fission gas release from LWR UO2 fuel under reactivity-initiated accident (RIA) conditions. Inputs are pellet-average burnup, peak fuel enthalpy, the ratio of peak enthalpy to pulse width, fission gas release during base irradiation, and fuel grain size. It was trained on pulse-irradiation test data from the CABRI and NSRR test reactors. It supports fuel-rod integrity analysis and source-term assessment in RIA safety analysis.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline ANN surrogate for RIA fission gas release has no actuation path, but it feeds fuel-rod integrity margins and radiological source-term assessments in the safety case. Its main implicit threats are non-conservative extrapolation from a small, heterogeneous test-reactor dataset, opacity and over-trust, and a qualification and configuration-control gap. The main adversarial threats are tampering with the training data or model artifact, and manipulation of analysis inputs. All of these end in an understated release fraction that looks like ordinary model scatter.

Small-data extrapolation failure -- implicit, exploitable
The ANN is trained on tens to low hundreds of CABRI/NSRR pulse tests (sodium or capsule conditions) and has no extrapolation guard, so it returns confident, non-conservative FGR for high-burnup, doped, large-grain or ATF fuel and for plant pulse widths outside its envelope. The sparse high-release tail is also poorly fitted. An adversary could steer or time inputs into these unflagged regions, or hide a data or weight bias inside the model's normal error band.

Omitted variables and mean-trend objective -- implicit, exploitable
Five aggregate inputs omit cladding state, rim microstructure, pulse shape and coolant conditions, and the fit objective gives a best-estimate trend rather than the bounding value licensing needs. The resulting unexplained error looks like irreducible scatter, so an adversary could pass a small manipulation off as natural model error.

Opacity and analyst over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
The network cannot show whether its sensitivities to burnup, enthalpy and grain size are physically monotonic, and a good fit to the test data invites acceptance over bounding correlations or mechanistic codes. Reviewers lose independent fuel-behaviour judgment. An insider could use that misplaced trust, especially in re-licensing windows, to introduce small changes that are defensible on their face.

Qualification and configuration-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
A literature-fitted ANN without independent hold-out validation or uncertainty quantification does not map onto deterministic nuclear software QA. Retraining non-determinism and weak version control also allow silent changes to the model. An adversary could swap or retrain the artifact with no provenance trail to expose it.

Training-data poisoning and integrity erosion -- adversarial
Because the dataset is small, altering a few high-burnup or high-release records, units or normalisation values in the compiled database or curated spreadsheet shifts the fit substantially where it matters. The result is a hidden downward bias in source-term and rod-integrity results that propagates through the vendor or licensee analysis chain.

Model and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
An insider or a compromised vendor, ML framework, notebook or exported model file could alter the weights to under-predict release in a narrow input region while still passing a small validation set. The ANN's opacity conceals the change until a real transient.

Input-deck manipulation -- adversarial
An insider or a compromised engineering workstation could alter burnup, enthalpy, pulse-width or base-irradiation FGR inputs within plausible ranges so that predicted release falls below a failure or source-term threshold. The model has no plausibility check, so the erroneous outputs look credible.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline design and licensing-analysis surrogate, not a control or protection function, so the downstream path runs through the safety analyst and the regulatory submission rather than any real-time actuation. Harm needs two things: a wrong FGR prediction that is accepted into RIA source-term or rod-integrity analysis, and then a failure of the independent barriers around that analysis. Those barriers are code-to-code benchmarking, conservative regulatory limits on enthalpy and burnup, licensing review, and in-plant safety margins. The real exposure is quiet erosion of analysis margin. A non-conservative FGR estimate would feed dose and source-term calculations, core-loading or burnup-limit decisions, and emergency-planning inputs. The model rests on a small and heterogeneous CABRI/NSRR dataset, so its weak spots are extrapolation and over-trust, which no adversary is needed to create.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Small-data and extrapolation failure. CABRI and NSRR pulse tests number only in the tens to low hundreds, and they differ in coolant conditions (sodium, water at ambient or capsule conditions), pulse widths, and rod designs. An ANN has no physical constraint to stop it extrapolating. Applied to high-burnup, new cladding or fuel (doped, large-grain, MOX-adjacent, or ATF concepts) or to pulse widths outside the training envelope, it can return smooth, plausible and non-conservative FGR values. It gives no warning that it has left its validated domain. The consequence is an understated release fraction, which feeds into the radiological source term. (2) Automation trust and opacity. The five-input model hides which mechanisms (grain-boundary inventory, HBS/rim effects, enthalpy-driven grain-boundary separation) it has captured. Analysts may accept it because it fits the test data well, and the fit hides the fact that the dataset does not show the scatter or the rare high-release outliers. A mean-trend predictor is not a bounding one, and the licensing basis needs bounding values. (3) Qualification mismatch. Static test-reactor data stand in for the dynamic power-plant transient, and base-irradiation FGR is itself an uncertain input from another code. That error is then amplified by the ANN, which was never qualified as a safety-analysis tool under nuclear QA. ADVERSARIAL OR EXPLOITABLE THREATS. (4) Training-data or artifact tampering, or supply-chain compromise of the model, spreadsheet or script. A subtle bias in the response surface in a region of interest would be hard to detect by inspection, and it would propagate through the fuel-vendor or licensee analysis chain into several safety cases. This is a low-probability, high-leverage path to an understated source term. It would be caught only if independent mechanistic code runs and experimental comparison still happen. (5) Manipulated inputs. Altered burnup, enthalpy or base-irradiation FGR values in analysis input decks would produce erroneous outputs that look credible. The model offers no plausibility check. (6) Exfiltration of proprietary or export-controlled test data, since the model weights can leak the data they were trained on. This is a minor concern next to the others. Existing practice (conservative regulatory acceptance criteria, mechanistic fuel-performance codes, regulatory review, defense in depth) mitigates most of this, provided the ANN stays a screening or supporting tool and is not allowed to replace bounding analysis.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small-tabular-data regression ANN, not a large or agentic system, so its fragility sits in the data and in extrapolation. CABRI and NSRR pulse tests number in the low hundreds at best. They were run on a limited set of fuel designs, cladding types, burnups and pulse widths, and with test-loop conditions (sodium or water capsule, room-temperature or hot-standby) that differ from PWR/BWR RIA transients. Five inputs summarize a complex transient. They omit cladding state, pellet microstructure (the high-burnup rim structure), pulse shape, and coolant conditions. Any dependence on these omitted variables shows up as irreducible, unflagged error. An ANN also has no built-in extrapolation guard, so new fuel types (high-burnup, doped or Cr-coated, ATF) or burnups beyond the test envelope will receive a confident-looking number with no sign that it is out of distribution. Because the output feeds source-term and fuel-failure assessment, the pipeline's weak points are the provenance and curation of the test database, the model's validity envelope, and the lack of uncertainty quantification.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Small-data and low-base-rate problem: there are few high-burnup pulse tests, and the highest-FGR cases are the ones that matter for source term. The network may interpolate well in the dense middle of the data while being unreliable at the tail. Overfitting, split sensitivity and training non-determinism (random initialisation, small validation sets) can give different weights, and so different predictions, from nominally identical retraining (OP.C0202, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0403). (2) Out-of-distribution and transferred-data mismatch: the model was trained on test-reactor data (CABRI sodium or water loops, NSRR capsule conditions, pulse widths and enthalpy-deposition rates that differ from commercial-reactor RIAs) and is applied to a different plant, fuel design or burnup. New fuel, cladding or additive designs, and the high-burnup rim structure, produce a shift the model cannot detect. The result could be non-conservative underprediction of release, which would understate the source term and cladding-failure consequences in design-basis safety analysis (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0203). (3) Omitted-variable and objective misalignment: five aggregate inputs ignore pulse shape, cladding condition and coolant state, and the model's fit to test data is not the same as conservatism for licensing. Without UQ or bounds, its output could be used as a best-estimate value that no one has qualified. The network is also opaque, so a reviewer cannot confirm that its sensitivities to burnup, enthalpy and grain size are physically monotonic and consistent with mechanistic fuel-performance codes (OP.C0301, OP.C0401, OP.C0303). (4) Qualification and governance gap: nuclear QA frameworks for safety-analysis codes assume deterministic, validated, version-controlled software. An ANN fitted to published literature data, and not validated against an independent hold-out or integral-test benchmark, does not map cleanly onto them. Silent retraining or database updates would change results without formal change control (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504). (5) Automation trust: analysts may take a clean ANN output as better than a bounding correlation, so the error goes unchallenged (OP.C0101.04).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. Exposure is concentrated in the training and lifecycle pipeline, not in an inference API. (a) Data poisoning or integrity erosion of the compiled CABRI/NSRR database, such as altered records, units, or burnup or enthalpy values, or a tampered curated spreadsheet, before retraining. Because the dataset is small, a few altered high-burnup, high-release points would shift the fit substantially in exactly the region that matters, and a downward bias would be hard to see (AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0010.002). (b) Model or weight tampering and supply-chain compromise of the ML framework, notebook or exported model file, with backdoor-like behaviour in a narrow input region that stays accurate on validation cases and is hard to find with a small test set (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076). (c) Input manipulation at the analysis step: an insider or compromised engineering workstation changing burnup, enthalpy or grain-size inputs, or nudging inputs inside the plausible range, so that predicted release falls below a failure or source-term threshold (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0031). (d) Public documentation of the architecture and inputs makes proxy models easy to replicate, so an adversary can predict where the model is least conservative and time or target manipulation accordingly (AML.T0000, AML.T0005). The consequence in every case is a non-conservative source term or rod-integrity result, passed into design and licensing analysis, that nobody can distinguish from ordinary model error.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is a low-value direct target. It is an offline, design-stage regression model with five numeric inputs and no actuation path, and a nation-state would find easier routes to the same end. Its value as a target lies in what it feeds: RIA fuel-rod integrity margins and source-term assessments that underpin licensing and safety-analysis conclusions. An insider or supply-chain adversary could influence those conclusions quietly, in a way that stays latent until a real transient. The main exposures are integrity of the model and its training data, and a trust concentration that is easy to over-extend. The ANN is trained on a small, heterogeneous CABRI/NSRR dataset and then used for extrapolation.
