That makes it opaque, hard to qualify, and hard for a reviewer to challenge, so a subtle bias would look like normal scatter.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity attack on model or data. An insider, a compromised analysis-tool vendor, or a poisoned shared dataset or pretrained artifact could alter the weights, the training or test records, or the input normalization (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). The failure mechanism is a model that systematically under-predicts fission gas release in a specific region of the input space, for example high burnup or high enthalpy-to-pulse-width ratio. The dependency is source-term assessment and fuel-failure and rod-integrity margins in the RIA safety case. The consequence is non-conservative dose and source-term figures, eroded safety margin, and possibly a flawed licensing basis that stays hidden until a real event. Because the training set is small, a few altered records could shift the fit without being visible, and the ANN's opacity helps conceal this. (2) Stepping-stone and trust concentration. If the model is embedded in a larger analysis workflow or sits on shared engineering servers or cloud tooling, it becomes a pivot point for lateral access to design data, and a place to hide manipulated results among legitimate outputs. Model-extraction and training-data inference are low risk here, since the data is public, though proprietary vendor data may be added to the training set. (3) Insider timing and review erosion. Analysts who find the ANN consistent with the code and the literature will grow less vigilant. An insider can use that complacency to introduce small, defensible-looking changes during design or re-licensing windows, when scrutiny is lowest. IMPLICIT (no adversary needed, but exploitable). (a) Extrapolation failure. The CABRI/NSRR data cover limited fuel designs, cladding types and pulse shapes, and test-reactor conditions (sodium or water capsule, pulse width) differ from plant transients. Modern high-burnup or accident-tolerant fuels fall outside the training distribution, so predictions can look confident yet be wrong (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0202). (b) Qualification gaps. Without an AI-specific QA basis, the model may be used in safety analysis beyond its validated range, and an ANN offers no mechanistic traceability (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0303). (c) Over-trust and skill fade. Reviewers may defer to a fast surrogate and lose independent mechanistic fuel-behavior judgment (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). (d) Reproducibility. Retraining non-determinism and weak version control make silent model swaps hard to detect (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502). An adversary would exploit the lack of provenance and configuration control, not the algorithm itself.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on small-data extrapolation, opacity and over-trust, the qualification gap, and a training-data and model integrity attack that understates source term. I dropped the minor extraction and inversion, proxy-model and lateral-pivot threats as low-value or weakly argued, and kept the input-manipulation path, which the nuclear and AI engineers both raised.

evidence.citation: "Artificial neural network modeling for fission gas release in LWR UO2 fuel under RIA conditions," Journal of Nuclear Materials (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper builds an ANN fission gas release model for UO2 fuel in reactivity-initiated accidents. It uses five fuel and pulse parameters and test data from the CABRI and NSRR reactors. It frames the model as a tool for analysing fuel rod integrity and assessing the radioactivity source term if fuel fails. The ANN is distinct from steady-state fuel-performance-code surrogates, because it covers transient accident conditions.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a hidden downward bias in predicted fission gas release (from poisoned data, tampered weights, or manipulated inputs), which erodes fuel-rod integrity margins and understates the radiological source term in the safety case; this is a safety-margin and source-term-assessment harm, but it is indirect, offline and has no actuation path, so it falls short of a direct release.

reproducibility.why: Small-data extrapolation failure is a systematic, near-deterministic property of this ANN class whenever inputs fall outside the training envelope (high burnup, ATF fuel, plant pulse widths), and a data or weight bias reliably propagates to every downstream result once present.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (training-data poisoning, model or supply-chain tampering, input-deck manipulation) need insider or vendor-level access to curated databases, model artifacts or engineering workstations, and the effect only matters if a reviewer relies on the output; the implicit failures need no adversary at all.

affected_users.why: A biased surrogate propagates through the vendor and licensee analysis chain into rod-integrity and source-term assessments for many fuel designs and plants, but it remains an offline analysis tool and does not couple to plant systems, so impact is broad in licensing terms without being facility-wide operationally.

discoverability.why: The model's architecture, five inputs and CABRI/NSRR training data are described in open literature, and small-data extrapolation, opacity and QA gaps are well-documented for this class of ML surrogate, so an outsider can readily infer where the weakness lies, though locating the specific artifacts or data pipelines needs more knowledge.

use_case: Stacked-regression ensemble (machine-learning chemometric model) applied to laser-induced fluorescence and Raman spectra. It simultaneously quantifies U(VI), samarium (a fluorescent fission-product surrogate), nitric acid and solution temperature in nitric-acid process solutions. It is meant for near-real-time in-line monitoring of reprocessing separation streams, and the source also notes it could indicate burnup of irradiated fuel.
incurred_insecurity:
This in-line spectroscopic ensemble gives near-real-time U(VI), acidity, Sm and temperature readings in reprocessing streams. It was validated only on clean laboratory solutions, and it could also feed a burnup indication. The main threats are silent lab-to-plant generalization failure, unvalidated surrogate-to-burnup inference, operator over-trust, weak qualification and change control, and adversarial tampering with the model, calibration data or spectral inputs. Together they could bias process and accountancy readings without any alarm.

Lab-to-plant generalization failure -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on bench solutions of four analytes, the regressors return confident point estimates on real streams carrying Pu, Np, Ru, organics, radiolysis products, fouled windows and darkened fibres, with no out-of-distribution flag. This produces biased U and acid readings that distort process control and the material balance. An adversary could time a manipulation or diversion to known poor-performance regimes, or hide a deliberate bias inside what looks like ordinary drift.

Cross-output error propagation -- implicit, exploitable
All four outputs share one feature set and meta-learner, so one corrupted spectral channel or a temperature-driven band shift biases U, acid and temperature together and removes independent cross-checks. An adversary needs to corrupt only one input path to mislead several parameters at once.

Surrogate-based burnup inference -- implicit, exploitable
Sm fluorescence stands in for the real fission-product inventory, and the inference may fail amid Eu, Gd, Am, Cm and a high radiation background. A falsely reassuring burnup or composition figure could mislead safeguards verification, and an adversary could rely on it as a deniable channel that conceals a discrepancy or material substitution.

Over-trust, skill fade and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Decimal-precision readings with no uncertainty estimate from an opaque ensemble invite operators to drop confirmatory grab sampling and, if tied to alarms or setpoints, to let a biased reading act as a control input. An adversary or slow drift can exploit this complacency because a subtle bias goes unchallenged.

Qualification, repeatability and change-control gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Non-deterministic retraining, recalibration after instrument maintenance and the absence of an AI-specific V&V basis let model behaviour change silently. Weak change control gives an insider an uncontrolled update path and hides honest drift from review.

Training-data scarcity and surrogate data -- implicit
Hot, Pu-bearing, high-dose training data are scarce, so the model rests on simulated or surrogate mixes whose small sets are easily dominated by errors. No distinct adversarial gain beyond the poisoning threat below.

Training, calibration and model tampering -- adversarial
A poisoned calibration or retraining set, a compromised chemometric library or a tampered serialized model or meta-learner can embed a small systematic bias in U(VI) or acid readings that still agree with sparse grab samples. This could mask diversion or a process upset, and the ensemble's opacity makes it hard to detect.

Spectrum and data-path manipulation -- adversarial
Altering spectra, the optical path, reference standards or the probe-to-model link, or adding a fluorescent contaminant, can steer the regression output while raw-signal sanity checks pass. Public availability of the method lets an attacker build a proxy model to craft such inputs, and the instrument PC may also offer a route to the process network.

Monitor denial and information exposure -- adversarial
Compromising the spectrometer or network, or attacking in a known weak regime, forces a fall-back to slower lab sampling and degrades monitoring cadence. Exfiltrating or querying the model and its outputs could also reveal throughput, fuel type or burnup characteristics.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a reprocessing operations and safeguards view, this is an in-line analytical advisory tool. It sits beside the established controls: sampling and lab analysis (DA/ICP-MS/titration), nuclear material accountancy, and criticality safety limits on concentration, geometry and acidity. The facility depends on it for faster process awareness, such as U concentration and acidity in separation streams, and potentially for burnup and Pu/U flow-sheet verification inputs. If it is wrong, delayed or manipulated, the main danger is that operators or downstream automation start trusting it as a primary measurement. The model was only demonstrated on clean laboratory samples. Real streams contain Pu, Np, Tc, Ru, Zr, radiolytic species, organics (TBP/dodecane carryover), entrained solids, radiation-darkened optics and fouled windows, so extrapolation is a serious implicit risk. Harm needs the independent criticality, accountancy and lab-verification layers to fail too, so the likely consequences are degraded process control, off-spec product, misleading material balances and loss of safeguards confidence, not direct criticality.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Lab-to-plant generalization failure: the training data are bench-prepared binary or quaternary solutions. Real streams add interfering species, different matrix and fluorescence quenching (nitrate, chloride, Fe, Ru, organics), radiolysis, and optical-path changes from window fouling, fiber darkening or laser and detector aging. The regressors can output confident but biased U(VI) or acid values with no indication they are outside the calibration domain. A stacked ensemble gives no natural out-of-distribution flag, and its predicted temperature may be coupled to the other outputs, so one corrupted spectral feature can propagate into all four quantities (cascading and intra-system bias). Plausible consequence: undetected under-reading of U concentration or acidity in a stream, with delayed detection of flow-sheet excursions, misrouted product or solvent-extraction upsets. Criticality control still rests on independent measurements and procedure, so the main harm is process and accountancy error. (2) Automation trust and skill fade: near-real-time numbers displayed with decimals invite over-trust. Operators may stop doing confirmatory sampling, and if the model is tied to alarms, setpoints or feed control, a biased reading becomes a control input (mode and clumsy-automation issues). (3) Samarium is a surrogate: using Sm fluorescence to infer burnup or fission-product content assumes Sm behaves like the real inventory, and in actual spent-fuel solutions with Eu, Gd, Cm, Am and other interferents the inference may fail. Declaring burnup or material attributes from it without a qualified basis risks a safeguards misinterpretation. (4) Qualification and repeatability gaps: ensemble hyperparameters and retraining are non-deterministic, there is no V&V basis for safety-related use, and recalibration after instrument maintenance can silently change model behavior. Version control and change management are weak points. (5) Small data and nuclear data scarcity: hot, Pu-bearing, high-dose training data are scarce, expensive and often classified or proprietary, so the model is likely built on surrogates and simulated mixes. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training and calibration data poisoning or supply chain compromise: a tampered calibration set, model file or retraining pipeline could embed a small systematic bias in U or acid readings. This is hard to see because plausible-looking readings still agree with sparse grab samples, and it could mask diversion-relevant concentration changes or hide a process anomaly. Calibration drift is a natural cover story for the bias. (7) Spectrum-level manipulation: an adversary with access to the spectrometer, fiber, or data link between the probe and the model could inject or alter spectra (a small perturbation to a few channels) so the regressors give wrong outputs while raw-signal sanity checks pass. A physical or optical interference, such as an added fluorescent contaminant in the stream, could do something similar with no cyber access. Safeguards-wise, this could be used to hide a material or solute-concentration discrepancy from in-line monitoring and to reduce confidence in the data. (8) Denial of the monitor through spectrometer or network compromise, or timing an attack around its known weak regime (high acidity, high temperature), forces a fall-back to slower lab sampling and degrades the monitoring cadence. (9) Cloud or remote model hosting and vendor-update channels would add a data-exfiltration route for plant composition data and an update path for tampering. Existing practice (independent redundant measurements, periodic calibration verification against lab assays, safeguards-approved measurement systems with authentication and tamper indication) mitigates most of these, but only if the ML output is kept advisory and its inputs and models are placed under the same authentication and change control as other safeguards or safety-relevant instrumentation.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a multi-output stacked regressor (PLS, SVR, tree ensembles and a meta-learner) trained on lab-prepared spectra of a small, factorial grid of U(VI), Sm3+, HNO3 and temperature. It is meant to run in-line on a real reprocessing stream. The key fragility is the gap between the training distribution and the deployment distribution. Lab samples are clean, with only four analytes, and were measured on one bench instrument. A real separation stream has Pu, Np, Tc, Ru, Zr, Nd and other lanthanides, TBP/dodecane degradation products, radiolysis products, and gamma-induced optical-fibre darkening and window fouling. None of these appear in the training data. The model also gives no structural signal that it is out of distribution. A stacked ensemble returns a confident point estimate for any spectrum, so a wrong input yields a plausible-looking number. Interferents, instrument ageing and probe replacement all move the spectra, and the ensemble has no built-in OOD or calibration-transfer layer. Because the four outputs share one feature set and one meta-learner, an error from one cause (for example a temperature-driven band shift) can leak into the U and acid estimates.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift and an unmodelled matrix (OP.C0302, C0302.01, C0302.03, C0201.01/.04). Training used lab-prepared simulated solutions, so real-stream interferents, fluorescence quenching by nitrate, Cl- and other quenchers, radiolytic changes and spectral baseline drift produce silently biased U(VI) and HNO3 estimates. The facility depends on these numbers for process control and for nuclear material accounting. Consequences are off-spec separations, a distorted material balance, and a degraded safeguards measurement. (2) Surrogate-to-real mismatch (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0303). Sm is a fluorescent surrogate. Its behaviour may not map to burnup indicators in irradiated fuel, which carries real fission-product spectra and a very different radiation background. The burnup extension is therefore an unvalidated transfer. A burnup figure with no tie to reference data could mislead operators or safeguards users. (3) Calibration transfer, sensor ageing and recalibration (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0204). Fibre-optic and probe degradation under radiation, laser power drift and temperature coupling require retraining or calibration transfer. Retraining on small new datasets creates non-repeatability (OP.C0402.01) and a requalification burden (OP.C0501), which a facility is tempted to skip. (4) Automation trust and opacity (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0403). Stacked ensembles are hard to explain, and no uncertainty is reported. Operators may trust multi-analyte outputs and fall out of the habit of cross-checking against grab-sample analysis. This is a risk because the inference gives no flag for being out of range (OP.C0102). (5) Cascading propagation (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). A shared feature pipeline and meta-learner mean one corrupted channel affects all four outputs at once.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Input-level evasion or manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043, T0041). An adversary with physical or network access to the spectrometer, fibre path or acquisition PC could add spectral artifacts, such as a small baseline, a fluorescence background or a band shift. This could pull U or acid readings toward a target while process reality stays unchanged. That would hide diversion or a process upset. It needs no model knowledge beyond a surrogate model trained on public data. The ORNL paper is open, and the model family and feature type are inferable (AML.T0000, T0005, T0013/T0014, T0002.000). (7) Supply chain and artifact integrity (AML.T0010.001/.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0059, T0076). Compromised chemometric libraries, a poisoned retraining dataset, or a tampered serialized model could shift predictions systematically in a narrow concentration window. Sparse retraining data makes small poisoned sets influential, and the shift is hard to see against normal drift. (8) Integrity of the data path and availability (AML.T0029, T0031, T0046). The model runs near real time, so tampering with timestamps, scaling, or the spectra-to-model interface, or denying the service, breaks monitoring. Operators then have to fall back to manual sampling, which is slower and less continuous. An adversary could time an attack around this gap or around known recalibration. (9) Model-reliance that creates a gap in safeguards (OP.C0701, OP.C0703). A model trusted for burnup or inventory indication, with scarce validation data, gives an adversary a deniable error channel where an apparently AI-verified measurement conceals a discrepancy.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this model is a trusted, continuous, non-destructive source of U(VI) concentration, acidity and a burnup proxy in a reprocessing stream, which is exactly where process monitoring and nuclear material accountancy intersect. Its value to an adversary is mainly indirect. An insider or a supply-chain compromise could quietly bias the numbers so that diversion, or a process upset such as an acidity excursion or off-spec feed, goes unnoticed or is explained away as 'model noise'. It is also a plausible weak link because it was built and validated on clean laboratory samples, so the gap between the lab data and a real radiolytic, multi-species plant stream is a natural failure mode an adversary could time an action around. Compared with attacking the DCS or the safeguards instrumentation directly, targeting the model is a cheap, low-visibility route to degrade or mislead an operator's confidence, especially while operators grow dependent on it.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or data tampering by an insider or supply chain: poisoning the training spectra or calibration set, or altering the stacked ensemble's weights or meta-learner, can give a small systematic bias in U(VI), HNO3 or temperature. The facility depends on these outputs for in-line process control and as a cross-check on accountancy, so the consequence is masked material loss or diversion, undetected loss of process control, or a falsified burnup indication that undermines safeguards verification. Public availability of the method (peer-reviewed, OSTI) lowers the barrier for building a proxy model and crafting inputs that move the output predictably. The ensemble's opacity makes a subtle backdoor or bias hard to spot. (2) Input-side manipulation: the model sits downstream of optical and spectrometer hardware, so tampering with spectra, the optical path, reference or calibration standards, or the data link can mislead the regression without touching the model itself. This is also a path to the process network via the instrument PC or the analytics host. (3) Concentrated trust in a single multi-output model: one model reports several correlated parameters at once, so a single compromise or fault corrupts all of them together and removes independent cross-checking. (4) Sensitive-information exposure: the model and its data can reveal throughput, fuel type or burnup characteristics, a proliferation-sensitive inference, if the outputs or training data are exfiltrated or the model is queried.

IMPLICIT, AND EXPLOITABLE AROUND. (5) Lab-to-plant generalization gap: the validation is on laboratory samples, with Sm as a surrogate. Real streams have radiolysis, other fission products and actinides, organic carryover, varied temperature and acidity, and spectral interferents, so there is a risk of out-of-distribution error, drift and a mismatch with the qualification conditions. An adversary can time an action around periods of known poor model performance. (6) Burnup extrapolation: inferring burnup from a surrogate fluorescent species is an unvalidated leap, and material substitution or unusual composition could give a falsely reassuring figure. (7) Automation trust and skill fade: continuous in-line readings tend to displace grab-sample analysis and operator chemistry judgement, producing complacency that an adversary or a slow drift can exploit. (8) Qualification, repeatability and governance gaps: no established AI-specific QA regime exists for safeguards-relevant chemometrics, and retraining or recalibration needs change control. Uncontrolled updates are an insider path, and weak change control also hides honest drift.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on lab-to-plant generalization failure, surrogate-based burnup inference, over-trust, qualification gaps, and poisoning/tampering and spectrum manipulation. I dropped speculative or weakly argued items (cloud hosting, model extraction, valid accounts, and several other codes) and kept the adversarial-versus-implicit split explicit for each threat.

evidence.citation: "Simultaneous quantification of uranium(VI), samarium, nitric acid, and temperature with combined ensemble learning, laser fluorescence, and Raman scattering for real-time monitoring," The Analyst (Royal Society of Chemistry), 147(18), 4014–4025, 2022. Authors are from Oak Ridge National Laboratory, and the page is the OSTI record.
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper builds and tests a stacked regression ensemble on combined LIFS and Raman spectra of laboratory samples. It reports prediction errors for U(VI), Sm3+, HNO3 and temperature, and compares the ensemble with conventional partial least squares regression. The paper presents the method as relevant to real-time monitoring in nuclear reprocessing and to estimating burnup from fluorescent fission products.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is the surrogate-based burnup and material-balance inference, plus tampering that hides a systematic bias; together these could falsify safeguards or accountancy readings and conceal diversion or a process upset. Direct radiological release is less likely because grab sampling and other controls remain.

reproducibility.why: Lab-to-plant generalization failure and cross-output bias propagation recur reliably whenever real streams contain interferents outside the lab training distribution. Deliberate tampering depends on access, but the implicit failure modes dominate.

exploitability.why: Credible adversarial paths (poisoning calibration data, tampering with the serialized model, manipulating the optical path or data link) need insider or privileged access to an in-plant instrument and its network. Only the weak-regime timing and public-method proxy-model threats are easier.

affected_users.why: The effect covers one in-line monitoring system, but shared feature sets bias all four outputs, which feed process control, material balance and safeguards verification. It is not clearly facility-wide.

discoverability.why: The method is published in the open literature, with its lab-only validation and burnup application stated, so the weakness class (generalization, surrogate inference, ensemble opacity) is widely known. Specific deployment details would still need partial inference.

use_case: Three-layer perceptron neural networks for acoustic leak monitoring at the VVER-440 reactor pressure vessel head. Features come from acoustic-emission sensor RMS values. The networks localize the leak position and, in a separate network, estimate the leak rate. They were tested on simulated leaks, including positions not seen in training.
incurred_insecurity:
A small three-layer perceptron fed a few acoustic-emission RMS values localizes and sizes leaks at the VVER-440 vessel head, a reactor coolant pressure-boundary location. It was validated only on simulated leaks. The main implicit threats are a simulation-to-reality gap with rare-event data scarcity, fragile RMS normalization, and opaque output that invites over-trust or disuse. The adversarial threats are sensor-level masking or spoofing, tampering with weights or normalization constants, and denial of the monitor. The function is supplementary to diverse leak-detection channels, so the main exposure is degraded defense in depth and misdirected or delayed response rather than direct loss of coolant.

Simulation-to-real gap and rare-event scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
The networks were trained and tested on simulated leaks, so real flow noise, pump and control rod drive vibration, thermal transients, sensor ageing and new leak geometries fall outside the training distribution. The MLP extrapolates silently, giving missed, mislocated or underestimated leaks, or nuisance alarms. Real vessel-head leaks are too rare to calibrate thresholds or false-alarm rates statistically. An adversary could time a manipulation to noisy operating states or to leak positions between training points, where model confidence is least justified.

Normalization and preprocessing fragility -- implicit, exploitable
Leak-rate estimation needed its own network because the RMS features required different normalization, so scaling statistics are a hidden coupling between the sensor chain and the model. A gain change, recalibration or sensor replacement silently biases the rate estimate, and a shared biased input degrades both the localization and rate outputs with no cross-check. An adversary could shift scaling constants or sensor gain so the bias passes as ordinary drift, or act just after sensor maintenance.

Opacity, no uncertainty and automation trust -- implicit, exploitable
A plain perceptron gives a point estimate with no calibrated uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag, so it always outputs a plausible location and rate. Operators may over-trust it when quiet, with skill fade in manual leak detection, or discount it after repeated false alarms. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust, or induce nuisance alarms until the monitor is disregarded.

Qualification and configuration-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
There is no established I&C qualification path for an ML monitor, so retraining, preprocessing and weight changes can escape configuration control, and retraining on new simulations can change behaviour without re-qualification. This weakens integrity baselines, so tampering with weights or constants would look like an ordinary model update.

Sensor-signal masking or spoofing -- adversarial
The low-dimensional RMS input carries little redundancy to separate a leak from injected acoustic or electrical interference, or altered sensor coupling. Someone with physical or maintenance access could suppress a real leak signature or fabricate a localization, hiding pressure-boundary degradation or inducing spurious inspections or outages.

Model, weights and data tampering -- adversarial
A poisoned simulation or retraining set, corrupted weights or altered normalization constants could bias localization or rate in ways hard to see given the model's opacity and few real validation events, or could add a condition-triggered backdoor. An insider or supply-chain route to an auxiliary, weakly integrity-checked model is a low-effort, low-visibility lever.

Monitor host compromise and denial -- adversarial
The workstation or historian hosting the model is an I&C-adjacent node, and compromising it provides a foothold to shape what operators see about vessel-head integrity or to deny the service. Removing the monitor during real degradation strips an early-warning layer.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is an advisory leak-monitoring function at the VVER-440 RPV head, a pressure-boundary location where the actual protection is leak-detection requirements, inventory balance, humidity and activity monitoring, and Technical Specification action limits. The acoustic ANN is a supplementary indicator, so a wrong output requires several layers to fail before real harm occurs. The risk is therefore less a direct safety-function failure than delayed or misdirected response, such as an operator or maintenance crew trusting a localization or rate estimate that is wrong. The documented evidence base is small: simulated leaks, RMS-only features, and interpolation to unseen positions. That is a weak basis for claiming robustness against real flow noise, the thermal, mechanical and operating-mode backgrounds of a running plant, and sensor aging.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulated-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0303). Simulated leaks are not a real through-wall crack or flange or seal leak. Real leak spectra, coolant conditions, and transient noise (pump, CRDM, boiling, valve actuation, outage activity) differ from the simulated leaks. Sensor couplant degradation, sensor replacement, and temperature drift change the RMS amplitude. The network may then produce confident but wrong localization or rate, or it may miss a real leak. The consequence is a delayed or false-negative indication at a pressure-boundary location, or a false positive that triggers unnecessary investigation or outage actions. (2) Rare-event scarcity (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Real vessel-head leaks are very rare, so field validation, false-alarm calibration, and detection thresholds cannot be established statistically. (3) Generalization over positions (OP.C0302.03). Success on unseen simulated positions does not show performance at geometries, or with multiple simultaneous leaks, that were not simulated. Leak-rate estimation needs separate normalization, which suggests sensitivity to amplitude scaling and gain changes. A change in sensor gain or a recalibration can silently bias the rate estimate (OP.C0101.03 mode error, OP.C0304.03 omission of uncertainty). (4) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0401). A point estimate with no uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag can be over-trusted for dispatching inspection. Alternatively, repeated nuisance outputs cause disuse and alarm complacency, so that a genuine early indication is dismissed. (5) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0502). There is no established I&C qualification path for an ML monitor, so retraining, firmware, and preprocessing changes may escape configuration control. Mitigation is that existing diverse leak-detection channels remain the licensing basis and the ANN is only supplementary.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. These are lower likelihood but plausible where the monitor feeds plant networks. (a) Manipulation of sensor or acquisition data (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0046). Injected or masked acoustic-emission signals, or tampering with RMS preprocessing, could suppress a real leak signature or fabricate one. This could hide pressure-boundary degradation, or induce spurious investigations and outages. Because the input is a low-dimensional RMS vector, there is little redundancy to flag implausible inputs. (b) Model or supply-chain tampering (AML.T0010, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0031). A poisoned retraining set, a corrupted weights file, or altered normalization constants could bias the localization or rate estimates, or be set to fail only under specific conditions such as a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004). (c) Availability (AML.T0029). Denial of the monitoring service during a period of real degradation removes an early-warning layer. Physical consequences still depend on the independent leak-detection systems also failing or being ignored, which engineering practice normally prevents, so the main exposure is reduced defense in depth and delayed response rather than direct loss of coolant.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small, shallow MLP regression/localization system trained on simulated leaks and fed a very low-dimensional feature (AE sensor RMS). The central ML fragility is the sim-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202). Real vessel-head leaks are rare events, so there is almost no field ground truth, and AE RMS depends heavily on the leak's physical geometry, fluid phase, flange and gasket path, background flow noise, sensor coupling and temperature. None of these can be fully covered by a simulated leak source. Held-out-position testing shows interpolation across positions, but it does not show robustness to a new leak mechanism, a new noise regime, or a degraded sensor. The paper's own finding that leak-rate estimation needed a separate network because of different RMS normalization shows how sensitive the pipeline is to preprocessing: the scaling statistics are baked in as part of the model, and any gain drift, sensor replacement or recalibration changes the input distribution without any visible failure. A plain MLP also gives no calibrated uncertainty and no out-of-distribution flag, and it will always output a plausible location and rate.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and distribution shift (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202). Failure mechanism: the model was trained on simulated or bench leaks, and at inference it sees plant-specific operational noise, such as pump and flow-induced AE, thermal transients, and sensor ageing or re-mounting. It extrapolates silently. Dependence: the leak detection and localization function, and the leak-rate estimate that supports operator decisions on whether to continue operating or shut down. Consequence: missed or late detection of a pressure-boundary leak, a mislocated leak that sends inspection to the wrong place, or an underestimated rate that delays response. False alarms from noise would instead cause unnecessary outages and operators ignoring the system (OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102). (2) Preprocessing and normalization fragility (OP.C0303, OP.C0502). The RMS scaling is a hidden coupling between the sensor chain and the model. A calibration change or sensor replacement shifts the features and breaks the rate network, while the localization network may look fine, so the two outputs become inconsistent (OP.C0603). (3) Opacity and no uncertainty (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0501). Operators cannot judge when to trust the output, and qualification of a small ML model for safety-relevant monitoring lacks an established basis. This invites over-trust (OP.C0101.04) or a role that is never clearly defined. (4) Retraining and lifecycle gaps (OP.C0204, OP.C0402.01): few real events exist to validate or update the model, and retraining on new simulations can change behavior non-deterministically without re-qualification.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Sensor-input manipulation and evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0041). Features are only a few RMS scalars, so an adversary with physical or signal-chain access could inject acoustic or electrical noise, or alter sensor coupling or gain, to mask a real leak or fabricate a localization. A small MLP is easy to probe, and a surrogate (AML.T0005) could be built from published literature (AML.T0000). The consequence is concealed degradation of the pressure boundary or induced spurious shutdowns. (6) Model or data integrity (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031). Poisoned simulation data, tampered weights, or altered normalization constants in the deployed pipeline would bias localization or rate estimates in ways that are hard to see, given opacity and few real validation events. (7) Timing: an adversary could exploit known drift or blind periods, such as after sensor maintenance, to act when model confidence is least justified.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this is a small, low-glamour model (a three-layer perceptron fed by a few acoustic-emission RMS channels), so a nation-state would be unlikely to target it for its own sake. It matters as a stepping stone and as a vigilance-shaper. It sits on the reactor coolant pressure boundary, where leak detection informs operator decisions about shutdown and inspection. If operators come to rely on its localization and leak-rate outputs, an adversary or an unlucky natural fault can hide a real leak or provoke a false one at a chosen time. The most plausible adversary routes are cheap and indirect: insider or supply-chain tampering with the sensor chain, the normalization parameters or the model weights, or physically injecting acoustic noise that the RMS features cannot tell from a leak. The non-adversarial weaknesses are what an adversary would time an attack around. The model was validated only on simulated leaks, it is poorly explainable, and the leak-rate network needs its own normalization.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Sensor-level evasion or spoofing. The input is a low-dimensional RMS summary of acoustic-emission channels, so it carries little information to separate leak signatures from other acoustic sources. Someone with physical or maintenance access could inject acoustic or electrical interference, or mask or mimic a leak signature (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0041). The consequence is either a suppressed real leak, which delays response on the pressure boundary, or a spurious localization or leak-rate alarm that triggers needless outages or inspections, and the outage can be timed to coincide with other activity. (2) Insider or supply-chain tampering with weights, scaler and normalization parameters, or the training and calibration data (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0020, AML.T0076). The leak-rate network is especially sensitive to normalization, so a small shift in the scaling constants could bias leak-rate estimates in a way that looks like ordinary drift. Few facilities have integrity checks or independent baselines for such an auxiliary model, so this is a low-effort, low-visibility lever. (3) Pivot and trust concentration. The monitoring workstation or data historian that hosts the model is an I&C-adjacent node, and compromising it (AML.T0012, AML.T0112) offers a foothold and a way to shape what operators see about vessel head integrity. IMPLICIT, adversary-exploitable. (4) Simulation-only validation and a small training set (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0302.03). The reported tests used simulated leaks, including unseen positions. Real leaks, with varying temperature, flow noise, pump and control rod drive vibration, and sensor aging, may fall outside the training distribution (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303). Adversaries can exploit known blind spots, such as leak positions or rates that fall between training points, or can time an action to coincide with noisy operating states. (5) Automation trust and vigilance erosion (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). An always-quiet monitor breeds complacency and skill fade in manual leak-detection practice, so a quiet period can pass for assurance. Conversely, frequent false positives may lead to disuse (OP.C0101.05), and an adversary could induce nuisance alarms until operators discount or disable the system. (6) Opacity and qualification gap (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0502). Operators cannot easily tell whether a perceptron output is trustworthy, and there is no AI-specific qualification regime for it. Tampering or silent degradation would therefore go unnoticed, and weight or version control may be informal. (7) Cascading effects (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). The leak-rate network depends on the localization result and on shared inputs, so one biased input propagates to both outputs, and a single compromised sensor channel degrades both outputs with no cross-check. Overall, the tampering and masking risk is modest but real, and the more serious concern is that an unqualified, simulation-validated monitor could be given decision weight on a safety-relevant boundary without an independent diverse backup.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulation-to-real gap, normalization fragility, opacity-driven trust problems, qualification gap, sensor masking and weight/data tampering. I dropped weakly argued or speculative codes (reconnaissance, proxy-model, T0046, T0076, T0005) and kept host compromise and denial as one distinct adversarial threat.

evidence.citation: "A neutral network approach for acoustic leak monitoring in the VVER-440 pressure vessel head," Progress in Nuclear Energy (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The journal paper (the title's "neutral" is the publisher's spelling) reports neural networks built to localize leaks and estimate leak rate at the VVER-440 vessel head. It was tested in experiments with simulated leaks. Three-layer perceptrons worked best, and leak-rate estimation needed an additional network because the RMS features of the acoustic-emission sensors required different normalization. The search result gave only the abstract, so I did not read the full text.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is masking or spoofing, or silent degradation, of leak monitoring at a reactor coolant pressure-boundary location, which erodes defense in depth and delays response; because the function is supplementary to diverse detection channels, direct radiological release is unlikely, so this is operational disruption and safety-margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Silent extrapolation outside the simulated training distribution and normalization bias occur reliably once conditions such as sensor changes, noisy states or new leak geometries arise, but the adversarial paths depend on specific access and timing.

exploitability.why: Credible adversarial paths (physical or maintenance access to sensors, insider or supply-chain access to weights and normalization constants, compromise of an I&C-adjacent host) need privileged access and domain knowledge, and are not routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Impact is confined mainly to one monitoring function at the vessel head (localization and rate outputs sharing biased inputs), with limited propagation to other systems because diverse leak-detection channels exist.

discoverability.why: The weakness classes (sim-to-real gap, normalization sensitivity, opacity of small MLPs, sensor spoofing) are well documented in the open literature and the approach is published, but system-specific deployment, configuration and integration details would need to be inferred by a capable outsider.

use_case: Multi-agent LLM 'Regulatory Context Protocol' (an agent-to-agent communication standard) that automates the Request for Additional Information (RAI) exchange between NRC reviewers and advanced-reactor applicants. It is grounded in a corpus of NRC ADAMS advanced-reactor docket documents (RAI responses, audit reports, topical reports, submissions). Human oversight is kept at safety-significant decision points. It aims to shorten licensing review time and cost.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case places an LLM multi-agent pipeline, grounded in a small public ADAMS corpus, between the NRC reviewer and the applicant, where it shapes which safety questions get asked and which answers are accepted. The main threats are adversary-influenced text flowing into reviewer-side agents, poisoning of the precedent corpus, compromise of the protocol and model supply chain, aggregation and leakage of sensitive design information, and implicit content-fidelity, data-scarcity, drift, human-factors and qualification weaknesses. The physical consequence is indirect and delayed: a latent gap in the licensing basis that survives only if downstream staff review, ACRS review and inspection also fail.

Indirect prompt injection via applicant submissions -- adversarial
Applicant RAI responses, attachments and topical reports are untrusted text that reviewer-side agents summarize and reason over. Embedded instructions or crafted framing can poison agent context, so a deficiency is downplayed, an item is marked resolved, or an issue is routed as non-significant and bypasses human review.

Corpus and retrieval poisoning -- adversarial
An adversary who can submit or influence docketed ADAMS material, or tamper with the local mirror, index or embeddings, can shape the precedent the agents treat as authoritative. Biased retrieval and fabricated or altered citations make skewed outputs look verified, and a poisoned precedent can be reused in later reviews.

Agent-to-agent protocol spoofing and tool abuse -- adversarial
A new, immature inter-agent standard exposes impersonation, message injection and unintended tool invocation. A spoofed or compromised agent can alter or suppress RAI messages, so the regulator-applicant record loses integrity, and agent configuration can be silently changed.

Model and tooling supply chain -- adversarial
Backdoored open-weight models, fine-tunes, agent frameworks or protocol libraries inside a regulator-trusted pipeline can silently skew outputs or hold a latent trigger. This is a quiet route to manipulating licensing outcomes.

Information aggregation and leakage -- adversarial
The system concentrates proprietary design data, export-controlled and security-related information, and reviewer deliberations in prompts, RAG stores and inter-agent logs. Leakage gives an adversary design-weakness intelligence and insight into review strategy, and public-corpus security models do not fit these non-public submissions.

Reconnaissance and volume flooding of the reviewer agent -- adversarial
The public preprint, protocol spec and corpus let an applicant model the reviewer-agent's behavior and tailor submissions to pass it. High-volume or chaff submissions can also overload the agents and reviewers, or stall a specific applicant's review.

Content fidelity failure -- implicit, exploitable
Hallucinated or misattributed precedent, mistranslated regulatory terms, and omitted limiting conditions in RAI drafts and summaries can make an incomplete safety case look complete, and errors cascade because every downstream agent consumes them. An adversary can rely on reviewers seeing only the digest, hiding a safety-relevant nuance in material the summarizer is likely to drop.

Automation bias and undefined oversight boundary -- implicit, exploitable
Fluent drafts and schedule pressure from the time-and-cost goal erode reviewer vigilance and independent skill, and the undefined 'safety-significant' threshold lets upstream non-flagged steps bypass review. An adversary can keep issues below that threshold or time a deficient submission for high-volume periods to exploit reviewer fatigue.

Small-corpus and out-of-distribution weakness -- implicit, exploitable
A corpus of about 1,236 documents covering few, heterogeneous advanced-reactor designs gives thin precedent, so the model may apply LWR-style reasoning or read the absence of past RAIs as absence of an issue. The agents are least reliable on novel features, which an adversary can exploit by presenting a novel design feature where the agent has no precedent to flag.

Regulatory and corpus drift -- implicit, exploitable
Changing rules (Part 53, risk-informed guidance) and docket content leave a frozen model and corpus encoding superseded positions, or shift behavior through uncontrolled retraining. An adversary can cite stale precedent the agents still treat as authoritative.

Non-determinism, opacity and weak qualification -- implicit, exploitable
Stochastic multi-agent inference, version changes and opacity make it impossible to reproduce why a question was or was not raised, and no AI-specific QA framework exists, with evidence limited to a non-peer-reviewed preprint and modeled savings. This weakens the auditable regulatory record and hinders detecting manipulation or assigning accountability.

Goal misalignment toward closing RAIs -- implicit
Optimizing for review time and cost can push agents toward closing RAIs rather than surfacing real gaps. A realistic adversary gains little beyond what the automation-bias pathway already provides.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a licensing-engineering lens, the RAI exchange is where the regulator probes whether the safety case holds together, so an LLM that drafts or answers RAIs sits upstream of the technical basis for a license. If a reviewer-side agent omits a question, or an applicant-side agent writes a confident but unsupported response, the error does not hurt anyone at once. It travels into the SER and the licensing basis, where it becomes a latent design or analysis deficiency. Existing practice does guard against much of this: staff technical review, audits, ACRS review, inspection, and commissioning testing. But the stated purpose is to cut review time and cost, and that pushes toward thinner human scrutiny, so the safeguards are exactly what get eroded. The corpus is also small (1,236 documents), drawn from public ADAMS records, and covers a young set of non-LWR designs, so the AI's grounding is thin where the physics and precedent are least settled. The pilot is a non-peer-reviewed preprint whose savings are modelled, not measured.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT: (1) Content fidelity failure. Hallucinated or misattributed precedent, such as citing a prior docket or regulation that does not support the claim, or omitting a limiting condition from a topical report, can make an incomplete safety case look complete. Reviewers may then close an RAI with an applicant analysis (thermal-hydraulics, source term, fuel qualification, PRA assumptions) that was never actually verified. The consequence is a licensing basis with a hidden gap. It would only surface in inspection or operation, after capital is committed. (2) Automation bias and skill fade. Staff reviewing agent-drafted RAIs may anchor on the agent's framing and stop asking novel questions. The 'safety-significant decision points' are not defined, so the boundary between what is automated and what is escalated is itself a weakness. Under schedule pressure, mode errors and rubber-stamping are likely. (3) Data scarcity and OOD generalization. A small corpus of advanced-reactor dockets, in which few designs are mature, means precedent is thin and heterogeneous. The model may apply LWR-style reasoning to novel designs, or treat the absence of past RAIs as evidence that no issue exists. Non-determinism makes review records hard to reproduce, which is a problem for a regulatory record that must be auditable and defensible. Qualification is also immature, since no AI-specific QA framework exists for NRC use. (4) Corpus drift. Regulations are changing (Part 53, risk-informed frameworks), so a corpus of past dockets can encode superseded positions.

ADVERSARIAL: (5) Corpus and RAG poisoning. ADAMS is public and applicants write the documents. An applicant, a competitor, or a state actor could seed submissions with content that steers agent reasoning (indirect prompt injection in PDFs), or manipulate which precedents are retrieved. The consequence is biased or softened RAIs, or a skewed regulatory interpretation. (6) Agent-to-agent protocol exploitation. Impersonating or masquerading as an agent, injecting instructions through a message, or manipulating context across the exchange could alter the substance of RAIs, suppress questions, or exfiltrate pre-decisional or proprietary and security-related information such as export-controlled design data and Safeguards Information. Mixing proprietary applicant data with an LLM pipeline raises a data-governance problem: public-corpus security models do not fit non-public submissions. (7) Supply chain risk from the open-weight model, the protocol libraries, and the tools. Backdoored weights or poisoned tools in a regulator-trusted pipeline would be a quiet route to manipulating licensing outcomes. (8) Denial or delay of the service to stall a specific applicant's review, or an adversary using exposed agent outputs for reconnaissance of design weaknesses and of what the regulator considers sensitive. The physical consequence is indirect and delayed. It depends on downstream human review and independent verification also failing, which is the main mitigating factor.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a RAG-plus-multi-agent LLM pipeline whose fragility sits in the pipeline rather than the facility. Its entire epistemic basis is a small (1,236-document) public ADAMS corpus. Those documents record historical outcomes on a few advanced-reactor dockets, not ground truth about safety adequacy. Agent-to-agent protocols add a text-mediated trust boundary: each agent consumes another agent's output, and in this case the applicant-side agent's text is adversary-influenced by design. The open-weight local model avoids cloud dependency but adds model-provenance, version-pinning and qualification problems. The reported savings come from a reconstructed baseline and a briefly described pilot, so the evidence does not show that outputs are faithful, repeatable or robust.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Indirect prompt injection and agent-to-agent trust abuse: applicant submissions, attachments and RAI responses are untrusted text that flows into reviewer-side agents and the retrieval context. Embedded instructions or crafted phrasing could steer summaries, suppress or downplay a technical gap, or trigger unintended tool calls, and it would be hard to attribute (AML.T0051.001, T0053, T0080, T0110). A protocol standard also lets message spoofing or impersonation between agents propagate across the whole chain (T0073, T0074). The consequence is regulatory findings that rest on manipulated analysis, which erodes licensing-basis integrity and, in the worst case, lets safety-relevant deficiencies pass. (2) RAG and corpus poisoning: ADAMS content is public and ingested continuously. An adversary or careless party can shape what gets retrieved by submitting or crafting documents, or by tampering with the index or embeddings (T0070, T0071, T0066, T0020, T0010.002). The result is biased precedent retrieval, and a poisoned precedent can be reused in later reviews. (3) Supply chain: open-weight model weights, fine-tunes, agent frameworks and protocol libraries could be backdoored or swapped silently (T0010.001, T0010.003, T0018.000, T0109). The effect is a latent trigger or systematically skewed outputs inside a regulator workflow. (4) Information exposure: aggregated RAI context, reviewer queries and applicant proprietary or security-sensitive information (SUNSI/export-controlled) could leak through LLM data leakage, memory or RAG stores, or inter-agent logs (T0057, T0085.000, T0025). (5) Reconnaissance: the public preprint, protocol spec and corpus let an applicant model reviewer-agent behavior and tailor submissions to pass it (T0000, T0005, T0043.003).

IMPLICIT. (1) Content fidelity: hallucinated or misattributed citations, mistranslation of regulatory terms, and omission of conditions or caveats in RAI drafts (OP.C0304.01, .02, .03). Because every downstream agent consumes the output, these errors cascade (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). (2) Data scarcity and provenance: a small advanced-reactor corpus covers a handful of designs and mixes outcome-bearing and procedural text, so there is little ground truth on what a correct RAI looks like (OP.C0202, C0203, C0201.05). Novel designs fall outside that distribution, and the system is least reliable exactly where licensing risk is highest (OP.C0302, C0302.03). (3) Drift: regulations, guidance, review standards and docket content change (concept drift). A frozen model and corpus, or an uncontrolled retrain, quietly shifts behavior (OP.C0302.01, .02, C0503). (4) Qualification and repeatability: stochastic inference, multi-agent path dependence, prompt and model version changes, and opacity make reviews hard to reproduce, audit or defend in an adjudicatory record (OP.C0402.02, C0401, C0501, C0303, C0504). (5) Human factors: 'human oversight at safety-significant points' is vulnerable to automation bias, rubber-stamping, skill fade and mis-scoped definition of what counts as safety-significant, so errors in upstream non-flagged steps bypass review (OP.C0101.04, .06, .01, C0102). (6) Goal misalignment: optimizing for time and cost can push the system toward closing RAIs rather than surfacing real gaps (OP.C0301). An adversary can time submissions around these weaknesses, for example flooding with volume to exploit reviewer fatigue and chaff (T0046, T0029).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this system is not a plant-control target but a high-value trust-concentration point in the licensing chain: it sits between regulator and applicant, ingests applicant-authored text that the regulator's agent must treat as input, and its outputs shape what safety questions get asked and what answers are accepted. A deliberate adversary (a hostile applicant, a competitor, a state actor seeking design intelligence or a weakened review) gains leverage by influencing the questions that are never asked, rather than by crashing anything. The agent-to-agent protocol also creates a machine-readable channel where applicant content flows into the reviewer's context, which is a classic indirect-injection and context-poisoning surface. Human oversight 'at safety-significant decision points' is the control an adversary would aim to bypass, either by keeping issues below the threshold the system labels significant or by exploiting reviewer fatigue as throughput rises.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Indirect prompt injection and context poisoning via applicant submissions (AML.T0051.001, T0080, T0093): the applicant agent's RAI responses, attachments and topical reports are content the reviewer-side agents summarize and reason over. Embedded instructions or crafted framing could cause the reviewer agent to downplay a deficiency, mark an item resolved, or route an issue as non-significant. The dependency is the reviewer's completeness and adequacy judgment, and the consequence is a licensing basis with unresolved safety gaps. (2) Corpus and retrieval poisoning (AML.T0070, T0066, T0020, T0010.002): grounding on public ADAMS documents means an adversary who can submit or influence docketed material, or who tampers with the local mirror or index, can shape precedent the agents treat as authoritative. This could skew what counts as acceptable resolution, and fabricated or altered citations (T0067.000) make the output look verified. (3) Protocol-level attack surface: a new agent-to-agent standard is immature software with impersonation, spoofing and tool-invocation risks (T0073, T0053, T0010.005, T0081). A spoofed or compromised agent could inject, alter or suppress RAI messages, so the record of regulator-applicant exchange loses integrity. (4) Information aggregation and exfiltration (T0085, T0057, T0025): the system concentrates proprietary design data, security-related and export-controlled information, and reviewer deliberations, making it a richer espionage target than scattered documents. Leakage would reveal design weaknesses or review strategy. Local open-weight inference helps, but model supply chain (T0010.003, T0018) and the access governance around it still matter. (5) Insider angle: a reviewer or applicant staffer with legitimate access can tune prompts or agent configuration, or select which corpus is used, in ways that are hard to audit. IMPLICIT, adversary-exploitable. (6) Automation trust and complacency (OP.C0101.04, C0101.01, C0102, C0101.06): faster cycles and fluent drafts erode reviewer vigilance and independent technical skill, and a patient adversary can time a deficient submission for high-volume periods. (7) Hallucination, omission and oversimplification (OP.C0304.01, C0304.03) can drop a safety-relevant nuance in summarization, with the human seeing only the digest. (8) Data limits: the corpus of about 1,236 documents is small and skewed toward past designs, so novel advanced-reactor features are out of distribution (OP.C0202, C0203, C0302) and the agent will be least reliable exactly where novelty matters. (9) Non-determinism, opacity and weak qualification (OP.C0402.02, C0401, C0501, C0504): the evidence is a non-peer-reviewed preprint with modeled savings, so the reviewer cannot reproduce or audit why a question was or was not raised, which hinders detecting manipulation and attributing accountability. (10) Governance scope (OP.C0503, C0505): a pilot-derived tool may be adopted without a threat model for the licensing process itself, with the 'safety-significant' threshold left poorly defined and therefore gameable. Overall, a sophisticated adversary would more likely exploit this as a low-cost route to influence regulatory outcomes or collect design intelligence than attack the plant directly, and the integrity of the licensing record is the asset at stake.

I dropped low-fit candidates (e.g., T0092, T0109, T0110, T0082) and kept single-panelist items such as reconnaissance and chaff flooding, and the goal-misalignment point, where they were distinct and argued.}

evidence.citation: "Overcoming the Regulatory Bottleneck via Agent-to-Agent Protocols: A Nuclear Case Study," arXiv (Argonne National Laboratory authors; preprint, not peer reviewed)
evidence.note: The authors propose a multi-agent LLM protocol that structures regulator-applicant RAI exchanges. They calibrate it on 1,236 NRC advanced-reactor docket documents retrieved from ADAMS and report a working multi-agent pilot, with local inference using an open-weight LLM. This is an arXiv preprint and has not been peer reviewed. Its cost and time savings are modelled against a reconstructed baseline, and the pilot is only briefly described.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is manipulation of licensing outcomes (injection, corpus poisoning, supply-chain backdoor), which can leave a latent gap in the licensing basis; the entry itself says the physical consequence is indirect and delayed and needs downstream staff review, ACRS review and inspection to also fail, so the harm is mostly safety-margin erosion and loss of regulatory record integrity, plus sensitive-information leakage.

reproducibility.why: Prompt injection, content-fidelity errors, automation bias and drift are reliably reproducible in LLM pipelines, but turning them into a surviving licensing gap depends on stochastic model behavior, human oversight points and downstream review, so the full end-to-end outcome is conditional.

exploitability.why: Applicants submit text through a routine channel, so indirect injection and chaff need no insider access, but corpus tampering, protocol spoofing and supply-chain compromise need privileged access or substantial resources, and the applicant must be able to craft submissions that evade human review.

affected_users.why: Errors cascade across all agents in the pipeline and a poisoned precedent can be reused in later reviews, which affects multiple licensing dockets and the regulatory record, but the impact stays in the licensing process and does not reach plant-wide coupled systems.

discoverability.why: The preprint, protocol spec and public ADAMS corpus are public and the weakness classes (prompt injection, RAG poisoning, hallucination, automation bias) are well documented for LLM agent systems, so a capable outsider can readily infer that the weaknesses exist, though system-specific internals remain non-public.

use_case: Tool-using large-language-model agent that assists operators of an integral PWR simulator. It uses retrieval-augmented generation over the plant manual and procedures, and an LSTM predictive module for reactor power. It responds to a boron-concentration anomaly and drafts new operating procedures, executing commands and adjusting operating parameters directly in the simulator.
incurred_insecurity:
An LLM agent with write authority over simulator parameters, grounded in a retrieval corpus and trusting an LSTM power predictor, collapses the separation between advice and actuation. The main threats are corruption of the retrieval corpus and tool layer, which steers the agent into unsafe actions or wrong procedures; compromise of the predictor and model supply chain; and implicit failures of content fidelity, trust, generalization, repeatability and qualification. Nothing physical is at stake in the simulator demonstration, but the pattern sets a precedent for training simulators, digital twins and operator-support tools, where protective barriers would erode.

Retrieval corpus poisoning and indirect injection -- adversarial
Anyone who can edit the plant manual, procedures, logs or tool-returned text can plant content in the RAG index or injected instructions that steer the agent's boron response or its newly drafted procedures. The agent executes with delegated authority, so a low-privilege document write becomes an unsafe parameter change or an authoritative-looking wrong procedure.

Agentic tool and configuration abuse -- adversarial
The function-call interface lets a jailbreak, injected instruction, poisoned tool definition or altered agent configuration turn a conversational channel into command execution. Embedded tool credentials add a lateral-movement prize, and in a plant-coupled analogue the result would be unauthorized parameter manipulation that bypasses two-person verification and weakens defence-in-depth.

Predictor and sensor-feed manipulation -- adversarial
Poisoned LSTM training data, a backdoored checkpoint, or falsified boron and power telemetry can bias the agent's picture of the plant. This can mask a real anomaly or provoke an unnecessary response, and an attacker can time it to coincide with a genuine transient.

Model supply chain and hosted-API dependence -- adversarial
A hosted foundation model, agent tools or dependencies can be compromised or silently changed, altering agent behaviour with no retraining event visible to the facility. Cloud dependence also sends procedures and operating state to a third party, creating a collection and leakage target and an availability dependency during anomalies.

Procedure and design knowledge exposure -- adversarial
Agent logs, system prompts, the indexed manual and generated procedures reveal plant response logic and operator workflows. This gives reconnaissance value for planning later attacks, even from a simulator.

Content fidelity failure in diagnosis and procedure drafting -- implicit, exploitable
The LLM can hallucinate setpoints, retrieve the wrong section or revision, or omit preconditions such as boration versus dilution direction, and because the agent actuates directly, the error becomes a state change rather than a suggestion. Newly drafted procedures bypass V&V and configuration control, and an adversary can rely on operators trusting these plausible drafts to slip in a subtly wrong step.

Automation trust erosion -- implicit, exploitable
Fluent end-to-end handling of anomalies invites over-trust, skill fade, out-of-the-loop operators, and confusion over who is in control, weakening the independent human barrier in rare anomalies. An adversary can time a manipulation to this complacency or rely on it to leave a wrong action unchallenged.

Simulator-to-plant generalization gap -- implicit, exploitable
The LSTM and agent behaviour are validated on idealised simulated transients with few boron anomaly cases, so sensor noise, ageing, faults and operating-mode differences are out-of-distribution, and the LLM propagates the predictor's confident errors. An adversary can induce or exploit out-of-envelope conditions where the predictor is unreliable and its errors go unflagged.

Non-repeatability and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
The same anomaly can yield different action sequences across runs, and the reasoning gives no reliable audit trail, which defeats verification and forensic reconstruction. An adversary's manipulation can hide among normal run-to-run variation and be hard to attribute.

Qualification and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
No accepted QA, regulatory or data-security regime exists for an LLM agent with write authority, and index, prompt or model-version changes are handled as ordinary content edits. An adversary can time an attack around such uncontrolled changes, or benefit from a demonstrator quietly promoted into operations without qualification.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a simulator demonstration, so nothing physical is at stake today. The vulnerability class that matters is what happens if the pattern migrates toward a training simulator, an operator-support tool, or a plant digital twin. The agent has write authority: it executes commands and adjusts parameters directly. It also drafts procedures with an LLM, and it works on boron concentration, which controls reactivity in a PWR. In a real plant, boron dilution and boration are tightly procedurized, interlocked and alarmed, and the licensed operator is the legal decision-maker. A wrong agent action therefore needs several independent barriers to fail before it causes harm: operator review, procedure verification and validation, interlocks and the protection system, and the shift supervisor. The real risks are that these barriers erode through automation bias and that an agent with direct actuation access reduces the independence of those barriers.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Content fidelity failure in procedure generation and anomaly diagnosis. The LLM may hallucinate setpoints, misread the manual through RAG retrieval of the wrong section or revision, or oversimplify conditional steps such as boration versus dilution direction, limits and preconditions. Plausible-looking drafts from an agent shown to work on a simulator invite unvalidated use. Procedures normally go through V&V, human-factors review and simulator validation, and an agent that writes them without that process breaks configuration control. (2) Automation trust failure: operators who see the agent succeed in a few scenarios may over-trust it. Over time this causes skill fade, out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity and monitoring complacency, which matter most in rare anomalies where the agent is least tested. (3) Simulator-to-plant transfer. The LSTM power predictor and agent behaviour are trained or validated on simulator data with idealised noise, sensors and dynamics. Plant drift, sensor faults, aging and operating-mode differences are out-of-distribution for it, and the surrogate may show poor fidelity during abnormal transients. Few boron anomaly cases are available, which is a small-data problem. (4) Non-determinism and opacity: the same anomaly may yield different action sequences on different runs, and the reasoning is hard to audit, so qualification and repeatability under nuclear QA are difficult. The agent's tool calls could also be mis-sequenced, with mode errors or cascading parameter changes that exceed what a single reviewing operator can follow. (5) Governance gap: no accepted qualification path exists for an LLM in the control or procedure loop. If a vendor model changes or the agent is hosted off-premises, there are unannounced version changes and a dependency on external availability.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Corrupted knowledge base: poisoned or altered plant manual, procedure or RAG index content, including indirect prompt injection through documents, logs or alarm text, could steer the agent toward unsafe parameter changes. The result is a subtly wrong boron or power action or a wrong procedure that looks legitimate, and an insider with document access could do this. (2) Tool and function abuse: if the command interface is not scoped, a jailbreak or injected instruction becomes direct actuation, which is excessive agency. Physical consequences are bounded by interlocks and the protection system, so the main concern is the erosion of defence-in-depth and, on a training simulator, corrupted training. (3) Manipulated inputs to the LSTM or sensor feeds could produce false predictions that lead the agent to the wrong anomaly diagnosis and delay or misdirect operator response. (4) Denial or degradation of the agent during an anomaly, with operators who have lost familiarity. (5) Supply chain compromise of the model, agent tools or hosted API. (6) Leakage of plant procedures and design data through the LLM, which is a security-of-information risk. The best mitigations are read-only or advisory operation, human-in-the-loop approval with independent verification, whitelisted bounded commands, and keeping the agent entirely outside safety-related I&C.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML-pipeline view, this is a composite system: a general-purpose foundation LLM (not trained on plant data, no qualification basis) orchestrating a RAG index, tool/function calls with write access to the simulator, and an LSTM trained on simulator-generated transients. Each seam is a separate fragility point: the LLM's reasoning is non-deterministic and unverifiable, the RAG corpus is the sole grounding for 'plant truth', and the LSTM is only valid inside the simulated operating envelope it was trained on. The architecture collapses the usual separation between advisory output and actuation, because the agent writes parameters directly, so a content-fidelity error becomes a state change rather than a suggestion. The documented work is a simulator demonstration, and the 'no extra training' procedure-generation claim means there is no fine-tuning or evaluation harness bounding behaviour on novel scenarios. Any plant-facing migration would inherit the simulator-to-plant data gap, the LLM API/version lifecycle, and a tool layer that is a new cyber attack surface.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Indirect prompt injection / RAG poisoning (AML.T0051.001, T0070, T0071, T0066): the agent ingests plant manuals, procedures and possibly operator logs or tool outputs. Altered or planted text in the retrieval index, or in any tool-returned string, can steer the agent's reasoning, for example reframing a boron dilution step or inserting a procedure clause. The agent executes with delegated authority, so the consequence is unsafe parameter changes (reactivity or boron setpoints in a simulator now, a real control path later) and corrupted drafted procedures that operators then trust. (2) Tool-layer abuse (AML.T0053, T0110, T0099, T0081, T0010.005): the function-call interface is the privileged attack surface. Poisoned tool definitions, modified agent configuration, or hijacked tool calls convert text-channel compromise into command execution; if the system were later coupled to real plant interfaces this would also open an IT-to-OT pathway. (3) Model and supply-chain integrity (AML.T0010.001/.003, T0018, T0109): a hosted foundation model can change silently under the operator (version rug-pull, a poisoned or altered LSTM checkpoint, a compromised dependency), changing behaviour with no retraining event visible to the facility. Cloud API dependence also exposes procedure content and operating state to third parties (T0057, T0029; OP.C0601). (4) Sensor/input manipulation (AML.T0043, T0031, T0046): falsified or noisy boron and power telemetry can push the LSTM forecast and the agent's anomaly diagnosis toward wrong actions, or toward suppressed responses to a real anomaly. IMPLICIT: (5) Hallucination and content-fidelity failure (OP.C0304.01/.03, OP.C0402.02): the LLM can misread a manual, omit a precondition, or invent a step, and stochastic inference means the same anomaly may get different responses, which defeats repeatability and V&V. Drafted 'new procedures' have no qualification pathway, so they are unvalidated safety-significant documents. (6) Simulator-derived data and OOD (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0203): the LSTM is trained on simulated transients, so it is not exposed to sensor noise, ageing or real plant heterogeneity, and it can extrapolate confidently outside the training envelope; the LLM treats its output as ground truth, so errors propagate (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). A static-benchmark qualification would not capture agentic closed-loop behaviour. (7) Human-AI interaction (OP.C0101.01/.04, OP.C0401): fluent, confident explanations encourage over-trust, out-of-the-loop operators and skill fade, while opacity of chain-of-thought gives no reliable audit trail for why parameters were changed. (8) Governance gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504): no accepted software QA regime exists for LLM agents with write authority, and retrieval-index and prompt-template changes are treated as ordinary content edits rather than configuration changes to a safety-relevant system. The adversary needs only to time an attack around these weaknesses, such as an index update or model version change.
