security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this is a research simulator demonstrator, but it is the architectural template for the pattern that matters: an LLM agent with write-capable tool access to plant parameters, grounded in a document corpus and a learned predictor that it trusts. It has no plant deployment today, so a nation-state would not target it directly. It matters as a stepping stone and a design precedent. If the pattern migrates to training simulators, digital twins, or advisory systems at operating plants, it creates a new insider-accessible pathway with two properties. A retrieval corpus becomes a low-privilege write channel that influences high-consequence actions. A fluent agent concentrates operator trust in a component whose reasoning is opaque and non-repeatable. Even in simulation, the exposure of simulator-derived procedures, operator-response baselines and training scenarios has real reconnaissance value.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Retrieval/procedure poisoning. The agent grounds decisions in the plant manual and procedures through RAG. Anyone who can edit or add documents (a technical writer, a contractor, a compromised document-management account) can steer the agent's recommended boron response or newly drafted procedures without touching the model or the control system (AML.T0070, T0071, T0066, T0051.001 indirect injection via document content). The facility dependency is the procedure corpus as a trusted source. The consequence is a subtly wrong but authoritative-looking action sequence that operators may follow or that the agent executes itself. (2) Agentic tool abuse. The agent executes commands and changes parameters directly, so prompt injection, a jailbreak, or tool-definition tampering turns a conversational interface into an actuation channel (AML.T0053, T0054, T0051, T0081, T0110). The privilege boundary between 'advise' and 'act' is the key vulnerability. Credentials embedded in the agent's tool configuration are a lateral-movement prize (T0083, T0098). The consequence in a simulator is corrupted training and qualification outcomes. In any real-plant analogue it is unauthorized parameter manipulation that bypasses normal two-person and procedure-verification culture. (3) Predictive-module manipulation. The LSTM power predictor is a trusted input, so poisoned training data, a backdoored model, or manipulated sensor/simulator feeds can bias the agent's picture of the plant (T0020, T0018.000, T0043, T0010.003). A bad prediction fed to a confident agent can mask a real anomaly or provoke an unnecessary response, and an adversary can time an attack to coincide with a genuine transient. (4) Supply chain and third-party dependency. Commercial LLM APIs or hosted models raise cloud-dependency, data-leakage and rug-pull risks (T0010, T0109, T0057, OP.C0601). Procedures and plant design details sent to an external service become a collection target. (5) Stepping-stone and knowledge theft. Agent logs, system prompts, the indexed plant manual and generated procedures reveal plant response logic and operator workflows (T0085.000, T0056, T0064), and are useful for planning later attacks. Procedures drafted in a simulator could also be carried into real procedure sets with unvalidated provenance.

IMPLICIT (exploitable without an attacker). (1) Automation trust and out-of-the-loop effects. A fluent agent that handles a boron anomaly end to end invites over-trust, skill fade, and mode confusion over who is in control (OP.C0101.01, .03, .04, .06; OP.C0102). An adversary can time an action around the resulting complacency. (2) Content fidelity. The agent can hallucinate, misattribute procedure steps, or oversimplify, and a newly drafted procedure is exactly the case where no reference exists to check against (OP.C0304.01, .03). Inference non-repeatability means the same anomaly may yield different actions, which undermines verification and forensic reconstruction (OP.C0402.02, OP.C0401). (3) Qualification and generalization gaps. The system was validated on two simulator experiments, with no AI-specific QA basis and heavy dependence on simulated data. Its behavior outside those scenarios, under sensor faults, or on real plant data is unknown (OP.C0501, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0302, OP.C0303, OP.C0301). (4) Governance. There is no defined data-security model for AI-held procedures and no clear regulatory scope for agentic write access (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0503, OP.C0504). Without an enforced separation between simulator and plant networks, a demonstrator pattern could be quietly promoted into operations.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on RAG poisoning with indirect injection, agentic tool abuse, supply chain and cloud dependence, and the implicit set of fidelity, trust, simulator-to-plant and qualification failures. I kept the predictor manipulation threat and the knowledge-exposure threat as distinct, and dropped lower-confidence codes such as T0046, T0031 and T0018 root as restatements.

evidence.citation: "Large language model agent for nuclear reactor operation assistance," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Korean Nuclear Society / Elsevier)
evidence.note: The authors built an LLM agent architecture that combines documentation retrieval, callable functions and a predictive module, and connects to a nuclear reactor simulator. Two simulator experiments tested it: handling a boron concentration anomaly, and generating a new procedure parallel to the provided manual without extra model training. The work is a simulator demonstration, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is agentic tool abuse or retrieval poisoning that turns advice into unauthorized parameter changes and wrong procedures; this erodes defence-in-depth and could affect reactivity control in a plant-coupled analogue, though the demonstrated scope is a simulator, so it falls just short of a direct radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Indirect injection, RAG poisoning and LLM non-determinism are generally reliable once the agent ingests tainted content or holds write authority, though outcomes vary across runs.

exploitability.why: Poisoning documents or tool text needs some write access to corpora or the tool layer, which is a modest insider or supply-chain position, but injection and jailbreak classes need little specialized tooling.

affected_users.why: In a plant-coupled analogue, a compromised agent with write authority could propagate across coupled systems and operator teams, but the demonstrated scope is a single simulator and its operators, and the precedent effect is only prospective.

discoverability.why: RAG poisoning, prompt injection, tool poisoning, supply-chain compromise and LLM hallucination are extensively documented in open literature, and the source paper is public, so the weaknesses are evident to an adversary.

use_case: Ensemble of artificial neural networks that predicts irradiation-induced ductile-to-brittle transition temperature shift in light-water-reactor pressure vessel steels. Inputs are chemical composition, neutron flux, fluence and irradiation temperature, taken from US surveillance data (the NUREG database) and IVAR test-reactor data. The trained networks are also used to probe single-variable trends, such as the flux and temperature effects, and to assess existing embrittlement models. This supports vessel integrity assessment for long-term plant operation.
incurred_insecurity:
This offline ANN ensemble predicts irradiation-induced DBTT shift for vessel integrity and long-term-operation assessment. It is not a control function, so its main exposure is quiet erosion of the brittle-fracture margin rather than a plant transient. The main threats are non-conservative extrapolation, heterogeneous and sparse training data, spurious trends read from black-box sweeps, and a qualification gap that lets over-trust and undetected change go unchecked. Adversarially, the realistic route is poisoning of the data, code or weights, plus a stepping-stone foothold through the ML toolchain.

Extrapolation beyond training coverage -- implicit, exploitable
The ensemble interpolates smoothly with no physical monotonicity or saturation constraint, and its spread understates epistemic uncertainty at high fluence, low flux and unusual compositions. The result can be a non-conservative DBTT shift feeding PTS screening and P-T limits for 60-80 year operation. An adversary could hide a deliberate optimistic bias inside this region, where error is expected and unverifiable.

Heterogeneous, sparse and transferred data -- implicit, exploitable
Small, clustered NUREG surveillance data are merged with accelerated IVAR test-reactor data whose transfer to power-reactor flux is unvalidated, and heats leak across naive train/test splits. The network can learn dataset artefacts and overstate skill. Because no ground truth exists for decades, a tampered record would be indistinguishable from natural scatter.

Spurious trends from black-box probing -- implicit, exploitable
Single-variable sweeps push inputs into combinations absent from the training data, producing unphysical flux or temperature dependences that are then used to assess existing embrittlement models. A false trend could discredit a conservative model or favour a less conservative one. An adversary could rely on analysts' trust in this authoritative-looking evidence to steer technical or regulatory positions.

Automation trust and anchoring -- implicit, exploitable
Analysts may treat a smooth ANN prediction as independent corroboration of a regulatory correlation, or favour whichever model fits training data best. This weakens the independence of the integrity check. An adversary or a licensee seeking relaxed limits could use the tool selectively for life-extension justification.

Qualification, reproducibility and change-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
Training non-determinism, unversioned data cleaning and retraining, and the absence of an accepted ML qualification path in Reg. Guide 1.99 or ASTM E900 practice leave the tool outside safety-software configuration and cyber regimes. A silent shift in predictions cannot be told apart from retraining noise. An adversary could hide unauthorised model or data changes behind that noise.

Training-data, code and weight poisoning -- adversarial
Altering surveillance or test-reactor records, preprocessing scripts or unit conversions, or tampering with the retrained ensemble or stored weights, can bias the learned flux or temperature effect for chosen composition or fluence regions. Plausible but non-conservative outputs would erode vessel-integrity margin and could wrongly justify life extension. Backdoor-style tampering could also yield evidence for or against a flux-effect hypothesis. An insider with workstation or notebook write access is the most credible actor.

Input falsification -- adversarial
Falsified or selectively reported plant-specific inputs such as Cu content or fluence can steer a trusted prediction toward a lower shift. The low-dimensional tabular input makes this trivial and needs no crafted perturbation.

Toolchain supply-chain foothold -- adversarial
Compromised open-source ML libraries or shared model files give code execution on an engineering network holding proprietary surveillance and fracture-toughness data. That data is useful for reconnaissance and sabotage targeting. Model extraction adds little, since the data are public.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an offline engineering-analysis tool, not a control or protection function. Its output (a predicted DBTT shift) feeds vessel integrity assessment for long-term operation, meaning pressurized thermal shock (PTS) screening, pressure-temperature limit curves and license renewal. The downstream danger is therefore slow and epistemic: a biased or over-trusted embrittlement prediction that erodes the margin to brittle fracture. Reasonable-looking numbers would have to pass through surveillance-capsule programs, regulatory correlations such as Reg Guide 1.99 and the ASTM E900 form, and conservative margins, and those safeguards are what keep an error from becoming physical harm. The residual risk is that an ANN is trusted beyond its training envelope, especially at extended fluence, at low flux or at unusual compositions, and that its 'insights' on flux and temperature trends quietly shift which embrittlement models are accepted.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (dominant). (1) Extrapolation and OOD failure: the networks are trained on US surveillance data and IVAR test-reactor data. Long-term operation (60-80 years) needs predictions at fluences, flux ranges and compositions that are sparse in those data. The flux effect is where test-reactor and power-reactor data disagree, so mixing the two creates operational heterogeneity. The ANN interpolates smoothly and gives no warning, so the predicted shift can be non-conservative exactly where the margin matters most (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0204, OP.C0201.05). (2) Data quality and provenance: the surveillance database is small and heterogeneous, with inconsistent chemistry, temperature records and fluence uncertainty, and high-fluence data are scarce. Test-reactor accelerated data are transferred to power-reactor conditions without validation, so the network may learn artefacts rather than physics (OP.C0201.03, OP.C0201.05). (3) Opacity and spurious trends: single-variable sweeps of a black-box model can give unphysical flux or temperature dependences. If these are used to 'assess' mechanistic models, a false trend could be read as evidence against a conservative model, or in support of a less conservative one (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03). (4) Qualification and regulatory gap: no accepted pathway exists for using ANN predictions in safety-significant integrity assessment. Ensemble spread may be read as true uncertainty although it only reflects training variance and not model-form error (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0402.01). (5) Automation bias: analysts may favour a model that fits well on training data, and consultants or licensees might use it selectively to justify relaxed limits or extended life (OP.C0101.04). A positive output is not checked against a physical interpretation.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS (secondary, mostly integrity-focused). Poisoning of the training data or database (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059), whether surveillance records, composition entries or test-reactor data, or tampering with stored model weights (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076), could bias predictions non-conservatively. A subtle bias would be hard to detect because surveillance data are sparse and the model is opaque. The consequence is erosion of integrity margin, a possible wrongly justified life extension or relaxed P-T limits, and misdirected research or regulatory arguments (AML.T0031). Because the model is small and offline with no real-time coupling, confidentiality and availability attacks matter little. Compromised software or data supply chains for the open datasets and ML libraries are the realistic entry points (AML.T0010.001). Existing practice (independent surveillance capsule testing, conservative margins, deterministic regulatory correlations, peer review) mitigates most of this, but the tool shifts risk when it is used to underpin or replace those checks.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small-data tabular regression ensemble whose real exposure sits in the data pipeline and in how its outputs are interpreted, not in the architecture. Surveillance data (the NUREG database) is sparse, heterogeneous and clustered: a few hundred to a few thousand points, concentrated in specific heats, at low flux and moderate fluence, and with strongly correlated inputs. IVAR is a test-reactor dataset at much higher flux and with a different spectrum, so the model merges two distributions whose flux-effect confounding is exactly what the networks are then asked to resolve. Using the trained networks to 'probe' single-variable trends and to judge other embrittlement models turns a predictor into a scientific instrument. Partial-dependence sweeps push inputs into combinations (high flux with low fluence, or unusual Cu/Ni/P/Mn pairings) that never occur in the training data. Ensembles extrapolate smoothly and confidently there, so a spurious trend can be mistaken for physics and used to rank or validate regulatory-grade models. The model's prediction uncertainty is reportedly only comparable to existing literature models, so it adds little accuracy while adding opacity and qualification burden.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution and extrapolation failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0403): long-term operation assessments need predictions at fluence beyond 60-year surveillance coverage, at new compositions and at different fluxes. An ANN ensemble has no physical constraint to keep it monotone or saturating there, and ensemble spread underestimates epistemic uncertainty off-manifold. The consequence is non-conservative DBTT shift estimates feeding pressurized thermal shock and P-T limit margins, a safety consequence from AI mechanism, not from facility conditions. (2) Data provenance and quality (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0202, OP.C0204): the surveillance data are field data with measurement scatter, inconsistent Charpy fit methods, uncertain fluence and temperature histories and repeated measurements from the same heat. Naive train/test splits leak heats across folds and overstate skill. IVAR is accelerated test-reactor data whose transfer to power-reactor flux (OP.C0201.03) is itself the open question. The database is also a frozen public snapshot, so new surveillance capsules, different alloys or new-build and subsequent-license-renewal conditions are not represented (OP.C0203, OP.C0302.01). (3) Interpretive misuse and automation bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03): trends read from black-box sweeps, and used to validate or discredit established embrittlement models, may encode dataset artefacts such as correlated flux and fluence or composition clusters. Engineers may over-trust a data-driven explanation, which could bias model selection in integrity programs. (4) Qualification and lifecycle gaps (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502): training non-determinism, ensemble seeds and unversioned data cleaning make results irreproducible, and there is no accepted regulatory qualification path for ML in embrittlement trend curves such as those in Reg. Guide 1.99 or ASTM E900. A retrained model could silently shift predictions. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training-data and supply-chain integrity (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0059): public datasets and literature tables are the sole inputs, so subtle alteration of records, unit conversions or a poisoned derived copy could bias the learned flux or temperature effect without detection, because no ground truth exists to check it. Tampering with the trained weights or preprocessing code (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0076) could similarly shave predicted shift for chosen compositions. Poisoning would be hard to separate from natural scatter, which makes it a good fit for an adversary seeking to erode margin or to discredit a competing model. (6) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0031): falsified or selectively reported plant-specific inputs, such as Cu content or fluence, can steer a trusted prediction to a lower shift. Low-dimensional tabular input makes this trivial, with no crafted perturbation needed. Model exfiltration and inversion are low concern given public data. The dominant overall risk is quiet, non-conservative bias that is hard to detect and that carries over into integrity decisions through human trust.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modelling view this is a low-value direct target but a credible quiet one. The ANN ensemble is an offline, advisory analytical tool, and the decisions it informs (vessel integrity margins and license-renewal or long-term-operation arguments) are slow, reviewed and normally rest on regulatory embrittlement correlations and surveillance capsule results. A nation-state would find it far easier to attack plant control systems. The real concern is a different one. A subtly biased trend or margin estimate would be hard to detect because no ground truth exists for decades. It would also be hard to attribute, because ANNs are opaque and their errors look like ordinary scatter. Both the data and the model are built almost entirely from public literature, so an insider or supply-chain adversary can reconstruct the training pipeline. The adversary's goal would be to shift engineering judgement, not to cause a spike or alarm. It would work by eroding the evidential basis for a long-term-operation decision, or by undermining confidence in a legitimate embrittlement model when the ANN is used to assess existing models.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Data and model integrity: the NUREG surveillance dataset and the IVAR data are small, public and curated. Poisoning or selective alteration of these records, of preprocessing scripts, or of the retrained ensemble (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0018.000, T0059) could skew predicted transition-temperature shifts in specific composition, flux or fluence regions. The outputs are non-conservative but plausible, and the vessel-integrity and long-term-operation case then rests on an optimistic margin. An insider with write access to the analyst's workstation or a shared notebook environment is the most credible actor. (2) Trusted-trend manipulation: single-variable probing (flux and temperature effects) is used to judge existing embrittlement models. A tampered or backdoored ensemble (AML.T0043.004) could produce authoritative-looking evidence for or against a flux-effect hypothesis. That steers regulatory or utility technical positions, which is a persuasion attack on the safety case, not on the plant. (3) Stepping-stone and supply-chain exposure: open-source ML toolchains and pre-trained or shared model files (AML.T0010.001, T0011.000) give a foothold on an engineering network that holds proprietary fleet-specific surveillance and fracture-toughness data. This is a data-theft and reconnaissance route (AML.T0025, T0035) into plant structural-integrity information, which has value for sabotage targeting. (4) Model extraction is of little value, since the data is public.

IMPLICIT, exploitable by timing. (a) Small, clustered data with sparse coverage of high-fluence, low-flux and long-term-operation conditions (OP.C0202, C0302, C0201.03) means the ensemble extrapolates exactly where long-term-operation decisions are made, and ensemble spread may understate that uncertainty. This hides both natural error and tampering. (b) Opacity and non-determinism (OP.C0401, C0402.01) make it hard to tell retraining noise from manipulation. (c) Automation trust and anchoring (OP.C0101.04) arise when analysts treat a smooth ANN prediction as corroboration of a regulatory correlation, so the check is less independent than it appears. (d) There is a qualification and governance gap: such research-grade tools lack AI-specific QA, version control and change control (OP.C0501, C0502, C0504). That makes unauthorised model or data changes hard to detect, and it leaves the tool outside the cyber-security and configuration regime applied to safety-related software. (e) Transferring test-reactor data (IVAR) to power-reactor conditions is a standing generalisation limit that can mask a deliberate bias.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on non-conservative extrapolation and data heterogeneity as the dominant implicit risk, and on data/model poisoning as the main adversarial route. I kept input falsification (AI engineer) and the toolchain stepping stone (security) as distinct, and dropped model extraction as low-value.

evidence.citation: "Reactor pressure vessel embrittlement: Insights from neural network modelling," Journal of Nuclear Materials (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The authors train an ensemble of ANNs on two literature datasets, US power-reactor surveillance data and the IVAR test-reactor experiment, to predict RPV steel embrittlement. They use the networks to examine how each input variable affects embrittlement and report that prediction uncertainty is similar to that of literature-based models.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is quiet non-conservative erosion of the brittle-fracture margin (via extrapolation, poisoning, or falsified inputs) feeding PTS screening and life-extension justification; this falls short of a direct radiological release because the tool is offline and sits behind other regulatory checks, but it is a safety-margin erosion in a primary-boundary integrity assessment.

reproducibility.why: Extrapolation and sparse-data failures recur reliably whenever inputs fall outside training coverage, but poisoning or falsification only produces a consequential outcome if the output actually drives a regulatory or integrity decision without independent checks.

exploitability.why: The credible adversarial routes (altering data, scripts, or weights; insider write access to workstations) need insider position or supply-chain compromise, though falsifying low-dimensional tabular inputs is simple for a party that already reports them.

affected_users.why: Impact would reach vessel integrity assessments, P-T limits, and life-extension positions for a plant or fleet using the model, but it stays confined to the integrity-assessment function and does not propagate across coupled operational systems.

discoverability.why: The model architecture, datasets (NUREG, IVAR), and the limits of ML extrapolation and sparse data are in the open literature, and the gap in ML qualification under Reg. Guide 1.99 and ASTM E900 practice is publicly evident, so an outsider can readily infer where the weaknesses lie.

use_case: Convolutional neural network (ConvNet) that classifies which PWR fuel assembly locations are susceptible to crud-induced power shift (CIPS). It is trained on measured plant data from Catawba Unit 1 together with calculated core design information. It predicts the onset and peak of CIPS in a CIPS-prone cycle, avoids false alarms in a clean cycle, and uses Monte Carlo dropout to quantify prediction uncertainty. It supports anticipating and managing axial-offset anomalies during core operation.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory ConvNet for crud-induced power shift susceptibility is trained on a very small, single-unit dataset and fed by a mix of plant measurements and calculated design-code data. It is not in the protection path, and Technical Specification limits, flux mapping and excore monitoring bound the safety consequence. The main threats are quiet integrity manipulation of the data and model, plus implicit generalization, calibration and trust failures that mislead reload, chemistry and power-maneuver planning. The consequence is mainly operational and economic, with an indirect margin effect if axial-offset anomalies arrive unanticipated.

Training and input data integrity -- adversarial
An insider, compromised engineering workstation or tampered historian/design-code pipeline could poison or alter training data or input tensors, biasing per-assembly susceptibility maps toward false 'clean' results or false alarms. This could hide a developing axial-offset anomaly from planners or induce needless derates and chemistry changes, and per-assembly maps are hard to attribute because the bias looks like physics.

Model and supply-chain tampering -- adversarial
Research-grade weights, code and ML dependencies passing from a national lab to utility or vendor can be altered or backdoored so that specific assembly locations are misclassified. Manipulated Monte Carlo dropout outputs could keep confidence looking plausible and conceal the tampering.

Model and data exfiltration -- adversarial
Model artifacts, fine-tuning sets and core-design/operating histories encode proprietary loading patterns, power histories and fuel performance. If held on shared research or cloud infrastructure, they can be collected and give an adversary unit-specific insight, and the environment bridging historian and compute widens the IT/OT boundary.

Single-unit generalization and drift -- implicit, exploitable
Trained on few CIPS-prone versus clean cycles at Catawba 1, the model may be confidently wrong on other plants, new fuel designs, uprates, chemistry changes or loading strategies, and 92% accuracy hides weak minority-class performance. An adversary could time a manipulation or coincident fault to a known drift window, where missed CIPS onset passes as model error.

Overconfident uncertainty and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Monte Carlo dropout captures only approximate model uncertainty, not covariate shift or label noise, and opaque ConvNet features resist physics-based review. Operators may take a narrow band as assurance, and an adversary could rely on that misplaced trust to make tampered or degraded outputs go unchallenged.

Hybrid data provenance and noisy labels -- implicit
Blending measured plant data with calculated design-code inputs and indirectly derived CIPS labels lets code bias or changed nodal models propagate silently, and the model may learn design-code artifacts or cycle identity rather than crud mechanisms. No realistic adversary gains much beyond what data-integrity tampering already offers.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Reliance on a seemingly accurate tool may erode independent checking of axial-offset trends, crud and chemistry expertise. An adversary or coincident fault could time an anomaly when the tool reports 'clean'.

Qualification and repeatability gap -- implicit
Static offline validation, retraining non-determinism and the lack of an AI QA basis for an O&M decision aid weaken licensing credibility and make degradation or tampering hard to detect. It offers an adversary little by itself beyond the masking already described.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this is an advisory O&M tool for core-follow and cycle planning. CIPS (axial offset anomaly) is managed by existing layers: in-core flux mapping, excore detector axial offset monitoring, Technical Specification AFD/ΔI limits, reactor protection system trips, and water chemistry/crud-control programs. A wrong output therefore most plausibly becomes a degraded operating or planning decision (unneeded power reductions or chemistry changes, or unwarranted confidence in a cycle that later develops CIPS), not a direct safety-limit challenge. The more serious concerns are implicit: a model trained on one unit (Catawba 1, with its own fuel, chemistry and loading-pattern history) and about 92% accuracy on a low-base-rate phenomenon may not generalize to other plants, and its inputs from core design codes and plant measurements are trusted data paths. The physical backstops are strong, but the AI could still bias fuel management, shutdown-margin and thermal-margin assumptions, or anticipated outage scope if its output is treated as authoritative.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Generalization and drift failure: trained on one unit's data (small, single-site, few CIPS-prone vs clean cycles). Applied to other plants or later cycles with new fuel designs, power uprates, chemistry regimes (zinc, pH, boron), or loading patterns, it may miss CIPS onset (false negative, giving the operator a false sense of security about axial offset and thermal-margin penalties, and possibly delayed chemistry/cleaning/power-shaping action) or flag clean assemblies (false positive, costing power derates, unnecessary outage cleaning, and eroding trust). Low base rate of CIPS cycles means headline accuracy hides poor minority-class performance. (2) Data provenance mixing: measured plant data blended with calculated core design data (simulated/surrogate inputs); design-code error or changed nodal models propagate silently into predictions. (3) Uncertainty quantification limits: Monte Carlo dropout gives approximate, often overconfident uncertainty especially out of distribution; operators may read a narrow band as a safety assurance, which is automation over-trust. Non-repeatability across retrains and opacity of ConvNet features limit qualification and licensing credibility; it should remain outside safety-related classification. (4) Human factors: reliance may erode in-house crud/chemistry expertise, and predictions may anchor core-follow decisions. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Integrity manipulation of the input path (plant process/flux-map data, core design files, or training datasets, via supply chain or an insider/compromised engineering workstation) could bias predictions toward under- or over-predicting CIPS: a quiet way to induce unwarranted derates, hide a developing anomaly from planners, or mask other axial power distribution issues. Evasion-style perturbation is a poor fit physically, but data poisoning/model tampering of a research-grade model with weak software hygiene is plausible. (6) Exfiltration of fuel-cycle, loading pattern, and operating data (proprietary and potentially sensitive) from the training sets or model; if hosted on cloud or shared research infrastructure, this widens the attack surface into the IT/OT boundary. (7) Denial of the tool is low-consequence given manual and existing monitoring fallbacks. Overall consequence is chiefly economic and operational, with safety impact bounded by independent TS limits and protection systems, unless the output were allowed to displace those defenses or feed automated control.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a spatial-map classifier (a ConvNet over core-loading-pattern-like grids) trained on an extremely small, single-plant dataset: one unit (Catawba 1), a handful of cycles, and only a few CIPS-prone vs. clean cycles, which gives few effective independent samples (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03). Its inputs mix measured operational data (excore detector axial offset, chemistry, power history) with calculated core-design data (neutronics and thermal-hydraulics predictions, e.g., from design codes, with their own biases), so data provenance is hybrid and any error in the design-code inputs flows through as a confident-looking prediction (OP.C0201.01/.05, OP.C0603). The ~92% accuracy headline hides class imbalance (most assembly locations are not susceptible) and cycle-level leakage risk, so reported performance likely overstates what will happen on a new cycle, a new fuel design, or a different plant. Monte Carlo dropout gives an approximate, poorly calibrated uncertainty that tends to be overconfident out of distribution, which is exactly where it is needed. The system is advisory, but its architecture makes it fragile at the points where operators will lean on it hardest.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT threats: (1) Generalization and distribution shift (OP.C0302, .01, .03): new fuel designs, power uprates, changed water chemistry (e.g., zinc injection, boron/pH strategy), different loading-pattern philosophies, or other plants will shift the joint distribution of inputs and the CIPS physics, so a model fit to one unit may mispredict onset or peak. Failure mode: confident wrong maps, with MC-dropout variance not signalling the shift. Dependence: the operator's anticipation of axial-offset anomalies and power-shape management. Consequence: missed CIPS leads to unplanned power reductions and AO limit challenges, reducing safety margin; false alarms lead to unnecessary derates or chemistry changes. (2) Small-data and label problem (OP.C0202, OP.C0203): CIPS labels are derived from indirect, noisy evidence (AO deviations, post-cycle crud scrapes or inspections), so the ground truth is itself uncertain and the model may learn proxies, such as design-code artifacts or cycle identity, rather than crud mechanisms. (3) Uncertainty calibration (OP.C0403, OP.C0401): MC dropout is not a guarantee of coverage, and opaque convolutional features limit physics-based review, which promotes automation trust failure (OP.C0101.04) or, after false alarms, disuse (OP.C0101.05). (4) Qualification gap (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0402): static offline validation versus a dynamic cycle-by-cycle use, with retraining non-determinism and no established AI QA basis for an O&M decision aid. Static validation also misses concept drift as fuel and chemistry evolve (OP.C0302.02). (5) Data continuity and governance (OP.C0204, OP.C0505): plant-proprietary measurements and design data are shared with the research model, and utility data-sharing limits hinder refresh and multi-plant retraining. ADVERSARIAL threats: (a) Training or inference data poisoning or integrity erosion (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0059, T0031): subtle manipulation of historian or design-code outputs, or of the prepared input tensors, can shift predictions (suppress an alarm before a real CIPS event, or induce false alarms that cause derates). Motive: economic disruption, or masking a power-shape anomaly during another action. Since the model is advisory but may inform chemistry and power-maneuver decisions, this is a quiet integrity attack that evades safety-system defences. (b) Model or supply-chain compromise (AML.T0010.001/.003, T0018.000, T0058): the research code, pretrained weights, and ML frameworks come from academic or open-source stacks, and a backdoored model or dependency could introduce triggered misclassification of specific assembly locations (AML.T0043.004). (c) Evasion at inference (AML.T0015, T0043): although only an insider or someone with access to the data pipeline could craft inputs, small perturbations to input maps could flip classifications; the same adversary could time an attack around a known drift window. (d) Exfiltration (AML.T0024, T0035, T0037): trained models and data encode proprietary core design and operating history, a commercial and sensitive-information exposure if the tool is hosted or shared (OP.C0601). Primary exposure is data and model integrity rather than direct plant control, because the tool is advisory; the severity depends on how far operators let it influence the chemistry and power-maneuver decisions.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team standpoint, a CIPS susceptibility classifier is a poor direct target. It is advisory, it sits in core-design and operations-engineering workflows rather than the protection system, and a nation-state would find easier ways to affect plant output. Its main significance is as a trust-concentrating decision aid and a stepping stone. It draws on measured plant data and core design data (loading patterns, power histories, chemistry), which are sensitive and sit in the engineering and fuel-vendor data pipeline. Its outputs can shape reload design, chemistry, and power-maneuver decisions, so an adversary or an ordinary failure could mislead planning at a time when operators are least vigilant. The more realistic concerns are a quiet integrity attack on the data or model, and the way a well-calibrated-looking tool dulls engineering skepticism about axial-offset anomalies.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training and operating data integrity (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059): the model depends on plant measurements such as ex-core/in-core axial offset and flux maps, plus calculated core design inputs from vendor or lab codes. An insider or a compromised engineering workstation or data pipeline could subtly bias this data. Retraining or fine-tuning on a CIPS-prone cycle would then skew susceptibility maps, producing false 'clean' results (a missed CIPS onset leading to an unplanned axial-offset anomaly, power derate, or reduced shutdown-margin confidence) or false alarms (unnecessary derates, chemistry changes, or economic harm). Because the output is a per-assembly map and not a trip signal, tampering is hard to attribute and may look like physics. The consequence is mostly economic and operational, with a possible indirect safety-margin effect if axial-offset limits are approached unexpectedly. (2) Model and artifact tampering and supply chain (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0076): research-grade code and weights moving from a national lab to a utility or vendor, with Python/ML dependencies, give a software supply-chain path. Weights can be altered without obvious signs, and tampered uncertainty (Monte Carlo dropout) outputs could hide the tampering by keeping confidence plausible. (3) Reconnaissance and exfiltration value (AML.T0000, AML.T0024, AML.T0035, AML.T0036): the published paper and a model trained on Catawba data disclose which design and operating parameters matter. Model artifacts or fine-tuning data could leak proprietary core-design and fuel-performance information or operating history that gives an adversary insight into unit-specific loading and power-maneuvering patterns. This is lower priority than the direct leakage risk from the core-design data itself. (4) Stepping-stone access (AML.T0012, AML.T0052): an ML environment that bridges plant historian data, design-code output, and a research or cloud compute environment widens the IT/OT boundary, so a foothold there could provide lateral movement toward more valuable engineering data. IMPLICIT. (5) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102): the reported accuracy (~92%) and uncertainty estimates invite reliance. Engineers may stop independently checking axial-offset trends and flux-map physics, which an adversary or a coincident fault could exploit by timing an anomaly when the tool says 'clean'. (6) Generalization and drift (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0202): training is on one unit (Catawba 1) with few CIPS-prone cycles. Transfer to other plants, new fuel designs, power uprates, chemistry changes, or different loading strategies is unvalidated. The model may be confidently wrong out of distribution, and MC dropout captures model uncertainty but not covariate shift or label scarcity. (7) Opacity and qualification gap (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303): a ConvNet cannot easily be checked against physics-based CIPS codes, and no AI-specific QA basis exists, so tampering or degradation would be hard to detect. (8) Data governance (OP.C0505, OP.C0201.01): calculated design inputs mix simulated and measured data and flow across lab, vendor, and utility boundaries, making provenance and access control uncertain.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on data/model integrity attacks and on single-unit generalization, calibration and trust failures; I merged them. I dropped weakly argued items (evasion perturbation, denial, phishing/valid accounts, reconnaissance via the paper) as poor fits or restatements, and kept exfiltration as a distinct lower-priority threat.

evidence.citation: "Predicting PWR Fuel Assembly CIPS Susceptibility with Convolutional Neural Networks: Performance and Uncertainty Quantification," Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) research output; Proceedings of the International Conference on Physics of Reactors (PHYSOR 2024)
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed conference paper describes a top-down ConvNet trained on Catawba Unit 1 measurements plus core design data to predict crud-induced power shift in PWR assemblies. It reports about 92% overall accuracy and uses Monte Carlo dropout for uncertainty. A journal extension of the work appears in ScienceDirect (Energy), which also came up in the search.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is quiet data or model tampering that hides a developing axial-offset anomaly or triggers needless derates, but the tool is advisory, outside the protection path, and bounded by Tech Specs, flux mapping and excore monitoring, so harm is mainly operational/economic with minor indirect margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Single-unit generalization failure and overconfident uncertainty will reliably appear once the model meets out-of-distribution fuel, chemistry or loading conditions, but deliberate poisoning or backdoor outcomes depend on the attacker obtaining access, so reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: Tampering with training data, historian/design-code pipelines or model supply chain requires insider access, a compromised engineering workstation or supply-chain position, though exfiltration from shared research or cloud infrastructure is somewhat less demanding.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly confined to one unit's planning decisions (reload, chemistry, power maneuvers) for a decision aid, with only indirect effects on core operation, and no propagation across coupled safety systems.

discoverability.why: The approach, dataset origin, accuracy and Monte Carlo dropout method are in open peer-reviewed literature, and small-data drift, overconfidence and data-poisoning weaknesses are well documented for this class of ML system, though specific deployment details would not be public.

use_case: U-Net image-segmentation model that finds and removes twin grain boundaries in backscattered-electron micrographs of the silicon carbide layer of TRISO fuel particles. Removing them allows grain size and shape to be measured quantitatively for QA/QC in coated-particle fuel fabrication. The model was trained on EBSD crystallographic data.
incurred_insecurity:
This prototype U-Net sits in the QA/QC measurement chain for the SiC layer of TRISO fuel, the main fission-product barrier, and reports grain statistics from twin-removed boundary maps. Its main threats are silent measurement-integrity failures. These are an aggregate-versus-local fidelity gap, distribution shift under cross-modality label transfer, loss of independent EBSD cross-checks, and a missing qualification basis. Adversarial threats are quiet tampering with weights, labels or micrographs, and theft of proprietary data. The consequence is mainly biased lot acceptance and unreliable QA records, not direct actuation of a safety system.

Aggregate-versus-local fidelity gap -- implicit, exploitable
Grain area and boundary-pixel counts agree with EBSD within 1% while pixel-wise metrics are low, so missed and over-removed boundaries can cancel in the aggregate. The pixel-loss training objective also differs from the QA objective of grain-size and shape statistics, so tail or shape biases pass acceptance unseen. An adversary could hide a small systematic manipulation of the model or its inputs inside this unmeasured error headroom.

Distribution shift and small-data label noise -- implicit, exploitable
The model learns crystallography from BSE channeling contrast using a small EBSD-labelled dataset with imperfect registration. Changes in deposition conditions, SEM voltage, detector, charging or polish, and artifacts such as scratches or pores, can silently mis-segment the process-excursion lots QA exists to catch. An adversary could time a manipulation to such a shift, or alter acquisition conditions to push the model into this unreliable regime, with failures looking like plausible grain maps.

Automation over-trust and loss of independent verification -- implicit, exploitable
Once the tool is faster and more repeatable than EBSD or manual analysis, analysts stop spot-checking and lose familiarity with twin-boundary morphology, so one software artifact determines the pass/fail record. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust and the missing crystallographic cross-check to make a later tampering event go unchallenged.

Qualification and change-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
A research prototype has no measurement-system qualification, model versioning, retraining change control or audit trail. Because training is non-deterministic and twin removal redefines grain size relative to legacy specifications, retraining can shift the accepted measurand and break lot-to-lot comparability without re-baselining. An adversary could make unauthorised model changes that are indistinguishable from routine retraining.

Model, label and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor could alter model weights, pretrained components, EBSD labels or pre/post-processing so that grain metrics are biased toward in-spec, optionally under a trigger such as specific image metadata. This would let marginal SiC lots pass, or good lots fail, and leave QA records that no longer support a fuel-performance or licensing claim.

Micrograph and acquisition manipulation -- adversarial
Someone with access to sample preparation, SEM settings or image storage could subtly alter contrast, noise or the image files so the segmentation errs predictably. With no per-image ground truth, this is a low-observable way to mask sub-spec coating.

Data and model exfiltration through the AI toolchain -- adversarial
Weights, EBSD datasets and micrograph libraries encode proprietary fuel microstructure and process-quality information. Shared repositories and GPU workstations, plus valid insider accounts, widen the attack surface of the QA lab and enable IP theft.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the fuel-fabrication floor, this model sits in a QA/QC measurement chain. Its output (twin-removed grain boundary maps, grain size and shape statistics) could inform acceptance of SiC coating batches, which are the main fission-product barrier in TRISO fuel. The reported result is aggregate agreement within 1% of EBSD-derived values, while pixel-wise segmentation metrics were low. That means the model can look right on batch averages while mislocating individual boundaries, so errors in grain-shape distributions and tails could go unseen. It is a prototype and not deployed. The realistic risk is therefore a future qualification and automation-trust gap, not a present failure. Existing practice already provides some defence in depth: destructive and non-destructive coating QA, IPyC/SiC thickness and density checks, burn-leach and failure-fraction testing, and in-pile qualification and irradiation data. A wrong grain-size number alone would need to coincide with weak process control and unchallenged acceptance before it caused a release-relevant outcome.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Aggregate-versus-local fidelity gap. The 1% match on area and boundary pixel counts hides low pixel-wise accuracy. If the model misses or over-removes boundaries in particular microstructural regimes, grain size and aspect-ratio distributions can be biased in ways that matter, such as a fine-grained or columnar layer, or a different polytype or stoichiometry. Downstream, process engineers could mistake a coating-parameter drift for a good batch, or a good batch for a bad one, and either accept marginal fuel or reject conforming fuel (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403, OP.C0401). (2) Distribution shift. EBSD-derived training labels come from a limited set of samples, conditions and imaging settings. Changes in deposition conditions, vendor or lab, SEM detector, voltage, charging, polishing artifacts, or new fuel designs (new-build, advanced TRISO variants) can silently degrade the model. Twin and grain boundaries may be confused with scratches, pores or polishing damage. The consequence is a drifted QA metric that nobody notices because the output looks plausible (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0201.04/.05, OP.C0303). (3) Automation trust and qualification. Once the tool is faster and more repeatable than manual analysis, analysts may stop spot-checking against EBSD, so skill fade and over-trust set in. Unless the model is qualified under nuclear QA (NQA-1-style software and measurement-system validation, change control, versioning), retraining or a model update could shift the accepted measurand with no re-baselining (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0402). (4) Measurand mismatch. Removing twins changes the definition of grain size relative to historical specifications and irradiation-performance correlations, so results may not be comparable with legacy data (OP.C0301, OP.C0702).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. These are lower-probability but credible for an insider or supply-chain actor. (a) Tampering with the model weights, the preprocessing pipeline or the EBSD ground-truth and retraining data (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0031) could bias grain metrics toward in-spec, or produce selective false passes on targeted lots, hiding a deliberate or accidental coating-quality degradation. (b) Image-level manipulation of micrographs, or of the acquisition settings, could evade segmentation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043) and mask sub-spec material. (c) Compromise of the QA data system, rather than the model, could swap records. This is a hazard to fuel integrity and, through falsified QA records, to safeguards and material-accountancy confidence. It is not a direct reactor-safety lever.

Mitigation context: independent EBSD or manual checks on sampled lots, statistical process control, other coating-integrity tests, and in-reactor and post-irradiation data all limit consequence. The main residual risk is slow, systematic bias that stays inside every check's tolerance, not an abrupt failure.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a supervised U-Net segmentation model whose ground truth (twin vs. non-twin boundaries) comes from EBSD crystallographic labels, and whose deployment input is BSE contrast images in which twins are only weakly or ambiguously visible. The pipeline is therefore a cross-modality label transfer: the model learns to infer crystallography from channeling contrast. That makes its fragility specific. Training data is small, from a few coating batches and imaging conditions, and EBSD-to-BSE registration is imperfect, so label noise sits exactly at the boundaries being segmented. The reported 1% agreement on aggregate grain area and boundary-pixel counts alongside low pixel-wise metrics suggests errors that cancel in aggregate. Aggregate agreement can hide systematic bias that shows up only when inputs shift, and the prototype has no qualification regime for that.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift at inference: BSE contrast depends on accelerating voltage, detector, tilt, polish and etch quality, charging, and SiC microstructure (grain size, stacking-fault density, twin fraction). These vary with deposition parameters, so a model trained on one process window can mis-segment a process-excursion lot, which is exactly the lot QA/QC is meant to catch. Failure is silent, since the output looks like a plausible grain map. Mechanism: OOD or drift plus small data and label noise. Consequence: grain-size statistics biased toward acceptance or rejection, so out-of-spec SiC (a pressure-retaining and fission-product barrier layer) could be accepted, or good lots scrapped. (2) Proxy-metric weakness: the 1% aggregate agreement is not per-boundary correctness. Missed or over-removed twins that offset each other can pass acceptance checks, and a mean-grain-size metric hides tail changes. The training objective (pixel loss) is also misaligned with the QA objective (grain statistics). (3) Automation bias and skill fade: once the model runs routinely, analysts stop doing manual or EBSD cross-checks, losing independent verification, and low pixel-wise scores give little per-image confidence signal. (4) Qualification gap: no established way exists to qualify a segmentation model as a measurement instrument for fuel acceptance (uncertainty quantification, repeatability across retrains, version control, non-deterministic training). Retraining on new EBSD data could shift outputs and break lot-to-lot comparability. EBSD ground truth is expensive, which restricts revalidation and drift monitoring. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Training-data or label poisoning and supply-chain compromise: an insider or compromised pipeline could alter EBSD labels, image-registration steps, model weights, or pretrained U-Net and library dependencies so the model systematically biases grain-size measurement in one direction or under a trigger, such as specific imaging metadata. This is a quiet, persistent way to mask a degraded coating process or falsify QA records. Integrity of measurement records matters for safety and for material accountability and proprietary process data. (6) Input manipulation: someone with access to the microscope or image store could alter acquisition settings or images so that contrast features push the model into predictable errors. Because a segmentation model is highly sensitive to texture, this is easier than attacking a human reviewer. (7) Model and data exfiltration: weights, EBSD datasets, and micrograph libraries encode proprietary fuel microstructure and process-quality information, and the AI toolchain (GPU workstations, shared repositories) widens the attack surface of an otherwise air-gapped QA lab. Overall, the exposure is mainly measurement-integrity risk (undetected bias in a QA decision) rather than a direct safety-system actuation.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team lens, this is a low-value direct target but a meaningful quiet-integrity target. A U-Net sitting in the QA/QC measurement chain for coated-particle fuel decides what 'grain size' a SiC layer reports, and that number is a proxy for fission-product retention and layer integrity. Nobody would attack it for dramatic effect. The realistic adversary is an insider or supply-chain actor who wants substandard or non-conforming fuel to pass inspection, or who wants to undermine confidence in the QA record. The documented result also matters here: pixel-wise metrics were low while aggregate grain area and boundary counts landed within 1% of the EBSD values. That means the model can be wrong at the pixel level, even substantially, and still pass the acceptance check. A saboteur would find that headroom attractive, and a human reviewer would have little chance of noticing a small shift. The prototype is not yet deployed, so the best time to build in controls is now, before the trust and the attack surface exist.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity attack on the measurement chain (AML.T0018.000, T0020, T0010.002/.003, T0076, T0031). The weights, the EBSD-derived training labels, or the preprocessing and post-processing code are altered. A small, systematic bias in what counts as a twin boundary shifts reported grain size or shape. This would be done to make marginal or non-conforming SiC lots look conforming, or to reject good lots. The AI failure mechanism is silent model corruption. Fuel fabrication depends on the output for lot release, and the consequence is degraded fuel quality assurance that is hard to detect. In the worst case, fuel performance and the fission-product barrier are compromised, and fabrication records no longer support a safety or licensing claim. (2) Evasion through the micrographs (AML.T0015, T0043, T0043.003). The segmentation model is sensitive to imaging conditions, so someone with access to sample prep, SEM settings or image files could subtly alter contrast, charging or noise, or edit images, to steer the output. Because there is no per-image truth, this is a low-observable route for an insider. (3) Concentrated, uncorroborated trust. If the model replaces EBSD, a slow and expensive method, then the independent crystallographic cross-check that would catch tampering disappears. This is both a security and a safeguards-of-quality concern, because one compromised software artifact then determines the pass/fail record. (4) Credential and access pathways (T0012, T0055, T0112.001). Model files, training sets and QA records on lab or shared research networks, perhaps with weaker controls than production systems, give an insider or an intruder a stepping-stone into the wider QA and fabrication IT environment. Moving from research code to production QA also brings the use case under tighter data-security expectations. Proprietary micrograph and process data would carry commercial and export-control sensitivity, so exfiltration for IP theft is plausible (T0025, T0035).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable by timing. (a) The pixel-metric gap and the 1% aggregate agreement (OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03) show the model is opaque and may omit or oversimplify boundary detail. The acceptance criterion is therefore weakly sensitive to tampering or error, and compensating errors can cancel in aggregate. (b) Training on EBSD from a limited set of materials and conditions invites drift or out-of-distribution failure when the deposition process, SEM, detector or sample prep changes (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0201.04). Process excursions are exactly the events QA should catch, and an adversary or a plain process change can occur while the model is least reliable. (c) Automation trust failure and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Once the output is routinely accepted, analysts lose their feel for twin-boundary morphology and stop spot-checking, which leaves a window for a later tampering event. (d) Governance gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0504). A research prototype lacks model version control, retraining-change control, a qualification basis and audit trails, so unauthorized or accidental model changes may not be traceable. Mitigation direction: retain periodic independent EBSD verification, treat model files and labels as controlled QA artifacts with integrity checking, and define acceptance on per-image and per-feature metrics as well as aggregates.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the aggregate-versus-pixel gap, distribution shift, automation over-trust and qualification gaps, and on quiet integrity tampering of weights, labels and images. I kept exfiltration as a distinct threat, dropped the speculative credential and measurand-mismatch items as separate entries (folding measurand shift into qualification), and omitted T0076, T0024.002 and T0055 as redundant or weakly traceable.

evidence.citation: "Methods development towards automated, physics-informed, quantitative quality control of TRISO-SiC," Journal of Nuclear Materials (Elsevier), vol. 626, art. 156591, 2026; Oak Ridge National Laboratory (via DOE PAGES/OSTI)
evidence.note: The ORNL authors describe the initial development, training and testing of an ML image-segmentation model that identifies twin grain boundaries in SEM micrographs of TRISO SiC and removes them. They report that grain area and grain-boundary pixel counts after twin removal come within 1% of values calculated from crystallographic data, even though pixel-wise metrics were low. The model is a prototype and has not been deployed in production QA/QC.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is tampering with the model, labels or micrographs so that marginal or sub-spec SiC coating passes QA. This undermines fission-product barrier quality assurance and fuel-performance or licensing claims, which is significant safeguards-adjacent integrity damage. It stops short of a direct release, since it is mediated by downstream controls and does not actuate a safety system.

reproducibility.why: The implicit failures (aggregate-versus-local gap, distribution shift, over-trust) recur reliably once the model is in use. Adversarial biasing requires specific conditions such as insider access or a trigger, so reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: The credible adversarial paths (altering weights, labels or pipeline code, or manipulating sample preparation, SEM settings or image storage) need insider or supply-chain position in a fuel fabrication QA lab. They also need enough ML knowledge to bias outputs quietly, which is not achievable by routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: A biased measurement tool would affect every lot it assesses and the QA records built on it, across the fabrication QA chain and downstream fuel-performance claims. It remains confined to one measurement step and does not propagate across coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: Aggregate-versus-local metric gaps, distribution shift, over-trust and the general classes of model and data tampering are well documented in the open literature. The ORNL publication also reports the low pixel-wise metrics. Exploiting them against a specific deployment would still require partial knowledge of the QA workflow, which makes this inferable by a capable outsider rather than evident to anyone.

use_case: K-nearest-neighbour classification of main control room operator fatigue in a nuclear power plant. Features are eye blink rate and PERCLOS from a webcam, plus mouse-movement velocity from a hidden logging program. The classifier gives a fatigue-level estimate in real time to support operator fitness-for-duty and human-error prevention.
incurred_insecurity:
A KNN fatigue classifier fed by a webcam and a hidden mouse logger in the main control room is an advisory human-performance tool, not a safety-system component, so its harm acts through operators, supervisors and administrative decisions rather than directly on reactor state. The main threats are poorly validated fatigue labels and generalization, misplaced trust in its output, evasion or tampering with its inputs and stored reference set, a new always-on collection agent and biometric data store near the control-room network, and governance gaps around covert monitoring.

Label and generalization failure -- implicit, exploitable
A KNN trained on a small lab or simulator cohort with proxy fatigue labels (self-report, induced sleep loss) has no calibrated uncertainty or out-of-distribution signal, so lighting, glasses, camera changes, per-person baselines and task phase (mouse velocity confounded by workload) produce confident but wrong fatigue classes, with biased misses and false flags per operator. An adversary or impaired operator could exploit the predictable blind spots by choosing the person, shift or condition in which fatigue goes unflagged.

Automation trust and complacency -- implicit, exploitable
A 'not fatigued' status can be treated as clearance, so supervisors reduce direct observation and the roughly 8% error band, with false negatives hidden inside it, goes unnoticed; frequent false flags cause disuse, and an unvalidated score may become a de facto fitness-for-duty determination. An adversary could time an action to a crew the tool has falsely reassured, or rely on a distrusted tool being ignored.

Qualification, drift and objective gap -- implicit, exploitable
The model estimates a fatigue state while the decision it supports is fitness-for-duty, and a non-safety tool has no AI-specific qualification regime, versioning of reference-set updates, or repeatable accuracy across sites. Interface changes, camera replacement or silent feature dropout degrade it without notice, and an adversary could hide behind this unaudited degradation when tampering with the reference set or inputs.

Input evasion and spoofing -- adversarial
An operator or insider who knows the features (blink rate, PERCLOS, cursor speed) can mask fatigue through deliberate blinking, scripted mouse motion, replayed video or altered camera angle, or conversely induce false fatigue flags to disrupt staffing or discredit an individual.

Reference-set poisoning and model tampering -- adversarial
Because KNN's model is its stored labelled samples, an insider or compromised pipeline can add or relabel a few points to make a specific operator or shift persistently scored alert or fatigued, with little ability to audit the change.

Collection-agent foothold and chaff or denial -- adversarial
The hidden logger, webcam stack and classifier host form a new always-on endpoint near the HMI network that can be compromised through supply-chain software, valid accounts or malicious updates, serving as a foothold or covert surveillance channel. The feed can also be flooded or disabled to blind the monitor and push the crew to manual processes at a chosen moment.

Biometric data exposure and covert monitoring -- implicit, exploitable
Continuous eye and behavioural records of named operators, collected by a hidden program with unclear consent and an inappropriate data-security model, reveal impairment history, shift rhythms and staffing weak points while damaging the reporting culture safety depends on. If exfiltrated they support coercion, social engineering and timing attacks against the least-alert crew, and covert monitoring itself fuels insider grievance.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view this is a decision-support and fitness-for-duty monitor sitting beside the operators, not in the safety-system chain. A wrong output does not directly move rods or trip the plant; it acts through people and procedures. The harm paths are therefore human-factors and administrative: missed fatigue leaves operators falsely reassured, and false alarms or misuse erode crew trust, add distraction, or drive unfair staffing and disciplinary decisions. Existing practice (shift-work and hours-of-service limits, two-person crews, shift technical advisors, independent safety systems, procedures) already bounds the physical consequence, so the main risks are degraded human reliability, workforce and privacy harms, and a new IT/OT-adjacent attack surface in the control room. The 91.8% accuracy comes from a small, lab or simulator study with an unknown ground-truth fatigue label, so field performance is uncertain.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Generalization and qualification gap: KNN trained on a small set of simulator or lab subjects with subjective or self-reported fatigue labels will not transfer across individuals, lighting, glasses, camera placement, ethnicity, and task types (monitoring vs. active transient). Distance-based KNN is sensitive to per-person baselines, and the model has no calibration to a real fatigue standard. 'About 91.8%' hides the false-negative rate that matters. Mouse velocity is also confounded by task and procedure phase (quiet steady-state vs. an upset), so the classifier can mistake workload for fatigue or the reverse. (2) Automation trust failure: a green 'alert' status could lead supervisors to skip normal observation, which is a complacency risk. Frequent false positives could cause alarm fatigue and disuse. Fatigue estimates could be used as a de facto fitness-for-duty determination without validation, which creates labour-relations and regulatory exposure. Adding an alarm-like cue during a transient also adds cognitive load at the wrong time. (3) Governance: no AI-specific QA or regulatory framework exists for biometric monitoring in a control room, and the covert, hidden logging program raises consent, privacy and data-governance problems. Sensitive health-adjacent biometric data and performance records are a retention and misuse risk, and the covert nature can damage the safety culture and reporting culture on which nuclear safety relies. (4) Data continuity: camera occlusion, failed logging, or operators changing posture can silently degrade or drop features, and the system may fail without anyone noticing.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Evasion or manipulation of inputs: an insider, or an operator who wants to avoid being flagged, can spoof the camera or the mouse signal (jiggling the mouse, deliberate blinking, a still image or video, a replayed feed), so a fatigued operator looks alert. Conversely, a malicious actor could induce false fatigue flags to force a crew change, cause staffing disruption, or discredit a particular operator. (b) Integrity compromise of the logging software, the model or its data store: a hidden logger and webcam that run on a control-room workstation expand the attack surface. If they are connected to the plant network, a compromise could be a foothold, a covert surveillance channel, or a vector for tampering with the model or its thresholds (poisoning, supply chain, valid accounts). The feeds also expose operator behaviour and presence patterns that support reconnaissance, such as knowing when the control room is fatigued or understaffed, which is useful for timing a physical or cyber attack. (c) Denial of service or chaff: flooding or disabling the monitor could force the plant back to manual supervision, which is a minor consequence in itself but could be used to distract. Overall the safety consequence is bounded by independent defence in depth; the realistic damage is to human performance, trust, privacy and the security posture of the control room network, so the system should stay advisory, isolated from the plant control network, and never be used as a sole fitness-for-duty determinant.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a small, simple model (KNN over a few hand-crafted features) whose main fragility is the data and the label, not the architecture. KNN stores the training set as the model, so the reference set is the attack surface and the drift surface. The reported ~91.8% accuracy most likely comes from a small cohort in a simulator or lab, with fatigue labels from induced sleep deprivation, self-report scales or task-time proxies. That provenance is unlikely to match real shift-work fatigue across individuals, lighting, cameras, glasses, ethnicity, shift timing and task phases. At inference, a webcam and a mouse logger feed unvalidated raw signals into a distance metric with no native out-of-distribution (OOD) signal, so a degraded input still returns a confident-looking fatigue class.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Label and ground-truth fragility. 'Fatigue' labels are proxies (self-report, KSS, induced sleep loss), so the model learns a proxy of a proxy. Accuracy from small-cohort, within-subject or window-leaky cross-validation overstates cross-operator generalisation (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0302.03). Per-person baselines for blink rate and PERCLOS vary widely, so false positives and false negatives are biased toward particular individuals, which carries fitness-for-duty and fairness consequences. (2) Drift and OOD. Lighting changes, camera replacement or auto-exposure, glasses, fatigue-unrelated blink changes (dry eyes, medication, display glare, task type) and changing mouse use (touchscreens, procedure changes, interface upgrades) shift the feature distribution. KNN has no calibrated uncertainty, and feature scaling set at training silently changes meaning (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303). A false 'alert' reading during a degraded state gives supervisors misplaced assurance (OP.C0101.04). A false 'fatigued' reading erodes trust, leading to disuse and alarm complacency (OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102). (3) Qualification gap. Mouse velocity as a fatigue marker depends on interaction style, and the model has no qualification regime for a non-safety human-performance tool. Retraining or reference-set updates are unversioned, and the accuracy claim is not repeatable across sites (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0402). (4) Objective misalignment. The model estimates a fatigue state, but the decision it supports is a fitness-for-duty judgment, which opens the door to administrative misuse of an unvalidated score (OP.C0301, OP.C0401).

ADVERSARIAL AND ADVERSARY-EXPLOITABLE THREATS. (a) Training or reference-set poisoning: because KNN's 'model' is its stored labelled samples, an insider or a compromised data pipeline that adds or relabels a few points can bias outcomes for target feature regions (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002). Result: a specific operator or shift is persistently scored alert or fatigued. (b) Evasion at inference: a person aware of the features can mask fatigue, for example with deliberate blinking, glasses, a camera angle or lighting change, or scripted or jiggled mouse input, so that fatigue is scored as alert (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003, AML.T0041). This is a low-sophistication route and is realistic for a fatigued operator hiding impairment or an adversary exploiting a known weak shift. (c) Input-stream tampering: a hidden mouse logger and webcam stream form a new endpoint-level attack surface on the control room network, where an agent running there could inject chaff or spoofed telemetry (AML.T0046, AML.T0112, AML.T0029). Impact: loss of the fatigue signal, or fabricated fatigue alerts used to remove or distract operators, or to time an attack for a period when the monitoring is blind or distrusted. (d) Data confidentiality and privacy: continuous biometric and behavioural records of named operators are sensitive, and the hidden logging adds a covert-surveillance and insider-targeting dimension. Exfiltrated profiles reveal staffing, shift patterns and individual impairment history (AML.T0025, AML.T0036, OP.C0505.01). (e) Supply chain: open-source vision and KNN libraries, pretrained face and eye landmark models and webcam drivers are all dependency points (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003).

security_specialist.argument: This system places a continuous camera and a hidden input-logging program on the people who hold the most safety-critical positions in the plant, and it produces a trusted real-time 'fit/fatigued' judgment about them. From a threat-surface view it creates three things that did not exist before: a biometric and behavioral data store about named operators, a new software and network pathway into the control-room environment (webcam driver, logging agent, classifier host), and a human-factors signal that supervisors may lean on and an adversary could shape. A nation-state would probably not target the classifier directly, since compromising it does not move reactor state. But it is a cheap stepping stone and a timing tool: it exposes operator identity, shift pattern, and alertness, and it sits on a workstation close to the HMI network. The non-adversarial weaknesses (a modest 91.8% accuracy, a small-sample KNN, and per-person variability) are also the ones an adversary could exploit by choosing when to act.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Stepping-stone and insider pathway: the hidden mouse-logging agent and webcam stack run on or beside control-room workstations. Whoever compromises them (supply-chain software, valid accounts, a malicious update) gains a foothold with keystroke-adjacent telemetry and a vantage point near the operator HMI. The AI-specific cause is a new always-on collection agent, and the consequence is lateral movement toward operational networks and reconnaissance on operator routines. (2) Data exposure: eye-feature and cursor-behavior streams, linked to named operators, reveal fatigue history, shift rhythms, health-adjacent traits, and staffing weak points. If exfiltrated or inferred from the model or its logs, they support targeted coercion, social engineering, or timing a physical or cyber action for the least-alert crew. The consequence is a security-culture and personnel-security harm. (3) Integrity manipulation: an insider or intruder who can alter the camera feed, feature extraction, or the KNN reference set (poisoning or backdoor trigger) can suppress 'fatigued' flags, or generate false ones to harass staff, delay shift handovers, or force staffing disruption. Because KNN keeps its raw training data, the model is easy to tamper with and hard to audit.
