A single operator who learns the feature dependence (blink rate, PERCLOS, cursor speed) could also deliberately evade it, for example by moving the mouse in a masking pattern. (4) Denial or degradation of the service could be used to push a crew toward manual fitness-for-duty processes at a chosen moment.

IMPLICIT. (a) Automation trust and complacency: if supervisors treat 'not fatigued' as clearance, real fatigue falls into the roughly 8% error band, and the tool lowers human vigilance exactly when an adversary would pick the moment. Over-reliance can also erode peer and supervisor observation (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). (b) Generalization limits: the model was trained on a small, lab or simulator cohort. It is sensitive to lighting, glasses, camera angle, individual baselines, and task type, and it drifts as workflows or interface designs change. The result is false alarms or misses that are uneven across individuals, which creates fairness problems and gives an adversary predictable blind spots. (c) Governance gaps: workplace surveillance, a hidden logger, consent, and the question of whether biometric data are covered by the plant's data-security regime. A 'hidden' program also undermines trust and invites insider grievance, which is itself an insider-threat driver. (d) Opacity and qualification: a non-safety-classified AI tool influencing fitness-for-duty decisions without qualification evidence, with 10-second real-time outputs that nobody can explain or replay deterministically.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on small-cohort generalization failure, automation over-trust, evasion by feature-aware operators, KNN reference-set poisoning, the hidden logger as an attack foothold, and biometric governance. I dropped speculative ATLAS codes with no clear mechanism here (e.g., T0036, T0112, T0024.000, T0043.004, T0010.002/.003, T0048.003) and omitted OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203 and OP.C0402 as weakly supported or redundant.

evidence.citation: "Detection of Operator Fatigue in the Main Control Room of a Nuclear Power Plant Based on Eye Blink Rate, PERCLOS and Mouse Velocity," Applied Sciences (MDPI)
evidence.note: The paper builds a non-invasive fatigue detector for NPP main control room operators. It combines webcam-derived eye features with mouse-velocity features, compares supervised classifiers over several time windows and feature sets, and finds K-nearest neighbour performs best at about 91.8% accuracy. The authors say it can flag fatigue within about 10 seconds.

damage.why: The tool is advisory and non-safety, so harm acts indirectly through degraded fatigue detection, wrongful fitness-for-duty decisions, and loss of reporting culture, producing operational disruption and erosion of human-performance safety margins rather than direct radiological release or safeguards falsification.

reproducibility.why: Label and generalization failures, automation complacency, and drift occur reliably given the described conditions (small proxy-labelled cohort, environmental or per-person variation), and input masking or reference-set edits work consistently once access exists.

exploitability.why: Evading the features needs only an operator's knowledge of them, but reference-set poisoning, collection-agent compromise, and biometric exfiltration require insider or privileged access to a system near the control-room network.

affected_users.why: Impact covers individual operators, shifts, and crews in the control room and the supervisory and staffing decisions that depend on the tool, but it does not propagate directly to coupled plant control systems.

discoverability.why: The features, model type, and accuracy are published in the open literature, and evasion and complacency weaknesses are well-known for this class of AI monitoring system, though deployment details and the presence of the hidden logger would be known mainly to insiders.

use_case: Three-layer feed-forward neural network models that infer canister internal helium pressure and peak cladding temperature from canister surface temperatures measured at five axial levels and four circumferential positions. The models were trained on data from a heated test apparatus that simulates a helium leak. They give confinement monitoring of spent fuel dry storage casks without a pressure-sensor penetration through the canister wall, and they flag rapid helium leakage.
incurred_insecurity:
Replacing a physical pressure measurement with a neural-network inference from 20 external surface temperatures makes confinement and cladding-temperature assurance for dry-storage casks depend on a model trained only on a heated bench rig. The main threats are a silent surrogate-to-field gap, transient blindness, over-trust in an unqualified inferred indicator, input manipulation that steers the estimate, and tampering with the model or its calibration pipeline. Acute consequences are limited by large thermal margins and independent surveillance, but undetected helium loss or false alarms would degrade safety and safeguards confidence.

Surrogate-to-field domain shift -- implicit, exploitable
The network was trained on rig data with a regulator-simulated leak and has no native out-of-distribution detection, so differences in decay heat, loading, vent geometry, solar and ambient loading, blockage and aging yield plausible but biased pressure and peak-cladding-temperature estimates. An adversary could use ordinary thermal variation or deliberate local thermal changes to sit in this blind region and hide a leak or vent blockage.

Transient and slow-leak blindness -- implicit, exploitable
Accuracy is reported only after thermo-fluidic stabilization, so the model is least reliable in the transients where a rapid leak occurs, and slow leaks or sensor drift may be absorbed as normal variation. An adversary could time interference around weather changes, loading or other transients, when anomalies are already expected and alarms are discounted.

Scarce leak data and unqualified indicator -- implicit, exploitable
Real leak events are essentially absent and no in-situ ground truth exists, so alarm thresholds cannot be tuned and the model gives no uncertainty bound, no explanation, and no regulatory qualification path. Operators may treat the number as a measurement, defer inspections, or suffer alarm fatigue, and an adversary could rely on that misplaced trust or deliberately provoke nuisance alarms to wear down vigilance before a real event.

Surface-temperature input manipulation -- adversarial
Local heating, insulation or shielding of the cask surface, thermocouple tampering, or injected data on a 20-channel fixed-input regression can drive the inferred pressure and peak cladding temperature toward normal while a leak proceeds, or fabricate a leak alarm. The result is concealed loss of confinement, a quiet window for diversion or sabotage preparation, or unnecessary cask handling and dose.

Model, data and update pipeline tampering -- adversarial
The weights, scaler parameters and recalibration data are small files that can be swapped or poisoned during retraining or vendor updates, embedding a bias or a trigger pattern that suppresses alarms. If one model is reused across casks of different design, a single bias or compromise propagates fleet-wide.

Alarm flooding and denial -- adversarial
Chaff or degraded data streams can flood or disable the leak alarm, pushing operators to ignore or switch off the monitor. A real leak is then discounted or goes undetected.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a dry-storage operations view, this model replaces a physical measurement (internal pressure) with an inference from external surface temperatures, so any error or manipulation leads directly to a wrong belief about confinement and cladding condition. It was trained on a heated test apparatus with a regulator-simulated helium leak. Real casks differ in decay-heat profile, loading pattern, vent and overpack geometry, ambient and solar loading, snow, debris, and aging. Reported accuracy is also only after the thermo-fluidic state stabilizes, so the model is weakest during transients, which is exactly when a rapid leak occurs. The downstream consequence is mainly a missed or false confinement alarm. A missed alarm means delayed detection of degraded helium backfill and higher cladding temperatures, with long-term cladding degradation and eventual release or retrievability issues. A false alarm means unnecessary inspections, dose, and cask handling. Existing practice (periodic surface and vent temperature surveillance, decay-heat limits, seal and weld QA, and conservative thermal analysis) limits acute harm because dry-cask thermal margins are large and degradation is slow. The AI therefore adds most risk through complacency, where it displaces inspections, and through a possible safeguards and surveillance blind spot.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT: (1) Domain shift from the test rig to real casks (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). The apparatus data is simulated or surrogate, with few leak scenarios and no real field leak data (OP.C0202). Different heat loads, ambient swings, wind, solar insolation, partial blockage of ventilation inlets, or fuel loading asymmetry can mimic or mask the thermal signature of helium loss. The result is a biased pressure and peak cladding temperature (PCT) estimate that looks plausible. (2) Transient-regime weakness: accuracy is claimed only post-stabilization, so slow leaks can be absorbed as drift, and rapid-leak alarms based on abrupt peaks or drops may produce false positives from weather or sensor faults (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0304.03). (3) Sensor drift, thermocouple or contact degradation, and loss of one of the 20 channels feeding a fixed-input network, with no physical redundancy to cross-check (OP.C0204, OP.C0603). (4) Automation trust and monitoring complacency: operators and regulators may reduce physical inspections or accept a 'pressure' number as measured (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). Opacity limits root-cause analysis when it disagrees with the thermal analysis (OP.C0401), and there is no regulatory qualification path for a non-safety inferred confinement indicator (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Fleet-wide reuse of one trained model across cask designs would propagate a common-mode bias (OP.C0602). ADVERSARIAL: (5) Manipulating the surface temperature inputs, through sensor spoofing, tampered cabling or DAQ, or physical thermal shielding or heating at the cask surface, to hold the model's output in the normal band while a leak or deliberate degradation proceeds, or to trigger nuisance alarms (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015, AML.T0041). This is a cheap, low-signature way to blind confinement monitoring on a passive system with sparse human presence, and it could cover diversion or sabotage preparation. Because the data path is simple, falsified inputs are plausible. (6) Training or calibration data poisoning, or tampering with model weights during retraining or vendor update, creating a bias or trigger in an alarm threshold (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003). (7) Alarm denial or flooding that desensitizes operators (AML.T0029, AML.T0046). Safeguards: the unattended, remote-monitoring architecture relies on trust in the data stream, so compromised monitoring weakens continuity-of-knowledge assurance, though dry casks remain under physical seals and surveillance. For harm to occur, independent surveillance (vent temperature checks, radiation survey, periodic inspections) and conservative thermal margins would also have to fail or be relaxed, so acute consequence is low, while the long-term consequence of undetected degradation is moderate.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small supervised regression model (3-layer FFNN, 20 surface-temperature inputs, 2 outputs) trained on a heated bench apparatus with a regulator-driven helium leak. Its fragility sits mostly in the data and the validity envelope, not in the architecture. The training data is lab-scale surrogate data (OP.C0201.01/.02/.04) with no field cask ground truth, since the whole point is that there is no pressure penetration to label real casks. The model therefore can never be validated in situ against the quantity it infers. The authors themselves concede accuracy only after the thermo-fluidic state stabilizes. At inference, the input space is dominated by factors the apparatus likely did not span: ambient and solar swings, wind, snow or debris blockage of vents, differing decay-heat loads and burnup profiles, cask designs, and thermocouple placement or failure. An FFNN has no native notion of out-of-distribution input and will return a confident number regardless. Because it is a regressor on correlated temperatures, it also cannot separate helium loss from other causes of a changed surface profile.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift and the surrogate-to-field gap: a model trained on a heated test rig is applied to real casks with different geometry, heat load, emissivity, fouling and ambient conditions. The failure mechanism is silent extrapolation, where the output is plausible but wrong. The monitored function is confinement assurance for spent fuel in dry storage, so the consequence is a false 'pressure nominal' reading that defers inspection, or a false alarm that triggers needless cask handling (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.01-.04, OP.C0303). (2) Transient blindness: accuracy is reported only for stabilized states, while the alarm function targets rapid leaks, which are exactly the transient regime. A static-trained model used dynamically gives a qualification mismatch and detection lag. Slow leaks and slow drift in surface temperature (aging, fouling, sensor drift) are likely absorbed as concept drift with no retraining signal (OP.C0303, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0202). (3) Low base rate: real leak events are essentially absent, so alarm thresholds cannot be tuned against real false-positive and false-negative rates, which breeds either alarm fatigue or complacency (OP.C0102, OP.C0101.04). (4) Opacity and qualification: there is no uncertainty estimate, no physics-consistency check, and no regulatory pathway for an AI confinement indicator, so operators may treat it as a measurement when it is only an inference (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Sensor-input manipulation: the model depends on only 20 thermocouple channels. Spoofing, biasing or locally heating or insulating a few surface sensors (physical or via the data path) can steer the inferred pressure and peak cladding temperature toward normal while real leakage proceeds, or fabricate a leak alarm. This is an evasion attack, and with a small, smooth model it can be crafted easily if the architecture or training range is learned (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041, AML.T0044). The security consequence is concealed loss of confinement or induced disruption, and a degraded safeguards and safety record for storage. (6) Pipeline integrity: the weights and scaler or normalization parameters are small, easily swapped files. A tampered or retrained model, poisoned recalibration data, or compromised supply chain could embed a blind spot or a backdoor trigger on a specific temperature pattern (AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0043.004, OP.C0502). (7) Fleet propagation: if one trained model is copied across casks of differing designs, one bias or one compromise propagates fleet-wide (OP.C0602). (8) Denial or chaff: noisy or flooded data streams degrade the model's usefulness, pushing operators to disable it (AML.T0046, AML.T0029).

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is a soft target mainly because of what it replaces: a physical penetration through the canister wall is swapped for an inferred value built on external thermocouples, and a leak alarm that operators will come to treat as the confinement indicator for casks that are rarely touched. The infrastructure is a handful of surface temperature channels and a small model. A deliberate adversary does not have to attack the neural network to degrade it. Thermal tampering at the cask surface, sensor spoofing, or a cable-level insider change could be enough, and the model would turn that into a plausible but false pressure and cladding-temperature estimate. The more interesting use is as a stepping stone or a cover. An adversary could build a false-reassurance window, or a false-alarm campaign that wears down operator vigilance. Either could be timed around a diversion, sabotage, or undeclared access to a cask, and the monitor's output is also a record that safeguards and safety staff may come to trust. The most important non-adversarial weakness is the training basis. A single heated test apparatus with a simulated leak, accurate only after thermal stabilization, will not generalize to real casks with different decay heat, ambient conditions, solar loading, and blocked vents. An adversary or an unlucky transient can sit in exactly the region where the model is blind.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
Adversarial. (1) Input manipulation: the model sees only 20 surface temperatures. Local heating or cooling, shielding or insulation, thermocouple relocation, or injected sensor data (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0015, AML.T0012) can shift the inferred pressure and peak cladding temperature, either hiding a real leak or vent blockage, or causing false alarms. The confinement consequence is delayed detection of helium loss and cladding degradation, plus unnecessary inspections or cask handling that add dose and exposure risk. (2) Trust concentration and timing: because direct pressure measurement is absent, the inferred value becomes the only confinement evidence. An insider or intruder who compromises the model, its weights, or its data path (AML.T0018, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0031) can create a quiet period for physical tampering or access to the stored material. A deliberate false-alarm flood (AML.T0046) can condition operators to dismiss alarms, so a real event is later discounted. (3) Integrity of the record: if the estimates enter inspection and safeguards records, falsified or drifted outputs undermine later assurance about cask condition. Targeting this is cheap for an insider, but a nation-state would more likely use it as a supporting deception than as a primary target.

Implicit. (a) Data scarcity and provenance: the training data come from a heated test apparatus with a regulator-simulated leak, not from real loaded casks (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Real leaks are slow, partial, and affected by ambient and solar variation, so rapid-leak detection does not demonstrate sensitivity to the leaks that matter. (b) Static and transient mismatch: accuracy is reported only after thermo-fluidic stabilization, so during transients such as loading, weather change, or blocked vents, outputs are unreliable (OP.C0303, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). An adversary can exploit these windows. (c) Over-trust and opacity: operators who adopt a pressure estimate with no uncertainty bounds, and who lack means to verify it, will drift toward automation trust failure and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0401). (d) Governance: there is no clear qualification path for a learned model as a confinement monitoring basis (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Model updates, retraining, and fleet-wide propagation across cask sites could spread a common bias or a single compromise (OP.C0602).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on rig-to-field domain shift, transient blindness, over-trust and opacity, input manipulation, pipeline tampering, and fleet propagation; I merged them. I dropped weaker or redundant codes (AML.T0012 valid accounts, AML.T0031, AML.T0044, OP.C0204) as not clearly instantiated by the text.

evidence.citation: "Transactions of the Korean Nuclear Society Autumn Meeting (paper on neural-network monitoring of canister internal pressure and peak cladding temperature from canister surface temperature in SNF dry storage)," Korean Nuclear Society
evidence.note: The conference paper proposes and tests neural network prediction models. Their inputs are canister surface temperatures from a test apparatus with a helium-pressure regulator that simulates a leak, and their outputs are canister internal pressure and peak cladding temperature. The authors report good accuracy once the thermo-fluidic state has stabilized after transients, and the model can alarm on abrupt peaks or drops from rapid helium loss. The search result did not show the paper's exact title, so the title field is descriptive and based on the proceedings page title and content.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is concealed loss of confinement or a leak/vent blockage hidden by manipulated or biased estimates, which gives a quiet window for diversion or sabotage preparation and erodes safeguards and confinement assurance, though large thermal margins and independent surveillance limit acute radiological consequences.

reproducibility.why: The surrogate-to-field gap, transient blindness and the absence of out-of-distribution detection are structural properties of a fixed-input regression trained on bench data, so they recur reliably under ordinary thermal variation or transients.

exploitability.why: Local heating, insulation or shielding of the cask surface needs physical proximity to the site, and pipeline tampering needs insider or vendor-level access, but passive exploitation of ordinary thermal variation and transients needs no special tooling.

affected_users.why: Impact is normally per cask or storage pad, but a single model reused across casks of different designs lets one bias or compromise propagate fleet-wide, which raises the breadth beyond a single component.

discoverability.why: Surrogate-to-field gaps, evasion of regression models and poisoning of small model files are well documented in the open literature, and the published conference paper describes the inputs and the training basis, but knowing how a given deployment is configured and where its blind regions lie requires partial inference by a capable outsider.

use_case: Random forest, artificial neural network and Gaussian naive Bayes classifiers that identify the level of damage to spent fuel assemblies inside a sealed dry-storage canister. Features come from the difference between the frequency response functions of an intact loaded canister and a damaged one. These are measured with accelerometers on the canister's outer surface during dynamic modal testing of a 2/3-scale canister mock-up. This gives non-invasive structural-integrity monitoring of stored fuel without access to the canister interior.
incurred_insecurity:
This classifier would become the main evidence of fuel integrity inside a sealed dry-storage canister that cannot be inspected, yet it is trained only on lab modal tests of a 2/3-scale mock-up with simulated damage (about 92% accuracy). Its main insecurities are a sim-to-real and baseline-drift gap that yields confident but wrong damage classes, misplaced operator trust with no independent ground truth, and governance gaps. An adversary can manipulate the physical sensing channel, the 'intact' reference data or the model files, so that degradation, diversion or substitution is masked or false alarms are provoked.

Sim-to-real and scale gap -- implicit, exploitable
Training on mock-up data with researcher-defined damage classes leaves the RF, ANN and GNB models producing confident class labels for out-of-distribution full-scale canisters, overpack coupling and real degradation modes. The result is a missed degradation or a spurious alarm that triggers needless canister handling and dose. An adversary who knows the published model and its weak sensitivity at small damage levels could act inside that blind spot.

Baseline and operational drift -- implicit, exploitable
FRF-difference features depend on a single-time 'intact' reference that shifts with temperature, decay-heat history, sensor remounting, boundary conditions and aging, so drift can mimic or hide damage and no interior ground truth exists to catch it. An adversary could time or disguise a physical change to the canister or its supports within this unmonitored drift band.

Over-trust, opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
A low base-rate damage event, uncalibrated outputs, a 92% accuracy figure that hides confusion between adjacent damage levels, and seed-dependent opaque models encourage operators to accept 'no damage' as a substitute for inspection. This erodes defense in depth and makes a tampered model hard to tell from a noisy one, so an adversary can rely on the misplaced trust and weak forensics.

Qualification, governance and data-continuity gaps -- implicit, exploitable
No AI-specific qualification or licensing route exists for ML structural-integrity evidence, research-grade code lacks software QA, and it is unclear whether models, baselines and data fall under safeguards-information security. Decades-long monitoring also risks sensor and format obsolescence. These gaps leave model changes and data loss unreviewed, which an adversary could use to alter the evidence chain unnoticed.

Sensor-channel manipulation -- adversarial
An insider or intruder with physical access to the outer-surface accelerometers, cabling or DAQ could alter coupling, mass, excitation or injected FRF data, shifting the features to mask real damage, removal or substitution of assemblies, or to fabricate damage alarms. The attack targets the physical signal rather than the model, and a proxy model built from the public paper could help tune it.

Baseline, data and model tampering -- adversarial
Alteration of the stored 'intact' reference FRFs, training labels or model files, including via the ML supply chain or a vendor or remote analytics path, silently biases all later decisions toward 'no damage'. Because the result is evidence about the contents of a sealed item, this compromises continuity of knowledge and can conceal degradation or diversion without any visible failure.

Concentration of trust across canisters -- adversarial
If the classifier replaces inspection, one compromised analysis workstation, vendor or shared model gives an adversary leverage over assurance for many canisters at once. The monitoring data pipeline can also serve as a stepping stone into wider plant networks.

Blind to material substitution -- implicit, exploitable
The classifier detects only damage-like dynamic changes, so dummy assemblies or removed material with similar mass and stiffness could present as intact. A state actor diverting or substituting fuel can rely on the false assurance, since no independent NDA or seals corroborate it.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations and safeguards view, this classifier would sit in a dry-storage monitoring chain, where the canister is sealed, welded, and effectively unobservable. Its output could feed decisions on inspection, retrieval, repackaging, transport readiness and continuity-of-knowledge records. The documented basis is a 2/3-scale mock-up, simulated damage, and about 92% accuracy. That is a long way from field qualification, because real canisters have different fuel loading, basket and gap conditions, thermal state, boundary conditions, concrete overpack coupling and decades of aging. The main downstream risks are false reassurance that defers a needed intervention, and false alarms that trigger unnecessary canister opening, handling, dose and cost. Neither outcome should cause an immediate accident on its own. Existing practice such as temperature and pressure monitoring, surveillance, inspections and conservative licensing limits sits behind it, but it can be eroded if the AI result is treated as authoritative evidence about the interior.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Sim-to-real and data-provenance gap: the classifier is trained on lab mock-up tests with simulated damage (OP.C0201.01/.02/.04, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). Real degradation modes such as cladding creep or failure, assembly shifting, basket deformation, hydride effects and fuel relocation have different structural-dynamic signatures. Damage classes are few, labeled by construction, and have no field base rate. The consequence is a confident but wrong damage class on a real canister, which means a missed degradation or a spurious alarm. (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303): the features are FRF differences against an 'intact loaded' baseline. Baseline shift from temperature, decay-heat history, boundary or support changes, sensor re-mounting, excitation differences, overpack or pad settlement, and sensor aging looks like damage or masks it. Because the baseline is itself a single point in time, it may be non-reproducible. The consequence is a drifting false-positive or false-negative rate, with no trustworthy ground truth because the interior can't be checked. (3) Opacity and automation bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0403): a random forest, an ANN and a naive Bayes model can disagree, and a ~92% accuracy figure hides class confusion, especially between adjacent damage levels (OP.C0304.03 oversimplification). Operators may over-trust a 'no damage' output as a substitute for inspection, or under-trust it and ignore it (OP.C0101.05). With no independent verification, errors are never discovered, which weakens defense in depth. (4) Governance gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0502): there is no accepted qualification pathway for ML-based structural-integrity evidence in dry-storage licensing. Model versioning, retraining and the validity envelope are often undefined. Regulators may not be ready to judge the evidence. (5) Fleet propagation (OP.C0602): a model qualified on one canister design and applied across a site's other designs or vintages propagates the same systematic bias.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Sensor or data-path manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0041, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020): an insider or intruder with physical access to the outer-surface accelerometers, cabling or DAQ could alter coupling, add mass, or inject or alter FRF data. This could mask real damage or manufacture false damage signatures, with the consequence of concealment of degradation or provoked intervention. The same applies to poisoning training or baseline data. (7) Baseline and model integrity (AML.T0018, AML.T0031, AML.T0076, AML.T0059): tampering with the stored 'intact' reference FRFs or model files shifts all later decisions invisibly. This is a safeguards continuity-of-knowledge issue, because the result is part of the evidence about the contents of a sealed item. If remote or vendor analytics are used (OP.C0601, AML.T0010), supply-chain and availability risks also arise (AML.T0029). (8) Safeguards deception: an adversary or state diverting or substituting fuel, or hiding a change in contents, could exploit a classifier that detects only damage-like dynamic changes. It would not detect material substitution or dummy assemblies with similar mass and stiffness (OP.C0702.01). Used as a safeguards tool, it provides weak assurance without independent NDA or seals. Mitigations lie in procedure: independent integrity checks, authenticated and logged data chains, multi-parameter corroboration, conservative treatment of a 'no damage' output, and periodic physical verification.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this system is fragile mainly because of where its training data comes from. All labels and features come from lab modal tests of a 2/3-scale mock-up, with damage that was simulated and introduced deliberately. The classifiers are small tabular models (RF, ANN, GNB) fed hand-built FRF-difference features. Their 0.916 accuracy comes from a small, controlled dataset, almost certainly with correlated repeated measurements and a limited set of damage configurations. Real deployment would hit a very different distribution: full-scale canisters, concrete overpack or storage-cask boundary conditions, temperature gradients, decay heat, aging, and real degradation modes. The difference-from-intact baseline adds a further dependency, because a trustworthy 'intact' reference FRF for each individual canister rarely exists, and the models have never been asked to say 'I don't know'.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and scale gap (OP.C0201.01/.02/.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03). Mock-up data is not field data. Damage classes were set up by researchers and probably do not match real fuel degradation, which is rare, gradual and poorly labeled. The mechanism is out-of-distribution input producing confident but wrong class labels, since RF, GNB and ANN all emit a class even for inputs far from training. Consequence: a canister with real damage is reported as intact, or a healthy one is flagged as damaged. The first gives false assurance on stored-fuel integrity and the second triggers unnecessary, costly and dosimetrically significant interventions. (2) Drift and baseline fragility (OP.C0302.01/.02, OP.C0303). The 'intact' FRF baseline shifts with temperature, humidity, sensor mounting, cask loading, concrete aging and instrument replacement. Static lab-qualified features will drift over decades of storage, and a drifting baseline can look like damage or hide it. A post-training change in measurement protocol (sensor placement, excitation) is a covariate shift that nobody monitors. (3) Evaluation optimism and limits of the metrics (OP.C0403, OP.C0401, OP.C0402). With a small dataset, the test split may share setups with training, so 0.916 accuracy and 0.920 Macro-F1 probably overstate generalization. A damage classification with a mid-range accuracy is also poorly calibrated for a safety-relevant decision. There is no uncertainty quantification, and RF and ANN training and inference are non-deterministic across seeds. (4) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04/.05, OP.C0102). Because the method is non-invasive and the interior cannot be inspected, there is no independent ground truth. Operators cannot readily check an 'intact' output, which encourages over-trust, and sporadic false alarms encourage disuse. (5) Governance (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0502). There is no AI qualification route for structural monitoring of storage casks, and the research code and models are unlikely to meet software QA expectations.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Evasion of the physical sensing channel (AML.T0015, T0043, T0041). Someone with physical access to the canister surface could change the mechanical coupling, damping or sensor mounting, or add excitation noise, shifting the FRF features so that damage is masked or false damage is created. The attack surface is the physical signal, not the model. Because the features are low-dimensional and the model class is known from the paper, a proxy model could be built from the public description (AML.T0000, T0005, T0002). (7) Data and pipeline integrity (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0031, T0018.000, T0059). Tampering with baseline FRF records, the training labels or stored model files would let an insider or supply-chain actor bias the classifiers or the 'intact' reference silently. Because the system is a monitoring layer, a successful compromise would degrade assurance rather than produce visible failure, and that gap could be used to conceal fuel degradation or tampering. A safeguards angle also exists: an apparently intact FRF could hide loss of fuel content, because the classifiers were never trained for material diversion or substitution.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this use case matters because a sealed dry-storage canister is a safeguards and safety 'black box': it is sealed precisely so no one can look inside, and this classifier would become the main evidence of fuel integrity, and possibly of continuity of knowledge, for material that cannot be inspected. That makes the classifier's output a high-value trust-concentration point. An adversary, or an insider with access to the accelerometer chain, the baseline 'intact' FRF reference, or the model, gains a way to shape what the facility believes about the canister's contents. The model is also weak in non-adversarial ways: it was trained on a 2/3-scale mock-up with simulated damage, it reaches about 92% accuracy, and it is a small-data, sim-to-real problem. A patient adversary could time an action around those gaps, and operators could grow complacent about a monitoring method that will rarely, if ever, report damage.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Baseline and measurement-chain integrity. The classifier works on the difference between an 'intact' reference FRF and the current FRF. An insider or a compromised sensor/DAQ/analysis pipeline could alter the stored reference, sensor placement or coupling, or the excitation. This would mask real damage or removal or substitution of assemblies, or it could fabricate damage alarms that trigger costly canister handling and radiological or dose exposure. The AI failure mechanism is evasion or poisoning of the input features (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0020, AML.T0059). Dependence: integrity or safeguards assurance for sealed fuel. Consequence: a false 'intact' reading, or a diversion or sabotage indicator that goes unseen. (2) Model and data supply chain. Tampering with the trained model, the training data, or open-source ML libraries could introduce a backdoor or bias toward the 'no damage' class (AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0076). The published paper and its methods are public, so a technically capable adversary can build proxy models and learn which damage levels and frequency bands the classifier is least sensitive to (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0013). This is cheap reconnaissance, although the physical-access barriers make direct attack hard. A nation-state might target the monitoring data pipeline as a stepping stone into wider plant networks rather than the classifier itself (AML.T0012, AML.T0025). (3) Concentration of trust. If the classifier is accepted as a substitute for inspection, a single compromised analysis workstation or vendor could undermine assurance across many canisters (OP.C0602).

IMPLICIT (exploitable or time-able by an adversary). (a) Sim-to-real and scale gap: the model is trained on a 2/3-scale mock-up with simulated damage, so it faces data scarcity, a transferred-data problem and operational heterogeneity (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0202, OP.C0203, OP.C0302.03). Real canisters differ in boundary conditions, loading, temperature, aging, concrete overpack coupling and burnup. Drift, or an unrepresentative case, can produce silent misclassification. An adversary who knows the model is only about 92% accurate and poorly characterized at small damage levels can act inside that blind spot. (b) Automation trust and complacency: damage is a very low base-rate event, so staff may over-trust a 'no damage' output (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06) and lose independent inspection and engineering skills. This erodes vigilance in a way an attacker could time around. (c) Opacity and non-repeatability: ANN and RF models are hard to explain and vary with training seed (OP.C0401, OP.C0402). That makes it hard to tell a tampered model from a noisy one, which weakens forensic detection. (d) Qualification and governance gaps: no AI-specific QA or licensing basis exists for using ML in spent-fuel structural monitoring, and it is unclear whether the model, baselines and data are covered by the security programs that protect safeguards-relevant information (OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0505). (e) Long data continuity: monitoring spans decades, so software, sensor and data-format obsolescence can create gaps (OP.C0204).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, baseline drift, automation trust, governance gaps, and adversarial sensor-channel and baseline/model tampering, so these were merged as single threats. Single-panelist points (data continuity, trust concentration, material substitution blindness) were kept as distinct, while the weakly argued cloud/vendor items (OP.C0601, AML.T0029) and generic ATLAS items such as T0013 were dropped.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning-aided damage identification of mock-up spent nuclear fuel assemblies in a sealed dry storage canister," Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence, vol. 128, 107484 (2024)
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper (Zhuang, Arcaro, Gencturk, Ghanem) trains and tests three ML classifiers on frequency-response-function difference features from experimental modal tests of a canister mock-up with simulated interior fuel-assembly damage. Random forest performed best, with a testing accuracy of 0.916 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.920. The URL is a ResearchGate listing of the journal article; the journal's own page is https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0952197623016688.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is baseline/model tampering or sensor-channel manipulation, or blindness to substitution, which would mask fuel degradation, diversion or substitution in sealed canisters and falsify safeguards continuity of knowledge, a safeguards-falsification category of harm.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real gaps and baseline drift would reliably produce confident misclassifications once the classifier is relied on in the field, but deliberate masking depends on specific physical or data-access conditions and on how small the damage or change is.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (physical access to canister sensors and cabling, tampering with stored baselines or model files, supply-chain compromise, or a state actor substituting material) need insider position, physical access to a controlled storage area, or state-level resourcing, though the implicit blind spots need no special access.

affected_users.why: A compromised shared model, workstation or vendor pipeline could undermine assurance across many canisters at once and give a foothold into plant networks, though the impact stays largely within the storage and monitoring domain rather than being facility-wide.

discoverability.why: The model type, features, accuracy and weak small-damage sensitivity are in a public peer-reviewed paper, and sim-to-real and drift limits are well-known for this class of ML. Exploiting them against a real deployment still needs partial knowledge of the system, so a capable outsider could infer the weakness but not the specifics.

use_case: Explainable machine-learning prognostics that predict a system-level remaining useful life (RUL) for a nuclear power plant subsystem under multiple concurrent component faults. Gradient boosting regressor, support vector regressor, fully connected neural network and LSTM models were compared on simulated plant degradation data, and the LSTM was the most repeatable. SHAP and LIME explanations show which signals drive each RUL prediction, to support trustworthy predictive-maintenance decisions.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory RUL predictor sits upstream of maintenance scheduling, outage planning and run-or-repair decisions, and was developed and shown only on simulated degradation. Its main threats are a sim-to-real gap that yields confidently wrong RULs, explanation layers that create false assurance, weak repeatability and qualification, and adversarial manipulation of the data, model and explanation chain. Direct safety consequence is bounded by independent surveillance and protection layers, but it grows if RUL is used to extend intervals or justify deferral.

Sim-to-real gap and missing ground truth -- implicit, exploitable
The models learn the simulator's fault-interaction physics and noise model, and concurrent multi-fault run-to-failure data barely exists in the field, so out-of-distribution inputs (novel fault combinations, sensor faults, post-maintenance resets) produce overconfident RULs that defer or force maintenance wrongly and stay latent. An adversary could wait for or induce operating conditions outside the training envelope, or hide a sabotage-related bias inside the model's unvalidated error band.

Drift after plant changes -- implicit, exploitable
Component replacement, uprates, sensor recalibration and changed operating regimes shift the signal-to-RUL mapping, and with no failures to compare against the stale model goes unnoticed. An adversary could time manipulation to such a change so that the resulting RUL error is attributed to benign drift.

Explanation-induced over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
SHAP and LIME are post-hoc approximations, LIME is unstable on sequential data, and attributions split credit between correlated interacting faults, so plausible explanations can validate a wrong RUL and misdirect maintenance to the wrong component. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, using a persuasive explanation to suppress operator scrutiny of a manipulated prediction.

Repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
The LSTM is only the most repeatable of four models, not deterministic or qualified, and retraining or seed variation changes RUL for the same plant state, with no established QA path for ML prognostics and weak version and access control over models and data. An insider's subtle tampering can hide inside this natural run-to-run variability, which weakens audit and makes manipulation hard to distinguish from noise.

Sensor and data-path manipulation -- adversarial
Slowly biased or crafted historian and sensor inputs can evade the model, pushing RUL up to mask real degradation ahead of sabotage, or down to force outages and give an insider physical access. Perturbations that mimic benign aging are stealthy, and can also steer SHAP/LIME attributions toward innocuous signals.

Training-data, simulator and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Poisoning the simulator, its parameters, retraining data, weights or ML and explainer libraries can embed a bias or backdoor triggered by specific fault combinations while benchmark metrics stay normal. Synthetic labels make poisoned values hard to detect against reality, and a shared or cloud-trained model could propagate one compromised update across units.

Model and degradation-data exfiltration -- adversarial
Trained models, fault-signature mappings and attributions reveal which components and signals the plant treats as critical and when it is vulnerable. This gives reconnaissance value and lets an attacker build a proxy model to rehearse evasion offline.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, a system-level RUL estimate feeds maintenance scheduling, outage planning, spare-parts ordering and run-or-repair decisions. A wrong or manipulated RUL therefore changes when and whether a degraded component is worked on. It does not directly actuate anything. Real harm needs several other layers to fail: condition monitoring, surveillance testing, Technical Specification limits, operator rounds and the safety-classified protection systems. Those layers keep the direct safety consequence small if this stays an advisory, non-safety tool. The credible concerns are a long-horizon erosion of maintenance rigor, and a hidden common-cause degradation (multiple concurrent faults) that the model was never trained to see. This use case is also a simulation-only study. Its main weakness is the gap between simulated degradation and real plant behavior, and that gap is something an adversary could exploit or time an attack around.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: the models are trained and validated on simulated degradation, so fault-interaction physics, sensor noise, operating-mode changes and repair history may not match a real plant. Compounding faults are rare in field data, so there are no real run-to-failure labels to calibrate against. The failure mechanism is out-of-distribution, overconfident RUL. The consequence is over-long RUL, which defers inspection or replacement and could erode margin on a degrading subsystem. Alternatively an over-short RUL drives unnecessary outages and intrusive maintenance, which carries its own human-error and dose risk. (2) Explanation artifacts: SHAP and LIME are post-hoc approximations, and the paper itself notes LIME is unstable on sequential data. Plausible but inconsistent attributions can lend false credibility to a wrong prediction. Maintenance staff may then chase the wrong component or accept an RUL because the explanation seems physically sensible (automation bias). Explanations also show correlation, not causation, in multi-fault cases. (3) Repeatability and qualification: the LSTM was only the most repeatable of the four, which is not the same as deterministic or qualified. Retraining and seed variation produce different RULs for the same plant state. This is hard to fit into software QA, nuclear-grade verification and configuration control for even non-safety-related decision support. (4) Drift: after component replacement, a power uprate, a changed operating regime or sensor recalibration, the learned degradation relationships go stale, and nobody may notice because there are no failures to compare against. Skill fade in manual trending and engineering judgment makes this worse.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Sensor or historian data manipulation (evasion or chaff, for example slowly biased signals) could steer RUL upward to hide real degradation, or downward to force outages or cause economic harm. It is stealthy because it looks like normal drift. Sabotage of a component combined with a suppressed RUL signal would be the dangerous case, since it defeats a trend-awareness layer. It would still need the independent protection and surveillance layers to fail as well. (6) Training-data or model supply-chain poisoning, including a compromised simulator, open-source ML libraries, pre-trained artifacts or a vendor-updated model, could embed a bias or backdoor that triggers on specific fault combinations. (7) Explanation interfaces and dashboards add an attack and integrity surface, including manipulated explanations that mask the true drivers. If the tool is cloud-hosted or fleet-shared, one compromised model update could propagate across units. Degradation data and RUL outputs also reveal asset condition and vulnerability timing, which is sensitive reconnaissance material. (8) Denial of the service during an outage window removes decision support and pushes staff back to conservative manual practice, which is a modest impact.

Overall severity is bounded by the advisory role and by existing defense-in-depth, but it rises sharply if RUL is later used to extend maintenance intervals or justify deferral without independent verification.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a simulation-trained model study, so the main exposure sits in the data and the lifecycle rather than the architecture. The RUL labels and degradation trajectories come entirely from a plant simulator. The model therefore learns the simulator's degradation physics, its fault-injection assumptions and its noise model, not real plant aging. The system-level RUL under concurrent faults has no ground-truth labels in the field, because run-to-failure data for safety-relevant subsystems barely exists. Fault-interaction patterns that were never simulated, such as novel combinations, sensor faults mimicking component faults, or maintenance interventions that reset degradation, fall outside the training distribution. The LSTM is a sequence model that is both opaque and sensitive to input history. Its 'most repeatable' status rests on a seed-variance metric in a closed benchmark, which says nothing about calibrated uncertainty or OOD behaviour. SHAP and LIME are post-hoc approximations. They give a sense of trustworthiness that may exceed what they warrant, and LIME is already shown to be unstable on sequential data. They also add an attack surface and a source of automation bias.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). The model is trained on simulated degradation with no field validation. In deployment, sensor noise, calibration drift, instrument replacement, operating-mode changes and unmodelled fault couplings shift the input distribution, and the LSTM extrapolates silently. The consequence is a confidently wrong RUL. An overestimate defers maintenance on a degrading subsystem and erodes safety margin. An underestimate triggers unnecessary outages and stresses components. Concept drift follows from aging, refurbishment and maintenance, which change the mapping from signals to RUL (OP.C0302.02, OP.C0303). (2) Low base rate and no ground truth (OP.C0202, OP.C0204). Concurrent multi-fault end-of-life events are rare, so predictions cannot be validated in operation and errors stay latent. (3) Explanation-induced over-trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02, OP.C0403, OP.C0501). SHAP and LIME attributions can look plausible even when the model is wrong, and LIME's local instability on sequences means explanations can disagree between runs. Operators may treat the explanation as validation and not as a diagnostic aid. There is no established qualification path for ML prognostics, and an explainer is not a verification method. (4) Multi-fault attribution is also fragile when features are correlated, because SHAP attributions can split or misallocate credit between interacting faults, which misdirects maintenance toward the wrong component (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0603).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Input manipulation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0031). An adversary with access to the sensor or historian path could craft small perturbations or slow drifts. A slow bias would mimic benign aging and shift RUL upward to hide real degradation, or downward to force costly outages. Such a perturbation is hard to separate from the implicit drift above, which gives an attacker cover. The explanations could be steered too, so they show benign signals as the drivers (SHAP/LIME are known to be manipulable). (b) Training-data and simulator integrity (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059). The simulator, its parameters and the retraining data are a supply chain. Poisoning them or inserting a backdoor trigger in sensor patterns would bias RUL in targeted regimes while benchmark metrics stay normal. Because the labels are synthetic, poisoned labels are hard to detect against reality. (c) Model and artifact theft or tampering (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0076, AML.T0010.001). The trained weights and the open-source explainer libraries (SHAP, LIME) are software supply-chain components. A proxy model (AML.T0005) lets an attacker rehearse evasion offline. Open publication of the architecture and simulation approach aids reconnaissance (AML.T0000). (d) Integration risk (OP.C0502, OP.C0601, OP.C0602). Cloud-hosted training or fleet-wide model propagation would spread one poisoned or drifted model across units. Maintenance-scheduling outputs may feed work planning, so a compromised RUL has downstream effects on outage planning and spare-parts decisions, which is a safety-margin and availability concern. It is not a direct protection-system function.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, a system-level RUL predictor changes the facility's attack calculus in a quiet way. It sits upstream of maintenance scheduling, outage planning and spare-parts decisions, so a deliberate adversary or insider who can bias its output gets a low-visibility way to steer human action without touching any safety-class I&C. The documented work is simulation-only, so the most important exposure is the gap between what was shown (a model that is repeatable on synthetic degradation data) and what a deployed advisory tool would face. That gap is where an adversary, or ordinary drift, can hide. The SHAP/LIME explanation layer is meant to build trust, which also makes it a trust-concentration point: persuasive explanations can mask a manipulated or degraded model and lower operator vigilance. A nation-state would probably choose easier targets first, but a prognostics feed is a plausible stepping stone for degrading plant availability, hiding real degradation, or inducing unnecessary outages.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity manipulation of the data and model chain. Prognostics depend on plant historian and sensor streams, plus training sets that may be simulator-derived. An insider or an adversary with a foothold in the OT/IT data path could poison training data, tamper with model weights or retraining pipelines, or subtly bias sensor inputs (T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0043, T0031). The aim would be to understate RUL for a degrading component, so a fault is overlooked or maintenance is deferred just before a time-chosen attack or sabotage. Or the aim would be to overstate degradation, forcing unneeded outages and costly inspections that also give an insider physical access. The safety-relevant consequence is a degraded or masked equipment-health picture. The security-relevant consequence is concealed sabotage preparation or targeted availability loss. (2) Explanation-layer deception. SHAP/LIME outputs can be made to look plausible even when the underlying prediction is manipulated. Adversarially crafted inputs can shift attributions toward innocuous signals (T0043, T0067, T0015). The explanation becomes a false assurance that suppresses operator scrutiny, so the trust-building feature is itself an attack surface. (3) Model and data exfiltration. Degradation models, fault-signature mappings and feature attributions reveal which components and signals the plant treats as critical and how it reasons about weak points. This is reconnaissance value for a later physical or cyber attack (T0024.002, T0035, T0085, T0025). (4) Supply chain and tooling. ML libraries, pretrained artifacts and explainability packages entering the plant's analytics environment widen the software-supply-chain exposure near OT-adjacent networks (T0010.001, T0011.001). If the tool is vendor-hosted or cloud-trained, it also creates an off-site dependency and a possible bridge into plant data (OP.C0601, T0012).

IMPLICIT (no adversary required, but exploitable or timeable). (a) The training data is simulated degradation. This is a provenance and sim-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). Real plants have few run-to-failure examples, and multiple concurrent faults are rarer still. Models can be confidently wrong under real operating heterogeneity, and an adversary can wait for or induce conditions outside the training distribution (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). (b) Automation trust failure. Maintenance planners may over-trust a clean RUL number with an explanation attached, so independent condition monitoring and engineering judgment skill fade (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Predictable over-reliance is the vigilance erosion an adversary would time an attack around. (c) Explanation instability. LIME was reported to be less stable on sequential data, and LSTM repeatability is only relative. Run-to-run variation in explanations or predictions weakens audit and makes tampering hard to tell from noise (OP.C0402.02, OP.C0401, OP.C0304.03). An insider's subtle manipulation hides inside this natural variability. (d) Governance gaps. There is no established AI-specific qualification path for advisory prognostics. Model versioning, retraining control and access control over models and data are therefore likely to be weak, and they are rarely treated as security-significant assets (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0503, OP.C0505). Overall severity depends on how far outputs are allowed to influence maintenance deferral. Modest as a pure advisory tool, it grows sharply if RUL is used to extend intervals or justify skipped inspections.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the sim-to-real gap, explanation-induced over-trust, input manipulation, and data/model supply-chain poisoning; I merged restated versions and dropped the minor denial-of-service and weakly argued items (T0067, T0012, T0011.001, T0029, T0076, T0024.001). I kept model exfiltration as distinct reconnaissance and left out cloud-dependency codes as secondary.

evidence.citation: "Explaining System-Level Prognostics with Established Machine Learning Methods," Nuclear Technology (Taylor & Francis / American Nuclear Society)
evidence.note: The paper simulates nuclear power plant operation to model how components degrade. It then trains and compares four ML models (GBR, SVR, FCNN, LSTM) to predict a new system-level RUL parameter under concurrent faults. The LSTM was the most repeatable. SHAP gave consistent global explanations, while LIME gave local explanations that were less stable on sequential data. The work is a simulation-based model study, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The worst credible threat is a manipulated or poisoned RUL that masks real degradation or forces wrong maintenance and outages, causing operational disruption and some safety-margin erosion; independent surveillance and protection layers bound direct radiological consequence, so it does not reach 5.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution inputs, drift after plant changes and explanation-induced over-trust reliably produce wrong or unvalidated RULs once the conditions occur, though a deliberate backdoor or sabotage-masking outcome depends on additional conditions.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (data-path manipulation, simulator or model supply-chain poisoning, insider tampering) need privileged access to historians, training pipelines or model artifacts, which is well beyond routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly a single subsystem's maintenance and outage decisions, but a shared or cloud-trained model propagating one compromised update across units could extend it to multiple units or fleet-wide.

discoverability.why: Sim-to-real gaps, drift, post-hoc explanation weaknesses and evasion or poisoning of ML models are well documented in the open literature, and this study is itself published, so an outsider can readily infer the weaknesses even without plant-specific details.

use_case: Faster R-CNN (Inception-v2 backbone) deep-learning detection of surface scratches on nuclear fuel assemblies from digital images. It was trained and tested on images of a 15×15 mock fuel assembly with randomly made scratch defects. It replaces manual visual inspection, which depends on personnel experience and attention, for assembly appearance quality checks. It was designed to separate real scratches from false positives such as water stains.
incurred_insecurity:
Replacing manual visual inspection with a Faster R-CNN scratch detector makes one unqualified model the acceptance barrier for assembly surface quality at a fuel fabrication plant. The evidence comes only from a single mock assembly with randomly made scratches, so the main threats are silent missed defects from lab-to-plant generalization failure, erosion of human oversight, and a missing qualification basis. Adversarial threats are model or data poisoning, physical or input-side evasion exploiting the stain-versus-scratch boundary, and tampering with the image chain. The implicit weaknesses make the adversarial ones harder to detect.

Lab-to-plant generalization gap -- implicit, exploitable
The detector was trained on surrogate data from one mock assembly, and the roughly 0.98 TPR at 0.1 FPR was measured on that same setup. Real defect morphology, finishes, lighting, camera ageing and residues are untested, so recall on real defects can fall silently and defective assemblies pass as accepted. An adversary who learns or infers these blind spots, through reconnaissance or insider knowledge, can place damage where the model does not look and have it attributed to ordinary drift.

Rare-defect scarcity and operating-point trade-off -- implicit, exploitable
Real critical defects are rare and underrepresented in training, and the reported metrics say nothing about subtle, small or low-contrast scratches. A 10% false-alarm rate on a low-prevalence line pushes staff toward threshold changes or overrides, and an adversary can use that alarm fatigue to bury a genuine detection or a deliberate defect.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Once the detector replaces experienced inspectors, reliance on 'no detection' grows, human inspection skill erodes, and no independent reference remains to notice systematic misses. An insider can rely on this misplaced trust, since a defect that evades the model will rarely be questioned.

Qualification, opacity and update-path gap -- implicit, exploitable
There is no AI-specific QA basis, no defined detection limits per defect class, and no explanation of why a region is rejected as a water stain. Retraining or backbone changes can alter behaviour without a regression suite tied to acceptance criteria. Silent degradation therefore looks the same as tampering, and an unvetted update path becomes a way to introduce a malicious change unnoticed.

Model and data poisoning -- adversarial
Tampered training images or labels (for example scratches labelled as stains), a poisoned public pretrained backbone, or a modified model file can implant a trigger-conditioned blind spot that ordinary test-set accuracy will not reveal. The result is defective fuel accepted with a clean-looking quality record, enabling sabotage or quality fraud.

Physical and input-side evasion -- adversarial
Because the model was explicitly trained to separate scratches from water stains, anyone controlling lighting, camera position, coatings or markings can craft inputs that push a real scratch into the benign class or trigger a planted backdoor. Insiders at the inspection station can do this cheaply and without touching the model.

Image-chain tampering -- adversarial
The model trusts whatever images reach it, so altering, replacing or replaying images between camera and inference defeats the check without touching the model. The same tampering can falsify inspection records and hide surface evidence that other processes reuse for traceability.

nuclear_engineer.argument: In a fuel fabrication plant, visual inspection of assembly surfaces is a quality-assurance barrier. It is meant to catch scratches or cladding and grid damage that could lead to fretting, corrosion, or fuel failure in service. The documented system was validated only on a 15x15 mock assembly with deliberately made random scratches, so real fabrication defects, real lighting, real surface finishes and real water-stain or oxide artifacts are all untested. The harm is a missed defect (false negative) passing as accepted. A real assembly gets released to a reactor operator with a latent flaw, and the AI result may be the only independent surface check once manual inspection is retired. The headline 0.98 TPR at 0.1 FPR also implies roughly 2% misses and 10% false alarms. That is acceptable for screening but not for a sole acceptance barrier, and the figures say little about rare, subtle or novel defect types.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Lab-to-plant generalization gap: the model was trained on a mock assembly with randomly made scratches (simulated/surrogate data). Real defects differ in morphology, depth, orientation and location. Real fuel rods have different oxide and finish conditions, and the plant has different cameras, illumination, reflections, water residue and handling marks. Recall on real defects could be far below the reported figure with no visible warning. Cause: distribution shift and surrogate data. Consequence: undetected scratches in accepted assemblies. (2) Drift and heterogeneity: camera ageing, lens contamination, lighting changes, new assembly designs (different lattice sizes, grid types, cladding alloys or coatings) and process changes degrade the detector silently, and no one retrains or requalifies it. (3) Automation bias and skill fade: once inspectors rely on the detector, vigilance falls and manual inspection skill erodes. Inspectors may accept 'no detection' as clearance, and the tool was explicitly designed to dismiss 'water stains', so a real shallow scratch could be classified as benign. Where the 10% false-positive rate causes alarm fatigue, staff may override genuine detections. (4) Qualification and opacity gap: a CNN's bounding-box output is hard to explain, repeatability across retraining is uncertain, and no AI-specific QA basis exists (quality-assurance codes, NQA-1-style software qualification, regulator acceptance). Criteria for detection limits, minimum scratch depth and probability of detection per defect class are undefined, so a safety-relevant acceptance decision rests on an unverified tool. (5) Rare-defect scarcity: the rare critical defects, such as deep gouges or debris-fretting precursors, are exactly the ones with the least training data.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Data or model poisoning in the supply chain: tampered training images or labels (for example, scratches labeled as stains), a compromised pretrained backbone, or a modified model file could create a blind spot for specific defect patterns. A trigger-style backdoor could suppress detection, enabling a sabotage or quality-fraud scenario in which a defective assembly is accepted. (7) Physical or input-side evasion: an insider or intruder who controls the lighting, camera position, surface coating or markings could cause systematic misses, for example by making a defect resemble a water stain. The same access could degrade image quality to cause denial of service, or flood the line with false positives to slow production. (8) Integrity of records: tampering with the inspection images, results or logs in the quality database would undermine traceability. This also matters for safeguards, because the same imaging and records infrastructure also supports item identification and accountancy.

MITIGATING FACTORS: downstream controls (ultrasonic/eddy-current testing, dimensional gauging, reactor-side inspection, and in-service monitoring) exist, and a detector can run as a second reader alongside manual inspection. Harm requires the AI to be the sole barrier. Even so, if the AI replaces manual inspection as the document says, those layers become the only defence, and their independence from surface defects is limited.

ai_engineer.argument: From the ML pipeline view, the main fragility is the gap between what this detector learned and what it would see in a real fuel fabrication line. It was trained and evaluated on 18,816 images of one 15x15 mock assembly with randomly made scratches, so the training data is simulated or surrogate, not field data. The roughly 0.98 TPR at 0.1 FPR was probably measured on a test split drawn from the same mock-up, lighting, camera, and surface finish. Real defects (drawing marks, handling scratches, oxide or contamination, pellet-stack or grid-spacer artefacts) have different morphology, frequency and base rate. Water stains were the only named confounder. A detector built around that narrow class boundary will have unknown behaviour on other confounders. Because the model is a pixel-based CNN detector operating on a mechanical-quality gate, the exposure comes from the model's input-distribution assumptions, its thresholding, and the lack of an independent qualification basis, more than from the facility around it.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Surrogate-to-production generalization failure (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03): random artificial scratches on a mock assembly do not match the distribution of real scratch mechanisms, and the model has never seen real rod cladding finish variation, different alloys or batches, or production-line contamination. A shift in camera, illumination, standoff distance, rod surface oxidation or coolant residue is covariate shift. It could silently reduce recall for the real defect class, so a defective assembly passes the appearance check. (2) Low base-rate and operating-point problem (OP.C0202): real defects are rare, so a 0.1 FPR that looks fine on a balanced test set could produce a huge false-alarm load, which pushes operators to raise the threshold or ignore alerts (OP.C0101.04/.05, OP.C0102). Alternatively an over-tuned threshold hides missed detections. The reported metrics say nothing about the miss rate on small, low-contrast or partially occluded scratches. (3) Automation trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06): replacing experienced inspectors with a detector removes the human reference needed to notice systematic misses, and the model gives no explanation of why it rejects a candidate region as a stain (OP.C0401). (4) Qualification and lifecycle gaps (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0402): no accepted way exists to qualify a CNN detector against fabrication QA standards. Retraining on new production images, or swapping backbones, can change behaviour non-deterministically with no regression suite tied to defect-size acceptance criteria. Labels are also a weak point: ground truth came from the authors' constructed scratches, not from a metrology reference.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS AND OPENINGS. (5) Evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043): a physical or digital perturbation, such as a surface coating, a texture or sticker that looks like a water stain, or targeted lighting changes, could push a real scratch into the 'false positive' class. Because the system was explicitly trained to discriminate stains from scratches, that decision boundary is a known and exploitable weakness for anyone with access to the model, its outputs (AML.T0063, AML.T0040) or a proxy (AML.T0005). Commodity open detector architectures make such a proxy easy to build. (6) Data and model integrity (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000/.004, AML.T0059, AML.T0031): the image corpus, labels, pretrained backbone weights (usually pulled from public checkpoints) and annotation tooling are supply-chain surfaces. Mislabelled or backdoor-triggered training images, a poisoned pretrained checkpoint, or tampered retraining data would leave a trigger-conditioned blind spot that standard test-set accuracy would not reveal. (7) Image-pipeline tampering (AML.T0043.003, AML.T0041): the model trusts whatever images it is given. Altering, replacing or replaying acquired images between camera and inference, or manipulating capture conditions, defeats the check without touching the model, and the AI integration adds a software path that manual inspection did not have. Implicit weaknesses make these harder to detect: no OOD detector, no confidence calibration on the real distribution, and a lack of independent sampling audit mean that an adversary or a slow drift can degrade detection with no alarm.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, a scratch detector on fuel assemblies is a low-value direct target but a high-value quiet one. It replaces a human inspector whose attention and experience were the control, so the detector becomes the single point of trust for cladding and structural-surface acceptance at a fuel fabrication facility. An adversary, whether an insider or a supply-chain actor, gains little by crashing it. The payoff comes from making it quietly wrong in a chosen way: suppressing detections of a particular defect class, or flagging benign features so that inspectors learn to ignore it. The documented evidence is a laboratory mock-up with randomly made scratches, not a plant deployment, so the gap between lab and production conditions creates blind spots that an adversary could exploit and that also hide non-adversarial failures.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or data integrity compromise (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004, T0076). The model, its weights and the labelled image set are small, static and rarely reviewed. A poisoned or backdoored model, or a tampered training set, could be built to pass assemblies carrying a specific scratch pattern, location or lighting signature. The facility depends on the detector for surface acceptance of assemblies, so the consequence is defective fuel entering the supply chain with a falsified quality record, which is a safety issue and a quality-assurance integrity issue. Insiders with access to the inspection station, camera or image pipeline could trigger it physically with a patch, marking or lighting change (AML.T0041, T0043.003, T0015). (2) Image-chain manipulation. Altering, replaying or substituting images upstream of the detector (AML.T0010.000, T0073) can defeat it without touching the model, and it could also hide diversion-relevant or tamper-relevant surface evidence if the same imagery is reused for records. (3) Detector as stepping stone. An inspection workstation joined to plant IT, model-update channels or vendor tooling gives lateral-movement access (AML.T0012, T0010.001), and the low-profile asset is less likely to be monitored than primary process systems. IMPLICIT, WITH ADVERSARY TIMING. (4) Automation trust failure and skill fade (OP.C0101, C0101.06, C0102). With a reported 0.98 TPR at 0.1 FPR, inspectors will drift into reliance while their own visual-inspection skill erodes. The residual miss rate then becomes a predictable window, and a 10% false-positive rate pushes toward alarm fatigue or override habits. (5) Lab-to-plant generalization gap (OP.C0302, C0302.03, C0201.01, C0202). A single mock assembly with random scratches and 18,816 images has little coverage of real defect morphology, different assembly designs, surface finishes, lighting, water residue, camera aging and rare critical defects. Systematic misses go unnoticed, and an adversary who learns the blind spots through reconnaissance or insider knowledge can place damage there. (6) Drift, opacity and governance (OP.C0401, C0501, C0503, C0302.01). Without drift monitoring, re-qualification after retraining and independent spot-check sampling, silent degradation is indistinguishable from tampering, so both persist. Model updates also become an unvetted change path (OP.C0502). Overall, a sophisticated adversary would target this only as part of a quality-fraud or sabotage-by-defect scheme, but an insider with modest access would find it easier than defeating human inspection plus procedural controls.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the lab-to-plant generalization gap, automation trust and skill fade, the qualification and opacity gap, poisoning or backdoor, and stain-mimicking physical evasion; I merged them accordingly. I folded image-chain tampering into one threat and dropped the security specialist's lateral-movement 'stepping stone' threat as speculative given the documented laboratory-only setup; I also left out generic ATLAS candidates such as AML.T0012, AML.T0073, AML.T0076, AML.T0029 and AML.T0005 as weakly traceable.

evidence.citation: "Defect detection of nuclear fuel assembly based on deep neural network," Annals of Nuclear Energy, Vol. 137 (2020), Elsevier
