evidence.note: The authors built and tested a Faster R-CNN scratch detector on a labelled image set of 18,816 images of a mock assembly with scratches. They compared it with other detectors (SSD, R-FCN, other Faster R-CNN backbones). Faster R-CNN with Inception-v2 performed best, reaching about 0.98 true-positive rate at 0.1 false-positive rate. This is a laboratory mock-up test, not a reported plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a poisoned or evaded detector (or falsified inspection records) letting defective fuel assemblies be accepted with a clean quality record. That is a quality-fraud and sabotage category with downstream fuel-integrity implications, but surface scratches are a quality barrier rather than a direct release pathway, so it falls short of the top score.

reproducibility.why: The generalization gap, rare-defect scarcity and automation over-trust are structural and recur reliably once the model replaces inspectors. Poisoning and evasion depend on access and conditions, but once those are met they are fairly dependable.

exploitability.why: Image-chain tampering and physical or input-side evasion by insiders at the inspection station need only modest access and no model changes. Poisoning the training data or model file requires deeper insider or supply-chain access, so the class sits mid-to-high.

affected_users.why: Defective assemblies accepted at the quality barrier can propagate into downstream fuel handling, reactor use and traceability records, spanning many assemblies and multiple processes. The detector covers one inspection step, so impact is not facility-wide in the sense of coupled control systems.

discoverability.why: The vulnerability classes (adversarial evasion, data poisoning, distribution shift, over-trust) are well documented in the open literature, and the source paper is public and describes the model and its stain-versus-scratch design. Exact blind spots at a given plant would still need reconnaissance or insider knowledge.

use_case: Neural-network surrogate of CASMO5 lattice calculations that predicts spent-fuel decay heat and nuclide concentrations. Inputs are initial enrichment, burnup, cooling time between cycles, mean boron concentration and fuel temperature. The surrogate is used for fast sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification of spent-fuel characteristics for waste management and safeguards.
incurred_insecurity:
This NN surrogate of CASMO5 lattice calculations sits off the control path but concentrates trust: its decay-heat and nuclide-inventory outputs feed cask thermal limits, shielding and criticality source terms, and safeguards inventory cross-checks. The main threats are silent extrapolation beyond a narrow validation set, inherited simulation bias with understated uncertainty, qualification and over-trust gaps, and adversarial tampering with the model, its training data or its inputs. Independent code-of-record calculations and cask measurements limit direct physical harm, but systematic bias common to many studies would pass through them.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
The network returns smooth, confident decay-heat and isotopic values for MOX, high-burnup, long-cooling, BWR or irregular-history fuel outside its UO2 two-PWR validation envelope, with no extrapolation flag. Small systematic non-conservative errors then enter thermal margins and safeguards inventories, and an adversary could place an atypical assembly or diversion scenario in this unflagged blind spot so it reads as model-consistent.

Simulated-teacher bias and understated UQ -- implicit, exploitable
The network learns CASMO5 outputs as ground truth, inheriting lattice-code and nuclear-data bias and the loss of history effects from five compressed inputs, while sparse measured validation and unpropagated surrogate error make the UQ bands falsely tight. An adversary could rely on these tight, apparently validated bands to justify reduced margins or to hide a small inventory discrepancy inside the unrecognised error.

Over-trust, opacity and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Speed encourages analysts to run thousands of cases, treat outputs as validated, and drop physics-code cross-checks, while network opacity and fading expertise hinder detection of subtle inventory anomalies. An adversary could count on this misplaced trust so that a quiet manipulation of results goes unreviewed.

Qualification and configuration-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
No established V&V route exists for NN surrogates, and retraining, framework versions, random seeds or a CASMO5 library change can shift outputs without audit trail, eroding repeatability needed for licensing. Weak version control lets an adversary swap or retrain a model and present it as the validated version.

Fault propagation across assemblies and sites -- implicit, exploitable
A single surrogate bias replicates across many assemblies, casks and any sites or tools sharing the model, so one flaw biases many inventories at once. An adversary compromising one shared instance gains fleet-wide leverage with a single alteration.

Model and training-data tampering -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor poisons the weights, CASMO5 training database or scaling files, or plants a trigger on specific burnup and cooling-time inputs, producing narrow under-prediction of decay heat or Pu content that sparse spot-checks will not reveal. The result is eroded thermal margins in storage and transport and masked fissile inventory in safeguards reconciliation.

Input and UQ-range manipulation -- adversarial
Falsified burnup, enrichment or cooling-time records, or narrowed sensitivity input distributions, yield plausible but wrong inventories and artificially tight uncertainty bounds, since the surrogate cross-checks nothing against operator records or measurements. This targets the analysis workflow and can justify reduced margins or conceal diversion.

Model extraction and artifact exposure -- adversarial
The low-dimensional input space makes proxy replication easy, and stolen weights or training sets can leak fuel design, plutonium content and operating history. A proxy lets an adversary rehearse which declared inputs pass safeguards plausibility checks, and cloud or collaborative hosting widens exposure.

nuclear_engineer.argument: As a nuclear engineer, I see this as an analysis-support tool, not a control function. A wrong output cannot directly challenge a safety barrier, but spent-fuel decay heat and nuclide inventory feed cask loading-pattern limits, canister thermal licensing margins, storage pool and dry-cask heat-load planning, criticality and shielding source terms, and safeguards inventory verification. The surrogate is trained on CASMO5 lattice-level data, so it inherits the lattice code's simplifications (no axial or radial core-history detail, only mean boron and fuel temperature) and adds an interpolation error that is hard to see. Its fast, cheap UQ is also its main hazard: it will be trusted for sensitivity studies and uncertainty bounds far outside the narrow validation set of UO2 assemblies from two PWRs. Real harm requires several independent checks to fail. These include conservative bounding margins in cask thermal analysis, qualified code-of-record calculations (ORIGEN, SCALE), burnup credit and loading verification, and measured cask surface temperatures and dose rates. Those barriers make a single bad output unlikely to cause physical harm, but they do not catch systematic bias that is common across studies or hidden inside UQ statistics.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution use (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303): the surrogate was validated on UO2 PWR assemblies within a given enrichment, burnup and cooling range. A user could apply it to MOX, high-burnup or extended-cooling fuel, BWR assemblies, or irregular irradiation histories (power shaping, mid-cycle shutdowns). It would return smooth, plausible numbers with no warning of extrapolation. The consequence is non-conservative decay heat or isotopic estimates feeding cask heat-load limits, shielding or criticality source terms, or safeguards declarations, and the error would be small and systematic, so it can go unnoticed. (2) Fidelity inheritance and compounding error (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0603): the training data are simulated CASMO5 results, not measurements. The surrogate carries lattice-code bias and nuclear-data errors, then adds approximation error. The reduced inputs (mean boron, fuel temperature) discard history effects. Because the network is validated against few measured decay-heat points (OP.C0202), the UQ output may understate true uncertainty, and that false confidence matters more than a point-estimate error. (3) Automation bias and misuse of UQ (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401): analysts may adopt the narrow surrogate-derived uncertainty bands in safety-case arguments. A black-box network is hard to review for regulators, and explainability is limited. (4) Qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0402.01): there is no established V&V route for NN surrogates in a nuclear-QA framework. Retraining, framework versions or random seeds can change outputs without configuration control, which erodes the repeatability that licensing calculations need. (5) Safeguards-specific: a nuclide-inventory surrogate used to cross-check declared spent-fuel content or support non-destructive-assay interpretation could shrink the apparent detection margin for diversion or substitution (OP.C0701.01, OP.C0702.01). A fuel assembly with an atypical history would be reported as consistent with the model.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Model or training-data integrity (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0076, AML.T0031): the model weights, the CASMO5 training database, or the normalization and scaling files could be tampered with, or a poisoned model could enter through a shared repository or an academic-code supply chain. A bias confined to certain burnup or cooling-time regions would be very hard to detect, since the model is only spot-checked against the physics code. The consequence is quiet under-prediction of decay heat or distortion of the plutonium inventory, which could undermine thermal margins in storage and transport planning or mask material accountancy discrepancies. (7) Input and workflow manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015): an insider or an attacker who has compromised the analysis workstation could tamper with the input assemblies' burnup and cooling-time records. Nothing in the surrogate would cross-check them against operator records or measurements. (8) Information exposure (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0085): model and UQ results for specific assembly inventories reveal isotopic composition, such as plutonium content and inferred reactor operating history, which is safeguards- and proliferation-sensitive. Cloud or collaborative hosting (OP.C0601, OP.C0505) could expose it. These risks are mitigated by independent verification against code-of-record calculations and by measurements at cask loading, so the main concerns are systematic bias reaching safety-case and safeguards inputs and uncertainty bounds being treated as validated when they are not.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a regression surrogate trained on CASMO5 lattice outputs, so it inherits every assumption of the lattice code (2D infinite-lattice, depletion chain, nuclear data library, boundary conditions) and has no independent physical grounding. Its 5-dimensional input space (enrichment, burnup, cooling time, mean boron, fuel temperature) is a heavy compression of real irradiation history. Power history, spectral shifts, burnable absorbers, axial and radial gradients, and MOX or other fuel types are all absent. The model is only trustworthy inside the sampled hull of the training grid, yet its stated purpose, fast sensitivity analysis and UQ, drives it to sample inputs densely and to the edges of that hull and beyond. Because the surrogate is reused for waste management and safeguards, its outputs become inputs to downstream decisions on cask loading, thermal limits, and declared-versus-calculated inventory comparison, and no one downstream sees the training envelope. The main fragility lies in the training data, the extrapolation behavior, and the UQ semantics, not in the facility around it.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution and extrapolation failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). The NN gives smooth, confident outputs outside the training envelope, for example at higher burnup, extended cooling times, unusual enrichment, or different assembly designs and reactor types. Nothing in a plain feed-forward net flags this. The resulting error in decay heat or nuclide inventory feeds thermal analysis for cask loading and storage, or safeguards inventory verification. (2) Data provenance and the surrogate-of-a-simulation problem (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.03). Labels are CASMO5 outputs, not measurements. Lattice-code bias, nuclide-data errors, and missing 3D and history effects are learned as ground truth. Validation against a limited set of measured decay heat from two PWRs is a small-data check (OP.C0202), so it cannot support claims of generality. The surrogate also cannot be independently better than its teacher, and its reported UQ may understate true uncertainty because it captures only parametric input variation and ignores model-form and nuclear-data uncertainty. (3) UQ semantics and ML-theoretic limits (OP.C0403, OP.C0401). Surrogate approximation error is rarely propagated into the UQ results. Nuclide concentrations must obey mass and decay-chain consistency, which an NN regressing each output does not enforce. Opacity makes it hard to qualify individual predictions. (4) Qualification and lifecycle (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0402.01). There is no established qualification path for an NN replacing a code in a licensing or safeguards chain. Retraining after a CASMO5 version or nuclear-data library change, or on a different random seed, can shift outputs without a clear audit trail, and the surrogate can silently drift out of sync with the reference code (OP.C0302.02). (5) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0304.03). Fast results invite over-trust. Analysts may run thousands of cases, treat the outputs as validated, and drop the physics-based cross-checks. Skill in running the full code also fades (OP.C0101.06). (6) Cascading propagation (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). One surrogate error can be replicated across many assemblies and many casks, and a fleet-wide shared model can propagate the same bias across sites (OP.C0602).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Supply-chain and model or data tampering (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059). Training-set generation, model weights, or the input libraries could be altered so that predictions are biased in a narrow region, for instance underestimating decay heat or shifting plutonium inventory for particular burnup and cooling-time bins. That would let an insider or an upstream compromise hide thermal margin erosion, or mask diversion by making declared-versus-calculated inventories reconcile. A backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004) on specific input combinations would be hard to find because validation covers only sparse test points. (b) Manipulation of inputs and metadata. Operator-declared burnup, enrichment, or cooling time are the model's only inputs, so falsified or perturbed records (AML.T0043, AML.T0015) produce a plausible but wrong inventory without any detectable anomaly. The surrogate cannot check consistency against measured signatures. (c) Model extraction and reconnaissance (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0013, AML.T0044). A small, low-dimensional input space makes a proxy model easy to replicate (AML.T0005), and a proxy lets an adversary learn which declared inputs would pass a safeguards plausibility check. (d) Integrity of the validation reference (AML.T0031, AML.T0076). Quietly corrupting the reference runs or the stored model degrades the surrogate while it still looks good against stale validation sets. Together these show that the exposure is concentrated in a small, hard-to-audit regression model whose training provenance, input-domain boundary, and UQ meaning determine whether downstream waste and safeguards decisions are sound.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view this surrogate is a poor direct target for a nation-state, because it sits off the safety-critical control path and its outputs feed analysis rather than actuation. Its value to an adversary is as a trust-concentration and falsification point. Nuclide inventories and decay heat from a fast, opaque model feed cask loading and thermal limits, transport and storage licensing margins, and safeguards declarations of Pu and actinide content. An adversary who can bias the surrogate quietly, or who exploits its known weaknesses, could shift those downstream conclusions while the output looks plausible and physics-derived. The insider pathway is the main concern: a few people with access to the training data, weights or UQ input ranges can alter results without the review a CASMO5 rerun would get, and routine use for sensitivity studies erodes the habit of cross-checking against the physics code.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or training-data tampering by an insider or supply-chain actor (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0059). A small bias in predicted Pu-239 or other fissile content, or in decay heat at particular burnup/cooling combinations, is very hard to detect because the network has no mechanistic transparency and its verification set is sparse. Consequences: understated decay heat or reactivity margin in cask loading and storage or transport calculations (safety); and understated or masked fissile inventory in assembly characterization, which is a safeguards and diversion-concealment concern, since nuclide-content estimates are used to cross-check operator declarations. (2) Manipulated inputs or UQ ranges (AML.T0043, T0015). Because the surrogate is used for sensitivity and UQ, an adversary or compromised analyst who narrows or shifts the input distributions (burnup, boron, temperature) can produce artificially tight uncertainty bounds that justify reduced margins. The attack targets the analysis workflow rather than the model weights. (3) Model-file and artifact exposure (AML.T0035, T0024.002, T0044). Weights and training sets derived from CASMO5 runs for specific assemblies may leak fuel design and operating-history information that is proprietary or safeguards-sensitive, and a stolen proxy lets an attacker rehearse what outputs will pass review. (4) Spoofed provenance: a replaced or retrained surrogate is presented as the validated version (AML.T0073, T0074), made easier by weak configuration control. IMPLICIT, and exploitable by timing. (a) Extrapolation and OOD failure (OP.C0302, C0302.03): the network is trained on a bounded range of enrichment and burnup, but waste-management work involves high burnup, MOX, other designs and very long cooling times, and no out-of-domain flag is built in, so an adversary or an honest error can sit in the blind spot. (b) Small-data validation (OP.C0202, C0201.01/.02): measured decay-heat data come from a few PWR assemblies, while most training data is simulated, so agreement with the code or measurement does not prove accuracy where it matters. (c) Automation over-trust and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0401): speed encourages use in place of the physics code, so errors propagate quietly into licensing and safeguards records and nobody retains the ability to notice a subtle inventory discrepancy. (d) QA and governance gaps (OP.C0501, C0502, C0303): no AI-specific qualification, version control or retraining rules, and no clear decision on whether safeguards uses of the output are in scope. (e) Cascading dependence (OP.C0603, C0602): if the same surrogate is shared across sites or tools, one compromised or flawed instance biases many inventories at once.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on OOD extrapolation, simulated-teacher bias with understated UQ, over-trust, QA gaps, and model/data tampering and input manipulation as the core threats. I merged duplicates, kept extraction/exposure as distinct, and dropped speculative or weakly argued codes such as OP.C0701.*, OP.C0702.01, AML.T0085 and AML.T0013.

evidence.citation: "Fast uncertainty quantification of spent nuclear fuel with neural networks," Annals of Nuclear Energy (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper trains a neural network on CASMO5 lattice-calculation data to replace the physics-based code for spent-fuel decay heat and nuclide inventories. It validates the network against physics-based decay-heat simulations and measured decay heat from uranium oxide assemblies in two PWRs. The network is then used for sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification at much lower computational cost. An arXiv version (2308.08391) also exists, but this citation is the peer-reviewed journal article.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoned or biased surrogate outputs that erode cask thermal and criticality margins and mask fissile (Pu) inventory in safeguards reconciliation, which edges toward safeguards falsification; independent code-of-record calculations and cask measurements limit direct radiological consequence, so this stops short of 5.

reproducibility.why: Unflagged out-of-distribution extrapolation, inherited teacher bias and configuration drift occur reliably whenever inputs fall outside the narrow validation envelope or the model is retrained, though targeted backdoor or poisoning attacks are more conditional.

exploitability.why: Input falsification and exploiting the unflagged blind spots need only access to analysis workflows or records, but model or training-data tampering and fleet-wide compromise need insider or supply-chain position.

affected_users.why: A single shared surrogate bias propagates across many assemblies, casks, studies and potentially multiple sites or tools, biasing thermal, shielding and safeguards inventories together, though it stays off the control path and does not affect the whole facility.

discoverability.why: The approach is published in the open literature with the architecture, the five inputs and the limited validation set described, and the weaknesses (OOD behavior, simulated-teacher bias, no V&V route for NN surrogates) are well-known for this class of AI system, so an outsider can readily infer where blind spots lie.

use_case: Supervised fine-tuning of a large language model (NuLLM-FTG, the Nuclear LLM Fault Tree Generator) to draft fault trees for nuclear power plant probabilistic risk assessment. The model is trained on a purpose-built textual fault-tree data structure and a dataset of several thousand examples. It was tested with few-shot prompting and compared against GPT-4. Its output was integrated with the RiskSpectrum PRA software so that non-expert analysts can build fault trees.
incurred_insecurity:
NuLLM-FTG drafts fault trees that feed RiskSpectrum PRA models used for licensing, risk-informed decisions and plant-change evaluation, and it is aimed at non-expert analysts. The main threats are plausible-but-incomplete trees that quietly understate risk, erosion of the human review that would catch them, weak generalisation and qualification, and adversarial corruption of the fine-tuning pipeline or the RiskSpectrum handoff. Consequences are indirect, landing through the safety case and licensing basis rather than plant equipment.

Incomplete or hallucinated fault-tree content -- implicit, exploitable
The fine-tuned LLM produces syntactically valid trees that omit common-cause groups, support-system dependencies or human-error events, invent or misattribute basic events, or mis-specify AND/OR gates, so cut sets and CDF/LERF come out non-conservative. Surface-similarity evaluation against GPT-4 and experts cannot detect absences, and an adversary can hide deliberate omissions among these expected errors, where they are hard to distinguish from honest model error.

Over-trust and skill fade among non-expert analysts -- implicit, exploitable
The tool lowers the expertise needed to draft trees, so analysts anchor on the model's output and the pool of people able to challenge it shrinks, which weakens PRA peer review. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust and thin review to get a subtly biased tree accepted into the licensing basis.

Small-data and out-of-distribution generalisation failure -- implicit, exploitable
A few thousand examples from a limited set of plants and systems cannot cover novel designs, new-build or advanced reactors, or plant-specific configurations, and the model answers confidently without calibrated uncertainty. An adversary could target unusual or novel configurations, where wrong logic is expected and least likely to be questioned.

Non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit
Sampling variance, few-shot prompt sensitivity, opacity and silent base-model or integration version changes give different trees for the same input, and no accepted nuclear QA basis exists to qualify a stochastic generator. This undermines traceability and defensibility in licensing submittals; an adversary gains little directly beyond lax verification that masks other problems.

Fine-tuning data and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
A small fine-tuning corpus, adapters or a third-party base model can be poisoned or backdoored so that particular components or phrasing trigger systematic omissions, such as a dropped dependency or a wrong gate. The result is a persistent, hard-to-attribute understatement of risk in the PRA that supports licensing.

Prompt injection and RiskSpectrum integration abuse -- adversarial
Altered design documents, few-shot examples or retrieved text can steer tree structure through indirect prompt injection, and malformed or hostile generated output imported into RiskSpectrum can corrupt PRA project files without an obvious trace. Compromised accounts or insiders with write access to the pipeline give a route from an AI service into a safety-analysis environment.

Leakage of risk-dominant sequence information -- adversarial
The corpus, prompts and logs hold plant-specific fault trees that map the failure combinations leading to core damage, and extraction, inversion or an off-site hosted LLM could expose them. This would give an adversary prioritised sabotage targets, a sensitivity that conventional design-information controls may not anticipate.

Fleet-wide propagation of a shared model -- implicit, exploitable
Reuse of one model or its recycled outputs across plants spreads a single systematic bias or compromise into multiple PRAs. An adversary compromising one shared model gains leverage across a fleet.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a PRA/licensing standpoint, a fault tree is a safety-case artifact. It feeds core damage frequency, risk-informed licensing submittals, technical specification changes and configuration risk decisions. An LLM that drafts trees for non-expert analysts moves the main risk away from the model itself and toward what the analyst accepts. A plausible but incomplete tree (missing common-cause failures, wrong gate logic, omitted support-system dependencies, wrong success criteria) is the failure that matters most. It looks credible and can pass a cursory review, and it understates risk in a direction that favors the licensee. Existing practice helps: PRA peer review against the ASME/ANS standard, regulatory review, and independent quantification checks. But those barriers assume the analyst-and-reviewer team has the skill to find omissions, and this tool is explicitly meant to lower the skill needed to draft. Its value proposition therefore erodes the barrier that would catch its errors.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Completeness and content-fidelity failure: the LLM generates plausible fault trees that omit failure modes, common-cause groups, human-error events, or cross-system dependencies, or that invent or misattribute components and basic events. The result is quietly non-conservative risk numbers. The facility dependency is the PRA model used for licensing, risk-informed applications and plant change evaluation. Harm would require the peer review and regulator review to also miss the omission. That is more likely when reviewers see a clean, well-formatted tree and judge only what is shown, not what is absent. (2) Automation bias and skill fade among non-expert analysts. Comparison with experts on a benchmark does not show the tool performs on plant-specific systems with unusual configurations. Anchoring on the model's tree narrows the analyst's independent thinking and over time reduces the in-house expertise needed to challenge it. (3) Data scarcity and out-of-distribution generalization. A few thousand examples, likely from a limited set of plant designs and systems, cannot represent the diversity of reactor types, plant-specific modifications, and new-build or advanced designs. Performance may drop sharply on unfamiliar systems, and the model gives no reliable signal when that happens. (4) Non-determinism and weak qualification. Different runs can give different trees. Few-shot prompt sensitivity, the lack of an AI-specific QA basis under nuclear QA programs, and opacity make the tool hard to reproduce and defend in a licensing submittal. Version changes, whether to the model or to the RiskSpectrum integration, can silently alter outputs. (5) Benchmark limitations: comparing against GPT-4 and a small panel of experts does not establish correctness. Similarity to training-style trees is not the same as technical adequacy.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data or fine-tuning-set poisoning, or a compromised base model or supply chain, could bias the model to omit or downplay specific failure paths, for example by systematically dropping a dependency or common-cause link. This is subtle, persistent sabotage of a safety analysis, aimed at undermining the licensing basis, and it need not trigger any alarm. (7) Prompt or context manipulation, including injection through imported plant documents or few-shot examples, could steer a tree toward a wrong structure. (8) Integration risk: the output feeds directly into RiskSpectrum, so malformed or manipulated model output could corrupt PRA project files, and tampering anywhere in that chain can alter a safety-significant model without leaving an obvious trace. (9) The fine-tuning corpus and the prompts hold sensitive plant-specific system-vulnerability information. If an external or cloud-hosted LLM is used, this creates an exposure path for security-sensitive design and PRA information, and a possible aid to adversary target selection through knowledge of risk-dominant sequences. Fleet-wide reuse of one model would spread any bias or compromise across multiple plants' PRAs.

MITIGATING CONTEXT: this is an offline analysis tool with no direct control of plant equipment, human peer review is mandatory, and the PRA is a decision-support product and not a protection function. Consequences are therefore indirect, and they land through licensing and operational risk decisions. The residual concern is slow, hard-to-detect degradation of the safety case, not an immediate physical event.

ai_engineer.argument: NuLLM-FTG is a supervised fine-tune of an LLM on a few thousand examples in a bespoke textual fault-tree serialization, and its output feeds RiskSpectrum, a PRA tool whose results support licensing and regulatory arguments. The ML fragility is concentrated in four places. First, the training corpus is small and was probably derived from a limited set of plant PRAs, so it covers a narrow slice of system designs and failure logic. Second, the output format is a custom structured text that must parse into a PRA tool, so any malformed or subtly wrong generation becomes a silently wrong model rather than a visible error. Third, the evaluation (few-shot comparison with GPT-4 and expert judgment of 'comparable to professionals') measures surface plausibility and structural similarity, not logical or quantitative correctness. Fourth, the intended users are non-expert analysts, which removes the human check that would catch plausible but wrong gate logic. The facility-level consequence is real, but the primary exposure is the pipeline: fine-tune data provenance, the base-model dependency, and the untested handoff into the PRA tool.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Content fidelity failure: the LLM can hallucinate or omit basic events, common-cause failure groups, support-system dependencies, or mis-specify AND/OR gate logic. The tree is syntactically valid and domain-plausible but incomplete or wrong. Cut sets and CDF/LERF contributions then come out non-conservatively, which undermines the licensing basis. Few-shot and expert-preference evaluation do not detect this, because there is no formal verification of tree logic against system design documents. (2) Small-data and out-of-distribution generalization: a few thousand examples from a narrow set of plants and system types means weak performance on novel designs (SMRs, advanced reactors, new-build designs with little operational data), unusual configurations, or plant-specific dependencies. The model will still answer confidently, with no calibrated uncertainty or abstention. Provenance matters: the data may be synthetic, reformatted from published or legacy PRAs, or have train/test leakage that inflates the reported performance. (3) Automation trust and skill fade: the tool targets non-expert analysts, who cannot validate the output. Over-trust, anchoring on the draft, and erosion of PRA expertise follow, so independent review shrinks and reviewers are pulled into rubber-stamping. (4) Non-repeatability: sampling variance and base-model version changes produce different trees from the same prompt, which breaks PRA QA requirements for reproducibility and traceability. If the base model is an API-hosted or upgraded checkpoint, behavior changes silently with no requalification. (5) Qualification gap: PRA software is qualified under nuclear QA regimes, while an LLM front-end falls outside existing software QA, and there is no accepted way to qualify a stochastic generator. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training data and supply-chain poisoning: the fine-tune corpus, base model weights, or adapters can be tampered with, planting subtle systematic omissions (for example, dropping a failure mode or a dependency class) or a backdoor triggered by particular component names or phrasing. Such poisoning would be hard to detect because outputs look normal, and it would bias risk results in a consistent direction. (7) Prompt or input manipulation: if analysts feed system descriptions, procedures, or retrieved documents into the model, indirect prompt injection or crafted descriptions can steer tree structure. Examples are an altered design document or a trojaned input file that causes basic events to be pruned. (8) Integration attack surface: model output flows into RiskSpectrum via a generated text format, so malformed or hostile output (injection into import parsers) and a model hosted off-site or accessed through third-party APIs add a data-exposure path. Plant design and PRA content is sensitive security information and could leak via prompts, logs, or model memorization. (9) Model extraction or inversion could expose proprietary fault-tree content from the fine-tuning set. (10) Integrity erosion over time: if outputs are later recycled into training or reference sets, systematic errors compound and spread across plants or fleets that share the same model.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this is an attractive stepping stone and not an attractive direct target. A fault-tree generator sits upstream of the PRA that supports licensing submissions, design-change justification and risk-informed decisions, so an adversary who can bias its output never has to touch a plant system. Quiet, plausible-looking omissions in a safety case could be worth more than a noisy attack. The use case is explicitly aimed at non-expert analysts, which means the human checking layer is weakest where the tool's trust is highest. That combination (concentrated trust, thin review and a durable artifact that outlives the model) is what makes it worth a patient adversary's attention, including an insider with PRA-model write access or access to the fine-tuning pipeline.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model integrity (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0043.004): the model is trained on a purpose-built fault-tree text structure and a few-thousand-example dataset. A dataset this small is cheap to poison, and a backdoor could tie a trigger, such as a particular system, component or phrasing, to subtly altered logic. Examples would be a dropped common-cause failure, an AND gate where an OR belongs, or an optimistic failure-mode assumption. Third-party base models and fine-tuning tooling add supply-chain exposure. The AI failure mechanism is a corrupted model. The facility dependency is the PRA used for licensing and safety-significance classification. The consequence is an understated risk profile that is hard to attribute later. (2) Integration surface (AML.T0049, T0053, T0012, T0051.001): the RiskSpectrum link creates a new path from a text-generating model into a safety-analysis software environment. If generated structures are imported with insufficient validation, malformed or injected content, or compromised accounts, could reach or alter the PRA model database. This gives a route from an enterprise-style AI service into a safety-related analysis environment. (3) Information leakage (AML.T0024.000/.001, T0057, T0035, T0036): the training corpus and the prompts hold plant-specific system designs, failure data and vulnerability-relevant logic. Fault trees are effectively a map of what combinations of failures lead to core damage, which is also a map of sabotage targets. Extraction from the model, from logs, or from a hosted API would hand an adversary prioritized target sets, a sensitivity that conventional design-information controls may not anticipate (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0601). (4) Trust and process exploitation (AML.T0073, T0067, T0031): an adversary could time subtle manipulation around the periods when analysts are most reliant on the tool.

IMPLICIT. Automation over-trust and skill fade among non-expert analysts (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102) mean wrong trees get accepted. This is the weakness an adversary would rely on, and it also hides honest errors. Hallucinated or omitted basic events and mis-specified gates (OP.C0304.01/.03) are plausible, and evaluation against experts and GPT-4 on a limited benchmark does not show completeness for rare or novel configurations (OP.C0202, C0302, C0303). Opacity and inference non-repeatability (OP.C0401, C0402.02) weaken audit and regulatory acceptance, since the same prompt can yield different trees. The qualification gap for AI-assisted safety analysis (OP.C0501, C0504) means that no accepted standard exists for validating the tool, so inadequate verification would not itself be a visible violation. Reuse across plants or fleets (OP.C0602) would spread a single flaw or compromise widely. Because the tool lowers the expertise needed to produce PRAs, the pool of people able to detect subtle manipulation shrinks over time.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on non-conservative incomplete trees, analyst over-trust, data scarcity, qualification gaps, poisoning and integration/leakage risks; I merged these and kept fleet propagation as a distinct threat. I dropped weakly supported or speculative ATLAS candidates (Valid Accounts, Tool Invocation, Impersonation, membership inference) and kept only codes traceable to the text.

evidence.citation: "A Text Intelligence-Based Approach for Automatic Generation of Fault Trees in Nuclear Power Plants," ASME (Proceedings of the International Conference on Nuclear Engineering, ICONE31)
evidence.note: The ICONE31 paper describes a fine-tuned LLM that generates fault trees for nuclear power plants. It was evaluated with real operators and domain experts and judged comparable to experienced fault-tree professionals. It was also integrated with RiskSpectrum v14.0 to show it works in practice. I read only the abstract, not the full paper.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a systematic, hard-to-attribute understatement of risk in PRAs (via poisoning or undetected omissions) that feeds licensing and risk-informed decisions, plus leakage of risk-dominant sequences that could support sabotage targeting. This erodes safety margins and could undermine the licensing basis, but the harm is indirect and not a direct release or material-control loss.

reproducibility.why: Incomplete or hallucinated trees, over-trust, and out-of-distribution failures are inherent to fine-tuned LLMs and recur reliably given the described use, while deliberate poisoning or injection depends on gaining access to the pipeline.

exploitability.why: The implicit failure modes need no special access, but deliberately corrupting the fine-tuning pipeline, base model, or RiskSpectrum handoff requires supply-chain or insider-level access, and an adversary must also get a biased tree through peer review.

affected_users.why: A biased PRA propagates into licensing, plant-change evaluation, and risk-informed decisions across the plant, and fleet-wide reuse of a shared model can extend the effect to multiple plants, though impact stays within the analysis and licensing layer.

discoverability.why: LLM hallucination and omission, over-trust, data poisoning, prompt injection, and extraction are all well documented in open literature, and the published paper and the RiskSpectrum integration make the tool class visible, though plant-specific pipeline details are not public.

use_case: Deep semantic-segmentation network (fully convolutional network with a VGG16 encoder, called FPCD, with a crack-weighted loss to handle class imbalance) that segments surface cracks pixel by pixel in images of nuclear fuel pellets. It supports quality inspection and the decision to reject pellets on the fuel fabrication line.
incurred_insecurity:
A pixel-level crack segmentation network at the accept/reject gate for fuel pellets, trained and validated only on about 2,240 images of ceramic pellet imitations (F1 ~89%, IoU ~80%), incurs a risk of silent false accepts that let cracked or chipped pellets into fuel rods. The main threats are an unvalidated surrogate-to-real gap, rare-defect and drift blind spots, over-trust that erodes human inspection, and deniable adversarial tampering with the model, data, imaging chain or records. The consequence is a latent fuel-integrity and quality-record problem, bounded by independent QA layers rather than an immediate radiological event.

Surrogate-to-real transfer gap -- implicit, exploitable
The network learned crack appearance on non-radioactive ceramic imitations, so real sintered pellets with different texture, reflectance, chips and grinding marks can produce under-segmented cracks (false accepts) or spurious ones (scrap, pressure to relax thresholds), with no validated false-negative rate. An adversary could hide a deliberate defect behind this known uncertainty so that a quality escape reads as ordinary model error.

Rare-defect and class-imbalance blind spots -- implicit, exploitable
Sparse, varied real cracks (hairline, closed, end-cap or lamination defects) and a crack-weighted loss tuned on imitation data mean the aggregate IoU hides a weak thin-crack tail, and a small pixel boundary bias moves a pellet across the size-based reject limit. An adversary could target defect morphologies the model is weakest on, knowing misses will be attributed to expected error.

Drift and absent qualification regime -- implicit, exploitable
Camera and lamp ageing, optics contamination, sintering-lot and pellet-geometry changes shift inputs, and F1/IoU is not tied to a crack-size acceptance criterion, per-lot monitoring or re-qualification path. Gradual adversarial degradation of imaging or lighting could be masked inside this unmonitored drift band.

Opacity, non-repeatability and no uncertainty output -- implicit, exploitable
Dense per-pixel masks come with no calibrated uncertainty or out-of-distribution flag, and training or GPU inference can vary between versions, so QA cannot explain or reproduce a miss. This makes forensics hard and lets tampering be passed off as honest model error.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Clean-looking masks and good benchmark scores invite inspectors to defer to the model, shrinking manual inspection and the ability to spot defect types the model never saw. An adversary could rely on this erosion of independent verification and time an attack to a period of low reject rates and complacency.

Error propagation into process records -- implicit
Incorrect masks flow into SPC trends, lot disposition and feedback to sintering and grinding, creating false or hidden process trends. No distinct adversarial gain beyond the false-accept pathway above.

Model, weights and training-data tampering -- adversarial
An insider or compromised vendor or retraining pipeline could poison masks, swap the public-sourced VGG16-derived weights, or alter crack weighting or the reject threshold, or implant a trigger keyed to a texture or marker, so chosen pellets or crack sizes pass while headline accuracy stays plausible.

Physical and imaging-chain evasion -- adversarial
An actor with line access could alter lighting, surface coatings, markings, camera geometry or pixel-to-millimetre calibration to suppress crack features or shift measured size under the reject limit, passing defective pellets without any software change.

Inspection service denial and record falsification -- adversarial
Disabling the service forces slower manual fallback that invites bypass, and altering stored images or masks can falsify quality and traceability records, concealing defects or substitution.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the fabrication-line side, this is a quality-inspection aid sitting at the accept/reject gate for sintered UO2 pellets. The documented evidence is thin for that role: about 2,240 images of ceramic pellet imitations, with F1 around 89% and IoU around 80%. That means roughly one crack pixel in ten is mis-segmented, and the pixel-level crack size is the quantity that drives the reject decision. The main downstream consequence is a defective pellet passing into a fuel rod, where chipped or cracked pellets raise concerns about pellet-cladding interaction, fission gas release and fuel performance. This is a latent quality or integrity defect, not an immediate safety event. Existing practice (sampling inspection, dimensional and density checks, rod-level QA, and in-reactor margins) limits direct harm, but it can erode if operators start treating the network as the primary detector. Over-rejection is also a real cost, producing scrap with fissile content and extra material-accountability and recycle burden.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Surrogate-to-real transfer gap: the model was trained on imitation ceramic pellets, not real sintered UO2. Real pellets differ in surface texture, color, reflectivity, chips, grinding marks, dishing, chamfers and lighting in the inspection station. The result is missed or false cracks, and no validated performance exists for the real population (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302, OP.C0203). (2) Low base-rate and class imbalance: the crack-weighted loss trades recall against precision in ways that were tuned on imitation data. Reject thresholds set on that tuning may not hold on real defect rates (OP.C0202, OP.C0301). (3) Drift: camera ageing, lamp output, powder lot or sintering changes, pellet geometry changes for new fuel designs, and contamination or dust on optics shift the input distribution silently. Without a per-lot performance check, degradation goes unseen (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (4) Qualification gap: an F1 or IoU figure is not an acceptance criterion tied to a crack-size reject limit. Pixel-to-millimetre calibration errors, fixed-threshold sensitivity and non-repeatable outputs undermine the size-based decision. The model also has no uncertainty output and is opaque to QA inspectors (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0403). (5) Automation bias and skill fade: inspectors may defer to a clean-looking segmentation mask. This shrinks manual inspection and the ability to recognise unusual defect types, such as end-cap chips, laminations or non-crack anomalies the model never saw (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (6) Error propagation: bad mask output flows into SPC trends, lot disposition records and process feedback to the sintering and grinding steps, so false trends or masked ones can mislead process control (OP.C0603).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Insider or supply-chain tampering with model weights, the loss weighting or the decision threshold, or with the imaging software stack, could bias the system toward passing defective pellets selectively (e.g., for a specific lot) or toward mass rejection that disrupts production. A subtle recall shift would be hard to detect against an F1 of ~89% (AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0076, AML.T0031). (b) Physical-domain evasion: surface markings, coatings, lighting changes or camera tampering that suppress crack features could hide real cracks from a segmentation net (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). This requires access to the line, which makes it mostly an insider scenario. (c) Training-data or retraining-pipeline poisoning, including mislabelled crack masks during any later fine-tuning on real pellets, would degrade the model quietly (AML.T0020, AML.T0059). (d) Denial or degradation of the inspection service, or alteration of stored inspection images and records, would hurt traceability and could affect quality-assurance and accountancy reconciliation (AML.T0029, AML.T0112.001). Overall severity is moderate and bounded by independent QA layers, but the surrogate-only validation and reject-gate role make silent false-accepts the key concern.

ai_engineer.argument: FPCD is a VGG16-encoder FCN trained on about 2,240 self-acquired images of ceramic pellet imitations, then proposed to drive reject decisions on real sintered UO2 (or MOX) pellets. The main fragility is therefore the data. The training set is surrogate data with a different surface texture, reflectance, color, and crack morphology from real pellets. It is also small, and the crack-weighted loss patches class imbalance without fixing the lack of diversity. An F1 of about 88.9% and IoU of about 80.3% are in-distribution numbers on imitation pellets. They say nothing about operational generalization, and they are not a qualified false-negative rate for a safety-relevant accept/reject gate. The architecture itself, a dense per-pixel classifier with no calibrated uncertainty, no out-of-distribution detector, and a crack-size output used against a threshold, means silent failure is the default behavior when inputs shift.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Surrogate-to-real domain gap (OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). The model learned crack appearance on ceramic imitations. Real pellets differ in grain texture, chips, pits, lubricant or dust residue, grinding marks, and lighting response. Inference on those inputs can under-segment real cracks (false accepts, so a defective pellet enters the fuel rod and cladding integrity and fuel performance are compromised) or over-segment benign features (false rejects, with yield loss and pressure to relax thresholds). (2) Small-data and low base-rate problem (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Real cracks are rare and varied, so the model may fail on unseen morphologies such as hairline, closed, or sub-pixel cracks. The reported aggregate IoU hides the thin-crack tail. Pixel-level width and length estimates feed the reject decision, so a systematic boundary bias translates directly into threshold misclassification. (3) Drift and lifecycle (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0303). Pellet recipe changes, sintering-lot variation, camera or lens aging, illumination changes, and new enrichment or MOX lines will shift the input distribution. A static weights file validated once has no monitoring or retraining path, and any retraining requires re-qualification (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402). Segmentation masks are hard to explain, and nondeterministic training or GPU inference can give different masks across versions. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). High benchmark scores invite automation over-trust, and inspectors may stop reviewing images and approve whatever the mask shows. Skill fade then reduces the human backstop that should catch model misses.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (5) Evasion at inference (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). An actor with physical or line access, or one who can alter lighting, surface coatings or markings, or the image stream, can craft perturbations or physical patterns that suppress crack segmentation. A defective pellet would pass without the defect being visible. A dense-prediction CNN with a public VGG16 backbone is susceptible, and the backbone is easy to replicate as a proxy (AML.T0005, AML.T0002.001). (6) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0076). ImageNet-pretrained VGG16 weights come from public sources, and the training data and weights are mutable files. Poisoning or a backdoor trigger (AML.T0043.004) keyed to a specific texture or marker could make chosen pellets pass. Tampering with weights, the loss weighting, or the post-processing threshold gives the same effect without touching the network's apparent accuracy. (7) Pipeline manipulation (AML.T0031, AML.T0029). Altering the image acquisition or preprocessing, or the pixel-to-millimeter calibration, shifts crack size estimates across the reject threshold. Denial of the service forces a fallback to manual inspection with less throughput, which in turn invites bypass.

CONSEQUENCE. Cause (model failure or manipulation) is separate from effect. The effect is that defective pellets are accepted into the fuel assembly, a quality-assurance record is falsified in effect, and defect statistics used in process control are corrupted. That is a safety and fuel-integrity risk, plus a regulatory and quality-record problem, rather than a direct radiological release at the inspection station.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this is a quality-gate AI sitting between fuel fabrication and the reactor. Its output decides which pellets are accepted into fuel rods. An insider or supply-chain adversary does not need to touch reactor safety systems to gain leverage. They only need to bias what the segmentation network reports about cracks. The model was trained on only ~2,240 images of ceramic pellet imitations, not real radioactive pellets, and reports F1 ~89% and IoU ~80%. That leaves a large, quietly exploitable gap between lab validation and production, and an adversary could time an attack around it or hide behind it as plausible deniability. A deliberate defect (cracks, chips, or substituted pellets) could be disguised as ordinary model error, so a quality-escape attack looks like drift and attribution is hard. Compared with attacking hardened reactor protection systems, this offline, inspection-line AI is a softer target. It is likely on a less segregated IT/OT network and has a small, easily poisoned data pipeline.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model and data integrity compromise (AML.T0010.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0059, T0076): a small, bespoke training set and a crack-weighted loss are easy to tamper with. An insider or a compromised vendor or retraining pipeline could poison labels, shift the crack-weight or threshold, or swap weights so that specific crack morphologies or sizes fall below the reject criterion. Consequence: defective pellets pass inspection, causing latent cladding-failure or fuel-integrity risk in-core. Because the model is a pixel-level estimator, small shifts in the mask area can move a pellet across the reject boundary without any visible alarm. (2) Evasion and physical-world manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043, T0041): lighting, surface finish, coating or imaging-geometry changes could cause systematic misses without touching software. This is accessible to anyone with line access. A backdoor trigger (T0043.004) could be a physical marking. (3) Concentrated, unwitnessed trust: if the AI becomes the primary reject decision, operators lose independent inspection capacity and skill (OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.04). That erodes the two-person and independent-verification culture an insider would otherwise have to defeat. A low reject rate also breeds complacency (OP.C0102) that an adversary can time an attack around. (4) Image and record integrity: tampered inspection images or segmentation outputs can falsify quality records. This supports hiding defects, or in a safeguards context covering material diversion or substitution (OP.C0703, OP.C0702.01). IMPLICIT, exploitable. (5) Training on non-radioactive imitation pellets creates a simulated-to-real gap, with different texture, reflectivity, and crack morphology (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0202). The class-imbalance handling hints at rare cracks and a low base rate, so false negatives on rare, safety-relevant defect types are likely. Reported F1/IoU on the same lab distribution overstate field performance. (6) Drift and heterogeneity across production lots, cameras, and lighting (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03) are not tied to a qualification regime (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0504). They provide cover for adversarial degradation. (7) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402) make post-incident forensics hard, so tampering is difficult to distinguish from honest error. (8) Pipeline hygiene (OP.C0502, OP.C0505): model files, annotation data, and pre-trained VGG16 weights from public sources (AML.T0002.001, T0010.001) widen the supply-chain surface. Net: the more the line relies on the model, the more valuable a quiet, deniable compromise becomes, and the lab-grade validation makes it harder to detect.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the surrogate-to-real gap, drift, qualification gap, over-trust, and model/data tampering and physical evasion as the core threats. I dropped weakly supported codes (proxy-model, safeguards imagery OP.C0703/OP.C0702.01, OP.C0502/OP.C0505, OP.C0504) and the training-time non-determinism, and kept record falsification under a single threat.

evidence.citation: "A surface cracks detection method for nuclear fuel pellets using an improved fully convolutional network," Journal of Nuclear Science and Technology (Taylor & Francis)
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests a deep FCN-VGG16-based network (FPCD) for pixel-level segmentation of fuel pellet surface cracks. Training and evaluation used a self-acquired set of about 2,240 crack images of ceramic pellet imitations, not real radioactive pellets. It reports an F1-score of about 88.9% and an IoU of about 80.3%. The authors say pixel-level crack size is needed to decide whether to reject a pellet.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a false accept that lets cracked pellets into fuel rods, or falsified quality and traceability records. This is a latent fuel-integrity and QA-record problem bounded by independent QA layers, not an immediate radiological release, so it sits at operational disruption and safety-margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Surrogate-to-real gap, thin-crack blind spots and drift are systematic properties of the model class and recur reliably once the model runs on real pellets. Deliberate tampering outcomes depend on the attacker's position and on how well QA layers catch the result.

exploitability.why: The most credible adversarial paths need insider or line access, such as model or weight tampering, a poisoned retraining pipeline, or physical alteration of the imaging chain, in a controlled fuel fabrication facility. Only the implicit weaknesses are exploitable without special access, and exploiting them still requires knowing the line.

affected_users.why: Impact spans the pellet lots passing the inspection gate, downstream fuel rods, and SPC and lot-disposition records feeding sintering and grinding feedback. It is limited to one inspection line and its QA records, not a facility-wide coupled system.

discoverability.why: The architecture, surrogate training data, and accuracy figures are published in the open literature, and surrogate-to-real gaps, class-imbalance weaknesses, drift and over-trust are well-documented generic weaknesses of segmentation models. Specific line details and thresholds remain non-public.

use_case: Cascade-forward neural network combined with a decision tree that detects fuel cladding failure in an operating PWR. It takes the specific activities of fission-product nuclides measured in the primary coolant as input. It classifies the degree of failure, including telling intact rods apart from rods with small defects. It supports decisions on identifying and discharging defective fuel. Sensitivity analysis ranks the most important nuclides so the network can be simplified for practical radiation detectors.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory fuel-failure classifier is trained only on simulated Booth-diffusion and first-order-kinetic release data, so its blind spots are fixed by model assumptions rather than plant reality, and they are knowable from the open paper. The main threats are a simulation-to-reality gap, loss of redundancy from pruning the network for practical detectors, over-trust in an opaque categorical output, weak lifecycle qualification and fleet propagation, and adversarial manipulation of inputs, model or training data to mask real fuel degradation or force needless discharge. Independent Technical Specification chemistry limits, sipping and inspection bound the severity, but a silently wrong output can delay defective-fuel handling and raise coolant activity, dose and cost.

Simulation-to-reality gap -- implicit, exploitable
The network learns idealized release physics and can misgrade defect size or miss failure onset under real conditions (tramp uranium, cleanup and letdown, power transients, multiple defects, mixed burnup), with scarce real failures to validate the intact versus small-defect boundary. An adversary who reads the open paper can infer these blind spots and hide a developing defect or trigger spurious alarms inside the misclassification band.

Drift and operational heterogeneity across plants -- implicit, exploitable
A model qualified statically on simulated cases is used dynamically across cycles, burnups, coolant-treatment regimes and transients such as iodine spiking, and may be reused across a fleet of similar PWRs, so one bias or bad update propagates systematically. An adversary could time a manipulation to transient periods when anomalous outputs look like normal model error, or exploit a shared update path to spread one bias to many plants.

Pruned-network loss of redundancy -- implicit, exploitable
Sensitivity-based reduction to a few top-ranked nuclides removes the redundant ratios that would expose a drifting, miscalibrated or misidentified gamma-spectrometry channel, so one bad channel dominates the grade. The published ranking tells an adversary which few channels to falsify, and simplified deployments widen the instrument-level attack surface.

Opacity and operator over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
A one-hot grade from a neural network plus tree, with no physical rationale or calibrated uncertainty, invites deference to a clean 'intact' output and erosion of independent chemistry and iodine-spiking trend review. An adversary can rely on that misplaced trust, and on the difficulty of distinguishing tampering from natural error, to let a coincident sampling or chemistry action go unchallenged.

AI qualification and lifecycle gap -- implicit, exploitable
Training-time non-determinism, retraining without regression qualification and weakly governed pretrained weights or vendor libraries leave model changes unverified for decisions on fuel discharge. A stealthy weight, threshold or library change could pass as routine retraining.

Input and data-path manipulation -- adversarial
An insider or intruder altering nuclide activities, spectra, sample records or preprocessing can push the classifier to grade a failing rod as intact, delaying detection, or an intact core as failed, forcing power reduction or discharge. The low-dimensional, physically structured input makes plausible perturbations easy to craft once the important nuclides are known.

Model and training-data poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with the synthetic-data generator parameters, the training or retraining set, or the deployed weights and tree thresholds can embed a persistent blind spot for a nuclide-ratio pattern, masking fuel degradation until an independent check catches it. Compromised software, data or model supply sources provide the entry path.

Open-literature reconnaissance and proxy building -- adversarial
The published architecture, training approach and nuclide-sensitivity ranking let an adversary build a proxy of the classifier and optimize evasion offline. Core-specific coolant activity histories and the model itself are also commercially sensitive and could be exfiltrated.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a plant-operations view, this classifier sits in an advisory chain: primary coolant sampling or detector spectra feed the network, and its output informs reactor engineering decisions on defective-fuel identification, power restrictions, coolant chemistry and discharge at outage. The documented training data comes from a Booth diffusion model and first-order kinetic release model, not from measured failures. That is a significant weakness, because real defect geometry, burnup, power history, tramp uranium, iodine spiking during transients, coolant cleanup and letdown, and detector efficiency all differ from the idealized model. Existing practice (Technical Specification limits on dose-equivalent I-131, chemistry trending, sipping, ultrasonic examination) provides independent defence-in-depth, so the likely harm is a wrong operational or economic decision, not an immediate safety event. The residual risks are automation bias toward a 'small defect' or 'intact' call, a missed or late detection that lets secondary hydriding or fuel degradation and coolant contamination progress, and unnecessary shutdowns or discharges that waste fuel and outage time.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulation-to-reality gap: the network is trained on Booth/kinetic-model data (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302). Operating plants differ in coolant cleanup rates, power maneuvers, tramp uranium contamination, multiple concurrent defects, and mixed burnup cores, so the classification of 'degree of failure' may be systematically biased (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302.01). Real failure data is scarce (OP.C0202, OP.C0204), so there is little ground truth for validating the small-defect versus intact boundary. Here the consequence is a missed small defect that progresses to larger failure with higher coolant activity and occupational dose, or false positives that trigger needless power reductions or early discharge. (2) Simplification for practical detectors: pruning to a few top-ranked nuclides via sensitivity analysis reduces redundancy, so a drifting or poorly calibrated gamma-spectrometry channel, or a nuclide misidentified in a spectrum, has more influence on the output (OP.C0603, OP.C0303). Resolution, efficiency calibration and sampling-time delay differ from the training assumptions. (3) Human factors: operators and fuel engineers may over-trust a categorical, one-hot output without explainability on why a rod class was chosen (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401), while the decision tree and network combination complicates qualification (OP.C0501, OP.C0402.01). The tool is non-safety-related, so the main safeguard is the independent technical-specification chemistry and sipping/inspection regime, which must not be relaxed because the AI gives a 'clean' output. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (4) Manipulating input data (AML.T0043, AML.T0020, AML.T0031, AML.T0010.002): an adversary with access to the plant's chemistry or radiochemistry data network, the lab information system, or detector software could alter nuclide activities or spectra so a developing failure appears intact, delaying detection, or so that intact fuel appears failed, inducing forced shutdown or discharge, which is an economic or availability attack. Poisoning the training or retraining dataset or the model file (AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.003) could embed a blind spot for a particular nuclide-ratio pattern. This does not directly defeat safety barriers, but it could mask fuel degradation during the period before an independent check catches it, and it erodes trust in the monitoring chain. (5) Model/IP and data exposure (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025): coolant activity histories reveal core-specific operating and fuel performance information, which is commercially sensitive and could inform where fuel defects are occurring. (6) Supply-chain and lifecycle risk: pretrained weights, third-party software libraries and vendor-provided analysis packages are weakly governed (OP.C0502, AML.T0010.001). Since the same model could be deployed across a fleet of similar PWRs, a single bad update or bias would propagate (OP.C0602). Overall severity is moderate and mitigated by independent chemistry limits and outage inspection, but undetected degradation of the advisory output could delay defective-fuel handling and increase source term, dose and cost.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this system is trained on simulated data. The Booth-type diffusion and first-order kinetic models generate the coolant fission-product activities, and no labelled real-world failure data appears to be involved. Real operating PWRs have very few labelled failures, especially the small-defect cases the classifier is meant to separate from intact rods. The network therefore learns the physics model's assumptions, not plant reality, and the sim-to-real gap is its central weakness. Inference inputs are noisy detector measurements affected by tramp uranium, coolant cleanup, power transients, spectrometry error and changing burnup. These are exactly the conditions where a cascade-forward net with a decision-tree stage can give confident but wrong classes, with no calibrated uncertainty and little explainability. The 'simplify the network for practical detectors' step adds a second fragility: pruning by sensitivity ranking narrows the input space and removes redundancy that could have caught sensor faults or tampering.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and OOD failure: the training data are synthetic and encode idealized release physics (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0202, OP.C0302). The model may misgrade defect size or miss the onset of failure when real coolant chemistry, power history, multiple defects, fuel-type differences, tramp-uranium background or purification-system effects differ from the simulation assumptions. The consequence is a false negative (late discharge of defective fuel, higher coolant activity, radiological and dose burden, possible secondary degradation) or a false positive (unnecessary outage or premature discharge). (2) Operational heterogeneity and drift across plants, cycles, burnup and coolant-treatment regimes (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). The model is qualified statically against simulated cases but used dynamically in transients such as power changes or shutdown spiking. (3) Opacity and over-trust: a neural net plus tree gives a grade with no physical rationale, so operators may defer to it or discount it (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.05). (4) Reduction for practical detectors discards redundant nuclide ratios, reducing robustness to a failed or biased measurement channel (OP.C0403, OP.C0304.03). (5) Training non-determinism and retraining without regression qualification on safety-relevant decisions (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0501).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. The system adds an attack surface at the gamma-spectrometry and sampling data path, as well as the model artifact. (a) Evasion by manipulating the inputs, such as spectra, nuclide activities or sample records, so that real failures are graded as intact or intact rods appear failed (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0043.003). The model's low-dimensional, physically structured input makes it easy to craft plausible perturbations once the important nuclides are known, and the published sensitivity ranking tells an adversary which ones. (b) Poisoning or tampering with the synthetic-data generator parameters, the training set, or the deployed weights or tree thresholds, which gives a stealthy persistent bias (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0076). The effect could be delayed detection that conceals fuel degradation, or manufactured failure alarms that force outages. (c) Open publication of the architecture and method eases proxy-model building (AML.T0000, AML.T0005.001, AML.T0002.001). The consequences range from availability and economic loss to degraded safety margin from masking real fuel damage.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this classifier sits on a trusted, low-bandwidth data path: primary-coolant fission-product activities, whose output informs decisions to discharge or keep fuel. It is an advisory O&M tool, not a protection system, so a nation-state would not target it directly. It is still a plausible stepping stone or cover mechanism. A compromised or silently biased classifier could hide fuel degradation, trigger unnecessary discharge and outage costs, or erode operator vigilance on chemistry and radiological trends. The tool was trained on Booth-diffusion and first-order-kinetic simulated data, so its blind spots are fixed by modeling assumptions and are knowable to anyone who reads the open paper. That lets an adversary or an opportunistic insider reason about which input patterns it handles poorly.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Integrity of inputs and model. The network consumes nuclide activities from coolant sampling or detectors, and an insider with access to the gamma-spectrometry data, preprocessing or the model file could manipulate the data or poison the model (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043, AML.T0031). Mechanism: nuclide ratios or the training set are altered so the classifier under-reports defect severity or flags healthy fuel. Dependency: the discharge and defect-identification decision, plus the chemistry team's reliance on the classification. Consequence: a failure that escalates unnoticed, with higher coolant activity, worker dose and release potential, or conversely spurious discharges that cost money and disrupt operations. The 'simplified network for practical radiation detectors' extends this surface to more instrument-level deployments, each with its own firmware and data-path risk (AML.T0010.000). (2) Trust concentration and timing. Operators who rely on a clean 'intact' output may stop cross-checking iodine spiking and activity trends (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). An adversary could time another action, such as tampering with sampling or a coolant chemistry excursion, to a period when the classifier makes anomalies look benign. (3) Open-literature reconnaissance. The architecture, nuclide-sensitivity ranking and training approach are public (AML.T0000, AML.T0001, AML.T0005). A white-box or proxy model of the classifier is easy to build, and the sensitivity ranking tells an adversary which nuclides matter most to the classifier's output.

IMPLICIT: (1) Simulated-data dependence (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0202). Real failures are rare and heterogeneous, and the Booth and kinetic models make assumptions about defect geometry, burnup, power history and release paths. In-plant behavior (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302.01) can therefore fall outside the training distribution, giving misclassification between intact and small-defect rods and false assurance. An adversary can exploit this by masking a defect or by relying on the model's known weaknesses. (2) Transferred-model risk. Reuse across plants with different fuel, coolant chemistry or tramp-uranium contamination (OP.C0602, OP.C0302.03) can cause systematic errors. (3) Opacity and qualification gap (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). Operators cannot easily tell a manipulated output from a naturally wrong one, which hinders detection of tampering and incident attribution. (4) Simplification risk. A reduced-nuclide network loses redundancy, so a single faulty or tampered detector channel has more influence on the result (OP.C0603). Overall this is low-priority as a direct target, but it could hide a developing fuel-integrity issue or mislead decision-makers, so it warrants integrity controls on data and model, retained independent human trend review, and out-of-distribution flagging.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulation-to-reality gap, loss of redundancy from pruning, opacity and over-trust, and input and model manipulation to mask or fake fuel failure. I dropped the more speculative or generic codes (e.g. AML.T0005.001 replaced by root AML.T0005, OP.C0101.05 and OP.C0101.06 omitted) and kept the exfiltration and IP exposure as a minor threat folded into reconnaissance.

evidence.citation: "Fuel failure detection with a cascade-forward neural network and decision tree (Frontiers in Energy Research, 2022, article 851848)," Frontiers in Energy Research (Frontiers Media)
evidence.note: The paper proposes and tests a neural network that takes coolant fission-product specific activities and outputs one-hot-encoded degrees of fuel failure. It was trained on data built from a Booth-type diffusion model and a first-order kinetic model, and it was more accurate and responsive at detecting the onset of failure than an earlier neural network. The title is my own descriptive label, because the search result gave no exact title.

damage.why: Worst credible case (input or data-path manipulation, or poisoning, masking real fuel degradation) delays defective-fuel handling and raises coolant activity, dose and cost, which is operational disruption with some safety-margin erosion; independent Technical Specification chemistry limits, sipping and inspection bound it well short of a radiological release.
