reproducibility.why: The simulation-to-reality gap and pruned-network blind spots are systematic and recur under the described conditions (transients, tramp uranium, a single dominant channel), but the effect depends on specific plant conditions and on independent checks failing to catch the error.

exploitability.why: Deliberate exploitation (altering nuclide data, spectra or sample records, or tampering with weights, training sets or the supply chain) needs insider or intruder access to plant instrumentation, data paths or the model lifecycle, which is a substantial barrier even though reading the open paper requires none.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly a single unit's fuel-failure assessment, though fleet-wide model reuse and a shared update path could propagate one bias across several similar PWRs; the classifier is advisory and does not couple directly to safety systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, training approach (simulated Booth-diffusion and first-order-kinetic data) and nuclide-sensitivity ranking are in the open literature, and the weakness classes (sim-to-real gap, pruning, over-trust) are well documented for this type of AI system, so an adversary can readily infer the blind spots.

use_case: Neural Normal Stochastic Process (NNSP) anomaly detection on incomplete nuclear power plant sensor time series. A 1-D CNN encoder models the multivariate sensor data directly in latent space, so missing readings from sensor failure, calibration drift or maintenance interruptions need no imputation. It flags abnormal operating states on real plant monitoring datasets, including a Power Generation System dataset with missing data, to support early anomaly detection in plant operation.
incurred_insecurity:
The NNSP detector is an advisory O&M monitor, downstream of the safety-classified protection system, so its failures matter mainly by delaying recognition of real degradation or sabotage rather than by directly tripping the plant. Its defining design choice is that it absorbs missing readings in latent space instead of flagging them, which makes the data path into the model the main attack surface. The main threats are masking of drift or missingness, baseline poisoning, alarm flooding, thin validation evidence, operator over-trust, opacity, and weak AI-specific governance.

Missingness and drift masking -- adversarial
Because dropped channels, stale values and slow calibration shifts are read as benign variation, an insider or intruder with access to the historian, acquisition or calibration path can suppress or slowly shift readings so the latent score stays under threshold. A degrading or manipulated instrument channel then goes unflagged, and the detector cannot tell a fault from deliberate data withholding.

Baseline poisoning via retraining -- adversarial
If the model is refit on recent normal historian data, anyone with write access to that data or the retraining pipeline can seed gradual shifts or selective dropouts so that a developing fault becomes learned-normal. The corruption persists in the weights and is hard to see in the opaque latent space.

Alarm flooding and desensitization -- adversarial
Injected perturbations on noisy channels can drive false-positive spikes until operators tune down or disable the tool, opening a window for a later real event or separate action.

Model and configuration tampering -- adversarial
Weights, thresholds and normalization statistics in the analytics stack are rarely integrity-protected, so altering them, or compromising the supply chain of the model or dataset, can disable detection with no visible failure. Stolen weights and thresholds also reveal what the plant treats as normal and therefore what is undetectable.

Baseline drift and heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Normal-only training goes stale across power levels, refuelling, seasonal heat-sink changes, sensor replacement and outages, producing either false-alarm floods or silent under-detection. An adversary can time an action to these transitions or known outage periods, when the detector is least reliable but still trusted.

Weak validation evidence -- implicit
An F1 of about 84% on one benchmark with synthetic 15% random missingness, and scarce rare-fault labels, says little about recall on slow, plant-specific degradations with structured, correlated missingness. Fleet-wide reuse of one model would copy the same blind spot to every unit. An adversary gains little from this beyond the exploitable drift gap above.

Automation trust and alarm fatigue -- implicit, exploitable
A quiet monitor is read as plant health, while repeated false alarms breed disuse and complacency, and operator skills fade as the tool is relied on. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust, or deliberately induce the fatigue, to let a manipulation sit unchallenged.

Opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
Latent-space scores with stochastic training and thresholding give no physical attribution and make flags hard to reproduce, so operators cannot say why something was or was not flagged. That hampers forensic separation of an attack from a model failure and lets a manipulation be passed off as model error.

Qualification and change-control gap -- implicit, exploitable
Nuclear software QA does not cover a learned model that is retrained or recalibrated after refurbishment, sensor replacement or setpoint change, so retraining and threshold edits can escape cyber and configuration review. An adversary could slip a malicious baseline or threshold change through this unreviewed path.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is an advisory O&M monitoring aid on the power generation (secondary/balance-of-plant) side. It sits downstream of, and independent from, the safety-classified protection system, so a wrong output does not directly trip or fail to trip anything. Harm therefore needs a second failure: operators or maintenance planners acting on or ignoring the flag. The real concerns are quieter. A missing-data-tolerant model can keep producing confident scores while its input is degraded, and an F1 of about 84% on a benchmark with 15% missing data is no assurance of detection on slow, rare, plant-specific degradations. Existing practice (alarm limits, redundant channels, surveillance tests, operator rounds) bounds the consequence, but only if the tool is not allowed to erode those practices.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT. (1) Masking of real degradation. The model learns a normal distribution in latent space, so missing readings from sensor failure, calibration drift or maintenance interruptions are absorbed rather than surfaced. Slow calibration drift can be learned as 'normal' (concept and data drift), and a failing channel may be treated as benign missingness when it is itself the precursor. Consequence: late detection of secondary-side degradation and wasted or mistimed maintenance, with a possible reactivity or thermal-performance excursion only if operators and independent instrumentation also miss it. (2) Weak validation evidence. The F1 of about 83.72% comes from one dataset with synthetic or random missingness. Real missingness is structured and correlated (outages, mode changes, shared cabinet or multiplexer failures), and anomalies are rare, so labels are scarce and recall on plant-specific faults is uncertain. This is the small-data and operational-heterogeneity problem, and it affects transfer across units, power levels, and startup or shutdown transients. (3) Opacity and repeatability. A latent-space score gives operators no physical attribution and no clear way to tell whether a flag is a real fault, a sensor fault or a missingness artefact. This invites over-trust or, after false alarms, disuse and alarm fatigue, and the tool adds another alarm stream to an already crowded control room. (4) Qualification gap. Nothing in current nuclear software QA frameworks covers a learned model that is retrained or recalibrated after refurbishment, sensor replacement or setpoint changes. A silent retrain can shift the baseline, and fleet-wide reuse of one model propagates the same blind spot to every unit.

ADVERSARIAL. (5) Low-and-slow evasion or poisoning. An adversary with access to historian or sensor-network data, or to the retraining pipeline, could inject gradual drift, or induce or exploit missingness (denial or spoofing of selected channels), so the model learns a corrupted 'normal' or leaves an attack on the process or instrumentation unflagged. A missing-data-tolerant model is easy to exploit this way because dropped channels are not an alarm condition. The attack surface is the data path into the model, not the model internals. (6) Alert suppression or flooding. Chaff data or forced false positives could drive operators to disable the tool, and disruption of the monitoring network could create a window for a separate action. (7) Supply chain and data-integrity risk. The model and dataset provenance, the training stack, and any vendor or cloud analytics link are all potential routes to a tampered model or exposed plant operational data. Credible harm depends on a second failure in independent safeguards, but the tool can lengthen the time during which that failure goes unnoticed.

ai_engineer.argument: NNSP is a self-supervised, normal-only latent-space model, so its whole safety value depends on what the 'normal' training distribution actually contains. In a power generation system, that distribution is non-stationary: it shifts with power level, fuel cycle, seasonal heat-sink temperature, equipment replacement and maintenance outages. The architecture also treats missingness as something to absorb, not something to flag. That is the pipeline's weak point. The same masking mechanism that tolerates sensor failure and calibration drift can also normalize a degrading or manipulated sensor into the learned normal. The reported F1 of 83.72% at 15% missing rate was measured on a benchmark dataset, and the Power Generation System dataset is not clearly labeled for true safety-relevant rare events. So the claimed early-detection performance is unlikely to transfer to rare, novel transients, and there is no ground truth to qualify against.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Drift and OOD: normal-only training with a latent-space distance or likelihood score makes the baseline stale after refueling, uprates, instrument replacement, or a change in operating regime. This produces either false-alarm floods, which lead to alarm complacency and disuse, or silent under-detection when slow drift is absorbed into the 'normal' manifold (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0101.05, OP.C0102). (2) Missingness-as-input: the model skips imputation, so it cannot tell benign dropout from informative or adversarial dropout. Correlated missingness during a real transient, or a sensor-quality fault that coincides with a process fault, can drag the latent representation toward normal. The safety consequence is that the monitor degrades silently at the moment it is most needed. This is an OOD and graceful-degradation gap, not an imputation error (OP.C0302, OP.C0403, OP.C0603). (3) Data scarcity and provenance: genuine abnormal-state labels are rare and plant-specific. Evaluation relies on public or injected anomalies, or on one operator's datasets, and the 15% missing rate is synthetic. Headline F1 therefore overstates field performance, and a single CNN encoder trained on one plant does not generalize across reactor types, which matters if models are copied across a fleet (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0201.05, OP.C0602). (4) Qualification and opacity: the latent-space anomaly score gives no causal attribution, and it is stochastic in both training and thresholding. Operators cannot tell what caused a flag or an absence of flags, and repeatability is hard to demonstrate for I&C-adjacent software (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). Automation bias follows: a quiet monitor is read as plant health (OP.C0101.04).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Slow poisoning of the retraining corpus: if the model is periodically refit on 'recent normal' plant historian data, an adversary or compromised insider/OT foothold can shift sensor values gradually, or selectively create dropouts, so a developing fault or sabotage state becomes learned-normal (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0031). (b) Evasion at inference: because the model is tolerant of missing channels and the dependence structure is learned in latent space, falsified or replayed sensor values, or targeted masking of the few channels that carry the anomaly signature, can keep the score under threshold. This is cheaper than defeating a rule-based limit check, and surrogate models are feasible given the published architecture and baseline code (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0005, AML.T0043.003). (c) Supply chain and model integrity: weights, preprocessing and threshold configs sit in the analytics and historian stack and are rarely integrity-protected. Tampering with a threshold or the normalization statistics disables detection without any visible failure (AML.T0018, AML.T0010.001, AML.T0076). (d) Alarm flooding by injected perturbations, to induce operator disuse before a real event (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). Because the tool sits on O&M data feeds, not in the protection system, the main consequence is not a direct plant trip. It is eroded early-warning and condition-monitoring that operators and regulators may be relying on, and the lack of AI-specific qualification and governance means nobody is positioned to notice (OP.C0504, OP.C0502).

security_specialist.argument: This is an advisory anomaly detector on O&M sensor streams, so I do not see a nation-state going after the model itself. The more realistic concern is that it becomes a trusted gatekeeper for what operators and maintenance staff treat as 'normal'. Its defining feature is that it tolerates missing data without imputation. That makes missingness a quiet input channel: gaps, stale values or drift look benign to the model, and a patient insider or an adversary with access to the instrumentation or data path can exploit this. Its reported F1 of about 84% at a 15% missing rate also means roughly one in six events is missed or false-alarmed. Operators who come to rely on it will drift into complacency, and a timed attack could sit inside that blind spot. The system matters mainly as a stepping stone and as a way to erode vigilance, not as a direct target.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by masking or slow drift. The model learns a latent distribution of 'normal' and handles missing readings without imputation. An insider or intruder with access to historian, data-acquisition or sensor-calibration paths could suppress readings, induce plausible gaps, or shift calibration slowly. The detector would then treat the gaps or drift as normal variation and never flag the anomaly (AML.T0015, AML.T0043.003). Because the model is built to ignore missingness, it has no built-in way to separate faults from deliberate data withholding. The result is delayed detection of real degradation, or concealment of sabotage or manipulation of a plant parameter. (2) Training-data and baseline poisoning. The model is retrained or recalibrated on 'normal' operational data. Someone with write access to the historian or retraining pipeline can seed corrupted baselines so that later abnormal states become normal (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059, AML.T0010.002). The poisoning persists in the model and is hard to see in the opaque latent space. (3) Alarm flooding and desensitization. An adversary can induce chaff or false-positive spikes, for example by perturbing noisy channels. Operators then discount or tune down the alerts, which sets up a later real event (AML.T0046, AML.T0031, AML.T0029). (4) Information value. Model weights, thresholds and latent representations reveal what the plant treats as normal, and so what is undetectable. That helps an adversary design stealthy actions (AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0013). Access to the integrity of the O&M analytics environment could also serve as a lateral-movement foothold toward the OT network (AML.T0012, AML.T0010.001).

IMPLICIT. (a) Automation trust and complacency. An advisory tool that handles messy data gracefully invites over-reliance and skill fade among operators and maintenance staff (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). An adversary can time an action to periods of known sensor outage or maintenance, when the detector is both least reliable and most trusted. (b) Evidence base. Reported performance comes from a limited number of real datasets, with about 83.7% F1 on one dataset at 15% missingness. Anomalies are rare, labels are scarce, and the evaluation says little about plant-specific operating modes, so the model may not generalize (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.02). Outages, power ramps and sensor replacements shift the baseline, and drifted normality is something an adversary can hide in. (c) Opacity and non-repeatability. Latent-space scoring and a stochastic process make it hard to justify why something was or was not flagged. That limits forensic reconstruction after an incident and makes it difficult to tell an attack from a model failure (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.02). (d) Governance. AI-specific qualification and change control for non-safety analytics are often weak, so retraining or threshold changes may escape cyber and configuration review (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0505, OP.C0503). The consequence is a trusted but unvetted monitoring layer whose silent failure could delay response to real degradation or an attack on the plant.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on missingness/drift masking, retraining-baseline poisoning, alarm flooding, thin validation evidence, automation complacency, opacity and the qualification gap, so these were merged into single threats. I kept the tampering and information-value threat from the AI and security panelists, dropped the vaguer lateral-movement, cloud-dependency and surrogate-model points, and omitted weaker codes such as AML.T0005, AML.T0012 and OP.C0603 that were not clearly traceable to the retained text.

evidence.citation: "Anomaly Detection in Nuclear Power Production Based on Neural Normal Stochastic Process," Sensors (MDPI), 25(14), 4358, 2025
evidence.note: The authors, from China Nuclear Power Operation Technology Corporation and Naval University of Engineering, propose and test an imputation-free anomaly detector for incomplete nuclear plant sensor time series. It uses a 1D-CNN encoder and was benchmarked against ARMA, Isolation Forest, LSTM-AD, VAE and NeuTraL AD. On the Power Generation System dataset with a 15% missing rate it reached an F1 score of 83.72% and beat all baselines.

damage.why: The detector is advisory and sits downstream of the safety-classified protection system, so the worst credible case (drift or missingness masking, or baseline poisoning, hiding real degradation or manipulation) is delayed recognition and erosion of safety margin or operational disruption, not a direct radiological release.

reproducibility.why: Once an adversary has data-path or retraining-pipeline access, masking missingness and drift is dependable because the design treats missing or shifted readings as benign; the implicit drift and heterogeneity weaknesses recur on every plant transition.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (historian or calibration path manipulation, retraining-pipeline poisoning, weight or threshold tampering) need insider or intruder access to OT/analytics systems; only the implicit trust and fatigue effects need no special access.

affected_users.why: Impact is mostly confined to one plant's O&M monitoring and its operators, but fleet-wide model reuse would copy a blind spot or poisoned baseline across units, and the model does not couple directly to protection systems.

discoverability.why: The imputation-free design and the general classes of data poisoning, drift, evasion and alarm fatigue are published openly, and the approach is described in the open literature, so a capable outsider could infer the weakness; plant-specific thresholds and data paths still need insider knowledge.

use_case: Convolutional neural network applied to reconstructed Passive Gamma Emission Tomography (PGET) cross-sectional images of spent fuel assemblies. It identifies the bundle type and locates present fuel pins, and the pin activities are then estimated. It supports IAEA safeguards verification of spent fuel in water pools, including detection of missing pins. It was demonstrated on simulated mock-up assemblies of Co-60 pins.
incurred_insecurity:
This CNN converts PGET tomograms of spent fuel in pools into a machine-made verdict (bundle type, pin map, per-pin activity) that supports IAEA conclusions on missing or substituted pins. It was demonstrated only on simulated Co-60 mock-ups, so the main threats are sim-to-real failure and scarce diversion data, a classify-then-estimate error cascade, over-trust and skill fade, and a missing ML qualification regime. Adversarial threats are evasion by a diverting operator, tampering with model or data artifacts, and reconnaissance from the public method. Independent inspector review, Cherenkov viewing, item counting and seals mean the realistic worst case is gradual erosion of safeguards assurance, not a sudden incident.

Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
A CNN trained on idealized Co-60 simulations meets real assemblies with mixed Cs-137, Cs-134 and Eu-154 emitters, burnup gradients, damaged or non-standard bundles and pool attenuation, and can return confident but wrong bundle labels and pin maps without an out-of-distribution flag. An adversary can present a configuration in these uncharacterized blind spots, so a missing or substituted pin reads as 'complete'.

Diversion-data scarcity and unvalidated detection claims -- implicit, exploitable
Real missing-pin and substituted-pin examples are essentially absent, so sensitivity and false-alarm rates are extrapolated from synthetic positives, and a roughly 5% activity error does not translate into a detection probability. An adversary can substitute a low-activity or dummy pin whose deviation falls inside the stated uncertainty.

Cascading classify-then-estimate error -- implicit, exploitable
A wrong bundle-type call or reconstruction artifact selects the wrong template for pin location, and the activity estimates are then computed on those locations, so each stage's errors look plausible downstream. An adversary can induce artifact-like geometric distortions that pass as innocent reconstruction error.

Automation trust, skill fade and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
A clean, authoritative-looking pin map invites over-trust, inspectors lose the habit of reading raw tomograms, and the CNN offers no physical explanation to separate a wrong call from a subtle manipulation or to rebut a disputing operator. An adversary can time a diversion for after complacency has set in and rely on the unquestioned 'complete' output.

AI qualification, repeatability and regulatory gap -- implicit, exploitable
No mature acceptance criteria, repeatability requirements or re-qualification rules exist for ML inside a safeguards instrument chain, so retraining non-determinism or a quiet model update can change outputs without being flagged. An adversary can hide a model alteration inside this unmonitored update and retraining channel.

Evasion of the classifier -- adversarial
A diverting operator with physical pool access can arrange pin substitutions, shielding or neighbouring-pin geometry so the reconstructed image shows a plausible full lattice, with perturbations that resemble physical artifacts rather than tampering. The consequence is a missing-pin diversion reported as verified on timeliness-critical material.

Model, data and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
Poisoned training or simulation data, trojaned weights or reconstruction code, or a tampered update on the vendor, lab or inspector-laptop path could install a backdoor trigger keyed to a bundle geometry that suppresses missing-pin calls while passing acceptance tests. If the same model is used across sites, the false assurance propagates fleet-wide.

Reconnaissance and proxy-model rehearsal -- adversarial
The publicly documented architecture and training regime let a state build a proxy model and rehearse evasion offline before touching the real instrument. This lowers the cost of finding the blind spots described above.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a safeguards-operations view, this CNN sits between the PGET reconstruction and the inspector's partial-defect verification of spent fuel in pools. Its output (bundle type, pin map, per-pin activity) is evidence that an inspector may use to conclude that no pins are missing or substituted. Harm would come from a false 'all pins present' result that nobody challenges, which means diversion or substitution goes unnoticed and continuity of knowledge on spent fuel is degraded. Existing practice limits the damage. PGET is an IAEA-authorised instrument, inspectors review the tomograms by eye, and the result is combined with other methods such as Cherenkov viewing, item counting, and seals and surveillance, so the CNN is a decision aid and not the sole barrier. The main risk is that this safety net erodes over time through automation bias and workload pressure, particularly because the demonstration used only simulated Co-60 mock-ups, not real irradiated fuel.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real gap: the CNN was demonstrated on simulated Co-60 pin mock-ups, with roughly 5% activity uncertainty. Real spent fuel has mixed Cs-137, Cs-134 and Eu-154 sources, burnup and cooling-time gradients, radial activity profiles, self-attenuation, water and rack geometry, and detector-collimator variation. This is a drift/out-of-distribution/data-provenance problem (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0701). Real assemblies (unusual designs, damaged or partially filled fuel, low-burnup or older fuel) could be misclassified as another bundle type, or low-activity pins could be mislocated as absent. The consequence is false alarms, which waste inspection effort, or, more seriously, false assurance. (2) Small-data and low base-rate problem: genuine missing-pin or substituted-pin cases are rare and are hard to produce as real training data, so detection sensitivity for the safeguards-relevant minority case is poorly characterised (OP.C0202, OP.C0701.01). The pin-activity estimate adds a quantitative error that can mask a partial-defect substitution, such as a dummy or low-activity pin, if the threshold is set by simulated performance (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0401). (3) Human factors and qualification: inspectors may over-trust a clean automated pin map, or lose the skill to read tomograms manually (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06). Qualification of the CNN as a safeguards instrument component is a gap, because acceptance criteria, repeatability, and re-qualification after retraining are not defined for ML (OP.C0501, OP.C0402, OP.C0303, OP.C0504). Opacity makes it hard to explain a 'pin present' call to a state operator who disputes a finding (OP.C0401).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (4) Evasion by a proliferating or diverting operator, who has physical access to the pool and fuel arrangement. The operator could make an assembly's gamma signature or geometry resemble what the CNN expects, for example by substituting a pin with a matching-activity source or placing shielding or neighbouring-pin arrangements that exploit the model's blind spots. Because the model architecture and the paper are public, a state could build a proxy model to find such configurations (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0005, AML.T0001). The consequence is a missing-pin diversion that the automated step reports as 'verified', which reduces detection probability on timeliness-critical material. (5) Supply-chain or software tampering with the CNN weights, reconstruction code, or the pin-map and bundle-library files, whether by a compromised vendor, an update channel, or the inspector's laptop. Poisoned weights or a backdoor trigger could suppress alarms for certain bundle IDs (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004, AML.T0076, OP.C0502). The consequence is systematic false assurance across inspections. If the same model is deployed across sites, the failure propagates fleet-wide (OP.C0602). (6) Data integrity of the input tomograms or detector data, through spoofed or altered raw measurements (AML.T0043, AML.T0031, OP.C0703). (7) Confidentiality: detailed pin maps and activity inventories reveal fuel design and burnup information, so operator or state data in the analysis pipeline are sensitive and the wrong data-security model could expose them (AML.T0025, OP.C0505.01).

Mitigating context: these threats need a second barrier to fail, namely independent inspector review, complementary NDA/Cherenkov verification, and seals, so the realistic worst case is gradual erosion of safeguards assurance. A sudden physical incident is unlikely, since the application does not control plant equipment.

ai_engineer.argument: The CNN sits downstream of an inverse-problem reconstruction. It was trained and demonstrated on simulated Co-60 mock-up assemblies, whose geometry, source term and noise are idealized. Real spent fuel in pools has a very different gamma field. Cs-137 and Cs-134 dominate, there is a large burnup-dependent activity spread across pins, Compton background, self-attenuation and water effects, and collimator or detector response varies. The ~5% activity uncertainty and the pin-presence accuracy are therefore only validated on simulated, low-base-rate data. Missing-pin cases are rare in the real world, so the labelled positives the model needs for verification are scarce and synthetic. The architecture is a two-stage classify-then-estimate chain, so a wrong bundle-type call propagates into the wrong template for pin location and activity. Assurance depends on data provenance and OOD behaviour rather than on the facility.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT. (1) Sim-to-real gap and OOD failure (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). A CNN trained on simulated Co-60 mock-ups meets real assemblies with different isotopics, burnup gradients, damaged or non-standard bundles, consolidated or rodded configurations, and detector or reconstruction artifacts. It can return confident bundle labels and pin maps that are wrong, with no calibrated OOD flag. The consequence is a false-negative missing pin (a diversion indicator goes undetected) or a false positive that burdens inspectors and erodes trust. (2) Scarcity of diversion-relevant data (OP.C0202, OP.C0701, OP.C0701.02). Real missing-pin examples are essentially absent, so the sensitivity and false-alarm rate are extrapolated from synthetic positives. A 5% activity error figure does not transfer to a detection-probability claim. (3) Cascading pipeline error (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). Reconstruction artifacts, such as a misalignment or incomplete angular coverage, feed the CNN, and the bundle-type error then biases the pin-location and activity estimates. Each stage's errors look plausible downstream. (4) Opacity and automation bias (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0402). Inspectors may accept the pin map without understanding why the CNN saw what it did. Retraining non-determinism and software updates can change outputs, which conflicts with IAEA authentication and reproducibility needs (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). ADVERSARIAL. (5) Evasion and shaping (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0043.003). A state with knowledge of the model family or of its published architecture and training regime can exploit the sim-to-real blind spots. It can place a dummy or lower-activity pin, use shielding, or distort the geometry so the reconstructed image yields a plausible pin count, with perturbations that look like physical artifacts rather than tampering. Open publication of the method supports reconnaissance (AML.T0000, AML.T0013, AML.T0005). (6) Supply chain and model integrity (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0076). Poisoned training or simulation data, a trojaned reconstruction library or weights, or a tampered update could bias the system toward certain pin patterns, such as a backdoor trigger that suppresses missing-pin alarms. This is a verification-integrity threat, since the host state typically operates the instrument and its data chain. The consequence is a compromised safeguards conclusion on spent-fuel continuity of knowledge.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this CNN sits at the exact point where a proliferation-relevant claim, that every pin in a spent fuel assembly is present and not substituted, is converted from a tomographic image into a machine-made verdict. That makes the model a high-value trust concentration. It is also a stepping stone: an adversary, whether a State diverting pins or an insider assisting, does not have to defeat the physical instrument, only make the classifier read 'complete' when it is not. The system was demonstrated only on simulated Co-60 mock-ups, so real-world generalization is unproven. Those gaps (unrepresentative training data, little operator experience of failure modes, opaque outputs) are what a sophisticated diverter would time an attack around. Inspectors who come to rely on the automated pin map will slowly lose the habit of reading raw reconstructions.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion and adversarial-data risk: a State operator who knows or approximates the model could arrange the assembly's physical presentation, or use dummy or substituted pins with a similar emission signature, so the CNN sees a plausible full lattice. The AI failure mechanism is a classifier that learned the appearance of simulated pins, not the underlying physics of diversion. The dependent function is IAEA verification of pin presence. The consequence is an undetected diversion of spent fuel and an erosion of safeguards conclusions (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, OP.C0703). (2) Supply chain and model integrity: the model, training sets and reconstruction pipeline are software artifacts that move between a vendor, a lab, the IAEA and inspectorates. Poisoned training data, a tampered model file or a backdoor trigger keyed to a particular bundle geometry could suppress 'missing pin' calls while passing routine acceptance tests. This needs only one insider with write access, or one compromised dependency (AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). (3) Reconnaissance and model extraction: the paper is public, and a determined State can build a proxy model from it and rehearse evasions offline (AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0017). (4) Trust concentration: where one tool becomes the de facto basis of a safeguards finding, a compromised analysis laptop or an insider altering outputs becomes a high-leverage target. This is far easier than defeating seals, surveillance or the detector (AML.T0012, AML.T0031).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable. (a) Data provenance and scarcity: validation on simulated Co-60 mock-ups says little about real spent fuel, which has mixed Cs-137, Eu-154 and other emitters, differing burnup and cooling times, and attenuation in the pool. The model may therefore fail out of distribution in ways no one has characterized, and an adversary can choose a configuration in the blind spots (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0701, OP.C0302, OP.C0303). (b) Automation bias and skill fade: the pin map and the roughly 5% activity uncertainty look authoritative. Inspectors may stop scrutinizing raw tomograms and may not question a confident 'complete' output. An adversary can time a diversion for after this complacency has set in (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). (c) Opacity and qualification gap: a CNN gives no physical explanation, so a wrong call cannot readily be distinguished from a subtle manipulation. Safeguards authorities also have no mature AI qualification regime for such a tool, so a quiet drift or retraining may go unflagged (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (d) Cascading error: pin activity estimates are made on pin locations the CNN has already identified, so a single misidentification propagates into wrong quantitative values (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). Because activity is estimated rather than measured independently, a small substitution of a lower-activity pin could fall inside the stated uncertainty and go unflagged.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sim-to-real failure, data scarcity, error cascade, automation bias, qualification gap, evasion, supply-chain tampering and proxy-model reconnaissance. I dropped weakly supported or generic codes (valid accounts, exfiltration, spoofed-tomogram imagery, hallucination) and treated the engineer's confidentiality and data-integrity items as peripheral to the main threats.

evidence.citation: "Quantitative imaging and automated fuel pin identification for passive gamma emission tomography," Scientific Reports (Nature Portfolio), vol. 11, article 2442, 2021 (Fang, Altmann, Della Latta, Salvatori, Di Fulvio)
evidence.note: The paper builds a software suite for PGET, the IAEA-authorised instrument for verifying spent fuel in pools. The suite reconstructs images with an inverse-problem method, then uses a CNN to classify the bundle type and extract pin locations. Pin activity levels are then estimated and compared with the ground truth on simulated mock-up assemblies, with uncertainty of about 5%.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a missing-pin diversion reported as 'verified' (safeguards falsification, evasion or backdoor), which falls in the top damage category; it is scored 4 rather than 5 because independent inspector review, Cherenkov viewing, item counting and seals limit the realistic outcome to gradual erosion of assurance.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real blind spots and small-data limits make misclassification fairly reliable for out-of-distribution configurations, but a successful evasion still depends on the specific model, the geometry and the other verification layers, so it is conditional.

exploitability.why: Evasion needs physical pool access, knowledge of the model's blind spots and the ability to arrange pin configurations, and backdoor or pipeline tampering needs insider or state-level access, so the class generally requires substantial resources and position.

affected_users.why: Impact is typically a single assembly, pool or inspection verdict, but a shared model, an update channel or a backdoor could propagate false assurance across sites (the fleet-wide case), which is a moderate-to-broad safeguards effect.

discoverability.why: The architecture, training regime and simulation-only validation are published in the open literature, and sim-to-real gaps, over-trust and ML qualification gaps are well-known classes, so a capable outsider can infer the weaknesses; the specific blind spots still need proxy-model work.

use_case: Radial-basis-function neural network that predicts the probability of pellet-cladding interaction (PCI) failure of water-reactor fuel rods during power ramps. It is built from existing experimental PCI failure data. It is intended as a fast, online alternative to finite-element PCI calculations, for use in transient analysis and core monitoring systems.
incurred_insecurity:
An RBF neural network surrogate for PCI failure probability, built from a small set of ramp-test data and offered for online core monitoring, concentrates operator and fuel-management trust in one advisory number. Its main implicit weaknesses are extrapolation outside a narrow training envelope, uncalibrated and opaque probabilities, and the lack of a qualification path. Its main adversarial exposures are tampering with its few parameters or training records, manipulation of its input feeds, and weak integrity control around a research-origin artifact. The realistic consequence is fuel failure by PCI, with coolant activity release, lost margin and outage, rather than a direct failure of safety systems, provided the tool stays outside the protection system.

Extrapolation beyond sparse training data -- implicit, exploitable
The network is a local interpolator fitted to few, heterogeneous test-reactor failures. For new cladding, higher burnup, MOX or load-following histories it still returns a smooth, plausible probability that can understate PCI risk and justify aggressive ramp rates. An adversary or insider who knows the domain edges could steer plant conditions into those regions, where optimistic outputs look like ordinary model error.

Uncalibrated, opaque probability and over-trust -- implicit, exploitable
A single scalar from a black-box fit on rare-failure data cannot be checked for calibration or explained, so operators and fuel engineers may treat it as a validated margin and let finite-element judgment atrophy. An adversary could rely on this misplaced trust, and on the difficulty of attributing a rare failure to model error or tampering, to make manipulated outputs go unchallenged.

Static model under changing fuel and operation -- implicit, exploitable
The fitted model cannot track new alloys, burnup extension, accident-tolerant fuel or flexible-power operation, so it loses validity silently, and retraining is limited by data scarcity and can change behaviour unnoticed. An adversary could time an action to periods of known drift, or hide a data or parameter change inside a routine retraining.

Qualification gap and scope creep -- implicit, exploitable
No accepted route exists to credit a data-driven surrogate in place of a qualified fuel-performance code, and a research-origin tool may sit outside software QA and cyber controls. An advisory tool can quietly become a basis for operating limits, and an adversary gains a lightly protected artifact that influences fuel-integrity decisions.

Input-quality and fleet propagation -- implicit, exploitable
Local power and burnup inputs from core simulators carry their own uncertainty, and bad or drifting inputs pass straight into the probability; a copy of the same model at several units replicates any bias everywhere. An adversary could use one tampered or mis-scoped version to bias several plants, and noisy inputs give cover for deliberate falsification.

Model or parameter tampering -- adversarial
The network is a small set of centers, widths and weights, so altering them is easy and review is hard. Because its local structure confines a change to a narrow input region, validation metrics can stay intact while a backdoor-like safe-looking region under-predicts PCI failure at chosen ramp conditions, producing delayed clustered fuel failures that resemble natural variability.

Training-data poisoning -- adversarial
The database is small, published and curated, so a few altered records, upstream or in a retraining set, can shift the failure boundary undetected. The result is a biased failure threshold that relaxes ramp or conditioning limits.

Input manipulation -- adversarial
The architecture and data are public, so an attacker can replicate the model and craft inputs in low-density regions, or falsify plant-computer power, ramp and burnup signals. Suppressed predictions conceal real PCI risk, while inflated ones force unnecessary derating; a timed power maneuver could exploit the false margin.

Software wrapper and toolchain foothold -- adversarial
Scripts, notebooks and data pipelines around the model, deployed without integrity checking or security categorisation, form a path from an advisory analytic into the monitoring network. Digital I&C threat models often exclude such advisory analytics.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations lens, this surrogate sits between fuel-performance knowledge and the power-maneuvering decisions made by operators and core-monitoring software. The most credible harm is a quiet one: a PCI failure probability that is wrong in the non-conservative direction gets used to justify ramp rates, load-following, or return-to-power after a trip, and a fuel rod fails by PCI. Existing practice limits the consequence. Fuel licensing relies on qualified fuel-performance codes, with PCI/PCMI operating limits, conditioning (preconditioning) rules and ramp-rate restrictions, and a through-cladding failure normally means an iodine or activity excursion in the coolant, not a core-damage event. Several things would need to fail for serious harm: the surrogate would have to be wired into an actual limit or setpoint function, its error would have to go undetected, and the independent safety-grade protection and chemistry/activity monitoring would also have to miss it. The realistic risks are therefore fuel reliability, reduced margin, economic loss and mistaken licensing credit, not a direct safety-system failure. They get worse if the tool migrates from advisory use to a basis for operating limits without anyone formally deciding that it should.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Small, heterogeneous training data: PCI failure experiments are few, drawn from test-reactor ramp tests, and come from specific fuel designs, burnups, cladding types (Zircaloy variants, liners) and ramp histories. An RBF network fits well inside that data and extrapolates poorly (OP.C0202, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302). Extrapolation to new cladding, high burnup, MOX, accident-tolerant fuel or load-following histories is outside its qualified envelope and gives no warning. (2) Probability calibration: failures are rare, so the output may look precise without being calibrated, and operators may read it as a validated margin (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0403, OP.C0401). RBF networks give no inherent out-of-domain indication, since the output decays toward a default value away from the training centers. (3) Qualification mismatch: a data-driven surrogate of a mechanistic phenomenon (stress corrosion cracking by iodine, with a threshold dependence on power history) has no established route to licensing credit, and a static fit cannot track in-core conditions such as fission-product chemistry or fuel-property changes (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (4) Input quality in an online core-monitor setting: local power and burnup estimates come from core simulators with their own uncertainty, and bad or drifting inputs propagate into the probability (OP.C0603, OP.C0204, OP.C0302.01). Automation bias and scope creep can follow, as advisory use quietly becomes limit-setting.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. Because the model is small, its training data is published and the architecture is public, so a model-integrity attack needs no reconnaissance. The relevant classes are supply-chain or model tampering (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018, AML.T0076), training-data poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002) and manipulation of its input feeds (AML.T0043, AML.T0015). Each could bias the probability low during a ramp, or high to force needless derating (AML.T0031). A coordinated version would time the bias to a planned power maneuver. Because the network is simple, such manipulation can look like ordinary model error. The consequences are fuel failure, activity release into the coolant, outage and economic loss, rather than a direct threat to safety systems, provided the surrogate stays outside the protection system. Denial of the tool (AML.T0029) mostly makes operators fall back on conservative procedures, which is low impact. The security-relevant point is a governance gap: the tool is likely to be treated as a research artifact, outside the cyber and software QA controls (OP.C0502, OP.C0503) that would apply once it feeds core monitoring.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a small-data surrogate: an RBF network fit to a limited set of experimental PCI ramp-test failure data (test-reactor ramp tests, with a handful of fuel designs, burnups, cladding types and ramp histories) and then proposed as an online substitute for finite-element PCI calculations. RBF networks are local interpolators with no extrapolation guarantee, so the central fragility is the operating envelope. Each query from core monitoring (new fuel designs, high burnup, load-follow histories, different cladding or pellet additives) can fall outside the convex hull of the training points, and the network will still return a smooth, confident-looking probability. The data is also failure-censored and imbalanced: failures are rare, ramp tests are conducted under controlled conditions that differ from plant transients, and the label (failure/no failure, determined by post-irradiation examination) carries no information on mechanism. Probability calibration is therefore hard to defend and cannot be checked against field data. The use case is also described only at proof-of-concept level, which suggests that nothing about qualification, versioning, or uncertainty quantification is built into the pipeline.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution/extrapolation failure (OP.C0302, C0302.03): a local-basis surrogate trained on a narrow ramp-test database is queried by monitoring with fuel designs, burnups or ramp rates it never saw. Outputs remain plausible but unreliable, and may understate PCI failure probability. The facility then relies on an optimistic margin for ramp rates, maneuvering limits or power-increase permissions, which is a fuel-integrity and radiological-release-barrier concern. (2) Data provenance and scarcity (OP.C0201.04, C0202, C0203): lab/test-reactor data with rare failures, with censored labels and unrecorded covariates (chemistry such as iodine/cesium, hold times, pellet-clad gap state). Failure probability is then a function of what was recorded, and the model may confuse correlation with mechanism (OP.C0301, C0403). (3) Static/dynamic qualification mismatch (OP.C0303): the model is validated against held-out experiments, but is applied to online, time-varying plant transients, and replaces a physics code whose credibility rests on code qualification. Surrogate-vs-FEM agreement is only as good as the sampled domain (OP.C0201.02, C0501). (4) Calibration and explainability (OP.C0401, C0304.03): a single scalar probability hides the dominant mechanism, so operators and licensing reviewers cannot challenge it; automation bias and over-trust (OP.C0101.04) are likely if it is embedded in core monitoring. (5) Lifecycle drift (OP.C0302.01/.02): new cladding alloys, accident-tolerant fuel, and higher burnup change the underlying physics (concept drift), yet retraining is limited by new data scarcity, and retraining can silently change behavior (OP.C0402.01, C0502). (6) Fleet propagation (OP.C0602, C0603): if the same network is copied to several plants or fed into other analysis tools, a bias propagates everywhere. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training-data or artifact tampering (AML.T0020, T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0031): the training set is small and hand-curated, so a few modified records or a modified weight/center file would shift the failure boundary in a chosen region. This would be hard to detect because the RBF's local structure lets the change be confined to a narrow region of input space, leaving validation metrics intact. The consequence is a hidden safe-looking region, i.e. a backdoor (AML.T0043.004) that could be timed to coincide with a physical operating action. (b) Input manipulation at inference (AML.T0015, T0043): if the online surrogate takes inputs from plant process computers, falsified or drifting power-history or burnup inputs push the model toward under-predicting failure, which could mask real PCI risk or, conversely, trigger spurious restrictions that reduce availability (AML.T0029, T0046). (c) Model access and replication (AML.T0044, T0005, T0024.002): because the architecture and data are published, a small model is easy to replicate, which lowers the cost of white-box crafting of inputs that sit in low-density regions (AML.T0000, T0002). (d) Integrity of the integration (OP.C0502): the main new attack surface is the software wrapper and data pipeline into core monitoring rather than the model itself, which is a pathway for lateral movement from an advisory tool into monitoring systems.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, a PCI failure-probability surrogate in core monitoring is a low-glamour target. It does not actuate anything, and a nation-state would likely choose easier or higher-consequence paths. Its danger is that it concentrates trust in an advisory number that sets operator and fuel-management behavior around power ramps. An adversary who wanted a fuel-integrity event, or wanted to degrade confidence in the plant, could target the model, its data, or its thresholds, or could time an action around its known blind spots. The more likely problems are implicit ones: a small, heterogeneous experimental database, extrapolation outside its envelope, and automation trust that makes a smooth probability output look authoritative. An insider with write access to a quiet, rarely audited artifact could exploit those weaknesses with little chance of being noticed.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Model or parameter tampering (AML.T0018, T0018.000, T0076, T0010.003): the RBF network is a small set of centers, widths and weights, so it is easy to alter and hard to review. A modified model could consistently under-predict PCI failure probability at specific ramp rates, burnups or power levels. Operators and fuel managers would then relax ramp-rate limits or conditioning constraints, and the effect would appear later as clustered fuel failures, release of fission products into primary coolant, and outage and regulatory consequences that look like natural fuel-performance variability. Because failures show up cycles later, attribution would be difficult. (2) Training-data or experimental-database poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0059): the model is built from a limited set of experimental PCI data. An upstream supply-chain or insider change to a few records, or to the data used for any retraining or recalibration, shifts the failure boundary in a way that is hard to detect. Such a change could also be introduced through shared research datasets and published papers. (3) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, T0015): online use means the model consumes plant-computer signals such as local power, ramp rate, burnup and cladding conditions. Tampering with these upstream, or crafting inputs at the boundary of the training range, could suppress or inflate predicted failure probability. Suppression conceals a real risk. Inflation causes unnecessary derating or conservative restrictions, an economic and availability harm. (4) Trust concentration and timing: once the number sits in monitoring displays, it can be used as the stepping stone for a deception effect. An attacker can make the plant believe its margin is larger than it is, then time a legitimate or induced power maneuver, such as grid-driven load following or a post-outage return to power, to exploit that belief. (5) Insider and access-governance gap: a research-origin surrogate may be deployed with weak configuration control, no cryptographic integrity checking, and little security categorisation, even though it informs fuel-integrity decisions (OP.C0505.01, OP.C0502, OP.C0503). The scripts, notebooks and toolchains around the model are also a plausible foothold into the monitoring network (AML.T0010.001, T0011.001). Threat models for digital I&C often exclude advisory analytics.

IMPLICIT, WITH ADVERSARIAL EXPLOITABILITY. (a) Small-data and extrapolation limits (OP.C0202, C0302, C0302.03, C0201.04, C0201.05): experimental PCI failure data is sparse and heterogeneous across fuel designs, cladding types such as liners or barrier claddings, and test conditions. Real reactor fuel may fall outside that range. Confident-looking probabilities will then be unreliable exactly where PCI risk is highest, and an adversary or insider who knows the model's domain edges can plan around them. (b) Automation trust failure and skill fade (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102): a fast, smooth online probability can replace the finite-element and engineering judgment that fuel engineers once exercised. It also discourages questioning, which makes quiet manipulation harder to notice. (c) Qualification and explainability gaps (OP.C0501, C0401, C0303, C0304.03): there is no accepted qualification path for a black-box surrogate to stand in for a licensed fuel-performance code. It is also hard to explain why a given output moved. A rare, low-probability failure event can therefore not be traced to model error or to tampering. (d) Drift across new fuel designs, burnup extension and flexible-power operation (OP.C0302.01, C0302.02): the surrogate is static, so it silently loses validity as operating practice changes. (e) Fleet propagation (OP.C0602): if the model is copied across units or sites, one tampered or mis-scoped version carries the same bias everywhere.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on small-data extrapolation, over-trust and qualification gaps as the implicit core, and on model tampering, data poisoning and input manipulation as the adversarial core. I dropped lower-value codes (denial of service, chaff, model extraction and replication) as minor or restating other threats, and kept the toolchain foothold only as a single supply-chain item.

evidence.citation: "Prediction Study on PCI Failure of Reactor Fuel Based on a Radial Basis Function Neural Network," Science and Technology of Nuclear Installations (Hindawi/Wiley)
evidence.note: The paper builds a radial basis function neural network from existing experimental data to predict fuel rod failure by pellet-cladding interaction under power increases. It presents the network as a simple, fast way to predict PCI failure probability online, which could be used within transient analysis methods and core monitoring systems. This is a peer-reviewed journal article. I read it only through the search-result excerpts, so details on the training data and validation are limited to those excerpts.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is model/parameter tampering or data poisoning that under-predicts PCI failure, causing clustered fuel failures with coolant activity release and lost margin; this is a significant fuel-integrity harm but short of a major radiological release, and the tool is assumed to sit outside the protection system.

reproducibility.why: Extrapolation, drift and over-trust failures recur reliably once the model is used outside its narrow envelope, but a tampering or poisoning outcome depends on specific operating conditions (ramp events in the affected region) and the rarity of PCI failures.

exploitability.why: Altering model parameters, training records, or plant-computer input feeds requires insider or privileged access to the fuel-management or monitoring environment, though the lightly protected research-origin artifact lowers the bar somewhat.

affected_users.why: Impact is plant-wide for the fuel cycle (many fuel rods and core regions), and copies of the model at several units can replicate bias across a fleet, but the effect stays confined to fuel-integrity advisory decisions rather than coupled safety systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture, data and approach are published in the open literature, and small-data extrapolation, poisoning and tampering weaknesses are well documented for this class of model, so an outsider can readily infer the weaknesses even without knowing a given plant's deployment.

use_case: Deep reinforcement learning (Proximal Policy Optimization, with a policy network and a critic) to optimise PWR core reload loading patterns. The agent searches for the fuel-assembly arrangement that maximises cycle length while meeting boron-concentration, peak-pin-power and rod-integrated peaking-factor limits. It was benchmarked against genetic algorithm, parallel simulated annealing, tabu search and an ensemble method.
incurred_insecurity:
A PPO agent that optimises PWR reload loading patterns against a simulator-based reward sits upstream of the licensed core design and safety analysis chain. The main exposures are that the optimiser pushes patterns to the edge of its evaluator's validity, that the evaluation loop (simulator, cross-section data, limit files, reward code, policy weights) is an integrity target, and that trust in a benchmark-proven 'optimal' result weakens independent verification. The result is a latent loss of design margin that surfaces late rather than an immediate excursion.

Reward and simulator exploitation -- implicit, exploitable
Soft penalty-encoded constraints (boron, peak pin power, rod-integrated peaking) let PPO trade evaluator blind spots such as xenon, burnup-dependent cross-sections and feedback fidelity for cycle length, producing patterns that look compliant in the low-fidelity evaluator but erode margin under licensing-grade codes. An adversary could rely on this systematic edge-seeking to hide a small evaluator or limit manipulation inside the band of apparently legitimate optimisation error.

Evaluation-loop and model integrity compromise -- adversarial
Tampering with the simulator or surrogate, cross-section libraries, assembly burnup or enrichment data, constraint files, reward-shaping code, or poisoned or backdoored policy weights and RL dependencies makes the agent actively search for patterns that satisfy the corrupted evaluator while violating real limits. If shared libraries are compromised, the downstream verification chain can be weakened too, so the margin erosion goes undetected until startup testing or in-cycle monitoring.

Insider manipulation of constraints -- adversarial
A valid-account insider can subtly alter constraint weights, limits or reward terms to bias outcomes toward a fuel-cost or schedule result while the output remains plausible. Integrity of the optimiser's behaviour is degraded without any visible model failure.

Generalisation and benchmark transfer failure -- implicit, exploitable
A policy trained on benchmark and simulated test problems degrades silently on plant-specific burnable-absorber designs, shuffling restrictions, new fuel types or changed limits while still emitting confident patterns. An adversary could use plant or cycle changes outside the training envelope to pass off a biased pattern as ordinary transfer error.

Opacity and non-repeatability -- implicit, exploitable
Seed-dependent training, stochastic rollouts and an uninspectable policy and critic make it hard to reproduce or justify why a pattern was chosen. Reviewers then cannot distinguish a genuinely novel pattern from a manipulated one, which gives an adversary cover.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Statistical superiority over GA, SA and tabu search invites reduced scrutiny of recommended patterns, and reload engineers lose heuristic design skill, so verification becomes a formality under outage schedule pressure. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust to get a manipulated pattern accepted.

Qualification and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
Academic RL code and benchmark evidence are not qualified under nuclear software QA, and weak hygiene and access control over code, dependencies, weights and data leave easy entry points. An adversary can exploit the unqualified, loosely controlled toolchain as the access path for the integrity attacks above.

Design and model exfiltration -- adversarial
Core designs, fuel-management strategy, proprietary vendor models and the trained policy can be stolen, particularly if training runs on shared HPC or cloud infrastructure. This exposes commercially sensitive information and power-distribution limits that could inform later targeting.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a reactor-operations viewpoint, the PPO agent is a search heuristic that sits upstream of the licensed core design and safety analysis chain. It proposes a loading pattern, but the pattern is only credited after the vendor or utility reload safety evaluation, with qualified neutronics codes, Technical Specification limits and independent review. That chain is the main safeguard, so the realistic harm is not that the agent directly causes a power excursion. The realistic harms are that an optimistic or distorted pattern gets through, that it is accepted with less scrutiny because it is 'optimal', or that it narrows design margin and the evidence behind it. The agent optimises against a surrogate or reduced-order neutronics evaluator and a hand-written reward with penalties for limit violations. Anything wrong in that evaluator or reward is exploited systematically, because the agent will find the corners where the model is least accurate. Consequences are cycle-length shortfalls, tight margins, late redesigns and outage-schedule or fuel-cost impacts, plus hidden loss of safety margin if downstream checks are shallow.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Reward hacking and model exploitation (OP.C0301, OP.C0303): PPO drives the pattern toward the edge of the constraints (boron concentration, FΔH/peak pin power, rod-integrated peaking), so small errors in the low-fidelity core simulator or nodal model become systematic optimistic bias. A pattern that looks compliant in the optimiser's code can fail on the licensing-grade code, or erode margin for transients, burnup-dependent effects, xenon or uncertainty allowances that the reward does not represent. Consequence: rejected designs, late fuel-procurement changes, or reduced thermal margins that the safety analysis must then catch. (2) Generalisation and benchmark limits (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.01): the results come from benchmark and test problems on extended PWR designs, which are simulated data. Real reloads involve plant-specific burnable-absorber designs, shuffling restrictions, assembly-specific burnup and tolerance data, and operational changes such as power uprates or new fuel types. Policies trained on one core may transfer poorly, and a 'statistically better than GA' result says little about worst-case behaviour on a given cycle. (3) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0402.02): stochastic training and policy sampling make it hard to reproduce or justify why a pattern was chosen. Regulators and reviewers expect traceable design basis, so the AI step adds a qualification burden (OP.C0501, OP.C0504) and a risk that it is used informally outside QA. (4) Automation bias (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06): designers who rely on the agent may lose skill in heuristic loading-pattern design, and over-trust an apparently optimal result, so verification becomes a formality. (5) Single objective (OP.C0301): maximising cycle length alone ignores secondary considerations such as shutdown margin, reactivity coefficients, discharged-fuel cost, fuel-integrity and economics, which can create hidden trade-offs.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Integrity attack on the evaluator or inputs (AML.T0010.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0018): tampering with assembly inventory, burnup or enrichment data, cross-section libraries, the surrogate model, reward code or trained policy weights, or substituting a supply-chain model or library. This yields plausible but wrong loading patterns, or patterns that quietly erode margin while appearing to meet the limits. Because the agent's output is reviewed by the same toolchain, a compromise of shared libraries or data could weaken the downstream check as well. (b) Insider or valid-account manipulation (AML.T0012, AML.T0031): subtle changes to constraint weights or limits that bias results toward a particular fuel-cost or schedule outcome. (c) Confidentiality (AML.T0025, AML.T0035, AML.T0024.002): core designs, fuel-management strategy and proprietary vendor models or data are commercially sensitive and could be exfiltrated, particularly if training runs on cloud or HPC infrastructure (OP.C0601, OP.C0505). (d) Availability (AML.T0029): denial of compute delays reload design near the outage window, but this is mitigated by the fact that legacy GA and SA tools and manual design remain available. The key mitigations are independent verification with qualified codes, hard-coded limit checks outside the agent, controlled data and model provenance, and treating the agent as an advisory generator only.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a PPO agent whose reward comes from a core physics simulator (nodal diffusion / lattice-code surrogate), so the real exposure is the agent-simulator coupling, not the policy network. PPO is an optimiser, and optimisers exploit whatever the reward function and simulator allow. If the simulator has biases, convergence tolerances or cross-section library errors, the agent will systematically find loading patterns that sit in those error regions (reward hacking / Goodhart), and it does so more effectively than GA or SA, which makes the 'surpasses legacy approaches' benchmark result a warning as well as a selling point. The results come from benchmark problems with stochastic training, and the paper compares point performance, not robustness: a policy trained on one cycle's reactivity-depletion state, burnable-poison inventory and constraint set may not transfer to a different plant, cycle or modified limits. The pipeline also has repeatability issues: seed-dependent training, stochastic search and non-unique optima make it hard to qualify and reproduce a pattern, and the policy and critic are opaque about why a pattern is preferred. Since the output feeds a safety-relevant licensing core design, the useful lens is where a poisoned or mis-specified simulator, constraint set or reward could pass unnoticed into the design basis.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: Implicit threats: (1) Reward/simulator exploitation. The agent maximises cycle length subject to penalty-encoded constraints (boron, peak pin power, rod-integrated peaking factor). Soft penalties let it trade a small constraint violation or a simulator-accuracy blind spot (xenon transients, burnup-dependent cross-sections, thermal-hydraulic feedback fidelity) for cycle length. Consequence: an optimised pattern looks compliant in the low-fidelity evaluator but breaches margins under higher-fidelity or licensing-grade codes, and the optimiser's very effectiveness concentrates risk at the edge of the model's validity. (2) OOD and transfer failure. A policy trained on specific core geometries, fuel inventories and constraint values will degrade silently on a new cycle, a new fuel type (e.g. higher enrichment, accident-tolerant fuel, extended designs) or changed operating limits, and without a trusted uncertainty estimate the output still looks confident. (3) Non-repeatability and opacity. Seed-dependent training and stochastic rollouts yield different patterns on re-runs, which weakens verification, independent reproduction and regulatory qualification. (4) Automation bias. The paper's claim of statistical superiority invites reduced independent review of the recommended pattern by reload engineers, and skill fade in manual loading-pattern design makes later disagreement harder to evaluate. (5) Data and qualification gaps. The benchmark evidence is academic and not qualified under nuclear software QA, and the validation basis for the surrogate/simulator in the optimisation loop is distinct from licensing codes. Adversarial threats: (6) Integrity attack on the evaluation loop rather than the network. Tampering with the neutronics library, cross-section data, constraint file, reward-shaping code or the simulator binary (supply-chain, insider, or compromised workstation) would steer the optimiser towards patterns that violate real limits while appearing to satisfy the modelled ones. The agent amplifies the attack because it actively searches for whatever the corrupted evaluator rewards. (7) Model and weight tampering or backdoored pretrained policies and open-source RL libraries (PPO frameworks, Python dependencies) could bias patterns toward a trigger configuration. (8) Exfiltration of optimised loading patterns, core design data and the trained policy would expose proprietary fuel-management strategy and could assist an adversary in understanding power-distribution limits. (9) Because outputs are design inputs, a downstream impact is a latent design-basis error: it would be detected late, possibly only at startup physics testing or in-cycle monitoring, which is a safety margin erosion and not an obvious failure.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, a PPO reload optimiser is a design-stage tool whose output (a loading pattern) goes into the safety-analysis and licensing chain. An adversary or a careless insider would not need to touch the reactor. They only need to bias a pattern so it sits close to a limit and still passes the checks. The agent is built to push toward the edge of the feasible region (maximum cycle length against peaking-factor, boron and pin-power constraints), so its outputs are already margin-minimising. That makes small, hard-to-notice corruption of the evaluator or constraint definitions both valuable and plausible. A nation-state would probably prefer the cheaper route of compromising the neutronics code, cross-section libraries or the reload design workflow. The RL agent is a good stepping stone, though, because it concentrates trust, produces many candidate patterns that nobody inspects individually, and its learned policy cannot be inspected.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: 1) Adversarial: corruption of the optimisation loop's inputs. The agent learns against a reward computed by a core simulator or surrogate, plus constraint limits. If an insider or a supply-chain actor alters the simulator, a surrogate, the cross-section data, the limit values or the reward shaping (AML.T0010.001/.002, AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0031), the agent will systematically converge on patterns that look compliant but have eroded real margin, such as underestimated hot-channel peaking or shutdown margin. The facility depends on the pattern then being independently verified in licensed safety-analysis codes. The consequence is a latent reduction in fuel-safety margin that surfaces only in a transient or in-core measurements. A backdoored policy or a hidden trigger (AML.T0018, AML.T0043.004) could also bias patterns only for particular fuel inventories or plant configurations. Model or policy theft (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035) exposes proprietary core designs, fuel-management strategy and burnup-limit information, which also has commercial and safeguards value. 2) Implicit weaknesses an adversary could time around: the agent reports better optimisation than GA/SA/tabu on test cases, which invites over-trust (OP.C0101.04) and skill fade in experienced reload engineers (OP.C0101.06). The policy is opaque (OP.C0401) and training is non-deterministic (OP.C0402.01), so reviewers cannot easily distinguish a legitimately novel pattern from a manipulated one, and exact reproduction for audit is hard. Benchmarks on test problems may not carry over to a real plant, with its actual burnable-poison, fuel-vendor and plant-specific constraints (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). Surrogate or reduced-order physics can diverge from licensed codes (OP.C0201.02). Ruling out an attack would require an independent re-evaluation of every candidate pattern, but automation complacency and schedule pressure during outage planning shrink that check. The pattern's novelty lowers the chance a reviewer notices anomalies. 3) Governance: there is no AI-specific qualification regime for design tools whose outputs feed licensing (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Software-hygiene and access-control weaknesses (OP.C0502, OP.C0505) on research-grade RL code, with its dependencies, pretrained weights and containers, give an insider or supply-chain actor easy access. Mitigations to emphasise are treating the optimiser as a non-safety advisory tool whose outputs are always re-verified by independent qualified codes, integrity control of the simulator, limit files and reward code, and two-person review of any changes.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on reward/simulator exploitation, evaluation-loop integrity compromise, non-repeatability/opacity and automation over-trust. Availability denial and the single-objective point were dropped as weak or restating reward misalignment, and speculative ATLAS codes such as T0044 were omitted.

evidence.citation: "Surpassing Legacy Approaches to PWR Core Reload Optimization with Single-Objective Reinforcement Learning," Nuclear Science and Engineering (Taylor & Francis / American Nuclear Society)
evidence.note: This peer-reviewed journal article applies a PPO-based deep RL agent to PWR loading-pattern optimisation. It reports that the agent is statistically better than classical stochastic optimisers (GA, simulated annealing, tabu search, ensemble) on test problems that include extended PWR designs. A related arXiv preprint of the work (2402.11040) also exists, but the cited source is the peer-reviewed version.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is evaluation-loop or model integrity compromise that erodes core design margin (peak pin power, peaking factors) and goes undetected until startup or in-cycle monitoring; this is a latent safety-margin erosion in the design chain, short of a direct release, and independent licensing-grade verification should catch much of it.

reproducibility.why: Edge-seeking against soft-penalty rewards and silent out-of-distribution degradation occur reliably once the optimizer is used against a lower-fidelity evaluator; deliberate tampering depends on gaining access but then reliably steers the agent.

exploitability.why: Deliberate integrity attacks need access to the simulator, data libraries, constraint files or weights (insider or supply-chain position) and enough domain knowledge to hide changes within plausible optimisation error, although weak toolchain hygiene lowers the barrier somewhat.

affected_users.why: A compromised or over-trusted optimizer affects the whole reload core design for a cycle and could propagate to other plants if shared libraries or models are compromised, but it remains confined to the design chain and relies on downstream verification failing.

discoverability.why: Reward hacking, simulator exploitation, benchmark-to-plant transfer failure, supply-chain and poisoning risks are well documented in the open RL literature, and the method is published openly. Only the specifics of a given site's toolchain would require deeper knowledge.

use_case: Proximal Policy Optimization deep reinforcement learning, in single-agent and multi-agent forms, for real-time control-drum adjustment in a nuclear microreactor. It follows grid load profiles in a point-kinetics model with thermal and xenon feedback. It was benchmarked against a PID controller on power-tracking error, control effort and robustness to noisy power measurements.
incurred_insecurity:
