A PPO policy that moves control drums in real time becomes a new, opaque, trusted decision-maker acting directly on core reactivity, and it was validated only in a reduced-order simulation against Gaussian noise. The main threats are sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure, reward misalignment, unverifiable and non-repeatable behavior, operator over-trust, and adversarial attacks through the sensor path, the training pipeline and the deployed weights, with fleet-wide propagation across identical microreactors. Independent protection systems would normally bound the worst consequences, so the credible harms are power excursions, trips, equipment wear and a loss of qualification confidence.

Sensor-channel adversarial inputs -- adversarial
The policy was tested only against random Gaussian noise, so structured, physically plausible spoofed or biased power, flux or temperature readings can steer a neural policy into confidently wrong drum motion that a PID would handle in a more bounded way. The attacker needs no model access, can time the attack to a grid event or xenon transient, and the effect depends on whether the protection system shares the same sensor path.

Training-pipeline and model compromise -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor who poisons the training simulator, reward function, pretrained checkpoint, ML library or deployed weights can embed a trigger-conditioned backdoor that behaves nominally in load-following benchmarks and then drives drums to erode reactivity margin under a particular power or xenon state. The weights are hard to audit, so the tampering is difficult to find in acceptance testing and can be mistaken for drift or retraining variation.

Simulation-to-reality and drift failure -- implicit, exploitable
The policy learns a point-kinetics model with lumped thermal and xenon feedback that omits spatial flux effects, drum-worth nonlinearity, actuator backlash and burnup-dependent coefficients, so off-distribution states produce confident but wrong drum commands, oscillation or xenon-driven power swings toward trip limits. An adversary could time an attack around these known weak regimes, such as xenon transients and ramp extremes, and hide a manipulation inside the resulting error band.

Reward misalignment -- implicit, exploitable
The reward trades tracking error against control effort without encoding shutdown margin, rate limits or fuel and coolant temperature margin, so the agent can learn aggressive or simulator-exploiting drum motion that looks optimal in simulation but erodes real safety margin. An adversary could use those under-weighted margins as a ready lever, nudging the plant toward the regimes where the agent is already running close to limits.

Opacity, non-repeatability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A stochastic neural policy has no stability or boundedness proof, PPO training varies across seeds, and multi-agent coordination adds emergent behavior such as one agent masking another's fault, so the policy cannot be qualified with deterministic I&C methods. A malicious weight change is then hard to distinguish from retraining variation, and weak configuration control means integrity checks may not be enforced.

Operator over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Good routine performance and the favorable PID comparison can lead operators of a small, lightly staffed or remote microreactor to disengage, lose manual-control skill and be slow to take over when the policy degrades. An adversary could time an attack to periods of lowest attention and rely on the misplaced trust to make the manipulation look like ordinary controller misbehavior.

Fleet propagation and remote update path -- implicit, exploitable
Cloning one trained policy across many microreactors, with retraining or updates delivered from offsite or cloud pipelines, turns a single flaw into a common-cause failure and creates an update channel that conventional PID control lacks. An adversary who compromises one artifact or the update channel gains fleet-wide reach, or can force fallback transitions by denying the inference or compute path.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a simulation-only study of a PPO controller driving control drums in a point-kinetics model with thermal and xenon feedback. The facility-side question is what happens if such a policy is ever put in the loop for load following. Control drums are reactivity-control devices, so a bad action from the agent acts directly on core power. Existing engineering practice would still sit between the agent and harm: the reactor protection system, scram and drum-speed or rate limits, and operator supervision. The agent therefore does not remove those barriers, but a trained policy could erode them in subtle ways, for instance by running the plant close to trip setpoints or by teaching operators to stop watching. Since the agent is trained on a reduced-order plant model, the main risks are the gap between that model and the real core, and the agent being a poorly explainable, hard-to-qualify controller in a safety-relevant loop. Adversarial exposure is mostly through the sensor and data path, model artifacts, and the training environment, and not through the model weights alone.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Simulation-to-reality gap: the policy is trained and benchmarked on a point-kinetics model with lumped thermal and xenon feedback. Real microreactor behavior involves spatial flux effects, drum-worth nonlinearity, temperature and burnup reactivity coefficients, sensor lag and actuator backlash that the model may omit. The policy could be confidently wrong, producing oscillation, xenon-driven power swings or overshoots toward trip limits. Benchmarking against PID on simulated tracking error does not demonstrate safety margin. (2) Drift and out-of-distribution operation: fuel burnup, coefficient changes, component aging and load profiles outside the training set shift the plant away from the policy's training distribution, and a neural policy extrapolates unpredictably. Robustness shown only for Gaussian measurement noise says little about bias, dropout, stuck sensors, frozen signals or correlated faults. (3) Opacity and qualification: a stochastic or opaque policy cannot be analysed with the deterministic methods used for I&C qualification, and PPO training is non-repeatable across seeds. In the multi-agent form, emergent coordination among drum agents adds further unverifiable behavior, such as one agent compensating for another's fault and masking it. (4) Reward misalignment: optimizing tracking error and control effort can trade away unmodelled objectives such as thermal stress, drum wear, fuel temperature margin and the reactivity margin needed for shutdown, and it can exploit simulator quirks. (5) Human factors: if the agent performs well routinely, operators may become complacent, lose manual-control skill, and be slow to take over when it degrades. Meanwhile, autonomous control in small, minimally staffed microreactors reduces the human oversight that would otherwise catch a fault.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Sensor and measurement manipulation: spoofed or biased neutron-flux or temperature signals, or crafted perturbations (AML.T0043, AML.T0015), could steer the policy into drum movements that depart from what the real state requires. Because the agent trusts its observations, it amplifies a data-integrity attack that a conventional PID would handle in more bounded ways. The end effect is limited if the protection system uses independent, diverse sensors, so the key question is whether the agent and the protection system share any sensor or data path. (7) Supply chain and training-pipeline compromise: a poisoned simulator, reward function, hyperparameter set, pretrained policy or ML library (AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004) could embed a latent backdoor, for example a trigger-conditioned bad action under particular load or xenon conditions. Because behavior is hard to inspect, this would be difficult to find in acceptance testing. (8) Fleet propagation: if one trained policy is cloned across many microreactors, a single compromise or flaw becomes a common-cause failure (OP.C0602). (9) Availability and update path: denial of the inference or compute path (AML.T0029) forces fallback transitions, and retraining or update channels are a new attack surface on a control system that conventional PID does not have. The credible consequences are power excursions, thermal transients, equipment wear, unplanned trips and loss of generation, and the likelihood of reaching core damage is low where independent protection exists. The more significant consequences are operational and regulatory: lost availability, and loss of confidence in the qualification basis.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a PPO policy trained entirely in simulation, on a point-kinetics model with lumped thermal and xenon feedback, to move control drums. The ML fragility sits in the sim-to-real gap and in the policy's lack of guarantees outside its training distribution. A policy trained on a low-order surrogate learns that model's dynamics and reward shaping, including its simplifications such as no spatial effects, idealized drum worth curves, ideal actuators and Gaussian-only sensor noise. It can score well on tracking error and control effort and still behave unpredictably on real drum backlash, non-Gaussian or biased sensor faults, burnup-dependent reactivity coefficients, or load profiles it never saw. The benchmark against PID with Gaussian noise is a narrow robustness test. It says little about adversarial or structured perturbations, and a neural policy has no stability proof or bounded-output guarantee comparable to a classical controller. Multi-agent PPO adds non-stationarity, coordination fragility and weaker repeatability across seeds.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure (OP.C0302, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0303). The policy is trained on simulated data from a reduced-order model. Plant parameters drift with burnup, xenon history and temperature coefficients, and these were fixed or randomized only within the training range. Off-distribution states can produce confident but wrong drum commands. The consequence is poor power tracking, thermal excursions or xenon-driven instability, with the margin to limits eroded before anyone notices. (2) Reward misalignment (OP.C0301). The reward trades off tracking error against control effort and does not encode safety limits such as rate limits, shutdown margin, or peak fuel and coolant temperature. The agent can exploit the reward, for example with aggressive drum motion that looks optimal in simulation. (3) Opacity and non-repeatability (OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0403). Seed-dependent training means a retrained policy may behave differently. There are no formal stability or boundedness guarantees, and this undermines qualification against deterministic I&C standards (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Multi-agent coordination adds emergent failures and cascading faults (OP.C0301.01, OP.C0603). (4) Automation trust (OP.C0101). Operators of a small, possibly remote or autonomous microreactor may be out of the loop and have little experience of taking over if the policy degrades. Skill fade and over-trust follow from the benchmark's favorable PID comparison. (5) Data scarcity (OP.C0203). Microreactors have little operational data, so validation cannot be done against field data.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Sensor-input evasion (AML.T0015, AML.T0043). The policy has only been tested against Gaussian noise. An adversary who can alter or spoof power or flux measurements, or who knows the observation structure, can craft small structured perturbations that push the policy into harmful drum actions. PID is more predictable under such perturbations, but the RL policy is vulnerable to crafted inputs of this kind, and the attacker needs no access to the model itself. Attack effort is further reduced by publication of the architecture and training setup (AML.T0000, AML.T0005). (7) Supply-chain and model integrity compromise (AML.T0010, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). A trained policy is a weight file that is hard to audit. Poisoned simulator parameters, a tampered training environment, a backdoored policy or compromised RL libraries could keep the policy behaving nominally until a trigger state occurs. (8) Model tampering at deployment (AML.T0076, AML.T0031). Corrupting or swapping weights or the normalization statistics is hard to distinguish from drift. (9) Remote and cloud dependencies (OP.C0601) for retraining or updates would widen the attack surface to a control-relevant system and could propagate a compromised policy across a fleet of identical microreactors (OP.C0602). Adversaries can also time attacks around known weak regimes, such as xenon transients or ramp extremes, where the policy's sim-to-real error is largest.

security_specialist.argument: Seen as a threat surface, a PPO policy that moves control drums in real time is a new, trusted actuator-side decision-maker that did not exist under PID. Its trained weights, reward function, simulator, and sensor inputs become valuable targets. A deliberate adversary, insider or supply-chain, could use the policy to cause unsafe reactivity excursions or load-following failures that look like ordinary model misbehavior. The documented system is a simulation study using a point-kinetics model with xenon and thermal feedback, and it was tested only against benign Gaussian noise. So the real exposure is the gap between that benign validation and a deployment where measurements can be manipulated, which an adversary could exploit or time an attack around. Microreactors are often remote or autonomous, with minimal staffing, which heightens the concern. Fewer operators means less human vigilance over the controller and more reliance on the AI's integrity.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL: (1) Model or training-pipeline compromise. The policy weights, reward shaping, and the point-kinetics training simulator are artifacts an insider or supply-chain actor (ML framework, pretrained checkpoints, containers) could tamper with. A poisoned or backdoored policy could behave normally across load-following benchmarks but respond to a specific trigger state, such as a particular power or xenon trajectory, by driving drums in a way that stresses reactivity margins. Because the policy is opaque, this is much harder to detect than a modified PID gain. (2) Sensor-channel adversarial inputs. The only robustness evidence is Gaussian noise. Structured, physically plausible false power readings (spoofed or subtly biased signals, crafted within the noise envelope) can push a neural policy into confidently wrong drum motion. Such inputs are not covered by random-noise testing, and a PID has different, more analyzable failure behavior. The consequence is power-tracking loss, possible excursions, or a trip, and an attacker could time this to a grid event or transient. (3) Multi-agent coordination. Agents that share observations or communicate create more channels to corrupt, and one compromised agent can degrade the others. (4) Trust concentration. If the AI replaces PID without independent diverse backup, compromising one model compromises the whole control function. It may also hide the attack by making it look like drift or poor tuning. (5) Fleet propagation. A policy replicated across a microreactor fleet means one tampered artifact has fleet-wide reach. Offsite or cloud training and update pipelines widen the exposure.

IMPLICIT (exploitable or timeable by an adversary): (a) Sim-to-real gap. A point-kinetics model omits spatial effects, drum-worth nonlinearity, and sensor and actuator dynamics. The policy may fail out of distribution, and an adversary or opportunistic event can exploit known transients. (b) Opacity and non-determinism. Stochastic training and policy variability make verification and repeatability weak, so a malicious change is hard to distinguish from retraining variation. (c) Automation complacency and skill fade. In a lightly staffed microreactor, operators lose the ability to notice or take over from a degraded controller, so an attack can be timed to when attention is lowest. (d) Reward misalignment. Optimizing tracking error and control effort may under-weight safety margins, creating exploitable behaviors. (e) Qualification gap. There is no established regulatory pathway for qualifying learned controllers, so integrity controls such as configuration management and hashing of weights may not be enforced. The consequence in all cases is degraded reactivity control and loss of operational assurance, with possible safety-relevant transients.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on sensor-path evasion, training-pipeline backdoors, sim-to-real drift, opacity and qualification, reward misalignment, operator complacency and fleet propagation, which I merged into one threat each. I dropped candidate codes without a distinct threat behind them (AML.T0031, AML.T0048, AML.T0012, AML.T0044, AML.T0059, AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0076) and kept the denial-of-service pathway as a single sentence tied to AML.T0029.

evidence.citation: "Nuclear microreactor transient and load-following control with deep reinforcement learning," Elsevier (Energy Conversion and Management: X), with Idaho National Laboratory and University of Michigan authors
evidence.note: This peer-reviewed paper builds and tests RL controllers, both single-agent and multi-agent, for microreactor control-drum load following. In simulation they matched or beat a PID controller across load-following scenarios, and they held up better when Gaussian noise was added to the power measurements. It is a simulation study, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a backdoored or spoofed-input-driven policy eroding reactivity margin, but the entry itself notes that independent protection systems would bound consequences to power excursions, trips, equipment wear and loss of qualification confidence, which is operational disruption with minor safety-margin erosion rather than release.

reproducibility.why: Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failures reliably occur in known weak regimes such as xenon transients and ramp extremes, but adversarial triggers depend on the protection system's sensor-path sharing, trigger conditions and the plant state, so reliability is conditional.

exploitability.why: The credible severe threats (training-pipeline or weight poisoning, update-channel compromise, and sensor spoofing on an instrumentation path) require insider or supply-chain position or access to the plant's instrumentation, not routine external interaction.

affected_users.why: Fleet propagation of a cloned policy and update channel turns a single flaw into a common-cause failure across identical microreactors, though each plant's protection systems limit per-site impact.

discoverability.why: Weaknesses of RL policies such as adversarial sensor inputs, poisoning, sim-to-real gap and reward misspecification are well documented in open literature, and the study is published, but knowing which plants deploy such a policy and how its sensor and update paths are built needs partial outside inference.

use_case: Gradient-based optimisation of Hanford low-activity-waste glass formulation that uses machine-learning property models (Gaussian process regression, support vector regression and artificial neural networks) with uncertainty quantification. The models predict glass properties from batch composition. They are embedded in a Gekko optimisation that sets glass-former additions to maximise waste loading within property constraints. In the demonstration they outperformed the current partial quadratic mixture models.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case puts ML property surrogates (GPR, SVR, ANN) with uncertainty quantification inside a gradient-based optimiser that sets glass-former additions for each Hanford LAW batch and pushes waste loading to the edge of the durability, viscosity, conductivity and crystallinity envelope. The optimiser concentrates and amplifies any surrogate error, whether it comes from natural extrapolation or from deliberate tampering, so the main threats are boundary-seeking extrapolation error, miscalibrated uncertainty margins, qualification and trust gaps, and integrity attacks on data, models and optimiser configuration. Consequences are mainly off-spec glass, melter upsets, rework and waste-form acceptance failures that surface late, not criticality or release. The demonstration is on a simplified problem, so the risk is prospective.

Optimiser-exploited extrapolation error -- implicit, exploitable
The optimiser drives solutions to the corner of the feasible region where lab-melt training data is sparsest, so surrogate error is largest where it is exploited and recipes pass model constraints but fail real durability or processing limits. Tank-to-tank and campaign feed variability worsens this, and an adversary could hide a small manipulation of data or inputs inside this expected model-error band, which would look like ordinary prediction error.

Miscalibrated uncertainty and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
ANN and SVR uncertainty intervals can be too narrow out of distribution, so margins sized from them are illusory. The ML models also lack the qualification history of the partial quadratic models and are non-repeatable across retraining, which blocks regulatory crediting or invites unjustified trust. An adversary could rely on this misplaced confidence and the weak review and change control around a recipe tool to slip in altered models or margins.

Automation trust under batch time pressure -- implicit, exploitable
Recipes are needed minutes after batch composition is known, so engineers have little time to cross-check against legacy models. Over-trust and skill fade follow, and the more aggressive loading objective removes the conservatism that used to hide model error. An adversary could wait for this complacency to set in before introducing a subtle bias.

Training data and model poisoning -- adversarial
A small, targeted bias in glass-property datasets, retraining records or model artefacts (including tampered libraries or model files) shifts the predicted constraint boundary, particularly for durability. The optimiser steers to the false boundary and produces plausible but unsafe recipes at scale, detected only at glass sampling or release testing and hard to attribute because it resembles model error.

Input and optimiser configuration tampering -- adversarial
Falsified batch-composition or analysis inputs, or edits to Gekko constraint bounds, uncertainty confidence levels and margins, silently convert safety margin into waste loading. The effect is similar to model tampering and is hard to separate from drift, and insiders with configuration access are the realistic actors.

Input error propagation and shared-model propagation -- implicit
Analytical bias in tank-waste batch composition is amplified by the optimiser, and a single model or constraint library reused across lines or sites spreads one flaw widely. Adversaries gain little beyond what direct tampering already offers.

Optimiser availability denial -- adversarial
Denying the optimiser or its compute forces fallback to the older quadratic models. This is a low-consequence delay provided the fallback is maintained.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a process-safety lens, this use case sets glass-former additions for each Hanford LAW melter feed batch and pushes waste loading toward the edge of the property envelope. The AI output is a recipe, not an advisory. The dangerous failure is a model that is confidently wrong near a constraint boundary, because the optimiser deliberately drives toward the boundaries (durability, viscosity, electrical conductivity, crystallinity/liquidus, sulfate and salt limits). Downstream consequences are mostly off-spec glass, melter upsets, rework and schedule loss, plus a waste-form compliance and repository-acceptance problem. These are serious but rarely acutely hazardous, and existing practice (waste form qualification, sampling and analysis of the melter feed and glass, conservative margins, the Hanford WTP compliance strategy, operator and engineer review of recipes) already provides layered defenses. The demonstration is on a simplified problem, so most risk is prospective, but the batch-by-batch minutes-scale timing is exactly where automation trust and thin review matter.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and distribution shift: GPR/SVR/ANN property models trained on historical lab-melt glass databases are being asked to predict at new Hanford waste compositions, and the optimiser seeks the corner of the feasible region where training data is sparsest. Model error is therefore concentrated exactly where it is exploited (optimiser's curse). The consequence is a recipe that passes the model's constraints but fails real durability or processing limits, producing off-spec glass or melter problems. Relevant: OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0201.04/OP.C0201.05 (lab-melt data transferred to plant conditions), OP.C0303. (2) Uncertainty quantification miscalibration: the UQ methods are only as good as their assumptions, and an ANN or SVR may report narrow intervals out of distribution. If the margin is sized from that UQ, the safety margin is illusory. This is OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0402 (retraining or seed non-repeatability changes the recipe for the same feed). (3) Automation trust under time pressure: recipes are needed minutes after the batch composition is known. Operators and engineers have little time to second-guess, which invites over-trust. Skill erosion in the mixture-model and glass-chemistry judgment compounds this, and a more aggressive waste-loading objective reduces the conservatism that earlier hid model error. Relevant: OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0301 (the objective rewards loading over margin). (4) Qualification gap: the existing partial quadratic models have a regulatory and qualification history, while ML models do not, and Gekko solver convergence or local-optimum behavior is a further unverified layer. Relevant: OP.C0501, OP.C0504, OP.C0502. (5) Input errors propagate: batch composition from tank-waste sampling and analysis carries analytical error, and an optimiser amplifies bias in it (OP.C0603, OP.C0204). Drift of the waste feed over the campaign is another concern (OP.C0302.01).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training or lab-data poisoning or supply-chain tampering (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059, AML.T0031): subtle bias in the property datasets or in the model files, aimed at one property such as durability, would produce plausible but unsafe recipes, and the optimiser's boundary-seeking behavior would exploit it. Because the effect is a gradual or batch-specific drift in glass quality rather than an alarm, detection could lag until glass sampling or release testing, and the harm is a repository-compliance or integrity problem for the waste form. (b) Tampering with the batch composition input or constraint and limit files fed into the optimiser (the Gekko model, bounds, UQ confidence levels) has an effect similar to model tampering and would be hard to distinguish from drift. Relevant: AML.T0081-style configuration modification, AML.T0043 in the input sense, AML.T0076. (c) Availability: denial of the optimiser or its compute (AML.T0029) forces fallback to the older models, which is a low-consequence delay, provided the fallback is maintained. The key judgement is that consequences are mainly quality, schedule and compliance, not criticality or release, and independent glass sampling, property verification and margin to limits are the safeguards that must also fail for real harm, so the risk grows if these are relaxed because the ML models appear better.

ai_engineer.argument: The core ML fragility is that a gradient-based optimiser is an adversarial search against its own surrogate. Maximising waste loading under property constraints pushes the solution to the boundary of the feasible region, which is also where the training data is sparsest (glass compositions near the edge of the qualified envelope). GPR, SVR and ANN surrogates are interpolators, so they are weakest in precisely the region the optimiser selects. The ML models beat the partial quadratic mixture models on a simplified problem, but that gain probably comes from flexibility fitted to lab-melt and legacy test-matrix data. The models were not shown to be valid for extrapolated, drifting or off-nominal feedstock. Calibration of the uncertainty quantification is the critical unknown: UQ methods are often overconfident out-of-distribution, and the chance-constraint margins are only as good as that calibration. Because glass formulation is the control that bounds product durability, a silent surrogate error does not show up as a plant fault. It shows up later as a nonconforming waste form.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Optimiser-exploited surrogate error and OOD extrapolation (OP.C0302, OP.C0403). Maximising loading drives the solution to the edge of the training envelope. Feedstock chemistry varies from tank to tank and changes as retrieval and pretreatment change (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). The models are trained on lab-melt or simulated test matrices (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.04, OP.C0201.03), not full-scale melter operating data. Sparse coverage of rare compositions (OP.C0202) produces confidently wrong predictions on durability, viscosity or conductivity constraints. The consequence is out-of-spec glass, rework, or a disposal-acceptance problem that is detected late because product verification is sampled. (2) UQ miscalibration and qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401). The regulatory basis for glass formulation rests on validated, explainable mixture models with documented applicability bounds. ANN and SVR models are opaque, and their retraining is non-deterministic (OP.C0402.01). The qualification and applicability-domain basis would have to be re-established. Without it the system either cannot be credited (disuse) or is over-trusted (OP.C0101.04) because 'uncertainty-aware' outputs look rigorous. Short decision windows, with composition known minutes beforehand, encourage automation bias and skill fade among the formulation engineers. (3) Lifecycle drift and static versus dynamic mismatch (OP.C0302.02). Melter, feed and glass-former supply changes shift the property relationships. Without a monitoring and retraining plan the models degrade silently, and unversioned retraining can alter safety margins between campaigns.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (4) Data and artefact poisoning (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0059). Small, curated glass-property datasets are easy to bias. A subtle shift in a few property measurements, or in the lab-database records used for retraining, moves the surrogate's predicted constraint boundary. The optimiser then amplifies this by steering to the false boundary, so an adversary needs only a small, targeted perturbation to cause out-of-spec glass at scale. (5) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0015). Falsified or biased batch-composition or sampling-analysis inputs would be treated as ground truth by a system that adds additives within minutes. Because the models are differentiable, gradients also expose where the surrogate is most sensitive, which makes crafting inputs easy for anyone with model access (AML.T0044, AML.T0024.002). (6) Supply chain and software hygiene (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, OP.C0502). The pipeline depends on open-source ML and optimisation libraries (Gekko, scikit-learn-style or deep-learning stacks) and pretrained or retrained artefacts. A tampered library or model file affects the formulation of every batch (OP.C0602, OP.C0603). A compromised surrogate also gives plausible-looking output that is hard to distinguish from honest model error, which supports deniability.

security_specialist.argument: Seen as an adversary would see it, this use case is a poor direct target. It is an advisory, offline-style recipe optimiser for vitrification, and it has no obvious route to a radiological release or to nuclear material diversion. The threat is quieter. The optimiser sits upstream of the physical glass-former recipe, and its whole value is that it pushes waste loading to the edge of the property-constraint envelope. A small, undetected bias in the property models, whether from poisoned data, tampering or ordinary drift, would therefore be turned directly into recipes that sit closer to or beyond the limits for durability, viscosity, electrical conductivity and crystallinity. It also invites automation trust: batch composition is known only minutes before the recipe is needed, so time pressure discourages independent checking. An insider or supply-chain actor who can alter the training data, the model artifacts or the Gekko constraint definitions would gain a low-visibility way to cause off-spec glass, melter upsets, or waste forms that fail acceptance criteria. This would be hard to attribute because it looks like model error.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity attack on the property models or their training and test data (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0059, T0031). The mechanism is a slight, targeted bias in GPR/SVR/ANN predictions, or in the uncertainty estimates, in the high-loading region the optimiser seeks. The facility depends on those predictions to keep glass within durability and processing limits. The consequence is off-spec glass, melter or process upsets, rework, or waste-form acceptance and long-term performance failures that may only surface after the glass is poured. The optimiser's drive toward constraint boundaries amplifies small perturbations, and ML models are opaque enough to hide the manipulation as ordinary prediction error. (2) Tampering with the optimisation layer: modification of Gekko constraint bounds, uncertainty margins, or confidence-level settings (AML.T0081, T0076, T0010.001). This is a trivially small edit with large effect, since loosening a margin silently converts safety margin into waste loading. Insiders with configuration access are the realistic actors. Many facilities treat a recipe tool as non-safety business software, so access control and change management may be weak (OP.C0502, OP.C0505.01, OP.C0503). (3) Timing and vigilance exploitation: operators who see a long run of good recommendations may stop cross-checking against the legacy quadratic model, particularly under minutes-scale batch timing. An adversary could wait for that complacency before acting (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). (4) Stepping-stone and denial risks: a model-serving or optimisation host on the plant network becomes a foothold, and degrading the tool (AML.T0029) forces fallback to conservative recipes, reducing throughput on a schedule-critical mission. This is low-value for a sophisticated actor compared with easier targets, so I would rate it moderate rather than high. IMPLICIT. (5) Extrapolation and drift: the models are trained on limited, lab-measured or simulated glass data, and Hanford waste compositions are heterogeneous, so a new waste stream or the pull toward higher loading can leave the training envelope, where GPR/ANN predictions degrade and uncertainty estimates can be miscalibrated (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0201.01/.04, OP.C0202). An adversary could exploit or time an attack around this. (6) Qualification gap: a demonstration on a simplified problem is not qualified for the full property-constraint set or for regulated waste-form acceptance, and non-determinism across training runs and UQ methods complicates repeatability and review (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0401). (7) Concentrated trust: if one validated model set or constraint library is reused across lines or sites, a single flaw or compromise propagates widely (OP.C0602, OP.C0603).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on boundary-seeking extrapolation error, UQ miscalibration, qualification gap and poisoning or tampering of data, models and configuration. I dropped speculative codes with weak support (e.g., AML.T0044, AML.T0024.002, AML.T0015) and kept narrow items like denial and propagation as brief separate threats.

evidence.citation: "Machine Learning with Gradient-Based Optimization of Nuclear Waste Vitrification with Uncertainties and Constraints," Processes (MDPI); PNNL-authored work
evidence.note: The paper addresses how to choose glass-former additions for each batch at the Hanford LAW vitrification facility when batch composition is known only minutes beforehand. It builds GPR, SVR and ANN property models with several uncertainty-quantification methods and implements them in Gekko. In a simplified waste-loading maximisation problem, the ML models performed better than the partial quadratic mixture model. This is a demonstration on a simplified optimisation problem, not a plant deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is training data or model poisoning, or configuration tampering, that silently converts safety margin into waste loading. This yields off-spec glass, melter upsets, rework and late waste-form acceptance failures. The entry itself says consequences are not criticality or release, so this is operational disruption and erosion of waste-form margin.

reproducibility.why: Optimiser-driven boundary seeking reliably concentrates surrogate error in sparse-data regions, and tampering with data or constraint bounds reliably shifts the recipes once access exists. Detection of the resulting failures at sampling is a separate matter.

exploitability.why: Realistic adversarial paths (poisoning datasets or retraining records, editing optimiser constraints and margins) require insider or privileged access to data pipelines and configuration, and the entry names insiders as the realistic actors. The implicit weaknesses need no exploitation to occur, but deliberately timing around them still takes access.

affected_users.why: One flawed model or constraint library reused across lines or sites can spread a flaw widely, so the effect can cover a whole vitrification line or campaign. The impact stays within the waste-form and melter domain and does not propagate across coupled safety systems.

discoverability.why: Surrogate extrapolation error, miscalibrated uncertainty, over-trust and data poisoning are well documented in the open literature. The source paper is public and describes the architecture and the use of ML property models with an optimiser. Specific data and configuration details remain internal, but the weakness class is evident from public information.

use_case: Quality-control classification of fabricated nuclear fuel pellets as good or defective. Features are extracted from photographed and scanned pellet images and fed to three neural network types: supervised backpropagation, supervised fuzzy ARTMAP, and unsupervised ART2-A. The aim is to automate manual pellet inspection on the fuel fabrication line, with higher accuracy and speed and lower worker radiation dose.
incurred_insecurity:
Automating the good/defective release decision on fuel pellets turns a human-vigilance barrier into a small, opaque, data-dependent software decision that is only a feasibility result on one plant's samples. The main threats are silent false acceptance of defective pellets through drift and rare-defect blindness, erosion of independent human and sampling checks, non-repeatable and unqualified model behaviour, and adversarial manipulation of training data, models, imaging inputs or logged results.

Distribution shift and silent drift -- implicit, exploitable
Camera ageing, lighting, powder lot, furnace profile or new pellet design changes shift the extracted image features, so the networks keep emitting confident labels while defective pellets pass; unsupervised ART2-A categories and fuzzy ARTMAP category proliferation make this worse. An adversary could hide a gradual manipulation of inputs or training data inside the drift band, since anomalous pass rates get attributed to process variation.

Small-data and low base-rate blindness -- implicit, exploitable
A feasibility set of limited plant samples with rare, long-tail defects (including subsurface cracks that photographs cannot show) makes headline accuracy overstate recall, leaving the false-accept rate on rare or novel defects uncharacterised and allowing escaped pellets to cause latent cladding or fuel-performance problems in-reactor. An adversary could introduce a defect type or surface appearance outside the thin training coverage, knowing the model has no basis to flag it.

Automation trust and erosion of independent checks -- implicit, exploitable
Once the AI pass decision becomes the de facto release authority, inspectors lose skill and complacency sets in, and the dose-saving goal pushes toward reduced manual or gauging sampling, removing the independent check that would catch drift or tampering. An adversary could time a quiet poisoning or evasion to this complacency, relying on the misplaced trust in the classifier.

Qualification, opacity and non-repeatability gap -- implicit, exploitable
Random initialisation in backpropagation, presentation-order dependence in ARTMAP and the vigilance parameter in ART2-A mean retraining yields different decision boundaries, and the opaque outputs resist audit or root-cause analysis, so the method is not a qualified nuclear QA inspection. An adversary could use unexplained model changes and the lack of a validated baseline to pass a tampered retrain as routine version variation.

Training data, model and toolchain poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or compromised vendor or engineering workstation can alter training images, labels, retraining data, weights or feature-extraction code, or embed a trigger such as a surface marking, so that a chosen defect class reliably passes while average accuracy stays high. The consequence is a persistent, deniable route to defective fuel entering rods.

Evasion at the imaging and feature layer -- adversarial
Manipulating lighting, camera or scanner settings, pellet surface treatment or placement, or perturbing the hand-engineered features can push defective pellets across the decision boundary into acceptance, or push good ones to reject to disrupt throughput. Physical access to the imaging station is sufficient and bypasses the QA barrier.

Model and image-archive exfiltration -- adversarial
Insider access to pellet image archives, labels and model internals exposes fabrication tolerances and throughput, and extracting the model reveals defect thresholds an adversary can then tune evasion against.

Classification-record manipulation and diversion masking -- adversarial
If reject and scrap counts are logged from classifier output, falsified or mislabelled results can hide a rejected batch or disguise diverted enriched pellets as defective scrap, degrading material accountancy. Denial or corruption of the service additionally forces fallback to manual inspection with the dose and throughput costs the system was meant to avoid.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From the fuel-fabrication floor, this classifier sits at a quality gate: its output decides which sintered pellets go on to rod loading and which are rejected. A false 'good' call on a cracked, chipped, end-capped or dimensionally out-of-spec pellet is the dangerous error. That pellet could become a latent cladding-interaction or fuel-performance problem that only shows up in-reactor, years later. The feasibility study used plant-supplied samples with high success rates, but defect classes are rare in production, imaging conditions vary between lines, and lighting, camera and sintering-furnace changes shift the image statistics. The real hazard is therefore quiet acceptance of marginal pellets, not a dramatic failure. Existing practice offers partial protection: dimensional gauging, density and chemistry sampling, rod-level gamma scanning and X-ray or helium-leak checks, plus lot acceptance statistics. These only help if the AI is not allowed to displace them or to reduce the sampling rate.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift and drift: camera ageing, illumination changes, pellet-surface or powder-lot changes and furnace-profile changes alter the extracted features. The network then silently misclassifies. Unsupervised ART2-A is especially exposed because its category formation can drift or create unintended clusters, and fuzzy ARTMAP is prone to category proliferation and order-dependence. (2) Small-data and low base-rate: defects are rare and the feasibility sample is small, so reported accuracy hides poor recall on rare or novel defect types, such as subsurface cracks that photographs cannot show. Accuracy is the wrong metric. The consequence is escaped defective pellets entering fuel rods, which is a fuel-integrity and licensing problem rather than an immediate radiological event. (3) Automation bias and skill fade: inspectors who stop looking closely once the AI is trusted, together with reduced manual sampling justified by the dose-saving goal, remove the independent check that would catch drift. (4) Qualification gap and opacity: a feasibility result on lab-photographed samples is not a qualified QA method under nuclear quality assurance (for example, 10 CFR 50 Appendix B-type programs). Non-deterministic training, such as random initialisation and presentation order in backpropagation and ART, makes retraining non-repeatable and complicates configuration control. Feature-extraction preprocessing errors can also propagate unnoticed. (5) Over-rejection or under-rejection from a misaligned threshold can cause throughput and cost pressure that pushes operators to loosen it.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) An insider or supply-chain actor could poison the training set, alter labels or retraining data, tamper with the model or feature-extraction code, or modify camera or lighting parameters. This would bias the classifier toward accepting a specific defect type, which is a plausible sabotage route for degrading fuel quality or undermining a customer's confidence. Physical access to the imaging station is enough to craft inputs, for example surface treatments or placement that evade detection. (7) Manipulating logged classification results could hide a rejected batch or falsify records. This also touches safeguards: pellet counts and rejects feed material accountancy, so a classifier that mislabels or silently diverts 'defective' pellets to scrap or rework streams can mask diversion of enriched material. (8) Denial of the AI service, or tampering with it, forces fallback to manual inspection and the associated dose and throughput costs. Overall, the consequences are bounded by independent downstream checks, but only if those checks are retained, so the main vulnerability is organisational erosion of defence-in-depth around a model that is hard to audit.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small-data, imbalanced, image-feature classifier in which the pipeline matters as much as the model. The feasibility study used a limited set of pellets from one plant, photographed and scanned under controlled conditions, with hand-engineered features feeding three shallow networks. Real fabrication lines have a very low defect base rate and a long tail of defect types (chips, cracks, end-capping, density and surface anomalies), so a high accuracy figure on a curated balanced sample says little about recall on rare defects in production. The deeper fragility is the gap between a feasibility dataset and a qualified production inspector: lighting, camera, lot, powder and sintering-process drift all move the feature distribution, and the three architectures fail differently. Backprop is opaque and overconfident out-of-distribution. Fuzzy ARTMAP is order-dependent, so training is not repeatable and it can proliferate categories. ART2-A is unsupervised, so its clusters need not map to good versus defective, and a vigilance parameter silently decides what counts as 'new'.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Distribution shift and drift (OP.C0302, .01, .03). Camera or lighting changes, new pellet geometries, new enrichment or MOX or gadolinia lots, and sintering changes all alter the extracted features. The failure is silent: the classifier still emits confident labels, and defective pellets pass into fuel rods. The consequence is a latent fuel-quality defect, with possible in-reactor cladding or thermal-performance problems, and a degraded quality-assurance record. (2) Small-data and low-base-rate problem (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.05). Few real defect examples, one plant's samples and balanced evaluation sets overstate performance. False-accept rate on rare defects is the safety-relevant metric and is statistically poorly characterised. (3) Repeatability and qualification (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0401, OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0403). ARTMAP is sensitive to presentation order, backprop to initialisation, and ART2-A to vigilance. Retraining therefore produces a different decision boundary, which is hard to qualify under fuel-fabrication QA regimes built around fixed, validated inspection methods. Opaque decisions hinder audit and root-cause analysis. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). Once manual inspection is displaced, inspector skill fades and the AI's pass decision becomes the de facto release authority, with no independent check on its blind spots. (5) Goal misalignment (OP.C0301). Optimising overall accuracy or throughput rather than defect-miss cost, and unsupervised clusters being read as quality classes.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Data and model integrity (AML.T0020, T0018.000, T0010.002/.003, T0031, T0059). Training or retraining images and labels are an integrity-critical asset. Poisoning, label flipping or a backdoor trigger (T0043.004), such as a subtle surface pattern, could make a class of defective pellets reliably pass. Because the model is small and its data flows are on-site, an insider or a compromised engineering workstation or vendor toolchain is the realistic vector. (7) Evasion (AML.T0015, T0043). Hand-crafted features are easy to reverse-engineer. Someone with access to the imaging station or the model could cause imperceptible changes to images or sensor inputs that shift the features across the decision boundary. This is also possible via the physical environment (T0041) through lighting or surface treatment. The consequence is concealed substandard fuel, a sabotage or fraud route that bypasses QA. (8) Availability and manipulation of the inspection chain (AML.T0029, T0076). Corrupting model files or the preprocessing pipeline, or denying the service, forces a fallback to manual inspection, with the dose and throughput costs the system was meant to avoid. Implicit weaknesses such as drift and unexplained confidence give an adversary cover, because anomalous pass rates are readily attributed to 'process variation'.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this classifier makes a pellet's accept/reject decision a software outcome, and that is the real security change. Pellet defects (cracks, chips, density or dimensional faults, enrichment or material mix-ups) are a quality and safety barrier for downstream fuel performance. An insider or supply-chain adversary who can touch the training images, labels, feature extractor or model weights could create a persistent, deniable way to let chosen defective pellets through. They could also cause mass false rejects to disrupt production. A nation-state would more likely pick easier routes (the fabrication process, supplier records, accounting data), so the AI is best viewed as one point where inspection trust concentrates, and where a human inspector's vigilance is replaced and then fades. The same inspection images and counts also feed material accounting, which creates a safeguards-adjacent concern. The source is only a feasibility study on plant-supplied samples, so deployment gaps in qualification, drift and governance are what an adversary would time an attack around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Poisoning or backdoor of the classifier: an insider or compromised vendor alters labelled training images, labels, or weights (a trigger such as a surface pattern, lighting artifact or marking) so a specific defect class is passed as good. Dependency: the fuel-quality acceptance barrier. Consequence: defective pellets enter rods, which reduces fuel integrity and may cause later cladding or performance failures. This is hard to detect because average accuracy stays high. (2) Evasion at the imaging/feature-extraction layer: the physical scene, lighting, camera or scanner settings, or the feature pipeline is manipulated so defective pellets look good, or good pellets look defective to cause throughput denial. Consequence: bad pellets accepted, or the line disrupted. (3) Compromise of the software and model supply chain, such as training code, libraries, and the retraining and update path, plus the unsupervised ART2-A network's self-organizing categories, which an adversary can bias gradually by feeding skewed input. (4) Insider access to image archives and model internals: images of pellets and the line expose fabrication specifications, tolerances and throughput, which is proliferation-sensitive and commercially sensitive, and model extraction or inversion could expose defect thresholds an adversary could then tune against. (5) Material accounting and diversion masking: if pellet counts, rejects and scrap are logged by the classifier, then manipulated reject/scrap records could hide diverted pellets as rejected scrap, so the model's outputs become a trusted record in a safeguards chain.

IMPLICIT, EXPLOITABLE. (a) Automation trust and skill fade: once manual inspection is displaced, inspectors lose skill and stop second-checking, so rare defects or a quiet poisoning go unnoticed (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102). An adversary can time action to this complacency. (b) Small-data and low-base-rate problems: defects are rare, labelled samples from a single plant are few, and the model is validated on limited samples rather than production lines, so the model misses novel defect types (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.05). (c) Drift and heterogeneity: new batches, tooling wear, lighting changes, new fuel designs or enrichment variants shift the images and degrade accuracy silently (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). (d) Qualification and governance gap: neural networks, particularly the opaque backprop and unsupervised variants, lack an established qualification basis for a quality barrier, and are hard to explain or reproduce (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402.01, OP.C0504). (e) Data access governance: image and label stores treated as ordinary QA data rather than security-relevant (OP.C0505.01).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on drift, small-data blindness, automation trust and qualification/opacity as the implicit threats, and on poisoning, evasion and supply-chain integrity as the adversarial core; I kept the security specialist's distinct exfiltration and records-manipulation threats. I dropped speculative or weakly argued codes (e.g. OP.C0301, OP.C0603, AML.T0012) and the cross-framework overlap in the list of integrity techniques was kept only where traceable to text.

evidence.citation: "Nuclear fuel pellet inspection using artificial neural networks," Journal of Nuclear Materials (Elsevier)
evidence.note: The paper studies whether neural networks can replace manual visual inspection of fabricated fuel pellets. It compares backpropagation, fuzzy ARTMAP and ART2-A networks on sample pellets supplied by a fuel fabrication plant, and finds that a well-trained supervised network classifies good versus bad pellets with a high success rate. This is a feasibility study on real pellet samples, not a production deployment.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is classification-record manipulation and diversion masking, which degrades material accountancy by disguising diverted enriched pellets as scrap; defective fuel escaping into rods and causing latent in-reactor fuel-performance problems is a close second. Neither is a direct radiological release, so this falls just short of the maximum.

reproducibility.why: Drift, rare-defect blindness and a classifier that is not fully characterised are systematic properties of this class of AI system and recur reliably. Poisoning and evasion also work reliably once access exists, though the insider position is a conditional factor.

exploitability.why: The adversarial threats (data and model poisoning, record falsification) generally require insider or supply-chain access to the fabrication line. Imaging-station evasion needs only physical access, and the implicit drift and complacency weaknesses need no special tooling, so the class sits at a moderate level.

affected_users.why: Impact spans the fuel fabrication line's QA and accountancy for every affected pellet batch, and defective fuel could propagate downstream to fuel rods and reactor operation. It is still confined to one inspection function and facility rather than coupled plant-wide systems.

discoverability.why: Drift, small-data blindness, non-repeatability, automation complacency and image-classifier evasion are well documented in the open literature, and the source paper is public and describes the networks used. Learning of a specific plant's data coverage or controls would still need some inside knowledge.

use_case: Robotised retrieval and sorting of legacy UNGG reactor waste from Silo 130 at Orano La Hague. A 3D vision system and laser reconstruct each extracted waste piece in 3D. A tree-based machine-learning classifier then identifies the piece as aluminium, magnesium or graphite. This lets operators quantify and regulate the magnesium content of each waste container, which limits hydrogen release during later storage.
incurred_insecurity:
This use case turns a safety-relevant physical property, magnesium content per waste container, which bounds hydrogen generation in storage, into a number produced by a tree-based classifier. The classifier was trained and exercised on simulants, not on real Silo 130 debris, and it infers material only from 3D shape. The main threats are a simulant-to-field generalisation gap, drift in the sensing and waste population, closed-set overconfidence, over-trust in aggregated inventories, an immature qualification regime, and an insider or supply-chain integrity attack that biases Mg declarations. A deliberate bias would look like ordinary model error, so the implicit weaknesses and the adversarial path reinforce each other.

Simulant-to-field domain shift -- implicit, exploitable
Training and validation on simulants leaves the model's accuracy on corroded, oxidised, sludge-coated, fragmented and irradiated Mg, Al and graphite pieces unknown, so out-of-distribution errors can systematically under-call Mg. The container Mg budget then understates later hydrogen generation, a late and silent storage-safety consequence. With no real-waste baseline, an adversary could hide a deliberate bias inside this expected error band.

Operational and sensor drift -- implicit, exploitable
Waste composition changes as retrieval goes deeper, and lighting, laser reflectivity, radiation-degraded cameras and calibration drift shift the 3D features without any model change. A slow shift can go unalerted against a static validation. An adversary could cause or time a perturbation of the scene or calibration to ride this unmonitored drift.

Closed-set overconfidence and proxy limits -- implicit
Shape-to-material correlation is not causal, Mg and Al fragments can look alike, and a three-label tree classifier has no reject option, so steel, sludge, composites and unknown items are forced into one class with confident labels. Errors are correlated rather than random, so they accumulate into a biased container inventory. An adversary gains little here beyond what the domain-shift weakness already offers.

Over-trust, skill fade and error propagation -- implicit, exploitable
Operators and regulators may treat per-container Mg totals as measurements rather than estimates with uncertainty, and manual cross-checks and identification skills may fade. One bias then propagates into the container records, the storage safety case and waste-acceptance decisions. An adversary could time a manipulation to this complacency window, relying on the misplaced trust to avoid independent sampling.

Qualification, versioning and repeatability gap -- implicit, exploitable
There is no clear AI-specific qualification regime, retraining or revalidation trigger, or version control for a model behind a safety-relevant waste parameter, and small retraining changes can move tree boundaries unpredictably. This weakens waste-package traceability and gives an adversary an unchallenged channel for changing the model or data.

Model, data and supply-chain integrity attack -- adversarial
An insider or compromised contractor with access to simulant datasets, feature code, serialized tree models or calibration could poison data, alter thresholds or insert a trigger-based bias that under-calls Mg only under certain geometries. This would evade simulant acceptance testing and cause under-declared Mg inventories, with delayed hydrogen-related storage hazards and regulatory non-compliance.

Sensor-stream and scene manipulation -- adversarial
Tampering with vision or laser inputs, calibration targets, or the surface or lighting of pieces can cause targeted misclassification or force operator intervention, with no cyber access to the model itself.

Record falsification and denial -- adversarial
Classification logs and container ledgers underpinning declared contents can be falsified, undermining waste accountancy and safeguards-relevant inventory declarations. Denial or corruption of the classifier would stall the retrieval campaign, a lesser availability harm.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a waste-operations view, the classifier is a quantitative control on a real process hazard: magnesium content per container drives radiolytic and corrosion hydrogen generation in later storage, so a systematic misclassification (Mg called Al or graphite) shifts the inventory estimate that underpins container loading limits. The model was developed over about five years and exercised on nuclear-waste simulants, not on the real Silo 130 population, which is old, corroded, fragmented, oxidised, possibly coated with sludge, and radiologically hot. Visual and 3D shape cues are an indirect proxy for material identity, since Mg and Al cladding fragments can look alike, so the model's real-world error rate is uncertain and an unmeasured bias could accumulate across hundreds of containers. Existing practice (conservative Mg assumptions, container limits, venting/hydrogen monitoring, periodic sampling) offers a barrier, but only if the AI-derived numbers are treated as an estimate with a quantified uncertainty and not as a measurement.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Simulant-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01/.02/.03, OP.C0302, OP.C0203): training and validation on simulants means the classifier meets surface degradation, contamination, debris, lighting/camera fouling by radiation, and piece geometry never represented. The failure mechanism is out-of-distribution misclassification. The dependence is the per-container Mg inventory. The consequence is underestimated Mg, hence higher-than-assumed hydrogen generation and corrosion in storage, with possible overpressure or flammable-gas accumulation if downstream hydrogen controls are also inadequate. Overestimating Mg instead causes unnecessary container use, dose, and cost. (2) Operational drift (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303): waste composition changes as retrieval proceeds deeper into the silo, and sensor degradation or recalibration shifts the 3D reconstruction. Static validation does not capture this, and nothing may alert operators to a slow shift. (3) Small-data and base-rate issues (OP.C0202, OP.C0701): rare materials or ambiguous pieces are poorly represented, and ground truth for real legacy waste is hard to obtain (destructive assay is difficult on highly active pieces), so the verification of true accuracy is itself weak. (4) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0401): operators and the regulator may over-trust a tree-based model that appears interpretable, and errors that are correlated (the same pieces misclassified the same way) will not average out across a container. Fewer manual cross-checks over time (skill fade) would remove the compensating barrier. (5) Governance (OP.C0501, OP.C0502): a lack of AI-specific qualification for a model supporting a safety-relevant waste acceptance parameter, plus retraining or model version changes during a multi-year campaign, creates a traceability and repeatability gap for the waste package records.

ADVERSARIAL threats. Ultimately a lower-probability class, because the system is likely air-gapped within a hot-cell environment, but consequential. (a) Integrity attacks on the model, training data or software supply chain (AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0059, AML.T0076) could introduce a subtle, targeted bias (for example, misclassifying Mg as Al only under certain geometry or size conditions) that evades acceptance testing on simulants, silently degrading the hydrogen-limiting control and producing a latent hazard or later regulatory and records-integrity problem. (b) Manipulating the sensor stream or the 3D reconstruction (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, physical access under AML.T0041) could produce misclassification at scale or force excessive operator intervention. (c) Denial or corruption of the classifier or its data (AML.T0029, AML.T0031) would stall the retrieval campaign, with an operational consequence for a legacy-risk reduction programme. An insider or maintenance-channel actor is the most plausible path. For all of these, the realistic harm depends on the failure of independent barriers (conservative Mg margins, sampling audits, hydrogen venting and monitoring), so these barriers should be kept independent of the model's output and used to verify it.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this is a small tabular/geometry-feature classifier (tree-based, likely random forest or gradient boosting on 3D-reconstruction descriptors) whose most fragile element is data provenance: it was developed over about five years and exercised on nuclear-waste simulants, not on real Silo 130 debris. Real UNGG waste (Mg-alloy cladding, graphite sleeves, Al components) has decades of corrosion, oxidation, sludge coating, fragmentation, deformation and underwater or dry-storage surface states that simulants likely cannot reproduce. The classifier is therefore operating under a systematic simulant-to-field domain shift (OP.C0201.01/.02/.03, OP.C0302). The classifier also sees only geometry and shape, so it infers material from a proxy: shape-to-material correlation is not causal, and that is the core ML-theoretic limitation. The output feeds a quantitative safety parameter (Mg inventory per container, which is tied to hydrogen generation), so a small per-piece error rate accumulates into a biased container-level inventory, and tree models give confident discrete labels with no native out-of-distribution signal.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Simulant-to-field domain shift: training and validation on simulants means true accuracy on corroded, coated, fragmented, occluded or unforeseen waste is unknown. Mg is the safety-critical class, so systematic misclassification of Mg as Al or graphite (or vice versa) biases the container Mg budget and understates hydrogen-generation potential during later storage; this is a safety consequence that appears late and silently (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (2) Small-data and class-imbalance problems: rare piece types, mixed or composite objects, and non-trio materials (steel, concrete, sludge, unknown items) are forced into one of three labels because a closed-set tree classifier has no reject option; this leads to overconfident output for OOD inputs (OP.C0202, OP.C0403, OP.C0302). (3) Sensor-to-model coupling: the 3D reconstruction depends on lighting, turbidity or dust, laser reflectivity of metal surfaces, radiation-induced camera degradation, and calibration drift; any feature-distribution shift upstream changes the model's inputs without any model change (OP.C0302.01). (4) Aggregation and automation bias: operators regulate container loading by per-piece labels and may treat the quantified Mg content as ground truth rather than a probabilistic estimate with an error bar; without confidence propagation or periodic independent verification (sampling, NDA, destructive assay), errors are not caught (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401, OP.C0603). (5) Lifecycle and qualification gap: a five-year bespoke development with no clear AI-specific qualification regime, retraining or revalidation trigger, or versioning and reproducibility controls for a safety-relevant classification (OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0402.01). Small changes to the retraining set or hyperparameters can shift tree boundaries unpredictably. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training-data or model poisoning and supply-chain compromise: the simulant datasets, feature-extraction code and serialized model files are small, high-value artifacts; tampering such as shifting thresholds or a subtle label bias toward under-calling Mg would be hard to detect and would be consistent with plausible drift, so an insider or compromised vendor (Siléane/Orano/consultant toolchain) could degrade the Mg inventory accuracy (AML.T0020, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0031). (7) Evasion and sensor-level manipulation: tampering with vision/laser inputs, calibration targets or point-cloud preprocessing could cause targeted misclassification without touching the model (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). The attack surface is small and mostly insider or supply-chain, but the consequence, a falsified Mg inventory that could cause a later hydrogen-related storage incident or waste-acceptance non-compliance, is material. (8) Record integrity: classification logs that underpin the declared container content are a target for falsification (AML.T0059), which also undermines waste-package traceability and regulatory inventory declarations.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, the classifier is a quiet control point. It converts a safety-relevant physical property (magnesium inventory per container, which bounds hydrogen generation in storage) into a software-derived number that operators and regulators will come to trust. An insider or supply-chain adversary does not need to touch the robot or the waste. Biasing the Mg/Al/graphite decision, or the training and calibration data behind it, could silently shift the declared inventory of every container. The effect would only surface years later as a storage-safety or waste-acceptance problem, long after the attacker could be identified. Non-adversarial weaknesses make this worse. The model was trained on simulants and not on real, corroded, contaminated and irradiated legacy pieces, and the documented source gives little performance detail. An adversary could therefore hide deliberate manipulation inside what looks like ordinary distribution shift, and the facility would struggle to tell the two apart. I would rate this a medium-value target for a nation-state, because Silo 130 is a legacy site and the main prize would be undermining confidence or causing delayed safety and regulatory consequences, not direct release. For an insider it is an attractive and low-visibility lever.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
1) Integrity attack on the classifier or its inputs (adversarial). The mechanism is poisoning of training or simulant data, tampering with model files or the tree-ensemble thresholds, or manipulation of vision or laser calibration and the 3D reconstruction pipeline. Alternatively, a backdoor trigger could be tied to a surface or shape feature. The facility dependency is the per-container magnesium quantification used to regulate hydrogen release. The consequence is systematic under-declaration of Mg, leading to containers that exceed hydrogen-generation assumptions in later storage. That is a delayed safety and regulatory-compliance failure, with possible fire or explosion hazard, and it is hard to attribute to an adversary because it looks like model error. The supply-chain exposure is real here: a bespoke model developed over about five years by a contractor and integrator involves several parties with write access to data, code and calibration. Valid accounts and insider access to the model, the training set or the container ledger are the most plausible paths. A reconstruction-stage attack is also plausible, since a physical or optical perturbation of the scene (surface coating, lighting, occlusion) can bias classification without any cyber access (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0010, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0012).

2) Implicit weaknesses that an adversary can exploit or time an attack around. The classifier was trained on nuclear-waste simulants, which are surrogate data (OP.C0201.02). Real UNGG waste is heterogeneous, degraded, oxidised and contaminated, so out-of-distribution pieces are likely (OP.C0302.03, OP.C0302). The few public performance figures and the small, imbalanced real data volume (OP.C0202) mean that nobody has a strong baseline against which to detect drift. As a result, a deliberate bias would be indistinguishable from expected error. Operators who learn to trust the sorter are likely to over-trust it (OP.C0101.04) and stop checking pieces. Skill fade in manual identification would then remove the fallback (OP.C0101.06). An adversary could time a manipulation to this complacency window, or to an outage in which operators are rushed or out of the loop (OP.C0101.01). A tree-based model is fairly interpretable, but the vision-to-feature pipeline is not, so opacity at the reconstruction stage limits forensic review (OP.C0401). Qualification of ML for a safety-relevant waste-characterisation role is immature (OP.C0501, OP.C0303), so there may be no standard against which to demand model integrity, version control and change control (OP.C0502).

3) Concentration of trust and cascade. Classification errors propagate into the container record, the storage-safety case and downstream waste-acceptance decisions, and one bias affects all containers (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). Confusing Mg with Al (similar appearance, and the two are materially different in hydrogen risk) is the key class-level confusion (OP.C0702.01). The records are also a data-integrity target: falsified inventory data can affect waste accountancy and safeguards-relevant material declarations as well as safety (AML.T0059, OP.C0505). Denial of the service (AML.T0029) would be a lesser, availability-oriented threat that stalls retrieval, but because retrieval is a legacy-clean-up activity it is unlikely to be a priority target. Mitigation themes are independent physical verification sampling, signed and versioned models and datasets, separation of duties between model developers and operators, and monitoring of class-proportion statistics for anomalies.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the simulant-to-field gap, Mg under-declaration and insider or supply-chain integrity attacks; I merged overlapping drift, small-data and trust items and kept the sensor-manipulation and record-falsification paths as distinct. I dropped OP.C0701 (safeguards-model scarcity) and OP.C0401 as weak fits, and treated AML.T0043.004 as the backdoor-trigger variant raised by the security specialist.

evidence.citation: "Machine Learning - Based Sorting Nuclear Fuel Waste," Institute of Nuclear Materials Management (INMM) & ESARDA Joint Annual Meeting proceedings, 2021 (Orano / Siléane / Picq Consulting)
evidence.note: The abstract describes a robotised solution from Siléane and Orano that combines 3D vision and laser with machine learning, to sort waste retrieved from Silo 130. Each retrieved piece is classified by a tree-based classifier that took about five years to develop and has been run using nuclear-waste simulants. The source is an abstract, so it gives little quantitative performance detail.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a biased or deliberately under-called Mg declaration (via model, data or record tampering) that understates hydrogen generation in storage and falsifies waste-package inventory declarations; this is a delayed storage-safety and accountancy harm, short of a direct release, so it scores just under the maximum.

reproducibility.why: Simulant-to-field shift, drift and forced closed-set labelling are systematic and recur reliably once real debris and sensor ageing are present, while the adversarial paths depend on access and are more conditional.

exploitability.why: The most consequential adversarial paths (data or model poisoning, backdoor triggers, log falsification) need insider or contractor access to datasets, models or records; scene manipulation needs less cyber access but still needs physical access to a controlled nuclear facility.

affected_users.why: A biased classifier propagates systematically across all container inventories, the storage safety case and waste-acceptance decisions for the whole retrieval campaign, though it stays within one waste-retrieval workflow rather than coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The general weakness classes (simulant-trained models, drift, closed-set overconfidence) are well documented in the open literature and the project's use of simulants is publicly stated in an abstract, but exploiting them needs insider knowledge of the system's data, models and configuration.

use_case: Deep Operator Network (DeepONet) virtual sensor for a pressurized water reactor hot leg, inside a digital twin. Trained on high-fidelity CFD simulations of AP1000 hot-leg flow, it maps operating conditions and measurements at a single pipe location to the spatial distribution of key thermal-hydraulic parameters such as pressure, velocity and turbulence. These fill gaps where physical sensors cannot reach. The aim is real-time tracking of degradation conditions and component integrity, without frequent retraining and at a small fraction of CFD run time.
incurred_insecurity:
A DeepONet virtual sensor inside a hot-leg digital twin creates inferred pressure, velocity and turbulence fields where no instrument exists, so nothing physical can contradict them. The panel agrees the main implicit threats are CFD-to-plant transfer failure, unverifiable and opaque output, over-trust, and error propagation into downstream integrity models.
