The main adversarial threats are manipulation of the single-location input, poisoning or tampering with the model and its data, denial of the twin, and extraction or exposure of design-sensitive information. The sensor is not a protection-system input, so consequences are mostly slow erosion of inspection and remaining-life decisions rather than prompt accidents.

Input manipulation of the virtual sensor -- adversarial
The model extrapolates the whole hot-leg field from one measurement point plus operating conditions, so a spoofed, biased or replayed input, or a perturbation within sensor noise, shifts the entire inferred field. This can mask or fabricate stratification, fatigue loading or flow-induced vibration, biasing inspection scope and integrity decisions or concealing a physical or cyber action.

Training-data and model supply-chain poisoning -- adversarial
Poisoned CFD datasets, tampered pre-trained weights or compromised ML libraries can embed a regime-specific trigger that yields non-conservative fields only at chosen operating states. Because validation is against the same CFD that generated the training data, aggregate error tests would not reveal it.

Model and pipeline integrity tampering -- adversarial
Modifying weights, normalisation constants or the inference pipeline silently changes the inferred fields while the twin still appears healthy. Without hashing and behavioural regression checks, the corruption looks like ordinary model error.

Denial of the twin -- adversarial
Flooding or chaff on the input stream, or disruption of the compute environment, forces fallback to conventional monitoring and removes coverage in locations with no physical backup. It could be timed to coincide with another event.

Model extraction and design-data exposure -- adversarial
The weights, CFD data and twin aggregate AP1000 hot-leg geometry and operating envelopes, so inference access or compromise of the twin allows model extraction and reconnaissance of thermal-hydraulic weak points. Cloud or off-premises hosting widens this surface.

Sim-to-real and out-of-distribution failure -- implicit, exploitable
The network is trained only on simulated CFD of a pristine AP1000 geometry and is frozen without frequent retraining, so aging, fouling, uprates, off-normal transients and inherited turbulence-model bias push it outside its envelope while it still returns smooth, confident fields. An adversary could act in these poorly characterised regimes, or deliberately push the plant into them, because a manipulated output is hard to distinguish from legitimate model error.

Static training versus transient dynamics -- implicit
Steady or quasi-steady training may not represent transient thermal-hydraulic dynamics, so transient loading and stratification onset can be mis-estimated. An adversary gains little distinct from the out-of-distribution weakness.

Opacity, unverifiability and qualification gap -- implicit, exploitable
A black-box neural operator has no routine ground truth in the gaps it fills, no mature uncertainty characterisation and no established nuclear QA basis, so systematic errors persist unseen. An adversary gains plausible deniability and long dwell time for a subtle manipulation, and the advisory classification may leave it outside the cyber and QA controls applied to safety systems.

Automation trust and degraded integrity decisions -- implicit, exploitable
A fast, plausible field map invites staff to treat it as measurement and to defer or de-scope inspections, extend intervals or accept fatigue margins, eroding defence in depth when an independent barrier also fails. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust so that a manipulated field goes uncross-checked.

Error cascade and fleet propagation -- implicit, exploitable
Twin outputs feed downstream fatigue, structural and prognostic models, and a model reused across units spreads one bias to every plant. An adversary who poisons or biases the shared model or upstream fields obtains correlated, multi-plant effects from a single compromise.

Non-reproducibility and configuration control -- implicit
Training and inference variation across retraining, library versions and hardware complicates configuration control and regression baselines. It offers an adversary little beyond a modest additional cover for tampering.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From an operations lens, this virtual sensor produces inferred field values (pressure, velocity, turbulence) at locations with no instrument, so nothing physical can contradict the output at those points. It sits in a digital twin used to track degradation (thermal fatigue, flow-induced vibration, erosion/corrosion, thermal stratification) and component integrity. The consequences are therefore mostly slow and indirect: wrong inspection scoping, wrong remaining-life estimates, and missed or false degradation indications. It is not a protection-system input, and reactor protection, TS-required instrumentation, ISI/NDE and chemistry programs are independent barriers. That limits the safety consequence, but it does not remove the risk. Plant staff may come to treat a fast, plausible-looking field map as measurement, and the model is trained only on CFD of one geometry, so its validity envelope is narrow and hard to see from the control room.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution failure and CFD-to-plant transfer. The training data are simulated AP1000 hot-leg CFD, with no plant data for the unmeasured fields. Real plants differ in as-built geometry, fouling, roughness, transients, power uprates, startup/shutdown and off-normal flow, aging and sensor bias. The network can return smooth, confident, physically plausible fields outside its training envelope, with no uncertainty indicator. Without frequent retraining it also drifts from the real plant over time. Any CFD modelling error (turbulence-model bias, mesh, boundary conditions) is inherited and then hidden by the fast inference speed. Candidate codes: OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.03, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0203. (2) Unverifiable output. Virtual sensors fill gaps where no physical sensor exists, so validation cannot be done routinely. This limits calibration and anomaly checking, and a systematic error can persist unseen. The DeepONet's opacity makes it hard to tell when it is wrong. Candidate codes: OP.C0401, OP.C0403, OP.C0501. (3) Automation bias and degraded integrity decisions. Operators and engineers may use the fields to defer or de-scope inspections, extend intervals, or accept fatigue-usage margins. A model that under-predicts thermal stratification or turbulence loading yields non-conservative fatigue and remaining-life estimates. Over-prediction drives unnecessary outages. The harm needs an independent barrier to fail as well (ISI, leak detection, monitoring), so the main danger is erosion of defence in depth over a long period, not a prompt accident. Candidate codes: OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102, OP.C0301. (4) Propagation. The twin may feed outputs into downstream fatigue, structural and prognostic models, so the errors cascade. A model trained on one reference design and reused across a fleet creates correlated errors. Candidate codes: OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01, OP.C0602.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Manipulation of the single-location input. The model extrapolates the whole field from one measurement point and the operating conditions. Spoofing, biasing or replaying that sensor, or the historian/OPC data path into the twin, can steer the inferred field. This can mask a real degradation condition or fabricate a false one, and it is a stealthy way to influence maintenance decisions or cause costly outages. It may also hide an ongoing physical attack or sabotage condition. The attacker needs no AI knowledge, only data-path access. Candidate codes: AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0046. (b) Model and data supply chain compromise. Poisoned CFD training sets, tampered weights or surrogate-model files, or compromised ML libraries could embed a bias or a trigger in specific operating regimes, giving silent non-conservative output. Candidate codes: AML.T0010.002, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004. (c) Model integrity erosion and tampering. Modifying weights or normalisation constants, or altering the inference pipeline, would change results while the twin still looks healthy. Candidate codes: AML.T0031, AML.T0076, AML.T0018. (d) Denial or delay of the twin. Lost real-time tracking forces fallback to conventional monitoring. This is usually benign, but it could be timed around another event. Candidate code: AML.T0029. (e) Information exposure. Weights and data could reveal AP1000 hot-leg geometry, operating envelopes and vulnerability-relevant thermal-hydraulic behaviour, which is proprietary or sensitive. Candidate codes: AML.T0024.002, AML.T0025. Governance gap: the use is likely outside safety-system qualification, which weakens the QA applied to it. Candidate codes: OP.C0501, OP.C0502, OP.C0505, OP.C0601.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this DeepONet is a surrogate trained entirely on simulated CFD of an AP1000 hot leg (OP.C0201.01/.02), then asked to infer fields at locations where no physical sensor exists. That makes the output unverifiable against ground truth at inference time, so errors are silent. Low reported test error is measured in-distribution against the same solver that generated the training data, so it says little about off-nominal transients, degraded geometry (wall thinning, fouling, stratification onset), sensor faults, or mesh and turbulence-model bias inherited from the CFD (RANS/LES closure). The 'no frequent retraining' goal is the core fragility: the model is frozen while the plant ages, and the branch-net input (a single-location measurement plus operating conditions) is the only link to reality. That input path is both a drift channel and an adversarial or fault-injection surface, since the model never checks whether its input is plausible for the learned manifold.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT threats. (1) Out-of-distribution and drift failure (OP.C0302, .01, .03): the operator is trained on a finite grid of CFD operating conditions and a pristine as-designed geometry. Real plants have aging, instrument bias, power uprates, off-design transients and differing unit behavior, so the outputs extrapolate with no uncertainty estimate. DeepONets give a smooth, confident-looking field even when wrong. The consequence is a mis-estimated degradation or integrity margin (e.g. thermal fatigue or stratification, flow-accelerated corrosion loading) that appears credible. (2) Sim-to-real data provenance gap (OP.C0201.01/.02/.03, OP.C0203, OP.C0202): there is little or no field data for a new-build AP1000 to validate against, and rare degraded states are poorly represented. Validation is solver-to-surrogate, not surrogate-to-plant, so CFD modeling error is learned as truth. (3) Static/dynamic qualification mismatch and opacity (OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0403): steady or quasi-steady training may not represent transient dynamics, and a black-box operator is hard to qualify under nuclear QA. A neural-operator generalization guarantee is not a safety-case argument. (4) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102): because virtual sensors fill gaps where no instrument exists, operators and the digital twin's downstream health-assessment logic cannot cross-check, which invites over-trust, and a plausible wrong field propagates into integrity or maintenance decisions (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). Also OP.C0402 for reproducibility of training and for floating-point or hardware variation across deployments.

ADVERSARIAL threats. (a) Input manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043, T0043.000/.001): the single measurement location is a low-dimensional, high-leverage input. Spoofed or subtly biased sensor data, or a crafted perturbation, can shift the predicted field and hide or fabricate a degradation signature. White-box or proxy-model attacks are easier because DeepONet is differentiable and the architecture is published (AML.T0002, T0005, T0000). The consequence is masked degradation or false alarms that drive unnecessary outages. (b) Training-data and supply-chain poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0043.004): CFD datasets, solver configs, pre-trained weights and ML libraries come from vendors or collaborators. A poisoned dataset or backdoored model could embed a trigger that suppresses anomalies under particular operating conditions, and it would pass aggregate error tests. (c) Model or twin integrity (AML.T0018, T0076, T0031): weight tampering in the twin pipeline is hard to detect without hashing and behavioral regression tests, and it degrades integrity silently. (d) Availability (AML.T0029, T0046): chaff or flooded input streams can force the twin to fall back or to stale outputs. (e) Information exposure (AML.T0024.002, T0035, T0048.004): the model and its CFD data encode proprietary plant geometry and flow characteristics, which enables extraction and reconnaissance of thermal-hydraulic weak points. Cloud or offsite hosting of the twin (OP.C0601) widens these surfaces, and a fleet-wide model reused across units (OP.C0602) would spread one poisoning or bias to every plant.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, a DeepONet virtual sensor is attractive because it creates trusted measurements where no physical sensor exists. Operators and degradation-tracking workflows have no independent instrument to cross-check against in exactly those locations, so the model's output stands in for ground truth. An adversary does not need to attack the reactor. Manipulating a digital-twin input, or the model or its data supply chain, could hide or fabricate degradation signals in the hot leg and bias integrity or inspection decisions. A realistic adversary would likely prefer the easier route of corrupting inputs or artifacts feeding the twin over defeating plant protection systems. The implicit weaknesses (out-of-distribution failure, opacity, over-trust) set the windows an adversary could time an action around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Input manipulation: the model maps a single-location measurement plus operating conditions to full fields. One compromised or spoofed input channel, or a subtle perturbation within plausible sensor noise, shifts the entire inferred field (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). The result is a masked or invented thermal-hydraulic anomaly, such as thermal stratification, fatigue loading or flow-induced vibration. Dependent decisions are degradation tracking, maintenance scheduling and component-integrity assessment. The consequence is deferred inspection or unnecessary outages, mainly an integrity and economic risk, but it could also be timed to coincide with a physical or cyber action. (2) Supply chain and model integrity: weights, CFD training datasets, surrogate-model libraries and twin integration software are an insider- or vendor-accessible pathway. Poisoning or backdooring could add a trigger condition that yields benign-looking output only at specific operating states (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043.004). Because the model is validated against the same CFD it was trained on, a narrow backdoor would be hard to detect. (3) Trust concentration and lateral pathway: the digital twin aggregates plant data, so it is an attractive reconnaissance and stepping-stone target. Compromising it exposes design-sensitive AP1000 geometry and operating data, and a model with inference access can be extracted or inverted (AML.T0024.002, AML.T0035, AML.T0036, AML.T0025). A bridge between OT and the twin's compute environment, especially if cloud-hosted, adds a network pathway toward plant networks (OP.C0601, AML.T0012). (4) Denial or degradation of the virtual sensor (AML.T0029) forces a fallback to manual procedures or removes monitoring in gaps with no physical backup.

IMPLICIT, adversary-exploitable. (a) Data scarcity and simulation-only provenance: the training data is CFD, not plant measurements, so there is an unquantified sim-to-real gap (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0203, OP.C0302). Off-nominal transients, sensor degradation and geometry changes such as aging or weld repairs fall outside the training envelope, and the model can still return confident, smooth fields. (b) Automation trust: because it replaces an unavailable sensor, over-trust and out-of-the-loop unfamiliarity are likely (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102). The speed advantage of real-time inference encourages removing human cross-checks. (c) Opacity and qualification gaps: neural operators lack a mature qualification basis, and uncertainty is weakly characterized (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0303). Non-determinism across retraining and library versions complicates configuration control (OP.C0402, OP.C0502). Together these mean a manipulated or drifting output is hard to distinguish from a legitimate model error, which gives an adversary plausible deniability and a long dwell time. (d) Regulatory scope drift: because the tool is classed as advisory or monitoring, it may fall outside the cyber and QA requirements applied to safety-related systems, leaving a lower-security path into decisions that affect integrity (OP.C0503, OP.C0504).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on out-of-distribution/sim-to-real failure, unverifiable opacity, over-trust, input manipulation, supply-chain poisoning, tampering, denial and extraction. I dropped speculative codes such as AML.T0012, AML.T0005 and AML.T0002, and kept AML.T0043.003 over the white-box and black-box variants because a spoofed or biased single-sensor input is a manual modification rather than a model-optimised one.

evidence.citation: "Virtual sensing-enabled digital twin framework for real-time monitoring of nuclear systems leveraging deep neural operators," npj Materials Degradation (Nature Portfolio)
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests DeepONet as a virtual sensor that predicts thermal-hydraulic fields in a PWR hot leg. It reports low prediction error and inference about 1400 times faster than CFD, so the model can run in real time within a nuclear digital twin to monitor degradation. The AP1000 detail comes from the paper's arXiv version (arXiv:2410.13762), which the search also returned.

damage.why: The worst credible threat is silent corruption or poisoning of inferred hot-leg fields (non-conservative output, error cascade into fatigue and remaining-life models), which erodes inspection and integrity margins; the sensor is advisory and not a protection-system input, so prompt radiological release is not credible and the harm stays at operational disruption or safety-margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution failure from a frozen, simulation-only model, and bias propagation from over-trust, occur reliably once the plant leaves the training envelope; input manipulation reliably shifts the inferred field because everything is extrapolated from one point; backdoor triggers are more conditional.

exploitability.why: The most severe credible threats (supply-chain poisoning, weight or pipeline tampering, spoofing the plant input) need privileged access to the training pipeline or OT/instrumentation networks, which is usually insider-level or well-resourced, though extraction or chaff against exposed or cloud-hosted twins is easier.

affected_users.why: Twin outputs feed downstream fatigue, structural and prognostic models, and a model reused across units spreads a single bias to multiple plants (error cascade and fleet propagation), so impact can span coupled systems and sites even though the sensor is advisory.

discoverability.why: The architecture, CFD-to-plant transfer gap, black-box opacity and sim-to-real limits are documented in open literature (the cited paper and its arXiv version), and the general weaknesses of neural surrogates and adversarial ML are well known; only facility-specific deployment details are non-public.

use_case: Supervised machine-learning regression (multilayer perceptron, random forest, support vector regression, k-nearest neighbours, with linear regression as baseline) predicts the equilibrium nitric acid concentration in the TBP organic phase of the PUREX solvent-extraction process. Inputs are the initial aqueous acid concentration and the TBP concentration, across several diluents. The models were trained on solvent-extraction data compiled from the literature. They are meant to improve understanding and control of PUREX separations in spent-fuel reprocessing, and to help design experiments.
incurred_insecurity:
This advisory regression surrogate for organic-phase nitric acid in PUREX has no actuator authority, so its main exposure is a quiet, plausible-looking error that biases flowsheet or experiment decisions in a reprocessing plant. The dominant threats are implicit: out-of-distribution failure, weak data provenance, and a qualification and governance gap that lets a proof of concept drift into operational use. Adversarial threats (poisoning of the compiled dataset or model artifact, insider tampering, falsified inputs) are secondary but would exploit those same weaknesses, and the model is also a stepping stone to a looser R&D network.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
With only initial acid and TBP concentration as inputs, the model cannot represent U/Pu/fission-product loading, temperature, solvent degradation products (DBP/MBP) or salting-out. Random forest and MLP therefore return smooth, confident numbers with no uncertainty or out-of-envelope flag, which can mis-set acid-scrub or stripping conditions and erode margin to third-phase formation, Pu/U partitioning limits and red-oil conditions. An adversary could attribute a deliberate process deviation to model error, or hide a biased input or output inside this unflagged, unexplained error band.

Literature data provenance and quality -- implicit, exploitable
The corpus mixes bench-scale measurements from different labs, temperatures, diluents and units, with transcription errors, sparse high-acid and high-TBP corners, and correlated records that inflate cross-validation scores. Real accuracy is therefore overstated, and an adversary altering a few points in a sparsely corroborated region would be hard to distinguish from existing noise.

Static validation and governance gap -- implicit, exploitable
Test-set accuracy on equilibrium data is not qualification for dynamic cascade use, and there is no AI-specific QA, version control, seed control or defined boundary of use. Analysts may over-trust the data-driven output and stop cross-checking against titration or thermodynamic codes, and unversioned retraining can shift predictions in safety-relevant regions undetected. An adversary or insider could rely on this misplaced trust and lack of change control to swap or retrain the model unnoticed. Skill fade in chemists who previously used thermodynamic models would deepen the dependence.

Training-data and model-artifact poisoning -- adversarial
Altering the compiled literature dataset, a derived repository, or the pickled model artifact and its dependencies can bias predictions in a narrow region while remaining smooth and plausible. The consequence is mis-set extraction and scrub conditions, distorted Pu/U stream expectations and degraded design margin.

Insider tampering and input manipulation -- adversarial
One insider can swap or retrain a lightly governed model, and if it is later connected to live acid or TBP measurements, falsified inputs would produce wrong but plausible outputs with no anomaly detector to catch them. This gives deniability for process excursions or cover for a diversion-relevant process change.

R&D environment stepping stone -- adversarial
The notebooks, Python packages and shared data sit on a loosely governed R&D network adjacent to process data and recipes. Compromising them gives a foothold toward more valuable facility information rather than any direct effect on the process.

nuclear_engineer.argument: This is a low-dimensional regression (two inputs, one output: organic-phase HNO3) trained on literature data, and it is advisory. It is meant for understanding and experiment design, not as a protection-system input. The facility consequence is therefore mostly indirect. A wrong prediction would bias flowsheet set-points, solvent-loading and acid-balance assumptions, or experiment design. It would do this without any alarm, because the output looks plausible. Real harm needs several other things to fail: the process model and operator margin, online acid and density measurement, criticality-safe geometry and concentration limits, and the red-oil/thermal runaway controls. Those controls make direct physical harm unlikely. The more credible risks are quiet erosion of margin and misplaced confidence if the proof of concept is promoted into an operating tool.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT (main weaknesses). (1) Data provenance and heterogeneity: literature data come from different labs, temperatures, ionic strengths and diluents. They are bench-scale, mostly fresh-solvent measurements with no uncertainty or metadata, and they are not plant data. Real PUREX solvent carries dissolved U/Pu/Zr/Tc, radiolytic and hydrolytic degradation products (DBP/MBP), and high-burnup fission-product nitrates. HNO3 uptake also depends on temperature and on metal-nitrate competition and salting-out. A model fit on two inputs cannot represent these, so prediction is out-of-distribution in real operation (OP.C0201.04, OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202). Tree and kernel methods also extrapolate badly outside the training envelope and give no warning when they do (OP.C0403, OP.C0401). Predictions at extreme acidity or at high TBP fraction may look smooth but be wrong. (2) Consequence of error: acid in the organic phase affects Pu/U/Np extraction and stripping behaviour, scrub-section acid balance, and third-phase formation boundaries. Systematic underprediction could mislead acid-profile, loading or scrub design. This could reduce the margin to third-phase or heavy-organic splitting, which has criticality-control implications because Pu-bearing organic could accumulate. It could also affect the nitrate/nitric acid inventory relevant to the red-oil and solvent-thermal hazard. In safeguards terms, mis-specified partitioning could distort expected Pu/U stream balances and so shift material-accountancy expectations. (3) Automation bias and scope creep: an apparently accurate test-set R² invites use as a soft sensor or control reference. Static test-set validation does not equal qualification for dynamic, closed-loop use (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Without explicit operating-envelope documentation, an advisory proof of concept can drift into a de facto control input. Retraining on new data without version control or repeatability checks adds further risk (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0502). Skill fade in chemists and process engineers who used to rely on thermodynamic models and measurement is a long-term concern (OP.C0101.06). ADVERSARIAL (secondary, plausible but modest). (a) Training-data poisoning or supply-chain tampering: the corpus is compiled from public literature and curated datasets. Subtle bias injected into published data, or into the compiled dataset, could shift predictions in a specific region (for example, lower acid uptake at a given TBP fraction) without obvious outliers. This is a slow, low-visibility way to degrade design margin (AML.T0019, AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059). Model or code tampering in a shared repository belongs to the same class (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000). (b) Manipulated inputs: if later connected to live acid or TBP measurements, falsified sensor values would produce plausible-looking but wrong outputs (AML.T0043, AML.T0031). Because this is a smooth regression with no anomaly detector, the model cannot flag them. (c) Reconnaissance value: published model details reveal little beyond the open literature, so the information-leak risk is low. Overall the existing defences are strong: independent online measurement, chemistry-based flowsheet codes, and criticality controls independent of the model. The gap lies in the process of qualifying and bounding the model's use, not in the model's physics.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a small-tabular-data regression model (two or three features, trained on literature-compiled equilibrium data) used as a surrogate for a thermodynamic distribution relationship. The weak points are in the data and the lifecycle, not the architecture. Literature data is heterogeneous: measurement methods, temperatures, ionic strength, diluent purity, TBP degradation state and units all differ, and the model usually has no feature for those variables. Nitric acid extraction into TBP is non-monotonic and nonlinear, with third-phase formation, TBP·HNO3 complexation and a strong dependence on uranium/plutonium loading. A flexible learner such as an MLP or random forest will therefore interpolate well inside the training envelope and fail silently outside it. Random forests cannot extrapolate at all, and MLPs extrapolate unpredictably. A model that fits well on a random train/test split of compiled data gives little assurance for a real plant, because of duplicate or near-duplicate points from papers citing each other, leakage between split sets, and no representation of metal-loaded, irradiated, or degraded solvent.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution inference. The inputs are only initial acid and TBP concentration, so the model cannot see the variables that dominate real plant behavior: U/Pu/fission-product loading, temperature, radiolytic and hydrolytic solvent degradation products (DBP/MBP), diluent composition, and salting-out effects. The model returns a plausible number with no uncertainty or out-of-envelope flag. If it is used to inform acid-scrub or stripping setpoints or to design experiments, the result is mispredicted acid partitioning and, downstream, errors in Pu/U separation, a criticality-relevant concentration profile, or conditions that favor third-phase formation or red-oil-type hazards. This is a process-safety and potentially criticality-safety consequence. (2) Data provenance and quality. Literature compilation has uncontrolled provenance, with transcription and unit errors, digitized figures, simulated or fitted values mixed with measured ones, and sparse coverage of high-acid and high-TBP corners. Small-data overfitting is hidden by optimistic cross-validation from correlated records. Corresponds to OP.C0201, OP.C0202, OP.C0302 and OP.C0302.03. (3) Qualification mismatch. Equilibrium (static) predictions are applied to a dynamic, non-equilibrium contactor cascade with finite stage efficiency and kinetics. There is no established qualification route for ML surrogates beside validated thermodynamic codes, so the numbers could be over-trusted by analysts because they appear data-driven (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0101.04, OP.C0401). Non-determinism across MLP seeds and random-forest resamples also causes repeatability gaps (OP.C0402.01). (4) Model-version and retraining drift. If retrained as new data are added without regression testing, the predictions in safety-relevant regions can shift without anyone noticing (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0502). ADVERSARIAL THREATS (lower probability, but they exploit the above weaknesses). (a) Poisoning of the literature or compiled dataset, or of the pipeline (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002, AML.T0059). An attacker or a careless contributor who alters a few points in the sparse high-acid region could bias the model where there is little corroborating data. (b) Model or artifact tampering via supply chain: pickled scikit-learn or PyTorch artifacts and Python dependencies are an execution risk (AML.T0010.001, AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0011.000). (c) Input manipulation (AML.T0043, AML.T0031). Where the model is wired to plant data or process-control historians, falsified acid or TBP measurements would drive wrong predictions and mask drift from the real operating point. Because the model is cheap and its predictions look smooth, a bias attack would be hard to detect. (d) Reconnaissance and information leakage. Model behavior and the compiled dataset reveal the PUREX operating envelope. This is mostly low-sensitivity open literature but could become more sensitive if facility-specific data are added (AML.T0024.001, OP.C0505). The main exposure is a quiet, plausible-looking error in a region where the model has no support, which is then used for experiment design or process decisions, rather than an overt cyberattack.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view this is a low-value direct target but a meaningful stepping stone. It is an offline, literature-trained regression model with two inputs (aqueous acid and TBP concentration) and one output (organic-phase acid), with no actuator authority. An adversary would not bother attacking it for immediate effect. The risk comes if it migrates from 'help design experiments' into advisory or setpoint-support roles in a reprocessing flowsheet. Acid loading in the organic phase drives Pu/U distribution, third-phase formation, and solvent degradation, so a quietly biased predictor becomes a trusted number that an insider or supply-chain actor could shift. The proof-of-concept status means it likely has no qualification, change control, or independent verification, which is the gap a patient adversary would exploit. The same accessible literature dataset and model also tell an outsider something about how a process might be tuned.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity: ADVERSARIAL: (1) Training-data and supply-chain poisoning. Training data is aggregated from open literature with heterogeneous provenance and diluent and temperature conditions. Someone who can alter the compiled dataset, a derived repository, or the model artifact could bias predictions in a narrow region, such as high acid or high TBP, with little chance of detection. The AI mechanism is a corrupted model or dataset that still looks plausible. The facility dependence is experiment design or flowsheet tuning that assumes a given acid loading. The consequences are mis-set extraction/scrub conditions, off-normal Pu/U partitioning, third-phase or solvent-degradation risk, and possibly distorted material-accountancy or process-monitoring baselines. Because the model is smooth and low-dimensional, there is no obvious red flag. (2) Insider and trust concentration. A small model that engineers consult informally is easy for one insider to swap or retrain, with no code signing, versioning, or review. Quietly changing its outputs would create plausible deniability for process excursions or help mask a diversion-relevant process change. (3) Low-effort stepping stone. The ML environment (notebooks, Python packages, shared data) typically sits on a more loosely governed R&D network adjacent to process data. Compromising it gives a foothold toward process data and recipes, so the model is a path to something more valuable rather than the objective. IMPLICIT, exploitable by an adversary: (4) Extrapolation and drift. Literature data is bench-scale and mostly clean. Real plant solvent is irradiated, degraded, and carries fission-product and metal loading (Pu, U, Zr, Tc) that shift acid extraction. The model has no uncertainty estimate, and its out-of-distribution behavior is opaque, especially for MLP and random forest. Overconfident predictions in unmodeled regimes give an adversary cover, because a deviation can be blamed on the model. (5) Automation-bias and vigilance erosion. Operators who learn the predictions usually match experience may stop cross-checking with titration or measurement, which creates a window in which a manipulated or drifting model goes unchallenged. (6) Governance gap. As a research proof of concept, it has no AI-specific QA, reproducibility controls (random seeds, non-deterministic training), or defined boundary of use. That makes scope creep into operational support likely and leaves no way to detect tampering.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on out-of-distribution extrapolation, literature data provenance, and the qualification/governance gap, and on poisoning and tampering as the main adversarial class. I dropped the information-leak and model-inversion item as low value, kept the insider and stepping-stone threats from the security specialist as distinct, and omitted AML.T0035, AML.T0011.000 and other codes whose pathways were only weakly supported.

evidence.citation: "Machine Learning Prediction of Nitric Acid Extraction Behavior in PUREX Process," ACS Omega (American Chemical Society); PNNL-affiliated work
evidence.note: The authors compiled literature data on nitric acid extraction by TBP. They built and benchmarked five supervised regression models, and the random forest and MLP models fit best. The work is a proof of concept for ML-based prediction to improve understanding and control of the PUREX solvent-extraction process.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a biased, plausible surrogate output (or tampered model) that mis-sets scrub/strip conditions and erodes margin to third-phase, Pu/U partitioning and red-oil limits, or masks a diversion-relevant process change; the model is advisory with no actuator authority, so damage stops short of direct release or falsification.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution extrapolation with confident, unflagged outputs recurs reliably whenever inputs fall outside the two-variable training envelope, and unversioned retraining or over-trust reliably produces undetected shifts.

exploitability.why: The adversarial paths (poisoning the dataset or pickled artifact, insider swap or retrain, falsified live inputs) need insider or privileged access to the R&D environment, though the implicit OOD failure needs no special access.

affected_users.why: The surrogate is an advisory tool for a narrow set of analysts and experiment or flowsheet decisions, and its effects stay local unless it is later integrated into operations or the R&D network is used as a foothold.

discoverability.why: The work is published in the open literature with its model types, inputs and data sources described, and OOD, data-quality and governance weaknesses are well-documented for this class of ML surrogate, though specific deployment details are not public.

use_case: Convolutional neural network surrogate of 3D finite-element models of a nuclear fuel pellet. It takes 13 input features, such as pressure, Young's modulus and temperature, and predicts the FE stress response (e.g. von Mises stress maps). It replaces slow finite-element runs for pellet-cladding interaction and mechanical interaction analysis in the fuel performance framework of nuclear power plants.
incurred_insecurity:
A CNN surrogate of 3D pellet finite-element runs feeds pellet-cladding interaction margin assessment and could drift from a screening tool into a basis for operating decisions. The main implicit threats are silent extrapolation outside the sampled 13-feature envelope, simulation-only label fidelity that hides peak-stress errors, qualification and repeatability gaps, over-trust with erosion of full-FE skills, and fleet-wide propagation of one bias. The main adversarial threats are poisoning or backdooring of the training data, weights or dependencies, manipulation of the input stream, and extraction of proprietary fuel data. Direct safety consequence is bounded by independent barriers (licensed codes, protection limits, coolant activity monitoring) only while the surrogate stays advisory.

Out-of-distribution extrapolation -- implicit, exploitable
The CNN interpolates inside its sampled design-of-experiments but gives no uncertainty or input-range warning for high burnup, power ramps, novel fuels or transients, producing confident non-conservative stress maps and PCI margins. An adversary could aim a manipulation at these known-weak regimes, where a plausible but wrong output draws no suspicion.

Simulation-bound fidelity and peak-stress error -- implicit, exploitable
Labels come only from FE runs, so the surrogate inherits the FE model's mesh, material and boundary-condition errors and was never checked against irradiation measurements; averaged metrics such as MSE can hide large errors at contact points and crack tips that govern failure. An adversary could tune a poisoning or input bias to stay inside this unmeasured error band and pass aggregate validation.

Qualification, opacity and retraining drift -- implicit, exploitable
The CNN lacks the nuclear QA basis of licensed fuel performance codes, is hard to explain, and retrains non-deterministically as FE correlations are updated, so versions silently shift and are hard to requalify. An adversary could hide a weight or data tampering inside this routine version churn.

Automation trust, scope creep and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Speedup and the real-time monitoring framing push analysts from FE spot checks to routine reliance, eroding full-FE skills and independent cross-checking. An adversary could time a manipulation for reload or ramp decisions where no FE cross-check remains, relying on that misplaced trust.

Fleet propagation and data scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
One transferred model applied to dissimilar fuel designs, new-build or advanced fuels with scarce data spreads a single bias across units, and errors propagate into coupled fuel-performance calculations. A compromised or biased shared model would give an adversary multi-unit reach from one tampering.

Training data, weight and supply chain poisoning -- adversarial
Tampering with FE datasets, serialized weights, preprocessing code or ML framework dependencies, often held on contractor or GPU infrastructure outside operator-grade cyber controls, can bias stress low in a chosen input region, or backdoor it for specific input signatures, while aggregate validation stays acceptable. The result is eroded cladding-failure margin or unwarranted power restrictions, discovered only after the fact.

Input stream manipulation -- adversarial
Small changes to the 13 inputs (temperatures, pressures, material-property tables) from upstream data chains, or crafted inputs exploiting CNN sensitivity, shift the stress output while staying inside plausible ranges and range checks. The surrogate inherits the trust of the instrumentation chain that feeds it.

Model and data extraction, toolchain foothold -- adversarial
Query or file access to the model and training set can leak proprietary or export-controlled fuel design and material data, and compromised GPU workstations or cloud training services give a foothold near fuel-margin data. 

Cloud and GPU dependence and denial -- implicit, exploitable
Reliance on GPU or off-premises compute makes the surrogate service a dependency that can be disrupted, which matters most once FE capability has atrophied. An adversary could deny the service to force reliance on stale outputs or to coincide with another action.

nuclear_engineer.argument: A CNN surrogate of a 3D pellet FE model sits in the fuel performance framework, so its output informs PCI/PMI margin evaluation, power-ramp and maneuvering guidance, and fuel-integrity assessments. It does not directly actuate anything. Harm needs a chain: a wrong stress map is believed, margin is wrongly assessed, and the independent barriers then fail to catch it. Those barriers are licensed fuel performance codes, conservative core-protection limits, Technical Specification limits, reactor protection, and cladding failure detection through coolant activity. Those barriers make a direct safety consequence unlikely if the surrogate stays advisory. The credible risks are non-conservative error in a rarely seen corner of the input space, an erosion of margin that nobody notices, and a gradual shift from 'screening tool' to 'basis for real-time decisions', which the paper's own framing encourages. Adversarial exposure is mainly through training data, model artifacts and input pipelines. Those could make the surrogate quietly optimistic about stress in exactly the regimes where PCI-driven failure matters, and a plausible-looking number is hard to spot.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Extrapolation and out-of-distribution failure. The surrogate is trained on a bounded FE design-of-experiments over 13 features. Real operation brings burnup-dependent properties, power ramps, pellet cracking and relocation, and off-normal transients that lie outside that envelope. CNNs interpolate well and extrapolate with no warning, and they give no native sign of being out of domain. The result is a non-conservative stress or PCI margin estimate. (2) Surrogate fidelity is bounded by the FE model. The FE model is itself a simplification and is validated against limited irradiation data, so the CNN inherits its errors and adds approximation error. Averaged accuracy metrics can hide large local errors at stress peaks, such as pellet-cladding contact points or crack-tip regions. Those peaks are the quantities that govern failure, so a low mean error does not bound peak-stress error. (3) Qualification mismatch. Fuel performance codes are qualified under nuclear QA and surrogates generally are not. The result is an unqualified tool informing licensing-adjacent or operating margins, with gaps in explainability, repeatability across training runs and GPU hardware, and version control. (4) Automation bias and scope creep. Large speedups and 'real-time monitoring' framing invite operators and analysts to move from verification-by-FE spot checks to routine reliance. Skill and practice in running the full FE then fade, and independent cross-checking is dropped. (5) Data scarcity and fleet propagation. Dissimilar fuel designs, new-build or advanced fuels, and different vendors' properties may be handled by one transferred model, so a single bias can spread across units or sites. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Poisoning or tampering with the FE training dataset, the surrogate weights, or the preprocessing and normalization code, including through the supply chain of ML frameworks and pretrained components. This can bias stress predictions in a targeted regime, for example to hide high-stress conditions or to cause unnecessary power restrictions. The chosen bias is designed to stay inside the plausible range and so avoid review. (7) Manipulation of the 13-feature input stream, such as material-property tables and temperature or pressure data from upstream plant-data systems. Because the CNN is smooth and sensitive, small perturbations can produce outsized output shifts that a human reviewer would not notice. (8) Integrity of the GPU or cloud training and inference environment, and denial of the surrogate service. Denial matters little if the FE fallback is retained, but it does matter if FE capability has atrophied. Overall, safety consequence is bounded by the independent barriers, but the integrity of fuel-margin assessment and economic or operating-flexibility decisions is exposed. The risk is greatest if the surrogate is allowed to replace, rather than screen ahead of, qualified analysis.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a supervised regression surrogate whose training labels come entirely from simulation (3D FE runs), not plant measurements (OP.C0201.01/.02). Its fidelity is therefore bounded by the FE model's own assumptions, and it can only be trusted inside the sampled 13-dimensional design-of-experiments envelope. CNNs on structured stress maps interpolate smoothly but have no built-in notion of physical admissibility or of being out of distribution. They tend to be most unreliable exactly where PCI analysis matters most: stress concentrations, pellet cracking and contact transitions, and extreme transients. The pipeline's value proposition is speed and 'real-time monitoring and decision-making', and this pushes it from offline analysis toward operational use. Surrogate error then enters decisions about margins and limits without the validation that the original FE code had.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Out-of-distribution extrapolation (OP.C0302, C0302.03): inputs such as high burnup, power ramps, or novel fuel or cladding designs that fall outside the sampled 13-feature hypercube produce confident but wrong stress maps. There is no uncertainty output and no input-range guard. Nothing on the surrogate side flags the departure, and the consequence is non-conservative PCI margins and a safety-analysis gap. (2) Fidelity inheritance and error compounding (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0303): the labels are FE outputs, so mesh, material-model and boundary-condition errors are baked in. Aggregate metrics such as MSE or R² can hide large local errors at the peak von Mises locations, which are the ones that matter. Errors can then propagate into downstream fuel-performance coupling (OP.C0603, OP.C0301.01). (3) Drift and lifecycle (OP.C0302.01/.02, OP.C0501): the FE model gets updated (new material correlations, irradiation data) and the surrogate silently goes stale. Retraining is non-deterministic (OP.C0402.01), so the versions are hard to requalify under nuclear QA, and the qualification regime for ML in safety-related codes is immature (OP.C0504). (4) Opacity and automation bias (OP.C0401, OP.C0101.04): fast, plausible-looking stress maps invite over-trust and displace the FE cross-check, which causes skill fade (OP.C0101.06). Physical plausibility is hard to audit in a CNN.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Supply chain (AML.T0010.001/.003, T0018.000, T0011.000): pretrained weights, serialized model files and GPU/ML framework dependencies are all attack surfaces. A tampered or backdoored surrogate could under-predict stress only for specific input signatures (AML.T0043.004). (2) Training-data and FE-dataset integrity (AML.T0020, T0059, T0010.002): subtly corrupted simulation batches or input-parameter files could bias the surrogate while leaving aggregate validation metrics acceptable. (3) Inference-time input manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043): the 13 inputs are low-dimensional but physically meaningful. If they come from plant data feeds, small manipulations of sensor or parameter values could steer outputs toward low stress without tripping range checks. This is a risk of integrity rather than of physical access. (4) Model/IP theft (AML.T0024.002, T0035): the model and training set encode proprietary fuel design and material data, and could be extracted by anyone with query or file access. (5) Availability: GPU or cloud dependence (OP.C0601, AML.T0029) could create operational reliance on an infrastructure that is attackable. Adversaries could also time attacks around the known-weak OOD regions.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, this is a low-value direct target but a meaningful stepping stone. A fuel-performance surrogate sits in the analytical chain that informs PCI margins, power-ramp limits and operating envelopes, so it concentrates trust in a number nobody re-derives once the FE run is gone. The adversary-relevant change is that quiet bias in a stress map would not trip any alarm and would reach licensing and operating margin decisions through a trusted-looking, fast tool. A nation-state would more likely use the model-development pipeline (training data, weights, GPU/cloud environment) as an access path or a long-dwell integrity attack than attack the plant through this model in real time. Non-adversarial weaknesses such as extrapolation, drift and eroded FE expertise are also what an adversary could time an attack around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model integrity: the surrogate learns from FE simulation datasets and weights that are often held on research or contractor GPU infrastructure, outside operator-grade cyber controls. An insider or supply-chain actor who poisons the data, the weights or the pretrained and framework dependencies could bias predicted stress or strain low in a specific region of the 13-dimensional input space, for example high-burnup or high-ramp conditions. The AI failure is a trusted but systematically non-conservative surrogate. The dependent functions are PCI/PMI margin assessment, ramp-rate guidance and fuel-performance-code outputs. The consequence is eroded cladding-failure margin, possible fuel failure with fission-product release, or a challenge to licensing-basis claims, and it could be exposed only after the fact. Because the output is a smooth field with no ground-truth check at inference, the manipulation is hard to detect. (2) Input-side manipulation: the 13 inputs (temperature, pressure, material properties) come from upstream data chains. Tampering with a few of them, or crafting adversarial inputs that exploit CNN sensitivity, would give plausible but wrong outputs. This is a stepping stone because the surrogate inherits trust from the instrumentation and code chain feeding it. (3) Stepping-stone and access risk: GPU workstations, shared model repositories, and cloud training services connect the engineering network to external environments. Compromise of the AI toolchain gives a foothold near fuel-design and operating-margin data that may be proprietary or export-controlled. Model extraction or inversion would also leak that data. (4) Concentration of trust and vigilance erosion: once FE runs are replaced for speed, people stop doing independent checks. An adversary could time a manipulation for when the surrogate is used for reload or ramp decisions with no FE cross-check.

IMPLICIT. (a) Out-of-distribution and extrapolation failure: surrogates trained on a finite set of simulated FE cases degrade silently outside the training envelope, such as new fuel designs, accident-tolerant fuels, unusual burnup or transients. The result is confident wrong stress maps with no uncertainty signal. (b) Simulated-data provenance: the surrogate inherits every error and idealization of the FE model, so it is validated only against its own teacher and not against measurement. (c) Opacity and qualification gaps: CNN stress predictions are hard to explain, there is little accepted qualification basis for safety-relevant surrogates, and local peak stress near singularities (pellet-cladding contact) is where CNNs tend to smooth out extremes. (d) Skill fade and automation trust: speed gains encourage real-time use and reduce the FE analyst skills needed to catch errors. (e) Version and retraining drift: undocumented retraining or non-deterministic training can silently change outputs, and an adversary can hide changes within that normal churn.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on OOD extrapolation, FE-bounded fidelity, qualification gaps, automation trust and skill fade, and training-data/weight poisoning plus input manipulation. I kept model extraction and cloud/denial as distinct but secondary threats, and dropped lower-confidence candidates (T0012, T0011.000, OP.C0502, OP.C0301.01, OP.C0302.02) as weakly traceable to the final text.

evidence.citation: "AI-Powered Convolutional Neural Network Surrogate Modeling for High-Speed Finite Element Analysis in the NPPs Fuel Performance Framework," Energies (MDPI)
evidence.note: The paper builds and tests CNN surrogates trained on a dataset of 3D fuel pellet finite-element simulations with 13 input features. It reports large computational-time savings, especially with GPU training, while keeping accuracy. The authors present this as a way to support real-time monitoring and decision-making in plant operations. The evidence comes from the paper's abstract and figure and section captions, because I did not retrieve the full text.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a poisoned or biased surrogate that silently eroded cladding-failure margin or forced unwarranted power restrictions, but the entry itself notes that independent barriers (licensed codes, protection limits, coolant activity monitoring) bound the safety consequence while the tool is advisory, so this stays at operational disruption or minor safety-margin erosion.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution extrapolation and simulation-bound peak-stress error occur reliably whenever inputs leave the sampled envelope, but the adversarial poisoning and backdoor threats depend on specific conditions (access to data, weights or dependencies, and a particular decision context), so reliability is moderate.

exploitability.why: The most credible adversarial threats (training data, weight or supply-chain tampering, and manipulation of upstream instrumentation or property-table inputs) generally need privileged or supply-chain access to contractor, GPU or plant data chains, while only the extraction and denial paths are comparatively accessible.

affected_users.why: Fleet propagation of a single biased or compromised shared model, plus errors feeding coupled fuel-performance calculations, could affect multiple units, though impact is limited to fuel margin assessment rather than the whole facility.

discoverability.why: Surrogate extrapolation failure, simulation-only fidelity, data poisoning and adversarial-input risks are well documented in the open literature, and the surrogate's architecture, 13-feature input set and benefits are described in a public paper, though an attacker still needs deployment-specific knowledge to find where a given system is weak.

use_case: Deep neural network classification of motorized rotating pancake coil (MRPC) eddy-current signals from steam generator tubes in nuclear power plants. The network labels flaws as axial or circumferential, using signals from tube specimens with deliberately introduced defects. The signals are preprocessed and augmented before training. It is meant to automate analysis of the very large signal volumes in time-limited in-service inspections.
incurred_insecurity:
A DNN trained on specimen tubes with artificial defects is meant to triage MRPC signals that decide steam generator tube integrity, a primary pressure-boundary barrier, under outage time pressure. The main insecurities are a bench-to-field generalization gap, a missing qualification path with eroding human review, and adversarial corruption of the training data, model or signal pipeline that would produce quiet, deniable misclassification of real flaws. Fleet-wide reuse and the tool's concentrated trust amplify every one of these.

Specimen-to-field generalization gap -- implicit, exploitable
A closed-set classifier trained on machined or EDM defects, with augmentation adding variety but not real crack morphology, will confidently output axial or circumferential labels for stress-corrosion, mixed-mode, wear, deposit or noisy signals it has never seen, with no abstain path. Misread or missed degradation leaves a flawed tube in service; an adversary could hide a manipulation or flaw signature inside this predictable out-of-distribution blind spot.

Small-data base rate and inflated validation -- implicit
Real flaws are rare and plant-specific, and augmented copies of the same specimen signal can leak across train and test splits, so reported performance overstates the false-negative rate that matters for safety-significant flaws. An adversary gains little directly from this beyond the general misplaced trust it creates.

Preprocessing brittleness and drift -- implicit, exploitable
Features keyed to filtering, normalisation or calibration choices degrade when probes, instruments or acquisition settings change between outages, shifting error rates without visible alarm. An adversary could alter calibration or preprocessing parameters to push real indications across the decision boundary under cover of this expected drift.

Qualification gap and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Eddy-current analysis relies on performance demonstration and qualified procedures that do not map onto an opaque, training-non-deterministic DNN, so version-to-version changes and error ownership cannot be traced. This makes a backdoor or tampering indistinguishable from honest error and defeats forensic verification of the model.

Automation bias and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Outage schedule pressure leads analysts to accept the label, eroding the independent two-analyst review and manual orientation judgement that is the main detection layer for model failure. An adversary can rely on this misplaced trust so that a corrupted label passes without scrutiny.

Oversimplified two-class output and scope creep -- implicit
An axial/circumferential label covers only one decision in a chain that also includes detection, sizing, depth and location, and it can be quietly extended to other tasks or reused across units, probes and vendors. A single flawed or compromised model then propagates its bias fleet-wide, which is the amplifier an adversary would target.

Training data and model poisoning -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor with write access to specimen signals, labels, augmentation scripts or weights could plant a backdoor trigger or systematic blind spot that labels certain flaw signatures benign or as the wrong orientation. The result is latent pressure-boundary degradation that stays invisible past outage closure and risks tube leak or rupture.

Raw-signal and pipeline tampering -- adversarial
Adversarial perturbation, substitution or chaff in eddy-current files, or tampering with preprocessing and analysis code, can push real flaws below the classifier's threshold while looking normal to a reviewer. The data path is contractor-operated and weakly monitored, and the same manipulation can instead force costly repeat inspections and outage delay.

Model theft and reconnaissance -- adversarial
Published architecture and performance details let an adversary build a proxy model and rehearse evasion offline, or extract a deployed model to find its blind spots. This lowers the cost of crafting inputs that will be mislabeled.

nuclear_engineer.argument: Steam generator tubes are the reactor coolant pressure boundary, so a missed or misclassified flaw during an outage inspection can leave a degraded tube in service. In the worst case that is a tube rupture or an SGTR-type bypass of containment. The documented classifier is trained on specimen tubes with deliberately introduced (EDM-notch or machined) defects, so the main implicit weakness is a gap between lab and field. Real degradation such as stress corrosion cracking, pitting, wear, denting, deposits, support-plate and tubesheet geometry, and probe wobble produces different, noisier, and often mixed-orientation signals. Axial versus circumferential is only one decision in an analysis chain that also covers detection, sizing, depth, and location. If the tool is positioned as a first-pass screen to cope with time-limited outages, the real danger is automation bias and schedule pressure eroding the independent human analysis (the two-analyst, qualified-procedure practice under EPRI guidelines). Existing practice limits some of that risk: qualified analysts, performance-demonstration programs, and the burden of proof on any new technique. That protection only holds if the AI is formally qualified and not quietly used as the decision-maker.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT: (1) Specimen-to-field generalization failure. Training on artificial defects, augmented and preprocessed, gives a model that scores well on lab data but misreads real cracking morphology, branched or mixed-mode cracks, and signals affected by noise, deposits, geometry, or different probe, instrument, or tube-material setups. The consequence is a false 'axial' or 'circumferential' label, or a missed flaw. Circumferential cracking is the more structurally consequential, so it matters which way the errors fall. (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202; the augmentation can also hide the gap by making the validation set look like the training set.) (2) Small-data and rare-flaw base rate. Real flaws are rare and plant-specific, so the apparent high performance may not predict the false-negative rate that matters. (OP.C0202, OP.C0403) (3) Qualification gap. Standard NDE performance demonstration (POD, blind testing with qualified procedures and analyst qualification) does not map neatly onto a DNN, and opaque, non-repeatable features make it hard to prove which signal features drive the decision. (OP.C0501, OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0303) (4) Human factors. Under outage time pressure, analysts may accept the label without independent review, which turns a single-point model error into a pressure-boundary decision. Skill fade follows if analysts stop practicing signal interpretation. (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102) (5) Scope creep and fleet propagation: a tool validated for one defect distinction is extended to other tasks, or a single model is reused across units and vendors with different probes and calibrations. (OP.C0602, OP.C0101.03) ADVERSARIAL: (6) Training-data or pipeline poisoning. An insider or supply-chain actor who can alter the specimen signals, labels, augmentation scripts, or model weights could introduce a backdoor, for example a pattern in which a certain signal signature is always labeled benign or as the less significant orientation. (AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004) (7) Manipulation of acquisition data. Tampering with raw eddy-current files, calibration or preprocessing parameters, or adding chaff or small perturbations could push real flaws below the classifier's decision boundary without alarming a human reviewer. This gives an attacker a quiet way to hide degradation. It would be hard to combine with physical sabotage, but it could also simply cause costly repeat inspections and outage delay. (AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031, AML.T0059, AML.T0029) (8) Model-integrity and IT/OT surface: the classifier adds software, GPU, and data-transfer dependencies to inspection vendor and plant networks. This is a new route for compromise of inspection records. Cloud or vendor-hosted analysis would also add a data-confidentiality exposure about tube condition. (AML.T0010.001, OP.C0601, OP.C0502) The key mitigation context is that the final disposition (plugging, repair, or continued operation) is still governed by qualified Level III analysts and regulatory rules. The harm path therefore requires the AI output to displace, not just supplement, that independent review.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view, this classifier is trained on signals from laboratory tube specimens with deliberately introduced defects (EDM notches or machined flaws), then augmented, and is meant to be applied to field MRPC data. That is a bench-to-field transfer problem. Artificial flaws have cleaner geometry and different electromagnetic signatures from real stress-corrosion cracks, and they lack the noise sources of a real steam generator: denting, deposits, support plate and tube sheet geometry, magnetite, probe wobble, and cable and instrument variability. Augmentation widens the apparent training distribution but does not add real flaw morphology. Reported high axial/circumferential performance therefore reflects in-distribution validation on specimen data, and it says little about calibration, out-of-distribution behaviour or rare flaw types in service. The task is also narrow (a binary orientation label), so it sits inside a larger detection and sizing chain that the model does not cover, and errors upstream or downstream would be hidden by the classifier's apparent competence.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Bench-to-field domain shift (OP.C0201.01/.04, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03). The mechanism is a model trained on specimen signals with artificial defects that sees real-flaw signals, geometry confounders, probe or instrument changes, and different tube materials or plants at inference. A closed-set softmax classifier will still output confident axial or circumferential labels for inputs that are neither (volumetric wear, deposit signals, mixed-mode cracks, noise), with no abstain path. The plant dependency is flaw characterisation for tube plugging and repair decisions. The consequence is misclassified or under-characterised degradation, which reduces the integrity margin of a pressure-boundary barrier. (2) Small-data and low base rate (OP.C0202, OP.C0203). Real flaw examples are scarce and plant-specific, and augmentation can create leakage between train and test splits (augmented copies of the same specimen signal on both sides), inflating reported performance. Rare, safety-significant flaw classes are the least represented. (3) Augmentation and preprocessing artefacts. Learned features may key on preprocessing choices (filtering, normalisation, calibration-standard handling), which makes the model brittle when acquisition settings or calibrations change between outages, a concept/data drift case (OP.C0302.01/.02). (4) Qualification mismatch (OP.C0303, OP.C0501, OP.C0401). Eddy-current analysis runs under qualified procedures with performance demonstration. A DNN has no established qualification path, limited explainability, and training non-determinism (OP.C0402.01), so version-to-version behaviour can change without a traceable reason. (5) Automation bias and skill fade (OP.C0101.04/.06, OP.C0102). Time-pressured outage schedules push analysts to accept the machine label, and manual orientation judgement erodes. Unlike the model, human analysts notice unusual signals, so disagreements are the main detection layer for model failure. ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Training or fine-tuning data poisoning and label manipulation (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0059). The dataset is small, curated, and shared between vendors, utilities and research groups, so a few altered labels or a backdoor-style trigger signature (T0043.004) could bias orientation calls, or degrade performance on selected tube regions. This exploits the weak provenance controls typical of lab data. (7) Model or pipeline tampering and supply chain (AML.T0010.001/.003, T0018, T0076). Weights, preprocessing code and third-party deep learning libraries sit within the inspection analysis workflow. Silent modification could shift decision thresholds without visible failure. (8) Data-integrity attacks at inference (AML.T0015, T0043). Altering stored or transmitted eddy-current files, or exploiting a model with known blind spots, could cause a particular indication to be mislabeled. This needs access to the acquisition or analysis network, which is more plausible given the concentration of inspection data on vendor laptops and shared drives. The cause is the AI classifier's lack of input validation and integrity checking. The effect is concealed or mischaracterised degradation of a safety-relevant barrier, with a further regulatory-trust consequence (OP.C0504) if an AI-assisted analysis is later found unreliable. (9) Cross-fleet propagation (OP.C0602). A single model reused across units or vendors spreads any bias or compromise widely.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-surface view, an MRPC flaw classifier concentrates trust at the one point where steam generator tube integrity (a primary-pressure-boundary barrier) is decided under outage time pressure. Once analysts rely on it to triage very large signal volumes, it becomes a high-value target for an insider or supply-chain actor. Quietly suppressing or mislabeling a handful of indications is easier and more deniable than any physical sabotage, and the damage appears later as an in-service tube leak or rupture. A sophisticated adversary would more plausibly take the cheap routes (training-data or model tampering, or exploiting the pre-outage window) than attack the plant directly. The non-adversarial weaknesses matter too: a model trained on machined-specimen signals is brittle on real degradation, and that gap is what an adversary can hide behind or time an attack around.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Training-data and model integrity: the model learns from specimen signals with deliberate defects, then preprocessing and augmentation. Anyone with write access to the specimen datasets, augmentation scripts, labels, or model weights (a vendor insider, an inspection-contractor employee, or a compromised third-party tool) could plant a backdoor or a systematic blind spot. An example is a signal feature or geometry that causes certain flaw types or orientations to be labeled benign or misclassified. The facility depends on correct axial/circumferential and flaw-present calls to trigger plugging, repair, and re-inspection decisions. The consequence is undetected degradation of the pressure boundary, with possible tube leak or rupture, and latent damage that stays invisible until after outage closure (ATLAS AML.T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004, T0076). (2) Raw-signal and pipeline tampering: eddy-current data passes through acquisition, preprocessing, and inference, and manipulating it at any point (adversarial perturbation or substitution) could evade the classifier while appearing normal to a human reviewer. Inspection data pipelines are often OT-adjacent, contractor-operated, and weakly monitored (T0015, T0043, T0031). (3) Concentrated trust and shared tooling: if the same vendor model or analysis workflow is reused across plants, one compromise propagates fleet-wide (T0010, OP.C0602). (4) Reconnaissance and model theft: published architecture and performance details help an adversary build a proxy model and rehearse evasion offline (T0000, T0005, T0024.002).

IMPLICIT, and exploitable around. (a) Specimen-to-field gap: deliberate machined defects differ from real stress-corrosion cracking, fretting, denting, deposits, and noise from support structures. Augmentation adds synthetic variety but not real-world fidelity, so the model fails on out-of-distribution signals, and a skilled adversary can exploit that predictable blind spot (OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0302, OP.C0202, OP.C0303). (b) Automation trust: time-limited outages push analysts to accept the classifier's labels. Skill fade and complacency erode the independent double-analyst review that would be the last line of defense against both error and tampering (OP.C0101.04, .06, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.01). (c) Opacity and non-repeatability: a DNN's logic cannot be audited, so a backdoor or drift is hard to distinguish from honest error. Run-to-run training variation also undermines forensic verification of the model (OP.C0401, OP.C0402, OP.C0403). (d) Qualification gap: eddy-current analysis is governed by qualified procedures and personnel. An unqualified AI tool sits outside this framework and creates ambiguity over who owns an erroneous call (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). A two-class axial/circumferential output also oversimplifies the real flaw taxonomy (OP.C0304.03). Overall, the highest-value adversary action is subtle, deniable corruption of the training data or model combined with erosion of human review, not a disruptive attack.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on specimen-to-field generalization failure, qualification gap, automation bias, and poisoning/pipeline tampering; I merged these and kept the security specialist's model-theft point as distinct. I dropped the weakly supported cloud and software-hygiene codes (OP.C0601, OP.C0502) and the denial-of-service and mode-error codes, which no threat in the text clearly instantiates.

evidence.citation: "MRPC eddy current flaw classification in tubes using deep neural networks," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Korean Nuclear Society / Elsevier, ScienceDirect)
evidence.note: The paper describes a five-step workflow: MRPC probe data acquisition on tube specimens with deliberate defects, signal preprocessing, data augmentation, DNN training, and a demonstration of the trained network. The network separated axial from circumferential defects with high performance. The authors conclude it could serve as an automated data-processing tool for steam generator tube eddy-current testing.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is poisoning or pipeline tampering that causes real flaws in steam generator tubes (a primary pressure-boundary barrier) to be misclassified or missed, risking tube leak or rupture; this is serious safety-margin erosion and possible primary-to-secondary leakage, though a release would need further failures, so it falls just short of 5.

reproducibility.why: The specimen-to-field generalization gap, drift and automation bias reliably recur once the tool is deployed on real signals under outage pressure, while the adversarial threats depend on the attacker holding the right access.

exploitability.why: The most severe threats (training-data or model poisoning, and tampering with the contractor data pipeline) need insider or supply-chain write access; only the reconnaissance and proxy-model threat is achievable from outside.

affected_users.why: A compromised or biased model reused across units, probes and vendors propagates fleet-wide and affects tube-integrity decisions for many steam generators, though it stays within one inspection function rather than across all plant systems.

discoverability.why: The architecture and performance are published in the open literature, and the weaknesses of closed-set classifiers (out-of-distribution blind spots, drift, automation bias) are well documented for this class of AI system, so an adversary can readily infer that they exist.

use_case: Residual neural network (ResNet) image classification of surface corrosion on stainless-steel dry storage canisters for used nuclear fuel. Camera images of the canister are cropped into small tiles. The ResNet flags corroded tiles, which show iron-oxide discoloration, pitting and stress corrosion cracking and where on the canister it occurs. The per-image count of corroded tiles then classifies each image as corroded or intact. This is meant to automate and speed up canister inspections, cut inspection cost, and partly replace on-site human inspection, which lowers personnel radiation dose.
incurred_insecurity:
Using a tile-based ResNet to flag corrosion and stress corrosion cracking on dry storage canisters, and partly replace on-site human inspection, makes the classifier's verdict the de facto integrity record for a long-lived confinement boundary. The main threats are silent false negatives from scarce, surrogate training data and poorly transferring field conditions, a fragile tile-count decision rule, erosion of human cross-checks, evasion and tampering that hide real degradation, compromise of the model and its supply chain, and disruption or reconnaissance against the inspection pipeline. The realistic harm is delayed detection of degradation and loss of credibility of the aging-management and regulatory record, not a sudden release.

Scarce, surrogate training data -- implicit, exploitable
