Real SCC-bearing canister images are rare and low base-rate, so a model trained on lab, mock-up or small field sets learns colour and texture shortcuts and misses fine cracks while flagging benign staining, welds and deposits. An adversary could rely on these known blind spots, using coatings, deposits or lighting that look like normal variability, to hide degradation as an apparently successful inspection.

Field drift and heterogeneity -- implicit, exploitable
Camera, standoff, vent-channel geometry, illumination, surface finish, canister design and marine or inland deposition all shift the input distribution, and the tile scores and fixed count threshold do not transfer or flag out-of-distribution inputs, so the model is confidently wrong. An adversary could time manipulation to such periods, where tampering is indistinguishable from environmental or equipment variation.

Tile-count aggregation and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
Thresholding the count of corroded tiles lets early, localised SCC fall below the image-level cutoff, and tile cropping discards crack continuity, while saliency maps cannot show why a tile was judged intact. An adversary, or an insider, could shift the threshold slightly or confine an effect to few tiles, producing systematic misses that look like normal binary output.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
Reduced on-site inspection leaves inspectors out of the loop, deskilled, and treating a confident intact label as clearance, with no independent ground truth for canisters never directly examined. An adversary can exploit this misplaced trust and vigilance gap, knowing nobody is positioned to notice a discrepancy.

Qualification, configuration and fleet gaps -- implicit, exploitable
There is no established qualification path for an ML classifier in an aging-management program, retraining is non-deterministic and may be uncontrolled, and one model reused across sites propagates the same blind spot fleet-wide. An adversary could use weak change control to slip in a modified model, or target a single common-cause weakness across many storage sites.

Evasion of the classifier -- adversarial
Physical changes to what the camera sees (coatings, contamination, lighting, positioning) or digital perturbation of images in transit or storage can push corroded tiles below the threshold without changing the canister. The result is a degraded canister recorded as intact, undermining safety and containment-and-surveillance style records.

Model and pipeline compromise -- adversarial
Poisoned training or labelling data, backdoored or swapped pretrained ResNet weights, compromised frameworks or tooling, or altered thresholds, scores and stored images can bias the classifier toward intact on chosen features. An insider with valid accounts on a system with weaker access control than safety instrumentation is the most plausible path, and publication of the architecture eases proxy-model crafting.

Denial and erosion of confidence -- adversarial
Chaff images, induced false positives or disruption of the analysis pipeline erode trust in the tool or force reversion to manual inspection, with unplanned dose, cost and schedule impact.

Inspection-record reconnaissance -- adversarial
Image archives, coverage maps and findings reveal which canisters and surfaces were examined and where degradation is developing, useful for planning against a storage site. Such archives and any cloud processing may carry a weaker data security model than the physical site.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a dry cask storage operations view, this is an inspection-support tool. Its output feeds decisions on canister integrity, aging-management actions, and whether a human has to go look at a canister at all. The main downstream danger is a false negative that goes unchallenged. Chloride-induced SCC on austenitic stainless canisters is a rare, slow, safety-significant event, and the classifier was probably trained on limited lab or surrogate imagery and then applied to real, heterogeneous field conditions. Once the tool is credited with partly replacing on-site inspection, the compensating safeguard (a human inspector, supplemented by surface sampling and NDE such as eddy current) gets thinner, and the dose-saving rationale creates pressure to trust it. Harm still needs several further failures: the aging-management program must miss the degradation, and the corrosion must progress toward through-wall penetration. Existing practice (periodic inspections, a confinement boundary that is not the only barrier, and licensing-basis inspection requirements) limits near-term consequences. The realistic harm is therefore erosion of the safety case and delayed detection of degradation, not a sudden release.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Training-data scarcity and provenance: real SCC-bearing canister images are very scarce and low base-rate. Models are likely trained on lab-simulated or surrogate corrosion, or on small field sets from a few sites, and may learn discoloration or lighting cues rather than actual cracking. The result is false negatives on real fine cracks and false positives on benign staining, dust, weld marks, and deposits (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01/.02, OP.C0203, OP.C0302.03). (2) Drift and operational heterogeneity: camera type, standoff distance, vent-path geometry, illumination, surface finish, canister vendor and design, and the site environment (marine vs. inland salt deposition) all shift between deployments. Performance validated on one set does not transfer, and accuracy numbers from a paper are not a qualification (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303, OP.C0501). (3) Aggregation logic: classifying an image by a threshold on corroded-tile counts creates a tunable decision boundary. Small early-stage SCC covers few tiles and may fall below the threshold, which is exactly the case that matters. Tile cropping also loses global context such as crack continuity (OP.C0304.03, OP.C0403). (4) Automation bias and skill fade: if the tool reduces human inspection, inspectors become out of the loop and less able to catch what the model misses. A confident 'intact' result becomes a de facto clearance (OP.C0101.01/.04/.06). (5) Opacity: tile-level heatmaps help, but they do not show why a tile was judged intact, which limits the reviewer's ability to challenge it (OP.C0401). (6) Fleet propagation: one model reused across many sites carries the same blind spot everywhere, a common-cause weakness across the storage fleet (OP.C0602). Retraining without configuration control adds software-hygiene risk (OP.C0502).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Adversarial or physical perturbation: patterns, coatings, or lighting changes that suppress corrosion features could hide real degradation from the classifier (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). That needs physical access to an inspected canister, which in a licensed facility is a high bar. (b) Data and model integrity: poisoning of the training set or model, or a supply-chain compromise of the classifier or its tooling, could bias it toward 'intact' on particular features (AML.T0020, AML.T0018, AML.T0010, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). (c) Image-pipeline tampering: manipulating images or results in transit or storage between camera, robot or crawler, and inspection record could falsify the integrity record. This also affects inspection records used by regulators, a safeguards-adjacent record-integrity concern (AML.T0031). (d) Denial or delay: disrupting the tool pushes the operator back to costly manual inspection, with dose and schedule consequences (AML.T0029). The main adversary value is quietly degrading confidence in canister integrity or the inspection record, not causing immediate harm. The key mitigations are retained human review of flagged and sampled 'intact' results, independent NDE, controlled test sets with real SCC, and configuration-controlled models.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a tile-level ResNet classifier with an image-level decision rule (count of flagged tiles above a threshold), so its fragility sits in the data, the cropping and thresholding pipeline, and the gap between the lab-built training set and field imagery. Real corroded dry-storage canisters are rare, and chloride-induced SCC at the severity of interest is scarcer still. The training set is therefore likely to be small, partly lab-produced or surrogate (corroded coupons, mock-ups, staged images) and weakly labeled. A tile-level model trained on this kind of data learns texture and color cues such as rust-like discoloration, and these cues transfer poorly to the field. The field has welds, heat tint, dust, salt deposits, water streaks, shadows, glare, vent-duct geometry, and variable camera, lens and lighting setups. Because the system is meant to partly replace on-site human inspection, a miss, meaning a false negative on a real SCC site, quietly removes the human check the system was supposed to supplement, and the failures concentrate on the rare, high-consequence cases.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Data provenance and scarcity (OP.C0201.01/.02/.04, OP.C0202, OP.C0204). A small, class-imbalanced dataset with surrogate or lab-derived corrosion images leads to shortcut learning on color and texture. Fine, tight SCC cracks and pitting are visually subtle and under-represented, so tile-level recall for the dangerous failure modes is probably far lower than headline accuracy suggests. Image-level accuracy is also inflated if tiles from the same canister or image leak across train and test splits. (2) Distribution shift (OP.C0302.01/.03, OP.C0303). Deployment images come from different canister designs, vendors, surface finishes, ages, camera systems (robotic crawlers or remote cameras in narrow vent channels), illumination, and coating or deposit states. Gradual drift in the camera or lighting, or in the environment, can silently change the tile score distribution. The fixed tile-count threshold is a second calibration point: tile size, image resolution, and canister coverage all change the count, so a threshold tuned on one dataset may not hold on another. The system gives no native out-of-distribution flag, so confident wrong outputs are likely. (3) Architectural and decision-rule weaknesses (OP.C0403, OP.C0401, OP.C0402). Aggregating tile counts hides single critical tiles, and a localized SCC crack could fall below the count threshold and the canister is labeled intact. Softmax confidence is poorly calibrated. Saliency explanations are weak evidence for subtle defects. Retraining non-determinism makes version-to-version behavior hard to reproduce for qualification. (4) Human factors (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102, OP.C0101.06). Over-trust in an 'intact' label, reduced inspector exposure and skill fade all remove independent verification. There is no ground truth for canisters that were never examined directly. (5) Governance (OP.C0501, OP.C0503, OP.C0504). There is no established qualification path for an ML classifier used in an aging-management or inspection program, and retraining or model updates may not be controlled as configuration changes.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Evasion through physical or digital perturbation (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). The classifier relies on color and texture, so surface contamination, coatings, lighting, or small image-level perturbations could push corroded tiles below the threshold. Tampering with the camera feed or image files in transit could do the same. The effect is concealment of real degradation, which defeats the safety and safeguards purpose of the inspection. (7) Supply chain and pipeline integrity (AML.T0010.001/.003, AML.T0018, AML.T0020/.T0010.002). Pretrained ResNet weights from public repositories (AML.T0002.001, AML.T0058), open-source frameworks, and the training and labeling data are all poisoning or backdoor entry points. A trigger pattern could make corroded tiles read as clean. Open publication of the architecture and approach (AML.T0000, AML.T0005) makes building a proxy model easy and lets an attacker craft adversarial inputs offline. (8) Integrity of the results and the data store (AML.T0031, AML.T0059, AML.T0076). Altering stored images, tile scores, or thresholds, or degrading retraining data, can hide degradation trends. Outsourced or cloud-based processing (OP.C0601) adds access and availability risk. (9) Denial of service (AML.T0029) on the analysis pipeline forces a return to manual inspection, which costs dose and schedule. Implicit weaknesses give an adversary a chance to time tampering with the pipeline around periods when human inspection is reduced.

security_specialist.argument: From an adversarial lens, this system matters less as a direct target than as a way to shape what humans never look at. It is meant to partly replace on-site visual inspection of dry storage canisters, so the classifier's verdict becomes the only record that a canister was inspected and found intact. An adversary, or a careless insider, who can influence the camera input, the tiling and thresholding pipeline, or the model artifact can hide real chloride-induced stress corrosion cracking, or flood the system with false alarms that wear down trust. Nobody is physically in the dose-limited area to notice a discrepancy. Dry storage is also a long-duration, low-attention domain, so a quiet integrity failure could go undetected for years, and the delay would favour an adversary who wants to shape the timing of a later event or undermine confidence in a licensed storage site.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (1) Input evasion and manipulation of the evidence chain. The mechanism is that a ResNet on small tiles, with an image-level decision from a tile count, is sensitive to input perturbation. Lighting, surface contamination, coatings, camera position, or digital tampering with images in transit or storage can push the tile count below threshold without changing the physical canister (AML.T0015, AML.T0043, AML.T0041). The facility depends on this output to schedule follow-up inspections and to support regulatory aging-management records for canister integrity. The consequence is that a degraded canister is recorded as intact. This is a safety and security consequence, and also a safeguards-adjacent one, because containment and surveillance records lose credibility. (2) Pipeline and model compromise. The model, weights, tiling code, thresholds and image archive sit in a supply chain of research code, pretrained ResNet backbones and possibly vendor or cloud tooling. Poisoned or backdoored weights, a swapped pretrained model, or a quiet change to the count threshold would produce systematic misses that look like normal operation (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018, AML.T0020, AML.T0076). Because the output is binary per image, a small threshold change is hard to see. An insider with valid accounts is the most plausible path, since these systems are rarely treated with the same access controls as safety-related instrumentation (AML.T0012). (3) Denial of confidence. Spamming the pipeline with chaff images, or inducing visible false positives, can force reversion to manual inspection and cause unplanned dose, cost and operator disruption, or erode trust in the tool (AML.T0046, AML.T0029, AML.T0031). (4) Reconnaissance value. The images, the inspection coverage map and the findings reveal which canisters and surfaces have been examined and where degradation is developing. That is useful intelligence for adversaries planning against a storage site (AML.T0036, AML.T0025). Image archives may get a weaker data security model than the physical site (OP.C0505.01).

IMPLICIT WEAKNESSES AN ADVERSARY COULD TIME AROUND. (a) Small-data, low base-rate problem. Real field cases of stress corrosion cracking on canisters are rare, and training relies on lab, simulated or surrogate imagery, so the model may miss real defects in field conditions (OP.C0202, OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02). Missed detections then look like successful inspections. (b) Drift and operational heterogeneity. Different canister designs, welds, dust, salt deposits, lighting and camera systems will shift the input distribution. Deposits can mimic or mask rust discoloration (OP.C0302.01, OP.C0302.03). This gives an adversary or an unlucky site a window in which the classifier is confidently wrong. (c) Automation trust and skill fade. Replacing on-site human inspection removes the human cross-check and lets inspector expertise erode (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0101.01, OP.C0102). A vigilance gap is exactly what a patient adversary would time an action around. (d) Opacity and qualification gaps. There is no AI-specific qualification regime for aging-management tools, and tile-level explanations may not support a defensible audit trail (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Together these allow a silent failure to persist, either because someone engineered it or because it arose naturally.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on false negatives from scarce surrogate data, drift, automation trust, and evasion or poisoning that hides degradation; I merged overlapping items and kept the tile-threshold, fleet propagation and reconnaissance points as distinct. I dropped weakly supported items (e.g. OP.C0204, OP.C0503) and kept ATLAS codes only where the pathway is an adversary action.

evidence.citation: "Automated detection of corrosion in used nuclear fuel dry storage canisters using residual neural networks," Nuclear Engineering and Technology (Elsevier / Korean Nuclear Society), Vol. 53, Issue 2, pp. 657-665, 2021
evidence.note: The peer-reviewed paper (Oak Ridge National Laboratory authors, with EPRI) trains ResNets on tiled canister images. It reports that the approach locates corrosion in small tiles and infers with high accuracy whether an image comes from a corroded canister. An earlier arXiv preprint (2003.03241) exists, but this cites the peer-reviewed journal version.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is evasion or model/pipeline compromise that records a degraded confinement canister as intact. This delays detection of stress corrosion cracking and falsifies the aging-management and safeguards-style record. The entry itself says the harm is delayed detection rather than a sudden release, so this falls just short of the maximum.

reproducibility.why: The implicit weaknesses (surrogate-data blind spots, field drift, a fixed tile-count threshold, over-trust) occur reliably whenever the stated deployment conditions hold. Deliberate evasion or tampering depends more on access and conditions, so this is slightly below the maximum.

exploitability.why: Physical-appearance evasion or exploiting known blind spots needs some site or physical access, and dry storage canisters are access-controlled. Model and pipeline compromise is most plausible via an insider with valid accounts. No single route is purely external and routine.

affected_users.why: A single model reused across sites propagates the same blind spot fleet-wide (common-cause weakness), and the corrupted integrity record undermines regulatory credibility across many canisters. The effect is not tightly coupled facility-wide, so it falls just short of 5.

discoverability.why: The architecture and method are published in an open peer-reviewed paper, and the failure modes of image classifiers (adversarial evasion, drift, data scarcity, supply-chain poisoning) are well documented in the open literature. Finding site-specific thresholds or deployment details would need more insider knowledge.

use_case: Convolutional neural network defect detection on eddy-current testing (ECT) scan data from stainless-steel (304L/316L) weld samples of spent nuclear fuel dry storage canisters. The 2D ECT scan maps are treated as images and split into fault-area and normal-area patches. The CNN classifies them to find weld cracks, which supports automated non-destructive inspection of canister welds.
incurred_insecurity:
A patch-level CNN that declares canister welds crack-free sits as a single point of trust over a confinement boundary that cannot be readily reopened or repaired. Its only documented evidence is one seeded-fault 304L sample with a waterjet slot. The main threats are a seeded-to-real-flaw generalization gap, patch-framing blind spots, opacity and missing qualification, automation over-trust, and adversarial integrity attacks on data, weights and supply chain, with evasion and data exposure as secondary routes. Each weakness makes concealed degradation harder to detect and easier to hide.

Seeded-fault training gap -- implicit, exploitable
The model learns the clean, high-contrast signature of an artificial slot from a tiny, low-base-rate dataset on one weld, one probe and one setup. Tight, branched real stress corrosion cracks, weld-metal permeability variation, lift-off and different probes fall outside that distribution, producing confident false negatives on real cracks or false positives on weld features. An adversary who understands this blind spot could tune physical damage or scan conditions to stay in the regions the model never saw, and the miss would look like natural model failure.

Patch-level framing blind spot -- implicit, exploitable
Splitting scan maps into fault and normal patches can fragment elongated indications and discards flaw length, depth and location, so a patch label does not map onto flaw-based acceptance criteria. Cracks that span tile boundaries or sit in marginal areas form a predictable blind spot an adversary could aim for.

Opacity and missing qualification -- implicit, exploitable
Uncalibrated softmax scores, no explanation of why a patch is called normal, and no probability-of-detection curve or code-accepted performance demonstration leave the evaluator unqualified for safety-significant dispositions. This weak assurance baseline means silent degradation or deliberate tampering with the model would go unnoticed, and an adversary can rely on the missing baseline to avoid detection.

Automation trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
If a normal label becomes the default screening outcome, analysts review fewer raw ECT signals and lose interpretive skill, so a missed crack with high confidence is accepted. An adversary could time tampering or sabotage to this period of reduced scrutiny and use the resulting false all-clear record to conceal damage.

Lifecycle and repeatability drift -- implicit
Retraining or changes to probes, hardware or software alter model behaviour and break repeatability against earlier inspection baselines. An adversary gains little from this beyond what the drift and qualification weaknesses already offer.

Training-data and model integrity attack -- adversarial
An insider or supply-chain actor could poison or mislabel the very small training set, insert a backdoor trigger, or swap or corrupt model weights or pretrained backbones so that real cracks are systematically classed normal. The consequence is undetected through-wall flaws in a containment boundary, a false inspection record, and untraceable loss of defense-in-depth.

Scan-data evasion and tampering -- adversarial
Crafted perturbations, altered probe or scan parameters, or edited raw ECT files can keep a real flaw below the classifier's decision boundary without touching the model. This yields a false all-clear for a canister that is physically degraded.

False-indication flooding and model degradation -- adversarial
Injected false indications or a degraded model could force unnecessary canister handling, repair and dose, or erode trust in the program. Real harm still requires independent failure of analyst review and redundant NDE.

Exposure of model and defect data -- adversarial
Theft of model weights, defect libraries or ECT datasets, including via cloud or vendor-hosted tooling, reveals which flaw types and sizes evade detection and helps an adversary design undetectable damage.

ai_vulnerability_atlas.atlas_name: Spamming AI System with Chaff Data

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a facility-operations view, this CNN screens ECT maps of 304L/316L canister welds for chloride-induced stress corrosion cracking (SCC) and fabrication flaws. The only documented evidence is one submerged-arc-welded 304L sample with an artificial waterjet-cut slot, so the model is trained on the easiest case: a clean, wide, geometrically regular defect. Real SCC is tight, branched and tortuous, with a weak ECT signal sitting on weld-metal permeability variation, delta-ferrite content, surface roughness, lift-off and probe-wobble noise. The dominant downstream risk is a false negative, because a missed crack gives false assurance and delays mitigation of a through-wall breach path in a canister that cannot be readily reopened or repaired. The cost of the opposite error, false positives, is mostly inspection burden and ALARA dose. Existing practice (qualified procedures, Level III analyst review, ASME-style performance demonstration, and aging-management programs with periodic re-inspection) would catch most of this if the CNN stays advisory. The vulnerability grows if it replaces the analyst, or if inspection frequency or scope is relaxed on the strength of its output.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS (no adversary needed). (1) Seeded-fault surrogate and data scarcity: a lab EDM or waterjet slot is not field SCC, and real cracked canister welds are very rare, so the training data is small and low-base-rate. Patch-level classification on a few scans likely overfits to the artificial notch signature. The result is poor sensitivity to tight, real cracks, and it creates missed-detection risk for the canister containment boundary (OP.C0201.01, OP.C0201.02, OP.C0202, OP.C0203). (2) Generalization and drift: the model may fail under different weld processes, heat-affected-zone geometry, 316L versus 304L, probe or instrument changes, surface condition, and remote-deployment effects such as crawler or robot scanning in a vent-path or narrow-gap environment (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). (3) Patch-based framing: splitting maps into fault and normal patches can break up elongated indications, so sizing and location are lost, and a patch decision may not match the acceptance criteria, which are about flaw depth and length (OP.C0301, OP.C0304.03). (4) Opacity and qualification: there is no explainability for why a patch is called normal. Qualification, performance demonstration with a probability-of-detection curve, and code acceptance of an AI evaluator are all lacking (OP.C0401, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (5) Automation bias: analysts see the CNN's call first and become complacent. Skill fades in manual ECT interpretation, and a high confidence score on a missed crack gets accepted (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0102).

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (6) Integrity attack on scan data or the model: a compromised acquisition or analysis chain (workstation, supply-chain model or software, or manipulated training or retraining data) could suppress or mask indications, either through crafted perturbation of the ECT maps or through a poisoned or backdoored model. Because the output is a pass/fail disposition, the consequence would be concealed degradation in a stored-fuel containment boundary. This is a safety and security concern, and it also bears on regulator trust and records for a licence-renewal case (AML.T0010.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0020, AML.T0043, AML.T0015, AML.T0031). (7) Record tampering and false-positive flooding: an adversary could inject false indications, or degrade the model, to drive unnecessary canister handling, repair, or dose, or to erode confidence and delay the program (AML.T0046, AML.T0029). Any actual harm still needs independent failure of analyst review, redundant NDE, and the monitoring and aging-management program. That is why the key control is keeping the CNN advisory, with a second-method or human verification of every negative call in safety-significant welds.

ai_engineer.argument: This is a patch-level image classifier trained on a very small, lab-generated dataset: a single submerged-arc-welded 304L sample with an artificial waterjet-cut slot. That is a poor proxy for real chloride-induced stress corrosion cracking (CISCC) in as-fielded 304L/316L canisters. The main fragility is data provenance and distribution shift, not model architecture. A waterjet slot has clean geometry and a sharp, high-contrast ECT signature. Real tight, branched, partly closed SCC cracks give weaker and more ambiguous signals, and they sit among confounders the training set never contained: weld-bead geometry, permeability variation from delta ferrite, surface roughness, lift-off, probe wobble, and different probe or frequency settings. Patch-level splitting into 'fault' and 'normal' areas invites leakage between train and test patches from the same scan, so the reported 'feasible and effective' result likely overstates generalization. The class imbalance is also extreme, because real cracks are rare.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
IMPLICIT THREATS. (1) Seeded-fault-to-real-flaw gap (OP.C0201.01/.02/.04, OP.C0202, OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0303). The model learns the signature of an artificial slot on one weld, one probe and one scan setup. Mechanism: at inference, real SCC, weld-geometry artifacts, instrument changes or different canister fabrication lots fall outside the training distribution. The CNN gives confident but wrong outputs, either false negatives on subtle cracks or false positives on weld features. Dependence: the canister integrity assessment and the aging-management inspection record. Consequence: missed through-wall or near-through-wall cracking in a confinement boundary that is hard to repair or inspect, or alternatively a flood of false calls that erodes trust. (2) Opacity and weak uncertainty calibration (OP.C0401, OP.C0403). CNN softmax scores are not calibrated probabilities and give no probability-of-detection (POD) curve. NDE qualification (e.g. ASME Section XI / EPRI-style performance demonstration) requires POD and sizing evidence that this approach cannot yet provide, which is a qualification gap (OP.C0501, OP.C0504). (3) Automation trust (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0102). If a 'normal' label becomes the default screening outcome, inspectors may skip manual review of raw signals, and their skill with raw ECT interpretation fades (OP.C0101.06). (4) Lifecycle issues: retraining after probe, hardware or software changes breaks repeatability (OP.C0402.01, OP.C0302.01), and patch-boundary effects can split a crack across tiles.

ADVERSARIAL THREATS. (a) Training-data or label poisoning (AML.T0020, T0010.002, T0059): a small number of mislabelled or manipulated scans in a tiny dataset has outsized effect, and the corpus may be shared across labs and contractors. It could make real cracks look 'normal' or insert a backdoor trigger (T0043.004). (b) Data-in-transit or at-rest tampering of ECT scan files, or of the stored model weights (T0018, T0076, T0031), can suppress indications without any adversarial-ML sophistication. This is a safeguards/integrity issue for the inspection record on a long-lived waste confinement boundary. (c) Evasion (T0015, T0043): an insider or supply-chain actor with knowledge of the model family (T0013/T0014, T0002.001) could shape signal-level artifacts, such as probe settings, lift-off or surface treatment, so that a flaw stays below the classifier's decision boundary while remaining in the physical canister. (d) Supply chain (T0010.001/.003): pretrained backbones or ML libraries introduced into the NDE software stack add an unqualified code path into an inspection chain that is otherwise tightly controlled. The adversarial risk is amplified by the implicit weaknesses above, because a fragile, poorly calibrated model with no POD baseline makes manipulation hard to detect.

security_specialist.argument: From a threat-modeling view, this CNN is a low-glamour but high-leverage target. It is a single point of trust that decides whether a canister weld is declared crack-free, and the consequence of a missed crack, such as chloride-induced stress corrosion cracking in 304L/316L heat-affected zones, is a long-lived integrity and confinement problem in a storage system that is hard to re-inspect. A nation-state would probably not attack the model directly if easier routes exist. But the pipeline (scan data, patch preprocessing, weights, vendor tooling) offers a cheap insider or supply-chain path to suppress true positives quietly. The published evidence is a single seeded-fault lab sample with a waterjet-cut crack, which is a large qualification gap. Anyone who understands that gap can predict where the model is blind, and natural failure and deliberate exploitation look the same afterward.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Integrity attack on the detection chain: an insider or supply-chain actor poisons training or labeling data, backdoors or swaps model weights, or tampers with the ECT map-to-patch preprocessing (AML.T0010.002/.003, T0018.000, T0020, T0043.004, T0076). The AI failure is a classifier that systematically labels real weld cracks as 'normal'. The facility depends on it to accept canisters for loading, storage and transfer, and the consequence is undetected through-wall or near-through-wall flaws, a delayed confinement failure, and a loss of defense-in-depth that no one can trace to a cause. (2) Evasion of the model: ECT maps are quantitative signals, and crack signatures that look like benign geometry, noise or lift-off variation can slip past a CNN trained on narrow data (AML.T0015, T0043). An insider with scan-acquisition access could alter probe settings, scan parameters or raw files without ever touching the model. (3) Concentrated trust and erosion of vigilance: once the CNN triages, human analysts review fewer scans, so an adversary can time tampering or a physical attack on a canister for a period of reduced human scrutiny. A false 'all clear' record may also be used to conceal prior damage or sabotage, and it undermines the inspection record on which safeguards and regulatory confidence depend. (4) Data exposure: weld ECT datasets, defect libraries and model weights reveal which flaw sizes and types evade detection, which helps an adversary design undetectable damage (AML.T0024.002, T0035, T0025). Documentation of inspection gaps also reveals canister vulnerabilities. (5) Remote and tooling paths: cloud or vendor-hosted training and inference, and third-party ML libraries, widen the IT/OT boundary (AML.T0010.001, T0012).

IMPLICIT, exploitable without any attacker. (a) Data scarcity and provenance: real cracks in fielded canister welds are rare, so the model depends on seeded or simulated defects such as waterjet cuts, which differ from real SCC morphology (OP.C0202, C0201.01/.02, C0302). An adversary who knows this can target real-crack signatures the model has never seen. (b) Generalization failure: variation in weld process, geometry, surface condition, probe and instrument hardware, and 304L versus 316L material can degrade the model's performance without warning (OP.C0302.03, C0303). (c) Automation trust failure and skill fade: analysts may defer to the classifier and lose their ability to read raw ECT data (OP.C0101.04, C0101.06, C0102). (d) Opacity and weak assurance: the CNN is hard to explain and the regulatory basis for qualification is thin, so a subtle compromise or silent degradation of the model may go unnoticed (OP.C0401, C0501, C0504). (e) Patch-level classification can miss flaws that span patch boundaries or sit in marginal areas, which gives a predictable blind spot (OP.C0304.03).

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on the seeded-fault-to-real-SCC gap, patch framing, opacity and qualification, automation trust, and insider or supply-chain integrity attacks that mask cracks. I dropped speculative or weakly tied codes (AML.T0012, OP.C0301) and the nuclear engineer's AML.T0059 and the AI engineer's T0013/T0014 recon, and kept exfiltration only as a distinct data-exposure threat.

evidence.citation: "Defect Recognition for Eddy Current Testing of Spent Nuclear Fuel Canister using Convolutional Neural Network," Oak Ridge National Laboratory / IEEE Industrial Electronics Society Annual On-Line Conference (ONCON 2023)
evidence.note: This peer-reviewed conference paper by ORNL-affiliated authors proposes a CNN that classifies 2D eddy-current scan data as defective or normal for canister welds. It was tested on a submerged-arc-welded 304L stainless-steel sample with an artificial waterjet-cut crack, where the experiments showed the approach was feasible and effective. The test used a seeded-fault laboratory sample, not a deployed system.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is the training-data and model integrity attack (or the seeded-fault generalization gap), which yields undetected through-wall flaws in a spent fuel confinement boundary and a false inspection record. This is a safeguards-adjacent record falsification and a potential long-term release pathway, but the harm is delayed and independent redundant NDE or analyst review could still intervene, so it falls just short of 5.

reproducibility.why: The seeded-to-real-flaw generalization gap and patch-boundary blind spots are structural and recur reliably once real, tight cracks or atypical scan conditions occur, while integrity attacks reliably cause misses once the model or data are altered.

exploitability.why: The adversarial routes (poisoning the small training set, swapping weights, editing raw ECT files, or timing tampering around reduced scrutiny) need insider or supply-chain access to a controlled inspection workflow, and exploiting the blind spots needs physical access to the canister or its scan process.

affected_users.why: A false all-clear affects the inspected canisters, and a compromised model or shared pretrained backbone could systematically affect every weld it screens, but impact stays within the inspection program and does not propagate across coupled plant systems.

discoverability.why: The CNN-for-ECT approach, its seeded-fault basis and general weaknesses such as small data, patch framing and opacity are in the open literature, and generic ML poisoning and evasion classes are well documented. Learning which flaw types evade detection in a specific deployment still needs partial inside knowledge.

use_case: Deep convolutional neural network that predicts uranium enrichment from handheld M400 CZT gamma spectra of UF6 cylinders (and U3O8 samples). It was trained on measured and generated spectra and tested against declared enrichments. It supports safeguards inspectors verifying enrichment declarations, and was compared with the GEM code.
incurred_insecurity:
A CNN that converts a handheld CZT spectrum into a single enrichment number sits at the point where an operator's declaration is checked against physical evidence. Its main threats are physical-world evasion by the inspected party, training-data and model supply-chain compromise, and tampering with the deployment chain. Implicit weaknesses make these easier to exploit: distribution shift, circular declared-value labels, a simulation-to-reality gap, scarcity of anomalous spectra, automation over-trust, and weak AI-specific qualification. The consequence is a false clearance of undeclared enrichment or a false alarm that damages inspector credibility. Formal safeguards conclusions rest on destructive and non-destructive assay, seals and material accounting, so the exposure is erosion of detection probability and timeliness.

Physical spectrum evasion -- adversarial
The operator controls the cylinder, its wall and contents, and the positioning, so added attenuators, liners, interfering gamma sources or substituted material can shift the measured spectrum until the CNN returns the declared enrichment. This needs no cyber access, and a learned regressor can be more sensitive to such perturbations than peak-ratio analysis.

Training-data and model poisoning -- adversarial
Poisoning of the generated-spectra pipeline, of declared-enrichment labels, or of distributed model weights can embed a bias at particular enrichment ranges or a backdoor triggered by a spectral feature. With little independent reference data the corruption is hard to detect, and one compromised release propagates to every inspector's device.

Deployment-chain tampering -- adversarial
Altering the model file, preprocessing, calibration or firmware on the handheld or analysis laptop can silently shift enrichment results while the inspection looks normal. This undermines the verification conclusion without any visible anomaly.

Proxy-model rehearsal from published details -- adversarial
Published architecture, data description and performance figures, or an extracted model, let an adversary build a proxy and rehearse evasion offline without probing limits before an inspection.

Distribution shift and no out-of-distribution flag -- implicit, exploitable
The model is trained on 0.2-4.95% UF6 and U3O8, and a regressor has no native unknown output, so high-assay or HEU material, other cylinder types, wall thickness, heels, temperature or gain drift, and unit-to-unit detector differences yield a confident wrong value. An adversary who knows where the training envelope ends can present material just beyond it and receive a plausible in-range number.

Circular labels and anomaly scarcity -- implicit, exploitable
Declared enrichments serve as both training labels and test ground truth, so agreement shows consistency with declarations, not truth, and the 0.03 pp error is an in-distribution figure rather than a detection-capability claim. There are almost no substitution, blended-lot or unusual-isotopics spectra, so a falsified declaration resembling the training population passes, and a misdeclaring operator gains from this blind spot.

Simulation gap and opacity -- implicit, exploitable
The CNN may learn simulation artifacts or proxies such as cylinder type or detector gain state instead of the 185.7 keV physics, and its opacity makes this hard to detect. An adversary could use these non-physical dependencies to craft spectra that steer the output.

Automation over-trust and skill fade -- implicit, exploitable
A precise-looking number that beat the GEM code encourages inspectors to defer to it, reducing independent spectral interpretation and cross-checks. An adversary can time an anomaly to this complacency or use a noisy output to dispute inspector findings.

Qualification and repeatability gaps -- implicit, exploitable
Non-deterministic training, retraining after hardware changes, and a GEM comparison in place of an independent qualification basis make versions hard to reproduce and a safeguards finding hard to defend. An adversary can exploit this to challenge the result's credibility or to hide a subtle version-to-version bias.

nuclear_engineer.argument: From a safeguards-operations view, this CNN sits in the verification chain for enrichment declarations at enrichment plants and cylinder stores. Its output is a number an inspector could use to accept or question an operator declaration. If it is wrong, biased, or manipulated, the likely harm is a missed diversion or misdeclaration (a false negative on enrichment), or a false alarm that burns inspection resources and credibility. Existing practice offers some protection. A handheld CZT screen is a non-destructive, attribute-level measurement, and the formal conclusion rests on DA/NDA with HPGe, mass spectrometry, sampling, seals, and material accounting. The real risk is the shift of a screening tool toward quasi-quantitative authority, especially when its reported error of about 0.03 percentage points comes from a narrow, favourable test set. That narrowness matters more than any attack on the model itself.
nuclear_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT. (1) Distribution shift and unrepresentative validation. The model was trained on measured plus generated spectra and tested against declared enrichments, over a range of 0.2–4.95%. Real inspections will differ in cylinder wall thickness, fill and heel, cylinder type, container corrosion or deposits, temperature and detector gain drift, individual detector units, count time, geometry and operator handling. The accuracy figure may not carry over. Out-of-range cases, such as HEU or high-assay LEU above 5%, can be mapped by the CNN onto a plausible in-range number, because a regressor has no built-in 'unknown' output. That gives a confident but wrong value in precisely the cases that matter most for safeguards. (2) Circular ground truth. Declared enrichments are the labels, so a systematic operator-side bias or misdeclaration is baked into both training and test. Agreement with declarations then shows consistency, not truth. It cannot show the system detects a falsified declaration. (3) Simulated-data gap. Generated spectra can embed simulation assumptions (response function, shielding model) that the CNN learns as artifacts. Opacity means it is hard to tell when it relies on non-physical features. (4) Automation bias. A low reported error and a win over the GEM code encourage inspectors to treat a single-point output as authoritative, with deskilling in physics-based interpretation and cross-checks. Reporting without uncertainty or a confidence indicator makes this worse. Non-repeatability across retrains and versions also complicates qualification and inspector-to-inspector comparability. (5) Scarcity of anomalous or diversion-relevant spectra. There is little data for material substitution, mixed or blended lots, non-UF6 matrices, or unusual isotopic compositions such as reprocessed uranium with U-232/U-236. A model tuned to natural-to-LEU enrichments could miss these. ADVERSARIAL. (6) Evasion and spoofing: a state or operator with knowledge of the measurement geometry could alter the spectrum (extra attenuators, liners, added gamma sources, a different material in the cylinder) so the CNN reports the declared enrichment while the true content differs. Learned models can be sensitive to perturbations that physics-based analysis would flag. This is a physical-world adversarial-input problem requiring no cyber access. (7) Supply-chain and integrity attacks: poisoning of training or generated-spectra pipelines, a tampered model file or software on the handheld, or firmware and calibration tampering could create systematic bias or a backdoor trigger on specific spectral features. This is credible mainly for a shared model deployed to many inspectors, where one compromised release propagates fleet-wide. (8) Confidentiality: the spectra and model hold information about facility declarations. Weights and training data could reveal sensitive facility or measurement information, and model extraction would help an adversary craft evasion. Consequence chain: bad output leads to an inspector accepting a false enrichment or raising an unwarranted discrepancy. For harm to occur, DA confirmation, seals, accountancy and containment/surveillance would also have to fail, so the main exposure is erosion of detection probability and timeliness, plus credibility damage to the safeguards conclusion.

ai_engineer.argument: From an ML pipeline view this is a regression CNN on low-resolution CZT spectra (M400 is a handheld, roughly 2-3% FWHM at 662 keV device), trained on a mix of measured and generated (simulated/augmented) spectra, then validated against operator-declared enrichments. Three structural fragilities follow. First, labels are declarations, not independent ground truth, so a model that matches declarations at 0.03 pp may be learning a proxy (cylinder type, wall thickness, geometry, detector gain state) rather than the 185.7 keV/daughter-line physics, and it cannot by construction detect a falsified declaration that happens to look like the training population. Second, the training distribution is narrow: 0.2-4.95% UF6 cylinders and U3O8 samples. HALEU, depleted or intermediate material, other cylinder sizes, heterogeneous or aged heels, different daughter ingrowth, temperature-dependent CZT gain drift and unit-to-unit detector variation are all out-of-distribution, yet a CNN regressor will return a confident point estimate with no native OOD flag. Third, the generated-spectrum component creates a sim-to-real gap and a dependence on the simulation tool chain (and a comparison against GEM, itself a model with assumptions), so provenance of each training sample is hard to audit.
ai_engineer.proposed_incurred_insecurity: IMPLICIT: (a) Distribution shift and domain gap (OP.C0302, .01, .03; OP.C0201.01/.02/.05; OP.C0202): spectra from new cylinders, new detector units, gain or temperature drift, different matrix or shielding, or enrichments outside 0.2-4.95% produce silently wrong enrichment values. The inspector sees a precise number and has no uncertainty or OOD indicator, which risks false assurance (an undeclared higher-enrichment cylinder judged consistent) or false alarms that burden inspections. (b) Label circularity and sample scarcity (OP.C0701, OP.C0701.01): ground truth comes from declared values and a limited set of cylinders, so low-base-rate diversion-like or anomalous cases are essentially absent. The reported 0.03 pp is an in-distribution figure that should not be read as a detection-capability claim. (c) Qualification and opacity (OP.C0501, OP.C0303, OP.C0401, OP.C0402): the model needs periodic retraining and recalibration as hardware or firmware changes, and non-deterministic training makes versions hard to reproduce. Saliency in a CNN can't readily show which spectral features drive the output, and comparison against GEM as the benchmark does not establish an independent qualification basis for safeguards conclusions. (d) Automation bias (OP.C0101.04, .06): inspectors may defer to the CNN over physics-based analysis, and skill with traditional peak analysis may erode. ADVERSARIAL: (e) Evasion by physical or data manipulation (AML.T0015, T0043, T0043.003, T0041): a facility operator, the party being verified, can alter the measurement geometry, add shielding or attenuating or interfering sources, or present spectra crafted to move the regression output. Because the device is handheld and the operator controls the cylinder and positioning, adversarial inputs are physically realizable, and a CNN is more sensitive to such perturbations than peak-ratio analysis. Knowledge of the published architecture and data lets the adversary build a proxy model (AML.T0005, T0000, T0043.002). (f) Training-data and supply-chain poisoning (AML.T0010.002/.003, T0020, T0018.000, T0043.004): if training data are contributed or generated across labs or by the host State, or models are shipped from a central repository to inspectors' devices, a poisoned dataset or backdoored weights could bias outputs for a particular signature (OP.C0602 for fleet-wide propagation). (g) Integrity of the deployment chain (AML.T0076, T0031): tampering with the model file, calibration or preprocessing on the handheld or the analysis laptop could undermine verification without any visible anomaly. The consequence is erosion of safeguards conclusions about enrichment declarations, a core safeguards concern for enrichment plants.

security_specialist.argument: From a red-team view, this model sits at the point where a state's declaration is checked against physical evidence. Its output (enrichment as a number with about 0.03 pp reported error) could carry more weight than the underlying handheld spectrum, which a human inspector can't easily interpret. A host-state adversary who wants to conceal enrichment above declared levels, or to sow doubt about an inspector's finding, gains more from shaping what the model sees and says than from defeating the CZT detector. The case is attractive for three reasons. The adversary controls the measured object (the cylinder, its wall, its contents). The model is a narrow, qualitatively unfamiliar classifier trained on limited, partly generated data. And a single trusted number can both close an anomaly and trigger a dispute.
security_specialist.proposed_incurred_insecurity:
ADVERSARIAL. (1) Evasion by the inspected party: a facility operator knows the measurement geometry, the cylinder, the shielding and wall conditions, and any matrix or impurity (e.g., minor isotopes, reprocessed-feed signatures, deliberate shielding or spectral perturbation). The operator can present spectra that fall outside the training distribution, or that are tuned so the CNN returns a declared-consistent enrichment. A physical-world adversarial example needs no network access. The model's low-error headline on in-distribution UF6 cylinders gives false assurance, and a CNN has no physics-based confidence bound the way an analytic code like GEM does. This maps to AML.T0015, AML.T0043 (including black-box optimization and manual modification) and AML.T0041. (2) Training-data and model supply chain: the model is trained on a mix of measured and generated spectra, so poisoning or backdooring the simulation pipeline, the labeled declared-enrichment data (declarations are themselves possibly falsified ground truth), or pretrained weights could embed a bias at specific enrichment ranges or a trigger spectral feature. Corruption of this kind is hard to spot because there is little independent reference data. See AML.T0020, AML.T0010.002/.003, AML.T0018.000, AML.T0043.004 and OP.C0201.01/.02. (3) Compromise of the handheld or analysis chain: tampering with the model file, preprocessing or firmware on an inspector laptop or detector, which would silently shift results while looking like a normal inspection. See AML.T0010.001, AML.T0018, AML.T0076 and AML.T0112.001. (4) Model and data exposure: the published approach, training framework and performance numbers, plus any extractable model, let an adversary build a proxy and rehearse evasion offline before an inspection, with no limits on probing. See AML.T0000, AML.T0005, AML.T0024.002 and AML.T0063. (5) Discrediting: a manipulated or noisy output can be used to dispute inspector conclusions or to sow doubt, since the model is opaque. 

IMPLICIT (exploitable or timeable). Automation over-trust and skill fade: inspectors may defer to a precise-looking number and stop doing independent spectral interpretation or cross-checks, and an adversary can time anomalies to that complacency (OP.C0101.04, OP.C0101.06, OP.C0401). Out-of-distribution failure: enrichments above the tested 4.95%, other detectors, cylinder types, wall thickness, temperature, detector aging or gain drift and different geometries are poorly covered, and the adversary knows where the training distribution ends (OP.C0302, OP.C0302.03, OP.C0202, OP.C0701). Reliance on generated data creates a simulation-to-reality gap (OP.C0201.02). Inference non-repeatability and AI-specific qualification gaps make the tool hard to defend in a safeguards finding (OP.C0402, OP.C0501, OP.C0504). Weak data governance of sensitive inspection spectra and declarations may drive both leakage and mislabeled training data (OP.C0505). A false alarm or false clearance carries a safeguards consequence: a false clearance can hide undeclared enrichment (diversion or misuse), while a false alarm creates a diplomatic and credibility cost the adversary can exploit.

red_team_panel.synthesis_notes: All three panelists converged on physical-world evasion, poisoning and supply-chain compromise, and the distribution-shift, circular-label and over-trust implicit cluster. I dropped the lower-support ATLAS items (T0000, T0063, T0112.001, T0031) and the OP codes for governance and mislabeled data (C0504, C0505, C0702.01), whose pathways were weakly argued or restated other threats.

evidence.citation: "Machine learning framework for predicting uranium enrichments from M400 CZT gamma spectra," Nuclear Instruments and Methods in Physics Research Section A (Elsevier); work from Oak Ridge National Laboratory (Bae & Hu, 2024)
evidence.note: The paper describes a framework for collecting, generating and processing gamma-spectrum data, and uses it to train CNN models that predict enrichment. The models were tested on measured spectra from UF6 cylinders (0.2–4.95%) and U3O8 samples. For UF6 cylinders the reported error was about 0.03 percentage points, and the model outperformed the GEM code. The work is aimed at safeguards inspections and is part of the NNSA-sponsored 'Gamma Rodeo' project.

damage.why: The most severe credible threat is a false clearance of undeclared or misdeclared enrichment (safeguards falsification, e.g. evasion or deployment-chain tampering), though the entry notes formal conclusions also rest on DA/NDA, seals and accounting, so the harm is eroded detection probability rather than a direct release.

reproducibility.why: Out-of-distribution inputs reliably yield confident wrong values from a regressor with no unknown output, and circular labels and anomaly scarcity are persistent structural properties, so the weakness recurs whenever the stated trigger conditions are met.

exploitability.why: Physical spectrum evasion needs no cyber access and is within the inspected party's routine control of the cylinder and its positioning, but achieving a targeted result takes some spectroscopy expertise, and poisoning or deployment-chain tampering needs insider or supply-chain access.

affected_users.why: A compromised model release or shared training pipeline propagates to every inspector's device and every verification using it, though the impact is confined to enrichment verification measurements rather than the whole facility.

discoverability.why: The architecture, training range (0.2-4.95%), data description and performance are published, and distribution shift, simulation gap and circular labels are well documented for ML regressors, so a capable outsider can readily infer where the weaknesses lie.
